dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: unnamed verse ×3; Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad); Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); a poet of Banū Saʿd (undated)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root ء-ر-ض (ʾ-r-ḍ) as having three separate origins: one productive origin that branches, plus two isolated meanings that follow no analogy and are simply fixed usages of the Arabs.

The two isolated meanings:
1. al-arḍ = a head-cold / catarrh. A man with a cold is maʾrūḍ (= mazkūm). Shāhid: a verse of the Hudhalī poet mocking someone who imagined he had caught cold when he had not.
2. arḍ = trembling / shivering. "Fulān has arḍ" means he has a tremor. Shāhid: Dhū al-Rumma, on a mount that senses a sound, or is subject to trembling, or has the mūm disease.

The principal (productive) origin: whatever lies low and faces the sky. Hence a horse's upper body is called its samāʾ ("sky") and its legs its arḍ ("ground") — illustrated by a verse contrasting a horse's lush "sky" (upper parts) with its barren "ground" (legs). From the same origin comes al-arḍ, the earth we stand on; its plural is araḍīn, though Ibn Fāris notes it never occurs in the plural in the Qurʾān.

Branches of the principal origin:
- arḍ arīḍa = soft, good, fertile land (shāhid: Imruʾ al-Qays).
- rajul arīḍ li-l-khayr = a man well-suited/disposed to good, by likeness to fertile land.
- taʾarraḍa al-nabt = a plant grown enough to be mown; jady arīḍ = a kid old enough to graze it.
- al-irāḍ = a large carpet of fur or wool.
- ibn arḍ ("son of earth") = a stranger (shāhid cited).
- taʾarraḍa fulān = he clung to / kept to the ground (shāhid from a poet of Banū Saʿd: a companion who rose promptly and did not cling to the ground).

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: ضِعْف 11x "double"; يُضَٰعِفُ 9x "will be doubled"; ضَعِيف 8x "weak"; ٱسْتَضْعَفُ 8x "were oppressed"; مُّسْتَضْعَفُون 5x "and the ones who are weak"; ضَعْف 4x "weakness"; ضَعُفَ 2x "so weak"; أَضْعَف 2x "(is) weaker"; مُّضَٰعَفَة 1x "multiplied"; ضِعَٰف 1x "weak"; مُضْعِفُون 1x "(will) get manifold"
text:
al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's entry for the root ḍ-ʿ-f (ضعف).

1. Core sense — weakness. الضَّعْف (al-ḍaʿf) is the opposite of strength. The verb ضَعُفَ = "to become weak," the adjective ضَعِيف (ḍaʿīf) = "weak" (Q 22:73, "weak are the seeker and the sought"). Weakness may lie in the soul, the body, or one's outward circumstances. Two vowellings, ḍaʿf and ḍuʿf, are noted as dialectal variants (Q 8:66; Q 28:5).

2. A finer distinction (from al-Khalīl). ḍuʿf (with u) = weakness of the body; ḍaʿf (with a) = weakness of intellect and judgement — hence Q 2:282, where the debtor may be "feeble-minded or weak."

3. Forms. Plurals of ḍaʿīf are ḍiʿāf and ḍuʿafāʾ (Q 9:91). The form X verb istaḍʿafa / istaḍʿaftu = "to find or treat someone as weak," hence al-mustaḍʿafīn = those deemed weak or held down (Q 4:75; 4:97; 7:150). This word is set as the opposite of istikbār ("arrogant self-magnification") in Q 34:33, the "deemed-weak" vs. the "arrogant."

4. The three-fold cycle of Q 30:54 ("created you from weakness, then strength, then weakness"). al-Rāghib argues each of the three ḍaʿf/quwwa refers to a distinct life-stage: the first weakness = origin from a fluid drop or dust; the second = the frailty of embryo and infant; the third = the frailty after old age ("the most abject part of life"). The two strengths = (a) the infant's capacity to move, seek milk, and cry off harm, and (b) the strength that follows puberty. His grammatical proof: each ḍaʿf is indefinite (munakkar). A repeated indefinite noun signals a NEW referent, whereas a referent already named is reintroduced as definite (as in "I saw a man… then the man said…"). On the same principle Ibn ʿAbbās read Q 94:5–6 ("with hardship comes ease" twice): the one definite "hardship" cannot overcome the two indefinite (hence doubled) "eases."

5. Two further glosses on weakness. Q 4:28, "man was created weak" — his weakness = the multitude of his needs, which the angels ("the highest assembly") do not share. Q 4:76, "Satan's plotting is weak" — weak only relative to God's servants over whom Satan has no authority (Q 17:65).

6. Second sense — ḍiʿf, "the double / multiple." This is a correlative term (like "half" and "pair"): it names the combining of two equal quantities and applies specifically to number. The verbs aḍʿafa, ḍaʿʿafa, ḍāʿafa all = "to add to a thing its like or more." Some hold ḍāʿafa is stronger than ḍaʿʿafa, which is why most reciters read the multiplying forms in Q 33:30 and Q 4:40; compare Q 6:160 ("tenfold"), so "multiplication" here reaches tenfold.

7. Grammar of ḍaʿf vs. ḍiʿf. ḍaʿf is the verbal noun (maṣdar), ḍiʿf the noun (ism) — parallel to thany/thiny; the passive participle is maḍʿūf. The ḍiʿf of a thing is what doubles it. Annexed to a number it means that number plus its like: "the ḍiʿf of ten" = twenty, "of a hundred" = two hundred, uncontested. A cited verse of poetry (unattributed) uses ḍiʿf al-widd, "double the affection."

8. The arithmetic of ḍiʿfayn. "Give him the ḍiʿfayn of one" = one plus twice it = three (the one and the two that pair with it). But un-annexed, al-ḍiʿfayn behaves like "a pair" (al-zawjayn): each doubles the other, so it means only two. Annexed to "one" (ḍiʿfay al-wāḥid), however, it yields three.

9. Qurʾānic applications of ḍiʿf. Q 34:37, "the recompense of the double." Q 3:130, "do not consume usury, doubled and multiplied" — one view: the two words are for emphasis; another view (al-Rāghib notes): the "multiplication" here is really from ḍaʿf (loss), not ḍiʿf (gain) — what the usurers count as increase is in truth diminution, echoing Q 30:39 (usury "does not increase with God") and Q 2:276 ("God blots out usury and grows charity"). A poet caught the same paradox: "an increase of grey hair — yet it is a decrease of my [life's] increase."

10. The "double punishment" verses (Q 7:38). فَآتِهِمْ عَذاباً ضِعْفاً — they ask for a doubled punishment: one for their own straying, one for leading others astray (cf. Q 16:25, bearing their own burdens plus some of those they misled). And لِكُلٍّ ضِعْفٌ ("for each is a double") means either "each has double your punishment," or "each of you and them has double what the other can see" — since punishment is both outward and inward, and each perceives only the other's outward part.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
quran_words: حَسَدَ 3x "are they jealous"; حَسَد 1x "(out of) jealousy"; حَاسِد 1x "(of) an envier"
poets_named: Shamir b. al-Ḥārith al-Ḍabbī (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse
text:
Root ḥ-s-d (حسد) as recorded by al-Zabīdī in Tāj al-ʿArūs.

1. Syntax. The verb takes the envied thing either as a direct object (ḥasadahu al-shayʾ) or with the preposition ʿalā. The direct-object construction is attested in a pre-Islamic-style verse by Shamir b. al-Ḥārith al-Ḍabbī describing jinn who come to his fire; their spokesman says: "We envy mankind the food" — with "the food" as a second accusative object.

2. Forms. Imperfect yaḥsudu (with ḍamma) is the well-known form; yaḥsidu (with kasra) is reported by al-Akhfash from some speakers. Verbal nouns: ḥasad (vowelled sīn, the commoner form), ḥasd (allowed by the author of al-Miṣbāḥ), ḥusūd, and ḥasāda. There is also an intensive form ḥassada / taḥsīd.

3. Core sense. To wish that another's blessing and excellence be transferred to oneself — a variant copy reads "away from him" — or that he be stripped of them. A cited verse: "You see the intelligent man much-envied, though he has reviled no one, while his own honour is reviled."

4. Definitions al-Zabīdī gathers:
 - al-Ṣiḥāḥ: to wish the removal of the envied person's blessing so that it passes to you.
 - al-Nihāya: a man sees a blessing his brother has and wishes it to leave him and belong to himself instead.
 - al-Asās: to wish the removal of the envied person's blessing.
 - al-Shihāb (Sharḥ al-Shifāʾ): the ugliest kind is wishing another's blessing gone when it will not come to oneself.

5. Ḥasad versus ghibṭ. Per al-Nihāya, ghibṭ is wishing to have the like of another's blessing without wishing its removal from him. Al-Azharī treats ghibṭ as a lighter species of ḥasad, citing the reply attributed to the Prophet when asked whether ghibṭ does harm: "Yes, as khabṭ (beating leaves from a tree) does harm."

6. Etymology. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: the root sense of ḥasad is qashr — stripping or peeling off bark.

7. Idioms from al-Asās: "he envied him for God's blessing"; "every possessor of a blessing is envied"; "envy eats the body"; "what invites envy invites ruin."

8. Agent nouns and plurals. ḥāsid, plural ḥussad, ḥussād, ḥasada (pattern of ḥāmil / ḥamala); and ḥasūd, plural ḥusud; the feminine takes no tāʾ.

9. A reported oath. Ibn Sīda, from al-Liḥyānī: the Arabs said "May God ḥasad me if I envy you" — which al-Zabīdī calls strange, parallel to another idiom with nafisa, and objectionable in wording since God is above such an attribute. He construes it as "may God punish or requite me for envy," comparing Q 3:54, "they schemed and God schemed."

10. Reciprocal. taḥāsadū: they envied one another.

11. Appended items. ḥisdil (with kasra): a tick — the lām being an augment on this root (al-Azharī from Ibn al-Aʿrābī). And form IV aḥsadtuhu: "I kept his company and found him to be an envier."

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: جَعَلَ 340x "we made"; جَاعِل 6x "and i will make"
poets_named: Abū Zubayd (Umayyad); al-Asadī (undated); Ṭufayl (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse ×2
text:
Ibn Sīda's account of the root ج ع ل (j-ʿ-l).

Verbal senses of جَعَل:
1. To put or place. جَعَل and اجتَعَل both mean "to place." Shāhid — Abū Zubayd, of a lion that has "made itself a refuge among the soft papyrus in the thicket."
2. To make or fashion (ṣanaʿa).
3. To lay down / stack. Sībawayh glosses "I made your goods, one part above another" as "I laid it down" — and, alternatively, "I worked it." (He notes the nominative in baʿḍuhu stands because the clause occupies the place of a circumstantial qualifier.)
4. To transform X into Y (ṣayyara): "he made the clay into pottery, the ugly into the beautiful."
5. To suppose X to be Y (ẓanna): "he made [=took] Basra to be Baghdad."
6. To begin / set about doing (with a following verb): "he set to doing such-and-such." (with shāhid).
7. To attribute or assign a relation. Al-Zajjāj: "I made Zayd your brother" = I related him to you.
8. Qur'anic usages, per al-Zajjāj: in "We have made it an Arabic Qur'ān," jaʿala means "We made it plain (bayyannāhu)"; in "they made the angels... females," al-jaʿl carries the sense of asserting or passing a judgment about something — as in "I have made Zayd the most learned of men," i.e. I described and ruled him so.
9. تَجاعَلوا الشيءَ: they placed/apportioned it among themselves.
10. To stipulate a fee: جَعَل له كذا على كذا = he contracted with him for it; likewise assigning a worker his due.

Nouns of hire and reward:
- الجِعالة / الجُعالة / الجَعالة, and الجَعِيلة: a fee assigned for someone's work (variant vowelling on al-Liḥyānī's authority).
- الجَعالة (fatḥ): a bribe (al-Liḥyānī).
- الجُعالة also, specifically: the payment to a substitute warrior — when raiding is obligatory on a man and he pays another to go in his place. Shāhid by al-Asadī (narrated with both jiʿāla and juʿāla).
- أجْعَلَه جُعْلاً / أجْعَلَه له: he gave it to him.
- الجِعالة: what men mutually contribute at the time of military levies, or under a burden imposed by the authority.

Household and animal senses:
- الجِعال / الجِعالة: the rag (or the like) used to lift a hot cooking-pot off the fire (shāhid by Ṭufayl); أجْعَل القِدرَ = he took the pot down with it.
- أجْعَلَت / استَجْعَلَت: (of a bitch, she-wolf, lioness, any clawed animal) to be in heat, desiring to mate; the animal is مُجْعِل.

Palm-tree senses:
- الجَعْلَة: a young palm-shoot (fasīla) — variously said to be the wadiyya, a short palm, or a palm beyond the reach of the hand. Plural جَعْل (with shāhid).
- الجَعْل (of palms): like al-baʿl — palms that grow unirrigated, drinking by their roots.

The beetle and its figurative uses:
- الجُعَل: a beetle (said to be "Abū Jiʿrān"); plural جِعْلان.
- ماء جَعِل / مُجْعِل: water in which beetles have died; أرض مُجْعِلة: land full of beetles.
- رجل جُعَل: a man black and ugly/squat, likened to the beetle; also said to mean the obstinate man, since the beetle is proverbially stubborn.
- جُعَل الإنسان: one's clinging watcher. Proverb: "his juʿal clung to a man" — of someone seeking privacy for a need whom another pesters and hinders (with shāhid). All such usages are figures drawn from the beetle.

Other:
- الجَعْوَل: a young ostrich (Yemeni usage).
- جُعَيْل: a man's name. Banū جِعال: a tribe.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats sh–ʾ–m as one root whose core notion is **the left-hand side**.

1. **Left side.** الْمَشْأَمَة (al-mashʾama) is the left side, the opposite of الْمَيْمَنَة (al-maymana), the right side.

2. **Geographic name.** الشَّأْم (al-Shaʾm, Syria/the Levant) is so called because it is the land lying on the left of the qibla. The form is given as both الشَّأْم and الشَّآم. The gentilic (place-adjective) is شَآمٍ for a man and شَآمِيَة for a woman. He cites a verse of poetry using the form: "Head for a Syrian [place], since we have no Iraq — a people we would love, since our own folk are harsh."

3. **Ill omen.** رَجُلٌ مَشْئُوم (mashʾūm) is an ill-omened man, from الشُّؤْم (shuʾm), ill fortune.

The entry is compact: it derives the place-name and the notion of ill omen alike from the single "left side" sense, without further elaboration.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats sh-ʾ-n as one root whose core idea is seeking and aiming at something.

1. Seeking, aiming at an object. شَأَنْتُ شَأْنَهُ means "I aimed at what he aimed at." He cites a verse of poetry — "O seeker of generosity, generosity is a noble trait; not miserliness from you, nor is generosity part of your شَأْن" — and reports that شأنك here was explained as "your seeking."

2. One's concern or pursuit. مَا هَذَا مِنْ شَأْنِي, "this is not my شَأْن," is glossed as "this is not among the things I seek and want."

3. الشُّئُون (singular شَأْن): the spaces between the plates of the skull. Ibn Fāris explains the name from the same root idea: these are the channels along which tears run, as though the tear were seeking them out and making them its watercourse.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: al-Kumayt (Umayyad); unnamed verse ×3; Abū Duʾād (pre-Islamic); al-Ṭirimmāḥ (Umayyad)
text:
ROOT sh-ʿ-b (ش‑ع‑ب) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha (d. 1004 CE)

Ibn Fāris states that this root has two distinct original meanings: (1) separation/division, and (2) gathering/union. Grammarians disputed how to explain this: some (including al-Khalīl explicitly) classed it among the aḍdād — a single word carrying two opposite meanings. Others, including Ibn Duraid, held it isn't a true antonym-pair at all, just two different dialectal usages that happen to share a form. Al-Khalīl called it one of the "wonders" and evidence of Arabic's breadth that shaʿb can mean both separating and joining.

**1. Separation** (the sense Ibn Fāris himself treats as basic)
- A crack or split in something is a shaʿb.
- From this comes shaʿb = a "people" — literally a branch that has split off from the Arab and non-Arab tribes; plural shuʿūb. He cites Qur'an 49:13, "We made you into peoples (shuʿūb) and tribes (qabāʾil)."
- Shaʿb can also mean a great tribe or clan.
- Mashʿab al-ḥaqq = "the path of truth" — cited from a verse of al-Kumayt contrasting loyalty to the family of Aḥmad with following the path of truth.
- Roads that diverge, or a tree's branches that split off, are both described with this root (inshaʿabat).
- Shuʿab al-faras — a horse's raised, prominent parts (neck, withers, etc.) — with a supporting verse describing a lofty stallion.
- A gazelle whose two horns splay far apart is ashʿab — with a terse citation from Abū Duʾād whose precise wording Ibn Fāris does not further explain.
- Al-shiʿb (different vowel pattern) = a mountain pass, the gap between two mountains.
- Shaʿūb = death/fate — because it scatters people; "death scattered them (shaʿibathum) and they dispersed."
- Al-shaʿīb = a worn, leaky waterskin — named because it "disperses" the water it holds rather than keeping it in, with a supporting verse comparing a weeping eye to such a skin.
- Ibn Duraid: the month Shaʿbān is named for people's dispersing in it to search for water.
- A hadith is cited using the same root: "What is this ruling that has scattered (shaʿʿabat) the people?" — i.e., divided them.

**2. Gathering**
- Shaʿaba al-ṣadʿ = to mend a crack (i.e., rejoin it).
- Shaʿaba al-ʿuss = to repair a large bowl.
- An awl or drill is called a mishʿab, from mending/joining.
- Ibn Fāris notes it's possible that shaʿb ("tribe/people") was actually named for union rather than division — the alternative etymology for the same word discussed under sense 1.
- Support: "the shaʿb of Banū So-and-so broke apart" implies shaʿb itself named a state of unity (that then broke). A verse of al-Ṭirimmāḥ: "the tribe's unity (shaʿb) scattered after having been joined."
- Two place-names are noted as belonging to this root-cluster by form even though not true derivations: Shaʿabʿab (with a supporting verse) and Shuʿabā.

Note: Ibn Fāris treats "peoples" (shuʿūb, as in Q. 49:13) as a lexical outgrowth of "separation" — a group that has branched off from a larger tribal stock — while also flagging the rival view that the same word could instead derive from "gathering." He offers this purely as a linguistic/etymological question, not a statement about how tribes or peoples should be understood theologically or socially.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) on the root sh-ʿ-l:

Core meaning: spreading and dispersing outward from a single thing, on its various sides.

1. Fire/kindling sense: ashʿala al-nāra fī al-ḥaṭab means "he kindled the fire in the firewood"; ishtaʿalat al-nār means "the fire blazed/flared up." By extension, ishtaʿala al-shayb describes gray hair "spreading" through the head — the image behind the Qur'anic verse he cites, "wa-shtaʿala al-raʾsu shayban," "and the head has flared up with gray" (Maryam 19:4).

2. Al-shuʿla means a flame — the fire kindled in a lamp-wick; he notes it is a well-known word needing no further explanation.

3. Extended "scattering" sense: ashʿalnā al-khayla fī al-ighāra, "we sent the horses out scattered/dispersed in the raid." Similarly, tafarraqa al-qawmu shaʿālīl means "the people scattered into separate bands," as if they had "blazed apart."

4. Al-shaʿal is a patch of white in a horse's forelock and tail (the horse itself is called ashʿal, feminine shaʿlāʾ) — again the idea of something spreading or showing through against the surrounding color.

5. Shaʿl is also recorded as a personal epithet, and as a woman's name.

6. An outlier that does not fit the core sense: al-mishʿal, a four-legged leather vessel used for steeping nabīdh (a fermented drink). Ibn Fāris cites a line of the poet Dhū al-Rumma describing women who deliberately let prayer times pass and instead kept company with the mashāʿil (these leather vessels) and wine-jars.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَشْعُرُ 25x "perceive"; شَاعِر 5x "(is) a poet"; شَعَٰئِر 4x "(the) symbols"; يُشْعِرُ 2x "and let not be aware"; شِّعْر 2x "and their hair"; مَشْعَر 1x "the monument"; شِّعْرَىٰ 1x "(of) sirius"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ش ع ر (sh-ʿ-r) as two distinct roots: one meaning firmness/growth, the other meaning knowledge and marking.

ROOT ONE — firmness/growth (hair and things covered or bristling):
1. شَعْر — hair (well known). Plural أَشْعَار (a plural of a plural); singular شَعْرَة (one hair). A man who is أَشْعَر has long hair on head and body.
2. شَعَار — trees/thicket; "land rich in shaʿār" means densely wooded.
3. أَشْعَر — the ring of hair-fringe growing around a hoof at the skin's edge; plural أَشَاعِر.
4. شَعْرَاء — (a) a downy variety of peach, named for its fuzz (contrasted with a smooth variety, القَرْعَاء); (b) a fly seeming to have down on its forelegs; (c) a dense stand of trees; a meadow (رَوْضَة) or sand-tract (رَمَلَة) that is شَعْرَاء is thick with vegetation.
5. Idiom: دَاهِيَة شَعْرَاء / وَبْرَاء — a "hairy, furry" calamity, i.e. a grave one. Ibn Durayd cites the saying, when someone says something momentous: "I have brought it hairy, possessed of fur."
6. Related by likeness: شَعِير (barley); شَعِيرَة, the small iron pin that fastens a knife-blade, named after a barley-grain; شَعَارِير, small cucumbers.
7. شِعَار — the garment worn next to the body, because it touches the hair on the skin.

ROOT TWO — knowledge and marking:
1. شِعَار also = the watchword troops call out in war to recognize one another.
2. Core sense: شَعَرْتُ بِالشَّيْء — I perceived/became aware of a thing; لَيْتَ شِعْرِي — "would that I knew." Some derive this awareness-sense from شَعْرَة, paralleled with دُرْبَة (skill) and فِطْنَة (acuteness).
3. شَاعِر (poet) — so called because he perceives (yafṭin) what others miss. Cited proof: ʿAntara's line "Have the poets left any patch to re-mend?" — i.e. poets have overlooked nothing.
4. مَشَاعِر الحَجّ — the sites of the rites, called this because they are the landmarks (maʿālim) of the Ḥajj. شَعِيرَة (sing. of شَعَائِر) = the landmarks and observances of the Ḥajj; Ibn Fāris cites Q 2:158, "Ṣafā and Marwa are among the shaʿāʾir of God."
5. شُعَيْرَة also = a sacrificial animal (badana) offered up. Its إِشْعَار (marking) is to gash the base of its hump so blood flows, signaling it is an offering (hady). Hence of a slain caliph they say قَدْ أُشْعِرَ ("he was marked/stricken") — used of him alone among the slain.
6. الشِّعْرَى — a well-known star (Sirius).
7. أَشْعَرَ فُلَانٌ فُلَانًا شَرًّا — he overwhelmed him with evil; أَشْعَرَهُ الحُبُّ مَرَضًا — love afflicted him with sickness. Ibn Fāris notes this can fit either root: the "marking" root (evil set on him like a mark) or the "covering" root (made a garment upon him).

Note: Ibn Fāris judges تَفَرَّقَ القَوْمُ شَعَارِيرَ ("the people scattered every way") to be a case of letter-substitution (ibdāl), the original form being شَعَالِيل.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris gives withholding (al-manʿ) as the root meaning of sh-ḥ-ḥ, which then comes to mean a withholding combined with greed (ḥirṣ).

1. **al-shuḥḥ**: avarice combined with greed. Two men are said to tashāḥḥa over a matter when each wants to win it and keeps it from the other. He cites Q 59:9: "whoever is guarded against the shuḥḥ of his own self, those are the ones who thrive."

2. **A fire-stick that yields no fire** is called zand shaḥāḥ. He cites a line by Ibn Harma about leaving the bounty of the most generous and striking with his own two hands "a fire-stick that is shaḥāḥ".

These, he says, give the root meaning of the doubled form sh-ḥ-ḥ. The reduplicated form shaḥshaḥ is, in his account, close to it, and is used of four kinds of person:

3. **One who keeps constantly at something.** Ibn Fāris reasons that such constancy is nothing other than stinginess over the thing (shuḥḥ).

4. **The jealous man (ghayūr)**, by the same reasoning: when he is jealous, he withholds.

5. **The brave man**, as the one who guards what lies behind his back.

6. **One who presses on (māḍī) in his khiṭba** (vowelled in this copy as "proposal of marriage"; the same letters read khuṭba mean "a speech"). Ibn Fāris explains this use as modelled on the brave man, the one being likened to the other.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: sh-ḥ-m (شحم), from Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha.

Core meaning: this root denotes a category of flesh — namely fatty tissue.

Senses derived from it:
1. الشَّحْم (ash-shaḥm) — "fat," a well-known, ordinary word needing no further gloss.
2. شَحْمَةُ الأُذُن (shaḥmat al-udhun) — "the earlobe," named because it is the fleshy part of the ear where an earring hangs.
3. A man described as مُشْحِم (mushḥim) is one who has a lot of fat (i.e., is fat/fatty).

Ibn Fāris then draws a set of morphological distinctions for related descriptive words, each tied to a different relationship the man has to fat:
- شَحِم (shaḥim) — a man who loves/likes fat.
- شَاحِم (shāḥim) — a man who feeds fat to his companions.
- شَحَّام (shaḥḥām) — a man who sells fat (the intensive/occupational pattern, marking it as his trade).

The entry is a short, self-contained root note: one core sense (a type of fatty flesh) with a small cluster of derived nouns/adjectives distinguished by grammatical pattern and by the person's relation to fat (possessing it, loving it, giving it to others, or trading in it).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats sh-ḥ-n as two unrelated roots, one meaning "filling," the other "distancing/driving off."

1. Filling. شَحَنْتُ السَّفِينَةَ — "I loaded the ship," i.e. filled it. Under the same head he places أَشْحَنَ لِلْبُكَاءِ, said of someone on the point of tears: he had readied himself for weeping, as though it had gathered and filled up in him.

2. Driving away. الشَّحْنُ means expulsion: شَحَنَهُمْ — "he drove them off." A very sour thing is described as إِنَّهُ لَيَشْحَنُ الذِّبَّانَ, "it drives the flies away," i.e. repels them. To this sense he also assigns الشَّحْنَاء, enmity, and عَدُوٌّ مُشَاحِنٌ, an enemy who holds himself apart — his reasoning being that enmity is itself a mutual distancing.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root sh-ṭ-ʾ (شطأ) from two unrelated senses.

1. Shaṭʾ (شَطْء) — a plant's "shoot": growth that comes up around the base of the main stem. Plural: ashṭāʾ. The verb is used as shaṭaʾati l-shajaratu, "the tree put out shoots." He cites the Qur'an: "like a seed-crop that has put forth its shoot" (al-Fatḥ 48:29).

2. Shāṭiʾ (شَاطِئ) — the "bank" or "side" of a valley/riverbed (shāṭiʾ al-wādī = jānibuhu, "its side"). From this comes the verb shāṭaʾtu al-rajula, "I walked the bank alongside the man" — meaning each of the two walked along a different bank, one on each side.

Ibn Fāris explicitly notes these two senses (the plant-shoot and the riverbank) are mutabāyinatān — mutually distinct, not derived from one another.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris traces sh-ṭ-ṭ to two sound root meanings (aṣlān ṣaḥīḥān): distance (al-buʿd) and inclining (al-mayl).

**First root meaning: distance.**

1. **Being far away.** Shaṭṭati al-dār (tashuṭṭu, shuṭūṭan): the dwelling became far away. Al-shaṭāṭ is distance.

2. **Tallness.** Al-shaṭāṭ (or al-shiṭāṭ) is tallness. Ibn Fāris counts it under distance, because the top of what is tall is far from the ground.

3. **Going too far, exceeding measure.** Ashaṭṭa fī al-sawm: to go too far in naming a price, committing shaṭaṭ, which is exceeding the measure. He cites the Qur'anic "wa-lā tushṭiṭ" (Q 38:22) here. Likewise ashaṭṭa al-qawm fī ṭalab fulān: the people pressed on and went far in pursuing someone.

**Second root meaning: inclining.**

4. **Inclining in judgement.** Shaṭṭa and ashaṭṭa denote injustice (jawr) and leaning in judgement. Ibn Fāris allows that "wa-lā tushṭiṭ" (Q 38:22) may instead be cited under this meaning, as "do not incline". In the report of Tamīm al-Dārī, "surely you are unjust to me, so that I carry your strength on my weakness", the word is explained as "unjust in judging against me".

5. **Side of a camel's hump.** Al-shaṭṭ of the hump is one of its sides, and every hump has two. According to Ibn Fāris it is called shaṭṭ because it inclines to one side. A poet says: "as if beneath her torn shift there were a hump-side onto which you had thrown another hump-side." The she-camel called shaṭawṭā takes her name from this.

6. **River bank.** The bank of a river is called shaṭṭ for the same reason, because it lies on the two sides.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha), root ش ط ن (sh-ṭ-n). He treats it as a single sound root whose core meaning is remoteness / distance (al-buʿd).

1. Being far / withdrawing. شَطَنَتِ الدَّارُ (shaṭanat al-dār) = "the dwelling grew remote." نَوًى شَطُونٌ = "a far-off place of separation" — with a supporting verse of al-Nābigha on a distant parting from the beloved Suʿād.

2. Depth. بِئْرٌ شَطُونٌ = "a deep-bottomed well," where the distance down is great.

3. الشَّطَن (al-shaṭan) = a rope, especially a long one (so al-Khalīl). Ibn Fāris says this fits the root's logic, because the span between a rope's two ends is far. Illustrations: a Bedouin's description of a horse, "as if it were a shayṭān among ropes (ashṭān)"; and, of an unruly horse tied between two ropes, "it leaps between two ropes (bayna shaṭanayn)."

4. الشَّيْطَان (al-shayṭān). Ibn Fāris reports two derivations:
 (a) That it belongs to this root sh-ṭ-n, with the nūn as an original (radical) letter — so named for its "remoteness from the truth" and its rebellion (tamarrud); on this account any insolent rebel, whether jinn, human, or beast, is called a shayṭān (with a verse of Jarīr as evidence). On this reading the word is of the measure fayʿāl. The proof cited is a line of Umayya using the form شَاطِن (shāṭin, pattern fāʿil), which treats the nūn as radical. This root-meaning is also applied to Q 37:65, "its spathes are as though the heads of the shayāṭīn" — where it is further noted that shayṭān can mean a serpent (a serpent being so called), supported by a verse likening thongs to a coiling serpent.
 (b) That the nūn is instead an augment, the word being pattern faʿlān and derived from the root شَاطَ (sh-y-ṭ), discussed elsewhere.

Ibn Fāris records both views without deciding between them.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris analyses sh-ṭ-r (شطر) as TWO independent roots: one meaning the half of a thing, the other meaning distance and facing/being opposite.

FIRST ROOT — "half"
1. شَطَرَ الشَّيْءَ — to halve a thing; شَاطَرْتُ فُلَانًا الشَّيْءَ — to split something with someone, each taking half.
2. شَاةٌ شَطُورٌ — a ewe with one teat longer than the other; also a ewe with one teat dried up, and (of camels) a she-camel with two of her four teats dried up.
3. شَطَرَ بَصَرُهُ (verbal nouns شُطُورًا / شَطْرًا) — of a man who looks at you and at someone else at once. Ibn Fāris justifies placing this here: such a man gives each of the two a *half* (shaṭr) of his gaze.
4. The proverb حَلَبَ فُلَانٌ الدَّهْرَ أَشْطُرَهُ ("he has milked time's teat-pairs") means he has experienced varieties of time's good and evil. Its literal base: a she-camel has four teats, two front and two behind; each pair is one shaṭr, since two out of four is the half.

SECOND ROOT — "distance / facing"
5. الشَّطِير — the distant, remote one; شَطَرَتِ الدَّارُ — the dwelling became far off. Cited rajaz line: "Do not leave me among them a stranger far off."
6. شَطَرَ فُلَانٌ عَلَى أَهْلِهِ — he left his people in defiance and opposition.
7. الشَّاطِر — one who has exhausted his family by his wickedness. Ibn Fāris derives this by analogy from the same idea: in acting so, he has removed himself far from his group and the main body of their affairs.
8. شَطْر in the sense of the aim and direction of a thing. He cites Q 2:144 on the qibla — "wherever you are, turn your faces شَطْرَهُ" — glossing shaṭrahu as قَصْدَهُ, "its aim/direction." Two poetic witnesses support this: "set straight the breasts of the pale camels shaṭra (toward) Banū Tamīm," and "a terror has overshadowed you min shaṭri (from the direction of) your frontier." He closes by noting that "the shaṭr of your frontier" is necessarily what lies opposite it while remaining far from and separate from it — tying the directional sense back to the second root of distance-plus-facing.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مُتَشَٰبِه 6x "similar"; تَشَٰبَهَ 4x "(is) allegorical"; شُبِّهَ 1x "it was made to appear (so)"; مُشْتَبِه 1x "resembling"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats sh-b-h as one root whose core meaning is that one thing resembles or matches another — in colour and in description (tashābuh, "mutual likeness").

1. Basic sense — "likeness, resemblance." The forms shibh, shabah, and shabīh all mean "a like / the like of something."

2. Applied to substances — al-shabah names a metal that resembles gold (a gold-like alloy).

3. Applied to affairs — al-mushabbihāt are matters that are perplexing or ambiguous (mushkilāt); and ishtabaha al-amrān means "the two matters became confusable," i.e. hard to tell apart.

4. Exception — al-shabahān (a plant name) is noted as anomalous, standing outside the root's core sense of resemblance.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: شَدِيد 56x "severe"; أَشَدّ 31x "stronger"; أَشُدّ 8x "his maturity"; شَدَدْ 6x "and we strengthened"; ٱشْتَدَّتْ 1x "blows furiously"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats sh-d-d as a single root meaning strength in a thing, and holds that all its branches go back to that idea.

1. **Tying tight.** shadadtu al-ʿaqda, "I tied the knot tight" (verbal noun shadd, imperfect ashuddu).

2. **A single charge.** al-shadda is one instance of the act. By the same reasoning the word is used in war: yashuddu shaddan, "he charges." A verse: "What a charge we made, not a feigned one, against Sakhīna, had it not been for the night and the sanctuary!"

3. **The miser.** al-shadīd and al-mutashaddid can mean the miser (the word "miser" appears as an editor's bracketed supply in the text). Ibn Fāris cites Q 100:8, "and truly in his love of wealth he is shadīd," and a verse of Ṭarafa: "I see death choosing the noble and selecting the choicest part of the wealth of the tight-fisted miser (al-mutashaddid)."

4. **Hardship.** Abū Zayd reports aṣābatnī shuddā, "hardship (shidda) befell me."

5. **Strong mounts.** ashadda al-qawm: the people's riding animals were strong.

6. **Height of the day.** shaddu al-nahār is the day's rising, its advanced part.

7. **al-ashudd.** This is given as twenty years, or by another account forty. Some say the word has no singular; others give its singular as shadd.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: شَفَٰعَة 13x "the intercession"; شَفِيع 10x "any intercessor"; يَشْفَعُ 5x "intercedes"; شَٰفِعِين 2x "(of) the intercessors"; شَّفْع 1x "and the even"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats شفع (sh-f-ʿ) as a single sound root whose core idea is pairing or joining one thing to another.

1. Even vs. odd: الشَّفْع (al-shafʿ) means "even," the opposite of الوتر (al-watr, "odd"). Usage: "it was single, and I paired it." He cites Qur'an 89:3, {By the even and the odd}, and reports the exegetes' reading that al-watr is God and al-shafʿ is creation.

2. Pre-emption right: الشُّفْعَة (al-shufʿa), a claimant's right of pre-emption over a house, belongs here. Ibn Durayd's explanation: it is so named because through it a person adjoins/pairs the property to his own.

3. The ewe with young: الشاة الشافع (al-shāfiʿ) is a ewe accompanied by her offspring.

4. Standing as a second / intercession: شَفَعَ لفلان is to come as someone's "second," seeking his request and helping him.

5. The doubly-milked she-camel: ناقة شَفُوع (shafūʿ) yields two milkings in a single session — again the "pairing" idea.

6. Backing against someone: the phrase "so-and-so shafaʿu against me with enmity" means he lends support against the speaker — fitting the root's logic, as if he turns the hostile party into a paired ally.

7. An outlier the author flags as uncertain: امرأة مَشْفُوعَة, a woman struck by shufʿa in the sense of the evil eye. Ibn Fāris doubts its soundness and suggests it may really belong to the root سفع (with unpointed sīn).

He closes by noting Banū Shāfiʿ of the line of al-Muṭṭalib b. ʿAbd Manāf, including the jurist Muḥammad b. Idrīs al-Shāfiʿī.

dictionary: ʿAyn — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786)
text:
Root ش ف ه (sh-f-h), al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad al-Farāhīdī, Kitāb al-ʿAyn

1. al-shafah — the lip; a grammatical note on its irregular final letter (an elided hāʾ) and its two possible triliteral plural forms (shafahāt, more regular by analogy, or shafawāt, more common in actual use — compared to the plural of "year," sanawāt).
2. al-mushāfahah bi-l-kalām — speaking face-to-face, mouth to mouth, i.e. directly without an intermediary — the root sense behind the modern notion of a "lip-to-lip," in-person exchange.
3. māʾ mashfūh — water that is sought-after and heavily drawn upon, so that people's demand has exhausted all but a little of it (plural miyāh mashfūhah); ṭaʿām mashfūh — food that is scarce, by the same logic — extending "lip" imagery to something worn down by many mouths/hands seeking it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مُشْفِقُون 8x "fearful"; أَشْفَقْ 2x "and they feared"; شَّفَق 1x "by the twilight glow"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives شفق (sh-f-q) from a single core idea: thinness or fineness in something, from which the other senses branch.

1. Apprehension / tender concern: أَشْفَقْتُ مِنَ الْأَمْرِ means to be wary and cautious of a matter — a "softening" toward it out of concern. The form شَفِقْتُ is occasionally used, but most philologists hold that only أَشْفَقْتُ and the participle مُشْفِق ("anxious, solicitous") are correct. In the verse "as the dependents were shafiqa over the provisions," the sense is that they were grudging/stingy with it.

2. Of garments/things: al-Khalīl glosses al-shafaq as what is poor or inferior in quality.

3. The evening afterglow — al-shafaq: the glow seen in the sky as the sun sets, i.e. the redness. It is called this for its color and its faintness (linking back to the "thinness" idea). Cited authorities:
   - al-Khalīl: the redness between sunset and the later ʿishāʾ time.
   - Mujāhid (one report via Ibn Najīḥ): "daytime" (al-nahār), on Q 84:16 "So I swear by the shafaq"; but in another report (via al-ʿAwwām b. Ḥawshab) he says it is the redness.
   - Muqātil's tafsīr: the redness.
   - al-Zajjāj: the redness seen in the west after sundown.
   - al-Farrāʾ: the redness, and he cites an Arab saying "a dyed garment as though it were the shafaq" — a red garment — as a witness that shafaq means the redness.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib treats sh-f-w through shafā, the edge of a thing, and explains al-shifāʾ, healing, as reaching the edge of soundness.

1. **Edge, brink (shafā).** The shafā of a well or of anything else is its edge. It serves as a proverbial image for being close to destruction, as in the Qur'an's ʿalā shafā jurufin, "on the brink of a bank" (Q 9:109), and wa-kuntum ʿalā shafā ḥufratin mina l-nār, "and you were on the brink of a pit of fire" (Q 3:103). The verb appears in ashfā fulān ʿalā l-halāk, "so-and-so was at the brink of destruction", meaning he came to be on its edge.

2. **A small remainder (figurative).** Borrowed from this sense: mā baqiya min kadhā illā shafan, "nothing remained of such-and-such but a shafā", meaning only a little remained, like the edge of a well.

3. **Forms.** The dual of shafā is shafawān and the plural ashfāʾ.

4. **Healing (al-shifāʾ).** Healing from illness is reaching the edge of soundness (al-salāma); the word then became a name for recovery. Describing honey, the Qur'an says fīhi shifāʾun li-l-nās, "in it is healing for people" (Q 16:69). Describing the Qur'an, he cites hudan wa-shifāʾ, "guidance and healing" (Q 41:44); wa-shifāʾun li-mā fī l-ṣudūr, "and healing for what is in the breasts" (Q 10:57); and wa-yashfi ṣudūra qawmin muʾminīn, "and He will heal the breasts of a believing people" (Q 9:14).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ش-ف + weak letter as a single semantic node meaning "to be on the brink of, to overlook, to come to the edge of" something.

1. Core sense — being on the verge / looking down on. أَشْفَى عَلَى الشَّيْءِ (ashfā ʿalā al-shayʾ): to come to overlook a thing, to be on the point of it.

2. شِفَاء (shifāʾ, "cure") — derived from that core sense: healing is so called because it overcomes the illness and comes to stand over it. اسْتَشْفَى (istashfā): to seek a cure. The transitive form: "I gave you the thing to seek cure by" — but Ibn Fāris says the correct expression is أَشْفَيْتُكَ الشَّيْءَ (ashfaytuka al-shayʾ).

3. شَفَى of anything — its edge or brink. He notes two possible derivations: either it belongs to this same root-sense, or the fāʾ is a substitution (ibdāl) for an original yāʾ.

4. Extended use of "brink" — أَشْفَى الْمَرِيضُ عَلَى الْمَوْتِ: the sick man came to the edge of death. مَا بَقِيَ مِنْهُ إِلَّا شَفًى: only a small remnant of it is left.

5. Poetic witness — al-ʿAjjāj: "I fulfilled it before a shafan, or at a shafan." The commentators explained this as the moment when the sun has come to the brink of setting.

6. شَفَة (shafah, "lip") — two accounts of the missing third radical:
   (a) the elided letter is a wāw, evidenced by the plural ثَلَاث شَفَوَات (thalāth shafawāt); a رَجُل أَشْفَى (rajul ashfā) is a man whose lips will not close, comparable to al-arwaq;
   (b) the elided letter is a hāʾ, evidenced by the diminutive شُفَيْهَة (shufayhah), by مُشَافَهَة (mushāfahah, speaking face to face, mouth to mouth), and by شُفَاهِيّ (shufāhiyy, a man with large lips).
   Ibn Fāris allows both but prefers the first, because it fits the analogy he set out: the two lips "overlook" the mouth — they stand on its rim.

7. Outside the pattern — شَفَهَنِي فُلَان عَنْ كَذَا (shafahanī fulān ʿan kadhā), "he kept me occupied away from such-and-such," which Ibn Fāris marks as anomalous to this section.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats sh-gh-f (شغف) as expressing a single core idea: al-shaghāf, "the covering of the heart" — the membrane or outer casing that encloses it.

He supports this with the Qur'anic verse {qad shaghafahā ḥubban} (Yūsuf 12:30), which he glosses as meaning that love reached, or penetrated as far as, the shaghāf — the very casing of her heart. In other words, the verb shaghafa describes love (ḥubb) reaching so deep that it touches the heart's own enclosing membrane, not merely its surface.

The entry gives no other senses; the root's whole meaning, per Ibn Fāris, is anchored in this one image of "the heart's covering."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: شُغُل 1x "will be occupied"; شَغَلَتْ 1x "kept us busy"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root sh-gh-l (شغل) from a single core meaning: "the opposite of being empty/free" (khilāf al-farāgh) — i.e., being occupied, taken up, or engaged.

1. Basic verb pattern: shaghaltu fulānan — "I occupied/busied so-and-so"; the doer is shāghil ("occupier"), and the one affected is mashghūl ("occupied, busied") [this exact word is partly illegible in the source but is the expected passive participle].

2. shughiltu ‘anka bi-kadhā — "I was kept away from you, occupied by such-and-such" — given only in the passive voice (no named agent).

3. A usage note: the Form IV passive ushghiltu is said NOT to occur in the language, according to those he cites.

4. Intensifying phrase: shughlun shāghilun — "a thoroughly preoccupying business" (literally "an occupation that occupies").

5. Plural: the plural of shughl ("occupation, business") is ashghāl.

6. A further attested form: ishtughila fulānun bi-sh-shay' — "so-and-so became occupied/engaged with the thing," with the active participle mushtaghil ("one who is occupied/engaged").

7. Poetic citation: a verse is quoted where a woman greets someone and says that their group's departure "today" leaves them all mushtaghal ("occupied/preoccupied"), cited to support this participial usage.

8. A contradicting report: despite point 3 (that ushghiltu is not used), some people are reported to have said ashghalanī bi-l-alf ("it occupied me with/by the thousand"), i.e., they did use the Form IV verb ashghala. Ibn Fāris records this as a variant usage some people relate, without resolving the tension with his earlier note.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: شِهَاب 4x "a burning flame"; شُهُب 1x "and flaming fires"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats sh-h-b as one root meaning: whiteness set within something dark. He states as the defining constraint that shuhba is never pure white — it is always white mingled with darkness.

1. Coat colour. Shuhba in a horse is a whiteness mixed with black.
2. Massed iron. كَتِيبَةٌ شَهْبَاءُ (a shahbāʾ squadron) is said when the top of the formation shows the white of iron.
3. Cold weather. A day of cold and chill wind is أَشْهَب (ashhab), and a night is اللَّيْلَةُ الشَّهْبَاءُ — the same white-in-dark colouring applied to weather.
4. Drying crops. اشْهَابَّ الزَّرْعُ is said when a standing crop has dried out while patches of green still remain through it (pale streaked with dark).
5. Flame. Belonging to the same chapter is الشِّهَاب (shihāb): a blazing, shooting flame of fire.
6. Figurative use. "So-and-so is a shihāb of war" is said of a man well known and famous in war — Ibn Fāris compares this to the fame of the gleaming stars.
7. Blade. The النَّصْل الْأَشْهَب is reported to be a blade lightly filed until its blackness is gone.
8. Thinned milk. Shihāb is also reported for milk heavily watered down; Ibn Fāris explains the name by the water content becoming so great that it turned into whiteness with another colour mixed into it — i.e. the root sense again.

Method note: the author derives every branch, including the fire and star senses, from the single colour notion of white mixed with dark, and uses the thinned-milk case explicitly to demonstrate that derivation.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: شَهِيد 56x "a witness"; شَهِدَ 44x "bear witness"; شَهَٰدَة 23x "and the witnessed"; شَاهِد 21x "the witnesses"; أَشْهَدَ 7x "and take witness"; مَشْهُود 3x "and what is witnessed"; شَهَٰدَٰت 3x "testimonies"; ٱسْتَشْهِدُ 2x "then call to witness"; مَّشْهَد 1x "(the) witnessing"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ش-ه-د (sh-h-d) as a single root with one core meaning: presence, knowledge, and making-known. He holds that every derivative traces back to this, except one anomaly noted at the end.

1. **shahāda (testimony)** — the word that pulls together all three strands: being present, knowing, and declaring. Verb pattern: shahida / yashhadu / shahādatan.

2. **mashhad** — the place where people gather (a "presence" of people).

3. **shuhūd (sing. shāhid), a birth sense** — the fluid that appears on a newborn's head at birth; some say it means instead the caul/membrane (ghirs). A cited verse describes moist earth "not yet dried of its shuhūd." Related: a she-camel's shuhūd are the birth-traces (blood or afterbirth) left where she calved.

4. **shahīd (one slain in God's path)** — two proposed derivations: (a) because the angels of mercy attend (are present with) him; (b) because he falls to the earth, and the earth is itself called al-shāhida. (Ibn Fāris reports these as others' explanations.)

5. **shāhid** — can mean "the tongue," and can mean "the angel." Al-Aʿshā uses both senses in a single line: "my shāhid" = his tongue, and "shāhid Allāh" = the angel.

6. **Qur'anic usage** — On {shahida allāhu…} (Q 3:18), Ibn Fāris reports the scholars' reading that shahida here means God "made known" / "made clear" — parallel to a witness before a judge who makes clear where the right lies. The sense stays within knowledge + declaration.

7. **mushhid (of a woman)** — one whose husband is present, contrasted with mughīb (whose husband is absent).

8. **ashhada** — said of a man who emits pre-seminal fluid (madhy); linked back, by analogy, to sense 3 (the fluid at birth).

9. **Anomaly (outside the root's core): shuhd** — honey in the comb; plural shihād. A cited verse mentions fine wheat "kneaded with honeycomb (shihād)." Ibn Fāris marks this as deviating (shadhdha) from the presence/knowledge/declaration meaning.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: ش-ه-ق (sh-h-q)

Ibn Fāris states this root has one core meaning: height / elevation (ʿuluww).

1. Primary sense — height. Source of جَبَلٌ شَاهِقٌ (jabal shāhiq), "a towering/high mountain."

2. Derived sense — breathing. From the height-sense comes الشَّهِيق (al-shahīq), meaning "inhalation" (drawing the breath back/up) — the opposite of الزَّفِير (al-zafīr), "exhalation" (pushing the breath out). Ibn Fāris frames the two as a paired opposition: shahīq is breath drawn upward/inward, zafīr is breath sent out — the root's original "rising" sense underlies the shahīq side of that pair.

3. Derived sense — intense anger. Some lexicographers cited by Ibn Fāris used the phrase فُلَانٌ ذُو شَاهِقٍ ("so-and-so is dhū shāhiq") of a man whose anger had become intense. Ibn Fāris adds his own suggestion that this state may also involve an accompanying sound (a loud groan or gasp), tying it back to the shahīq/breathing sense.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats sh-h-r as a single sound root meaning clarity/manifestness in a matter and the giving of light. From this core he derives:

1. الشَّهْر (month): in Arab speech the word first meant الهِلال, the crescent/new moon; a period of thirty days was then named after the crescent and called a "month." He notes that Arabs and non-Arabs (ʿAjam) agree in this, since the ʿAjam likewise name a thirty-day span after the crescent in their own language. He cites Dhū al-Rumma as evidence — a verse describing someone keen-eyed who sees the crescent-month before others while it is still thin.

2. الشُّهْرَة (shuhra): the clear manifestness/publicity of a matter; hence مَشْهُور (renowned) and شُهِرَ … بكذا (to become well-known for something), شَهَرُوه (they made him publicly known).

3. شَهَرَ سيفَه: to unsheathe or bare one's sword (= انتضاه).

4. أَشْهَرْنا بالمكان: we stayed somewhere for a month.

5. شَهْرَان (Shahrān): the name of a tribe.

All senses trace back to the root idea of something becoming clear, visible, or brought out into the open.

quran_words: ٱشْتَهَتْ 8x "they desire"; شَّهَوَٰت 3x "(of) the (things they) desire"; شَهْوَة 2x "lustfully"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root sh-h-w (shīn, hāʾ, and a weak final letter) as yielding a single core notion: al-shahwa, meaning appetite, craving, or desire.

Derived forms he cites:
- رَجُلٌ شَهْوَانُ (shahwān) — a man marked by strong craving or eager appetite.
- شَيْءٌ شَهِيٌّ (shahiyy) — a thing that is desirable or appetizing.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: شَجَرَة 19x "[the] tree"; شَجَر 7x "and the trees"; شَجَرَ 1x "arises"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats sh-j-r as two overlapping roots so close he combines them. The shared idea has two strands: (a) one thing interpenetrating another, part entering part; and (b) height and elevation. He derives the whole entry from these two notions.

1. شَجَر — trees / woody plants. Singular شَجَرَة (a tree), which always involves height and interlacing branches. Related forms: وَادٍ شَجِرٌ (a tree-filled valley); this land is أَشْجَر (more wooded) than another. He defines shajar as every plant that has a stem (sāq), citing Q 55:6 "and the najm and the shajar bow down."

2. شَجَرَ بَيْنَ الْقَوْمِ — a matter arises in dispute among people; they differ and quarrel (tashājarū). A dispute is called mushājara because the disputants' words interpenetrate one another. اِشْتَجَرُوا = they contended. Cited with Q 4:65 "…until they make you judge in what has arisen in dispute (shajara) between them."

3. شَجْر of a person — one view: the opening/parting of the mouth. Al-Aṣmaʿī: the chin itself. Ibn Fāris judges the two close, since the jawbones "interlock" (ishtajarā) when they meet — matching the root's interpenetration sense. اِشْتَجَرَ الرَّجُل = a man rests his hand on his shajr (chin), with a poetic citation of a sleepless man propping his chin, eyes as if stung by the bitter ṣāb plant.

4. شَجَرْتُ الشَّيْءَ — to raise up something that hangs down (the elevation sense).

5. الشِّجَار — the wooden frame of a camel-litter (hawdaj); it carries both senses at once (height + interlacing). المِشْجَر is so named for its interlocking parts.

6. تَشَاجَرَ الْقَوْمُ بِالرِّمَاح — they thrust spears at one another (mutual interpenetration).

7. الأَرْض الشَّجْرَاء / الشَّجِرَة — land abounding in trees. Ibn Durayd notes one does not say wādin shajrāʾ (this feminine form is not used for "valley").

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats sh-k-k as a single root whose derivatives all come from one another, and he says its one meaning is interpenetration: one thing entering into another.

1. **Piercing.** shakaktuhu bi-l-rumḥ means "I pierced him with the spear", when the spearhead enters his body. A verse is cited: "So I pierced his garments through with the solid spear; the noble man is not held sacrosanct from the lances." The same idea covers joining two things together by piercing through them.

2. **Doubt.** al-shakk, the opposite of certainty (yaqīn), belongs here. Ibn Fāris explains the name this way: the doubter is as if two matters had been skewered together for him on one skewer, and he is certain of neither. Compare shakaktu bayna waraqatayn, "I pinned two leaves together", said when you push a twig through both and so join them.

3. **Weaponry.** al-shikka is the weaponry a person wears, and a man is called shākk fī l-silāḥ, "clad in arms". It gets the name either because one pierces with it, or because its parts seem pierced into one another.

4. **A slight limp.** In a verse of Dhū al-Rumma describing a scarred wild ass leaping "as though he had a manifest shakk or were afflicted in the side", shakk is said to mean a slight limp: baʿīr shākk, "a limping camel", and shakka shakkan, "it limped". Ibn Fāris calls this a sound analogy, since it is a pain that enters into the animal. Others say shakk here is the upper arm sticking to the side; if that is correct, he says, it fits the analogy even more clearly.

5. **Groups of people.** al-shakāʾik (singular shakīka) are groups or factions of people. They are named so, he says, because when they split apart, the members of each group are intermingled with one another.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root sh-k-l — core idea: matching, resembling, binding/hobbling.

1. Mushākala (correspondence/resemblance): matching in outward form and shape; matching in kind/genus (nidd); matching in quality (shabah). Cited for Q38:58, "others of its kind, in pairs" — meaning resembling something else in form and in the act performed.

2. Shikl: sometimes glossed as "coquetry" or a charming manner, but al-Rāghib holds that it really names the mutual familiarity/intimacy that exists between two similar things sharing the same manner. Hence the saying: "people are kinds, and they pair up with their own kind" (al-nāsu ashkālun wa-allāf).

3. Etymological core — hobbling: mushākala is said to derive from shakl meaning "to hobble a riding-animal" (tie its legs) — shakaltu al-dābba, "I hobbled the animal." Al-shikāl is the hobble-rope itself. By metaphor this gives shakaltu al-kitāb, "I placed diacritics on the book" — likened to fettering/fixing the text in place. A riding-animal is said to "have shikāl" when its white leg-markings sit on one hind leg and one foreleg, forming the same crossed pattern as a hobble-rope.

4. Shākila (Q17:84, "each works according to his shākila"): means one's innate disposition (sajiyya), which binds/constrains a person the way a hobble binds an animal — because, as al-Rāghib notes (pointing to his own book al-Dharīʿa ilā Makārim al-Sharīʿa for fuller discussion), the pull of one's innate nature over a person is overpowering. He likens this to a saying attributed to the Prophet: "Everyone is made easy toward that for which he was created."

5. Ashkila: a need or compulsion that constrains a person.

6. Ishkāl ("difficulty/ambiguity" in a matter): a metaphorical extension of the same root — parallel to how ishtibāh ("confusion") is derived from shabah ("resemblance").

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: شَكَرَ 46x "be grateful"; شَاكِر 14x "the grateful ones"; شَكُور 10x "(and) grateful"; مَّشْكُور 2x "appreciated"; شُكُور 2x "to be thankful"; شُكْر 1x "(in) gratitude"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats sh-k-r as four separate roots that, in his view, share no common underlying sense.

1. Shukr — praise or thanks given to a person for a kindness done to you. He notes a reported view that its essence is "contentment with little," citing the usage farasun shakūr, a "grateful" horse that stays fat on scant fodder. Shawāhid: a line of al-Aʿshā describing a summer raid so harsh it exhausts even a hardy, easily-kept mare; and the proverb "more grateful than a barwaq plant," which greens at the sight of a cloud without any actual rain.

2. Fullness and abundant yield. A milch animal is shakira when good pasture makes it give copious milk (ashkara al-qawm, shakirat al-ḥalūba). By extension a tree is shakira when its foliage/shade grows thick.

3. Shakīr — the tender new shoots that sprout from a tree's trunk, and by extension the first growth of any plant. Shāhid: a poet's line comparing a fledgling nestling to curly shakīr shoots.

4. Shakr — sexual intercourse; also said to mean a woman's vulva. Shāhid: the saying of Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar to a man sued by his wife — that if she demands the "price" of her shakr and his shabr (intercourse), he takes to cheating her of her due and paying her off in dribs and drabs.

dictionary: ʿAyn — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786)
text:
Root ش ك س (sh-k-s), al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad al-Farāhīdī, Kitāb al-ʿAyn — the shortest of the four entries on this root (companion to al-Rāghib's, al-Zamakhsharī's, and Ibn Manẓūr's)

1. al-shikis/al-shakas — bad-tempered, difficult in dealing (mubāyaʿah) and otherwise; al-shakas is the verbal noun.
2. Figurative extension: al-layl wa-l-nahār yatashākasān — night and day "are at variance," i.e. oppose each other and do not align — the same idiom found in al-Zamakhsharī's entry on this root.
3. Qur'anic citation, al-Zumar 39:29: "shurakāʾu mutashākisūn" — quarrelling partners — cited here as the paradigm example of the root's core sense.
4. rajul shakis bayyin al-shakas — a man clearly difficult in temperament, illustrated with a line of poetry describing oneself as created "shaksan ashwasa" (difficult, sidelong/fierce in bearing).

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
quran_words: أَشْكُوا 1x "i complain"; مِشْكَوٰة 1x "(is) like a niche"; تَشْتَكِى 1x "and she directs her complaint"
text:
Root Š-K-W / Š-K-Y, as treated by al-Zabīdī in Tāj al-ʿArūs.

1. To lay a grievance before someone. شَكَا (imperfect يَشْكو) — "he laid his case before God," i.e. he informed Him of the weakness of his condition. The verbal nouns are many: شَكْوى, شَكاة, شَكاوة, شَكِيَّة, and شِكاية.

2. Grammatical note on شِكاية. The wāw of the root became a yāʾ here because most فِعالة verbal nouns from weak roots belong to the yāʾ class (compare جِراية "allowance", ولاية "guardianship", وِصاية "trusteeship"); wāw-forms of this pattern are rare, so شِكاية was assimilated to the commoner type. Al-Zabīdī compares the parallel alteration in عَلاية, noting that a proper name is more open to such change.

3. To complain about a person. شَكَى فلاناً — to report the wrong someone has done to you. تَشَكَّى and اشْتَكَى carry the same sense as شَكَا. تَشاكَوْا: to complain to one another. شاكاهُ: to complain of him, or report harm received.

4. The image behind the word (al-Rāghib). شِكاية is the making-visible of inward distress (بَثّ). Its origin is "opening the شَكْوة" — a small skin water-bag — and showing what is inside; the usage is taken as an original metaphor, parallel to "I poured out for him what was in my vessel" and "I shook out for him what was in my bag," both said of disclosing what is in the heart. Qurʾānic citations given: "I only complain of my anguish and grief to God" and "and she complains to God."

5. Sickness itself. الشَّكْو, الشَّكْوى, الشَّكْواء (long form, from al-Azharī), الشَّكاة, الشَّكاء all denote the illness itself, not only the complaining. Abū al-Mujīb asked his cousin "What is your ailment?" and was answered, "The ending of the term and the expiry of the span." A cited verse: "A brother — if he complains of hurt I am his fold; and if that ailment is mine, my brother is my cure." تَشَكَّى / اشْتَكَى also simply means "he fell ill." الشَّكْو is used of longing or passion as well.

6. Derived nouns. الشَّكِيُّ: the one complained of (the فَعِيل form can be read as active or passive) — al-Ṭirimmāḥ: "My mark is complained of and my tongue is fierce." It also denotes one who sickens at the very slightest thing, as does الشاكِي (per al-Muḥkam). الشَّكِيَّة: the thing complained of (like رَمِيَّة "the thing shot at"), plural شَكايا; شَكْوى pluralises as شَكاوى.

7. The IV-form أَشْكى — with opposite senses (a ضِدّ, auto-antonym).
 a. To find someone complaining or ailing; per al-Tahdhīb, to come upon one's beloved complaining.
 b. To obtain redress for someone from another (Ibn Sīdah).
 c. To give someone more cause for complaint: شَكانِي فأَشْكَيْتُه — "he complained of me, so I gave him more to complain of." Al-Ṣiḥāḥ: to act toward someone so as to drive him to complain of you.
 d. To remove someone's cause of complaint — al-Ṣiḥāḥ: to satisfy him and strip away his grievance. Al-Miṣbāḥ explains the hamza here as privative, which is what makes the verb an auto-antonym. Cited report: "We complained to the Messenger of God of the burning ground against our foreheads, and he did not relieve us," i.e. did not remove the grievance.
 e. أَشْكاهُ also: to pour out one's complaint and endured longing to someone. And (per Ibn al-Qaṭṭāʿ) to take up a شَكْوة.

8. To be accused. هو يُشْكى بكذا — "he is suspected/accused of it." Cited verse: a fair, bright-eyed woman "accused of flirtation."

9. الشَّكْوة — the skin bag. A hide vessel for water and milk; al-Rāghib: a small vessel for water. Al-Ṣiḥāḥ: the hide of a suckling kid, used for milk — the hide of a yearling or older is a وَطْب instead. Al-Muḥkam: a hide vessel in which water is cooled and milk kept. Al-Tahdhīb gives the graded terminology: while still suckling its hide is a شَكْوة, after weaning a بَدْرَة, at yearling stage a سِقاء. Plurals: شَكَوات, شِكاء, and also شُكِيّ; diminutive شُكَيَّة.

10. Denominal verb from the bag. شَكَّتِ النِّساءُ / اشْتَكَتْ — Thaʿlab preferred تَشَكَّتِ النِّساءُ: the women took up the شَكْوة to churn milk, precisely because the bag is small and only a little can be churned in it. A cited verse describes a season of plenty: the goat frisking with fat, the antelope lying sated with folded neck, and "the husbandless women took up their milk-skins" — i.e. milk was so plentiful that even a woman without a husband had a surplus to store.

11. Other lexical items. الشَّكْو: a small lamb (Ibn Sīdah). شَكْو: also the name of an Arab clan (Ibn Durayd). شَكَّى: a village in Armenia, source of the "Shakkī" bridles and hides.

12. المِشْكاة. A recess or window in a wall that does not pass through (al-Muḥkam; al-Jawharī from al-Farrāʾ; al-Asās: a small unpierced opening). Ibn Jinnī held its alif to be converted from wāw, since it is sometimes inflected on the wāw pattern, as صلاة is. Cited: "like a niche in which is a lamp." On origin: al-Zajjāj reports a claim that it is Abyssinian, while noting it is current Arabic speech; Ibn al-Jawālīqī lists it among loanwords, as does al-Khafājī. On sense, al-Zabīdī records competing exegetical opinions: the majority (Ibn Jubayr, Saʿīd b. ʿIyāḍ) take it as the blind wall-recess, which concentrates light so a lamp shines brighter there; Mujāhid, as the column the lamp stands on, or (alternatively) the iron hook the lamp hangs from; Abū Mūsā, as the iron or lead fitting holding the wick; al-Azharī, as the glass tube where the wick sits, likened to a niche. Ibn ʿAṭiyya judged Ibn Jubayr's view soundest. Al-Suhaylī transmits an exegetical reading of the verse as God's light in the believer's heart, dispelling darkness and doubt; Kaʿb's reading takes the niche as Muḥammad's breast, the lamp his tongue, the glass his mouth. (These are reported as the views of named exegetes.)

13. Homonym from a different root. شاكِي السِّلاح — a man of sharp and formidable weaponry — belongs with شَوْكة "point, prowess"; al-Akhfash treats شاكِي as a metathesis of شائِك. الشاكِي is also a name for the lion. الشُّكِّيّ, an arabised weapon-term, belongs under ش ك ك, and al-Zabīdī notes (following al-Ṣāghānī) that al-Jawharī misplaced it here.

14. Textual correction. The Qāmūs text شَكَّى شاكِيَهُ ("he desisted from him / set his mind at ease") is judged by al-Zabīdī a bad scribal corruption; the correct reading, per al-Takmila, is سَلَّى شاكِيَه — he consoled the one complaining over what had befallen him. Relatedly, سَلَّى شاكِيَ أرضِ كذا: he left a land alone and did not approach it.

15. Further supplementary senses. الشِّكاة: a fault or blemish — hence Ibn al-Zubayr's retort when taunted about his mother "of the two waistbands": "That is a reproach whose shame passes clear of you." Of a camel worn out by travel, stretching its neck and moaning, it is said قد شَكا — "My camel complained to me of the long night-march: patience, fair patience; both of us are afflicted." شَكا فلانٌ also: his nails split (al-Azharī). ذو الشَّكْوة ("the man with the water-skin") was a byname of Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Kaʿb b. Thaʿlaba al-Qaynī, present at Ajnādayn with Abū ʿUbayda b. al-Jarrāḥ, who used to carry a شَكْوة into battle.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: شِّمَال 8x "the left"; ٱشْتَمَلَتْ 2x "contains"; شَمَائِل 2x "and to the left"
poets_named: Abū al-Najm (Umayyad); Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad); unnamed verse
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ش-م-ل (sh-m-l) from two regular roots, plus a few outliers.

FIRST ROOT — encircling something and taking hold of it from every side:
1. شَمَلَهُمُ الأمر — a matter "encompassed" them, became general to all; hence أمر شامل, an all-encompassing matter.
2. الشَّمْلَة (shamla) — a cloak one girds and wraps oneself in.
3. جَمَعَ اللهُ شَمْلَه — a prayer that God bring a person's scattered affairs together; when things unite, each "wraps around" the other.
4. شِمَال — a pouch fitted over a ewe's udder so it encloses it; likewise "wrapping" a fruit-shedding palm by tying its clusters in cloth.
5. المِشْمَل (mishmal) — a small sword a man conceals by wrapping his garment over it.

SECOND ROOT — the side opposite the right:
1. اليد الشِّمال — the left hand.
2. الريح الشِّمال — the north wind, so called because it comes from the left of the qibla for someone facing the qibla of Iraq. Plural of شِمال is أشْمُل (shāhid: Abū al-Najm, "it comes to it from rights and lefts").
3. الشَّمُول (shamūl) — wine; two explanations: either it has a gust like the north wind's, or it "takes hold of" the intellect.
4. غدير مشمول — a pool chilled by the north wind; hence wine is called mashmūla, "cold-tasting."
5. A verse of Dhū al-Rumma on "the shamāʾil of Jillān" is read two ways: either the hunters' blinds/hides (sing. shimāla, likened to the udder-pouch above), or simply "the region of the left/north."

OUTLIERS (fitting neither root):
1. الشَّمَلة — leftover ripe dates on a palm; shamālīl = the last remnants, or the offshoots of branches.
2. الشَّمْلَلة — swiftness; hence a swift she-camel is called shimlāl / shimlīl (shāhid: a verse describing a lean, inbred, long-necked, swift she-camel).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the whole root ش م س from a single core idea: changeableness and restlessness — something that shifts and will not stay put.

1. al-shams (the sun): named from this idea because it never stays fixed but is always in motion. He supports this with the Qur'anic reading "and the sun runs — no fixed resting-place of its own."

2. Verb of weather: shamasa yawmunā / ushmisa — "our day turned sunny / its sun grew strong."

3. shamūs of an animal: a beast that can hardly be kept still — skittish, restive (verbal noun shimās).

4. shamūs of a woman: one who shies away from anything improper or suspect and will not settle near it (plural shumus). He cites a line praising such women as too aloof to reward a lewd, jealous man's expectations.

5. shamūs of a man: one with no steady character, unsettled and inclined to be difficult.

6. shamisa lī fulān: "he turned shamis toward me" — i.e. he showed open hostility; Ibn Fāris ties this back to the same idea of a shifting, unstable temperament.

He labels all the above the root's regular sense-pattern (qiyās). He then adds proper names formed from it, on the authority of Ibn Durayd: the name ʿAbd Shams; a report from Ibn al-Kalbī (which Ibn Fāris notes no one else records) that al-Shams was an ancient idol; another view that Shams was a known water-spring; and the tribal name ʿAbshams (of Banū Tamīm), source of the relative adjective ʿAbshamī.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ش-م-ت (sh-m-t). Source: Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004 CE).

Ibn Fāris treats sh-m-t as a single sound root, but flags that some of its derived uses are obscure and don't obviously connect back to the core sense.

**1. Core sense — gloating over an enemy's misfortune.** شَمِتَ بِهِ (shamita bihi) = "he gloated over him," rejoicing at a calamity that has struck someone hostile to him. أَشْمَتَهُ اللَّهُ بِعَدُوِّهِ (ashmatahu Allāhu bi-ʿaduwwihi) = "God made him one gloated over by his enemy," i.e. let the enemy have cause to gloat over him. He cites Qur'an 7:150, {فَلَا تُشْمِتْ بِيَ الْأَعْدَاءَ}, "so let not the enemies gloat over me," as an instance of this root.

**2. Idiom "the night of the gloaters."** بِلَيْلَةِ الشَّوَامِتِ (bi-laylati l-shawāmit) describes spending a night of misfortune — the kind that gives one's gloaters (al-shawāmit) something to gloat about. A poetic line is quoted: a man startled by hunting hounds spends the night "at the mercy of the gloaters, from fear and from cold."

**3. "Returning disappointed."** رَجَعَ الْقَوْمُ شَمَاتَى/شِمَاتًا (rajaʿa l-qawmu shamātā/shimātan) — "the people returned [in a state of] shamātā/shimātan," said of a party that came back from its destination empty-handed or thwarted. Attributed to the poet Sāʿida (the verse itself isn't quoted in this entry).

**4. Obscure usage — the sneezing blessing (tashmīt al-ʿāṭis).** This is the custom of saying "yarḥamuka Allāh" ("God have mercy on you") to someone who sneezes. Ibn Fāris quotes a ḥadīth: two men sneezed before the Prophet; he gave the blessing (tashmīt) to one but not the other, explaining that the first had said "al-ḥamdu lillāh" (praised God) and the second had not. Al-Khalīl (an earlier lexicographer Ibn Fāris cites) held that tashmīt al-ʿāṭis is simply a prayer of good for the person — anyone who prays good for someone is a "mushammit" for them. Ibn Fāris is explicit that he cannot see how this usage derives from the "gloating" core sense, and suggests the connecting knowledge has simply been lost over time.

**5. A separate, unrelated word — "legs of an animal."** شَوَامِت (shawāmit) is also used as a name for the legs of a four-legged riding/pack animal. Al-Khalīl says it's just a name, with no further explanation. Abū ʿAmr cites a curse: "lā taraka Allāhu lahu shāmitatan" — "may God leave him no shāmita [i.e., no standing leg]." Ibn Fāris again flags this as unexplained: no analogical (qiyās) reasoning accounts for why an animal's leg would be called shāmita.

Ibn Fāris closes with "wa-Allāhu aʿlam" ("and God knows best") — his standard formula for entries he considers unresolved.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ش-م-خ (sh-m-kh) from a single core sense: self-magnification paired with physical height.

1. Height/loftiness — used of a mountain: jabalun shāmikh, "a lofty/towering mountain," meaning ʿālin, "high."

2. Haughty pride, expressed through the nose — shamakha bi-anfihi, literally "he raised his nose," used of someone who became inwardly conceited or self-important.

3. Proper name — Shamkh is also recorded as a man's name.

Ibn Fāris ties senses 1 and 2 together as one underlying idea: both height (of a mountain) and pride (of a person, expressed by an upturned nose) are instances of the same root meaning of elevation/self-exaltation.

dictionary: ʿAyn — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786)
text:
This is a very short entry from Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl's dictionary, arranged by which combinations of the three root letters ش (sh), م (m), ز (z) are actually used in Arabic. The ʿAyn notes that of all possible orderings of these three letters, only ش‑م‑ز is attested — the rest are unused arrangements, a bookkeeping note typical of this dictionary's method.

Under the entry itself, the book records two related items:

1. The noun at-tashmīz (from a verb shammaza) — the entry states this word is not [correct/pure] Arabic, but notes it is nonetheless used, giving the example "shammazat al-arḍ tashmīzan" — the earth "did tashmīz" (i.e., some action or state affecting the ground; the word given without further gloss).

2. The verb ishmaʾazza — used, the text says, "when it contracts" (idhā taqabbaḍa), i.e., to describe something drawing itself together or shrinking/recoiling.

The entry gives no shawāhid (citations) beyond these two brief usage notes, and no further grammatical or morphological detail.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ش-ن-أ as a single root whose core idea is hatred together with shunning or keeping away from something.

1. **Core sense — hatred / revulsion and avoidance.** The root points to *bighḍa* (hatred) and to turning away from a thing.

2. **شَنُوءَة (shanūʾa) — fastidious disgust.** Defined as *taqazzuz*, squeamish revulsion at something. Ibn Fāris derives the tribal name أَزْد شَنُوءَة (Azd Shanūʾa) from this word.

3. **The verb.** شَنِئَ فُلَانٌ فُلَانًا — "so-and-so hated so-and-so."

4. **Verbal nouns.** The verbal noun is شَنَآن (*shanaʾān*), sometimes lightened (hamza dropped) to شَنَان (*shanān*). شَنْء (*shanʾ*) carries the same meaning. A cited verse uses the lightened form: "Life is only what you enjoy and desire, even if the man of hatred blames you for it and calls you a fool."

5. **مِشْنَاء (mishnāʾ) — an intensive form on the pattern مِفْعَال.** Said of a man whom people hate.

6. **A further usage, left unresolved.** Ibn Fāris also notes the expression شَنِئْتُ لِلْأَمْرِ / شَنِئْتُ بِهِ in the sense of "I acknowledged, admitted [the matter]," with the supporting verse: "Had this affair happened in a *jāhiliyya*, you would have acknowledged it — or its drinker would have choked on the water." The text of the entry breaks off at this point, so his explanation of how this sense relates to the root is not given.

poets_named: Labīd (lived into Islam); Al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); unnamed verse
text:
Ibn Fāris treats sh-q-q as one sound root meaning a splitting open in a thing, with further words derived from it by metaphor.

1. **Splitting, cracking.** shaqaqtu al-shayʾ, ashuqquhu, shaqqan: "I split the thing", when you cleave it. shuqūq are cracks in the hand; shuqāq is cracking in a riding animal. The root, he stresses, is one.

2. **Splinter.** al-shiqqa is a splinter split off from a board or piece of wood.

3. **Dissension.** al-shiqāq is disagreement: the community cracks and divides. Hence "they split the staff of the Muslims", and "the people's staff has split after being joined", when their affairs fall apart.

4. **Half.** al-shiqq is the half of a thing.

5. **Hardship.** shiqq and mashaqqa are severe difficulty, as if its severity splits a person. Qur'anic example: "to a land you would not reach except with the shiqq of your souls" (al-Naḥl 7, Q 16:7).

6. **Side.** al-shiqq is also the side of a mountain, as in the ḥadīth "he found me among owners of a few sheep at a shiqq".

7. **Full brother.** shiqq is also shaqīq, a full brother: "my brother, my shaqīq, the shiqq of my own self". The image is of a piece of wood made into two halves.

8. **Anger.** Of an angry man: "he flared up and a splinter (shiqqa) flew off him", as if he split from rage. Ibn Fāris calls all these figurative expressions.

9. **Long journey.** al-shuqqa is a long journey to a distant land, "an arduous shuqqa". Qur'anic example: "but the shuqqa was too far for them" (al-Tawba 42, Q 9:42).

10. **Piece of cloth.** al-shuqqa of cloth is a familiar term.

11. **Veering in argument.** ishtaqqa fī al-kalām: in disputes, to go right and left and abandon the straight course, as if now on this side (shiqq), now on that.

12. **Leaning horse.** A horse that is ashaqq leans to one side when it runs. Ibn Fāris says the analogy in all of this is one.

13. **Strip of land between sand ridges (al-shaqīqa, pl. shaqāʾiq).** A gap between sands that grows vegetation. The authorities he quotes differ: Abū Khayra, a soft strip within rough ground, as long as the sand-ridge; al-Aṣmaʿī, rough ground between two sand ridges, or rough patches between every pair of ridges; Abū Hishām al-Aʿrābī, what lies between two amīls (amīl = ḥabl, a sand ridge); al-Naḍr's version, hard ground between two mountains along their length, where water collects, one or two bowshots wide. Labīd uses the word of a wild cow that lost her calf and kept roaming and lowing "across the breadth of the shaqāʾiq".

   Ibn Fāris adds a personal comment: were it not that lexicographers dwell at length on these terms and he follows their method, time would be better spent on something more useful; there is little benefit in knowing what such a thing is, still less in knowing people's disagreements over it. He says much of his book is like this, especially for words of more than three radicals, but it is the scholars' established way.

14. **Camel's bray-bladder.** al-shiqshiqa is the lahāt a male camel pushes out, so called because it looks split. An eloquent orator is called a shiqshiqa, likened to the stallion. Al-Aʿshā: "I cut off the shiqshiqa of the roarer." A ḥadīth says "much oratory is the shaqāshiq of Satan."

15. **Exception.** Ibn Fāris lists as departing from the root's meaning al-shaqīq, said to be a stallion that has become firm and strong, citing the verse "your father is a shaqīq, with sharpened spurs".
