quran_words: شَقِيّ 4x "unblessed"; شَقُ 4x "so (that) you would suffer"; أَشْقَى 3x "the wretched one"; شِقْوَت 1x "our wretchedness"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root شقو (sh-q-w) as follows:

1. Core sense: the letters sh-q-w point to hardship and suffering — the opposite of ease, and the opposite of felicity/well-being (saʿādah). So الشِّقْوَة (shiqwah) means the opposite of felicity.

2. Applied to a person: رَجُلٌ شَقِيٌّ (shaqiyy) is a wretched, hard-pressed man; the abstract state is named variously شَقَاء (shaqāʾ), شِقْوَة (shiqwah), and شَقَاوَة (shaqāwah).

3. Related form: المُشَاقَاة (mushāqāh) is said to mean hard toil and sustained exertion or practice. The unifying idea is of someone taking on strain and being worn down or made wretched by it.

4. Hamzated variant (a different root): when the final letter is hamzated — شقأ — the meaning shifts. شَقَأَ نَابُ الْبَعِيرِ means the camel's canine tooth broke through / emerged. The شَاقِئ (shāqiʾ) is such a tooth that has not yet hardened into full firmness.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī defines شِرْذِمَة (shirdhimah) as: a group that is broken off or detached — a small, cut-off band.

He cites the Qur'an's use of the word: "إِنَّ هؤُلاءِ لَشِرْذِمَةٌ قَلِيلُونَ" — "Indeed, these are but a small band" (al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:54).

He then grounds the word's core sense by pointing to ordinary usage: Arabs would say ثوبٌ شَرَاذِمُ (a garment [that is] shirdhim/sharādhim), meaning a garment torn into pieces (مُتَقَطِّع). So the root idea is "a piece torn/separated off from a whole" — applied to cloth it means tatters or shreds, and applied to people it means a small splinter-group broken off from a larger body, not an integral whole.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: شَرَعَ 2x "he has ordained"; شِرْعَة 1x "a law"; شُرَّع 1x "visibly"; شَرِيعَة 1x "an ordained way"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ش-ر-ع as one single root, with a core idea he states plainly: something that is opened up, with an extension or stretch to it. Everything else in the entry is derived from that image.

1. The watering-place. الشَّرِيعَة (sharīʿa) is the place of access to water where the drinker comes down to drink. This is presented as the primary, concrete sense, backed by a verse of poetry about a wounded animal driven to water: "And when she saw that the watering-place was her whole concern, and that the white of her flanks was running with blood."

2. Derived usage in religion. From that watering-place sense, Ibn Fāris says, شِرْعَة (shirʿa) and شَرِيعَة were derived for what pertains to الدِّين (dīn). He cites Q 5:48 ("For each of you We appointed a shirʿa and a minhāj") and Q 45:18 ("Then We set you upon a sharīʿa of the matter"). He gives no further definition of the religious sense beyond this derivation from the point of access to water.

3. Bringing to water / drinking. شَرَعْتُ الْإِبِلَ — to give camels access to the watering-place. الْإِبِلُ الشُّرُوعُ — camels that have come down to water and drunk their fill. حِيتَانٌ شُرَّعٌ — fish lowering their heads to drink.

4. Opening a way. أَشْرَعْتُ طَرِيقًا (also شَرَعْتُ) — to open a road and make it a through-way.

5. Levelling a spear. أَشْرَعْتُ الرُّمْحَ نَحْوَهُ إِشْرَاعًا — to point/level a spear at someone; the form without the alif (شَرَعْتُ) is also reported.

Ibn Fāris then marks a deliberate extension: after the water sense, the root was applied to anything drawn out or extended, whether upwards or otherwise.

6. Strings of an instrument. الشِّرَع, singular شِرْعَة; الشِّرَاع is a plural of the plural. Shāhid: "as a singing-girl shone brightly with the strings."

7. A ship's sail. شِرَاعُ السَّفِينَةِ — extended upward. By that likeness, a camel raising its neck is said to شَرَعَ عُنُقَهُ or "extend its sail" (مَدَّ شِرَاعَهُ). On the same basis, Q 7:163 (fish coming "shurraʿan" on the Sabbath day) is glossed by some exegetes as "raising their heads." Related: رُمْحٌ شِرَاعِيٌّ, "a long spear," in a line attributed to al-Hudhalī.

8. Splitting a hide. Returning to the "opening" sense he began with, he reports from Ibn al-Sikkīt: شَرَعْتُ الْإِهَابَ — to slit the hide, splitting what lies between its two legs.

Method note: the entry's argument is etymological throughout — one physical image (an opened access-way / an extended thing) is stated first, and each later usage, including the religious one, is explicitly derived from it rather than defined independently.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats sh-r-ḥ as one small base-root with a single sense: opening up and making clear.

1. Core sense — opening and clarification. The consonants shīn, rāʾ, ḥāʾ form what he calls a minor root (uṣayl) pointing to "opening" (fatḥ) and "making evident" (bayān).

2. Applied usage — sharaḥtu al-kalāma wa-ghayrahu sharḥan, "I explained speech, or something else": that is, you made it plain. The verbal noun is sharḥ.

3. Derivation — he traces the word to tashrīḥ al-laḥm, the slicing open of meat, so the sense of explaining is drawn from the physical act of laying something open.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: unnamed verse ×2; Ḥassān [ibn Thābit] (lived into Islam); al-ʿAjjāj (Umayyad); Jarīr (Umayyad)
text:
ROOT sh-r-ṭ (شرط) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core sense: a sign or mark (ʿalāma/ʿalam), and anything that approximates a sign.

1. al-sharaṭ = "sign, mark." Ashrāṭ al-sāʿa, "the signs of the Hour," takes its name from this — also used this way in a ḥadīth referring to the Hour's signs.

2. The shuraṭ (armed guards/police) are so called because they adopted a distinguishing sign/badge by which they were recognized.

3. Idiom: ashraṭa fulānun nafsahu li-l-halaka, "he exposed himself to ruin" — literally, he made himself a marker for destruction. Related: ashraṭa min ibilihi wa-ghanamihi, "he set some of his camels/sheep aside" (for sale). Illustrated by a verse: a man "commits himself" to a venture, casting down his lifelines and trusting in God.

4. sharṭ al-ḥājim, "the cupper's incision" (the cut made in cupping/bloodletting) — belongs here because it leaves a visible mark/trace. (Also: ashrāṭ al-sāʿa is said to mean its earliest portents.)

5. al-sharīṭ = the cord used to hobble/tether young lambs — named because tying with it leaves a trace.

6. al-sharaṭ = a small watercourse (about ten cubits long) — named because it leaves a mark in the ground, like the cupper's incision.

7. al-sharaṭān = two stars identified as "the two horns of Aries" — well-known celestial landmarks.

8. jamal shirwāṭ = "a huge camel" — called this because among other camels it stands out like a landmark. A verse of Ḥassān [ibn Thābit] uses ashrāṭ for companions "roused after the slumber-time of al-ashrāṭ" (i.e., the stars/watch of the night).

9. Ibn Fāris then surveys competing explanations of ashrāṭ in that verse: (a) the two sharaṭān-stars plus a third counted with them, giving "the three ashrāṭ" (supported by a verse of al-ʿAjjāj); (b) "the night-guards" (al-ḥaras); (c) "the lowly/common folk" (sifilat al-qawm) — illustrated by a satirical verse calling a tribe's members "scraps of the dregs of Ṭayyiʾ," sons of a man literally named Ashraṭ.

10. sharaṭ al-miʿzā = the culled, inferior goats — from a verse of Jarīr mocking a people whose women's dowries are paid in worthless goats.

11. Ibn Fāris closes by weighing two theories of how al-shuraṭ (police) got their name: either from sense 10 (they were regarded as low-grade men), or from sense 2 (they marked themselves out with a badge). He reconciles this with the "inferior" sense by noting that such men are tushraṭ — always thrust forward first into danger ahead of the main body — which circles back to the idiom in point 3: to be "marked" for destruction.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: شَرِبَ 15x "and drink"; شَرَاب 11x "a drink"; شَّٰرِبِين 5x "to the drinkers"; مَّشْرَب 3x "their drinking place"; شِرْب 3x "(is a share of) drink"; أُشْرِبُ 1x "and they were made to drink"; شُرْب 1x "(as) drinking"
text:
Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's account of the root **sh-r-b (شرب)**:

**1. al-shurb — the taking in of liquid.** The base sense is consuming any liquid, water or otherwise. Cited in contrasting Qur'anic settings: the Garden's people are given "a pure drink" (Q76:21), the Fire's people "a drink of scalding water" (Q10:4). The plural of sharāb ("drink") is ashriba. The verb (sharibtu, with verbal nouns sharban/shurban) appears in Q2:249 ("whoever drinks from it… so they drank from it") and Q56:55 ("drinking as the thirst-stricken camels drink").

**2. al-shirb (with kasra) — a share/allotment of water.** A distinct vocalization meaning one's turn or portion of water: Q26:155 (the she-camel's water-share against the people's) and Q54:28 ("every water-share is attended").

**3. al-mashrab.** Serves three grammatical functions: the verbal noun, the noun of the time of drinking, and the noun of the place of drinking (a drinking-place). Cited from Q2:60 ("each people knew their drinking-place").

**4. al-sharīb and shārib.** al-sharīb = a drinking-companion, and also "drink." By a visual likeness, the hair of the upper lip is a shārib ("mustache"), and the vein inside the throat is likewise called shārib; the shared plural is shawārib — the two being pictured on the model of the paired mustaches. A line of al-Hudhalī describing a wild ass is cited.

**5. "They were made to drink the calf into their hearts" (Q2:93).** Al-Rāghib gives two explanations of this striking phrase:
- (a) From ashrabtu al-baʿīr, "I tethered the camel" (bound a rope on its neck) — cited with a supporting verse. On this reading the calf was, as it were, tied fast in their hearts through their infatuation.
- (b) The love of the calf was "made to be drunk into" their hearts. He notes an Arab idiom: to express love or hatred saturating a person, they borrow the vocabulary of drinking, because drink penetrates the body most thoroughly (illustrated by a verse: "it penetrated where no drink reached, nor grief, nor joy"). Naming the calf itself (rather than "love of the calf") heightens the force: their infatuation fixed the calf's very image ineffaceably in their hearts.

**6. A proverb.** ashrabtanī mā lam ashrab, "you made me drink what I did not drink" — i.e., you alleged against me what I never did.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris treats sh-r-d (ش ر د) as expressing a single core idea: scaring or driving something away to a distance, and — closely related — an animal's shying-away/bolting together with scattering into dispersal.

1. Basic usage: sharada al-ba'iru shurudan — "the camel bolted" (fled in fright). sharradtu al-ibila tashridan — "I scattered/drove off the camels."

2. Qur'anic citation — Q8:57, {fa-sharrid bihim man khalfahum}, "so by them, scatter/disperse those behind them." Ibn Faris glosses this as nakkil bihim wa-sammi' — "make an exemplary, deterrent punishment of them, and publicize it" — i.e., use the punishment of these people to scare off and disperse those who might follow their example.

3. Why the two senses connect: when an offender sins and is punished, that punishment "scatters" (deters) everyone else — they see what happened to him, become wary of the same fate, and so shy away from committing the same offense.

4. Closes with the standard scholarly formula, "And God knows best."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَشْرَكَ 71x "they associate (with him)"; مُشْرِك 44x "the polytheists"; شَرِيك 40x "partners"; شِرْك 5x "your association"; مُشْرِكَٰت 3x "and the polytheist women"; مُشْرِكَة 2x "a polytheistic woman"; مُشْتَرِكُون 2x "sharing"; شَارِكْ 1x "and be a partner"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ش-ر-ك from two distinct roots:

1. **Association / not being alone.** The core noun is shirka (partnership): a thing held between two people, with neither possessing it by himself. Usage: shāraktu fulānan fī l-shayʾ = "I shared in the thing with him," i.e. I became like him in it; ashraktu fulānan = "I made him my partner (sharīk)." He cites the Qur'an, from the story of Moses: "and make him a sharer in my affair" (Ṭā-Hā 32). He also cites a supplication: "O God, make us sharers in the believers' prayer," i.e. partners with them in it. The verb form sharika…ashraka is noted.

2. **Extension / straightness.** Here sharak means the main travelled part of a road (laqam al-ṭarīq), also called its shirāk. The strap of a sandal (shirāk al-naʿl) is named by analogy to this. Likewise the hunter's snare (sharak al-ṣāʾid) is so called because of its extension (imtidād).

(Note: this entry treats only the literal senses of sharing and of extension; it does not define shirk in any theological sense.)

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مَشْرِق 11x "the east"; مُّشْرِقِين 2x "(at) sunrise"; شَرْقِيّ 1x "eastern"; شَرْقِيَّة 1x "(of the) east"; إِشْرَاق 1x "and [the] sunrise"; أَشْرَقَتِ 1x "and (will) shine"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ش-ر-ق (sh-r-q) as a single root meaning illumination and opening.

1. Rising and shining of the sun. شَرَقَتِ الشَّمْسُ (sharaqat al-shams) = the sun rose; أَشْرَقَتْ (ashraqat) = it gave light; الشُّرُوق (al-shurūq) = its rising. Illustrated by the oath "I will not do that as long as a shāriq scatters its light" — meaning as long as the sun rises.

2. أَيَّامُ التَّشْرِيقِ (the days of tashrīq). Named, on one account, because sacrificial meat is spread out in them to dry in the sun; some instead derive the name from the saying "Shine forth, O Thabīr, that we may set out."

3. Directional terms. الْمَشْرِقَانِ (the two easts) = the sun's rising-points in summer and winter; الشَّرْق (al-sharq) = the east.

4. Red meat as شَرْق (sharq). Reported by some; if correct, Ibn Fāris explains it from the root's "shining" sense, its redness making it seem to glow (mushriq).

5. الشَّاةُ الشَّرْقَاءُ (al-shāt al-sharqāʾ) = a ewe with a slit ear. Placed under the "opening" sense of the root.

6. An outlier: choking. شَرِقَ بِالْمَاءِ (shariqa bi-l-māʾ) = he choked on water (verbal noun شَرَق, sharaq). Ibn Fāris marks this as deviating from the root's main sense, citing a verse of ʿAdī [ibn Zayd] on choking.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats sh-r-r as a single root meaning spreading out and flying about, and he derives each of its uses from that idea.

1. **Evil.** al-sharr is the opposite of khayr (good); a wicked man is shirrīr. Ibn Fāris calls this the root sense, explaining it by evil's spreading and abundance.

2. **Spreading in the sun.** al-sharr is also spreading something out in the sun, and al-ishrāra is the thing on which it is spread.

3. **Sparks.** sharāra (plural sharār) and sharar (singular sharara) are what flies up from fire, as in Q 77:32: "It throws up sparks (sharar) like the qaṣr."

4. **Cutting and shaking out.** sharshara l-shayʾ means he cut it up. al-sharshara is shaking something out of your mouth after biting it.

5. **Dripping meat.** shiwāʾ shirshār is roast meat whose fat drips.

6. **Tail-ends.** sharāshir al-adhnāb are the dangling ends of tails, as in a verse of animals (the verbs are feminine) that howl and strike with "the sharāshir of their tails".

7. **The self.** "He threw his sharāshir on it" means he threw himself on it out of eagerness and love, as in the half-verse "an error on which one's whole self is thrown". Ibn Fāris answers the objection that this does not fit the root: sharāshir here is not the body but the self, meaning the aspirations and desires within it. To "throw one's sharāshir" is to gather one's scattered aspirations onto one thing and give all one's concerns to it. So it fits the idea of spreading.

8. **Imputing evil.** ashrartu fulānan: I attributed evil to someone. Ṭarafa: "my drinking of wine went on until my friend imputed evil to me".

9. **Bringing into the open.** ashrartu l-shayʾ: I brought it out and displayed it. Examples: "until the maṣāḥif were raised up in the palms"; "when it is asked which tribe is worst, the fingers point out Kulayb"; and Imruʾ al-Qays, passing guards and men eager against him, "if only they could bring my death out into the open".

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris analyzes the root sh-r-ā (shīn + rāʾ + a weak final letter) as three distinct roots.

1. Reciprocal exchange between two parties — taking and giving on a basis of equivalence.
   - شَرَى / اشْتَرَى (sharā / ishtarā): to take a thing from its owner for a price, i.e. to buy. But شَرَى can also mean the opposite — "to sell." Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 12:20, {وَشَرَوْهُ بِثَمَنٍ بَخْسٍ}, "they sold him for a paltry price."
   - The idea of equivalence/likeness: هَذَا شَرْوَى هَذَا ("this is the like of that"); فُلَانٌ شَرْوَى فُلَانٍ ("X is the equal of Y"). Illustrated by a saying of the judge Shurayḥ about a man who broke another's bow — he ruled "شَرْوَاهَا," its equivalent (in compensation).
   - أَشْرَاء of a thing: its sides/regions (singular شَرًى), so called because each is "like the other side." Note that الشِّرَى is maqṣūr (shortened final alif): شَرَى الشَّيْءَ شِرًى.

2. A plant.
   - الشَّرْي (al-shary): said to be الحنظل, colocynth (the bitter gourd).
   - الشَّرْيَة: a palm that sprouts from a date-stone; cited from the poet Ruʾba: "a shrya-palm in a settlement."
   - الشَّرَى: a place full of thickets and lions — with a verse on "the lions of Sharā" meeting "the lions of Khafiyya."
   - الشِّرْيَان: a tree from which bows are made.

3. Agitation, excitement, or rising up in a thing.
   - شَرِيَ الرجل: a man carried away by rage (as though "made to fly" with anger).
   - شَرِيَ البعير: a camel quickening its pace.
   - شَرِيَ البرق: lightning flashing/spreading — with a verse describing lightning that "dies down for a moment and flashes forth for a moment."
   - اسْتَشْرَى: to persist doggedly in something.
   - شَرِيَ زمام الناقة: the she-camel's nose-rein thrashing about restlessly.
   - Proverb: "كل مُجْرٍ في الخلاء يشرى" — "anyone racing in open, empty ground grows spirited/reckless."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats sh-t-t as a root (aṣl) indicating dispersal and separation (tafarruq, tazayyul).

1. **Scattering.** tashtīt is the scattering of something dispersed.

2. **A community breaking up.** shatta shaʿbuhum shatātan wa-shattan (with the verbal nouns shatāt and shatt), "their united body was scattered", means that their gathered company dispersed. He cites al-Ṭirimmāḥ: "The clan's united body was scattered after it had been joined together, and the abode grieved you, the abode of residence."

3. **Arriving in separate groups.** jāʾa al-qawmu ashtātan: "the people came in scattered groups."

4. **Gapped teeth.** thaghr shatīt describes handsome front teeth with gaps between them (mufallaj). Ibn Fāris places this under the same idea: it is as though the teeth were said not to be crowded on top of one another.

5. **shattāna, "far apart!"** The wording shattāna mā humā, "far apart are the two of them!", is said to be the most eloquent, and a verse is recited for it: "Far apart are my day upon her camel-saddle and the day of Ḥayyān, the brother of Jābir!" People sometimes said shattāna mā baynahumā, "far apart is what lies between the two", but the first form is the more eloquent.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
1. Core meaning — a season of the year: al-shitā' ("winter"), the opposite of al-ṣayf ("summer"). The singular/instance-noun is al-shatwah, a single winter season.

2. Place-noun — al-mashtāh and al-mashtā, "winter quarters," the place where winter is spent. Ibn Fāris cites a line of Ṭarafah illustrating the word in use: at the winter camp, the hosts call everyone to the feast without exception — no stingy host among them picks and chooses whom to invite. (This line demonstrates the place-noun al-mashtāh; Ibn Fāris does not himself gloss the poem's vocabulary — the parenthetical sense given for al-ādib/al-jafalā/yantaqir reflects the verse's well-known standard reading, not the dictionary's own commentary.)

3. Grammatical note, from al-Khalīl: shitā'/shatwah follow the same regular derivational pattern as shakwah/shikā' (a waterskin, singular/plural) — a sound analogy (qiyās), not an irregular formation.

4. Verb forms:
- ashtā al-qawm — "the people entered winter" (of the season's arrival)
- shataw — "winter struck/befell them" (of people being overtaken by it)

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats sh-w-ẓ (شوظ) as a single, sound triliteral root with one core meaning — no branching senses.

**Core meaning**: al-shuwāẓ (الشُّوَاظ) is the pure flame-tip of a fire — a blaze that gives off no smoke with it. That is, it names fire's smokeless blazing flame specifically.

**Qur'anic citation**: he cites {shuwāẓun min nār}, "a shuwāẓ of fire" (Q 55:35, Sūrat al-Raḥmān), as the attestation of this word in use.

The entry is very brief — Ibn Fāris gives no further derivations, related forms, or additional shawāhid beyond this single Qur'anic verse.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root š-w-b (شوب) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: a single underlying sense — "mixing" (al-khalṭ).

1. Verb usage: shubtu ash-shayʾa ashūbuhu shawban — "I mixed the thing / I mix it / a mixing."

2. Honey as shawb: philologists (ahl al-lugha) reported that honey (al-ʿasal) was itself called shawb, because it was used among them as a mixing-agent (mizāj) stirred into other drinks.

3. shiyāb: the general name for whatever substance is used to mix into something else.

4. Idiom: mā ʿindahu shawbun wa lā rawbun — "he has neither shawb nor rawb," i.e. he has nothing at all. Ibn Fāris glosses the two terms: shawb = honey; rawb = curdled/soured milk (al-laban al-rāʾib).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ش-و-ك (sh-w-k) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core idea: roughness combined with a sharp point or tip on something.

1. Thorn (al-shawk) — the primary, well-known sense: the sharp spike-point on a plant. A thorny tree is called shawikah, shā'ikah, or mushīkah (three interchangeable adjective-forms). "The thorn pricked me" = shākanī l-shawk. "I pricked/hurt someone with a thorn" = ashaktu fulānan (causative Form IV).

2. Sprouting/pointed growth, by extension — used for anything that puts forth a sharp point:
   - A fledgling bird's feathers beginning to sprout (spike-like) = shawwaka l-farkh.
   - A woman's breast becoming erect with a pointed tip = shawwaka thadyu l-mar'ah.
   - A camel's canine teeth growing long = shawwaka l-ba'īr.

3. al-Shawkah — derived abstractly from the same root: intensity or strength of military might/fighting power (the "sting" or "point" of force).

4. Idiom of abundance — "he came with thorn and tree" (jā'a bi-l-shawki wa-l-shajar), meaning he came in great, abundant number.

5. Roughness of texture — burdatun shawkā' describes a cloak rough to the touch, either because it is still new (stiff) or, on another view, because of its coarse weave.

Ibn Fāris ties all these together under one unifying sense: roughness + a sharp/pointed extremity, whether literal (a thorn, a growing feather, a tooth, a nipple) or figurative (fighting strength, abundance, coarse texture).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: تَشَاوُر 1x "and consultation"; شَاوِرْ 1x "and consult them"; أَشَارَتْ 1x "then she pointed"; شُورَىٰ 1x "(are conducted by) consultation"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ش-و-ر as two steady root-senses:

1. **Bringing out, displaying, putting on show.**
 - شُرْتُ الدابةَ شَوْرًا — "I paraded the animal", i.e. displayed it for inspection.
 - مِشْوَار — the ground where animals are shown off. Hence the proverb he quotes: "Beware of public speeches — they are a show-ground with much stumbling."
 - He reports a view of some lexicographers that شَوَّرَ به ("he shamed him") belongs here via الشُّوَار, a man's genitals — as in the imprecation "May God expose his shuwār". On that reading, "he shamed him" is literally "he exposed his shuwār until he was ashamed."
 - الشَّوَار is also reported as household goods. If that is sound, Ibn Fāris explains it as what a man keeps and guards.

2. **Taking / drawing something out.**
 - شُرْتُ العسلَ أشُورُه — "I gathered the honey" (from the hive). Some permitted the alternative form أَشَرْتُ العسل, citing the verse ending "…وحديثٍ مثل ماذيِّ مُشَارِ" ("talk like the clear honey of a gathered hive"). Al-Aṣmaʿī corrected the reading to مَاذِيِّ مَشَارِ, taking it as a genitive construction instead.
 - مَشَار — the hive from which honey is taken.
 - Consultation belongs here: شَاوَرْتُ فلانًا في أمري ("I consulted so-and-so about my affair") is, on the view he cites, derived from the gathering of honey — the one seeking counsel *draws* an opinion out of another.
 - Also derived: a camel called مُسْتَشِير, meaning one that can tell a pregnant female from a non-pregnant one — supported by the line "He startled away from her every mustashīr, and every rutting, vicious young stallion." An alternative gloss he records is simply "the fat one".

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَشْوِى 1x "(which) scalds"; شَّوَىٰ 1x "of the skin of the head"
text:
Root ش-و-ي (sh-w-y) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris gives this root one core sense: al-amr al-hayyin — something easy, minor, or trifling.

1. al-shawā — the inferior/least valuable part of one's property, illustrated with a verse about eating the shawā until only its best remaining bits are pointed out.

2. al-shawā (a homonymous plural, of shawāh) — the scalp-skin; and, separately, al-shawā also means the extremities/limbs, and more broadly anything on the body that is NOT a vital, fatal-wound location. "Every trifling matter is shawā" ties this back to the core sense.

3. A rhyming phrase: ʿayiyy shawiyy — helpless and trifling. Ibn Durayd traces shawiyy here to the same "inferior" sense.

4. Hunting usage: ramaytu al-ṣayda fa-ashwaytuhu — I shot the game and only wounded its extremities, i.e. hit it non-fatally rather than killing it outright.

5. al-shawāyā — the surviving remnant of a people who perished (singular shawiyya), named for their fewness and insignificance. Similarly, al-shawwāya is a small piece cut from something large, like a cut of meat from a sheep; and "nothing remained but a shawāya" means only a trifling amount was left.

6. Etymology of "roasted meat": Ibn Fāris states with confidence that al-shiwāʾ (roasted meat) derives from this same root — because roasting "diminishes" the meat. He raises and answers his own objection: if boiled or cubed meat is also "diminished," why isn't it also shiwāʾ? He replies that etymology only traces usage to one consistent pattern — it cannot account for every extension of the logic.

7. Verb forms for roasting: shawaytu al-laḥma / ishtawaytuhu — I roasted the meat; mushtawin — one roasting. inshawā al-laḥm — the meat got roasted — illustrated with two verses about roasting meat over a fire.

8. Al-Khalīl (cited) explains al-ishwāʾ as "leaving a remainder" — as in "so-and-so ate supper and ashwā from it," meaning he left food over. A closing verse plays on the same idea: certain speech "has no shawā to it" — once it slips off the tongue, nothing remains; it cannot be recalled.

Ibn Fāris closes by reaffirming that all these senses trace back to the single root-meaning he established at the outset.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha entry for the root sh-kh-ṣ (شخص).

Core meaning: the three letters shīn-khāʾ-ṣād point to one single idea — "elevation" or "rising up" in something (irtifāʿ fī shayʾ). Every sense below branches from this one core.

1. Al-shakhṣ ("a person/figure/silhouette") — the dark outline of a human being as it rises into view / becomes visible to you from a distance. This is the root sense the word "shakhṣ" (person, individual) comes from: literally, a shape that "rises up" (into your line of sight).

2. Shakhaṣa min baladin ilā baladin — "he set out/departed from one town to another." Ibn Fāris explicitly notes this is derived by analogy (qiyās) from the core "rising" sense — i.e., setting out on a journey is treated as a kind of "rising" or "moving off."

3. Shukhūṣ al-baṣar — the eyes becoming fixed and raised, staring without blinking. Again tied to the "rising" sense: the gaze "lifts" and locks.

4. Shakhīṣ (masc.) / shakhīṣa (fem.) — describing a man or woman as "bulky, large-bodied" (jasīma). The bodily bulk is what "stands out"/rises to notice.

5. Ashkhaṣa al-rāmī — an archer "overshoots": his arrow flies past the target, passing above it. Such an arrow is called sahmun shākhiṣ, a "rising/overshooting arrow" — again the arrow "rises" past its mark.

6. Shukhiṣa bihi — said of someone struck by a distressing matter that unsettles him. Ibn Fāris explains the logic: when a person is disturbed, his usual place becomes uncomfortable to him, so he "rises" (cannot stay settled/still) — tying emotional agitation back to the same core image of "rising."

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
text:
al-Zamakhsharī's Asās al-Balāgha records the figurative and idiomatic uses of the root ش ي أ (sh-y-ʾ), tied to شيء (shayʾ, "thing") and the verb شاء / شيَّأ.

1. Idioms of nothingness: أنت في لا شيء ("you are in nothing") and رأى غير شيء ("he saw nothing") — shayʾ used to express worthlessness or negation.

2. Adverbial use: تأخرت عنه شيئاً ("I fell back from him a shayʾ") means "a little, slightly."

3. Exclamatory يا شيء / يا شيء ما: al-Kisāʾī reports يا شيء مالي (yā shayʾa mā lī) as an expression of regret or longing over something, with a supporting verse ("whoever lives long, time and its turns destroy him"). Zuhayr b. Masʿūd uses يا شيء ما as an exclamation of admiration ("what men they are, when a distressed caller summons them to the day of terror").

4. مشيَّأ (mushayyaʾ): said of a boy of misshapen, uneven build — "as if there were something of every ugliness in him." The related verb appears in شيَّأ الله خلقه ("God formed/shaped his make"), i.e. shayyaʾa = to fashion or form.

5. Polite dismissal: to someone whose departure is wished, one says إذا شئت ("whenever you wish").

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ش ي ع (sh-y-ʿ) from two distinct roots: (I) support and aid, and (II) spreading and diffusion.

ROOT I — support / accompanying:
1. شَيَّعَ (shayyaʿa) — to escort or see someone off at his departure.
2. By extension of "accompanying," one says "I'll come tomorrow or its shayʿ," meaning the following day — as if the second day escorts the first into the past. Cited verse: "The companion said tomorrow is our parting, or the day after — will you not bid us farewell?"
3. الْمُشَيَّع (al-mushayyaʿ) — a title for a brave warrior, as though his strength is reinforced or "backed up" by another.
4. Two reported minor senses Ibn Fāris does not endorse: (a) that شَيْع is a lion's cub — he notes he never heard this from a scholar by direct transmission; (b) that شَيْع means a measure or approximate amount, as in "he stayed a month or so." He affirms the correct sense is that the mushayyiʿ is one who aids and accompanies another.
5. الشِّيعَة (al-shīʿa) — helpers and supporters.

ROOT II — spreading / diffusion:
1. شَاعَ الْحَدِيثُ (shāʿa al-ḥadīth) — a report spread, became widely known.
2. شَيَّعَ الرَّاعِي إِبِلَهُ — the herdsman shouted among / drove his camels. Related noun الشِّيَاع (al-shiyāʿ), the reed-pipe the herdsman blows. Cited: "...like the yearning of the old she-camels that thrill to the shepherd's pipe."
3. سَهْمٌ شَائِعٌ (sahm shāʾiʿ) — an undivided share; the holder is imagined as "spread" throughout the whole, just as a report spreads among people until it reaches everyone.
4. شَيَّعْتُ النَّارَ فِي الْحَطَبِ — to make fire spread/blaze through the firewood, i.e. to set it ablaze.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: شَيْب 1x "(with) white"; شَيْبَة 1x "and gray hair"; شِيب 1x "gray-haired"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats š-y-b as a near-neighbour of the root š-w-b, both turning on the idea of one thing being mixed into another.

1. Grey hair. The core use is shayb, the greying of the head; the verb is shāba / yashību ("to go grey"). A man who has gone grey is ashyab. Al-Kisāʾī records that "grief" can be made the agent of the greying, in two verb forms (shayyaba, ashāba) and with two constructions — either taking "his head" as a direct object or governing it with the preposition bi-.

2. Snow-capped mountains. Al-shīb is used of mountains on which snow falls, which Ibn Fāris derives from the greying sense. He cites a verse describing them as "elders that go grey when winter comes, and greyness is no defect upon them," explaining that the poet means mountains turned white by snow.

3. shayb versus mashīb — a disputed distinction. A commentary on the poetry of ʿUbayd, on the line "greyness is a blemish for him who goes grey," treats shayb and mashīb as identical in meaning. Al-Aṣmaʿī, by contrast, distinguishes them: shayb is the whiteness of the hair itself, while mashīb is a man's crossing over into the class of the shīb — the aged, grey-haired men.

4. "Whitened," not "mixed." On ʿAdī's line "and the head — greyness has shābahu it," Ibn al-Sikkīt holds that the verb here means "whitened it," not "mingled with it." A supporting verse is quoted: "greyness fell upon greyness and shāba-hu" — that is, it turned what was black of it white. (This qualifies the mixing-idea Ibn Fāris opened with, for this particular usage.)

5. Names of the coldest months. Shībān and Milḥān are the two months called qimāḥ, the coldest of winter, so named because the ground turns white with hoar-frost — again the whiteness sense.

6. An anomalous usage. Ibn Fāris marks as falling outside the section the expression "she passed a shaybāʾ night," used of a woman whose virginity was taken; the contrasting phrase for the opposite case is "a ḥurra night."

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
text:
Root ش ي د (Sh-Y-D) — Tāj al-ʿArūs (al-Zabīdī, d. 1791 CE)

1. Core verb — shāda al-ḥāʾiṭa yashīduhu shayḍan: "he plastered/coated a wall with al-shīd" (a plastering substance). Al-shīd is defined as what a wall is plastered with — gypsum (jiṣṣ) or similar. Al-Jawharī had glossed it as "clay," or in another version "gypsum or balāṭ (paving-stone)"; al-Zabīdī rejects "stone" here, since stone (balāṭ) isn't itself a plastering material — only clay/mortar (malāṭ) is — though he notes a defender's reading in which balāṭ means the stone after it's been burned into gypsum, which would make the phrasing figurative rather than wrong.

2. المشِيد (mashīd, pattern of amīr): "that which is worked/finished with al-shīd," i.e. plastered/coated. Two Qur'anic citations anchor this sense: {وَقَصْرٍ مَّشِيدٍ} "a mashīd palace" (22:45) and {فِي بُرُوجٍ مُّشَيَّدَةٍ} "in mushayyada towers" (4:78). A line of poetry is quoted describing a structure plastered with marble and coated with lime, high enough for birds to nest in its heights.

3. المُشَيَّد (mushayyad, pattern of muʾayyad): according to Abū ʿUbayd, this means "the elongated/heightened building" — a distinct sense from "plastered."

4. A technical grammatical dispute follows over whether mashīd is the singular form and mushayyad the plural, or vice versa, and whether the plural mushayyada derives from mashīd or from mushayyad. Al-Jawharī, citing al-Kisāʾī, is accused (via Ibn Barrī) of a transmission error on this point. Several authorities weigh in — Ibn Sīdah defends al-Kisāʾī's standing as too eminent to have erred; al-Azharī offers a reconciling explanation (mushayyad and mashīd can be near-synonyms, both meaning "plastered with shīd," except that mashīd simply never takes the plural tāʾ ending — a case of one word standing in for another's missing form, comparable to how tarak replaced wadaʿa in usage). Al-Farrāʾ separately explains the underlying grammar of doubled (mushayyad) vs. undoubled (mashīd) forms: doubling marks an action that is repeated or drawn out (as building is), which is why qaṣr mashīd can also take the doubled form mushayyad — building, unlike a single act such as slaughtering, is a prolonged, recurring action.

5. Figurative (majāz) branch — الإشادة (al-ishāda): "raising the voice about something its subject dislikes," close to public shaming (al-tandīd) — al-Layth's definition. Ashāda bi-dhikrihi is used for publicizing someone, in both praise and blame (al-Jawharī restricted it to the positive sense only, "raising someone's repute"). A ḥadīth is cited: whoever exposes ("ashāda") a Muslim's faults without right will be disgraced by God on the Day of Resurrection. The image is explicitly derived from ashadtu al-bunyān / shayyadtuhu, "I built something high" — transferred metaphorically to "raising the voice."

6. Al-ishāda also means: (a) publicly announcing a lost/stray animal (taʿrīf al-ḍālla) — al-Aṣmaʿī notes that whatever you raise your voice about, whether a stray animal or anything else, you have "ashadta" it; and (b) destruction/ruin (al-ihlāk), again a figurative, exaggerated extension of al-tandīd.

7. الشِّياد (al-shiyād), with kasra — two further, unrelated senses: (a) calling out loudly to camels (from al-Aṣmaʿī); (b) rubbing perfume into the skin (also called al-tashayyud/al-tashyīd in variant copies).

8. shāda yashīdu shayḍan, said of a man: "he died/perished" — transmitted from al-Ṣāghānī.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: ʿAbīd ibn al-Abraṣ (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse ×2; Jadhīma al-Abraṣ (pre-Islamic)
text:
**Root sh-y-kh — Ibn Manẓūr, *Lisān al-ʿArab***

1. **Core sense — an aged man.** A *shaykh* is one in whom age has become visible and on whom grey hair has appeared. Ibn Manẓūr records disagreement on the threshold: from fifty onward; or from fifty-one to the end of life; or the span from fifty to eighty.

2. **Forms.** Unusually many plurals: *ashyākh, shīkhān, shuyūkh, shiyakha, shīkha, mashyakha, mashikha, mashyūkhāʾ,* and *mashāyikh* (this last rejected by Ibn Durayd). A ḥadīth phrase *shīkhān Quraysh* shows the *shīkhān* plural, formed like *ḍayf* → *ḍīfān* ("guest"→"guests"). The feminine is *shaykha*, attested in a verse of the pre-Islamic poet ʿAbīd ibn al-Abraṣ comparing a swooping eagle (to which he likens his mare) to an old woman anxiously watching her child; the commentary glosses *ʿadhūb* as "having eaten nothing" and *raqūb* as a woman fearful her child will die.

3. **Verb.** *shākha / yashīkhu* "to grow old," with verbal nouns *shayakh, shuyūkha, shuyūkhiyya, shaykhūkha, shaykhūkhiyya*; form II *shayyakha* likewise means "to grow old."

4. **Morphological argument for *shaykhūkha*.** The *yāʾ* was originally vowelled and then made silent, because Arabic has no *faʿlūl* pattern. Comparable words from *wāw*-roots — *kaynūna, qaydūda, hayʿūʿa* — go back to doubled forms (*kayyanūna*) later lightened; without that account one would expect *kawnūna, qawdūda*. Words from *yāʾ*-roots (*ḥaydūda, ṭayrūra, shaykhūkha*) need no such restoration.

5. **Form II as address and as insult.** *shayyakhtuhu* = "I called him *shaykh*" as a mark of honour. But Abū Zayd pairs *shayyakhtu l-rajula* with *sammaʿtu bihi* and *naddadtu bihi* — all meaning "to expose or disgrace someone"; and *shayyakha ʿalayhi* = "he denounced him." Abū al-ʿAbbās notes the abstract nouns *tashayyukh*, *tashyīkh*, *shaykhūkha* used of a *shaykh*.

6. **Diminutive.** *shuyaykh* (also with kasra, *shiyaykh*); the form *shuwaykh* is explicitly excluded.

7. **Astronomical use — *ashyākh al-nujūm*.** Glossed as the bright fixed stars (*al-darārī*). Ibn al-Aʿrābī: those stars that do not lodge in the lunar mansions. Ibn Sīda takes him to mean the fixed stars. Thaʿlab dissents, reading instead *asnākh al-nujūm*, "the stars' roots," on which the planets' revolution turns.

8. **Figurative uses in verse.** A riddling piece describes a milk-skin that "the ignorant man takes for a *shaykh* on his chair, wearing a turban" — mute, so not really a man; Sībawayh treats one of its forms as poetic licence, comparing a line of Jadhīma al-Abraṣ. In another line, *shaykh* is said to denote a mountain goat.

9. **Plant and tree names.** *al-shīkha*: a plant so called for its whiteness, parallel to *al-haram* used of a kind of saltbush. Abū Zayd: *al-shaykh* is also a tree, called "the tree of the shaykhs," whose fruit is a pod like that of the *khirrīʿ*; he identifies it as the safflower plant, growing in meadows and watercourses.

10. **A related form.** *al-shākha*: "the well-proportioned/upright one." Ibn Sīda reasons that its long *ā* must derive from *yāʾ* rather than *wāw*, since no root *sh-w-kh* exists — otherwise a middle *wāw* would have been expected.

11. **Place-name.** *Shaykhān* (with fatḥa) in the Uḥud narrative: a spot near Medina where the Prophet camped the night he set out for Uḥud and reviewed his men. An editorial note cites Ibn al-Athīr on the vowelling and Yāqūt, who reads it as the dual of *shaykh* and adds that *Shīkha* is a white sand-tract in the territory of Asad and Ḥanẓala.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḏ–ʾ–b as a single root whose core idea is **instability of movement** — a thing that does not travel in one fixed direction.

1. **The wolf (الذِّئْب, ḏiʾb).** Ibn Fāris derives the name from this root: the wolf is so called because of its تَذَؤُّب — its roving, coming at things from no single quarter. Plurals: أَذْؤُب (aḏʾub), ذِئَاب (ḏiʾāb), ذُؤْبَان (ḏuʾbān).

2. **ذُئِبَ الرَّجُل (ḏuʾiba r-rajul)** — passive: said of a man when the wolf gets in among his sheep.

3. **تَذَأَّبَتِ الرِّيح (taḏaʾʾabat ar-rīḥ)** — of wind: it came from every side. The verb applies the wolf's multi-directional motion to the wind, showing the root-idea working outside the animal itself.

4. **أَرْضٌ مَذْأَبَة (arḍ maḏʾaba)** — a land full of wolves (the place-noun pattern).

5. **ذَؤُبَ الرَّجُل (ḏaʾuba r-rajul)** — of a man: he turned into a malignant wolf, i.e. became wolfish in character.

6. **تَذَاءَبْتُ النَّاقَة (taḏāʾabtu n-nāqa)**, verbal noun تَذَاؤُب, on the reciprocal pattern تَفَاعَلَ. A herding practice: to get a she-camel to adopt a calf not her own (ظَأَرَ), the herdsman disguises himself before her as a wolf, so that fear makes her more tender toward the young one.

7. **الْإِذْآب (al-iḏʾāb) = fleeing.** Ibn Fāris attributes this sense to an unnamed group, and cites a line of verse (poet unnamed) as evidence: "Truly I, when a people's lion has taken flight, / and his pride has fallen and he has run off…"

8. **Extended/metaphorical use.** Having stated the root-meaning, Ibn Fāris notes that things are then likened to the wolf. So الذِّئْبَة (aḏ-ḏiʾba) of the camel-saddle (قَتَب) is the hollow beneath where the two saddle-bows meet, the part that sits on the animal's withers.

Method to note: Ibn Fāris's *Maqāyīs* argues from a single abstract root-idea (here: unfixed, multi-directional motion) outward to the concrete words — the wolf, the wind, fleeing, and finally a saddle-part named by resemblance.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ذ أ م (dh-ʾ-m), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: dislike/aversion combined with fault.

1. adhaʾtanī ʿalā kadhā — you compelled me, against my will, to such-and-such; dhaʾamtuhu — I disdained/despised him.
2. al-dhaʾm — fault, blemish; one so described is madhʾūm.
3. A grammatical note: Ibn Fāris explicitly rejects al-dhān (spelled with nūn) as a genuine separate root — he argues its nūn is simply a substitution for mīm, i.e. it's the same word as al-dhaʾm in disguise, illustrated with a line of poetry using the nūn-spelled variant.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ذعن (ḏ-ʿ-n) from a single core sense: following along / compliance and submission.

1. Verb usage: The form actually used in speech is aḏʿana (Form IV) — "he complied/submitted" (yuḏʿinu, iḏʿānan = compliance). Ibn Fāris notes a grammatical subtlety: the underlying base pattern (bināʾ) of the root is the plain Form I ḏaʿana, but in practice people only use the Form IV verb aḏʿana.

2. Animal usage: nāqatun miḏʿānun — a she-camel described as miḏʿān, meaning one that is easy-headed and submissive: it goes along compliantly wherever led, without resistance.

So the whole entry rests on one idea — yielding/going along with another's lead — applied first to a person who submits, then to a camel that is docile and easily led.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
Root ذ-ب-ب (dh-b-b), from Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr). This is an unusually long entry covering many distinct senses that share the consonant root but diverge widely in meaning:

**1. To defend / drive away.** الذَّبّ (al-dhabb) = to repel, ward off, or drive away. ذَبَّ عنه = "he defended/warded off harm from him" — used especially of defending one's family or honor (cited in a ḥadīth of ʿUmar comparing undefended women to meat left exposed). ذَبَّبَ = to defend repeatedly/vigorously. A مِذَبّ or ذَبَّاب is a man who staunchly defends his household. الذَّبِّيّ = a bailiff or watchman.

**2. To wander restlessly, not settle in one place.** Said of a camel (بعيرٌ ذَبّ) that won't stand still — with a grammatical note that the form ذَبَّة (with tāʾ marbūṭa) proves it's a true adjective, not a frozen verbal-noun.

**3. The wild bull**, called الذَّبّ or ذَبّ الرِّياد, named either because it restlessly roams and never settles, or because it constantly "comes and goes." Several early poets (Ibn Muqbil, al-Nābigha) are cited using this name for the wild bull. Commentators debate whether "riyād" refers to the bull's roaming mate or to its own grazing. By extension, "ذَبّ الرياد" is also used of a man who frequently visits/courts women — illustrated with two verses about a man who used to "open locked doors" to women.

**4. To dry up, wither, grow pale.** ذَبَّتْ شَفَتُه = his lip dried and cracked from severe thirst (or another cause); similarly of a withered tongue, a body grown thin and wasted, a withered plant, a pool drying up at season's end, or a man's complexion turning sallow. Several verses illustrate each usage.

**5. Residue / remainder (ذُبابة).** Camels returning from water still show ذُبابة — a lingering trace of thirst. ذُبابةُ الدَّين = the remainder of a debt; generally, ذُبابة anything = its leftover remnant (also used of leftover river-water). Poetic citations (a rajaz verse; Dhū al-Rumma) support this. ذَبَّبَ النهار = the day had only a remnant left before ending.

**6. Plague; madness.** الذُّباب can mean "the plague" (الطَّاعون) or "madness" (الجُنون); ذُبَّ الرجل = "he went mad" — with a supporting verse.

**7. The insect — housefly and bee — and its many idioms.** الذُّباب is the ordinary black housefly (plural ذِبَّان; the singular ذُبابة is correct, ذِبَّانة is not) and is also used for bees, with a grammatical note on rarer variant forms. A ḥadīth of ʿUmar concerning honey-hives at Ṭāʾif uses "ذُباب غيث" (rain's bee) for bees, since they live off what rain causes to grow. Al-Tahdhīb confirms the singular ذُباب has no tāʾ, and cites the Qurʾān, "وَإِن يَسْلُبْهُمُ الذُّبَابُ شَيْئًا" (22:73, "and if the fly should rob them of anything"), noting the grammatical plurals أَذِبَّة (paucal) and ذِبَّان — with Sībawayh's technical discussion of why this word's plural pattern isn't restricted the way similar words are, including a rare assimilated plural ذُبّ in the Tamīmī dialect. A ḥadīth states the fly lives forty days and "is in the Fire" — explained as not punishment for the fly itself, but so it can be used to torment the damned. Arabs nicknamed a man with bad breath "Abū Dhubāb" (this stuck to the caliph ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān). Other idioms: ذَبَّ الذُّباب = to shoo a fly away; "feared for the fly" = feared for his ignorance; "a stinging fly befell him" = harm befell him; مَذَبَّة/مَذْبوبة = fly-infested land; a camel "struck by flies" (مَذبوب/أَذَبّ) is one that sickens and dies on entering rich pastureland (illustrated with a verse). المِذَبَّة = a horsehair fly-whisk. A ḥadīth uses "dhubāb" (of a long-haired man) to mean "ill omen," giving رجل ذُبابيّ = ill-omened; الذُّباب can also mean "persistent/lasting evil," as in a ḥadīth of al-Mughīra.

**8. Sharp tip or point (by extension from "edge/point").** ذُبابُ العين = the pupil (by likeness to a fly); also a dark speck in a horse's eye. ذُبابُ أسنان الإبل = the sharp edge of a camel's teeth. ذُبابُ السيف = the point of a sword between its two blade-edges, with a detailed description of the sword's anatomical terms (ظُبتان, عَيْر, غِراران); a ḥadīth treats a broken sword-tip as an omen fulfilled by Ḥamza's death. الذُّباب من الأذن = the sharpened tip of the ear. ذُبابُ الحِنّاء = the first bud of henna blossom.

**9. Hurrying travel.** A مُذَبِّب rider travels hurriedly and alone (verse of ʿAntara cited). ذَبَّبْنا لَيْـلَتَنا = we wore ourselves out traveling by night. قَرَبٌ/ظِمْءٌ/خِمْسٌ مُذَبِّب describe hard, hurried stretches of travel toward water, with a verse of Dhū al-Rumma.

**10. أَذَبّ البعير** = the camel's canine tooth (with a verse likening its creak to a pulley).

**11. Swaying / dangling motion.** الذَّبْذَبَة = the to-and-fro sway of something hanging in the air. الذَّباذِب = ornaments hung on a howdah or camel's head for decoration (singular ذُبْذُب). الذَّبْذَب is glossed as "the tongue," or (in a ḥadīth about guarding oneself from "the evil of one's ذَبْذَب and قَبْقَب") as the private parts, with قَبْقَب as the belly — a variant ḥadīth promises Paradise to one guarded from it, the term explained as the penis, named for its "swinging." الذَّباذِب elsewhere = the genitals generally, or specifically the penis (for the same reason), or, per another view, the testicles.

**12. Wavering between two loyalties.** مُذَبْذِب/مُتَذَبْذِب = a man torn between two people or courses, settled with neither. This is the sense used in the Qurʾān's description of the hypocrites, "مُذَبْذَبِينَ بَيْنَ ذَلِكَ لَا إِلَىٰ هَـٰؤُلَاءِ وَلَا إِلَىٰ هَـٰؤُلَاءِ" (4:143) — which Ibn Manẓūr glosses as "driven off and repelled from both sides," tracing it to sense (1), "to drive away." A ḥadīth about an unmarried man being "of the مُذَبذَبين" (driven off from both believers and monks) is read the same way, though Ibn al-Athīr allows the word may instead derive from plain motion/agitation (تَذَبْذُب), a sense confirmed by other examples: a swaying suspended object, a ḥadīth describing swinging sleeves, and a ḥadīth of Jābir describing a fringed cloak (ذَباذِب = fringes/tassels, singular ذِبْذِب, so named because they swing as the wearer walks). A verse of Abū Dhuʾayb uses ذَبْذَبَا for "they kept [rivals] dangling/trailing behind."

**13. An obscure food term**, "ذُبَيْباء," mentioned by Abū Ḥanīfa among foods "with nothing good in them," left unexplained; possibly identical to "الذُّنَيْناء" (discussed elsewhere).

**14. A place name.** "Dhubāb" is also recorded as a mountain near Medina, the site of a crucifixion mentioned in one ḥadīth.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: ذُبِحَ 5x "i will surely slaughter him"; يُذَبِّحُ 3x "slaughtering"; ذِبْح 1x "with a sacrifice"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ذ-ب-ح as a single root whose one underlying idea is splitting or cleaving open (al-shaqq). He then lists the derived forms:

1. الذَّبْح (dhabḥ) — the verbal noun of ذَبَحْتُ الشَّاةَ, "I slaughtered the sheep": the act of slaughtering, i.e. cutting/cleaving the throat.

2. الذِّبْح (dhibḥ, with kasra) — the passive sense: the thing slaughtered, the slaughtered animal itself, as distinct from the act.

3. الذُّبَّاح (dhubbāḥ) — cracks or fissures in the skin at the bases of the fingers. A splitting of a quite different kind, showing the root's core sense outside any slaughter context.

4. ذُبِحَ الدَّنُّ — said of a large wine-jar that has been broached, i.e. pierced or tapped so its contents run out; the jar is spoken of as "slaughtered".

5. المَذَابِح (madhābiḥ) — small run-off streams that cut channels through the ground, cleaving it.

6. سَعْدٌ الذَّابِح ("the slaughtering Saʿd") — one of the stars/asterisms known as the Suʿūd.

7. الذِّبَح (dhibaḥ) — a plant name; Ibn Fāris flags this one as possibly anomalous (shādhdh), i.e. not reducible to the root's cleaving sense.

The entry's method is his standard one: assert a single semantic core, then show ordinary and marginal usages fitting it, and mark the one item that resists the pattern rather than forcing it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: al-Nābigha (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse ×4; Ibn Muqbil (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats dh-b-b, in its doubled form, as having three separate root meanings: a small flying creature (the fly), to which other things are then compared; edge and sharpness; and agitation and movement.

1. **The fly, and things likened to it.** al-dhubāb is the fly; one fly is dhubāba, and adhibba is the "plural of the plural", the form in al-Nābigha's words "much given to striking at the flies with her lip". By likeness, dhubāb al-ʿayn, "the fly of the eye", is the pupil. dhababtu ʿanhu means "I defended him", as though driving off the flies that trouble him. A madhbūb camel is one whose nostril flies get into, and madhbūb is also said of a fool, as though he were compared to such a camel.

2. **Edge and sharpness.** The dhubāb of a camel's teeth is their edge; for this he cites a verse in which "you hear the dhubāb, when it sings, like the warbling of doves upon the branches". The dhubāb of a sword is its edge.

3. **Agitation and movement.** Under this third root he places the following.

(a) Swinging and wavering. dhabdhaba is the swinging of something suspended in the air, and a mudhabdhab man is one who wavers between two courses. dhabdhab is the penis, "because it swings to and fro", and dhabādhib are things hung on a howdah or on a camel's head. dhabb is the wild bull, also called dhabb al-riyād; Ibn Muqbil pictures it as a Persian youth wearing two bracelets and bearing a lance. It was given that name, "they said", because it comes and goes and never stays in one place.

(b) Withering. dhabbat shafatuhu is said when someone's lip has withered from thirst; a cited verse speaks of being given drink "after the tongue had shrivelled and withered". dhabba l-nabt means the plants wilted, and dhabba jismuhu means his body grew lean.

(c) Hurrying. dhababnā laylatanā means "we wore ourselves out travelling through the night", and a qarab mudhabbib is a hurried journey to water ("they reach the water only by a qarab mudhabbib"). Two cited verses use the word: one has mudhabbiba, "hastening", worn down "by my early-morning starts and my travelling in the midday heat, when the gazelle takes its noon rest"; the other has "Ward hastens (yudhabbibu) on his track".

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ذهب (ḏ-h-b) as a small root whose core sense is beauty and freshness/bloom (ḥusn wa-naḍāra), plus one further, separate root meaning "to go away."

1. Gold — الذهب (al-ḏahab), the familiar metal. It can be treated as feminine (ذهبة, ḏahaba) and takes the plural الأذهاب (al-aḏhāb).

2. Gilded things — المذاهب (al-maḏāhib): straps plated with gold, or decorative fittings on swords. Anything gold-plated is مذهب (maḏhab). Cited: verse of Qays comparing a faded encampment-trace to streaming gilded straps.

3. Related usages — a man is ذهب (ḏahib) when he is dumbstruck at the sight of a gold mine; a bay horse is مذهب (muḏhab) when its coat is overlaid with a reddish-to-yellow (gold-like) sheen.

4. Generous rain — الذهبة (al-ḏihba), plural ذهاب (ḏihāb). Ibn Fāris singles this out as the true analogical center of the root, since such rain makes the earth and plants flourish and bloom — the "freshness" idea. Cited: verse of Ḏū al-Rumma pairing the rains with blossoms.

5. A second, distinct root — ذهاب الشيء (ḏahāb al-shayʾ), a thing's going or passing away: ذهب يذهب ذهاباً وذهوباً (ḏahaba, "to go"). Also used figuratively: قد ذهب مذهباً حسناً — "he took a fine course/way."

text:
Ibn Fāris identifies a single core meaning for the root dh-h-l (ذهل): being distracted or occupied away from something, whether by fright/terror (dhu'r) or by some other cause.

1. Core sense: dhahiltu 'ani sh-shay' ("I dhahal-ed from the thing") means you forgot it, or were kept preoccupied and so drawn away from it. The causative adhhalanī 'anhu ("it dhahala-ed me from it") means something distracted me away from it. Ibn Fāris marks this as the base meaning of the root.

2. A secondary usage, reported from the grammarian al-Liḥyānī: dhuhl or dhahl can denote a stretch/portion of the night — as in "he came after a dhuhl of the night had passed," parallel to the phrase "a hud' of the night passed" (hud' likewise meaning a period of night). Ibn Fāris suggests this sense may connect back to the core meaning: because of the night's darkness, one becomes unaware of things (yudhhalu) during that stretch.

3. An irregular/anomalous derivative outside the root's normal semantic pattern: dhuhlūl, used for a swift, excellent horse. Ibn Fāris flags this explicitly as not following from the "distraction/forgetting" sense.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives ذ-ك-ر from two distinct roots.

FIRST ROOT — maleness:
1. al-mudhkir: a female who has borne a male; al-midhkār: a female who habitually bears males. Cited: a line of ʿAdī [b. Zayd] describing a powerful she-camel "like the smith's anvil," a bearer of males.
2. al-midhkār is also land that produces the "male" (coarse) type of herbage.
3. al-mudhakkara (of she-camels): one whose build and temperament resemble a [male] camel's.
4. al-Farrāʾ records "kam al-dhikara min waladik?" — "how many males among your children?"
5. sayf mudhakkar: a well-tempered sword with fine sheen ("water"); dhū dhukr: sharp, cutting.
6. dhukūr al-baql: the coarse herbs (e.g. lavender, chamomile), as opposed to aḥrār al-buqūl, the delicate choice ones. Al-Shaybānī noted the "males" tend toward bitterness.

SECOND ROOT — recollection and mention:
7. dhakartu al-shayʾ: "I remembered it," the opposite of "I forgot it." From this the sense of al-dhikr as verbal mention (remembrance "with the tongue") was derived.
8. Idiom: ijʿalhu ʿalā dhukr (with ḍamma) — "keep it in mind, do not forget it."
9. al-dhikr also means eminence and honor — which Ibn Fāris treats as the analogical outgrowth of this second root.
10. rajul dhakir / dhikkīr: a man of good memory, keen and astute.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats dh-k-w (dhāl, kāf and a weak letter) as a single, consistent and regular root whose meaning is sharpness and penetration in a thing.

1. **Blazing: sun and fire.** The sun is called Dhukāʾ because it blazes (tadhkū) as fire does, and the morning is "the son of Dhukāʾ" because it comes from her light. dhakkaytu l-nār and dhakawtuhā both mean "I made the fire blaze". adhkaytu is also said of kindling war and fire, and dhukwa is what a fire is kindled with.

2. **Slaughter.** dhakkaytu l-dhabīḥa, "I slaughtered the animal", belongs to the same set of words.

3. **The mature horse.** al-faras al-mudhakkī is a horse a year past its qurūḥ, its coming to full growth; the verb is dhakkā yudhakkī. The Arabs say "the running of mature horses is ghilāb", a contest of mastery, also told as ghilāʾ, a contest of outdistancing.

4. **Keenness of mind.** al-dhakāʾ is keenness of the heart and quickness of understanding; the verb is dhakiya yadhkā. A poet, not named, says that when two strive their hardest, what gives one the advantage is "his full age and his keenness".

text:
Ibn Fāris treats dh-l (in its doubled forms and the reduplicated dhaldhal type) as a single root meaning submission, humble yielding and softness.

1. **Abasement, the opposite of might.** Al-dhull is the opposite of al-ʿizz. Ibn Fāris calls this a sound pairing of opposites that shows a wisdom peculiar to the Arabs among the nations: ʿizz derives from ʿazāz, hard, firm ground, whereas dhull is the contrary of hardness and difficulty. From this sense: rajul dhalīl, an abased man, marked by dhull, madhalla and dhilla.

2. **Tractability, yielding.** A saying is reported: "a little dhill (with i) better preserves family and wealth." From this: dābba dhalūl, a tractable, docile animal.

3. **Trodden ground.** The well-trodden part of a road is called dhill.

4. **Hanging low.** Dhullila al-qiṭf tadhlīlan is said of a fruit cluster when it softens and hangs down.

5. **The course of things.** The idiom "run matters along their adhlāl" means along their straight course, the way in which they go willingly and yield.

6. **Hems.** The dhalādhil of a shirt are the parts of its lower edge next to the ground; singular dhuldhul or dhildhil. Ibn Fāris counts this within the root.

7. **Hurrying.** Idhlawlā al-rajul idhlīlāʾan means "the man hurried"; he also counts this within the root.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats dh-m-m as a single root (aṣl wāḥid) whose every use, he says, points to the opposite of praise.

1. **Blame.** One says dhamamtu fulānan, adhummuhu, "I blamed so-and-so". The person is then dhamīm or madhmūm, "blamed", meaning he is not praiseworthy. The saying "do such-and-such, and blame (dhamm) has passed you by" means no blame will be on you.

2. **A well with little water.** Ibn Fāris places here al-dhamma, a well with little water, plural dhimām. A ḥadīth says "he came upon a dhamma well", and Dhū al-Rumma likens eyes to "the dhimām of wells that the water-drawers have drained". Ibn al-Aʿrābī reports biʾr dhamīm in the same meaning, with a verse describing a sandgrouse hurrying in search of the last seepings of stale pools "whose water is dhamīm".

3. **The covenant.** A covenant (ʿahd) is called dhimām because a person is blamed for letting it be lost. Ibn Fāris calls this an established Arab way of naming, like ḥāmī al-dhimār, "protector of the dhimār", one who guards whatever provokes anger, and ḥāmī al-ḥaqīqa, one who guards what he is duty-bound to defend. ahl al-dhimma are "the people of the compact". Abū ʿUbayd glosses dhimma as a guarantee of safety (amān) in the Prophet's words wa-yasʿā bi-dhimmatihim, "and [he] may extend their guarantee of safety". It is also said that they are called ahl al-dhimma because they paid the jizya and so were made secure in their lives and property.

4. **The claim a pledge creates (madhamma).** For the pledge sense one says madhamma or madhimma; for blame, only madhamma. In a ḥadīth a man asks the Prophet what will remove from him "the madhamma of suckling", and is told: a ghurra, a male or female slave. The phrase means the claim of the woman who nursed him. al-Nakhaʿī explained that people liked to give the nurse a small gift beyond her wage when the child was weaned; on this reading the man was asking how to pay her right in full. The Arabs likewise say "remove their madhamma with something", meaning give them something, since they have a claim on you.

5. **Other verbal and adjectival uses.**
- adhamma bi-fulān: he made light of so-and-so.
- adhamma bihi baʿīruhu: his camel fell behind and was cut off from the rest of the camels.
- shayʾ mudhimm: a faulty thing.
- rajul mudhimm: a man who cannot stir.

6. **Remaining items, "if sound".** Ibn Fāris ends with material that, if it is sound, comes near the root's pattern: al-dhamīm as pustules that come out on the nose; and, as Ibn Qutayba reports, al-dhamīm as the urine that trickles from a he-goat's penis. A verse of Abū Zubayd follows: "you see from her teats, behind her, a flow (nasal) like the dhamīm upon the small yaʿāmīr". Nasal, said of milk, is what flows out, and quzm means small. al-Shaybānī said he did not know the word yaʿāmīr, and no one asked could explain it; it is said to mean young sheep.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
poets_named: unnamed verse ×2; Abū ʿUbayda (unnamed); Ibn Muqbil (lived into Islam); ʿAmr b. Shaʾs (pre-Islamic); al-Afwah al-Awdī (pre-Islamic); Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad)
text:
Zamakhsharī's Asās al-Balāgha treats the root dh-n-b (ذنب) in two blocks: literal senses, then figurative (majāz) extensions, all built on the core idea of a "tail" / rear / hind part.

LITERAL SENSES
1. Tail and tail-hair of an animal: a horse "long of tail (dhanab) and tail-hair (dhunābā)"; seizing a bird "by its tail-feathers"; a horse called dhanūb has thick, abundant tail-hair (hulb).
2. To follow at the rear: dhanaba / istadhnaba the camels = to come behind them (with a verse of a hired driver following the riding-camels).
3. Specialized verbs from "tail": the locust dhannaba = thrust its tail into the ground to lay eggs; the ḍabb-lizard dhanaba = stuck out its tail when hunted, and the hunter dhannabahu = grabbed it by the tail.
4. Moral sense: adhnaba = committed a dhanb (fault/sin); the servant "sought God's forgiveness for [his] sins (dhunūb)." Also tadhannaba against someone = to impute a fault to him (like tajannā, tajarrama). [Zamakhsharī glosses dhanb simply as fault/offense, not any defined category of sin.]
5. Water/vessel words: dhanūb / dhināb = a bucketful of water ("pour me some of your dhanūb"); the midhnab = a ladle; and (plural madhānib) a narrow watercourse in low ground, or a channel on a mountain-slope.

FIGURATIVE SENSES (majāz), all playing on "tail = rear/last/lowest part"
- Lowly followers: adhnāb / dhunābā / nadhāʾib = the "tail-end" people, hangers-on.
- The outer corner of the eye: to look at someone "with the tail of the eye" (its hinder part), with several vowel-variants (dhunāba / dhunābata, kasra and ḍamma).
- The far end of things: water reaching "the tail of the valley/river"; following "the tail-end" of a people or a caravan.
- Idioms of fortune and time: to "ride the tail of the wind" = to outstrip others and not be caught; to "ride the tail of the camel" = to settle for a shrunken share; to be past fifty is for the fifty "to turn its tail to you"; to "plant one's tail" = to settle immovably (image drawn from the egg-laying locust); to "follow the tail of a matter" = to keep grieving over what is already gone.
- Enmity: "between me and him is the tail of the ḍabb" (the lizard's crooked tail) = we are at odds.
- Virility: of an old man, "his tail has gone slack" = his potency has failed (with a verse by Abū ʿUbayda where a woman shuts her door once the man's wealth and "tail" are gone).
- Trailing clouds: one cloud "tails" (yudhnibu) another; a cloud-mass described as mutually trailing (with a rain verse).
- Approach and dress: tadhannabtu the valley = I came at it from its lower (tail) end (verse of Ibn Muqbil); a turban-wearer tadhannaba = he let a "tail" of the cloth hang down.
- Ripening dates: a date dhannaba = ripened from its tail-end first (busr mudhannib; the state called tadhnūb).
- Speech: dhannabtu his words = I latched onto their "tails," their loose ends/details.
- Share/portion: "they have a dhanūb of it" = a share (verse of ʿAmr b. Shaʾs, where a king answers "yes, and buckets more"; and a verse of al-Afwah al-Awdī using aḏniba, buckets — aslām/salm being a bucket with a single handle).
- Anatomy: the dhanūb of the back = the back muscles ("jerboas of the back"); a verse of Dhū al-Rumma describes hair hanging over "the two dhanūbs" (flanks) of the back.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats dh-q-n as a single notion from which every derivative in the section descends. He does not state that notion abstractly, but the senses he lists all cluster around the chin/jaw area and, by extension, a lopsided tilt.

1. الذَّقَن (al-dhaqan) — the chin: the point where the two jawbones meet, in a human being or in any other creature.

2. نَاقَة ذَقُون (nāqa dhaqūn) — a she-camel that bobs her head as she walks.

3. الذَّاقِنَة (al-dhāqina) — the protruding tip of the windpipe. Ibn Fāris cites the report from ʿĀʾisha that the Prophet died "between my chest and my throat, my ḥāqina and my dhāqina," pairing the term with ḥāqina as two adjacent points of the throat.

4. ذَقَنْتُ الرَّجُلَ / أَذْقُنُهُ (dhaqantu / adhqunu) — verb: to strike someone with a closed fist on the side of the jaw.

5. دَلْو ذَقُون (dalw dhaqūn) — a bucket that is not evenly made: bulky and tilted to one side.

The form ذَقُون (dhaqūn) thus serves both for the head-tossing camel and for the lopsided bucket, linking the chin-sense to the idea of tilting.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats dh–r–ʾ as two separate root-meanings, plus one irregular usage.

1. Whiteness of colour. الذُّرْأَة (dhurʾa) is whiteness — the white of grey hair or of anything else. Derived forms: مِلْح ذَرَآنِيّ / ذَرْآنِيّ (white salt); a man أَذْرَأ (grey-haired), a woman ذَرْآء. Al-Shaybānī cites شَعْرَة ذَرْآء ("a white hair"), noting it follows the pattern of ذَرْعَاء. The verb is ذَرِئَ / يَذْرَأُ. He also reports that a ذَرْآء ewe or goat is one with a white ear.

2. Scattering seed / sowing. They say ذَرَأْنَا الْأَرْض, "we sowed the land"; a sown crop is زَرْع ذَرِيء, on the فَعِيل pattern. He cites a verse of poetry as evidence: "You split the heart, then sowed your love in it; so it was stitched up and the fissures closed."

Ibn Fāris places the divine usage under this second (sowing/propagating) sense: ذَرَأَ اللهُ الخَلْق — God brought forth or propagated the creation — citing Qurʾān 42:11, {يَذْرَؤُكُم فيه} ("He multiplies you thereby").

Irregular, outside both roots:
- أَذْرَأْتُ فلاناً بكذا — "I made him keen on / set upon it."
- Reported from Ibn al-Aʿrābī: ما بيني وبينه ذَرْء — "between me and him there is a barrier."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats dh-r-ʿ as one root meaning extension and forward movement; every derived usage, on his method, traces back to that base.

1. Forearm. الذِّرَاع (dhirāʿ) is the human forearm — the well-known word, and the anchor of the whole family.

2. Measuring. الذَّرْع (dharʿ) is the verbal noun of "I measured the garment, the wall, etc." (by the cubit). From this comes ضاق بهذا الأمر ذرعاً — literally "his reach became narrow at this matter" — said of someone who takes on more than he can manage and fails.

3. Outstripping. ذرعه القيء: vomit "got ahead of" him, overtook him.

4. Legs and wading. مَذَارِع of a beast are its legs (sing. مِذْرَاع). تذرّعت الإبل الماء: the camels waded in with their forelegs. ذرعتُ البعير: I trod on the camel's foreleg so my companion could mount.

5. Sides of a land. مَذَارِع الأرض are its outlying sides — as if each side were a forearm reaching out.

6. Drawing along the arm. تذرّعت المرأة الخوص: a woman sorts palm-leaf strips by drawing them along her forearm. Shāhid: تذرّعُ خِرصانٍ بأيدي الشواطب ("the drawing-out of shafts in the hands of the palm-leaf splitters").

7. الذَّرِيعَة: a she-camel the archer walks beside and shoots game from behind — so called because he paces along with her.

8. Speech. تذرّع الرجل في كلامه: a man spreads himself out at length in speech; الإذْرَاع is talking a great deal.

9. Stride and nimbleness. فرس ذريع: a horse of wide stride, showing ذَرَاعَة; قوائم ذَرِعَات: light, nimble legs.

10. Stars. الذِّرَاعَان: two stars, called "the two forearms of the Lion."

11. Of a woman quick-handed at spinning: ذِرَاع — attributed by Ibn Fāris to al-Kisāʾī.

12. Markings. ثور مُذَرَّع: a bull with black patches on its forelegs. مطر مُذَرِّع: rain that, when dug after, has soaked the ground about a cubit deep.

13. Mixed parentage. المُذَرَّع of men: one with an Arab mother and a base non-Arab father — named, Ibn Fāris says, by analogy with the two marks on a mule's foreleg, which come from the ass's side.

14. Idioms of nearness. "It is yours from me على حبل الذراع" — said when promising something immediate. ذراع العامل: the fore-part of a spear-shaft.

15. Place-names and nearby places. الذِّرَاعَان also denotes two hills; shāhid: إلى مشرب بين الذراعين بارد ("to a cold watering-place between the two Dhirāʿs"). المَذَارِع: settlements close to the big towns, e.g. al-Qādisiyya relative to al-Kūfa; and, of palms, those growing near the houses.

16. زِقّ مِذْرَاع: a long, bulky skin-vessel.

17. Form II uses. ذرّع لي فلاناً شيئاً من خبر: he passed me some news. ذرّع الرجل في سعيه: he ran using his arms, swinging them. And of a herald signalling with his hand: قد ذرّع البشير — the sign that good news is coming.
