text:
Ibn Fāris treats dh-r-r (with doubled r) as a single root that indicates fineness and spreading out.

1. **Small ants.** al-dharr are tiny ants; one ant is a dharra.

2. **Sprinkling.** dharartu means "I sprinkled", said of salt and of medicine. al-dharīra, a well-known powdered perfume, also belongs here. Ibn Fāris says all of these follow a single analogy.

3. **Sunrise.** dharrat al-shams, with the verbal noun dhurūr, is said when the sun rises; he explains it as a fine light that spreads. Hence the expressions "I will not do it as long as a rising sun rises" (mā dharra shāriq) and "as long as the edge of the sun rises" (mā dharra qarnu l-shams).

4. **Sprouting plants.** Abū Zayd reports dharra l-baql, "the herbage came up from the ground". Ibn Fāris counts this within the root, because young plants are small and scattered.

5. **A bad-tempered she-camel (disputed).** People say dhārrat al-nāqa, "the she-camel became ill-tempered" (participle mudhārr), and some report it with a doubled r. Ibn Fāris says that if this is correct it departs from the root meaning he has established. But al-Ḥuṭayʾa used dhārat bi-anfihā ("she turned up her nose") with a single r, and Ibn Fāris thinks this is the correct form. On that view it would come from dhaʾirat, "she became angry", with the hamza softened. He then notes that Abū Zayd reported "in so-and-so's soul there is dhirār", meaning turning away in anger, like the she-camel's dhirār, and this supports the first view (the doubled form). He closes with "God knows best".

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: تَذْرُو 1x "it (is) scattered"; ذَّٰرِيَٰت 1x "by those scattering"; ذَرْو 1x "dispersing"
text:
Ibn Fāris analyses ذ–ر–و (dh–r–w, with a weak third letter) as two separate roots.

Root 1 — one thing rising above another and overshadowing it:
1. ذِرْوَة / ذُرْوَة (dhirwa/dhurwa): the top of a camel's hump, and by extension the summit of anything; plural ذُرًى (dhuran).
2. ذَرَا (dharā): anything one takes cover behind — hence "I am in so-and-so's shade" means in his shelter.
3. مِذْرَوَانِ (midhrawān): the upper edges of the buttocks, so called because they overlook what lies between them.

Root 2 — something falling away in scattered pieces:
4. ذَرَا نَابُ الْجَمَلِ: said of a camel's tusk when its point breaks off. Cited from the poet Aws: "When a breeding-stallion of ours has the edge of his tusk broken away, another stallion's tusk rages among us."
5. ذَرَتِ الرِّيحُ الشَّيْءَ: the wind scattered or winnowed something; ذَرَا (dharā) is also the noun for what the wind has scattered.
6. أَذْرَتِ الْعَيْنُ دَمْعَهَا: the eye shed its tears; ذَرَى (dharā) is reported as a name for tears that are poured out.
7. أَذْرَيْتُ الرَّجُلَ عَنْ فَرَسِهِ: I flung the man off his horse.
8. ذَرْوٌ مِنْ قَوْلٍ: a "scattering" of speech — fragments a person lets drop from the edges of his talk, reaching the hearer incomplete.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) gives the root dh-w-d two possible original meanings, which he suggests may in fact go back to one:

1. To drive/repel something away — the verb ḏāda-yaḏūdu-ḏawdan. Examples he cites: ḏudtu fulānan ʿani-sh-shayʾ ("I drove so-and-so away from the thing") — repelling a person from something; and ḏudtu ibilī ("I drove my camels") — the same verb (masdar forms ḏawd or ḏiyād) used for herding/driving camels. A derived causative form, aḏadtu fulānan, means "I helped him drive his camels" (i.e., assisted him in the ḏiyād of his herd).

2. A small group of camels — the noun al-ḏawd, used for livestock/camels as a collective term. He quotes the philologist Abū Zayd specifying the precise range: al-ḏawd denotes a group of camels numbering from three to ten.

No Qur'anic citations appear in this entry; it is a purely lexical/philological note on the root's two senses and their possible common origin.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: ذَاقُ 36x "taste"; أَذَاقَ 22x "we will make him taste"; ذَائِقَة 3x "(will) taste"; ذَائِقُوا 2x "(will) certainly taste"
text:
Ibn Fāris's account of the root ذ-و-ق (ḏ-w-q):

1. Core meaning: the letters ḏāl, wāw, qāf share one root sense — testing or examining a thing by tasting it. Ibn Fāris treats tasting as the literal base from which the other uses branch metaphorically.

2. Literal use: ذُقْتُ الْمَأْكُولَ ("I tasted the food"), with the verbal noun ذَوْق.

3. Metaphorical "testing": ذُقْتُ مَا عِنْدَ فُلَانٍ ("I tasted what so-and-so has") = I tried/tested him to find out what he possesses.

4. Undergoing hardship: quoting al-Khalīl's Kitāb al-ʿAyn — anything unpleasant that befalls a person is said to be something he has "tasted." (This is the sense behind experiencing suffering as "tasting" it.)

5. Testing a bow: ذَاقَ الْقَوْسَ ("he tasted the bow") = he checked how much draw/give it has and how strong it is. Ibn Fāris cites a line of verse (poet unnamed) picturing an archer who "tastes" (tests) his bow, finds it supple enough, and notes it can drive the arrow deep. The verse is defective/cut off in the source.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ذ-خ-ر (dh-kh-r) from ONE core meaning: securing and keeping something safe.

1. Core sense — "to store/hoard": ذَخَرَ (dhakhara), "he stored a thing," verbal noun ذَخْر (dhakhr). The Form VIII reflexive is ادَّخَرَ (iddakhara), "he laid something up for himself" (the geminated-d form is how iftaʿala surfaces from this root).

2. Related noun — الْمَذَاخِرُ (al-madhākhir): a word for the inside of a body — a person's (or animal's) belly/interior and its veins, i.e. what "stores" fluid inside it. He cites the poet Manẓūr describing a she-camel: after she was given a milk-and-water drink (al-ʿakīs), "her innards (madhākhirihā) filled up and her neck-vein swelled with sweat/oozing." He also notes the everyday expression "the camel filled its madhākhir," meaning its belly.

3. Excluded look-alike — الْإِذْخِرُ (al-idhkhir), the name of a plant, is explicitly said NOT to belong to this root, despite the shared letters.

4. Extended (four-letter) forms — Ibn Fāris says words longer than the three root-letters that resemble this root are few, and point toward "setting off, going away," but their derivation is too obscure for him to treat in detail. He lists some anyway:
   - الذِّعْلِبَة (al-dhiʿlibah) — a swift she-camel. Related verbs: تَذَعْلَبَتْ ("she moved off swiftly"), اذْلَوْلَتْ ("she slipped away swiftly" — a stealthy departure). He adds that some say al-dhiʿlibah properly means the ostrich, and the she-camel was named by comparison to it.
   - الذَّعَالِب (al-dhaʿālib) — scraps of torn rag, illustrated by a line of verse: "running off swiftly, save for scraps of rag [it shed]."
   - اذْلَعَبَّ (idhlaʿabba) — said of a camel moving swiftly on its course; close in meaning to idhlawlā above.

He closes with the standard scholarly formula: "God knows best what is correct."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ذ-ي-ع (dh-y-ʿ) from a single core meaning: something becoming manifest, appearing, and spreading abroad.

1. Core sense — spreading/becoming known: One says dhāʿa al-khabar ('the news dhāʿa'), meaning it spread and became widely known, verbal noun dhuyūʿ.

2. Agent noun — a man who cannot keep a secret is called midhyāʿ (plural: madhāyīʿ) — literally 'a spreader.'

3. Citation — a ḥadīth attributed to ʿAlī describes certain people as 'not the masāyīḥ (those who roam about spreading slander) nor the madhāyīʿ al-budhur (the blabbermouths who scatter secrets).'

4. Extended usage — Ibn Fāris notes a related expression built on the same 'spreading' logic: adhāʿa al-nās mā fī al-ḥawḍ ('the people adhāʿū what was in the trough') is said when people drink a water-trough completely dry among themselves — i.e., they used it all up. The link to the core sense is that the water is 'dispersed'/exhausted by being spread among many drinkers, just as news is dispersed by being spread among many mouths.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris's Maqayis al-Lugha treats the root '-sh-r as a single root whose core meaning is hiddah - sharpness, keenness, intensity. He traces this one idea through several derived usages.

1. A person described as ashir is batir (exultant, insolent from excess/high spirits) and mutasarri' (hasty, impetuous) - someone with a sharp, excitable temperament. The verb is ashira - ya'sharu. A man in this state is called ashir or ashur.

2. A she-camel with this same sharp/spirited quality is called mi'shir (pattern mif'il, from al-ashar). Ibn Faris cites a line of the poet Aws ibn Hajar describing such a she-camel as bred from closely related stock (her brother is her father, her paternal uncle is her maternal uncle) and calling her a big-cheeked, mi'shir she-camel.

3. Al-ushur names a fineness and sharpness at the edges/tips of the teeth - finely serrated tooth-edges. Ibn Faris quotes Tarafa's line comparing sun-bleached teeth to polished white hailstones with fine serrated edges.

4. The expression ashartu l-khashabata bi-l-mi'shar (I sawed the wood with the saw) is derived from the same root - the mi'shar (saw) takes its name from the sharpness/serration of its teeth, the same underlying idea of hiddah running through the whole entry.

So for Ibn Faris, one root-meaning - sharpness/keenness - covers a sharp-tempered person, a spirited camel, serrated tooth-edges, and a toothed saw.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: إِذْن 39x "by (the) permission"; أَذِنَ 23x "permits"; أُذُنٌ 18x "their ears"; ٱسْتَـْذَنَ 12x "ask your permission"; أَذَّنَ 3x "called out"; مُؤَذِّن 2x "an announcer"; تَأَذَّنَ 2x "declared"; ءَاذَن 2x "we announce (to) you"; أَذَٰن 1x "and an announcement"
text:
Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's account of the root اذن (A-dh-n):

1. الأذن (al-udhun) — the ear as a bodily organ. Because of its ring-like shape, the word is extended to a pot's "ear" (its handle) and similar loops.

2. By metaphor it names a person who listens a great deal and repeats what he hears: "they say he is an ear [all ears]; say: an ear of good for you" (9:61) — i.e. his listening serves your good. In "in their ears is a heaviness" (6:25) the point is their ignorance, not that they cannot physically hear.

3. أَذِنَ (adhina) — to listen, to give ear: "and it gave ear to its Lord, as is fitting" (84:2). It also covers knowledge gained through hearing — being informed or put on notice: "then take notice of a war from God and His Messenger" (2:279).

4. الأُذن / الأذان — what is heard; and by extension, knowledge, since for us hearing is the source of much of what we know. Related: ائْذَنْ لِي ("give me leave," 9:49) and تَأَذَّنَ رَبُّكُمْ ("your Lord proclaimed / gave notice," 14:7). The verbs أَذَنْتُهُ بكذا and آذَنْتُهُ both mean "I informed him of it."

5. المُؤَذِّن (muʾadhdhin) — anyone who announces something by a call or proclamation: "a herald proclaimed: O caravan…" (12:70); "a herald proclaimed among them" (7:44); "proclaim among the people the ḥajj" (22:27). And الأذين is the place that such a proclamation reaches.

6. الإِذن (idhn) — to make known that a thing is permitted, to grant license for it. Hence "We sent no messenger but to be obeyed by God's leave" (4:64), i.e. by His will and command; likewise 3:166, 2:102, and 58:10 ("harms them only by God's leave").
   - Some gloss idhn here as "by His knowledge," but al-Rāghib distinguishes the two: idhn (permission) is narrower than ʿilm (knowledge). It is used only where God's volition (mashīʾa) is involved — whether or not He approves of the act itself.
   - In "no soul can believe except by God's leave" (10:100), His volition and command are plainly present. In "they harm none by it except by God's leave" (2:102), His volition enters in one respect: God created in the human the capacity to be affected by a wrongdoer's blow — not making him a stone that feels no pain — and creating that very capacity is God's act; in that sense the harm inflicted by a wrongdoer occurs "by God's leave." A fuller treatment, he notes, belongs elsewhere.

7. الاستئذان (istiʾdhān) — asking permission: "only those who do not believe in God ask your leave" (9:45); "when they ask your leave" (24:62).

8. Grammar of «إِذَنْ» (idhan) — a particle of response-and-consequence ("then, in that case"). It calls for an answer, and the surrounding speech carries a consequential sense. Its governing effect on a following imperfect verb depends on position: if idhan opens the clause and an imperfect verb follows, it necessarily takes the accusative (إذن أخرج); if speech precedes it, both accusative and nominative are allowed (أنا إذن أخرج / أخرج); if it follows the verb or has no imperfect verb with it, it governs nothing (أنا أخرج إذن). Qur'anic instance: "then you would be like them" (4:140).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the letters hamza–dhāl–yāʾ as a single root with one core idea: something you find loathsome and cannot settle at ease with.

1. Verbal usage: آذَيْتُ فُلَانًا أُوذِيهِ — "I harmed/annoyed So-and-so, I harm him." The sense is causing distress or irritation.

2. Applied to animals: بَعِيرٌ أَذٍ (a restless male camel) and نَاقَةٌ أَذِيَةٌ (a restless she-camel) describe a beast that will not stay put in one place even though it is in no pain — as if it were being made uneasy (يَأْذَى) by wherever it stands. This extends the core idea from inflicting distress to being oneself unable to settle.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root: أحد (a-ḥ-d). Entry by al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī.

Al-Rāghib divides اَحَد (aḥad) into two distinct usages, one in negation and one in affirmation.

1. In negation only. Here aḥad sweeps up the entire class of rational beings — few or many, taken together or apart. "There is no one (aḥad) in the house" means: not one, not two, not more; neither as a group nor as individuals. Because of this all-encompassing force, al-Rāghib argues it cannot be used in affirmation: you may deny two contradictory things at once, but you cannot assert them both at once. To say "in the house is aḥad" would simultaneously assert a single lone person and assert more-than-one — which is absurd. And because in negation it also covers "more than one," the following word can take a plural form: فَما مِنْكُمْ مِنْ أَحَدٍ عَنْهُ حاجِزِينَ ("not one of you could have shielded him" — al-Ḥāqqa 69:47), where the participle is plural.

2. In affirmation, in three ways:
   - As the unit in compound numbers: أحد عشر (eleven), أحد وعشرين (twenty-one).
   - In a genitive construct, meaning "the first (one)": أَمَّا أَحَدُكُما ("as for one of you two" — Yūsuf 12:41); and يوم الأحد (Sunday = "the first day"), paired with يوم الاثنين (Monday).
   - Absolutely, as a bare descriptive attribute — which al-Rāghib says occurs only in describing God: قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ ("Say: He is God, One" — al-Ikhlāṣ 112:1).

Etymology: al-Rāghib holds that aḥad originates from وحد (waḥd), but notes that waḥd is applied to things other than God, citing a line of al-Nābigha in which waḥd describes a solitary wild oryx at day's end.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī treats the root أصل (ʾ-ṣ-l) under two connected senses:

1. **Evening / late afternoon.** In "in the mornings and the آصāl" (al-Aʿrāf 7:205), آصāl means the evenings. The singular for evening is أَصِيل (also أَصِيلَة). Plurals: أَصِيل → أُصُل and آصَال; أَصِيلَة → أَصَائِل. Compare "morning and evening" (بُكْرَةً وَأَصِيلًا, al-Fatḥ 48:9).

2. **Root / foundation of a thing.** أَصْل is a thing's base or footing — such that if you imagine the base lifted, everything above it rises with it. He cites "its root firmly fixed and its branch in the sky" (Ibrāhīm 14:24).

Derived usage: تَأَصَّلَ ("to become firmly rooted"), أَصَّلَ ("to root/establish"), مجد أصيل ("deeply-rooted glory"), and the idiom فلان لا أصل له ولا فصل ("he has neither root nor branch," i.e. no lineage).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: al-Ḥuṭayʾa (lived into Islam); al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʾ-ṣ-r as a single root whose derivatives all stay close in meaning.

1. Core notion. The root's basic sense is aṣr: holding or confining something (ḥabs), and inclining or bending toward something (ʿaṭf) — plus whatever falls under those two.

2. Covenant and kinship. On this basis a covenant or compact is called iṣr, and a kinship tie is called āṣira; in his account every binding tie, kinship bond, and covenant counts as iṣr — the whole family of words expresses one idea.

3. Attested usage. The Arabs say "mā taʾṣirunī ʿalā fulānin āṣira" — "no āṣira draws me toward So-and-so," i.e. no kinship inclines me toward him. He cites al-Ḥuṭayʾa: they showed him favour "without any āṣira — for the awāṣir [ties] have grown great," which he glosses as: they inclined toward me without covenant or kinship between us.

4. Maʾṣar. The maʾṣar (a barrier or check-post) belongs here because it is a thing by which something is held back.

5. A heavy covenant. As for calling a burdensome covenant an iṣr, he derives this from the same core: a covenant and a kinship tie carry an iṣr — a binding weight that has to be borne.

6. Verb. aṣartuhu means "I confined/held him back."

7. Iṣār. Also from this root is iṣār, the tent-rope (ṭunub), plural uṣur; another report makes it the peg to which the tent-rope is fastened. He quotes a line of al-Aʿshā in which one man prepares fresh fodder for the animals while another sets the iṣār among them.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
Root ء ب ب (Abb) — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr

**1. al-abb = herbage / pasturage.** The base sense the entry establishes: al-abb is fodder-plant growth — "the pasture" (Ibn Durayd), or more fully "all the herbage that livestock feed on" (al-Zajjāj). This is the word in the Qur'an, "wa fākihatan wa abban" — "and fruit and abb" (Q 80:31).

Several early authorities are cited on what exactly it covers:
- Abū Ḥanīfa (al-Dīnawarī): God named all pasture "abb."
- al-Farrāʾ: whatever the cattle/livestock eat.
- Mujāhid draws the contrast explicitly: fruit is what people eat, abb is what cattle eat — abb is to animal pasture what fruit is to human food.
- Thaʿlab and ʿAṭāʾ broaden it further: everything the earth puts forth of plant growth.

A line of poetry is quoted using abb alongside makraʿ (a watering place), as things a tribe's territory provides.

A hadith about Anas is recorded: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb read this Qur'anic verse aloud, asked "what is al-abb?", then answered his own question by saying "we are not obligated to know this" — i.e., he let the point go rather than press for a ruling on it.

A second, narrower nuance: al-abb can also mean pasture specifically ready for grazing and cutting — illustrated by a saying attributed to Quss b. Sāʿida, who "grazed on abb and hunted a lizard."

**2. abba (verb) = to make oneself ready to travel.** "Abba li-l-sayr" — he prepared and equipped himself for departure. Illustrated with a verse by al-Aʿshā comparing a man resolved to leave to one who has already cut ties. The Form VIII verb iʾtabba carries the same meaning. Related nouns: abāb / ibāba / abāba, meaning one's travel-gear or state of readiness.

A parallel form, al-wabb, is noted (in al-Azharī's Tahdhīb) for readying oneself to charge in battle — "habba wa wabba" — with the note that wabb derives from abba by turning the hamza into a wāw. Ibn al-Aʿrābī adds two further verbal senses: abba said of something that "moved/stirred," and abba said of routing an enemy with a charge that is fully committed, "with no feint in it."

**3. al-abb = longing for one's homeland.** "Abba ilā waṭanihi" — he yearned toward his home. Ibn Durayd is cited as preferring the vowel pattern ibāba here. A verse is quoted picturing someone at an encampment feeling this pull homeward just as the camp's ropes are being struck for departure.

**4. Minor idioms built on the same root:**
- "Abba yadahu ilā sayfihi" — he drew his hand back to his sword, readying to draw it.
- "Abbat abābatu al-shayʾ" — its course/way became straight.
- A saying about gazelles at water uses abāb/ʿabāb wordplay to mean "they neither reached it nor prepared to seek it" (the ʿabāb side of this pairing belongs under the separate root ʿ-b-b).

**5. al-ubāb — a related noun** meaning either water or a mirage (per Ibn al-Aʿrābī), illustrated by a verse about boats/litters cutting through its "surging crests" (explained as a metaphor calling camels "ships of the land"). It can also mean the surge or foam of the sea, synonymous with ʿubāb. Ibn Jinnī specifically rejects deriving this ubāb from ʿubāb by letter-substitution; he analyzes it instead as the pattern fuʿāl built directly from abba ("to make ready").

**6. A final, separate note**: istaʾabba aban, "to adopt someone as a father" — flagged as a grammatically irregular (rare) formation; the expected regular form would be istaʾbi. This entry appears to be about the unrelated word ab ("father"), included here in passing rather than as part of the abb (pasturage) discussion proper.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ʾ-b-d from two core ideas: (1) length of duration, and (2) wildness or becoming feral.

1. Duration. الأَبَد (al-abad) means time / an unbounded stretch of time (glossed as al-dahr), plural آبَاد (ābād). The Arabs form an intensifying doublet أَبَدٌ أَبِيدٌ ("endless age"), parallel to دَهْرٌ دَهِيرٌ. From this sense, الأَبْدَة (al-abda) is a deed that endures permanently.

2. Wildness / becoming feral. تَأَبَّدَ البَعِيرُ = the camel reverted to a wild state. Ibn Fāris cites a ḥadīth that these domestic beasts have "awābid" (ones that bolt) like wild animals. Extended to places: تَأَبَّدَ المَنْزِلُ = the dwelling fell empty and desolate — supported by Labīd's line on the effaced abodes at Minā (Ghawl and Rijām left deserted).

Related items the entry records:
- الإِبِد (al-ibid), per Ibn al-Aʿrābī: livestock that breeds yearly (e.g. the slave-woman, mare, she-ass), because they bear young every year.
- تَأَبَّدَ وَجْهُهُ = his face became blotched or discolored (freckled/spotted).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: unnamed verse ×3; Labīd (lived into Islam); ʿAdī (pre-Islamic); al-Shammākh (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root ʾ-b-l as resting on a small set of basic ideas: camels; doing without water (self-sufficiency); heaviness; and overcoming. His entry then gathers the usages under these headings.

1. Camels (الإبل). Per al-Khalīl, the word is common knowledge. إبل مؤبَّلة = camels formed into successive herds — a description reserved for camels. A camel-owner is آبِل. Abū Zayd: إبل covers both the mature animals and the young, has no singular of its own form, and pluralizes as آبَال (with a verse: "Their camel-herds have drunk by means of fire… and fire may cure burning thirst").

2. Skill with camels. Ibn al-Aʿrābī distinguishes آبِل (owner of camels) from أَبِلٌ, on the pattern فَعِل (expert at pasturing them), verb أَبِلَ يَأْبَلُ. "He is of آبَل الناس" = the most expert of people with camels; hence the proverb "more expert with camels than Ḥunayf al-Ḥanātim."

3. Abundance of camels. الإِبِلَات = camels. أَبَّلَ الرجل = his camels grew numerous (so he is مُؤَبِّل); مال مُؤَبَّل is used only of camels, denoting their multitude and their crowding one on another. "لا يأتبل" = he cannot keep his seat on camels. Al-Aṣmaʿī glosses إبل مؤبَّلة simply as "many," on the model of غنم مغنَّمة, بقر مبقَّرة, and reports another gloss, "kept as acquired property." Ibn al-Aʿrābī: ناقة أَبِلَة = a strong she-camel. Saying: "he has neither هابِل nor آبِل" — the first the resourceful provider, the second the herdsman.

4. Tending camels (الأَبَلَة). From al-ʿĀmirī: أَبَلَة is careful, honouring husbandry of camels, tending them well. Abū Nukhayla's dictum, quoted here, praises such property: it stanches bloodshed (as blood-payment), dowers women, and by it God in heaven is served; its milk a cure, its urine a remedy, its ownership eminence.

5. "A hundred camels." Abū Zayd: "so-and-so has إبل" means he owns a hundred — the word became a name for that number, like هُنَيْدَة. Ibn Fāris cites the Prophet's saying, "People are like a hundred camels among which there is not one riding-beast."

6. Magnifying / heaping up. Al-Farrāʾ: "يُؤَبِّل على فلان" = he piles things up against him; the underlying sense is magnification and aggrandizement (verse: a good companion "assented and did not heed the word of the exaggerator"). Al-Farrāʾ derives the name الإبل itself from this, because of the animal's great bulk.

7. Doing without water; abstaining (الاجتزاء). Al-Khalīl: بعير آبِل = a camel that stays in one place and needs no water. تأبَّل الرجل عن المرأة = a man holds off from a woman as a wild animal holds off from water; hence the report that Adam kept apart from Eve for days over his slain son. Labīd's verse refers to a wild ass "that has gone without water." Verb: أَبَلَ يَأْبِلُ / يَأْبُلُ, verbal noun أُبُول; al-ʿAjjāj uses the plural الأُبَّال. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: أَبَلَتْ تَأْبِلُ أَبْلًا = they grazed on herbage fresh and dry alike; eating only the fresh is called الجَزْء. Abū ʿUbayd gives the participles أوابل, أُبَّل, أُبَّال = "those that do without water."

8. Qurʾānic use. On {طَيْرًا أَبَابِيلَ} (105:3), al-Khalīl explains أبابيل as "some of them following others" (i.e. in successive flocks), the singular being إِبَّالَة or إِبَّوْل.

9. الأَبِيل. Al-Khalīl: a title of one of the chief men of the Christians, also أَبِيلِيّ. Al-Aʿshā's أيْبُليّ is explained as a metrically forced transposition of أَبِيليّ, on the analogy of أَيْنُق for أَنْوُق. ʿAdī swears "by an abīl who cried aloud whenever he prayed."

10. Mourning. Some hold تأبَّل على الميت = he grieved over the dead man, and أَبَّلْتُ الميت parallels أَبَّنْتُ (I eulogized him).

11. مُسْتَأْبَل. In one cited verse (a man "forsaken" by his own two tribes), مُسْتَأْبَل is said to mean the man who is wronged.

12. Grudge, claim, need (أَبَلَة / أَبِلَة). Al-Farrāʾ: الأَبَلَات = rancours, singular أَبَلَة. Al-ʿĀmirī: "قضى أبلته من كذا" = he settled his need of it, adding that the word belongs to the vocabulary of evil, not good. Abū Zayd: "ما لي إليك أَبِلَة" = I have no need of you; and "أطلبه بأَبِلَة" = I pursue him for a blood-claim (تِرَة).

13. Place-name. Per Yaʿqūb, أُبْلَى is a place, attested in a verse of al-Shammākh.

14. Overcoming (الغَلَبَة). أَبَلَّ الرجل يَأْبِلُ أَبْلًا = he prevailed and held out against others.

15. Heaviness (الثِّقَل). الأَبَلَة = weight or burden; Ibn Fāris cites the report, "Every property whose zakāt has been rendered — its burden (أَبَلَة) is gone." Related: الإِبَّالَة, a bundle of firewood.

poets_named: unnamed verse ×2; al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); Ruʾbah (Umayyad); Zuhayr (pre-Islamic)
text:
Root ء-ب-ق (ʾ-b-q) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha (d. 1004 CE)

Ibn Fāris derives two core senses from this root:

1. A slave fleeing/absconding (ibāq).
- Base verb: أَبَقَ (abaqa), "he [a slave] fled/absconded," imperfect يَأْبِقُ, verbal nouns abqan/abaqan.
- A rajaz-metre verse uses the active participle ābiq ("one who is fleeing"), comparing the fleeing man to lightning flashing over "the land of the ghouls."
- A habitual absconder is called ʿabd abūq or abbāq (intensive adjective patterns — "a chronic runaway slave").
- A related form, تَأَبَّقَ (taʾabbaqa), is glossed by the philologist Abū Zayd as "he hid/concealed himself." Two poetic citations use it this way: al-Aʿshā says death came upon a man "not hiding," and another poet asks Bahān why he hides himself, adding that ease/comfort does not suit him.
- Ibn Fāris also records a colloquial extension: when accused of some trait or asked about a woman, a man replies "mā ataʾabbaqu" — meaning "I do not deny it/her." So the sense of "concealing oneself" shades into "disavowing/denying."

2. Hardness or toughness in a matter (al-tashaddud fī al-amr).
This branch is illustrated through al-abaq, the bark or husk of hemp (qinnab):
- al-Khalīl defines al-abaq simply as the husk of hemp.
- Abū Ziyād describes the process: hemp stalks are pounded until the bark separates out, yielding qinnab (hemp fiber).
- Two verses show the resulting product — hemp cordage: Ruʾbah compares eight lean animals to "ropes of hemp," and Zuhayr describes rope-nooses of rawhide and hemp being pulled taut/firmly secured. The toughness of hemp rope is the link Ibn Fāris draws to the root's second meaning, "hardness/toughness."

No sense of "the five ritual acts" or any later technical usage appears here — this entry is purely about (a) a slave's flight/self-concealment and (b) hemp fiber and its toughness.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: ابَاء 64x "our forefathers"; أَبٌ 46x "to his father"; أَبَوَان 7x "his parents"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʾ-b-w as pointing to one idea: rearing and nourishing.

1. **To nourish.** Abawtu l-shayʾ, ābūhu, abwan means "I nourished the thing." Ibn Fāris says it is for this reason that the father is called al-ab.

2. **Relative adjective.** The adjective formed from ab is abawī ("paternal, of a father").

3. **An ailing goat.** A she-goat is called abwāʾ when she falls ill from smelling the urine of mountain goats.

4. **The father and its plurals (al-Khalīl).** Al-Khalīl calls al-ab a familiar word and gives two plurals, ābāʾ and ubuwwa, citing a verse in which the poet calls a tribe "the forefathers (ubuwwa) of my fathers."

5. **Taking someone as a father.** One says taʾabbaytu aban, "I took someone as a father," on the same pattern as tabannaytu ibnan ("I adopted a son") and taʾammahtu umman ("I took someone as a mother").

6. **Poetic and plural forms (al-Khalīl).** In poetry, abāka and abīka can stand for abawāka / abawayka, "your two parents." A verse speaks of a man being "ransomed with fathers (al-abīna) and a maternal uncle," using al-abīna as a plural. The plural abūn is also allowed, so hāʾulāʾi abūkum means "these are your fathers."

7. **Being a father to someone (Abū ʿUbayd).** "You were not a father, and now you have become one (ubuwwa)." Abawtu l-qawm means "I was a father to the people." A verse says: "We lead them and father them all together, as straps are cut from the hide."

8. **Caring for an orphan (al-Khalīl).** Fulān yaʾbū l-yatīm: he nourishes the orphan as a father nourishes his child.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root أ-ب-ي (a-b-y), per Ibn Fāris. Core sense: refusal, holding back, declining (al-imtināʿ).

1. To refuse. أَبَيْتُ الشَّيْءَ آبَاهُ = "I refused / I refuse the thing." From this: قَوْمٌ أَبِيُّونَ / أُبَاةٌ = people who refuse to submit, who will not be wronged (plurals abiyyūn, ubāh). Shāhid: "one who refuses injustice, from a band of men who refuse to be wronged" (أَبِيُّ الضَّيْمِ مِنْ نَفَرٍ أُبَاةٍ).

2. الإِبَاء (al-ibāʾ): refusal to accept — when something is offered to a man and he declines it. The verbal noun is heard with both ḍamma (ubāʾ) and kasra (ibāʾ). The verb follows the pattern faʿala yafʿalu.

3. Extensions to animals: الأَبِيَّة is the intractable, hard-to-handle she-camel. Al-Liḥyānī: a man is أَبَيَان (abayān) when he habitually refuses things; مَاء مَأْبَاة is water that camels refuse. Ibn al-Sikkīt: أَخَذَهُ أَبَاء = he was seized by [a condition making] him refuse food.

4. الأَوَابِي (Abū ʿAmr): young she-camels (of the ḥiqāq, jidhāʿ, thinnāʾ age-classes) that the stallion has covered but which have not conceived; they keep this name until they conceive once, then no longer. Singular آبِيَة.

5. الأُبَاء (al-ubāʾ): possibly from the same root-logic — an ailment that strikes goats from smelling the urine of wild mountain-goats (arwā). Shāhid: "…for it is ubā — I do not think the sheep will come through it safe."

6. الأَبَاء (al-abāʾ): the tips of reeds/canes; singular أَبَاءَة. By extension a reed-bed/thicket is called أَبَاءَة (compared to calling a copse أَرَاكَة). In one verse the word may instead mean spears, likened to reeds for their abundance. A second shāhid compares battle-slaughter to "the crackling of burning reeds" (كَمَعْمَعَةِ الأَبَاءِ الْمُحْرَقِ).

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
Root أ د د (a-d-d), Ibn Manẓūr, Lisān al-ʿArab

1. al-idd/al-iddah — a wonder, a monstrous/terrible matter, a calamity (also al-add, same sense). The entry's central citation is Qur'an Maryam 19:89, "laqad jiʾtum shayʾan iddā" — "you have certainly come up with a monstrous thing" (God's response to those who claim He has a son) — with a grammatical note on a minority reading (add instead of idd) attributed to Abū ʿAmr, and a bawdy line of poetry (attributed to Ibn Durayd) illustrating the word's general sense of "something enormous."
2. addahu al-amru — a matter struck/afflicted someone with calamity; a hadith of ʿAlī describes a dream of the Prophet, asking what "great calamities and crookedness" (al-idād wa-l-awad) he had faced since. al-add is also used for overpowering strength, illustrated with a line of poetry about lost vigor.
3. Animal sounds, a separate cluster: addat al-nāqah — a she-camel's repeated yearning-cry; adda al-baʿīr — a camel bellowed.
4. addu al-shayʾ/al-ḥabl — to stretch or pull something taut (a rope); adda fī al-arḍ — to go off/depart; adad al-ṭarīq — a road's well-worn track; al-add — also the sound of footsteps, illustrated with a line of poetry about jinn-haunted land and its eerie sounds.
5. al-adīd — natural constitution/character; shadīd adīd — a fixed intensifying word-pair.
6. Closing onomastic material: Udd/Udad as the name of ʿAdnān's ancestor (with Ibn Durayd's etymological speculation that the hamzah derives from an original wāw, related to wudd, "love"), and a separate Udad as ancestor of a Yemeni tribe; al-Azharī notes that Quraysh also worshipped an idol named Wudd, sometimes pronounced with a hamzah as Udd — the same root-letters, different referent entirely.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يُؤَدِّ 5x "he will return it"; أَدَاء 1x "[and] payment"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʾ-d-y as having one single root idea: **getting something to reach something else** — either delivering a thing to its destination, or the thing arriving there by itself.

1. **Arriving at a state (of milk).** On the authority of Abū ʿUbayd: the Arabs use أَدَى / يَأْدِي / أُدْيًا of milk when it has "arrived" at the point of turning — i.e. when it has thickened and curdled. This is the intransitive side of the root: something reaching its state on its own.

2. **Delivering / discharging what is owed.** On the authority of al-Khalīl: أَدَّى (form II) — "so-and-so renders what is due from him," with the two verbal nouns أَدَاء (adāʾ) and تَأْدِيَة (taʾdiya). This is the transitive, causative side: making a thing reach its rightful recipient.

3. **Comparative form.** فُلَانٌ آدَى لِلْأَمَانَةِ مِنْكَ — "so-and-so is more reliable than you at delivering up a trust" (ʾādā, the elative built on this root, construed with li- and the thing entrusted).

**Citation.** A line of verse quoted from an unnamed reciter uses the form II verb of conveying a message: "He conveyed to Hind her greetings … and said, 'This is from the farewell of Bikr.'"

Note the method: Ibn Fāris derives all of the above from one abstract notion (reaching/causing to reach) rather than listing unrelated senses, and supports it with a transmitted usage (milk), a lexicographer's paradigm (al-Khalīl), an idiom, and a poetic witness.

dictionary: ʿAyn — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786)
text:
**Root ʾ-f-f — Kitāb al-ʿAyn (al-Khalīl, d. 786 CE)**

1. **The interjection and the act of uttering it.** *Uff* and *afaf* both belong to *taʾfīf* — the act of saying "*uff*" [an exclamation of annoyance or disgust]. The ʿAyn gives the verb: *affaftu fulānan*, "I said *uff* to so-and-so," i.e. you said *uffin* to him.

2. **Vocalisation (three dialectal forms).** The word is heard with a final kasra, ḍamma, or fatḥa when it takes no tanwīn; the entry rates the kasra form the best of the three.

3. **Grammatical note — with tanwīn it is a noun.** If you add tanwīn, the word goes into the nominative: *uffun*. The book's reasoning is that with tanwīn it has become a full noun, parallel to *waylun lahu*, "woe to him."

4. **The feminine form *uffatun lahu*.** The Arabs also say *uffatun lahu*, feminine and nominative. This form occurs only with tanwīn — either nominative or accusative. The accusative is explained by an implied verb (a cognate accusative), as if one said *affaftu affan*.

5. **A separate concrete sense, paired with *tuff*.** In the pairing *al-uff wa-l-tuff*: *uff* is earwax, and *tuff* is the dirt under the fingernails.

6. **Attested usage.** The phrase *ʿalayhim al-laʿna wa-l-taʾfīf* — "upon them be the curse and the saying of *uff*."

The entry closes with the book's colophon: the *fāʾ* chapter ends here with the *lafīf* section, which has no four-letter or five-letter roots.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أُفِكَ 16x "are they deluded"; إِفْك 9x "a lie"; مُؤْتَفِكَة 3x "and the overturned cities"; أَفَّاك 2x "liar"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats أ-ف-ك (a-f-k) as one root with a single core idea: turning a thing over and diverting it from its proper direction.

1. Overturning / being turned: أُفِكَ الشَّيْءُ — "the thing was turned over."

2. Lying: أَفِكَ الرَّجُلُ means "the man lied," i.e. spoke falsehood; and الْإِفْك (al-ifk) is "the lie, falsehood." (On his analysis, a lie is speech turned away from its true direction.)

3. Diverting someone: أَفَكْتُ الرَّجُلَ عَنِ الشَّيْءِ — "I turned the man away from the thing." He cites Qur'an 46:22: "Have you come to divert us (li-taʾfikanā) from our gods?" — the verb here meaning to turn/divert away. A verse of poetry uses the same sense: one "turned away" (maʾfūk) from the best is among others who have likewise been turned away (ufikū).

4. Shifting winds: الْمُؤْتَفِكَات (al-muʾtafikāt) are winds whose directions of blowing keep changing. He notes the saying: "When the shifting winds are frequent, the earth thrives."

All four uses trace back to the one sense of turning/diverting from the proper course.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَفَلَ 3x "it set"; ءَافِلِين 1x "the ones that set"
poets_named: unnamed verse; Al-Farazdaq (Umayyad); Ihāb ibn ʿUmayr (undated)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʾ-f-l as having two independent base meanings.

1. Going out of sight / disappearing. أَفَلَتِ الشَّمْسُ = the sun set, went from view; نُجُومٌ أُفَّلٌ = stars that set. He states the rule broadly: anything that disappears from view is آفِل (āfil). His poetic witness plays on the Pleiades, which come into conjunction once and then sink away — a figure for a separation that grants nearness only briefly.

He also records, on al-Khalīl's authority, an extension of this sense: when the impregnating seed settles into the womb, it is said to have "afala" — i.e. to have gone in and become hidden.

2. Young camels. الأَفِيل (afīl) is the young weaned camel-calf (faṣīl); plural الإِفَال (ifāl); feminine أَفِيلَة (afīla). Al-Farazdaq's verse contrasts the breeding stallion coming on ahead of the herd's young ones. Al-Aṣmaʿī narrows the term: an afīl is a camel in its second or third year (ibn al-makhāḍ, ibn al-labūn); once it passes that age the word no longer applies.

A further verse, by Ihāb ibn ʿUmayr, is glossed for two words: ثَامِنَة means coming to water on the eighth day, and مُثُول means standing upright.

The entry closes with the proverb "the mighty stud-camel comes only from the calf," which Ibn Fāris reads as: what is great begins in what is small.

Note on method: Ibn Fāris does not link the two senses to each other — he presents them as two separate origins under one consonantal root.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʾ-f-q as a single root with one core idea in two aspects: the wide distance between a thing's outer extremities, and the reaching of an utmost limit.

1. Horizons / outer regions. الآفاق (al-āfāq) are the far regions and outermost parts. Of a Bedouin tent, its āfāq are its sides, as opposed to its roof height. A cited verse speaks of "the alternating horizons of the sky." From this sense comes أَفَقَ الرَّجُل (afaqa l-rajul): a man travelled far out into the land.

2. Abū Ḥanīfa al-Dīnawarī's distinction (reported by Ibn Fāris): the sky has horizons and the earth has horizons.
   - Horizons of the sky: the furthest point sight reaches along the earth's surface in every direction — the boundary between the hidden part of the celestial sphere and the visible part of the earth. Rising and setting of stars happen on this line, hence the rajaz line "before the horizon drew near to al-Jawzāʾ" (i.e. before al-Jawzāʾ rose); another verse has the sun "on the horizon like the eye of a squinting man"; another describes the western sky running with blood from the sun's redness "when the horizon made away with her" — the entry glosses "making away with" as causing her to disappear.
   - Horizons of the earth: its outer edges, from wherever they encircle the observer; cited with a rajaz line contrasting home-threshed grain with "visiting the horizons."
   - Derived adjective: a man from a distant region is أُفُقِيّ / أَفَقِيّ, and so is a star whose course stays near the horizon and never reaches the zenith. (End of Abū Ḥanīfa's material.)

3. Reaching the limit / pre-eminence. الآفِق (al-āfiq) is a man who has reached the utmost in generosity; feminine آفِقَة. Al-Aʿshā uses آفِقًا of a man to whom the tribute of everything between ʿUmān and Malaḥ is brought. Abū ʿAmr: al-āfiq equals al-fāʾiq (the surpassing one); the verb أَفَقَ يَأْفِق أَفْقًا means to overcome or surpass, and الأُفُق in this usage means superiority/victory. فَرَسٌ أُفُقٌ (pattern fuʿul) is a splendid mare.

4. A disputed line of al-Aʿshā about King al-Nuʿmān "granting written allotments and yaʾfiqu": al-Khalīl reads it as "he takes from the far regions," noting the singular of āfāq is أُفُق, a region of the earth.

5. Morphological note. Ibn al-Sikkīt: أَفَقِيّ for "one of the people of the far regions" is formed irregularly (against analogy); أُفُقِيّ is also attested.

6. Road sense. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: أَفَقُ الطَّرِيق is the road's beaten course — "I sat on the afaq of the road and its open track."

7. Bodily sense. Ibn al-Aʿrābī also places here الأَفَقَة, the flank, collective الأَفَق, with a verse about the shoulder-muscle and the flank suffering, and the phrase "I drank until I filled my two flanks."

8. Bucket and hide. Abū ʿAmr and others: دَلْوٌ أَفِيق is a bucket that exceeds other buckets — "it is no mere bucket; it is the afīq." For the same reason tanned hide is called أَفِيق, plural أَفَق (also أُفُق). Ibn Fāris marks this as the end of the strictly lexical and derivational material.

9. Yawm al-Ufāqa (a proper name, not a lexical sense). Ibn Fāris appends the battle-day of the Arabs called Yawm al-Ufāqa — also known as the Day of al-ʿUẓālā, the Day of Aʿshāsh and the Day of Mulayḥa — Ufāqa being a place. Bisṭām b. Qays lay in wait with three hundred horsemen for the Banū Yarbūʿ; the Banū Zubayd camped at the grove of al-Ufāqa. Bisṭām, scouting, learned from a youth where the other clans were and urged his men to seize the isolated Zubayd clan, saying "safety is one of the two spoils." They mocked him and said they would pick the clans off like truffles; he warned that a spear-thrust would make them forget the plunder. A mare sensed the horses; her rider Usayd b. Ḥinnāʾa raised the alarm cry to the Banū Yarbūʿ, and battle was joined at al-Ghabīṭ before mid-morning. Al-Uḥaymir b. ʿAbd Allāh — nicknamed "breaker of spears" because his spear always shattered — charged Bisṭām, who fled with his men after losses. Verses are quoted blaming the army of al-ʿUẓālā more than that of al-Ghabīṭ and mocking Abū al-Ṣahbāʾ for casting off his armour. The entry identifies this day with the Day of al-Iyād named in a line of Jarīr.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats أ-ه-ل as two unrelated roots.

FIRST ROOT — الأهل (family / people belonging to one):
1. On Khalīl's authority: a man's أهل is his wife; التأهُّل means "to marry." More broadly, a man's أهل are the people most closely bound to him.
2. أهل البيت = the dwellers of a house. أهل الإسلام = those who profess Islam as their religion.
3. Grammar/plurals: the plural is أهلون; الأهالي is a "plural of the plural" (a collectivity of groups). Shāhid: a verse of al-Nābigha using أهلين.
4. Verb form أهَّل (verbal noun تأهيل) = to make someone fit or qualified for a task.
5. آهِل / مأهول = "inhabited, populated" (of a place), with two poetic citations describing once-peopled dwellings now deserted.
6. Any animal that grows accustomed to a place is آهِل / أهلِيّ = domestic, tame — cited with the ḥadīth forbidding the flesh of "domestic donkeys."
7. An idiom: آهَلَكَ اللهُ في الجنّة (verbal noun إيهال) = "may God give you a spouse in Paradise."

SECOND ROOT — الإهالة (melted fat):
On Khalīl's authority, الإهالة is fat-tail and the like — taken, cut up, and rendered/melted down. Also called الجميل and الجُمالة.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
text:
Al-Zamakhsharī's entry for the root ʾ-J-J, arranged as literal senses followed by figurative extensions.

1. Fire and blazing. ajjaja al-nār = to kindle a fire so that it blazes up (fa-taʾajjajat); the fire "roars" (ajjat). The verbal noun ajīj denotes the roaring blaze of fire.

2. Intense heat. The same word covers scorching heat: "the ajjah of the summer season grew intense." A hajīr ajāj is a burning midday heat, in which the sun has its mujāj — literally "the sun's spittle," the shimmering exudation seen in such heat.

3. Bitter/salt water. māʾ ujāj (ajāj) is water described as burning by reason of its saltiness.

4. Figurative uses, explicitly marked by the author as majāz:
   - Of a person's movement: "he passed by ajj-ing in his gait" — i.e. moving so that he makes a rushing, rustling sound like the roar of a flame; compared to "the ajjah of the male ostrich" (its rushing rush of movement).
   - Of a crowd: "I heard the ajjah of the people" — the rustle of their walking and their agitated commotion.

The organising idea across the entry is a roaring, rushing, burning quality: applied to flame, to searing heat, to water that burns the mouth with salt, and by extension to the rushing sound of rapid movement.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَجَل 52x "a term"; أَجَّلَ 2x "you appointed"; مُّؤَجَّل 1x "determined"; أَجْل 1x "time"
poets_named: Khawwāt ibn Jubayr (lived into Islam); unnamed verse
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʾ-J-L (أجل) as five separate root-meanings, holding that none can be derived from another by analogy — each is an independent origin.

1. الأَجَل (ajal) — a fixed term, the end-point of a span of time: the due-date of a debt and the like. Al-Khalīl inflected it (أَجِلَ … يَأْجَل). The derived noun الآجِل ("the deferred / that which is to come") is the opposite of العاجِل ("the immediate"), and الأَجِيل is what is postponed to a set time (cited: "the end of the deferred one is the pit of destruction"). The reply-word أَجَلْ ("yes, indeed") belongs here too, as if to say a matter "has reached its end / its mark."

2. الإِجْل (ijl) — a herd of wild oxen; plural آجال. The verb تأجَّل (of the drove) means it gathered into a herd.

3. الأَجْل (ajl) — the verbal noun of أَجَلَ عليهم شرًّا, "he brought / perpetrated an evil upon them, stirred it up." Shāhid: a line of Khawwāt ibn Jubayr using آجِل in the sense of "the perpetrator (jānī)" of a matter.

4. الإِجْل (ijl) — a pain in the neck. Cited from Abū al-Jarrāḥ: "I have an ijl, so treat me for it" (فأجِّلوني = cure me).

5. المَأْجَل (maʾjal) — a wide basin in which well- or channel-water is dammed for some days and then let out onto the crops; plural مآجِل. Related usage: أَجِّلْ لنخلتك = "make a basin for your palm-tree."

Two further usages Ibn Fāris appends:

- أَجَلوا مالَهم ("they held/confined their property") he explains as a case of letter-substitution (ibdāl), the original form being with zāy, أزَلوه. He notes its sense may be one with the maʾjal (water-basin), since water is likewise confined there.

- مِن أجْلِ ذلك ("because of that…") he traces to أجَلْتُ الشيء ("I brought it about"), so the phrase means roughly "out of what was brought about, I did [it]."

Finally, أَجَلَى (Ajalā), on the pattern faʿalā, is simply a place-name — and place-names, he notes, are mostly non-analogical labels; he closes with a verse locating Sulaymā "at Ajalā."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَجْر 105x "(is) a reward"; ٱسْتَـْجَرْ 2x "you (can) hire"; تَأْجُرَ 1x "you serve me"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʾ-j-r as two roots that can be linked in meaning.

1. Wage for work. The core sense of the first root is payment for labor: al-ajr and al-ujra ("wage, recompense"). Ibn Fāris cites al-Khalīl that al-ajr is "the recompense of work." Morphology: the verb ajara / yaʾjuru / ajran, with the passive participle maʾjūr ("recompensed"). Al-ajīr is the hired worker; al-ujāra is what one pays as a wage. Another authority extends this sense to a woman's dowry, adducing Q 4:24, {so give them their ujūr} (here "their wages/bridal-gifts").

2. Setting a broken bone. The second root means to mend a fracture: ujirat yaduhu ("his hand was set/healed"), with a variant ajarat yaduhu.

Linking sense. Ibn Fāris proposes that the two roots meet in one idea: a worker's wage is, as it were, something that mends his condition after the toil his labor cost him — i.e., payment "sets" him as a splint sets a bone.

Excursus on al-ijjār ("flat rooftop/terrace"). Ibn Fāris judges this a Levantine dialect word, occasionally used by the Ḥijāzīs, and deliberately excludes it from the root's core analysis because it is not genuine Bedouin speech. He notes a variant injār, which he says weakens its standing further. He cites a hadith — whoever sleeps on an ijjār lacking a parapet loses his protection — and pre-empts the objection that the Prophet's use proves it Arabic: he parallels it with the Prophet's use of sūr ("wedding-feast"), which is Persian, not Arabic. As a poetic attestation he quotes Ibn Durayd's line likening horses' necks to Abyssinians ranged in a row upon a rooftop.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَكَلَ 93x "eat"; أُكُل 7x "(are) its taste"; أَكْل 4x "devouring"; ءَاكِلُون 3x "will surely eat"; أَكَّٰلُون 1x "devourers"; مَّأْكُول 1x "eaten up"
poets_named: unnamed verse; Aws b. Ḥajar (pre-Islamic); al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root أ ك ل (hamza–kāf–lām) as a large family of words all tracing to one core notion: **diminishing / consuming** — eating being the central case.

1. **Eating and eaters.** al-akl = eating; al-aklah (fatḥa) = a single act of eating; al-ukalah (ḍamma) = a morsel, like luqmah. A heavy eater is akūl. ākil = an eater; its plural is akalah, as in the saying "they are but head-eaters" (so few they could share one head). al-akīl = one who eats with you (a table-companion).

2. **Food and feeding.** al-maʾkal = food (what is eaten); al-muʾkil = one who feeds; al-maʾkalah = a food-source or portion. A prophetic report curses "the one who consumes ribā (usury) and the one who feeds it." "I tasted no akāl" = nothing edible.

3. **A grant of provision.** Per Ibn al-Aʿrābī, al-ukl was a stipend of estates (like villages) that kings gave to nobles; plural ākāl — with a verse citing lords "of the pavilions and the estates."

4. **False accusation.** "You made me eat what I did not eat" (Abū ʿUbayd) = you falsely charged it to me.

5. **Animals defined by eating.** al-akūlah = a ewe kept to be eaten, not sold or bred — hence "pasture but no akūlah" = wealth hoarded with no one to spend it. akīl/akīlah al-dhiʾb = a wolf's prey (what is eaten); Abū Zayd: al-akīlah = a lion's prey. akāʾil al-nakhl = palms reserved to eat from. al-ākilah (pattern fāʿilah) = a grazing animal (also al-iklah). al-akilah (pattern faʿilah) = a she-camel harmed by her unborn young's fur growing inside her.

6. **Blazing, glowing, corroding — the "consuming" sense.** iʾtakalat al-nār = the fire blazed up; iʾtakala al-rajul = a man's anger flared. An ember tataʾakkal (glows); a sword's watered pattern shimmers (yataʾakkal) — with a line by Aws b. Ḥajar comparing the blade's shimmer to a silver basin. Strongly wafting perfume also taʾakkal. Fire "eats" firewood; ākaltuhā = I fed the wood to it.

7. **Consuming reputation / discord.** ākaltu bayn al-qawm = I stirred up strife. "Do not let so-and-so eat your honor" = do not quarrel and let him consume it. al-muʾkil = a slanderer; "he has an uklah among people" = he backbites them.

8. **One's worldly share.** al-ukl = a man's lot/portion in life; men of fortune are dhawū ākāl (with a line by al-Aʿshā). By extension: a garment "of uklun" = thickly woven with much yarn; a man "of uklun" = of sound judgment and intellect; likewise a fruitful palm or crop.

9. **Itching and decay.** al-ukāl = itching ("an itch struck his head"). al-akal in leather = a thin spot that looks sound but shows its flaw when worked. Teeth with akal = corroded/decayed.

10. **A knife; a small pot.** al-Farrāʾ: a knife is ākilat al-laḥm ("meat-eater") — as in ʿUmar's warning that a man who strikes his brother with such a blade should not assume he escapes retaliation. Abū Ziyād: al-miʾkalah = a small cooking-pot, easy for the clan to use.

11. **Fruit.** ukul al-shajarah = a tree's fruit — Ibn Fāris closing with the Qurʾānic phrase "it gives its fruit every season by its Lord's leave" (Ibrāhīm 14:25).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَلْف 14x "a thousand"; أَلَّفَ 5x "then he made friendship"; إِلَٰف 2x "for (the) familiarity"; مُؤَلَّفَة 1x "and the ones inclined"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ء-ل-ف as one root meaning the joining of one thing to another — and, relatedly, a large number of things.

1. "A thousand" (alf), plural ālāf. Derived verbs mean "to reach/make a thousand": ālafat al-ibil = the camels became a thousand; ālaftu al-qawm = I made them a thousand; ālafū = they became a thousand. Ibn al-Aʿrābī notes parallel forms akhmasū (became five hundred) and amāʾū (became a hundred). Ibn Fāris judges this a sound derivation, since a thousand is simply an aggregation of hundreds — tying "thousand" back to the root's core idea of things joined together.

2. Familiarity / attachment. aliftu al-shayʾ = I grew familiar with or attached to a thing (participle ālif). The verbal noun ulfa means mutual affinity or concord — the noun of iʾtilāf (harmonious coming-together). Your ilf or alīf is the one you are attached to (companion/mate). Al-Aṣmaʿī records both aliftu (I became familiar) and the causative ālaftu (participle muʾlif). Shāhid: a line of Dhū al-Rumma describing a white gazelle "of those that keep to the sand."

3. Causing attachment. Abū Zayd (Ḥijāzī usage): ālaftu al-makāna wa-l-qawm = I became attached to a place and people; ālaftu ghayrī = I made another become attached.

4. Birds that keep to a place. Al-Khalīl: awālif al-ṭayr are birds that stay put at Mecca and elsewhere; they are called muʾlifāt because they do not leave. Cited with a verse about doves keeping to Mecca.

5. Composition. To join parts together is allafa … taʾlīfan (to put together, compose).

6. On the Qur'anic li-īlāfi Quraysh (106:1): Ibn Fāris gives only Abū Zayd's lexical note — that al-maʾlaf is a sap-yielding tree game draws near to out of familiarity — connecting the verse's word to the root's sense of habitual attachment rather than expounding the sūra.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris's account of the root ʾ-l-h (أله):

1. Core meaning. The three letters hamza–lām–hāʾ trace to a single root sense: worship/devotion (al-taʿabbud).

2. al-ilāh. On this basis al-ilāh denotes God (Allāh), so called — in this author's explanation — because He is the one worshipped (maʿbūd).

3. Derived verb. taʾallaha al-rajul means "the man devoted himself to worship." Ibn Fāris cites Ruʾba as a witness: women glorify God and utter the pious "return" formula in astonishment at the speaker's devotion (taʾalluh).

4. al-ilāha = the sun. A separate noun, al-ilāha, means the sun, said to be so named because a certain people used to worship it. Cited witness: a hemistich, "So we hastened before al-ilāha [the sun] should set."

5. A verb he excludes. The verb aliha / yaʾlahu meaning "to be bewildered/perplexed" is judged NOT to belong to this root: its initial hamza is originally a wāw (i.e. it belongs to w-l-h / walaha), and it is treated under that other chapter.

dictionary: ʿAyn — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786)
text:
Al-Khalil's Kitab al-Ayn records several distinct senses under the root A-L-L:

1. Al-ill equals lordship/divinity (rububiyyah). Illustrated by Abu Bakr's remark on hearing Musaylimah's rhymed oracular speech: "This didn't come out of ill" -- meaning it carried nothing of true divine lordship or inspiration.

2. Al-ill in Qur'an 9:8 ("neither ill nor dhimmah") -- some tafsir, per this entry, glosses it there as meaning Allah, mighty and exalted.

3. Al-ill equals closeness of blood-kinship. A cited verse likens someone's claimed "ill" (kinship) with Quraysh to the "kinship" of a baby camel to an ostrich chick -- meaning no real kinship at all.

4. Ilal is a mountain near Mecca, identified as Mount Arafah, supported by a verse describing camels visiting it.

5. The verb alla (ya'illu/ya'ullu) means to feel the ache of fever or similar pain in the body, short of actual groaning; the noun is al-alilah/al-alil. Two verses illustrate this dull bodily-ache sense, one of them about the "pain" of debt.

6. Alla, said of a man, means to hasten, to hurry.

7. Alla, said of a color, means to become clear and gleam.

8. Al-allah is a weapon or war-implement in general, and specifically a spear or spearhead-shaped blade; plural al-all / al-ilal, with a supporting verse ("standing with spears and with al-ilal"). Al-Khalil explains the name comes from its being fine and slender.

9. Al-ta'lil means tapering or sharpening something to a point, the way a reed pen's nib is trimmed; a two-edged knife-tip is called mu'allal. An ear called mu'allalah (pointed, pricked-up) signals good breeding -- illustrated with a line by the poet Tarafah comparing such ears to a sheep's.

10. Al-alal / al-alalan denotes the two flat faces of a knife, or of anything broad and flat rather than round (a spearhead, a divination/gambling arrow, etc.); it is also used for the two meeting surfaces of any paired things -- two fingers, two front teeth, or two matching leaves growing from one point.

Al-Khalil treats these as related but separate senses of the same root, moving from abstract notions (lordship, kinship) to concrete ones (a mountain, bodily pain, speed, sharpened objects, and paired flat surfaces), each anchored to a verse or saying.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root ʾ-l-m as having a single meaning: pain (al-wajaʿ).

1. Core sense and verb. Citing al-Khalīl, al-alam is "pain." The verb is alima ("to be in pain"), and the one experiencing it is alim.

2. The form alīm and its morphology. The related adjective alīm follows the pattern faʿīl but carries the force of the active/causative pattern mufʿil — i.e. "causing pain," not merely "pained." Ibn Fāris draws a parallel with wajīʿ, which likewise means mūjiʿ ("causing pain"). He supports the faʿīl-for-active point with a poetic line ("...the caller who is made to hear"), where samīʿ ("hearing") stands in for musmiʿ ("one who makes another hear").

3. Both directions attested. Ibn al-Aʿrābī notes that alīm can be active — ʿadhāb alīm ("painful punishment") = muʾlim ("pain-causing") — while rajul alīm and muʾlam describe a man who is afflicted with pain.

4. Reflexive usage. Per Abū ʿUbayd, one may say alimta nafsaka ("you pained yourself"), on the model of safihta nafsaka ("you made yourself foolish").

5. Proverb. An Arab saying: "The free man gives, while the slave's heart aches."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris records a single, unified core meaning for the root ء-ل-ت (Alt): deficiency or diminution (النقصان).

- Verb pattern: alata / ya'litu (أَلَتَ / يَأْلِتُ), meaning "to diminish [something], to deprive [someone] of [something]." He glosses it directly with the synonym naqaṣa (نَقَصَ), "to lessen, reduce, take away from."
- Qur'anic citation: "lā ya'litkum min a'mālikum shay'an" (Q52:21) — glossed as lā yanquṣukum, "He will not diminish/reduce you in anything [of your deeds]."

The entry is brief: it gives no further derived forms, no plural patterns, and no additional shawāhid beyond the single Qur'anic verse.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
quran_words: ءَالَاء 34x "(of the) favors"; يُؤْلُ 1x "swear (off)"; يَأْلُ 1x "they will spare you"; يَأْتَلِ 1x "let swear"
poets_named: unnamed verse ×7; Al-ʿArjī (Umayyad); Ḥassān (lived into Islam); ʿAntara (pre-Islamic); Al-Nābigha (pre-Islamic); al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); Bishr b. Abī Khāzim (pre-Islamic); Ruʾba (Umayyad); Labīd (lived into Islam)
text:
The Lisān's article on a-l-w gathers several distinct word groups: a verb meaning both "to fall short" and "to be able / to exert oneself", the oath (with the Qur'anic verb yaʾtali), the buttock or fatty tail (alya), aloeswood (aluwwa), favours (ālāʾ), a bitter tree (alāʾ), and a mourner's rag (miʾlāt).

**1. Falling short, being slow.** alā, yaʾlū (verbal nouns alw, uluww, uliyy, iliyy), allā and iʾtalā mean to fall short and be slow. Verses show sons who "did not fall short" (mā allā) and a bound captive blamed though "he did not fall short" (mā-ʾtalā). Abū ʿAmr: muʾallin is one who falls short. A hunting dog or falcon that fails at its quarry is said to allā. A rajaz verse, explained by Ibn al-Aʿrābī through Thaʿlab, uses allā of a loaf that was "slow to cook through" and came out ash-smeared and raw. Ibn Sīda notes that Ṭufayl's ghayra muʿtalī stands for ghayra muʾtalī, with ʿayn replacing hamza. A Hudhalī verse calls women who would not mourn with full effort awālī.

Grammar: al-Kisāʾī (via al-Liḥyānī) reports lā yaʾlu without the wāw, like Sībawayh's lā adri. The noun is aliyya, as in the proverb "If not favour, then no slackening", said of a wife out of favour who keeps trying to win people over.

**2. Leaving off, being able, exerting oneself.** mā alawtu dhālika: "I could not do that"; mā alawtu an afʿalahu: "I did not leave off doing it"; alawtu fīhā: "I exerted myself in it". Al-Aṣmaʿī accepts mā alawtu jahdan ("I spared no effort") and calls the common people's mā ālūka jahdan an error. lā ālūka nuṣḥan: "I do not flag in advising you". Al-Jawharī gives the participles ālin, āliya, plural awālin.

Qur'an and ḥadīth: Ibn al-Aʿrābī explains lā yaʾlūnakum khabālan (Q 3:118) as "they do not fall short in corrupting you". A ḥadīth speaks of a ruler's evil intimates who "do not fall short in ruining him". In the ḥadīth of ʿAlī's marriage the Prophet tells Fāṭima, "I have not fallen short with you or with myself." In a saying of al-Ḥasan, mā yaʾla lahum is glossed from yāla / ayāla lahu, "the time has come for him, it is fitting", like nawluka an tafʿal.

**3. A word of opposite meanings.** Abū l-Haytham counts al-alw among the aḍdād: alā, allā and iʾtalā mean to flag and weaken, and alā, allā and taʾallā also mean to exert oneself. His example is "what an effort she made". Abū ʿAmr takes allaytu as "I was slow"; Abū Manṣūr derives it from uluww, "falling short". Ibn Jinnī cites a Hudhalī verse for alawtu as "I was able", and one says huwa yaʾlū hādhā l-amr, "he can manage this matter".

**4. Oath.** ulwa, alwa, ilwa, aliyya and aliyyā all mean an oath, plural alāyā, as in a verse praising a man "sparing of oaths" who keeps them. The verbs are ālā / īlāʾ, taʾallā and iʾtalā, "to swear".

- On wa-lā yaʾtali ulū l-faḍli minkum (Q 24:22), Abū ʿUbayd takes it from alawtu, "let them not fall short". Al-Farrāʾ takes iʾtilāʾ as swearing. He cites a Medinan reading wa-lā yataʾalla, which differs from the written text, and connects the verse to Abū Bakr's oath to stop supporting Misṭaḥ and his kin after they spoke of ʿĀʾisha; Abū Bakr then resumed. On a report from Ibn al-Aʿrābī that al-alw is capability, falling short and effort, the verse is taken as "let him not fall short in giving to kin"; it is also said to mean "let him not swear".
- Ḥadīth on taʾallī ʿalā llāh ("swearing against God"): God belies whoever swears about Him, for example "God will surely put So-and-so in the Fire". Woe to the mutaʾallīn, who declare who is in the Garden and who is in the Fire.
- Anas reports that the Prophet ālā min nisāʾihi shahran, "swore not to go in to his wives for a month". The verb takes min because it carries the sense of abstaining. The entry adds that in fiqh īlāʾ has specific rulings without which the term does not apply. ʿAlī: "there is no īlāʾ in setting things right", because īlāʾ belongs to harm and anger.

**5. lā darayta wa-lā-ʾtalayta.** This phrase occurs in the ḥadīth of Munkar and Nakīr. Ḥadīth transmitters say wa-lā talayta, but the entry calls iʾtalayta correct.

- Ibn Sīda: "you did not know, nor were you able", from alawtu = "I was able".
- Al-Farrāʾ: "nor did you fall short in seeking".
- Other variants: wa-lā alayta (an echo of darayta) and wa-lā atlayta ("may your camels not bear following young").

The ḥadīth "whoever fasts perpetually, lā ṣāma wa-lā allā" is read either as a curse ("nor was he able to fast") or as a statement ("he neither fasted nor fell short"). Al-Khaṭṭābī rejects the variant wa-lā āla ("nor returned").

**6. Ibn al-Aʿrābī's five senses of al-alw.** He lists falling short, withholding, exertion, capability, and gift. For "gift" he cites "Khālid, I give you (lā ālūka) nothing but an Indian blade and a bull-hide shield". A Bedouin told to make his camel kneel replied lā ālūhu, "I cannot". Al-ʿArjī's grooms, who "are able only to say 'halā!'" to an unruly horse, illustrate alāhu = "he was able to do it". The entry also records alā as "to be proud" (and laʾā as "to be slow"). Al-Azharī calls "proud" a strange word he heard only from Ibn al-Aʿrābī. It also says al-aliyy is a man of many oaths.

**7. aluwwa: aloeswood.** aluwwa or uluwwa is incense wood; al-Liḥyānī also gives liyya and luwwa. The plural alāwiya takes hāʾ to mark foreignness. Al-Aṣmaʿī thinks it is Persian arabicised; Abū Manṣūr thinks it is neither Arabic nor Persian but Indian. A ḥadīth says the censers of the people of the Garden burn aluwwa, and Ibn ʿUmar perfumed himself with it. Verses by Ḥassān and an anonymous Bedouin ask why the Prophet was not buried in a casket of aluwwa. Aluwwa is also given as al-ghalwa (a bowshot) and al-sabqa (a race stake). The idiom lā ātīka alwata Abī Hubayra means "never": the name stands for "time", and alwa is accusative like an adverb of time (Thaʿlab).

**8. alya: rump, fatty tail, fleshy pads.** alya is the buttock of people and animals, and the sheep's fat tail; plurals are alayāt and irregular alāyā. liyya and ilya are called mistakes for this sense.

- A ḥadīth says people used to cut the tails off live sheep.
- Another says the Hour will not come until the women of Daws sway round the idol-house Dhū l-Khalaṣa again, having turned back from Islam.
- Adjectives: kabsh alayān / alyān / alan / ālin, plural ulyun. Ibn Sīda discusses why ālin is pluralised as fuʿl.
- For women the scholars disagree. Abū Isḥāq says ʿajzāʾ, not alyāʾ, and al-Jawharī says some do use alyāʾ. Ibn Sīda says Abū ʿUbayd erred here, and Ibn Barrī traces alyāʾ to al-Yazīdī.
- Abū Zayd gives the dual as alyān, like khuṣyān, and Ibn Barrī cites alyatān from ʿAntara. The seller of tail fat is allāʾ.
- Extended uses: the back of a hoof; the pad of the foot under the little toe; the ball at the base of the thumb, paired with the ḍarra, as in the ḥadīth of the Prophet wiping ʿAlī's eye and al-Barāʾ's "prostrate on the two alyas of the palm"; and, per al-Fārisī, the calf of the leg. Al-Layth gives a somewhat different layout of the hand.
- alya also means fat, and famine (from Kurāʿ). al-Tahdhīb gives laʾāt / alāt for the wild cow.

**9. liyya: kin.** Ibn al-Aʿrābī defines liyya as a man's kin and intimates, citing a verse he explains as giving to Yemen and Syria. liyya is also the incense wood.

**10. ilya: one's own accord.** Ibn al-Aʿrābī says ilya means one's own side. A ḥadīth says no one should be made to leave his seat unless he rises min ilyati nafsihi, "of his own accord". Abū Manṣūr takes the word as originally wilya, from waliya.

**11. ālāʾ: favours.** ālāʾ means favours; the singular is alan, ilyun or ilan. Ḥadīth: "Reflect on God's favours, not on God." Al-Nābigha pairs ālāʾ with niʿam. Ibn Sīda reads al-Aʿshā's ilā either as a singular of ālāʾ or as lightened from ill, "covenant". Ibn al-Anbārī derives ilā from wilā and alā from walā.

**12. alāʾ: a bitter tree.** alāʾ is a tree fair to look at and bitter to taste. Bishr b. Abī Khāzim compares praising Bujayr to praising it. Abū Ḥanīfa describes it as an evergreen sand tree that is eaten fresh and used for tanning once hard. Land rich in it is maʾlaʾa, and a waterskin tanned with it is maʾliyy or maʾluww. Ruʾba shortens the word to alā, which Ibn Sīda calls metrical licence.

**13. Names.** Ilyāʾ is a city (the text reads "bayna l-Maqdis"), and Iliyyā is a man's name.

**14. miʾlāt: the mourner's rag.** miʾlāt (plural maʾālī) is the rag a wailing woman holds; the verb is ālat, "she took a miʾlāt". In ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ's oath it means a menstrual rag: he denies being born of fornication or conceived at the end of a period. Labīd compares lightning in the clouds to flashing swords, or to wailing women clapping their hands.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
text:
**Root أ-م-د (A-M-D) — Tāj al-ʿArūs of al-Zabīdī**

**1. أَمَد (amad), vowelled a-ma-d — an end-limit / span of time.** Al-Zabīdī quotes al-Rāghib (al-Mufradāt): the word is used with reference both to a *goal or end-point* and to *time*; it is general enough to take in both the terminus and the starting-point, and is then extended figuratively to mean a stretch of duration in general.

**2. The terminus of a lifetime.** One asks ما أَمَدُك؟ — "what is your amad?" — meaning: where does your lifetime end. The entry cites the Qurʾān here (Q 57:16), though the quoted wording is missing from the text as preserved. Shamir defines amad as the end-point of the أَجَل (appointed term), and adds that a human being has *two* amads: the first is the beginning of his creation, which becomes visible at birth; the second is death. As an instance of the first usage, al-Ḥajjāj asked al-Ḥasan "what is your amad?" and he answered "two years of ʿUmar's caliphate" — i.e. he was born when two years of that caliphate remained. So the word can point to either terminus of a life.

**3. أَمَد = anger.** The verb أَمِدَ عليه (conjugated like فَرِحَ), and likewise أَبِدَ, means "he became angry at him."

**4. آمِد (āmid), pattern of صاحب — filled up.** Filled with good or with evil (reported from al-Ṣāghānī). Abū ʿAmr gives a concrete use: a *laden ship*; the variants آمِدة, عامِد and عامِدة carry the same sense.

**5. آمِد (Āmid), the town.** A frontier town in Diyār Bakr, bordering Byzantine territory. Al-Zabīdī quotes al-Marāṣid: the name is a Byzantine (Greek) word; the town is ancient and strongly fortified, built of black stone on high ground, with the Tigris curving around most of it like a crescent, and watered from nearby springs. Some vocalize the mīm with ḍamma; al-Zabīdī notes that pronunciation is the one current in speech. A line of verse — "at Āmid once, and at Raʾs ʿAyn, and at times at Mayyāfāriqīn" — leaves the name without tanwīn, because the poet treated it as a *tract of land* (feminine place-name) rather than as a masculine town-name. The scholar Abū Muḥammad Maḥmūd b. Mawdūd b. Sālim, titled Sayf al-Dīn, takes his nisba from it. A separate note at the end reports that the city is said to be named after a man, Āmid b. al-Balandā b. Mālik b. Duʿr.

**6. Derived forms** (all reported from al-Ṣāghānī):
- **تَأْميد (taʾmīd)** — specifying an amad, exactly as تأجيل means specifying an أَجَل (a set term).
- **سِقاءٌ مُؤَمَّد** (pattern مُعَظَّم) — a waterskin holding no more than a mouthful of water.
- **أُمْدة (umda)**, with ḍamma — a leftover remnant of anything.
- **أَمَدٌ مَأْمود** — an end-point that is actually reached.

**7. أَمَد in horse-racing.** For horses run for a wager, the amad is the point they contend over and the finishing limit they race to reach first. Al-Nābigha's line "like the outstripping of the courser when it takes command of the amad" is glossed: it prevailed over the finishing point by winning. This is the concrete, physical use behind the temporal senses.

**8. إِمِّدان (immidān) — a disputed form.** With a doubled mīm, on the pattern of إِسْحُمان and إِضْحِيان: a place-name, and also (per Kurāʿ) water lying on the surface of the ground; Ibn Sīda remarks that he is not confident of this. The claim that these three words have no fourth of their pattern is traced to Ibn al-Qaṭṭāʿ's Kitāb al-Abniya, which lists إِفْعِلان nouns: إِسْمِحان (a named mountain), ليلة إِضْحِيان (a moonlit night), and إِمِّدان (a place). Ibn al-Qaṭṭāʿ distinguishes إِمِدّان, with a doubled *dāl*, meaning water that seeps up to the surface — supported by Zayd al-Khayl's line about gazelles that shun "the pools of al-imiddān."

**The morphological objection.** Al-Zabīdī reports his teacher's criticism: if the mīm is doubled and the hamza is therefore augmentative, the word's radicals are م-م-د (both mīms being root letters, first and second radical), so it belongs under the letter mīm — which is in fact where the author of al-Qāmūs also lists it, among augmented forms. But if the hamza were a radical, as its placement in the hamza chapter implies, its pattern would be فِعِلاّن, and it would belong neither to this root nor to the إِفْعِلان class. Either way there is a manifest inconsistency in both al-Qāmūs and Ibn al-Qaṭṭāʿ. And if one follows Ibn al-Qaṭṭāʿ's doubled-dāl reading with an augmentative hamza, the radicals are م-د-د and the word has no business in this entry at all — which is how al-Jawharī treats it, filing it under م-د-د and identifying the pattern as إِفْعِلان, whereas al-Qāmūs cites it without assigning any pattern.

**Overall shape of the entry:** the core is a spatial finishing-line (the racecourse limit) extended to the terminus of a lifetime and then to duration generally; alongside it sit an unrelated sense "anger," a sense "filled/laden," the place-name Āmid, and a long grammatical dispute over إِمِّدان that concerns pattern and root-assignment rather than meaning.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: أمل (a-m-l) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris finds two unrelated senses under this root.

1. Steadying oneself / watchful waiting
al-Khalīl (Ibn Fāris's source) defines الأَمَل (al-amal) as "hope" (al-rajā'), with the verb forms أمّلته / أمَلته ("I hoped for/expected it"). Ibn Fāris adds that this sense carries "something of waiting" in it — hope here is bound up with anticipation, not pure wishing.

From the same root comes التَّأَمُّل (al-ta'ammul), "looking carefully / deliberately" — steadying one's gaze rather than glancing. Two verses illustrate this:
- "Look carefully, my friend — do you see any travelling parties who set out from the high ground above Jurthum?"
- Al-Mirrār's line contrasts someone now told to "look carefully" with how he used to be a qaṭāmī (a falcon) — a bird content with a single glance, i.e. formerly quick and inattentive, not one who lingers over a look.

2. A sand-ridge
Separately, الأَمِيل (al-amīl) names a long ridge of sand standing apart from the main sand-mass (pattern faʿīl; plural umul). Citations show it used in poetry ("I forced my way across the amīl..."; "like lightning crossing a well-known amīl") and in the proverb "there was a resting-place between the two amīls," which al-Aṣmaʿī glosses as meaning there was open room/space in the land. The biggest such ridge is called "amīl al-umul."

Ibn Fāris treats these as two separate, unconnected roots sharing the same three letters — he does not derive one sense from the other.
