text:
Ibn Sīda's account of the root ʾ-m-m (أمم) in al-Muḥkam. The organizing idea he returns to throughout is qaṣd — "aiming at, heading for" — from which he derives most of the senses.

1. Core sense — aiming/heading for. أَمَّهُ ("he headed for it, intended it"), with variant forms أتمّه, تأمّمه, and by sound-substitution يمّه, تيمّمه. From this he derives al-tayammum, the ablution performed with dust, since one "aims at" the earth to wipe with it (Qurʾān: "so head for [tayammamū] clean ground," al-Nisāʾ 43, al-Māʾida 6). A guiding camel is miʾamm/miʾamma because the guide heads purposefully.

2. immah / ummah — way, state, bounty. al-immah covers: a state or condition; a way and religion (shirʿa wa-dīn) — Qurʾān "we found our fathers upon an umma," al-Zukhruf 23, with a variant reading immah; a blessing/ease of living (with a verse of al-Aʿshā and one of Ibn al-Zubayr); outward bearing; and one's affair or standing. It also = established custom (sunna); to "take something as an immah" is to make it one's model.

3. Leading and the imām. أمّ القوم = "he went before / led the people," and that act is imāma. The imām is whoever is followed — a chief or anything else; plural aʾimma (Qurʾān "the leaders of disbelief," al-Tawba 12; "leaders calling to the Fire," al-Qaṣaṣ 41). Ibn Sīda adds a long grammatical excursus: the hamza in aʾimma becomes yāʾ because two successive original hamzas are avoided in Arabic; the Kufan reading with two hamzas is anomalous, as are Abū Zayd's rare examples.

4. imām = manager/rectifier and model. The imām of a thing is its overseer and setter-right: he names the Qurʾān the imām of the Muslims, the Prophet the imām of the community, the caliph the imām of the subjects, and an army's commander its imām. Concrete extensions: a boy's daily lesson; a copied pattern; and the builder's plumb-cord stretched to build straight upon (a verse likens a smooth arrow to it).

5. imām = road/direction/guide. The qibla's direction, the camel-driver (a guide even from behind), and the road itself: Qurʾān "the two are upon a clear imām" = a plain road that is headed for (al-Ḥijr 79). On "make us an imām for the God-fearing" (al-Furqān 74) he reports Abū ʿUbayda's view that a singular can stand for a plural, and alternative views that imām here is itself a plural.

6. ummah = community/kind. A prophet's umma = all sent to him, believer and unbeliever alike. More broadly it is the generation or species of any living thing (Qurʾān "communities like yourselves," al-Anʿām 38; a ḥadīth uses umma of dogs). A person wholly upon the true religion, alone against all others, is himself "an umma" — as Ibrāhīm was, and as Zayd b. ʿAmr b. Nufayl is said to be, having believed before the Prophet's mission.

7. ummah — further senses. A man who gathers goodness; a span of time (Qurʾān "to a reckoned umma" = a fixed term, Hūd 8; "he remembered after an umma" = after a while, Yūsuf 45); stature and face ("of good umma" = well-built); obedience; a scholar; one's people (ummat al-rajul); and God's creation (ummat Allāh).

8. amam — moderation and nearness. The middle, moderate course; nearness ("their house is amam" = near); a trifling amount; and, of an affair, "clear, within due measure" (muʾāmm = close/fitting), illustrated by a verse of al-Ṭirimmāḥ about a doe stretching her neck in slight alarm.

9. umm = mother. al-umm / al-ummah = the mother; plurals ummāt and ummahāt (the hāʾ augmentative), with a reported distinction of ummahāt for rational, ummāt for non-rational beings. أمّت أمومةً = "she became a mother"; one may "take a woman as a mother." A morphological note: umm is fāʾ-ʿayn-lām = hamza + mīm + mīm (pattern fuʿl like durr, jull), against the author of al-ʿAyn who treated the hāʾ as original.

10. umm = origin/source. Used of the mother-stem of a palm, tree, or banana, and generally of the origin and support of anything (Ibn Durayd: whatever things attach to is their umm). Hence the fixed expressions: umm al-qawm (their chief); umm al-kitāb (the Fātiḥa — because a prayer opens with it — or, per al-Zajjāj, the foundation of the Book, said also to be the Preserved Tablet); umm al-nujūm (the Milky Way, where stars cluster); umm mathwā al-rajul (a man's landlady); umm al-rumḥ (the banner on a spear); umm al-qurā = Mecca (as the earth's middle, or the qibla all head toward; Qurʾān al-Qaṣaṣ 59); and umm al-raʾs = the brain, or the membrane over it.

11. Head-wound family. أمّه = "he struck his skull-membrane"; the man is maʾmūm/amīm, and a wound reaching that membrane is āmma/maʾmūma — extended figuratively to grief ("my belly is amīm from the heat of parting"). al-amīma = stones for crushing heads; a maʾmūm camel is one with a ruined back.

12. al-ummī. One who does not write; per al-Zajjāj, one left on the nation's natural constitution, untaught in writing (Qurʾān "unlettered ones who do not know the Book," al-Baqara 78). Also a tongue-tied, coarse man of few words.

13. amām and names. al-amām = "in front" (opposite of "behind"), noun and adverb; grammarians note its gender and its use in warning ("amāmak!"). al-Aʾimma is given as a name of Kināna. Umayma/Umāma is a woman's name (with a verse of Abū Dhuʾayb), Umayma being the diminutive of umm; Umāma is also used for three hundred camels.

14. Particles. أمّا = a particle of inception, marking statement/detailing; إمّا of condition is a compound of in + mā; إmmā of doubt is the counterpart of aw ("or").

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʾ-m-n as two closely related root meanings (aṣlān mutaqāribān): amāna, trustworthiness, the opposite of khiyāna (betrayal), whose meaning he gives as "stillness of the heart"; and taṣdīq, affirming something as true. He repeats that the two meanings are near each other.

**First meaning: trust, safety and trustworthiness**

1. Al-Khalīl is quoted: amana (security) comes from amn (safety); amān is the granting of security; amāna is the opposite of betrayal.

2. Verb forms: amintu al-rajula, "I felt safe with the man, trusted him", with the verbal nouns amn, amana and amān; and āmananī, yuʾminunī, īmānan, "he gave me safety", with īmān as its verbal noun.

3. The Arabs call a man ummān when he is amīn, trustworthy. Al-Aʿshā speaks of "the trustworthy (ummān) merchant, his drink much frequented". One also says "he was not trustworthy, and now he has become so", using the verb amuna.

4. Abū Zayd: amīn means muʾtaman, "one who is trusted". Al-Nābigha: "You were his trusted one, had you not betrayed him; but there is no good faith (amāna) in the Yemeni."

5. In Ḥassān's line about a trusty one (amīn) who was given the speaker's secret and kept it "as the amīn keeps [it for] the amīn", the entry explains the first amīn as passive in sense (muʾtaman, the one entrusted) and the second as active (muʾtamin, the one who entrusts). In a verse recited by al-Liḥyānī, "I have sworn an oath that I will not betray my amīn", "my amīn" is glossed as āminī, the one who trusts me.

6. A bayt āmin, "safe house", is one that has safety. Q 14:35: "My Lord, make this land secure (āminan)."

7. Al-Liḥyānī and others distinguish two forms: umana, a man people trust and whose treachery they do not fear; and amana (with fatḥa, the vowel a, on the first letter), a man who believes whatever he hears, calls nothing a lie and trusts people.

8. The expression "I gave him from the āman of my wealth" is explained as "from what is dearest of it to me". Ibn Fāris comments that even so, it keeps the meaning of the whole section, since what is dearest to a man is what his soul rests in. A verse is cited: "We shield our honour with the most prized (āman) of our wealth, and in the fray we leave the spears trailing [in the foe] and call out [our lineage]."

9. The proverb "It is from where he feels safe (maʾman) that the wary man is overtaken", and the saying "The Balawī is your brother, yet do not trust him", meant as a warning.

**Second meaning: affirming as true (taṣdīq)**

1. Q 12:17, "you are not one to believe us" (bi-muʾminin lanā), is glossed as "not one who credits what we say" (muṣaddiq lanā).

2. On al-Muʾmin as an attribute of God, two views are reported. Some scholars say it means that He is true to the reward He has promised His servant. Others say He is muʾmin to His friends (awliyāʾ) in that He gives them safety from His punishment and does not wrong them. Ibn Fāris notes that this second view has gone back to the first meaning, and cites al-Nābigha's line as an instance of it: "the one who gives safety (al-muʾmin) to the birds that seek refuge, which the riders of Mecca stroke between al-Ghīl and al-Saʿad."

3. Āmīn. With the hedge "God knows best", Ibn Fāris places āmīn, the word said in supplication, under the second meaning. It is explained as "O God, do [it]", and is also said to be one of the names of God. A verse shows the short form amīn: "Fuṭḥul and his mother's son have drawn away from me; amīn, and may God add to the distance between us." Sometimes it is lengthened to āmīn, as in: "O Lord, never strip me of the love of her; and may God have mercy on a servant who says āmīn."

text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ʾ-m-r (أمر) from five distinct base meanings: (1) "matter/affair," (2) command (the opposite of prohibition), (3) al-amar, with a fatḥa on the mīm, meaning growth and blessing, (4) landmark/sign, and (5) the astonishing.

1. Matter, affair (umūr). One says "this is a matter I approve of" and "a matter I do not approve of." Proverbs: "it is some matter that brought you here," and "it is for a reason that the one who becomes chief is made chief."

2. Command (opposite of prohibition). The basic form is "do such-and-such." Al-Aṣmaʿī: "I have over you one command to be obeyed" (a single order that must be obeyed). Al-Kisāʾī: "he consults his two selves" — one self urges one course, another self a different one; and "he is much given to commanding good and forbidding wrong," said of a people (plural umur). From this sense come imra / imāra (authority, governorship), whose holder is an amīr or muʾammar. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: ammartuhu = "I made him a commander"; the forms amartuhu and āmartuhu carry the same meaning; and amura ʿalā qawmihi = "he became commander over his people." Also from this root is the immar: per al-Aṣmaʿī, a weak-minded fool who keeps asking others' opinions and cannot decide whose advice to follow — illustrated by a verse ("I am no feeble witless follower who, led against his will, meekly complies") and a saying that one should not send out with one's camels "a male or female immara," i.e. a man with no sense.

3. Growth and blessing (al-amar). Al-Khalīl: al-amar = increase and blessing; a woman described amira is one who brings blessing/fertility to her husband; amira l-shayʾ = "the thing became abundant." Sayings: "whoever is few is abased, whoever is many prevails"; and "So-and-so's clan grew numerous (amirū) and their livestock multiplied." A verse of Labīd links being numerous with eventual ruin. Al-Aṣmaʿī cites the proverb "the best property is a well-pollinated palm-row or a mare of much offspring (maʾmūra)" — meaning one blessed with many young. One says amara/āmara Llāhu mālahu = "God multiplied his property"; hence muhra maʾmūra ("a much-breeding mare"). Ibn Fāris reads Qurʾān 17:16 {amarnā mutrafīhā} under this sense ("We made its affluent ones increase/multiply"); on the variant reading ammarnā the meaning is instead "We set [them] in authority."

4. Landmark, sign, appointed time (amāra / amār). Al-Khalīl: amāra = an appointed time (with a verse of al-ʿAjjāj). Al-Aṣmaʿī: amāra = a sign/token — "set between me and you a token"; illustrated by a verse making sunrise the agreed sign for exchanging greetings. Amār also = the waymarks of a road (singular amāra), with a verse of Ḥumayd b. Thawr. The forms amar and yaʾmūr likewise mean a marker; a single word (amār) can cover a set sign, time, appointment, or term.

5. The astonishing (al-ʿajab). Illustrated by Qurʾān 18:71 {laqad jiʾta shayʾan imran} — "you have done an astonishing/dreadful thing."

text:
Root: أ م ت (Amt), from Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha.

Ibn Fāris states that hamza-mīm-tā' forms a single, non-generalizable root — meaning the root has only this one sense, with no broader pattern to extrapolate from. That one sense is al-amt.

He cites its Qur'anic occurrence: "You will see therein no crookedness ('iwaj) and no amt" (Ṭāhā 20:107).

Two glosses are given for al-amt:
1. Al-Khalīl [ibn Aḥmad al-Farāhīdī]: al-'iwaj ("crookedness") and al-amt are synonymous — the same meaning.
2. Others (which Ibn Fāris treats as essentially the same meaning): al-amt describes a place that is thick/rough in one spot and thin/smooth in another — i.e., unevenness of surface, a rising-and-falling irregularity in terrain.

text:
The article under أما (root ʾ-m-w) deals first with al-amah, "the bondwoman", with her plurals and verbs and the names Umayya and Amah, then with the particles amā, ammā and immā, and ends with a verb for a cat's cry.

**1. al-amah, the bondwoman.** Al-amah (الأَمَة) is the woman who is owned, the opposite of the free woman (al-ḥurra). Al-Tahdhīb describes her as a woman in servitude who has acknowledged her status as a bondwoman (al-umuwwa). A curse reported by Ibn al-Aʿrābī runs "May God pelt him with a stone from every amah"; Ibn Sīda thinks the true wording is "from every amt".

**2. Plurals.** The plurals given are amawāt, imāʾ, āmin, imwān and umwān; imwān and umwān drop the added letter, on the pattern Sībawayh compares to akh, ikhwān ("brother, brothers"). Al-Tahdhīb, quoting Ibn Kaysān, gives amatu llāhi ("God's bondwoman"), the dual amatā llāhi, the plurals imāʾu llāhi, umwānu llāhi and amawātu llāhi, and allows the shortened amātu llāhi. The same passage shows āmin in its three case forms ("they are / I saw / I passed by bondwomen of Zayd") and says that when the women are many, the words are imāʾ, imwān and umwān. Al-Layth's example is thalāthu āmin, "three bondwomen".

**3. Poetic evidence.** Several verses attest these plurals. An unnamed poet and al-Qattāl al-Kilābī both speak of the moment "when the sons of bondwomen (banū l-imwān) hurl disgrace at one another", al-Qattāl adding "as for bondwomen, they do not call me their child"; al-Liḥyānī transmits the phrase as banū l-umwān. Āmin appears in a ruined camp where "nothing remains but bondwomen left behind"; in al-Sulayk's valley holding "only male slaves and bondwomen among small herds of camels"; in ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib's line "you were slaves ... sons of bondwomen"; in a line where the birds are left "hopping upon him, as bondwomen trot to the shelters"; and in al-Kumayt's ostriches that walk "the way load-bearing bondwomen walk together" (cited by al-Azharī).

**4. How amah and its plural āmin are formed.** The article gathers a long grammatical discussion.
(a) Abū l-Haytham: āmin is a plural like nakhl from nakhla ("palms" from "a palm"). Amah was originally amwa, and its weak final wāw fell away. A plural on the nakhl pattern would have been the two-letter am; to avoid that without leaving a wāw at the end of the word, where pausing on it is heavy, the wāw was moved forward and became the long ā between the hamza and the mīm.
(b) Al-Layth: in thalāthu āmin, āmin has the measure afʿul. Abū Manṣūr notes that al-Layth says no more, and prefers the account al-Mundhirī passed on to him, since he knows of no transposition that shifts two letters. His own analysis: āmin is afʿul, its first ā being the prefix of afʿul and its second the first radical; the final wāw of āmuwin dropped and the mīm took the vowel i, as ajruwin became ajrin, the plural of jirw ("whelp"). He also calls Abū l-Haytham's view a good one.
(c) Al-Mubarrad: amah is faʿala, with a vowel on the middle radical. Every two-letter noun has lost a letter, recoverable from its plural, its dual or a related verb, since a word has at least three radicals; the lost letter here is wāw, as umwān shows. The plural āmin has the measure afʿul, like akama, ākum ("hillock, hillocks"), which a faʿla noun with a vowelless middle radical does not take; imwān parallels ikhwān.
(d) Sībawayh, as Ibn Sīda reports, also took amah to be faʿala because of the plural āmin.
(e) Ibn Jinnī explains why a faʿala noun can take the plural afʿul. The vowel on the middle radical and the feminine ending replace each other: words for ailments have the vowel without the ending (ramathan) and lose it with the ending (ḥaqlatan), and jafna ("large bowl") takes the vowel in its plural jafanāt once the ending is dropped. When both occur together, as in faʿala, they cancel each other out, so the word behaves as if it were faʿl, and faʿl regularly takes the plural afʿul.
(f) Al-Jawharī: the original form is amawa, since the plural āmin (afʿul, like aynuq, "she-camels") is not formed from faʿla nouns with a vowelless middle radical.

**5. Verbs.** Istaʾmā amatan and taʾammā amatan mean to take a woman as one's bondwoman ("take a bondwoman other than your own"); Ruʾba speaks of people "content with enslavement and the taking of bondwomen". Ammāhā means he made her a bondwoman (Ibn Sīda). Amat, amiyat and amuwat (the last from al-Liḥyānī), with the verbal noun umuwwa, mean she became a bondwoman: "she was not a bondwoman, and now she has become one".

**6. yaʾtamī.** Ibn Barrī records huwa yaʾtamī bi-Zaydin as the same as yaʾtammu bihi, "he follows Zayd's lead", citing a verse about a man who, "as for God, is wary of Him, and as for the deeds of the righteous, takes them as his lead".

**7. Names and relative adjectives.** The relative adjective from amah is amawī, and its diminutive is umayya. Banū Umayya are a clan of Quraysh. Their relative adjective is umawī (regular, according to Ibn Sīda), sometimes amawī (irregular); Sībawayh reports umayyiyy, built on the unreduced form, which is not the commoner form and is said only by some, and al-Jawharī notes that it "combines four yāʾs". Al-Jawharī says Umayya was originally a man's name: there were two, the elder and the younger, sons of ʿAbd Shams ibn ʿAbd Manāf by different mothers. From the elder come Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb, al-ʿAnābis and al-Aʿyāṣ; the younger are three brothers whose mother was named ʿAbla, known as al-ʿAbalāt. Banū Amah are a clan of Banū Naṣr ibn Muʿāwiya.

**8. The short particle amā.**
(a) An opening word like alā, meaning "truly"; this is why Sībawayh allows both amā innahu and amā annahu after it. Someone reports hamā wa-llāhi, with h in place of the hamza.
(b) As a question, amā is the interrogative a- joined to the negative mā. Al-Layth calls it an "interrogative of denial": amā tastaḥī mina llāh? ("are you not ashamed before God?").
(c) It emphasizes statements and oaths (al-Layth): amā innahu la-rajulun karīm ("indeed, he is a noble man"); amā wa-llāhi ... ("by God, ...").
(d) It affirms what follows as true in reality, not figuratively: amā inna Zaydan ʿāqil, "truly, Zayd is intelligent".

**9. mā as a connective with conditional force.** Al-Farrāʾ reads mimmā khaṭīʾātihim (Q 71:25, "because of their sins [they were drowned]") with mā as a connective where a conditional sense is intended. He saw the mā in a later position in the codex of ʿAbd Allāh, which he takes as evidence for this, as in that codex's ayya l-ajalayni mā qaḍaytu ("whichever of the two terms I complete", Q 28:28), and he compares ḥaythumā takun akun ("wherever you are, I will be") and mahmā taqul aqul ("whatever you say, I will say").

**10. ammā ("as for") and immā ("either ... or", "if").**
(a) Al-Kisāʾī, as al-Farrāʾ reports: ammā, with a, is used when commanding, forbidding or informing: "as for God, serve Him", "as for wine, do not drink it", "as for Zayd, he has gone out". Immā, with i, is used for a condition ("if you insult him, he will bear it patiently"), for doubt ("I do not know who stood up, either Zayd or ʿAmr"), for offering a choice ("learn either fiqh or grammar") and for making one ("either I will live in it or I will sell it").
(b) Ammā opens speech, and its answer must take fa- (ammā ʿAbdu llāhi fa-qāʾim, "as for ʿAbd Allāh, he is standing"), because it implies a condition: "whatever may be the case, ʿAbd Allāh is standing".
(c) Al-Mubarrad: a before nouns, i before verbs, as in "whether you stay (immā aqamta) or are on a journey (wa-ammā anta dhā safarin), God guards what you do and what you leave". Ibn Kaysān explains "O Abū Khurāsha, ammā anta dhā nafarin" as "when you are a man with a band of kin".
(d) The Basrans: ammā is an joined to mā, the mā standing in for the verb, and it means "since" (idh): "since you are standing, I stand with you". Before a verb it becomes immā ("if you set off, I set off with you"). A following future verb takes the added nūn (immā tadhhabanna, "if you go"), or, without it, the jussive ("if the wolf eats you, I will not weep for you").
(e) Al-Zajjāj: the immā of choice is likened to an joined to mā, as in "either you punish, or you take toward them a way of goodness" (Q 18:86). It is written with alif; alā is also written with alif, since with a final y it would look like ilā ("to").
(f) Al-Farrāʾ: some Arabs use immā for the conditional ammā, and al-Kisāʾī recited to him a verse with one mīm changed to y: "Would that our mother had departed, īmā to a garden, īmā to a fire." Al-Jawharī says that īmā and aymā both stand for ammā; he cites the half-line with aymā, from a verse he attributes to al-Aḥwaṣ, and says it may also take i. Ibn Barrī corrects him: īmā is right because it comes from immā, whereas aymā would come from ammā ("as for"), and the coordinating immā only ever has i.
(g) Al-Farrāʾ on Q 76:3, "We guided him to the way, immā grateful wa-immā ungrateful": immā is conditional, "whether gratitude or ingratitude"; or it matches the immā of Q 9:106, "either He punishes them or He turns to them", as though He had said "We created him wretched or happy".
(h) Al-Jawharī: the coordinating immā equals aw ("or"), except that with aw the speaker starts in certainty and doubt comes afterwards, while with immā he starts in doubt, and immā must be repeated ("either Zayd or ʿAmr came to me"). The conditional immā is a different word: in ("if") with a redundant mā, needing no repetition, as in Ḥassān ibn Thābit's "if you see my head, its colour changed with grey", in immā taʾtinī ukrimka ("if you come to me, I will honour you"), and in Q 19:26, "and if you should see any human being".

**11. A cat's cry.** Al-Jawharī: amati l-sinnawru taʾmū umāʾan, "the cat cried out", like māʾat tamūʾu muwāʾan.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats hamza–nūn–fāʾ (ʾ-n-f) as **two** basic senses, from which everything in the chapter branches; he adds that the root's regular associated idea is **coming to a point / being sharpened** (taḥdīd).

**Root sense 1 — taking a thing from its beginning.**
1. Citing al-Khalīl: اسْتَأْنَفَ = to start something over, to go back to its beginning; ائْتَنَفَ (verbal noun iʾtināf) is the same. مُؤْتَنَفُ الأمر = the point at which an affair is begun.
2. From this comes آنِفًا "just now, a moment ago" — as though referring to the beginning of the speech. Ibn Fāris cites Q 47:16, "What did he say just now (āinifan)?"

**Root sense 2 — the nose (al-anf).**
3. The organ itself: paucal plural آنُف, plural أُنُوف.
4. بعير مأنوف: a camel driven by its nose, because the nose-peg (khishāsh) makes it tractable once it wounds it. Also بعير أَنِف / آنِف (both the shortened and lengthened forms). He cites the ḥadīth that the muslimūn are "easy and gentle, like the nose-led camel: if led, it follows; if made to kneel, it kneels."
5. Derived personal descriptions: أُنافِيّ = big-nosed; أَنَفْتُ الرجل = I struck his nose; امرأة أَنوف = a woman whose nose smells sweet.

**Sense 2a — disdain, derived from the nose.**
6. أَنِفَ مِنْ كذا ("he disdained/scorned it") Ibn Fāris derives from the nose, comparing the idiom for an arrogant man, "his nose swelled." The nose is singled out because one says شَمَخَ بأنفه, "he raised his nose," i.e. lifted his head in pride — a gesture connected to anger. Verse cited: "he is not provoked when his nose has swelled," i.e. one does not address a man in his anger.
7. Proverb: "his pain is where the charm-reciter does not put his nose" — said of an incurable ill.

**Sense 2b — the nose as honour.**
8. Two competing accounts of the clan-name Banū Anf al-Nāqa ("Sons of the She-camel's Nose"), Banū Jaʿfar b. Qurayʿ: per Abū ʿUbayda, Jaʿfar arrived late to a slaughtered spoil-camel and only the nose was left, so he carried it off and the name stuck; per al-Kalbī, his father sent meat to his other three wives but not to Jaʿfar's mother, and when Jaʿfar came only the nose remained. The name was an insult until al-Ḥuṭayʾa's line — "a people who are the nose, while others are the tails; who equates the tail with the she-camel's nose?" — turned it into praise.
9. Hence فلان أنفي = "he is my glory and my boast," with a supporting verse.

**Sense 1 extended — the "nose" as the foremost or first part of anything.**
10. Al-Khalīl: أنف اللحية = the tip of the beard (verse cited); أنف كل شيء = the first/front part of anything.
11. أنف الجبل = the mountain's projecting front, what first appears of it (verse on Harshā: take its front or its back, both sides are a road).
12. Yaʿqūb: أنف البرد = the sharpest of the cold; يعدو أنف الشدّ = running at its hardest; أنف الأرض = the hard open ground that faces you.
13. رجل مئناف = a man who travels in the first part of the day.
14. خمرة أُنُف = wine of the first drawing, untouched (verse: "first-drawn, aged, like a gazelle's blood…"); جارية أُنُف = a girl in the first flush of youth.

**The taḥdīd (sharpening) strand.**
15. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: أنَّفْتُ السراج = I sharpened and evened its tip. Hence, in praise of a horse, أُنِّفَ تأنيف السير — "shaped as a leather thong is shaped," i.e. cut and made even.
16. Al-Aṣmaʿī: سنان مؤنَّف = a spearhead sharpened to a point (verse comparing an arrow to "the sharpened sword of the Ḥimyarite").
17. التأنيف in a horse's hock is its sharp, tapered definition, considered a desirable trait.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
Ibn Manẓūr's article on ʾ-n-m is short: it defines al-anām and records a discussion of how the word is used in Q 55:10.

1. **Al-anām.** Al-anām is whatever of all creation is on the face of the earth. In poetry the form al-anīm is also allowed.

2. **Al-anām in Q 55:10.** On wa-l-arḍa waḍaʿahā li-l-anām, "and the earth He has laid down for al-anām" (Q 55:10), the exegetes said that al-anām here are the jinn and humankind. The proof given for their view is that right after mentioning al-anām, God continues up to "... and the fragrant plants. So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?" (Q 55:12–13), with its "you two", although the jinn had not been mentioned before that point; He names al-jānn only afterwards: "He created the human being from ringing clay like pottery, and He created al-jānn from a flame of fire" (Q 55:14–15). The jinn and humankind together are al-thaqalān, "the two thaqal".

3. **Addressing two parties before naming them.** Another explanation is also reported: the two thaqal may be addressed before both have been named, because they are named right after the address. A verse of al-Muthaqqib al-ʿAbdī is cited as a parallel: "I do not know, when I make for a land seeking good, which of the two will come to me: the good that I am seeking, or the evil that is seeking me?" The poet says "which of the two" although evil is not mentioned until after that line is complete.

text:
Root أ‑ن‑س (Ans), as treated by al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī in his glossary of Qurʾanic vocabulary.

1. Core terms. الإنس (al-ins) means humankind, as opposed to the jinn. الأنس / al-uns names the quality of sociability or being at ease — the opposite of shying away and aversion (nufūr).

2. الإنسيّ (al-insī). The adjective from al-ins. It describes a person of abundant sociability, and more broadly anything one keeps company with or is put at ease by. From this comes a spatial usage: the insī side of a riding-beast is the side next to the rider, and the insī side of a bow is the side facing the archer. Generally, the insī of a thing is the part toward the human, while its waḥshī side is the part turned away.

3. Plural. The plural of ins is أَناسيّ (anāsiyy), cited from Q 25:49, "and many human beings."

4. Idiom. ابن إنسك (ibn insik, "son of your familiar") is used to mean the self or soul.

5. The verb ānasa. Al-Rāghib reads the Qurʾanic uses through the sense of perceiving/discerning by way of familiarity: Q 4:6 "if you ānastum right judgment in them" = if you perceive it; Q 20:10 "I ānastu a fire" = I perceived a fire; and Q 24:27 istaʾnasa = to find a sense of welcome or familiarity (before entering).

6. الإنسان (al-insān, "human being") — three suggested derivations:
   (a) From ins (mutual sociability): the human is made so as to subsist only through people's dependence on one another — hence the saying "the human is social by nature," since no one can meet all his needs alone.
   (b) From uns (taking comfort): because he grows familiar and at ease with whatever he becomes accustomed to.
   (c) On the pattern ifʿilān, originally insiyān, linking the word to nasiya ("to forget") — named thus because God laid a covenant on him and he forgot.

text:
Ibn Sīda's account of the root أ‑ن‑ث (ʾ-n-th):

1. Core sense — female. al-unthā ("female") is the opposite of the male. Plural ināth; unuth is a further plural of ināth (pattern ḥimār → ḥumur). He notes the Qur'anic reading of Q4:117 as unuthan ("they call on nothing but unuth"); those who read it ināthan are said to mean "nothing but lifeless things," since all inanimate things take feminine grammar.

2. Grammatical feminine. al-taʾnīth (making a word feminine) is the opposite of al-tadhkīr (masculine); the abstract noun is al-anātha.

3. al-unthayān (the dual). Several senses:
 - the two testicles;
 - the two ears — a Yemeni usage; illustrated by al-Farazdaq's line about striking a man "beneath the unthayān" (= the ears), because the ear is grammatically feminine;
 - by extension, feminine objects: al-ʿAjjāj uses "unthā carrying stones" for the mangonel (feminine), and uses the dual (diminutive) of a mare's thighs' fleshy masses;
 - two Arab clans, Bajīla and Quḍāʿa (from Abū al-ʿAmaythal), with a supporting line from al-Kumayt.

4. Bearing females. ānathat al-marʾa = the woman gave birth to females; she is muʾnith, and miʾnāth if this is habitual.

5. "Soft" land — and an etymological claim. ard miʾnāth / anītha = soft, fertile, plant-bearing land; balad anīth = soft/easy land (Ibn al-Aʿrābī), in the idiom "a land anīth, damīth" (smooth, productive, soft-timbered). Ibn al-Aʿrābī held that a woman is called unthā precisely from this "soft land" sense — because she is softer than a man — so that, on his view, the underlying meaning of the whole root is anīth = "soft."

6. "Soft" (non-hardened) metal and blades. ḥadīd anīth = iron that is "not male"; an anīth sword is one of such non-male iron, said to be near a blunt blade (kahām). Shāhid from Ṣakhr al-Ghayy contrasting a keen blade with an anīth one. al-muʾannath carries the same "soft" sense; Thaʿlab cites a line contrasting a muʾannath sword with one that cuts through bone. sayf miʾnāth / miʾnātha (from al-Liḥyānī): the feminine form is used because one intends "the blade" (shafra), "the iron piece" (ḥadīda), or "the weapon" (silāḥ), all feminine nouns.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root أنى (hamza + nūn + weak letter) to four basic senses: (1) slowness and its kin (forbearance, deliberation); (2) an hour of time; (3) a thing's reaching or ripening; (4) a vessel.

1. Slowness / deliberation. Per al-Khalīl, al-anāh is forbearance (ḥilm); its verbs are taʾannā / taʾayyā ("to take one's time"), and al-taʾannī is deliberating carefully in affairs. Shawāhid: al-Kumayt ("take your time, for you are not lowly"); the Prophet's words to a man who climbed over people on Friday — «you caused harm (ādhayta) and delayed (ānayta)» — glossed as "you came late and were slow"; and al-Ḥuṭayʾa on a long-drawn-out (al-anāʾ) evening meal. Related forms: a deliberate man is aniyy, "possessed of anāh"; even a camel's slow impregnation is called aniyy, and a man whose benefit is slow in coming has "aniyy good." Al-anā likewise means unhurried composure (al-tuʾada). To say a man is dhū anāh is to say he does not rush, being deliberate (ānin) and grave (waqūr); staʾnaytu fulānan = "I did not hurry him" (cf. al-Nābigha: "deliberation is felicity — proceed deliberately and you will succeed"). A forbearing, blessed woman is an anāh (plural anawāt); Abū ʿUbayd: an anāh is a woman with a languor when she rises.

2. An hour of time. Al-inā / al-anā is an hour, especially of the night; plural ānāʾ, each inā being an hour. Ibn al-Aʿrābī gives the plural uniyy, with a verse praising a companion "laughing at any hour (al-aniyy)" — i.e. found cheerful whenever one comes to him.

3. Reaching / ripening. Al-inā is a thing's becoming ready: inā al-laḥm = "the meat's being cooked." mā anā laka / lam yaʾni laka = "the time has not come for you" (verb āna yaʾīnu), cited from {a-lam yaʾni li-lladhīna āmanū} [al-Ḥadīd 16]. staʾnaytu al-ṭaʿām = "I waited for the food to be ready." Applied to heat: {ḥamīm ānin} [al-Raḥmān 44] is water whose heat has peaked (verb anā al-māʾ yaʾnī, of heated water), likewise {ʿaynin āniyah} [al-Ghāshiya 5], with a supporting verse from ʿAbbās on scalding fluid. Ibn al-Aʿrābī notes the parallel forms āna yaʾīnu aynan and anā yaʾnī anyan ("the time came"), and the idiom āyinatan baʿda āyinah = "at times after times" (like tāratan baʿda tārah). Cited also: {ghayra nāẓirīna ināhu} [al-Aḥzāb 53], "its being ready."

4. A vessel. Al-ināʾ (with long final alif) is a container, from al-āniyah (vessels); al-awānī is a plural-of-a-plural — the pattern fiʿāl pluralized as afʿilah.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مَـَارِب 1x "(are) uses"; إِرْبَة 1x "having no physical desire"
poets_named: Qays (pre-Islamic); Labīd (lived into Islam); Ibn Muqbil (lived into Islam) ×3; al-Kumayt (Umayyad); al-Mutalammis (pre-Islamic); Aws (pre-Islamic); Ibn Aḥmar (lived into Islam); al-Farazdaq and Jarīr (Umayyad)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) analyzes the root ء-ر-ب (hamza-rāʾ-bāʾ) as having four core senses, from which all its derived words branch out:

1. Need (al-ḥāja)
Al-arab means "need" (al-Khalīl): "mā arabuka ilā hādhā" — "what do you need this for?" The nouns maʾraba, maʾruba, and irba likewise all mean "need." The entry cites Qur'an 24:31, {ghayri ulī l-irbati min al-rijāl} ("...those among men who have no irba..."), as an instance of this sense — the verse is placed under "need" without further gloss — alongside the proverb "arabun lā ḥafāwatun" ("need, not warm regard"): said of someone whose visit is prompted by need rather than affection.

2. Intellect ('aql)
Al-irb also means "intellect." Ibn al-Aʿrābī notes that the same words, irb/irba, serve both for "need" and for "intellect." The adjective is arīb, "intelligent/shrewd"; the verb is aruba, "to be intelligent." From this branch come:
- Skill/mastery: aribtu bi-sh-shayʾ, "I became skilled at it" (illustrated with a verse of Qays on growing skilled at repelling war).
- Triumph: ārabtu ʿalayhim, "I prevailed over them" (with a verse of Labīd on a soul pledged to a winning throw).
- al-muʾāraba, "outwitting, cunning" (al-Khalīl), cited in a ḥadīth: "muʾārabatu l-arībi jahlun" — "to try to outwit the shrewd man is folly."

3. A share or portion (naṣīb)
Grouped together with "limb" ('uḍw), since both denote "a part of something." Al-urba is the winner's share of the slaughtered camel in the game of maysir (illustrated with a verse of Ibn Muqbil about people who do not gloat when they win, nor withhold the loser's due share). A ḥadīth uses irb for "limb": "kāna amlakakum li-irbihi" — "most in command of his own body/limbs." ʿUḍwun muʾarrabun is a limb full and complete in flesh (with a verse of al-Kumayt). Ariba can mean "his limbs fell away from him" (i.e. he was dismembered/maimed) — as in ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb's rebuke to a man who questioned him: "aribta min yadayka" ("may your hands be maimed") — "do you ask me something I myself asked the Prophet?"

4. Binding / tightening ('aqd)
Ariba – yaʾrabu: to grow strict, tight-fisted, and hard-bargaining (Abū Zayd). Related words in this branch:
- al-taʾrīb, "incitement" (arrabtu ʿalayhim, "I incited them against [someone]").
- taʾarraba ʿalaynā, "he turned obstinate and difficult with us."
- taʾarrabtu fī ḥājatī, "I was firm/insistent about my need" (al-Aṣmaʿī); arrabtu l-ʿuqdata, "I tightened the knot" — the kind that will not loosen until deliberately undone.
- A dog's or horse's collar is called urba because it is knotted around the neck (with verses of al-Mutalammis and a citation from Ibn al-Aʿrābī, who says al-urba is the opposite of al-unshūṭa, a slip-knot — i.e. it is a knot that holds fast). Al-Khalīl adds that mustaʾrib describes a strong, well-made bowstring.
- A line of Ibn Muqbil pairing the casting of gambling arrows with taʾrīb "ʿalā l-khaṭar" was explained two ways: either "completing their share in full," or "holding firm over the stake." A further verse of his repeats the "not withholding the loser's due share" idea, glossed as: they are generous people whom no hardship corrupts.
- rajulun aribun: a man sound and firm in his conduct (Ibn al-Aʿrābī).
- aribtu bi-kadhā, "I sought help by means of such-and-such" (with a verse of Aws on seeking relief from worry via a sturdy she-camel).
- al-urabā: a dreaded, hard-to-fathom calamity — said to be named for the "tight knot" (taʾrīb) of its predicament, as though it can never be undone (with a verse of Ibn Aḥmar).

A closing note: Irāb is also a place name, source of "the Day of Irāb" — a battle-day between al-Hudhayl ibn Ḥassān al-Taghlibī's raid on Banū Yarbūʿ, and a later related raid-and-truce between Juzʾ ibn Saʿd al-Riyāḥī's people and Bakr ibn Wāʾil, commemorated in verses by al-Farazdaq and Jarīr.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: Ruʾba (Umayyad); Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam); Kuthayyir (Umayyad); unnamed verse
text:
Ibn Fāris treats أ-ر-ك as two independent roots, from which everything else branches:

1. A TREE — الْأَرَاك (al-arāk), a well-known tree.
   - Singular: أَرَاكَة (arāka); a woman is also named Arāka.
   - Verb: ائْتَرَكَ الْأَرَاكُ — "the arāk became firmly established/grew thick." Cited from the poet Ruʾba: "of the thorn-trees and the well-established arāk."
   - Camels that browse on arāk are أَرَاكِيَّة (arākiyya) and أَوَارِك (awārik) (reported from Abū ʿAmr). A ḥadīth is cited in which the Prophet was brought, at ʿArafa, the milk of awārik camels.
   - أَرْضٌ أَرِكَةٌ (arḍ arika): land full of arāk. Camels grazing it are likewise أَرِكَة — formed on the same pattern as ḥāmiḍ ("feeding on ḥamḍ-plants") from ḥamḍ. Shāhid from Abū Dhuʾayb on choosing "the milk of the ārikāt in summer."

2. STAYING / REMAINING IN PLACE — الْإِقَامَة, verbal noun أُرُوك (urūk); verb أَرَكَ, imperfect يَأْرِكُ or يَأْرُكُ.
   - Al-Kisāʾī derived the arākiyya camels from this sense of staying. Abū Ḥanīfa (al-Dīnawarī) disputes that: the word is not taken from arāk (the tree) and does not mean staying among arāk specifically — it applies to remaining anywhere, including a man staying in his own house.
   - Shāhid from Kuthayyir describing women's litters, comparing them to "the white antelopes of the athīl-trees, the awārik."
   - Ibn Fāris's supporting argument for Abū Ḥanīfa: the couch or bed set inside the curtained canopy (ḥajala) is called أَرِيكَة (arīka), plural أَرَائِك (arāʾik) — i.e. a thing of settled repose, from this second root.
   - An objection is raised from Abū ʿUbayd, who used أَرَكَ ... أُرُوكًا of a wound that mends and improves. Ibn Fāris assigns this to the second root as well: when a wound heals over, its swelling and its rising above the skin subside — i.e. it settles down.
   - The place-name أَرِيك (Arīk) is derived from this same section, with a line of poetry placing a traveller "by the side of Arīk at evening."

Closing note on a neighbouring form: أ-ر-ل is neither a root nor a branch; although the mountain-name أَرُل (Arul) is said, it properly has a kāf (أَرُك).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَسِف 2x "and grieved"; أَسَف 2x "alas, my grief"; ءَاسَفُ 1x "they angered us"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats أ-س-ف (ʾ-s-f) as a single root whose core notion is something being missed or lost, and the keen regret that follows — loss plus lamenting over it.

1. Regret/grief. أَسِفَ عَلَى الشَّيْءِ – يَأْسَفُ – أَسَفًا: to grieve or feel bitter regret over something. He glosses it with تَلَهَّفَ, to lament keenly over what is gone.

2. Anger. الأَسِف means "the angry one." He cites Q 7:150, "And when Mūsā returned to his people, angry (ghaḍbān) and asif," and a verse of al-Aʿshā describing "a man of them asīf, as though pressing to his flanks a hand dyed [red]" — on which, he reports, it is said that asīf here means the angry man.

3. Barren land. الأُسَافَة (also vocalised al-asāfa): land that grows nothing. Ibn Fāris ties this back to the root notion — vegetation has "passed it by," i.e. it has missed out on growth.

4. A lean camel. الجَمَل الأَسِيف: the camel that scarcely puts on fat — the same idea of something failing to be attained.

5. An excluded homonym. The use of أَسِيف for a follower or subordinate, he says, does not belong to this root at all: there the hamza is a substitution for an original ʿayn (i.e. it belongs to ʿ-s-f), and he has treated it under that entry.

Method note: Ibn Fāris derives the senses from one abstract kernel (fawt, "missing out") and explicitly separates a phonetically similar word on morphological grounds.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root أ س ن (a-s-n), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Two distinct roots:

First — change/spoiling. asina al-māʾ — water changes/spoils (becomes stale). Qur'anic citation, Muhammad 47:15: "min māʾin ghayri āsin" — "from water unaltered [in taste or smell]" (describing a river of Paradise). asina al-rajul — a man overcome/fainting from a well's foul vapor. Ibn Fāris flags two further words as not genuinely belonging to this root despite the resemblance: al-usun ("residual fat"), which he explains is really ʿusun with the hamzah substituted for ʿayn; and taʾassana ("to grow ill and slow"), which Abū Zayd argued is actually a corruption of taʾassara (with rāʾ, not nūn).

Second — ropes/cords. al-āsān — ropes, illustrated with a line of poetry about the ropes/bonds of parting being cut. This is metaphorically extended in the idiom "huwa ʿalā āsānin min abīhi" — "he follows in his father's āsān," meaning his ways or paths.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَسِير 4x "(as) captives"; تَأْسِرُ 1x "and you took captive"; أَسْر 1x "their forms"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats hamza–sīn–rāʾ as a single root with one regularly applicable sense: confining, holding fast, restraining.

1. Captive — أَسِير. Ibn Fāris derives it from the practice of binding a prisoner with a thong of untanned hide, called إِسَار. The name then broadened: anyone taken/seized was called أَسِير even if he was not actually tied up.

2. Poetic witness. Al-Aʿshā: poetry "has fettered me in its bayt (house/verse) as the binding cords fetter the wild ass." Ibn Fāris reads this as the poet saying he is inside poetry's house — meaning he has reached its furthest limit.

3. Ordinary usage — أَسَرَ قَتَبَهُ, "he bound his camel-saddle frame," i.e. tied it tight. The root is used of physical fastening, not only of prisoners.

4. Qur'anic witness — Q 76:28, "and We made firm their أَسْر." Ibn Fāris reports two interpretations without deciding between them: (a) أَسْر means the bodily frame/constitution; (b) it refers to the passage of what issues from the two outlets of the body.

5. Kin-group — أُسْرَة, a man's close kin, so called because he is strengthened by them (a bond that holds him together).

6. Grammar/plurals — أَسِير pluralises as أَسْرَى and, with fatḥa, أَسَارَى.

7. أُسْر — retention or blockage of urine, i.e. the body holding back what should be released.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
text:
Root ʾ-s-s, as al-Zamakhsharī presents it in Asās al-Balāgha — a short entry organised, as this dictionary always is, by first giving the plain concrete use and then the figurative extensions.

1. Literal sense — the foundation or base of a built thing. His examples: "he built his house on its original foundation" (أساس), and "he tore it out from its base" (أُس) — i.e. uprooted it at the footing rather than merely damaging what stood above.

2. Figurative (majāz) — the base of time. The idiom "so-and-so has never stopped being mad ʿalā āsti/ʾussi l-dahr" is glossed by the author as "throughout its whole course," so the "base" of time here carries the sense of the entire stretch or run of it.

3. Figurative — the foundation of a person's conduct. "So-and-so: the foundation (asās) of his affair is lying," i.e. falsehood is what the whole matter rests on.

4. Figurative — the founding of rule. "Whoever does not found (yuʾassis) his dominion on justice has already demolished it": building without this foundation is itself the act of tearing down.

Across all four, the constant is the lowest supporting layer on which something stands, applied by extension to time, to a person's character, and to political authority.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: Al-Ḥuṭayʾa (lived into Islam); Al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats أ-س-و as a single root meaning to treat/heal and to set right.

1. To treat a wound. أَسَوْتُ الْجُرْحَ (asawtu l-jurḥ) = "I doctored the wound," with the verbal nouns أَسْو (asw) and أَسًا (asan). From this the healer gets his name — the text is damaged at the word itself ("the physician is called al-…", i.e. الآسي, al-āsī). Two poetic witnesses:
   - Al-Ḥuṭayʾa: "They are the ones who treat the umm al-raʾs [deep head wound] when the physicians and the healers passed it off on one another" — the الْإِسَاء (al-isāʾ) of the line being glossed as "those who apply treatment"; Ibn Fāris credits this reading to al-Umawī.
   - Al-Aʿshā: "With him are goodness and restraint, and the mending of the rift, and the carrying of back-breaking burdens" — أَسَا الشَّقِّ (asā l-shaqq), healing a split/breach.

2. To reconcile. أَسَوْتُ بَيْنَ الْقَوْمِ (asawtu bayna l-qawm) = "I put things right between the people" — the same "mending" applied to a social rupture rather than a body.

3. An example to follow. Ibn Fāris places أُسْوَة / إِسْوَة (uswa/iswa) here: لِي فِي فُلَانٍ أُسْوَةٌ = "so-and-so is a قُدْوَة (qudwa) for me," i.e. "I model myself on him."

4. To console. أَسَّيْتُ فُلَانًا (assaytu fulānan) = "I offered him condolence," derived from the same idea: one tells the afflicted person, "Take so-and-so as your uswa — the same thing befell him" — a parallel case that reconciles him to his loss.

5. Fellow-feeling in person. Also of this root: آسَيْتُهُ بِنَفْسِي (āsaytuhu bi-nafsī), standing by someone / sharing with him personally. The entry ends here.

The organising logic of the entry: mending a wound → mending a quarrel → a parallel case one is measured against (uswa) → consoling by supplying such a parallel → sharing another's burden oneself.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: اتَى 271x "were given"; أَتَى 264x "then bring"; اتِي 9x "(is) surely coming"; إِيتَاءٌ 3x "and giving"; مُؤْتُون 1x "and the ones who give"; مَأْتِيٌّ 1x "sure to come"
poets_named: unnamed verse ×3; Labīd (lived into Islam); al-Nābigha (pre-Islamic); al-Aṣmaʿī (unnamed)
text:
Ibn Fāris's account of the root أ-ت-ي (Aty):

1. Core sense — "to come." أَتَانِي فُلَانٌ = "so-and-so came to me." Its verbal nouns are إِتْيَان، أَتْي، and (for a single instance) أَتْيَة / أَتْوَة. Ibn Fāris notes a grammatical point: the "one-instance" noun should follow the verb's own pattern, so إِتْيَانَة ("one coming," with -āna) is irregular and used only under metrical necessity — al-Liḥyānī nonetheless records it. A poet's line on الأَتْي is cited as a shāhid.

2. Dialectal imperatives (from Abū Zayd) for "come to me / bring me": تِنِي (to one man), تِيَانِي (to two), تُونِي (to a group), تِينِي (to a woman), تِينَنِي (to women).

3. مَأْتَى / مَأْتَاة = the point or way of approach to something: أَتَيْتُ الأمرَ من مَأْتَاهُ ("I approached the matter by its access-point"), supported by a verse.

4. Form III مُؤَاتَاة (from al-Khalīl): آتَيْتُ فلانًا على أمرِه = to comply with or accommodate someone — "good compliance." The variant واتَيْتَه (with wāw) is dismissed as a coarse Yemeni usage. A morphological aside: verbs like آسَيْتُ، آكَلْتُ، آخَيْتُ take a wāw only through lightening of the hamza (يُوَاكِل, etc.).

5. اسْتِئْتَاء (from al-Liḥyānī): استأتيناك = "we reckoned you slow in coming and asked you to come." And تَأَتَّ لهذا الأمر = "go about it gently/gradually."

6. الإِيتَاء = "giving" (آتَى يُؤْتِي إِيتَاءً). The imperative هَاتِ ("give/hand over") is related to آتِ, with a hāʾ placed over the alif.

7. تَأَتَّى / تَأْتِيَة = a matter coming about smoothly. تَأَتَّى لفلانٍ أمرُه = "his affair went smoothly"; أَتَّاهُ اللهُ = "God brought it about / made it easy." Cited verses (including Labīd) use تَأْتَى as a lightened form of تَأَتَّى.

8. الأَتِيّ (water sense, from al-Khalīl): (a) debris — wood or leaves — that falls into a river and dams the water (أَتِّ لهذا الماء = "ease its flow"); (b) in common usage, the channel/canal carrying water to a trough, plurals أُتِيّ and آتَاء; (c) a torrent/flood coming from another land. A line of al-Nābigha is cited, with two interpretations of أَتِيّ (the watercourse of a tent-trench, or the debris damming it). أَتَّيْتُ للماء = "I directed a channel for it."

9. الأَتِيّ (of a person): "effective, penetrating" (al-Liḥyānī); or a stranger/newcomer among a people not his own — also أَتَاوِيّ (al-Khalīl). Supported by a line al-Aṣmaʿī recited and by the ḥadīth of Thābit b. al-Daḥdāḥ, «إنما هو أتيٌّ فينا» ("he is only a newcomer among us").

10. الإِتَاء = growth, increase, yield of crops and palms: نخلٌ ذو إتاءٍ = "palms that bear well." Al-Farrāʾ: أَتَتِ الأرضُ والنخلُ, and أتى الماءُ إتاءً = "it became abundant." Two further verses cite الإتاء in the sense of yield/abundance.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); unnamed verse ×2; al-Akhṭal (Umayyad); Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam)
text:
Root أ ث ل (a-th-l), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: the root/origin of a thing, and its accumulation.

1. al-athl — a literal tree, described by al-Khalīl (resembling tamarisk, but larger, with better wood used for fine cups) and Abū Ziyād (a tall, thornless, fine-fronded thorn-tree).
2. Figurative idiom: "huwa mūlaʿun bi-naḥti athlatihi" — "he is fond of carving at his athlah," meaning fond of maligning/reviling someone — illustrated with a line of poetry by al-Aʿshā daring an opponent to keep trying and failing to harm him.
3. athtala fulānun — his wealth grew and his condition improved; al-mutaʾaththil — one who accumulates wealth upon wealth; "athtala Allāhu mulkaka" — an idiom for "may God make your reign great and abundant." Abū ʿAmr glosses al-athal itself as either "glory" or "wealth."
4. athalatu kulli shayʾ — the root/origin of anything; taʾaththala fulānun — he acquired a foundation of wealth; extended to tree-branches, al-mutaʾaththil describes a thick, luxuriant growth, illustrated with a line of poetry contrasting an uneven root and branch.
5. Further idioms from al-Aṣmaʿī: athaltu ʿalayhi al-duyūn — to pile up debts on someone; athaltuhu bi-rijāl — to strengthen someone with men, illustrated with a line of poetry by al-Akhṭal reproaching an ingrate. Also: taʾaththaltu li-l-shitāʾ — to prepare oneself for winter.
6. Onomastic note: Uthāl, a mountain's name (per Abū ʿUbaydah); and a line of poetry (via Ibn al-Aʿrābī) using tuʾaththilu for persistently imposed judgment/fate.
7. Closing sense: taʾaththala al-biʾr — to dig a well, illustrated with a line of poetry by Abū Dhuʾayb — which Ibn Fāris notes fits the root's core logic, since digging a well "brings out" what has accumulated/settled within it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: إِثْم 35x "sin"; أَثِيم 7x "sinful"; اثِم 3x "any sinner"; تَأْثِيم 2x "sinful (speech)"; أَثَام 1x "a penalty"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ʾ-th-m (أثم) from a single core sense: slowness and lagging behind.

1. Literal base sense — slowness / lagging. A she-camel that falls behind the others is called آثِمَة (āthima). He cites al-Aʿshā's line "when the lagging she-camels belie the midday heat" as a poetic witness.

2. الإِثْم (al-ithm, "sin") as a derivative. In his account, ithm comes from that base sense: the person who bears sin is one who is "slow toward the good and lags behind it."

3. Verb forms (from al-Khalīl). أَثِمَ (athima) = to fall into sin. The reflexive تَأَثَّمَ (taʾaththama) means the opposite — to shrink back and hold oneself off from sin. He gives a parallel pair: ḥarija (to fall into constraint) versus taḥarraja (to keep clear of it), showing how the ta- form flips the meaning to avoidance.

4. Intensive adjectives (from Abū Zayd). أَثِيمٌ (athīm) and أَثُومٌ (athūm) describe a man deeply given to sin.

5. A disputed sense — ithm as "wine." Some transmit from al-Akhfash that al-ithm means wine (khamr), reading Qurʾān 7:33 ("...and al-ithm") accordingly, and citing a verse: "I drank al-ithm until my mind went astray; thus does al-ithm do to minds." Ibn Fāris explicitly flags that he does not know whether this attribution is sound, but notes that if it is, it fits the root logic, since wine drives its drinker into sin.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَثَر 14x "their footsteps"; اثَرَ 5x "you prefer"; أَثَٰرَة 1x "a trace"; يُؤْثَرُ 1x "imitated"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root أ-ث-ر from three fundamental meanings: (1) giving something precedence, (2) mentioning or reporting something, and (3) the lasting mark or trace a thing leaves behind. The entry's material falls under these three heads.

**1. Precedence / preferring (تقديم)**
- أَثِرْتُ بِأَنْ أَفْعَلَ ("I resolved to do") — a firm intention (from al-Khalīl).
- آثِرًا مَا / آثِرَ ذِي أَثِيرٍ — "do this first of all / in preference." Ibn al-Aʿrābī: "do it before everything else." Cited in a line of ʿUrwa b. al-Ward.
- الأَثِير: someone dear whom you single out with your favor; feminine أَثِيرَة; verbal noun الأَثَرَة (pattern فَعِيل; per Abū Zayd, man = أَثِير, plural أُثَرَاء).
- الأَثَرَة / الإِثْرَة: self-preference — taking for oneself. "أخذت بلا أَثَرَة عليك" = "I took it without preferring myself over you" (Abū ʿAmr). A man who does this is أَثُر (pattern فَعُل). Ḥadīth: «سَتَرَوْنَ بَعْدِي أَثَرَةً» — "you will see people take the spoils (fayʾ) for themselves." Ibn al-Aʿrābī: آثَرْتُهُ إِيثَارًا, "I preferred him," with a supporting verse.
- اسْتَأْثَرَ اللهُ بفلان — "God took him to Himself" (of a death with paradise hoped for). Ḥadīth: when God "reserves a thing to Himself" (forbids it), turn away from it.

**2. Reporting / transmitting (ذكر)**
- أَثَرْتُ الْحَدِيثَ = "I transmitted the report"; حَدِيثٌ مَأْثُورٌ = a transmitted report.
- ʿUmar's ḥadīth «ما حلفت بعدها آثِرًا ولا ذاكِرًا»: آثِر = reporting another's oath ("so-and-so swore…"); ذاكِر = swearing on one's own account. He denies doing either.

**3. Mark / trace / remnant (رسم الباقي)**
- الأَثَر: the visible remnant of anything, or the lingering residue of what is not seen; variant form الأَثَار (paired like فَلَاح/فَلَح). Following behind is also الأَثَر / إِثْر — no verb derives from it in that sense; one says ذَهَبْتُ فِي إِثْرِهِ ("I went in his track"). Proverb: «تدع العين وتطلب الأثر» — leaving the spring for the track, i.e. forsaking ease for hardship.
- أَثَرُ السَّيْفِ = a sword's stroke; proverb «من يشتري سيفي وهذا أثره» for the tried-and-tested.
- Tracks of beasts: الأَثِير = a beast leaving a large track; المِئْثَرَة = a knife that marks a camel's foot-pad so its trail is recognized (plural المَآثِر).
- الأَثْر (also أَثَر) in a sword = the فِرِنْد, its watering/damascene pattern; hence a sword is مَأْثُور, and أَثَرْتُ السَّيْفَ = "I polished it till the pattern showed" (al-Khalīl, with a dispute between al-Farrāʾ and others over the vowelling, and two supporting verses).
- الْمَأْثُورَة (of wells): an old well dug and buried before your time that you chance upon, recognizable by the marks of old ropes (al-Naḍr). طَرِيقٌ مَأْثُورٌ = a road freshly marked with tracks (Abū ʿAmr).
- أُثِرْتُ بهذا المكان = "I stayed fixed here" (al-Kalbī, with a verse).
- الأُثْر (also kasra per Yaʿqūb; plural الأُثُور): milk that has separated and been purified from butter (Abū ʿUbayd, al-Aṣmaʿī), with a verse.

**Qurʾānic citation:** الأَثَارَة = a remnant of a thing (plural أَثَارَات), as in {أَوْ أَثَارَةٍ مِنْ عِلْمٍ} "or a remnant/trace of knowledge" (46:4). Al-Aṣmaʿī also records الإبل على أَثَارَة = camels "upon old fat," with a supporting verse.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives the whole root أ-و-ب (hamza–wāw–bāʾ) from a single core idea: returning (rujūʿ). Every branch traces back to it, even ones that sound distant.

1. Basic sense — to return. Per al-Khalīl, آب فلان إلى سيفه = he brought his hand back to draw his sword.

2. Al-awb = the back-and-forth swing of a traveller's (or camel's) arms and legs in motion. Cited in two lines of Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr (the swing of forelegs; the swinging hands of a grieving woman).

3. The verb is al-taʾwīb. Hence daytime travel is called taʾwīb (night travel = isʾād); a single instance is a taʾwībah. Supported by a poetic line contrasting a day of councils with a day of taʾwīb toward the enemy.

4. Al-taʾwīb also = glorifying/praising (tasbīḥ), which Ibn Fāris links to the Qurʾanic "O mountains, echo/return [praise] with him, and the birds" (Saba 34:10).

5. Related evening senses (al-Aṣmaʿī): أوّبت الإبل = I drove the camels home to their resting-place at evening; تأوّبني = he/it came to me by night (poetic shāhid of an old malady returning at night).

6. A recorded scholarly dispute on whether "return" implies nighttime. Al-Aṣmaʿī read every poetic al-iyāb ("return") as night-bound. Abū Zayd objected that iyāb just means returning at any time (قد آب المسافر = the traveller has returned), citing ʿAbīd's line "every absent one returns…" and the Qurʾan's "to Us is their return" (al-Ghāshiya 88:25); al-Aṣmaʿī fell silent — yet Abū Zayd concedes most usage does fit al-Aṣmaʿī's evening reading.

7. Al-maʾāb = the place of return. أبت القوم (Abū Ziyād) = I returned to the people. Abū ʿUbayd: the mill's flour-outlet is called al-maʾāb because the ground meal "returns" to it.

8. Of the sun: آبت الشمس إياباً = the sun set into its maʾāb (place of setting) — al-Khalīl, with a line of Umayya. Al-Naḍr: the sun is al-muʾawwibah, its taʾwīb being its daily run from east to west, returning at sunset.

9. جاءوا من كل أوب = they came from every direction/quarter — also from this root.

10. Al-awb = bees, so named (al-Aṣmaʿī) because they keep returning to the hive from their pastures; the singular is like āyib. Compare the curse آبك الله = أبعدك الله ("may God remove you"), with a closing poetic line.

text:
Root أ و د (a-w-d), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: bending and curving.

1. udtu al-shayʾa — I bent something; taʾawwada al-nabt — a plant bent/curved, illustrated with a line of poetry about a stem too slight to bend even under a light weight.
2. From this comes ādanī al-shayʾu yaʾūdunī — an idiom for something weighing heavily on you, "as though it grew heavy upon you until it bent you."
3. Onomastic notes: Awd, a tribe-name, which Ibn Fāris suggests plausibly derives from this root; and Ūd, a place-name, illustrated with a line of poetry naming several locations.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris opens by flagging this as an anomaly: the letters hamza-waw-ha do not form a true triliteral root that other words can be derived from by regular analogy - this is essentially an interjection/exclamation, not a root with a stable core meaning.

1. Base sense - a moan/sigh of grief. The verb ta'awwaha means "he uttered a sigh," specifically by saying "awwah" or "awhi". Ibn Faris notes this is genuine Arabic usage ("the Arabs do say this"), and supports it with a line of verse describing a she-camel that, when saddled for a night journey, "moans the moan of a grieving man" - i.e. she groans as if in sorrow.

2. Qur'anic form - awwah, Q9:114 (Abraham). Citing "Indeed Abraham was la-awwah, halim," Ibn Faris glosses awwah as ad-Da'daa' - one who supplicates/invokes (God) frequently, an intensive noun of habitual action built on the same root as the sighing/moaning sense above.

3. Recorded pronunciation variants. Ibn Faris lists the dialectal forms in which this exclamation was said, distinguished by vowel length and consonant doubling: long alif with doubled waw; short alif with doubled waw; long alif with single waw; plus "awhi", "awwih", "aahi", "aawi", and the derived form "awwataahu".

The entry is purely lexical/phonetic in focus: it treats the root as an onomatopoeic interjection of grief/lament, and explains the Qur'anic epithet awwah applied to Abraham as "one who supplicates much," on that same basis - Ibn Faris does not attach any further doctrinal content to the word.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ء-و-ل from two base ideas: (1) the beginning of a matter, and (2) its end / return.

FIRST BASE — beginning (al-awwal, "first"):
1. أَوَّل (awwal) is the outset of a thing. Feminine الأُولَى (al-ūlā) on the patterns afʿal / fuʿlā; its plural is ulayāt (paralleling al-ukhrā, "the other/last"). Plural of awwal is al-awāʾil.
2. Etymological note: some derive awwal from the letters hamza-wāw-lām (Ibn Fāris's preferred view); others from two wāws plus a lām.
3. Feminine form أَوَّلَة (awwalah), plural awwalāt; used of a camel's forebears (a shāhid on a proud-bred camel). Abū Zayd: a she-/he-camel is awwalah/awwal when it leads the herd.
4. Morphology of the plural: analogically awāwil, but a wāw ending after a quiescent alif turns into hamza.
5. Adverbial/indefinite use (al-Khalīl): عَامًا أَوَّلَ ("last year"), diptote because awwal is afʿal-pattern; with tanwīn it is treated as indefinite (shawāhid from Abū al-Najm). Ibn al-Aʿrābī records phrases meaning "before everything."
6. الصَّلَاة الأُولَى ("the first observance") is so named simply because it was the first performed. Abū Zayd: pre-Islamic Arabs called Sunday al-awwal (an old weekday-naming scheme, with a supporting verse).

SECOND BASE — return / end (آلَ يَؤُولُ, "to revert, come back"):
1. الأَيِّل (ayyil), the male mountain-goat (pl. ayāʾil), is named for "returning" (yaʾūlu) to the mountain for refuge (shāhid, Abū al-Najm).
2. آلَ اللَّبَن — milk thickens/curdles, so called because it does so only at the final stage; likewise tar thickening, and a man's body growing lean (each a "reverting" to a condition). الإِيَال is a vessel where drink is kept to mature.
3. Core verb آلَ = "returned." أَوَّلَ الحُكْمَ إلى أهله = restored a judgment to its people (al-Aʿshā).
4. الإِيَالَة = governance/statecraft, because subjects' recourse is to their steward. Al-Aṣmaʿī: āla raʿiyyatahu = governed them well. Proverb: أُلْنَا وإِيلَ عَلَيْنَا ("we governed and were governed"). Related: taʾtāluhu (Labīd) = "sets it right"; آيِلُ مالٍ = a property-manager/steward; radadtuhu ilā āyilatihi = to its innate nature.
5. آل الرجل = a man's household/kin, because their destination is to him and his to them — the sense of the vocative يَالَ فُلَان ("O people of…", shāhid, Ṭarafa). Ibn Fāris argues this āl is a lightened form of awwal.
6. آل also = a person's self; and by extension the āl of anything. Kin can stand for the man: "āl Abī Bakr" meaning Abū Bakr himself (a point Ibn Fāris grants is slightly obscure).
7. Further physical senses (from al-Khalīl and shawāhid): āl al-jabal = a mountain's edges/flanks; āl al-baʿīr = a camel's broad frame-bones/prominences; āl al-khayma = tent-poles; الآلَة (āla) = state/condition.
8. تَأْوِيل of speech = its outcome, what it "comes back to." Ibn Fāris reads Q 7:53 {هل ينظرون إلا تأويله} as "what it comes to at the resurrection," and cites al-Aʿshā using taʾawwul for "return/outcome" — all from آلَ يَؤُولُ.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ʾ-w-y (أوي) from two base meanings: (1) gathering / coming together, and (2) tenderness / compassion.

Sense 1 — betaking oneself, sheltering, gathering:
- أَوَى (awā): a person betakes himself to his dwelling; آوَى (āwā): to give shelter to another. Verbal nouns: أُوِيّ (uwiyy — the preferred form), إِيوَاء (īwāʾ), and إِوَاء (iwāʾ). Al-Khalīl is cited for this.
- Qurʾānic witnesses (as Ibn Fāris adduces them): "when the youths betook themselves to the cave" (18:10); "and We gave the two of them refuge on an elevated ground" (23:50).
- المأوى (al-maʾwā): the place to which anything betakes itself or takes shelter, by night or day.
- The verb also describes camels returning to their owners (آوِيَة, āwiya).
- التأوّي (al-taʾawwī): gathering — used of birds flocking together (أُوِيّ, مُتَأَوِّيَات). A poetic line likens hearth-stones drawing together to gathering kites: "as the gathering kites draw near one another."

Sense 2 — compassion:
- أَوَيْتُ لِفُلَانٍ (awaytu li-fulān): to feel tenderness and mercy toward someone; verbal noun مَأْوِيَة (maʾwiya) or أَيَّة (ayya).
- Abū ʿUbayd is cited: اسْتَأْوَيْتُ فُلَانًا (istaʾwaytu) means "I asked him to take pity on me," with the line: "had I sought his compassion, he would not have pitied me."

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʾ-kh-dh as one root meaning, whose branches all stay close to it. In his account the core of akhadha is taking possession of a thing: gathering it in and collecting it (akhadhtu al-shayʾa, ākhudhuhu, akhdhan, "I took the thing").

**1. Taking.** al-Khalīl defines akhdh as the opposite of giving, that is, taking hold of something.

**2. Binding by a charm.** al-Khalīl says al-ukhdha is a charm that "takes hold of" the eye and the like. al-muʾakhkhadh is a man whom a woman binds away from his own judgement and away from other women, as though he were held back from them.

**3. The water-hollow (ikhādha / ikhādh).** A place where water collects, like a pool. Abū ʿUbayd gives the form without the final -a. al-Khalīl explains the name by the fact that a person takes such water for himself. A further possibility is also given: the hollow may be named for the way it takes in water. The plural is ukhudh. His citations are:
- a line by ʿAdī ibn Zayd describing rain, recited by Abū ʿUbayd and others, in which the pools are "not sparing with the ikhādh";
- a line by al-Akhṭal about a watcher who sees the pools grown hot and thinks their water has run low;
- Masrūq ibn al-Ajdaʿ's comparison of the companions of Muḥammad to such pools, some of which are enough for one rider, some for two, and some for a large company of people.

**4. What "takes hold" of a body.** Ibn Fāris says the same analogy covers ailments that take hold in things, and some other things as well:
- al-ākhidh, plural al-awākhidh, is a camel in which fatness has "taken hold" (al-Khalīl).
- akhida al-baʿīr (the camel is akhid, with the verb's middle consonant undoubled) describes a kind of madness that seizes a camel. It also affects sheep and goats (al-Khalīl).

**5. Eye inflammation: ukhudh and istaʾkhadha.** Ibn Fāris raises an objection himself. Some say al-ukhudh means eye inflammation (ramad) and al-akhid means someone suffering from it, so does that break the analogy? His answer is that ailments get this name because they take hold of a person. As support he gives the Hudhayl commentators' reading of a line by Abū Dhuʾayb. In that line a wild ass looks toward what is hidden with a lowered gaze, like the mustaʾkhadh, a man whose eye inflammation has taken firm hold of him, so that he droops his head or, some say, closes his eyes. Ibn Fāris notes that istaʾkhadha, "to take firm hold", is a well-known word, and he cites Ibn Abī Rabīʿa: "when will sleep take hold of them?"

**6. The "stars of taking" (nujūm al-akhdh).** These are the mansions of the moon. They are named on the same analogy, because each night the moon takes up one of these mansions. A poet says these stars "failed" and brought only small trickles, the trickles of a drought that do not moisten the ground.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: اخِر 155x "the hereafter"; اخَر 70x "another"; أَخَّرَ 15x "and give you respite"; يَسْتَأْخِرُ 6x "you can postpone"; تَأَخَّرَ 3x "delays"; مُسْتَـْخِرِين 1x "the later ones"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats أ-خ-ر (ʾ-kh-r) as a single root whose meaning is the opposite of precedence or coming-forward.

1. Core sense. Following al-Khalīl, al-ākhir ("the last, the latter") is the contrary of "the one going before," and al-ukhur ("backwardness, going to the rear") is the contrary of qudum ("forward motion"): one says "he went forward" (maḍā quduman) versus "he drew back" (taʾakhkhara ukhuran).

2. Front vs. rear of objects. The pairing runs through concrete nouns: ākhira / muʾakhkhar al-raḥl is the rear part of the camel-saddle, opposed to its front (qādima / muqaddam).

3. Morphological note. The lightened (undoubled) form muʾkhir occurs, al-Khalīl says, in only one expression: muʾkhir al-ʿayn, the outer corner of the eye (paired with muqdim al-ʿayn, the inner corner).

4. Deferral / lateness. From the same root: biʿtuka bi-akhiratin, "a sale on deferred payment (credit)"; and mā ʿaraftuhu illā bi-akharatin, "I did not know it until lately / at last."

5. Idiom of remoteness. Al-Khalīl records faʿala Allāhu bi'l-akhir, glossing al-akhir here as al-abʿad, "the most remote one" — used as an imprecation.

6. "The rear / hindmost." jiʾtu fī ukhrayātihim ("I came among the hindmost of them"), ukhrā al-qawm ("the rear of the people"), with the cited line "I am the one born in the rear of the camels" (ukhrā al-ibil).

7. Ibn Durayd's variant. Ibn Durayd defines al-ākhir as "that which follows the first." Ibn Fāris notes this is close to the foregoing, but that usages like "the latter of the two men" (ākhiru al-rajulayni) fit Ibn Durayd's definition better.

8. Plural. ukhar is the plural of the feminine ukhrā ("others").

dictionary: ʿAyn — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786)
quran_words: أَخ 75x "his brother"; أُخْت 14x "a sister"; إِخْوَةٌ 7x "brothers and sisters"
text:
Al-Khalīl's entry on the root ʾ-kh-w (أخو) covers two clusters of meaning:

1. Kinship — "brother." أَخ (akh, brother); dual أَخَوان (akhawān, two brothers); plurals إِخوة (ikhwa) and إِخوان (ikhwān). The abstract noun for the relationship is أُخُوَّة (ukhuwwa) or إِخاء (ikhāʾ), "brotherhood": "between me and him there is brotherhood." The verb "to make/take as a brother" is آخَيْتُه (āākhaytuhu), with a variant واخَيْتُه (wākhaytuhu) in the dialect of Ṭayyiʾ. A phrase like "this is a man of my brethren" uses ākhāʾ (pattern afʿāl). Al-Khalīl notes a grammatical point: the standard form āākhaytu keeps the original root-structure, whereas the Ṭayyiʾ form wākhaytu is treated as derived from wikhāʾ.

2. Feminine. The feminine of akh is أُخْت (ukht, sister); its final tāʾ was originally a hāʾ. Dual أُخْتان (ukhtān), plural أَخَوات (akhawāt).

3. A distinct concrete sense — الأَخِيَّة (al-akhiyya): a peg or crosspiece of wood fixed into a wall to which an animal is tethered; plural أَواخِيّ (awākhiyy). Used figuratively for a secure position: "so-and-so has a firm akhiyya (standing) with the commander." From it come the verbs akhkhaytu ("I fixed such a peg," verbal noun taʾkhiya) and taʾakhkhaytu ("I made one for myself"). Al-Khalīl derives these from ākhiyyat al-ʿūd (the wooden tethering-peg), which he analyses as pattern fāʿūla; a lighter variant ākhiya (without doubling) is also used throughout.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَيَّدَ 9x "and we supported him"; أَيْيد 2x "with strength"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats أ-ي-د (ʾ-y-d) as one root carrying two linked ideas: strength and protection.

1. Strength (qūwa). The verb أَيَّدَهُ (ayyadahu) means "he strengthened him"; أَيَّدَهُ اللَّهُ = "God strengthened him." He cites Qurʾān 51:47, "And the heaven — We built it with might (bi-aydin)," as an instance of this sense.

2. Protection/guarding (ḥifẓ). From the same root comes الْإِيَاد (al-iyād): any barrier or screen that shields something and keeps it safe. As a witness he quotes the poet Dhū al-Rumma, describing how a raised mound of earth had gathered around a bird's fair eggs to protect them (bi-iyād).

text:
Root ء-ي-م (Aym) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris treats hamza-yāʾ-mīm as covering three unrelated meanings: smoke, the snake, and the spouseless person.

**1. Smoke.** Al-Khalīl gives al-īyām as "smoke." The poet Abū Dhuʾayb pictures a beekeeper smoking out a hive: the bees "withdraw into groups, humiliated and dejected" once he clears them out with smoke. Al-Aṣmaʿī supplies the verb: āma / yaʾūmu / iyāman means to smoke a hive so the bees leave and the honey can be harvested. The smoker is an āʾim; the smoked-out bee/hive is muʾawwama.

**2. The snake.** Al-aym is a name for the white snake. Two poetic citations use it as a simile: a she-camel's nose-rein compared to a swaying white snake, and a description of soft, quivering haunches likened to a snake's smooth belly. Yūnus glosses it as al-jānn, a small white snake; the tribe of Tamīm instead say ayn (with n). Al-Aṣmaʿī notes the word's fuller form has a doubled consonant — ayyim alongside the lighter aym — on the same pattern as hayyin/hayn ("easy"). A further verse uses ayyim mutaghaḍḍif ("a coiling snake") for a nighttime watering-place.

**3. The person without a spouse.** Al-ayyim is a woman without a husband, or a man without a wife. Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'an, "And marry off the ayāmā among you" (Q24:32), as the attestation. The related verb āmat / taʾīmu, with the maṣdars ayma and uyūm, means "she became without a husband." A closing verse of poetic address to a woman named Fāṭima uses the imperative taʾayyamī ("become husbandless") and observes that "every woman becomes ayyim" eventually — i.e., every woman at some point ends up without a husband.

Grammatical note preserved from the entry: ayyim and aym are treated as a doubled/undoubled pair of the same word (like hayyin/hayn), not as separate roots.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
