text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ʾ-y-y (hamza–yāʾ–yāʾ) from two distinct origins.

1. Looking / waiting deliberately (النظر). The verb تَأَيَّا means to tarry, wait, or act unhurriedly. Shawāhid: a verse pairing "halt at the dwellings... and tarry, for you are not abased"; Labīd's line, glossed as "I departed unhurriedly"; and, per Ibn al-Aʿrābī, تَأَيَّيْتُ [الأمرَ] = "you waited for the moment it became possible" (with a verse of ʿAdī). Related: لَيْسَتْ هذه بدارِ تَئِيَّةٍ — "this is no place to stay."

2. Aiming at / purposing something (التعمّد). تَآيَيْتُ (pattern تفاعلت) means to aim deliberately at a thing's mark and figure ("with it I aim at every matter and parting").

From this second origin comes آية = a sign or mark (علامة). One says آيةٌ مَأْيَاةٌ, "a well-marked sign," parallel to علامةٌ معلَمة; and أَيَّيْتُ, "I set up a mark" (with a verse addressed to Banū Tamīm "by the sign that you love food").

Etymology/morphology of آية: its underlying form is said to be أَأْيَة (pattern أَعْيَة) with two hamzas; the second was lightened and stretched into a long vowel. Sībawayh judged its middle radical to be a wāw, on the statistical ground that roots of the shape wāw-then-yāʾ (e.g. شَوَيْتُ) are commoner than yāʾ-then-yāʾ ones (e.g. حَيِيتُ).

Additional recorded senses of آية:
- A person's figure or self (al-Aṣmaʿī: آيةُ الرجل = شخصُه).
- A whole company or group (al-Khalīl: خرج القومُ بآيتهم = "with their whole company," supported by a verse of Burj b. Mus'hir).
- On this last basis Ibn Fāris explains آية القرآن (a Qurʾānic āya) as "a group of letters"; its plural is آيٌ.

Finally, إياةُ الشمس = the sun's light/radiance, placed under this root because the sun's radiance functions like a mark or sign of it (with a supporting verse).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: the mother of Yazīd b. al-Ṭathriyya (Umayyad); unnamed verse ×2
text:
**Root ازف (a-z-f) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha**

Ibn Fāris assigns the root a single core idea: **nearness, drawing close**.

1. **To draw near, be imminent.** أَزِفَ الرَّحِيلُ — "the departure has drawn near," i.e. it has come close. He cites Qur'an 53:57, {أَزِفَتِ الْآزِفَةُ} ("the Impending has drawn near"), and glosses الآزفة as the Resurrection.

2. **مُتَآزِف (mutaʾāzif) — short, with a compact frame.** Ibn Fāris derives this from the same principle: the man's bodily parts are "close together." He cites a line by the mother of Yazīd b. al-Ṭathriyya describing a youth "cut to the cut of a sword — not *mutaʾāzif*, nor flabby in chest and shoulder-flesh," where the word stands opposite a lean, well-proportioned build.

   - **A disputed second reading.** Al-Shaybānī glossed *mutaʾāzif* as "narrow/mean of **character** (khuluq)" and quoted a verse in support ("large in the breast-bones, not *mutaʾāzif*… nor stiff-handed and squat"), in which مُجَذَّر means "short" and جَاذِي means "stiff/dry." Ibn Fāris rejects the inference: the verse says nothing about character (khuluq) — it is about **physical build** (khalq), and the poet meant simply "short." The distinction turns on the near-identical pair khuluq / khalq.

3. **تَآزَفَ الْقَوْمُ** — of people: to draw near one another, close the distance between them.

4. **أَزَفَ (transitive, form IV pattern in use) — to hurry someone.** On al-Shaybānī's authority: أَزَفَنِي فُلَانٌ, "so-and-so made me hasten"; imperfect يُؤْزِف, verbal noun إِيزَاف.

5. **مَأْزَفَة, plural مَآزِف — filthy places.** Illustrated by a line likening a man in his two cloaks to a dung-beetle snorting about such spots. Ibn Fāris ties this back to the root idea with a closing remark: such filth hardly collects except in a **narrow, confined** place — narrowness being a form of things being pressed close together.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats hamza-zāʾ-rāʾ (أزر) as a single-meaning root: "strength" and "intensity."

1. Verbal use — taʾazzara: said of a plant when it grows strong and thick/dense. He supports this with a line of poetry (transmitted via al-Qaṭṭān from Thaʿlab) describing vegetation grown so thick that the hillocks looked blurred/veiled and sheep sleeping in it were hidden from sight — vividly illustrating "strength/density" as abundant growth.

2. Nominal use — al-azr: simply "strength" or "power." He cites al-Baʿīth's line: "I braced my azr [my strength/support] for him with a resolute man's firm resolve, in a grave matter of his that had worsened" — azr here meaning the speaker's own strength/backing lent to someone in a difficult situation.

So the entire entry rests on one core sense, strength/intensity, shown first in a plant growing vigorous and dense, then as an abstract noun for personal strength or support lent to another.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
text:
Al-Zamakhsharī's Asās al-Balāgha entry for the root أزز (azz), which distinguishes literal from figurative (majāz) usage:

1. Core/literal sense — a seething, hissing sound: "the cooking-pot azzat" (boiled/seethed), and its azīz (أزيز) is the sound of its nashīsh — the sizzling/hissing noise it makes while cooking.

2. Extended to other loud droning or rumbling sounds:
 - "the azīz of thunder alarmed me" — a rumbling roar.
 - "the azīz and hazīz of the millstone split my head" — the whirring/grinding noise of a millstone, said to be head-splitting (i.e., headache-inducing).

3. Verb, transitive (azzahu ʿalā kadhā — "he azza'd him toward such-and-such"): to incite or goad someone into something, driving him to it through agitation or harassment (izʿāj).

4. Verb, reflexive (huwa yaʾtazzu min kadhā — "he yaʾtazzus from such-and-such"): to feel aggrieved and agitated/perturbed because of something.

5. Explicitly marked by al-Zamakhsharī as figurative (min al-majāz): "his belly/insides have an azīz" — a rumbling sound in the stomach, extending the "seething/hissing noise" sense metaphorically to the body.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḍ-ʾ-n (ضأن) as a sound, genuine triliteral root whose core sense is a kind of livestock — specifically sheep.

1. **Core noun**: الضَّأْن (al-ḍaʾn) = sheep (as a flock/kind of livestock).

2. **Verb usage**: one says أَضْأَنَ الرَّجُلُ (aḍʾana al-rajul), "the man became aḍʾan," said of a man whose sheep multiplied/became numerous — i.e. a denominative verb meaning "to come to have many sheep."

3. **Singular form**: الضَّائِنَة (al-ḍāʾina) is the singular of al-ḍaʾn — one ewe/sheep.

4. **Extended idiom (reported, not the author's own attestation)**: some transmitters relate the expression فُلَانٌ ضَائِنُ الْبَطْنِ (fulānun ḍāʾinu l-baṭn), "so-and-so is ḍāʾin of belly," explained as مُسْتَرْخِيهِ (mustarkhīhi) — meaning someone whose belly is slack or loose. This appears to extend the sheep-sense metaphorically to describe bodily slackness.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris groups ḍ-ḥ-k close to the preceding root-section and assigns it one core idea: uncovering and coming into view.

1. الضَّحِك (ḍaḥik) — laughter, the laughing of a human being. A variant vowelling الضَّحْك (ḍaḥk) also exists, but ḍaḥik is the more eloquent form.

2. الضَّاحِكَة (ḍāḥika) — any tooth, among the front teeth and molars, that becomes visible when one laughs.

3. Of clouds (from Ibn al-Aʿrābī): a ḍāḥik cloud is like a cloud on the horizon, except that when it flashes with lightning it is said "to laugh" (ḍaḥika) — the flash being a kind of showing-forth.

4. الضَّحُوك (ḍaḥūk) — a clear, plainly visible road.

5. أَضْحَكْتَ حَوْضَكَ ("you made your trough laugh") — you filled the watering-trough until it overflowed.

6. الضَّاحِك (ḍāḥik) (from Ibn Durayd) — a brightly glittering stone, of any color, that shows out in a mountain.

7. Laughter-related forms: الأُضْحُوكَة (uḍḥūka) = a thing laughed at; رَجُلٌ ضِحْكَة (ḍiḥka) = a man who is laughed at; ضُحَكَة (ḍuḥaka) = one who laughs often.

8. الضَّحْك (ḍaḥk) is also reported to mean honey, cited by a verse of poetry ("a blend... it is aḍ-ḍaḥk, except it is the work of bees"). It is likewise said to mean fresh dates (balaḥ). Al-Shaybānī: the palm-spathe (ṭalʿ) is both al-kāfūr and aḍ-ḍaḥk at the moment it splits open — again the sense of opening and emerging into view.

dictionary: ʿAyn — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786)
quran_words: ضُحًى 6x "by the morning brightness"; تَضْحَىٰ 1x "exposed to the sun's heat"
text:
Al-Khalīl's entry for the root ḌḤW, in his chapter grouping ḥāʾ and ḍād with the weak letters.

1. Times of the morning. الضَّحْو (al-ḍaḥw) is the day's rising; الضُّحى (al-ḍuḥā) is slightly later; and الضّحاء (al-ḍaḥāʾ, with a long ending) is when the day has drawn out and is nearly half gone. So the root marks a graded sequence of forenoon times, distinguished by vowel length.

2. Being struck by the sun. ضَحِيَ (ḍaḥiya) is for the sun's heat to fall on a person. The ʿAyn cites the Qur'anic phrase "you shall not thirst therein, nor taḍḥā" and glosses it: the sun's heat does not harm you. The imperative اضْحَ (iḍḥa) means "come out into the sun." Two conjugations are given: ḍaḥā / yaḍḥū / ḍuḥuwwan, and ḍaḥiya / yaḍḥā / ḍaḥan and ḍuḥiyyan.

3. The sun itself. الضّحاء (al-ḍaḥāʾ) is sometimes used as a name for the sun.

4. Doing something at the ḍuḥā hour. الأُضْحِية (al-uḍḥiya) is the animal offered in sacrifice, and ضَحِّ (ḍaḥḥi) is to offer it. أَضْحِ بصلاة الضُّحَى (aḍḥi bi-ṣalāt al-ḍuḥā) — with the verbal noun إضحاء (iḍḥāʾ) — is, in the entry's wording, to postpone that ṣalāt until the ḍuḥā has climbed high. نتضحَّى (nataḍaḥḥā) is to take the forenoon meal, equated with نتغدّى (nataghaddā).

5. Forenoon grazing. تَضَحَّتِ الإبِلُ (taḍaḥḥat al-ibil): the camels grazed from the day's beginning, paired against تعشّت (taʿashshat), grazing at night; hence the command ضَحْها وعَشِها ("pasture them morning and night").

6. The exposed outer part. الضّاحية (al-ḍāḥiya) of a town is its open, outward-facing side, contrasted with its interior (الجوّ / الباطنة, al-jaww / al-bāṭina): some people settle in the inner quarter, others in the ḍawāḥī, the outskirts. Likewise ضواحي الحوض (ḍawāḥī al-ḥawḍ) are the outer sides of a watering-basin — a poetic fragment ("...and no ḍawāḥī") is glossed simply as نواحي (nawāḥī, "sides").

7. A sun-exposed place. المضحاة (al-miḍḥāt): ground the sun scarcely ever leaves.

8. Openly, in plain view. فعلتُ ذلك ضاحيةً (faʿaltu dhālika ḍāḥiyatan) means doing something openly and manifestly. The text cites a verse: "There has come to us the going-down to the fire, ḍāḥiyatan (openly), truly and certainly, though the coming-back-up has not yet reached us."

9. Sacrifice vocabulary. الضَّحيّة (al-ḍaḥiyya) equals الأُضْحية (al-uḍḥiya), plural الضّحايا / الأضاحي (al-ḍaḥāyā / al-aḍāḥī): the sheep sacrificed on يوم الأضحى (yawm al-aḍḥā) at Minā and elsewhere. Kitāb al-ʿAyn adds a grammatical observation: the Arabs treat الأضحى (al-aḍḥā) as feminine.

10. Cloudless brightness. ليلة إضحيانة (laylatun iḍḥiyāna) and يوم إضحيان (yawmun iḍḥiyān): a night or day that is luminous, with no cloud in it.

Running through the entry is one image: full daylight — hence sunlight falling on a body, the hour when the sun has climbed, the outward and exposed side of a place, plain visibility, and cloudless brightness.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ض ب ح (ḍ-b-ḥ), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Two sound roots gathered under this spelling:

First — a sound. ḍabaḥa al-thaʿlab — a fox "ḍabaḥa," its cry called al-ḍubāḥ, illustrated with a line of poetry about a yelping fox-cub. The entry's central subject is Qur'an al-ʿAdiyat 100:1, "wa-l-ʿādiyāti ḍabḥan" — "by the racers, panting/breathing." Ibn Fāris weighs two readings: the more analogically sound one takes ḍabḥan as the sound of the racing horses' breath; an alternative reading takes it instead as a gallop faster than al-taqrīb, originally spelled ḍabaʿa ("to extend the forelegs to the fullest stride") — which, if correct, would make ḍabḥ a letter-substitution (bāʾ for ʿayn) of that word.

Second — color-change from fire. al-ḍabḥ — scorching the top/end of a stick with fire; al-ḍibḥ — ash; al-ḥijārah al-maḍbūḥah — flint-stones used for striking fire, so called because they look scorched, illustrated with a line of poetry about splintered, scorched flint-nodules. al-indibāḥ — the changing of a color to black.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris holds that ḍ-d gives two words that do not share a common derivational basis (qiyās).

**1. al-ḍidd (with i): the opposite.** The ḍidd of a thing is its opposite. Two things that are al-mutaḍāddān ("mutual opposites") cannot exist together at one and the same time, like night and day.

**2. al-ḍadd (with a): filling.** One says ḍadda l-qirba, "he filled the waterskin", with the verbal noun ḍadd.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: unnamed verse; Jarīr (Umayyad); Labīd ibn Rabīʿah (lived into Islam)
text:
Root: ḍ-f-d-ʿ — "frog." Not a Qur'an-specific term; this is a general lexical entry (Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr).

1. **Basic word and vocalizations.** The word for "frog" has two equally correct classical forms: ضِفْدِع (ḍifdiʿ, on the same vocalization pattern as "little finger") and ضَفْدَع (ḍafdaʿ). A third, less common form, ضِفْدَع (ḍifdaʿ), is also attested (al-Jawharī). The feminine is ḍifdiʿah/ḍafdaʿah.

2. **Grammatical note (al-Khalīl).** The vowel-pattern kasra-fatḥa-sukūn (fiʿlal) is very rare in Arabic — attested in only four words: dirham ("coin"), hijraʿ ("tall man"), hiblaʿ ("glutton"), qilʿam ("huge/old/tall"). This is cited because of the rarer ḍifdaʿ pronunciation just mentioned.

3. **Plural.** Normally ضَفادِع (ḍafādiʿ, "frogs"). Al-Azharī notes a poetic variant ضَفَادِي (ḍafādī), where the middle root-letter ʿ is swapped for a y — the same swap seen in arānī for arānib ("rabbits"). A citation is given: "and for the frogs of its pool there is croaking" (using this ḍafādī form).

4. **Idiom for hunger.** "The frogs of his belly croaked" (naqqat ḍafādiʿu baṭnihi) means a man became hungry — parallel to the idiom "the sparrows of his belly chirped," i.e. his stomach growled.

5. **Unrelated anatomical sense.** With a specific vocalization (ḍifdiʿ, kasra on the dāl), the same word names a bone on the underside of a horse's hoof — what is called in English the "frog" of the hoof.

6. **Denominal verb ḍafdaʿa.** Used of a man, it can mean: he shrank/huddled up in fear; or (two further glosses given) he defecated, or he broke wind — i.e. a euphemism for cowardly loss of bodily control. Illustrated with a line attributed to the poet Jarīr (with a manuscript note that his Dīwān has a slightly different word form): mocking the tribe of Mujāshiʿ as weak horsemen who "ḍafdaʿū" when they eat a meat-and-fat dish called khazīr.

7. **Poetic citation — Labīd.** A verse by the poet Labīd ibn Rabīʿah describes travelers heading to springs at Lubnā or Ajā that are muḍafdiʿāt ("frog-filled") and muṭaḥlibah ("moss/algae-covered") — Ibn Manẓūr glosses this simply as "waters abundant in frogs."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ضغن (ḍ-gh-n) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris gives this root one core meaning: covering/concealing something together with a leaning or crookedness — and he notes explicitly that this root never indicates anything good.

1. Rancor/malice: al-ḍighn/al-ḍaghan — the chief derived sense, meaning concealed ill-will or grudge (a heart that "covers" hidden hostility, matching the root's core image).

2. A horse called ḍāghin withholds its full running speed unless struck — its capability is "concealed" until forced out.

3. "So-and-so's chest ḍaghina" — harbored resentment.

4. A crooked spear-shaft is qanāh ḍaghina.

5. A she-camel "possessing ḍighn" strains and yearns toward her home territory when led away — restless longing, again framed as a kind of concealed pull.

6. Al-Khalīl (cited) applies the same word to a pregnant wild she-ass resisting the wild ass: she has shaghb (obstinacy) and ḍighn.

7. "So-and-so ḍaghana toward the world" — he leaned into worldly life; "my ḍighn is toward so-and-so" — my inclination is toward him. (Here the word carries a neutral "inclination" sense, without the negative charge of "rancor.")

8. The clearest evidence for the root's core sense of "covering": al-iḍṭighān means wrapping oneself in a garment — illustrated with a verse describing someone as though carrying a child wrapped against his side, and the phrase "I iḍṭaghantu the thing under my armpit." A verse of Ibn Muqbil uses the same verb for tucking a weapon at one's flank-strap.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḍ-gh-th as one root whose single idea is things being mixed up and tangled together, one part with another. From that core he lists:

1. **Jumbling a dream.** To a person who has dreamt one says aḍghathta al-ruʾyā — "you have muddled the vision." Correspondingly, aḍghāth are dreams that are confused and run together.

2. **A bundle held in the hand.** A ḍighth is a handful of twigs or of grass — i.e. stalks gathered and intermixed in one grip. He notes that al-Khalīl likewise took this as belonging to the one root.

3. **A she-camel of uncertain condition.** A nāqa ḍagūth is one whose fatness you are unsure of, so you feel her by hand to test whether she has ṭirq (flesh/fat, condition) — the sense of uncertainty and mixture again.

4. **Working a thing about by hand.** Ḍaghth is described as being like mars — soaking or kneading something and mixing it about.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
ROOT ضها / ضهأ (Ḍahā / Ḍahaʾa) — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr

Core sense: resemblance, matching one thing to another.

1. Al-muḍāhāh = to resemble or match something (also said with hamza, ضاهأ). "ضاهيتُ الرجل" = I resembled him — or, in another reading, I opposed/rivaled him. "فلان ضهيّ فلان" = so-and-so is the counterpart of so-and-so.

2. Qur'an 9:30, "يُضاهُونَ قَوْلَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِن قَبْلُ" (they resemble the saying of earlier disbelievers). Al-Farrā' glosses yuḍāhūn as yuḍāriʿūn — they echo the earlier disbelievers' saying (their calling on "al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā"); some Arabs read it with hamza (yuḍāhiʾūn), a reading of ʿĀṣim. Abū Isḥāq explains it as: they resembled the earlier disbelievers' saying, i.e. they said it only in imitation of them — citing as support the verse that they "took their rabbis and monks as lords besides God," meaning they accepted from them that the Messiah and ʿUzayr are sons of God.

3. Etymology (Abū Isḥāq): thought to derive from "امرأة ضهياء" — a woman whose breasts do not show, or (another view) who does not menstruate — so she resembles a man. A long technical discussion follows on the word's exact morphological pattern (is the hamza or the yā' the added letter; is it فَعْلأ or فَعْيَل, etc.), with scholars disagreeing on the fine details but generally accepting the derivation from "resemblance."

4. The noun الضَّهْياء / الضَّهْيأ (describing a woman) carries several overlapping senses across authorities: one whose breasts have not developed; one who does not menstruate; one who neither menstruates nor conceives (or conceives without menstruating). A variant form الضَّهْواء carries similar meanings. Plural: ضُهْي; verb: ضَهِيَتْ تَضْهَى ضَهًى. Two shawāhid illustrate the word: a woman's plea to al-Ḥajjāj describing herself as "al-ḍahyāʾ, al-dhannāʾ" regarding her imprisoned son, and a poetic exchange (poets before ʿAbd al-Malik, completed by al-Rāʿī) where "ḍahyāʾ" names a prized young she-camel.

5. الضَّهْياءُ من النُّوق — of she-camels, one that never goes into heat and has never conceived.

6. الضَّهْيا (without hamza) also has unrelated senses: barren land that grows nothing; or a very thorny shrub with reddish fodder and leaves like the samur tree (al-Jawharī records الضَّهْياء as the name of a different tree; Abū Zayd compares a form of it to the sayāl tree). "أضهى فلان" = his camels grazed on this fattening plant.

7. الضَّهْوة = a pool of water, plural أضْهاء (Abū ʿAmr).

8. "ضَهْيَأَ فلانٌ أمرَه" = he let a matter drag on unresolved, without deciding it (Ibn Buzurj).

9. "ضاهَأَ الرجلَ" = he was gentle/lenient with him (al-Umawī) — a separate sense recorded alongside "resemble."

10. Khālid ibn Janbah: al-muḍāhāh can also mean "to follow/imitate" — "فلان يضاهي فلانا" = he follows him.

11. A ḥadīth: "the people most severely punished on Judgment Day are those who yuḍāhūn God's creation" — explained as rivaling or opposing God's creative act through their own work; understood to refer to makers of images/sculptures.

12. ʿUmar's remark to Kaʿb, "ضاهيتَ اليهودية" (you have resembled Jewish practice), applies the same "resemble/parallel" sense to conduct.

13. ضُهاءٌ is recorded as a place name (with a supporting verse by a Hudhalī poet); Ibn Sīdah judges its hamza to represent an original yā' as the root's final letter, based on the parallel forms ضَهْيَأ and ضَهْياء.

Second heading, ضهأ:
14. "ضاهَأَ الرجلَ" = he was gentle with him (again, via al-Umawī).
15. المُضاهَأَة = resemblance — the same core sense as المُضاهاة above.
16. Ṣāḥib al-ʿAyn records both "ضاهأتُ الرجلَ" and "ضاهيتُه" for "I resembled him," with or without hamza, and notes the Qur'anic verse was read both ways.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḍ–j–ʿ as a single root whose core idea is lying flat against the ground on one's side; every other use, in his account, is carried over from that image.

1. Basic verb: ḍajaʿa, verbal noun ḍujūʿ — to lie down on one's side. The noun of a single instance is ḍajʿa (one lying-down). The form VIII iḍṭajaʿa (verbal noun iḍṭijāʿ) carries the same sense.

2. Derived persons and manner: ḍajīʿuka is the one who lies down beside you. Ḥasan al-ḍijʿa means "of goodly posture in lying down" — the fiʿla pattern here denoting the mode of an act, exactly as rikba denotes one's manner of riding.

3. Extended to slackness: ḍajjaʿa fī al-amr (form II) is to fall short in a matter — as though the person never took it up but lay down away from it. From the same idea, a man called ḍajūʿ is weak in judgement, and a ḍujaʿa is someone helpless who scarcely stirs from where he is.

4. Applied to animals: al-ḍajūʿ is a she-camel that grazes off to one side — stated again at the end of the entry as one that pastures apart and lies down alone. Al-ḍājiʿa and al-ḍajʿāʾ mean a large flock of sheep or goats; Ibn Fāris admits this belongs to the root only because such animals graze and then lie down.

5. Applied to weather and terrain: taḍajjaʿa al-saḥāb (form V) is said of clouds that settle and linger persistently over a place — a usage he locates in the poetry of the tribe of Hudhayl. An akama ḍajūʿ is a hillock that lies low, pressed against the ground.

6. Proper names from the root: al-Ḍujūʿ is one specific hillock, and al-Ḍawājiʿ is a place, cited from the poetic fragment "…Rākis, then al-Ḍawājiʿ."

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḍ-l(-l) as a sound root with one meaning: a thing being lost and going off where it ought not to go.

1. **Forms.** ḍalla has two dialectal present tenses, yaḍillu and yaḍallu. al-ḍalāl and al-ḍalāla mean the same thing.

2. **Straying from the course.** Anyone who swerves from the right, intended course is ḍāll, "astray." A man who is ḍillīl or muḍallal is one given to error and falsehood.

3. **Evidence for the core sense of loss.** Ibn Fāris supports his claim with usages where "going astray" plainly means "disappearing":
- uḍilla al-mayyit, "the dead man was made lost," means he was buried, as if he had gone missing. A verse speaks of the men who buried someone (his muḍillūn) returning with certainty, leaving resolve and generosity behind at al-Jawlān.
- ḍalla al-laban fī al-māʾ, "the milk was lost in the water," which is also expressed as "it was absorbed."

4. **Losing and failing to find (from Ibn al-Sikkīt).** aḍlaltu baʿīrī, "I lost my camel," is said when it has wandered away from you. ḍalaltu al-masjid wa-l-dār, "I could not find the mosque and the house," is said when you cannot find your way to them, and likewise of any fixed thing you cannot locate.

5. **Places of straying.** A land where people lose their way is maḍilla or maḍalla. "They fell into the valley of Tuḍullil" means they fell into such a place of straying.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḍ-m-m as a single root (aṣl wāḥid) whose meaning is a fitting-together (mulāʾama) of two things.

1. **Joining.** ḍamamtu l-shayʾa ilā l-shayʾ means "I joined one thing to another"; the present tense is aḍummuhu and the verbal noun is ḍamm.

2. **A group.** An iḍmāma of horses is a group of them, and a horse called sabbāq al-aḍāmīm is one that outruns the groups (aḍāmīm, the plural). An iḍmāma of books is like an iḍbāra, a bundle.

3. **The lion.** Ibn Fāris places here, under the same root, the lion called ḍamḍam and ḍumāḍim: one that gathers in (yaḍummu) everything.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris (Maqayis al-Lugha) says the root d-m-r has two distinct, sound senses:

1. Leanness / thinness of body
- damara (verb), dumur (verbal noun): said of a horse (or anything else) growing lean, from lightness of flesh, sometimes from wasting/emaciation.
- al-midmar: the training-ground where horses are conditioned down to leanness, i.e. a racecourse/training track.
- A man called damr: slight/light of body.
- al-lu'lu' al-mudtamir ('contracted pearl'): a pearl with a slight compression or dent in its middle.

2. Absence / concealment
- al-dimar: wealth or property that is absent and not expected to be recovered. More generally: anything absent from you that you cannot be sure of counts as dimar.
- He cites an anonymous verse about travel-worn camels made to kneel at a man named Sa'id's dwelling, arriving by night and leaving at dawn, praising the visit because what they received from him was a real gift, not merely a promise that stays unfulfilled ('idatan dimaran).
- From this same sense of concealment comes admartu fi damiri shay'an, 'I hid something in my damir [inner self]', because a person conceals such a thing in his heart and breast. This is the origin of damir as 'the hidden inner mind/conscience'.

Ibn Faris links the two senses only by their shared root-letters, not by a common underlying idea: one is physical (a body or object becoming thin/compressed), the other is abstract (something withheld from view or certainty, including one's inward thoughts).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris identifies the letters ḍ-n-k as forming two distinct, valid roots (with few derived words):

1. Narrowness / constriction
- aḍ-ḍank (الضَّنْكُ) — narrowness, constriction.
- imra'atun ḍināk (امرأةٌ ضِنَاكٌ) — a woman "compact/firm in flesh," so described because compacted flesh presses in on itself (the same idea of things being pressed tightly together underlies both words).

2. Sickness (specifically catarrh)
- al-maḍnūk (المَضْنُوكُ) — a person afflicted with catarrh (a head-cold).
- aḍ-ḍināk (الضِّنَاكُ) — the catarrh/head-cold itself.

He closes with the standard formula "wa-llāhu a'lam" ("God knows best"), signaling the entry's conclusion rather than adding content.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḍ-n as a sound root (aṣl ṣaḥīḥ) that indicates stinginess with a thing.

1. **To be grudging of something.** ḍanintu bi-l-shayʾ, aḍannu bihi: "I was grudging of the thing, I am grudging of it"; the verbal nouns are ḍann and ḍanāna. Sometimes the verb was said with a on the nūn instead of i (ḍananta, ضَنَنْتَ).

2. **The grudging man.** A rajul ḍanīn is a stingy man.

3. **A treasured thing.** A valued possession is called ʿilqu maḍanna or ʿilqu maḍinna when it is precious and one is grudging of it.

4. **A treasured friend.** fulānun ḍinnī min bayni ikhwānī, "so-and-so is my ḍinn among my brothers", is said of the precious one of whom one is grudging.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَتَضَرَّعُ 3x "humble themselves"; تَضَرُّع 3x "humbly"; تَضَرَّعُ 1x "they humbled themselves"; ضَرِيع 1x "a bitter thorny plant"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḍ-r-ʿ as a single sound root whose core idea is softness or pliancy in a thing. From that he derives the following senses:

1. **Lowliness, submission.** ḍaraʿa al-rajul, verbal noun ḍarāʿa — for a man to become abased or humble himself.

2. **Weakness in a person.** A rajul ḍaraʿ is a weak man. He cites a line of Ibn Waʿla contrasting patience with slackness: the speaker is "neither the slackener nor the weak, inexperienced one" (al-ḍaraʿ al-ghumr).

3. **The udder.** ḍarʿ of a ewe or other animal — named, on his account, for the softness in it.

4. **Milk coming down.** aḍraʿat al-nāqa: the she-camel's milk descends as her time to give birth approaches.

5. **Resemblance (muḍāraʿa).** Similarity between two things. He reports that some scholars derive this from ḍarʿ (udder) — as if the two resembling things had suckled from one and the same udder.

6. **Large-uddered.** A ewe described with the adjective from this root (the text here is defective; the expected form is ḍarʿāʾ), and also ḍarīʿa, means one with a big udder.

7. **Emaciated in body.** ḍāriʿ is said of someone thin or wasted. His witness is a saying of the Prophet about Jaʿfar's two sons: "Why is it that I see the two of them ḍāriʿayn?"

8. **Anomalous: al-ḍarīʿ, a plant.** He marks this as deviating from the chapter's core idea, then suggests it can still be brought under it: named for its weakness, since it "neither fattens nor avails against hunger." He closes with an unattributed verse picturing camels left in a stretch of ḍarīʿ growth, "every one of them hump-backed, with bleeding forelegs, scant of milk."

Method note: the entry works by positing one abstract sense (softness) and then showing each concrete usage — udder, milk-descent, humility, thinness, resemblance, a barren plant — as a specialisation of it, with an explicit flag when an item resists the derivation.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḍ-r-b (ضرب) as one root meaning — "to strike a blow" — from which every other sense is drawn by metaphor.

1. Core: ضَرَبَ = to strike, inflict a blow on another. رَجُلٌ مِضْرَب = a hard-hitting man. مَضْرِب السَّيْف = the striking-part of a sword.

2. Travel: الضَّرْب فِي الأَرْض = striking out into the land — journeying, for trade or otherwise. He cites Qur'an 4:101, "when you journey through the land, no blame to shorten the prayer." Related: swift travel is also ḍarb (poetic shāhid: scouts "striking" toward them with news); الطَّيْر الضَّوَارِب = birds ranging in search of food.

3. Minting / shaping (صِيغَة): الضَّرْب = a stamp or mould, because to form a thing is to "strike" it. Hence هَذَا مِنْ ضَرْبِ فُلَان = "of so-and-so's stamp." From this:
   - الضَّرِيب = the like or equal, as if two things struck from one mould.
   - الضَّرْب = a sort or kind (struck on the same pattern as its fellows).
   - الضَّرِيبَة = innate character/nature, as if a person were cast in that mould.

4. Things "struck" onto something:
   - الضَّرِيب = hoarfrost/rime (as if the sky struck the earth with it); the frost-bitten thing is مَضْرُوب (poetic shāhid supplied).
   - الضَّرِيب of milk = fresh milk mixed into curdled, one struck upon the other.
   - الضَّرِيب = honeycomb, as if formed (struck) by bees.
   - الضَّرَب = thick honey, as if struck (compare nafaḍ, the shaken-off thing).

5. Imposition: الضَّرِيبَة = a levy imposed on a person — jizya (tribute) and the like — "struck" upon him. Likewise ضَرَبَ عَلَى يَدِ فُلَان = to place under interdiction/restraint, as if striking down a hand reaching out.

6. Restraint / desisting: أَضْرَبَ عَنِ الأَمْر = to turn away from, desist — from the idea of holding back. Abū Zayd's reported أَضْرَبَ الرَّجُلُ فِي بَيْتِه ("he kept to his house") follows the same analogy.

7. Animal breeding: ضِرَاب الفَحْل = the stud covering the she-camel; أَضْرَبْتُ النَّاقَة = I set the stallion to her.

8. Gaming arrows: الضَّرِيب = the man entrusted with the qidāḥ (gambling arrows), named as a companion of the one who casts them (like qaʿīd, jalīs, "seat-mate").

9. Further metaphors: a lean, light-bodied man is ضَرْب, likened to the lightness of a blow (poetic shāhid); الضَّارِب = a broad open stretch in a valley, as if a track "striking" through it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَضُرَّ 19x "will they harm"; ضُرّ 19x "the adversity"; ضَرّ 10x "any harm"; ضَرَّاء 9x "and hardship"; ٱضْطُرَّ 7x "(is) forced"; يُضَارَّ 3x "harm them"; ضَارّ 2x "at all [be those who] harm"; ضِرَار 2x "(to) hurt"; مُضَارّ 1x "(being) harmful"; ضَّرَر 1x "[the] disabled"; مُضْطَرّ 1x "(to) the distressed one"
text:
Ibn Fāris says ḍ-r-r goes back to three root meanings (uṣūl): the opposite of benefit, the gathering together of a thing, and strength.

**I. The opposite of benefit**

1. **Harm.** Al-ḍarr is the opposite of benefit (nafʿ): ḍarrahu yaḍurruhu ḍarran, "he harmed him." Ibn Fāris says everything of the same kind as this, or close to it, is then carried over onto this meaning.

2. **Emaciation.** Al-ḍurr is bodily wasting (huzāl).

3. **Marrying onto a co-wife.** Al-ḍirr is a woman's being married to a man who already has a wife: "she was married ʿalā ḍirr," that is, onto a woman who was there before her. Al-Aṣmaʿī gives both ʿalā ḍurr and ʿalā ḍirr. He says iḍrār means the same, and such a man is muḍirr.

4. **The co-wife (ḍarra).** Ibn Fāris derives ḍarra from ḍarr (harm), as though each co-wife harms the other just as the other harms her. The two stones of a hand-mill are likened to two co-wives and so are called al-ḍarratān.

5. **Necessity.** Iḍṭarra, "to be driven to something," comes from ḍarūra, necessity. Poets also use the form ḍārūra, as Ibn al-Dumayna does: "Reward a man in dire need (akhā ḍārūra), over whom even enemies have grown pitying, and whose excuses before a true friend have grown few."

6. **Mutual harm, jealousy.** Al-ḍarīr is mutual harming (muḍārra), used mostly of jealousy: "how fierce is his jealous harshness over her!"

7. **The blind or wasted.** Al-ḍarīr is also someone harmed by the loss of his sight or by the wasting of his body.

**II. Gathering together**

8. **Udder and thumb.** Ḍarrat al-ḍarʿ is the flesh of the udder. Abū ʿUbayd defines al-ḍarra as the udder that is never empty of milk, and Ibn Fāris says it is so named because it is gathered together. Ḍarrat al-ibhām is the flesh gathered beneath the thumb.

9. **Abundant wealth.** A muḍirr is someone who has a ḍarra, a gathered mass, of property. The word describes much wealth, as in the verse: "It is enough for you among the people that they know that among them you are rich, muḍirr."

**III. Strength**

10. **Endurance.** Al-ḍarīr is strength of soul. "So-and-so is dhū ḍarīr in a matter" means he has the endurance to bear its hardship. Jarīr uses it, in a verse quoted only in part: "… boldness and endurance (ḍarīr)."

11. **A horse on the bit.** Of a horse one says aḍarra ʿalā faʾs al-lijām when it clamps down on the bit-bar of its bridle.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḍ-w-ʾ as a single sound root whose one meaning is light.

1. Core sense — light. The nouns الضَّوْء (ḍawʾ) and الضُّوء (ḍūʾ) are two vocalisations of the same word, meaning the same thing: light, equivalent to ضِيَاء (ḍiyāʾ, radiance) and نُور (nūr, light).

2. Qur'anic witness. He cites 2:17, "and when it lit up what was around him" (fa-lammā aḍāʾat mā ḥawlahu), for the verb form.

3. Grammatical note on the fourth-form verb أَضَاءَ. On the authority of Abū ʿUbayd, the verb works both ways: أَضَاءَتِ النَّارُ, "the fire shone" (no object — the thing itself gives light), and أَضَاءَتْ غَيْرَهَا, "it lit up something else" (taking an object).

4. Poetic witness for the transitive use, quoted by Abū ʿUbayd: "The fire lit up for us a radiant face, entangled with the heart in deep entanglement."

The entry is brief and records no sense for this root other than light and illumination.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḍ-y-ʿ (ضيع) as a single sound root meaning the loss, disappearance, and perishing of a thing.

1. Core sense: ضَاعَ (ḍāʿa, imperfect yaḍīʿu) = "to be lost, to slip away, to perish," with the verbal nouns ḍayāʿ and ḍayʿa. The causative أَضَاعَ / أَضَعْتُ (aḍāʿa / aḍaʿtu) = "to cause something to be lost, to let it go to waste."

2. On ḍayʿa meaning "estate / landed property": Ibn Fāris judges this usage not to be part of the original language but a later coinage (muḥdath). He notes a report that an estate is called ḍayʿa because, left untended, it is "lost" (ḍāʿat) — which, if true, he takes as further proof that the sense is a later development, not root-original.

3. أَضَاعَ فَهُوَ مُضِيعٌ (aḍāʿa, so he is muḍīʿ) = a person who wastes or neglects much, when his losses grow many.

4. A note on substitution (ibdāl): al-Shammākh's verse ("O ʿĀʾisha...") uses a related-looking word that does not actually belong to this root. Ibn al-Sikkīt records تَضَيَّعَتِ الرِّيحُ (taḍayyaʿat al-rīḥ, "the scent diffused") as a variant of تَضَوَّعَتْ (taḍawwaʿat) — a case of yāʾ substituting for wāw, so it belongs to a different root.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: ضَيْف 5x "(of the) guests"; يُضَيِّفُ 1x "offer them hospitality"
poets_named: Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); Abū Zubayd (Umayyad); al-Farazdaq (Umayyad); unnamed verse ×5
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḍ-y-f as a single sound root whose one meaning is: one thing inclining or leaning toward another. Everything else in the entry is derived from that.

1. Inclining, leaning, propping. أَضَفْتُ الشَّيْءَ إِلَى الشَّيْءِ — "I made one thing lean toward another." Of the sun, ضَافَتْ / تَضَيَّفَتْ means it inclined, specifically toward setting; he cites a ḥadīth forbidding the ṣalāh when the sun has so inclined toward setting. Imruʾ al-Qays: "when we entered it, we propped our backs against every new striped Ḥīran cushion" — aḍafnā here = we leaned/propped.

2. Swerving aside. ضَافَ السَّهْمُ عَنِ الْهَدَفِ — the arrow veered off the target. Abū Zubayd: a volley either hits, "or swerved aside, not far off."

3. Guest and host — from the same inclining. ضِفْتُ الرَّجُلَ = I presented myself to a man so he would take me in; أَضَفْتُهُ and ضَيَّفْتُهُ = I lodged him with me; يَتَضَيَّفُ النَّاسَ = he trails after people so they will host him (al-Farazdaq speaks of "the guest-seeker who hopes for his bounty"). Grammatical note: ضَيْف serves for both singular and plural, and also takes the plurals أَضْيَاف and ضِيفَان.

4. Side, flank, and closing in from the sides. ضِيف is the side of a valley; the dual ضِيفَانِ is its two sides. تَضَايَفْنَا الْوَادِيَ = we came at the valley from both its sides; تَضَايَفَ الْكِلَابُ الصَّيْدَ = the dogs came at the quarry from its flanks ("a white antelope closed in on by low-necked dogs"). تَضَيَّفُوهُ = they converged on him from all sides ("when they closed in on him from the sides, he slipped away").

5. الْمُضَاف: the man surrounded/hemmed in during battle — "he protects the beset man when he calls out, when the thick-maned one flees." Ibn Fāris counts this under the same analogy of being pressed from the sides.

6. ضَيْفَة in the verse about a castaway conceived while his mother "was a ḍayfa" is, he says, simply the ordinary word from ضِيَافَة (being a guest).

7. Rejected sense: some claim ضَافَتِ الْمَرْأَةُ means a woman menstruated. Ibn Fāris dismisses this outright — no analogy supports it and it is not worth pursuing.

8. Anomalous sense: أَضَافَ مِنَ الشَّيْءِ = he dreaded something. He judges this shādhdh (irregular) relative to the root's core meaning. He records a possible forced derivation — as though the fearful man has gone off to the ḍīf, the side, rather than keeping to the middle — but calls it far-fetched and prefers simply to class it as anomalous; the usage itself is well attested ("the reproach was that you should dread and cry aloud"; a Hudhalī verse where تُضِيفُ = she is apprehensive).

9. Abū Saʿīd's report: ضَافَ الْهَمُّ, of anxiety descending on a person. Ibn Fāris brings it back to the root: what descends upon someone has inclined toward him.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
quran_words: ضَاقَ 7x "and (was) straitened"; ضَيِّق 2x "tight"; ضَيْق 2x "distress"; ضَائِق 1x "and straitened"; تُضَيِّقُ 1x "to distress"
text:
Root ض ي ق (Ḍ-Y-Q), as recorded by Ibn Manẓūr in Lisān al-ʿArab.

Core sense: ضِيق (ḍīq) is the opposite of "roominess" — narrowness, straitness.

1. Verb forms. ضاقَ ("became narrow"), with verbal nouns ḍīq and ḍayq; also the reflexive taḍayyaqa / taḍāyaqa ("grew narrow"). Transitive: ḍayyaqa ("made narrow"); Ibn Jinnī also records aḍāqa. A "straitened matter" is amr ḍayyiq.

2. ḍayq vs. ḍīq (per Abū ʿAmr and al-Farrāʾ). ḍayq is the narrow thing itself; ḍīq is the abstract verbal noun. Al-Farrāʾ refines this: ḍayq is what constricts the breast (emotional), while ḍīq is narrowness in something that physically expands and contracts, like a house or a garment. maḍīq = a narrow place; plural maḍāyiq.

3. Extended senses.
 - ḍayqa / ḍayqāt: poverty and hard circumstances (al-Aʿshā: God "lifted the ḍayqa [hardship] from us").
 - ḍāqa (of a person) = became miserly.
 - Idiom ḍiqtu bihi dharʿan ("my capacity for it was straitened") = to be unable to bear something.
 - taḍāyaqa l-qawm = people who make no room for one another, in temperament or in space.
 - "In so-and-so's breast is ḍīq against us" = ill-feeling.

4. Doubt. ḍayq (variant ḍayaq, with a vowel on the y) can mean the doubt that arises in the heart — cited for Qurʾan 16:127, "Be not in ḍayq over what they scheme." Ibn Manẓūr notes ḍayq is the commoner form for this sense.

5. Grammar and morphology.
 - Adjectives for a narrow place: ḍayyiq, ḍayq, and ḍāʾiq.
 - ḍāqa is given as the plural of ḍāʾiq (Zuhayr's line "narrow of resting-ground"), on the pattern of sāda as plural of sāʾid.
 - Superlative feminine "narrowest" appears as ḍīqā and ḍūqā (the y shifts to w after a ḍamma). ḍūqā is fuʿlā from ḍīq (originally ḍuyqā), paralleling khūrā from "good" and kūsā from "cleverness." Kurāʿ took ḍūqā as a plural of ḍayyaqa; Ibn Sīda doubts this, since fuʿlā is not normally a plural pattern.
 - Qurʾanic shāhid for the adjective: Qurʾan 11:12, "...and your breast being straitened (ḍāʾiq) by it."
 - When ḍayq stands where ḍīq is expected, it is explained either as a plural of ḍayqa or as a lightened form of ḍayyiq (like hayn, layn from hayyin, layyin).

6. Livelihood. aḍāqa (so one is muḍīq) = one's living became straitened, or one's wealth ran out.

7. Astronomical sense. ḍīqa is the gap between two stars, and specifically two small stars close together between the Pleiades (al-Thurayyā) and Aldebaran (al-Dabarān). As al-Ḍīqa it names a lunar station beside the Pleiades toward Aldebaran, reckoned by the Arabs an unlucky spot. Al-Akhṭal alludes to it (a beautiful woman wed to an ugly man, "the night you came... at Ḍīqa between the Najm and the Dabarān"). Ibn Qutayba (from Abū Ziyād al-Kilābī): the moon sometimes falls short of Aldebaran and lodges at this Ḍīqa. Abū Manṣūr notes al-Akhṭal treats Ḍīqa as an undeclined proper name of the place, whereas Abū ʿAmr read it as a common adjective, "the narrowness between the Najm and Aldebaran." ḍayqa / ḍīqa can also denote the moon itself.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḍ-y-r as a single-meaning root: its three letters (ḍād, yā', rā') all trace back to one underlying sense, which he equates with al-ḍayr and al-maḍarra — "harm."

1. Core sense: to harm, to cause injury. The verb yaḍīru is given as equivalent to yaḍurru ("to harm"): "lā yaḍīrunī kadhā" = "lā yaḍurrunī" — "such-and-such does not harm me."

2. Qur'anic citation: he cites Q3:120 (Āl ʿImrān), "And if you are patient and are mindful [of God], their scheming will not harm you (lā yaḍurrukum) at all," as the attested instance grounding this sense of harm.

The entry is brief and gives no further senses or derivational notes beyond identifying ḍ-y-r as synonymous in effect with ḍ-r-r ("harm").

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris notes up front that this root (Ḍ-Y-Z) has already been discussed once before, under the root with wāw (و) — since some say ḍ-y-z actually derives from ḍ-w-z. Others, however, class it among the yāʾ-type weak roots, so he repeats it here as well, under yāʾ.

1. Core sense — qisma ḍīzā ("a ḍīzā division/share"): a deficient apportionment, i.e. a share that shortchanges someone, an unjust division.

2. Verb usage — ḍiztuhu ḥaqqahu, "I denied him his right": used when you withhold something owed to someone.

3. Variant form — some transmitters report the hamzated form ḍaʾaza with the same meaning, supporting it with a line of verse: "so your right is denied [maḍʾūz], and your nose is humbled" — i.e., you are cheated of what is due you and left disgraced.

Ibn Fāris closes by stating that this chapter contains nothing beyond this single sense.

poets_named: Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad); unnamed verse; Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); Zuhayr (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ʿ-sh-r from two sound bases: (I) a specific number — "ten" — which is then extended to other things, and (II) mingling and entering-into.

ROOT I — "ten" and its extensions

1. Core numeral: عَشَرَة "ten" (masc.), عَشْر (fem.).
2. To make/become the tenth: عَشَرْتُ الْقَوْم = "I became their tenth"; كُنْتُ عَاشِرَ عَشَرَةٍ = "I was the tenth of ten," i.e. they were nine and I made them ten.
3. Taking a tenth: عَشَرْتُ الْقَوْم also = "I took a tenth (عُشْر) of their wealth" (also عَشَّرَ, تَعْشِير); hence the tithe-collector is called الْعَشَّار.
4. A tenth-part: الْعُشْر = one part of ten; synonyms الْعُشَيْر, الْمِعْشَار.
5. Camel-watering cycle: الْعِشْر = camels coming to water on the tenth day; إِبِل عَوَاشِر = camels watering at that interval. Dual/plural عِشْرَان, عِشْرُون, each ʿishr being counted as nine days. (Shāhid: Dhū al-Rumma, on sandgrouse watering at a five-day interval, khīms.)
6. Distributive "ten by ten": per al-Khalīl, عُشَارَ عُشَارَ / مَعْشَرَ مَعْشَرَ, parallel to أُحَادَ أُحَادَ ("one by one") and مَثْنَى مَثْنَى ("two by two"); Ibn Fāris adds مَوْحَدَ مَوْحَدَ as valid though al-Khalīl omitted it.
7. Donkey's bray: تَعْشِير الْحِمَار — al-Khalīl says الْمُعَشِّر is a loud-braying donkey, reportedly so called because it brays up to ten times in succession. Ibn Fāris accepts it only on the authority of the transmitters, noting it is analogically sound if the report is true. (Shāhid supplied.)
8. Pregnant she-camel: نَاقَة عُشَرَاء = one near delivery, named for completing ten months of pregnancy; she stays ʿushrāʾ until she gives birth. Plurals عُشَرَاوَات (counted), عِشَار. An alternative account: عِشَار covers she-camels some already delivered and some awaiting delivery; these have no milk and are called ʿishār only because they are newly delivered (maṭāfīl). (Shawāhid from an unnamed poet and al-Farazdaq.)
9. Broken fragments: الْعُشْر = a shard breaking off a cup or pot. Al-Khalīl notes the singular عِشْر is rarely used; قُدُور أَعْشَار / أَعَاشِير = "pots [broken] into ten pieces." Extended to a shattered heart (Imruʾ al-Qays: "the shattered pieces — أَعْشَار — of a slain heart") and to a broken sword-sheath (أَعْشَار).
10. Length: الْعُشَارِيّ = something ten cubits long.
11. Calendar: عَاشُورَاء = the tenth day of al-Muḥarram (given here simply as a date).

ROOT II — mingling / association

12. الْعِشْرَة, الْمُعَاشَرَة = keeping company, association. عَشِير = one who associates with you. Al-Khalīl: no heard plural for ʿashīr — they use مُعَاشِرُون instead.
13. عَشِيرَة (kin-group) is so named from members' mutual association; even a husband is his wife's عَشِير. Cited in a hadith about women: "you curse much and are ungrateful to the ʿashīr [companion/husband]" (reported by the author).
14. عَاشَرَهُ مُعَاشَرَةً جَمِيلَة = kept fine company. (Shāhid: Zuhayr, on long companionship breeding weariness.)
15. الْمَعْشَر = any group united in one affair — e.g. "the maʿshar of the Muslims"; mankind is one maʿshar and the jinn another; plural مَعَاشِر.
16. Homonym noted in passing: الْعُشَر = a [named] plant.

poets_named: al-Ḥuṭayʾa (lived into Islam); unnamed verse; al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); Zuhayr (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Fāris takes the root ʿ-sh-w (ʿayn, shīn, and a weak final letter) as a single sound root meaning darkness and lack of clarity in a thing; the other senses branch out from this core.

1. ʿishāʾ — the first darkness of nightfall. ʿashwāʾ al-layl is the night's darkness. The verb ʿashawtu ilā nārihi means to grope one's way toward a fire in the dark — used only of blundering toward it through darkness (shāhid: al-Ḥuṭayʾa, on coming to a generous man's fire). al-ʿāshiya is anything that moves by night toward firelight.

2. al-taʿāshī — feigning ignorance, pretending not to notice something (shāhid: a verse mocking one who treats such feigned blindness in her religion as "guidance").

3. al-ʿashiyy — the end of the day (late afternoon/evening). The feminine ʿashiyya refers to one specific day's evening ("I met him on the evening of such-and-such a day"). Ibn Fāris notes al-Khalīl restricted ʿashiyya to a single day, but Ibn Fāris holds the more correct view is that ʿashiyy works the same way as ʿashiyya, since ʿashiyy simply means the end of the day. It is also said that everything after the sun's decline (zawāl) is ʿashiyy. Diminutive: ʿushayshiya.

4. al-ʿashāʾ (lengthened, hamzated, ʿayn vowelled with a) — the meal eaten at the end of the day and start of the night (supper).

5. al-ʿashā (shortened form) — per al-Khalīl, the verbal noun of al-aʿshā: night-blindness. Such a person sees by day but not by night; feminine ʿashwāʾ, plural ʿushw; verb ʿashiya / yaʿshā / ʿashan (shāhid: al-Aʿshā).

6. al-ʿashwāʾ of she-camels — one that appears not to see what is ahead and so tramples/blunders into everything with her forelegs; said to result from the keenness of her heart. Zuhayr's famous line likens the fates (al-manāyā) to the random trampling of such a night-blind she-camel — whom they strike they kill, whom they miss lives to grow old. Hence the idiom innahum la-fī ʿashwāʾ min amrihim ("they are in blind confusion about their affair").

quran_words: عَذَاب 322x "the punishment"; عَذَّبَ 41x "he will punish you"; مُعَذِّب 4x "punish them"; مُعَذَّبِين 4x "will be punished"; عَذْب 2x "(is) fresh"
poets_named: Nābigha al-Jaʿdī (lived into Islam); unnamed verse; Zuhayr (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Fāris opens by noting that this root (ʿ-dh-b) is a genuine, sound root, but unusually its words do not follow analogy and cannot be reduced to one underlying meaning — which, he says, proves that language as a whole is not governed by analogy, even though most of it is. He then lays out five separate, unrelated "chapters" of usage:

1. Sweetness of water. عَذُبَ الْمَاءُ (ʿaḏuba, verbal noun ʿuḏūba) = the water became sweet/pleasant; the adjective is عَذْب (ʿaḏb, "sweet"). أَعْذَبَ الْقَوْم = the people's water became sweet; اسْتَعْذَبُوا = they drew and drank sweet water.

2. Abstaining from food through thirst. عَذَبَ الْحِمَار (ʿaḏaba, of a donkey) = it stopped eating from severe thirst; the animal is عَاذِب / عَذُوب. By extension أَعْذَبَ عَنِ الشَّيْء = he desisted from a thing and left it; cited in a ḥadīth, "Refrain (aʿḏibū) from the mention of women," and in a verse using أَعْذِبُوا for "desist." A horse (or other animal) that spends the night neither eating nor drinking is called عَذُوب, because it holds itself back.

3. Being exposed to the open sky. عَذُوب / عَاذِب = that which has no covering between it and the sky. Ibn Fāris cites Nābigha al-Jaʿdī (a beast lying under the bare sky "like Suhayl [Canopus] when the other stars leave it alone") and a second verse ("We passed the night exposed while gnats stung us…"), noting the second could mean either "no cover from the sky" (this sense) or "spending the night without food or drink" (sense 2). He adds al-Khalīl's report that عَذَّبْتُهُ = "I weaned him" (faṭamtuhu), which Ibn Fāris files under the idea of being kept from food and drink.

4. Torment / punishment (al-ʿaḏāb). The verb is عَذَّبَ (ʿaḏḏaba, "to torment"). Ibn Fāris reports that some hold the original sense of ʿaḏāb to be "striking/beating," citing Zuhayr (a beast that "when she fears the ʿaḏāb [the beating] stretches out her back and neck"), and that the word was then extended metaphorically to any hardship. He gives this as others' view, not as established fact.

5. Whip-tip and related tips. عَذَبَة = the thong at the tip of a whip (plural عَذَب), with a supporting verse. عَذَبَة also names the tip of a camel's rod. Finally, الْعُذَيْب is a place-name.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَعْتَذِرُ 5x "make excuse"; مَعْذِرَة 3x "their excuse"; عُذْر 2x "(as) justification"; مُعَذِّرُون 1x "the ones who make excuses"; مَعَاذِير 1x "his excuses"
text:
Ibn Fāris opens by stating a method-point: the root ʿ-dh-r has many branches but no single unifying meaning — each cluster stands on its own, so he treats them as separate "sections."

1. Excuse / apology (al-ʿudhr). The core, well-known sense: a person's attempt, by speech, to set right something for which he has been blamed. ʿadhartuhu = "I excused/exonerated him." The idiom ʿadhartuhu min fulān = "I held him blameless and blamed the other"; man yaʿdhirunī minhu = "who will take my side against him?" A poet: "I want his gift, he wants my death — take up your plea against your friend of Murād."
   - ʿadhīr can also mean the thing a man aims at and is excused for doing. Al-Khalīl's anecdote: al-ʿAjjāj, mending his saddle for a trip, tells his wife not to "disapprove of my ʿadhīr," i.e. don't deny what I'm attempting.
   - Verb of apologizing: iʿtadhara ("he made excuse for his sin"); noun al-maʿdhira. Qur'anic shāhid: "qālū maʿdhiratan ilā rabbikum" — "as an excuse before your Lord" (7:164). aʿdhara = "he gave a valid excuse and escaped blame."
   - ʿadhdhara (form II) = to make a show of exerting oneself while actually slacking. Qur'anic shāhid: "wa jāʾa al-muʿadhdhirūn mina al-aʿrāb" (9:90), with a variant reading al-muʿdhirūn. Grammarians: al-muʿdhirūn (light) = those with a genuine excuse; al-muʿadhdhirūn = those with no excuse who fake one. Ibn Fāris regards even the "one who falls short" (muʿadhdhir) as still tied to ʿudhr, since he slacks by leaning on an excuse.

2. Proving difficult (taʿadhdhara al-amr) — a matter that "does not go right." Shāhid from Imruʾ al-Qays: she "proved hard against me and swore an unbreakable oath."

3. The bridle's cheek-strap (al-ʿidhār) — also any lengthwise brand or scratch on the cheeks. ʿadhartu al-faras = "I bridled the horse"; aʿdhartu al-lijām = "I fitted it with a cheek-strap." Figurative extension: of a man plunged into wrongdoing, khalaʿa al-ʿidhār — "he cast off the cheek-strap" (threw off restraint).

4. A celebration meal (al-ʿidhār) given on a happy occasion; verb aʿdharū. Said specifically to be the circumcision feast: ʿudhira al-ghulām = "the boy was circumcised"; two people "of one year's ʿidhār" were circumcised the same year.

5. al-ʿadhawwar — per al-Khalīl, wide-bellied and fiercely biting (of a donkey); used figuratively for broad, expansive dominion (a poet praising a "spacious ʿadhawwar kingdom"), and, in another verse, for a host bustling ill-temperedly until the cooking-pots are ready.

6. al-ʿudhra — the maidenhead; a girl ʿadhrāʾ is one no man has touched. Ibn Fāris links this to the "ʿudhra" of circumcision in sense 4.

7. al-ʿudhra — a throat ailment; the sufferer is maʿdhūr. Shāhid from Jarīr comparing a squeeze to "the physician pressing the throat-glands of the maʿdhūr."

8. al-ʿUdhra — a star whose rising brings fierce heat: "when al-ʿUdhra rises, not an unripe date is left in ʿUmān."

9. al-ʿudhra — a lock of hair, and a horse's forelock/mane-tuft.

10. al-ʿadhira — the forecourt of a house. Ḥadīth: "the Jews are the foulest of creatures in ʿadhira," i.e. in their courtyard. Excrement later came to be called ʿadhira because it used to be thrown into the forecourts.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-ḍ-ḍ as one sound root: holding on to a thing with the teeth. Everything that resembles this, he says, is named from it by analogy, so that what is severe, what is hard and the cunning man are all called by words of this root.

1. **Biting.** The primary use is biting with the teeth: ʿaḍiḍtu, aʿaḍḍu ("I bit, I bite"), with the verbal nouns ʿaḍḍ and ʿaḍīḍ; the biter is ʿāḍḍ, and a dog or a horse given to biting is ʿaḍūḍ. One declares oneself "clear of ʿiḍāḍ", biting as a fault in an animal; Ibn Fāris notes that most faults of riding animals take the pattern fiʿāl, like khirāṭ (pulling free of the halter) and nifār (bolting).

2. **Attacking a person.** By extension, "you bit the man" means you set upon him with what is improper.

3. **Something to eat.** Al-Naḍr reports "we have no ʿaḍāḍ", nothing to bite, just as maḍāgh is what is chewed. Ibn al-Aʿrābī reports "I have not tasted ʿaḍāḍ", anything to eat.

4. **Harshness and difficulty.** A "biting time" is severe and ravening: "To you I complain of a biting time; whoever escapes it comes away broken." A "biting well" is one so deep that drawing water from it is hard on the one who draws; a verse speaks of spending the night at "the biting water". A "biting bow" is one whose string clings to its middle.

5. **Kinds of person called ʿiḍḍ.** Al-Khalīl gives a man of bad, objectionable character, as in "I was never a ʿiḍḍ among the drinking-companions, much blamed." It also names a person of cunning, "a ʿiḍḍ from whom nothing slips away", explained as the tight-fisted one who bites down on whatever falls into his hand; it is likewise said that al-ʿiḍḍ is the cunning one among men, with a verse on the many tales of ʿĀd and Jurhum stirred up by "the two ʿiḍḍs, Zayd and Daghfal". "A ʿiḍḍ of evil" is a man given to evil, its companion. For Abū Zayd, "a ʿiḍḍ of travel" or "a ʿiḍḍ of property" is one strong at it and experienced in it, and the verb is ʿaḍḍa bi-mālihi ("he bit on his property"), verbal noun ʿuḍūḍ. For al-Farrāʾ, a ʿiḍḍ man, and a ʿiḍḍa woman, is defiant and rebellious (mārid). Finally, "this one is that one's ʿiḍḍ" means his equal and his match.

6. **An outlier.** Ibn Fāris lists as departing from the root, "if it is authentic", al-ʿuḍḍāḍ, the bridge of the nose, cited in a verse about one bridled "with the bit-iron of humiliation" who "lowered his eyes over the ʿuḍḍāḍ of a cropped nose".

7. **Fodder and thorn-trees.** Ibn Fāris says he has already said enough about the plant names in this root, but records several reports. Al-ʿuḍḍ (with u) is the fodder of villagers and townspeople: date-stones, qatt (dried fodder) and the like; al-Aʿshā describes choice white camels "hardened by ʿuḍḍ, by grazing the reserved pasture, and by long barrenness". Al-Shaybānī says al-ʿuḍḍ is fodder. Others say it is the thorn-trees ṭalḥ, samur and salam, which are called the ʿiḍāh.

Al-Farrāʾ says people are muʿiḍḍūn when they pasture on the ʿiḍāh, as in the verse "my people pasturing on arāk, hers muʿiḍḍūn: if she moves on, how shall I go?" The entry explains that this is allowed only because the ʿiḍāh are trees, not herbage, so camels that stay in one place on them are like animals fed at home on date-stones, ʿuḍḍ being the fodder of the farmland. Only on this interpretation may muʿiḍḍ be formed from ʿiḍāh; properly, a muʿiḍḍ is one whose camels eat ʿuḍḍ. Some say al-ʿiḍḍ (with i) is the ʿiḍāh.

A camel is called ghāḍ when it is fed it or pastured on it. A verse addresses a man who threatens the poet and walks about between ṭaylasān-cloaks and white garments: the poet does not know whether he is "a camel of ʿuḍḍ, swollen in the neck-glands and coarse of lip, or a ghāḍ camel". Abū ʿAmr says al-ʿuḍḍ is barley and wheat. The verse is explained this way: ʿuḍḍ is the fodder of the towns and ghaḍā the fodder of the desert, so the poet is saying he does not know whether the man is an Arab or a hajīn, one of mixed descent.

8. **Back to gripping.** A woman described as ʿaḍūḍ is one in whom the man's member can scarcely penetrate. "A ʿiḍāḍ of living" is one who endures hardship. "There is no maʿaḍḍ in this matter" means there is nothing to hold on to. Al-Aṣmaʿī's proverb, "You are like one who turns back to the one who bites", comes from a young camel that hurt its mother's udder while suckling, was bitten by her, and came back all the same; it is said of a man who is refused and returns.

text:
ROOT ʿ-ḍ-d (عضد) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha (d. 1004 CE)

Ibn Fāris states the three letters ʿ-ḍ-d form a sound root pointing to a bodily organ, and that this is then used metaphorically for strength and for a helper/supporter.

1. The upper arm, and "support" by extension
- Al-ʿaḍud is the upper arm (elbow to shoulder); grammatically feminine; plural aʿḍād.
- By metaphor, al-ʿaḍd means help/support — "ʿaḍadtu fulānan" = "I supported him." The entry cites Qur'an 18:51, "Nor was I to take the misleaders as a supporter [ʿaḍudan]," attributed by the author to al-Khalīl's usage.
- Ibn al-Aʿrābī: a man's "ʿaḍud" can also mean his people/clan — his backing. Hence the idiom "it breaks his ʿaḍud" for undermining someone's support.
- A weak or unhelpful person could be mocked as "the chipped ʿaḍud" (a Bedouin saying quoted here).
- Al-ʿaḍad (different vowel) names a disease of the upper arm/foreleg, illustrated with a verse of al-Nābigha and said by some to occur specifically in camels; related terms: ʿaḍida (an afflicted she-camel or a short/thin upper arm), muʿaḍḍada (camels branded on the upper foreleg).
- An armlet worn on the upper arm is called miʿḍad/miʿḍād/ʿiḍād; the same word ʿiḍād also names a money-pouch strapped to the arm.
- By extension, "aʿḍād" describes any supporting structure built around something — e.g. the stone slabs set around a water-trough's rim (with a verse of Labīd on a ruined trough). The word also names parts of a camel-saddle (the wood pieces beside its crosspiece) and a door's two jambs (ʿiḍāda).
- Al-ʿaḍīd: a palm tree short enough to pick by hand, perhaps named because the arm can reach it. Al-ʿuḍādī: a man muscular in both upper arms (illustrated with a verse).
- Al-ʿāḍid: a rider who flanks a camel caravan on either side (caravans need two, since the driver goes behind) — illustrated with a verse from Ibn al-Aʿrābī's citation. The same word also names an arrow that veers off and misses its target, and (per Ibn al-Sikkīt) a male camel that comes alongside a female to make her kneel for mating.
- The verb "ʿaḍada ʿan al-ṭarīq" means "he swerved from the road."

2. Cutting (the second, unrelated root-sense)
- Al-ʿaḍd also means cutting a tree, done with a tool/sword called al-miʿḍad, used for felling wood.
- Al-ʿāḍid here means "the cutter." A ḥadīth about Medina is quoted: "its trees are not to be cut [lā yuʿḍad]."
- A poetic verse plays on miʿḍad as a crude cutting-blade contrasted with a fine sword that needs only one stroke.
- Ibn al-Aʿrābī: a sharp sword can be called miʿḍad, miʿḍād, or ʿaḍḍād. The verb "ʿaḍḍadtu al-shajara" means "I pruned the tree"; what is cut off is called al-ʿaḍīd or al-ʿaḍad — illustrated with a verse of al-Hudhalī comparing the sound of a striking blow to an axe cutting wood in the rain.

3. Outlier, unconnected to either sense
- Al-thawb al-muʿaḍḍad — a striped garment — is noted as not derived from either the "upper arm/support" or "cutting" root-meanings, with a supporting verse.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives the whole root ʿ-ḍ-l from one core idea: intensity/hardship combined with twistedness — something that resists being straightened out or resolved.

1. Muscle (al-ʿaḍalah). Al-Aṣmaʿī: any hard, solid piece of flesh set within a sinew is called ʿaḍalah. Verb: ʿaḍila yaʿḍalu ʿaḍalan, "to become muscular/sinewy." A muscular, strong man is called al-ʿaḍal.

2. A formidable difficulty. ʿUḍlah (pl. ʿuḍal) means a serious calamity or intractable problem — the sense of bodily strength extended by analogy to "something too tough to handle."

3. The intractable/baffling. Al-dāʾ al-ʿuḍāl = an incurable disease; al-amr al-muʿḍil = a matter so hard it defeats every attempt to fix it. Verb: aʿḍala, "to become insoluble." Illustrated by a verse attributed to Dhū l-Iṣbaʿ, who couldn't get his people to pay one wife's dowry and quipped that a single wife's dowry had already defeated them — so how could they manage four?

The same verb is used transitively: aʿḍalahu l-amru / aʿḍala bihi, "the matter overwhelmed/wore him out." Ibn Fāris cites ʿUmar's remark that the people of Kufa had worn him out (aʿḍala bī) — they wouldn't accept any governor, and no governor would put up with them. Al-muʿḍilāt = severe crises.

4. Preventing a woman from marrying. ʿAḍaltu l-marʾata / ʿaḍḍaltuhā — to unjustly bar a woman from marrying. Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'anic verse "So do not ʿaḍl them from marrying their husbands" (Q 2:232), glossing ʿaḍl here as taḥbis — "restrain/confine," i.e. withhold them by force from a marriage they wish to enter.

5. Difficult childbirth. ʿAḍḍalat is also used of a woman when the child becomes lodged in the womb and cannot easily come out; a ewe in the same difficulty is muʿaḍḍilah (plural maʿāḍīl).

6. A land choked with people. ʿAḍḍalat al-arḍu bi-ahlihā — the land became overcrowded and constricted by the sheer number of its inhabitants, illustrated with a line of poetry by Aws describing a plain "sickened" and "constricted" by a huge host.

7. A hard year. Sanatun ʿiḍl — a hard, difficult year, with a supporting citation.

8. Twisted fortune. Al-Farrāʾ: "So-and-so's good news never reaches us except muʿḍilan" — i.e. tangled up with hardship and bad luck.

9. Tribal name. ʿAḍal, the name of a tribe, is said to derive from this same root.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
**Root ʿ-ḍ-w — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha**

Core sense: a single idea runs through this root — dividing a thing into parts.

1. **ʿiḍw / ʿuḍw (عِضْو، عُضْو)** — "a limb," i.e. a bodily part. Both vocalizations of the word are recorded.

2. **taʿḍiya (تعضية)** — cutting up a slaughtered animal into its limbs/pieces (أَعْضَاء).

3. **ʿiḍah (عِضَة)** — a piece or portion of anything in general. The verb form is illustrated: "ʿaḍḍaytu al-shayʾ" — "I portioned it out / distributed it."

4. **Poetic citation (Ruʾba):** "the religion of God is not something fragmented" (بِالْمُعَضَّى) — glossed as "not something split apart." Used to show ʿaḍḍā/muʿaḍḍā carrying the sense of fragmenting/splitting.

5. **Qur'anic citation, via al-Khalīl (Q15:91):** "those who made the Qur'an ʿiḍīn." Al-Khalīl explains ʿiḍīn as "portion by portion" — they split the Qur'an up, accepting part of it and rejecting part of it. The abstract noun for this act is taʿḍiya.

6. **Ḥadīth citation:** "there is no taʿḍiya in an inheritance" — meaning one must not divide up an inheritance item that cannot bear division without ruining its value, giving a sword or a pearl as examples.

Throughout, the entry ties every derived form (ʿiḍw, taʿḍiya, ʿiḍah, ʿiḍīn) back to the single underlying notion of splitting/portioning a whole into parts.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-ṣ-b as one sound root whose single idea is BINDING one thing to another — either lengthwise or by wrapping round. Every branch of the chapter, he argues, traces back to that one analogy.

1. Sinew (al-ʿaṣab). Per al-Khalīl, the cords at the joints that hold them together — distinct from al-ʿaqab (tendon). Hence لحم عصب, firm compacted flesh full of sinew; معصوب الخلق, a man of tightly packed build, "as though twisted into a twist"; and حسن العصب said of a man or a woman. Shāhid: Ḥassān — men are "people of ʿaṣb and manliness."

2. Tight folding/twisting (al-ʿaṣb). The ʿaṣīb made of sheep's entrails is so named because it is bound and folded up.

3. Hunger and want. A hungry man is called maʿṣūb. Ibn Fāris rejects the explanation that his bowels nearly "dry up," holding instead that he has bound up his belly against hunger; عصبهم = he starved them. Three views on al-muʿaṣṣab are recorded: Ibn al-Aʿrābī — the needy man, from "hunger bound him," explicitly not one who ties on a stone; Abū ʿUbayd — one who binds himself with rags from hunger; Abū Zayd — one whom drought years have bound, i.e. eaten up his wealth. Ibn Fāris prefers Abū ʿUbayd's, both on his own analogy and because it is better known among the learned, and accepts Abū Zayd's as sound (loss of wealth reduces a man to the state of the hungry man tying on rags).

4. ʿAṣb cloth. Al-Khalīl: a kind of striped cloth (burd) whose yarn is bound/tied in bundles, then dyed, then woven. It takes no plural of its own: only برد عصب / برود عصب, because ʿaṣb here is annexed as a verbal noun. Related: al-ʿaṣṣāb, the spinner — "the analogy," since thread is bound; shāhid on the "burds of the ʿaṣṣāb."

5. Head-binding. Al-ʿiṣāba is what the head is bound with against a headache; the form with tāʾ marbūṭa is reserved for the head, while ʿiṣāb (without it) is what you bind anything else with — a deliberate distinction. اعتصب is used of putting on a crown or turban (poetic shāhid: the crown binding itself about the parting, over a brow like gold); حسن العصبة = good at binding on. عصّب رأسه بالعصا والسيف, to strike the head with staff or sword, is taken as derived from ʿiṣāba. Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣ b. Umayya was called Dhū l-ʿiṣāba because when he wore his turban no Qurashī would wear one, out of deference — with a verse on Abū Uḥayḥa's turban.

6. Binding trees and gathering people. Branches are bound so the leaves fall off; hence al-Ḥajjāj's threat to "bind you as the salama-tree is bound." Al-ʿiṣāb are the bindings used on a tree. Ibn Aḥmar's verse — haze and cold "ʿaṣaba the people" — is glossed as gathering and drawing them together.

7. Camels. A she-camel's thigh is bound to make her yield milk; the ʿaṣūb is the camel that will not yield until bound. A verse turns this into a boast: "we do not yield milk to one who binds," i.e. we give nothing under compulsion.

8. Gelding. ʿAṣb also means binding a beast's testicles until they drop off; it is then maʿṣūb.

9. Mouth. عصب الفم: saliva gathering on the teeth from dust or severe thirst — likened in a verse to thick cream clinging to the lips of a milk-skin.

10. Bands of ten and more. Al-ʿuṣba per al-Khalīl is ten men, and nothing fewer is called that; it is so named because it is "bound," as if tied one to another. ʿUṣba and ʿiṣāba are used of people, birds and horses (al-Nābigha: bands of birds circling over armies, guided by other bands). اعصوصب القوم = they formed a band; اعصوصبت = they gathered.

11. Severity. يوم عصيب / يوم عصبصب, a hard day; اعصوصب اليوم, the day grew hard.

12. Clinging and encircling. Abū Zayd: anything joined to something has "ʿaṣaba" to it — عصب القوم بفلان, they thronged about him; and anything that circles and surrounds a thing has ʿaṣiba to it. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: عصب/عصّب به = went round it and kept to it (verse of camels pressing round water); عصب الماء = kept close to the water. Abū Mahdī: عصبت الإبل بالماء عصوبًا, the camels circled and hovered over it. Also negatively: "I neither kept close to that place nor came near it."

13. Kin and inheritance. From this encircling sense, per Abū Zayd, comes al-ʿaṣaba: a man's paternal kin and paternal cousins. Al-Khalīl reports its technical use: those who inherit by kalāla, without parent or child; in the fixed-share system, anyone whose share is not named is ʿaṣaba and takes what remains after the fixed shares. Al-Khalīl adds that al-ʿaṣabiyya (partisan solidarity) is derived from this.

14. The best of a group. Ibn al-Sikkīt: رجل من عصب القوم, a man of their best — which Ibn Fāris takes as fitting the chapter's analogy, since affairs are bound fast by means of such men.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-Ṣ-F (عصف) as a single sound root whose core notion is lightness and speed. He derives every sense from that.

1. ʿaṣf — chaff and dry plant matter. The husk of straw on the grain, and the dried, crumbling leaf on the stalk of a standing crop. He cites Q 105:5, "so He made them like eaten ʿaṣf," and reports that some commentators explain ʿaṣf as any crop whose grain has been eaten and whose straw is left, while Ibn al-Aʿrābī held it to mean the foliage of any growing plant. Related forms: ʿaṣaftu l-zarʿ = to cut off and eat the tips of a crop, as with herbage; makān muʿṣif = a place abounding in ʿaṣf, illustrated by a verse in which a well-vegetated watering-place adorns the poet's precincts when the rains of Jumādā fail. Synonyms for ʿaṣf: ʿaṣīfa and ʿuṣāfa; al-Farrāʾ notes that once the ʿaṣīfa has been stripped from the crop, the crop is said to have been uʿtuṣifa.

2. ʿāṣif — a violent, sweeping wind. Cited from Q 10:22, "a ʿāṣif wind came upon them," a sense he attributes to al-Khalīl. He explains the link to the root idea: such a wind makes things light and carries them off (taʿṣifu bihā). Variants: muʿṣif, muʿṣifa; al-ʿAjjāj's line on gale-winds "never ceasing to move with a rocking gait."

3. A grammatical distinction. Scholars, he reports, separate two epithets: rīḥ ʿāṣifa is a participle built on the verb (ʿaṣafat, "it blew violently"), whereas rīḥ ʿāṣif is a possessive-type adjective meaning "possessed of gale-blowing (ʿuṣūf)," not implying the verb — formed like lābin ("having milk") and tāmir ("having dates").

4. Extension by analogy: swift, sweeping motion. A nāqa ʿaṣūf is a she-camel who sweeps along with her rider like a wind in speed (verb also aʿṣafat); war "sweeps away" a people, as in al-Aʿshā's line about a dense army that carries off armoured and unarmoured men alike; and a naʿāma ʿaṣūf is a swift ostrich. He restates the governing idea: ʿaṣf is lightness and speed.

5. Earning a living. ʿaṣafa / iʿtaṣafa = to earn or gain, which he explains as fitting the root because the earner is brisk and light in his exertion; cited with the half-line "with no earning and no gaining." Hence dhū ʿaṣf = a resourceful man.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-ṣ-m as one sound root with a single core idea in three shades: holding back, preventing/withholding, and clinging/adhering. Everything under the root is analogized back to this one sense.

1. Protection / taking refuge. al-ʿiṣma: God's preserving His servant from an evil he might fall into. iʿtaṣama bi-llāh = he shielded himself [by holding to God]; istaʿṣama = he sought refuge. aʿṣamtu fulānan = I gave someone a handhold to cling to. Shāhid: al-Nābigha — the frightened sailor clings to the rudder-pole in dread and thunder.

2. al-muʿṣim (of a horseman): one poor at riding, who clutches his horse's mane to keep from falling. Shāhid: the brave rider does not go to battle as a feeble "clinger."

3. al-ʿiṣma also = anything you hold fast to. ʿaṣamahu al-ṭaʿām = the food sustained him / kept him from hunger.

4. al-ʿaṣīm: the dried crust of tar-salve and urine on a she-camel's thigh; also the trace of dye. al-muʿṣam: a hide left with its fur/hair still clinging (because useless to strip). All still "adhering."

5. al-ʿuṣm (per al-Aṣmaʿī): the trace of a dye-stuff — wars, saffron, henna, or khalūq perfume left on the hand. Ibn Fāris's own correction: al-Aṣmaʿī is inconsistent — the woman who asked for "the ʿuṣm of your henna" wanted the scraped henna substance, not merely a trace; so ʿuṣm properly = the henna clinging to the dyer's hand, and its residue afterward is ʿuṣm too, because it lasts and adheres.

6. al-ʿuṣma: white marking on an animal's pastern/foreleg — hence al-waʿil al-aʿṣam (white-legged mountain-goat), plural ʿuṣm; likewise ghurāb aʿṣam (a crow with a white spot, rarely found). Ibn al-Aʿrābī: in horses, whiteness on the forelegs (not hind), so aʿṣam al-yadayn. Same analogy — the white blaze "clings" to the leg like henna. Shawāhid from an unnamed poet and al-Aʿshā on ibexes brought down from the heights.

7. al-ʿiṣma = a necklace, because it clings to the neck; Labīd pluralizes it aʿṣām (of hunting-hounds' collars/leashes).

8. ʿiṣām: a binding-cord — of a camel-litter (its fastening), or of a water-skin (a two-cubit cord threaded through the eyelets to join them); aʿṣamtuhumā = I fitted them with a ʿiṣām. Shāhid: Taʾabbaṭa Sharrā. Note: a bucket has no ʿiṣām.

9. miʿṣam: a woman's wrist — the seat of the bracelets — so named for "holding" the bracelet, and remains a miʿṣam even with no bracelet. Shāhid on a woman's coquetry today, her wrist another's tomorrow.

10. Idioms and names: aʿṣama bihi wa-akhlada = he clung and cleaved fast to it. ʿiṣām as a man's name; the proverbial question "What is behind you, O ʿiṣām?" (from al-Nābigha) used when seeking news; and "The self of ʿiṣām ennobled ʿiṣām" — said of one noble by himself, not through his forebears.
