poets_named: Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse ×9; Aws (pre-Islamic); Ibn Aḥmar (lived into Islam); Ṭarafa (pre-Islamic); Abū Duʾād (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-ṣ-r as three separate sound roots: (1) an age or stretch of time; (2) squeezing something until its liquid runs out; (3) clinging to something and taking hold of it for protection.

FIRST ROOT — TIME

1. ʿaṣr = time, an age (dahr). Cited from the Qur'an: "By al-ʿaṣr, man is indeed in loss" (103:1). A variant plural/form ʿuṣur occurs; Imruʾ al-Qays: "Good morning to you, O worn ruin — but can one greet with good morning a man of the ages gone by?"

2. al-ʿaṣrān (the two ʿaṣrs) — per al-Khalīl, night and day, with the verse: "The two ʿaṣrs, a day and a night, will not be slow, as they alternate, to overtake what they aim at." The same dual is also used of morning and evening: "those who feed people through the alternation of the two ʿaṣrs."

3. On this basis, Ibn Fāris reports, the ʿaṣr prayer is so named because it is "pressed back," i.e. deferred after the ẓuhr. He also cites a ḥadīth in which "keep to the two ʿaṣrs" is explained as a prayer before sunrise and one before sunset — understood as the ṣubḥ and ʿaṣr prayers. (These are the author's reports of usage, given as the sense the name carries.)

4. Time-of-day verbs: aʿṣara l-qawm — the people reached the ʿaṣr hour (paired by Ibn al-Aʿrābī with aqṣarū, from ʿaṣr and qaṣr); ʿaṣṣarū — they lingered/held back until the ʿaṣr.

5. muʿṣir, of a girl: al-Khalīl and others — a girl who perceives in herself the swelling of youth has "aʿṣarat," having reached the ʿaṣr (season) of her youth and maturity. Abū Laylā: one who has come of age and is near menstruation. Shāhid: "A girl whose home is at Safawān — she has become muʿṣir, or her iʿṣār draws near." One group explained the name as her having changed from her ʿaṣr; others gave a different explanation, which Ibn Fāris says he treated elsewhere. He judges the derivation from "time/season" plausible.

SECOND ROOT — PRESSING OUT LIQUID

6. ʿuṣāra = what runs out of a thing you press; the same as ʿaṣīr (pressed juice). Shawāhid: "the ʿuṣāra of the bread that exuded"; "The stalk — its liquid is pressed out; and every set of stalks has its ʿuṣāra." Ibn al-Sikkīt records the proverb "I will not do it so long as oil is pressed," and Aws: "There is no recovery from Ḍabbāʾ while oil is still pressed."

7. Figurative use: ʿuṣāra and muʿtaṣar stand for a man's good and his giving — "he is generous of ʿuṣāra and generous of muʿtaṣar."

8. Grammatical/valency distinction: ʿaṣarta l-ʿinab = you pressed the grapes yourself; iʿtaṣartahu = it was pressed for you specifically. The miʿṣār (instrument noun) is a nosebag-like container in which grapes are placed and pressed.

9. Rain sense, by extension from pressing: al-muʿṣirāt = clouds that bring rain — "And We sent down from the muʿṣirāt water pouring forth" (78:14); uʿṣira l-qawm = rain came to them. A variant reading of "in it people are given relief and in it yuʿṣarūn" is glossed as rain reaching them. Ibn Fāris derives all of this from the pressing of grapes and the like.

10. Winds called muʿṣirāt: he allows this as belonging to the same section by adjacency — the winds stir up the rain-bearing clouds, so they too are called muʿṣirāt and iʿṣār. Shāhid: "As though the scouring of the muʿṣirāt had clothed it with the dust of plains and hollows, sifted through a sieve."

11. iʿṣār = dust rising in a circling column (whirlwind); plural aʿāṣīr. Shāhid: "While a man is among the living, envied, suddenly he is in the grave, effaced by the whirling dust." Also used of billowing dust generally: "Then an iʿṣār containing fire struck it and it burned" (2:266).

12. ʿaṣra = a waft of perfume that rises and spreads — "so-and-so passed and his clothes had an ʿaṣra" — which Ibn Fāris derives from iʿṣār. A ḥadīth: "A perfumed woman passed by; her hem had an ʿaṣra."

13. Extracting/exacting: al-Khalīl defines iʿtiṣār as getting wealth out of a person by a fine or some other means. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: "the sons of so-and-so exact the gift." al-Aṣmaʿī: the muʿtaṣir is one who takes and obtains something from a thing; Ibn Aḥmar: "Life is only in its prime, and you draw out something from its branches."

14. Produce: ʿuṣāra is also used of crop yield (ghalla). "And in it they yaʿṣirūn" (12:49) was explained as "they draw produce from their lands" — Ibn Fāris calls this an analogy, since produce is as if pressed out the way grapes are.

15. Giving: al-Khalīl gives ʿaṣr the sense of a gift/giving, with Ṭarafa: "Were there among our rulers one who yaʿṣiru among us as you do" — glossed "as you give."

THIRD ROOT — REFUGE

16. ʿaṣar = a place of refuge; iʿtaṣara bi-l-makān = he took shelter in it. Abū Duʾād: "a pouring one, from which the mountain hollow gives the wild ass no refuge."

17. Two patterns are noted: ʿuṣra (fuʿla) and ʿaṣar (faʿal), both meaning refuge — "you have no ʿuṣra from this affair"; and the shāhid "and he was indeed a refuge for the distressed."

18. maʿāṣir in a line of invective ("...when you cast away the maʿāṣir"): some glossed it as turbans, others as black garments; Ibn Fāris holds the correct sense to be coats of mail, derived from ʿaṣr in the sense of refuge, since one shelters behind them. He closes with "God knows best."

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: عَصَا 10x "with your staff"; عِصِيّ 2x "and their staffs"
text:
Al-Rāghib treats ʿ-ṣ-w through the staff (al-ʿaṣā). He derives disobedience (ʿiṣyān) from it.

1. **The staff.** Al-ʿaṣā is a staff or stick. Its third radical is originally wāw, as the dual ʿaṣawāni shows. Its plural is ʿiṣiyy. Qur'anic examples: "cast down your staff" (Q 27:10); "so he cast down his staff" (Q 7:107); "he said: it is my staff" (Q 20:18); "so they cast down their ropes and their staffs" (Q 26:44).

2. **Striking.** ʿAṣawtuhu means "I struck him with the staff." For striking with the sword, the form ʿaṣaytu is used.

3. **Settling down.** "So-and-so cast down his staff" means he halted and settled. The image is of a traveller who has come home. A poet says: "so she cast down her staff, and her destination settled with her."

4. **Disobedience.** ʿAṣā (verbal noun ʿiṣyān) means to leave obedience. Al-Rāghib says its origin is resisting or holding out with one's staff. Qur'anic examples: "and Adam disobeyed his Lord" (Q 20:121); "whoever disobeys God and His messenger" (Q 4:14); "now? when you disobeyed before" (Q 10:91).

5. **Splitting the staff.** Of someone who has separated from the community one says "he split the staff" (shaqqa al-ʿaṣā).

text:
Ibn Manẓūr treats ʿ-ṣ-y / ʿ-ṣ-w in two large blocks: first al-ʿaṣā, the staff, with its many figurative uses, and then al-ʿiṣyān, disobedience, with a set of extended senses.

**1. al-ʿaṣā: the staff.** A stick of wood; the word is feminine. Qur'anic example: "It is my staff; I lean upon it" (Q 20:18). Dual ʿaṣawān; plurals aʿṣin, aʿṣāʾ, ʿuṣiyy and ʿiṣiyy (the kasra of ʿiṣiyy is assimilation to the following vowel). Sībawayh rejected aʿṣāʾ, saying aʿṣiyā was used instead. Al-Azharī notes the variant ʿaṣāt (with tāʾ marbūṭa), which some disliked; al-Aṣmaʿī's source forbids both the tāʾ and a lengthened form, and al-Farrāʾ calls "hādhihi ʿaṣātī" the first solecism heard in Iraq.

**2. Why it is called ʿaṣā.** Al-Aṣmaʿī reports from a Baṣran that the staff is so named because the hand and fingers gather around it, from ʿaṣawtu al-qawm, "I gathered the people together" (for good or ill). Abū ʿUbayd likewise says the root sense of al-ʿaṣā is gathering and concord.

**3. The staff and the herdsman.** "Hard of staff" (ṣulb / shadīd al-ʿaṣā) describes a herdsman who is rough with his camels, or, per al-Azharī, strong and in firm control of them; Ibn Barrī adds it can mean simply a hard man. "Soft of staff" or "weak of staff" describes a gentle manager who rarely beats his animals, which is praise (Ibn al-Aʿrābī); verses of Maʿn ibn Aws and al-Rāʿī illustrate it. Ibn al-Aʿrābī says the Arabs blamed herdsmen who beat camels as harsh, citing verses urging herders to brandish the staves rather than strike.

**4. Verbs from the staff.**
- ʿaṣāhu yaʿṣūhu ʿaṣwan: he struck him with the staff (the well-known form, per Ibn Sīda and Ibn al-Aʿrābī); ʿaṣaytuhu and ʿaṣītuhu are dialect variants. Al-Kisāʾī reports some preferred ʿaṣītu, and that the usage was extended to the sword by analogy. Ibn Sīda uses the form ʿaṣaytuhu to argue the final radical can be yāʾ.
- ʿaṣā bihā: he took hold of it; ʿaṣiya bi-sayfihi: he gripped or struck with his sword as with a staff (Jarīr's verse "others wield them").
- Abū Zayd: ʿaṣiya fī al-qawm bi-sayfihi: he ran amok among them with his sword. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: ʿaṣiya yaʿṣā: he played with the staff as with a sword.
- iʿtaṣā al-shajara: he cut a staff from the tree; iʿtaṣā bi-l-ʿaṣā: he leaned on it (again Q 20:18); yaʿtaṣī bi-l-sayf: he makes his sword a staff.
- ʿāṣānī fa-ʿaṣawtuhu (al-Liḥyānī, without explanation): the text suggests "he contended with me with it and I overcame him".
- ʿaṣṣāhu al-ʿaṣā: he gave him the staff (Ṭurayḥ: "the staff of the Messenger he gave you").

**5. Casting down and raising the staff.** "The traveller cast down his staff": he arrived and settled. The key verse, "So she cast down her staff and her journey came to rest", is told of a woman who would not settle with any husband until she found one she accepted; it became a proverb for anyone who finds what suits him and stays. Ibn Barrī records disputed attributions (ʿAbd Rabbih al-Sulamī, Sulaym ibn Thumāma al-Ḥanafī, and via al-Āmidī, Muʿaqqir ibn Ḥimār al-Bāriqī). Another view: to cast down the staff is to drive in tent-pegs and camp. Conversely, "he raised his staff" means he set out.

**6. The staff as discipline.** On Abū Jahm, "he never puts his staff down from his shoulder", two readings are given: he disciplines his household by beating, or he travels constantly. On the Prophet's words "Do not lift your staff from your family", al-Kisāʾī and others say no literal staff or beating is meant: it is a figure for not neglecting their discipline and keeping them together in obedience to God and away from corruption. "Slaves of the staff" are people humbled and beaten (al-Azharī, Ibn Sīda); Yazīd ibn Mufarrigh: "the slave is beaten with the staff; for the free man reproach suffices." "He struck him with the staff of blame" means he censured him severely, whence taqrīʿ, "rebuke". The proverb "the staff was rapped for the man of forbearance" refers to an aged Arab arbiter whose son rapped a staff to alert him when he erred.

**7. The staff as unity: "splitting the staff".** Because the staff stands for togetherness, "splitting the staff" means breaking up a community: the Khawārij "split the staff of the Muslims"; "beware of the one slain of the staff" means beware of killing or being killed in such a split; "the staff split" means discord broke out. Abū al-Haytham adds that its splitting stands for a separation with no reunion, since a split staff is no longer called a staff. Ibn Barrī discusses the grammar of a related verse (the wāw of "wa-l-Ḍaḥḥāka" having the sense of bāʾ). A man who has settled and got his affairs together "has cast down his staff".

**8. Proverbs and other figurative uses.**
- "The staff is from the little staff" (al-Aṣmaʿī, on a son resembling his father); Abū ʿUbayd thinks it should be the reverse, unless it means great things start small; al-Jawharī: one part of a matter comes from another.
- "The slave's staff" in a verse: the stick for stirring baking-ashes.
- "The staff of separation" in a verse recited by Ibn al-Aʿrābī.
- yuṣallī ʿaṣā fulān (Abū Saʿīd): he manages someone's affairs; al-Azharī traces it to straightening a crooked staff by holding it to the fire.
- "Better than the separated pieces of the staff": a broken staff becomes pins, the pins become pegs, the pegs become the small sticks for tying udder-bags.
- aʿṣā al-karm: the vine put out shoots ("staves") without fruit.

**9. Bones and other objects.** al-ʿiṣiyy: the bones of the wing; ʿaṣā al-sāq: the shin-bone, by comparison with a staff (Dhū al-Rumma). ʿaṣawā al-biʾr: the two cross-sticks over a well-bucket (Ibn Barrī, citing Dhū al-Rumma). Ibn Barrī also gives al-ʿunṣuwa, a lock of hair.

**10. Miscellaneous verbs.** yaʿṣī al-rīḥ: he faces into the wind and does not expose himself to it; ʿaṣā: he became hard (al-Azharī thinks this is ʿasā with sīn turned to ṣād); ʿaṣawtu al-jurḥ: I bound the wound; iʿtaṣat al-nawāt: the date-stone hardened.

**11. al-ʿiṣyān: disobedience.** Defined as the opposite of obedience. ʿaṣā al-ʿabdu rabbahu: the servant disobeyed his Lord, going against His command. Verbal nouns ʿaṣy, ʿiṣyān, maʿṣiya; the doer is ʿāṣin or ʿaṣiyy; ʿāṣāhu means the same. Sībawayh explains that the mafʿil pattern here appears only with the final -a (maʿṣiya), since without it the form would be weak. istaʿṣat ʿalayhi: a group rebelled against the ruler.
- A ḥadīth: the Prophet rebuked a preacher who said "whoever disobeys them both [God and His Messenger]", telling him to name God and then the Messenger explicitly; the entry takes this as evidence that wāw can indicate sequence.
- "Were it not that we disobey God, He would not 'disobey' us": that is, He would not withhold His answer; the response is called ʿiṣyān by correspondence, like "they schemed and God schemed" (Q 3:54).
- The Prophet changed the name al-ʿĀṣī because obedience is the believer's mark; the "ʿUṣāt of Quraysh" are men named al-ʿĀṣī, of whom only Muṭīʿ ibn al-Aswad became Muslim.
- istaʿṣā ʿalayhi al-shayʾ: the thing proved hard for him, "as if from ʿiṣyān".

**12. Extended senses of al-ʿāṣī.** A young camel that does not follow its mother, as though disobeying her; a vein that will not stop bleeding (ʿirq ʿāṣin), as though refusing to stop, with verses of Dhū al-Rumma and one cited by al-Jawharī on the "disobedient veins" of the belly. ʿaṣā al-ṭāʾir: the bird flew (al-Ṭirimmāḥ).

**13. Names.** Ibn Abī ʿĀṣiya, a poet mentioned by Thaʿlab; Ibn Sīda classes the name under yāʾ because its opposite, Muṭīʿ (as in Muṭīʿ ibn Iyās), is also used as a name. al-ʿAṣā was a famous horse, variously said to belong to ʿAwf ibn al-Aḥwaṣ, to Qaṣīr ibn Saʿd al-Lakhmī, or (al-Azharī) to Jadhīma al-Abrash, one of the swiftest of Arab horses; hence the proverb "Qaṣīr rode al-ʿAṣā". ʿUṣayya is a clan of Sulaym.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ʿ-ṭ-f (ع-ط-ف) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

**Core meaning:** Ibn Fāris states this root has one single sound sense: bending and curving.

1. **Basic verb.** ʿaṭaftu al-shayʾ = "I tilted/bent the thing." inʿaṭafa = "it curved/bent" (on its own). The verbal noun of ʿaṭafa is al-ʿuṭūf.

2. **Extended to inclination/compassion.** taʿaṭṭafa bi-l-raḥma = "he inclined [toward someone] with mercy." ʿaṭafa Allāh fulānan ʿalā fulān = "God inclined so-and-so toward so-and-so" — i.e. the physical sense of bending toward something extends to inclining favorably toward a person.

3. **Concrete physical use.** A man "bends" (yaʿṭifu) a pillow, meaning he folds it over, when he rests his elbow on it. Ibn Fāris cites a line of the poet Labīd using ʿāṭif in exactly this sense — "one who folds the cushion" (the citation is brought only to attest the word, not for its full poetic scene, which is difficult to render).

4. **The body's sides (al-ʿiṭfān).** The two sides of a person are called al-ʿiṭfān because a person leans on them. From this comes the idiom thanā ʿiṭfahu, "he bent his side" — said of someone who turned away from you and treated you with coldness/disdain.

5. **Derived adjectives of temperament.** A man who is inclined toward kindness in war and in good deeds is called ʿaṭūf or, more intensively, ʿaṭṭāf.

6. **Animal usage.** A doe (ẓabya) is called ʿāṭif when she crouches down and bends her neck.

7. **Gait.** Someone described as yataʿāṭafu fī mishyatihi sways from side to side as he walks.

8. **Clothing.** A person yataʿaṭṭafu bi-thawbihi — drapes his garment over himself in the manner of a wrap over one shoulder (tawashshuḥ). The outer wrap/cloak itself (al-ridāʾ) is called ʿiṭāf precisely because it is folded/draped around the body.

9. **Extended metaphor to the sword.** By further extension of this same idea, the sword too came to be called ʿiṭāf, because — like the cloak — it is slung across the body in the same position.

In short: every sense Ibn Fāris records — the physical bend, the folded pillow, the body's sides, turning away in disdain, inclining with compassion, the swaying gait, the draped garment, and even the sword — traces back to one image: something bending, curving, or folding around/toward something else.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ʿ-Ṭ-L (عطل) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core sense: emptiness, vacancy — something left devoid or unattended.

1. Left empty / unattended. "ʿuṭṭilat al-dāru" — a house left empty, abandoned. Camels left without a herdsman are "ʿuṭṭilat." A well not visited or drawn from is described the same way. Two Qur'anic examples are cited: "an abandoned well" (Q22:45), and "when the ten-months-pregnant she-camels are left untended" (Q81:4). Ibn Fāris generalizes the sense: anything without a keeper is "ʿuṭṭila" — hence "taʿṭīl al-thughūr," leaving frontier garrisons unmanned.

2. Without jewelry. "Al-ʿaṭal" — the source text has a gap here, but the following material makes the sense plain: a woman is called "ʿāṭil" (plural "ʿawāṭil") when she wears no jewelry. A cited verse describes women's necks as not "ʿawāṭil" (not bare of ornament) — i.e. they are in fact strung with pearls.

3. A bow without a string. "Qaws ʿuṭul" — a bow with no bowstring on it.

4. Horses without neck-bands. "Khayl aʿṭāl" — horses wearing no collars.

5. An outlier flagged by the author. "Al-nāqah al-ʿayṭal" — a she-camel (occasionally also said of a woman) that is tall and comely, i.e. long-necked. Ibn Fāris explicitly notes this word does not fit the root's "emptiness" sense. He illustrates it with a line by Dhū al-Rummah describing a she-camel as "timid of heart, fine of face, long-necked (ʿayṭal)."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَعْطَىٰ 8x "they are given"; عَطَاء 5x "(the) gift"; تَعَاطَىٰ 1x "and he took"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the whole root ʿ-ṭ-w from a single sound meaning: taking, and handing or passing something over. Every use in the section stays within these two ideas.

1. ʿaṭw (العَطْو) — reaching for or taking something with the hand. Imruʾ al-Qays uses the verb taʿṭū of a woman reaching out with soft fingers (described as she cleans her teeth with a siwāk). The same verb is used of a gazelle that raises its forelegs and stretches up to a tree to reach the leaves — illustrated by a second verse where the animal strips fruit from an arāk with its horns and reaches up with its hooves when the branch is too high.

2. iʿṭāʾ (الإعطاء, "giving") — al-Khalīl's view, cited here, is that the sense of "giving" is derived from this root of reaching/handing. Related forms: muʿāṭāh (المُعاطاة) = handing things to one another; the phrase ʿāṭā al-ṣabiyyu ahlahu = "the boy served his family," i.e. worked and passed them what they wanted.

3. ʿaṭāʾ (العَطاء) — a noun for the thing given; equivalently ʿaṭiyyah (العَطِيَّة, "a gift"). Plural ʿaṭāyā, and the plural of that in turn is aʿṭiyah. A cited verse uses tuʿāṭīhi ("she passes to him") of freely given rain-water/saliva likened to honeyed ginger.

4. taʿāṭī (التعاطي) — a narrowed, negative use: taking or reaching for what one has no right to. Example: "So-and-so yataʿāṭā the wronging of another" (undertakes to wrong him). Ibn Fāris cites Qurʾān al-Qamar 54:29, {fa-taʿāṭā fa-ʿaqara} ("then he reached out and hamstrung [the she-camel]"), for this "reaching out" sense.

5. Proverb: "ʿāṭin bi-ghayr anwāṭ" — literally "reaching out with nothing to reach for." It describes someone who aspires to a thing while having no means to attain it, like a person grasping where there is nothing to grasp.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ع-ظ-م (ʿ-ẓ-m) as one sound root meaning largeness and strength. From this single sense he derives the following:

1. al-ʿiẓam — "largeness, greatness," given as the verbal noun (maṣdar) of al-ʿaẓīm ("the great/mighty thing"). The base verb is ʿaẓuma / yaʿẓumu / ʿiẓaman ("to become great").

2. Derived verb forms:
   - ʿaẓẓamtuhu — "I magnified it."
   - aʿẓamtuhu and istaʿẓamtuhu — "I deemed/found it great," used specifically when something looms large "in your eyes."

3. muʿẓam al-shayʾ — the greater or main part of a thing.

4. ʿaẓmat al-dhirāʿ — the thick, stout part of the forearm.

5. al-ʿaẓīma — a grave, severe calamity that befalls. He cites a verse of poetry: "If you escape from it, you escape from something of grave moment; and if not, I do not think you will be saved."

6. al-ʿaẓm — "bone," which he says belongs to this root because a bone is named for its strength and hardness.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ʿ-b-ʾ (عبأ) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris gives ONE core meaning for this root (including its weak-letter variant ʿ-b-w/y): a coming-together under weight — things gathered up in a way that makes them heavy or bulky.

1. Load / burden — al-ʿibʾ (عِبْء), plural al-aʿbāʾ (أَعْبَاء): any load, whether a debt (ghurm) or a surety one has taken on for another (ḥamāla). Cited verse: a poet speaks of "bearing the load off the necks of my people."

2. "I don't care" — the idiom mā ʿabaʾtu bihi shayʾan ("I gave it no ʿabʾ at all") means "I didn't care about it" — as if it carried no weight for you.

3. Preparing perfume — ʿabaʾtu al-ṭīb, "I mixed/prepared the perfume," illustrated by a verse comparing scent on someone's chest and shoulders to perfume a bride stayed up preparing.

4. Arraying an army — a related but distinct usage: to organize/marshal troops is ʿabbaytu al-katība (without hamza) or, per Ibn al-Aʿrābī, ʿabbaʾtu al-jaysh (with hamza). Ibn Fāris notes Arabs kept this word for armies distinct from the "perfume" usage above.

5. The cloak — al-ʿabāʾa, a type of garment/mantle, is derived from the same root because — in his words — it "envelops its wearer and gathers him in," fitting the core sense of gathering/enclosing under bulk.

Closes with the standard formula "wa-Llāhu aʿlam bi-l-ṣawāb" (God knows best).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: عَبْد 131x "his slaves"; عَبَدَ 122x "worship"; عَابِد 11x "(are) worshippers"; عِبَادَت 9x "his worship"; عَبَّد 1x "you have enslaved"; عَٰبِدَٰت 1x "who worship"
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) on the root ع ب د (ʿ-b-d).

He treats it as two sound but seemingly opposite roots: one meaning softness and lowliness, the other strength and hardness.

FIRST ROOT — softness / lowliness:
1. al-ʿabd = an owned person (al-mamlūk). Collective plural al-ʿabīd; small-number plural aʿbud (as in "three"); another plural al-ʿibād. al-Khalīl notes common usage separates ʿibād Allāh ("servants of God") from al-ʿabīd ("owned slaves"). One says a slave is "of manifest ʿubūda (servitude)."

2. No verb is derived for the state of being a slave. Were one coined it would be ʿabuda ("he became a slave / acknowledged servitude"), but that verb fell out of use.

3. The verb ʿabada / yaʿbudu / ʿibāda, per al-Khalīl, is said only of one who worships or serves God. Related forms: taʿabbada ("to devote oneself"), the mutaʿabbid being one wholly given to ʿibāda; istaʿbada ("to take someone as a slave"). Notably, ʿabada is NOT used for merely serving a human master.

4. taʿabbada X ("he made X like a slave to himself, though X was free") — with a verse where the speaker complains Nimr ibn Saʿd has "enslaved" him though outwardly Nimr obeys him. aʿbada = "to make someone a slave."

5. Usage note: polytheists are called ʿabadat al-ṭāghūt wa-l-awthān ("worshippers of false powers and idols"); Muslims are ʿubbād who worship God. Some record the pair ʿābid / ʿabada like khādim / khadama ("servant" / "he served"). Feminine of ʿabd is ʿabda. al-ʿibiddāʾ = slaves born into servitude.

6. Extended concrete senses tied to "lowering/humbling": al-baʿīr al-muʿabbad = a camel smeared with tar (which degrades it) — cited from Ṭarafa's line about being cast out like a tarred camel; muʿabbad also = a broken-in, docile camel; and al-ṭarīq al-muʿabbad = a well-trodden, smoothed (literally "humbled") road.

SECOND ROOT — strength / hardness:
7. al-ʿabada = strength and firmness. A garment "with ʿabda" is thick and strong. Hence the name ʿAlqama ibn ʿAbada (with fatḥa on the b).

8. By the same sense, al-ʿabad = disdain / indignant anger (like al-anaf and al-ḥamiyya): "he is indignant at this matter." On this basis Ibn Fāris reports an interpretation of Q 43:81, {…fa-anā awwalu l-ʿābidīn}, as "I am the first to be angered by / to disdain such a claim" — reading ʿābid here as "indignant rejecter" rather than "worshipper." Supporting citations: a saying attributed to ʿAlī, ʿabidtu fa-ṣamattu ("I was angered, so I kept silent"); a verse where an ignorant man "rages" (yaʿbadu) uselessly after losing his case; and a line, "I disdain (aʿbadu) that Kulayb be lampooned by Dārim."

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī records one strand of explanation for ʿabqar/ʿabqariyy:

1. It is said that ʿAbqar is a place associated with the jinn, and that anything unusually excellent or extraordinary — a person, an animal, or a piece of cloth — used to be attributed to it, as if it came from there. This is why the saying arose about the caliph ʿUmar: I have not seen an ʿabqarī like him (i.e., no one so exceptional).

2. The Qur'anic citation: wa-ʿabqariyyin ḥisān, and fine ʿabqarī [things] (Qur'an 55:76, Surat al-Rahman).

3. Al-Raghib further reports that ʿabqariyy denotes a kind of furnishing or carpet, and that God used the word as a likeness (mathal) for the furnishings of Paradise, i.e. in the verse it describes cushions or carpets of Paradise, named after this proverbially excellent, jinn-associated ʿAbqar.

The entry is short and gives no further sense beyond these two connected strands: the rare/excellent thing from ʿAbqar idiom, and the specific Qur'anic use for fine paradise furnishings.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: عِبْرَة 6x "surely (is) a lesson"; عَابِرِى 1x "(when) passing"; تَعْبُرُ 1x "interpret"; ٱعْتَبِرُ 1x "so take a lesson"
poets_named: al-Ṭirimmāḥ (Umayyad); Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse; Al-ʿAjjāj (Umayyad); Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad); al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-b-r as a single sound root whose core idea is passing through something and going on across it. From that one image he derives the senses below, and marks off at the end the ones he cannot fit.

1. Crossing over; a bank. عَبَرْتُ النَّهْرَ عُبُورًا — "I crossed the river." عَبْر of a river is its bank. A she-camel constantly travelled on is نَاقَة عُبْر أَسْفَار; al-Ṭirimmāḥ: "I have ridden a swift she-camel, worn to journeying, muffled of grunt."

2. Related forms of the crossing-place. الْمَعْبَر — the stretch of bank prepared for crossing; الْمِعْبَر — the boat by which the river is crossed.

3. Passing along a way. عَابِر سَبِيل is one who is merely passing through. Cited from Q 4:43: "nor in a state of janāba, except as passers-by along the way."

4. Tears. Ibn Fāris reports from al-Khalīl that عَبْرَة is the running of a tear, and also the tear itself; Imruʾ al-Qays: "my cure is a flow of tears, if I pour it out — yet is there at an effaced camp-trace anything to lean on?" Ibn Fāris says this fits the root exactly, because a tear "crosses over," i.e. passes through and runs.

5. Tearful grief. عَبِرَ … عَبَرًا is to grieve; the man is عَبْرَان, the woman عَبْرَى or عَبِرَة; Ibn Fāris notes this word is used only where there is actual weeping. اسْتَعْبَرَ = his tears ran; امْرَأَة عَابِر = a woman in tears. A cited verse: "The Jarmī says: will you take me up behind you? — how should a routed man ride pillion? Your mother is in tears."

6. A riverside lote-tree. عُبْرِيّ is the kind of sidr that grows on riverbanks — so named, on his account, because a bank is a thing crossed and crossed to. Al-ʿAjjāj: "about it twine the ashāʾ (young palm-shoots) and the ʿubrī." He reports that the ʿubrī is always tall, while the smaller sort is الضَّال; Dhū al-Rumma pairs the two: "the kinds of sidr — ʿubrī and ḍāl." An alternative report makes ḍāl the inland variety.

7. Interpreting a dream. عَبَرَ الرُّؤْيَا (verbal nouns عَبْر, عِبَارَة) and عَبَّرَ (تَعْبِير) mean to explain it. Ibn Fāris's reasoning: crossing a river means going from one bank (ʿibr) to the other, and the dream-interpreter likewise carries the image from one side to another — asked about water, he answers "life."

8. Speaking on another's behalf / expression. From al-Khalīl: عَبَّرْتَ عَنْ فُلَان is to state a man's argument for him when he is tongue-tied. Ibn Fāris fits this to the root: the man could not push his speech through, so another pushed it through for him.

9. اعْتِبَار and عِبْرَة (taking heed). He proposes that both come from the two facing banks of a river: each bank is the counterpart (ʿibr) of the other. To say اعْتَبَرْتُ الشَّيْءَ is to look at a thing and set what concerns you alongside it as its counterpart, so the two match in your estimation. He calls this his own account of the derivation, and reads Q 59:2 "So take heed, O you possessed of insight" accordingly: look at those who acted and were punished, and avoid doing the like lest the like befall you. In support he cites al-Khalīl's عَبَّرْتَ الدَّنَانِير — weighing coins one dinar against another — and al-Khalīl's definition of عِبْرَة as drawing a lesson from what has passed.

10. Uses he judges anomalous. الْمُعْبَر of camels: thick-furred. الْمُعْبَر of boys: uncircumcised — of which he says plainly that he does not see how it fits the root; a hemistich of Bishr b. Abī Khāzim uses it. Also anomalous: الْعَبِير, said by some to be saffron and by others to be a mixture of perfumes; al-Aʿshā: "cool as a bride's mantle in summer, sprinkled with ʿabīr."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-b-s as one sound root whose core notion is aversion or repugnance toward something.

1. Concrete origin: al-ʿabas is dung and similar matter that dries and cakes onto the coarse hair of an animal's tail. He notes it is to camels what al-wadaḥ (caked dung on the wool) is to sheep.
   - Shāhid, Abū al-Najm: the caked summer filth on the camels' raised tails looked like stags' horns.
   - Ḥadīth citation: camels were passed by that had become "ʿabasat" — crusted over in their own urine.
   - Shāhid, Jarīr, describing a herdswoman: the year-old caked filth, black on her wrist, served her as bracelets — not ivory ones.

2. From that concrete sense he derives al-yawm al-ʿabūs, "the scowling day," meaning a day that is harsh and repellent.

3. From it likewise the verb ʿabasa / yaʿbisu / ʿubūs — to scowl; and the participle ʿābis al-wajh, "sour-faced," which he glosses as angry.

4. And the intensive form ʿAbbās is used of someone in whom this scowling is frequent.

The entry's method is derivational: the physical caking of filth is taken as the base image, and the facial/temporal senses of scowling are presented as extensions of it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) on the root ʿ-b-th:

He states this is one sound root with a single core meaning: mixing (al-khalṭ).

1. Literal/concrete sense — mixing: "ʿabatha al-aqiṭ" = he mixed/worked the dried curdled milk (aqiṭ); "anā aʿbithuhu ʿabthan" = I am mixing it. The thing so mixed is called "ʿibbīth" — it is mixed together and then dried in the sun. "Al-ʿabīth" is his general term for "any mixture." He also cites the expression "fī hādhā al-wādī ʿabīthah" — "in this valley there is an ʿabīthah" — meaning a mixture of two tribes/clans settled together.

2. Derived sense — purposeless action: By analogy from "mixing," the word "al-ʿabath" came to denote an action done without evenness or soundness — i.e., not done properly or purposefully. Verb: "ʿabitha yaʿbathu ʿabathan." Someone who is "ʿābith" is occupied with something that does not concern him and is not on his mind — aimless, trifling activity.

3. Qur'anic citation: Ibn Fāris cites Q23:115 — "Did you then think that We created you in ʿabathan?" — and glosses ʿabathan here as laʿiban ("in play/sport," i.e., without purpose).

He closes by stating that one and the same analogical principle (qiyās) — mixing, extended to an act lacking proper order or purpose — underlies every usage given above.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: أَعَدَّ 20x "and he has prepared"; عِدَّة 11x "their number"; عَدَّ 7x "you count"; مَّعْدُودَة 6x "numbered"; عَدَد 6x "(in) number"; عَدّ 2x "a counting"; عُدَّة 1x "(some) preparation"; مَّعْدُود 1x "limited"; عَادِّين 1x "those who keep count"; تَعْتَدُّ 1x "(to) count concerning them"; عَدَّدَ 1x "and counts it"
text:
Al-Rāghib treats ʿ-d-d from its basic sense of number and counting, then follows its figurative uses through the Qur'anic verses where the root occurs.

1. **Number (al-ʿadad).** Units put together, or the putting together of units; al-Rāghib says the two definitions are the same. Examples: "the number of the years and the reckoning" (Q 10:5). In "We struck upon their ears in the cave for years, a number" (Q 18:11), he says the mention of number signals that the years were many.

2. **Counting (al-ʿadd).** Joining numbers one to another. Examples: "He has enumerated them and counted them" (Q 19:94); "ask those who count" (Q 23:113), meaning those who keep number and reckoning; "how long did you tarry on the earth, in number of years?" (Q 23:112); "a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count" (Q 22:47).

3. **Figurative use: "counted" meaning few.** A thing that is "counted and enumerated" (maʿdūd) is few, as opposed to what is too much to count, the kind of thing meant by "without reckoning" (Q 2:212). So "except for days counted" (Q 2:80) means a few days. Al-Rāghib explains that they said they would be punished only for the days in which they worshipped the calf.

4. **Figurative use in the opposite sense: many.** An ʿadīd army is a large one, and "they are people of number" means there are so many of them that they have to be counted. So something small is called "not counted". Al-Rāghib says "years, a number" (Q 18:11) can bear either meaning. Related expressions:
   - "this is not taken into account" (ghayr muʿtadd bihi);
   - "he has ʿudda", meaning a great deal of wealth, weapons and the like, as in "they would have prepared some preparation for it" (Q 9:46);
   - "ʿidd water", which he lists without explaining.

5. **Al-ʿidda: the thing counted, a number.** "We have not made their number" (Q 74:31) means their count. "Then a number of other days" (Q 2:184) means the person owes as many days as he missed, kept at a time other than Ramaḍān. Also "the number of the months" (Q 9:36).

6. **The ʿidda of a woman.** Al-Rāghib defines it as the days after which it becomes lawful for her to marry. Examples: "you have no ʿidda over them to count" (Q 33:49); "divorce them at their ʿidda and enumerate the ʿidda" (Q 65:1).

7. **Making ready (al-iʿdād).** Al-Rāghib derives it from counting in the same way that isqāʾ ("giving to drink") comes from saqy ("watering"). "I made this ready for you" means "I placed it so that you can count on it and take it as you need it." Example: "prepare for them what you can" (Q 8:60). He reports a view that aʿtadnā, "We have prepared" (Q 4:18; Q 25:11), and aʿtadat, "she prepared a reclining-place for them" (Q 12:31), also belong to this root.

8. **Further Qur'anic uses of counted days.**
   - "then a number of other days" (Q 2:184): the number of days missed;
   - "that you complete the number" (Q 2:185): the number of the month;
   - "days counted" (Q 2:184): he says this refers to the month of Ramaḍān;
   - "remember God in days counted" (Q 2:203): he says these are the three days after the day of sacrifice, while the "known days" are the first ten of Dhū al-Ḥijja.

   Some jurists instead count the day of sacrifice and the two days after it as the "counted days". On their view, the day of sacrifice belongs to both the "counted" and the "known" days.

9. **Al-ʿidād.** The counted time at which pain recurs. The Prophet is quoted: "The morsel of Khaybar has kept coming back to me at intervals (tuʿāddunī)."

10. **ʿIddān of a thing.** Its period and time.

text:
Root ʿ-d-l (عدل), per Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha). He treats it as two sound roots that are near-opposites: one meaning evenness/straightness, the other meaning crookedness/deviation.

FIRST ROOT — evenness, equality, straightness:
1. Of a person, ʿadl = one who is approved and straight in conduct; upright. The noun can stay unchanged for one, two, or many ("this is ʿadl," "the two are ʿadl"), but also inflects (dual ʿadlān, plural ʿudūl). A verse of Zuhayr uses ʿadl of trusted arbiters who are "accepted, and just." One says a man is "manifestly upright" (bayyin al-ʿadl wa-l-ʿudūla).
2. ʿadl = judging by equity, deciding evenly.
3. Equality/counterpart: something that equals another is its ʿidl; ʿadaltu bi-fulānin fulānan = "I made one the equal of the other"; yuʿādiluhu = "counterbalances him." Ibn Fāris applies this to the mushrik who yaʿdilu bi-rabbihi — treating another as equal to his Lord.
4. Related concrete nouns: al-ʿidlān = the two panniers/loads on a pack-animal, named for being equal in weight; al-ʿadīl = the person who rides balancing you on the other side of a camel-litter.
5. ʿadl = the value or ransom of a thing. He cites Q 2:123 "and no ʿadl shall be accepted from it," glossing ʿadl there as fidya (ransom). All these senses come back to muʿādala = making-equal.
6. ʿadl = the opposite of wrongdoing/tyranny (jawr): "he ruled justly among his subjects."
7. muʿtadil = balanced/temperate — a day whose heat and cold are equal, or food that is moderate.
8. ʿadaltuhu ḥattā iʿtadala = "I straightened it until it stood straight"; supported by a poetic line about gripping/steadying the earth so it does not lean.
9. al-muʿtadila among she-camels = one whose limbs are well-proportioned.
10. The ship-name ʿadawliyya: Ibn Fāris allows it could fit this root (such ships being even and well-balanced), but notes al-Khalīl's view that it is instead a place-name adjective (from a place called ʿAdawlā), citing Ṭarafa's verse.

SECOND ROOT — crookedness/deviation:
11. ʿadala / inʿadala = to curve, swerve, turn aside. He cites Dhū al-Rumma: "had I yielded to my glance it would not have turned aside."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris opens by stating that ʿ-d-s, as a triliteral root, has no single underlying sense that unifies its uses — it is not a "true" root with one core meaning. He then records two separate, unrelated usages that Arabic speakers attached to these letters:

1. **The grain**: the well-known legume — lentils — is called "ʿadas."

2. **A mule-driving cry**: Arabs say "ʿadas!" as a goading call (zajr) to drive mules forward.

He supports the second usage with two citations:
- A verse of poetry in which a rider taunts a mule with "ʿadas! ʿAbbād has no authority over you... you have escaped, and the one you carry is now free" — using the cry as if it were the mule's own name.
- A line, "When I load my gear upon ʿadas," where "ʿadas" stands for the female mule herself — she is nicknamed "ʿadas" simply because that is the cry used to drive her.

In short: this is a "no-derivation" entry — Ibn Fāris flags ʿ-d-s as a root without a unifying lexical meaning, and instead catalogues two disconnected conventional uses (a plant name, and an onomatopoeic driving-call that came to double as a name for the mule).

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-D-W as one sound root whose whole family turns on a single idea: going beyond something, overstepping the limit at which one ought to stop.

1. Running (al-ʿadw). To run/gallop: ʿadā yaʿdū ʿadwan; the runner is ʿādin. Al-Khalīl notes two verbal-noun forms — ʿadw (like ghazw) and ʿuduww (like ḥuḍūr, quʿūd).

2. Overstepping / transgression (al-taʿaddī, al-ʿudwān). Going past one's proper bounds. Qurʾān 6:108, "lest they revile God ʿadwan," is read two ways — ʿadwan and ʿuduwwan. The ʿādī is one who assaults people wrongfully (ẓulman wa-ʿudwānan). Related: "he overstepped his measure" (ʿadā ṭawrahu); al-ʿudwān is glossed by al-Khalīl as manifest injustice, and iʿtidāʾ (aggression) is derived from it. Of a horse, ʿadawān = a strong, frequent runner; of a wolf, one that preys on people (with a poetic citation).

3. The exceptive particle. Mā raʾaytu aḥadan mā ʿadā Zaydan ("no one except Zayd"), which al-Khalīl explains as "not passing beyond Zayd."

4. Al-ʿadwā. Two senses: (a) seeking redress — your appeal to a ruler or judge to act (yuʿdiyaka) against one who wronged you; (b) contagion — what is said to pass on from mange or disease; cited with the ḥadīth "No ʿadwā, and nothing transmits [disease] to anything." Ibn Fāris ties this to the core idea: a disease that does not pass beyond its bearer to you.

5. Assault / robbery (al-ʿadwa). The onslaught of a thief or raider: ʿadā ʿalayhi ("he set upon him and took his property," or "struck him with his sword") — here the sense is wrongdoing, not running on foot.

6. Preoccupation / distraction (al-ʿadāʾ, al-ʿādiya). Something that diverts you (yaʿdūka) from your business. "Hold your ʿādiya (harm) back from us." Cited with Zuhayr, where a distraction (ʿadāʾ) kept the poet from his beloved.

7. Coursing two quarries (al-ʿidāʾ, with kasra). When a horse, dog, or hunter takes two prey in succession, felling one after the other (cited with Imruʾ al-Qays) — also from "running." A variant ʿadāʾ (fatḥa) means a single burst/heat of running.

8. The side / length of a thing (al-ʿadāʾ). The extent along which something's breadth or length runs: "I kept to the length of the river"; "a road running along the mountainside." Variant ʿidwa; the hāʾ may drop (ʿidw), plural aʿdāʾ al-nahr / al-ṭarīq ("the banks/edges"). Morphological note: taʿdāʾ is on the pattern tafʿāl. A related word ʿudawāʾ can name a way-station; cited with Dhū al-Rumma. Al-Khalīl adds ʿindaʾwa (crookedness, difficulty), which he also traces to al-ʿadāʾ.

9. Turning/moving on (verb form II, ʿaddā). "He passed on from the matter to another"; "you put the worry aside from me"; "turn from this matter to something else" (cited with al-Nābigha). Also taʿaddaytu al-mafāza ("I crossed the desert"), and ʿaddaytu al-nāqa ("I urged the she-camel on," with a poetic citation).

10. Enemy (al-ʿaduww). Derived from the same root; the one form serves singular, dual, and plural. Cited with Qurʾān 26:77 (Abraham: "they are an enemy to me, except the Lord of the Worlds"). Plurals/related: ʿidā, ʿudā, ʿādī, ʿudāt.

11. Hard, dry ground (al-ʿudawāʾ). So named because a settler must "pass on beyond" it. Al-Khalīl: it may be hit inside a dug well, sometimes as rock they veer aside from (cited with al-ʿAjjāj, of a wild bull that hit hard ground and swerved off).

12. Valley-bank (al-ʿudwa). A firm part of a valley's edge, named because it "opposes" (tuʿādī) the river — as if the two banks were contending opponents.

13. Summer pasture (al-ʿadawiyya, pattern faʿaliyya). Summer plants that green up after spring has passed, grazed by camels: "the camels found ʿadawiyya."

quran_words: يَسْتَعْفِفْ 3x "then he should refrain"; تَّعَفُّف 1x "(their) restraint"
text:
Ibn Fāris traces ʿ-f-f to two sound root meanings: refraining from what is foul, and the scantness of something.

1. **Restraint.** al-ʿiffa is refraining from what is not fitting. A restrained man is ʿaff or ʿafīf; the verb is ʿaffa, yaʿiffu, with the verbal nouns ʿiffa, ʿafāfa and ʿafāf.

2. **A small remainder of milk.** al-ʿuffa, also called al-ʿufāfa, is the milk left in the udder. al-Aʿshā speaks of a young one that nothing nourishes but an ʿufāfa or a fuwāq. The command taʿāffa nāqataka means: milk your she-camel after the first milking, then let her young one suck what is left. ʿaffaftu fulānan means "I gave him the ʿufāfa to drink."

Ibn Fāris sets apart the expression jāʾa ʿalā ʿiffāni dhāka, "he came at its due time": he explains ʿiffān as a case of letter substitution for iffān, which he treated earlier.

poets_named: al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); unnamed verse ×2; Jarīr (Umayyad); Kuthayyir (Umayyad); Labīd (lived into Islam); al-Kumayt (Umayyad)
text:
**Root ʿ-f-r (عفر) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha**

Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-f-r as one sound root branching into five distinct senses.

**1. A color — dust-red.**
Al-ʿufra names a color: dust-gray shading into red. From this, plain earth/soil itself is called al-ʿafar. Related verb forms: "ʿaffara" (to roll something in the dust), "iʿtafara" (to fall into the dust) — used of a woman's loose hair-locks trailing on the ground when let down. Ibn Duraid glosses al-ʿafar as the bare dust on the earth's surface. A gazelle is called aʿfar for its dust-toned color (so too dust-red sand); al-yaʿfūr, the fawn, is named for how often it lies close to the ground. Al-ʿafīr is meat sun-dried on sand, and by extension sawīq (a roasted-grain drink) drunk "ʿafīr" means plain, without oil or ghee.
A separate, possibly-related idiom, "waqaʿū fī ʿāfūri sharrin" ("they fell into a pit of trouble"), may come from this same dust-sense, or may be an unrelated word with a substituted letter; Ibn al-Aʿrābī derives it from "throwing someone down and rolling him in dust." Abū ʿUbayda's report that "ʿafarū" can mean "they sowed seed" is tentatively linked here too, since seed is cast into the soil. A ḥadīth about Hilāl b. Umayya using "ʿaffarnā" is connected to palm-pollination (al-ʿafār).
Other extensions: al-ʿufr for moonlit/white nights (the month's 13th night is "ʿafrāʾ"); al-ʿufr also said of white, hairless sheep, with owners called muʿfirūn — the tribe of Hudhayl alone bears this description. A saying: "there's nothing like it on the face of the earth." And in a ḥadīth, the Prophet, when finishing the prayer's salutation, held his upper arms out from his sides so the whiteness under his armpits (ʿufrat ibṭayhi) showed from behind.

**2. A tree — al-ʿafār.**
A fire-rich tree used to make fire-sticks (for kindling by friction). A proverb pairs it with markh-wood for fire-making. Cited in verse by al-Aʿshā, both for the tree/fire-sticks and possibly as the origin of the woman's name "ʿAfāra" (and its diminutive "ʿUfayra"). Some say al-ʿufur is simply the plural of this tree-name, again tied to fire-striking imagery ("markh and ʿafār earned the most credit for fire").

**3. Strength and ferocity.**
A strong, bold, or cunningly wicked man is "ʿifr" — hence "shayṭānun ʿifriyatun / ʿifrītun" (a devilish, formidable one), plurals al-ʿufāriya, al-ʿafārīt; also glossed as "clever and sharp." A rebellious, untamable man is likewise ʿifr (pl. aʿfār). Lions are called ʿifirr, ʿafarnā (fem. ʿafarnāh) for their ferocity, illustrated in verse. A burrowing creature is nicknamed "layth ʿifirrīn" (lion of ʿifirrīn) because it digs into dust and flings it up when disturbed — tying this sense back to sense 1. Al-Khalīl also records "layth ʿifirrīn" as an honorific for a man at the peak of maturity, age fifty, quoted within a folk-saying charting a man's character through each decade of life up to a hundred. Abū ʿUbayd records "al-ʿifriya al-nifriya" for a detestable, wicked person, and a ḥadīth condemning God's dislike of such a person — glossed as one who has never once suffered loss of wealth or health. Some also link al-ʿafarfar, a lion-epithet for one that throws down and dust-rolls its rival, back to sense 1. "ʿAfār" is also recorded as a man's name after whom a type of arrowhead was named, and al-ʿifirr is alternatively called ʿufāriya (cited in Jarīr's verse).

**4. A stretch of time.**
"I met him ʿan ʿufr" means "after a month had passed." Said of an old, established nobility: "his rank is not recent [ʿan ʿufr] but ancient" — illustrated by a verse of Kuthayyir about inherited nobility maturing over generations. Also connected here: the practice of leaving a pollinated palm tree unwatered for forty days (ʿafār al-nakhl), and al-taʿfīr, a nursing mother's practice of suckling her child intermittently rather than continuously (illustrated by a verse of Labīd about an abandoned/intermittently-fed fawn). Al-Farrāʾ explained al-ʿafīr (of a woman) as one who never gives gifts, deriving it from that same intermittent-suckling idea; Ibn Fāris judges this a poor fit and instead argues al-ʿafīr describes a woman whose gift-giving was once constant but became occasional — a reading he says better fits the "time" sense, supported by a verse of al-Kumayt (also cited by al-Farrāʾ) where a woman's once-steady generosity turns "ʿafīr."

**5. A part of an animal's body.**
Al-ʿifriya (also al-ʿifrāh, a dialect variant, like nāṣiya/nāṣāh) is the hair on the crown/middle of the head — illustrated by a verse picturing time "climbing up" to a man's ʿifrāh and shaving it away [i.e., old age and baldness]. By extension/comparison, a rooster's comb is also called ʿifriya, and Abū Zayd records that the nape-hair of a human is likewise called al-ʿifriya.

poets_named: al-Kumayt (Umayyad); Labīd (lived into Islam); Zuhayr (pre-Islamic); al-Ṭirimmāḥ (Umayyad)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ʿ-F-W (عفو) from TWO base ideas: (1) leaving/abandoning a thing (tark), and (2) seeking a thing (ṭalab). He argues nearly every usage traces back to "leaving," and that even "seeking" ultimately reduces to it.

FIRST ROOT — LEAVING / ABANDONING

1. al-ʿafw — pardon. God's ʿafw toward His creation is His leaving them unpunished, as a bounty. Al-Khalīl: whoever deserves punishment and you leave him, you have "ʿafawta ʿanhu" (pardoned him). Ibn Fāris adds a nuance: one can ʿafā over something in the sense of simply leaving it, with no desert involved — as in the Prophet's "I have pardoned you as to the ṣadaqa of horses," meaning "I have left off imposing it," not remitting a deserved penalty.

2. al-ʿāfiya — God's protecting/defending of the servant from harm: ʿāfāhu / aʿfāhu Allāh (God kept him well).

3. al-istiʿfāʾ — asking to be excused from a task someone imposes on you.

4. Camel usage: ʿafā ẓahr al-baʿīr — the camel's back was left un-ridden (aʿfaytuhu, I left it so).

5. al-ʿifāwa — food set aside as a gift for someone; from ʿafw (leaving), since it was left un-eaten. He cites al-Kumayt's line about the starving girl "possessor of the ʿifāwa" and rejects the reading that ties it to giving away surplus wealth, preferring "the gift-food that hard times ended."

6. al-ʿāfī of broth — what the borrower of a cooking-pot returns; called ʿāfī because it was left un-eaten.

7. al-ʿafw — untrodden ground; hence arḍ ʿafw (land with no trace, ungrazed) and ṭaʿām ʿafw (fresh food no one has touched, al-unuf).

8. ʿafā = became effaced/obliterated (of ruined abodes), because a thing left un-tended fades over time. Shāhid: Labīd's "The abodes are effaced… left desolate (taʾabbada)." Ibn Fāris explicitly denies that ʿafā is one of the aḍdād (meaning both "effaced" and "increased"); for him the single underlying sense is "leaving."

9. ʿalayhi al-ʿafāʾ — a curse; al-ʿafāʾ as either "dust" (undisturbed dust) or "effacement." Shāhid: Zuhayr. Verb forms: ʿafat al-dār, taʿaffat al-dār (the abode was effaced); Ibn al-Aʿrābī: dust thickening over a dwelling until it covers it.

10. al-ʿafw / al-ʿufuww (pl. ʿifāʾ) — young asses; female ʿafwa; named so because left un-ridden and unloaded. A grammatical aside: the plural form ʿifawa is the only case in Arabic of a moving wāw after a moving letter at a word's end, adopted because "ʿifāh" was disliked. Al-Farrāʾ gives variant vocalizations (ʿifw/ʿufw, ʿify/ʿufy) for the donkey's foal.

11. al-ʿifāʾ — abundant, long fur or feather (left un-plucked, un-sheared): nāqa dhāt ʿifāʾ; the ostrich's and birds' overgrown plumage (singular ʿifāʾa, needing thickness to qualify). Shawāhid: al-Ṭirimmāḥ (describing a rooster) and a she-camel description. Al-Khalīl extends it to cloud resembling nap/fringe (a simile from thick fur).

12. Of hair: ʿafawtuhu / ʿafaytuhu — leaving it to grow long and thick. Qurʾānic shāhid: {ḥattā ʿafaw} (al-Aʿrāf 95), glossed "until they grew and multiplied," which Ibn Fāris takes as confirming that the base sense is "leaving." Also ʿafā al-māʾ (water untrodden/unmuddied, its ʿafwa), and ʿafwat al-sharāb (a drink's best, undiminished part) — Abū Zayd.

SECOND ROOT — SEEKING

13. al-ʿufāt / al-muʿtafūn — seekers of bounty; iʿtafaytu fulānan = I sought his favor. Ibn Fāris notes that if the "kindness" sought is itself the ʿafw (freely given surplus, not hoarded), then this root collapses back into "leaving." Abū ʿAmr: aʿṭaytuhu al-māl ʿafwan = I gave it unasked. Al-Aṣmaʿī: iʿtafāhu = ʿafāhu; the seekers also called al-ʿuffā.

14. al-ʿāfiya (second sense) — a collective for seekers of sustenance/foragers. Hadith shāhid: reviving dead land, "what the ʿāfiya eat of it is a ṣadaqa." Ibn al-Aʿrābī: the many "comers" (ʿāfiya) to a water source; ibil ʿāfiya (camels that reject trodden pasture and seek fresh). Al-Naḍr: istaʿaffat al-ibil — camels lipping dry herbage up off the dust.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: عَهْد 29x "the covenant"; عَٰهَدَ 11x "you made a covenant"; عَهِدَ 6x "and we made a covenant"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives every branch of the root ʿ-h-d (عهد) from a single core idea, which he credits to al-Khalīl: guarding or keeping something, and renewing one's contact with it.

1. Injunction / charge. عَهِدَ (ʿahida) means to enjoin or charge, akin to a bequest (waṣiyya) — so called because a ʿahd is something that ought to be kept. From this comes the ʿahd written out to appoint a governor (a commission or warrant); plural ʿuhūd.

2. Pledge / covenant. الْعَهْد is a binding pledge or solemn compact (mawthiq); plural ʿuhūd.

3. Contact / acquaintance. ʿahd can mean meeting and frequenting: قريب العهد به = "recently in contact with it," since frequenting a thing is itself a form of keeping. العَهِيد is a thing whose time has grown old.

4. Familiar abode. الْعَهْد (and مَعْهَد, plural maʿāhid) is the dwelling a people keep returning to after they leave — attested by a verse of Ruʾba about tracing the effaced ruins of such a place.

5. Covenanted people. أهل العهد / المُعَاهَدُون are those bound under covenant regarding the jizya due from them (verbal noun muʿāhada). Ibn Fāris keeps this within the one core sense — a matter "held in trust" for them — and notes the term drops away if they accept Islam.

6. Tending / attending to. al-iʿtihād, al-taʿāhud, and al-taʿahhud all mean to tend or attend to something (al-Khalīl), with a verse of al-Ṭirimmāḥ on a man who "does not tend to" what God made binding on him. عَهِيدُك is one who mutually covenants with you (illustrated by a verse contrasting the Turks' faithfulness with Nizār's).
   - Grammatical dispute: Abū Ḥātim held that تعهّدتُ ("I tended") is correct but تعاهدتُ is not, because taʿāhud requires two parties. Ibn Fāris counters that al-Khalīl knows Arab speech better than al-Naḍr, and that forms like تغافل ("feigned heedlessness") and تجاوز ("passed over") also take this pattern without implying two agents.

7. Liability document / warranty. العُهْدَة is the deed securing a sale. "There is a ʿuhda not yet made firm" = something still needs securing. The sale-formula "المَلَسَى لا عُهدة" ("a slipping-away, no liability") means both parties are clear with nothing left to tighten. "In his affair there is a ʿuhda" hints at a weakness — the same underlying idea.

8. Stipulation. Making a condition is sometimes called استِعْهَاد (istiʿhād), because a stipulated condition is something to be kept; supported by a verse on exacting a pledge from a husband.

9. Qur'anic citation. {أَلَمْ أَعْهَدْ إِلَيْكُمْ} (Yā Sīn 60): Ibn Fāris glosses it — "God knows best" — as "did I not set before you, and make binding on you to keep, the matter I enjoined."

10. Rain (kept within the same analogy). العَهْد is rain that follows the earliest autumn rain (the wasmī), also called al-waliyy. Ibn Fāris likens it to "tending" an estate: the rain first marks the land, then returns to attend to it. When spring follows the wasmī with rain after rain — the later reaching the moisture of the earlier — that is ʿahd, plural عِهَاد; indeed any rain following rain is ʿihād. A meadow so watered is مَعْهُودة (rained-upon); attested by al-Ṭirimmāḥ (watered chamomile) and Ibn al-Aʿrābī (ʿahd clouds alongside الفُتُوح, the broad copious rains). Others define ʿihād as early spring before the cold intensifies (singular ʿahda), or as the stored first rains that make roots strike and greenery spread — called al-ḥayāʾ (life-giving rains) if further rains follow, otherwise of no account.

11. Era / time. كان ذلك على عهد فلان وعِهْدانه = "that was in so-and-so's time," with a verse using عِهْدان for one's era.

text:
Root Ehn (ain-ha-nun) - Ibn Faris, Maqayis al-Lugha.

Core meaning per the author: softness, ease, and scantiness of sustenance/substance in a thing.

Senses recorded, each traced to a named authority:

1. Ready wealth (al-Khalil): al-ahin = property regularly on hand for its owner, "the ready, present" wealth. "He gave him from the ready portion (ahin) of his wealth." A verse pairs "wealth for ready wealth (mal ahin), undivided."

2. The immediate/prompt (al-Shaybani): al-ahin = al-ajil, "the swift." "How prompt is what came to you!" A saying distinguishes a cash sale from a credit sale: "did you sell ahin [cash-in-hand] or on credit?"

3. In hand / within one's power (Ibn al-A'rabi): something "ahin" is in your grasp, at your disposal (verb: ahina ya'hanu 'uhunan). A verse uses it of a woman's favor being "present and abiding."

4. To emerge/come forth (Abu Zayd): good or news "ahana" - came forth - from someone (he flags uncertainty over which exact word was cited).

5. To hasten (al-Nadr): "i'hin lahu" = hurry it up for him; "ahana lahu ma arada" = what he wanted came to him promptly.

6. Speaking carelessly (Ibn Habib): "he throws his speech on its awahin" - speaking without care, or purely from conjecture, without certainty. Ibn Faris notes this fits the root's logic: such speech is not held back with care or verified.

7. Broken/bent, and weakness: a "qadib ahin" is a cracked, bent rod; an "uhna" is a partial break - looks sound but bends when shaken. A poor man is likewise called "ahin," from this same idea of weakness. Related verb: "ahantu l-qadiba" = I bent/broke the rod.

8. The awahin of the palm-tree: one report (Abu al-Jarrah) claims this means the fronds once they dry out - Ibn Faris rejects this as an error, since it does not fit the root's pattern. The correct account, he says (following Ibn al-A'rabi): the awahin are the fronds closest to the palm's growing heart - still moist and soft, not yet hardened. This is backed by a hadith in which the Prophet tells a companion to bring him palm-fronds but avoid the awahin, "because they are moist," and by Hijazi dialect usage naming these same soft inner fronds "al-awahin."

9. A rejected reading: some said al-ahin means "the one who holds back/restrains" (al-habis), citing a line of al-Nabigha where a camel is urged on because "short of the watering-place there is no ahin to hold you back." Ibn Faris judges this an error too, and reinterprets the line by his own root-logic: the ground short of the watering-place is easy going, not barred - consistent with the root's sense of "ease," not "restraint."

10. Possibly (if a report from Ibn al-Sikkit is reliable): al-awahin also names certain veins/ligaments in a she-camel's womb, per a verse of Ibn al-Riqa' describing the womb binding tightly around the fetus. Ibn Faris suggests the poet is comparing these veins to the soft palm-fronds.

11. Al-ihn - dyed wool: Ibn Faris judges it plausible that this word too belongs to the same root-family, since dyeing makes wool soft.

The entry closes with "wa-llahu a'lam" (God knows best).

text:
Ibn Fāris derives ʿ-j-b (عجب) from two sound roots: one about deeming something great/being conceited, the other a part of an animal's body.

1. Wonder / self-conceit (al-ʿujb, al-ʿajab). Al-ʿujb is a person magnifying himself inwardly — "he is conceited about himself" (muʿjab bi-nafsihi). From the sense of wonder: ʿajiba yaʿjabu ʿajaban ("to marvel"), and amr ʿajīb ("a wondrous matter") — used when a thing is deemed great and momentous.

2. Degrees of wonder (per al-Khalīl). Al-Khalīl distinguished al-ʿajīb (also al-ʿajab) — the matter one wonders at — from al-ʿujāb, which exceeds the ordinary bound of the wondrous. His analogy: ṭawīl ("tall," common among people) versus ṭuwāl ("excessively, ungainly tall"). Intensive phrase: ʿajab ʿājib ("wonder upon wonder").

3. Intense astonishment (al-istiʿjāb). The strongest form of marvelling; one is mustaʿjib or mutaʿajjib at what he sees. Shāhid — Aws [ibn Ḥajar]: "and one astonished at the composure he sees in us — yet had war shoved him, he would not have stirred."

4. Being pleased / impressed (aʿjaba). aʿjabanī hādhā l-shayʾ ("this thing pleased me"), uʿjibtu bihi ("I was impressed by it"), and shayʾ muʿjib ("a pleasing thing") — said of something exceedingly beautiful. Also qiṣṣa ʿajab ("a wondrous tale").

5. The rump (al-ʿajb) — the second, physical root. In any beast, the base of the tail set into the rear of the hindquarters, where the two haunches meet. By likeness, the thinning tips of sand-dunes are called ʿujūb — shāhid from Labīd. A she-camel is ʿajbāʾ when the top of her rear is thin and her hip-bones protrude — an unsightly conformation.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) treats ʿ-j-f as having two distinct, unrelated core senses.

1. Leanness / emaciation (al-ʿajaf)
- The word means the loss of fatness, thinness.
- Adjective forms: masculine aʿjaf, feminine ʿajfāʾ, plural (for both sexes) ʿijāf.
- Verb: ʿajifa yaʿjafu ("to become lean").
- A grammatical curiosity he flags: no other Arabic word of the pattern afʿal takes a broken plural on the pattern fiʿāl except this one (ʿijāf) — the Arabs modeled it on simān, "fat ones."
- Usage: aʿjafa al-qawm — "the people('s livestock) grew lean," said when a people's herds become emaciated; such people are called muʿjifūn.
- Al-Kisāʾī cites the extended, figurative use shafatān ʿajfāwān, "two ʿajfāʾ lips," meaning fine or delicate lips — not literally starved.
- A grammatical note from Abū ʿUbayd: the expected past-tense pattern for an afʿal/faʿlāʾ adjective pair is faʿila (compare ʿarija/aʿraj, "to limp"/"lame"), so ʿajifa is the analogically correct form; but ʿajufa is also used. He lists this word among a small set of exceptional verbs that instead take the pattern faʿula (he names samura, ḥamuqa, raʿuna, ʿajufa, kharuqa — though he says there are six such words, only five are given in this text). Al-Aṣmaʿī reports a parallel case: ʿajuma for al-aʿjam ("the inarticulate/non-Arabic-speaking one").
- The sense is further extended metaphorically to land: arḍ ʿajfāʾ, "lean/barren land" — land with no good in it and no vegetation, as in the scout's report "I found a barren land."
- And to an arrowhead: naṣl aʿjaf, meaning a thin, slender arrowhead. He quotes a verse by Ibn Abī ʿĀʾidh describing arrows as ʿijāf al-niṣāl, "lean/slender of arrowhead."

2. Restraint of the self, endurance toward or away from something
- ʿajaftu nafsī ʿani l-ṭaʿām — "I held myself back from food," i.e., restraining yourself from something you still desire. He notes that using this verb for restraining someone else (ʿajaftu ghayrī) is rare. A verse is cited using the related noun taʿjīf ("forced abstention") alongside small food-measures (mudd, half-mudd, a few dates) that did not nourish someone.
- ʿajaftu nafsī ʿalā l-marīḍ — "I devoted/restrained myself to the sick person," meaning bearing with him patiently and nursing him. A verse is cited in which the speaker, though mocked for his own emaciation (nuḥūl), says he still holds himself in patient service to a close friend, offering affection and generosity.

Ibn Fāris presents these as two separate root-meanings under one triliteral shape, connected only by the shared letters, not by a shared concept — one is physical thinness (and its figurative extensions to land and arrowheads), the other is self-restraint or patient devotion.

poets_named: Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad); unnamed verse; al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam) ×2; al-Khansāʾ (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ʿ-j-l from two distinct sound roots: (1) haste/speed, and (2) a particular animal (the calf).

FIRST ROOT — haste (al-isrāʿ):
1. Core sense: al-ʿajala = haste in a matter. The agent adjective has two forms, ʿajil and ʿajul (both "hasty"), attested in a line of Dhū al-Rumma.
2. Verbs: istaʿjala someone = urged him on; ʿajila someone = outstripped/got ahead of him. Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'an, al-Aʿrāf 7:150, "Did you hasten [ahead of] the command of your Lord?"
3. ʿujāla = anything taken in haste; proverb: "the traveller's quick provision is dates and sawīq (parched-barley meal)." Al-Khalīl's reported sense of ʿajal (hurried food served before the meal is ready) Ibn Fāris rejects: he judges the supporting verse fabricated and the word baseless, though he grants the morphological analogy is sound. The verb ʿajaltu al-qawm = "I gave people a quick bite" (like lahhana).
4. ʿājil = the opposite of ājil (the deferred). Hence this world = al-ʿājila (the hastening/present) and the hereafter = al-ājila (the deferred) — Ibn Fāris attributes this pairing to "the lexicographers."
5. Proper name: al-ʿAjlān (Kaʿb b. Rabīʿa b. ʿĀmir), said to be named for hurrying his slave, with a supporting verse.
6. She-camels: al-muʿajjil / al-muʿjil = one that calves before full term yet whose young survives.
7. Extended by "carrying onto" the haste-sense — objects associated with quick motion:
   - al-ʿajala = ox-cart; also the water-drawing wheel/hoist (manjanūn), pl. ʿajal, ʿajalāt. Abū ʿUbayd: a beam across a well's two posts from which the bucket hangs. Abū Zayd: the well-pulley (maḥāla), with a cited verse.
   - al-ʿijla = a small water-skin (pl. ʿijal), so named because it is light and its bearer moves quickly with it; verse of al-Aʿshā cited.
8. al-ʿajūl (al-Khalīl) = a she-camel maddened by the loss of her young; pl. ʿujul; shawāhid from an anonymous line and from al-Khansāʾ. The word is sometimes applied to a bereaved human mother too (al-Aʿshā cited). Ibn Fāris explains the tie to the root as the agitation and haste that grip the grief-stricken — noting that, unlike thakila from thukl (bereavement), no verb ʿajilat was actually attested from the Arabs, even though the underlying sense is the same.

SECOND ROOT — the calf:
al-ʿijl = the young of the cow; dialectal variant ʿijjawl; plural ʿajājīl; feminine ʿijla / ʿijwala. A man was also named ʿIjl from this.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root ʿ-J-M (عجم) — al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān

Core idea, as this entry sets it out: ʿujma is the opposite of clear expression (ibāna), and iʿjām is leaving something obscure or indistinct.

1. Muteness / absence of clear response. To say istaʿjamtu l-dār is to find a dwelling unresponsive — its people gone, with no ʿarīb left in it, i.e. no one who returns an intelligible answer. Al-Rāghib cites an Arab saying, "I went out from lands that speak," as a figure for lands that are inhabited and cultivated.

2. ʿajam as the non-Arabs. ʿAjam is the counterpart of ʿArab, and ʿajamī is the adjective of relation to them. But aʿjam denotes anyone whose speech is indistinct, Arab or not — the label is extended from the fact that little is understood from the ʿajam.

3. Qurʾānic citations. 26:198, "had We sent it down upon one of the aʿjamīn" — al-Rāghib notes the form is contracted from al-aʿjamiyyīn by dropping the yāʾs. 41:44, "had We made it an aʿjamī recitation they would have said: why are its signs not set out distinctly? An aʿjamī and an Arab?" And 16:103, "him to whom they incline is aʿjamī."

4. ʿajmāʾ — the dumb beast. An animal is called ʿajmāʾ because it cannot make itself clear in words as a speaker does. Al-Rāghib quotes two sayings using the word: "the daytime prayer is ʿajmāʾ," meaning the recitation in it is not said aloud; and "the wound caused by a beast carries no compensation."

5. Two opposed verbs. Aʿjamtu l-kalām ("I made speech indistinct") is the opposite of aʿrabtu ("I made it clear / gave it Arabic inflection"). By contrast aʿjamtu l-kitāba means "I pointed the writing," i.e. removed its obscurity — a privative use of the same form, which he compares to ashkaytuhu, "I removed his grievance."

6. ḥurūf al-muʿjam. Al-Rāghib reports from al-Khalīl that these are the disconnected letters, so called because they are "aʿjamiyya" (indistinct). He adds an explanation offered by some: letters standing alone do not signify what letters joined together signify.

7. bāb muʿjam — a door shut fast, i.e. something left closed off or obscure.

8. ʿajam — date-stones and the like, singular ʿajama. He gives three possible motivations for the name: they are hidden in the fold of the fruit that holds them; or parts of them are concealed under the pressure of chewing; or they are taken into the mouth and hidden while being bitten. Related: ʿajm is the act of biting on such a stone, and "so-and-so is ṣulb al-maʿjam" (hard at the biting-place) means he proves firm when tested.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives ʿ-J-Z (عجز) from two sound roots: (1) weakness/inability, and (2) the hind-part or rear of a thing.

ROOT 1 — inability, weakness:
1. عَجِزَ عن الشيء ("to be unable to do something"), verbal noun عَجْز; the agent is عَاجِز ("incapable"), i.e. ضَعِيف ("weak").
2. Hence عَجْز ("incapacity") is called the opposite of حَزْم ("resolve"), because such a person's judgement is weak. Proverb: "a man inevitably grows incapable."
3. أَعْجَزَنِي فلان = "he eluded me," i.e. I could not pursue and overtake him. So too "nothing can render God incapable" — God is never unable to act when He wills. Qurʾānic shawāhid: al-Jinn 72:12 (لن نعجز الله... ولن نعجزه هربا) and al-ʿAnkabūt 29:22 (وما أنتم بمعجزين في الأرض).
4. Grammar/pronunciation: the verb also occurs as عَجَزَ (fatḥa on the jīm). Ibn Fāris relays, through Thaʿlab from Ibn al-Aʿrābī, the view that عَجِزَ (kasra) is used only of large buttocks growing — linking the two senses.
5. Also from this root: عَجُوز ("old woman"), plural عَجَائِز, verb عَجَّزَتْ ("she grew old"). عَاجَزَ فلانٌ فلانًا = "he evaded/outran him," went off out of reach — cited with Sabaʾ 34:38 (معاجِزين). Extended uses: wine is sometimes called عَجُوز because of its age, as if an old woman; and عِجْزَة / ابن العِجْزَة = an old man's last-born child (poetic citation, "named Maʿbad").

ROOT 2 — the rear / hind-part:
6. عَجُز = the back or rear of a thing, plural أَعْجَاز; extended to عَجُز الأمر / أعجاز الأمور ("the tail-ends of affairs"). Proverb: "do not busy yourselves with the tail-ends of matters whose fronts have already passed."
7. عَجِيزَة = a woman's buttocks, specifically when large; adjective عَجْزَاء (large-buttocked), plural عَجِيزَات. Al-Khalīl noted one avoids the plural عَجَائِز here, to prevent confusion with the plural of عَجُوز. Poetic shawāhid: Dhū al-Rumma and Abū al-Najm (both describing a shapely, large-hipped woman).
8. العَجَز = a disease striking a beast in its hind-quarters; the affected female is عَجْزَاء, the male أَعْجَز.
9. By likeness within this root: العَجْزَاء of sand = a high dune resembling a mountain (plural العُجْز), likened to a woman's buttocks, just as buttocks are likened to sand-dunes; العَجْزَاء of eagles = one light in the hind-part (citation from al-Aʿshā).

Ibn Fāris notes he omitted further examples to avoid repetition, all tracing back to these two roots. Finally, he reports on hearsay that عَجُوز may mean a sword's blade — if sound, named (like the old woman) for its age and the passing of time over it.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-K-F as a single sound root carrying two linked ideas: facing or turning toward something (muqābala), and holding back or confining (ḥabs).

1. Staying turned toward something. The verb ʿakafa (imperfect either yaʿkufu or yaʿkifu; verbal noun ʿukūf) means to face a thing and not turn away from it. Two shawāhid illustrate the sense of persistent gathering around an object: a verse describing figures that "keep about it… like the gathering of the Nabaṭ playing the fanzaj [a dance]", and the phrase ʿakafat al-ṭayr bi-l-qatīl, "the birds kept hovering about the slain man". A line attributed to ʿAmr adds: "We left the horses staying over him, their reins hung on their necks, standing [motionless]."

2. The participle. al-ʿākif is glossed simply as al-muʿtakif — the one who keeps himself to a place or thing. Ibn Fāris gives no further definition of the term here.

3. Form II — fixing gems in place. From the same root comes the usage for a strung ornament once the jewels are set on it: ʿukkifa taʿkīfan. The supporting verse likens bead-strings "held in place by the thread" on either side of a long-necked woman's neck. The gems are both arranged facing along the string and held fast by it — both halves of the root's sense at once.

4. Passive participle — held back. al-maʿkūf means al-maḥbūs, the one detained or prevented. Ibn al-Aʿrābī records the idiom mā ʿakafaka min kadhā, "what held you back from such-and-such?"

5. Qur'anic shāhid for that second sense: Q 48:25, "and the offering held back (maʿkūfan) from reaching its place."

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-l-m as a single sound root whose core meaning is a mark or trace on a thing by which it is told apart from others; he reduces every sense back to this.

1. ʿalāma — a sign or mark. ʿallamtu ʿalā al-shayʾ = "I put a mark on the thing." aʿlama al-fāris = a horseman who wears a distinguishing mark in battle; muʿlim = one who goes out bearing such an emblem.

2. ʿalam — (a) a banner or standard (pl. aʿlām); (b) a mountain, and by extension any landmark (maʿlam), the opposite of a trackless, unmarked place (majhal); its plural is also aʿlām. Poetic witness: al-Khansāʾ likens her brother Ṣakhr to a fire-topped mountain (ʿalam) that travelers' guides steer by.

3. ʿalam — a cleft in the upper lip (such a man is aʿlam, hare-lipped). Same logic: the cleft is like a mark on the person.

4. ʿullām — reported to mean henna, because dyeing with it leaves what is like a mark.

5. ʿilm — knowledge, the opposite of ignorance (jahl). Ibn Fāris holds it follows the same root-logic as ʿalam/ʿalāma. As evidence he cites a variant Qur'anic reading of Q 43:61, "la-ʿalamun li-l-sāʿa" (a marker for the Hour) alongside the standard "la-ʿilmun" (knowledge of the Hour); those who read it thus, he reports, took it to refer to the descent of Jesus, by which the Hour's nearness is known.

6. taʿallama — to learn, i.e. to acquire knowledge (ʿilm) of a thing; and the idiom taʿallam anna… used to mean "know that…" (equivalent to iʿlam), attested in a line of Qays ibn Zuhayr.

7. al-ʿālamūn — the "worlds," i.e. the kinds of creation, because each genus of creation is itself an indicator and sign (maʿlam/ʿalam). Others instead derived it from ijtimāʿ (being gathered together). Ibn Fāris cites Q 6:45, "Lord of the ʿālamīn," which "they" gloss as all created beings entirely, plus two verse-fragments (one anonymous, one on Khindif as "head of this world"). He judges the "gathering" derivation not far-fetched, noting the kindred word ʿaylam, said to mean the sea or a water-abundant well.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-l-n as a single sound root whose core sense is a thing's being made manifest, being pointed to, and becoming apparent (the opposite of being hidden).

1. Base verb: عَلَنَ الأمرُ / يَعْلُنُ (ʿalana / yaʿlunu) — a matter becomes public, comes out into the open.
2. Causative: أَعْلَنْتُهُ (aʿlantuhu) — "I made it public, disclosed it."
3. Derived noun: العِلان (al-ʿilān) is glossed as المُعَالَنة (al-muʿālana) — dealing or acting openly between parties, in the mutual (form III) sense.
