text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-l-q as one large, sound root with a single underlying idea: **that a thing be hung on, or fastened to, something above it**. Every later use, he says, traces back to that. Basic forms: ʿallaqa / taʿlīq ("to hang something up") and ʿaliqa bi- ("to cling to, stick fast to").

1. **Well-gear.** al-ʿalaq is what the pulley hangs from on the well's frame — or, per one report, the pulley's tackle itself. "The well needs its ʿalaq." Abū ʿUbayda: al-ʿalaq is the pulley with all its fittings, excluding the rope and bucket. Al-Liḥyānī: "his well keeps going on ʿalaq" = it is never drawn dry (it has two buckets, a frame and a rope); "a frame with no ʿalaq" = with no rope hung on it.

2. **Clotted blood.** al-ʿalaq is congealed blood; a single piece is ʿalaqa. Ibn Fāris says the analogy holds because such blood clings. Shāhid: "he leaps upon his worn rags from the clotted blood." A threat-formula: "Do it, or you will choke on a clot" — i.e. a threat of killing.

3. **Yoking / pulling water.** al-ʿalaq is also binding two camels with a rope to draw water when the bucket is large; aʿlaqtu bi-l-gharb baʿīrayn = to couple two camels to the end of its rope.

4. **Catching fast.** Al-Khalīl: al-ʿalaq is one thing catching in another. Jarīr: "When his talons fasten on an adversary, he strikes the heart or rends the midriff."

5. **Quarrelling.** ʿaliqa bi-fulān = he fell to disputing with him. ʿalāqa = litigation/quarrel. Al-Khalīl: a miʿlāq is a fierce disputant — Muhalhil: "…and a stubborn adversary, one of miʿlāq." Another transmission reads it with ghayn (miḡlāq), the adversary with whom an opponent's pledge is forfeited beyond redemption.

6. **Love and attachment.** al-ʿalaq = passion. Proverb: "a glance from one possessed of ʿalaq" — one whose heart has fastened to his beloved. Al-Aʿshā: "I was made to love her by chance, and she was attached to another man, and he to yet another woman." ʿalāqa = love that clings to the heart; al-ʿalūq (of women) = one who loves her husband.

7. **Browse and bare sustenance.** al-ʿalāq = the scant pasturage on which livestock make do until spring — al-Aʿshā: "a waste like the back of a shield, where the only ʿalāq is the cud." A doe "ʿalaqa, ʿulūq" = takes from a tree with her mouth; in the ḥadīth of the martyrs the birds "browse (taʿluq) in the Garden." al-ʿulqa = winter-hardy shrubs camels get by on; "he eats only an ʿulqa" = only enough to keep alive. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: al-ʿulqa is any small quantity, plural ʿulaq. "The milker left the camel no ʿulqa" = drew her udder dry. Related: al-ʿalūq is what grazing animals browse of leaf or fruit — "the browse laid a redness on them," camels growing fat and reddish on ṭalḥ leaves.

8. **The leech.** al-ʿalaqa is a small water creature (plural ʿalaq) that fastens on a drinker's throat; a man is maʿlūq when leeches seize his throat; a beast "ʿaliqat ʿalaqan" when a leech takes hold as it drinks.

9. **Blood-guilt (metaphorical).** "So-and-so's blood has clung to so-and-so's clothes" = he is his killer; "so-and-so's blood is on his garment." Abū Dhuʾayb: "She disavows the slain man's blood and his gear, though her wrapper has caught it" — with the note that izār is both masculine and feminine in Hudhayl, and bazz = his weapons. Some hold the line is proverbial ("you bore his blood in your garment" = you killed him), analysed as two clauses run together.

10. **Hanging things.** taʿlīq of a door = setting it up. maʿālīq / aʿālīq = hanging clusters of grapes and the like (aʿālīq has no singular). ʿilāqa = a whip's thong. maʿālīq of a necklace or ear-ornaments = the pendants added to adorn them.

11. **Livelihood.** ʿalāqa also = the means by which one keeps oneself going in living. Proverb: "the one who scrapes by is not like the one who picks and chooses" — a man of scant living is unlike a fastidious man who takes what he pleases. Someone content with a matter short of completion is mutaʿalliq.

12. **Fodder / drink.** al-ʿalīq = fodder, from aʿlaqtuhu → ʿalīq, on the pattern of aʿqadtu l-ʿasal → ʿaqīd. Al-Khalīl is reported to have said drink is called ʿalīq; Ibn Fāris doubts he would say such a thing, especially on the strength of the cited verse: "…we call drink nothing but ʿalīq."

13. **Taking hold / setting about.** ʿaliqat al-fasīla = the palm-shoot took root. ʿaliqa yafʿalu kadhā = he set about doing something, as if attaching himself to it. "Old age has fastened on him at its holds." al-ʿalāqiya = a man who, once he fastens on a thing, hardly lets go. dhū maʿlaqa = a raider who fastens on everything ("I fear a grasping raider will fasten on her").

14. **Proverb of the two ropes.** "ʿaliqat maʿāliqahā wa-ṣarra l-jundab" — a man hooked his rope to a well's rope and on that basis claimed the owner's protection; told to leave, he said this, meaning: the bucket is caught in its fastenings and the heat has come, so departure is impossible.

15. **Medical use.** iʿlāq: a mother pressing up with her hand for a child's ʿudhra (a painful swelling near the uvula) — so called, Ibn Fāris suggests, because in lifting it she "hangs" it up.

16. **The precious object.** ʿilq (pl. aʿlāq, also ʿulūq) = a prized thing, as though everyone who saw it became attached to it; ʿilq maḍinna = an object jealously guarded. By extension wine is called al-ʿilq ("when you taste her mouth you say: buried ʿilq, meant for a chieftain, left in a cellar"). aʿlaqtu = I chanced on a precious ʿilq. Al-Kumayt: "he has sold cheap among precious things, at a dear price." al-ʿalāʾiq also = trade goods, and = neck-collars.

17. **Calamity.** jāʾa bi-ʿulaqa fulaqa = he came with a disaster; aʿlaqa wa-aflaqa. So called because it is a calamity that fastens on everyone. Death itself (al-maniyya) is called ʿalūq (Abū ʿAmr: al-ʿalūq is what fastens on a person) — "death had already fastened on Thaʿlaba."

18. **Trapping.** ʿaliqa l-ẓabyu fī l-ḥibāla = the gazelle caught in the snare; aʿlaqathu l-ḥibāla; aʿlaqa l-ḥābil = the trapper made a catch. "You have made a catch, so come and take it." Dhū al-Rumma: "…its locusts leaping like the leaping of things hung up."

19. **The withholding she-camel.** Al-Kisāʾī: al-ʿalūq is the she-camel that refuses to take to her young (also maʿāliq): "how does it profit, what the ʿalūq gives by way of a mere sniff of affection, when the milk is withheld?" Ibn Fāris: the analogy holds, as though she kept her milk fastened up so it can scarcely be got from her.

20. **The bramble.** al-ʿullayq — a thorn tree that never grows large; whatever catches in it can hardly get free, its thorns being sharp and hooked; hence the name.

21. **Long-tailed.** "This is a report long of ʿawlaq" = long-tailed.

22. **Conception.** ʿaliqat al-marʾa = the woman conceived.

23. **The short shift.** al-ʿilqa — per Ibn al-Sikkīt, a shirt reaching to the navel or halfway to it, the same as the baqīra: "she was in nothing but a waist-wrap and an ʿilqa…". Ibn Fāris notes this too follows the root-analogy: not being a full wide garment, it is as though a thing merely hung on a thing. Abū ʿAmr: a garment slit for the head, its sides unsewn, worn by a girl down to the waistband — the shawdhar.

24. **Qur'anic citation.** On {fa-tadharūhā ka-l-muʿallaqa} ("so that you leave her as one suspended," al-Nisāʾ 4:129), Ibn Fāris glosses: the woman who is neither husbandless nor possessed of a husband, as though her affair were unsettled. He pairs it with the ḥadīth of Umm Zarʿ: "If I speak I am divorced; if I keep silent I am left suspended."

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ع-ل-و (with its weak final letter as yāʾ, wāw, or alif) as a single root meaning loftiness and elevation, from which nothing departs. Its core nouns are al-ʿalāʾ (eminence) and al-ʿuluww (height).

1. Core sense — rising / being high. تَعَالَى النَّهَارُ = "the day climbed high." To someone who stumbles: لَعًا لَكَ عَالِيًا ("up you rise, high and firm"). عَالَيْتُهُ فَوْقَ الْبَعِيرِ = "I set him up on the camel."

2. Al-Khalīl's distinction of the derivatives: al-ʿuluww is the base; al-ʿalāʾ specifically means elevation of rank, while al-ʿuluww can mean greatness and overbearing tyranny — عَلَا الْمَلِكُ فِي الْأَرْضِ ("the king exalted himself arrogantly in the land"), as in Q 28:4 of Pharaoh.

3. Honor / nobility. رَجُلٌ عَالِي الْكَعْبِ ("high of ankle") = noble. A grammatical note: for mere rising one says عَلَا يَعْلُو, but for the sense of rank and honor one says عَلِيَ يَعْلَى. Related: al-maʿlāt = winning honor (pl. maʿālī); ʿilyat al-nās = the elite; ʿilw / sifl = the top and bottom of a thing.

4. Overpowering / mastering. اعْتَلَاهُ, اسْتَعْلَى عَلَيْهِ / بِهِ = to dominate, equivalent to اسْتَوْلَى; used of a racehorse that "masters" the finish line. عَلَوْتُ حَاجَتِي = I prevailed over my need. Poetic evidence (Aws, Umayya b. Abī al-Ṣalt read by al-Aṣmaʿī): al-ʿālī = a grave, crushing affliction; al-ʿāfī = the easy, al-ʿālī = the severe. Ibn al-Sikkīt: muʿtalin bi-ḥimlihi = fully equal to his load.

5. Idioms of "get off / move up." عَالِ / اعْلُ عَنْ ثَوْبِي = "get up off my garment"; عَالِ عَنْهَا = "move aside." Conversely أَعْلِ / عَالِ عَلَيَّ = "load it onto me." تَعْلُوهُ الْعَيْنُ / تَعْلُو عَنْهُ الْعَيْنُ = the eye rejects and recoils from him.

6. A noted counter-pair: عَلَا الْفَرَسَ = mount the horse, yet أَعْلَى عَنْهُ = dismount. Ibn Fāris defends this as logical though seemingly opposite: to descend from a thing is truly to "part and rise away" from it — the Arabs marked the two senses by two word-forms.

7. Places / geography. al-ʿalyāʾ = a mountain-top or high ground (Zuhayr); al-ʿāliya = the upper part of a spear-shaft (pl. ʿawālī); al-ʿĀliya = a Ḥijāzī district (nisba in use: ʿulwī; Ibn Durayd: also called ʿuluww). al-ʿulliyya = an upper chamber (morphological pattern discussed: fuʿliyya or fuʿlūla).

8. ʿilliyyīn (Q 83:18). Al-Farrāʾ: "elevation upon elevation without limit." Its wāw-nūn plural marks an unbounded, uncountable thing (not a real singular/dual), like the colloquial maraqīn ("broth on broth") and wābilīn ("downpour on downpour"). Also ʿulyā / ʿulā for "highest" (as in al-samāwāt al-ʿulā, the high heavens; sing. ʿulyā).

9. Adverbs of "from above." جِئْتُ مِنْ أَعْلَى / مِنْ عَلَا / مِنْ عَالٍ / مِنْ عَلِ, with مِنْ عَلُ sometimes fixed as an indeclinable "limit" (Ibn Rawāḥa's line on the Messenger being sent by the One "above the heavens, from on high"). al-Aʿshā's مِنْ عَلْو can be voweled three ways (-u, -a, -i). Abū Zayd even records جِئْتُ مِنْ عَلَيْكَ = "from your presence."

10. Milking term. al-mustaʿlī = the milker holding the vessel / milking from the she-camel's left; al-bāʾin milks from the right.

11. Size / stature. ʿilyān = tall and massive (of camel, man, or a loud voice); muʿālan / ʿūliyat = built tall. Al-Farrāʾ notes ʿilyān as a rare kasra-initial adjective serving both genders; Abū ʿAmr denies it for the male (only jamal nabīl).

12. تَعَالَ ("come!"). From ʿuluww — originally "ascend to me" — later generalized so even one below says it to one above; used only in the imperative, obsolete elsewhere.

13. Loads and directions. al-ʿilāwa = a man's head-and-neck, also an extra load piled on a camel; muʿallā = a load's carrying-place. عُلَاوَة الرِّيح = the windward side.

14. Further specialized senses: al-muʿallā = the seventh and best gambling arrow (seven shares, seven notches); al-muʿallī = one who hauls up the bucket, or who resets a rope slipped off the pulley. Of a woman cleansed after childbirth-bleeding (nifās): تَعَلَّتْ — said, they claim, only in that case (Jarīr).

15. ʿulwān al-kitāb (a book's heading): defended as a valid variant of ʿunwān — both post-classical (muwallad); ʿunwān from (ʿ-n-n), ʿulwān from ʿuluww since it tops the book.

16. Miscellaneous: al-ʿalāt = the anvil, a simile for a hard she-camel; the name ʿAlī (pattern faʿīl, nisba ʿalawī) and the clan Banū ʿAlī of Kināna; and Abū Saʿīd's مَا أَنْتَ إِلَّا عَلَى أَعْلَى وَأَرْوَحَ ("you are in full ampleness and height").

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-m-d as a large root with many branches all returning to a single idea: **straightness in a thing — either standing upright or extending lengthwise — and the same straightness in opinion and in intending something.**

1. **To head for / intend deliberately.** عَمَدْتُ فلاناً, "I made for him," i.e. aimed at him on purpose. Hence الْعَمْد, the opposite of خطأ (accident/error) in killing and in other matters; it is called ʿamd, he explains, because one's intention toward the act is "straight" or settled (استواء الإرادة). Al-Khalīl adds that ʿamd is to take on a matter with earnestness and certainty: فعلتُه عَمْداً وعَمْدَ عَيْنٍ ("I did it on purpose, of set purpose"), تَعَمَّدْتُ له, فعلتُه مُعْتَمِداً. Also الزَمْ عُمْدَتَك — "keep to your aim."

2. **To prop, and the prop itself.** Al-Khalīl: ʿamd is to hold a thing up with a عِمَاد that supports it and on which it rests. Ibn Durayd: عَمَدْتُ الشيءَ = I leaned/propped it. The thing leaned against is a عِمَاد (pl. عُمُد); also عَمُود and عَمَد. A عَمُود of wood or iron (pl. أَعْمِدَة) includes the tent-pole. Tent-dwellers who live in nothing else are called أهل عَمُودٍ / أهل عِمَادٍ ("people of the tent-pole"). Abū ʿUbayd: عَمَدْتُ الشيءَ = I set it upright (so it is مَعْمُود), and أَعْمَدْتُه = I put supports under it.

3. **Extended uses of "column/mainstay."** عَمُود السِّنَان — the middle ridge of a spearhead between its two blades (al-Khalīl). عَمُودَان — the two legs of the male ostrich. عَمُود الأمر — the mainstay of an affair, without which it does not stand straight. عَمِيد القوم — a people's chief and the one they rely on, to whom they run when a matter presses them hard. عَمُود الأُذُن — the main frame of the ear.

4. **The propped-up invalid, and the broken heart.** A sick man is called عَمِيد: the lexicographers say he is المَعْمُود, one who cannot sit up from illness until he is propped with cushions on his sides. From this, they say, comes القلب العَمِيد — the heart broken and shattered by passion, "like a thing propped with something." Al-Akhṭal's line is cited: "Suʿād has departed, and the eye's sleep is sleeplessness / and the heart is downcast, burning, propped up." Forms: عَمِيد, مَعْمُود, مُعَمَّد.

5. **The broken camel-hump.** السَّنَام العَمِد (عَمِدَ يَعْمَدُ عَمْداً): Ibn Fāris refers this back to sense 4 — a hump that is huge and fat, then loaded until it is broken and its fat dies inside it, so it never sits straight again; compared to a wound that goes bad (يَعْمَد) when squeezed before it ripens, so it swells. Hence بعيرٌ عَمِدٌ, ناقةٌ عَمِدَةٌ, سنامها عَمِدٌ.

6. **Qurʾānic attestations.** On {فِي عَمَدٍ مُمَدَّدَةٍ} (104:9): "in something like tents of stretched-out fire"; the variant reading فِي عُمُدٍ is noted, عُمُد being the plural of عِمَاد. On {إِرَمَ ذَاتِ الْعِمَادِ} (89:7): al-Mubarrad's sense — رجلٌ مُعْمَدٌ means "tall," and الْعِمَاد means tallness/height — so "possessed of loftiness." He supports this with the ḥadīth phrase "he is lofty of column, long of sword-belt."

7. **Bodily "columns."** الْعَمُود = the vein that feeds the liver; the aorta is عَمُود السَّحْر; عَمُود البطن = a vein-like cord stretched from the breastbone cartilage to just above the navel, along which a sheep's belly is slit. Others say عَمُودَا البطن are the back and the spine — so called because each of the two rests upon the other.

8. **Full-bodied youth.** الْعُمُدّ (ʿayn and mīm with ḍamma, dāl doubled): a young man brimming with youth; also الْعُمُدَّانِيّ (pl. -ون), and امرأةٌ عُمُدَّانِيَّةٌ, a woman of bulk and stoutness.

9. **Rain-soaked soil.** ثَرًى عَمِدٌ, soil the rains have soaked. Abū Zayd: عَمِدَتِ الأرضُ, the rain sank down to the moist layer so that a handful cakes and clumps in the palm. A verse is cited on gathering alāʾ-roots "in soil rain-soaked and clumped."

10. **One unexplained expression, left open.** Ibn Fāris closes by saying the chapter has run straight in root and branches except for one phrase whose meaning and derivation he does not know, and which he suspects belongs to speech that died out with those who knew it: Abū Jahl's reported words when struck down, أَعْمَدُ من سيدٍ قَتَلَه قومُه. Others glossed it "Is it more than a chief slain by his own people?" — but he objects that the word does not support that reading, and says outright that he does not know. A line of Ibn Mayyāda using the same construction is cited, glossed "Have we done more than suffice our brothers?" He also reports al-Naḍr's view that أَعْمَدُ means "more astonishing" (the Arabs say أنا أَعْمَدُ من كذا, "I am more astonished at it"), which he judges even further off than the first, ending: "God knows best how it is."

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-m-h as a single sound root with one meaning: bewilderment and a poor ability to find one's way.

1. Core sense — being at a loss, unable to get oriented. Ibn Fāris cites al-Khalīl for the verb عَمِهَ / يَعْمَهُ / عَمَهًا: a man is described this way when he casts about back and forth, not knowing which direction to take.

2. Qur'anic citation — the entry gives al-Aʿrāf 7:186, "and He leaves them in their overreaching, wandering blindly (yaʿmahūn)," as an attestation of that same sense.

3. Derived usage for lost livestock — quoting Yaʿqūb, the phrase ذَهَبَتْ إِبِلُهُ الْعُمَّيْهَى (with a doubled mīm) is used of a man whose camels have gone off and he has no idea where they went. The bewilderment here belongs to the one who cannot trace them.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-M-L (عمل) as a single sound root with one general sense: it covers every act or deed that is performed.

1. Core verb. عَمِلَ means "to work, to act"; the agent is عامِل ("worker, doer"). The reflexive اعْتَمَلَ means to do the work oneself — illustrated by a line of verse: the noble man labours with his own hands when he has no one else to lean on.

2. Derived nouns of labour and dealing:
- عِمَالَة (ʿimāla): the wage paid for work done.
- مُعَامَلَة (muʿāmala): the verbal noun of عَامَلَ, "to deal/transact with someone."
- عَمَلَة (ʿamala): a body of manual labourers doing various tasks — digging, coiling, and the like.

3. A specialised, concrete sense: عامِل / عامِلة of a spear is the part just below the lower socket (ثَعْلَب), adjacent to the blade (سِنَان) — its fore-part or "breast." Ibn Fāris cites a battle line describing this part of the spear swaying in a wide wound.

4. The root's verb forms spread across usages: a man works for himself (يَعْتَمِل), works for others (يَعْمَل لِقَوْم), employs someone else (يَسْتَعْمِل), or "puts to work" his opinion, his speech, or his spear (يُعْمِل). A builder likewise "employs" (يَسْتَعْمِل) the mud-brick he builds with.

5. Morphology/derivation: يَعْمَلَة (yaʿmala), a working she-camel, takes its name from عَمَل ("work"); plural يَعْمَلَات, and يَعَامِل is also allowed. The word is used only of the female. A verse (attributed to Dhū al-Rumma or another) mentions these work-camels enduring sore feet, but the line is garbled in the source. Ibn Fāris closes with "and God knows best."

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-m-m as one sound root which, in his account, indicates tallness, abundance and height. He sorts the material under these ideas, adds the turban and its figurative uses as belonging to the same chapter, and sets apart one name he can derive only by forcing it.

1. **Tallness and full growth.** Citing al-Khalīl: al-ʿamīm is the tall among plants; a tall palm is nakhla ʿamīma (plural ʿumm), and a plant that "stands at its ʿamam" has reached its completeness. A tall girl is jāriya ʿamīma, and a full-statured body is jism ʿamam, as in Ibn Shaʾs's line about "the dark one with the full (ʿamam) shoulder". Ibn al-Aʿrābī gives rajul ʿamam and imraʾa ʿamam for a man and a woman of full stature. Tall herbage is ʿushb ʿamīm, and of it one says iʿtamma, "it has grown tall"; al-Hudhalī compares the tall and thick growth (ʿamīm, jamīm) of open land to the shades of a dark night.

2. **Tall palms.** Some say a tall palm is ʿamma, plural ʿamm, citing Labīd's tall, lush palms (ʿamm) with vines between them. Abū ʿAmr places the ʿamīm palm above the jabbār. A verse pairs "a tall one (ʿumm) for your tall one" with "a little one for your little one", explained as the palm's small ones for your small ones and its big ones for your big ones. Abū Duwād's line "swaying, gentle, full-limbed, like a tall (ʿamīma) papyrus in the rafḍ" is glossed: ʿamīma is the tall one, and rafḍ is a little water.

3. **The turban.** Also in this chapter is al-ʿimāma, the turban (plural ʿimāmāt and ʿamāʾim). One says taʿammamtu or iʿtamamtu for putting it on, and ʿammamanī ghayrī, "someone else turbaned me"; a man who is ḥasan al-ʿimma is good at wearing it. A verse speaks of racing camels whose muzzles are "turbaned" with curly foam.

4. **Made a chief.** ʿummima, "he was turbaned", means he was made a chief (suwwida), because turbans are the people's crowns: where non-Arabs say tuwwija, "he was crowned", Arabs say ʿummima. Al-ʿAjjāj's "when the turban-wearer was turbaned" is explained as being made a chief and clothed in the turban of chiefship.

5. **"Turbaned" animals.** A sheep or goat that is muʿammama is black-headed. Abū ʿUbayd calls a horse muʿammam when the white of its forelock runs down to the roots of the forelock and the head around them, and a blaze (ghurra) muʿammama when it is the same. In piebald colouring, taʿmīm means white on the top of the head (al-hāma) but not on the neck, hence ablaq muʿammam.

6. **Groups.** Returning to the idea of a gathering named at the head of the chapter: al-Khalīl and others say al-ʿamāʾim are groups, singular ʿamm. Abū ʿAmr gives al-ʿamāyim, with yāʾ, for groups (qawm ʿamāyim) and says he knows no singular for it; al-ʿAjjāj speaks of "the throngs (ʿamāyim) of Ḥimyar" streaming. For Ibn al-Aʿrābī al-ʿamm is a group of people, as in a verse, explained as meaning the Black Stone, where the throng brings it their needs "though it owns no wealth", and another where the throng call to one another as evening wanes.

7. **Being general.** From the idea of gathering comes ʿammanā hādhā l-amr, yaʿummunā ʿumūman, "this matter has included us all", said when something befalls the whole people. al-ʿāmma, the common body of people, is the opposite of al-khāṣṣa, the select few.

8. **ʿummiyya.** inna fīhi la-ʿummiyyatan means "there is pride (kibr) in him"; if so, Ibn Fāris says, it belongs to the sense of height. Al-Naḍr instead explains dhū ʿummiyya as a man who extends his support to all his companions (yaʿummu) rather than singling some out (yakhuṣṣu), and a verse speaks of "the brave man of ʿummiyya" driving others off.

9. **Pure stock.** Al-Aṣmaʿī: "he is of their ʿamīm and their ṣamīm", meaning pure, not of mixed stock (muʾtashab).

10. **Frothing milk.** By way of comparison, ʿammama l-laban, "the milk turbaned", means it frothed, which happens only when it is pure at the moment of milking. Labīd speaks of guests' bowls filled with pure milk that is muʿammam, "turbaned".

11. **ʿAmmān.** Ibn Fāris lists ʿAmmān, the name of a place, among words that have no analogy except by forced reasoning; Abū Wajza's verse has al-Qaṭāt, his she-camel, yearning at its gates.

text:
Ibn Fāris identifies ʿ-m-q (عمق) as a root recorded by Ibn al-Aʿrābī with one core, physical sense — depth/farness downward — that then extends to a figurative sense of "going deep" in speech, plus a cluster of unrelated place-names and a plant-name that he includes for completeness even though he notes they don't really fit the root's analogical pattern.

1. Depth/distance (the core sense), per Ibn al-Aʿrābī:
   - Said of a road: al-ʿumq means "distance, farness" (al-buʿd).
   - Said of a well: al-ʿumq means the length/extent of its dug shaft.

2. "Deep well" — per al-Khalīl: a biʾr ʿamīqah is a well whose bottom lies far down; one says aʿmaqahā ḥāfiruhā, "its digger dug it deep." Similarly the saying mā abʿada ʿamāqata hādhihi r-rakiyyah, "how deep this well is!" — literally "how far its bottom is."

   Illustrative citation: an eloquent Arab quoted by Ibn al-Aʿrābī said, "I saw a khalīqah [a freshly-dug well], and never saw one deeper."

3. Figurative extension — taʿammaqa fī kalāmihi, "he went deep in his speech," meaning he was over-elaborate or affected (tanaṭṭaʿa), pressing subtlety or refinement to excess.

4. Unrelated items Ibn Fāris appends, while explicitly flagging that they don't derive from the root by normal analogy:
   - ʿAmq — a tract of land belonging to the tribe Muzaynah, cited in a line of poetry by Sāʿidah [ibn Juʾayyah] comparing a distant echo to the rumble of a muzzled stud-camel.
   - Al-ʿImqā — a place-name, cited in a verse of Abū Dhuʾayb about grief and a dense shīḥ (wormwood) shrub.
   - Al-ʿimqā — also the name of a plant (spelled with the fixed alif maqṣūrah ending). Yūnus is quoted: a camel called ʿāmiq is one that grazes on this plant.
   - Uʿāmiq — another place-name, cited in a verse by al-Akhṭal describing a beloved campsite he used to range around.

In short: the lexical core of ʿ-m-q is physical depth (of a well or a road's distance), extended metaphorically to intellectual over-elaboration in speech; the place-names and the plant-name are appended as loosely-related homonyms rather than true derivations of the root.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-m-r as having two sound root meanings: (1) remaining and the extension of time, and (2) something that rises high, a sound or otherwise. He lists a few words as standing outside both.

**1. Remaining, length of life**

- al-ʿumr, also al-ʿamr: life. The oath laʿamruka ("by your life") swears by a person's life.
- ʿamraka llāha: "I adjure you by God to do such-and-such", i.e. "I remind you of God"; you make the person swear by God while asking long life for him.
- ʿamira al-nās: the people lived long. ʿammarahum Allāh taʿmīran: God gave them long life.
- In the same category is ʿimārat al-arḍ, inhabiting and cultivating the land: the people ʿammarū the land, they yaʿmurūnahā, and it is ʿāmira and maʿmūra. ʿĀmira is formed from ʿamarat al-arḍ (the land flourished); maʿmūra from ʿumirat (it was inhabited). The noun and verbal noun is al-ʿumrān.
- istaʿmara Allāh al-nāsa fī l-arḍ: God settled people in the land so that they would inhabit and cultivate it.
- Ibn Fāris says the whole category comes back to this meaning.

**2. Rising high, raised voice**

- al-ʿawmara: shouting and clamour.
- iʿtamara al-rajul: a man declared the ihlāl for his ʿumra, which is raising his voice with the talbiya for the ʿumra.
- In Ibn Aḥmar's line "its riders raise their voices at al-Farqad, as the riding muʿtamir raises his voice", some take muʿtamir as the one raising his voice for the ʿumra; others take it as muʿtamm, one wearing a turban. Ibn Fāris says that either way it belongs to height and rising.
- al-ʿamār: according to the people of language, anything placed on the head: turban, cap, circlet, crown and the like. Al-Aʿshā: "we bowed down to him and raised our ʿamār." Some say ʿamār can also be made of sweet basil.
- Ibn al-Sikkīt says al-ʿamār means greeting: ʿammaraka Allāh means "may God greet you". Ibn Fāris suggests this may come from raising the voice.
- He also suggests that a large tribal community is called ʿimāra because of the clamour in it, citing: "Every people of Maʿadd has an ʿimāra, a region and a side to which they take refuge."

**Outside both root meanings**

- al-ʿamr (sometimes al-ʿumr): a kind of palm tree; someone used its fruit-stalks to clean his teeth.
- al-ʿamr: the visible part of the gums, plural al-ʿumūr. The name ʿAmr is said to be derived from this.

quran_words: أَعْمَىٰ 21x "the blind"; عَمِىَ 7x "(are) blinded"; عَمُون 2x "(are) blind"; عَمًى 2x "blindness"; عُمِّيَتْ 1x "but (it) has been obscured"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the whole root ع-م-ي from a single idea: covering and concealment. The senses follow from it.

1. Blindness (al-ʿamā): loss of sight in both eyes together (verb ʿamiya, yaʿmā, ʿaman; a rarer form iʿmāyya is built on the sound-verb pattern, like idhāmma). The adjective is aʿmā (m.) / ʿamyāʾ (f.); the plural for women is ʿamyāwāt. The term is not used of just one eye — instead one says "both his eyes went blind."

2. Figurative blindness (of the heart): a man is ʿamin, a people ʿamūna, when blind in understanding. Grammatical note: for this inner sense one may exclaim mā aʿmāhu ("how blind he is!"), but not for physical blindness. Ibn Fāris (citing al-Khalīl) explains the rule: the exclamatory mā afʿalahu form is reserved for hidden qualities, whereas physical blindness is a visible, shared fact, so exclaiming it over a person present is unseemly.

3. al-taʿmiya (from al-Khalīl): to obscure something for someone, confusing it for him.

4. As a noun ʿaman can be pluralized as aʿmāʾ ("obscured/effaced tracks"), attested in a line of al-ʿAjjāj describing a trackless land.

5. Proverbial figurative use: "your love of a thing blinds and deafens"; "love is blind." aʿmaytu al-rajula = "I found the man blind" (attested in verse). A variant plural ʿumyān for blindness follows the pattern of ṭughyān.

6. al-ʿummiyya / al-ʿimmiyya: error, misguidance. In a hadith God is said to have removed "the ʿimmiyya of the Jāhiliyya," which the transmitters glossed as pride/arrogance (al-kibr). Related: being "in ʿamyāʾ" = not perceiving the truth; qatīlun ʿimmiyyan = a slain man whose killer is unknown. al-ʿamāya = going astray, tied to obstinacy (lajāja).

7. al-ʿamāʾ: thick, closed-over cloud (single piece ʿamāʾa); by extension darkness (per al-Kisāʾī, being "in ʿimāya and ʿamāʾ" = in the dark). Also given as "dust" (a line of al-Murrār on a dust-laden west wind).

8. al-maʿāmī (per the lexicographers): neglected, untraced tracts of land with no sign of cultivation — attested in the Prophet's letter to Ukaydir claiming "the untilled tracts and untraced lands."

9. al-ʿamy (pattern of ramy): waves casting up debris and foam on their surface — which Ibn Fāris notes fits the root's core sense, since foam covers the water's face. Attested in verse. Likewise a braying camel "casts" (ʿamā) its froth over its head.

10. Idiom ṣakkata ʿumayya: the fierce noonday heat. Two glosses: Ibn al-Aʿrābī — the hour when heat nearly blinds; al-Mubarrad — when the gazelle reaches its lair unable to see for the heat.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿayn–nūn as a small, sound root with two unrelated meanings: a well-known fruit, plus one other word.

1. The fruit — grapes (ʿinab). The unit-noun for a single grape is ʿinaba, and Ibn Fāris notes this is cited as the only word in Arabic on the pattern fiʿala. Variants and derivations he records:
- al-ʿinabāʾ, an alternative word for grapes, with a poetic citation: "the choice grapes and figs."
- al-aʿnāb, a plural sometimes used for ʿinab.
- rajul ʿānib, "a man rich in grapes," formed like tāmir ("rich in dates") and lābin ("rich in milk").

2. The unrelated word — al-ʿanabān (pattern faʿalān): the long-horned mountain ibex, with a poetic citation: "it charges as the veering ʿanabān charges." The same word is also used of a brisk, lively gazelle. Ibn Fāris notes no verb is derived from this second sense.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives the whole root ع-ن-د (ʿ-n-d) from a single core idea: passing beyond a limit and leaving the straight path — i.e. deviation.

1. Basic sense (per al-Khalīl): ʿanada, of a man (participle ʿānid, verbal noun ʿunūd) — to act insolently and tyrannically and to exceed one's proper measure.

2. muʿānada — obstinacy: a man knows a thing yet refuses to accept it. Related: ʿanada ʿan al-amr = to swerve/turn aside from a matter.

3. ʿanūd — the aloof or solitary one. Of a camel, one that will not mingle with the herd but stays off to one side; of a person, one who keeps to himself and does not mix with people (two verse-citations illustrate the aloof companion and the solitary client).

4. ʿanīd — the arrogant tyrant; this word is from tajabbur (haughty domineering). Ibn Fāris notes the language deliberately distinguishes three forms: ʿanīd (the tyrant), ʿanūd (the aloof one), and ʿānid (the deviating one).

5. Applied to a vein: al-ʿirq al-ʿānid (per al-Khalīl) is a vein that gushes blood and will not stop/clot; ʿanada ʿirquhu = his vein bled unstoppably. Yaʿqūb adds that such a vein's blood "runs off to one side."

6. Of a road/she-camel (per Ibn Durayd): a ʿānid road is one that slants or veers; a ʿanūd she-camel swerves off the track from sheer vigor. A rajaz line uses al-ʿunnad for such wayward mounts.

7. mā ʿanhu ʿundad / ʿandad — an idiom for "there is no avoiding it, no turning aside from it," used memorably of death (Jundal's couplet).

8. Further usages: aʿnada fī qayʾihi = his vomiting would not stop; istaʿnada al-baʿīr = the camel overpowered its driver at the halter and dragged him; the poetic ʿanadahu = a side/direction of a thing that one keeps watch over.

9. Proverb: "Beneath his soft manner (ṭirrīqa = gentleness) lies an ʿindaʾwa" — i.e. under apparent mildness hides pride, overstepping and transgression.

10. The preposition ʿinda ("at/with," as in "Zayd is ʿinda ʿAmr") Ibn Fāris tentatively traces to the same root-idea: as if the person had inclined away from everyone else toward this one until he came close and cleaved to him.

text:
Root ʿ-n-k-b — "spider" (Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī)

1. Headword: al-ʿankabūt = "the spider."

2. Dialect variants: the ʿAyn notes that in the Yemeni dialect the word is instead al-ʿankaboh or al-ʿankabāh.

3. Plural: al-ʿanākib.

4. Definition: a small creature that spins a thin, loosely-woven (flimsy) web — described as weaving "in the air," over the mouth/head of a well, and in similar places.

5. Poetic citation: the entry cites a line by the pre-Islamic/Umayyad-era poet Dhū al-Rummah describing spiders weaving between the mathāb — the standing-place or coping at the head of a well. The line as quoted here has a gap in the middle (marked by an ellipsis in the source), so its full sense and the referents of "it/its" are not recoverable from this entry alone.

text:
ʿ-N-Q (عنق) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core sense: Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-n-q as a single sound root meaning extension in something — either extension upward (height) or extension outward (spreading, stretching along).

1. ʿunuq — the neck, the link between head and body. Grammatically usable as masculine or feminine; plural aʿnāq. Derived descriptions of height: aʿnaq (long-necked man; a towering mountain; a lofty upland), ʿanqāʾ (a tall hill; a long-necked woman), muʿniqa (a lofty hill). Cited verse: a lofty long-necked height whose only companions are grey doves, its herbage never grazed. Al-Aṣmaʿī: muʿanniqāt is equivalent to muʿniqāt (shāhid from ʿUmar b. Lajaʾ). Abū ʿAmr: muʿanniq = "tall", with the shāhid "a high hump like the towering dune".

2. al-ʿanqāʾ as a bird — Abū ʿAmr reports it "as is said" to be a bird of which only the name survives, named for a white band on its neck. Hence the proverb for the unobtainable: "the ʿanqāʾ has flown off with it."

3. ʿunuq = a group of people. Ibn Fāris judges this analogically sound, since a group is a thing whose parts are joined together. He applies it to Q 26:4, "so their aʿnāq became khāḍiʿīn [submissive]", reading aʿnāq as "their company". His grammatical argument: the Qurʾān uses khāḍiʿīn, the masculine plural used of persons; had actual necks been meant, khāḍiʿatan or khāḍiʿāt would have been used. He attributes this reading to Abū Zayd. Two rival explanations are recorded: (a) the grammarians — because the necks are annexed to the people, the predicate is referred to the people, not the necks; (b) Muḥammad b. Yazīd (al-Mubarrad) — since the people's submission consists in their necks' submission, the statement is made about the people, the meaning reverting to them. Idiomatic support: "my neck became lowly / bowed to him" = I submitted; and the opposite, "he turned his neck away from me and his neck-veins did not soften toward me" = he neither submitted nor yielded.

4. Putting something on a neck. Ibn Durayd: aʿnaqtu l-kalb = to put a collar or cord on a dog's neck; miʿnaqa = the dog's collar.

5. Extended (metaphorical) necks. aʿnāq al-riyāḥ = the rising columns of wind; "the wind raised the dust." Al-Khalīl: a beast stuck in mud is uʿtuniqat when it thrusts its neck out; Ruʾba's line gives muʿtanaq = the place where mountain "necks" emerge from the mirage.

6. Embracing vs. grappling. iʿtināq and muʿānaqa share one derivation, but usage separates them: muʿānaqa belongs to affection, iʿtināq to war — "they closed neck-to-neck in battle" uses iʿtanaqū, not taʿānaqū. When one party alone is the agent, only ʿānaqa fulānun fulānan is used; iʿtanaqa is sometimes used of a single person, as in Zuhayr's line describing a fighter who spears, then strikes, then finally grapples.

7. ʿanaqtu l-baʿīr (Yūnus b. Ḥabīb) = to strike a camel's neck, on the pattern of raʾastuhu, "I struck its head".

8. ʿāniqāʾ — a burrow packed with soft earth used by the hare and the jerboa when frightened. Al-Khalīl: taʿannaqa l-arnab, said because the animal drives its head and neck into the loose soil and pushes on until it is underneath it. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: the ʿāniqāʾ is the earth of the jerboa's lughayzā (its two side-diggings) and of its run.

9. Anatomical "necks". Quṭrub: ʿunuq al-raḥim, the narrowed part of the womb next to the vulva. Abū Ḥātim: ʿunuq al-kirsh, the lower part of the rumen — and he equates ʿunuq with qibba.

10. Palm-produce. ʿannaqat kawāfīr al-nakhl: the palm's spathes grow long without splitting open (the verbal noun is taʿnīq). A busra muʿanniqa is a date whose unripened band around the calyx remains like a signet-ring, when ripening has come close to the calyx.

11. Proper names from neck-length. al-Aʿnaq = Qays b. al-Ḥārith b. Hammām, named for his long neck; his descendants Banū l-Aʿnaq, a clan of Wāʾil b. Qāsiṭ. A Yemeni people are Banū l-ʿAnqāʾ. Al-Khalīl: al-ʿAnqāʾ = Thaʿlaba b. ʿAmr b. Mālik of Khuzāʿa, said by some to be named for his long neck, the feminine form following the feminine gender of ʿunuq — parallel to "ʿAntara al-Falḥāʾ", feminized because "lip" (shafa) was in mind. A verse naming him is cited.

12. Proverbial inseparability. Quṭrub: of something that never leaves you, "he is to you as the dove's neck" — i.e. its ring-collar, which never comes off.

13. ʿanaq — a gait: the long, stretching-out pace of riding animals; the animal is called ʿanīq or miʿnāq (a swift hack; a stretching pace), with a verse contrasting a once-swinging stride now reduced to a crawl. Abū ʿUbayda: al-ʿanaq is the outstretched pace — which Ibn Fāris flags as direct confirmation of his opening claim that the whole root turns on extension. Ibn al-Sikkīt: aʿnaqa l-faras = to go at a light quick walk; proverb: "I shall make its slow-stepper catch up with the swift-paced one."

14. Restless camels. Abū Ḥātim: miʿnāq is the light camel that heads for pasture but does not graze; the maʿānīq are camels never satisfied with their pasture, from ill-nature and lack of good, so their herdsman is never free of toil — the point being that they are always stretching their necks toward what lies ahead (verse cited on the labour of watering, herding, and chasing them). Other lexicographers: aʿnaqat = they ranged about their pastures without grazing, in search of other herbage. Ibn al-Aʿrābī on Ibn Aḥmar's line about "the daughters of Aʿnaq": he takes it to mean any beast, horse or camel, that goes at the ʿanaq pace — the line actually describing a pearl, with mounts kept saddled morning and evening to go and look at it.

15. ʿanqāʾ = calamity, so called (Ibn Fāris explains) to make it repugnant and frightening, as though it were some long-necked creature; cited with ʿanqafīr in a list of disasters.

16. muʿniq of hard ground: a firm raised strip with level land around it, running about a mile or less in length; plural maʿāniq.

17. ʿanāq — a female kid of goats; plural ʿunūq (verse of Jamīl on a herdsman anxious over a sick kid). Proverb for a man fallen from high station to low: "she-kids after she-camels" — you now herd kids where once you herded camels. Age range disputed: Ibn al-Aʿrābī puts it from birth until it becomes a jadhaʿ two months after weaning, at five months old; Abū ʿUbayda extends it from birth until a full year, when it becomes an ʿanz. A shāt miʿnāq is a ewe/goat that bears she-kids (verse cited). ʿanāq al-arḍ is an animal smaller than the leopard (the caracal).

18. ʿanāq = disappointment/failure. Ibn Fāris explicitly excludes this from the root's core meaning. His explanation: the Arabs sometimes attach a nickname to a thing to allude to it — as treachery is nicknamed "Kaysān" — and so used ʿanāq (also ʿanāqa with hāʾ) for failure. Two verses are cited using it in that sense; he glosses aws in the first as "gift, compensation". He also assigns Ibn al-Sikkīt's report that ʿanāq means "calamity" to this same figurative category (verse: "they meet from him the two ears of disaster").

19. Rejected material. On the saying "this water of yours is ʿanāq al-arḍ", said to be "the water of lying", and the report transmitted with it, Ibn Fāris dismisses it as the kind of tale by which stories are multiplied and books padded — with, in his judgment, no meaning and no benefit.

quran_words: عَنِ 3x "distresses you"; أَعْنَتَ 1x "surely he (could have) put you in difficulties"; عَنَت 1x "committing sin"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-n-t as one sound root meaning hardship and things like it; he states explicitly that it does not point to soundness or to ease.

1. Core sense — hardship (mashaqqa). Al-Khalīl: al-ʿanat is hardship that falls upon the tongue. عَنِتَ فُلَانٌ = "he met with ʿanat," i.e. hardship.

2. Causative form IV — أَعْنَتَهُ إِعْنَاتًا: to bring hardship upon someone.

3. Form V — تَعَنَّتَهُ تَعَنُّتًا: to question someone about something with the aim of confusing him and making things hard for him (trapping him with a question).

4. Coercion. Ibn Durayd: al-ʿanat is oppressive force and compelling someone to what he dislikes; verb أَعْنَتَ / يُعْنِت / إِعْنَات.

5. Extension by analogy to wrongdoing. From the above, it is said of one who sins: عَنِتَ عَنَتًا — he incurred culpability (maʾtham).

6. Qur'anic citation, 4:25 — "That is for whoever among you fears al-ʿanat." Ibn Fāris records four readings of what ʿanat means there:
   - Al-Farrāʾ: the dispensation to marry bondwomen applies when a man fears he will fall into illicit sexual conduct.
   - Al-Zajjāj: linguistically al-ʿanat is severe hardship — hence أَكَمَةٌ عَنُوتٌ, "a toilsome hillock" (a hill hard to climb).
   - Al-Mubarrad: here it means destruction (halāk).
   - An unnamed authority: it means fearing that desire will drive one to fornication and so incur grave sin in the hereafter.

The adjectival form عَنُوت (ʿanūt, "arduous"), used of a hill, is the entry's one non-Qur'anic attestation of the root's basic "hard going" sense.

text:
This is a single chapter (bāb) of al-Khalīl's Kitāb al-ʿAyn covering nine root-permutations of the letters ʿ, n, w/y together, as this dictionary's method requires: عنو, عني, عون, عين, نعو, نعي, وعن, نوع, ينع.

1. عنو (ʿ-n-w) — "captive / submission"
- Al-ʿānī = a captive. Two verbal nouns are given for the state of captivity: al-ʿunuww and al-ʿanāʾ. A verse has a man calling himself "your captive" to the sons of Umayyah, his ʿanā being only that he trembles, near death. The verbs are ʿanā–yaʿnū and ʿaniya–yaʿnā, "to become entangled in bondage." "Aʿnūhu" = keep him captive.
- By extension al-ʿānī also means anyone submissive or self-abasing. The dictionary cites Qurʾān 20:111, "and faces are humbled before the Living, the Self-Subsisting" (wa-ʿanati l-wujūhu…), as an instance of this sense, with the verb taʿnū ʿunuwwan. "I came to you ʿāniyan" is glossed as coming submissively, like a captive held hostage by his own offenses.
- Al-ʿunwa = forcible subjugation ("he took it ʿunwatan" = by force of the sword); al-ʿānī is said to derive from this word, i.e. from abasement.
- Al-ʿunwān, a letter's heading/title: three dialect verb-forms (ʿanwantu, ʿannantu, ʿayyantu), said to derive from al-maʿnā, "the sense" — which leads into the related root ʿ-n-y: "the matter ʿanānī" = concerned/occupied me, so I am maʿniyy (concerned) with it; "iʿtanaytu bi-amrihi" = I attended to it. Al-maʿnā of a thing is defined here as its miḥna (trial) and the state its affair comes to.
- Al-ʿanāʾ = toil and hardship (verb ʿannaytuhu tuʿannīhi). Al-muʿannā names a Jāhiliyya custom: once a man's camel-herd reached a hundred, the camel that brought it to that number had its back ritually disabled — stripped of spinal projections, its hump cut — so it could never be ridden or worked again, marking the owner's wealth. A Farazdaq verse and an Aws b. Ḥajar verse (on al-ʿaniyya, a tar or thickened-urine compound used on camels) are cited as further attestation.

2. عون (ʿ-w-n) — "help / midway"
- Al-ʿawn = anyone or anything that helps or is sought for help (e.g. "fasting is an ʿawn toward worship"); same form for masculine/feminine/plural, plural aʿwān. Verbs: aʿantu ("I aided"), taʿāwanū ("they aided each other"); miʿwān = a man good at giving aid. Al-maʿūna is analyzed grammatically two ways: pattern mafʿula (if from al-ʿawn) or faʿūla from al-māʿūn.
- Al-ʿawān = something "middle-aged": a cow of middling age, a middle-aged woman, or (metaphorically) a second war fought after an initial one (ḥarb bikr), each subsequent war being fiercer.
- Al-ʿāna = a herd of wild asses (plurals ʿānāt, ʿūn); ʿĀnāt is also a place-name in the Jazīra that gives its name to "ʿāniyya wine." A man's ʿāna = his pubic hair (diminutive ʿuwayna).

3. عين (ʿ-y-n) — "eye" and its many extensions
- The literal eye; "ʿayn of water" (a spring); "ʿayn of the knee." A directional cloud-sense: clouds arising from a certain quarter (called al-ʿayn) rarely fail to bring rain. "ʿAyn of the sun" = its blazing heat.
- Ready cash ("ʿayn, not dayn/debt"); a man "of ʿayn" (cash-rich); a proverb, "I will not seek a trace after ʿayn" (don't chase indirect evidence once you've seen firsthand); al-ʿayn can also mean a gold dinar (with a supporting verse).
- The evil eye: "ʿintu l-shayʾa bi-ʿaynihi" (I struck it with the [evil] eye), maʿyūn/maʿīn (afflicted), miʿyān (a man with a malevolent eye) — illustrated with a verse about a chief "eye-struck."
- Technical senses: the deviation-point of a balance-scale; a spy (dhū l-ʿuyaynatayn, "the two-eyed one," with dialect variants); "ʿiyānan" = with one's own eyes; a waterskin or large skin wearing thin (taʿayyana), with a Qaṭāmī verse; al-ʿīna, a credit-sale arrangement; al-ʿīn, wild cattle/oryx as a collective noun (like al-ʿīs for camels).
- Descriptive forms for wide/fine eyes (ʿaynāʾ for cow/woman, aʿyun for man, disputed for a bull); al-ʿayan = largeness combined with wideness of the eye's black. Al-aʿyan can also simply be a proper name for the wild bull.
- Social senses: aʿyān = the nobility/chief men of a people, or full brothers (as against half-brothers by other mothers); banū aʿyān = a man's children by free wives. Al-māʾ al-maʿīn = visibly flowing water. Thawb muʿayyan = a garment patterned with small squares like animals' eyes.

4. نعو (n-ʿ-w) — al-naʿw = the slit in a camel's upper lip, attested with a line from al-Ṭirimmāḥ.

5. نعي (n-ʿ-y) — "death announcement"
- naʿā–yanʿā nuʿyan = to announce a death; naʿiyy = the news, or the man who delivers it (with a supporting verse). Al-istinʿāʾ = a kind of startled scattering — used of a frightened group breaking up, or a she-camel bolting with her rider.
- "Yā naʿāʾi l-ʿarab" is an old exclamatory formula ("O announcer of the Arabs' [downfall]"), illustrated with a verse of al-Kumayt lamenting the tribe of Judhām's change of lineage-affiliation — which the ʿAyn glosses explicitly as what the verse is about. A parallel dialect form, nuʿyān, is also a verbal noun of the same verb.

6. وعن (w-ʿ-n) — al-waʿna/al-wiʿān = barren white patches of ground marking an ants' valley; "tawaʿʿanat al-ghanam" = sheep began fattening in spring. A fragment of an old Jāhiliyya pilgrimage-chant (talbiya) is quoted as an example of the word's ritual use.

7. نوع (n-w-ʿ) — al-nawʿ/al-anwāʿ = "kind, sort, type" of anything — garments, fruit, even speech. A separate word al-nūʿ is discussed as meaning hunger, though the author argues it more likely means thirst, since Arabs paired it with al-jūʿ ("hunger") in set phrases — and pairing a word with its exact synonym would be pointless repetition. He notes some grammarians instead defend such doublets (different wording, one meaning) as intentional for emphasis.

8. ينع (y-n-ʿ) — yanaʿat al-thamra = the fruit ripened (verbal nouns yunʿ, yanaʿ; also aynaʿa); the descriptive adjectives given are yāniʿ and mūniʿ, "ripe."

quran_words: عَٰقِبَة 32x "(the) end"; عِقَاب 20x "(in) the penalty"; عَقِب 8x "your heels"; عُقْبَى 6x "(is) the final attainment"; عَاقَبَ 6x "he was made to suffer"; يُعَقِّبْ 2x "look back"; عَقَبَة 2x "the steep path"; أَعْقَبَ 1x "so he penalized them"; مُعَقِّبَٰت 1x "(are) successive (angels)"; مُعَقِّب 1x "adjuster"; عُقْب 1x "(for) the final end"
text:
Ibn Fāris on the root ʿ-q-b (عقب). He identifies two sound roots: (I) a thing's delay and its coming after another; (II) elevation, intensity, and difficulty.

ROOT I — COMING AFTER / SUCCESSION

1. Basic sense (al-Khalīl): whatever follows a thing is its ʿaqīb, like night and day, each the successor of the other. When night comes, day goes: ʿaqaba al-laylu al-nahāra. They "take turns" (yuʿaqqibān, yataʿāqabūn). Some exegetes read the muʿaqqibāt of Q 13:11 as the angels of night and day, because they relieve one another in turn.

2. Taking turns / alternating: the ʿaqīb is one who rides a mount in alternation with another; aʿqabtahu = you dismounted to give him his turn. ʿāqaba bayna rijlayhi = he shifted his weight from one leg to the other.

3. Redress and requital: ʿaqiba ʿalayya ʿaqab = a claim (darak) fell on me over goods; al-taʿqibah = that redress. ʿāqabtu al-rajula (I requited/punished him) → ʿuqūba, ʿiqāb, punishment. It is called ʿuqūba because it comes last, following on (is "second to") the offense (a usage ascribed to Banū Asad). al-muʿāqib (per Ibn al-Aʿrābī) = one who has taken his blood-vengeance; illustrated by verses on avenging a slain kinsman "in the span between a sneeze and its blessing."

4. Outcome / end (al-Khalīl): the ʿāqiba of anything is its end (plural ʿuqab). istaʿqaba... khayran aw sharran = to reap good or ill as the sequel of a deed; istaʿqaba nadaman = to reap regret. taʿaqqaba = to trace someone's track. "You'll find the sequel (ʿaqib) of the matter good or evil" = its ʿāqiba. Of a man struck dumb: "if he had an ʿaqib (a reply) he would speak."

5. Succession in time and rank: ʿaqabtu al-rajula = I became his successor. The Prophet was called al-ʿĀqib because he came after the earlier prophets. faʿaltu bi-ʿāqiba = I did it finally. jiʾtu fī ʿaqib/ʿuqb al-shahr = I came at/after the month's end (Abū Zayd and al-Khalīl distinguish the vowellings: ʿaqib = the very end; ʿuqb = when it has ended and the next has begun). al-Aṣmaʿī: ʿāqiba of birds = birds each alighting where the one before it flew off.

6. Substitution / leavings: akhadhtu ʿuqba min asīrī = I took a substitute for my captive. ʿuqbat al-qidr = what a borrower leaves in the bottom of a returned pot (the "last / remainder"). taṣaddaqtu ṣadaqatan laysat fīhā taʿqibah = a gift with no reservation attached.

7. Offspring / posterity: laysa li-fulānin ʿāqiba = he has no ʿaqib (progeny). al-miʿqāb = a woman who habitually bears a boy after a girl.

8. Repetition and turning back: whoever repeats a thing is muʿaqqib. In Q 27:10 {wa lam yuʿaqqib} = "he did not turn round" (yaʿṭif). al-taʿqīb = a raid following a raid. ʿaqqaba fī l-ṣalāt = to stay praying after others have finished. (A grammatical debate on Labīd's line: Ibn al-Sikkīt takes al-muʿaqqib as "the defaulter/delayer" and the grammatical object; al-Khalīl explains the case-ending by the wronged claimant standing in its position.)

9. Following and traces: aʿqaba = he came back (right on the heels of his going). al-muʿqib (al-Duraydī) = a star rising just after another. ʿuqbat al-sarw wa l-jamāl = the trace (athar) of nobility and beauty upon someone — "trace," because a thing's mark comes after it.

10. The heel and its idioms: ʿaqib al-qadam = the heel; hence the proverb "your son is the one who bloodied your heels" (the true mother is she who bore him), traced to a story of ʿAqīl ibn Mālik and his adoptive vs. birth mother. muwaṭṭaʾ al-ʿaqib = one with many followers (his heel is trodden), as in ʿAmmār's ḥadīth praying that a liar become a much-followed ruler. min ayna jāʾat ʿaqibuka = whence have you come.

11. Withholding after sale: al-muʿtaqib (per al-Nakhaʿī) = a seller who withholds goods until paid and bears the loss if they perish; iʿtaqabtu al-shayʾ = I held it back. al-iʿqāba = a livestock brand, also a flap of skin left behind the ear.

ROOT II — ELEVATION / HARDNESS / DIFFICULTY

12. Height and hard climbs: al-ʿaqaba = a mountain road (plural ʿiqāb); to it are referred all things of height or difficulty. In well-work, the lining is reinforced (yuʿqab) with stones at its back — aʿqābuhā, and al-muʿqib packs gravel into the gaps to strengthen it (al-Kisāʾī); al-ʿuqāb = pottery wedged between the bricks to firm the lining (Abū ʿAmr). al-ʿuqāb (al-Khalīl) = a jutting ascent in a mountain flank, or a rock the water-drawer stands on, or the channel feeding water to the trough.

13. Sinew: al-ʿaqab = the sinew used to bind spears and arrows. Unlike ʿaṣab (which yellows and is useless), ʿaqab tends white and is the harder, stronger of the two — which Ibn Fāris takes as proof that this root's principle is strength.

14. Hardening plant: ʿaqiba al-ʿarfaj = the ʿarfaj-shrub hardened — its stalk thinning and fruit yellowing, after which it only dries out.

15. The eagle: al-ʿuqāb (eagle), a bird of prey, so named for its strength and power (plural aʿqub, ʿiqbān). ʿuqāb ʿaqabnāt = swift to swoop; a verse describes an eagle with blackened beak and shank, to which the war-banner is likened, "flying as it flies."

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-q-d as one root meaning "to tie, bind" and, by extension, "firmness of hold." He states explicitly that every branch of the section returns to that single sense.

1. Architecture. عَقْد = an arch or vault (plurals أَعْقَاد, عُقُود). Al-Khalīl reported no verb for it, but Ibn Fāris allows that عَقَّدَ تَعْقِيدًا ("he built an arch") would be admissible.

2. Literal knotting. عَقَدَ الْحَبْلَ = he knotted the rope; the rope انْعَقَدَ (became knotted); the knot itself is عُقْدَة.

3. Thickening. With the added hamza — a form used, he notes, to keep the senses apart — أَعْقَدَ الْعَسَلَ = he boiled honey down thick; عَسَلٌ عَقِيدٌ / مُنْعَقِد = thickened honey. Verse cited: boiled-down grape syrup running down the sides of a huge beast. Related: عَقِيد, a food thickened with honey.

4. Binding agreements. عَاقَدَهُ is equated with عَاهَدَهُ (to covenant); the noun is عَقْد, plural عُقُود, cited with Q 5:1 "fulfil the ʿuqūd." عَقْد also covers the binding of an oath, cited with Q 5:89 "the oaths you have bound fast." عُقْدَة النِّكَاح — and of anything else — is its becoming binding and being confirmed; in a sale, عُقْدَة is what makes it binding. Ibn Fāris defines these as the tying/confirming of an undertaking; he does not expand them into legal categories.

5. Property and acquisition. عُقْدَة also = an estate (plural عُقَد); اعْتَقَدَ عُقْدَةً = he acquired one; اعْتَقَدَ مَالًا وَأَخًا = he got and kept property, or a brother.

6. Inner fixity. عَقَدَ قَلْبَهُ عَلَى كَذَا = he fixed his heart on something and does not turn from it. اعْتَقَدَ الشَّيْءُ = it hardened; اعْتَقَدَ الْإِخَاءُ = brotherhood became firmly established.

7. Stringing beads. مَعَاقِد = the tie-points in a string of beads (verse: "the tie-points of its thread are not joined"). عِقْد الْقِلَادَة = the necklace-string, measured to the neck's length. Al-Duraydī: مِعْقَاد = a thread for stringing beads.

8. Heaped sand. Al-Khalīl: عَقَد الرَّمْل = sand heaped and gathered (plural أَعْقَاد; rarely عَقِد/عَقِدَات, though allowed). Verse of Dhū al-Rumma on a sand-heap grown with shrubs. Three proverbs turn on it: "more foolish than the soil of the ʿaqad" (foolish because the soil will not hold but collapses), "thirstier than a sand-heap," and "more drinking than a sand-heap" — it soaks up every rain that reaches it.

9. Conception. Al-Khalīl: نَاقَةٌ عَاقِدٌ, a she-camel that has conceived (i.e. held).

10. Thickets and land. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: عُقْدَة of trees = enough to sustain livestock for a year; another authority: trees gathered with firmly rooted stock — also the name for a densely wooded place. Ibn Fāris insists all such uses reduce to the one sense and refuses to multiply entries by repetition. Proverb: "more attached than the crow of the ʿuqda" — its crow never flies off, because it finds there what it wants. Also اعْتَقَدَتِ الْأَرْضُ حَيَا سَنَتِهَا: the land held its year's rain, so deeply that a digger's arm sinks to the shoulder in compacted moist soil. Ibn al-Aʿrābī derives عُقَد of dwellings and lands from عُقَد of pasturage, since both hold sufficiency.

11. Drying/setting. عَقَدَ الْكَرْمُ: the vine's wood has spent its sap; and عَقَدَ الْإِقْط (curd set).

12. Speech impediment. عَكَد (also said عَقَد) of the tongue = thickness in its middle; a man is عَقِد / أَعْقَد when there is a knot in his tongue.

13. Animals with knots or twists. ظَبْيَةٌ عَاقِدٌ = a doe twisting her neck; أَعْقَد of he-goats and gazelles = one with a knot in its horn. Al-Nābigha's verse on "the neck-twisting gazelles" is cited.

14. Character. Ibn al-Sikkīt: لَئِيمٌ أَعْقَدُ, a base man not easy of temper — with a verse of al-Ṭirimmāḥ lampooning such a man of ignoble stock; some say أَعْقَد here means "dog," used as a likeness.

15. Firm build. نَاقَةٌ مَعْقُودَةُ الْقَرَى = a firm-backed she-camel (verse cited); جَمَلٌ عَقْدٌ = a tightly twisted, compact build, with al-Nābigha's line on a firmly twisted bond "that the treacherous cannot undo."

16. Clouds. تَعَقَّدَ السَّحَابُ: clouds massing as though into a built arch.

17. Anger. "His knots have come undone" = his anger subsided; "he has knotted his forelock" = he grew angry and made ready for harm (verse: "a people who have knotted their forelocks").

18. Dogs. تَعَاقَدَتِ الْكِلَابُ: they locked together in coupling.

19. Obscure speech. Al-Duraydī: عَقَّدَ كَلَامَهُ = he made his speech obscure and abstruse.

20. Sorcery. الْمُعَقِّد is said to be the sorcerer, because he knots the magic; verse cited on a glance that "ties the magic of the two Babylonians." Ibn Fāris cites Q 113:4, "those who blow on knots," glossing it as sorceresses who tie knots in threads.

21. A valley destroying a people: عَقَدَ عَلَيْهِمْ, when it closes over them.

22. Resembling the root: أَعْقَد for a short man — because he is like a knot; عُقْد = short ones, with a verse contrasting well-aimed spears that are "neither stubby nor crooked."

text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root ʿ-q-l (عقل) as having one consistent core meaning: a holding-back or restraint (ḥubsa) in a thing, or something close to it. Every sense below is derived from that core.

1. Intellect / reason (al-ʿaql): that which restrains a person from blameworthy speech and action. Al-Khalīl defines it as the opposite of ignorance (jahl): one "ʿaqala" when he grasps what he did not know before, or holds himself back from what he had been doing. Plural ʿuqūl. A man of reason is ʿāqil (pl. ʿuqalāʾ, ʿāqilūn); ʿaqūl describes someone of keen understanding. "Mā lahu maʿqūl" = "he has no sense." Illustrated by a verse ("it has given them reason and admonition, for one with wit"), the proverb "many a simpleton is really shrewd," and "so-and-so retains what he hears well."

2. Fortress / stronghold (al-maʿqil, al-ʿaql; pl. ʿuqūl): a refuge one holds fast in. A verse by Uḥayḥa uses "al-ʿuqūl" to mean fortresses.

3. Blood-money (al-ʿaql, the diya): "ʿaqaltu al-qatīl" = I paid the blood-money for the slain (so Al-Aṣmaʿī). "ʿaqaltu ʿan fulān" = I paid the fine for his offence — and the author notes the judge Abū Yūsuf once failed to distinguish these two constructions until it was explained to him. The ʿāqila are the killer's near paternal kin and brothers, over whose property the blood-money is apportioned in an accidental killing. Related usages: "the blood of X became a liability (maʿqula) on his people"; a woman shares blood-money equally with a man up to one-third of her diya, after which her diya is half of his; clans held inherited "grades in blood-monies" (maʿāqil, sg. maʿqula) from pre-Islamic times. Two explanations for why diya is called ʿaql: because the camels paid were tied up (tuʿqal) in the slain man's courtyard (the name sticking even when paid in coin); or because it "holds back" (restrains) the blood [i.e. further bloodshed].

4. Tithe / alms in kind (ʿiqāl): Al-Khalīl — a collector who takes a full year's camel-ṣadaqa "took an ʿiqāl" (two years = ʿiqālayn), i.e. the levy itself, not a cash price. Philologists extend ʿiqāl to alms generally ("appointed over the ʿiqāl of the tribe" = over their alms). Said to be called ʿiqāl because it holds back from the payer both the demand upon him and the sin. Ibn Fāris records the debate over Abū Bakr's vow to fight those who withheld "even an ʿiqāl" of what they paid the Prophet: some read ʿiqāl as a year's alms, others as a trivial thing (the camel-rope) used proverbially for the least item; others still say the collector handed over the camels together with their tethers.

5. Binding / constipating: Al-Aṣmaʿī — a gazelle "ʿaqala" when it takes refuge on a mountain; food "ʿaqala the belly" when it constipates; a binding medicine is ʿaqūl.

6. Tucking / locking a limb: iʿtaqala a lance = wedge it between stirrup and shin; iʿtaqala a ewe = pin its leg to milk it; a wrestler's "ʿuqla" is a leg-lock; ʿaqaltu the camel = hobble its foreleg with the ʿiqāl (tether). Proverb: "the stallion guards his herd even when hobbled." A tongue is "ʿuqila" when held back from speech.

7. The choice/noble one (ʿaqīla): a woman who is the pride of her people; also used of a chief. The ʿaqīla of anything is its finest — the pearl is "the ʿaqīla of the sea." Two explanations for the word: Ibn al-Aʿrābī — she "held back" her peers from reaching her rank; Al-Khalīl — she was kept secluded (ʿuqilat) in her chamber. Abū ʿUbayda notes ʿaqīla is used for male and female alike. Cited with verses of Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyāt and Imruʾ al-Qays.

8. Knock-kneedness (al-ʿaqal): the knocking-together of the knees; a camel so afflicted is aʿqal. Al-ʿuqqāl (also ʿuqāl) is a leg disease of beasts (mostly sheep) making the animal seem to wrench its legs off rock. Abū ʿUbayda: a woman ʿaqlāʾ has thin shins and thick calves.

9. Tangle / crookedness (al-ʿāqūl): of a river, valley, or affair — that which is entangled and winding (Al-Khalīl).

10. Shallow well (al-ʿiqāl): reported (secondhand) from Ibn al-Aʿrābī and Abū ʿUbayda — so called because its water lies near, as if drawn with a short rope.

11. Heaped/coiled sand (al-ʿaqanqal; pl. ʿaqāqīl): a piled dune, named for its heaping. Also the lizard's coiled intestine (with a proverb, "feed your brother from the lizard's gut," meant as praise by some and mockingly per Al-Aṣmaʿī). The core idea is coiling and twisting; hence twisted vine-shoots are also called ʿaqāqīl.

12. Proper names from this pattern (possibly still analogical): ʿĀqil, a mountain (and Banū ʿĀqil, a royal clan named for settling there); Maʿqula, a desert place (a depression in al-Dahnāʾ, per Al-Aṣmaʿī); and Dhū al-ʿUqqāl, a well-known horse — each attested with a verse.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-q-m as a single root whose core idea is obscurity, narrowness, and severity. He derives every sense from that one notion.

1. Severity / no relief. حَرْب عَقَام (ʿaqām war): so fierce that no one turns aside to help anyone else. دَاء عَقَام: an illness from which one does not recover.

2. Narrowness of temper. رَجُل عَقَام: a man of constricted character. Cited verse: "You are ʿaqām — no wish of his can be met — a man of resolve when it comes to delay, and a waster."

3. Barrenness of the womb. عَقِمَتِ الرَّحِم: he explains it as a depression or hollow occurring in the womb, so that it does not receive the child. Both عَقِمَتِ الْمَرْأَة (active form) and عُقِمَتْ (passive form) are used; he judges the passive the better. He cites a report that the backbones of the hypocrites are "made ʿaqīm" so they cannot prostrate — here he glosses the sense as stiffening of the joints.

4. Forms and plurals. رَجُل عَقِيم, plural عُقَمَاء; of women عَقِيمَات, عَقَائِم, عُقُم. Abū ʿAmr: عُقِمَتِ الْمَرْأَة = she does not bear. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: verbal noun عَقْم; the woman is مَعْقُومَة or عَقِيم, and a man likewise عُقِمَ, so he is عَقِيم or مَعْقُوم.

5. A causative use tied to sorcery: عَقَمْتُ فُلَانَة — "I bewitched her so that her womb was closed and she does not bear."

6. Figurative "fruitless." Al-Khalīl: عَقْل عَقِيم, an intellect that yields its owner nothing. Ibn Fāris relays the saying that intellect is of two kinds — barren (that of the man of this world) and fruit-bearing (that of the man of the hereafter). Likewise الْمُلْك عَقِيم, "sovereignty is barren," because a man will kill his own father over rule — i.e. it shuts the door on preserving kinship; and الدُّنْيَا عَقِيم, this world returns no good to its owner.

7. The barren wind. الرِّيح الْعَقِيم: the wind that fertilises neither tree nor cloud. He cites Q 51:41, "when We sent against them the barren wind," and notes the view that it is al-dabūr, the west wind. Al-Kisāʾī gives the verb عَقِمَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ الرِّيحُ ... عُقْمًا.

8. Digging at the sides. عَقِيم of land is ground you have dug into (iʿtaqamtahā). Al-Khalīl: الِاعْتِقَام is digging into the sides of a well; a verse of Rabīʿa ibn Maqrūm describes beasts digging/working at the sides of a stagnant desert pool. Ibn Fāris explicitly ties this back to the root idea: it is called iʿtiqām because it is at the side, which indicates the narrowness he posited.

9. Constraining in argument. الْمُعَاقِم is the adversary in dispute — so called, he explains, because he hems his opponent in with words.

10. Archaic speech. Al-Shaybānī used كَلَام عُقْمِيّ for speech of the Jāhiliyya that is no longer known; he reported asking a man of Hudhayl about a rare Hudhalī word and being told, "This is ʿuqmī speech" — pre-Islamic language not spoken today.

11. A technical item: the مِعْقَم is the barrier separating straw from grain when produce is winnowed.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-Q-R as **two unrelated roots**, each internally consistent: (1) wounding — or a dent/breach that resembles a wound; (2) fixity and permanence.

**FIRST ROOT: wounding, hamstringing, disabling**

1. **Hamstringing an animal.** Per al-Khalīl, ʿaqr is a kind of wounding: ʿaqartu al-faras = "I struck the horse's legs with the sword." Hence faras ʿaqīr / maʿqūr (a hamstrung horse), plural khayl ʿaqrā. Ziyād: "when you pass his grave, hamstring there the fat white camels and every swift courser." Labīd compares a vulture raising its wing-feathers to "the hamstrung one, weaponless."

2. **Bringing a camel down to slaughter it.** The she-camel is hamstrung until she collapses; once down, the man slaughters her with full command of her. Imruʾ al-Qays: "the day I hamstrung my mount for the maidens."

3. **Galling, chafing.** ʿaqartu ẓahra al-dābba = I galled the beast's back; al-ʿaqqār is a man rough with his camels, careless of their saddle-frames until their backs are sore. Imruʾ al-Qays: "You've galled my camel, Imruʾ al-Qays — get down!" Related: sarj miʿqar / ʿuqara / ʿaqqār / miʿqār (a galling saddle); kalb ʿaqūr (a biting dog).

4. **Immobilising, detaining.** "ʿaqarta bī" ("you kept me long") is not a mere synonym for delay: Ibn Fāris insists the sense is that one is held as though his she-camel had been hamstrung, so he cannot travel. So too a verse on Umm al-Khazraj "hamstringing" a people. And taʿaqqara al-ghayth = the rain settled and stayed, "as though it were something hamstrung and cannot leave."

5. **Barrenness.** ʿāqir = a woman who does not conceive — placed here because "she is like one who has been hamstrung." Plural ʿawāqir. The verb is given as ʿaqarat/taʿqiru, but the form ʿaqirat/taʿqaru is judged better; al-Khalīl's reason: this is something that befalls her from outside, not an act of her own. Abū Zayd allows both ʿaqarat and ʿaqirat, and rajul ʿāqir for a man; he notes that strict analogy would want ʿaqurat, since the verb is intransitive like ẓarufa ("was elegant") and karuma ("was noble"). A ḥadīth phrase ʿujuz ʿuqqar (barren old women) is cited, and the proverb "more barren than a she-mule." A poet likens an eagle preparing her nestling's bed to "a beautiful barren woman" preparing for her husband — the explanation given being that she is the more assiduous in adorning herself for him, having no child to boast of and nothing to distract her. Also laqiḥat al-nāqa ʿan ʿuqr = she conceived after long barrenness (parallel to ʿan ʿuqm).

6. **ʿUqr as compensation, then as dower.** The compensation paid for a woman's private part when she has been taken by force is called ʿuqr. Ibn Fāris files this under the Arabs' habit of naming one thing by the name of a neighbouring thing; the dower (mahr) is then likewise called ʿuqr "because it is taken by reason of the ʿuqr."

7. **The last of a kind.** bayḍat al-ʿuqr is the hen's final egg, after which she lays no more — proverbial for anything with no successor of its type.

8. **A gap.** Al-Khalīl reports a bedouin of al-Ṣammān saying that any gap between two things is ʿaqr / ʿuqr; he laid his hand on two table legs and said "what is between them is ʿuqr."

9. **Cutting off growth.** A palm-tree is ʿuqirat when its crown is cut so nothing ever sprouts again from the trunk (nakhla ʿaqira). kalaʾ ʿaqār = pasture that injures and kills camels. A bedouin's "I neither plucked at the matted pasture nor ʿaqartuhā" = nor did I finish it off. Proverbially, ʿuqarat al-ʿilm al-nisyān — forgetting is what "wounds" knowledge (pattern of tukhama, "indigestion").

10. **The raised voice (ʿaqīra).** rafaʿa ʿaqīratahu = he raised his voice in song or recitation. Explained as adjacency: a man whose leg had been severed laid it across the other and cried out at full voice; ʿaqīra properly is the severed leg, and the voice took its name from the circumstance.

11. **The slain notable.** "I have never seen an ʿaqīra like so-and-so" for a man of rank derives from what was said over an eminent slain man: "never have I seen such an ʿaqīra in the midst of a people."

12. **Imprecation.** ʿaqran lahu wa-jadʿan (wounding and mutilation to him). To a woman: ḥalqā ʿaqrā — read either as "may God wound her body and give her pain in her throat," or, per some, as calling her ill-omened, one who "shaves and wounds" her own people. ʿaqqartu al-rajul = I said ʿaqrā ḥalqā to him.

13. **Drugs.** Compounded medicines are ʿaqāqīr, singular ʿaqqār, so called as if the drug "wounds" the belly.

14. **A fright-sickness.** al-ʿaqar: an affliction that grips a man in terror so he cannot move and his legs give way beneath him.

**SECOND ROOT: a fixed base, a standing place**

1. **A stronghold.** al-ʿaqr is the castle that the villagers depend on and take refuge in — Labīd likens something to "the ʿaqr of the Hajarī," built of ashbāh, i.e. bricks moulded to one pattern. Abū ʿUbayd generalises: al-ʿaqr is any elevated building.

2. **The home ground.** Per al-Khalīl, ʿuqr al-dār is a people's settled place between house and watering-trough, built up or not — Aws b. Maghrāʾ: "when we drove them from the ʿuqr of their abode." More broadly, al-ʿuqr is **the root or base of anything**.

3. **The trough's standing place.** ʿuqr al-ḥawḍ is where camels stand when they come to water (plural aʿqār, in a line of Dhū al-Rumma about lean ticks there). A camel that drinks from the trough's ʿuqr is ʿaqira; one that drinks from its front (izāʾ) is aziya.

4. **The heart of a fire.** ʿuqr al-nār is where the embers collect (cited in a verse on blade-points).

5. **Property.** Per al-Khalīl, al-ʿaqār is a man's landed estate, plural ʿaqārāt — "he has neither house nor estate." Ibn al-Aʿrābī instead glosses ʿaqār as treasured household goods, with rajul muʿqir = one rich in goods.

6. **al-ʿUqayrā.** Per al-Qutaybī, a name formed from ʿuqr al-dār; hence Umm Salama's words to ʿĀʾisha, "settle in your ʿuqayrā and do not take it into the open," i.e. keep to your house.

7. **A cloud (by likeness to the castle).** al-ʿaqr is also cloud rising from the direction of the spring/eye and veiling the sun's disc and its surroundings — a line of Ḥumayd.

8. **Wine.** ʿuqār is said to be so named because it "clung to" (ʿāqarat) the jar, i.e. kept fast to it.

9. **Barren sand.** al-ʿāqir of sand is sand that grows nothing, like sifted flour. Ibn Fāris closes the second origin here.

**Place-names** (possibly derived from the above): ʿAqārāʾ (in a wine verse of Ḥumayd); al-ʿAqr near Bābil, where Yazīd b. al-Muhallab was killed — hence Yawm al-ʿAqr, taunted by al-Ṭirimmāḥ; and ʿAqrā, a watering-place.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-r-sh (عرش) as a single sound root whose core sense is elevation/height in a built thing, then extended metaphorically.

1. al-ʿarsh — a raised seat. Per al-Khalīl, "the king's seat/throne" (سرير الملك); cited from Q 12:100, "and he raised his parents upon the throne."

2. Metaphorical extension to a person's standing. A man's affair and the support that sustains him is called his ʿarsh; when it collapses one says "his ʿarsh was toppled" (ثُلَّ عرشه) — shāhid from Zuhayr.

3. Trellising / shade-structures. taʿrīsh al-karm = trellising a vine (raising and securing it). al-ʿarīsh = a frame of rods raised and made fast to cast shade; at Badr the Prophet was asked, "Shall we build you an ʿarīsh?" Any shade-giving structure is ʿarsh or ʿarīsh.

4. Roof of a house — ʿarsh; cited from Q 22:45, "fallen down upon its roofs" (عروش): the roof collapses and the walls fall in upon it.

5. A woman's camel-litter — al-ʿarīsh, resembling a howdah. Shawāhid from Ruʾba (of old age bending him like a curved ʿarīsh-frame) and al-Khansāʾ (a collapsed ʿarsh once shade-giving). Al-Ṭirimmāḥ's "maʿrūsh al-ḥaṣīrayn": some read it as this litter, its ḥaṣīrān being its two sides; others say maʿrūsh means a camel firm in the flanks.

6. Vine climbing. ʿarashtu / ʿarrashtu al-karma = I trellised the vine; iʿtarasha al-ʿinab = the grape climbed the trellis.

7. Wooden tents/shelters — al-ʿurūsh, singular ʿarīsh (with a shāhid glossing al-dawāmij as "those entering").

8. Lining a well — ʿarsh al-biʾr. In sandy wells that won't hold a stone lining, the top is framed with wood laid piece on piece so water-drawers can stand and draw; the mathāba is the standing-spot at the well-top. A related sense: the ʿarsh at the well's mouth on which the drawer stands (shawāhid cited, incl. al-Shammākh; al-huwiyya = the spot from which one plunges/falls).

9. A verb of the wild ass — ʿarrasha bi-ʿānatihi: charging his herd with head raised and mouth open (per al-Khalīl); tied to the root by the "raising of the head."

10. Anatomy of the neck — al-ʿursh: the two ʿurshān flanking a vertebra, holding the akhdaʿ veins; two elongated pieces of flesh along the neck (shāhid from Dhū al-Rumma). Some vocalize it ʿarshān (fatḥa).

11. Anatomy of the foot — al-ʿarsh: the region between the ʿayr and the toes on the top of the foot; plural ʿirasha. Ibn Fāris notes further near-identical reports on al-ʿurshayn that he omits for brevity.

12. Astronomy — ʿarsh al-simāk: four stars below al-ʿAwwāʾ shaped like a bier (naʿsh), also said to be the rump of Leo (shāhid from Ibn Aḥmar; "shariyat" = it persisted with rain).
