text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-r-ḍ as a root with a great many branches which, he says, all go back to one root meaning: al-ʿarḍ, breadth, the opposite of length. He holds that close study bears this out, and he explains most of the derived uses as pictures of breadth, such as showing a thing's broad side, laying something crosswise, setting one breadth against another, or coming at a thing from the side.

1. **Breadth itself.** ʿAruḍa, yaʿruḍu, verbal noun ʿiraḍ, "to be broad", gives the adjective ʿarīḍ, "broad". Abū Zayd gives the verbal noun ʿarāḍa and cites a verse in which the breadth and length of Ibn Laylā's character outdo everyone who races for noble deeds. A qaws ʿurāḍa is a broad bow. A woman who aʿraḍat her children bore broad ones, as aṭālat is said of bearing tall ones. ʿArraḍa, and aʿraḍa as al-Khalīl reports it, mean "to make broad".

2. **Displaying and reviewing.** ʿAraḍa al-matāʿ (yaʿriḍu, verbal noun ʿarḍ) is to display goods, as though showing their breadth. ʿArḍ al-jund, reviewing troops, is having them pass before one, as though looking at what shows of their condition; whatever is displayed in this way is called ʿaraḍ, with a vowelled r, just as qabaḍ is used of things seized. ʿAraḍūhum ʿalā al-sayf, "they put them to the sword", pictures the sword taking in the people's whole breadth, so that none escaped.

3. **Laying crosswise.** To lay a stick across a vessel is ʿaraḍa with the imperfect yaʿruḍu (vowel u); a ḥadīth asks why a vessel was not covered "even with a stick you lay across it". Otherwise the imperfect is yaʿriḍu (vowel i). One lays a spear crosswise (ʿaraḍa al-rumḥ; al-Nābigha: "when they lay the Khaṭṭī spears across the withers"), lays sticks across one another so that they "lie crosswise" (iʿtaraḍat), and a weary man lies across his camel (aʿyā fa-ʿtaraḍa ʿalā al-baʿīr). Abū Duwād likens feathers riding on water, lying over one another, to arrowheads laid across each other like a cross.

4. **Getting in the way; accosting.** Mā ʿaraḍtu lahu, "I did not get in his way", and lā taʿriḍ lahu, "do not get in his way", are explained as setting one's breadth against another's. Iʿtaraḍa fī al-amr is to thrust oneself into a matter; taʿarraḍa lī bi-mā akrahu means "he accosted me with what I dislike", and a man given to this is ʿirrīḍ. Iʿtaraḍa ʿirḍa fulān is to malign someone, doing what takes in the breadth of his ʿirḍ. Al-Khalīl: one who is ʿurḍa li-l-nās is someone people never stop assailing, because they come at his side.

5. **Going sideways, not straight.** A horse that ʿaraḍa in its running goes sideways, as though showing the onlooker its breadth; this is explained as running with the breast turned sideways or the head inclined (verse: "he goes sideways until he raises his muzzle"). Iʿtaraḍa al-faras is said of a horse that will not go straight for the one leading it; al-Ṭirimmāḥ says he had been "a man of arrogance and iʿtirāḍ" when the Sovereign showed him his right course. Yamshī al-ʿiraḍnā, in which the n is an added letter, is to veer sideways while running (al-ʿAjjāj: their horses run al-ʿiraḍnā in troops). A nāqa ʿurḍiyya is an intractable she-camel that goes crosswise instead of straight, and a man who has ʿurḍiyya against his enemies is tough with them.

6. **Exchange, matching, keeping abreast.** ʿAraḍa min silʿatihi is to barter some of one's wares, giving one thing and taking another (verse: "the one who barters with you gives back in exchange"). ʿAraḍtu lahu min ḥaqqihi thawban, "I gave him a garment against his due", sets the breadth of the one against the breadth of the other. ʿĀraḍtuhu fī al-sayr is to travel abreast of someone; ʿāraḍtuhu mithla mā ṣanaʿa is to do to him the like of what he did, and from this comes muʿāraḍa, "matching, countering": the breadth of what one does is like the breadth of what came to one (Ṭufayl: "I kept pace alongside them at an easy gait"). The same holds for ʿāraḍtuhu on the road and ʿāraḍtuhu bi-l-kitāb, collating by a book. Ibn Fāris says of these, "this is the qiyās", the root's analogy.

7. **Turning away.** Aʿraḍa ʿan, to turn away from a person or a matter, and aʿraḍa bi-wajhihi, to turn one's face away, keep the same meaning: whoever turns away turns his breadth toward the other. Al-ʿāriḍ too, he says, derives from ʿarḍ as breadth.

8. **Coming into view; offering a target.** Aʿraḍa laka al-shayʾ min baʿīd: a thing "shows itself" to you from afar and is then muʿriḍ, because you have seen its breadth (ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm: "al-Yamāma came into view and towered high, like swords in the hands of men drawing them"). Anything that gives you a hold on its breadth is muʿriḍ (vowel i): aʿraḍa laka al-ẓabyu fa-rmihi, "the gazelle has shown you its breadth, so shoot", like afqara and aʿwara.

9. **Without discrimination.** Aʿraḍta al-qirfa, "you have made the suspicion broad", is said to someone who, asked whom he suspects, names a whole tribe; some said aʿraḍta al-furqa, which the entry calls perhaps better. Istaʿraḍa al-khawārij al-nās: the Khawārij killed without caring whom. A ḥadīth, "eat cheese ʿurḍan", means take it as it comes and do not ask about it. Al-muʿriḍ is one who accosts people and borrows from whoever he can, as in ʿUmar's report that Usayfiʿ of Juhayna "borrowed muʿriḍan". Iʿtaraḍtu uʿṭī man aqbala wa-adbara: "I set about giving to all who came and went".

10. **By chance.** ʿAliqtu fulānan ʿaraḍan, "I became attached to someone ʿaraḍan", means through a chance crossing, without preparing for it or intending it, as with the unled mating of camels (verse: "I became attached to her by chance, while I kill her people"). A sahm ʿaraḍ is a stray arrow whose shooter is unknown, as though it came crosswise without being aimed, like the miʿrāḍ arrow. To look at or see someone ʿarḍa ʿayn is to catch a glimpse of him: he crossed before one's eye.

11. **Unled mating.** A stallion covers a she-camel ʿirāḍan when he does so without being led to her. This is referred to iʿtaraḍa, "to come at a thing from the side", as though he came at her crosswise from among the other she-camels (al-Rāʿī: noble she-camels that conceive only ʿirāḍan and are bought only at high prices). Al-Liḥyānī: laqiḥat al-nāqatu ʿirāḍan, "the she-camel conceived ʿirāḍan", when she went to a stallion she had not been led to.

12. **Al-ʿirḍ: a person's honour or self.** Some say a person's ʿirḍ is his ḥasab (standing and merit), others his self (nafs); either way, Ibn Fāris says, it comes from ʿarḍ. When al-ʿirḍ is said to mean a person's odour, good or bad, he calls this an extension (mujāwaza): the odour is named after the ʿirḍ it comes from. He cites the Prophet's saying about sweat that runs "from their aʿrāḍ", that is, their bodies, as confirming this. Those who take ʿirḍ as "self" adduce Ḥassān's verse: "my father, my mother and my ʿirḍ are a shield for Muḥammad's ʿirḍ against you". Naqiyy al-ʿirḍ describes someone far from being reviled or faulted.

13. **Oblique speech.** Maʿārīḍ al-kalām is speech that comes out in a guise (miʿraḍ) other than its plain wording, like the miʿraḍ of a girl, the garment in which she is displayed. Some claim the Arabs also say "I recognized it in the ʿarūḍ of his speech", meaning in its oblique turns.

14. **A vast army; mountains and clouds.** Al-ʿarḍ is a huge army, by comparison with the ʿarḍ of clouds, cloud that blocks the horizon with its breadth. A verse speaks of leading an ʿarḍ against a people, explained as an army like a mountain or a horizon-blocking cloud, and Durayd speaks of "the ʿarḍ of an army, vast, for which the open tracts of the earth grow narrow". Ibn al-Aʿrābī: al-aʿrāḍ are mountains, valleys and clouds, singular ʿirḍ (also transmitted from him as ʿarḍ). Abū ʿUbayda: al-ʿarḍ is the face (sanad) of a mountain; al-Aṣmaʿī recited a line about boulders rolling down "from the ʿarḍ".

15. **Al-ʿāriḍ: cloud, and whatever faces you.** Al-ʿāriḍ is cloud (Q 46:24: "They said: this is an ʿāriḍ that will bring us rain"), and the ʿāriḍ of anything is what faces you. Abū ʿUbayda: it is the cloud that appears across one quarter of the sky in the evening and by morning has mounted up and levelled out; it is also called al-ʿānn. So too "an ʿāriḍ of locusts" is one that fills the horizon.

16. **The middle.** The ʿurḍ of a wall, of property or of a river is its middle (Labīd: the two "made for the middle of the stream").

17. **Prosody (ʿarūḍ).** Some derive ʿarūḍ al-shiʿr, the prosody of poetry, from al-ʿarūḍ, "side, region", as though it were a region of knowledge, citing a verse in which every people of Maʿadd has an ʿarūḍ to which they resort. Others say al-ʿarīḍ is a difficult road on a mountain's flank, which brings it into line with the rest of the chapter; they connect it with the intractable nāqa ʿurḍiyya, which goes crosswise rather than straight (verse: "I gave her my words despite her waywardness").

18. **Al-ʿāriḍa and al-ʿawāriḍ: strength, face, teeth, beard.** For shadīd al-ʿāriḍa, al-Liḥyānī gives "strong of side" and al-Khalīl "possessed of endurance and firmness"; Ibn Fāris finds the two close: what such a man presents to people is strong. ʿĀriḍat al-wajh is what shows of the face in laughing, and it is claimed that a woman's teeth are called al-ʿawāriḍ (a verse of ʿAntara is cited). Khafīf al-ʿāriḍayn means light on the two sides of the beard. Abū Laylā: the ʿawāriḍ are the teeth that show in laughing, being in the breadth of the face. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: a man's two ʿāriḍs are the hair of his cheeks, so one does not say to a beardless youth "wipe your ʿāriḍs".

19. **Mishap, worldly goods, property.** Al-ʿaraḍ is a mishap of time such as illness, so called because it comes across a person and takes hold of him in some part of his body. Al-ʿaraḍ is also the lure of this world, little or much, because it shows you its side (verse: let not the ʿaraḍ of the world be a care to one who hopes for a lasting without end; saying: "the world is a ready ʿaraḍ from which the righteous and the wicked alike take"). In the Prophet's saying "richness does not come from abundance of ʿarḍ", Ibn Fāris reports the word as heard only with an unvowelled r: ʿarḍ is any property other than coin, plural ʿurūḍ. ʿAraḍ, with a vowelled r, is what a person obtains of his share of this world (Q 7:169: "if a like ʿaraḍ comes to them, they take it").

20. **The miʿrāḍ arrow.** The miʿrāḍ is an arrow with four thin vanes that goes crosswise when shot; al-Khalīl: an arrow shot without feathers that travels broadside.

21. **Beams, cloth, bulk, wealth.** Al-Khalīl: al-ʿawāriḍ are the broad roof-pieces of a camel-litter whose ends rest in its two ʿāriḍs, together forming its roof, and likewise a house's roof-pieces when laid crosswise; ʿāriḍat al-bāb is the beam that holds the two door-posts together from above. Al-ʿarḍī is a kind of cloth, "and perhaps it has breadth" (Abū Nukhayla: "a stature that strains the ʿarḍī"). A woman who is ʿurḍa is bulky, spread out in breadth by her fatness. The proverb fulān ʿarīḍ al-biṭān, "broad of girth-strap", is said of one who has grown rich.

22. **The young goat.** Al-ʿarīḍ is a kid that mounts or is about to mount, that is, has reached maturity; plural ʿurḍān. Ibn Fāris refers this too to ʿarḍ.

23. **Camels, provisions, travel.** Al-taʿrīḍ is the provisions or travel-food carried on camels, so called because they are offered to whoever may need them; ʿarriḍū min mīratikum means "feed us from your provisions". A verse calls a red provision-camel "one of those that make offerings to the crows": she runs ahead of the other camels, her loads come open with her speed, and crows light on them. Al-ʿurāḍāt are camels whose tracks run far because they take a broad course across the land (saying: when the star al-Shiʿrā rises at first light and you see no rain, send the ʿurāḍāt out to seek you a place to live). A nāqa ʿurḍa li-l-safar is a she-camel strong for travel, always put forward for it.

24. **Al-ʿāriḍa: an animal slaughtered when stricken.** Al-ʿāriḍa is a she-camel or sheep slaughtered because something has befallen it (verse: roast meat "not from an ʿāriḍa"). In Ibn Fāris's view this is an active participle standing for a passive one, as in sirr kātim, a "concealing" secret for a concealed one: the animal is one befallen by illness. Usage then extended this until the verb was built on the animal itself, ʿaraḍat, "she was stricken" (verse: when a fat one among them is stricken, do not give it away but preserve its meat).

25. **Places.** Al-ʿirḍ is a valley, and al-ʿIrḍ is a particular valley in al-Yamāma (al-Aʿshā: its hollow "has become palms, growing crops and clover"; al-Mutalammis: "the season of al-ʿIrḍ, when its flies have come alive"). Al-maʿāriḍ, plural of maʿraḍ, are lands in which livestock are put out to graze.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ʿ-r-b (عرب) from three independent base meanings:

1. Clarifying and making plain (al-ināba wa-l-ifṣāḥ).
- أَعْرَبَ عَنْ نَفْسِهِ = "he expressed himself, made himself clear." Cited via the Prophetic saying that a previously-married woman's "tongue speaks out for her" (yuʿribu ʿanhā lisānuhā), and a report recommending that a child, "when he begins to speak clearly" (yuʿribu al-ṣabiyy), say the shahāda seven times — i.e. when he can make himself understood.
- Grammatical iʿrāb (inflection) is not the same thing, yet Ibn Fāris says it belongs to the same underlying sense: inflection is what distinguishes meanings — subject vs. object, negation, wonder, interrogation, etc.
- He suggests the people called al-ʿArab may be named from this sense, "because their tongue is the most clarifying of tongues." Supporting evidence: a saying that "Arabic is not a single category but a speaking tongue," and the idiom مَا بِهَا عَرِيبٌ ("there is not a soul in it," i.e. no one who could speak out for himself).
- On al-Khalīl's authority: al-ʿArab al-ʿāriba = the pure/genuine Arabs; al-aʿārīb = plural of al-aʿrāb (bedouin); aʿraba = to speak eloquently; ʿarabāniyy al-lisān = eloquent; aʿraba al-faras = a horse whose Arabian pedigree is pure and free of any suspicion of mixed breeding; al-ibil al-ʿirāb = Arabian camels; al-ʿArab al-mustaʿriba = those who entered later and became arabized.

2. Liveliness and cheerfulness of soul (al-nashāṭ wa-ṭīb al-nafs).
- al-ʿarūb (pl. al-ʿurub) = a woman who laughs readily and is cheerful. This is the sense Ibn Fāris attaches to Q 56:36, {عُرُبًا}; he reports that the exegetes glossed it as women "lovingly devoted to their husbands."
- al-ʿarb (rāʾ vowelless) = liveliness/eagerness — a verse describes horses "pulling eagerly at their reins."
- al-ʿarab (rāʾ with fatḥa) = a trace or mark; verb ʿariba yaʿrabu ʿaraban.

3. Corruption in a body or organ (fasād).
- عَرِبَتْ مِعْدَتُهُ = "his stomach became upset/spoiled." From this, امْرَأَةٌ عَرُوبٌ can also mean a corrupt/depraved woman — supported by a line of Ibn al-Aʿrābī (via Thaʿlab). Note that ʿarūb thus carries opposite valences: cheerful (sense 2) and corrupt (sense 3).

Appendix on Friday: al-ʿarūba was an old name for Friday, which Ibn Fāris treats as lying outside his three analogies. He notes the Qurʾān and ḥadīth use only al-jumʿa, cites two lines of poetry that mention yawm al-ʿarūba, and concludes that this material "is not to be relied upon as sound."

text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ع-ر-ف from two sound base meanings: (1) the successive following of a thing, one part joined to the next; (2) stillness and tranquility.

FIRST BASE — successive following:
1. al-ʿurf: a horse's mane — so called because the hair runs strand after strand along it. Related idiom: "the sandgrouse came ʿurfan ʿurfan" (in file, one flock behind another).
2. al-ʿurfa (pl. ʿuraf): a raised, sloping strip of fertile land between two sandy tracts, likened to a horse's mane. (A supporting verse is cited but dropped in the source.)

SECOND BASE — stillness/settling of the soul:
3. al-maʿrifa / al-ʿirfān: knowing, recognizing (ʿarafa X ʿirfānan wa-maʿrifatan; "a known matter," maʿrūf). Ibn Fāris ties this to the second base: the soul settles toward what it recognizes, whereas whoever rejects something shies away and recoils from it.
4. al-ʿarf: a sweet fragrance — fitting the base because the soul settles toward it ("how sweet its scent"). He reads Qur'an 47:6, {ʿarrafahā lahum}, as "He made it (the Garden) fragrant/pleasant for them," and cites a verse praising a woman "of sweet fragrance."
5. al-ʿurf = al-maʿrūf: kindness / good conduct — so named because souls settle toward it. Supported by al-Nābigha: "no wrong is counted good, nor is kindness lost."
6. al-ʿarīf: (per al-Khalīl) the overseer set over a group — called ʿarīf because he is "known" by the office; alternatively the office (ʿirāfa) is like a governorship, and he is so named so he may know the people's circumstances.
7. ʿArafāt (place name): three explanations reported — (a) Adam and Eve came to know one another (taʿārafā) there; (b) when Gabriel taught Abraham the rites of the ḥajj he asked "Have you understood? (aʿarafta)"; (c) it is a hallowed, exalted place, as though "made fragrant/sanctified" (ʿurrifa), paralleling 47:6. The standing there (wuqūf) is called taʿrīf.
8. al-taʿrīf: publicly announcing a stray animal or lost property — calling out "Who knows/recognizes this?"
9. iʿtarafa bi-: to acknowledge or confess — as if one made a thing known and thereby admitted it.
10. al-nafs ʿarūf: a soul that, set to a task, yields and becomes settled to it (with al-Nābigha-style verse on women "submissive/resigned after shelter and veiling"; wijāḥ = veil).
11. al-ʿārif: the patient/steadfast one (ṣābir) — "a calamity struck him and he was found ʿarūf," i.e. enduring; al-Nābigha uses ʿārifāt of war-mares "steady for the thrust," bearing wounds.

text:
Ibn Fāris analyses ʿ-r-j into three separate roots: (1) inclining and limping, (2) a number, and (3) height and ascent.

**1. Inclining, bending aside, limping**
- ʿaraj is the verbal noun behind aʿraj, "lame." ʿarija yaʿraju ʿarajan = to become lame. He notes a distinction in the two verb patterns: ʿarija yaʿraju is used of lameness that belongs to a creature's natural make; ʿaraja yaʿruju is used of walking with a limping gait.
- ʿarjāʾ ("the lame one, fem.") is a name for the hyena, since the limp is part of her build; plural ʿurj. The plural of aʿraj for people is ʿurjān. The crow is called aʿraj because it hops as it walks.
- taʿarruj / taʿrīj: halting riding-camels at a couching- or stopping-place, turning them aside toward it. Shāhid — Dhū al-Rumma: "O you two neighbours of the daughter of Faḍḍāḍ, have you no mind to halt awhile until we may speak with her?" Ibn al-Aʿrābī glosses ʿarrajtu ʿalayhi as "I halted my mount at him," and cites the phrase "I have no halting nor stopping-place at it."
- inʿaraja: of a road or a valley, to bend; its munʿaraj is the point where it swings right and left. inʿaraja l-qawm ʿan al-ṭarīq = a group turned aside from the road.
- ʿurayjāʾ is reported to mean the midday heat; Ibn Fāris accepts this only conditionally ("if this is sound"), reasoning that everything then bends aside toward shade. Shāhid: "But Suhayya knows that I am a male, at the ʿurayjāʾ, when the waist-wrappers were soaked." Al-Aṣmaʿī gave ʿurayjāʾ a different sense: a watering pattern in which camels drink one day in the morning and the next in the evening — hence "we have watered by the ʿurayjāʾ pattern."
- al-ʿArjāʾ is also a known hill, cited from Abū Dhuʾayb; one explanation given is that the road winds past it.
- amrun ʿarīj: an affair still not straightened out — still crooked.

**2. A number of camels**
- Some hold ʿarj to be a herd of eighty to ninety; at a hundred the word is hunayda. Plurals: ʿurūj, aʿrāj. Shāhid — Ṭarafa: "On the day the fair women uncover their shins and the horses sweep up the herds of camels." Another report puts ʿarj at a hundred and fifty.
- Ibn Fāris suggests this sense could be folded back into the first: the owner of such a herd "halts by it" (yuʿarriju ʿalayhi) and is satisfied with it.

**3. Going up, ascending**
- ʿurūj = ascent. Verb: ʿaraja yaʿruju, verbal nouns ʿurūj and maʿraj; maʿraj is the place of ascent.
- Qurʾānic shāhid: Q 70:4, "The angels and the Spirit ascend (taʿruju) to Him."
- On the line "until, when the sun was minded to ʿaraj," others glossed ʿaraj as the sun's setting. Ibn Fāris judges that gloss true but imprecise: the point is that in setting the sun is pictured as having gone up into the sky. He supports this with a second line, "and the mansions of the sun sent the night up," and concludes that this is the sound analogical reading.

Root '-r-j-n (عرجن), William Edward Lane, Arabic-English Lexicon

A companion English-language treatment of the same root covered in al-Zabidi's Arabic entry. 1. 'arjanahu — to strike someone with an 'urjun-stalk or staff, or to decorate a garment with figured palm-cluster images, or to smear someone with blood, saffron, or dye. 2. 'urjun (the entry's central noun) — a date-palm's raceme, especially once dried and curved. This grounds the entry's central Qur'anic citation, Qur'an 36:39, comparing the waning crescent moon to "the old 'urjun," sharing its slenderness and curve — with a grammatical note establishing (via a verse of Ru'bah) that the word's final nun is an original root-letter, not a mere suffix. 3. A separate, unrelated sense: a white, truffle-like fungal growth, pleasant when fresh. 4. Closing: mu'arjan, a garment figured with palm-cluster imagery, as in the cited verse of Ru'bah.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-r-m as one sound root meaning intensity and sharpness.

1. Fierceness/severity in a person. ʿAruma yaʿrumu ʿarāmatan = to become fierce or unruly; such a person is ʿārim. A cited verse praises a man who defends what is sacred to him "with an outstretched hand and a fierce (ʿārim) tongue." Having that quality is called ʿurām.

2. The onslaught of an army. ʿUrām al-jaysh is an army's vigor, sharpness, and sheer numbers — cited in a verse about "a host possessing ʿurām." This is why a formidable army is called jaysh ʿaramram ("mighty army"). Ibn Fāris explains the extra letters in ʿaramram as the normal Arabic device of lengthening a word to intensify its meaning — the word is built up from ʿarama and ʿarara. A further verse illustrates ʿaramram describing an abundant host/herd.

3. Sayl al-ʿarim — the Qur'anic "flood of al-ʿarim." Ibn Fāris gives two possible senses of ʿarima (plural ʿarim): (a) it is a dam/dike — fitting, he says, because dammed-up water builds up ʿurām, i.e. destructive force, from its accumulated volume; or (b) it is a threshed, still-unwinnowed heap of grain shaped like a vault — fitting because such a heap, too, is dense and massed, like water with ʿurām.

4. Al-ʿurma — a separate, irregular sense: the white patch on a ewe's muzzle (shātun ʿarmā'), and likewise a viper marked in this way (afʿā ʿarmā'). Ibn Fāris flags this sense as an anomaly (shādhdh) that doesn't fit the "intensity/sharpness" core meaning, and offers a speculative explanation: perhaps the rā' here is a substitute for a lām, so the word was originally ʿalmā' ("marked one"), the whiteness functioning as a distinguishing mark (ʿalāma). He calls this plausible, not certain, and supports it with a verse mentioning "marked (al-ʿurm) viper-heads" in their lurking places.

5. He rejects, as baseless, a claim reported that al-ʿarim means "the male rat," saying such a claim deserves no attention.
