text:
al-Rāghib explains the word ʿizīn and reports two accounts of where it comes from.

1. **Meaning.** ʿizīn means "groups in dispersion". Its singular is given as ʿizza.

2. **First account: descent.** The word comes from ʿazawtuhu fa-ʿtazā, "I traced his descent and he claimed it". On this account the ʿizīn are groups whose members are linked to one another by descent, whether by birth or by marriage. From the same sense comes al-iʿtizāʾ in war: saying "I am the son of so-and-so" or "the companion of so-and-so". He cites the report: "Whoever makes the claim of descent of the Jāhiliyya, make him bite his father's 'thing' (hun)."

3. **Second account: consolation.** It has also been said that ʿizīn comes from ʿaziya ʿazāʾan, "to be patient", with taʿazzā meaning to bear patiently and take solace. On this account the word names a group whose members take solace in one another.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: عَزِيز 101x "(is) the all-mighty"; عِزَّة 11x "the honor"; أَعَزّ 3x "and stronger"; تُعِزُّ 1x "and you honor"; عِزّ 1x "an honor"; عَزَّزْ 1x "so we strengthened them"; عَزَّ 1x "and he overpowered me"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-z-z as one sound root meaning hardness and strength, and what resembles them, such as overcoming and subduing. He derives all the senses below from that claim.

1. **Might and being made mighty.** Al-Khalīl says al-ʿizza (might) belongs to God, and relates it to the name al-ʿAzīz. ʿAzza al-rajul means a man became mighty after weakness. Aʿzaztuhu means "I made him mighty". Iʿtazza bī and taʿazzaza mean he gained might through me, or made himself mighty. Al-Farrāʾ gives aʿzaztuhu and ʿazzaztuhu in the sense "I strengthened him", and cites fa-ʿazzaznā bi-thālith, "so We strengthened [them] with a third" (Q 36:14).

2. **Scarcity, restated.** Al-Khalīl says ʿazza al-shayʾ means a thing became so scarce it can hardly be found. Ibn Fāris accepts this but prefers to phrase it as "what can hardly be got hold of". The same sense is in the proverbs of the form "rarer (aʿazz) than …": rarer than the eggs of al-anūq, than the pregnant piebald male, than the white-legged crow, and than a gnat's marrow.

3. **Overcoming.** ʿAzzahu ʿalā amr (present tense yaʿuzzuhu) means he overcame him in an affair. The proverb man ʿazza bazza means "whoever overcomes, plunders". Al-muʿāzza is contending for mastery: "he strove with me for mastery and I overcame him (ʿazaztuhu)". A poet describing grey hair and youth says: "When I saw the vulture overcome (ʿazza) Ibn Dāya and nest in his two nests, my soul was stirred." The proverb "When your brother is hard (ʿazza), be pliant" means "if he makes things difficult, make them easy for him".

4. **Hard to bear.** Uʿziztu bi-mā aṣāba fulānan, from al-Khalīl, means "what befell so-and-so was grievous and hard for me". Al-Farrāʾ also gives ʿazaztu ʿalayhi (aʿizzu ʿizzan wa-ʿazāzatan), and ʿazza ʿalayya kadhā, "it was hard for me". Asked "Do you love me?", one may reply la-ʿazza mā, meaning "how intensely!".

5. **Severe illness and death.** Ustuʿizza ʿalā l-marīḍ means the illness grew severe. Al-Aṣmaʿī calls a gravely ill man miʿzāz, and says istaʿazza bihi l-maraḍ, "the illness overpowered him". A ḥadīth says the Prophet stayed three days with the sick Kulthūm ibn al-Hidm on arriving in Medina. Then ustuʿizza bi-Kulthūm, glossed "he died", and the Prophet moved to Saʿd ibn Khaythama.

6. **Being overpowered in other ways.** A maʿzūz man is one whose wealth has been swept away and taken. Istaʿazza ʿalayhi al-shayṭān means the devil overcame him and his reason. Istaʿazza ʿalayhi al-amr means he persisted obstinately in the matter.

7. **The narrow-teated animal.** A ʿazūz she-camel or ewe has a narrow teat-opening and yields milk only with effort. The verbs are taʿazzazat, ʿazzat taʿuzzu ʿuzūzan, and ʿazuzat ʿuzuzan; the plural is ʿuzuz. A proverb calls the wealthy miser "a narrow-teated she-goat with abundant milk".

8. **Hard ground.** Al-Khalīl defines al-ʿazāza, and al-ʿazāz, as firm ground without stones on which water does not stand. Others describe it as rough, level ground that hardly grows anything even after rain. Abū Ḥātim says this sense was derived from taʿazzaza laḥm al-nāqa, "the she-camel's flesh grew firm". Abū Zayd gives aʿzaznā, "we came onto such ground", and al-Farrāʾ gives arḍ ʿazzāʾ for hard ground. Istaʿazza al-raml means sand holds together and does not pour away, and Ruʾba uses the verbal noun istiʿzāz for this firmness.
   A saying of ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba, as al-Zuhrī reports it, uses this sense figuratively. Al-Zuhrī stopped standing up for his teacher, thinking he had learned all he had. ʿUbayd Allāh told him: "You are still in the ʿazāz, so stand", meaning "you are still at the edges of knowledge, not its middle". Abū Ḥātim explains that ʿazāz ground lies at the edges of a land, while its middle is soft.

9. **The hard year.** Al-ʿazzāʾ is a hard year, as in the verse about a man who slaughters his great-humped camels in the hard year when guests come by night.

10. **Heavy rain and torrent.** Al-ʿizz of rain is heavy, abundant rain. Ground struck by it is maʿzūza. Abū ʿAmr gives ʿazza al-maṭar, "the rain was heavy". Ibn al-Aʿrābī allows aṣābanā ʿizz min al-maṭar, but says the word is not used of a torrent (sayl). Ibn al-Sikkīt, by contrast, gives both maṭar ʿizz, "heavy rain", and sayl ʿizz, "an overwhelming torrent". According to al-Khalīl, rain ʿazzaza the ground, meaning it packed it down. Al-ʿazāza is also said to be a surge driven into a valley a spear's height deep.

11. **Part of a horse.** Al-ʿuzayzāʾ is the part of a horse between the root of the tail and the haunch; it is also said to be the two ends of the hip. Thaʿlaba al-Asadī's verse describes a horse whose two ʿuzayzāʾ are firm. Ibn Fāris notes that the word ends in a long vowel with hamza (mamdūd); the poet may have shortened it for the metre, and the dual ʿuzayzāwān shows the long form. In the same verse, kurūm (singular karma) are the rounded heads of the thighs.

12. **Morphology of the elative.** Al-ʿuzzā is the feminine of al-aʿazz, with the plural ʿuzaz. Al-ʿuzzān is given as a plural of ʿazīz, paired with al-dhullān as a plural of dhalīl, "lowly", as in "the mighty ones have come to you".

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: حَشَرَ 37x "you will be gathered"; حَٰشِرِين 3x "gatherers"; حَشْر 2x "gathering"; مَحْشُورَة 1x "assembled"
text:
al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's account of the root ḥ-sh-r (حشر):

1. Core sense — al-Ḥashr: driving a group out of their settled place and dislodging them, urging them away toward war or the like. It applies both to humans and to others. A cited saying — «النساء لا يُحْشَرن» ("women are not driven out") — is glossed as: they do not go out to the raid. An idiomatic use: حَشَرَتِ السنة مال بني فلان, "the drought drove off the wealth of such-and-such a tribe," i.e. stripped it away from them.

2. Grammatical restriction — the term is used only of a collective/group, never of a single individual.

3. Qurʾānic usage (this being a Qurʾān-specific lexicon, al-Rāghib strings the sense through its attestations):
- Mustering/summoning people: "send into the cities gatherers/musterers" (al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:36).
- Herding creatures together: birds "gathered together" (Ṣād 38:19); "when the wild beasts are gathered/herded" (al-Takwīr 81:5).
- Driving out / mass expulsion: "at the first gathering-out; you did not think they would go out" (al-Ḥashr 59:2).
- Marshalling of hosts: Solomon's assembled ranks of jinn, men, and birds (al-Naml 27:17).
- The Resurrection assembly: mankind "gathered" (al-Aḥqāf 46:6); "He will gather them all to Himself" (al-Nisāʾ 4:172); "We gathered them and left not one behind" (al-Kahf 18:47).

4. Name of the Day — the Day of Resurrection is called yawm al-ḥashr (the Day of the Gathering), paralleling its other names, the Day of the Raising (al-baʿth) and the Day of the Dispersing (al-nashr).

5. Derived physical idiom — رجل حَشْرُ الأذنين, "a man ḥashr of the ears," describes ears marked by a spread/flare and a fine sharpness (breadth with a pointed edge).

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-dh-r as a single root meaning to guard oneself and to be alert/vigilant.

1. Core verb: ḥadhira / yaḥdharu / ḥadharan — to be cautious or wary. The agent nouns ḥadhir, ḥadhūr, and ḥidhriyān all describe a man who is vigilant and on his guard.

2. Imperative form: ḥadhāri functions as a command meaning "beware!" (equivalent to iḥdhar). Shāhid — a line of verse: "Beware of our spears, beware!"

3. Qurʾānic citation with two readings of al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:56: the reading ḥādhirūn was glossed as "fully prepared/equipped" (mutaʾahhibūn); the variant reading ḥadhirūn means "fearful" (khāʾifūn).

4. Related noun: al-maḥdhūra means fright or dread.

5. al-ḥidhriya denotes rough, rugged ground — which Ibn Fāris suggests may be so named because one is wary of walking on it, tying the sense back to the root's core notion of caution.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-ḍ-ḍ as having two root meanings (aṣlān): rousing someone to something, and low-lying ground.

1. **Urging.** One says ḥaḍaḍtuhu ʿalā kadhā, "I urged him to such-and-such," when one has urged him on to it (ḥaḍḍaḍa) and incited him (ḥarraḍa). Ibn Fāris quotes al-Khalīl on the difference between ḥaḍḍ and ḥathth (spurring on): ḥathth is used of travelling, of driving beasts, and of anything at all, but ḥaḍḍ is not used of travelling or driving.

2. **Low ground.** al-ḥaḍīḍ is the bottom of the land. A quoted line uses it: "I came down to him, standing on the low ground (bi-l-ḥaḍīḍ)."

text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) on the root ح-ض-ر (ḥ-ḍ-r).

Core sense: bringing a thing forth, its arriving/coming, and its being witnessed or present. Several derived senses drift far from this, though Ibn Fāris holds the origin is single.

1. Settled vs. nomadic life. al-ḥaḍar = settled/town life, opposite of al-badw (desert/nomadic life). The settled state is al-ḥiḍāra (civilization/settledness). A cited verse debates the vowelling: Abū Zayd read ḥiḍāra (kasra), al-Aṣmaʿī ḥaḍāra (fatḥa).

2. Running/galloping. al-ḥuḍr = a gallop, tied to the root because a horse "brings forth" the speed it has. aḥḍara l-farasu = the horse galloped; a swift horse is miḥḍīr or miḥḍār. ḥāḍartu l-rajula = I raced alongside him.

3. Being frequented/afflicted (esp. by jinn). "Milk is maḥḍūr" = prone to blight, because jinn are said to attend it; likewise privies are called "frequented" (maḥḍūra). On this basis some read Qurʾān 23:97 ("lest they yaḥḍurūni") as "lest they afflict me with harm" — i.e., the devils "attend" a person with harm. (Ibn Fāris attributes this reading to "some people.")

4. A large settled community. al-ḥāḍir = the great settled tribe. Shāhid from Ḥassān ("a populous ḥāḍir…"), with a variant reading ("peaks of Raḍwā") that Quraysh rejected as nonsensical.

5. A small band. al-ḥaḍīra = a group that is not large (poetic shāhid of watering sand-grouse).

6. Contending before authority. al-muḥāḍara = overcoming/contending; ḥāḍartu l-rajula = I disputed with him kneeling before a ruler or judge.

7. Afterbirth. A ewe "casts its ḥaḍīra" = discharges the placenta after birth. Ibn Fāris calls this a sound analogy, since such things are termed al-shuhūd ("the witnesses").

8. Other nominal senses: ḥaḍrat al-rajul = a man's courtyard/frontage; al-ḥaḍīra also = pus gathered in a wound; al-ḥaḍr = fat on and above the flank.

9. Grammar note on "the prayer came." ḥaḍarat al-ṣalāt (the prayer arrived); the Medinan dialect says ḥaḍirat, yet all say the imperfect taḥḍuru. Ibn Fāris flags this as a rare instance of the pattern faʿila–yafʿulu among sound (non-defective) verbs.

10. rajul ḥaḍir = a man unfit for travel; compared to rajul nahir, fit for day-work not night (poetic shāhid).

Anomalies outside the root's core:
- al-Ḥaḍr = a fortress (verse of ʿAdī referencing the Tigris and Khābūr).
- Ḥaḍāri = a star; the Arabs say "Ḥaḍāri and al-Wazn are muḥlifān" (they induce swearing), because people swear the two are Suhayl/Canopus, which they resemble. muḥlif = anything that forces one to swear an oath (poetic shāhid).
- ḥiḍār al-ibil = the white camels (Hudhalī shāhid).

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
The article ḥ-ṣ-ṣ also contains the reduplicated verb ḥaṣḥaṣa, the verb of Q 12:51. It records the following senses.

1. **Hard running; breaking wind.** Al-ḥaṣṣ and al-ḥuṣāṣ are running hard and fast (ḥaṣṣa, yaḥuṣṣu). Al-ḥuṣāṣ is also breaking wind. A ḥadīth of Abū Hurayra says that when Satan hears the call (al-adhān) he turns his back "with ḥuṣāṣ". Asked what ḥuṣāṣ means, ʿĀṣim ibn Abī l-Najūd described a donkey that pricks up its ears, whisks its tail and runs; al-Azharī calls this the correct explanation.

2. **Scorching.** Frost that ḥaṣṣa the plants burns them; this is a dialect form of ḥassa.

3. **Shaving and loss of hair.** Al-ḥaṣṣ is shaving the hair, or its loss by chafing, as a helmet wears its wearer's head bare; it is also defined as removing hair from the head by shaving or by illness. Of the hair itself, ḥaṣṣa (verbal noun ḥaṣaṣ) and inḥaṣṣa mean that it came away, went bare and fell out. A verse of Abū Qays ibn al-Aslat: "The helmet has worn my head bare, so I taste no sleep but a doze."

4. **Al-ḥāṣṣa, a disease.** Al-ḥāṣṣa is the disease that strips the hair and makes it fall out. In a ḥadīth, a woman tells Ibn ʿUmar that her daughter, a young bride, is losing her hair and that she has been told to dress it with wine; he answers that if she does, God will cast al-ḥāṣṣa into her head. Abū ʿUbayd: al-ḥāṣṣa is what shaves the hair entirely away.

5. **Falling leaves.** Leaves that inḥaṣṣa (like inḥatta) have fallen from the tree.

6. **Aḥaṣṣ, ḥaṣṣāʾ: bare of hair.** The adjective aḥaṣṣ (feminine ḥaṣṣāʾ, plural ḥuṣṣ) is used of a man whose hair has gone (al-Yazīdī: gone entirely, a woman then being ḥaṣṣāʾ), who has little hair on his head, or who has none on his chest; of a beard whose hairs break and grow short (the beard inḥaṣṣat, and the condition is called al-ḥaṣaṣ); of a hairless tail, "like a stirring-stick"; of a bird "bare of wing" (a verse of Taʾabbaṭa Sharran); of a she-camel with no fur; and, in a verse of Imruʾ al-Qays, of the hungry dogs of two well-known hunters, called ḥuṣṣ because their hair has come away. Al-Kisāʾī cites a line on "every orphan with a shaven (maḥṣūṣ) nape".

7. **Shedding animals; horses.** A donkey or camel that taḥaṣṣaṣa has shed its hair, and al-ḥaṣīṣ is the shed hair. Al-ḥaṣīṣa is what is gathered from shaving or plucking; it is also the hair and fur of the ear, shaved or not, or, by a less-known account, hair and fur in general. On a horse, al-ḥaṣīṣa is the sparsely haired part above the hair-line round the hoof. A horse that is aḥaṣṣ or ḥaṣīṣ has little hair on the fetlock-tuft and tail, which counts as a defect (noun: al-ḥaṣaṣ). Al-aḥaṣṣ is also the chronically infirm one whose hair does not grow long.

8. **Worn bare (taḥaṣḥaṣa).** Ibn al-Aʿrābī gives taḥaṣḥaṣa for fur and nap that have worn bare, citing a rajaz about a stripped fibre rope that "had worn bare".

9. **The proverb "the tail was stripped".** Abū ʿUbayd cites ufilita wa-nḥaṣṣa l-dhanab ("he got away, and the tail was stripped") for a coward who escapes destruction after coming to the brink of it. He relates it to Muʿāwiya, who sent a Ghassānī envoy to the king of the Rūm, promising him three blood-prices if he gave the call (al-adhān) on entering the king's audience. The patricians rushed to kill him, but the king stopped them: Muʿāwiya, he said, wanted him to kill an envoy treacherously so that he could do the same to the king's own people under safe-conduct. He sent the man home equipped. Muʿāwiya greeted him with the proverb, meaning the tail had been cut off; the envoy answered that it still had its hair, and on hearing the story Muʿāwiya said the king had hit upon what he intended.

10. **A barren year.** In a ḥadīth, a year that ḥaṣṣat everything carried everything off. A sana ḥaṣṣāʾ is a barren year with little vegetation, or, some say, none; al-Ḥuṭayʾa describes a ḥaṣṣāʾ year that "left not a lopping short of the staff". Al-Jawharī glosses it as a bare year with no good in it and cites Jarīr on those driven "by the ḥaṣṣāʾ year and the wolf"; the entry comments that Jarīr seems to have meant "the hyena", a name for the drought year, and put the wolf in its place for the rhyme.

11. **A cold, cloudless day.** A day that is aḥaṣṣ is bitterly cold and cloudless. An Arab asked which days are coldest answered "al-aḥaṣṣ al-azabb". The aḥaṣṣ day has a clear north wind and a reddened horizon, and its sun rises without any warmth being felt; the azabb day has neither sun nor rain, while the nakbāʾ cross-wind drives thin, rainless clouds.

12. **A clear wind.** A ḥaṣṣāʾ wind is clear and free of dust (a verse of Abū l-Duqaysh).

13. **Severed kinship.** A man who is aḥaṣṣ cuts his ties of kinship (ḥaṣṣa raḥimahu). A kinship that is ḥaṣṣāʾ or ḥāṣṣa has been cut, so that the relatives no longer keep up ties on its account.

14. **Ill-natured, ill-omened.** Al-aḥaṣṣ is also the churlish, ill-omened person.

15. **"The two aḥaṣṣ".** These are the slave and the ass, because their prices keep pace with them until they grow decrepit; then their prices fall and they die.

16. **Share.** Al-ḥiṣṣa is a share of food, drink, land or anything else (plural ḥiṣaṣ). Taḥāṣṣa: (of a group) to divide up their shares. Ḥāṣṣahu (verbal nouns muḥāṣṣa, ḥiṣāṣ): to divide with someone, each taking a share. Ḥaṣṣanī minhu kadhā: "so much of it fell to me as my share". Aḥaṣṣa l-qawm: to give people their shares.

17. **Lodging.** Aḥaṣṣahu l-makān: to lodge someone in a place; a phrase of an orator is cited for it.

18. **Falling short.** In a line of Abū Ṭālib, "a balance of equity that does not yaḥuṣṣu a barley-grain" means one that does not fall short by a grain.

19. **A dye.** Al-ḥuṣṣ is wars, used for dyeing (plurals aḥṣāṣ and ḥuṣūṣ), cited in lines of ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm and al-Aʿshā. Al-Azharī accepts the sense wars as well known and sound, notes that some say saffron, and reports that some say pearls, a sense he neither confirms nor recognises. The entry adds that Sībawayh gives no fuʿūl plural for doubled nouns of the pattern fuʿl, only fiʿāl (as in khifāf and ʿishāsh).

20. **Tracking details; number.** A ḥuṣḥuṣ or ḥuṣḥūṣ is a man who tracks down the fine details of affairs, learns them and keeps count of them. "The ḥaṣīṣ and baṣīṣ of the people" is their number.

21. **Proper names.** Al-Aḥaṣṣ is a known watering-place. Al-Azharī tells how Kulayb ibn Wāʾil kept it for himself against Bakr ibn Wāʾil and refused them water; when Jassās had stabbed him and he asked for water, Jassās answered "You have gone past al-Aḥaṣṣ", i.e., your power over it is gone. Verses of al-Jaʿdī recount the exchange, and al-Aṣmaʿī says it was said in mockery. Banū Ḥaṣīṣ is a clan; al-Ḥaṣṣāʾ is the horse of Ḥazn ibn Mirdās; al-Ḥaṣḥāṣ and Dhū l-Ḥaṣḥāṣ are places, the latter in a Ḥijāzī's line about "the gazelles at Dhū l-Ḥaṣḥāṣ", meaning women.

22. **Ḥaṣḥaṣa: going off.** Al-ḥaṣḥaṣa is going off into the land: "when he saw me out in the open, he ḥaṣḥaṣa".

23. **Ḥaṣḥaṣa: working in until settled.** It is also movement in something until it settles, takes hold and stays fixed, or moving one thing about in another until it lodges. So of a camel that plants its knees to rise under a heavy load (Ḥumayd ibn Thawr: it worked its knee-pads into the hard pebbles). ʿAlī's saying that he would rather turn two live coals over in his hands than two knucklebones belongs here. It is also said that ḥaṣḥaṣa is moving a thing about, turning it over and shaking it back and forth. In a ḥadīth of Samura ibn Jundub about an impotent man tested with a slave-girl, the man claims he kept on "until it ḥaṣḥaṣa in her", explained as "I moved it until it took hold and settled"; al-Azharī spells out the sexual meaning. The girl said he had done nothing, and the report ends with "Let her go, O muḥaṣḥiṣ!"

24. **Moving earth.** Ḥaṣḥaṣtu l-turāb: to move earth about, scraping it right and left.

25. **Clinging to the ground.** Taḥaṣḥaṣa (like taḥazḥaza): to cling to the ground and lie flat.

26. **A fettered gait.** Ḥaṣḥaṣa (with dahmaja): to walk like a man in fetters.

27. **Hovering and pressing.** Ibn Shumayl: someone "taḥaṣḥaṣa only around this dirham" in order to take it; al-ḥaṣḥaṣa is sticking close to a person, coming at him and pressing him importunately.

28. **The truth coming out (Q 12:51).** Al-ḥaṣḥaṣa is the truth becoming clear after being concealed. The verb is used only in the active, ḥaṣḥaṣa; one does not say ḥuṣḥiṣa. On al-āna ḥaṣḥaṣa l-ḥaqq, the entry explains that when the women were summoned and cleared Yūsuf, the wife of al-ʿAzīz said that nothing was left but for them to turn on her for a confession, and she confessed; her words mean that the lie has swerved off and the truth is plain. It is also said that it means the truth appeared and came into the open. Abū l-ʿAbbās says al-ḥaṣḥaṣa is going to the utmost (ḥaṣḥaṣa l-rajulu: the man went to the utmost in his affair). It is also said that the word derives from al-ḥiṣṣa, "share": the share of truth became distinct from the share of falsehood.

29. **Stones and dust.** Al-ḥiṣḥiṣ (with kasra) is stones; it is also said to be earth or dust. Al-ḥiṣḥiṣ and al-kithkith both mean stones. Al-Liḥyānī reports the curse al-ḥiṣḥiṣa li-fulān, "dust to so-and-so!", put in the accusative like al-turāba laka, "dust to you!", which is explained as treating the noun like a verbal noun; likewise bi-fīhi l-ḥiṣḥiṣ, "dust in his mouth".

30. **Speed and distance.** Al-ḥaṣḥaṣa is also hastening on a journey. A qarab (journey to water) that is ḥaṣḥāṣ is a far one; it is also, like ḥathḥāth, one without pause, and sayr ḥaṣḥāṣ is fast travel without flagging.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
quran_words: حَاصِب 4x "a storm of stones"; حَصَب 1x "(are) firewood"
poets_named: Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam); Labīd (lived into Islam); Al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad); unnamed verse ×3; al-Rāʿī (Umayyad)
text:
Ibn Manẓūr's entry for the root Ḥ-Ṣ-B (Lisān al-ʿArab) gathers several connected senses around the ideas of pebbles, pelting, and things thrown.

**1. A skin eruption.** ḥaṣba / ḥaṣaba / ḥaṣiba (the ṣād may be vowelless, or take a or i): the pustules that break out on the body and show on the skin. Verb: ḥaṣiba jilduhu ("his skin broke out"), imperfect yaḥṣabu; passive ḥuṣiba, participle maḥṣūb. A report from Masrūq mentions visiting ʿAbdallāh among people struck by smallpox (judarī) and by ḥaṣba.

**2. Pebbles and gravel.** ḥaṣab and ḥaṣba mean stones and pebbles, with the irregular unit-noun ḥaṣaba. ḥaṣbāʾ is the standard word for gravel — unit ḥaṣaba, on the pattern qaṣaba / qaṣbāʾ; Sībawayh classes ḥaṣbāʾ as a collective noun rather than a plural. In a report about al-Kawthar, what is drawn "from its ḥaṣbāʾ" means the pebbles on its bed.

**3. Pebbly ground.** arḍ ḥaṣiba / maḥṣaba: land full of gravel. Al-Azharī distinguishes maḥṣaba (having ḥaṣbāʾ) from maḥṣāt (having ḥaṣā). Abū ʿUbayd instead takes arḍ maḥṣaba as land where the ḥaṣba disease is found, parallel to majdara (where smallpox is found); for him makān ḥāṣib is the gravelly place.

**4. Pebbles under the worshipper.** A prohibition is reported against touching the gravel during ṣalāt: people prayed directly on the mosque's gravel and would smooth it with their hands when prostrating. Ibn Manẓūr explains the ban as barring an action not belonging to the prayer, idle motion invalidating it if repeated; another report allows touching it once, the dispensation resting on its being unrepeated.

**5. An adjective without a verb.** makān ḥaṣib, "a gravelly place," is formed by attribution (nisba), since no verb has been heard for it. Abū Dhuʾayb: they drank at pools of sweet cold water, the watercourses pebbly, hooves sinking out of sight in them.

**6. Pelting.** ḥaṣb is pelting someone with gravel: ḥaṣabahu yaḥṣibuhu ḥaṣban (a marginal note records the verb as ḍaraba-class, and qatala-class in one dialect). taḥāṣabū: they pelted one another. ḥaṣbāʾ covers both small and large stones. Reports: during the killing of ʿUthmān men pelted each other in the mosque until the sky was hidden; Ibn ʿUmar pelted two men who talked while the imām preached, to silence them.

**7. Kicking up stones.** iḥṣāb: throwing up pebbles while running. Al-Liḥyānī notes it of horses and other running animals: aḥṣaba al-farasu.

**8. Laying down gravel.** ḥaṣṣaba al-mawḍiʿ: to strew a place with small pebbles. ʿUmar is reported to have ordered the taḥṣīb of the mosque — softer underfoot for the worshipper, and better at covering the litter, threads and filth dropped in it; another report has him gravelling the mosque as "more concealing" of spittle. (aqshāb = shreds falling from rags and similar refuse.)

**9. Al-Muḥaṣṣab, a place-name from the same root.** Either the stone-throwing ground at Minā, or the ravine opening onto al-Abṭaḥ between Mecca and Minā where a traveller sleeps part of the night before going on to Mecca — both named from their pebbles; the throwing-ground is also called ḥiṣāb. Al-Azharī defines taḥṣīb as that brief night's sleep in the ravine, and reports that the Prophet camped there without making it a practice for people, so it is optional. ʿĀʾisha is quoted as saying "taḥṣīb is nothing," meaning that halt. ʿUmar is reported urging the family of Khuzayma (Quraysh, who do not leave in the first departure) to "perform taḥṣīb," i.e. stay at al-Muḥaṣṣab. Abū ʿUbayd describes it as stopping at al-Abṭaḥ on the way from Minā to Mecca to doze an hour before entering the city, adding that it was once done and later abandoned; he identifies Khuzayma as Quraysh and Kināna, not Asad. Al-Qaʿnabī takes taḥṣīb simply as halting at al-Muḥaṣṣab, citing a verse on no parting being more scattering than the parting at al-Muḥaṣṣab. Al-Aṣmaʿī takes al-Muḥaṣṣab as the stone-throwing site, citing a verse on a three-day stay there, and a line of al-Rāʿī ("known at Mecca and at al-Muḥaṣṣab") in the same sense.

**10. Ḥāṣib — the pelting wind.** A violent wind carrying dust and gravel; also said of scattered fine hail and snow. Qurʾān: "We sent against them a ḥāṣib." The form ḥaṣiba is used likewise, as in Labīd's line about every gusting pebble-driving wind trailing its skirts over an abandoned camp. On the Qurʾānic phrase Ibn Manẓūr records two readings: a punishment that pelts them with stones of sijjīl, or a wind so strong it tears up the gravel. ʿAlī's words to the Khawārij, "may a ḥāṣib strike you," are explained as a punishment from God, the literal sense being pelting with stones from the sky. A cloud flinging down hail or snow is equally a ḥāṣib. Al-Aʿshā's "we have a ḥāṣib like a swarm of locust-young" is glossed as stone-throwers; al-Azharī reads the same line as meaning a great mass of foot-soldiers. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: ḥāṣib dust is dust with gravel in it. Ibn Shumayl: ḥāṣib is the gravel carried in the wind ("our day was a ḥāṣib day"). Hence rīḥ ḥāṣib, verb ḥaṣabatnā ("it pelted us"), and rīḥ ḥaṣiba, a wind holding gravel — Dhū al-Rumma: a gust "whose beard is pebble-laden."

**11. Ḥaṣab — what is thrown into a fire.** Anything cast into a fire, firewood or otherwise. Qurʾān: "You and what you serve apart from God are the ḥaṣab of Jahannam." Al-Farrāʾ reports that in Yemeni speech ḥaṣab means firewood (ḥaṭab), and a reading of ʿAlī has ḥaṭab jahannam. On this account nothing is ḥaṣab until the fire is actually stoked with it; al-Azharī likewise restricts it to wood put into an oven or fuel, not wood lying unused. Some hold ḥaṣab simply means firewood in general. Verb: ḥaṣaba al-nāra bi-l-ḥaṣab, "he kindled the fire with fuel." Ibn Manẓūr also links it to the pelting sense: since ḥaṣabtuhu is "I pelted him" and the thrown stone is called ḥaṣab (a passive-sense noun like nafaḍ from nafaḍtu), "ḥaṣab of Jahannam" means they are flung into it as wood is flung into a fire. Al-Farrāʾ adds that in Najdī speech ḥaṣab is whatever you throw into the fire. ʿIkrima claimed the word is Abyssinian for "firewood"; Ibn ʿArafa answers that this is acceptable only if the Arabs adopted it so that it became Arabic, since on his view the Qurʾān contains nothing but Arabic.

**12. Going off.** ḥaṣaba fī al-arḍ: he went away into the land.

**13. Names.** Ḥaṣaba is recorded by Ibn al-Aʿrābī as a man's name, with a verse mentioning "ʿĀmir ibn Ḥaṣaba." Yaḥṣab is a tribe; some vocalise Yaḥṣub, deriving it from ḥaṣabahu bi-l-ḥaṣā ("he pelted him with pebbles"), which Ibn Manẓūr judges weak. Al-Ṣiḥāḥ gives Yaḥṣib with i, a Yemeni clan, whose relative adjective is Yaḥṣabī with a, on the model Taghlib → Taghlabī.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: حَصِيد 4x "(for) the harvest"; حَصَاد 1x "(of) its harvest"; حَصَد 1x "you reap"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-ṣ-d as two distinct root-senses, which he says diverge from each other:

1. Cutting something.
   - حَصَدْتُ الزَّرْعَ (ḥaṣadtu al-zarʿ) — "I reaped the standing crop," and likewise other things; verbal noun ḥaṣd. The harvest season is called both الحَصَاد (al-ḥaṣād) and الحِصَاد (al-ḥiṣād), two vowellings of the same word.
   - He cites a prophetic report: "Does anything topple people onto their nostrils in the Fire other than the harvests (ḥaṣāʾid) of their tongues?" He glosses ḥaṣāʾid as the plural of ḥaṣīda, meaning whatever is said about people with the tongue and by which a verdict is cut against them — the cutting sense applied to speech.
   - The verb occurs in form I (ḥaṣadtu) and form VIII (iḥtaṣadtu); the agent noun is muḥtaṣid, "reaper." A line of verse he quotes: "We are only like the tender stalk of a crop — whenever it falls due, its reaper comes to it."

2. Making something firm, tight, closely compacted.
   - حَبْلٌ مُحْصَدٌ (ḥablun muḥṣad) — a rope tightly twisted and firmly plaited.
   - Belonging to the same chapter: شَجَرَةٌ حَصْدَاءُ (shajaratun ḥaṣdāʾ), a tree thick with leaves; دِرْعٌ حَصْدَاءُ (dirʿun ḥaṣdāʾ), a coat of mail closely and soundly woven; and اِسْتَحْصَدَ الْقَوْمُ (istaḥṣada al-qawm), said when a group draws together into a compact body.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ح ص ل (ḥ-ṣ-l), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One sound, analogically regular root: gathering something together. Ibn Fāris explicitly ties the name of a bird's crop (al-ḥawṣalah) to this root, since food is gathered there.

1. ḥaṣṣaltu al-shayʾa — I gathered/extracted something. Some philologists (per Ibn Fāris) hold that al-taḥṣīl originally meant extracting gold or silver from ore-bearing stone or mine-dust — the practitioner called al-muḥaṣṣil — illustrated with a line of poetry whose exact sense is unclear from the fragment given. Ibn Fāris notes: if this mining sense is indeed the origin, then it is the root's core analogy, and the whole chapter of related words builds on it.

2. al-ḥaṣal — unripe dates before they harden and before their calyxes show, singular ḥaṣalah — illustrated with a line of poetry about dates falling (paired with a near-synonym, al-sadā, withered unripe dates). Ibn Fāris links this sense back to the core meaning too: such dates are what has been "gathered/extracted" (ḥuṣṣila) from the palm tree.

3. An outlier Ibn Fāris flags explicitly as not fitting the pattern, admitting he does not know its derivation: ḥaṣila al-faras — said of a horse whose belly ails from eating dirt.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مُحْصَنَٰت 8x "and the chaste women"; أَحْصَنَتْ 5x "guarded"; مُّحْصِنِين 2x "desiring to be chaste"; تَحَصُّن 1x "chastity"; حُصُون 1x "their fortresses"; مُّحَصَّنَة 1x "fortified"
poets_named: unnamed verse; Ḥassān ibn Thābit (lived into Islam) ×2
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-ṣ-n as a single, regular root meaning protection, guarding, and safekeeping.

1. Core sense — protection/safekeeping. From it comes al-ḥiṣn, a "fortress" or stronghold (plural ḥuṣūn).

2. A chaste woman. al-ḥāṣin / al-ḥaṣān is the woman who is chaste and guards herself. Two poetic witnesses support this: an anonymous line ("No chaste woman of Rabīʿa bore me, if I were to side with desire...") and a verse of Ḥassān ibn Thābit praising a woman who is "chaste and grave, never suspected of any fault," who abstains from backbiting ("rises hungry from the flesh of heedless women"). The verb is ḥaṣuna.

3. A grammatical distinction from Thaʿlab (Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā): a chaste woman may be called both muḥṣana and muḥṣina, but a married woman is called muḥṣana only.

4. Extended sense — anything withheld or made inaccessible (mamnūʿ) is called muḥṣan; some also apply muḥṣan to a lock (qufl).

5. Morphological note: one says aḥṣana l-rajul ("the man became fortified/chaste"), yielding the participle muḥṣan. Ibn Fāris flags this as one of the irregular cases where a verb of the aḥṣana (afʿala) form takes a participle on the passive mufʿal pattern (muḥṣan) rather than the expected active form.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أُحْصِرُ 2x "you are held back"; حَصِرَتْ 2x "and besiege them"; حَصُور 1x "and chaste"; حَصِير 1x "a prison-bed"
poets_named: Ibn Mayyāda (Umayyad); al-Akhṭal (Umayyad); Jarīr (Umayyad); Labīd (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-ṣ-r as one root with a single core idea: gathering together, confining, and preventing. He then shows how each usage traces back to that idea.

1. **al-ḥaṣīr — the flank/side of the body.** Abū ʿAmr glosses it simply as "the side" (al-janb). Al-Aṣmaʿī defines it more narrowly: the area bounded by the vein that runs crosswise on the flank of a camel or horse, and everything above it to where the flank ends. Ibn Fāris notes that either definition fits the root, because this is where the ribs gather.

2. **al-ḥaṣr — being tongue-tied, unable to speak fluently**, as though speech had been shut off from the speaker and withheld.

3. **al-ḥaṣar — tightness of the chest.**

4. **al-ḥuṣr — retention of the bowels (constipation)**; the verbs used are the passives ḥuṣira and uḥṣira.

5. **nāqa ḥaṣūr — a she-camel with a narrow teat-orifice**, so the milk is held back. Ibn Fāris remarks that the underlying analogy is the same in all these cases.

6. **al-iḥṣār — a pilgrim being kept from the House by illness or the like.** Some speakers distribute the two verb forms: illness ḥaṣara-hu, an enemy aḥṣara-hu. But Abū ʿUbayd, citing Abū ʿAmr, gives both forms for the same sense, "the thing confined me," with a line of Ibn Mayyāda in which "preoccupations have confined you" (aḥṣaratka) is used of ordinary hindrance. Ibn Fāris states plainly that the ḥaṣara/aḥṣara question is, in his judgement, extremely confused: some authorities merge the two, others separate them. He declines to settle it, observing that neither position damages the root analogy — every use points to confining.

7. **al-ḥaṣūr — a man who does not go in to women.** Ibn Fāris records two competing morphological analyses: (a) the form faʿūl carrying a passive sense (mafʿūl), so the man is one who has been held back; (b) an active sense, one who refuses women, holding himself back. He supports the second by a parallel idiom: a man is called ḥaṣūr when he withholds his share and fails to contribute what drinking companions contribute — illustrated by a line of al-Akhṭal contrasting a generous cup-companion with "the withholder."

8. **ḥaṣir bi-l-sirr — one who locks a secret away**, i.e. keeps it close. Jarīr's line describes slanderers probing him and finding him tight-lipped and grudging with his beloved's secret.

9. **Qur'anic usage.** In Q 17:8, "and We made Hell for the deniers ḥaṣīr," Ibn Fāris glosses ḥaṣīr as the place of confinement, a prison.

10. **al-ḥaṣīr — the king**, as in Labīd's phrase "standing at the door of the ḥaṣīr."

11. **al-ḥiṣār — a stuffed cushion** fitted to the front of a camel-saddle; the denominal verb iḥtaṣara al-baʿīr means to fit a camel with one.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: أَحْصَىٰ 10x "we have enumerated it"; أَحْصَىٰ 1x "best calculated"
poets_named: Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam); al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); Sāʿida ibn Juʾayya (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Sīda arranges the root ḥ-ṣ-y (ḥāʾ, ṣād, yāʾ) as follows.

1. حَصَاة (ḥaṣāt), "pebble" — the base sense: a well-known kind of small stone. Plurals: ḥaṣayāt, ḥaṣan, ḥuṣiyy. He cites Abū Dhuʾayb, describing a spear-wound that gushes so hard it would sweep pebbles from its path.

2. Verbal/derived forms of the physical sense: حَصَيْتُه (ḥaṣaytuhu) = "I pelted him with pebbles"; أَرْض مُحْصَاة (arḍ muḥṣāt) = "pebble-strewn ground."

3. حَصَاة (ḥaṣāt), medical sense — a bladder disease in which the urine thickens and hardens into a pebble-like stone; the sufferer is said to be ḥuṣiya.

4. حَصَاة القَسْم (ḥaṣāt al-qasm) — the stones people use when portioning out (rationing) water among themselves.

5. حَصَى (ḥaṣā), "a large number" — used figuratively for a great count, by analogy with the abundance of pebbles. Shāhid: al-Aʿshā, "you are not the more numerous among them, for might belongs to the more numerous."

6. حَصَاة (ḥaṣāt), "intelligence and steadiness / gravity of judgment." Idioms: ذُو حَصَاةٍ وأَصَاةٍ = "a man of sense and sound judgment"; مَاله حَصَاةٌ ولا أَصَاةٌ = "he has no settled opinion to fall back on."

7. حَصَاة (ḥaṣāt) — also "a piece of musk."

8. أَحْصَى (aḥṣā), "to encompass / comprehend fully." He anchors it in Qur'an 72:28, "and He has encompassed everything in number," and cites Sāʿida ibn Juʾayya; the line's yuḥṣī is glossed as "leaves a mark/effect" (in the left / the north-wind).

The entry thus threads a single image — the countable pebble — through concrete stone, a stone-like bladder ailment, "great number," sound reckoning of mind, and finally the verb aḥṣā, "to comprehend by count."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-ṭ-ṭ as having one root meaning (aṣl wāḥid): bringing a thing down from a height. The verb is ḥaṭṭa (imperfect yaḥuṭṭu, verbal noun ḥaṭṭ). He files the following under that meaning ("from this category"):

1. **ḥiṭṭa in the Qur'an.** For the word ḥiṭṭa in Q 2:58 he reports an explanation given by others ("they said"): it means "O God, put our burdens (awzār) down off us."

2. **A woman's figure.** A girl called maḥṭūṭat al-matnayn is one whose two sides of the back look as though they had been pressed down (ḥuṭṭa) with the miḥaṭṭ, an implement. A verse describes a fair, plump woman, full in the haunches, "maḥṭūṭat al-matnayn," not worn by bearing children one after another.

3. **A short man.** A small, short man is called ḥuṭāʾiṭ, as though he had been pressed down.

4. **A fast camel.** A swift thoroughbred she-camel is called ḥaṭūṭ, as though she never stops setting down a saddle in some land.

Ibn Fāris names one word that departs from this root meaning: al-ḥaṭāṭ, a pustule on the face. He cites al-Hudhalī on a face "clear, smooth-cheeked, not a coarse one with ḥaṭāṭ," and gives a variant reading of the line's second half: "like the horn of the sun, not one with ḥaṭāṭ."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ḥ-ṭ-b (Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha)

Core meaning: fuel — al-waqūd, i.e. firewood/kindling. Every other use below is built on this base sense by resemblance or extension.

1. Literal sense: al-ḥaṭab = "firewood" (a well-known word). Verb: ḥaṭaba – yaḥṭibu – ḥaṭban, "to gather firewood." Cited: Imruʾ al-Qays' line where children say "come, let's gather firewood until the game arrives."

2. Idiom — "ḥāṭib layl" ("a night wood-gatherer"): said of someone who talks in a confused, indiscriminate way, mixing sense and nonsense — like a person gathering wood in the dark who can't tell good sticks from bad.

3. "ḥaṭabanī ʿabdī" = "my slave brought/gathered firewood for me."

4. An anonymous verse describes a greedy, lazy man who cries from hunger yet "neither gathers firewood for the people nor gives them water" — i.e., does nothing useful for others.

5. "makān ḥaṭīb" = a place rich in firewood.

6. "nāqa muḥāṭiba" = a she-camel that eats dry thorns (an extension of the "firewood" sense to dry, wood-like fodder).

7. Qur'anic connection (Q111:4): on "his wife, the carrier of firewood" (ḥammālat al-ḥaṭab), Ibn Fāris reports that scholars ("they said") read this as a kināya — a figurative, euphemistic expression — for namīma, talebearing/slander, not literal wood-carrying. Correspondingly, "ḥaṭaba fulān bi-fulān" means "he went about spreading tales about / slandering so-and-so." Ibn Fāris presents this as an interpretive gloss he is transmitting, not as the root's own literal sense.

8. "al-aḥṭab" / "al-ḥaṭib" = a person who is extremely gaunt or emaciated — likened to dry, shriveled firewood.

9. As further support for the slander-sense, he cites a poet's line praising a woman who "did not walk among people with wet firewood" — read as meaning she did not go about spreading smoldering, mischief-stirring gossip.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: حُطَٰم 3x "debris"; حُطَمَة 2x "the crusher"; يَحْطِمَ 1x "lest not crush you"
text:
Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's entry for the root Ḥ-Ṭ-M:

1. Core sense — ḥaṭm is breaking something, of the same order as hashm (crushing, smashing). From there it was extended to any breaking that is complete or carried to its extreme. Qur'anic citation: "Let not Solomon and his troops crush you" (27:18).

2. Grammar — the transitive ḥaṭamtuhu ("I broke it") pairs with the reflexive/passive form inḥaṭama ("it broke apart"), verbal noun ḥaṭman.

3. Applied to a person — sāʾiq ḥuṭam, a camel-driver who "breaks" his camels by driving them too hard.

4. Al-Ḥuṭama — the name given to the blazing fire (al-jaḥīm), cited from "And what will make you know what al-Ḥuṭama is?" (104:5).

5. Transferred use — a voracious eater is also called ḥuṭama, likening him to that fire; al-Rāghib grounds the image in a poet's line, "as though in his belly there were an oven."

6. Derivation by nisba — dirʿ ḥuṭamiyya, a type of coat of mail, named after either its weaver or the man who wore it.

7. Proper names — Ḥaṭīm and Zamzam are given simply as two places, without further comment.

8. Al-Ḥuṭām — what crumbles apart because it has dried out. Qur'anic citation: "then it withers and you see it turned yellow, then He makes it ḥuṭām (broken debris)" (39:21).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-ẓ-ẓ as a single root meaning (aṣl wāḥid): share, and good fortune.

1. **al-ḥaẓẓ**: a share or portion; fortune (al-jadd).

2. **Derived forms**: "so-and-so is aḥaẓẓ than so-and-so" means more fortunate, having a greater share; a fortunate person is maḥẓūẓ.

3. **Plurals**: al-ḥaẓẓ has the plural aḥāẓin, which Ibn Fāris notes is irregular. Abū Zayd also gives the plural aḥuẓẓ.

4. **Abū Zayd's usage**: a man is called ḥaẓīẓ jadīd ("fortunate") when he has a share of provision (rizq). One also says, of the verb, ḥaẓiẓtu fī l-amr, aḥaẓẓu, "I was fortunate in the matter".

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مَحْظُور 1x "restricted"; مُحْتَظِر 1x "(used by) a fence builder"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ḥ-ẓ-r (حظر) from one core meaning: prevention / forbidding (al-manʿ).

1. Core verb sense — ḥaẓartu al-shayʾa ("I forbade/fenced off the thing") → I am ḥāẓir ("one who forbids"), and the thing is maḥẓūr ("forbidden/withheld"). Cited: {And the gift of your Lord is not withheld (maḥẓūran)} (17:20).

2. Concrete sense — ḥiẓār: a fence or enclosure built around sheep (or other livestock) out of branches or wood, usually made while the wood is still moist, since it later dries out. The person who builds such an enclosure is called al-muḥtaẓir. Cited: {And they became like the crumbled stubble of al-muḥtaẓir} (54:31) — Ibn Fāris explains this as the sheep-pen builder, whose enclosure material dries out and crumbles.

3. Idiom — jāʾa bi-l-ḥaẓiri al-raṭb ("he came with the moist ḥaẓir") is said of someone telling an outrageous, shameless lie.

4. Idiom — huwa yūqidu fī al-ḥaẓr ("he is lighting a fire in the enclosure") is said of a gossip/tale-bearer; Ibn Fāris notes that the supporting citation for this was already given earlier in the dictionary (under a different entry).

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
quran_words: حَبِطَ 12x "became worthless"; أَحْبَطَ 4x "and he will make worthless"
text:
Ibn Manẓūr's Lisān al-ʿArab on the root ح ب ط (ḥ-b-ṭ). The entry ties a cluster of concrete senses — festering, bloating, swelling — to the abstract Qurʾānic sense of a deed being rendered void.

**1. Aftermath of a wound.** al-ḥabaṭ is grouped with al-ʿarab: the traces left by a wound. Per al-Jawharī, حَبِطَ الجرحُ means a wound festered and relapsed.

**2. Bloat in grazing animals.** The core physical sense: a belly disease of camels and livestock. An animal eats pasture that disagrees with it, or simply over-eats, until its belly swells and nothing passes out of it (ḥabiṭa, so it is ḥabiṭ; plural forms ḥabāṭā, ḥabaṭa). A sheep bloats from eating al-dhuraq (sweet clover). Al-Azharī: the belly ḥabiṭa when it swells up.

**3. The Prophetic hadith on spring pasture** (given at length by al-Azharī because, cut short, it becomes obscure): "Among what spring grows is that which kills by bloat, or nearly so." The disease is al-ḥubāṭ (some read it with khāʾ, from takhabbuṭ, "thrashing"). In the full report the Prophet warns of the seductions of worldly wealth. It carries two parables:
- The over-eater that bloats and dies = the greedy hoarder who amasses the world and withholds others' rightful due; he perishes in the Hereafter.
- The "eater of al-khaḍir" (green summer pasture) that grazes moderately, fills its flanks, then relieves itself and grazes again = the person moderate in gathering and spending wealth, who escapes its harm. Al-Azharī's botanical point: al-khaḍir is summer growth (al-janba), grazed little by little, so it does not cause bloat — unlike the lush tender herbs of spring. He cites Ṭarafa ("...when summer sprouts the shoots of al-khaḍir") to fix it as a summer plant. Grammatically, illā ākilat al-khaḍir here means "but/rather the eater of al-khaḍir." "This wealth is green (khaḍira) and sweet" uses khaḍira in the sense of soft/fresh; the point urges giving to the poor and orphan from it.

**4. Swelling in general.** Beyond bloat, al-ḥabaṭ covers swelling anywhere, from disease or otherwise — mild swelling in an udder, a swollen skin, a horse swollen in the flanks (faras ḥabiṭ al-quṣayrā; cited with al-Jaʿdī's verse). Note: a horse is called ḥabiṭ only when the word is attached to "flank" or the like, since its ḥabaṭ specifically means belly-swelling.

**5. The augmented forms iḥbanṭaʾa / al-ḥabanṭā.** From this root, with augmentative letters (nūn, hamza, alif, bāʾ) added to make the form parallel a quadriliteral like safarjal: iḥbanṭaʾa = one's belly swelled; al-ḥabanṭaʾ = a thick, short, big-bellied man; al-muḥbanṭiʾ = one swollen or filled with anger. Ibn Manẓūr gives the morphology in detail — the various vowellings (ḥabanṭan, ḥibanṭan, with or without hamza), the rules for forming the diminutive, and the option to compensate or not for a dropped augmentative letter. Ibn Barrī corrects al-Jawharī: the word belongs under ḥabaṭ, not a separate entry ḥabṭaʾ, because its hamza is augmentative, not a root letter. Two senses are distinguished for al-muḥbanṭiʾ: with hamza = physically swollen/big-bellied; without hamza = angry, sullen. In the hadith of the miscarried fetus "remaining muḥbanṭī at the gate of Paradise," Ibn al-Athīr glosses it as angry and impatient — or one who holds back as a petitioner does, not as a refuser. A separate sense: al-muḥbanṭiʾ = one clinging to the ground.

**6. The abstract Qurʾānic sense: a deed made void.** ḥabiṭa (ḥabṭ, ḥubūṭ) = one did a deed then spoiled it; God made it void (aḥbaṭahu). Cited from Revelation: "so He made their deeds void" (fa-aḥbaṭa aʿmālahum). The standard reading is ḥabiṭa ʿamaluhu (kasra), the verbal noun ḥabṭ taking sukūn on the bāʾ; al-Azharī notes a lone bedouin reading with fatḥa (ḥabaṭa) that he heard from no one else. Ibn al-Athīr derives this abstract usage directly from the animal sense — the beast that over-eats and dies.

**7. The tribal name al-Ḥabaṭ / al-Ḥabiṭ.** al-Ḥārith b. Māzin b. Mālik b. ʿAmr b. Tamīm, nicknamed for a bloat-like affliction (or a belly swollen from something he ate) that struck him on a journey. His descendants are the Ḥabiṭāt/Ḥabaṭāt; the nisba is ḥabaṭī (they fronted the vowel to fatḥa to avoid a run of kasras, as in salamī, shaqarī). Ibn al-Aʿrābī preserves Daghfal's genealogical image of ʿAmr b. Tamīm as "a crouching eagle," each sub-clan a part of the bird. Crucially, al-Azharī states his own view that the deed-nullifying sense (ḥabṭ) derives from belly-bloat (ḥabaṭ): as the bloated animal perishes, so the hypocrite's deed comes to nothing — the two being distinguished only by the vowel on the bāʾ.

**8. Further idioms.** ḥabiṭa dam al-qatīl = the slain man's blood went unavenged/wasted; ḥabiṭat al-biʾr = a well's water was lost; al-iḥbāṭ (Abū ʿAmr) = to drain a well's water so it never returns as before.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-b-b as having three root meanings: (1) holding fast and staying fixed, (2) the grain of anything that bears grain, and (3) shortness. He then sets out the grain sense first, followed by holding fast and shortness.

**1. Grain**

- al-ḥabb is the familiar grain of wheat and barley. al-ḥibb, with an i-vowel, is the seed of aromatic plants, singular ḥibba. The Prophet said of certain people that "they come out of the Fire and sprout as the ḥibba sprouts in the silt carried by the flood."
- An unnamed scholar says that the grain of anything that bears grain is called ḥibba, while wheat and barley are called only ḥabb.
- ḥabbat al-qalb, the heart's "grain", is its black core; some say its fruit.
- al-ḥabab is the teeth set evenly in rows. Ṭarafa: "when she laughs she shows ḥabab, like musk-sweet saliva with cool water."

**2. Holding fast, staying fixed**

- Ibn Fāris derives al-ḥubb and al-maḥabba, "love", from this sense: aḥabbahu means that one held fast to the thing.
- al-muḥibb (also al-muḥabb) is a camel that is worn out and stays fixed in its place. A verse says that a woman surpassed all other women, "so after that all of them are like the stalled camel."
- aḥabba al-baʿīr means that the camel stood still. It is reported that iḥbāb in camels is like ḥirān, balking, in other riding beasts. A half-verse speaks of "a beating like that of the bad camel when it stalls."
- Thaʿlab recited lines by a Bedouin girl asking her father to adorn her neck "until the suitors come with camels muḥabḥaba". Ibn Fāris explains that the camels are so fat that they stand still. There is also a variant with khāʾ, mukhabkhaba, which has a different meaning and is treated under its own root.
- Another verse: "stalled like a sick man stalls, yet all that afflicts him is grief that he sees no one to spring upon him."

**3. Shortness**

- al-ḥabḥāb is a short man. Its plural, al-ḥabāḥib, means "small ones", as in al-Hudhalī's verse about travelling by night "when the night grows dark over the joined, small ones". Here al-muqarrana means mountains so close together that they seem joined.
- **ḥabāb al-māʾ.** Ibn Fāris thinks that the ḥabāb of water belongs to this sense. He allows that it may instead belong to the grain sense, as though the bubbles were grains. Others say ḥabāb al-māʾ is the main body of the water, citing the verse "her breast cleaves the ḥabāb of the water."
- **al-Ḥubāḥib.** This is the name of a man, derived from one of the senses above. It is said that his fire was of no use to anyone, so every useless fire was named after him: "the fire of al-ḥubāḥib". Al-Nābigha has a verse describing how "they cleave doubled-woven Salūqī mail and kindle on the broad stones the fire of al-ḥubāḥib."

**An exception to the pattern**

- al-ḥubāb, "the snake", does not fit the root's meanings. Scholars say it is also given as the name of a shayṭān because the snake is a shayṭān. A verse compares something to "the writhing of a shayṭān in a desolate place of castor-oil plants."

text:
Root: h-b-k (Ibn Faris, Maqayis al-Lugha)

Core meaning: making something firm/well-knit along a stretched, extended, regular course -- firmness combined with regularity of pattern.

1. Applied to a camel: "mahbuk al-qara" -- "firm/well-knit along the back," i.e. strong-backed.

2. Related derivation: "al-ihtiba'" (tying the waist-wrap/izar around oneself) is said to come from "al-ihtibak" -- fitting the root's core sense of firm, regular binding.

3. Qur'anic use -- "wa-l-sama'i dhati l-hubuk" ("By the sky/heaven possessed of hubuk," 51:7). Ibn Faris records two views on hubuk here:
   - Some scholars: it means the sky is possessed of a good, well-ordered (muhkam) creation.
   - Others: hubuk means "tara'iq" -- tracks, paths, or streaks (singular: habikah) -- understood as referring to the paths/courses of the stars.

4. Also: "kisa' muhabbak" -- a cloak that is striped or streaked (mukhattat).

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-b-l as one root whose core idea is that something extends or stretches out. Everything else, in his account, is carried figuratively on that one idea.

1. ḥabl — a rope or halter (plural ḥibāl). This is the plain, well-known sense.
2. ḥabl al-ʿātiq — the cord or sinew of the shoulder.
3. ḥabl — a long, drawn-out ridge or stretch of sand.
4. ḥabl — a covenant or pact. Ibn Fāris marks this explicitly as the figurative extension of the rope. His witness is a line of al-Aʿshā about a traveller passing from tribe to tribe: the "ropes" of one tribe carry the rider along until she reaches the next, which then takes over. He glosses these ropes as safe-conduct and the covenants of protective escort (khifāra) — one tribe guarantees passage until the next takes up the guarantee.
5. ḥibāla — the hunter's snare; iḥtabala al-ṣayd, "he trapped the game with a snare." Al-Kumayt's line uses it for hoping the impossible: hoping for someone's affection is like hoping to snare the anūq (vulture) sitting on its eggs — the bird's nest cannot be reached at all.
6. muḥtabal — in a line of Labīd describing his mount, this means the pasterns of the animal, so called because that is where the hobbling rope sits.
7. ḥabīlu barāḥ — said of someone who holds his position and does not flee, as if he were roped in place. Ibn Fāris adds that some claim the lion is called by this name.
8. ḥibl (with i) — a calamity or disaster; plural ḥubūl in a cited verse addressed to ʿAzz, asking whether the slanderers brought honest advice or ruin. Ibn Fāris offers his own derivation here, flagged as his opinion: a person struck by disaster is as though snared, having fallen into the trap like hunted game — and he judges that connection not far-fetched.
9. ḥabal — pregnancy. He links it to the root idea because the days stretch out with it.
10. ḥablah / ḥabalah — the grapevine, belonging here because its growth resembles well-ropes.
11. ḥublah — the fruit of the ʿiḍāh (thorny acacia). He cites Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ, who recalled campaigning with the Prophet with no food but this fruit and samur leaves.
12. ḥublah — also an ornament strung in necklaces. Ibn Fāris marks this as his own conjecture ("I think"), suggesting the bead was likened to the acacia fruit, and quotes a verse describing a woman adorned at the throat with necklaces of ḥublah and sulūs.

Method worth noting: Ibn Fāris's argument is derivational throughout. He states the single semantic principle first (extension), then shows each sense — rope, sand-ridge, covenant, snare, pregnancy, vine, fruit — as a case of something stretched out or bound, and twice signals where he is reasoning rather than reporting.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-b-r as one root with a single, regularly applicable idea: **a mark or trace left in something, associated with beauty and splendour.**

1. **The base sense — a mark/trace.** الحَبَار (al-ḥabār) is a trace or mark. He cites a line describing a horse: the farrier has not worked over its hoof, and there is no chafe-mark on it from its ropes.

2. **Ink, and the man of ink.** From this branch: حِبْر (ḥibr) is ink; and حِبْر / حَبْر (ḥibr, ḥabr) is the man who writes with ink — that is, the learned man — plural أَحْبَار (aḥbār).

3. **Beauty and splendour.** الحَبْر (al-ḥabr) is comeliness and splendour. Hence the phrase ذُو حِبْرٍ وَسِبْرٍ (of good looks and good appearance). He quotes a ḥadīth about a man coming out of the Fire "whose ḥibr and sibr have gone," and a line of Ibn Aḥmar: "we wore its comeliness until we were called to account."

4. **Adornment, embellishment.** المُحَبَّر (al-muḥabbar) is a thing that has been adorned. The poet Ṭufayl al-Ghanawī was nicknamed Muḥabbir because he embellished and ornamented his verse.

5. **The mark without the beauty.** By the same analogy the root also covers unlovely marks: حَبِرَ الرَّجُلُ — a man whose skin sores have healed and left scars; and الحِبْر (al-ḥibr) — a yellow film on the teeth.

6. **Fine, new, well-finished.** ثَوْبٌ حَبِيرٌ — a garment new and handsome (Ibn Fāris assigns this to the first, "beauty" category). قِدْحٌ مُحَبَّرٌ — an arrow-shaft well pared.

7. **Gladness.** الحَبْرَة (al-ḥabra) is joy. He cites Q 30:15, "so they, in a meadow, are made glad (yuḥbarūn)."

8. **Abundance in nature.** أَرْضٌ مِحْبَارٌ — ground quick to sprout vegetation. الحَبِير of clouds — cloud heavy with water.

9. **Outside the pattern.** He marks as anomalous the idiom مَا فِيهِ حَبَرْبَرٌ, "there is not a thing in it."

10. **The ḥubārā (bustard).** Also outside the pattern: الحُبَارَى, a bird, and the proverb "he died of grief like the ḥubārā." The explanation given: it moults with the other birds but its feathers grow back slowly, so when the flock flies and it cannot, it dies of grief. He cites a line on Zayd "dead of grief like the ḥubārā," and three lines of al-Rāʿī: the bird caught in a hunter's snare can do nothing but roll its eye at the man rushing at it, kicking with its feet, its feathers fouled. The point of the oath is that the poet's being reviled will not go unanswered — he will not be left as helpless as the trapped ḥubārā, which Ibn Fāris calls among the most abject of birds. He adds glosses: المُعْزِب is the hunter, so called because he does not go home to his family; حَمْلَقَتْ is turning back the inner lid of the eye; تَنُوشُ بِرِجْلَيْهَا is striking with the feet; الغِسْل is marshmallow wash — the image being that the bird soiled its own feathers. He closes with a comparable line of al-Kumayt on the ḥubārā puffing itself up in threat, from a distance, at a grey hawk with blood-dyed talons.

text: Ibn Faris (Maqayis al-Lugha) gives the root h-b-s a single core sense: to hold something back, to restrain or detain it. All the words he lists under this root branch from that one idea. First, the verb habasa / habastuhu habsan means "I detained/confined him"; the verbal noun habs simply means a detaining, a holding-back. Second, al-habs as a thing is "that which is held back" (ma wuqifa) - something made to stand still or kept from moving or being used freely. Third, he cites the usage ahbastu farasan fi sabili Llah, "I withheld/set aside a horse in God's path" - an animal held back from ordinary use or disposal and dedicated to a particular purpose; he does not gloss this phrase further. Fourth, al-hibs is a structure built to hold back water, i.e. a dam or reservoir, plural ahbas. All four senses trace back to the one root idea of restraint or confinement - of a person, of movement, of an animal's normal use, or of water.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives the whole root ح-د-ب from one core idea: the rising or curving upward of something (irtifāʿ).

1. A rise in the land. Al-ḥadab means high ground — a hillock or elevation. Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 21:96, "{وَهُمْ مِنْ كُلِّ حَدَبٍ يَنسِلُونَ}" — "they issue forth swiftly from every ḥadab (rise in the ground)."

2. A hump on the back. The same word describes a curved/humped back. The verb ḥadiba and its intensive form iḥdawdaba both mean "he became hunched." A she-camel is called ḥadbāʾ when her hip-bones jut out (i.e., she's gaunt), and ḥidbār carries the same meaning; the plural expression is ḥudub ḥadābīr — worn-down, hump-backed she-camels.

3. To lean over someone in compassion. The idiom ḥadiba ʿalayhi ("he was tender/compassionate toward him") is explained as coming from this same root: the compassionate person is pictured as bending or leaning over the other out of concern — a posture Ibn Fāris likens directly to the physical curve (ḥadab) of a hump.

So the entry traces a single image — outward/upward curvature — from a rise in terrain, to a hump on a back or camel, to the bodily posture of leaning over someone in kindness.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-d-d as having two roots: first, prevention (al-manʿ); second, the edge of a thing.

**Root 1: prevention**

1. **Barrier.** The ḥadd is the barrier between two things.
2. **Withheld.** Someone who is prevented is maḥdūd. "He is luckless and maḥdūd" means he has, as it were, been withheld from provision.
3. **Doorkeeper.** A doorkeeper is called ḥaddād because he prevents people from entering. Al-Aʿshā speaks of a dark wine-jar "kept by its ḥaddād". Al-Nābigha has the King (al-malīk) tell Sulaymān to "restrain (uḥdud) creation from folly". Another poet prays that a man be given a wife who makes him "her ḥaddād as long as she lives", that is, her doorkeeper so that she does not run off.
4. **Iron.** Iron (ḥadīd) is named for its resistance, hardness and toughness. Istiḥdād means using iron.
5. **Mourning.** Ḥaddat or aḥaddat al-marʾa ʿalā baʿlihā: a woman withholds adornment and dye from herself in mourning for her husband.
6. **Opposition.** Muḥādda means opposing someone, as if it were mutual withholding. Ibn Fāris adds that it may instead belong to the second root.
7. **No escape; "God forbid".** "Mā lī ʿan hādhā al-amr ḥadad wa-muḥtadd" means "I have no way to turn aside from this matter, and no refuge." Ḥadadan means "God forbid", and it too comes from prevention. Al-Kumayt: "God forbid that your bounty among us be cut short or come in scant drops."
8. **The penalty.** The ḥadd for a disobedient person is called ḥadd because it prevents him from repeating the act.
9. **Inaccessible.** Al-Duraydī reports "amr ḥadad" for a matter that is inaccessible (manīʿ).

**Root 2: the edge**

10. **Blade's edge.** The ḥadd of a sword or a knife is its edge.
11. **Strength of a drink.** The ḥadd of a drink is its strength. Al-Aʿshā: "a cup like the eye of a rooster, whose ḥadd I met early in the morning."
12. **Might.** A man's ḥadd is his might, which Ibn Fāris calls a comparison (tashbīh).
13. **Sharp temper.** By extension, ḥidda is the sharpness of temper that comes over a person from irascibility: ḥadadtu ʿalā al-rajul aḥiddu ḥiddatan, "I became sharp with the man."

text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) traces the root ḥ-d-q to one core sense: something encircling or surrounding something else.

1. To surround (verb). "Ḥadaqa al-qawmu bi-l-rajuli" / "aḥdaqū bihi" — the people surrounded/encircled the man. Illustrated with a line of verse: death "encircled" the poet while his supporters were slow to arrive.

2. Pupil of the eye (ḥadaqah). Named from the same root because the black part of the eye "encircles" the tiny reflected image within it — what the Arabs called al-ṣabī, "the little one." Plural: ḥidāq. A second verse pictures an eye whose pupil has been gouged out with a thorn, left blind and weeping — again turning on this body part.

3. Intense gaze (taḥdīq). A derived noun/verbal-noun meaning a fixed, intense stare.

4. Garden (ḥadīqah). Land covered with trees. Ibn Fāris gives no explicit link here, but the word shares the root's underlying sense of enclosure/surrounding (land enclosed by trees or a wall).

5. Pupil, alternate word (ḥindīqah). Given simply as a synonym of ḥadaqah.

Note: the second poetic citation in the source shows a likely transcription irregularity ("كَأَن قَهَا"); it has been read as the expected "كَأَنَّ حَدَقَهَا."

text:
Ibn Fāris derives the whole root ح-د-ث (ḥ-d-th) from one core idea: a thing's coming into being after it was not — newness, coming-to-pass.

1. Core sense: to happen / come about. حَدَثَ أَمْرٌ = "a matter came to pass after it had not been."

2. الحَدَث (al-ḥadath), of a man: young, fresh in years.

3. الحَديث (al-ḥadīth), "speech / report": tied to the same root, because speech is where one thing arises after another — it comes forth bit by bit, i.e. a new thing continually being produced.

4. رَجُل حَدَث (rajul ḥadath): a man of good conversation (ḥasan al-ḥadīth).

5. رَجُل حِدْث نِساء (rajul ḥidth nisāʾ): a man who converses / keeps up talk with women.

6. Morphological note: حِدِّيثَى (ḥiddīthā), formed on the pattern of خِطِّيبَى (khiṭṭībā), also means al-ḥadīth (speech, talk) — as in هذه حِدِّيثَى حَسَنَة ("this is a fine piece of talk").

text:
Ibn Fāris derives all uses of the root ḥ-f-ẓ from one core idea: tending to or watching over something.

1. Core sense — guarding, keeping, preserving. حَفِظَ الشَّيْءَ = to guard or keep a thing (verbal noun ḥifẓ).

2. Anger. Anger is named ḥafīẓa (and also iḥfāẓ) from this root, because the angry state moves a person to be protective of something. أَحْفَظَنِي = "he angered me."

3. taḥaffuẓ — attentiveness / being on one's guard, glossed literally as "little heedlessness."

4. ḥifāẓ — muḥāfaẓa, keeping up or maintaining one's affairs.

The entry offers no poetic or Qur'anic citations; it is a brief etymological note tracing these senses back to the single idea of watchful care.

text:
Root ح ف د (ḥ-f-d), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning combining two ideas: lightness/swiftness in work, and gathering/coming-together.

1. al-ḥafadah — helpers/attendants (singular ḥāfid), so named because both senses of the root combine in them: they gather around a purpose, and they act with light, ready swiftness. Swiftness toward obedience is itself called ḥafd — the source of the qunūt supplication phrase "ilayka nasʿā wa naḥfidu" ("toward You we hasten and swiftly obey"), illustrated with a supporting line of poetry.
2. The entry's central Qur'anic citation: al-Nahl 16:72, "wa jaʿala lakum min azwājikum banīna wa ḥafadatan" — "and made for you, from your spouses, sons and ḥafadah." Ibn Fāris surveys three readings of ḥafadah: helpers/attendants (which he judges the sound view — al-ṣaḥīḥ); in-laws by marriage; or grandchildren (the offspring of one's offspring).
3. al-miḥfad — a measuring-vessel for grain. Returning to the "swiftness" sense: sayf muḥtafid — a swift-cutting sword; al-ḥafadān — a sustained, unbroken traveling pace.

text:
Ibn Fāris traces ḥ-f-f to three root meanings (uṣūl): a kind of sound, one thing going round another, and hardship in living.

1. **A sound.** al-ḥafīf is the rustling of trees and the like, and likewise the sound of a bird's wing.

2. **Going round, surrounding.** ḥaffa al-qawm bi-fulān is said when people go round someone. Ibn Fāris cites Q 39:75, "and you will see the angels surrounding (ḥāffīn), from around the Throne." He files here ḥifāfā, the two sides of anything, with a line of Ṭarafa: "As though the two wings of a maḍraḥī (a large bird of prey) flanked its two sides, pinned into the tail-bone with an awl." Also here: huwa ʿalā ḥafafi amr, "he is on one side of an affair", since every side of a thing goes round it; and the saying fulān yaḥuffunā wa-yaruffunā, as though the person encompasses us, giving to us and keeping us supplied.

3. **Hard, dry living.** al-ḥufūf and al-ḥafaf are hardship and dryness of life. Abū Zayd reports ḥaffat arḍunā wa-qaffat, said when the land's herbage has dried; it is like shaẓaf, a hard, meagre life. hum fī ḥafafin min al-ʿaysh: they live in straitness and dearth. Ibn Fāris says the usage was then carried further: a head is called maḥfūf or ḥāff when it has long gone without oil, and a woman is said to ḥaffat her face when she clears it of hair. He adds iḥtafaftu al-nabt, "I cut the plants."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ḥ-f-r (حفر) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris derives two distinct core meanings for this root.

**1. To dig / to wear away from below**

The basic sense is ḥafr — digging something, i.e. removing or pulling it out from underneath. "I dug the earth" is ḥafartu al-arḍa ḥafran.

- The horse's hoof (ḥāfir al-faras) takes its name from this root, as if the hoof "digs" the ground.
- The same root covers the wearing-away of teeth: "his mouth eroded" (ḥufira fūhu) uses the same verb, meaning tooth decay/erosion.
- Al-ḥafar is the earth dug out of a pit (like spoil from demolition), or, by extension, the name for the dug place itself — illustrated by a citation about a trench (khandaq) called al-ḥafar.
- A colt is said to uḥfira ("has been dug") when some of its milk teeth fall out as the permanent ones grow in — a technical term for that stage of a horse's dentition.
- A proverbial line: every pregnant female is "dug into" (worn down, made lean) by her pregnancy — except the she-camel, who fattens on it instead. Here "digs her" is glossed as "makes her thin."

**2. The first/former state (al-ḥāfira)**

The second root-meaning is "the beginning of a matter." From it comes al-ḥāfira, used in Qur'an 79:10 — "Are we indeed to be returned to al-ḥāfira?" Ibn Fāris reports this is explained as "the first/original state," i.e. "will we live again after we have died?"

He also gives a second derivation for the same word: from the expression "so-and-so returned upon his ḥāfira," meaning he retraced the path he had taken; and "the old man returned to his ḥāfira," meaning he became senile — reverted to a childlike former state.

**A related proverb**

"Payment at the hoof" (al-naqdu ʿinda al-ḥāfir): the horse doesn't leave until you've paid its price. Ibn Fāris explains that because Arabs held the horse in such high esteem, it was traditionally never sold on credit. The expression later spread to things other than horses.

text:
Kitāb al-ʿAyn groups this under one chapter covering several root-permutations built from ḥ, f, and a weak third letter (w/y). Only the first section (ḥafw/ḥafy) is the entry for the requested root ḥ-f-w; the rest are neighboring roots the book lists in the same chapter for completeness.

**Root ḥ-f-w / ḥ-f-y**

1. **Barefoot, footsore** — al-ḥifwah / al-ḥafā is the verbal noun behind al-ḥāfī, "barefoot": ḥafiya–yaḥfā = to be without sandal or boot. The same verb extends to a foot, a camel's pad, or a hoof grown sore and thin from walking. Cited in verse by al-Aʿshā (swearing not to pity a mount's "footsoreness") and by Ruʾbah (a beast "footsore, worn thin" from exhaustion).

2. **Form IV, aḥfā** — said of a man when his riding animal goes footsore. "Aḥfānī" = he wore me down by relentless pressing or repeated asking.

3. **Al-ḥifāyah / al-ḥafī — warm attentiveness** — describes someone gentle and solicitous toward you, who treats you kindly and takes warm interest in you (yaḥtafī bika). The entry attaches two Qur'anic citations to this sense:
   - Q19:47, "innahu kāna bī ḥafiyyan" — glossed there as "dutiful, gentle."
   - Q7:187, "ka-annaka ḥafiyyun ʿanhā" — glossed there as "as though you were preoccupied/concerned with it."
   A further verse uses ḥafiyy of someone earnestly inquiring after al-Aʿshā.

4. **Al-ḥafaʾ (hamzated — an unrelated homograph)** — green papyrus-reed, abundant and perennial where it grows; unit-noun ḥafaʾah; the verb iḥtafaʾa means to pull it up and take some.

**Neighboring roots in the same chapter (not the requested root, given here as the ʿAyn arranges them):**

- *f-ḥ-w:* al-faḥwā = the gist/drift of what is meant in speech; "fahhā bikalāmihi" = to hint toward something. Separately, al-faḥā = spices/seasoning ("faḥḥi qidraka" = season your pot).
- *ḥ-w-f:* al-ḥawf = "village" in some dialects (pl. aḥwāf); in the dialect of al-Jawf/al-Shiḥr, a howdah-like device a woman rides on a camel with. Al-ḥāfān = the two veins under the tongue. Ḥāfah = the edge/side of anything (diminutive ḥuwayfah).
- *ḥ-y-f:* al-ḥayf = bias or partiality in judgment.
- *f-w-ḥ / f-y-ḥ:* al-fawḥ = catching a pleasant scent ("fāḥa al-misk," musk gave off its scent — with a supporting verse). Al-fayḥ = the blazing forth of heat; also (with al-fuyūḥ) the lushness of spring across a wide land (a verse by Abū al-Najm cited). Al-fayḥ is also the verbal noun of al-afyaḥ, "a spacious place" — the text notes its verb (fāḥa–yafāḥu) is irregular; by normal analogy it should have been fayiḥa–yafyaḥu.
- *w-ḥ-f:* al-waḥf = thick black hair, or (of plants) lush and well-watered. Al-waḥfah = a black boulder jutting from a valley-side or slope (two verses cited, one by al-Aʿshā where al-Wiḥāf is used as a place-name); also, separately, the sound made by someone under duress. Al-waḥfāʾ = red land — though also said to mean black.

text:
**Root Ḥ-J-B — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha**

Ibn Fāris treats this root as having one single sense, from which everything else is derived by analogy.

**1. Core sense: to prevent, bar, withhold (al-manʿ).**
The example given is *ḥajabtuhu ʿan kadhā* — "I barred him from such-and-such," which he glosses simply as "I prevented him."

**2. Extended uses, all built on that one sense:**

- **ḥijāb al-jawf** — the internal partition that screens off the heart from the rest of the body cavity. (A literal screening barrier inside the body.)
- **al-ḥājibān** — the eyebrows: the two bones above the eyes together with their hair and flesh. Ibn Fāris marks this explicitly as a figure of likeness (*tashbīh*): they are named as though they screened off whatever might reach the eyes.
- **ḥājib al-shams** — "the brow of the sun," which he says is nothing more than a comparison with the human eyebrow.
- **al-ḥajaba** — the head of the hip-bone. Also an analogy, but here on the basis of its *ishrāf* — its jutting out or standing prominent — rather than its screening.

**Method to note:** Ibn Fāris's argument is that a single primitive meaning (barring) generates the anatomical and celestial vocabulary through visual resemblance, and he flags each derived term as figurative rather than as an independent sense. He records no sense here beyond barring and the things named for it.

text:
Ibn Fāris holds that ḥ-j-j has four distinct root meanings, and he tentatively links some derived words and even the second root back to the first.

1. **Setting out toward something (al-qaṣd).** In his words, "every qaṣd is ḥajj". A verse describes clans that "ḥajj" (make their way to) al-Zibriqān's saffron-dyed turban. According to Ibn Fāris, the word then became restricted to setting out for the Sacred House (al-bayt al-ḥarām) to perform devotional rites.
   - Al-ḥajīj and al-ḥujj: those performing the ḥajj. Verses speak of the ḥajīj clamouring at Mecca, and of ḥujj encamped below Dhū l-Majāz.
   - Proverbs: "he persisted, and so he ḥajja (prevailed)"; and "it is the pilgrims you have let hear", said of someone who spills a secret, since telling the pilgrims means telling everyone.
   - Al-maḥajjah: the main track of a road, the route one aims along. A verse warns someone that he is veering off "the straight course of the maḥajjah".
   - Al-ḥujjah (argument, proof): Ibn Fāris says it is possibly from this root meaning, either because a proof is what one aims at, or because through it one aims at the truth being sought. Ḥājajtuhu fa-ḥajajtuhu means "I argued with him and beat him with proof"; this is winning in a dispute. Plural ḥujaj; verbal noun al-ḥijāj.
   - Ḥajajtu al-shajjah: probing a head wound with a probe, since one is aiming to learn its depth. Others say it means pouring clarified butter on the wound's blood so that it rises and can be lifted off with cotton; Abū Dhuʾayb uses ḥajīj for a wound so treated.

2. **Al-ḥijjah: the year.** Ibn Fāris suggests this may join the first meaning, since the ḥajj comes only once a year, so the year may be named after the ḥajj in it. In a verse about women "breaking in stubborn pearls in every ḥijjah", some read ḥijjah as the year, others as the earlobe, and others as a bead or pearl hung in the ear; Ibn Fāris considers both of the latter views doubtful.

3. **Al-ḥijāj: the round bone around the eye.** A person with large eye-bones is aḥajj; the plural is aḥijjah. Abū ʿAmr claimed that a cave-like hollow, and part of a rock, is called ḥajjāj.

4. **Al-ḥajḥajah: drawing back.** "They charged at us, then ḥajḥajū" means they fell back. Related forms:
   - al-muḥajḥij: one who is incapable, as in a verse praising "a violent blow, not that of one who holds back";
   - "I do not uḥajḥij in this": I have no doubt about it; and "let no hesitation or faltering carry you off";
   - a ḥajḥaj man: a worthless, base man.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-j-r as one consistent root with a single core sense: prevention/withholding (manʿ) together with encompassing or surrounding a thing (iḥāṭa). He suspects the whole family ultimately derives from ḥajar ("stone"), because of its hardness and solidity.

1. al-ḥajr / ḥijr — a person's lap or bosom (the ḥāʾ takes either fatḥa or kasra).

2. Legal interdiction: ḥajara l-ḥākimu ʿalā s-safīh — "the judge placed a ban on the incompetent man," i.e. barred him from disposing of his own property.

3. ḥijr = the intellect/reason, so called because it holds one back from improper action — parallel to ʿaql ("reason"), which is likened to the ʿiqāl (a hobble). Shāhid: Qur'an, al-Fajr 89:5, "for one possessing ḥijr [reason]."

4. Ḥajr — the chief town of the region of al-Yamāma.

5. al-ḥajar — "stone"; smaller-number plural aḥjār, also the rare pattern ḥijāra (compared to jamal → jimāla).

6. al-ḥijr — a mare; guarded and prized.

7. al-ḥājir — a hollow that holds water; plural ḥujrān.

8. ḥajratu l-qawm — the quarter/edge of a people's dwelling, their protected precinct (ḥimā). Related: al-ḥujra, a building's chamber.

9. Circular/encircling senses: ḥajjara l-qamar — a halo rings the moon; ḥajjartu ʿayna l-baʿīr — to brand around a camel's eye with a round iron; maḥjiru l-ʿayn — the socket-rim around the eye, the part visible above a veil; al-ḥijr — the Ḥaṭīm of Mecca, the enclosure curving around the Kaʿba.

10. al-ḥijr = kinship (qarāba). Ibn Fāris ties this to the root's core: kinship is a covenant that is protected and guarded. Shāhid (poet): a kinsman is "of a lineage close to me and possessed of ḥijr."

11. al-ḥijr = the forbidden (ḥarām). In the sacred months a man fearing another would say ḥijran — "forbidden!" — meaning "it is unlawful for you to harm me." Ibn Fāris connects this to the Qur'anic ḥijran maḥjūran (al-Furqān 25:22): the polytheists cry it on the Day of Resurrection at the angels of punishment, imagining it will shield them then as such an appeal did in worldly life. Supporting verse: a spokesman pleads "I am under sanctuary (ḥājūr)."

12. al-maḥājir — gardens/orchards; singular maḥjir. Shāhid: Labīd, "a huge, powerful she-camel waters the gardens."
