poets_named: al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); Ibn al-Aʿrābī (unnamed); Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam); unnamed verse ×2; Ruʾba (Umayyad); Labīd (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Sīda's al-Muḥkam entry for the root ḥ-s-r (ح س ر).

1. Core sense — to strip/uncover. ḥasara (imperfect with both -i- and -u-, verbal nouns ḥasr, ḥusūr) is to peel or strip one thing off another; the reflexive inḥasara means to be stripped away or to recede. In poetry ḥasara can itself carry this passive-reflexive force.

2. Unarmored / bare. al-ḥāsir is the opposite of al-dāriʿ (the armored man) — i.e. one wearing no mail; plural ḥussar (a poet also formed ḥussarīn). A woman called ḥāsir has cast off her outer garment; more broadly any woman bare-headed and bare-armed is ḥāsir (plurals ḥussar, ḥawāsir). Cited: al-Aʿshā (an army "hurling forth the mailed and the unarmored alike"), Ibn al-Aʿrābī's verse, and Abū Dhuʾayb (mourning daughters standing "bare").

3. Exhaustion / fatigue. ḥasr, ḥasar, ḥusūr all mean weariness. A beast or she-camel ḥasarat / istaḥsarat = grew exhausted; a hard journey ḥasara-hā (also aḥsara-hā, ḥassara-hā) = wore it out. A worn beast is ḥāsir / ḥāsira / ḥasīr (same for male and female), plural ḥasrā. aḥsara l-qawm = fatigue struck the people. Shāhid attributed with the odd added kāf (muʿriḍi l-muḥassir).

4. Weary / dimmed sight. ḥasarat al-ʿayn = the eye tired or dimmed; a strong glare can weary the gaze. baṣar ḥasīr = dulled, exhausted vision — cited from the Qurʾān, "the sight returns to you humbled and it is ḥasīr" (67:4). Shāhid from Ruʾba on brightness wearying the eye.

5. Grief / regret (ḥasra). al-ḥasra is being overwhelmed by regret beyond all limit. ḥasira ʿalā (verbal nouns ḥasar, ḥasra, ḥasarān) = to grieve over something lost; the person is ḥasir / ḥasrān.

6. Ebbing of the sea. ḥasara l-baḥr = the sea receded from the seabed and shore, laying them bare.

7. Moulting; flesh settling. inḥasarat al-ṭayr = birds shed old plumage for new (the season is ḥasar); taḥassarat al-nāqa = the she-camel's flesh settled firmly into place (cited from Labīd).

8. Despised / worn-down man. muḥassar = one harmed and held in contempt. A ḥadīth describes an end-times figure ("Amīr al-ʿAṣab," or "Amīr al-Ghaḍab") whose followers are muḥassarūn — scorned, shut out from rulers' courts, gathering to him "like scattered autumn clouds."

9. Other derivatives. al-miḥsara = a broom. ḥasarū-hu = they begged of him until he gave away everything he had.

10. al-ḥasār (plant). A herb of level lowlands and hard ground, with a small spike; fine pasture, better dried than fresh, rising slightly off the ground and resembling zabād but coarser-leaved. Abū Ḥanīfa: a green herb spreading flat on the ground that livestock eat eagerly (with a shāhid describing wild asses grazing it in a trackless waste); Kalb Bedouin likened it to cress (ḥurf) growing in ground-running runners, and some said it resembles the carrot plant.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَحَسَّ 3x "you perceive"; تَحُسُّ 1x "you were killing them"; تَحَسَّسُ 1x "and inquire"; حَسِيس 1x "(the) slightest sound of it"
text:
Ibn Fāris says ḥ-s has two root meanings: (1) overpowering something, by killing or in some other way, and (2) a sound imitating a cry of pain.

**First root: overpowering, killing**

1. **Killing.** al-ḥass is killing. He cites "when you were cutting them down (taḥussūnahum) by His leave" (Q 3:152), the ḥadīth "cut them down with the sword", and a ḥadīth on locusts, "when the cold has killed (ḥassa) them". al-ḥasīs is a slain man; a verse of al-Afwah speaks of "every slain adversary" having fallen. Cold is called a maḥassa for plants, something that destroys them.

2. **Roasting meat.** ḥasḥastu the meat means putting it on the embers. The saying "do it before the ḥusās of the aysār" means "before the aysār put the meat of their slaughtered camel on the fire".

3. **Knowing and perceiving.** aḥsastu means "I came to know of something", as in "do you perceive (tuḥissu) any one of them?" (Q 19:98). Ibn Fāris links this to the first root through the idiom "I killed the matter in knowledge", meaning "I know it thoroughly". The five senses (touch, taste, smell, hearing, sight) are called al-ḥawāss. "Where did you ḥasista this news?" means "where did you learn of it?"

4. **Generosity.** A man who drives off hunger with his generosity is a ḥasḥās. A verse praises ʿUtba as "the generous one, the ḥasḥās".

**Second root: the cry of pain**

1. ḥassi is a word said when one feels pain.

2. **Pity.** ḥasistu lahu means "I felt tender pity for him", as if the heart ached with compassion.

3. **Birth pain.** al-ḥiss is the pain that seizes a woman in childbirth.

4. **Teeth.** inḥassat asnānuhu means "his teeth were pulled out". A verse describes an ancient royal line as "neither uprooted nor broken out".

5. **Bad character.** Ibn Fāris places al-ḥusās, bad character, in this chapter and "not far from" the root. A verse speaks of a drinking companion with ḥusās, whose company is like being cut with razors. al-ḥusās is also said to mean ill omen. Ibn Fāris says this could belong to either root, the first because ill omen takes good away.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ح ت م (Ḥ-T-M) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris opens by saying this is not, in his judgment, a genuine independent root. He treats it as a phonetic variant in which tāʾ stands in for kāf — so ḥatama is, for him, really a form of ḥakama ("to judge, decree," explained under that root elsewhere in the book). The core notion carried over is "making a thing firm/binding" (iḥkām).

1. To make binding / decree — ḥattama ʿalayhi: "he made it binding/obligatory on him." Traced back to ḥakama.

2. Al-ḥātim: one who settles or decides a matter.

3. From this sense, the crow/raven was called ḥātim, because the Arabs believed its cry "pronounces" (yaḥtimu) separation/parting — functioning like an omen handing down a verdict (ḥukm). Illustrated with an anonymous line of poetry in which the speaker says he used to go out at dawn without heeding omen-birds — neither the wāq nor the ḥātim.

4. A second, separate word sharing this shape: al-ḥutāmah, "what is left of food on the table/spread." Ibn Fāris assigns this one to a different substitution — tāʾ standing in for ṭāʾ, i.e. really from ḥaṭama ("to break, crush"). He glosses it as something that does not hold firm, but rather crumbles and breaks apart, matching his fuller discussion of ḥaṭama elsewhere in the dictionary.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris holds that ḥ-th-th goes back to two root meanings (aṣlān): urging someone toward a thing, and something dry, from among the dry remnants of a thing.

1. **Urging.** One says ḥathathtuhu ʿalā al-shayʾ, aḥuththuhu: "I urged him to the thing; I urge him."
   - **al-ḥathīth, "hastening".** From this sense: wallā ḥathīthan means "he turned away in haste." Salāmah's verse: "It turned away swiftly, and this grey hair seeks it; if only the racing of the partridges could overtake it."
   - **al-ḥathḥathah.** Also from this sense: the quivering of lightning in the clouds.

2. **Dry matter.** al-ḥuthth is dry debris; it is also said to be dry, coarse sand. A quoted line: "until ḥuthth is seen in the dry part of the moist earth."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ḥ-w-sh (حوش) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris treats this root as expressing one underlying idea, though he records it branching in two directions.

1. Wildness. Al-ḥūsh means "the wild [creatures]" (al-waḥsh); something wild-natured is called ḥūshī. He quotes ʿUmar's remark about the poet Zuhayr, that Zuhayr "did not crowd his rhymes together, did not resort to ḥūshī (uncouth/strange) speech, and praised a man only for what was truly in him" — ḥūshī speech here meaning coarse or alien diction.

Al-Qutaybī reported that "ḥūshī camels" (al-ibil al-ḥūshiyya) take their name from al-ḥūsh because they descend from stallions belonging to the jinn's herds that had covered ordinary camels, so the offspring were named after that stock. A line of Ru'ba's poetry ("our millstone was hauled from the lands of al-Ḥūsh") is cited as further attestation.

Ibn Fāris himself judges that this "wild" sense is really a metathesis of w-ḥ-sh (waḥsh, "wild") — the same phenomenon as jadhaba/jabadha ("to pull"), where two root letters swap places.

2. Gathering/collecting. If this second sense is sound, the true root-meaning is to gather or draw together. Evidence:
- ḥushtu al-ṣayd / aḥashtu-hu — "I drove the game," i.e. took it from all around and herded it together toward the snare.
- iḥtawasha al-qawmu fulānan — "the people encircled so-and-so," putting him in their midst.
- taḥawwasha ʿannī al-qawm — "the people withdrew/drew back from me."
- mā yanḥāshu fulānun min shay' — "so-and-so does not draw himself together/recoil from a thing," said of someone who feels little concern about it and so does not brace against it. A verse is quoted about a woman (and her mother) who do not shy away, their aversion (zawīl) dropping when they see the poet's people.
- al-ḥuwāsha is glossed two ways, both tied to this "drawing back" sense: (a) a sinful matter — because a person draws in on himself and recoils from it, illustrated by a verse rebuking someone who "wanted a sinful thing (ḥuwāsha), was ignorant of the truth, and chose jesting instead"; (b) bashfulness/shame (al-istiḥyā') — because a shy person likewise draws himself away from the thing.
- al-ḥawsh: eating from the edges of a dish until it is used up.
- al-ḥā'ish: a grove/cluster of palm trees, a word with no singular form.

Ibn Fāris's own analysis, then, is that the "wild beast" sense is a transposed form of a different root (w-ḥ-sh), while the root ḥ-w-sh proper centers on gathering, encircling, and — by extension — recoiling or shrinking away (from sin, from shame, from company).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root حوذ (ḥ-w-dh) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris gives this root one core sense: lightness, speed, and briskness in handling a matter.

1. Driving swiftly: al-iḥwādh — swift travel; ḥādha al-ḥimāru utunahu — a donkey drives his females along forcefully, illustrated with a verse of al-ʿAjjāj about a driver's skill (ḥūdhiyy).

2. A capable, quick person: al-aḥwadhiyy — someone nimble and quick in affairs, who has mastered and perfected what he does. ʿĀʾisha is quoted praising ʿUmar as "an aḥwadhiyy, peerless of his kind."

3. A bird's wings: al-aḥwadhiyyān — the two wings of the sand-grouse, illustrated with a verse about taking flight — the same root-image of speed and lightness applied to flight.

4. Religious usage: istaḥwadha ʿalayhi al-shayṭān — "Satan istaḥwadha over him," meaning Satan overpowered him and drove him toward misguidance — the root's "driving/overpowering" sense applied to spiritual seduction.

5. Two usages Ibn Fāris flags as irregular, not fitting the root's core pattern: khafīf al-ḥādh — "light of ḥādh," describing an agile, capable person (illustrated with a verse praising someone as swift-tracking and a devoted companion, not an ordinary servant); and al-ḥādh, the name of a particular tree — unrelated in meaning, sharing only the letters.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَحَاطَ 17x "they encompass"; مُحِيط 9x "all-encompassing"; مُحِيطَة 2x "(will) surely surround"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-w-ṭ (حوط) as a single core idea: one thing surrounding or encircling another.

1. Core sense — to surround, encompass, guard. The verbal noun al-ḥawṭ comes from ḥāṭahu ("he surrounded/guarded it").
2. Extended to gathering/keeping together: the male donkey "yaḥūṭu" his herd of she-asses, meaning he gathers them.
3. ḥāʾiṭ ("a wall / walled enclosure"), from ḥawwaṭtu ("I walled in") — the enclosing structure.
4. al-ḥuwāṭa — reportedly an enclosure built to store grain.
5. al-ḥawṭ — also a round silver ornament a woman hangs on her forehead.

All the senses trace back to the one image of encircling.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ح و ب (ḥ-w-b), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One root branching into three closely related senses: sin, need, and destitution.

1. al-ḥūb/al-ḥawb — sin. Qur'anic citation, al-Nisaʾ 4:2 (cited twice, in two related forms): "innahu kāna ḥūban kabīrā" — "indeed it is ever a great sin" (regarding misappropriating orphans' property).
2. al-ḥawbah — what a person sins in by failing a duty owed to someone, such as one's mother; yataḥawwabu min kadhā — to avoid something out of a sense of sin, illustrated with a hadith citation asking God to accept repentance and forgive sin (ḥawbah).
3. al-taḥawwub — also used for moaning/lamenting in pain or grief, illustrated with a line of poetry by Ṭufayl about shared suffering and lament.
4. "alḥaqa Allāhu bihi al-ḥawbah" — an idiom meaning need and destitution befell someone.
5. A grammatical aside: Ibn Fāris addresses why al-ḥawbāʾ ("the soul/self") shares this root, explaining that it fits perfectly — a person's tender concern for his own soul is his most dominant, most frequent concern, so the word for "soul" naturally derives from the same root as sin/need/destitution.
6. Closing methodological note: the camel-driving call "ḥawb" is explicitly excluded from this root — Ibn Fāris reiterates his general position that such imitative sounds are not derived from any semantic root, but simply invented and spread by usage. A related word, al-ḥawʾab, is noted as discussed separately under its own entry.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ḥ-w-j (ح و ج) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris states that this three-letter root has a single core meaning: being driven by necessity toward something — i.e., need.

1. Core noun: al-ḥājah (a need), plural al-ḥājāt (needs). A variant noun form, al-ḥawjāʾ, carries the same meaning of "need."

2. Verbs meaning "to need":
   - aḥwaja (form IV) = iḥtāja, "he needed / was in need."
   - ḥāja – yaḥūju (form I) is also used with the same sense, "to need."

3. Illustrative verse (unattributed in the entry): the poet says that when he had grown wealthy/self-sufficient, he did not turn away those who came asking of him; and when he himself was in need (ḥujtu), he did not scratch/scrape at people with his fingers — an image for begging persistently. The line is cited to show ḥujtu used as "I was in need."

4. A noted exception: the word al-ḥāj, denoting a type of thorny plant, shares the same three root letters but is explicitly flagged by Ibn Fāris as unrelated in meaning — an anomaly (shādhdh) that falls outside this root's core sense of "need."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: حَوْل 17x "(are) around it"; حَالَ 3x "and a barrier will be placed"; تَحْوِيل 3x "any alteration"; حِيلَة 1x "plan"; حِوَل 1x "any transfer"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the whole root ḥ-w-l from one core idea: movement within a turning or cycle (taḥarruk fī dawr). From this single sense he draws the following:

1. Time turning round. al-ḥawl = "the year," because the year turns/revolves (yaḥūl means yadūr, "goes round"). Hence ḥālat / aḥālat / aḥwalat al-dār = "a full year passed over the dwelling," and aḥwaltu / aḥaltu bi-l-makān = "I stayed a year in the place."

2. Physical movement / shifting. ḥāla al-rajul fī matn farasihi (verbal noun ḥawl / ḥuʾūl; also aḥāla) = "he vaulted onto his horse's back." ḥāla al-shakhṣ = "the figure moved," and by extension anything that changes from one state (ḥāla) to another. From this same idea comes istaḥaltu al-shakhṣ = "I watched to see whether it would move."

3. Cunning and contrivance. ḥīla (stratagem), ḥawīl, and muḥāwala (effort, contrivance) all follow the same logic: a person circles around (yadūr ḥawālay) a thing in order to get at it.

Poetic witness: a line of al-Kumayt describes a bird "of two names… deemed foolish, though its cunning (ḥawīl) is plain." Ibn Fāris explains that this is the Egyptian vulture, called both rakhma and anūq. It is thought foolish yet is in fact shrewd, because it nests on mountain peaks, is first among migrating birds to leave and first to return, loves its young, broods its eggs, and lets none but its mate near it.

4. A further derivative: al-ḥuwalāʾ = the membrane/afterbirth expelled with a newborn, so named because it encompasses (muṭīf) the child.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: حَوَارِيُّون 5x "the disciples"; حُور 4x "(to) companions with beautiful eyes"; يُحَاوِرُ 2x "was talking to him"; تَحَاوُر 1x "(the) dialogue of both of you"; يَحُورَ 1x "he would return"
text:
Ibn Fāris organizes ح-و-ر (ḥ-w-r) under three base meanings, plus one word he sets aside as not belonging.

1. A COLOR — whiteness. al-ḥawar is intense white of the eye against intense black of it. Abū ʿAmr held it means the eye being wholly black, as in gazelles and wild cattle; on his view humans do not truly have ḥawar, and women are called ḥūr al-ʿuyūn only by likeness to those animals. Al-Aṣmaʿī, by contrast, said he did not know what ḥawar in the eye is. From "whitening" come: ḥawwara al-thiyāb (to whiten garments); the ḥawāriyyūn, Jesus's companions, so named because they whitened clothes — this is the origin, after which any helper/supporter came to be called ḥawāriyy (cited in a hadith calling al-Zubayr the Prophet's ḥawāriyy); al-ḥawāriyyāt, white(-skinned) women (with a verse of poetry); ḥuwwārā, whitened/refined food; iḥwarra, to become white (with a poetic citation about a fat-whitened bowl). The planet Jupiter is called al-Aḥwar by some. Ibn Fāris tentatively attaches here al-ḥawar meaning soft hide tanned without qaraẓ, suggesting it too may carry a color-sense (with a line by al-ʿAjjāj).

2. RETURNING / REVERTING. ḥāra = to return. He cites Qurʾan 84:14, "he thought he would never return (yaḥūra) — nay!" The idiom al-bāṭil fī ḥūr means falsehood is in decline; ḥūr denotes any reversion or diminishment (poetic citation). al-ḥawr is the verbal noun of this ḥāra; the saying "[refuge] from al-ḥawr after al-kawr" means decrease after increase (also ḥāra baʿda mā kāra). A reply/answer is ḥawār, ḥiwār, maḥūra, or ḥawīr — as in "I spoke to him but he gave me no answer (ḥawār)."

3. TURNING / ROTATING. al-miḥwar is the wooden axle-pin on which a pulley turns. ḥawwara al-khubza means to shape and turn a round of dough before setting it in the hot ashes.

ANOMALOUS: ḥuwār al-nāqa, a she-camel's young, which Ibn Fāris notes falls outside these three roots.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-w-t as one sound root with a single consistent sense that can be applied by analogy.

1. Core idea: restless agitation and swerving aside (iḍṭirāb and rawaghān) — movement that will not hold still and keeps veering.

2. الحُوت (al-ḥūt): the large fish. He derives the name from the core idea: such a fish is perpetually in motion and never settles in one place.

3. Verbal use, form III: حَاوَتَنِي فُلَانٌ ("so-and-so ḥāwatanī") is given as attested Arab usage meaning "he dodged about me / used evasive feints against me."

Citation for sense 3: "All day an ash-grey calamity kept dodging around me ... on the day of al-Thawiyya, [keeping me] from my family and my property." The verse is quoted anonymously, with no poet named.

The entry is brief and lists no other senses.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-w-y as a single root whose core meaning is "gathering, collecting" (al-jamʿ).

1. Base verb: ḥawaytu al-shayʾa aḥwīhi ḥayyan — "I gathered/collected the thing."

2. Al-ḥawiyyah (pl. al-ḥawāyā) — the intestines. Ibn Fāris derives this directly from the "gathering" sense (the gut as a coiled, gathered thing). A singular variant, ḥāwiyāʾ, is also used. He cites an (unnamed) poet's line comparing the crackling of grain inside the intestine to the hiss of vipers or the crackle of scorpions.

3. Al-ḥawiyyah (same word, different sense) — a cloth wound around a camel's hump so that a rider can sit on it.

4. Al-ḥayy — used of the tribal clans/encampments of the Arabs (i.e., a gathered group of people).

5. Al-ḥiwāʾ — a single dwelling or house.

Ibn Fāris closes by noting that every one of these senses fits the same underlying pattern (qiyās) of the root: things that are gathered, coiled, or brought together — intestines, a wrapped cloth, a clan, a dwelling.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ح و ز (ḥ-w-z), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: gathering and coming-together.

1. ḥawz/ḥawzah — a gathering-place, a district/territory; ḥamā fulānun al-ḥawzata — so-and-so protected his territory. The word became a proverbial figure for what a woman ought to protect and withhold, illustrated with a line of poetry about a woman defending her husband's honor in his absence.
2. taḥawwazati al-ḥayyah — a snake coiled/writhed, illustrated with a line of poetry by al-Qutāmī comparing someone drawing back in fear to a viper recoiling from a striker.
3. The general verb: ḥāzahu ḥawzan — to gather something to oneself, the root's most direct sense. By extension, ḥawz is also used for a man's inner nature/temperament.
4. al-ḥūzī — someone who withdraws from people and isolates himself; a disputed line of poetry by al-ʿAjjāj is cited (with a transmitted variant) describing a donkey that gathers and drives his mares.
5. Closing note: al-aḥwazī, describing men, is compared to the similar word al-aḥwadhī — Ibn Fāris notes both follow the same derivational logic.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-y-ḍ as having only one underlying meaning.

1. The base image is botanical: حَاضَتِ السَّمُرَةُ (ḥāḍat al-samura) is said of the samura (a species of acacia) when a red fluid seeps out of it.

2. From this, he derives the human application: a woman discharging blood (nufasāʾ) is called حَائِض (ḥāʾiḍ) because her blood is compared to that red tree-sap.

The entry gives no further senses, no grammatical or plural patterns, and no poetic or scriptural citations.

poets_named: unnamed verse ×2; a Hudhalī poet (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-y-ṣ as a single root with one core idea: swerving or turning aside — a movement away that carries both the sense of deviating from what is right and the sense of casting about in perplexity.

1. Swerving away, deviating. حَاصَ عَنِ الْحَقِّ (ḥāṣa ʿani l-ḥaqq), imperfect yaḥīṣu, verbal noun ḥayṣ: "he swerved away from the truth," i.e. he deviated (jāra). Two verse fragments are cited without named authors: "even if ʿĀmir swerves away from death," and a transmitted line describing "a true balance that does not swerve by so much as a barley-grain" — the latter showing the verb used of the smallest deviation from exactness.

2. Straits, being hemmed in. From the same root comes the idiom وَقَعُوا فِي حَيْصَ بَيْصَ (waqaʿū fī ḥayṣa bayṣa), "they fell into ḥayṣa bayṣa," which Ibn Fāris glosses simply as hardship or a tight spot. He supports it with a line by a Hudhalī poet: "I used to be one who went out and in freely, a shifter of affairs — the straits of ḥayṣa bayṣa did not close in on me."

Method note: the entry works by asserting one semantic origin and then showing that both the plain verb (swerving off course) and the fixed idiom (being boxed in) fall under it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha derives the whole root h-y-d from one core idea: leaning or turning away from a straight, even course.

1. Core verb: ḥāda ʿan al-shayʾ, "he turned away / swerved from the thing," yaḥīdu, with the verbal nouns ḥaydah and ḥuyūd.

2. Intensive form: al-ḥayūd describes something that deviates/shies away frequently; al-ḥayadā (a related pattern) carries the same sense.

3. Poetic citation: Ibn Fāris quotes al-Hudhalī describing a dark, stout, thickset creature (probably a wild animal such as a lion) as ḥayadā - "swerving/shying" - at pit-traps (diḥāl) set for it, illustrating the verb's use for evasive, wary turning-aside.

4. Extended concrete senses, all tied to the same "jutting/turning-aside" idea:
- al-ḥayd = a jutting outcrop or ridge on a mountain (plurals: ḥuyūd, aḥyād).
- al-ḥuyūd = the ridges or knots (ʿuqad) on a gazelle's horn.

Ibn Fāris closes by stating explicitly that all of these senses - the verb of turning away, the intensive adjective, the mountain ridge, and the horn's knots - trace back to the single underlying meaning of leaning/deviating from straightness.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris gives the root h-y-f a single core sense: to incline or lean away from the straight/proper line.

1. hafa alayhi yahifu - he leaned against him, i.e. he wronged/was unjust to him - injustice pictured as a deviation, a leaning away from what is right.
2. tahayyaftu al-shay'a - I took the thing from its sides/edges, said of taking something bit by bit from its margins rather than from its center or bulk.

He notes that sense 2 still fits the root's underlying logic (qiyas al-bab): taking from the sides is itself a leaning - a movement away from the thing's breadth/middle toward its edges.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ḥ-y-n from a single origin: time (zamān). Other meanings are then carried back onto this base.

1. Core sense — time: al-ḥīn means "time," whether a short or a long span.

2. Derived time-expressions:
- عَامَلْتُ فُلَانًا مُحَايَنَةً — "I dealt with him by fixed periods / on a time basis."
- أَحْيَنْتُ بِالْمَكَانِ — "I stayed in the place for a while (ḥīnan)."
- حَازَ حِينَ كَذَا — "it drew near." Illustrated by a verse on being consoled away from Jamīl: the hour "has not come, nor has its ḥīn (appointed time) arrived."

3. Pastoral usage (setting a fixed time): ḥayyantu al-shāta means to milk a ewe at set intervals, or to fix a milking-time for it. Its opposite, al-taʾfīn, is to milk it with no fixed time. A verse of al-Mukhabbal contrasts the two: milked without a set time (ufinat) her yield still feeds your dependents; milked at set times (ḥuyyinat) her yield overflows the waterskin.

4. Two grades of ḥīn (citing al-Farrāʾ): (a) an indefinite ḥīn whose limit is not fixed — the more common usage; and (b) a delimited ḥīn, as in the Qur'anic {giving its fruit every ḥīn} [Ibrāhīm 25], which al-Farrāʾ takes as fixed at six months.

5. Carried-on sense — perishing: calling destruction ḥayn is by analogy, since when it comes it must have its "time" (ḥīn); it is as if named after the verbal noun.

Grammatical note: the medial alif in this root goes back to either a wāw or a yāʾ, and Ibn Fāris says the branching words are treated in their own chapters (mostly under wāw), so he omits them here.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-y-q as having one core meaning: the befalling or descending of one thing upon another (nuzūl al-shayʾ bi-l-shayʾ).

Usage: ḥāqa bihi al-sūʾ, imperfect yaḥīqu — "evil befell / came down upon him."

Shāhid: he cites the Qurʾān, {and the evil scheming does not befall any but its own authors} (Fāṭir 35:43), where the sense is that the harm recoils upon the very people who devised it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives everything under ḥ-y-r from one core idea: wavering back and forth in a thing — not settling on one course. This is the root of al-ḥayrah, "bewilderment": ḥāra fī al-amr (he was bewildered about a matter), taḥayyara (he became confused/perplexed).

1. Physical sense — a place of swirling water: al-ḥayr / al-ḥāʾir names a hollow or basin where water collects and circulates back and forth rather than draining out. Ibn Fāris cites a line of poetry by Qays describing legs (or stems) like papyrus reeds, nourished by a rushing, abundant flow in the courtyard of such a ḥāʾir.

2. Extended sense — "brimming full": anything completely full is called mustaḥīr. Ibn Fāris explains this as a sound extension of the same core meaning: when something is filled up, its contents surge and jostle against each other internally, just as water in a ḥāʾir basin eddies back and forth once it is full. He supports this with a line from Abū Dhuʾayb: "and her youthful vigor became full/brimming" (wa-staḥāra shabābuhā) — youth reaching its full, surging bloom.

So the entry moves in one line from indecision/mental wavering, to a basin where water physically wavers/swirls, to anything so full that its contents wallow/surge within it.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
text:
Ibn Sīda's entry treats the word حَيْثُ (ḥaythu), "where," on the root ḥ-y-th.

1. Basic description: ḥaythu is an adverb of place with an indefinite/vague reference. Its standard final vowel is ḍamma (-u), though some Arabs pronounce it with fatḥa (-a).

2. Etymology — two accounts:
   - One claim: the word's original final consonant was wāw, later shifted to yāʾ simply for ease of pronunciation. Ibn Sīda judges this account weak.
   - The account he develops: the original form was حَوْثَ (ḥawtha). The wāw shifted to yāʾ because yāʾ commonly supplants wāw, giving ḥayth-. The word was then given a fixed (built-in) ending: ḍamma, forced by the meeting of two quiescent consonants. Ḍamma was chosen specifically because it is akin to the original wāw, so the ending itself hints at that lost wāw.

3. Case-like variation (from al-Kisāʾī): although the standard ending is -u, ḥaythu can take -a when a preceding element pulls it toward fatḥa. Al-Kisāʾī reports tribal usages:
   - Banū Tamīm (Banū Yarbūʿ and Ṭuhayya): fix the ending as -a in every syntactic position — genitive, accusative, or nominative alike; e.g. ḥaytha 'ltaqaynā ("where we met"), min ḥaytha lā yaʿlamūn ("from where they do not know"). The -u form is absent from their speech.
   - Banū Asad ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Thaʿlaba and all of Banū Fuqʿas: inflect it to match the position — genitive -i in a genitive slot, accusative -a in an accusative slot; e.g. min ḥaythi lā yaʿlamūn, and kāna dhālika ḥaytha 'ltaqaynā.

4. A further variant (al-Liḥyānī from al-Kisāʾī): some give it the genitive -i, saying bi-ḥaythi, as in the verse "a-mā tarā ḥaythi Suhaylin ṭāliʿan" ("do you not see where Suhayl is rising?"). Al-Kisāʾī notes this is not the preferred usage.

5. Poetic citation (via Ibn Durayd): "bi-ḥaythu nāṣā al-limama al-kithāthā / mawra al-kathībi fa-jarā wa-ḥāthā." Ibn Sīda suggests the poet's final word ḥāthā may stand for ḥathā ("heaped/poured [sand]"), by metathesis.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-y-y as having two root meanings: life, the opposite of death, and shame or modesty, the opposite of shamelessness.

**1. Life, the opposite of death**
- al-ḥayāt and al-ḥayawān mean life, the opposite of al-mawt and al-mawatān (death).
- Rain is called ḥayan because it gives the earth life.
- A she-camel is called muḥyin or muḥyiya when her young almost never die.
- The form aḥyā can mean "to find something alive": "I came to the land and aḥyaytuhā" means I found its plants living and fresh.

**2. Shame, modesty**
- istaḥyā minhu, verbal noun istiḥyāʾ, means to feel shame before someone.
- Abū Zayd reports the simple verb with the same meaning: ḥayītu minhu, aḥyā ("I felt shame before him").
- Ibn Fāris suggests that ḥayāʾ, the name for a she-camel's vulva, may belong here. He reasons that if the animal were capable of shame, it would be ashamed of that part being seen and exposed. He presents this as a possibility, not a certainty.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ḥ-z-b from a single core sense: the gathering-together of a thing. All the words below turn on that idea of things drawn into one mass.

1. ḥizb — a group or company of people. Cited from Qurʾān 23:53, "Every party (ḥizb) rejoicing in what it has."
2. ḥizb — by extension, a section or portion of anything. Hence the idiom "he recited his ḥizb of the Qurʾān," i.e. his set portion.
3. ḥizbāʾ — rough, hard ground.
4. ḥazābiya — a donkey compact and well-knit in build (its frame "gathered" together).
5. ḥayzabūn — an old woman. Ibn Fāris notes the added letters yāʾ, wāw, and nūn are a common device to intensify the intended description.

quran_words: يَحْزُن 37x "will grieve"; حَزَن 3x "the sorrow"; حُزْن 2x "the grief"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ḥ-z-n as a single root whose core sense is the roughness of a thing and a hardness or severity in it. From this one idea he draws:

1. al-ḥazn (الْحَزْن): rough, rugged ground — the concrete, physical application of "roughness."

2. al-ḥuzn (الْحُزْن): sorrow or grief, which he calls "well-known." The verb is ḥazananī al-shayʾu / yaḥzununī ("the thing grieved me / grieves me"); a fourth-form variant aḥzananī ("it caused me grief") is also attested.

3. ḥuzānatuka (حُزَانَتُكَ): one's family and those one grieves or feels concern for — grief extended to the people who are one's charge.

The entry thus unifies rugged terrain and inner sorrow under one notion of harshness/hardness, with no citations beyond the usage examples given.

quran_words: صَعِيد 4x "(with) earth"; تُصْعِدُ 1x "you were running uphill"; يَصَّعَّدُ 1x "he (were) climbing"; يَصْعَدُ 1x "ascends"; صَعَد 1x "severe"; صَعُود 1x "(with) a laborious punishment"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-ʿ-d as one sound root carrying two linked ideas: **rising/elevation** and **hardship**. His derived senses:

1. **Upward slope; to ascend.** ṣaʿūd is the up-gradient, the opposite of ḥadūr (the down-gradient); the verb is ṣaʿida / yaṣʿadu. iṣʿād is facing the downslope from a higher place.

2. **A steep, toilsome pass — hence difficulty itself.** ṣaʿūd is the "toilsome mountain pass" (al-ʿaqaba al-kaʾūd), and by extension hardship in any affair. He cites Q 74:17, "I shall burden him with a ṣaʿūd (steep ascent)," and a verse: "ʿUtba and al-Muʿallā forbade the Taymī, saying: the steep ascent will soon rebuff you."

3. **Roads.** ṣaʿadāt = thoroughfares, singular ṣaʿīd. He quotes the Prophet: "Beware of sitting in the roads, except one who renders their due." Morphology: ṣaʿīd → ṣuʿud → ṣuʿudāt, the last a plural of a plural, on the pattern of ṭarīq / ṭuruq / ṭuruqāt (road / roads / roads).

4. **ṣaʿīd — a disputed sense: "surface of the ground" vs. "dust."** Some hold it is the face of the earth. Al-Zajjāj held it is the face of the earth and the place, whether or not dust lies on it, and claimed the lexicographers agree ṣaʿīd is not turāb (dust/soil); Ibn Fāris notes the followers of Mālik b. Anas hold this too, and that it is his own school. He nevertheless rejects it on evidence: Abū ʿUbayd reported from al-Aṣmaʿī that ṣaʿīd *is* turāb, and the book ascribed to al-Khalīl glosses the phrase tayammam bi-l-ṣaʿīd as "take of its dust." (This is Ibn Fāris's own weighing of the two reports, not a settled definition.)

5. **A rising breath.** ṣuʿadāʾ is breathing out in pain — a breath that goes *up*, which he takes as fitting the root's analogy.

6. **ṣaʿūd of a she-camel.** One account: a camel whose calf dies, so she is brought back to her earlier offspring and yields milk to it — said to improve her milk. Another: one that miscarries her young. He offers this as the explanation of the line "She has the milk of the khaliyya and of the ṣaʿūd."

7. **To weigh heavily on someone.** taṣaʿʿadanī al-amr = the matter was hard on me. He cites ʿUmar — "the marriage address did not weigh heavily upon me" — and the saying, "Public address is an uphill climb, and on the man of sense it is heavier still."

8. **To set off through country.** Per Abū ʿAmr, aṣʿada fī al-bilād = he went off through the lands, in whatever direction he headed; illustrated by al-Aʿshā: "If you ask after me — many a questioner has asked eagerly about al-Aʿshā, wherever he set off."

9. **ṣaʿda, of a woman: upright of stature** — as though she were a ṣaʿda, the straight spear-shaft that grows even on its own and needs no straightening. Ibn Fāris marks this as a sense whose fit with the root's analogy is plausible rather than certain.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-ʿ-q (صعق) as a single root with one core idea: a violent striking together with an intense sound.

1. al-ṣaʿq (الصَّعْق) — an intense, powerful sound. Hence the phrase حِمَارٌ صَعِقُ الصَّوْتِ, "a donkey loud of voice," said when its braying is very loud.

2. al-ṣāʿiqa (الصَّاعِقَة) — the thunderbolt, i.e. the violent stroke that accompanies thunder.

3. al-ṣuʿāq (الصُّعَاق) — reported as another word for an intense sound.

4. ṣaʿiqa (صَعِقَ) — "to be struck down / to die," used of someone who dies as though a thunderbolt had struck him. Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an al-Zumar 39:68: "And the trumpet is blown, and whoever is in the heavens and on the earth is struck down (ṣaʿiqa), except whom God wills."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ص ع ر (ṣ-ʿ-r), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One consistent, regular root: a tilt/inclination in something.

1. al-ṣaʿar — a tilt in the neck. al-taṣʿīr — turning one's cheek away from looking at someone, out of self-conceit; sometimes a human or a male ostrich is naturally aṣʿar by constitution. The entry's central citation is Qur'an Luqman 31:18: "wa lā tuṣaʿʿir khaddaka li-l-nās" — "and do not turn your cheek away from people [in contempt]".
2. Ibn Fāris links this to al-ṣayʿariyyah — a camel's veering/swerving gait, and also the name of a brand-mark on she-camels' necks (possibly involving a curved shape), illustrated with a line of poetry by al-Musayyab.
3. Hadith citation: "there is none among them but aṣʿar or abtar" — glossed as: none but the conceited, or the lowly/disgraced.
4. sanām ṣayʿariyy — a huge hump, so named because great size brings a tilt/lean.
5. Closing outlier, explicitly flagged as not fitting the pattern: qarab muṣʿarr — a severe, forced pace, illustrated with a line of poetry, with Ibn Fāris himself expressing uncertainty ("God knows best").

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: أَصْحَٰب 78x "(the) companions"; صَاحِب 10x "to his companion"; صَٰحِبَة 4x "a companion"; صَىٰحِب 2x "o my two companions"; تُصَٰحِبْ 2x "but accompany them"; يُصْحَبُ 1x "can be protected"
text:
Ibn Sīda's entry for the root ص ح ب (ṣ-ḥ-b).

1. Core sense — to keep company. صحِبَه (with the verbal-noun variants ṣuḥba, ṣiḥāba, ṣaḥāba) means "he associated with / accompanied him." الصَّاحِب (al-ṣāḥib) is "the companion, the one who keeps company."

2. Grammatical note on صاحِب. Although it looks like an active participle, Arabic does not let it govern a direct object the way a participle does: one does not say "Zayd is companion-ing Amr." It is used like a noun in a construct (as غلام زيد, "Zayd's boy"), not like the participle ḍārib ("striking"), which can take either an accusative object or a construct. Ibn Sīda adds that in the construct-participle usage the form without tanwīn carries the same meaning as the form with it.

3. Plurals. Many: aṣḥāb, aṣāḥīb, ṣuḥbān, ṣiḥāb, and ṣiḥāba / ṣaḥāba (the last pair reported by al-Akhfash). The common usage is ṣiḥāb (kasra, no hāʾ) and ṣaḥāba (fatḥa, with hāʾ); the hāʾ can also attach to the kasra-form by analogy, added to mark the plural as feminine. ṣuḥba and ṣaḥb are collective nouns; al-Akhfash counted ṣaḥb a true plural, against Sībawayh.

4. Feminine plural. Of women: صواحبُ يوسُف ("the women around Joseph"). Al-Fārisī, from Abū l-Ḥasan, records a doubly-pluralised صواحبات, paralleled by poetic double plurals (ḥadāʾidāt, ṣarāriyyīn).

5. "One of the group." صاحب القوم means "a member of the people," like أخو القوم ("brother of the people") for one who belongs to them. Ibn Sīda cites Q 53:2, (ما ضَلَّ صاحِبُكم وما غَوَى) "Your companion has not strayed nor erred," glossing ṣāḥib as the Prophet.

6. Derived verb forms.
- اصطحب / تصاحب: two men became mutual companions.
- أصحب: (a) to come to have a companion; (b) of a man, his son grew to manhood and became like him — as though his companion.
- استصحب: to invite someone into companionship; and by extension, whatever suits or matches a thing "keeps its company" (a verse: musk sometimes keeps company with the cheaper rāmak base).

7. A second branch — to guard/protect. أصحب / اصطحب can mean "he guarded/protected him." Ibn Sīda reads Q 21:43, (ولا هم منّا يُصْحَبون), as "nor shall they be protected from Us," with a supporting verse ("my companion is guarded from the promptings of evil").

8. Related senses of submission and going straight.
- أصحب الشيءُ: a thing became tractable and obeyed after being difficult.
- المُصْحِب: one going straight on without tarrying. A cited verse contrasts al-mumārī (the disputer) with al-muṣāḥib (the compliant companion).

9. Physical/material senses of the muṣḥab pattern.
- أصحب الماءُ: water became covered with moss/algae.
- أديم مُصْحَب: a hide still bearing its wool, hair, or fur; قربة مُصْحَبة: a waterskin with some wool left in it; قضيب مُصْحِب: a rod still in its bark (with a verse of Kuthayyir ʿAzza).
- رجل مُصْحَب: a madman.

10. Miscellaneous.
- صَحَبَ المذبوحَ: to flay a slaughtered animal (a dialectal usage).
- تصحَّبَ من مجالستنا: he felt shy of sitting with us.
- Proper names: Banū Ṣaḥb — two sub-clans, one in Bāhila and one in Kalb; Ṣaḥbān — a man's name.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
**Root ṣ-ḥ-f (صحف) — Ibn Fāris, *Maqāyīs al-Lugha***

Ibn Fāris treats this as a "sound" (single, coherent) root whose core idea is **something spread out flat, and breadth/extent**. He then lists the uses that fall under that idea:

1. **صَحِيف (ṣaḥīf)** — reported as the *face*, i.e. the flat surface, of the earth.

2. **صَحِيفة (ṣaḥīfa)** — the outer skin of a man's face (again a flat expanse). He cites al-Buʿayth: every man of the tribe of Kulayb has a "face-skin" more abject under men's feet than a sandal.

3. **صَحِيفة (ṣaḥīfa)** — belonging to the same root-category, the flat surface *written upon*: a sheet or leaf. Two plurals are noted: **صَحَائِف (ṣaḥāʾif)**, and also **صُحُف (ṣuḥuf)**, which he explains morphologically as if it were formed as the plural of the shorter form *ṣaḥīf* rather than of *ṣaḥīfa*. An unnamed poet's line pairs "the ties of kinship and the written sheets" as both yearning toward the speakers.

4. **صَحْفة (ṣaḥfa)** — a wide, flattened-out serving bowl.

5. **صِحَاف (ṣiḥāf)** — on the authority of al-Shaybānī: small hollows or catch-basins made to hold water; plural **صُحُف (ṣuḥuf)**.

The organising method is visible throughout: Ibn Fāris derives the "written sheet" sense not as a separate meaning but as one more instance of a flat, spread-out surface — alongside the earth's surface, facial skin, a shallow bowl and a water hollow.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Raghib al-Isfahani derives several distinct senses from the root s-b-w/s-b-':

1. al-sabiyy - "child." One who has not yet reached puberty. A man with children is called musbin. Cited: Maryam 19:29, where the infant Jesus in the cradle is called sabiyyan.

2. sabaa/yasbuu (sabwah) - "to yearn, to incline." Said of someone who longs for something and acts as children do. Cited: Yusuf 12:33, where Yusuf says "I would incline (asbu) toward them and be among the ignorant" - expressing the pull toward temptation he seeks to avoid. Also notes the idiom asbaanii fa-sabawtu, "he made me incline, so I inclined."

3. al-sabaa - a named wind. The wind that blows facing the qibla, i.e. the east wind.

4. sabaytu (form III), used of weapons. Sabaytu al-sayf: to sheathe a sword upside-down. Sabaytu al-rumh: to tilt a spear, readying it for a thrust.

5. al-Sabi'un - the Qur'anic community name. Al-Raghib records two derivations: (a) from the people who were on the religion of Nuh (Noah); more broadly, some said anyone who leaves one religion for another is called sabi', on the model of saba'a naabu al-ba'ir - "the camel's tooth erupted/came out." On this view the reading "Sabiin" (without hamza) found in some recitations is explained as a softening (takhfif) of the hamza, comparable to al-khaati'un read as al-khaatun in al-Haaqqah 69:37. (b) Alternatively, from sabaa yasbuu (sense 2 above, "to incline"), without any hamza in the root at all. Both Qur'anic occurrences of the term are cited: al-Hajj 22:17 ("the Sabi'in and the Christians") and al-Baqarah 2:62 ("the Christians and the Sabi'in").

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ص ب ع (ṣ-b-ʿ) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-b-ʿ as a single root, with further senses derived from it by metaphorical extension (istiʿārah).

1. Core sense — the finger. Iṣbaʿ = "finger," singular of aṣābiʿ ("fingers"). Its grammatical gender was disputed: usually feminine, though sometimes treated as masculine. As evidence for the feminine usage he cites a hadith in which the Prophet, of his own bleeding finger, says: "Are you but a finger that has bled (damiti), and in God's path is what you have met?" — the feminine verb form damiti confirms iṣbaʿ as feminine here.

2. To point at someone while backbiting. Ṣabaʿa fulānun bi-fulānin, "so-and-so pointed at so-and-so," is said of gesturing at a person with the finger while speaking ill of him.

3. Metaphorical sense — a fine trace or good influence. Extended from "finger," al-iṣbaʿ can mean al-athar al-ḥasan, a visible good mark someone has left. Two illustrations are given:
   - A proverb: "So-and-so has an iṣbaʿ in his wealth" — he has left a fine, visible improvement in it.
   - Said of a skilled camel-herder: "He has an iṣbaʿ over [the camels]" — his good care shows in their visible condition. Ibn Fāris quotes the poet al-Rāʿī describing such a shepherd: frail-looking, with a thin staff and veins showing from age, yet his camels visibly bear the mark of his good care even in drought, when other people's herds do not.

4. Related verbal noun — al-ṣabʿ. The act of pouring out the contents of a vessel from between your two fingers.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-b-ḥ as a single coherent root whose core sense is a color — specifically redness (ḥumra).

1. Root sense — redness / light of dawn. He derives the family from redness: ṣubḥ (dawn) is so named for its redness, as is the miṣbāḥ (lamp) for its glow; from the same idea comes wajh ṣabīḥ (a bright, handsome face). Al-ṣabāḥ is \"the light of day.\" He names this the root, from which the other senses branch.

2. The morning drink. From \"morning\" derives al-ṣabūḥ, a morning draught, and the verb iṣṭabaḥa (to take one); such a draught is called al-jāshiriyya — illustrated by a verse boasting that after the morning draught the drinkers heed no chief. A related proverb, \"more lying than the morning-drinking captive\" (akdhab min al-akhīdh al-ṣabḥān), is explained by a story: captors questioned a prisoner about his tribe; he lied and pointed to a distant region, and when they stabbed him the milk of his morning draught ran out before the blood.

3. Further branch-senses tied to morning:
- al-miṣbāḥ: a she-camel that stays couched at her resting place until morning.
- al-taṣabbuḥ: sleeping in the morning.
- yawm al-ṣabāḥ: the day of a raid (attested in a line of al-Aʿshā about morning battle-dust).
- Idioms: uṣbūḥata kulli yawm (every morning); dhā ṣabūḥ (having a morning-drink).
- al-maṣābīḥ: the cups used for the morning draught.
- ṣubḥ / ṣibḥ khāmisa: \"the morning of the fifth [day],\" recorded with two vowelings.

4. Back to the color root. From the original sense of redness comes al-ṣabaḥ, intense redness in the hair, whence asad aṣbaḥ, a lion of reddish coloring.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-b-b as one root meaning, "the pouring out of a thing", and says that every branch of the chapter goes back to it.

1. **Pouring.** ṣababtu l-māʾa aṣubbuhu ṣabban: "I poured out the water".

2. **A downward slope.** By analogy, ground that slopes down is ṣabab (plural aṣbāb), as though it poured down in its descent. In a ḥadīth it is said of him (God bless him and his family and grant him peace) that when he walked it was as though he were going down a slope (ṣabab), and a rajaz line speaks of "a land of rises and descents (aṣbāb)".

3. **Troops and flocks.** al-ṣubbah is a troop of horses, as though they pour down in a raid; a flock of sheep is likewise called ṣabbah.

4. **Black snakes.** Black snakes are called al-ṣabb, because when they strike they pour themselves down on the one they bite.

5. **al-ṣabīb.** It is said to be the juice of sesame leaves, or else pressed henna juice. Ibn Fāris cites a verse in which stale water looks like "henna and ṣabīb together" as evidence that the first view is correct. Others say al-ṣabīb is pure blood, and extracted safflower dye.

6. **The remnant.** al-ṣubābah is the water left in a vessel. taṣābabtu l-ināʾ means drinking that remnant, and taṣābabtu l-shayʾ getting only a little of something, as in al-Shammākh's verse about a people "after whom I have had life only in its last drops".

7. **Love-longing.** al-ṣabābah comes from ṣabba ilayhi, "he yearned toward him"; a man is ṣabb when passion overcomes him, which Ibn Fāris explains as the heart pouring itself out.

8. **Heat and vanishing.** taṣabbaba l-ḥarr: the heat grew intense, as though poured upon the earth. taṣabṣaba l-shayʾ: the thing went away and was wiped out, as though it had been poured out.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root s-b-gh has one core meaning: to colour or dye something with some colour.

1. Basic verb sense: sabaghtuhu asbughuhu - "I dyed it / I dye it." The same word is used for a fresh date (rutaba) as it ripens: qad sabbaghat, "it has taken on colour" - i.e., begun to change colour as it ripens.

2. Quranic phrase sibghata Llah ("the sibgha of God," Q 2:138): Ibn Faris records two competing explanations current among scholars of his time, without adopting either as his own.
   - Some say it means God's fitra - the innate constitution/nature He gave His creation.
   - Others say it means anything at all by which a person draws near to God - i.e., sibgha there stands generically for "a means of nearness to God," not one specific act.

3. Al-asbagh (a term for a horse): a horse with white at the tip of its tail - a lesser/different marking than what is called al-ashkal (left unglossed in the entry itself). Ibn Faris explains the name as a metaphor: the tail-tip is figuratively "dyed" white, as if colour had been applied to its end.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives ص-ب-ر (ṣ-b-r) from three distinct roots: (1) restraint/confinement, (2) the top or upper parts of a thing, and (3) a kind of stone.

1. Restraint (al-ḥabs). Al-ṣabr means to hold or confine. One says "I held my soul to that matter" (ṣabartu nafsī), i.e. restrained it. A verse illustrates it: "So I held firm a noble soul… it stays anchored when the coward's soul rises up in panic." Related terms:
 - al-maṣbūra: an animal confined and held to be killed. Ibn Fāris notes the Prophet forbade killing any animal this way (ṣabr).
 - al-ṣabīr: a guarantor or surety, so named because he "endures" (yaṣbiru) the liability. Hence ṣabartu bihi = "I stood surety for it."
 - ṣabartu al-insān: to make someone swear by God with the most binding oath.

2. The top/upper parts. ṣubr of anything is its highest part. The aṣbār of a vessel are its sides or rims (singular ṣubr), as in the verse: "I filled it with blood up to its brims."

3. Stone. al-ṣubra of stones is what is hard and thick (plural ṣibār). Ibn Fāris cites Ibn Durayd: al-ṣubāra is "a piece of iron or stone," in al-Aʿshā's line "…that man was not created of stone." Ibn Durayd noted the Baghdadis read it "ṣabāra" and said he did not know their intent; Ibn Fāris explains they meant al-ṣibār (the hard, thick [stones]), as in another line of al-Aʿshā, "just before dawn, the sounds of the ṣibār," with the final hāʾ added as a plural marker. Abū ʿUbayd adds that al-ṣubr is pebbly-but-not-coarse ground, whence a lava-field is called umm ṣabbār; and onto this is carried the saying "the people fell into umm ṣabbūr," used when they land in a grave, momentous predicament.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
poets_named: Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad) ×2; unnamed verse ×2; Ibn Muqbil (lived into Islam); al-Hudhalī (lived into Islam)
text:
Root Ṣ-B-W (ص ب و), from al-Zamakhsharī's Asās al-Balāgha.

**Core sense: yearning / inclining, especially with youthful passion**
- "ṣabawtu ilayhi" = I yearned toward him; the noun ṣabwah is that longing or pull — the impulsive, youthful kind (often erotic infatuation).
- A ṣabwah "in" someone is glossed as "the heedlessness of youthfulness" (jahlat al-futuwwah).
- Passion is said to "aṣbā" or "taṣabbā" a person — to stir this youthful yearning in him. Dhū al-Rumma is cited using taṣabbā of even a wild mountain-goat moved by a call.
- "taṣābā al-shaykh" — an old man acting young.
- "ṣabā" (ṣibā) is also simply the noun for childhood/youth: "I saw him in his ṣibā."

**Children**
- ṣibyah, aṣbiyah, uṣaybiyah (diminutive plural), ṣibyān — all mean "young children."
- "aṣbat al-marʾah" — a woman's children multiplied.
- muṣbin / muṣbiyah / muṣbiyāt — a woman (or women) with many/young children.

**Overturning or tilting something**
- "ṣābā al-shayʾ" — he flipped or tilted it. A cited verse plays on this: builders raise a covering on bow-frames, and one onlooker accuses the builder of having "skewed" (ṣābā) the construction while another says it turned out fine.
- "ṣābā l-bayt" — said when a reciter fails to deliver a line of poetry correctly/metrically upright.
- "tuṣābī l-kalām" — to let speech run crooked, off its proper course.
- "ṣābā sayfahu/sikkīnahu" — to present a sword or knife tilted, not in its proper straight orientation. Related courtesy expressions: when handing someone a knife, turn it (ṣābihi) and offer the handle (niṣāb) toward them, not the blade.

**The ṣabā wind**
- "ṣabati l-rīḥ" — the wind blew as ṣabā (the east wind), paralleling janabat/shamalat for south/north winds. A verse describes wind alternating between blowing as ṣabā and as janūb (south wind) over something as it is led along. A related expression puns on the wind "pouring" (ṣabba) and "blowing as ṣabā" (ṣabā) — being spelled the same, so "when the winds blow as ṣabā" plays on "when the winds pour."
- One explanation given for the name: the ṣabā wind is called that because it blows facing the Kaʿbah directly, "as if it yearns for it" — explicitly tying the wind's name back to the root sense of longing.

**Metaphorical extensions (ومن المجاز)**
- ṣibyān al-jalīd / ṣibyān al-maṭar — the small beads of condensed frost, or the small droplets of rain, likened to tiny pearls. Several verses are cited describing droplets of frost or dew rolling down a surface "like strung pearls" (including one by Ibn Muqbil), with a note that some transmitters record the word differently as "ṣiʾbān" in one of these lines.
- ṣabiyyāhu (dual) — the two tapering ends of the jawbones nearest the chin; a verse of Dhū al-Rumma describes a worn camel as "bare" at these two points.
- ṣabiyy al-qadam — the instep of the foot, the area between its fleshy raised pad (ḥimārah) and the toes.
- ṣabiyy al-sayf — the part of a sword blade just short of its point/tip; a verse by al-Hudhalī praises a blow struck with "every sharp sword possessing a ṣabiyy and a gleam."

**Closing usage**, returning to the core sense: "so-and-so yaṣbū toward lofty matters" — noble qualities are said to "aṣbā" a person, giving him a ṣabwah toward them, so that "his soul yearns toward the good."

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-d-ʿ as one sound root whose core idea is a splitting or parting open in something.

1. Basic sense — to split. صَدَعْتُهُ فَانْصَدَعَ وَتَصَدَّعَ: "I split it, and it cracked / split apart" (the derived forms VII and V are the intransitive result).

2. Cutting across open ground. صَدَعْتُ الْفَلَاةَ, "I split the desert," meaning to traverse it; and a guide who opens the way is a مِصْدَع (miṣdaʿ).

3. Plant growth. الصَّدْع (al-ṣadʿ) is vegetation, so called because it splits the earth open. Ibn Fāris cites Q 86:12, "and the earth possessing the ṣadʿ."

4. Speaking out openly. Belonging to the same root-idea: صَدَعَ بِالْحَقِّ, to utter the truth openly and publicly. He cites Q 15:94, addressed to the prophet: "so declare openly what you are commanded."

5. A group breaking up. تَصَدَّعَ الْقَوْمُ, the people dispersed / split apart.

6. A detachment of camels. الصِّدْعَة (al-ṣidʿa) is a portion of camels, around sixty or so, as though it had split off from a large host.

7. Anomalous to the root-idea. Ibn Fāris marks الصَّدَع (al-ṣadaʿ), a young mountain goat, as falling outside the chapter's core meaning.

text:
Ibn Fāris holds that most of ṣ-d goes back to one idea, turning away and turning aside, and that some further words stand outside it.

1. **Turning away (the root meaning).** al-ṣadd is turning away; ṣadda, yaṣuddu is inclining toward one of two sides. Transitively, ṣadadtu fulānan ʿan al-amr means "I turned so-and-so aside from the matter."

2. **The sides of a valley.** al-ṣaddān are the two sides of a valley (singular ṣadd). Ibn Fāris says this fits the root, since a valley side necessarily slopes, that is, inclines.

3. **Words he regards as outliers.** Others report that al-ṣadad is what faces something ("this house is on the ṣadad of that one"), and that al-ṣadad is also nearness; that al-ṣuddād is the road to water; and that al-ṣadd is a mountain. Ibn Fāris says these are not a root in his view because they are far from the analogy, and if they are authentic they should be referred back to the root meaning.

4. **Crying out (sound, but a separate matter).** ṣadda, yaṣiddu (with i in the imperfect) means to cry out loudly. Ibn Fāris says this is sound but does not belong to this chapter. Some read Q 43:57 (al-Zukhruf) "when your people yaṣiddūn at it", and explained it as "they cry out".

5. **Ṣadīd.** al-ṣadīd is blood mixed with pus; aṣadda al-jurḥ means the wound produced it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-d-f as two separate bases: (1) inclining or turning aside, and (2) a concrete object.

Base 1 — inclining / turning away:
1. صَدَفَ عَنِ الشَّيْءِ (ṣadafa ʿan al-shayʾ): to incline away from something, turn from it and go off. He cites Qurʾān 6:157, "We shall requite those who turn away (yaṣdifūna) from Our signs."
2. الصَّدَف (al-ṣadaf) of a camel: a defect in which the foot-pad of a fore- or hind leg tilts toward the outer side; verb صَدِفَ (ṣadifa).
3. الصَّوَادِف (al-ṣawādif): camels standing behind the ones already at the trough, waiting for the drinkers to leave so they can take their turn. Verse cited: "the ones watching for their turn, the ṣawādif."
4. الصَّدَف (al-ṣadaf): the side or flank of a mountain — so called, he says, precisely because it slopes off toward one of the two directions.

Base 2 — the object:
5. الصَّدَف (al-ṣadaf): the sea-shell (maḥāra); Ibn Fāris notes only that it is well known and offers no derivation for it.
