quran_words: صَادِق 59x "truthful"; مُصَدِّق 19x "confirming"; صَدَقَ 15x "you have spoken the truth to us"; صِدْق 14x "sound"; صَدَّقَ 10x "found true"; صَدَقَٰت 8x "the charities"; تَصَدَّقَ 6x "and be charitable"; صَدَقَة 5x "charity"; صِدِّيق 5x "a man of truth"; أَصْدَق 2x "(is) truer"; تَصْدِيق 2x "a confirmation"; مُتَصَدِّقِين 2x "and the men who give charity"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ṣ-d-q from a single core idea: strength or firmness in a thing — whether in speech or otherwise. He connects every sense back to this notion of solidity.

1. ṣidq (truthfulness) — the opposite of lying (kadhib). Named for its inner strength: truth has firmness, whereas a lie has none and is void. The root's concrete origin appears in shayʾ ṣadq (a solid/hard thing) and rumḥ ṣadq (a firm spear). Hence ṣadaqūhum al-qitāl means "they stood firm/true against them in battle," its opposite being kadhabūhum.

2. ṣiddīq — one who cleaves constantly to truthfulness.

3. ṣadāq — a woman's dowry, so called because it is a firm, binding right. Variant forms: ṣadāq, ṣudqa, ṣaduqa. Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 4:4, "give women their dowries (ṣaduqātihinna) as a free gift," noting the variant reading ṣadqātihinna.

4. ṣadaqa — what a person gives away as charity from himself and his wealth.

5. muṣaddiq / mutaṣaddiq — Ibn Fāris records a usage dispute. Citing al-Qutaybī, he says people wrongly use "yataṣaddaq" both for one who gives and one who asks; correctly, the mutaṣaddiq is the giver, as in Qur'an 12:88, "and give charity to us" (wa-taṣaddaq ʿalaynā). He also cites al-Khalīl's contrary view that both feeder and asker are called mutaṣaddiq equally — but concludes that in the Qur'an the word means the giver. Separately, muṣaddiq also denotes the official who collects the alms (ṣadaqāt) on livestock such as sheep.

6. rajulu ṣidq — "a man of genuine worth/truth."

7. ṣadāqa (friendship) — derived from ṣidq in the sense of sincerity in affection. The word ṣadīq serves for a single person, two, a group, or a woman alike; occasional plurals are aṣdiqāʾ and aṣādiq. A line of verse is cited ending "...to a far-off land of few friends (aṣādiq)."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: صَدْر 44x "their breasts"; يُصْدِرَ 1x "take away"; يَصْدُرُ 1x "will proceed"
text:
Ibn Fāris identifies two sound roots under ص د ر:

1. Departing / going back — the opposite of al-wird (coming down to water). One says ṣadara ʿan al-māʾ ("he departed from the water") and ṣadara ʿan al-bilād ("he departed from the land"), meaning he had arrived there and then moved off. On the grammar, al-Aḥmar notes a vowel distinction: ṣadar (dāl vowelled) is the noun, while the verbal noun (maṣdar) takes a silent dāl — ṣadr. A cited verse uses ṣadr al-maṭiyya ("the mount's setting out") as this verbal noun.

2. The chest (ṣadr) — of a human and of other things; plural ṣudūr. Ibn Fāris cites Q 22:46, "but rather the hearts that are within the breasts (al-ṣudūr) grow blind." From this sense he derives:
   - ṣidār: a garment covering the head and chest.
   - ṣidār: a brand on a camel's chest.
   - taṣdīr: a rope girthing a camel at the chest so its load is not pushed backward.
   - muṣaddar: the lion, named for the strength of its chest.
   - maṣdūr: one who suffers from a chest ailment.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ص-د-ي (Ṣ-D-Y) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris opens by flagging this as a root whose words scatter across unrelated meanings — no single underlying idea ties them together. He then lists the senses:

1. Owl. Al-ṣadā is the male owl (plural: aṣdāʾ). A verse of poetry uses it in a line of scorn: people left behind are worth nothing — "nothing but owls (aṣdāʾ) and skulls (hām)."

2. Brain / hearing. Al-ṣadā also names the brain itself, or (on another account) specifically the seat of hearing within it — which is why one curses someone with "may God deafen his ṣadā."

3. Echo. On yet another account, this is really "the echo of sound" — the thing that calls back to you when you shout near a mountain. A poet uses it describing a ruined, abandoned dwelling: its echo has gone silent, its traces are worn away, it no longer answers a visitor's call.

4. Good steward. A man who manages his property well is called ṣadā māl ("a ṣadā of wealth") — but Ibn Fāris notes this word is only ever used attached to another noun (in construct), never on its own.

5. Thirst. Al-ṣadā also means thirst: a thirsty man is ṣadin/ṣādin, a thirsty woman ṣādiya.

6. To crane forward. The verb taṣaddā (as in taṣaddā li-l-shayʾ) means to lift oneself up and watch something intently, gazing toward it.

7. Clapping. Al-taṣdiya means clapping the two hands together. Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 8:35: "Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping (taṣdiya)."

8. Tall palms. Al-ṣawādī, said of palm trees, means the tall ones.

9. To conciliate. Ṣādaytu fulānan means you handled someone gently/diplomatically (dārayta-hu).

10. To repay in kind. A related sense — ṣādaytu fulānan muṣādātan — is glossed as treating someone exactly as he had treated you (this part of the source text appears to be an editorial reconstruction of a gap).

11. A different word entirely. Ibn Fāris adds a caution: if a hamza follows the dāl, this is a different root altogether — ṣadaʾ, meaning the rust of iron. From this comes the expression ṣāghirun ṣadiʾ, "lowly and rust-stained," using rust as a figure for disgrace.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
**Root ṣ-f-ḥ (صفح) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha**

Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-f-ḥ as a single sound root with one consistent idea running through it: **breadth / a wide flat side**. He then derives each usage from that core.

1. **Breadth, a broad flat face.** The *ṣafḥ* of a thing is its broad surface. A *muṣfaḥ* head is a broad one. A *ṣafīḥa* is a broad sword; the two *ṣafḥa*s of a sword are its two flat faces. Any broad stone is a *ṣafīḥa* (plural *ṣafāʾiḥ*) or a *ṣuffāḥ*. He cites al-Nābigha, whose line describes cleaving doubled-weave Salūqī mail and striking sparks — "the fire of al-ḥubāḥib" — off the broad stones.

2. **Clasping hands (*muṣāfaḥa*).** Ibn Fāris files this under the same idea: it is as if one presses his hand flat against the broad face of the other's hand.

3. **Side, flank.** *Ṣafḥ* means the side of the body; the two *ṣafḥ*s of anything are its two sides.

4. **Turning aside from an offence (*ṣafaḥa ʿanhu*).** Ibn Fāris explains this idiom — turning away from someone's wrongdoing — as belonging to the same root-sense and as a figure of speech: in turning away, a person has in effect turned his broad side and flank toward the other rather than his face.

5. **Refusing a request (*ṣafaḥtu / aṣfaḥtu al-rajul*).** When someone asks and you withhold, the same image applies: you showed him your side as you turned away.

6. **Driving camels past the trough (*ṣafaḥtu al-ibil ʿalā al-ḥawḍ*).** To pass them by it — as though you showed the trough their flanks, their broad sides.

7. **An outlier he flags as not fitting the root idea:** *ṣafaḥtu al-rajul ṣafḥan*, meaning to give a man a drink — any drink, at any time. Ibn Fāris marks this explicitly as anomalous (*shadhdha ʿan al-bāb*).

**Method note:** the entry is built on Ibn Fāris's characteristic argument that a whole family of apparently unrelated usages (broad stones, handshakes, pardoning, refusing, watering camels) all trace back to one physical image — width and the flat side — with any residue openly labelled as falling outside the pattern.

dictionary: Ibn ʿAbbās — Gharīb al-Qurʾān fī Shiʿr al-ʿArab, Attributed to ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās (d. 900)
text:
Root ص ف ص ف (ṢFṢF) — ṣafṣaf

This entry is a short question-and-answer exchange (the "questions of the Qurʾān's difficult words" format attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās), built around a single verse.

1. Meaning — "level, even ground." Asked about God's words fa-yadharuhā qāʿan ṣafṣafan, "then He will leave it a level plain" (Q20:106), Ibn ʿAbbās glosses both nouns in the phrase: al-qāʿ = smooth, bare ground; al-ṣafṣaf = even, level ground (al-mustawī).

2. Poetic proof. Asked whether the Arabs actually used the word this way, he quotes a line of verse describing a dense, grayish army or mass so solid that even the jagged peaks of Mount Raḍwā, if hurled against it, would be flattened — "turned level" (ʿāda ṣafṣafā). The citation establishes ṣafṣaf as ordinary pre-Qurʾānic Arabic for "made flat/level," not a specialized or invented term.

No etymology, wazn, or plural pattern is discussed — the entry is limited to this one gloss and its poetic attestation.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris identifies two distinct sound senses for the root ص ف د (ṣ-f-d):

1. **Giving, a gift** — al-ṣafad. The verb aṣfadtuhu means "I gave him [something]." An anonymous verse is quoted in which the speaker says he offered his praise/eulogy freely, not in exchange for a ṣafad (a gift or reward).

2. **Binding, fettering** — al-ṣafd means a fetter or shackle (equivalent to al-ghull), and is also said to mean the act of binding or restraining (al-taqyīd) more generally. Its plural al-aṣfād means "fetters" (aqyād). A near-synonym, al-ṣifād, likewise means "fetter." An anonymous verse is cited picturing a man named Maʿbad led away bound in a ṣifād, with the speaker reproaching the captor (a man of ʿĀmir) for showing his kinsman no mercy.

Ibn Fāris also notes the ḥadīth "When Ramaḍān begins, the devils are shackled (ṣuffidat al-shayāṭīn)" as an instance of this second, binding sense.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: صَفّ 7x "(in) rows"; صَٰفَّٰت 3x "by those lined"; مَصْفُوفَة 2x "lined up"; صَوَافّ 1x "(when) lined up"; صَّافُّون 1x "stand in rows"
text:
Ibn Fāris holds that ṣ-f-f has one root meaning: evenness in a thing, and two things standing level with each other in the same place.

1. **Row, rank.** al-ṣaff is a row. "The two stood in a row" is said when each stands beside the other. The people iṣṭaffū or taṣāffū when they line up together.

2. **Level ground as the origin.** Ibn Fāris says the source of this is al-ṣafṣaf, level ground. Hence maṣaff (plural maṣāff), the place where fighters stand when they have drawn up in ranks for battle.

3. **The ṣafūf camel.** al-ṣafūf is a she-camel that fills two milking-vessels at a single milking. The same word is also used of a she-camel that sets her forelegs evenly side by side when milked.

4. **An exception: al-ṣafīf.** Ibn Fāris lists al-ṣafīf as falling outside the chapter's pattern. He grants that some way of fitting it to the root meaning might be found, but says he dislikes a forced, contrived analogy. Some define al-ṣafīf as dried strips of meat; others as meat carried on journeys, stewed or roasted but not fully cooked. He cites the verse: "The meat-cooks kept on, some bringing to doneness strips of roast meat, or a hastened pot-dish."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ص ف ن (ṣ-f-n), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Two sound, distinct roots:

First — a way of standing. al-ṣufūn — a horse standing on three legs with the fourth raised, though its hoof-tip still grazes the ground; al-ṣāfin — one who stands with feet aligned. A hadith of al-Barāʾ describes the Companions standing behind the Prophet ṣufūnan (in this attentive posture). From this comes taṣāfana al-qawm — people sharing something (water) by turns, using al-ṣufn, a leather vessel for drawing water, illustrated with a line of poetry about sharing a waterskin in turn. Ibn Fāris notes this sharing was reportedly done by a careful eye-measure, giving each person just enough to cover the pupil.

Second — a receptacle. (Named in the opening but not elaborated separately in this excerpt beyond the al-ṣufn vessel above.)

Outlier: Ibn Fāris flags al-ṣāfin — a specific vein (the saphenous vein) — as not fitting either of the two established senses.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris analyses the root ṣ-f-r as having six distinct root-senses: (1) a colour, (2) emptiness, (3) a metal of the earth, (4) a sound, (5) a season/time, (6) a plant.

1. Colour — ṣufra is "yellowness." Banū al-Aṣfar ("sons of the yellow one") is a name for the Byzantine kings, said to be because a yellowness affected their ancestor. He also records al-aṣfar used for "black," citing a verse in which a poet's horses and riding-camels are called ṣufr, "their young ones like raisins."

2. Emptiness — ṣifr means "empty." He cites the curse-formula "may his vessel be emptied," i.e. may his livestock die. Under the same heading he places the phrase used of a madman, "he is in ṣufra / ṣifra" (vowelled either way), meaning he is in the days when his reason leaves him; Ibn Fāris judges this derivation sound, since the man is as though emptied of his intellect.

3. Metal — al-ṣufr is a mineral of the earth, said to be nuḥās (copper/brass). The variant vowelling al-ṣifr is also reported. On authority traced back to al-Aṣmaʿī: nuḥās can mean "natural disposition, origin," and nuḥās is also the ṣufr from which vessels are made — al-Aṣmaʿī vowelling it ṣufr (with u), while Abū ʿUbayd gave the same account but vowelled it ṣifr (with i).

4. Sound — ṣafīr is the whistling of a bird. The expression "there is not a ṣāfir in it" (i.e. no living thing) belongs here, as though the referent were something that makes a sound.

5. Time — Ṣafar is the name of the month. Citing Ibn Durayd: there were two months in the year called "the two Ṣafars," one of which came to be called al-Muḥarram in Islam. Related: al-ṣafarī is vegetation appearing at the start of autumn, and al-ṣafarī in animal breeding is the birth-season falling after al-yaqaẓī.

6. Plant — al-ṣafār is a plant, said to be the withered form of the pasture grass buhmā, with a verse describing men spending the night beside their colt "pulling al-ṣafār out from its two lips."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: ٱصْطَفَىٰ 12x "has chosen"; أَصْفَىٰ 2x "then has your lord chosen (for) you"; صَفْوَان 1x "(that of a) smooth rock"; مُصْطَفَيْن 1x "the chosen ones"; مُّصَفًّى 1x "purified"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ص-ف-و (ṣād, fāʾ, and a weak final letter) from a single idea: being clear and free of any admixture.

1. Core sense — الصَّفَاء (clarity, purity): the opposite of الكَدَر (murkiness). The verb صَفَا / يَصْفُو means "to become clear or unmixed."

2. The choice/select part: لَكَ صَفْوُ هَذَا الْأَمْرِ ("yours is the pure, best part of this matter"). Ibn Fāris applies this to Muḥammad as صِفْوَةُ اللَّه — God's chosen elect (khiyra) and muṣṭafā from among His creation (stated as this author's usage).

3. الصَّفِيّ / الصَّفِيَّة (plural الصَّفَايَا): the special portion a leader picks out for himself from war-spoils — illustrated by a verse listing a chief's shares ("Yours is the quarter and the choice picks…, the nashīṭa and the surplus"). The name comes from اصطفى, "to select."

4. Same words also denote a she-camel rich in milk or a palm-tree heavy with fruit (plural الصَّفَايَا) — again because the owner picks it out.

5. أَصْفَتِ الدَّجَاجَة (verbal noun إِصْفَاء): a hen ceasing to lay, as if "cleared" of eggs. Ibn Fāris notes the special form afʿalat marks it off from similar verbs, and adds that a poet whose verse dries up is likened to it.

6. الصَّفَا / الصَّفْوَان (singular صَفْوَانَة): smooth, bare stone, so called because it is clear of clay and sand. Al-Aṣmaʿī is cited that صَفْوَان, صَفْوَاء, and صَفَا are one word, with a verse on the smooth rock slipping underfoot.

7. يَوْمٌ صَفْوَانُ: a day of clear sunshine but bitter cold.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: صَٰغِرُون 5x "humiliated"; صَغِير 3x "small"; صَغِيرَة 2x "a small"; أَصْغَر 2x "smaller"; صَغَار 1x "a humiliation"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-gh-r as a single sound root carrying two linked ideas: smallness and lowliness/contemptibility.

1. Smallness. al-ṣighar is the opposite of al-kibar (largeness); al-ṣaghīr (the small one) is the contrary of al-kabīr (the large or great one).

2. Lowliness / submission. al-ṣāghir is one who accepts being wronged or subjected (ḍaym), with the verbal nouns ṣughr and ṣaghār.

3. Applied to a camel's cry. The verb is used of a she-camel: aṣgharat wa-akbarat. Here al-iṣghār is her low, soft yearning cry (ḥanīn) and al-ikbār is the high, loud one — smallness/largeness carried over into pitch. Cited from al-Khansāʾ: "She has two yearning cries, a low one (iṣghār) and a loud one (ikbār)."

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
al-Rāghib defines al-ṣaghw as inclining (al-mayl) and gives these uses.

1. **Inclining, tilting.** The stars and the sun are said to ṣaghā when they incline toward setting. A vessel is tilted: ṣaghaytu al-ināʾ, or aṣghaytuhu.

2. **Inclining the ear.** aṣghaytu ilā fulān means "I inclined my hearing toward him". Here he cites Q 6:113: "and so that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline toward it" (wa-li-taṣghā ilayhi afʾidatu …).

3. **Verb forms.** Reported forms are ṣaghawtu ilayhi with the imperfect aṣghū or aṣghā, and the verbal nouns ṣaghw and ṣughiyy. Others give ṣaghaytu with the imperfect aṣghā, and the derived form aṣghaytu with the imperfect uṣghī.

4. **Those who incline to a person.** A man's ṣāghiya are the people who incline toward him.

5. **A tilted vessel: a reduced share.** "So-and-so's vessel is tilted" (muṣghan ināʾuhu) means his share is diminished. The phrase is sometimes used as an indirect way of speaking of his perishing.

6. **A slant of the eye or jaw.** One says "his eye is ṣaghwāʾ toward such-and-such", that is, inclined toward it. al-ṣaghy is a tilt in the jaw (al-ḥanak) and in the eye.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يُصْهَرُ 1x "will be melted"; صِهْر 1x "and marriage relationship"
text:
Ibn Faris derives the root s-h-r from two distinct underlying senses.

1. Nearness / in-law kinship (qurba)
The noun al-sihr means al-khatan, a relation acquired through marriage.
- Al-Khalil distinguished the two sides: a man's own blood-household are called akhtan; the household on the woman's side (i.e., her husband's people, as seen from her side) are called ashar. Some Arabs, though, used ashar loosely for in-laws on either side.
- Ibn al-A'rabi defined al-ishar more broadly as a state of mutual inviolability/protection (al-taharrum) established by any of three means: living as neighbors (jiwar), blood kinship (nasab), or marriage (tazawwuj).
- This broader sense is illustrated by a poetic line praising a man for leading war-horses, forming marriage-alliances with kings (ishar al-muluk), and enduring hardships that would exhaust others.

2. Melting
The verb sahara means to melt something, e.g. sahartu al-shahmata, "I melted the fat." Al-suhara names the rendered/melted residue. A form-VIII variant, istahartu, carries the same meaning.
- A cited verse plays on this sense: praising someone as one who "melted" (tested/subdued) boys/youths as no one else could.
- Idiomatically, saharat-hu al-shams ("the sun melted him") describes intense heat's effect - used specifically of the chameleon (al-hirba') when its back shimmers from the sun's heat.
- Also idiomatic: la-asharannahu bi-yaminin murratin ("I will surely melt him with a bitter oath"), understood as equivalent to "I will surely make him melt" (la-udhibannahu) - i.e., break him down through a harsh oath.

Ibn Faris treats these as two separate original meanings of the same root, unified only by the shared consonantal form, not by a claimed semantic link between them.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-k-k as a root indicating two things meeting with force and vehemence, as though one of them strikes the other.

1. **Striking.** ṣakaktu al-shayʾ ṣakkan: "I struck the thing."

2. **Knocking knees.** al-ṣakak: a man's two knees knocking together.

3. **Slamming a door.** ṣakka al-bāb: he shut the door violently and forcefully.

4. **Compact and strong.** A camel is called miṣakkak when its flesh has been packed hard into it. A man who is miṣakk is strong, and the word is also used of horses, donkeys and others.

5. **ṣakkat ʿumayy.** In the saying jiʾtuhu ṣakkata ʿumayyin, "I came to him at ʿumayy's collision", Ibn Fāris explains the image as a blind man meeting another like him so that the two collide, each striking the other. The expression was coined specifically for the midday heat and the time when the heat is most intense.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
quran_words: صَٰلِح 65x "the righteous"; صَّٰلِحَٰت 62x "righteous deeds"; أَصْلَحَ 28x "and reforms"; صَٰلِح 9x "salih"; إِصْلَٰح 7x "its reformation"; مُصْلِح 5x "the reformers"; صُلْح 2x "a reconciliation"; صَلَحَ 2x "(were) righteous"
poets_named: Bishr b. Abī Khāzim (pre-Islamic); Ḥarb (or al-Ḥārith) b. Umayya (pre-Islamic)
text:
Root ص-ل-ح (ṢLḤ), as recorded by al-Zabīdī in Tāj al-ʿArūs.

1. Core sense. الصَّلاَح (ṣalāḥ) means "soundness / being in good and right order," the opposite of فَسَاد (corruption, spoiling). A variant is صُلُوح (ṣulūḥ). Zabīdī notes a scholarly dispute over whether prophets may be described by ṣalāḥ: the base view restricts it to ordinary people, while al-Subkī and others allowed it of prophets too.

2. Verb forms. The verb صَلَحَ (ṣalaḥa) is inflected like manaʿa (imperfect yaṣlaḥ) — held the most eloquent, being regular — and like naṣara (yaṣlaḥ / yaṣluḥ), with verbal nouns ṣalāḥ and ṣulūḥ; a further form ṣaluḥa (like karuma) is reported from al-Farrāʾ but judged unestablished by Ibn Durayd. Zabīdī faults al-Fīrūzābādī for omitting the common ṣalaḥa/yaṣluḥ form documented by al-Jawharī, al-Fayyūmī, Ibn al-Qaṭṭāʿ and others.

3. Agent nouns. One who is sound is ṣilḥ, ṣāliḥ, or ṣalīḥ; one who actively sets things right is مُصْلِح (muṣliḥ). Plurals: ṣulaḥāʾ, ṣulūḥ.

4. أَصْلَحَ (aṣlaḥa), "to set right / repair," the opposite of أَفْسَدَ (afsada, "to spoil"): to restore a thing after its corruption. Figurative extension: aṣlaḥa ilayhi = "to do good to," e.g. aṣlaḥa al-dābbah, to treat an animal well so that it thrives (ṣalaḥat).

5. الصُّلْح (ṣulḥ), "reconciliation, peace-making" between parties; equated with al-salm/al-silm ("peace"), used as both masculine and feminine. It also names a reconciled group: "they are a ṣulḥ to us" = at peace with us.

6. صَالَحَ (ṣālaḥa), "to make peace with," verbal nouns muṣālaḥah and ṣilāḥ. Related reflexive/reciprocal forms all mean the same "to reconcile mutually": iṣṭalaḥā, iṣṣālaḥā, taṣālaḥā, iṣtalaḥā. Shāhid: Bishr b. Abī Khāzim, "They seek reconciliation (ṣilāḥ) at Dhāt Kahf…," where the feminine agreement shows ṣilāḥ standing for muṣālaḥah.

7. Ṣalāḥ as a name of Mecca. صَلاح (Ṣalāḥ), indeclinable like Qaṭāmi (though sometimes declined), is recorded as one of the old names of Mecca — possibly from ṣulḥ (linked to the Qurʾānic "a secure sanctuary," Q 28:57) or from ṣalāḥ. Shāhid: verses of Ḥarb (or al-Ḥārith) b. Umayya inviting Abū Maṭar to safety and good living at Ṣalāḥ among Quraysh; Ibn Barrī cites them for the declension of the name.

8. المَصْلَحة (maṣlaḥah), "benefit, public interest"; plural maṣāliḥ, contrasted with mafāsid ("harms"): "the Imam saw the maṣlaḥah in it," "he looked into people's interests." اسْتَصْلَحَ (istaṣlaḥa), "to seek to set right," is the opposite of istafsada.

9. "Suitability / fitness." Figuratively صَلَحَ لِ- (ṣalaḥa li-) = "to be fit/suitable for": "this suits you," "this hide is fit for a sandal." The verbal noun of this fitness is ṣalāḥiyah (pattern ṭawāʿiyah). al-iṣṭilāḥ ("technical convention," per al-Khafājī) is the agreement of a particular group on a particular usage.

10. Idioms and metonymy. مَطْرة صَالِحة (maṭrah ṣāliḥah) = "abundant rain" (ṣāliḥ used for "copious," as in Ibn Jinnī's usage); "so-and-so's condition became good (ṣalaḥat)"; "a good thing (ṣāliḥah) came to me from him"; "his good deeds (ṣāliḥāt) are beyond count."

11. Names and places. The prophet Ṣāliḥ, whose people dwelt at al-Ḥijr (between Tabūk and the Ḥijāz). Fam al-Ṣilḥ, a canal at Maysān. Ṣāliḥān, a quarter of Isfahan. al-Ṣāliḥiyyah, settlements near Edessa, in Baghdad, outside Damascus, and in Egypt, named after Ayyubid rulers (Ṣalāḥ al-Dīn Yūsuf b. Ayyūb and others). Personal names of the root include Ṣalāḥ, Ṣulaḥ, Muṣliḥ, and Ṣulayḥ; Banū al-Ṣulayḥī were kings of Yemen; several traditionists bear al-Ṣilḥī / al-Ṣāliḥānī / al-Ṣāliḥī / al-Ṣulaḥī.

dictionary: Tuḥfa — Tuḥfat al-Arīb, Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī (d. 1344)
text:
Abū Ḥayyān's gloss on the root ṣ-l-ṣ-l covers only the Qur'anic word ṣalṣāl:

1. ṣalṣāl — dry clay that has not been fired (i.e. not baked into pottery).
2. The name is explained from the sound it makes: strike or tap it and it rings (ṭanna). Abū Ḥayyān adds the clarification "that is, it makes a sound," tying the word's form to an audible ringing rather than to any property of the clay itself.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يُصَلَّبُ 4x "and i will surely crucify you"; صُّلْب 2x "the backbone"; صَلَبُ 2x "he will be crucified"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-l-b as two independent roots: one meaning hardness and strength, the other a kind of grease or fat (wadak).

FIRST ROOT — hardness, strength

1. ṣulb — the hard, firm thing. The back (ẓahr) is called ṣulb because of its strength. A variant vocalisation ṣalab is reported with the same meaning, supported by the verse: "in a back (ṣalab) like a well-tanned rein."

2. al-ṣālib of fever — the violent, raging fever. Cited verse: "your sweet water — had I drunk it with the raging fever on me, it would have cured me."

3. ṣalabat ʿalayhi al-ḥummā (reported from al-Kisāʾī) — the fever settled on him persistently and grew severe; the sufferer is then called maṣlūb ʿalayhi.

4. al-ṣullabiyya — whetstone rock; hence sinān muṣallab, a spearhead honed sharp.

5. al-taṣlīb (verb ṣallaba) — fresh dates hardening as they reach dryness.

6. al-ṣalīb — a marker or standard (ʿalam) set up in the landscape. Cited from al-Nābigha: herded livestock spending the day beside "a ṣalīb set up on al-Zawrāʾ."

SECOND ROOT — bone-grease

7. al-ṣalīb — the fat or grease of bone. iṣṭalaba: to collect bones and render out their fat to eat with bread. Cited half-line: "the old man of the household passed the night rendering bone-grease."

8. Derivation of "crucified": Ibn Fāris reports that the maṣlūb (the one crucified/impaled) was named from this second root — as though fat were running down his face; and ṣalīb is likewise used for the crucified man. The structure on which the person is fixed came to be called ṣalīb only secondarily, by adjacency (mujāwara) — that is, the name transferred from the person to the object.

9. thawb muṣallab — a garment bearing a cross-figure design. He cites a ḥadīth that when the Messenger of God saw such a figure on a garment he cut it out (qaḍabahu).

Rejected item: the claim that ṣawlab means seed broadcast over the ground and then ploughed in — Ibn Fāris dismisses this as post-classical, newly coined usage (muwallad) with no genuine root.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ص ل د (ṣ-l-d), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha — companion entry to al-Khalīl's on the same root

One core meaning: hardness and dryness.

1. al-ḥajaru al-ṣald — the hard rock; extended to ṣalida al-zand — a fire-drill failing to produce a spark (with the causative asladtuhu, "I made it fail to spark").
2. al-raʾsu al-ṣald — a head that grows no hair, compared to barren land that grows nothing, illustrated with a line of poetry by Ruʾbah.
3. A stingy man is called aṣlad, traced (by Ibn Fāris) to either of the two images above — barren ground, or a fire-drill that won't spark.
4. Extended to livestock: nāqa ṣalūd — a she-camel giving little milk, with a thick udder-skin; faras ṣalūd — a horse that doesn't sweat; nāqa mislād — a she-camel that has given birth but has no milk.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: صَلَوٰة 83x "the prayer"; صَلَّىٰ 12x "send blessings"; مُصَلِّين 3x "those who pray"; مُصَلًّى 1x "(as) a place of prayer"
text:
Al-Rāghib treats this root under two heads: burning with fire (al-ṣaly), and al-ṣalāt, which he derives mainly from supplication.

1. **Burning, roasting.** The root meaning of al-ṣaly is kindling with fire. Ṣaliya bi-l-nār means to be afflicted by fire (and, by extension, by anything); iṣṭalā bihā means to warm oneself at it. Ṣalaytu al-shāh is "I roasted the sheep", and the roasted animal is maṣliyya. Al-ṣalāʾ is used both for fuel and for roasting / roast meat.

2. **Burning in the Fire (Qur'anic usage).** The Qur'an uses the verb for being burned in, or suffering, the Fire: "Burn in it today" (Q 36:64); "who will burn in the greatest Fire" (Q 87:12); "they will burn in a blazing Fire" (Q 88:4); "he will burn in a blaze" (Q 84:12, and Q 4:10, where sa-yaṣlawna is read both as sa-yuṣlawna and sa-yaṣlawna); "Hell is enough for them; they will burn in it" (Q 58:8). The causative form means to make someone burn in it: "I will make him burn in Saqar" (Q 74:26), "We shall make him burn in a Fire" (Q 4:30); the verbal noun taṣliya appears in "a burning in the Blaze" (Q 56:94). On "none will burn in it but the most wretched" (Q 92:15–16), one view is that it means none is scorched by it except the most wretched.
   - Al-Khalīl says ṣaliya al-kāfiru al-nār means the unbeliever suffered its heat.
   - Another view: ṣalā al-nār means to enter the Fire, and aṣlāhā ghayrahu to make another enter it.
   - In "those most deserving to burn in it (ṣiliyyan)" (Q 19:70), ṣiliyy is said to be the plural of ṣālin, "one who burns".

3. **Al-ṣalāt as supplication and blessing.** Many philologists, he reports, say al-ṣalāt means supplication, invoking blessing and glorifying. Ṣallaytu ʿalayhi means "I prayed for him and commended him". A saying of the Prophet illustrates this: when invited to a meal one should accept, and if fasting one should yuṣalli, that is, pray for the household. Qur'anic examples: "pray for them; your prayer is a source of tranquillity for them" (Q 9:103); "the prayers of the Messenger" (Q 9:99); "O you who believe, bless him" (Q 33:56).
   - When God is the subject, His ṣalāt on the believers is, al-Rāghib says, in reality His purifying and commending them: "upon those are blessings from their Lord, and mercy" (Q 2:157).
   - When angels are the subject, it is supplication and asking forgiveness, as it is from people: "God and His angels bless the Prophet" (Q 33:56).

4. **Al-ṣalāt as a specific act of worship.** The ṣalāt that is "the specific act of worship" gets its name from supplication, its root sense, in the way a thing may be named after one of its parts. Al-Rāghib states that no religious law has ever lacked it, though its forms differ from one law to another, and cites "the ṣalāt is for the believers a prescription at fixed times" (Q 4:103).
   - An alternative etymology from "some": ṣalāt comes from al-ṣalā, fire. Ṣallā would then mean that the worshipper wards off and removes from himself God's kindled fire through this act. The doubled verb form is compared to marraḍa, "to nurse", which means removing illness.

5. **Al-ṣalāt as a place of worship.** The place of worship is also called ṣalāt, which is why churches are called ṣalawāt in "cloisters, churches, ṣalawāt and mosques would have been demolished" (Q 22:40).

6. **"Establishing" versus merely "performing".** Al-Rāghib observes that wherever God praises or urges ṣalāt, the Qur'an uses iqāma, "establishing / keeping upright": "those who establish the ṣalāt" (Q 4:162), "establish the ṣalāt" (Q 2:43), "they established the ṣalāt" (Q 2:277). The plain participle al-muṣallīn, "those who perform ṣalāt", is used only of the hypocrites: "woe to those who perform ṣalāt, who are heedless of their ṣalāt" (Q 107:4–5); "they come to the ṣalāt only lazily" (Q 9:54). In his account iqāma signals that the aim is to fulfil the prayer's dues and conditions, not just to produce its outward form. He adds the reported saying: "Those who perform ṣalāt are many; those who establish it are few."
   - "We were not among those who performed ṣalāt" (Q 74:43) he glosses as "not among the followers of the prophets".
   - "He neither affirmed the truth nor performed ṣalāt" (Q 75:31) indicates, he says, that such a person did not even go through the outward form, let alone establish it.
   - "Their ṣalāt at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping" (Q 8:35): calling it mukāʾ and taṣdiya shows that their ṣalāt was void and counted for nothing. They were like birds that whistle and clap.

The entry ends by noting that ṣalāt is mentioned twice in the passage "the believers have succeeded, those who are humble in their ṣalāt … and those who guard their ṣalāt" (Q 23:1–2, 9). Al-Rāghib says he will explain why in a later work.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَصْلَى 13x "and they will be burned"; أُصْلِي 4x "we (will) cast him"; تَصْطَلُ 2x "warm yourselves"; صَالُوا 2x "(will) burn"; صِلِيّ 1x "(of) being burnt"; صَال 1x "(is) to burn"; تَصْلِيَة 1x "and burning"; صَلُّ 1x "burn him"
text:
Ibn Fāris holds that the root ص-ل-ي / ص-ل-و has two distinct origins.

FIRST ORIGIN — fire and what resembles it (including fever, الحُمَّى):
1. صَلَيْتُ العُودَ بِالنَّارِ — "I roasted/held the wood to the fire."
2. الصَّلَى — the scorching heat of fire.
3. اصْطَلَيْتُ بِالنَّارِ — "I warmed myself at the fire."
4. الصِّلَاء (al-ṣilāʾ) — that by which one warms oneself; the fuel with which a fire is fed and kindled. Shāhid (unnamed poet): a woman makes ʿūd-wood, aloewood (yalanjūj), and myrtle (rand) into ṣilāʾ (fuel/fire) on the brazier.

SECOND ORIGIN — a kind of devotion. Its base sense here is supplication (دُعَاء):
1. الصَّلَاة = duʿāʾ, prayer/petition. Evidence: the Prophet's saying that a fasting man invited to a meal should "yuṣalli" — which Ibn Fāris glosses as "let him pray for them with good and blessing."
2. Shāhid from al-Aʿshā: his daughter prays that ailments be kept from her departing father; he answers, "Upon you the like of what you have prayed" — ṣallā used for petition/blessing.
3. Second al-Aʿshā shāhid (on wine): the wind "prayed over" (ṣallā ʿalā) the wine-jar and made a sign over it.
4. Ibn Fāris then notes that الصَّلَاة is also what the Law (sharʿ) brought — bowing, prostration, and the rest of the ṣalāt's prescribed limits (he attributes this specifically to the Law's usage, distinct from the base sense of supplication).
5. When الصَّلَاة is ascribed to God, it means mercy (raḥma). Evidence: the ḥadīth "O God, ṣalli upon the family of Abū Awfā" = bestow mercy.

ANOMALOUS (outside the two origins): مَصَالِي (maṣālī), occurring in a ḥadīth alongside "snares" for Satan — glossed as traps (ashrāk), singular مِصْلَاة (miṣlāt).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ص م ع (ṣ-m-ʿ), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: fineness/delicacy combined with compactness/being drawn together.

1. Al-Khalīl's rule, cited approvingly: "everything drawn-together is mutaṣammiʿ" — from which the word for a monastic cell/tower, al-ṣawmaʿah, is derived.
2. al-ṣamaʿ, of the ears — aṣmaʿ describes ears pressed closely/flattened to the head; extended figuratively: qalb aṣmaʿ — a fine, sharp, intelligent heart/mind.
3. al-ṣamʿāʾ — a term for the buhmā grass when it has risen but not yet split open, because at that stage it is compact and delicate.
4. mutaṣammiʿ — anything smeared and clumped together, like blood-clotted arrow-feathers, illustrated with a line of poetry about a fatal shot on a barren gazelle-doe.
5. Closing: dogs described as "ṣumʿu al-kuʿūb" — small and fine of ankle-joint — illustrated with a line of poetry by al-Nābighah.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ص-م-د (Ṣ-M-D) — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004 CE)

Ibn Fāris derives two distinct core meanings from this root:

1. To head toward / aim at (al-qaṣd)
- al-ṣamd = heading toward or aiming at something; ṣamadtuhu ṣamdan = "I headed toward/aimed at him."
- A man called muṣammad (or ṣamad) is a chief (sayyid) whom people seek out and turn to for important matters — i.e., "the one resorted-to."
- Allāh is called al-Ṣamad, Ibn Fāris explains, because His servants turn/head toward Him in supplication and petition.
- Citation (unattributed in the entry): a line of verse addressing "Ḥudhayf" and calling him "the lord, the ṣamad" — the one people turn to.
- Citation (Ṭarafa, pre-Islamic poet): boasts that at the tribe's gathering he will be found at the top of "the lofty, muṣammad tent" — the tent everyone is drawn to.

2. Hard, solid ground (al-ṣalāba fī al-shayʾ)
- al-ṣamd here means any solid, hard patch of ground.
- Citation (Abū al-Najm): describes something leaving behind the ṣamd (hard ground), likening it to the smooth back of a hard rock (al-ajzal).

Method: Ibn Fāris's signature move — reducing a root to a small number of core senses and showing each with a shāhid. Here the two senses (motion-toward vs. physical hardness) are kept separate; he does not merge them or claim one derives from the other.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَصَمّ 12x "deaf"; صَمُّ 2x "and they became deaf"; أَصَمَّ 1x "so he made them deaf"
poets_named: Ibn Aḥmar (lived into Islam); Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-m-m as a single root meaning (aṣl) whose core is that a thing is closed tightly together, with no breach or opening left in it. He derives each word he lists from that idea.

1. **Deafness.** al-ṣamam is deafness of the ear: the ear is thought of as closed. The verb is ṣamimtu, "I became deaf" (imperfect taṣammu); ṣumma is sometimes used in the same sense. aṣmamtu al-rajula means "I found the man deaf". He cites Ibn Aḥmar: "The call of my blaming woman found [me] deaf; she holds fast to our later ones and forgets our earlier ones."

2. **Calamity.** al-ṣammāʾ is a calamity, as though from deafness: an affair with no opening in it. From this comes ishtimāl al-ṣammāʾ, a way of wrapping oneself in a garment and then throwing the left side over the right.

3. **The cry "ṣammī ṣamāmi".** The Arabs say this to make an affair out to be grave. Ibn Fāris traces it to the saying "a pebble went deaf with blood": in battle so much blood covers the ground that a thrown pebble makes no sound when it lands. He cites Imruʾ al-Qays, who, given ʿAdwān and Fahm in place of Wāʾil and Kinda, cries "be deaf, O daughter of the mountain!", meaning to stress how grave his situation is.

4. **Stopper.** The ṣimām of a flask is its stopper, named because it blocks the opening.

5. **Resolve.** ṣammama fī al-amr is said of someone who presses on in an affair headlong. Ibn Fāris fits this to the same analogy: set on his aim, he hears neither blame nor prohibition, as if he were deaf.

6. **The sword.** The sword called al-ṣamṣām or al-ṣamṣāma is derived from this.

7. **Biting fast.** ṣammama also means to bite into something and fix one's teeth in it.

8. **Hard ground.** al-ṣammān is a land. Some say any land beside a sand-tract is called ṣammāna. Ibn Fāris accepts this, because sand is full of gaps and the ṣammāna is not.

9. **Solid things: the heavy man, the lion, the crowd.** al-ṣimṣim is a thick-set man, as if his flesh had no gap or breach in it. The lion is called ṣimma, as if there were no way of getting at him from any side. al-ṣimṣima is a company of people, as if packed together so closely that no gap or breach is left.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ص م ت (ṣ-m-t), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha — companion entry to al-Khalīl's on the same root

One core meaning: vagueness/ambiguity and being sealed shut, extended most often to silence.

1. ṣamata/aṣmata al-rajul — to fall silent (two verb forms). Idiom: "I met so-and-so in the land of iṣmit" — a desolate wasteland with no one in it, as though it were itself silent.
2. "mā lahu ṣāmitun wa lā nāṭiq" — an idiom distinguishing wealth in precious metal (al-ṣāmit: gold and silver, "the silent kind") from wealth in livestock (al-nāṭiq: camels, sheep, horses, "the speaking kind").
3. al-ṣamūt — a soft, supple coat of mail that makes no sound when worn, illustrated with a line of poetry about fine, silent armor.
4. bāb muṣmat — a door made completely, seamlessly shut.
5. al-ṣāmit, of milk — thickened/curdled milk, named because it makes no sound when poured, unlike thin milk.
6. Idiom: "bittu ʿalā ṣimāti dhālika" — "I spent the night with intent toward that matter" — Ibn Fāris notes this may be an irregular derivation, possibly related instead to al-samt, "the way/path," illustrated with a line of poetry.
7. "ramāhu bi-ṣimātihi" — "he struck him with his ṣimāt," meaning with whatever silenced him; "aʿṭā al-ṣabiyya ṣumtatan" — to give an infant something to quiet him.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: صَنَعُ 15x "do"; صُنْع 2x "(the) work"; ٱصْطَنَعْ 1x "and i (have) chosen you"; صَنْعَة 1x "(the) making"; مَصَانِع 1x "strongholds"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-n-ʿ (صنع) as a single sound root whose core meaning is the making or doing of a thing (ṣunʿ).

1. Skill in craft: صَنَاع (of a woman) and صَنَع (of a man) describe someone deft and expert at what they make. He cites a verse describing a woman "clumsy at good, but skilled (ṣanāʿ) at causing harm among family and neighbor" — the same word for skill applied ironically to doing harm.

2. صَنِيعَة (ṣanīʿa): a kindness or good deed that one deliberately does for another.

3. تَصَنُّع (taṣannuʿ): fineness of bearing or good comportment.

4. فَرَس صَنِيع (a ṣanīʿ horse): a horse well tended and cared for by its owners — "made" by their attention.

5. مَصَانِع (maṣāniʿ): structures built — a well or the like — for watering/irrigation.

6. مُصَانَعَة (muṣānaʿa): from the same root, likened to a bribe.

7. Anomalous/deviant use: صِنْع (ṣinʿ), said to mean a roasting-spit or skewer (saffūd). Ibn Fāris introduces a supporting verse by al-Marrār, but the citation is cut off in the source text.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-n-m as a single, unbranched item:

1. The root yields only one word, صَنَم (ṣanam) — no secondary or derived senses grow from it.
2. He describes a ṣanam as an object fashioned out of wood, silver, or copper, which was then made an object of worship.

No poetic or Qur'anic citations, and no grammatical or morphological notes, are given in this entry.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris's Maqayis al-Lugha on the root s-n-w:

Core meaning: the root signals closeness between two things, whether by kinship or by physical distance.

Sense 1 - full brother / close kinsman. Al-sinw is a person's full brother (same mother and father). By extension a man's paternal uncle is called the sinw of his father, as a kind of counterpart to him. Al-Khalil is cited for the phrase 'so-and-so is the sinw of so-and-so,' said of full brothers.

The image behind this sense: two palm trees growing from one shared root-stock. Each tree alone is a sinw; together, sinwan (dual). This is the image the Qur'an uses: 'and palm-trees, joined and not joined' (Qur'an 13:4). Abu Zayd extends the word to two wells so close together that nothing (no trough) separates them.

Sense 2 - an unrelated usage. Ibn Faris separately notes that sinw also names a hollow or pit dug in the ground (diminutive sunayy), and flags this sense as not fitting the root's core meaning. He cites a line of poetry by Layla, addressed mockingly to the poet al-Nabigha and punning on his name (nabagha, 'to rise to prominence'): she says he never rose to prominence and was never first among poets, but was only a small, obscure hollow between two rock outcrops.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ص ر ع (ṣ-r-ʿ), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: something falling to the ground through a struggle between two — from which the whole chapter of related words is derived.

1. ṣaraʿtu al-rajula — I threw the man down; ṣāraʿtuhu — I wrestled him; rajul ṣarīʿ — a man thrown down. al-ṣarīʿ, of branches — one that droops and falls to the ground (plural ṣuruʿ); a bow made from such fallen wood is itself called ṣarīʿ.
2. Extended by analogy: "humā ṣirʿān" — an idiom meaning two things "fall together" simultaneously, a comparison rather than a literal fall. The two leaves of a door (miṣrāʿā al-bāb) are named on the same logic — two equal halves that meet/fall together.
3. al-ṣirʿān — two camel-herds moving at different paces (one going out as the other returns), so numerous that this alternation happens constantly — illustrated with a line of poetry about relieving hardship.
4. maṣāriʿu al-nās — people's "falling-places," i.e. their fates or points of death.
5. Abū Zayd's idiom "atānā ṣarʿay al-nahār" — "he came to us at the day's two ṣarʿ" (morning and evening) — Ibn Fāris traces this back to the same core sense of ṣarʿān as "two equal/matching counterparts," closing the entry by affirming the whole chapter follows one consistent analogy.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-r-ḥ as one regular root whose core notion is that something appears, stands out, becomes visible.

1. Plain / manifest. الصَّرِيح (ṣarīḥ) is the thing that is plain and open.

2. Pure, unmixed — of descent. ṣarīḥ is one of pure, unmixed lineage; plural صُرَحَاء (ṣuraḥāʾ). Al-Khalīl notes that of horses the plural used is الصَّرَائِح (al-ṣarāʾiḥ), and that anything unmixed at all is called ṣarīḥ. The quality is named with two verbal nouns, ṣarāḥa and ṣurūḥa: "he is of evident ṣarāḥa/ṣurūḥa."

3. Speaking openly. صَرَّحَ (ṣarraḥa) with what is in one's mind = to bring it out into the open, state it plainly.

4. Unmixed drink. كَأْسٌ صُرَاح — a cup not cut with any admixture. Wine "ṣarraḥat" when its froth has gone off it and it runs clear. Ibn Fāris cites al-Aʿshā: a dark-red wine that "discloses a redness ... when it clears after its frothing."

5. In the open, face to face. جَاءَ بِهِ صُرَاحًا = he brought it openly, publicly. To meet someone مُصَارَحَةً / صِرَاحًا is to meet him face to face, in open confrontation.

6. Truth coming uncovered. صَرَّحَ الْحَقُّ عَنْ مَحْضِهِ — the matter came out into the clear after having been hidden.

7. Place / open ground. الصَّرْحَة is "the place"; on another report, the firm raised tract (matn) of ground.

8. Cloudless day. يَوْمٌ مُصَرِّح — a day with no cloud in it; attested, he says, in the poetry of al-Ṭirimmāḥ.

9. Tall building. الصَّرْح (al-ṣarḥ) is a single edifice built standing on its own, massive and rising high into the sky — and, generally, any lofty building.

The whole entry is held together by the one idea he states at the start: something emerging into plain view, whether that is a truth spoken out, a liquid running clear of what clouded it, a sky clear of cloud, or a structure standing up alone above the ground.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
**Root ṢRR (صرر) — Ibn Manẓūr, Lisān al-ʿArab**

Ibn Manẓūr's article gathers two large clusters of usage — (a) sound/creaking/clamour, and (b) tying, binding, gathering — plus a cold sense, and he repeatedly notes that the base idea of ṣarr is "to gather and bind fast."

**1. Cold.** صِرّ (ṣirr) and صِرّة (ṣirra) = severe cold; Thaʿlab is cited for the broader sense "cold in general." Al-Layth: the cold that strikes vegetation. A ḥadīth forbids locusts killed by the ṣirr, i.e. by cold. صُرَّ النباتُ = the plants were struck by cold.

**2. رِيح صَرْصَر — two readings.** Of the Qurʾanic "بريح صرصر," al-Zajjāj takes ṣirr/ṣirra as intense cold, and explains ṣarṣar as a form with the rāʾ reduplicated; he lays down a general rule of the language: a single, non-repeated sound is ṣarra / ṣalla, a repeated one is ṣarṣara / ṣalṣala. Al-Azharī: "exceedingly cold." Ibn al-Sikkīt reports two derivations: (i) from ṣirr "cold," originally ṣarrar, with the first radical substituted for the middle rāʾ (compare تجفجف < تجفَّف, كبكبوا < كبَّبوا); or (ii) from ṣarīr al-bāb, a door's creak, and ṣarra "clamour." For "فأقبلت امرأته في صَرَّة," commentators are cited as glossing "in a clamour and a cry"; a line of Imruʾ al-Qays using فى صَرَّة is instead read as "in an undispersed body." On "كمثل ريح فيها صِرّ," Ibn al-Anbārī records three views: cold; sound and movement; and — reported from Ibn ʿAbbās — fire.

**3. Sound and crying out.** صَرَّ يَصِرُّ صريراً / صَرْصَرَ = to make a sound, to cry at the top of the voice. Al-Zajjāj: ṣarra is the loudest cry, used of birds, humans and others. Cited: Jarīr's elegy for his son Sawāda, ending "a falcon that screeches (يصرصر) above the high look-out" (also quoted by al-Aṣmaʿī). Thaʿlab's anecdote: a woman said the most hateful of women is "the one who, when she is loud, screeches." Related uses: the ear-canal ringing from thirst; a bird crying (some restrict ṣarṣara to hawk and falcon); a small yellow bird called ṣarr, named from its sound (ḥadīth of Jaʿfar b. Muḥammad); a sparrow chirping, a cricket, a creaking door, pen, or camel-litter; a ringing in the ear. A morphological point: a sustained sound is ṣarīr; a sound with a returning cadence takes the doubled form, صَرْصَرَ الأَخْطَبُ صَرْصَرَةً. In the ḥadīth of the palm-trunk that moaned when the Prophet took the pulpit, اضْطَرَّت is iftaʿalat from ṣarīr, its tāʾ turned to ṭāʾ after ṣād.

**4. Coin that rings.** درهم صَرِّيّ / صِرِّيّ = one that rings when struck (likewise a dinar); some limit the word to negative sentences. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: "ما لفلان صِرّ" = he has not a dirham or dinar — used only in negation. Khālid b. Janba treats صَرِّيّ as invariable (no dual, no plural).

**5. Clamour, throng, hardship, heat.** ṣarra = shout and uproar; also a throng or assembled body; also severity of distress or of war. Imruʾ al-Qays's line "في صَرَّةٍ لم تَزَيَّلِ" is read as "throng," as "hardship," or as bearing all three senses. صَرَّة القيظ = the peak of summer heat. ṣarra also = a bend or turning.

**6. Thirst.** صارَّة = thirst, plural ṣarāʾir (irregular), with Dhū al-Rumma's line on wild asses that "did not quench their thirsts." Ibn al-Aʿrābī distinguishes vowels: صَرَّ يَصِرُّ = to thirst; صَرَّ يَصُرُّ = to gather. قصع الحمارُ صارَّتَه = the ass quenched its thirst. Ibn Manẓūr notes a dispute: the plural ṣarāʾir was faulted (against Abū ʿAmr), some holding ṣarāʾir to be plural of ṣarīra while ṣārra pluralises as ṣawārr.

**7. Binding a she-camel's udder — ṣirār.** ṣirār is the cord tying the teat-guards on a she-camel's teats, the teats first smeared with fresh dung so the cord leaves no mark; صَرَرْتُ الناقة = I bound her so her young could not suckle. A ḥadīth forbids untying another's camel's ṣirār without leave, "for it is her people's seal." Ibn al-Athīr describes the custom: udders bound when the animals go to pasture, loosed at evening for milking — hence maṣrūra, muṣarrara. Verses of Mālik b. Nuwayra (refusing to send his tribe's alms) use مُصَرَّرة أخلافها. Ibn Manẓūr notes that al-Shāfiʿī's ruling on the muṣarrāt was construed on this sense. Related: plural aṣirra; الصَّرَّة = a ewe whose milk is left to build up; المُصَرَّاة = المُحَفَّلَة, by transposition of the doubled letter; ناقة مُصِرَّة = one that gives no milk (verse of Usāma al-Hudhalī).

**8. Purse, gathering, binding — the root idea.** صُرَّة = a tied purse of dirhams or dinars; صَرَرْتُ الصُّرَّة = I tied it. "The root sense of al-ṣarr is gathering and binding fast." Ḥadīth evidence: the Prophet to Gabriel, "you come to me ṣārr between your eyes," i.e. knitting the brows like a grieving man; to two litigants, "bring out what you are gathering up (تُصَرِّرانه) of speech in your breasts"; a variant reading تَنْصَرُّ in the ḥadīth of ʿImrān b. Ḥuṣayn (Ibn al-Athīr prefers تنضرج, "splits"). Hence a captive is مَصْرُور, his hands gathered to his neck — Ibn ʿUmar refused to kill a prisoner "while he is maṣrūr."

**9. Pricking or drawing back the ears.** صَرَّ الفرسُ أُذُنَيْه = he set his ears erect / drew them to his head; without an object, أَصَرَّ, said of a horse gathering its ears and bracing to run. Ḥadīth of Saṭīḥ: صَرَّار الأُذُن. جاءت الخيل مُصِرَّة آذانها of horses exerting themselves.

**10. Standing grain.** Ibn Shumayl: أصرَّ الزرع = when the awn-tips appear before the ear emerges (once the ear is clear, أَسْبَل); also, the crop is ṣarar when the leaf twists and the ear-tip dries even without grain. الصَّرَر = the ear after jointing, before it shows; Abū Ḥanīfa: the ear so long as no wheat is in it (sing. ṣarara). Also أَصَرَّ يَعْدُو = ran somewhat fast — Abū ʿUbayd transmits it with ḍād (أضرّ), which al-Ṭūsī called a scribal error.

**11. Resolve and persistence — أَصَرَّ.** أصرَّ على الأمر = he resolved firmly. The idiom "هو مني صِرِّي / أَصِرِّي" (with several vowellings) = a settled, earnest resolve; Abū Zayd glosses it "a certainty," with a verse of Abū Mālik. The anecdote of Abū al-Sammāl al-Asadī, who swore an oath when his camel strayed and, on finding her, said "God knew it was from me ṣirrā" — i.e. a firm resolve. Ibn al-Sikkīt derives it from أصررت على الشيء "I kept to and persisted in it," and cites the Qurʾanic "ولم يُصِرُّوا على ما فعلوا وهم يعلمون." Abū al-Haytham reads أَصِرِّي as an imperative, "resolve!", the speaker addressing himself. Al-Farrāʾ explains the final alif as an imperative shifted out of verbal force into a noun (comparable to نُهِيَ عن قِيل وقال, and to the idiom "من شُبَّ إلى دُبَّ," from childhood to doddering age). In moral usage, أصرَّ على الذنب = he did not desist; Ibn Manẓūr notes the word is used mostly of evil and sins, citing "ما أصرَّ من استغفر" — one who follows a sin with seeking forgiveness is not a muṣirr even if he repeats it — and "woe to the muṣirrīn."

**12. صَرُورة.** رجل صَرُور / صَرُورة = one who has never performed ḥajj — said to derive from ṣarr in the sense of restraint and withholding. Variants ṣarūrī / ṣārūrī inflect for dual, plural and feminine; Ibn al-Aʿrābī holds all forms inflect. A second sense: one who has not married; in al-Nābigha's verse the ṣarūra is the monk who has renounced women. On the ḥadīth "لا صَرُورة في الإسلام," Abū ʿUbayd takes it as celibacy and refusing marriage — "not of the manners of the Muslims, but the deed of monks." Ibn al-Athīr adds a second interpretation: one who kills in the sanctuary is killed and cannot plead "I am a ṣarūra, I never made ḥajj and did not know the sanctuary's inviolability" — recalling the Jāhilī practice of not molesting an offender who took refuge at the Kaʿba, when it would be said to the blood-avenger, "he is a ṣarūra, leave him." Grammatical note (Ibn Jinnī): the hāʾ in ṣarūra is not feminine but a marker of intensification; al-Liḥyānī allows only the form with hāʾ; al-Farrāʾ reports ṣarār (sing. ṣarāra) and ṣawārīr.

**13. Hoof.** حافر مَصْرُور / مُصْطَرّ = a narrow, contracted hoof; its opposite أرَحّ = over-broad — both are faults. Abū ʿUbayd: اصطرَّ الحافر = it is excessively narrow, with a verse of Abū al-Najm contrasting muṣṭarr (too narrow) with firshāḥ (too wide).

**14. Miscellaneous senses and names.**
- صَارَّة = a need; "لنا قِبَلَه صارَّة," pl. ṣawārr.
- مَصَارّ = the bowels ("he drank till he filled his maṣārr"), reported by Ibn al-Aʿrābī without further explanation.
- صَرارة = a canal drawn from the Euphrates.
- صَرَارِيّ = sailor (verse of al-Quṭāmī, where irtasama = he said the takbīr); pl. ṣarāriyyūn, no broken plural. Ibn Barrī argues the word belongs under the root ṣry: singular ṣārin, plural ṣurrāʾ, whose plural is ṣarārī; Abū ʿAlī had held ṣurrāʾ to be a singular (like ḥussān). Verses of al-Farazdaq, al-Musayyab b. ʿAlas (of a diver and his pearl) and Khalaf b. Jamīl show ṣarārī used both as plural and as singular. Al-Jawharī, seeing it used as a singular, took the yāʾ for a nisba (like ḥawārī) and so filed it under ṣrr. Ibn Barrī also corrects the recitation of al-ʿAjjāj's line to جَذْبُ (nominative), subject of the preceding line; kurūr = pl. of karr, the ship's rope in the sail.
- الصَّرّ = a bucket that slackens and so is bound tight and fitted with a mismaʿ, a loop inside opposite another loop (with a supporting verse).
- الصَّرَّة = a knotting of the face in distaste.
- الصِّرار = high ground the water does not cover; Ṣirār as a mountain name (verse of Jarīr), and — per Ibn al-Athīr on a ḥadīth — an old well three miles from Medina on the Iraq road, or a place.
- صارَّه على الشيء = he forced him to it.
- الصَّرَّة (fatḥa) = a bead women use as a binding-charm on men (al-Liḥyānī).
- صَرَّرَتِ الناقة = she went out in front (Abū Laylā, with a line of Dhū al-Rumma).
- صِرِّين = a place (verse of al-Akhṭal).
- صَرْصَر / صُرْصُر / صُرْصُور = huge camels; ṣurṣūr also = the Bactrian camel or its young (variant with sīn), and per Ibn al-Aʿrābī the choice stallion; also used of a ship, like qurqūr.
- صَرْصَرانِيَّة = camels crossed between Bactrian and Arabian, or the fawālij; ṣarṣarān = Nabatean camels.
- صَرْصَران(يّ) also = a large, smooth-skinned sea fish (with a verse).
- صَرْصَر = a small creature under the ground that chirps in spring; صَرَّار الليل = the cricket, larger than the grasshopper, called by some Arabs al-ṣadā.
- صَرْصَر = a river in Iraq; الصَّراصِرة = the Nabateans of Syria.
- From the Nawādir (via the Tahdhīb): صَرْصَرْتُه belongs with a set of verbs (kamhaltu, ḥabkartu, dabkaltu, ḥabḥabtu, zamzamtu, karkartu, kabkabtu) all meaning "I gathered it and folded back its scattered edges" — again the gathering sense.

text:
Root ص-ر-ط (ṣ-r-ṭ), as Ibn Fāris treats it:

1. Core sense: the root belongs to the category of letter-substitution (ibdāl) — the ṣād here standing in for a sīn — and it means "the road/path." Its regular treatment was given under sīn (i.e. سراط/صراط, ṣirāṭ). Shāhid: a verse using وَضَح الصِّرَاط, "the plain, open road," (the poet driving his enemies "onto the clear ṣirāṭ").

After this brief head-sense, our source runs into this entry Ibn Fāris's separate chapter for the whole letter ṣād on words of more than three letters: "carved" compound words (manḥūt) and words with an augmented letter. His method is to show that each is built from two shorter roots, or from a shorter root plus an extra letter:

Compounds carved from two roots (naḥt):
- اصْمَقَرَّ (milk turning sharply sour) ← ṣaqara + maqara (maqir = sour; ṣaqir = thick, whence molasses called ṣaqr).
- الصِّلْقَم (a hard biter) ← ṣalaqa + laqama (as if it turns the thing into a "morsel").
- الصَّهْصَلِق (loud, clamorous; of a woman) ← ṣahala + ṣalaqa. Shāhid: Ibn Aḥmar, "clamorous of voice … the swooping falcon has no hope of her."
- الصَّمْعَرَة (hard ground), الصَّمْعَرِيَّة (a malignant snake), الصَّمْعَرِيّ (a vile man) ← ṣamara ("grew hard") + maʿara ("its pasture grew scant").
- الصُّمَالِخ (thick clotted milk) ← ṣalakha + ṣamala (ṣamala = hardened; ṣalakha linked to ṣamam "deafness" — thick milk makes no sound when poured).
- الصِّلْدَمَة (a hard, strong mare) ← ṣalada + ṣadama (ṣald = hard, like hard rock; ṣadm = colliding).
- الصَّقْعَب (a tall man) ← ṣaqaba + ṣaʿaba (ṣaqb = tall; ṣaʿb = difficult).

Words traced to a shorter root with one letter added (ziyāda):
- الصَّعْنَب (small-headed): added bāʾ; base ṣ-ʿ-n (see ṣiʿwann).
- صَلْخَد / صَيْلَخُود (a tough camel): added lām; from ṣakhada (cf. ṣaykhūd, hard rock). The latter form Ibn Fāris credits to Ibn Durayd.
- الصِّرْدَاح / الصَّرْدَح (a strong she-camel): added dāl; from ṣarḥ, a tall strong building.
- اصْمَعَدَّ (went off into the land): added mīm; from aṣʿada.
- صَلْفَعَ رأسه (shaved his head): added fāʾ; from ṣalaʿ (baldness). A minority gloss: "struck his neck" — Ibn Fāris finds "shaved" more analogical.
- صَلْمَعَ: al-Aḥmar, "uprooted from the base"; al-Farrāʾ, "shaved the hair"; mīm added. Both ṣalmaʿa and ṣalfaʿa are also said to mean insolvency.
- الصِّمْرِد (a she-camel of little milk): added mīm; from ṣarada (taṣrīd = reducing).
- الصُّمَّلِك (very strong): added kāf; base ṣumull.
- الْمُصْمَئِلَّة (calamity): base ṣamala.
- الصَّفَارِيت (the poor; sing. ṣifrīt): added tāʾ; from ṣifr, "empty." Shāhid: Dhū al-Rumma.
- الصَّعْنَبَة (heaping tharīda into a peak): added bāʾ; from muṣʿann / ṣiʿwann.
- الصِّمْلَاخ (ear-hole/wax): added lām; from ṣimākh.
- الصِّقَعْل (dry dates): added ʿayn; from ṣaql (polishing) — dried, it looks polished.
- الصِّنْتِيت (a chief): via substitution, = ṣindīd.
- الصَّلْهَب (a tall man): either substitution (= salhab, ṣād for sīn) or augmentation (added hāʾ, from salib "tall").

Words Ibn Fāris regards as coined outright, not derivable by analogy (waḍʿ, ghayr munqās):
- الصُّنْبُور: four senses — a palm left standing alone with a thinning base; a cistern's water-spout; a solitary man with no child or brother; the iron or lead drinking-reed of a water-skin.
- الصِّنَّبْر (bitter cold): nūn and bāʾ added; from ṣirr.
- الصَّعَافِقَة (perhaps a nickname): people with no capital who haunt the markets and, when someone makes a purchase, muscle into his deal.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ص ر ف (ṣ-r-f) from a single core idea: the returning or turning-back of a thing. He groups the senses accordingly.

1. Core sense — turning (people) back: ṣaraftu al-qawm ("I turned the people back") and they inṣarafū (turned back / departed).

2. al-ṣarīf: milk at the moment it is milked and carried away.

3. al-ṣarf in the Qur'an: repentance (tawba) — because through it a person is brought back from the rank of the sinners. (This is Ibn Fāris's gloss of the Qur'anic usage.)

4. al-ṣarfa: (a) a star/asterism, named for the "turning away" of the cold at its rising; (b) a bead used as a love-charm on men, named because it supposedly turns a man's heart away from what he desires.

5. Exchange/money (from al-Khalīl): al-ṣarf is the surplus value of one dirham over another. Ibn Fāris's own explanation: something exchanged into another thing — as a dinar is "returned" into dirhams when you take its equivalent. Hence al-ṣayrafī (money-changer), and tasrīf al-darāhim = spending coins in trade.

6. ṣarf al-kalām (from Abū ʿUbayd): embellishing and expanding speech, so called because polished speech "turns" the ears toward it.

7. ṣarf / plural ṣurūf: the vicissitudes of time, named because time turns people about — overturning them and sending them back and forth.

8. al-ṣirāf: the rutting/heat of sheep, cattle, and dogs — fitted to the root because the animals go back and forth (taṣarraf) in it.

9. al-ṣarīf (second sense): the grinding sound of a camel's canine tooth, named because the animal reiterates the sound.

10. ṣarīf as "silver": in the line "O sons of Ghudāna, you are neither gold nor ṣarīf but earthenware," some took ṣarīf to mean silver; if so, it derives from "exchanging a dinar into dirhams," with no other basis.

Ibn Fāris flags two senses he considers anomalous (outside the core):

11. al-ṣarafān: (a) lead; and (b), disputed in the verse "or a cold, hard ṣarafān," some say lead, others a kind of dates — supported by lines about butter eaten with ṣarafān and dates prized by al-Zabbāʾ.

12. al-ṣirf: a dye for tanning leather (cited in a verse on a bay/reddish hue). From this comes ṣirf meaning "pure, unmixed," as in drinking wine ṣirfan — left on its own color and redness.

text:
Root ṣ-r-m — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: "cutting" (al-qaṭʿ). Every sense below is a variety of something being cut, cut off, or separated.

1. Cutting off relations — ṣurm al-hijrān, "the severing" of estrangement.

2. Firm resolve — [word partly illegible in the source, likely al-ṣarīmah]: determination on a matter, described as cutting off every attachment that would hold one back from it.

3. The last of the milk — al-ṣurām: milk drawn as a last resort after the herd's udders have been rested to build up supply. Cited in a proverb from the poet Bishr ("ṣurām has been milked"), meaning things have reached their worst — because the end of anything comes at the point it is "cut off."

4. The single daily meal — al-ṣayram / al-wajbah: called this because eating it "cuts off" the rest of the day from further food.

5. Grammar note — ṣaramtu-hu ṣarman ("I cut him off"): ṣarm (fatḥa) is the verbal noun; ṣurm (ḍamma) is the plain noun.

6. Dawn and night — al-ṣarīm is given as a name for both dawn and night, and Ibn Fāris says either fits the root's logic, since day and night each "cut off" from the other. He cites the Qur'an, {so it became like al-ṣarīm} [68:20], glossing it himself as "it burned and turned black like the night" — the reading that takes ṣarīm as "night." For the "dawn" sense he quotes a verse of Bishr describing darkness clearing "from its ṣarīmah."

7. A stretch of sand — al-ṣarīm: sand cut off from firm, level ground.

8. Date-harvest — al-ṣirām: the season for cutting date-clusters; aṣrama al-nakhl, "the palms became ready for harvest."

9. A group of camels — al-ṣirmah: a herd of roughly thirty camels.

10. Patches of cloud — al-ṣiram (sing. ṣirmah), illustrated with a line of al-Nābighah describing wind driving scattered cloud-patches through a cold night.

11. A detached encampment — al-ṣirm: a group of people who camp apart from the main water source with their camels; called ahl ṣirm.

12. A decisive man — al-rajul al-ṣārim: resolute in affairs, compared to a cutting sword (al-sayf al-ṣārim).

13. A "cut" she-camel — nāqah muṣarramah: her teat is cut/cauterized so the milk-duct dries up, which is said to strengthen her since milk no longer drains away; the process (al-taṣrīm) is done by cauterizing two teats.

14. Waterless land — al-ṣarmāʾ.

15. Harvested land — al-ṣarīmah is also given as a term for land whose crop has already been reaped.

16. The two aṣramān — in a verse about a bewildering desert overrun "when it turns hostile" by "the two aṣramān," Ibn Fāris identifies these as the wolf and the raven, named for being "cut off" from human company.
