text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-r-r as having four roots, plus two words he cannot fit into them.

**Root 1: tying, binding, gathering tight.**
- Ṣarra al-darāhim: to tie up coins; the cloth is a ṣurra (purse). The word the Arabs know is ṣirār, the rag bound over a she-camel's teats to stop her young from suckling.
- Iṣrār, resolve: he places it here because resolving on something and being fully set on it are one; iṣrār is also holding firm to a thing.
- Yamīn ṣirrī: an oath "in earnest", one held to firmly.
- Ṣarra: a group; Imruʾ al-Qays describes a herd's laggards "in a ṣarra that did not scatter".
- Ḥāfir maṣrūr: a contracted hoof. Ṣurṣūr: a huge herd of camels.

**Root 2: height and rising.**
- Ṣarra al-ḥimār udhunahu: the ass pricked up its ear. Without the ear one says aṣarra; with it, aṣarra bi-udhunihi, which he thinks rare.
- He takes the origin to be ṣirār, raised places that water hardly covers. Ṣirār is also the name of a mountain, cited in a verse: al-Farazdaq will not leave his baseness "until Ṣirār moves from the road".

**Root 3: cold, and also heat.**
- Ṣirr is cold that harms plants, and the chill of a cold wind.
- Some place heat here: ṣārra is said to be intense sun-heat. "The ass cut off its ṣārra" means it drank enough to break its thirst. Ṣārra is thirst (plural ṣawārr), and ṣarīra is thirst (plural ṣarāʾir); a verse speaks of wild asses "their thirsts unquenched".
- Abū ʿUbayd gives ṣārra with the plural ṣarāʾir; Ibn Fāris calls this an error.

**Root 4: sound.**
- Ṣarra is intense shouting; the cricket's ṣarīr and the akhṭab's ṣarṣara.
- Ṣarārī, a sailor, perhaps from raising his voice.

**Two anomalous words**, which he says may have an analogy hidden from him:
1. Ṣārra, a need: "I have a ṣārra with so-and-so" (plural ṣawārr).
2. Ṣarūra: one who has not made the ḥajj; one who has not married; or one who gives up marriage as a celibate. A ḥadīth says "there is no ṣarūra in Islam".

Ibn Durayd explains ṣarūra's history. In the Jāhiliyya, a man who had committed an offence and took refuge at the Kaʿba was left alone; if the blood-avenger found him in the sanctuary he was told, "He is a ṣarūra, do not touch him." The word then came to mean a devotee who avoids women and fine food, as in al-Nābigha's "grey-haired monk … a ṣarūra given to devotion". When Islam came and required the ḥudūd (prescribed penalties) to be carried out in Mecca and elsewhere, the name passed to the person who has not made the ḥajj. His neglect of the ḥajj was seen as like the old devotee's abstinence.

Ibn Fāris suggests that ṣarūra may come from ṣirār, the teat-binding, and closes with "God knows best."

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
quran_words: مُصْرِخ 2x "(be) your helper"; يَسْتَصْرِخُ 1x "cried out to him for help"; يَصْطَرِخُ 1x "will cry"; صَرِيخ 1x "(would be) a responder to a cry"
text:
Root Ṣ-R-KH — Ibn Manẓūr, Lisān al-ʿArab

1. Basic sense — a loud cry. ṣarkha is the loud cry uttered in fright or at a disaster. Another account makes ṣurākh simply a loud voice of any kind. Verb: ṣarakha / yaṣrukhu / ṣurākhan, "to cry out." A proverb uses it for something that strikes without warning: "it was like the cry of a pregnant woman."

2. The crier as one appealing for help. ṣārikh and ṣarīkh are given as the one who calls for aid. Proverb: "a slave whose rescuer is a slave-woman" — i.e. his helper is lowlier and weaker than he is.

3. A disputed pair of opposites. The entry lays out competing assignments of the participles:
   - ṣārikh = one seeking help; mustaṣrikh = one seeking help; muṣrikh = one giving help.
   - Another view: ṣārikh can itself mean the one giving help.
   Al-Azharī notes he heard that second view from al-Aṣmaʿī alone, and reports that everyone else holds ṣārikh and mustaṣrikh = seeker of help, muṣrikh = giver of help. Abū Ḥātim is cited for the verbal noun istiṣrākh carrying both senses, seeking help and giving it. Accordingly ṣarīkh is listed among the aḍdād — words carrying two opposite meanings, both "helper" and "help-seeker."

4. Qur'anic citation. "I am no muṣrikh of yours, nor are you muṣrikhs of mine." Abū al-Haytham glosses: "I am not your helper." He adds that ṣarīkh equals ṣārikh in the sense "helper," on the pattern qadīr/qādir.

5. Being summoned by a cry. In a report about Ibn ʿUmar, ustuṣrikha ("he was called out to") over his wife Ṣafiyya — the living being summoned on account of the dead, i.e. called on to help attend to the deceased; the ṣurākh is the sound of that appeal. Ibn al-Athīr: a person is ustuṣrikha when the cry reaches him informing him of an event so his help can be enlisted, or announcing a death. Separately, istaṣrakhtuhu means to make someone cry out.

6. Derived forms.
   - iṣṭarakha al-qawm, taṣārakhū, istaṣrakhū: they called out for help. iṣṭirākh is the iftiʿāl-form equivalent of taṣāruḫ.
   - taṣarruḫ: putting on or forcing a cry; said of sneezing, "affecting it is folly."
   - istaṣrakhanī fa-aṣrakhtuhu: "he sought my help and I helped him."
   - ṣarīkh also = the sound made by the one seeking help. One cries wā-ghawthāh! wā-ṣarkhatāh! ("O for rescue! O for a cry!").

7. Morphology. ṣarīkh may be faʿīl used with the force of the active mufʿil, like nadhīr for mundhir ("warner") and samīʿ for musmiʿ. The form ṣārikha (fāʿila) works as a verbal noun in two directions: "I heard the ṣārikha of the people" = the sound of their appeal; and ṣārikha = the act of giving aid, as in the verse "they would have destroyed the sons, had aid from a compassionate one not reached them in time." Al-Layth takes ṣārikha as equivalent to ṣarīkh, the helper.

8. Shāhid. Zuhayr: "When we hear a crier for help, lean grey-flanked mounts race with us toward his voice."

9. Names of criers. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: al-ṣarrākh is the peacock (as al-nabbāḥ is the hoopoe). A report has the Prophet rising at night on hearing the voice of "the ṣārikh," meaning the rooster, since it crows much at night.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-w-ʿ (ص و ع) as a sound triliteral root with two distinct branches of meaning.

**1. Scattering / splitting apart**
- تَصَوَّعُوا (taṣawwaʿū) — "they scattered/dispersed." Illustrated with a line from the poet Dhū al-Rummah describing a herd of wild game scattering away from him.
- تَصَوَّعَ شَعَرُهُ (taṣawwaʿa shaʿruhu) — "his hair taṣawwaʿa," said when it splits or cracks (i.e., gets split ends) — attributed to the lexicographer al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad.
- تَصَوَّعَ النَّبْتُ (taṣawwaʿa al-nabtu) — "the plant taṣawwaʿa," meaning it dried out / went to seed — also from al-Khalīl.
- اِنْصَاعَ الْقَوْمُ سِرَاعًا (inṣāʿa al-qawmu sirāʿan) — "the people inṣāʿa swiftly," meaning they went off/passed by quickly.

**2. A vessel**
- الصَّاعُ / الصُّوَاعُ (al-ṣāʿ / al-ṣuwāʿ) — a drinking vessel.
- The same word ṣāʿ also names a unit of measure (a measuring-cup/bushel). Ibn Fāris notes it belongs to the "wāw" class of roots and explains the name: it was called ṣāʿ because it is turned/rotated as the grain or substance is measured out.
- By extension, the verb yaṣūʿu describes a mailed warrior "coming at" his opponents by approaching them from the flanks, and a man "driving/rounding up" camels (yaṣūʿu al-ibil).
- Also under this branch: al-ṣāʿ as a hollow depression in the ground, supported by an unattributed half-verse ("with the two paws of a māqiṭ in a hollow"), and ṣāʿu juʾjuʾi al-naʿāmah — the hollow of an ostrich's breastbone, i.e. where its chest rests when it lowers itself to the ground.

Note: this second branch (vessel/measure) is the sense behind the Qur'anic term ṣuwāʿ, the king's drinking-cup/measuring-vessel in the Joseph narrative — though the Qur'an itself is not cited in this entry.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَصَابَ 64x "befalls you"; مُّصِيبَة 10x "disaster"; صَيِّب 1x "like a rainstorm"; مُصِيب 1x "will strike her"; صَوَاب 1x "(what is) correct"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ص-و-ب (ṣ-w-b) as a single sound root whose core meaning is something descending and settling firmly in its place.

1. Ṣawāb — rightness/correctness in word and deed: as if a matter has come down and settled firmly where it belongs. It is the opposite of khaṭaʾ (error).

2. Ṣawb — the falling of rain; also the thing that falls/descends itself. Ibn Fāris takes the fact that rightness (ṣawāb) is also called ṣawb as evidence that both senses trace to the one root. He cites a verse using ṣawbī ("my rightness") alongside khaṭaʾī ("my error").

3. Ṣayyib — a rain-bearing cloud (one "possessing ṣawb"), cited from Qurʾan 2:19, "or like a ṣayyib from the sky."

4. Ṣawb as descent/coming-down generally: illustrated by a verse describing an angel descending (yaṣūbu) from the sky.

5. Proverbial usage ṣābat bi-qurr ("it has settled with firmness / hit home"), said of a matter that has firmly settled; cited from Ṭarafa.

6. Taṣwīb — a raised hump set within a downward slope (only used in this configuration).

7. Ṣuyyāba — the choicest/best of anything, which he links to ṣawb in the sense of the pure water of a cloud, suggesting the word derives from that.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ص و ف (Ṣ-W-F) — from Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha (d. 1004 CE)

Ibn Fāris states that ṣād-wāw-fāʾ is a single, sound root whose core meaning is الصُّوف (al-ṣūf), "wool" — and every usage in the entry traces back to this one idea.

1. **Wool-bearing animals**: A ram described as aṣwaf, ṣawif, ṣāʾif, or ṣāf is one that has abundant wool.

2. **The nape-tuft**: The phrase "he took hold of the ṣūfa of his nape" refers to grabbing the hair that hangs down in the hollow at the back of the neck — that tuft is called ṣūfa by analogy with wool.

3. **Ṣūfa, the pre-Islamic group**: Ṣūfa was the name of a people in the Jāhiliyya who served the Kaʿba and were responsible for releasing the pilgrims to move on from their standing-place. Abū ʿUbayda is cited as saying they were made up of scattered offshoots from various tribes who banded together and became "interlocked" with one another the way wool fibers interlock — which Ibn Fāris implies is the reason for their name. A line of verse (partially quoted, with a gap in the source text) is given as evidence: the group does not leave its station at al-Taʿrīf (ʿArafāt) until someone calls out, "Let the family of Ṣūfān pass on!"

4. **A look-alike expression, explicitly set aside**: The phrase ṣāfin ʿani l-sharr ("turning aside from evil") looks like it belongs to this root, but Ibn Fāris says it does not — he classifies it instead as a case of ibdāl (interchange of letters) with the separate root ص و ب (ṣāba, "to incline/deviate"), which he says he has already covered under that root's own entry. So this sense is deliberately excluded from ص و ف.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: صِيَام 9x "then fasting"; يَصُمْ 2x "fast"; صَوْم 1x "a fast"; صَّٰئِمِين 1x "and the men who fast"; صَّٰئِمَٰت 1x "and the women who fast"
poets_named: Al-Nābigha (pre-Islamic); Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); Al-Shammākh (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-w-m as a single root meaning with two sides: holding back (imsāk) and staying still in one place (rukūd).

**1. Holding back**
- ṣawm of the one who fasts (al-ṣāʾim): his holding back from food, drink and everything else he has been forbidden.
- Holding back from speech is also called ṣawm. On Q 19:26, "Indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a ṣawm", Ibn Fāris reports that "they said" it means holding back from speech: silence.

**2. Staying still**
- One who stands still is called ṣāʾim. Al-Nābigha: "horses standing still (ṣiyām), and horses not standing still, beneath the dust-cloud, and horses champing the bits."
- al-ṣawm is also the dropping of the wind, when it becomes still.
- al-ṣawm is also the sun at its height at midday, as though it paused at the top of its circuit. So one says ṣāma al-nahār, "the day stood still", i.e. reached noon. Imruʾ al-Qays: "when the day stood still and the midday heat came on."
- maṣām al-faras, also maṣāma, is a horse's standing-place. Al-Shammākh: "whenever he sniffed at a standing-place of hers."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: صُّور 10x "the trumpet"; صَوَّرَ 4x "and he formed you"; صُورَة 3x "your forms"; صُرْ 1x "and incline them"; مُصَوِّر 1x "the fashioner"
text:
Ibn Fāris opens by declaring the root ص و ر (ṣ-w-r) a set of many words with unrelated origins — not a case governed by analogy or derivation. Only one strand can be brought under a rule; the rest are separate homonyms.

The rule-governed core — "leaning/inclining":
- صَوِرَ / يَصْوَرُ (ṣawira/yaṣwaru): to lean, incline.
- صُرْتُ الشَّيْءَ / أَصَرْتُهُ (ṣurtu al-shayʾa / aṣartuhu): to incline something toward oneself.
- تَصَوَّرَ (taṣawwara): said of someone struck, as if he leaned over and toppled.

The separate, standalone words:
1. الصُّورَة (ṣūra) — the form or shape of any created thing; plural صُوَر (ṣuwar). Hence God as al-Bāriʾ al-Muṣawwir (the Fashioner, the Shaper), and rajul ṣayyir = a man of beautiful form.
2. الصَّوْر (ṣawr) — a cluster/stand of palm trees (a ḥāʾish); it has no singular of its own wording.
3. الصُِّوار (ṣuwār/ṣiwār) — a herd of cattle or oxen; plural صِيرَان (ṣīrān). Backed by a verse describing spearing amid the herds of al-Ṣarīm.
4. الصُِّوار (ṣuwār/ṣiwār) — of musk: reported either as its scent or as its container. A cited love-couplet (which Ibn Fāris thinks is probably fabricated, though the words are genuine) plays on the word.
5. صَوْرَة (ṣawra) — in "I find a ṣawra in my head," meaning an itch.
6. عُصْفُور صَوَّار (ʿuṣfūr ṣawwār) — reported by al-Khalīl as a sparrow that answers when called. Ibn Fāris doubts it is Arabic; if genuine, he suggests it could fall under the "leaning" sense, since the bird inclines toward its caller.
7. صَوْر (ṣawr) — also the hair of a horse's forelock; possibly named by likeness to the ṣawr of palms. Supported by a poetic line.
8. الصَّارَة (ṣāra) — land that has trees.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-w-t as a single sound root with one core meaning.

1. Core sense — صَوْت (ṣawt), "sound, voice." He defines it as a generic category covering anything that lodges in the hearer's ear, i.e. any audible thing, not one particular kind of noise. Example of usage: هذا صوت زيد, "this is Zayd's voice."

2. Derived descriptions of a person by loudness. صَيِّت (ṣayyit) = a man of powerful voice. صَائِت (ṣāʾit) = one making a sound, said of someone shouting.

3. Morphological note on انْصَاتَ (inṣāta). The idiom "he was called and inṣāta" belongs to the same root: it is the infiʿāl (VII) pattern built on ṣawt — as if a sound was directed at him and he reacted to it — and the sense is that he answered the call.

4. صِيت (ṣīt) — good repute, a favourable mention of someone among people. Idiom: ذهب صيته, "his renown travelled / spread."

The entry is brief and cites no poetry or Qurʾānic verses; the semantic thread Ibn Fāris draws is audible sound → a voice raised → responding to a voice → the name one is spoken of by.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ṣ-kh-r (ص خ ر) is classed by Ibn Fāris as a "sound" root — a single, unified word rather than one built from overlapping senses.

1. Core meaning: al-ṣakhrah — a huge, massive rock (a boulder-sized stone), glossed as "the great stone."
2. Two attested vocalizations of the word are given: ṣakhrah (صَخْرَة) and ṣakharah (صَخَرَة).

The entry records no further senses or citations.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris says that ṣād and khāʾ (ṣ-kh-kh) form a root (aṣl) indicating a certain kind of sound, and he gives three examples.

1. **al-ṣākhkha:** said to be the cry that deafens the ears.

2. **ṣakhkh: the sound from a struck rock.** One says: "I struck the rock with a stone and heard a ṣakhkh from it."

3. **ṣakhkha, said of a crow: to jab with the beak.** ṣakhkha al-ghurābu bi-minqārihi fī dabarati al-baʿīr: the crow jabbed with its beak into the sore on the camel's back.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: unnamed verse; Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); Ruʾba (Umayyad); Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad); ʿUbayd (ibn al-Abraṣ) (pre-Islamic)
text:
Root صيح (ṣ-y-ḥ), from Ibn Manẓūr's Lisān al-ʿArab.

1. Core sense — crying out. الصِّياح (ṣiyāḥ) is "sound/cry"; per the Tahdhīb, "the sound of anything when it grows loud." The verb صاحَ / يَصِيحُ means "to cry out at the top of one's capacity," used of people and of other things. It has many verbal nouns: ṣayḥa, ṣiyāḥ, ṣuyāḥ, ṣayḥ, ṣayaḥān, plus the doubled form ṣayyaḥa. A cited verse: "The raven of separation cried out, and the staff split apart."

2. Crying to one another. المُصايَحة (muṣāyaḥa) and التصايُح (taṣāyuḥ): people crying out to each other.

3. الصَّيْحة as "the punishing blast/destruction." Ibn Manẓūr derives this from sense 1. He cites the Qurʾanic فأَخَذَتْهم الصَّيْحةُ ("the ṣayḥa seized them"), glossing ṣayḥa here as the punishment. Related idiom: صِيحَ في آلِ فلان ("a cry was raised over so-and-so's family") = they perished; the phrase means it destroyed them.

4. الصَّيْحة as a sudden raid. The attack that takes a tribe by surprise.

5. الصائِحة (ṣāʾiḥa): the cry of ritual mourning. Idiom: "they await nothing but the cry of a pregnant woman," i.e. an evil soon to overtake them. On وأَخَذَ الذين ظَلَموا الصيحةُ, Ibn Manẓūr notes a grammatical point: the verb أَخَذَ appears in the masculine because ṣayḥa here stands for the verbal noun ṣiyāḥ (crying); feminine agreement (أَخذت) would also be permissible if one attends to the feminine word ṣayḥa itself. Shāhid from Imruʾ al-Qays: "Leave off the plunder over whose fringes an alarm was cried…"

6. Idiomatic ṣayḥ + nafr. قبل كل صَيْح ونَفْر = "before any cry (ṣayḥ) and dispersal (nafr)," also used to mean "before daybreak." من غير صَيْحٍ ولا نَفْر = "for no reason at all" (nothing was cried out about); a cited verse glosses it as "over neither little nor much."

7. Applied to plants — صاحَ العُنقُود. The grape-cluster "ṣāḥa" when it has fully emerged from its sheaths and grown long while still tender. On Ruʾba's line "like the vine when it called out (nādā) from the spathe": Abū Ḥanīfa (al-Dīnawarī) held he really meant صاحَ ("cried"), but that would break the metre; Ruʾba substituted نادَى to keep the metrical foot intact (avoiding the ṭayy).

8. Drying and cracking — تَصَيَّحَ. Of herbage, wood, hair, etc., a variant of تَصَوَّحَ: to crack, split and dry out. صَيَّحَتْه الريحُ والحرُّ والشمسُ = the wind, heat, and sun dried/split it (= ṣawwaḥa). Shāhid from Dhū al-Rumma about a scorching day. تَصَيَّحَ الشيءُ = the thing broke and cracked apart; transitive صَيَّحْتُه = "I split it."

9. Splitting open — انْصاحَ. انْصاحَ الثوبُ: the garment split by itself. انْصاحَت الأرضُ: land partly covered with vegetation and partly bare, like a torn garment. Shāhid from ʿUbayd (ibn al-Abraṣ). Ibn Manẓūr notes this verse also appears under the root صوح.

10. الصَّيْحانيّ (ṣayḥānī): a kind of Medinan date. Per al-Azharī, black and firm to chew, named after Ṣayḥān, a ram tied to a palm in Medina that then bore this variety of date.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root ص ي ص (ṣ-y-ṣ), al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān

1. Qur'anic citation, al-Ahzab 33:26: "wa anzala alladhīna ẓāharūhum min ahli al-kitābi min ṣayāṣīhim" — "and He brought down those of the People of the Book who had supported them from their fortresses." Al-Rāghib glosses ṣayāṣī as fortresses.
2. General principle: anything one fortifies/protects oneself with is called ṣīṣah. On this same logic, a cow's horn is also called ṣīṣah, and so is the spur/spine a rooster fights with — both being the animal's means of self-defense.
3. Closing formula: "and God knows best His intent and the secrets of His Book" — a standard humility-marker before an interpretive extension.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-y-d as one sound root with a single core idea: moving straight ahead, head-on, without turning the head aside or veering.

1. **al-ṣayad** — the condition of a person who keeps his gaze straight in front of him (holding the head unturned).

2. **al-aṣyad** — reported by the lexicographers as a term for "king," plural **al-ṣīd**. They explain the name by how little such a person turns his head aside. Ibn Fāris adds that some people are aṣyad by natural build, not just by bearing.

3. **al-ṣayd (game, quarry)** — derived, on his account, from the same idea: the animal goes past in a straight, unswerving course. When it is caught one says *qad ṣīda* ("it has been taken as game"). He notes the direction of derivation: the verb comes from the noun, on the pattern of *raʾastu al-rajula* ("I struck his head," from raʾs) and *baṭantuhu* ("I struck his belly," from baṭn). So too *ṣidtuhu* — "I fell upon the game and took it."

4. **al-ṣaydāna** — cited from Ibn al-Sikkīt as a woman of bad character, so named (says Ibn Fāris) because she turns aside for nothing; he offers this as evidence that his single-meaning analysis holds. Under the same heading, al-ṣaydāna also denotes **al-ghūl** (the ghoul).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ص ي ف (ṣ-y-f), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Two distinct roots:

First — the season. al-ṣayf — the season after late spring (summer); rain falling in it is al-ṣayyif; a hot day/night is called ṣāʾif/ṣāʾifah. "ʿāmaltuhu muṣāyafatan" — I dealt with him for the summer season (by analogy with mushāharah, a monthly arrangement). al-ṣayfiyyūn — a man's children born after his old age ("late" children), illustrated with a line of poetry contrasting them with rabīʿiyyūn, children born in one's youth ("spring" children).

Second — turning away/veering. ṣāfa ʿan al-shayʾ — to turn away from something; ṣāfa al-sahmu ʿan al-hadaf — an arrow veering off target, illustrated with a line of poetry by Abū Zubayd about a volley of arrows, some hitting true and some veering off.

Closing: a place called Ṣāʾif, mentioned in a line of poetry by Aws — unrelated to either core sense, simply a proper name sharing the letters.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ص ي ر (ṣ-y-r) as a single sound root whose core meaning is an outcome and a place of return — where something ends up or comes back to.

1. Core verb: ṣāra / yaṣīru (verbal nouns ṣayr and ṣayrūra) — "to become, to come to be, to end up as."

2. ṣīr al-amr = the point a matter comes to. The phrase anā ʿalā ṣīri amrin means "I am on the verge of a matter being settled" — the ṣīr being what it resolves into. He cites Zuhayr's verse ("for eight years, over Salmā, upon the ṣīr of a matter neither bitter nor sweet"), glossing ṣīr al-amr here as the matter's outcome (maṣīr) and end-result (ʿāqiba).

3. ṣīra (pl. ṣīr) = a pen or enclosure built for cattle — named from the same root because the animals return/come to it.

4. ṣayyūr al-amr = the final part or end of a matter, again because it is what one arrives at. Hence lā raʾya li-fulānin wa-lā ṣayyūr = "he has neither judgment nor ṣayyūr," i.e. no resolve or firmness for him to fall back on.

5. taṣayyara fulānun abāhu = "he took after his father" in resemblance — as though he had "become" his father.

6. Marked as anomalous to the root (shādhdh): ṣīr meaning a slit or crack, as in the Hadith "whoever looks through the ṣīr [crack] of a door without permission, his eye is forfeit."

7. Also noted: ṣīr as a name for ṣiḥnāt (a fish-relish). Ibn Fāris judges this not to be genuinely Arabic and doubts the Arabs knew it; lexicographers record it, but he regards it as having no real [Arabic] basis.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: طَعَام 24x "food"; أَطْعَمَ 13x "and feed"; طَعِمُ 5x "you have eaten"; إِطْعَٰم 3x "then (the) feeding"; طَاعِم 1x "an eater"; ٱسْتَطْعَمَ 1x "they asked for food"; طَعْم 1x "its taste"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṭ-ʿ-m as a single regular root whose core sense is the tasting of a thing (one says طَعِمْتُ الشَّيْءَ, "I tasted the thing").

1. Core sense — tasting / food. طَعَام (ṭaʿām) is "that which is eaten," food. He notes that some philologists restricted ṭaʿām specifically to wheat (al-burr), citing Abū Saʿīd's report that in the Prophet's time the fast-breaking alms was given as a ṣāʿ of ṭaʿām or a ṣāʿ of another commodity.

2. Metaphorical extension beyond tasting. Things outside literal tasting are drawn into the "food" domain: اسْتَطْعَمَنِي الْحَدِيثَ means "he sought me to relate the story" (literally, sought its "food"). The ḥadīth "when the imam seeks 'food' from you, feed him" means: when he falters in recitation and seeks a prompt, supply the words for him.

3. Feeding (iṭʿām) covers anything ingested, even water. Cited: Qurʾān 2:249, {وَمَنْ لَمْ يَطْعَمْهُ فَإِنَّهُ مِنِّي} ("whoever does not partake of it is of me"); and the saying about Zamzam, "a food that nourishes and a cure for sickness." Khālid al-Qasrī was mocked for saying "give me water to eat," and verse was composed against him — but Ibn Fāris judges this no fault, since "feeding" legitimately extends to water.

4. Derived forms and descriptors.
- طَاعِم (ṭāʿim): a man well-off as to food, illustrated by al-Ḥuṭayʾa's line addressing "the well-fed, well-clothed one."
- مِطْعَام (miṭʿām): one who gives much hospitality.
- مُطْعَم (muṭʿam): one provided with sustenance, blessed in provision.
- طُعْمَة (ṭuʿma): a source of food or livelihood — "I made this estate a livelihood for so-and-so." Conversely خَبِيثُ الطُّعْمَة is one whose earnings are base.

5. Specialized/technical uses.
- Dhū al-Rumma's verse on a bow of shiryān-wood: read مُطْعَمَة, "provided with game (fortunate in the hunt)," or مُطْعِمَة, "one that feeds its owner game."
- مُطْعِمَة: the thick foremost talon of a bird of prey, so called because it "feeds" the bird its catch.
- مُطَعَّم (of camels): one in whose marrow the taste of fat is found, from fatness.
- أَطْعَمَتِ النخلة: said of a palm-tree when its fruit ripens ("it has come to bear").
- طَعُوم (ewe): one with some fat in it.

6. Tasting/appetite idioms. تَطَعُّم means tasting: تَطَعَّمْ تَطْعَمُ, "taste and you will crave it." And ادْنُ فَاطْعَمْ ("come eat") is answered مَا بِي طُعْم ("I have no appetite"), parallel to مَا بِي شُرْب ("I have no thirst") for drink.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ṭ-ʿ-n (ط ع ن) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris states the root is sound and regular, and gives its core meaning as: piercing or jabbing into something with an implement that goes through it. From this physical core, the root is then extended and used figuratively.

1. Core/literal sense: al-ṭaʿn bi-l-rumḥ — stabbing or thrusting with a spear.

2. Reciprocal forms: taṭāʿana al-qawm / iṭṭaʿanū — "the people stabbed each other" [in battle]. Those skilled or much engaged in this are called maṭāʿīn fī al-ḥarb, "stabbers in war."

3. Figurative extension — verbal attack: a man habitually assailing others' honor is called ṭaʿʿān fī aʿrāḍ al-nās (an intensive form: "one who constantly stabs at people's reputations"). Ibn Fāris supports this with a ḥadīth: "the believer is not a ṭaʿʿān" (not a habitual slanderer/reviler).

4. Some philologists reportedly kept the verbal noun for the figurative (verbal) sense distinct from the literal one: ṭaʿantu fī al-rajuli ṭaʿanānan ("I reviled the man") uses ṭaʿanān only, as if to mark it off from ṭaʿn, the noun used for the literal spear-thrust.

5. A supporting line of poetry (poet not named in the entry, and the source text shows an ellipsis mid-verse) uses ṭaʿanān for reviling: "the manifestness of enmity insists on nothing but ... reviling, and saying what should not be said."

6. A further figurative use: ṭaʿana fī al-mafāzah ("he plunged into the desert-waste") simply means dhahaba, "he went/set out [into it]" — no notion of stabbing survives here beyond "pressing into."

7. Morphological note: philologists distinguished the two senses by the vowel of the imperfect verb — ṭaʿana bi-l-rumḥ, yaṭʿunu (ḍamma) for the literal act of stabbing with a spear, versus ṭaʿana bi-l-qawl, yaṭʿanu (fatḥa) for assailing someone with speech.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ṭ-ḥ-w (طحو) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: "spreading out" and "extension."

1. Basic sense — al-ṭaḥw means "spreading," a near-synonym of al-daḥw. Ibn Fāris cites Q 91:6, "By the earth and Him who spread it out (ṭaḥāhā)," glossing ṭaḥāhā as "He spread it" (basaṭahā). He notes the parallel wording at Q 79:30, "the earth, after that, He spread it out (daḥāhā)," which uses the related root d-ḥ-w for the same idea.

2. Idiomatic extension — "ṭaḥā bika hammuka" ("your worry carried you off") describes a concern that draws a person along into a matter and prolongs their involvement in it. Illustrated with a line of poetry by ʿAlqama: a heart carried away by longing for beautiful women even as old age and gray hair were setting in.

3. al-mudawwima al-ṭawāḥī — a term for vultures or eagles wheeling/circling around the slain (e.g., on a battlefield), extending the same image of a sweeping, drawn-out motion.

4. A separate report from the lexicographer al-Shaybānī: ṭaḥaytu = "I lay down" — an additional attested usage, not obviously connected to the "spreading" sense.

5. al-ṭāḥī — a large crowd or multitude, said to be so named because it "drags" or sweeps over whatever it passes, comparable to the term jarrār ("the dragging/overwhelming host"). Supported by a poetic fragment describing an overwhelming throng.

Ibn Fāris closes with the standard formula: "And God knows best."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṭ-b-ʿ (طبع) as one sound root whose core image is a limit at which a thing reaches its end and is sealed shut.

1. Core sense — sealing. طَبَعْتُ عَلَى الشَّيْءِ (I set a seal on a thing). The seal-instrument is الطَّابَع (ṭābaʿ), the one who seals is الطَّابِع (ṭābiʿ).

2. Innate nature. From "sealing" comes طَبْع, a person's inborn nature and disposition — as if stamped into them.

3. Qur'anic usage. طَبَعَ اللَّهُ عَلَى قَلْبِ الْكَافِرِ (God sealed the disbeliever's heart): Ibn Fāris explains it as though a seal is set on the heart so that no guidance or light can reach it, and he is granted no success toward good.

4. Forging/striking. طَبْع of a sword or a coin: striking the metal until it is brought to completion.

5. Filling to fullness (the completion/closure idea). Filling a measure is called ṭabʿ (it is now complete and closed off). تَطَبَّعَ النَّهَرُ = the river filled up. A she-camel loaded with her full load is مُطَبَّعَة — illustrated by a verse asking "where is the load of the fully-laden she-camel?"

6. River/watercourse. Ibn al-Sikkīt: الطِّبْع = the river, plural الطِّبَاع, with a supporting verse likening languid walkers to river water-beasts near to sticking in mud. Ibn Fāris suggests the sense fits best if the river is understood as full.

7. A divergent sense — filth/tarnish (ṭabaʿ). Ibn Fāris marks this as departing from the core sense (though it might be forced into connection). رَجُلٌ طَبِعٌ = a soiled man. He cites the prophetic saying "Seek refuge in God from a greed that leads to defilement (ṭabaʿ)," and a verse praising jewelry with "neither flaw nor tarnish." From the same word: قَدْ طَبِعَ, said of a man who cannot carry a matter through (becomes dull/blocked).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
**Root ط ب ق (Ṭ-B-Q) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha**

Ibn Fāris treats this as one sound root with a single core idea: **laying something flat over something else of its own kind, so as to cover it.** He then derives every attested use from that one image.

1. **Covering / lid / matching layer.** *ṭabaq* is a cover. *aṭbaqtu l-shayʾa ʿalā l-shayʾ* = "I laid one thing over the other," the upper being a *ṭabaq* to the lower; *taṭābaqā* = "the two fitted one over the other."

2. **Unanimity.** *aṭbaqa l-nās ʿalā kadhā* — "people closed ranks on such-and-such." Ibn Fāris explains it as their statements being so equal that either could be laid over the other as an exact counterpart and still fit.

3. **State or stage.** *ṭabaq* = *ḥāl* (condition). He cites Q 84:19, *la-tarkabunna ṭabaqan ʿan ṭabaq* — "you shall mount stage upon stage."

4. **Calamity.** The idiom *iḥdā banāt Ṭabaq* ("one of the daughters of Ṭabaq") means a disaster — so called, he says, because it is general and covers everything.

5. **Ground-cover / overspreading rain.** Whatever rises over the earth until it covers it is *ṭabaq al-arḍ*. Shāhid: Imruʾ al-Qays on rain — a steady, long-fringed drizzle that is "a covering of the earth," seeking its mark and pouring.

6. **Hitting the mark exactly.** *ṭabbaqa l-ḥaqq* = "he hit upon the truth," i.e. his aim coincided with, matched, the truth. Extended: *ṭabbaqa* of one who strikes precisely at the joint without missing; then *ṭabbaqa ʿunuqahu bi-l-sayf* = "he took his neck clean off with the sword."

7. **Muṭābaqa as a gait.** The walk of a man in fetters, because his feet fall close together as if laid one on the other. Shāhid: al-Jaʿdī — "with the close tread of dogs treading on thorns."

8. **Anatomy.** *ṭabaq* is also the thin bone separating two vertebrae. And a hand is *ṭabiqa* when it has stuck fast against the side.

9. **Alignment, and a grammatical term.** *ṭābaqtu bayna l-shayʾayn* = to set two things on one and the same alignment. On that basis, Ibn Fāris notes, lexicographers call doubled (reduplicated) speech *muṭābaq* — e.g. *jarjara*, *ṣalṣala*, *ṣaʿṣaʿa*.

10. **A locust swarm** is a *ṭabaq*, likened to a covering spread over the ground.

11. **Successive births.** Sheep are said to give birth *ṭibqan wa-ṭabaqatan* when they bear one after another.

He states explicitly that the analogy behind all of the above is one and the same.

12. **Ṭabāqāʾ.** Used of a tongue-tied, ineffectual man, and of a stallion camel unable to cover the female. He fits this to the same analogy: it is as though the matter were shut off and closed over him, leaving him as one covered up. Shāhid: Jamīl — "a helpless dolt, who never stood among disputants nor led camels to their saddles."

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
1. **Of a fire: to go out.** ṭafiʾat al-nār (imperfect taṭfaʾu; verbal nouns ṭafʾ and ṭufūʾ), and also inṭafaʾat: the fire's flame went away. The form inṭafaʾat is reported from al-Zajjājī, who records it in Kitāb al-Jumal.

2. **To put out; by figure, to end a war.** aṭfaʾahā: he put the fire out. aṭfaʾa al-ḥarb, "he put out the war," is the same verb used figuratively. The Qur'an says: "Whenever they kindle a fire for war, God puts it out" (Q 5:64), explained as "He makes it die down until it grows cold." A verse is also cited: "Among the house of Banū ʿAdī there was strife, and Ziyād put it out."

3. **Stages of a dying fire.** A fire whose flame has died down but whose embers are still alive is khāmida. Once the flame has died down and the embers have gone cold, it is hāmida and ṭāfiʾa.

4. **Muṭfiʾ al-Jamr, "the quencher of the embers."** The name of the fifth of the "days of the old woman" (ayyām al-ʿajūz). A verse is cited that names it alongside Āmir, "his brother" Muʾtamir, and Muʿallil.

5. **Muṭfiʾat al-raḍf, "the quencher of the heated stones."** An emaciated sheep. On al-Liḥyānī's authority, the Arabs say ḥadasa lahum bi-muṭfiʾat al-raḍf, "he laid down for them [for slaughter] a quencher of the heated stones."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris says the letters ṭ-f point to the smallness of a thing, and explains most of the root's words from that.

1. **Slight.** Shayʾ ṭafīf: a slight, small thing.

2. **A full vessel; what is above it.** Ināʾ ṭaffān: a full vessel. What is above a vessel is called al-ṭafāf (or al-ṭifāf, al-ṭufāf) and al-ṭufāfa.

3. **Short measure.** Al-taṭfīf: making the measure and the balance short. One of the learned says it is so called because what is taken off is slight (ṭafīf).

4. **Bringing level with.** Ṭaffaftu bi-fulān mawḍiʿa kadhā: I raised someone up to a certain place and brought him level with it. A ḥadīth has "the horse ṭaffafa with me the masjid of Banū so-and-so", meaning the horse leapt until it almost came level with the masjid. Ibn Fāris explains this as a likening to what stands above a vessel (its ṭufāf or ṭufāfa), and says the underlying analogy is the same.

5. **Exceptions.** He lists as departing from the pattern aṭaffa bi-fulān, to watch someone slyly meaning to take him unawares, and with it ustuṭiffa l-amr, "the matter became feasible and was brought to completion." He classes this as letter substitution (ibdāl), treated in its own chapter.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṭ-f-l as a single sound root with one base meaning, from which the other uses are derived by analogy.

1. Core sense — the young child. The root's base meaning is "the small newborn." A male child is طِفْل (ṭifl), a female طِفْلَة (ṭiflah).

2. Applied to animals with young. المُطْفِل (al-muṭfil) is a doe that has her fawn with her, having recently given birth. The verb form II طَفَّلَ / تَطْفِيل is used of driving animals gently: "we ṭaffala-ed our camels" means their young were with them, so the travelling pace was eased for them. Ibn Fāris marks this animal/pastoral usage as belonging to the root sense itself, not as a later extension.

3. Derived sense — a soft, delicate woman. A tender woman is called طَفْلَة (ṭaflah), on the reasoning that she is compared, in softness and delicacy, to a little girl. The two words are then kept apart by vowelling: fatḥa in ṭaflah (the woman), kasra in ṭiflah (the girl).

4. Sense in, or near, the same chapter — early darkness. طِفْل الظَّلَام (ṭifl al-ẓalām) is the first onset of darkness, so called because it is slight and thin, coming before the main body of the night. Shāhid: Labīd — "Then I let myself down upon it, returning … while over the earth lay the shadows of the ṭafal."

5. Verbal use for nightfall. طَفَلَ اللَّيْلُ (ṭafala al-laylu) means its darkness came on.

6. A further citation is begun — a poet's line, "for a hollow which the ṭafal of the Pleiades watered" — but the entry as preserved breaks off before Ibn Fāris explains it.

Method: the account works by naming one attested base sense (the young child) and showing each further use — the doe with her fawn, easing the pace for young camels, the soft woman, the first thin darkness — as a likeness measured against it, with the vowel change (ṭiflah/ṭaflah) noted as the device that separates two of them.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ط ف ق (Ṭ-F-Q) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris treats this root as having a single, straightforward sense: it forms the verb ṭafiqa, meaning "he set about / began [doing something]."

He explains it by direct comparison to another common auxiliary verb: Arabic speakers say ṭafiqa yafʿalu kadhā ("he began doing such-and-such") exactly as they say ẓalla yafʿalu ("he kept on doing [it]"). So ṭafiqa works like ẓalla — a verb that, prefixed to another verb, marks the onset or continuation of an action, roughly "he began to..." / "he set to..."

He supports this with two Qur'anic citations of the verb in this same inceptive sense:
1. "then he began wiping/stroking the shanks and necks" (fa-ṭafiqa masḥan bi-l-sūqi wa-l-aʿnāq)
2. "and the two of them began sewing leaves of the Garden over themselves" (wa-ṭafiqā yakhṣifāni ʿalayhimā min waraqi l-jannah) — Q 7:22

No other senses or derivations are given; the entry is confined to this single grammatical/lexical function of the verb.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ط-غ-ي (ṭ-gh-y) as one sound, regular root whose core meaning is exceeding the limit in disobedience or rebellion.

1. Core sense: to overstep the bounds. A person who does this is طاغٍ (ṭāghin), a transgressor.

2. Extended to water: طَغَى السَّيْلُ (ṭaghā al-sayl) = the torrent overflowed, coming with a great volume of water. He cites Qur'an al-Ḥāqqa 69:11, {when the water overflowed}, glossing it (with the deferential "God knows best") as the water going out beyond its due measure.

3. طَغَى الْبَحْرُ (ṭaghā al-baḥr) = the sea raged, its waves surging.

4. طَغَى الدَّمُ (ṭaghā al-dam) = the blood became inflamed or overabundant (tabayyagha).

Grammar/derivation (on al-Khalīl's authority): the noun has two variant forms, طُغْيَان (ṭughyān) and طُغْوَان (ṭughwān); the verb accordingly appears as both طَغَيْتُ (ṭaghaytu) and طَغَوْتُ (ṭaghawtu).

Anomaly: Ibn Fāris notes one usage that falls outside this root's core meaning — الطَّغْيَة (al-ṭaghya), used for a smooth rock or slab (al-ṣafāt al-malsāʾ).
