text:
Ibn Fāris treats ط-ه-ر (ṭ-h-r) as a single, sound root with one core meaning: purity and the removal of filth. From it he draws the following:

1. الطُّهْر (ṭuhr) — "purity," the direct opposite of دَنَس (danas), "defilement."

2. التَّطَهُّر (tatahhur) — the reflexive verbal noun: keeping oneself clear of blame and of everything base or ugly. So the root carries a moral sense of self-cleansing, not only a physical one.

3. Idiomatic use: طَاهِرُ الثِّيَابِ ("pure of garment") describes someone undefiled. He cites a line of poetry on the Banū ʿAwf, whose "garments are pure and clean" and whose faces are radiant — where the plural form طَهَارَى (ṭahārā) is noted.

4. الطَّهُور (ṭahūr) — used of water, with the Qur'anic citation "We sent down from the sky pure water" (25:48). On the authority of the philologist Thaʿlab, ṭahūr is defined as that which is "pure in itself and purifying for something else" — i.e. an intensive form denoting water that is both clean and able to cleanse other things.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: طَّلَعَ 7x "mounts up"; طَلْع 4x "(are) layers"; طَلَعَت 2x "rising"; طُلُوع 2x "(the) rising"; يُطْلِعَ 1x "to inform you"; مَطْلِع 1x "(the) rising place"; مُّطَّلِعُون 1x "be looking"; مَطْلَع 1x "(the) emergence"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṭ–l–ʿ (طلع) as a single sound root whose core meaning is appearing, emerging, coming into view.

1. Rising (of the sun): طَلَعَتِ الشَّمْسُ, "the sun rose" (verbal nouns ṭulūʿ, maṭlaʿ). al-maṭliʿ is the place of rising. Qurʾān, al-Qadr 97:5: {حَتَّى مَطْلَعِ الْفَجْرِ}, "until the rising of dawn." He notes the reading variant: with fatḥa (maṭlaʿ) it is the verbal noun (the act); with kasra (maṭliʿ) it is the place it rises from.

2. Coming suddenly upon: طَلَعَ عَلَيْنَا فُلَانٌ, "So-and-so came upon us unexpectedly."

3. Making known / acquainting: أَطْلَعْتُكَ عَلَى الْأَمْرِ, "I informed you of the matter" (iṭlāʿ); أَطْلَعْتُكَ طِلْعَهُ, "I told you the inner knowledge of it."

4. al-ṭilāʿ: all the land the sun rises over. Ḥadīth: "Were I to have the earth's fill (ṭilāʿ) of gold."

5. Eager looking-out: a soul described as ṭulaʿa reaches out toward things; a woman called ṭulaʿa peers about / looks out frequently.

6. Palm spadix: al-ṭalʿ is the date-palm's flowering sheath, enclosing the white blossom (kāfūr); a palm that produces it "aṭlaʿat."

7. A bow "ṭilāʿ al-kaff": one whose grip just fills the hand — with a verse of Aws [ibn Ḥajar] describing such a bow, neither less than a handful nor too broad for the hand.

8. Further derivatives: istaṭlaʿtu raʾya fulān, "I sought out his opinion" (watching what emerges from him); ṭalʿat al-insān, a person's face/appearance, because it comes into view; "he shot and overshot," his arrow passing over the top of the target.

9. Scouting/access: ṭalīʿat al-jaysh, the army's scout who spies out the enemy's position; al-muṭṭalaʿ, the point of access/approach — "where is the muṭṭalaʿ of this matter?" i.e. how it is reached. He cites the Prophetic saying, "I would ransom myself from the terror of the muṭṭalaʿ" (the vantage/place one is made to look out from).

10. al-ṭulaʿāʾ: vomit; aṭlaʿa, "he vomited" — also placed under this root of coming-forth.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris identifies two distinct genuine meanings under the root Ṭ-L-Ḥ:

1. A kind of tree. Al-ṭalḥ is a well-known tree species; one single tree is a ṭalḥa. A place called Dhū Ṭulūḥ was, he suggests, likely named for having this tree growing there. Camels that sicken from eating this tree are described as ṭalāḥā or ṭaliḥa.

2. Leanness/exhaustion, and things like it. A she-camel worn thin and exhausted by travel is called "ṭilḥu asfār" (worn by journeys), and the verb ṭaliḥat means "she became exhausted/emaciated." The same word ṭilḥ is also used for an emaciated tick — illustrated with a line of poetry about a scrawny, disheveled tick that finds its way to a she-camel by following her breathing.

From this second sense comes al-ṭalāḥ, "badness" (the opposite of ṣalāḥ, "goodness/soundness") — Ibn Fāris treats this as figuratively extended from the idea of a bad, run-down, emaciated state.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَطْلُبُ 1x "seeking it"; طَلَب 1x "to find it"; طَّالِب 1x "(are) the seeker"; مَطْلُوب 1x "and the one who is sought"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṭ-l-b as one root with a single core sense: seeking after / going in quest of something (ibtighāʾ).

1. Basic verb: ṭalaba / yaṭlubu / ṭalab — to seek a thing. Related nouns: maṭlab, "what I seek, my object of pursuit," and ṭalibah, "my request, the thing asked for."

2. Fourth form (aṭlaba), sense A — to grant the seeking: aṭlabtu fulānan bi-mā ibtaghāhu, "I supplied so-and-so with what he was after," i.e. met his request.

3. Fourth form, sense B — the opposite: aṭlabtuhu can also mean "I put him in need of seeking," i.e. forced him to go looking for something.

4. Applied to terrain and water: aṭlaba al-kalaʾ — the pasture lay far from water, so people had to go searching for water; hence māʾ muṭlib, "water that makes you seek it," a distant, hard-won watering place.

5. Poetic evidence (shāhid), Dhū al-Rummah: two Kalbī shepherds lost their charge after turning back from a muṭlib — a remote watering place, reached only by a hard drive, to which those coming for water arrive in bands.

The entry is brief and stays within these usages; Ibn Fāris derives all of them, including the two contrary senses of the fourth form and the desert-water usage, from the one idea of seeking.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris says ṭāʾ and lām point to three root meanings: the tender freshness of a thing, overlooking (al-ishrāf), and nullifying something.

1. **Freshness.** al-ṭall is the weakest kind of rain; Ibn Fāris says it takes its name from the way it makes the ground beautiful. For the same reason a man's wife is called his ṭalla; some say this is because she is fresh in his eyes, as if she were ṭall. Taken over from al-ṭall, in the sense of scantiness, is the saying "the she-camel has no ṭull", meaning she has no milk, not even a little; here the ṭāʾ takes the vowel u (ṭull) to keep the word apart from the word for rain.

2. **Overlooking.** al-ṭalal is whatever still stands up visibly among the remains of dwellings, and a man's figure is called his ṭalal. From this comes aṭalla ʿalā l-shayʾ, "he overlooked the thing", said of looking down on it from above. The ṭalal of a ship is its covering (jilāl), plural aṭlāl. taṭālaltu means "I craned my neck to look at something far away", as in the verse: "It is grief enough that I craned to see the heights of the two landmarks of Damkh, and they would not show themselves."

3. **Nullifying.** iṭlāl al-dimāʾ is letting blood go for nothing, when no one pursues a claim for it. Blood declared of no account is called maṭlūl or muṭall.

**Outliers.** Among words that stand apart from these three meanings is the claim that al-ṭill means the snake; Ibn Fāris says he does not know how sound it is. The entry ends with al-ṭalāṭila, a disease that takes hold in the back.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: طَلَّقَ 10x "you divorce"; ٱنطَلَقَ 9x "proceed"; طَّلَٰق 2x "the divorce"; مُطَلَّقَٰت 2x "and for the divorced women"
poets_named: Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad); al-Nābigha (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse ×2; Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); al-Musayyab (pre-Islamic)
text:
al-Zamakhsharī arranges the root ط ل ق (ṭ-l-q) by its core idea of loosing/setting free, dividing literal from figurative (majāz) usage.

Literal senses:
1. Releasing a captive: أطلقت الأسير ("I freed the captive"); the freed man is a ṭalīq, and such men are the ṭulaqāʾ.
2. Loosing an animal: freeing a she-camel from its hobble; the freed camel is ṭāliq / ṭaliq (plural aṭlāq). A ṭāliq she-camel grazes wherever it likes, unrestrained. A gazelle that taṭallaqa runs off with legs unbound, turning aside for nothing. (Shawāhid from Dhū al-Rumma and an unnamed poet.)
3. Being unfettered generally: to imprison someone ṭalaqan is to hold him without shackles; انطلق = to set off (on an errand).
4. Loosening of the body: استطلق بطنه = his bowels ran; أطلقه الدواء = the medicine loosened him. A shepherd who "istaṭlaqa" a she-camel keeps it aside, unmilked with the herd.
5. Of horses: a ṭalaq (plural aṭlāq) is a single run or heat; the horses taṭallaqat = ran a course.
6. Childbirth: the ṭalq is the labor-pang; a woman in labor is maṭlūqa.

Figurative senses (majāz):
7. Divorce: a woman ṭuliqat/ṭaluqat is a ṭāliq (plural ṭawāliq); a man prone to divorcing is a miṭlāq / miṭlīq / ṭillīq. (Shāhid from al-Nābigha, of venom that alternately "lets go" and returns.)
8. Free/unencumbered ownership and lawfulness: ḥalāl muṭlaq or ṭilq = unrestricted lawful; "it is yours ṭalaqan" = yours unconditionally; the ṭalaq of one's wealth is its unencumbered part; the pairing ḥalāl ṭilq ("free lawful") vs. ḥarām ghilq ("locked-up unlawful").
9. Generosity: to "free the hand" (ṭallaqa/aṭlaqa yadahu) with good = to give freely; ṭalq al-yadayn = open-handed.
10. Fluent speech: ṭalq / ṭalīq / munṭaliq al-lisān = of ready, unhindered tongue.
11. A bright, open face: ṭalq / ṭalīq / munṭaliq al-wajh; the face ṭalaqa (grew bright, ṭalāqa). (Shāhid on lush pasture brightening the face.)
12. A horse that taṭallaqa = staled after its run (shāhid from Imruʾ al-Qays).
13. Mildness of weather: a ṭalq / ṭalqa night, a ṭalq day = gentle and fair.
14. Ease of mind: "my soul does not taṭṭaliq to this matter" = it does not open up / feel at ease with it.
15. An auxiliary idiom: انطلقت أفعل ("I set off doing…"), parallel to ذهب يقوم ("he went to stand"). (Shāhid: setting off to drive a mount onward.)
16. Horse markings: a limb muṭlaq is one left unmarked (free) of white, contrasted with muḥajjal (white-socked).
17. A share: a ṭalaq of someone's wealth = a portion — which al-Zamakhsharī traces back to the ṭalaq (heat/course) of the horse (shāhid from al-Musayyab).

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root ṭ-m-ʿ (طمع), from al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's al-Mufradāt.

1. Core sense: ṭamaʿ (طَمَع) is the soul's inclining toward something out of appetite or craving for it — hence "to crave, covet, or eagerly hope for."

2. Grammar/derivation: the verb runs ṭamiʿtu, aṭmaʿu, with the verbal nouns ṭamaʿ and ṭumāʿiya; the agent noun is ṭamiʿ or ṭāmiʿ ("one who craves/covets").

3. Qur'anic usage (as cited here): "Indeed, we crave/hope that our Lord will forgive us" (26:51); "Do you then covet/hope that they will believe you?" (2:75); and "in fear and craving/hope" (7:56) — the word covers both eager hope and covetous desire.

4. Moral note recorded by al-Rāghib: because such craving usually springs from caprice (hawā), the sayings arose "craving is [second] nature" (al-ṭamaʿu ṭabʿ) and "craving soils the hide" (al-ṭamaʿu yudannisu l-ihāb), i.e. it defiles one's character.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṭ-m-m as a sound root with one basic meaning: one thing covering another until it makes it level with it, be it the ground or something else. He derives the other uses from this.

1. **Filling in and levelling.** ṭamma al-biʾr bi-l-turāb means he filled the well with earth and levelled it.

2. **The sea.** By extension the sea is called al-ṭimm, as though the water had filled in and levelled that low ground. In the saying "he has al-ṭimm and al-rimm", al-ṭimm is the sea and al-rimm the moist earth.

3. **Rising over, prevailing.** ṭamma al-amr is said when a matter rises high and prevails. Ibn Fāris says this is why al-qiyāma, the Rising, is called al-ṭāmma.

4. **Trimming hair.** ṭamma shaʿrahu, said when a man takes some of his hair off, keeps the idea of levelling, he notes, though not that of covering.

5. **Unclear speech.** al-ṭimṭim is a man who does not speak clearly, as though he himself had been filled in, the way a well is.

**An exception.** Ibn Fāris counts as departing from this root something reported by Ibn al-Sikkīt: ṭamma is said of a horse when it rises up, and of a bird when it rises onto a tree.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: ٱطْمَأَنَّ 9x "find satisfaction"; مُطْمَئِنّ 2x "(is) content"; مُّطْمَئِنَّة 2x "who is satisfied"
text:
Root: ط م ن (Ṭ-M-N).

Ibn Fāris treats this as a small (minor) root whose usual forms take an added hamza.

1. اطْمَأَنَّ (iṭmaʾanna), imperfect يَطْمَئِنُّ, verbal noun طُمَأْنِينَة (ṭumaʾnīna): of a place, to become settled, still, and at rest.

2. طَامَنْتُ مِنْهُ (ṭāmantu minhu): to lower, calm, or quiet something — glossed as سَكَّنْتُ (sakkantu), "I made it still."

The shared sense is settling into stillness and calm.

dictionary: Ṣiḥāḥ — al-Ṣiḥāḥ, al-Jawharī (d. 1003)
text:
al-Jawharī's entry for ط م س (Ṭ-M-S) is brief:

1. Core sense — ṭumūs is effacement and obliteration: a thing being wiped out, worn away, its traces erased.

2. Grammatical note — the verb works both ways. Intransitively: ṭamasa al-ṭarīq, "the road became effaced/blotted out," and its imperfect is attested with either vowel on the middle radical (yaṭmusu and yaṭmisu). Transitively: ṭamastu-hu ṭamsan, "I effaced it," verbal noun ṭams.

3. Derived reflexive/passive forms — inṭamasa (form VII) and taṭammasa (form V) of a thing, meaning it became wiped out and worn away.

4. Qur'anic shawāhid — on "Our Lord, efface (iṭmis) their wealth," al-Jawharī glosses ṭams here as "alter it, change it," and cites alongside it "before We efface faces." He treats both as instances of the same root sense of obliterating/transforming beyond recognition.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ط-م-ث (Ṭ-M-Th) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: a sound root meaning "to touch something" (mass al-shayʾ) — a single unifying sense from which the specific usages below all branch.

1. General "touching." Al-Shaybānī: in Arabic usage al-ṭamth simply means "touch," applicable to anything at all. Example cited: "mā ṭamatha dhā l-martaʿi qablanā aḥad" — "no one touched this pasture before us." Anything can be "touched" (yuṭmath).

2. Menstruation. From the general sense comes al-ṭāmith, "the menstruating woman," with two attested verb forms: ṭamithat and ṭamathat.

3. Sexual touching. ṭamatha al-rajulu al-marʾata = "the man touched the woman," i.e. had intercourse with her. Ibn Fāris adds that the word in this usage is not restricted to intercourse alone, and cites the Qur'an as an instance of the word: {lam yaṭmithhunna insun qablahum wa lā jānn} — "whom no man has touched before them, nor jinn" (Q55:56).

4. Touching/binding an animal. Al-Khalīl: ṭamathtu al-baʿīr ṭamthan = "I hobbled the camel" (tied its leg). Also cited: "mā ṭamatha hādhihi l-nāqata ḥablun qaṭṭ" — "no rope ever touched this she-camel," meaning it had never been touched/tied.

5. Filth (a disputed reading). In a line of poetry by ʿAdī, "aw ṭamthi l-ʿaṭan" ("or the ṭamth of the pen/fold"), some scholars glossed ṭamth there as "filth, defilement" (al-danas) — Ibn Fāris reports this as others' interpretation, not his own assertion.

Overall: Ibn Fāris treats "touch" as the base sense; the menstruation, intercourse, and animal-hobbling usages are all specific applications of that one core meaning, while the "filth" sense (from the ʿAdī citation) is attributed to other scholars rather than stated as fact by him.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: ṭ-r-ḥ (ط ر ح)

Ibn Fāris gives one core sense for this root: casting a thing away, throwing it down or flinging it off.

1. Base verb — ṭaraḥa al-shayʾa yaṭraḥuhu ṭarḥan: "he threw/cast the thing away."

2. al-ṭaraḥ — a derived noun meaning "a distant place," i.e. a place something has been cast to.

3. Idiom of separation — "al-nawā ṭaraḥat bi-fulānin kulla maṭraḥ": al-nawā (the distance/parting brought by travel) is said to "cast" a person off to every far-flung place, scattering him away. Ibn Fāris cites a line of poetry: the poet asks to linger with [his beloved] Mayy before al-nawā "casts" them apart to some distant place, or before a parting takes her away.

4. faḥlun miṭraḥ — said of a stallion whose seed lands deep/far within the womb; "casting" applied to potency/reach.

5. Same root, other applications where something extends or juts out far:
 - nakhlatun ṭarūḥ — a palm tree with long fronds/spathes.
 - sanāmun iṭrīḥ — a long, protruding hump.
 - qawsun ṭarūḥ — a bow that propels/casts the arrow forcefully.

6. Ibn Fāris closes by noting that the underlying logic (qiyās) tying all these senses together is one and the same — each usage reduces to the idea of something being cast so that it reaches or lands at a distance.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: طَرَد 3x "send away"; طَارِد 2x "going to drive away"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ط ر د (ṭ-r-d) as a single sound root whose core notion is **putting at a distance, driving away**. From that one idea he derives every use he lists:

1. **Driving off, expelling.** طَرَدْتُهُ ṭaradtuhu — "I drove him away." With the ruler as subject, forms IV and II (أَطْرَدَهُ / طَرَّدَهُ) mean to banish someone from his town.

2. **Hunting.** الطَّرْد al-ṭard is the work of taking game — the driving that catches it — and الطَّرِيدَة al-ṭarīda is the quarry itself.

3. **Combat.** مُطَارَدَة muṭārada (form III) between opponents is their charging at one another; Ibn Fāris reports the explanation that it is so named because each one drives the other.

4. **Related nouns.** الْمِطْرَد al-miṭrad is a short spear; مَطْرَدَة maṭrada is the beaten middle of a road.

5. **Running on in sequence.** اطَّرَدَ iṭṭarada (form VIII) is said of a thing whose parts follow one after another. Ibn Fāris flags this explicitly as a **metaphorical extension**: it is as if the first part drove the next along. He cites the verse describing a deserted campsite: "Do you recognise a trace, like the running-on of streaked patterns, belonging to ʿAmra — desolate, save for a rider's halting-place?"

6. **A figurative epithet.** مُطَّرَد النَّسِيم muṭṭarad al-nasīm, "the run-way of the breeze," is a kenning for the nose, supported by a line transmitted through Ibn al-Aʿrābī comparing it, after exertion, to two hornets' nests.

7. **Going straight / extending.** اطَّرَدَ الأمر — the affair ran straight, went smoothly. Ibn Fāris then generalises the analogy: **anything that stretches out** belongs here, as in طَرِّدْ سَوْطَكَ, "draw out your whip" (extend it).

8. **Ṭarīd, the later-born brother.** الطَّرِيد al-ṭarīd is a child born after his brother: the second is the ṭarīd of the first. Again by likeness — as though he drove him on and followed after him. Grammatically he notes that ṭarīd here carries an **active** sense (= ṭārid, "driver"), not a passive one.

He closes by remarking that the chapter offers little to say, then adds an unrelated word, الطَّزِع al-ṭaziʿ, "a man with no jealous protectiveness," and ends with "God knows best."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: طَرْف 6x "(will be) companions of modest gaze"; طَرَف 5x "its borders"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ṭ-r-f from two distinct roots: (1) the edge or border of a thing, and (2) a movement of the eyelids. He adds one anomalous word that fits neither.

FIRST ROOT — "edge, extremity":
1. Core sense: ṭaraf = the edge/tip of a thing, a garment, or a wall. Plural aṭrāf.
2. nāqa ṭarifa: a she-camel that grazes the outer edges of the pasture and keeps apart from the herd.
3. ʿayn maṭrūfa ("struck eye"): an eye hit by the edge (ṭaraf) of a garment or the like, so that it fills with tears. Extended figuratively: ṭarafahā al-ḥuzn ("grief made it tear up").
4. karīm al-ṭarafayn ("noble in both extremities"): some say this means noble in both the father's and the mother's lineage. The phrase "which of the two extremities is longer is unknown" belongs here too.
5. A cited verse plays on aṭrāf meaning one's parents/kin: reviling them leaves no room for reconciliation.
6. ṭirāf: what is gathered from the tips of standing crops.
7. ṭawārif of a tent: the side-flaps one lifts to look out.
8. ṭārifat ʿayn: from ṭurifat al-ʿayn (the eye struck and brimming, so it can barely see) — used of something so abundant the eye is bewildered by it.
9. ṭarīf: a newly-acquired thing, opposite of talīd (old/inherited property) — something gained "now, at the edge of a past time." Verb iṭṭarafa = to acquire as new.
10. al-rajul al-ṭarif: a man who won't stay with one woman or friend — by analogy, because he keeps seeking new "extremities." al-marʾa al-maṭrūfa: a woman who won't stay with one man but roves after others (cited from al-Ḥuṭayʾa).
11. al-ṭirf: a fine/noble horse, as though freshly acquired; the newly-gained is prized over the inherited.

SECOND ROOT — "eyelid movement / glance":
12. ṭarf: originally the movement of the eyelids in looking; by extension it also names the eye itself.
13. A star is called al-ṭarfa, which Ibn Fāris supposes to be "the glance/eye of the Lion" (Leo).
14. Cited verse by Jarīr: eyes with a languorous "sickness" in their glance slay their lovers yet do not revive them.

ANOMALOUS:
15. al-ṭirāf: a tent made of hide — Ibn Fāris notes this does not fit either root.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: طَرِيقَة 5x "paths"; طَرِيق 4x "a path"; طَّارِق 2x "and the night comer"
poets_named: unnamed verse ×4; Ruʾba (Umayyad); al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ṭ-r-q from four base meanings: (1) arriving by night, (2) striking, (3) slackness/limpness, and (4) laying one thing over another.

FIRST — arriving by night (ṭurūq). The core sense is coming to a dwelling at night. A rajul ṭuraqa is a man who travels by night until he reaches his people after dark; the word is sometimes used of daytime arrival too, but night is the base. Ibn Fāris's proof that night is primary: the star is called ṭāriq ("night-comer") because it rises at night. Anyone who comes at night has "ṭaraqa." He cites a woman's line "We are the daughters of Ṭāriq," meaning her father is like a star in nobility and height. From this root he places ṭarīq (road), because it is trodden/come upon — though he notes it could instead belong to the fourth root. Also here: ataytuhu ṭarqatayn ("I came to him twice"), and ṭāriqat al-rajul, a man's kin-group, so called because it comes to him and he to it (with a supporting verse).

SECOND — striking (ḍarb): ṭaraqa/yaṭruqu. A miṭraq/miṭraqa is a hammer. Related senses:
- al-ṭarq = striking pebbles for divination; Ibn Fāris notes the ḥadīth forbidding it ("al-ṭarq, bird-augury, and omen-scaring are of al-jibt"). A woman diviner is ṭāriqa, plural ṭawāriq (with a verse: the pebble-diviners and bird-augurers do not know what God will do).
- al-ṭarq = beating wool with a rod (the rod is a miṭraqa); a soothsayer mixes cotton with wool when divining, hence the proverb "ṭaraqa wa māsha" (with a supporting verse).
- ṭaraqa al-faḥl al-nāqa = the stallion covers the she-camel; ṭarūqat al-faḥl = the female covered; istaṭraqa = to ask for another's stallion to cover one's camels, aṭraqahu = to grant it.
- "This arrow is the ṭarqa of one man" = the make/fashioning of a single craftsman.

THIRD — slackness (istirkhāʾ). al-ṭaraq = softness in a bird's feathers. aṭraqa = to lower the gaze / look down; al-muṭriq = one with a slack, lowered eye (two verses cited, incl. the serpent "lowering its head" then striking). al-ṭirrīqa = softness and pliancy/submissiveness; proverb "beneath his mildness lies some hardness" (i.e. softness with occasional difficulty). On al-ṭaraq some said it is a crookedness of the shank; others, a weakness of the knees — Ibn Fāris judges the latter more consistent with the theme of softness/slackness.

FOURTH — layering one thing over another (khaṣf). naʿl muṭāraqa = a sandal sewn in layers; khuff muṭāraq = a double-soled boot; any patch/layer is ṭirāq; turs muṭarraq = a shield overlaid with fitted hide. From this:
- al-ṭirq = fat and strength, as if layered on; "mā bihi ṭirq" = he has no strength. Ibn Qutayba: the base of ṭirq is fat, since strength comes mostly from it.
- al-ṭaraq = standing pools of water, by analogy to things piling up in layers (verse by Ruʾba).
- ṭarīq (road) also fits here, as something lying over the earth "patched" onto it; taṭāraqat al-ibil = camels came in single file; ṭarīq also = palm-trees in one row (verse by al-Aʿshā); rīsh ṭirāq = overlapping feathers.
- kharaja al-qawm maṭārīq = people set out on foot without mounts, each footprint layered on the one before; "camels came on a single track" is the same idea; a woman dyeing "ṭarqatayn" applies the dye twice, the second over the first.
- Derived from ṭarīq: ṭarraqat al-marʾa at childbirth = she "made a way" for the child — said specifically when half the child emerges, is held back, then delivers ("ṭarraqat, then delivered"); similarly ṭarraqat al-qaṭāt, of a sandgrouse straining to lay its egg and scratching the ground with its breast.

dictionary: ʿAyn — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786)
text:
Kitāb al-ʿAyn organizes entries by anagram-chapters: every root built from ṭ + r plus a weak letter or hamzah is treated together in one bāb. This record is that whole chapter; the target root ṭrw is the first and primary entry.

**ṭrw — freshness/moistness**
1. Ṭarāwah/ṭarāʾah (verbal nouns of ṭariya – yaṭrā) = the state of being fresh/moist/new. Al-Khalīl notes the verbal noun is rarely used, since freshness isn't treated as a "newly-occurring" event.
2. Aṭrā fulānan = to praise someone with the utmost praise one is capable of.
3. Al-muṭarrāh = a type of perfume; "ʿūd muṭarrā" = scented aloeswood.
4. Al-ṭarā, used idiomatically for a great multitude ("more numerous than al-ṭarā and al-tharā"). Two glosses given: (a) everything in creation too numerous to count; (b) everything on earth's surface that isn't part of the earth's own matter (i.e., not dust or pebbles).
5. Al-uṭriyah (also iṭriyah) = a Levantine food with no singular form — a noodle-type dish, likened to the word zibniyah.

**Sibling roots in the same chapter:**

- **ṭwr**: al-ṭūr = a well-known mountain (a man tied to it is "ṭūriyy/ṭūrāniyy"). Al-ṭawr = "an occasion/turn" ("time after time"); people described as "aṭwār" = of various kinds/stages (cited verse: man is created "stage after stages"). Al-ṭawār = running alongside/parallel to something (e.g., houses whose walls align). A separate verb, "ṭāra yaṭūru ṭawran" (homographic with "to fly"), means to hover near and approach something.

- **wṭr**: al-waṭar = any matter a person has real concern in — his purpose/business. Only recorded usage: "qaḍaytu waṭarī" = "I fulfilled my need." Plural: awṭār.

- **wrṭ**: al-wirāṭ = deception with livestock (manipulating flock counts by grouping/ungrouping them). Al-warṭah = a predicament one falls into; awraṭahu = he entangled him in one.

- **ṭyr**: al-ṭayr = the collective feminine noun for birds (singular ṭāʾir; feminine ṭāʾirah rarely used; plural-of-plural aṭyār). Al-ṭiyarah/ṭīrah = the verbal noun for taking an omen (rare grammatical pattern, paired only with khīrah "a choice"). "A person's ṭāʾir" = his fastened deed/fate, citing Qur'an 17:13 ("every person — We have fastened his ṭāʾir to his neck"). Al-ṭāʾir also names bird-divination/omen-reading generally. A citation on Qur'an 27:47 ("iṭṭayyarnā bika...") is glossed here as "we made them flee and delivered them" — this does not match the verse's ordinary sense of "we take you as a bad omen," and looks like a textual slip in the source, reproduced as given. Other usages: al-muṭayyar = cloth patterned with woven bird images; "fajr mustaṭīr" = the true dawn whose light spreads across the horizon (vs. the false, "elongated" dawn — with a ḥadīth distinguishing the two for fasting purposes); "ghubār mustaṭār" = dust scattered in the air; "kalb mustaṭīr" = a frenzied dog; "faras mustaṭār" = a spirited, swift horse.

- **ryṭ**: al-rayṭah = a single-piece woven wrap (not two joined pieces); plural riyāṭ.

- **ṭrʾ**: ṭaraʾa ʿalaynā = he came upon us suddenly from afar (root of al-ṭurʾāniyy). Ṭaraʾān = a mountain known for its pigeons ("ṭurʾānī" pigeons), which common people mistakenly call "ṭūrāniyyah."

- **ʾṭr**: al-aṭr = bending something by gripping one end and curving it (with a poetic citation about a spear bending in combat). Al-uṭrah = a sinew binding wound around an arrow's fletching. Al-iṭār = a rim or encircling frame — of a tambourine, a sieve, the ridge around the mouth (between mustache and lip), a house (like a girdle around it), or trellis-vines; generally, whatever surrounds a thing is its iṭār. Al-taʾaṭṭur = a woman staying confined to her house (with a poetic citation).

- **rṭā**: al-arṭāh = a tree the Persians call "sinjid"; collective form al-arṭā.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: أَطَاعَ 72x "obey"; ٱسْتَطَاعَ 42x "they are able"; طَوْع 4x "willingly"; طَاعَة 3x "obedience"; تَطَوَّعَ 2x "voluntarily does"; يُطَاعُ 2x "to be obeyed"; طَوَّعَتْ 1x "then prompted"; مُطَّوِّعِين 1x "the ones who give willingly"; طَائِعِين 1x "willingly"; مُّطَاع 1x "one to be obeyed"
text:
Ibn Sīda's entry for the root ṭ-w-ʿ (ṭawʿ):

1. Core sense — willing obedience. al-Ṭawʿ is the opposite of karh: compliance as against coercion. The verb ṭāʿahu (yaṭūʿuhu) and ṭāwaʿahu = "obeyed, complied with"; the verbal nouns are ṭawāʿa and ṭawāʿiya. An obedient man is ṭāʾiʿ, or (by metathesis) ṭāʿin — both equal muṭīʿ, though ṭāʿin has no verb of its own. Intensive forms miṭwāʿ / miṭwāʿa mean "highly compliant." The idiom "you shall do it ṭawʿan or karhan" = willingly or unwillingly. (Cited: a line swearing "by the House… or one obeying"; al-Mutanakhkhil al-Hudhalī on a most compliant lord.)

2. To yield / be pliant. ṭāʿa (yaṭāʿu) and aṭāʿa: to become soft and submit; also aṭāʿahu, inṭāʿa lahu. Extended agricultural uses: a plant "aṭāʿa" = did not resist its grazer (was freely available); a pasture aṭāʿa = spread out abundantly; dates aṭāʿa = ripened, their harvest-time came.

3. Idioms of submission. "I am ṭawʿu yadika" = at your command; a woman ṭawʿu al-ḍajīʿ = compliant to her bedfellow; a horse ṭawʿu al-ʿinān = easy of rein; a she-camel ṭawʿatu / ṭayyiʿatu al-qiyād = pliant to the lead. (Cited: al-Nābigha, where al-shawāmit = the dogs, or, it is said, the legs.)

4. To attempt / undertake. taṭawwaʿa (li-)l-shayʾ / taṭawwaʿahu: to try at, take on, something.

5. To be able. istaṭāʿahu, with the variant forms isṭāʿahu, asṭāʿahu, istāʿahu, astāʿahu: to have the power/capacity for something.

Grammatical analysis of the "able" forms (the entry's method): The base is istaṭāʿa. isṭāʿa (continuous hamza) drops the tāʾ for ease, since ṭāʾ is near it in articulation (compare dropping a lām in ẓaltu). asṭāʿa (cut hamza) puts the sīn in place of the ʿayn's vowel in aṭāʿa (original aṭwaʿa). Sībawayh held the sīn to be a substitute (ʿiwaḍ) for the lost vowel of the ʿayn, yet still an augment, since it replaces no lost letter. Al-Mubarrad objected: one compensates only for what is lost, and here the vowel was merely transferred to the fāʾ, not lost. Ibn Jinnī defended Sībawayh: the ʿayn, once made quiescent, is weakened and liable to elision (as in lam yuṭiʿ, aṭiʿ), so the sīn compensates that weakening; had the ʿayn kept its vowel (aṭwaʿa, yuṭwiʿu) it would not drop. He compares ahraqtu, where a hāʾ likewise compensates a lost vowel (original arwaqtu / aryaqtu; al-Kisāʾī's rāqa yarīqu argues the ʿayn is yāʾ) — so neither ahraqtu nor asṭaʿtu derives from istafʿala. Further variants: istaʿtu (drop the ṭāʾ); istaʿtu with tāʾ (ṭāʾ turned to tāʾ to match the whispered sīn); yastīʿu; mā astatīʿu (two tāʾs); mā astayiʿu; astāʿa yastīʿu. Sībawayh's summary: the sīn is added to compensate the loss of the ʿayn's vowel from afʿala.

6. Voluntary/supererogatory action. taṭāwaʿa li-l-amr, taṭawwaʿa bihi / -hu: to take pains to be able to do something. Qur'anic citation: "fa-man taṭawwaʿa khayran fa-huwa khayrun lahu" ("whoever volunteers good, it is better for him"). al-taṭawwuʿ = what a person does freely, beyond obligation — the tafaʿʿul form treated as a noun (like tanawwuṭ). al-muṭṭawwiʿa = those who volunteer for striving (jihād); Thaʿlab (Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā) reported the variant al-muṭawwiʿa, which al-Zajjāj rejected.

Proper name: Ṭawʿah.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ط و د (ṭ-w-d), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One sound root, containing a single word: al-ṭawd — the great mountain. The entry's core citation is Qur'an al-Shuʿaraʾ 26:63: "fa-nfalaqa fa-kāna kullu firqin ka-l-ṭawdi al-ʿaẓīm" — "and it [the sea] parted, and each part was like a great mountain" (the parting of the sea for Moses).

A secondary usage: "ṭawwada fī al-jabal" — to roam or traverse a mountain — which Ibn Fāris notes appears to be a verb derived from al-ṭawd itself, extending "mountain" into "to wander a mountainous area."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: طَائِفَة 24x "a group"; طَافَ 8x "and will circulate"; طَائِف 4x "for those who circumambulate"; يَطَّوَّفَ 2x "and circumambulate"; طُّوفَان 2x "the flood"; طَوَّٰفُون 1x "(as) moving about"
poets_named: al-ʿAjjāj (Umayyad); al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); unnamed verse
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) treats ṭ-w-f as a single authentic root meaning the circling of one thing around another, and a thing's being surrounded or encompassed. Other senses branch from this.

1. Core verb: طَافَ / يَطُوفُ (to go around), with the verbal nouns ṭawf and ṭawāf — e.g. going around the House (al-bayt). Related forms: iṭṭāfa and istaṭāfa.

2. طُوفَان (ṭūfān) — a flood: water that circles around things and envelops them. Al-Khalīl cites al-ʿAjjāj, who likened the darkness of night to a ṭūfān engulfing the trees (with a variant verb ghamma, "shrouded").

3. الطَّائِف (al-ṭāʾif) — one who goes the rounds at night, a patrolman.

4. الطَّيْف / الطَّائِف — something from the jinn that circles around a person: a touch of madness or an apparition; verbs ṭāfa and iṭṭāfa. Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'anic إذا مسهم طيف من الشيطان ("when a ṭayf from Satan touches them"), noting the variant reading ṭāʾif; and a line of al-Aʿshā describing a jinn-sent frenzy (awlaq).

5. Of the dream-phantom (khayāl) one says both ṭāfa and aṭāfa; a cited couplet speaks of the phantom "circling" (yuṭīf) a beloved, with a variant maṭāf.

6. الطَّائِفَة (al-ṭāʾifa) of people — a group that circles around one person or thing. The Arabs do not fix it to a set number. Ibn Fāris notes that jurists and exegetes variously make it four-or-more, or three, or even a single person, and debate it at length; but in the Arabic language proper, any group able to encircle a thing is a ṭāʾifa — and typically only a small one. (He reports these numeric definitions as the jurists'/exegetes' view, distinct from the language.)

7. Metaphorical extension: طَائِفَة من الثوب, "a ṭāʾifa of the garment," i.e. a piece of it — since a ṭāʾifa of people is likewise a faction or portion.

8. طَائِف القوس — the part of the bow adjoining its main body (abhar).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: طَوْل 3x "(of) wealth"; طَالَ 3x "grew long"; طَوِيل 2x "prolonged"; طُول 1x "(in) height"; تَطَاوَلَ 1x "and prolonged"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ط-و-ل (ṭ-w-l) as a single sound root meaning excess and extension in a thing.

1. Core sense — length/tallness. طَالَ … يَطُولُ طُولًا = "to be long/tall." Ibn Fāris cites Thaʿlab: al-ṭūl ("length") is the opposite of al-ʿarḍ ("breadth").

2. Comparative use. طَاوَلْتُهُ فَطُلْتُهُ = "I vied in height with him and outmatched him"; طَالَ فُلَانًا فُلَانٌ = one is taller than another. Shāhid: a line on al-Farazdaq, a rounded rock so tall the mountain-goats cannot reach it.

3. Extension by analogy — a rope. Because of its length, a tether is called al-ṭiwal. Shāhid: Ṭarafa likens death (as long as it spares a youth) to a slackened tether whose folds are still held in the hand.

4. Duration. طَوَالَ الدَّهْرِ = "for all time / ever," as in لَا أُكَلِّمُهُ ("I will never speak to him").

5. Physical application. جَمَلٌ أَطْوَلُ = a camel with a long upper lip.

6. Adjective and plural. al-ṭuwāl = al-ṭawīl ("tall/long"); al-ṭiwāl is the plural of al-ṭawīl. Some report qalānis ṭiyāl ("long caps") with a yāʾ.

7. Figurative sense — worthlessness. amr ghayr ṭāʾil = "a matter of no worth/avail," where there is no benefit; used for both masculine and feminine. Shāhid: "they imposed on me a course of no worth."

8. Other derived uses:
- تَطَاوَلْتُ فِي قِيَامِي = "I stretched up while standing," extending the legs to see farther.
- طَوِّلْ فَرَسَكَ = "let out your horse's tether" to graze.
- اسْتَطَالُوا عَلَيْهِمْ = "they got the upper hand over them," i.e. killed more of the enemy than they lost.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: طَاقَة 2x "strength"; يُطِيقُ 1x "can afford it"; يُطَوَّقُ 1x "their necks will be encircled"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṭ-w-q as a sound (genuine) root carrying the same idea as the root he treated just before it: going round, encircling.

1. Core sense — encircling. Anything that goes round about a thing is a ṭawq (an encircling band or collar).

2. Extensions from roundness:
   - ṭāq — a building's arch or vault, so called because it is round when arched over.
   - ṭāq — the ṭaylasān (a cloak), so called because it goes round upon the person wearing it.

3. Capacity / being able to bear. Expressions such as aṭāqa hādhā l-amra iṭāqatan ("he could manage this matter"), huwa fī ṭawqihi ("it is within his capacity"), and ṭawwaqtuka al-shayʾa ("I laid this on you as a charge") all belong here, on his reasoning: to be able to bear something is, as it were, to have encompassed it and gone round it on every side.

4. An outlier. ṭāqa used of "a single strand of thread" or "a single sprig of herbage" — the single individual unit — departs from this root idea. Ibn Fāris allows that one might force an analogy back to the encircling sense, but judges that far-fetched.

Method note: the entry works by positing one core sense and testing each usage against it, explicitly flagging the one usage that resists the analogy rather than absorbing it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṭ-w-r as a sound root with one core idea: extension or stretching out, in either space or time. From this single sense he derives:

1. Spatial extent. ṭawār al-dār is the ground that stretches alongside a house — its forecourt or precinct. Hence the expression ʿadā ṭawrahu, "he overstepped his ṭawr," i.e. he crossed the limit that properly belongs to him. This was then extended metaphorically to anything that is exceeded or transgressed.

2. al-Ṭūr (a mountain). It may simply be a proper name, or it may be named from this root because a mountain "extends" in length and breadth.

3. Temporal extent. The phrase faʿala dhālika ṭawran baʿda ṭawr, "he did it stage after stage," reflects the time sense — acting over one span of time after another.

4. Wildness. Calling wild birds and similar creatures ṭūriyy or ṭūrāniyy also belongs here: such an animal has turned wild and so "overstepped the ṭawr," keeping far from the boundary of the tame (al-anīs).

dictionary: Lane — Arabic-English Lexicon, Edward William Lane (d. 1876)
quran_words: طُوًى 2x "(of) tuwa"; نَطْوِى 1x "we will fold"; طَىّ 1x "like (the) folding"; مَطْوِيَّٰت 1x "(will be) folded"
text:
**Root ط و ي (Ṭ-W-Y) — Lane's Arabic-English Lexicon (d. 1876)**

**The core verb: طَوَى (ṭawā), verbal noun طَىّ (ṭayy)**

1. **To fold, fold up, or roll up** — a garment, a piece of cloth, or a written sheet. Lane gives طَوَى الصَّحِيفَةَ as the direct opposite of نَشَرَ (nashara, "to unfold, spread out"); this contrast between folding and unfolding organises much of the entry. A related verbal noun طِيَّة (with kesr, also lightly pronounced طِيَة) is recorded from Lh; صَحِيفَةٌ جَافِيَةُ الطِّيَة is "a sheet rudely folded."

2. **To make compact, as though folded; to round like a scroll.** طُوِىَ جِسْمُهُ — his body was compacted so that its flesh was firm; سَاقٌ حَسَنَةُ الطَّىّ — a shank well turned, well rounded.

3. **To make lean or lank.** طَوَاهُ السَّيْرُ — travel emaciated him. Related forms: انطوى بَطْنُهُ (of a camel or sheep, "its belly became lank"); the adjectives طَاوٍ, طَيَّانُ, طَوِى البَطْنِ, مُنْطَوِى البَطْنِ all describe a lean-bellied man or beast.

4. **To bend or fold a body part.** Of a gazelle: طَوَى عُنُقَهُ وَنَامَ آمِنًا — "he folded his neck and slept unafraid."

5. **To withdraw affection** (figurative). طَوَى كَشْحَهُ, literally "he folded his flank," means he turned away his love (S), or withdrew his countenance (M), or turned away forsaking someone (طَوَى كَشْحَهُ عَنِّى). Cited verse: "Many a companion has folded away his flank from me, and I said to him: this withdrawal of yours withdraws me from you."

6. **To conceal or to resolve** (figurative). طَوَى كَشْحَهُ عَلَى أَمْرٍ — he concealed an affair (K); or resolved upon it (M); or persevered in it (L). Likewise طَوَى عَنِّى الحَدِيثَ / السِّرَّ — he concealed the story or the secret from me; اِطْوِ هٰذَا الحَدِيثَ — "keep this story folded up."

7. **To pass on from one thing to the next without stopping.** Of a traveller: يَطْوِى مَنْزِلًا إِلَى مَنْزِلٍ فَلَا يَنْزِلُ — he goes from one halting-place to the next without alighting. Also طَوَى المَكَانَ إِلَى المَكَانِ, طَوَى حَدِيثًا إِلَى حَدِيثٍ (to drop one story and move to another), and طَىُّ الصَّوْمِ (passing from one fast on to the next). طَوَى البِلَادَ — he traversed the lands, country after country.

8. **To come to / pass by / sit with a people** — طَوَى القَوْمَ (IAar, K).

9. **To contract distance.** طَوَى اللّٰهُ البُعْدَ لَنَا (K) — may God fold up (make near) the distance for us; the T reads البَعِيدَ, "make the far near."

10. **To make life pass away.** طَوَى اللّٰهُ عُمُرَهُ — God made his life pass away. Poetic line: "the calamities of your age folded you up after an unfolding." And طُوِىَ فُلَانٌ وَهُوَ مَنْشُورٌ, said of one who has died but whose good repute survives — "he has been folded away, yet he stands unfolded." On this usage طَوَاهُ can mean "he destroyed / annihilated it." Lane notes that al-Bayḍāwī allows يَوْمَ نَطْوِى السَّمَآءَ (Q 21:104) to mean "the day we efface the heaven," but Lane judges "the day we fold up / roll up the heaven" the better rendering.

11. **To wind thread** — طَوَى الغَزْلَ عَلَى المِطْوَى, he wound the spun thread on the winder.

12. **To case a well** — طَوَى الرَّكِيَّةَ / البِئْرَ, to line a well with stones or baked bricks; likewise to set bricks in a building.

**The intransitive طَوِىَ (ṭawiya), verbal noun طَوًى / طِوًى (Sb)**
- Of a waterskin: folded up while still damp or with milk left in it, so that it spoiled, stank, and came apart.
- Of a person: **he was hungry** (so too Form IV أَطْوَى). Note the deliberate variant under Form I: طَوَى (i.e. طَوَى أَحْشَآءَهُ) — he went hungry on purpose.
- طَوِيَتْ طِيَّتُهُ — the place he meant to head for became distant (Lh).

**Derived forms**
- II طَوَّى — to fold repeatedly, to wind or coil.
- V تَطَوَّى — to be coiled or wound; تَطَوَّتِ الحَيَّةُ, the serpent coiled itself. Sībawayh cites: "I writhed with the coiling of the ḥaḍbah" (a kind of serpent, or a bowstring).
- VI تَطَاوَى — of several parties, to fold together mutually (Freytag, from the Hudhalī Dīwān).
- VII انطوى (and VIII اِطَّوَى, of the pattern افتعل, per Az and ISd) — to be folded, rolled up; the passive counterpart of "unfolding." Figuratively: انطوى عَلَى الحِقْدِ / الوُدِّ — the heart infolded rancour, or love.

**Nouns and the "fold" imagery**
- **طَىّ / طِىّ / طِوًى**, pl. **أَطْوَآء** — the lines, streaks and creases left by folding: in cloth, in a written sheet, in the belly, in fat, in guts, in a serpent. The synonym set **مَطْوًى / مَطَاوٍ** covers the same. Examples: "nothing was left in the creases of their guts"; مَطَاوِى الدِّرْعِ, the creases of a coat of mail drawn together; of a she-camel, the fat of her hump lies طَىٌّ فَوْقَ طَىٍّ, "fold above fold" (Layth); Abū Ḥanīfah applies أَطْوَآء to the jointed bends in a locust's tail.
- The same word gives the idiom of things **enclosed**: وَجَدْتُ فِى طَىِّ الكِتَابِ كَذَا, "I found such-and-such folded inside the letter"; الغِلُّ فِى طَىِّ قَلْبِهِ, malice folded inside his heart; أَدْرَجَنِى فِى طَىِّ النِّسْيَانِ, "he folded me into the fold of oblivion."
- **طَىّ** is also, concretely, a stone or brick **casing** — especially of a well.
- **طَيَّة** — one single act of folding.
- **طِيَّة** — (a) the *manner* of folding (pattern of جِلْسَة, رِكْبَة); Dhu-r-Rummah: "as letters are unfolded after being folded." (b) Equivalent to نِيَّة: a destination or an intention. Al-Khalīl says it may be the place one means to make for, or the object one aims at; the A defines it as the direction in which lands are traversed. Hence طِيَّةٌ بَعِيدَةٌ (a distant destination), مَضَى لِطِيَّتِهِ (he went off to what he purposed), لَقِيتُهُ بِطِيَّاتِ العِرَاقِ (in the regions of Iraq). (c) Also an object of need.
- **طَوًى** — a waterskin (سِقَاء), especially one folded up damp and spoiled; also **hunger**.
- **طُوًى** — Lane records two lines of interpretation for the Qurʾānic word (20:12; 79:16). Some take it like طِوًى, "a thing done twice, as though folded" — the Kashshāf and al-Bayḍāwī compare ثِنًى and gloss "twice sanctified" (of the valley); al-Ḥasan: "twice blessed and sanctified"; alternatively "twice called," referring to the calling of Moses in the context (so also ar-Rāghib). Lane observes that most, however, treat طُوَى / طُوًى there simply as the proper name of a valley, and he rejects Golius's renderings of the word as errors.
- **طَوِىّ** — (a) a bundle of cloth (so called from being folded); a variant reading has "of burd-cloth." (b) A well cased with stone or brick — فَعِيل in the sense of مَفْعُول; masculine, though it may be feminised to agree with بِئْر; pl. أَطْوَآء. (c) A short stretch of the night: "I came to him after a طَوِىّ of the night" (ISd).
- **طَوِيَّة** — the ضَمِير, the inner heart or mind: named so because it is folded over the secret, or because the secret is folded within it. Also a synonym of طِيَّة (intention).
- **طَايَة** — a flat house-roof one sleeps on (Az); a place where dates are laid out to dry; a large rock in sandy or stoneless ground (ISd). Also, in the plural, camels coming "in herds."
- **مِطْوًى** — a thread-winder; in later colloquial use, a small clasp-knife.
- **مَطْوِىّ** — folded, rolled up; hence "compacted, rounded" (اِمْرَأَةٌ مَطْوِيَّةُ الخَلْقِ, a woman of compact build — though Lane notes it could equally mean slender); بِئْرٌ مَطْوِيَّةٌ, a stone-cased well. On وَالسَّمٰوَاتُ مَطْوِيَّاتٌ بِيَمِينِهِ (Q 39:67), usually "the heavens rolled up in his right hand," Lane reports ar-Rāghib's explanation that it signifies their destruction.
- **شِعْرٌ طَاوِىّ** — verse rhyming on ṭāʾ; al-Khalīl notes its alif is originally yāʾ.

**Method visible in the entry:** Lane builds outward from one concrete physical act — folding cloth or a written sheet — and derives every extended sense from it: compacting a body, emaciating it, bending a neck, turning a flank away in estrangement, folding a secret out of sight, folding up stages of a journey or of life itself, and folding a well with a stone lining. He consistently marks which extensions the sources label tropical (مجاز) and which he infers, and he weighs competing readings (e.g. of طُوًى and of the Qurʾānic "folding" of the heavens) rather than settling them.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṭ-y-b as a single sound root whose core meaning is the opposite of al-khabīth (the foul or vile). Under it he records:

1. al-ṭayyib — "the good/wholesome," the antonym of al-khabīth. He cites the phrase سَبْيٌ طِيبَةٌ (sabyun ṭībah), "good/wholesome captives," i.e. ṭayyib.

2. al-istiṭāba — a term for al-istinjāʾ, cleansing oneself after relieving oneself; so named, he explains, because the person makes himself wholesome again (yuṭayyibu nafsahu), removing the filth (khubth) from himself. He notes the hadith forbidding a man to do this with his right hand.

3. al-aṭyabān ("the two most agreeable things") — eating and sexual intercourse.

4. Ṭaybah — a name of the Prophet's city (Medina).

5. Idiom of pleasure: هذا طعامٌ مَطْيَبَةٌ للنفس, "this food is a delight to the soul."

6. al-ṭayyib glossed as al-ḥalāl (the lawful) — this equation is Ibn Fāris's own.

7. al-ṭāb = al-ṭīb (fragrance/pleasantness), evidenced by a line of verse praising noble descent "in pleasantness upon pleasantness" between the houses of Abū al-ʿĀṣ and al-Khaṭṭāb.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ṭ-y-n as a single word: الطِّين (ṭīn), "clay" or "mud," a well-known thing.

Usages recorded:
1. طَيَّنْتُ الْبَيْتَ — "I plastered/coated the house" (with clay).
2. طِنْتُ الْكِتَابَ — "I sealed the letter" (closed it with a clay seal).
3. طَانَهُ اللَّهُ عَلَى الْخَيْرِ — "God fashioned/molded him upon goodness," i.e. shaped his natural disposition toward it (jabalahu).

Ibn Fāris connects this last sense back to "sealing a letter": as if God impressed a person upon goodness and sealed his affair with it — the imagery of clay taking and holding an imprint. He adds the caution "and God knows best."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: طَيْر 19x "the birds"; طَٰئِر 5x "a bird"; ٱطَّيَّرْ 3x "we consider you a bad omen"; يَطِيرُ 1x "(that) flies"; مُسْتَطِير 1x "widespread"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ṭ-y-r from a single core sense: the lightness of a thing in the air. From that core it extends by metaphor to anything swift.

1. Core / literal — flight. الطَّيْر (al-ṭayr, "birds") is the plural of طَائِر (ṭāʾir, "flyer"), named from this idea; the verb is طَارَ / يَطِيرُ / طَيَرَان ("to fly, flying").

2. Extended to speed. Anyone who moves lightly and fast is said to "fly": قَدْ طَارَ. Shawāhid: a hadith praising the warrior who, hearing an alarm, "flies to it," and a verse "so we flew/darted to them with horse-troops and spears."

3. Scattering / spreading. تَطَايَرَ = "scattered, dispersed"; اسْتَطَارَ الْفَجْرُ = "the dawn spread wide," and likewise anything that spreads. Qur'anic shāhid: al-Insān 76:7, a day whose evil is مُسْتَطِير ("widespread").

4. Taking an omen. تَطَيَّرَ ("to read an ill omen from something") is, per Ibn Fāris, derived from birds (al-ṭayr) — e.g. the crow and similar birds watched for omens.

5. A person's ṭāʾir. طَائِرُ الْإِنْسَانِ is glossed as his deed/work.

6. Wide-mouthed well. بِئْرٌ مُطَارَةٌ = a well with a wide mouth; poetic shāhid: "the rushing of the wind in a wide-mouthed well."

7. Anger. الطَّيْرَة = anger, so named because a person is "made to fly up" (provoked) by it.

8. Long-grown hair. خُذْ مَا تَطَايَرَ مِنْ شَعْرِ رَأْسِكَ = "take what has grown long of your hair"; poetic shāhid: "the growth of the tallest hump flew up [grew long]."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ظ-ع-ن (Ẓ-ʿ-N) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: setting out or departing from one place to another (al-shukhūṣ).

1. Verb — ẓaʿana / yaẓʿanu (verbal nouns: ẓaʿn, ẓaʿan) = 'to depart, set out, move on, journey.' Cited proof-text: Q16:80, where the hide tents are described as light to carry 'on the day of your ẓaʿn (journeying) and the day of your iqāmah (settling)' — i.e. easy to pack when moving camp, easy to pitch when settled.

2. Al-ẓaʿīnah — a disputed term. One group of scholars took it to simply mean 'the woman.' Another group held that al-ẓaʿāʾin (the plural) are the camel-borne litters/howdahs themselves, present whether or not a woman happened to be riding in one. Ibn Fāris judges the second view sounder, because the litter is classed among the equipment of travel — so the word belongs here on account of its role in journeying, not because it denotes women.

3. Al-ẓaʿūn — a camel kept and outfitted specifically for travel.

4. Al-ẓiʿān — the rope used to lash the pack-saddle onto a camel, so named because it too is one of the tools of travel and journeying.

Illustrative line of verse (poet not named in the entry): a camel is described whose neck twists around whatever is tied to it, and whose flanks wear through every ẓiʿān (binding-rope) — a vivid picture of the rope named in sense 4 actually being used and worn out.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ẓ-f-r (ظفر) as having two genuine underlying senses that he thinks may ultimately converge:

1. Triumph, success, overpowering (al-qahr, al-fawz, al-ghalaba)
- ẓafar = success, gaining/attaining something. Verb: ẓafira yaẓfaru ẓafaran, "he succeeded/triumphed."
- Causative: Allah aẓfarahu, "gave him victory." He cites Q48:24 (al-Fatḥ), "after He had given you victory over them" (aẓfarakum ʿalayhim), as a Qur'anic instance of this usage.
- muẓaffar = "one granted victory/success."

2. Strength/firmness in a thing, centered on the fingernail
- ẓufr = the human fingernail. Verb ẓaffara fī al-shayʾ = to dig/fix one's nail into something.
- aẓfar = "long-nailed" (formed the same way as ashʿar, "long-haired," from shaʿr, "hair").
- A proverbial phrase for a contemptible or spent man: kalīl al-ẓufur, "blunt of nail" — Ibn Fāris cites a line of Ṭarafa's poetry using this image (an old, worn-out figure vs. one still "sharp-clawed").
- ẓaffara (of a plant) = to sprout, because the new shoots push out forcibly like little nails/claws.

Extended, metaphorical uses he groups under the second sense:
- ẓafara(tun) — a thin film/membrane that grows over the eye — named this by resemblance to a nail; the affected eye is described as ẓufirat. He notes Abū ʿUbayd's confirmation that this is also called ẓufr.
- ẓufr al-qaws — the two notches at the tips of a bow's two curved ends (sīyatān), where the bowstring is fastened — again "nail" by resemblance.
- al-ẓafara can also mean a low, fertile patch of ground that puts out vegetation — another simile from the sprouting-plant sense.
- al-aẓfār ("the nails") is also used, by metaphor, for a group of small stars.

Finally, he notes the Yemeni city Ẓafār (ظَفَارِ) — with the adjectival form ẓafārī — as possibly connected to one of the senses above, though he leaves this tentative ("Allah knows best").

quran_words: ظَهْر 15x "their backs"; ظَهَرَ 10x "(is) apparent"; ظَٰهِر 8x "dominant"; أَظْهَرَ 8x "he may cause to appear"; ظَٰهَرُ 6x "pronounce zihar"; ظَهِير 6x "a helper"; تَظَٰهَرُ 2x "you support one another"; ظَٰهِرَة 2x "apparent"; ظِهْرِيّ 1x "backs"; ظَّهِيرَة 1x "noon"
poets_named: al-Farazdaq (Umayyad); Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam); unnamed verse
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ẓ-h-r (ظهر) from one core idea: strength and prominence/coming-into-view. He treats the human back (ẓahr) as the concrete origin from which the whole family branches, since a back combines both notions — it is what is prominent (as opposed to the belly) and what bears loads.

1. To appear / become visible: ẓahara (ظَهَرَ), verbal noun ẓuhūr, participle ẓāhir — a thing becomes uncovered and comes into the open. Hence ẓuhr (noon) and ẓahīra (the noon heat) are named, as the most prominent and brightest part of the day; and aẓharnā = "we travelled at noon."

2. To become informed of something: ẓahartu ʿalā kadhā = you came to know / were made aware of it.

3. The back and things derived from it: ẓahr also names a riding-mount (it carries loads on its back); muẓahhar = strong-backed man; ẓahir = a man complaining of his back; ẓahīr = a strong camel.

4. Helper / supporter: ẓahīr — as though he braces his back against yours. Related is the sense of gaining strength through a thing (yastaẓhiru), whence ẓaharah = household goods (a person "backs himself up" with them), and ẓahra = one's kinsfolk, so called because one is strengthened by them.

5. Overcoming / prevailing: ẓuhūr = victory, being uppermost. Cited: Qur'an al-Ṣaff 61:14, {fa-aṣbaḥū ẓāhirīn} ("so they became prevailing/uppermost").

6. Casting behind the back = neglecting: ẓihriyy is anything you put "at your back," i.e. forget and disregard. Cited: Qur'an Hūd 11:92, {wa-ttakhadhtumūhu warāʾakum ẓihriyyā} ("you took it, disregarded, behind your backs"). Same idiom: "so-and-so put my need at his back" (ignored it), with a supporting verse by al-Farazdaq.

7. Passing away / departing: "a matter whose disgrace is ẓāhir ʿanka" = one that goes away from you, as if it passes behind your back. Supported by a verse of Abū Dhuʾayb ("a complaint whose disgrace passes away from you").

8. Ẓihār (the disavowal formula): a man's saying to his wife "you are to me as my mother's back," a phrase pre-Islamic Arabs used intending separation. Ibn Fāris notes the "back" was singled out only because it is the place of mounting; otherwise her other limbs would carry the same prohibition. (He reports this as attested Arab usage, not as a legal ruling.)

9. Other specialised uses: ẓāhira = a bulging/protruding eye; ẓuhār of feathers = the part that shows on the wing; ẓāhira = camels watering daily at midday; "we took al-ẓahr" = the overland route (because it is open and visible); Quraysh al-Ẓawāhir = those who camp in Mecca's outskirts (with a supporting hemistich); aqrān al-ẓahr = those who come at you from behind.

10. An opposite-sense (aḍdād) usage from Ibn Durayd: taẓāhara al-qawm = the people turned their backs on one another; Ibn Fāris endorses the derivation, since each set his back toward the other. He closes with "and God knows best."

quran_words: ظِلّ 14x "shades"; ظَلَّ 9x "so we will remain"; ظُلَّة 6x "coverings"; ظَلَّلْ 2x "and we shaded"; ظَلِيل 2x "thick"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ẓ-l-l as a single root meaning: one thing screening another, which is what is called ẓill (shade). He traces every word of the root back to this idea.

1. **ẓill, shade.** The shade of a person or anything else. Ibn Fāris distinguishes it from fayʾ: ẓill can occur in the morning or the evening, while fayʾ occurs only in the evening. "The tree shaded me" is aẓallatnī al-shajara. A ẓill ẓalīl is lasting shade.

2. **Night as shade.** The night itself is a ẓill. A poet speaks of crossing unknown country "in the shade of a dark one", which Ibn Fāris explains as "under the cover of a dark night".

3. **aẓallaka, protecting.** "So-and-so shaded you" means he protected you with his shade, that is, his might and power to defend.

4. **miẓalla, a sunshade.** Mentioned as a well-known object.

5. **ẓulla, cloud or canopy.** aẓalla yawmunā means the day's shade lasted. Some say the ẓulla is the first cloud that casts shade. A ẓulla is also something shaped like a ṣuffa, a roofed shelter, as in Q 7:171: "when We raised the mountain above them as though it were a ẓulla."

6. **ẓalla, to keep doing something by day.** ẓalla yafʿalu kadhā is said of something done during the day, never at night. Ibn Fāris explains why he puts it under this root: things cast shade in the daytime, while the night is itself a shade.

7. **aẓall, the camel's foot-pad.** The underside of a camel's foot. Ibn Fāris says the analogy with the root holds: it may be named so because it screens what is beneath it, or because it is covered by what is above it. One verse describes a camel "bleeding in the aẓall". In another, "from aẓlal and aẓlal", the poet wrote out the doubled letter in full because the metre required it.

poets_named: Kaʿb (lived into Islam); Zuhayr (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ẓ-l-m from two sound roots.

1. Opposite of light. The base word is ظُلْمَة (ẓulma, darkness; plural ظُلُمَات), also called ظَلَام (ẓalām); the verb أَظْلَمَ means "the place grew dark." Idioms of nearness attach here: لَقِيتُهُ أَوَّلَ ذِي ظُلْمَةٍ ("I met him at the first onset of dark," reported from al-Khalīl as the first thing that blocks one's sight — a noun from which no verb is derived), and لَقِيتُهُ أَدْنَى ظَلَمٍ ("I met him quite near"). Ibn Fāris explains that such expressions ultimately go back to "darkness": Arabs figuratively treat a distant human figure as a patch of darkness — comparable to their calling a figure سَوَاد ("a black shape"). He notes this as an unusual basis for construing their speech.

2. Putting a thing out of its proper place, wrongfully. The verb ظَلَمَ / يَظْلِمُ / ظُلْم means to wrong. The core idea is misplacement, shown by the proverb مَنْ أَشْبَهَ أَبَاهُ فَمَا ظَلَمَ — "whoever resembles his father has not misplaced [the resemblance]," i.e. done nothing out of place — cited with Kaʿb's line ("...and whoever resembles his father has done no wrong").

Derived usages under this second root:
- ظَلَّمْتُ فُلَانًا = to accuse someone of wrongdoing.
- ظَلَمْتُهُ فَاظَّلَمَ / انْظَلَمَ = I wronged him and he bore / submitted to the wrong; illustrated by Zuhayr's line about a generous man "sometimes wronged, so he bears it" (fa-yaẓẓalimu), which Ibn Fāris notes is transmitted with both ẓāʾ and ṭāʾ.
- الْأَرْضُ الْمَظْلُومَة = land dug for the first time (never dug before); its disturbed soil is ظَلِيم — with a cited verse.
- A camel slaughtered with no cause/defect is said to be "wronged" (ظُلِمَ), backed by a poetic shāhid ("wrongers-of-slaughter-beasts").
- الظُّلَامَة = the redress one demands for one's grievance (maẓlama) from a wrongdoer.
- ظَلَمَ وَطْبَهُ = to draw milk from the skin before it has curdled and given up its butter; such early-drawn milk is called ظَلِيم (also ظَلِيمَة), with a closing verse. Ibn Fāris ends "and God knows best."

quran_words: ظَمَأ 1x "thirst"; تَظْمَؤُا 1x "will suffer from thirst"; ظَّمْـَان 1x "the thirsty one"
text:
Root: ẓ-m-w/y (weak-final) together with its hamzated counterpart ẓ-m-ʾ.

1. Core idea (Ibn Fāris): a single underlying sense — withering and scarcity of water/moisture — runs through both the non-hamzated and hamzated forms of this root.

2. Non-hamzated form, al-ẓamā: scantiness of blood in the gums.
   - "A woman ẓamyāʾ al-lithāt" = one with pale, thin (blood-scant) gums.
   - Extended to the eye: an "ẓamyāʾ" eye has a thin, delicate eyelid.
   - Extended further by analogy to the leg: a "ẓamyāʾ" shank is one with little flesh on it.

3. Hamzated form, al-ẓamaʾ: thirst. Verb pattern: ẓamiʾtu, aẓmaʾu, ẓamā ("I thirsted / I thirst / thirst[ing]").
   - Related noun al-ẓimʾ: the interval between two waterings (of a drinking animal).
   - Ibn Fāris notes the same underlying pattern (qiyās) governs all of these — scarcity or loss of water.

4. Figurative extension: a "spear (rumḥ) aẓmā" is one that is dark/tawny in color and slender. He explains this naming as arising from the loss of the spear's "water" — i.e., its moisture or sap has gone, leaving it dry and thin.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: ظَنَّ 47x "i think"; ظَنّ 21x "the assumption"; ظَّانِّين 1x "who assume"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ẓ-n-n as a sound minor root with two different meanings: certainty and doubt. He closes the article by saying the whole category is one.

**1. Certainty**

- ẓanantu ẓannan can mean "I was certain." His Qur'anic example is "Those who yaẓunnūna that they will meet God said…" (Q 2:249). He glosses yaẓunnūna, adding "and God knows best", as "they are certain". He says the Arabs use and recognise this sense and that it is frequent in the Qur'an.
- In a verse, "ẓunnū two thousand men armed head to foot, their chiefs in close-linked Persian mail," the command ẓunnū means "be certain of".
- **maẓinnah**: Ibn Fāris puts this under the same sense. The maẓinnah of a thing is its known mark and place, where it is to be expected. "It is a maẓinnah for such-and-such." Al-Nābighah: "the maẓinnah of folly is youth."

**2. Doubt**

- ẓanantu al-shayʾ: to hold something without being certain of it.
- **al-ẓinnah**: suspicion. **al-ẓanīn**: the suspected one.
- **iẓẓannanī fulān**: "so-and-so suspected me." A verse: "Not everyone who suspects me am I one to placate, nor do I say everything reported against me." Ibn Fāris notes that the form sometimes appears with ṭ, because the ẓ is assimilated into the t of the iftiʿāl pattern.
- **al-ẓanūn (person)**: someone who thinks ill of others.
- **al-taẓannī**: acting on ẓann. Its underlying form (aṣl) is al-taẓannun.
- **Usage note**: "I thought ill of him" is suʾtu bihi ẓannan without the article, but asaʾtu bihi al-ẓann with it. The form with an added alif (asāʾa) is used when al-ẓann carries the definite article.
- **al-ẓanūn (well)**: a well of which it is not known whether it holds water. It is illustrated by a verse about an uncertain well kept from the downpour of a thundering rain-cloud.
- **al-dayn al-ẓanūn**: a debt of which it is not known whether it will be repaid.

poets_named: al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); Baḥnah b. Rabīʿah (undated)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the whole root b-sh-r from one core idea: a thing appearing/coming into view together with goodness and beauty. His senses:

1. **Skin, surface.** al-basharah is the outer surface of human skin. From it comes bāshara ("a man had bodily union with a woman"), i.e. skin meeting skin. More broadly, mā aḥsana basharata al-arḍ ("how fine is the surface/greenery of the land"), and bashartu al-adīm ("I pared the face of a hide").

2. **Human beings.** al-bashar (mankind) are so named from their outward visibility (ẓuhūr) — tied back to the "appearing" core sense.

3. **Beauty, good looks.** al-bashīr = one of beautiful face; al-bashārah = comeliness. He cites al-Aʿshā: she saw grey hair had come upon him, and cheerfulness and comeliness had left him.

4. **Giving tidings.** bashshartu fulānan ("I gave someone good news"), pattern bashshara / tabshīr. This is properly for good news. Bad news is sometimes cast in the same form, which Ibn Fāris takes to be a kind of taunting. But used absolutely, bishārah is of good and nidhārah (warning) is of the opposite.

5. **Land bringing forth growth.** absharat al-arḍ = the land put out its vegetation.

6. **A "complete" man.** muʾdam mubshar describes a perfect man, as if combining the softness of the inner skin (adamah) with the roughness of the outer skin (basharah). Ibn Fāris quotes Baḥnah b. Rabīʿah, marrying off his daughter, telling his wife: "Prepare her, for she is al-muʾdamah al-mubsharah." (A variant abshartu al-adīm is noted for basharatu.)

7. **First light / winds.** tabāshīr al-ṣubḥ = the first gleams of dawn, and by extension the first beginnings of anything (no verb is formed from this). al-mubashshirāt are the winds that bring tidings of rain.

text:
Ibn Fāris: root ب‑ذ‑ر (b-dh-r)

**Core meaning:** one single idea — scattering and dispersing a thing (نَثْرُ الشَّيْءِ وَتَفْرِيقُهُ).

**1. Sowing seed.** بَذَرْتُ الْبَذْرَ أَبْذُرُهُ بَذْرًا — "I sowed the seed" (scattering it on the ground).

**2. Squandering wealth.** بَذَّرْتُ الْمَالَ أُبَذِّرُهُ تَبْذِيرًا — "I squandered/scattered the wealth," using the intensive verb form. Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'an: "And do not squander wastefully — indeed the squanderers (al-mubadhdhirīn) are brothers of the devils" (al-Isrāʾ 17:26). The same root-idea of scattering underlies both sowing seed and scattering money.

**3. People who can't keep a secret.** الْبُذُرُ (al-budhur) describes people who won't keep a matter concealed and don't guard their tongues — they "scatter" talk the way one scatters seed. Ibn Fāris quotes ʿAlī describing certain people (praisingly) as "lamps in the darkness — not gadabouts, and not blabbing broadcasters (al-madhāyīʿ al-budhur)." He glosses: al-madhāyīʿ are those who spread news around; al-budhur are the tongue-loose types just described.

**4. A place-name.** Baddhar is the name of a place, which Ibn Fāris guesses may derive from this same root. He supports this with a line of poetry naming several watering-places, one of which is "Baddhar" (poet unnamed in the entry).

text:
Root b-'-r (بأر), Murtada al-Zabidi, Taj al-'Arus fi Jawahir al-Qamus

1. Al-bi'r (the entry's central noun) — a well, discussed with detailed grammatical notes on its irregular plural forms (a metathesized pattern per Ya'qub and al-Farra'), and illustrated with a hadith of 'A'ishah about washing from three interconnected wells. A related hadith establishes a legal principle — "injury from a well carries no liability" — with two competing classical explanations (an ownerless ancient well versus a hired well-cleaner's fatal accident).
2. Ba'ara/ibta'ara (a distinct but related verb-sense) — to dig, extended figuratively to "hiding away" or "storing" something, especially good deeds performed in secret as a spiritual reserve for the Hereafter. This grounds a hadith criticizing a wealthy man who "stored up no good" — i.e., made no advance provision of righteous deeds — with two attested dialectal verb-forms for this same concept illustrated in a supporting verse about Quraysh's moral conduct.
3. Closing: al-bu'rah, a cooking-pit or hearth (and, by extension, any stored provision or reserve); and a final note distinguishing two similar-sounding roots — one for truthfully claiming an act, one for falsely claiming it.

text:
Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr) on the root ب أ س (b-ʾ-s). The entry treats one family of meanings — force/severity — branching into war, torment, hardship, and poverty, plus the separate blame-word biʾsa.

1. al-baʾs (بأس): core sense of force and severity. Al-Layth glosses it as (a) torment/punishment and (b) intensity in war; al-baʾsāʾ as a name for war, hardship, and striking. Ibn Sīda: it originally meant "war," then spread so widely that "lā baʾsa ʿalayk / lā baʾs" came to mean "no fear, no harm." Ibn al-Aʿrābī: baʾs and baʾis (pattern faʿil) = severe torment.

2. "lā baʾs ʿalayk" as safe-conduct: to say this to an enemy is to grant him security, since one negates baʾs from him. Ḥimyarī dialect renders it "lābāti" (لَبَاتِ), attested in their verse and reported by al-Azharī from Shamir. The verse of Qays b. al-Khaṭīm ("no bās upon you") shows baʾs with the hamza softened analogically, proven by the rhyme with "al-shams."

3. Bravery: a man is baʾis / baʾīs (pattern faʿīl) = courageous, one of great baʾs (baʾusa yabʾusu baʾsan, Abū Zayd). The Qurʾanic "a people of severe baʾs" (ulī baʾsin shadīd) is glossed by various reports as Banū Ḥanīfa, or Hawāzin, or Persia and Rome.

4. al-buʾs (بُؤْس): hardship and poverty. baʾisa yabʾasu buʾsan = to become poor and needy; the person is bāʾis = poor (shāhid from al-Farazdaq). al-baʾsāʾ and al-mabʾasa carry the same sense (shāhid from Bishr b. Abī Khāzim). Al-Zajjāj glosses Qurʾanic "baʾsāʾ wa-ḍarrāʾ" as hunger, versus affliction in wealth and lives. In the prayer-hadith "tabʾasu" = to show humility/neediness; ʿAmmār's "buʾsa ibn Sumayya" pities his hardship.

5. al-bāʾis (بائِس): the afflicted, sorely tried. Sībawayh classes it (like miskīn) among words spoken in compassion — one visited by calamity or destitution, pitied. Verbal noun al-buʾsā; shāhid from Taʾabbaṭa Sharran. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: "būsan / tūsan / jūsan lahu" are synonyms.

6. Grammar of al-baʾsāʾ / al-buʾsā: al-Akhfash notes baʾsāʾ is a noun on faʿlāʾ with no matching afʿal (compare aḥmad, which has no feminine). al-buʾsā is the opposite of al-nuʿmā (well-being); baʾsāʾ/buʾsā belong to the hardship sense, while al-baʾs proper belongs to courage/force. Sībawayh notes the imprecation "buʾsan lahu" (accusative by an implied, unused verb).

7. ibtaʾasa / mubtaʾis: "lā tabtaʾis" = do not grieve or complain; mubtaʾis = grieving or averse (shawāhid from Ḥassān b. Thābit and Labīd). Two readings of the Qurʾanic "fa-lā tabtaʾis": al-Zajjāj takes mubtaʾis as "poor and grieving" (so: do not grieve/be abased); Ibn Barrī prefers deriving it from baʾs "hardship" (so: let their conduct not weigh heavily on you), arguing "aversion" is only a derived nuance — what weighs on a person he comes to dislike. The Paradise-hadith "fa-lā tabʾusū" (never suffer) uses baʾusa yabʾusu = to grow severe; al-baʾūs = one plainly in buʾs.

8. biʾsa (بِئْسَ), the blame-verb (opposite of niʿma, the praise-verb). Frozen past-tense verbs that do not conjugate, having been shifted from their origins: niʿma from naʿima (to gain a blessing), biʾsa from baʾisa (to meet with hardship); resembling particles, they became invariable. Usage: "biʾsa l-rajulu Zayd." Al-Zajjāj/al-Khalīl: they govern only an indefinite genus-noun, not a proper name; a following genus-noun is accusative without the article, nominative with it ("biʾsa rajulan Zayd" / "biʾsa l-rajulu Zayd"). biʾsa may join mā (Qurʾanic "wa-la-biʾsamā sharaw bihi anfusahum"; hadith "biʾsamā... an yaqūla"), after which "an + verb" follows; then mā ranks as an indefinite noun.

9. The Qurʾanic "ʿadhāb baʾīs" (a grievous torment) — a catalogue of the qirāʾāt: baʾīs (faʿīl: Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, al-Kisāʾī, Ḥamza); biʾīs (fiʿīl: Ibn Kathīr, Shibl, Meccans); biʾs (fiʿl, hamzated: Ibn ʿĀmir); bīs (no hamza: Nāfiʿ, Meccans). All mean "severe." Ibn Sīda discusses the anomalous fayʿil form bayʾis (normally only in weak roots like sayyid/mayyit), plus bīs and bayyis as further reflexes.

10. al-abʾus (الأَبْؤُس): plural of baʾs (from "yawm buʾs / yawm nuʿm"), also used for "disasters." Ibn Barrī corrects the singular gloss "calamity" to the plural "calamities," since abʾus is itself a plural (faʿl → afʿul in the plural of paucity: kaʿb/akʿub, fals/aflus). It anchors the proverb "ʿasā l-ghuwayru abʾusan" ("perhaps the little cave holds disasters"), first spoken by al-Zabbāʾ when warned of Qaṣīr's trap: fleeing one baʾs, she feared falling into many (ʿasā here = apprehension, per Sībawayh). The proverb is applied to a suspected person (so ʿUmar to the man who brought a foundling) or to anything from which harm is feared (al-Aṣmaʿī); al-Ghuwayr is a watering-place of Kalb. Sense: perhaps you have come with a matter bearing suspicion and trouble.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ب-ض-ع as three separate roots: (1) a portion of a thing — a limb or anything else; (2) a patch of ground; (3) a thing being relieved or satisfied, by speech or otherwise.

FIRST ROOT — a portion cut off

1. Cutting into pieces. Per al-Khalīl: baḍaʿa l-laḥm ("he cut up the meat"), verbal noun baḍʿ; intensified form II baḍḍaʿa / tabḍīʿ — to reduce something to pieces. A baḍʿa is the resulting piece, a hunk of flesh.

2. Bulk of body. shadīd al-baḍīʿ wa-l-baḍʿa describes a man of solid frame and heavy flesh; the cited verse "khāẓī l-baḍīʿ…" is glossed "hard-fleshed." Yaʿqūb takes baḍīʿ as a plural of baḍʿ on the pattern of ʿabd → ʿabīd.

3. A detached part of a flock. bāḍiʿa = a portion split off from sheep; firq bawāḍiʿ = flocks in separated groups.

4. Plural patterns. Al-Aṣmaʿī: baḍʿa is a compact piece of meat, plural biḍaʿ (like badra → bidar), and also baḍʿ. Zuhayr's line pairs a carcass with birds hopping around it and "gobbets of flesh in a strip-cut hide."

5. Cutting a branch. baḍaʿtu l-ghuṣn = I severed it; Aws describes "a splinter cut away from the top of a summit."

6. Sexual intercourse, as a euphemism. mubāḍaʿa (form III from buḍʿ) is placed here by derivation, and Ibn Fāris calls it one of the elegant euphemisms. Al-Aṣmaʿī: bāḍaʿa l-rajulu mraʾatahu = he had intercourse with his wife, verbal noun bidāʿ. Proverb: "like a girl teaching her own mother about intercourse" — said of a man instructing someone who knows more than he does. Also mālik buḍʿihā, "the one who controls her buḍʿ," glossed as control of her marrying. A verse wishes that her husband, the holder of her buḍʿ, and all their father's sons had never been created. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: buḍʿ = nikāḥ (marriage/coition), bidāʿ = jimāʿ (copulation).

7. Trade goods (bidāʿa) — carried on the same "portion" analogy: a merchant's bidāʿa is a portion of his wealth. Al-Aṣmaʿī: abḍaʿa (form IV) = to put out goods as trading capital; and hence the proverb "like one carrying dates as merchandise to Hajar," said of someone bringing a thing to those who know it better and have more of it. Plurals: biḍāʿāt, baḍāʾiʿ. Abū ʿAmr: a bāḍiʿ is the man who brings in the tribe's trade-goods. Al-Aṣmaʿī also has ittakhadha ʿirḍahu bidāʿatan, "he made his honour a commodity," treating it as something bought and sold — and Ibn Fāris cites al-Aṣmaʿī's own wording as confirming the derivation: bidāʿa is so named because it is a piece (qiṭʿa) of wealth put into trade. Ibn al-Aʿrābī adds a further usage: baḍāʾiʿ like ʿalāʾiq, the led beasts driven alongside the camels — with two rajaz citations about consignments sent off and coming to ruin.

8. A wound classed as a "portion of the body": al-shajja al-bāḍiʿa, a head-wound that splits the flesh without exposing the bone; al-Aṣmaʿī: it splits the flesh only lightly. The report of ʿUmar flogging the man who had put Umm Salama under oath describes thirty lashes "every one of which tabḍaʿ and taḥdur" — splitting the skin and drawing the blood down.

9. Indefinite number: biḍʿ is what falls between three and ten; it is also said that biḍʿ is seven. Ibn Fāris reports that this is the explanation given for the Qur'anic phrase biḍʿa sinīn, "biḍʿ years" (Yūsuf 12:42).

10. Proverb: tushriṭu l-bidāʿatu — when a man is in need, he spends his stock and whatever he has.

SECOND ROOT — a place
al-Buḍayʿ is a locality, named in a line of Ḥassān alongside al-Jawābī and Ḥawmal. Bāḍiʿ is a place; Baḍīʿ is a mountain mentioned in Labīd's poetry. Al-Baḍīʿ is also the sea, per a Hudhalī verse in which the sun above al-Baḍīʿ looks like a thicket amid the rays. Ibn Durayd says al-baḍīʿ is an island cut off from the land into the sea; Ibn Fāris notes that if this is sound, the word has come back round to the first analogy of something cut off.

THIRD ROOT — drinking one's fill
baḍaʿtu min al-māʾ = I drank my fill of the water. māʾ baḍīʿ = sweet, wholesome water. Al-Aṣmaʿī: "he drank and did not baḍaʿ," i.e. was not satisfied. al-baḍʿ = the quenching of thirst. Al-Shaybānī gives the verbal noun buḍūʿ, on the analogy of naqaʿa.
