text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-ʿ-ḍ as having a single core meaning: the dividing or partitioning of a thing.

1. Core sense — "a part." Every portion of a thing is a baʿḍ ("part/some"). Ibn Fāris cites al-Khalīl: the baʿḍ of anything is a portion of it. Usage examples: jāriya yushbihu baʿḍuhā baʿḍan ("a slave-girl, one part of which resembles another") and hādhihi al-dāru muttaṣilun baʿḍuhā bi-baʿḍ ("this house, one part joined to another"). Grammatically he notes baʿḍ is masculine in gender.

2. Derived verb. baʿʿaḍa / tabʿīḍ = to break something up into portions, to separate it into parts.

3. baʿḍ as a connective particle. Ibn Fāris reports the view that Arabs may use bi-baʿḍ as a connective just as they use bi-mā, citing Qur'anic examples of mā so used — fa-bi-mā raḥmatin min Allāh (Āl ʿImrān 159) and mimmā khaṭīʾātihim (Nūḥ 25) — and applying the same to baʿḍ in wa-in yaku ṣādiqan yuṣibkum baʿḍu alladhī yaʿidukum (Ghāfir 28).

4. Reflexive/reciprocal usage. A bedouin's phrase raʾaytu ghirbānan yatabaʿḍaḍna ("I saw crows...") is understood as crows taking a part of one another.

5. Anomalous branch — the gnat (baʿūḍa). Ibn Fāris flags baʿūḍa ("gnat/mosquito," plural baʿūḍ) as deviating from the core sense. Related forms: a night thick with gnats is laylatun baʿiḍatun or mabʿūḍatun — he compares the pattern to sabiʿ/masbūʿ (a place of many lions) and dhaʾib/madhʾūb.
   - Proverb: kallaftanī mukhkha al-baʿūḍ ("you charged me with the marrow of the gnat"), said of an impossible demand, with supporting verses by Ibn Aḥmar.
   - Aṣḥāb al-Baʿūḍa ("the People of the Gnat"): a group killed by Khālid ibn al-Walīd in the Ridda wars, referenced in a line of elegy.

text:
Ibn Sīda's account of the root ب ع د (b-ʿ-d):

1. Core sense: al-buʿd is "distance / farness," the opposite of al-qurb ("nearness"). He cites Imruʾ al-Qays, reading a phrase as yā buʿda mutaʾammal ("how far off is the thing one hopes for!") — a cry of regret — and a parallel line by Abū al-ʿIyāl ("O calamity of his people…"), which he then glosses.

2. Qurʾānic figurative use: on «those are called from a distant place» (Q. 41:44), he takes "distant" as distant from their hearts — since people who take no heed are as if placed at the utmost remove; what is recited stays far from them.

3. Verb and derivatives: baʿuda / baʿida "to be(come) far," verbal nouns buʿd and baʿad; adjective baʿīd, also buʿād (per Sībawayh), plural buʿadāʾ; alternative plural buʿud (with a line of al-Nābigha for "the near and the far"). He notes the patterns faʿīl and fuʿāl behave alike as "sister" forms.

4. In imprecation: buʿdan lahu ("away with him / to perdition"), an accusative governed by an unspoken verb — meaning "may God set him far." The intensive buʿdun bāʿidun likewise prefers the accusative when used as a curse. A poetic line shows al-abʿad pronounced al-abʿadd (doubling the final consonant at a pause, then carried into continuous recitation — a licence permitted in verse).

5. Transitive/causative forms: bāʿada and baʿʿada "to set apart"; God "sets a distance between" people. The prayer «our Lord, make the stages of our journeys far» (Q. 34:19) is read with both bāʿid and baʿʿid. A mibʿad/mubʿid is a far-ranging traveller (with a line of Kuthayyir). Sībawayh notes buʿdaka warns someone of something behind him.

6. A distinct sense — perishing / being cut off: baʿida "to perish or be exiled," as in «as Thamūd were removed/perished» (Q. 11:68), with a deathbed line by Mālik b. al-Rayb. From this same sense, al-buʿd / al-biʿād also means "cursing, damnation"; abʿadahu llāh = "God removed him from good."

7. Idioms and shades: baʿīd used adverbially for "a far place"; the feminine can stay baʿīd ("hiya baʿīdun minka"), cf. Q. 11:83 «not far from the wrongdoers»; but baʿīdat al-ʿahd ("long past") takes the tāʾ. tanaḥḥa ghayra baʿīdin = "keep near"; ghayra bāʿidin = "abased"; ghayr abʿad = "of no worth"; dhū buʿdatin = "a man of judgment and resolve"; mā ʿindahu abʿad = "anything of consequence."

8. The adverb baʿdu ("after"), opposite of qablu ("before"): indeclinable when standing alone, inflected when in construct. On «to God belongs the command, before and after» (Q. 30:4), he explains — following Sībawayh's grammar — that these are ghāyāt (words whose annexed term is deleted, so the remainder becomes the "limit"); they are built on -u because they have become definite by an irregular route. He gives the contextual sense ("before the Romans were overcome and after"), then surveys variant readings: min qablin / baʿdin (indefinite, "from before and after"), which he rates weaker, and al-Kisāʾī's min qabli / baʿdi with kasra and no tanwīn (per al-Farrāʾ), whose supporting analogy he rejects as not parallel. A cited line tanwīns baʿdun by metrical necessity.

9. Further usages: the saying mā huwa bi-lladhī lā baʿda lahu wa-lā qabla lahu (per al-Liḥyānī). The oratorical formula ammā baʿdu is glossed "as for what comes after my prayer for you"; it is claimed David first used it (linked to «We gave him wisdom and decisive speech», Q. 38:20), while Thaʿlab attributes it to Kaʿb b. Luʾayy. Finally laqītuhu buʿaydāti baynin, "I met him after a while, then stayed away, then came again" — used only adverbially.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: unnamed verse; al-Ḥuṭayʾa (lived into Islam); Ibn Rawāḥa (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ب-ع-ل as three separate roots rather than one.

1. Companion / associate. This is the primary sense: صاحب, "the one who goes with." A husband is called baʿl. Ibn Fāris notes in passing that the Arabs also applied the name Baʿl to certain idols. Derived from the same root is بِعال (biʿāl), a man's playful, affectionate dalliance with his wife. He cites a ḥadīth on the days of tashrīq describing them as "days of eating, drinking and biʿāl," and a line of al-Ḥuṭayʾa in which a married woman ("possessed of a baʿl") is left with no one to dally with when night falls — the verb تُباعِل built on the same sense.

2. Bewilderment, being dumbfounded. بَعِلَ الرجل means "the man was stupefied, at a loss." Ibn Fāris tentatively ("perhaps") attaches to this the phrase امرأة بَعِلة, a woman who cannot manage to dress herself properly — i.e. a kind of helpless confusion.

3. High, rain-starved ground. baʿl of land is elevated terrain that rain only reaches once a year. He quotes an unnamed poet: climbing the back of a broad baʿl, one would imagine split eggshells strewn over the travellers — an image of glare and heat on the bare heights.

Attached to this third root (not made a fourth) is baʿl of plants: growth that drinks through its own roots from the ground, with no watering from the sky. Ibn Fāris supports this with a prophetic saying on what is due from date-palms — what drinks baʿlan, by its own roots, owes a tenth — and with a line of Ibn Rawāḥa contrasting "irrigated palms" with "baʿl palms."

The organising logic is that the husband-sense and the dalliance-sense belong together under "companion"; the confusion-sense stands alone; and the land-sense and the self-watering-plant sense are one idea of ground and growth that get no rain.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) treats the root ب-ع-ر (b-ʿ-r) as covering two distinct underlying senses:

1. Camels. The word بَعِير (baʿīr) means "camel," with plurals أَبْعِرَة (abʿira), أَبَاعِر (abāʿir), and بُعْرَان (buʿrān). He supports this with a verse attributed to "one of the thieves," in which the speaker says he is too ashamed before God to be seen leading a rope with no camel tied to it, or to beg a mean-spirited man for a camel, when his own Lord's camels are plentiful throughout the land — using baʿīr/buʿrān three times across the two lines.

2. Dung. الْبَعَر (al-baʿr), meaning dung or droppings (of camels and similar animals), which Ibn Fāris simply notes is "well-known," offering no further explanation since the word was common and self-evident.

No other senses are given for this root in the entry.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: بَعَثَ 52x "we sent"; مَّبْعُوثُون 9x "(will be) resurrected"; بَعْث 4x "(of) the resurrection"; ٱنبِعَاث 1x "their being sent"; ٱنبَعَثَ 1x "(was) sent forth"
poets_named: unnamed verse; Ḥumayd b. Thawr (lived into Islam); Ibn al-Aʿrābī (unnamed)
text:
Ibn Sīda's account of the root ب ع ث (b-ʿ-th):

1. To send. بَعَثَهُ (baʿathahu) = to send someone on his own; بَعَثَ بِهِ (baʿatha bihi) = to send him together with another. البَعِيث (al-baʿīth) = an envoy/messenger, plural biʿthān.

2. To dispatch troops. بَعَثَ الجُنْدَ = to send out and direct an army — treated as the same core sense. The dispatched force itself is called al-baʿth or al-baʿīth (plurals buʿūth, buʿuth). A verse laments military levies (buʿūth) that "ran upon us," leaving the speaker "between being flung far off and bearing loss."

3. To impel or loose upon. بَعَثَهُ على الشيء = to drive someone to do a thing; بَعَثَ عليهم البلاء = to loose affliction upon them. Cited from the Qur'an: "We sent/roused against you servants of Ours of great might"; and a sermon of ʿAbd al-Malik using the same verb of unleashing a commander on the people.

4. To set in motion / surge forth. Reflexive انْبَعَثَ / تَبَعَّثَ = to be driven forward, to rush ahead. Ibn Sīda gives the governing sense (taʾwīl) of baʿth as the removal of whatever was holding something back from acting or moving.

5. To rouse from sleep. بَعَثَهُ من نومه = to wake someone, with انْبَعَثَ = to wake up. Related descriptive forms: a man baʿith = one easily and often roused, whom sleep never overpowers; a man baʿth / buʿth / biʿth (plural abʿāth) = one whose anxieties keep him wakeful and stir him from sleep — illustrated by a line of Ḥumayd b. Thawr on a careworn man kept sleepless by his worries.

6. Of God raising creation. بَعَثَ اللهُ الخلق, which Ibn Sīda glosses as nasharahum ("spread/raised them forth"), listed as flowing from the same idea of setting in motion. He notes a variant vocalization baʿath (fatḥa on the ʿayn) is acceptable throughout.

7. To stir up a camel. بَعَثَ البعير = to untie its hobble and release it, or to rouse a kneeling camel so it rises; the intensive noun al-tabʿāth ("rousing/stirring") is a tafʿāl form, with a verse of Ibn al-Aʿrābī describing a herdsman "rough and vigorous in his stirring-up" of the beasts at night.

8. Names. Yawm Buʿāth = a famous pre-Islamic battle-day of the Aws and Khazraj. Al-Baʿīth and Bāʿith are used as proper names.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
According to Ibn Manẓūr's Lisān al-ʿArab, the root ب-ع-ث-ر (baʿthara) centers on the sense of overturning, scattering, and turning something inside-out or upside-down.

1. Qur'anic usage — "the graves are buʿthirat" (Q 82:4): al-Farrāʾ explains this as the graves' interior contents (gold, silver) being brought out, followed by the dead themselves coming out. He links it to a sign of the Hour: the earth disgorging "the choice pieces of its liver" — an idiom for its hidden treasures/riches. He notes buʿthirat and buḥthirat (with ḥ) are two dialect forms of the same word.

2. Al-Zajjāj glosses the same verse as: its soil was overturned and the dead within it were raised up.

3. General usage: "they baʿtharū / baḥtharū their belongings" means they overturned them, scattered them, and left them in a disordered heap, one thing tossed over another.

4. Figurative/bodily use: in a ḥadīth of Abū Hurayra, "my nafs tabaʿtharat" when he doesn't see someone — meaning his inner self churned, turned over, and felt nauseated/unsettled.

5. As a plain verb: baʿthara al-shayʾ = he scattered/dispersed a thing; baʿthara al-turāb wa-l-matāʿ = he overturned the soil and the goods.

6. Morphological note (Ibn Sīdah, citing Yaʿqūb): there is debate over whether the ʿayn in this root is a substitute consonant for the ghayn of a variant root بغثر (baghthara), or vice versa — i.e., the two roots are seen as phonetic variants of one another.

7. Extended sense: baʿthara al-khabar = he investigated or dug into a report/news, synonymous with baḥatha. Likewise baʿthartu al-shayʾ / baḥthartuhu = I extracted it and uncovered/exposed it.

8. Second Qur'anic citation — "when what is in the graves is buʿthira" (Q 100:9): Abū ʿUbayda glosses this as "stirred up and brought out" (uthīra wa-ukhrija). He adds the everyday expression "I baʿthara-ed my trough," meaning I demolished it, turning its bottom to the top — i.e., flipped it inside out.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: Umayya (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse ×2; al-Nimr ibn Tawlab (disputed date); Dhū l-Rumma (Umayyad)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ب ح ر (b-ḥ-r) from two base ideas.

FIRST ROOT — breadth, expanse, spreading out.
1. The sea (al-baḥr) is named for its istibḥār — its spreading out and vastness. From this: istabḥara fī l-ʿilm = to become vast in knowledge; tabaḥḥara fī l-māl = to grow immense in wealth; tabaḥḥara l-rāʿī = the shepherd ranging over wide pasture (cited from a verse of Umayya).
2. A generous man is called baḥr, because his hand overflows with giving as the sea overflows.
3. abḥara l-qawm = to embark on the sea (opposite of abarrū, to take to land) — cited from al-ʿĀmirī.
4. Water that turns thick and salt after being sweet is said to istabḥara; māʾun baḥr = salt water (with a supporting verse). Ibn Fāris notes the claim that all rivers are "seas" (biḥār).
5. al-baḥra: glossed variously as a meadow (al-Farrāʾ), a town/settlement (al-Umawī: "this is our baḥra"), or a wide open expanse of ground (with a verse of al-Nimr ibn Tawlab).

SECOND ROOT — a disease/ailment.
6. baḥirat al-ghanam / al-ibil: livestock sicken from eating dew-wet or rain-regrown herbage — bellies shrink, bodies waste, and (per al-Shaybānī) snake-like creatures emerge from the belly. al-Ḍabbī: this baḥar in sheep parallels suhām in camels, each term exclusive to its animal.
7. Of a person, baḥir = afflicted with consumption/wasting (sulāl) — Ibn al-Aʿrābī, with a verse. al-Ziyādī glosses al-baḥr as a yellowing of the complexion.

Ibn Fāris's method: he anticipates the objection — how does "disease" fit the root-idea of breadth? — and answers that the disease sense still traces back to al-baḥr (the sea), since sea-water and any salt water are undrinkable and cause illness if drunk. So both roots ultimately connect.

Further items he refers back to the first root:
- al-bāḥir = a fool, because he "spreads out" in his ignorance where a sensible man would not.
- baḥartu l-nāqa = to slit a she-camel's ear; such a camel is the baḥīra. Pre-Islamic Arabs did this after her tenth birth, then left her unridden and unused. Ibn Fāris cites God's prohibition of it: "God has not ordained any baḥīra" (Q 5:103) — attributing the practice and its ban as recorded, not endorsing it.
- al-dam al-baḥrānī (bāḥir blood): some said it means deep-red blood, but the sounder view (ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim) is that it is named from al-baḥr in the sense of the depth of the womb — so again back to the first root.
- baḥrānī as a relative adjective from al-Baḥrayn (per al-Khalīl), the form deliberately distinguished from baḥrī, "of the sea."
- The idiom laqītuhu ṣaḥrata baḥrata = "I met him face to face."
- In a verse of Dhū l-Rumma, al-baḥr = any salt water; and al-baḥr can also mean the cultivated riverside country (al-rīf).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ب ح ث (b-ḥ-th), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: stirring up a thing.

1. al-baḥth — searching for something in the dirt/soil (per al-Khalīl); extended to inquiring/seeking information about something — istabḥith ʿan hādhā al-amr / baḥathtu ʿan fulānin — to inquire about a matter or a person.
2. The proverb "like the one digging up [his own] knife" — said of someone whose destruction comes by his own hand — traced to a bull for whom a slaughtering-knife is buried in the ground; it digs the knife up unknowingly and is slaughtered by it, illustrated with a line of poetry warning against being "like the bull" in this way.
3. A grammatical/physical distinction: al-baḥth is specifically done with the hand; the equivalent action done with the foot is called al-faḥṣ.
4. Al-Shaybānī describes al-baḥūth, camels that kick dirt backward behind them as they walk, illustrated with a line of poetry.
5. baḥatha ʿan al-khabar — to seek out information/news.
6. Idiom (via al-Duraydī): "taraktuhu bi-mabāḥithi al-baqar" — "I left him where wild cattle have dug up the ground," meaning: somewhere his whereabouts cannot be known.
7. Closing note (via Abū Zayd): al-bāḥithāʾ — the earth a jerboa gathers while digging its burrow, plural bāḥithāʾwāt.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: ب-ص-ل (b-ṣ-l) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris treats this as a single, unitary root (not one that branches into multiple underlying senses, as he does with many other roots).

1. Core meaning: al-baṣal (البصل) is simply "the onion" — he calls it "well-known," i.e. it needs no further explanation.

2. Poetic citation: he notes that the pre-Islamic poet Labīd used the onion as a point of comparison for helmets (al-bayḍ). Ibn Fāris quotes Labīd's line:

"Massive, strong-scented, bound by its straps... of Qurdumānī and Turkish make, like the onion."

The line describes a helmet — heavy/thick in construction, with its own characteristic smell, held on by fastening straps, made in the Qurdumānī or Turkish style — and says it resembles an onion, evidently in its rounded, layered shape.

That is the entirety of the entry: the root simply denotes the onion, attested via this single Qur'an-unrelated poetic shāhid.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: بَصِير 51x "(is) all-seer"; بَصَر 48x "and the sight"; أَبْصَرَ 29x "see"; بَصِيرَة 7x "enlightenment"; مُبْصِر 4x "giving visibility"; مُبْصِرَة 3x "visible"; بَصُرَتْ 3x "they perceive"; مُسْتَبْصِرِين 1x "endowed with insight"; تَبْصِرَة 1x "giving insight"; يُبَصَّرُ 1x "they will be made to see each other"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives بصر (b-ṣ-r) from two distinct roots.

Root 1 — perception/knowledge of a thing.
- One says huwa baṣīr bihi ("he is perceptive/knowing of it").
- From this comes baṣīra ("insight").
- Also from it: a clot of blood that rounds into a disc when it falls to the ground — cited in a line by al-Asʿar (baṣāʾir carried on the shoulders, and a baṣīra borne off by a swift steed).
- baṣīra is also said to mean a shield (turs), and it means a proof or clear evidence (burhān).
- The unifying idea behind all these senses is the clarity or manifestness of a thing.
- Usage notes: raʾaytuhu lamḥan bāṣiran = "I saw it with an intent, fixed gaze"; baṣurtu bi-l-shayʾ = "to become perceptive/knowing of a thing"; abṣartuhu = "I saw it."

Root 2 — thickness / joining.
- buṣr of a thing is its thickness or coarseness.
- From it, al-baṣr is the joining of one hide to another, sewn together like the hem of a garment.
- baṣīra here also means the space between the two panels of a tent — though Ibn Fāris notes this sense sits closer to the first root.
- al-baṣra is soft stone; drop the final hāʾ and it becomes biṣr (with kasra on the bāʾ), which belongs to this second root.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: بَطَشْ 5x "you seize"; بَطْش 3x "(in) power"; بَطْشَة 2x "(with) the seizure"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-ṭ-sh as a single root with one meaning: taking hold of something by force, domination, and strength.

Qurʾanic witness: {إِنَّ بَطْشَ رَبِّكَ لَشَدِيدٌ} — "Indeed the grip (baṭsh) of your Lord is severe" (al-Burūj 85:12).

Usage example: يَدٌ بَاطِشَةٌ — "a seizing/gripping hand."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root b-T-' (ba, Ta, hamza), from Ibn Faris, Maqayis al-Lugha.

Ibn Faris states this root has one single core meaning: slowness in a matter.

Forms given:
1. abTa'a - 'he was slow / delayed,' with verbal nouns ibTa' and but'.
2. baTi' - adjective, 'a slow man' (rajulun baTi').
3. biTa' - the plural, 'a slow people' (qawmun biTa').

He supports this with one line of poetry (poet not named, introduced only by 'he said'), describing a scattered group (likely camels or a herd) spread out like a swarm of young locusts, in which the speaker turned back its slow ones from its swift ones - i.e. the group had both slow-moving (biTa') and fast-moving (sira') members, and the speaker managed the slower ones relative to the faster.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: بَٰطِل 26x "the falsehood"; مُبْطِلُون 5x "the falsifiers"; يُبْطِلَ 4x "render in vain"; بَطَلَ 1x "and became futile"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-ṭ-l as having a single core sense: a thing’s passing away and its failure to last. The verb baṭala / yabṭulu (verbal nouns buṭl, buṭūl) means “to become void, come to nothing.”

1. Void / false. From this, Satan is called al-bāṭil (“the false one”) because his deeds have no reality — nothing from him yields any return or can be relied upon.

2. The hero. Al-baṭal means “the courageous man.” Those who trace it to this root explain that a hero is so named because he throws himself into places of destruction; Ibn Fāris judges the derivation sound. Usage: baṭal bayyin al-buṭūla wa-l-baṭāla (“a hero of manifest valour”); of a woman, imraʾa baṭala (“a brave woman”).

3. The proverb “mukrahun akhūka lā baṭal” (“Your brother is coerced, not a hero”). Its origin is disputed. One account attributes it to Jarwal ibn Nahshal ibn Dārim, an imposing but cowardly man: during a raid on Banū Dārim he was captured by a man who, at first intimidated by his stature, then bound him and mocked him; brought before the commander (who knew his cowardice) and taunted for supposedly loving combat, Jarwal replied with this line — meaning he fought only under compulsion. Another account assigns the proverb to Bayhas, whose fuller story lies elsewhere.

4. Idleness / worthlessness. Rajul bayyin al-baṭāla means “a man plainly given to idleness/worthlessness.” And dhahaba damuhu buṭlan means “his blood went for nothing,” i.e. unavenged (hadar).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: بَطْن 17x "their bellies"; بَاطِن 3x "and the unapparent"; بِطَانَة 2x "(as) intimates"; بَطَنَ 2x "is concealed"; بَاطِنَة 1x "and hidden"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-ṭ-n as one stable root meaning the inner/intimate side of a thing, the side that faces inward.

1. Core sense — belly and interior. الْبَطْن (the belly) is the opposite of الظَّهْر (the back). بَطَنْتُ الرَّجُلَ means to strike a man in the belly; a saying runs, "when you strike a laden beast, strike it in the belly."

2. The inner reality of a matter. بَاطِنُ الْأَمْر is a matter's hidden interior, as opposed to its ظاهر (outward face). On this basis Ibn Fāris explains the divine name الْبَاطِن (the Inner) as meaning that God knows the inner nature of things thoroughly. بَطَنْتُ هَذَا الْأَمْرَ = "I came to know its inner reality."

3. Words describing the belly. الْبَطِين — big-bellied; الْمَبْطُون — sick in the belly; الْمِبْطَان — a heavy eater (glutton); الْمُبْطِن — lean of belly.

4. Extended, transferred senses (all tied to "inner side"):
   - الْبُطْنَان — the inner surfaces of an arrow's feathers.
   - الْبَطْن — a clan-subdivision ranking below the full tribe (qabīla).
   - الْبُطَيْن — an asterism, said to be "the belly of Aries."
   - الْبِطَان — the girth/cinch of a saddle, named because it lies against the animal's belly.
   - بِطَانَة — a man's close confidants who know his private affairs. Ibn Fāris cites Q 3:118, "Do not take intimates (biṭāna) from outside your own."

5. Verbal usage. تَبَطَّنْتُ الْكَلَأَ = "I ranged through the pasture," with a poetic citation: "I have roamed through it, beneath me a sturdy she-camel, the tendons at her elbows twisted like rope."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root meaning: "splitting/cutting."

1. The farrier (al-bayyar, also al-mubayyir) - one who lances or treats animals - is named from this root because his work is a kind of cutting. Ibn Faris quotes a line of poetry by al-Nabigha comparing a spear-thrust into a horse's flank muscle to a farrier's piercing motion when treating an ailment of the upper arm (al-adad).

2. Insolent excess (al-batar) is derived from the same root: defined as exceeding the proper limit in mirth or exultation - reckless excess born of high spirits, not arrogance in the abstract.

3. The idiom "his blood went for batar" (his blood-price went unclaimed) may not fit the root cleanly, Ibn Faris says, but can be explained as: the blood's channel was "split open" and so it was lost - i.e. used when a slain man's blood goes uncompensated.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ب د أ (b–d–ʾ) from a single core idea: the opening or commencement of a thing.

1. To begin. بَدَأَ / ابْتَدَأَ = to begin, commence (from ibtidāʾ). Of God are the names al-Mubdiʾ and al-Bādiʾ (the Originator/Beginner). Qur'anic examples: 85:13 "He originates and restores," and 29:20 "how He began creation."

2. A wonder. بَدِيّ = an astonishing matter — as if, from its marvel, one starts with it. Cited from the poet ʿAbīd: "neither a wonder nor a marvel."

3. A chief. الْبَدْء = the master/leader, so called because one begins by mentioning him (he is named first). Supported by a verse contrasting the true chief with a merely second-rank man.

4. To set out. أَبْدَأَ = to go forth from one land to another.

5. A share/portion. الْبُدْأَة = one's allotted portion — from the same idea, since a shareholder's portion is what is mentioned first and matters most to him. Supported by a verse (granting a choice portion to a watchman by the fire).

6. Finger-joints. الْبُدُوء = the knuckle-joints of the fingers (singular بَدْء, patterned like بَدْع). Ibn Fāris judges the hamza here secondary — not original — and links the word to the joints' protrusion and visibility, so it still belongs to the core "emerging/beginning" sense.

7. An anomalous sense (etymology unknown to Ibn Fāris). بُدِئَ / مَبْدُوء = to be stricken with smallpox or measles. Supported by a verse likening the pocked skin's surface to something scorched.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: بَدِيع 2x "(the) originator"; بِدْع 1x "a new (one)"; ٱبْتَدَعُ 1x "they innovated"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-d-ʿ as two separate roots.

1. Originating something without a prior model.
- أَبْدَعْتُ الشَّيْءَ (abdaʿtu al-shayʾ): to originate a thing, in word or deed — to begin it with no preceding pattern to copy.
- Hence the Qurʾanic phrase بَدِيعُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ, God as Originator of the heavens and the earth.
- Arab usage: ابْتَدَعَ فُلَانٌ الرَّكِيَّ — he was the first to dig out a well and draw its water.
- فُلَانٌ بِدْعٌ فِي هَذَا الْأَمْرِ — so-and-so is the first/an unprecedented case in this matter. Citing Q 46:9, "Say: I am no bidʿ among the messengers," he glosses bidʿ as "I am not the first."

2. Being cut off, breaking down, exhaustion.
- أُبْدِعَتِ الرَّاحِلَةُ (passive): the riding-animal gave out — worn down and disabled.
- أُبْدِعَ بِالرَّجُلِ: the man was stranded, his mounts having given out or been disabled, leaving him unable to continue. He cites a ḥadīth in which a man says, "O Messenger of God, I have been stranded (ubdiʿa bī), so carry me."
- A reported qualification: ibdāʿ is said to occur only through lameness (ẓalʿ).

Derivation: Ibn Fāris notes that بِدْعَة (bidʿa, "innovation") is derived from part of this material — he does not define the term further here.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: بَدَّلَ 23x "but changed"; تَبْدِيل 7x "any change"; يَسْتَبْدِلْ 3x "and will replace you"; يَتَبَدَّلِ 3x "exchange"; مُبَدِّل 3x "one (can) alter"; يُبْدِلَ 3x "he will substitute for him"; ٱسْتِبْدَال 1x "replacing"; بَدَل 1x "(is) the exchange"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-d-l as a single root whose core sense is one thing standing in the place of another that has gone.

1. The noun forms: بَدَل (badal) and بَدِيل (badīl) both mean the substitute or replacement of a thing — "this is the badal / badīl of the thing."

2. He distinguishes two verb forms by whether a replacement is actually supplied:
   - بَدَّلَ (baddala, form II) = to change or alter something, even when no substitute is brought in its place. He cites Qurʾān Yūnus 10:15, "Say: it is not for me to change it (ubaddilahu) of my own accord," as an instance of this "alter" sense.
   - أَبْدَلَ (abdala, form IV) = to replace something, i.e. to bring an actual substitute in its stead.

3. Poetic shāhid for the "replace" sense: the phrase "the deposing of the commander in favour of the commander put in his place (al-mubdal)."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: بَدَن 1x "in your body"; بُدْن 1x "and the camels and cattle"
text:
Root بدن (b-d-n) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core sense: the bulk/mass of a thing, as distinct from its extremities (shawā).

1. Basic anatomy: al-badan — a person's body/torso (plural abdān).

2. Extended to a large mountain-goat, called badan for its bulk — illustrated with a verse about a belted, laboring animal. Ibn Fāris explains: Arabs sometimes name something exaggeratedly typical of its kind by the name of the whole category — just as an exceptionally manly man might simply be called "a man" — so a notably large-bodied goat is called "a body."

3. Religious usage: al-badana, the sacrificial camel offered at the Kaʿba, is said to be named this because such animals were deliberately fattened up before sacrifice.

4. Age: a man called badan is an aged man — illustrated with a verse asking what the tears of a grey-haired badan are even worth.

5. Physical size: bādin and badīn describe someone large of body (verb baduna). A hadith has the Prophet saying "I have grown heavy/stout" — some transmissions instead give "baddantu." Separately, baddana means "to grow old" — illustrated with a verse listing grey hair and aging among life's distracting burdens.

6. A coat of mail is called al-badan because it encloses the body — a final extension of the root's "bodily bulk" image to something that wraps around it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ب د ر (b-d-r), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Two roots:

First — completeness/fullness. Anything complete is called badr; the full moon (al-badr) is named for its completeness and fullness. Ten thousand dirhams is a badrah, the "completion" of a round number; ʿaynun badrah — a full, brimming eye, illustrated with a line of poetry. A young goat's skin (also badrah) is explained on the same "holding a full amount" logic; ghulām badr — a youth full of vigor. Separately, Badr the place-name is noted as simply named after a man called Badr, unrelated to the "fullness" sense. al-bawādir (plural of bādirah) — the flesh between shoulder and neck, included in this sense-group because it is full/plump, illustrated with a line of poetry about reddened flesh on horses in battle.

Second — hastening. badartu ilā al-shayʾi / bādartu — to hasten toward something. Error/lapse is called bādirah because it "bursts forth" from a person in a moment of intensity or anger — illustrated with the idiom "kānat minhu bawādir," meaning he committed lapses. badarat damʿatuhu — a tear "badar"-ed, i.e. came first/rushed ahead — illustrated with a line of poetry by Kuthayyir about passion and rushing tears.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: يُبْدِىَ 15x "you reveal"; بَدَا 11x "and (will) appear"; بَادِى 1x "immature in opinion"; بَدْو 1x "the bedouin life"; بَاد 1x "and the visitor"; بَادُون 1x "living in (the) desert"; مُبْدِي 1x "(was to) disclose"
poets_named: al-Shammākh (lived into Islam); unnamed verse ×2; Ibn Aḥmar (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Sīda's al-Muḥkam on the root ب د و (b-d-w):

1. Core sense — "to appear": بَدَا (badā) = a thing appeared or became manifest; verbal nouns badw, buduww, badāʾ, and badan (the last from Sībawayh). The causative abdā = to make [something] appear.

2. "The first thing that shows": badāwat al-amr = the first of a matter to appear (from al-Liḥyānī). Related idioms: bādiya al-raʾy = the apparent/surface aspect of an opinion (from Thaʿlab); "You, bādiya al-raʾy, do such-and-such" = you, going by what first appears of the opinion (al-Liḥyānī, without hamza).

3. "A new view occurring to someone": badā lahu fī al-amr = a fresh idea or change of mind came to him about the matter (verbal nouns badw, badan, badāʾ), illustrated by al-Shammākh's line ("…a change of mind about that she-camel has occurred to you"). Sībawayh applies this to Qurʾān 12:35 ({ثم بدا لهم…} "then it appeared to them… that they should imprison him"), reading it as "there appeared to them an appearing (badāʾ)"; grammatically the clause layasjununnahu cannot be the verb's subject, since a subject cannot be a full sentence.

4. badānī bi-kadhā = he got ahead of / began before me in something (equivalent to the hamza-form badaʾanī).

5. Fixed adverbial phrase: bādiya badin / bādiya badā = "at the very first, first thing" (with a cited verse). Sībawayh gives the form bādiya badā without tanwīn, noting analogy would not actually forbid the tanwīn.

6. Desert / nomadic life (opposite of settled life, al-ḥaḍar): the nouns al-badw, al-bādiya, al-badāh, al-bidāwa, al-badāwa. The relative adjective badawiyy is irregular; badāwiyy / bidāwiyy is the regular (analogical) form, being a nisba to al-badāwa. Ibn Sīda notes he lists badāwiyy only because ordinary speakers know solely badawiyy, and argues that where a nisba can be read as either regular or irregular, the regular reading is preferable because analogy is broader.

7. Verb of going out: badā al-qawm badāʾan = the people went out to the desert. Cited for Qurʾān 33:20 ({…يودوا لو أنهم بادون في الأعراب} "they would wish they were out in the desert among the bedouin"). Ibn al-Aʿrābī notes this desert-dwelling is seasonal — during spring pasturing — while otherwise they stay settled at their water sources.

8. Plurals/collectives for desert-dwellers: qawm budda / buddāʾ = desert folk (= bādūn), with a supporting verse. In Ibn Aḥmar's line, badw is either a collective noun for bādin (paralleling rākib/rakb) or means "desert life" itself (as if "people of badw").

9. Other senses: badwatā al-wādī (Abū Ḥanīfa al-Dīnawarī) = the two sides of a valley. al-badā (shortened) = excrement from a man's rear; badā al-rajul = he relieved himself so it became visible. al-badā also = a human joint (plural abdāʾ), and = a chief/master (both cross-referenced to the hamza root). al-Badiyy and Wādī al-Badiyy are place-names; Badwa is a watering-place of Banū al-ʿAjlān.

10. Method note: Ibn Sīda states that any word of this chapter whose final weak letter does not surface is judged to be a wāw (not yāʾ), because the root ب د و is widely attested while ب د ي is narrow.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-gh-ḍ as one root with a single sense.

1. Core sense: the opposite of love — that is, hatred or detestation. The standard verb form he cites is the fourth form: أَبْغَضْتُهُ / أُبْغِضُهُ, "I detested him / I detest him."

2. A disputed poetic usage: he quotes a line of verse containing the word بِغْضَة (bighḍa) — roughly, "among the things that turn one aside is that she kept you off with bighḍa, and with hurling from her, and that you are being watched." Two readings were offered by earlier scholars: (a) bighḍa here stands for "the enemies"; (b) the poet meant ذَوِي بِغْضَة, "people who harbour hatred," with the possessor-word elided. Ibn Fāris reports both without choosing.

3. An idiomatic imprecation: بَغُضَ جَدُّهُ, literally "may his good fortune become hateful," which he compares to the formula عَثَرَ ("may he stumble / may his luck trip"). Here the verb takes the intransitive-stative pattern (baguḍa) rather than the transitive fourth form of sense 1.

He closes with the customary "and God knows best."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ب-غ-ل (b-gh-l) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core sense: physical strength/robustness in the body.

1. البغل (al-baghl, "the mule") is derived from this root. Two explanations are reported for the name:
   - It was named for the strength of its physical build.
   - It was named after at-tabghīl, a particular kind of gait (way of moving).

2. Ibn Fāris's own preferred position reverses the second explanation: he holds that the word tabghīl (the gait-name) is what derives from the mule's characteristic gait — not the mule's name from the gait.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ب-غ-ت (b-gh-t) as one simple root that generates no wider analogical pattern (lā yuqāsu ʿalayhi).

1. Core sense — al-baght: a thing happening suddenly, coming upon a person by surprise / unawares (yafjaʾ).

Supporting citation: he quotes a poetic line, "and the greatest of things is when the sudden onset takes you unawares," illustrating baght as an abrupt, unexpected occurrence.

text:
Ibn Sīda's account of the root ب غ ي (b-gh-y).

1. Core sense — to seek / desire. بغى الشيء = to seek a thing, whether good or evil; verbal nouns بغاء (better known) and بغي (per al-Liḥyānī). Poetic witness: "let me not hold you back from seeking good, for I have fallen upon a lion about to devour me."

2. Derived seeking-verbs. ابتغى، تبغّى، استبغى all likewise mean "he sought it." A cited verse uses تستبغي / تبغى ("she seeks them out yet finds them not") in a form lacking the usual compensating weak-letter.

3. Nouns from this sense. البُغية / البِغية = the thing sought, or a need; Thaʿlab treats both vowellings as verbal nouns. البُغية can also mean a sought-after stray animal.

4. Seeking on another's behalf. أبغاه الشيء = he sought it for someone, or helped him seek it; some distinguish بغاه (sought it for him) from أبغاه إياه (helped him get it). al-Liḥyānī: استبغى القوم فبغوا له = the people were asked to seek for him, and did.

5. Agent noun. الباغي = the seeker (plurals بُغاة، بُغيان).

6. To be feasible / fitting. انبغى الشيء = it became easy and feasible. Ibn Sīda reads the Qur'anic "We did not teach him poetry, nor does it ينبغي for him" as "nor is it made easy/fitting for him." ذو بَغاية = an acquisitive person, a good earner.

7. Illegitimacy and fornication. البُغية in a child = the opposite of legitimate birth. بغت (المرأة/الأمة), also باغت, verbal nouns بغاء / بغي; she is بغيّ = she fornicated. Reports differ: البغيّ = a slave-woman (fornicator or not); or = a fornicating woman, free or slave. On the Qur'anic "your mother was not a baghiyy" (of Mary's mother, who was certainly free), Thaʿlab generalized the term to any woman without specifying slave or free.
   - Abū ʿUbayd: البغايا originally = slave-women, because they used to fornicate; a verse of al-Aʿshā about gifting them (a free woman not being given as a gift) is cited, after which usage broadened to any fornicating woman, slave or free. al-Liḥyānī: the masculine رجل بغيّ is not said.

8. A separate sense: scout / vanguard. البُغية = a scouting party; witness from Ṭufayl on scouts signalling the approach of a large army.

9. Wrongdoing / transgression — a distinct major sense. بغى على فلان = he swerved from truth and overreached; = he rose against and wronged him. Qur'anic witnesses: "some of us wronged others"; "sin, and wrongful transgression (baghy)." A grammatical note: al-Kisāʾī's line drops the case-vowel off the yāʾ of البغي (Ibn Sīda: the kasra was felt heavy on the yāʾ, so its vowel shifted to the preceding letter). قوم بُغاء = people who wronged one another.
   - Related shades (al-Liḥyānī): بغى على أخيه = he envied him; بغى = he lied. The Qur'anic "O our father, mā nabghī" thus admits two readings: "what do we seek?" (mā interrogative) or "we neither lie nor wrong" (mā negating).

10. Further senses.
   - بغى في مشيته = he strutted and moved fast (also of a horse; but فرس باغٍ is not said).
   - البغي = heavy/abundant rain; بغي السماء = a downpour's violence and bulk.
   - بغى الجرح = the wound festered and suppurated; برئ على بغي = it healed with some remaining corruption (نغل).
   - جمل باغٍ = a camel that fails to impregnate (from Kurāʿ).
   - بغى الشيء = he looked to see how it was; بغاه = he watched and waited for it.
   - ما ينبغي لك أن تفعل = it is not fitting for you (لا نَوْلُك); al-Liḥyānī gives ما انبغى لك with the same meaning.
   - Idiom: إنك لعالم ولا تُباغ = "you are indeed learned — and may you not be struck by the evil eye."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ب-هـ-ج (b-h-j) as a single root with one core meaning: joy/gladness (surūr) paired with freshness or radiant beauty (naḍra).

1. Core sense: joy combined with freshness/radiance. He gives the example "a bahīj plant" (nabāt bahīj) — meaning one that is fresh, blooming, and beautiful.

2. Qur'anic citation: he quotes Qāf 50:7, "And We caused to grow therein every beautiful [bahīj] kind," as an attestation of this sense — a plant/growth so fresh and lovely it is a source of delight to look at.

3. Related derivative: ibtihāj ("rejoicing," from the same root) simply means surūr, "joy/gladness" — confirming that the root's two component ideas (visual radiance/freshness and inner delight) are bound together rather than separate.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
poets_named: unnamed verse; Ḥassān (lived into Islam); Labīd (lived into Islam)
text:
Root ب هـ ل (b-h-l), al-Zamakhsharī, Asās al-Balāgha

Literal senses
1. abhala al-nāqata — to leave a she-camel unmilked; nāqa bāhil — an unbound she-camel anyone may milk. Extended figuratively: abhala al-wāliya al-raʿiyyah — a governor leaving his subjects unattended; istabhalahum — to leave people unrestrained, doing as they please; abhala ʿabdahu — to leave a slave free to his own will; "mālun bahlalun sabahlalun" — wealth left free and unclaimed.

2. From "left free/unbound" comes a distinct sense: bahalahu — to curse someone; "ʿalayhi bahlatu Allāh" — "upon him is God's curse." bāhaltu fulānan mubāhalatan — two parties mutually invoking God's curse on whichever is the wrongdoer; tabāhala/ibtahala — to curse one another mutually. This is the entry's central Qur'anic citation, Al ʿImran 3:61: "thumma nabtahil fa-najʿal laʿnata Allāhi ʿalā al-kādhibīn" — "then let us invoke mutual cursing and place God's curse upon the liars" (the famous Mubāhalah verse).

3. bahlūl (plural bahālīl) — a noble, generous person, illustrated with two lines of poetry (one about a true knight; one by Ḥassān naming Jaʿfar, ʿAlī, and the Prophet Aḥmad as bahālīl).

Figurative senses (majāz)
4. rajul bāhil — a man wandering aimlessly, without occupation; rāʿin bāhil — a shepherd walking without a staff.
5. ibtahala ilā Allāh — to supplicate God fervently, striving in prayer — the root sense behind the modern word for earnest, imploring prayer — illustrated with a line of poetry by Labīd where Time itself "ibtahala" (strove/exerted itself) to destroy noble chiefs.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ب-ه-م (b-h-m), from Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha.

Core idea: something remains such that the way to approach or make sense of it is unknown. Hence hādhā amrun mubham, "this is an obscure/ambiguous matter."

Branches from this core sense:

1. Al-buhmah — a rock with no crack or opening in it. By extension, a brave man is called buhmah because he cannot be overcome from any direction he is attacked — like the solid, unbreachable rock. (Some lexicographers instead give al-buhmah as "a company of horsemen.")

2. Al-bahīm — a color not mixed with any other, whether black or another color; i.e. a solid, uniform color.

3. Abhamtu al-bāb, "I closed the door" — locking it renders it likewise "impenetrable/unclear," tying back to the core sense of something whose way in cannot be found.

4. Irregular offshoots the author flags as not fitting the core pattern: al-ibhām, "the thumb," and al-bahm, "young lambs/kids of sheep."

5. Al-buhmā — a type of plant; the land is said to "become buhmā" (abhamat) when this plant grows abundant there.

Ibn Fāris closes with a line of poetry describing the buhmā plant's growth as like a king's (qayl's) jealously-guarded carpets — flawless and unbroken (mubham), echoing the same root-sense of something whole and without a crack or blemish.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-h-t as having one single root sense, which he glosses as being stunned or struck dumb (dahash) and bewildered (ḥayra).

1. Core sense — stupefaction / bewilderment. The verb is given in the passive pattern: buhita al-rajul, yubhatu, verbal noun bahtan ("the man was confounded / left dumbstruck"). The noun al-bahta likewise means bewilderment.

2. Derived sense — falsehood. Al-buhtān, on this account, means a lie (kadhib).

3. Attested idiom. Ibn Fāris cites the Arabs' expression yā la-l-bahītati, which he explains as meaning "O what a lie!" — showing the form bahīta used for a falsehood.

The entry is brief and offers no further senses, poetic citations, or plural patterns.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ب ج س (b-j-s), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One meaning, specifically tied to water: the opening/bursting-forth of a thing, releasing water.

1. al-bajs (per al-Khalīl) — a split in a waterskin, stone, or ground from which water gushes forth; if nothing gushes, it isn't true inbijās — illustrated with a line of poetry by al-ʿAjjāj about a bucket splitting. Al-Khalīl distinguishes al-inbijās (general bursting-forth) from al-nubūʿ (specifically a spring's flow).
2. The entry's central Qur'anic citation, al-A'raf 7:160: "fa-nbajasat minhu ithnatā ʿashrata ʿaynā" — "and there gushed forth from it twelve springs" (Moses striking the rock).
3. Extended usage: tabajjasa al-gharb — a water-bucket splitting/leaking; "hādhihi arḍun tabajjasu ʿuyūnan" — land bursting forth with springs; "al-saḥābu yatabajjasu maṭaran" — a cloud bursting forth with rain.
4. Figurative, food-related extension (via Yaʿqūb): a bowl of tharīd (bread-and-broth) that "tatabajjasu" — oozes/bursts — with abundant fat.
5. Closing note: Ibn Fāris flags a report from an unfamiliar authority ("Abū Turāb, whom we do not know") using bajastu al-jurḥ ("I bajas-ed the wound") to mean lancing it — an attestation he records without vouching for its reliability.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-k-m as one root with few derivatives, its core meaning being muteness (khoras).

1. Muteness proper. Citing al-Khalīl: al-abkam is the mute person, one who does not speak.

2. Withheld speech. If someone refrains from speaking — whether from ignorance or on purpose — the verb is used: bakima ʿan al-kalām, "he held back from speech." This extends the root beyond a physical defect to a refusal or failure to speak.

3. Unclear speech. The word can also be applied to someone who does not speak clearly or express himself plainly: innahu la-abkam.

4. Exegetical usage. In tafsīr, Ibn Fāris notes, al-abkam denotes specifically one born mute.

5. Morphology. On the authority of al-Duraydī: bakīm is an alternative form with the same meaning as abkam; its plural is abkām, following the pattern of sharīf → ashrāf.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: بُكْرَة 7x "morning"; بِكْر 3x "and virgins"; إِبْكَٰر 2x "and the morning"
poets_named: unnamed verse; al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-k-r as one root meaning "the beginning / outset of a thing," from which two further branches grow (one derived, one by analogy).

1. Core sense — earliness / early morning. البُكْرة (bukra) is the early morning (pl. bukar). The verbs tabkīr, bukūr, and ibtikār all mean setting out early. الإبكار means "early morning" (paralleling iṣbāḥ for "morning"). bākartu / bakartu ʿalā = to do something early or set out early on an errand. Abū Zayd gives forms: to come early to water, to take the morning meal early, to make someone else go early (bakartu and abkartu both used). A habitual early-riser is a bakir / bakur (like ḥadhir, "cautious").

2. Extended to rain, plants, fruit (the "early" idea applied). Al-Khalīl: a "baker rain" (ghayth bākūr) is the first of the autumn rains, and also that which travels early in the night or day; a cloud that journeys by night and arrives early is bakūr. Al-Farrāʾ: a tree "comes early" (bakarat / abkarat / bakkarat) when it hastens to fruit and ripen (such a tree is bakūr; if habitual, mibkār). The first-ripe date is a bākūra (also bakīra, pl. bakāʾir). Early-yielding land is mibkār. Illustrated by verses of a Hudhalī poet and al-Akhṭal.

3. Derived branch — youth / firstness (from "beginning of life"). 
 - Camel: a bakr is a young male camel that has not yet cut its aging tooth (in the freshness of youth); once it does, it becomes a full-grown jamal. The female is bakra, becoming a nāqa when aged. Plural bikār; smallest number "three abkur." Two proverbs: ṣadaqanī sinnu bakrihi ("the tooth of his young camel told me the truth" — from a seller who lied about a decrepit camel's age), and arwā min bakri Habannaqa ("more watered than Habannaqa's camel," of a proverbial fool whose camel kept leaving and returning from water uselessly). Al-Tamīmī: called bakr from when it is first ridden until it cuts the four-year tooth.
 - Woman: al-Khalīl — a bikr is a woman never touched (a virgin); Abū ʿUbayd adds that a woman who has borne one child is also called bikr. bikr is used of a firstborn, boy or girl; proverb: "the strongest of people is a firstborn son of two firstborns." A bikr cow is a young cow that has not conceived.
 - Generalized: the bikr of anything is its first instance. "This affair is neither bakīr nor thanī" = neither first nor second (with a supporting verse: a "need that is bakr" = a new/first need). A bikr vine is one that has borne for the first time (verse of al-Aʿshā). ʿasal abkār is honey made by young bees (or, alternatively, tended by young slave-girls).

4. Third branch — by likeness. البَكَرة (bakara) is the well-pulley over which water is drawn; Ibn Fāris allows that it may be named by likeness to the young she-camel (bakra). Cited by a verse of Imruʾ al-Qays. Rings on a sword's ornament are likewise called bakarāt. All of these, he concludes, trace back to the single origin.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: بَكَتْ 5x "weeping"; بُكِيّ 1x "and weeping"; أَبْكَىٰ 1x "and makes (one) weep"
text:
Root b-k-y, as treated by al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī:

1. Verb and verbal nouns. bakā / yabkī, with two verbal nouns: bukan and bukāʾ.
   - bukāʾ (with the long ending) = tears flowing from grief accompanied by wailing. This form is used when the *sound* is the dominant element — it belongs to the same pattern Arabic uses for animal cries, e.g. ruġāʾ (a camel's grumbling) and thuġāʾ (bleating).
   - bukan (with the short ending) is used when the *grief* is the dominant element rather than the noise.

2. Plurals and morphology. The active participle al-bākī ("one who weeps") has the plurals bākūn and bukiyy. The Qur'an uses the second in Maryam 19:58, "they fell down prostrate and weeping" (sujjadan wa-bukiyyan). Al-Rāghib analyses bukiyy as originally the pattern fuʿūl — the same participle-to-plural pairing as sājid/sujūd, rākiʿ/rukūʿ, qāʿid/quʿūd — with the wāw shifted to yāʾ and then assimilated, exactly as in jāthin/juthiyy and ʿātin/ʿutiyy.

3. Range of the verb. bakā can denote grief and the shedding of tears together, or either one of the two on its own.

4. Qur'anic application. In al-Tawba 9:82, "let them laugh little and weep much," the pair points to gladness and sorrow as inner states — the laughing need not involve loud laughter, nor the weeping actual tears.

5. Figurative use. Al-Dukhān 44:29, "neither the heaven nor the earth wept for them," is reported with two readings: taken literally, which is the position of those who attribute life and knowledge to the heaven and the earth; or taken figuratively, with the implied sense "the people of the heaven did not weep for them."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) derives everything under ب-ل-ع from one core idea: swallowing something down (izdirād).

1. Core/literal sense — balaʿtu al-shayʾa, "I swallowed the thing." The base verbal sense of gulping something down.

2. Al-bālūʿ, "drain-hole" — a sink or drain is named from this root because it "swallows" the water that runs into it.

3. Saʿd Bulaʿ — the name of a star (one of the "Saʿd" asterisms/lunar mansions). Ibn Fāris notes this without further comment on how it connects to the swallowing sense — likely just a proper name built on the root.

4. Al-bulaʿ, on a pulley — the eye/hole bored in the upright post (qāmah) of a pulley (bakrah) is also called al-bulaʿ. Ibn Fāris explains the logic is the same as the core sense: the hole "swallows" the axle-piece of wood that threads through it.

5. Extended/figurative sense — "ballaʿa al-shaybu fī raʾsihi," said when gray hair has completely taken over someone's head. Ibn Fāris treats this as a close extension of the same root idea: once grayness has covered (shamila) the whole head, it is as if the head has been "swallowed" by it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad); Ibn al-Riqāʿ (Umayyad); unnamed verse ×2
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-l-d as one root whose senses all trace back to a single core: **the chest / breast** (al-ṣadr). From that center the branches radiate:

1. **Chest (core sense).** The she-camel "sets her balda to the ground" when she kneels — balda = her chest. Ibn Fāris cites Dhū al-Rumma's line of a camel casting her chest down in a silent place.

2. **Hand-to-chest in perplexity.** تَبَلَّدَ (tabalada): a man puts his hand on his chest when baffled by some matter.

3. **The space between the brows.** الْأَبْلَد (al-ablad) is a man whose eyebrows are not joined; the bare gap between them is called balda — linked to the root because it resembles open, bare ground.

4. **An asterism.** الْبَلْدَة (al-balda) is a star/star-group; "the balda of the Lion" means the Lion's chest.

5. **A settlement / region.** الْبَلَد is "the chest [central part] of the villages" — i.e. an inhabited place. He supports the extension with Ibn al-Riqāʿ's verse on decay enveloping "its abilād" (its tracts). An alternative view holds balad means "trace/mark" (athar), plural abilād — but Ibn Fāris judges the first (chest-based) account more consistent with the root's analogy.

6. **Clinging to the ground.** بَلَّدَ (ballada) = to stick fast to the ground. He cites a verse where night landmarks "cling low like hillocks," and a Tamīmī verse on a mublid — a watering-trough lying flat against the ground.

7. **Related verb.** أَبْلَدَ (ablada) means exactly the same as tabalada.

8. **Sword-fighting.** الْمُبَالَدَة (mubālada), fighting with swords, parallels mubālaṭa; some derive it from the "clinging" sense — as if combatants held their ground and fought on it.

9. **A resident.** الْبَالِد (al-bālid), by analogy, is one who dwells in a balad (settlement).

Method note: Ibn Fāris explicitly reasons by qiyās (analogical consistency), deriving each sense from the "chest → center → ground-hugging → inhabited place" line and preferring the reading that best fits that pattern.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: بَلَغَ 40x "he reached"; بَلَٰغ 15x "the conveyance"; بَلَّغْ 6x "convey"; بَٰلِغ 6x "reaching"; أَبْلَغُ 5x "i have conveyed to you"; بَٰلِغَة 3x "perfect"; بَلِيغ 1x "penetrating"; مَبْلَغ 1x "(is) their sum"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-l-gh as a single root whose core meaning is reaching or arriving at a thing.

1. Core sense — arrival. بَلَغْتُ الْمَكَانَ (balaghtu al-makān) = "I reached the place," i.e. arrived at it.

2. Extended to nearness. Being on the verge of something (al-mushārafa) can also be called bulūgh, on the strength of its closeness to arrival. He cites Q 65:2, "when they reach their term (balaghna ajalahunna)."

3. Attaining one's aim. The idiom aḥmaq bilgh / balgh describes a fool who, despite his foolishness, still reaches what he wants.

4. al-bulgha — a bare subsistence, the little one "gets by" on: as if a contented man thereby reaches the standing of someone with plenty.

5. al-balāgha (eloquence) — the praise given to a fluent speaker, so called because through it he reaches what he intends; and lī fī hādhā balāgh means "this is enough / a sufficiency for me."

6. ballagha al-fāris — of a horseman who stretches out his hand along the rein to make his horse run faster.

7. tabalaghat al-qilla bi-fulān — said when scarcity presses hard on someone, because the want has then reached its utmost extreme (al-ghāya) with him.

Throughout, Ibn Fāris keeps every usage tied to the one idea of reaching a limit or goal.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-l-s as a single root, and states that anything falling outside it carries no weight.

1. Core sense — despair. The root's basic meaning is يأس (yaʾs), losing hope. أَبْلَسَ (ablasa) = "he despaired." He cites Q 23:77, {إِذَا هُمْ فِيهِ مُبْلِسُونَ}, "when they are, in it, struck with despair."

2. Etymology of إبليس (Iblīs). He reports (attributing it to others: "they said") that the name Iblīs was derived from this root — as though the bearer had despaired of God's mercy.

3. Extended sense — falling silent. Still within the same section: أَبْلَسَ الرَّجُلُ means the man went silent. Applied to a she-camel, أَبْلَسَتِ النَّاقَةُ — she being called a مِبْلَاس (miblās) — describes one that does not bellow despite the intensity of her rut (الضَّبَعَة).

4. A poetic witness. On the line of Ibn Aḥmar, "Turn aside, O daughter of the balas, the mistrusted one — for the small thing grows and the break is mended," he notes it is said that البلس (al-balas) means الواجم (al-wājim), one struck silent by gloom — which links the citation back to the silence sense rather than to despair directly.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: بَلَوْ 20x "and surely we will test you"; ٱبْتَلَىٰ 8x "he try him"; بَلَاء 6x "(was) a trial"; مُبْتَلِي 2x "surely testing"; يُبْلِىَ 2x "and that he may test"
poets_named: Sībawayh (unnamed); Ṭarafa (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse ×4; Zuhayr (pre-Islamic); Jarīr (Umayyad)
text:
al-Zamakhsharī's Asās al-Balāgha organizes this material into literal and figurative (majāz) usage, and covers two clusters: moisture/recovery (b-l-l) and trial/knowing (b-l-w).

Moisture and recovery:
1. balla / istaballa: to recover from illness (Sībawayh's favorite line: one recovers from a disease and is thought saved, though the fatal illness is still in him).
2. balaltu bihi: to win or get hold of something (Ṭarafa's line on gripping a sword-hilt).
3. balbāl / balābil: agitation or anxiety in the breast — "whenever I call you to mind, I fall into turmoil."
4. Figurative: ballū arḥāmakum, "moisten your kinship ties" = keep them fresh and connected; paralleled by naddi raḥmaka. A verse asks God to "moisten" someone with a son.
5. From moisture of the tongue: billat al-lisān, praise for clear articulation; balīl al-rīq, "moist of saliva" = fluent, eloquent. "No moisture reaches you from him" = you get no good from him.
6. ibtalla / taballala: to recover good condition after wasting away.
7. ṭawaytuhu ʿalā billatihi, "I folded him up while still damp" = I put up with him despite his fault — the image is a waterskin rolled away wet, which then rots.

Trial, testing, and coming to know:
8. balawtu: to try/test someone (he proved "the best of those tried"); prayer: "try us only with what is best."
9. buliya / ubtuliya bi-: to be tried or afflicted; baliyya / balwā: a calamity that befalls one; balāʾ descends on the disbelievers. Hadith: refuge is sought from the hardship of balāʾ — except a balāʾ that carries elevation of rank with God.
10. Zamakhsharī links testing to knowing: yatabālayān = yatakhābarān, "they test/inform each other." Hence lā ubālīhi, "I do not reckon with him," from not troubling to inform oneself about him (Zuhayr: "she does not care"). An alternative derivation makes it a metathesis of a form from al-bāl (the mind): "I do not bring it to mind." Also lā ubālīhi bālatan.
11. nāqat bilwi safar: a she-camel worn down (tested) by travel.
12. ablaytuhu ʿudhran, "I made my excuse plain to him" — literally, I made him one who knows my excuse fully; likewise ablaytuhu yamīnan, to administer an oath (Jarīr's line on showing a ruler trustworthiness).
13. From the same root: ablā balāʾan ḥasanan, to show fine valor in war — to display might until people test and know you; a man's notable "feat" on a day; God tries the servant with a good or bad trial ("God tries and bestows").
14. ibtalaytu al-amr: I tested the matter = I came to know it (verse of a confined woman questioning the maids).
15. Figurative: balawtu al-shayʾ = shamamtuhu, "I smelled it" (verse on stagnant old water, its smell likened to pressed mustard).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-n-n, as a doubled root, as having one root meaning: sticking fast and staying in place (al-luzūm wa-l-iqāma). He says every word in the article goes back to it.

1. **Staying, settling.** Al-Khalīl defines al-ibnān as "sticking fast": abanna al-qawmu bi-maḥalla means "the people stayed at a place of settlement". One verse addresses riders "who stay" (al-mubinnūna) at a slope; a rajaz verse, cited for al-ibnān in the sense of staying, speaks of young she-camels that "do not wait for the man who lingers" (al-mubinn).

2. **Tethering an animal to fatten it.** Bannana al-rajulu is said when a man ties up a sheep to fatten it. A verse: "My people taunt me that I tether beasts for fattening; and has anyone but the noble ever tethered the lesser beasts?"

3. **Al-banān, the fingertips.** Al-Khalīl defines al-banān as the tips of the fingers of the hands. The singular banāna, for a single finger, is said to occur in poetry, as in the verse "no tribe has a banāna above them" (about the Banū Kināna), which is explained as: no one surpasses them by so much as a finger's measure. Another verse, cited for al-banān, describes a man whose colour is dusky and whose fingers are short.

4. **Al-banān in Q 8:12.** For "and strike every banān of them" (Q 8:12), two explanations are given. Right after al-Khalīl's definition, the article explains al-banān there as al-shawā, the hands and the feet. Al-Zajjāj says it means the fingers and all the other limbs, and gives banāna as the singular. The passage quoted from al-Zajjāj goes on to derive al-banān from abanna bi-l-makān, "he stayed in the place", because everything that serves staying and living is handled with the banān.

5. **Al-banna, a clinging smell.** Al-Khalīl defines al-banna as the smell of the lairs of cattle, sheep and goats, and gazelles. It is also used of a pleasant scent, as in "I find in this garment a pleasant banna of apple or quince". A verse speaks of tail-hair wetted with clinging dung (mubinn). Ibn Fāris says this too belongs to the first meaning, because a smell clings.

6. **Al-banīn, the steady man.** Abū ʿAmr says al-banīn is the sensible, careful man, and derives the word from al-banna.

7. **Al-bunāna, a meadow.** Al-bunāna is a meadow full of herbage and adorned. The name Thābit al-Bunānī comes from it; he is described as a descendant of Saʿd ibn Luʾayy ibn Ghālib who had a nurse called Bunāna. Ibn Fāris says this too comes "from that first" meaning, because such a meadow never lacks a pleasant smell.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: بُنَىّ 80x "(the) children"; ٱبْن 63x "son"; بَنَات 17x "and (the) daughters"; بَنَىٰ 11x "construct"; بُنْيَٰن 7x "his building"; بِنَاء 2x "a canopy"; ٱبْنَت 2x "(of) my daughters"; بَنَّاء 1x "builder"; مَّبْنِيَّة 1x "built high"
text:
Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, root ب-ن-ي (b-n-y)

Core sense: Ibn Fāris treats b-n-y as one root meaning to build or construct — to join one part of a thing to another. Example: بَنَيْتُ الْبِنَاءَ أَبْنِيهِ (banaytu al-bināʾa abnīhi, "I built the building, I build it"). By this sense Mecca is called الْبَنِيَّة (al-Baniyya, "the Built One").

1. Applied to a bow: قَوْسٌ بَانِيَةٌ (a "building" bow) is one that has "built upon" its string — a bow whose string nearly breaks because it clings so tightly to the bow. The tribe of Ṭayyiʾ use the variant بَانَاة (bānāt) instead of بَانِيَة, as in the line of Imruʾ al-Qays: "…not built close upon its string."

2. Word-forms (grammatical note): the derived nouns come in paired patterns — بُنْيَة / بُنًى (bunya / bunan) and, with kasra on the first letter, بِنْيَة / بِنًى (binya / binan). Ibn Fāris compares this to the parallel pairs جِزْيَة / جِزًى (jizya / jizan) and مِشْيَة / مِشًى (mishya / mishan).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: unnamed verse ×2; Bishr (pre-Islamic); al-Ḥuṣayn ibn Ḥumām (pre-Islamic)
text:
Root ب ق ع (b-q-ʿ), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning, to which all branches trace back (even if some seem distant): the mixing/variegation of colors, one against another.

1. ghurāb abqaʿ / kalb abqaʿ — a piebald crow or dog (black with white patches). Illustrated with an anecdote: someone described al-Ḥajjāj's opponents' cavalry as "buqʿ" (patched) because dire circumstances had forced them to patch their clothes. A hadith warns that "the buqʿān of the people of Syria" will soon be put in authority — glossed by Abū ʿUbayd as the Romans and Slavs, referring to their pale complexion.

2. al-buqʿah (per al-Khalīl) — a piece of land visually distinct from what's beside it (plural biqāʿ/buqaʿ; also al-baqʿah per Abū Zayd). al-abqaʿ, of a horse — one with scattered patches differing from its base color (per Abū ʿUbaydah). al-baqʿāʾ, of land — struck by rain unevenly, some parts wet and some dry (per Abū Ḥanīfah); a related but distinct reading takes arḍ baqiʿah as land patched with plant growth, or (a less-favored reading) barren land. Ibn al-Aʿrābī gives yet another sense: al-baqʿāʾ as stony, pebble-strewn hard ground.

3. al-baqīʿ (per al-Khalīl) — land containing the root-stumps of various trees; this is the origin of the name Baqīʿ al-Gharqad, the well-known burial ground in Medina. Abū Zayd broadens it further: any low-lying tract of land, illustrated with a line of poetry. A proverb, "a donkey's fatness saved it in al-Baqīʿ," plays on the irony of being spared because of the very trait that should have marked it for use.

4. al-bāqiʿah — calamity; "baqaʿathum bāqiʿatun" — a calamity struck them, explained as something that "clings until its trace is gone." sanah baqʿāʾ — a barren year (per Ibn al-Aʿrābī).

5. Onomastic note: Banū al-Baqʿāʾ, a clan descended from Hāribah ibn Dhubyān, named after their mother al-Baqʿāʾ bint Salāmān — illustrated with lines of poetry by Bishr and by al-Ḥuṣayn ibn Ḥumām on the clan's smallness and its standing. Separately, Baqʿāʾ is also recorded as the name of a village of al-Yamāmah, illustrated with a further couplet of verse.

6. Idiomatic extensions of the same sense: buqiʿa fulānun bi-kalāmi sawʾin — so-and-so was "pelted" with bad speech (per Ibn al-Sikkīt, traced to the same root sense). ibtuqiʿa lawnuhu / imtuqiʿa lawnuhu — his color changed, from grief or fright (per al-Kisāʾī) — possibly the same word, possibly a letter-substitution variant. lā adrī ayna saqaʿa wa baqaʿa — "I don't know where he went" (per Ibn al-Aʿrābī). baqaʿa fī al-arḍi buqūʿan — to vanish, one's trace disappearing.

7. Further idioms: al-buqʿah, of a man — one who talks excessively and aimlessly, "casting about" speech with no clear beginning or end (per some Bedouin informants). baqaʿa al-rajula — to swear an oath to someone. ʿāmun abqaʿu wa arbadu — a year with no rain in it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: Abū al-Najm (Umayyad); Abū al-Ṭamaḥān (lived into Islam)
text:
Root: ب ق ل (b-q-l) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris states this root has a single core meaning: plant growth. Every derived usage traces back to it.

1. Definition of al-baql (the noun): al-Khalīl defines baql as plant growth that counts as neither a small shrub nor a large, coarse shrub. The dividing line is stem thickness — shrubs have stalks tough enough that rain and wind don't break them, so they stand through the season; baql, by contrast, is the soft, non-woody growth.

2. Grazing on it: ibtaqala (of people) and tabtaqilu/tatabaqqalu (of camels) mean "to graze on/eat baql." A verse of Abū al-Najm is cited using tabaqqalat for grazing at the very start of the green season.

3. Land producing it: abqalat and baqalat, said of land, mean "it grew baql," making the land mubqila. Mabqala and baqqāla both mean land rich in baql. Al-Farrāʾ gives arḍun baqilatun for the same sense (land abounding in greens) — the parallel term here is partly illegible in the source. A line of poetry by Abū al-Ṭamaḥān uses bāqil descriptively of a lush place.

4. Animals eating it: al-Shaybānī records baqala l-ḥimār, "the donkey grazed on baql."

5. A related but distinct verb form: some say abqala l-makān for a place becoming covered in ramth (a desert shrub), giving the participle bāqil — but the lexicographer notes he knows of no unprefixed form "baqala l-makān" in this sense. This pattern (hamza-prefixed verb → participle without the prefix, e.g. aʿshaba → ʿāshib, awrasa → wārīs) is a recognized derivational quirk, not an exception to the baql root.

6. Extended sense — "first growth" of anything: Abū Ziyād generalizes baql to mean whatever sprouts first, of any kind. This licenses two extended, non-botanical uses: (a) a young man's first facial down is said to "baqala," and (b) a camel's canine tooth "baqala" when it first emerges.

7. A usage restriction: al-Shaybānī notes that khalā (green herbage) is only called baql while it is still moist/fresh — dried-out growth doesn't qualify.

8. Bāqil as first budding on trees: al-Khalīl describes al-bāqil specifically as the earliest spring buds on trees — tiny growths on the bark, before leaves are distinguishable, resembling locusts' eyes. The tree at that stage "has abqala," and the whole tree is then said to have "become a single baqla."

9. A staged growth sequence for ramth: Abū Zayd traces ramth's growth through named stages — bāqil (first sprouting after rain, when the shoots look like ants' heads — its best state), then ḥāniṭ, then wārīs (fully green); past that point it spoils and camels stop grazing it.

10. The proper name Bāqil: separately, "Bāqil" was a man so proverbially inarticulate that his name became a byword for speechlessness (al-ʿiyy) — Ibn Fāris flags this as unrelated to the botanical sense above.

quran_words: بَقَرَة 4x "(is) a cow"; بَقَر 3x "the cows"; بَقَرَٰت 2x "cows"
poets_named: unnamed verse ×4; Ibn Abī Ṭarafa (undated); Ṭufayl (pre-Islamic); al-Khuḍrī (undated); Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); al-Nābigha (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Fāris analyses b-q-r as **two distinct roots**, noting that some lexicographers merged them into one — a merger he rejects.

**Root 1 — cattle (al-baqar)**
1. **البقر (al-baqar)** is the collective noun of **البقرة (al-baqara)**, a single head of cattle. Other collective forms: **البقير (al-baqīr)**, **الباقر (al-bāqir)**, **الباقورة (al-bāqūra)**, and **أبقور (ubqūr)** — the last on the pattern of *umʿūz* (a herd of mountain goats). *Bāqir* functions for cattle the way *jāmil* does for camels (a herd word).
2. **Grammatical method.** These are treated as collectives without true singulars — *baqīr* is classed with *ḍaʾīn* (sheep) and *shawiyy*. Al-Aṣmaʿī notes **بواقر (bawāqir)** likewise has no recorded singular, though it could be the plural of *bāqira*.
3. **Gender.** Abū ʿUbayda: the male animal is also called *baqara*, just as a cock can be called *dajāja* ("hen") — the tāʾ marks the unit, not the sex.
4. **Shawāhid.** For *baqīr*: "they strike the tails of the cattle that shelter in their coverts." For *bāqir*: "And what is his fault, that a herd refused the water…". Ibn Abī Ṭarafa, for *bawāqir*: "So I quieted them with speech until they were as though they were hornless herds settled by the pastures."
5. **Derived verb.** **بَقِرَ (baqira)** is said of a man who suddenly sees a great mass of cattle and loses his wits.
6. **Extended usage.** *Baqara* is applied to a man's dependants: "So-and-so came driving a *baqara*" = a large household. Yūnus reports *al-baqara* used of a woman.

**Root 2 — opening, splitting, widening out**
7. The core sense is **بَقَرْتُ البطن (baqartu l-baṭn)**, "I slit the belly open." From it **التبقّر (al-tabaqqur)** = expanding and opening out.
8. **Applied to wealth:** al-Aṣmaʿī — *tabaqqara fulān fī mālihi*, he opened his wealth up wastefully, i.e. ruined it. Ibn Fāris refers here the report that the Prophet forbade *al-tabaqqur* in family and property.
9. **Applied to animals:** **ناقة بقير (nāqa baqīr)**, a she-camel whose belly is cut open to extract her young; **المهر البقير (al-muhr al-baqīr)**, a foal taken out this way when its mother dies before delivery. Abū Ḥātim adds a narrower use: a foal that emerges still enclosed in the foetal membrane (*salā*) and *māsika* is *baqīr*, the opposite term being *salīl*.
10. **Applied to strife:** **فتنة باقرة (fitna bāqira)** — a rending strife, likened to a disease of the belly.
11. **Applied to ground:** **بقّروا ما حولهم** — they dug up the ground around them; "how much have you dug for your palm-shoots?" From the same image, **البقّيرى (al-buqqayrā)** is a children's game in which small circles are beaten into the ground resembling hoof-prints. Ṭufayl: their playing-ground is "like the traces of the one who marks out circles"; al-Khuḍrī compares a hanging object to "the child's circle-marker (*baqqār*)."
12. **Etymology rejected.** Those who merge the two roots say cattle are called *baqar* because they cleave open the earth (ploughing). Ibn Fāris dismisses this: "that is nothing."

**Anomalous forms (shādhdh), outside both roots**
13. **بيقر (bayqara)**, reported with several unrelated senses: (a) to migrate from one land to another — cited with Imruʾ al-Qays, "that Imruʾ al-Qays son of Tamlik has *bayqara*"; (b) to expose oneself to destruction; (c) to come to the land of Iraq; (d) to run with the head hanging down from weakness — "as one who walks to al-Jalsad goes head-down." Ibn al-Aʿrābī glosses it: he drove himself on.
14. **Place-names** attached loosely to the above: **al-Baqqār**, a location — al-Nābigha: "as though, beneath the mail, they were the jinn of al-Baqqār"; and **Baqar**, the name of a sand-hill, cited in a verse about "the two sand-mounds of Baqar."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَبْقَىٰ 7x "and more lasting"; بَقِيَّت 3x "those possessing a remnant"; بَقِىَ 3x "he spared"; بَٰقِيَٰت 2x "but the enduring"; بَاقِين 2x "the remaining ones"; بَاقِيَة 2x "remains"; بَاق 1x "(will) be remaining"; تُبْقِى 1x "it lets remain"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-q-y as a single root meaning permanence / enduring (al-dawām).

1. Core sense — to endure, remain, last. On al-Khalīl's authority: بَقِيَ يَبْقَى بَقَاءً ("to remain, it remains, remaining"), the opposite of الفناء (perishing, passing away).

2. Dialect note (Ṭayyiʾ). The tribe of Ṭayyiʾ say بَقَى يَبْقَى with a final alif instead of yāʾ. This is a general habit: wherever a yāʾ follows a kasra-marked letter, they dislike the kasra-plus-yāʾ combination, so they put a fatḥa before the yāʾ and it shifts to an alif — hence جَارَاة for جَارِيَة (girl), بَانَاة for بَانِيَة (builder, f.), نَاصَاة for نَاصِيَة (forelock).

3. baqiyya / buqyā = sparing, clemency, mercy shown to someone. Illustrated by a verse (Khālid did not hold back from me "out of any baqiyya"), glossed as al-buqyā, mercy toward him. Related expressions: نَشَدْتُكَ اللَّهَ وَالْبُقْيَا ("I adjure you by God and by [your] clemency"), with the variant البَقْوَى.

4. istabqā = to keep/retain someone. Per al-Khalīl: to pardon a person's slip so as to preserve his affection. Shāhid from al-Nābigha: you will not "keep" a brother you never reproach for a fault, since no man is entirely faultless.

5. yabqī bi-baṣarih = to watch, keep one's eye on, lie in wait for. هو يبقي الشيء ببصره means to look fixedly at something and keep watch over it. Examples: al-Kumayt's line of a wild ass waiting atop a hillock for sunset to water its herd; باتَ يبقي البرقَ ("he spent the night watching the lightning") for where it flashes, with a supporting verse by al-Fazārī.

6. baqā / abqī = to watch for, tend, await. Per Ibn al-Sikkīt: بَقَيْتُ فلاناً = to heed and wait for someone; ابْقِ لي الأذانَ ("watch out for the call for me"), i.e. keep watch of it. A shāhid pictures watching departing travellers until they resemble threads a weaver draws in.

7. Link back to the core. The ḥadīth of Muʿādh «بَقَيْنَا رسولَ الله» ("we waited for the Messenger of God") uses this "waiting" sense. Ibn Fāris ties it back to the root's primary meaning: waiting is itself a form of steadfastness and continuance (thabāt wa-dawām).
