quran_words: بَرِىء 12x "free"; تَبَرَّأَ 5x "will disown"; بَارِئ 3x "your creator"; تُبْرِئُ 2x "and you heal"; بَرَاءَة 2x "freedom from obligations"; بَرَّأَ 2x "i absolve"; بَرِيَّة 2x "(of) the creatures"; مُبَرَّءُون 1x "(are) innocent"; بَرَاء 1x "disassociated"; نَّبْرَأَ 1x "we bring it into existence"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root b-r-ʾ from two base meanings.

1. Creating (الخلق). "بَرَأَ اللَّهُ الْخَلْقَ" — God created the creation. الْبَارِئُ (the Creator/Fashioner) is God, as in {فَتُوبُوا إِلَى بَارِئِكُمْ} "turn in repentance to your Creator" (al-Baqara 54). The poet Umayya pairs the term with al-Khāliq and al-Muṣawwir ("Creator, Fashioner, Shaper").

2. Withdrawing from a thing and parting from it (التباعد والمزايلة). All the following branch from this idea of separation:

• Recovery from illness — الْبُرْء = soundness from sickness. Both بَرِئْتُ and بَرَأْتُ are used. Ibn Fāris cites al-Liḥyānī on dialect: the Ḥijāz say "بَرَأْتُ من المرض أبْرُؤُ بُرُوءًا," while al-ʿĀliya say "بَرَأْتُ أبْرَأُ بَرْءًا."

• Declaring oneself quit / disowning — "بَرِئْتُ إليك من حقّك" (I release myself to you of your claim). Two dialect forms of the adjective: Ḥijāzī بَرَاء ("أنا بَرَاءٌ منك") and the more general بَرِيء ("أنا بَريءٌ منك"). Both occur in the Qurʾān: the Ḥijāzī form in {إِنَّنِي بَرَاءٌ مِمَّا تَعْبُدُونَ} "I am quit of what you worship" (al-Zukhruf 26), and بَريء in {إِنِّي بَرِيءٌ} (al-Anʿām 78). Grammatical note: بَرَاء is invariable — no dual or feminine ("نحن البَرَاءُ والخَلَاءُ من هذا"). بَرِيء inflects normally: dual بَريئان, plural بَريئون, and broken plurals بُرَآء, بُرَاء, بِرَاء.

• Being free of a fault — الْبَرَاءَة from a defect or from anything disliked; only the verb بَرِئَ / يَبْرَأُ is used here.

• Mutual release / settlement — بَارَأْتُ الرجل = each party releases the other. Used of a woman settling a separation with her husband (بارَأَت... على المفارقة), of settling with a business partner, and of discharging someone from a debt or a surety-guarantee (أبرأتُ من الدين والضمان).

• الْبَرَاء = the last night of the month, so called because the moon "parts" from the month. Cited verse: "يومًا إذا كان البَراءُ نحسا." Ibn al-Aʿrābī, by contrast, glosses "the barāʾ day" as the auspicious one — free (barīʾ) of what is disliked.

• الاسْتِبْرَاء (from al-Khalīl) — a buyer of a slave-girl refrains from her until she menstruates; it fits the root because she is thereby "cleared" of the doubt that would bar him.

• بُرْأَة الصَّائِد — the hunter's blind/hide (his nāmūs / qutra), plural بُرَأ; it fits the root because people withdraw away into it. Cited verse: "بها بُرَأٌ مثل الفَسيلِ المكمَّمِ."

text:
Root: ب ر ح (b-r-ḥ) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris derives all uses of this root from two underlying ideas.

**Sense group 1 — departure, emergence, coming into the open**

- بَرَحَ يَبْرَحُ بَرَاحًا (baraḥa) — to move away from one's place, to depart. A slow riding-animal is cursed by its rider: "may you never move to good effect."
- مَا بَرِحْتُ أَفْعَلُ ذَلِكَ ("I have not ceased doing that") = "I still do it" — baraḥa here functions like mā zāla, "not to cease." This is the sense in the Qur'anic citation {لَنْ نَبْرَحَ عَلَيْهِ عَاكِفِينَ} (Q 20:91, "we will never stop being devoted to it"), quoted here simply as speech Allah reports from certain people, glossed as "we will never cease."
- بَرِحَ الْخَفَاءُ ("the hidden thing became bariḥ") = it came out into the open, was disclosed.
- Al-Farrāʾ: baraḥa can also mean "it passed/went by" — the source of الْبَارِحَة (al-bāriḥa), "last night" (literally "the departed [night]"), a descriptive phrase that hardened into a fixed name.
- الْبِرَاح (al-birāḥ) = open confrontation/disclosure (Abū ʿUbayd).
- Ibn Fāris himself suggests الْبَارِح (al-bāriḥ) — an animal or bird crossing on the inauspicious side (opposite of al-sāniḥ, the auspicious side) — belongs here too, since it is something that "emerges and becomes visible." Al-Khalīl gives البُرُوح as the verbal noun for this. A cited proverb, "he is like the bāriḥ of the mountain-goat — rarely seen," describes something almost never witnessed, since mountain-goats live high in the peaks; some say the proverb carries a double ill-omen, since the goat is already inauspicious and its departing only deepens it.

**Sense group 2 — intensity, severity, greatness**

- مَا أَبْرَحَ هَذَا الْأَمْرَ ("how abraḥa this matter is") = it astonished/impressed him greatly; glossed by some as "made [it/him] great." (Cited from al-Aʿshā's poetry praising a lord and a neighbor as "great.")
- أَبْرَحْتُ بِفُلَانٍ (Ibn al-Aʿrābī) = I loaded someone with more than he could bear, so that he grew weighed-down and distressed by it.
- الْبَرِيح (al-barīḥ) = fatigue, exhaustion (cited in a line pairing it with sweat and clamor on an exhausted mount).
- أَبْرَحْتَ لُؤْمًا / أَبْرَحْتَ كَرَمًا = "you went to an extreme of baseness / of generosity." بَرْحَى لَهُ = an exclamation of astonishment at someone. بُرْحَة من البُرَح = a choice, select camel.
- بَرَّحَ فُلَانٌ تَبْرِيحًا — to harm someone through relentless persistence; the noun is البَرْح. Dhū al-Rumma: "passion is a harsh affliction (barḥ) on whoever pursues it."
- التَّبَارِيح = toil and hardship. ضَرْبٌ مُبَرِّحٌ = a severe blow. أَبْرَحُ عَلَيَّ مِنْ ذَاكَ ("more abraḥ upon me than that") = "more arduous" — used by Dhū al-Rumma to say the night's hardship exceeds the day's.
- Set intensifying idioms: لَقِيتُ مِنْهُ الْبُرَحِينَ / الْبَرَحَيْنِ / بَنَاتِ بَرْحٍ / بَرْحًا بَارِحًا, all meaning "I suffered severe hardship because of him."
- البَوَارِح — violent, dust-carrying winds — belong here too, named for the intensity of their blowing (cited in a Dhū al-Rumma verse).
- Finally, بَرْحَى, the cry when an archer misses his shot, is traced by Ibn Durayd (and others) to this same root, as if saying "a hard/severe turn of luck" (خُطَّةٌ بَرْحَى).

Ibn Fāris thus treats brḥ as bifurcating early into "moving off / coming into view" on one branch, and "severity / excess, whether painful or admirable" on the other — with the Qur'anic verb (lan nabraḥa, "we will not cease") drawn from the first branch's "not stopping" usage, cited here purely as an attested instance of ordinary Arabic speech, not glossed with any doctrinal content.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root برص (b-r-ṣ) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core sense: a patch on something that differs in color from the rest of it.

1. al-baraṣ — the skin condition (vitiligo/leprosy-like patches) that gives the root its name.

2. Extended to the moon: the Arabs sometimes called it abraṣ, for its patchy, uneven appearance.

3. al-barīṣ — a gleam or glint (like al-baṣīṣ), following the same pattern of a bright patch standing out — illustrated with a verse about a gleam on someone's cheek.

4. al-birāṣ — barren, flat sandy tracts that grow nothing (a patch of infertility in the land, by the same logic).

5. sāmm abraṣ — the well-known large gecko, named for its patchy/spotted coloring. Al-Qutaybī gives its plural as al-abāriṣ, illustrated with a self-deprecating verse about eating geckos. Thaʿlab records three attested case/number forms of the name in his grammatical work Kitāb al-Faṣīḥ.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-r-d as having four independent bases, with all derived forms tracing back to one of them: (1) the opposite of heat; (2) stillness and fixity; (3) a worn garment; (4) agitation and back-and-forth movement.

BASE 1 — coldness, the opposite of heat
- barada / bārid: to be cold, cold. "The water cooled the heat of my insides."
- Extended to relief from burning: a verse promises a she-camel that "will cool livers and set mourners weeping."
- baradtu ʿaynahu bi-l-barūd: to treat the eye with a cooling application.
- al-baradah: indigestion.
- saḥāb barid: a cloud carrying hail (barad).
- al-abradān (also al-bardān): the two cool ends of the day, evidenced by a verse on gazelles pillowed on the arṭā bush's "two cool sides."
- al-bawārid: swords. Two explanations are recorded — that they are the slayers, or simply that the touch of iron is cold. A verse on "thin-edged cold blades" is cited.
- jāʾū mubridīn: they came once the heat had died down.

BASE 2 — stillness, persistence, fixity
- al-bard as sleep, with Q 78:24 "they taste therein no bard nor drink" as the proof-text, plus a verse pairing bard with nuqākh (sweet fresh water).
- barada al-shayʾ: the thing lasted. Abū ʿUbaydah's line "today is a day whose hot wind is bārid" is glossed with bārid = dāʾim, unceasing.
- barada lī ʿalā fulān min al-māl kadhā: an amount became fixed/established as owed by someone.
- barada fī yadī kadhā: something came securely into one's possession.
- barada al-rajul: the man died. Ibn Fāris leaves the assignment open — it may belong to this base (fixity) or to the first (coldness).

BASE 3 — the garment
- al-burd, the mantle, described as well known; a verse mentions a cloak "from Salāmān, or a burd."
- burdā al-jarādah: the locust's two wings, by extension of the same image.

BASE 4 — movement to and fro
- al-barīd, the army courier, so named because he goes and comes back; a verse speaks of "a month's journey for the courier driven to and fro."
- Ibn Fāris suggests, as a possibility rather than a certainty, that al-mibrad (the file) belongs here, since the hand works it back and forth.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
Root ب-ر-ه-ن (b-r-h-n), as recorded by Ibn Manẓūr in Lisān al-ʿArab.

1. Core sense — decisive proof. Citing al-Azharī's Tahdhīb, Ibn Manẓūr glosses بُرْهان (burhān) as "the decisive, clarifying proof" — a demonstration that both settles a dispute and makes the matter plain. The Qur'anic shāhid is قُل هاتوا بُرْهانَكم إن كنتم صادقين, "Say: produce your burhān, if you are truthful."

2. Verbal use and morphology. The verb is بَرْهَنَ / يُبَرْهِنُ / بَرْهَنةً (barhana / yubarhinu / barhana­tan), used of someone who brings a conclusive proof to counter an opponent's obstinate wrangling (ladad); the agent noun is مُبَرْهِن (mubarhin), "one who adduces proof." With the preposition ʿalā — بَرْهَنَ عليه — it means "he established the proof for it." The plural of burhān is بَراهين (barāhīn).

3. A second shading: "to make clear." Al-Zajjāj is quoted for the retort said to a man who fails to substantiate his claim: "you are merely making a wish." On that basis he treated يُبَرْهن (yubarhin) as equivalent to يُبَيِّن (yubayyin), "to make manifest" — proof understood as clarification rather than only as adversarial argument.

4. Extended use in a ḥadīth. The entry cites الصَّدَقةُ بُرْهانٌ, "ṣadaqa (giving from one's wealth) is a burhān," and again glosses burhān as "proof and evidence." Two explanations are given, both as Ibn Manẓūr's reported material rather than as his own ruling: (a) it is a proof in favour of the one seeking reward, since it is an obligation (farḍ) that God requites and holds one to account for; and (b) it is evidence of the soundness of the giver's īmān, because he parts with his wealth willingly — significant given the attachment that exists between a person's soul and his property.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: بُرُوج 4x "constellations"; مُتَبَرِّجَٰت 1x "displaying"; تَبَرَّجْ 1x "display yourselves"; تَبَرُّج 1x "(as was the) display"
text:
Root b-r-j, as treated by al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī in his glossary of difficult Qurʾānic words:

1. Core sense — burūj (sing. burj): palaces, lofty towers. From this the "towers" of the sky are named, because of the stations assigned particularly to them. Qurʾānic evidence: "By the sky possessed of towers" (85:1) and "Blessed is He who placed towers in the sky" (25:61).

2. An ambiguous case — "even if you were in towers built high" (4:78). Al-Rāghib allows two readings, without deciding between them:
   - earthly towers (the literal sense); or
   - the towers of the stars — in which case calling them "built high" (mushayyada) is a metaphor.
   Each reading is anchored to a line of poetry. For the celestial reading, Zuhayr: whoever dreads the causes of death is overtaken by them even if he reaches the means of heaven by a ladder. For the earthly reading, another poet: even inside Ghumdān [the famed Yemeni stronghold], its gate guarded by Abyssinian footmen and tame lions, death would still find me, a guide leading it and a tracker on my trail.

3. Derived sense — display. A mubarraj garment is one with tower-figures depicted on it; the beauty of such a garment is what the verb picks up. Hence tabarrajat al-marʾa: the woman made herself like such a garment by putting her beauties on show. A second explanation is also reported: that she came out of her burj, i.e. her palace. Qurʾānic evidence for this sense: "remain in your houses, and do not display yourselves as the displaying of the former Jāhiliyya" (33:33), and "not displaying adornment" (24:60).

4. Related form — al-baraj: wideness of the eye together with its beauty, so named by comparison with a burj in both respects.

Method note: al-Rāghib works from the concrete sense (tower/palace) outward, deriving both the astronomical and the "display" senses from it, and uses pre-Islamic poetry as the test for which reading a Qurʾānic occurrence can bear.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: تَبَارَكَ 9x "blessed is he"; مُبَارَك 8x "blessed"; بَٰرَكَ 8x "we blessed"; مُّبَٰرَكَة 4x "blessed"; بَرَكَٰت 3x "and his blessings"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives all senses of ب-ر-ك from one core idea: the firmness or settling-down of a thing, which then branches into closely related meanings.

1. A camel kneeling / lying down: baraka al-baʿīr (the camel knelt). Al-Khalīl: al-bark are camels that have knelt at water or in the open desert, from the sun's heat or from being full; singular bārik, feminine bārika (with a cited verse describing kneeling camels under fierce windless heat, al-abt). Abū al-Khaṭṭāb restricts al-bark to a large herd that drinks then kneels in the watering-yard. Causative: abraktu al-nāqa fa-barakat (I made the she-camel kneel and she knelt).

2. The camel's breast: al-bark is also the breast-bone/chest with which the camel crushes what is under it (illustrated by a battle verse in which a she-camel presses its breast on the slain). Related: al-birka = the belly-and-chest skin nearest the ground in any beast, derived from mabrak, the kneeling-place (plural mabārik). Yaʿqūb defines the horse's birka anatomically (chest muscles down to the forearm veins). Abū Ḥātim: bark (fatḥa) = the chest, and adding the -a gives birka (kasra); some equate al-bark with al-qaṣṣ (sternum). Al-Aṣmaʿī notes Kūfans nicknamed Ziyād "hairiest of chest."

3. Idioms from kneeling = accepting / settling: "a matter my camels will not kneel upon" = I will not approach or accept it; "a matter the muzzled reddish camels will not kneel upon" = a matter grown grave — since camels bolt from what they dislike. Abū ʿAlī: camels are singled out because they only kneel on soft ground they have tested with their feet.

4. Onomastic / calendrical uses: al-burūk is a star-setting (nawʾ) of al-Jawzāʾ, so called because its cold and rain make camels kneel. Al-Burak was a man (ʿAwf ibn Mālik), named on the Day of Qiḍḍa for hamstringing his camel and standing his ground: "I am al-Burak; I kneel wherever I am overtaken."

5. Steadfastness in combat: ibtaraka fī ākhar = to revile another; ubturikū fī al-ḥarb = they knelt and fought on their knees; the noun barākāʾ = holding firm in battle (Bishr: nothing saves from battle's straits but standing firm, or flight); the command barāki barāki = "kneel!" More broadly, baraka/bāraka ʿalā al-amr = to persevere steadily at something, and ibtaraka al-faras = a horse straining hard in its run.

6. Rain: abraka (or, held more correct, ibtaraka) al-saḥāb = the cloud settled in and kept raining over a place.

7. Milking sense of al-birka: the milk that collects in a she-camel's udder overnight at her kneeling-place and is milked at dawn (only used of mornings) — "milk for us from the birak of your camels." Al-Kisāʾī: milk flowing while she kneels, so she is raised and milked. (Illustrated with lines of al-Kumayt.)

8. Pool / cistern: al-birka is a basin dug into the ground with no raised banks; the Kilābī usage equates it with a maṣnaʿa (reservoir), plural birak, the difference being that the birka is lined with baked brick while the maṣnaʿa is not.

9. Blessing (baraka): al-Khalīl derives baraka from increase and growth; tabrīk = to invoke baraka. On {تَبَارَكَ اللَّهُ} (al-Aʿrāf 7:54), Ibn Fāris reports it as glorification and magnification, also interpreted as "God is exalted" — adding "God knows best what He intended." Abū Zayd: ṭaʿām barīk = food possessed of baraka.

text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) derives four distinct base senses from the root ب-ر-م (b-r-m):

**1. Making something firm/tightly twisted.** Al-Khalīl: "abramtu al-amr" = I made the matter firm, settled it. Abū Ziyād: al-mabārim are the thick spindles a woman uses to twist her spun yarn (made of samur-acacia wood). "abramtu al-ḥabl" = I twisted the rope tight. Al-mubram (twisted yarn) is the opposite of al-saḥīl: mubram is twined from two strands, saḥīl spun from one.

**2. Weariness / being fed up.** "barimtu bil-amr" = I grew weary of it, worn out by it; "abramanī" = he exhausted/wore me out. Example saying: "I hope I won't tire of asking about such-and-such." Al-Khalīl adds "barimtu bikadhā" = I was irritated by it (verbal noun: baram). Several verses illustrate the sense — one poet excuses himself for being "worn out with my own scheme"; another (cited anonymously) speaks of being wearied of a soul as if infected with the love-sickness of the famous ʿUdhrī lover-poet ʿUrwa; Ibn al-Ṭathriyya describes being left speechless and worn down by a woman's words ("baramtu, and I found no answer for them").

**3. The blending of two colors/kinds.** Al-barīmayn = the two components of anything made of a mixture — like night's black shot through with day's white, or tears mixed with kohl (cited from ʿAlqama's verse on a gazelle-eyed woman's streaked tears). By the same logic, dawn's first light is called barīm, since its whiteness is still mixed with the night's darkness (per Abū Zayd, with a supporting verse). Al-Khalīl notes the Arabs call a motley group of people "barīmu qawmin" (their mixture of every kind), illustrated by a verse of Laylā about a mixed troop led from the Ḥijāz. The word also names: two contrasted parts of a roasted animal (liver and hump, per Abū ʿUbayd); a herd of gazelles; and a beaded, particolored waist-belt worn by women (illustrated by a verse of al-Farazdaq about a nursing woman's belt swaying).

**4. A plant name (al-baram).** The best-smelling variety grows on the salam-tree; the worst-smelling on the ʿurfuṭ (white like myrtle-blossom). Al-Shaybānī: "abrama al-ṭalḥ" describes the ṭalḥ-acacia's first fruiting. Abū Ziyād: al-baramah is the blossom preceding the ḥublah (fruit-cluster). Abū al-Khaṭṭāb extends the word to grape-pips once past the unripe stage, likened to tiny ants' heads.

**Outlier (not fitting the four bases):** al-burām, a large tick — used in the saying "he clings tighter than a tick" (wording of the saying is unclear in the source text). Also unrelated: al-burmah, the cooking pot.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-r-q as TWO independent roots, with everything else figurative and traceable back to them:
- Root A: a thing's flashing or gleaming.
- Root B: black and white combined in a thing.

ROOT A — FLASHING

1. Lightning. الْبَرْق (al-barq) is the flash of a cloud (al-Khalīl). Verb بَرَقَ, verbal nouns بَرْق and بَرِيق; أَبْرَقَ (form IV) is also attested as a variant. بَرْقَة (fatḥa) = one single flash; بُرْقَة (ḍamma) = a quantity of lightning. Proverbial: "I will not do it so long as a star flashes in the sky" — i.e. so long as one rises. أَتَانَا عِنْدَ مَبْرَقِ الصُّبْحِ = he came at daybreak's first flash. Al-Liḥyānī: أَبْرَقَ الرَّجُلُ = the man headed toward lightning on sighting it.

2. Anything that glitters. بَارِقَة = a cloud carrying lightning; بَارِق = anything whose color glitters. Swords are بَوَارِق ("flashers"); أَبْرَقَ بِسَيْفِهِ = he made his sword flash (al-Aṣmaʿī); "I saw the bāriqa" = the glint of swords. Also "a bāriqa passed us tonight" = a lightning-bearing cloud. Proverb: "sweeter than the water of the lightning-cloud."

3. إِبْرِيق (ibrīq) is applied to a sword and to anything with a gleam — even to a beautiful, glittering woman: "the abodes of the evening's ibrīq, the swaying-walking woman." Another verse likens a fleeing animal slipping off a slope "like an ibrīq." The ewer/pitcher called ibrīq belongs to this same section.

4. Rain by association. Abū ʿAlī al-Aṣfahānī: أَبْرَقَتِ السَّمَاءُ عَلَى بِلَادِ كَذَا (the sky flashed over such lands); أَبْرَقْتُ = I was caught by the sky / I was rained on in a given place.

5. Empty threatening. Al-Khalīl: of a man who piles on threats it is said أَبْرَقَ وَأَرْعَدَ (he lightened and thundered) — as in al-Kumayt's line "Lighten and thunder, O Yazīd; your threat does me no harm." The form-I pair بَرَقَ وَرَعَدَ is also used ("thunder there as much as you please, and lighten"). A recorded disagreement: al-Aṣmaʿī accepted only form I (بَرَقَ وَرَعَدَ) and rejected form IV, even after a Bedouin of Banū Kilāb, questioned by Abū Zayd, confirmed تُبْرِقُ وَتُرْعِدُ for intimidation.

6. False signalling in animals and people. أَبْرَقَتِ النَّاقَةُ = the she-camel flicks her tail (al-Khalīl); per al-Liḥyānī, specifically raising her tail deceptively and feigning pregnancy when not pregnant — she is مُبْرِق / بَرُوق, the opposite being الْمِكْتَام. Ibn al-Aʿrābī uses form I بَرَقَتْ / بَارِق for the same tail-flicking without conception. Correspondingly of people: بَرَّقَ الرَّجُلُ = he produced something with nothing to back it; the saying "بَرَّقْتَ وَعَرَّقْتَ" = you made a show of something unreal, and stinted on it.

7. Fear and dazzled sight. الْإِنْسَانُ الْبَرُوق = the perpetually frightened person ("he terrifies every weak, easily-startled man"). بَرِقَ بَصَرُهُ (with kasra) = his sight was struck with bewilderment; the man is بَرِق, alarmed and stupefied. Ibn Fāris ties this to the two readings of Q 75:7: those reading بَرِقَ (kasra) explain it as this dazed alarm; those reading بَرَقَ (fatḥa) explain it as the eye gleaming from the intensity of its fixed stare, unable to endure — illustrated by the verse in which a man's eye "flashed" out of wonder at a she-camel he was given. Also بَرَّقَ بِعَيْنِهِ = he made his eye glitter with hard staring (verse: a woman clapping and flashing her eye at the commander to get a divorce). Ibn al-Aʿrābī: بَرِقَ الرَّجُلُ = his eyes sank into his head, his mind went.

8. Making something gleam. Al-Yazīdī: بَرَقَ وَجْهَهُ بِالدُّهْنِ = he made his face shine with oil; likewise بَرَقَ/بَرَّقَ الْأَدِيمَ of tanned leather. Abū Zayd: بَرَقَ طَعَامَهُ بِالزَّيْتِ (or ghee, or melted fat) = he put a small amount of it into the food.

9. Heat-spoiled milk. Al-Liḥyānī: بَرِقَ السِّقَاءُ (verbal nouns بَرَق, بُرُوق) = heat reached the skin and its butter melted. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: زُبْدَةٌ بَرِقَةٌ, سِقَاءٌ بَرِقٌ = butter and skin broken down by heat; also زُبْدٌ مُبْرِق.

10. الْبَرْوَق (al-barwaq), a feeble plant (Abū Zayd). Proverb "more responsive than a barwaqa," because it greens at mere overcast sky, while heavy rain is said to kill it. Cited in verse as an image of flimsiness (severed hands flying like barwaq stalks) and of famine food. Yaʿqūb: بَرِقَتِ الْإِبِلُ = the camels' bellies sickened from it.

ROOT B — BLACK-AND-WHITE MIXED

1. The eye is called بَرْقَاء for its black and white (al-Khalīl and others); a verse speaks of the tear "descending from the head of a barqāʾ."

2. الْبَرَق is the verbal noun behind الْأَبْرَق, used of ropes and mountains: a rope firmly twisted from one black and one white strand; a mountain with white and black streaks. الْبُرْقَة is also the whitened portion in the twist of a black rope.

3. Terrain. الْبَرْقَاء of land = streaked ground, black stones mixed with white sand; each separate patch is a بُرْقَة, and when broad it is الْأَبْرَق / الْبَرَّاق, plural الْأَبَارِق (verse: "…then the sand-tracts, then the buruq"). Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī: الْبُرَق is what pushes out into the torrent from the mountain side. Quṭrub: الْأَبْرَق is a smooth unclimbable mountain fronting you for a day and a night. Abū Ziyād al-Kilābī: stony heights with sandy bases where people settle, classed with mountains. Other Bedouin: prime vegetation ground, half stones and half whitish-red earth with scattered red stones; sand-plus-stones is also أَبْرَق; as a feminine of land, بَرْقَاء; it can also be a tall two-colored landmark of stones, or of clay and stones. Plurals: الْبُرَق, الْبِرَاق, الْبَرْقَاوَات.

4. Grammatical note: because أَبْرَق became a predominant descriptive term (functioning as a name), it takes a noun-type plural, الْأَبَارِق — parallel to الْأَبَاطِح, الْأَدَاهِم (plural of أَدْهَم, "fetter"), and الْأَسَاوِد (plural of أَسْوَد, "snake"). Verse of al-Rāʿī cites the place Dhū l-Abāriq.

5. Proper name. Quṭrub: Banū Bāriq are a Yemeni clan of the Ashʿarīs; Bāriq's name was Saʿd b. ʿAdī, who settled at a mountain called Bāriq and was named after it.

6. Variegated creatures. Al-Aṣmaʿī: الْبُرْقَان is the locust once yellowed and streaked with black; singular بُرْقَانَة (on the pattern of ظَبْيَةٌ أُدْمَانَة / ظِبَاءٌ أُدْمَان). Abū Ziyād: it has black and white like the dappling of a sheep, and it emerges white for seven days, blackens seven, then becomes burqān. الْبَرْقَاء in sheep corresponds to الْبَلْقَاء (piebald) in horses.

quran_words: بَرّ 22x "the land"; بِرّ 8x "[the] righteousness"; تَبَرُّ 2x "you deal kindly"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-r-r (with the doubled rāʾ) as having four separate root meanings: truthfulness, the imitation of a sound, dry land as opposed to sea, and a plant.

**1. Truthfulness (al-ṣidq)**

- **Being true in word and oath.** "He spoke truly and was true" (ṣadaqa wa-barra). An oath that "came true" (barrat yamīnuhu) proved truthful; to abarra an oath is to carry it through in truth.
- **An accepted ḥajj.** "May God make your ḥajj true" (barra Allāhu ḥajjaka, abarrahu), and a ḥajj that is mabrūr: one accepted with the acceptance given to a truthful deed.
- **Being true to one's Lord.** yabarru rabbahu means he obeys Him, which Ibn Fāris also derives from truthfulness. A verse: "O God, were it not that Bakr stand before You, people would be true to You and would transgress against You." He places here Q 2:177: "al-birr is not that you turn your faces toward the east and the west." In al-Nābigha's line about dishevelled riders "heading for their birr", some said birr means obedience, others that it means the ḥajj.
- **The surpassing horse.** A swift, excellent horse is called al-mubirr because it proves true when it runs and when it charges. Ibn al-Aʿrābī reports a Bedouin's description: the excellent horse is lean-jawed like the wild ass, tapered like a leather thong, stretching long when it runs and standing erect when halted; the slow, base-bred horse has flattened hip-bones, a thick nose-tip, a thick neck and much clamour, and "when you hold it back it says 'let me go', and when you let it go it says 'hold me back'."
- **Prevailing.** The verb abarra ʿalā (to prevail over) is linked to overpowering and dominance, and Ibn Fāris says it too goes back to truthfulness. Ṭarafa: "they lift harm from the one among them who suffers it, and prevail over the refuser who would prevail."
- **Dutiful kindness to kin and parents.** "He treats his kinsman with birr" is, at base, truthfulness in love. Adjectives: barr and bārr (dutiful, true). Barirtu wālidī (I was dutiful to my father); barirtu fī yamīnī (I kept my oath). Abarra al-rajul: he fathered dutiful (abrār) children.
- **Barra as a name.** Abū ʿUbayda says Barra is a proper name for al-birr, definite and diptote, as in al-Nābigha's line: "I bore Barra (righteousness), and you took on Fajāri (wickedness)."

**2. The imitation of a sound**

- The proverb "he does not know hirr from birr": hirr is the call to sheep and goats, and birr the sound made at them when they are driven. Another explanation: he cannot tell who dislikes him from who treats him kindly.
- **al-barbara:** a flood of talk and noise with the tongue; a chatterer is barbār or barbāra. Ibn Fāris says the name al-Barbar may perhaps derive from this.
- In a verse of Ṭarafa, al-barābir is said to be the plural of burbur, the young of sheep and goats, a name also traced to sound, since barbara is the bleating of goats.

**3. Land, as opposed to sea**

- abarra: to be on land; abḥara: to be at sea.
- al-barriyya: the open desert. al-barr: the open, as opposed to shelter.
- Used indefinitely: "I went out by land (barran) / by sea (baḥran)." Q 30:41: "corruption has appeared on land and sea."

**4. A plant**

- **al-burr:** wheat; a single grain is burra. Al-Aṣmaʿī: abarrat al-arḍ, "the land became rich in wheat." al-burbūr: coarsely ground wheat. Bread is nicknamed Ibn Burra and Ibn Ḥabba ("son of the grain"). Al-Shaybānī cites the saying "shorter than a wheat-grain", the grain being the utmost in shortness.
- **al-barīr:** according to al-Khalīl, the fruit of the arāk tree (al-Nābigha: "she crops its barīr and roams in it"). Abū Ziyād al-Kilābī says its berries are smaller than the mard and kabāth, like little beads. Al-Aṣmaʿī says barīr names the ripened fruit of the ʿiḍāh trees, which turns deep black when fully ripe. So Bishr likens a woman's jet-black braided hair to "the crows of the barīr".

quran_words: بَرَزَ 5x "and they will come forth"; بُرِّزَتِ 2x "and will be made manifest"; بَارِزَة 1x "(as) a leveled plain"; بَٰرِزُون 1x "come forth"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-r-z as having one single meaning, from which he says every use follows without exception: a thing's becoming visible, coming out into the open.

1. Basic sense — to emerge, come into view. بَرَزَ الشَّيْءُ = the thing came out; the active participle is بَارِزٌ (visible, out in the open).

2. Stepping out from one's own group. The reciprocal form تَبَارَزَ is used of two horsemen coming out to fight each other in single combat. Ibn Fāris explains this as the same core idea: each man detaches himself from his company and goes out alone toward his opponent.

3. الْبَرَاز — open, wide ground. Named so, he says, because such ground lies exposed to view; it is expressly contrasted with three kinds of terrain that are hidden or sunken: a depression (غائط), a hole or burrow (دَحْل), and a pit (هُوَّة).

4. Applied to persons. امْرَأَةٌ بَرْزَةٌ is a woman of standing who comes out and sits in the open forecourt of her house. He also reports the pair رَجُلٌ بَرْزٌ / امْرَأَةٌ بَرْزَةٌ used for people characterized by conspicuous, imposing bearing together with sound judgement. From al-Khalīl's book he cites رَجُلٌ بَرْزٌ meaning pure, chaste, abstinent — and argues this still fits the root's single analogy, since a man with something to hide keeps himself concealed rather than out in the open.

5. To outstrip. The doubled form بَرَّزَ is said of a man or a horse that gets ahead of the rest; Ibn Fāris counts this under the same root-idea (the winner comes out clear of the field).

6. Causative. أَبْرَزَ / إِبْرَاز = to bring something out, put it on display.

7. الْمُبَرْوَز — an attested quadriliteral-shaped form, cited from a line of Labīd contrasting "the speaking mubarwaz" with "the sealed." Ibn Fāris glosses الْمُبَرْوَز as "what is out in the open / on display," the sealed document being precisely what is not on display. He notes another group glosses it as الْمَنْشُور, the unrolled or published writing, and calls that a good reading.

quran_words: بَسَطَ 16x "extends"; بَٰسِط 4x "stretched"; بَصطَة 2x "abundantly"; مَبْسُوطَتَان 1x "(are) stretched out"; بَسْط 1x "reach"; بِسَاط 1x "an expanse"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-s-ṭ as a single root whose core sense is the extension or spreading-out of a thing, whether in width or otherwise. From this he derives:

1. **What is spread out** — al-bisāṭ is a thing spread out (a carpet/spread).

2. **A flat expanse / the earth** — al-basāṭ is the earth, also called al-basīṭa (the flat expanse). One speaks of a makān basīṭ or basāṭ (a level, open place). He cites a verse describing "a wide expanse [basāṭ] for the feet of swift she-camels" lying between the speaker and al-Ḥajjāj's reach.

3. **Open-handedness** — yadu fulānin bisṭ ("his hand is outspread") is said of a generous, open-handed person (munfāq).

4. **Amplitude / breadth** — al-basṭa in anything means amplitude or ample scope: a person can be basīṭ (ample) in body, in reach (bāʿ), and in knowledge. He anchors this in Qur'an 2:247, {and increased him in amplitude [basṭa] in knowledge and body}.

5. **A freely-ranging she-camel** — traced back to the same root: the she-camel left free with her young and not kept from it is called buṣṭ / bisṭ (vocalised with either ḍamma or kasra).

text:
Root ب-س-ل (b-s-l) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: prevention / restraint — holding something back or blocking it.

1. Basl (بَسْل) = "forbidden," "off-limits." Arabs use this word for whatever is forbidden, and more broadly for anything that is prevented or withheld. Zuhayr's verse illustrates the sense: "If you two keep away from them, then they are basl [inaccessible/forbidden]."

2. Basālah (بَسَالَة) = "courage, valor." Ibn Fāris derives this from the same root idea, since courage is a form of resistance — refusing to yield to one's rival, holding one's ground against an opponent.

3. Absala (أَبْسَلَ, Form IV) = "to give something up / surrender it to ruin." absaltu al-shayʾ = "I consigned the thing to destruction." By extension, absaltu waladī = "I pledged/mortgaged my son" (handed him over as a hostage or security). Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 6:70 — "those who are ubsilū [given up, consigned] for what they have earned" — and a line of poetry by ʿAwf ibn al-Aḥwaṣ describing how he pledged his own sons though they had done no wrong and no blood had been shed.

4. Busla (بُسْلَة) = the fee paid to a ruqyah-practitioner (someone who recites incantations, e.g. over the sick). Ibn Fāris says this sense connects to the root's core meaning only with some stretching of the reasoning, and gives his own judgment that it is better regarded as an outlier that does not fit the main pattern of the root.

5. Basal (بَسَل), per Ibn al-Aʿrābī = a person disagreeable or grim of face. Ibn Fāris accepts this as a sound and consistent extension of "prevention/restraint" (a face that repels or holds others off).

text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-s-m as a single root with one core meaning: parting/baring the front of the mouth out of pleasure or delight — that is, smiling. He is explicit that this act is a lesser degree than laughing (ḍaḥik); the root denotes the smile, not the laugh.

He gives three verb forms in use, all meaning "he smiled": بَسَمَ يَبْسِمُ (basama–yabsimu, Form I), تَبَسَّمَ (tabassama, Form V), and ابْتَسَمَ (ibtasama, Form VIII).

The entry is very short — a single core sense with no further shawāhid, morphological notes beyond the verb forms listed, or etymological discussion.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ب س ق (b-s-q) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: "rising, height, elevation."

1. Palm-trees: "basaqat al-nakhlah" — the palm grew tall and reached full height (al-Khalīl). Qur'an 50:10, "wa-l-nakhla bāsiqāt" ("tall palm-trees"), is glossed simply as ṭawīlāt, "tall ones." Singular bāsiqah, plural bawāsiq, verbal noun al-busūq (Yaʿqūb).

2. People: "basaqa al-rajul" — a man grew tall. Figuratively, "basaqa fī ʿilmihi" — he rose/excelled in his knowledge.

3. Clouds: "ghamāmah bāsiqah" — a high, white cloud; "bawāsiq al-saḥāb" — the topmost parts of clouds (Abū Zayd).

4. A separate, unrelated usage — milk appearing before birth: Ibn Fāris addresses an objection that the word "basaqa" is also used in a sense that has nothing to do with "height." His answer: that other usage is not really this root — it is a sound-substitution (sīn standing in for ṣād), the true root being ب ص ق (baṣaqa, "to spit"). By analogy from that, Arabs call a ewe that lets down milk a month or more before lambing "mubsiq," and she can be milked. He explains the image: it is as if she produces "busāq" (spittle), compared to human "buṣāq" (spit/saliva) — supported by the observation that even a still-virgin girl can develop milk in her breast, described the same way. Abū ʿUbaydah adds the term "al-mibsāq" for such an animal, and cites a verse about a "mubsiq" being milked halfway through pregnancy — though Ibn Fāris suspects Abū ʿUbaydah composed that verse himself.

So the entry keeps one true sense for this root — rising/height (palms, people, clouds) — and explicitly separates out the milk-related usage as an unrelated homograph borrowed by letter-substitution from a different root (bṣq, "to spit").

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root b-s-r, per Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha.

Ibn Fāris derives two basic underlying meanings for this root:

1. Freshness, or a thing being before its proper/due time (not yet ripe/settled).
2. Stillness — a thing standing still with little movement. (Stated as the second root-sense, but the entry gives no examples for it.)

All the illustrations in this entry fall under sense 1, "before its time":

- busr - anything fresh or green; also used of a plant when it is moist and tender.
- ma' busr (water that is busr) - rain-water that has only just fallen, i.e. still close in time to the cloud it came from.
- ibtasara al-fahlu al-naqata - said of a stud camel covering a she-camel before she is actually in heat, i.e. acting prematurely.
- busrah - a name for the sun at the very instant of its rising.
- basara al-hajata (he "basara" the need) - to pursue a need through the wrong channel, not by the proper route. Ibn Faris says the logic holds because it amounts to seeking the thing before its due time, the same "before its time" idea as the other usages.
- al-basr, defined as "zulm al-siqa'" (wronging the waterskin) - drinking the milk in the skin before it has thickened or fermented (raba), again a case of taking something before it is ready.

No Qur'anic citations or shawahid appear in this entry; it is purely a lexical and etymological note.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: بُسَّتِ 1x "and will be crumbled"; بَسّ 1x "(with awful) crumbling"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-s-s as resting on two root meanings (aṣlān): driving (al-sawq), and crumbling a thing and mixing it.

**1. Driving.** His first example is Q 56:5, wa-bussati l-jibālu bassā ("and the mountains were bussat"), glossed as "they were driven along" (sīqat sawqan). A ḥadīth uses the verb in the same way: "A people will come from al-Madīna yabussūna (driving along), and al-Madīna is better for them, if only they knew." So does a line of Abū l-Najm, "and the snakes of the loose sand-heap inbassa," where inbassa is explained as insāqa, "were driven along."

Calling a she-camel to be milked, bassa bi-l-nāqa or abassa bihā, also belongs to this first meaning. A proverb says, "I will not do that as long as a slave calls a she-camel for milking" (mā abassa ʿabdun bi-nāqa). A poet says: "May God revile whoever among us seeks peace, as long as the caller (al-mubiss) goes round the black she-camel."

**2. Crumbling and mixing.** Bussati l-ḥinṭa means the wheat (or something else) was crumbled (futtat). Q 56:5 has also been explained in this second sense. What is so crumbled is called al-basīsa. A poet says, "Don't bake, you two; just mix (bussā)," which is explained as: do not bake and so be slow about it, but mix the sawīq (parched-grain meal) with water and eat.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يُبَتِّكُ 1x "so they will surely cut off"
text:
**Root: ب ت ك (b-t-k)** — Ibn Fāris, *Maqāyīs al-Lugha*

**Core meaning:** cutting (al-qaṭʿ). *Bataktu al-shayʾ* = "I cut the thing"; verbal noun *batk*.

1. **Cutting the ear.** Al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad specifies *al-batk* as cutting the ear, citing Qur'an 4:119, {فَلَيُبَتِّكُنَّ آذَانَ الْأَنْعَامِ} — "they will surely slit the ears of the cattle."

2. **The cutting sword.** Al-Khalīl also gives *al-bātik* as a term for a sharp, cutting sword.

3. **Tearing off hair or feathers.** *Al-batk* also describes gripping hair, feathers, or similar, then pulling until it tears loose from its root (*yanbatik* — is severed/plucked out). A single torn-off piece is a *bitka*, plural *bitak*.

**Poetic citation:** Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā uses the plural *bitak* for the tufts of feathers left in a boy's hand after a bird he grabbed for wrenches free and flies off.

All three senses (slitting an ear, a slicing sword, tearing out tufts) trace back to the one core idea of severing/cutting.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives everything under b-t-l from one core idea: separating or cutting a thing off from something else (ibānah).

1. Base usage: "bataltu l-shayʾa" — "I severed the thing," i.e. cut it off from the rest.

2. Divorce idiom: "ṭallaqahā battatan batlatan" — he divorced her with a battah/batlah, meaning a final, absolute (irrevocable) divorce — a clean cutting-off of the marriage tie.

3. Mary the Virgin is called "al-Batūl" precisely because she is described as separate/set apart — she had no husband.

4. "nakhlatun mubtil" — a palm tree is called mubtil when the small shoot that had been growing alongside it has become detached from it. Ibn Fāris supports this with a line from a Hudhalī poet, comparing camel-loads/she-camels to "al-mubtil" young she-camels — i.e. animals that stand apart or have been separated (the verse is terse and its exact picture is not fully spelled out).

5. "al-batīlah" (pl. batāʾil) is a limb that is thickly, compactly fleshed — so called because the sheer bulk of its flesh makes it look set apart from the limb next to it. From the same idea comes the phrase "imraʾatun mubattalatu l-khalq," a woman of compact, well-proportioned build.

6. "al-tabattul" — devoting one's intention sincerely to God and cutting oneself off exclusively toward Him. Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 73:8, "wa-tabattal ilayhi tabtīlā," glossing it simply as "cut yourself off to Him, a complete cutting-off" — i.e. undivided devotion, in this author's own gloss, not elaborated into any ritual prescription.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ب ت ر (b-t-r), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: cutting something short — before it is completed.

1. al-sayf al-bātir — a sharply-cutting sword. Extended to people: a man with no surviving offspring (to carry on his line) is called abtar; more broadly, anyone whose legacy of good deeds has been cut off is likewise abtar.
2. Hadith citation: "kill the two-striped [snake] and the short-tailed [abtar] one" — using abtar for a specific kind of snake, tied to the same "cut short" image.
3. Historical anecdote: the governor Ziyād's famous sermon is called "al-khuṭbah al-batrāʾ" ("the docked sermon") because he omitted the customary opening praise of God and blessing on the Prophet — an incomplete, "cut-short" beginning.
4. rajul ubātir — a man who severs his own kinship ties, illustrated with a line of poetry about someone quick and severing toward near relatives.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: بَثَّ 5x "and dispersing"; بَثّ 1x "(of) my suffering"; مُّنبَثّ 1x "dispersing"; مَبْثُوثَة 1x "spread out"; مَبْثُوث 1x "scattered"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-th-th as a single root meaning: the scattering of a thing and making it manifest.

1. **Scattering, sending out in all directions.** Raiders "baththū the horses" in a raid, sending them out on every side; a hunter "baththa his dogs" over the game. Al-Nābigha describes a hunter who "loosed them in all directions upon it," while the quarry ran on, carried by sound, compact-jointed legs. Ibn Fāris adds that God created the creatures and spread them (baththahum) over the earth for their livelihood.

2. **Spread out (mabthūth).** Goods and furnishings laid out along the sides of a house or dwelling are mabthūth. The Qur'an has "and carpets mabthūtha" (Q 88:16), which Ibn Fāris glosses as "many and spread about."

3. **Loose, turned over (from Ibn al-Aʿrābī).** Tamr bathth are dates lying loose, not packed and pressed together. Bathathtu al-ṭaʿām wa-l-tamr, "I baththed the food and the dates," means I turned it over and threw one part on another.

4. **Spreading talk abroad.** Bathathtu al-ḥadīth means I spread the talk around.

5. **Bathth as grief.** Ibn Fāris derives this sense from the same idea: grief is something complained of, poured out and made manifest. The Qur'an quotes one who said, "I only complain of my bathth and my grief to God" (Q 12:86).

6. **Form IV, abaththa / ibthāth: disclosing one's troubles (from Abū Zayd).** One says abaththa so-and-so his concerns and needs to someone else, meaning he complained to him of his poverty and destitution. A poet weeping at a dwelling says that from all he pours out to it (ubiththuhu), its stones and playgrounds almost speak to him. A woman told her husband that she had fed him her food with its relish and disclosed to him (abthathtuka) what she kept hidden, "like a she-camel left unbound, without a ṣirār," the cloth tied over the udder.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: بَاءَ 6x "and they drew on themselves"; بَوَّأَ 6x "and settled you"; يَتَبَوَّأُ 4x "to settle"; مُبَوَّأ 1x "(in) a settlement"
poets_named: Ṭarafa (pre-Islamic); Ibn Harma (Umayyad); unnamed verse ×4; Muhalhil (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root b-w-ʾ (bāʾ, wāw, hamza) from two base ideas: (1) returning to a thing, and (2) the equality or matching of two things.

FIRST SENSE — returning; settling; an abode.
- al-bāʾa / al-mabāʾa: a people's dwelling-place, where they settle (yatabawwaʾūn) at the head of a valley or the foot of a mountain. Hence tabawwaʾū (they settled) and bawwaʾahum Allāh manzila ṣidq (God settled them in a place of truth). Shawāhid: Ṭarafa ("goodly of dwelling…") and Ibn Harma ("she was lodged in the very core of her kin…").
- al-mabāʾa also = the fold where camels are made to kneel at watering-places. abaʾnā al-ibil = we brought the camels to kneel side by side (with the verbal noun ibāʾa, long vowel). Attested in two verses and by al-Aṣmaʿī (the herdsman "brought her to her resting-place and she settled into it").
- Abū ʿUbayd: fulān ḥasan al-bīʾa (of good dwelling — noun on the pattern fiʿla, from tabawwaʾtu manzilan, "I took up a dwelling"); bāta bi-bīʾati sawʾ (he spent the night in an evil lodging), with a supporting verse.
- Abū Mahdī: bāʾat ʿalā al-qawm bāʾatuhum = their camels came home to them at evening.
- Extended uses of "returning": abiʾ ʿalayhi ḥaqqahu = restore his right to him (like ariḥ ʿalayhi); abāʾahu ʿalayhi = he returned it to him.
- bāʾa bi-dhanbihi = he "returned bearing his sin," as though he went back to his abode carrying it. So buʾtu bi-l-dhanb (I came back bearing the sin), and bāʾat al-yahūd bi-ghaḍab Allāh (the Jews returned bearing God's wrath).

SECOND SENSE — equality / matching, especially in blood-retaliation.
- fulān la-bawāʾ bi-fulān = if killed in retaliation for him, he would be his equal (kufʾ).
- abaʾtu bi-fulān qātilahu = I killed his slayer in requital for him. istabaʾtuhum qātil akhī = I demanded they hand over/bind my brother's killer; istabaʾtu bihi = like istaqadtu (I sought retaliation). Shawāhid from an unnamed poet and from Zuhayr.
- bāʾa fulān bi-fulān = one is killed in retaliation for the other. When the two killings are made equal, "they have been matched" (bāʾat). Verse: "…lā yabwuʾ al-dam bi-l-dam" (before blood is set equal against blood).
- Wider "parity" uses: ajābūnā ʿan bawāʾ wāḥid = they all gave one and the same answer; hum … bawāʾ = they are equals and peers (sawāʾ). Ḥadīth: he ordered them "an yatabāʾaw," i.e. to be equal in retaliation (qiṣāṣ). Muhalhil's taunt to Bujayr b. al-Ḥārith: "buʾ bi-shisʿ Kulayb" (be slain as a mere match for Kulayb's sandal-strap); and the verse "buʾ bi-mriʾ lasta mithlahu…" (be killed as the match of a man you are not the equal of).

dictionary: Lane — Arabic-English Lexicon, Edward William Lane (d. 1876)
text:
Root ب و ب (b-w-b), as recorded by Lane's Lexicon.

Verb forms:
1. بَابَ لَهُ (Form I): to be, or become, a door-keeper or gate-keeper to someone (e.g. to a Sultan). The related noun for the office is بِوَابَةٌ.
2. بوّب (Form II) carries two clusters of meaning: (a) figuratively, to practise أَبْوَابُ الحَرْب (the stratagems of war), and by extension to charge or attack the enemy; (b) to sort things into distinct headings — to arrange, classify, or organize (e.g. an author dividing a book into chapters, بوّب المُؤَلِّفُ كِتَابَهُ).
5. تبوّب (Form V): to take on a door-keeper for oneself.

The core noun بَابٌ (originally بَوَبٌ):
Sense 1 (primary, literal): a door, gate, or place of entrance — and also the physical leaf (of wood, etc.) that closes it. Plurals: أَبْوَابٌ, بِيبَانٌ, and the anomalous أَبْوِبَةٌ (normally used only to match an accompanying word, as in Ibn-Muqbil's verse "a frequent enterer of doors"; grammarians note this plural pattern breaks the usual rule for a فَعَلٌ noun). Used in بَابُ الدَّارِ (door of the house), بَابُ البَلَدِ (gate of the town). Also applied to a water channel cut for irrigation (pl. أَبْوَابٌ), and (in Egypt) to a rock-hewn tomb-chamber, from Coptic βηβ.

From that literal sense Lane derives a chain of figurative uses:
Sense 2 (tropical): a means of access or attainment — "this science is a بَاب (gateway) to that science."
Sense 3: an expedient, trick, stratagem, or method for achieving something — hence أَبْوَابُ الحَرْب (the ploys of war), بَابٌ مِنَ النُّجُوم (a procedure of astrology/astronomy), بَابٌ مِنَ السِّحْر (a procedure of magic).
Sense 4: a mode, kind, sort, class, or category — "it is of this باب (kind)." A poet (Suweyd Ibn-Kuráa) uses the plural metaphorically for "kinds of rhymes."
Sense 5: a chapter, or a section of a chapter, in a book — conventionally, a block of material on matters of one kind.
Sense 6: a head or class of items in an account — "I explained his account to him بَابًا بَابًا (head by head)." In this accounting/legal register, both بَابٌ and بَابَةٌ can also mean an extreme limit (غَايَة), though the lexicographer IDrd was uncertain of this.

Related nouns:
- بَابَةٌ: a mode or manner (syn. وَجْه); هٰذَا مِنْ بَابَتِى = "this is the sort I want / this suits me." Also extended to mean a habit, quality, or natural disposition (syn. خَصْلَة), and a condition (syn. شَرْط). بَابَاتُ الكِتَابِ = the lines (or possibly the chapters) of a book; it has no attested singular.
- بَوْبَاةٌ: a desert, especially a waterless one (syn. فَلَاة); a variant of مَوْمَاةٌ, with ب shifting to م.
- بِوَابَةٌ: the office/occupation of a gate-keeper.
- بَوَّابٌ: a door-keeper, gate-keeper.
- Adjectival: أَبْوَابٌ مُبَوَّبَةٌ (categories arranged in order, like أَصْنَافٌ مُصَنَّفَة) and كِتَابٌ مُبَوَّبٌ (a book divided into chapters).

Overall, Lane organizes the root around one physical image — a door or point of entry — from which every figurative sense (access, method, category, chapter, account-heading) radiates, alongside the agent-noun بَوَّاب (gatekeeper) and its verb forms.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: Al-Farazdaq (Umayyad); Ibn Muqbil (lived into Islam); unnamed verse; ʿAdī (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats B–W–L as two separate roots: (1) fluid that seeps or flows out; (2) al-rūʿ — the inner part of a person into which a thought falls.

FIRST ROOT — flowing fluid
1. بَوْل (bawl) — urine; the base, well-known sense. بِيلَة (bīla) is the noun of manner from it ("So-and-so has a good bīla"), and بُوَال (buwāl) is said of someone seized by frequent urination.
2. By extension, bawl was used for offspring/progeny. Al-Farazdaq's line boasts that his forebear Mujāshiʿ was "he of abundant bawl … in every land where no stallion sires."
3. Al-Aṣmaʿī: the seed of mules is called أَبْوَال الْبِغَال ("mules' urine"), and from that the mirage got the same name — because a mule's discharge is deceptive and produces nothing, and the mirage is likewise. Ibn Muqbil's verse uses the phrase for the mirage of the Ḥimyarī uplands.
4. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: شَحْمَة بَوَّالَة — a lump of fat that melts fast, i.e. runs. Cited with a verse in which the نَثُول (the woman lifting the fat from the pot) tells the جَمُول (fat being cooked): "O daughter of fat, flow in the gullet."
5. زِقّ بَوَّال — a wineskin that bursts and gushes its drink; attested in ʿAdī's poetry.

SECOND ROOT — the inward self
6. بَال (bāl) means the bāl of the soul: مَا خَطَرَ بِبَالِي, "it never crossed my bāl," glossed as "it was not cast into my rūʿ (inward self)."
7. Ibn Fāris answers an objection: al-Khalīl defined bāl al-nafs as اكْتِرَاث (concern/being troubled), deriving مَا بَالَيْتُ ("I did not care") from it. Ibn Fāris replies that this is the same meaning — iktirāth is precisely being weighed down by what has fallen into one's soul, so it reduces to the sense he gave.
8. The verbal nouns are بَالَة (bāla) and مُبَالَاة (mubālāt). He cites Ibn ʿAbbās, asked about performing wuḍūʾ with milk: "I do not mind it in the least; be easy and you will be dealt with easily." The verb is also shortened in use: لَمْ أُبَالِ and لَمْ أُبَلْ.
9. Also referred to this root: بَال in the sense of ease and comfort of life — رَاخِي الْبَال ("of relaxed bāl"), نَاعِم الْبَال ("of comfortable bāl").

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zibaʿrā (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse ×2
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ب-و-ر from two distinct roots.

**Root 1 — perishing, and what resembles it: lying idle, standing empty.**
1. *Destruction/perishing.* On al-Khalīl's authority, البَوَار (bawār) is perishing. بَارُوا = "they perished"; بُورٌ (būr) describes people who are straying and doomed; أبارهم = "he destroyed them." He notes that بُور serves for singular and plural, feminine and masculine alike, citing Q 48:12, "and you were a doomed people."
2. *Going to waste / finding no taker.* Al-Kisāʾī connects to this the report of seeking refuge from بَوَار الأيّم — an unmarried woman's "going to waste," i.e. she becomes unsought and finds no husband.
3. *A corrupt, worthless person.* Yaʿqūb: البُور is the corrupt man with no good in him — shown by ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zibaʿrā's line, "my tongue is mending what I tore open when I was worthless." Abū Zayd adds the idiom في حُورٍ وبُورٍ, glossed as "in loss and ruin."
4. *Commercial stagnation.* البائر is what will not sell; بارت البِياعات = "the wares became unsaleable." Ibn Fāris places Q 14:28, "the abode of ruin" (دار البَوار), under this same head.
5. *Untilled or fallow land.* أرضٌ بَوَارٌ is land with no crop. Abū Ziyād: البُور is dead ground unfit to be brought into cultivation, plural أرَضُونَ أبوار — cited from the Prophet's letter to Ukaydir, "ours are the uncultivated land and the untraced waste." Al-Yazīdī gives a narrower agricultural sense: land rested for a year to be sown the next, called both بُور and بَوَار.
6. *A descending affliction.* On al-Aḥmar's authority, نزلت بَوَارٌ على الناس = "a calamity came down on the people," with the verse: "wronging one another among friends is ruin (بَوَار)."

**Root 2 — trying and testing.**
7. بُرْتُ فلانًا / بُرْتُ ما عنده = "I tested him / tested what he has."
8. Specialised camel-breeding use: بُرْتُ الناقةَ (imperfect أبُورُها) is to bring a she-camel near the stallion to see whether she is pregnant or barren; the stallion able to tell the two states apart is called مِبْوَر. One also says بار الناقةَ بالفحل. A verse is cited with تَبُورُها in this sense.
9. From the same testing sense Ibn Fāris explains the line "تُبارُ إليها المُحصَناتُ النجائبُ": choice, well-kept she-camels are bought by being measured against her — i.e. assessed, from بُرْتُ الناقةَ.

Method note: the entry works by tracing every attested usage — Qur'anic, prophetic report, proverb, and poetry — back to one of the two posited semantic origins, without merging them.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris gives ب-خ-ع a single core meaning: killing, and whatever comes close to it — humiliation and forceful subjugation.

1. Killing through grief/passion. Al-Khalīl: 'a man baxaʿa'd his own soul' means he destroyed it through rage born of intense grief or longing (al-wajd). Cited shāhid, Dhū al-Rumma: 'O you who kill yourself with grief, over something fate has carved out of your reach.' The author links this directly to Qur'an 18:6, '{fa-laʿallaka bākhiʿun nafsaka ʿalā āthārihim}' — 'perhaps you will destroy yourself with grief, following after them' — as an instance of this same sense.

2. Cutting through, at slaughter. Via a chain back to al-Ḍabbī: 'baxaʿtu al-dhabīḥata' — I cut clean through the neck-bone of the slaughtered animal (the resulting state is 'mabkhūʿah'; word partly garbled in the source text). This is distinguished from a related root, n-kh-ʿ ('nakhaʿtuhā'): that verb denotes a shallower cut, because al-nukhāʿ names the white cord running through the neck and spine (the spinal cord) — so this cut falls short of reaching bone. Separately, al-bikhāʿ (with bāʾ) names the vessel/artery running along the spine.

3. Exerting oneself to the limit. Abū ʿUbayd: 'baxaʿtu lahu nafsī wa-nuṣḥī' — I gave him my utmost self and sincerest counsel, i.e., I strove as hard as possible.

4. Land worked to its limit. 'arḍun mabkhūʿah' — land whose full productive capacity has been reached (exhausted) through cultivation.

5. Conceding a right. 'baxaʿa lī bi-ḥaqqī' — he acknowledged/submitted to my due (aqarra).

All five uses converge on the root idea: pressing something (a soul, flesh, land, a claim) all the way to its limit — through killing, cutting to the bone, total exertion, exhaustion of capacity, or forced acknowledgment.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-kh-l as expressing a single idea: miserliness / stinginess (recorded with two vocalizations, al-bukhl and al-bakhal).

Derived forms he gives:
1. بَخِيل (bakhīl) and بَاخِل (bākhil) — a miserly man / one who acts stingily.
2. بَخَّال (bakhkhāl) — the intensive form, used when stinginess is a person's fixed character or habit (a confirmed, habitual miser).

Poetic witness (shāhid): a line by the poet Ruʾba using bakhkhāl, associating the confirmed miser with tight-fisted "contracting" or shrinking in.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-kh-s as having a single underlying idea, and gives the entry in two moves:

1. Core sense — shortfall. The three letters bāʾ–khāʾ–sīn go back to one root meaning: نَقْص, deficiency or being made less. He cites Qurʾān 12:20, "and they sold him for a bakhs price," and glosses bakhs simply as "deficient" — a price short of what was due.

2. Extended usage — marrow that has dwindled. He places under the same heading the expression بَخَّسَ تَبْخِيسًا used of مُخّ (marrow): it is said when the marrow is left only in the سُلَامَى (the small bones of the hands and feet) and in the eye. His explanation is that this is precisely because the marrow has decreased and disappeared from the rest of the body — the last places it survives being the extremities and the eye. So the verb marks the end-stage of depletion, tying the usage back to sense 1.

Poetic witness. He supports this with an unattributed line: "They do not complain of the labour so long as they keep their marrow — as long as there is marrow in a small bone or an eye," i.e. camels keep working while any marrow at all remains.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's account of the root ب ي ض (b-y-ḍ):

1. Core sense — whiteness (bayāḍ), the opposite of blackness. Verb: ibyaḍḍa / yabyaḍḍu (to turn white), verbal nouns ibyiḍāḍ and bayāḍ; adjective abyaḍ (white), participle mubyaḍḍ. Qur'anic witness: \"On a Day when faces turn white and faces turn black… those whose faces turn white are in God's mercy\" (Āl ʿImrān 3/106–107).

2. abyaḍ (\"the white one\") is also the name of a vein, so called for its whiteness.

3. Whiteness as excellence — because whiteness was regarded as the finest of colours (a saying: \"whiteness the most excellent, blackness the most dreadful, redness the most beautiful, yellowness the most becoming\"), it came to stand for merit and nobility. Of someone untainted by any fault it is said, \"he is white of colour.\"

4. Whitening/blackening of faces as emotion — the whitening of faces (Āl ʿImrān 3/106) expresses joy, their blackening expresses grief. Compare: \"when one of them is given news of a female, his face remains darkened\" (al-Naḥl 16/58); and, in the sense of that brightening, \"faces that Day radiant\" (al-Qiyāma 75/22) and \"faces that Day bright, laughing, rejoicing\" (ʿAbasa 80/38–39).

5. Whiteness of fairness/clarity — \"your mother is white of Quḍāʿa\" (i.e. noble/fair); and of drink, \"white [wine], delicious to the drinkers\" (al-Ṣāffāt 37/46).

6. bayḍ (eggs), sing. bayḍa — named for its whiteness. A woman is figuratively called a bayḍa (egg), likened to it in colour and in being kept protected \"beneath the wing.\" The phrase bayḍat al-balad (\"the egg of the town\") is used both ways: in praise, of a protected, leading figure among his people — hence the verse, \"Quraysh was an egg, then split open, and its pure yolk went to ʿAbd Manāf\"; in blame, of a lowly person left exposed to anyone, like an egg abandoned in the open wilderness.

7. Anatomical extension — bayḍatā al-rajul (the two testicles), named by likeness to the egg in shape and whiteness.

8. Verb bāḍa (to lay an egg; the hen laid) also means to become firmly settled/established: \"it nested, then laid,\" and bāḍa al-ḥarr (the heat settled in). Also bāḍat yad al-marʾa — a woman's hand swelled in an egg-like shape. Forms: dajāja bayūḍ (a hen that lays much), dajāj buyuḍ (laying hens).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: بَيْع 7x "the business"; بَايَعْ 6x "they pledge allegiance"; تَبَايَعْ 1x "you make commercial transaction"; بِيَع 1x "and churches"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-y-ʿ as a single root whose core sense is the selling of a thing (bayʿ, "sale").

1. Core sense — selling. Verb بِعْتُ الشَّيْءَ بَيْعًا ("I sold the thing").

2. Overlap with "buying." The same word bayʿ is sometimes used for buying (shirā), the two being treated as one in meaning. Ibn Fāris cites the Prophetic saying "Let none of you sell over the sale of his brother," which the scholars glossed as "let none buy over his brother's purchase" — showing the two verbs standing in for each other.

3. Morphological note. The plain form بِعْتُ = "I sold." The fourth form أَبَعْتُهُ (af'ala) means to offer or put something up for sale rather than to complete the sale.

4. Poetic witness (shāhid): "I was well pleased with the bounties of the bay horse; so whoever may sell a horse — our steed is not for sale" — where بِمُبَاع ("for sale") is the passive participle of the fourth-form verb abāʿa, illustrating sense 3.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ب ي د (b-y-d) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core sense: something perishing or coming to ruin.
- bāda al-shayʾu baydan wa-buyūdan — "the thing perished/was ruined."

Derived word:
- al-baydāʾ — "the desert/wasteland," linked (Ibn Fāris says) to the "perishing" sense — the desert is a place where things come to ruin.
- al-baydāna — the she-ass that lives in the baydāʾ (desert).

A separate usage — bayda meaning "except/however":
The word bayda is also used with the sense of ghayr ("except, however, but"), as in: "such-and-such was done, bayda that such-and-such [else] was the case."

Citations given:
1. A hadith of the Prophet: "We are the last [nation], [yet] the foremost on the Day of Resurrection — bayda (however) that they [earlier nations] were given the Book before us, and we were given it after them."
2. A line of poetry: "Deliberately I did that — bayda that I think, had I perished, you would not have shown [grief] for me."

Ibn Fāris's own note: this "except/however" usage of bayda does not fit the root's core "perishing" sense — it breaks the expected analogy. He suggests it would not be unreasonable to treat it as a separate, independent root rather than a branch of the "perish" root.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: بَيْن 266x "between them"; مُّبِين 119x "clear"; بَيِّنَة 71x "with clear proofs"; بَيَّنُ 35x "makes clear"; تَبَيَّنَ 18x "(has) become clear"; بَيَان 3x "[the] speech"; مُّبَيِّنَة 3x "clear"; مُّبَيِّنَٰت 3x "clear"; تَسْتَبِينَ 1x "so that becomes manifest"; تِبْيَٰن 1x "(as) a clarification"; بَيِّن 1x "clear"; مُسْتَبِين 1x "the clear"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-y-n as a single root carrying two linked ideas: the distance/remoteness of a thing, and its becoming disclosed or manifest.

1. Separation. al-bayn = parting, separation (al-firāq). Verb: bāna / yabīnu, with the verbal nouns bayn and baynūna.

2. Depth/distance. al-bayūn = a well with a far-off bottom, i.e. a deep well.

3. Expanse of land. al-bīn = a stretch of ground as far as the eye can reach. Cited verse (poet unnamed): "In the highland of Ḥimyar... how did you cross that expanse (al-bīn) in the dead of night?"

4. Clarity/manifestness. bāna and abāna = to become clear and uncovered. Hence "so-and-so is abyan than so-and-so" means clearer in his speech.

5. A further sense, al-bāʾin used of milking, is introduced but the entry breaks off before defining it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: بَيْت 65x "houses"; بَيَّتَ 4x "surely, we will attack him by night"; بَيَٰت 3x "(at) night"; يَبِيتُ 1x "spend (the) night"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats b-y-t as one root with a single core sense: a shelter or dwelling — a place of refuge, a place to return to, and a place where people gather together. The noun is بَيْت (bayt, "house"), plural بُيُوت (buyūt) and أَبْيَات (abyāt).

1. Line of verse. A line of poetry is also called a bayt, by analogy, because it gathers words, letters, and meanings under a fixed condition — metre. He cites a verse in which a poet speaks of "building a bayt on the back of his camel" using "a brown one that bleeds," explaining that the "brown one" is the reed-pen.

2. Household. A bayt is a man's household and dependents — those with whom he spends the night. Hence the saying mā li-fulānin bītatu laylatin: "so-and-so hasn't even a night's provision (of food or the like) to get through the night on."

3. Contriving by night (bayyata al-amr). To plan or scheme a matter at night. He cites Qurʾān al-Nisāʾ 108, "when they contrive by night speech He does not approve," glossing it as their gathering in their houses — but noting the verb is specific to nighttime action (the daytime equivalent uses yaẓallu).

4. al-bayyūt. (a) Water left standing overnight. (b) A matter that keeps its owner awake and anxious through the night — with a supporting line from the poet Umayya.

5. Night-raid (al-bayāt / al-tabyīt). To fall upon the enemy by night, as though seizing him in his own house.

6. "Measured/determined" (buyyita). Ibn Fāris reports from Abū ʿUbayda that buyyita al-shayʾ means the thing was measured out or determined, likened to the scansion of poetic "houses" (verses). He judges this consistent with the root-principle he has laid down.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris (Maqayis al-Lugha) treats the root b-z-gh as a single root whose core meaning is something rising up and becoming visible or appearing.

He gives three attested usages, all traced to this one sense:

1. bazaghati l-shamsu - "the sun rose/dawned" - the sun's rising and coming into view.
2. bazagha nabu l-ba'ir - "the camel's canine tooth erupted" - a tooth breaking through and becoming visible, paralleling the sun's rising.
3. bazaghahu, said of a farrier/veterinary bloodletter, used when he opens a vein in an animal to let blood. Ibn Faris explicitly states this is not a separate meaning but an analogical extension (qiyas al-bab) of the same root idea: the vein is opened so that something (the blood) rises up and comes into view - matching the "rising and appearing" sense that unifies the entry.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: دَأْب 4x "like (the) way"; دَأَب 1x "as usual"; دَائِبَيْن 1x "both constantly pursuing their courses"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats د-أ-ب as a single root whose core idea is sticking persistently to something and keeping it up continuously.

1. **al-daʾb — habit, customary manner, one's affair.** From the root's sense of constancy comes the noun daʾb, glossed as ʿāda (settled habit) and shaʾn (manner, case, the way one goes about things).

2. **Derivation.** Ibn Fāris cites al-Farrāʾ: daʾb originally comes from the verb daʾabtu ("I toiled persistently"), but Arab usage transferred its sense over to shaʾn — that is, from the act of persisting to the settled manner that persisting produces.

3. **The verb — to exert oneself steadily.** daʾaba l-rajulu fī ʿamalihi is said of a man who works hard and keeps at it.

4. **Causative form IV.** adʾabtuhu (verbal noun idʾāb) — to keep someone at it, to drive him to sustained effort; the transitive counterpart of sense 3.

5. **al-dāʾibān, "the two constant ones"** — a dual epithet for the night and the day, named for their unceasing recurrence.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَدُعُّ 2x "they will be thrust"; دَعّ 1x "(with) a thrust"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats d-ʿ-ʿ as a single root, regular and consistent, whose meaning is movement, pushing and agitation.

1. **Pushing.** Al-daʿʿ means pushing or shoving: daʿaʿtuhu aduʿʿuhu daʿʿan, "I pushed him." He cites Q 52:13: "the day they are thrust into the fire of Jahannam with a thrusting."

2. **Shaking a measure (al-daʿdaʿa).** The doubled form al-daʿdaʿa is shaking a measuring vessel so that it takes in all of what is being measured. From this comes jafna mudaʿdaʿa, a large bowl filled full: it has been shaken until it filled up.

3. **Twisting run (al-daʿdaʿa).** Al-daʿdaʿa is also running with a twisting motion.

4. **Cries, set aside.** It is also said that daʿdaʿa is the cry used to drive sheep and goats, or the words "daʿ daʿ" said to someone who stumbles, like the call laʿan. Ibn Fāris does not count these: sounds and imitations of sounds hardly ever follow analogy, so they are not roots.

5. **Short man (daʿdāʿ).** The word daʿdāʿ for a short man, if it is authentic, is daḥdāḥ with ʿayn substituted for ḥāʾ.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: دَعَا 170x "invoke"; دُعَاء 22x "the call"; دَعْوَة 6x "a claim"; دَعْوَىٰ 4x "their plea"; دَاعِى 4x "(to the) caller"; دَّاع 3x "the caller"; يَدَّعُ 3x "call"
poets_named: Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse ×2; Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the whole root د-ع-و from one core idea: to incline or draw something toward yourself by means of a sound or speech that you produce. The base verb is دَعَا / يَدْعُو / دُعَاء (to call).

1. Vowelling distinguishes two nouns: دَعْوَة (fatḥa) = an invitation to a meal; دِعْوَة (kasra) = a claim of kinship/lineage. Ibn Fāris cites Abū ʿUbayda for this as the usage of most Arabs — with one tribe, ʿAdiyy al-Ribāb, reversing the two vowels.

2. iddiʿāʾ (ادِّعَاء), on al-Khalīl's authority, is to claim a right for oneself or another, whether the claim is true or false (ادَّعَى حَقًّا أَوْ بَاطِلًا). Shāhid: a line of Imruʾ al-Qays ("...the people do not claim that I flee").

3. In war, iddiʿāʾ means iʿtizāʾ — proclaiming one's descent as a battle-cry ("I am the son of so-and-so"). Shāhid: "in the fray we drag the spears and proclaim our lineage."

4. dāʿiyat al-laban (the milk's "caller") is the milk deliberately left in the udder so it draws down more milk after it — an explicitly figurative usage. Cited from a ḥadīth to a milker: "leave the milk's caller."

5. By analogy, further senses hang on the same root-idea of "drawing/inclining toward":
   - دَعَا اللَّهُ فُلَانًا بِمَا يَكْرَهُ — God brought some hardship down upon a person (shāhid: "may God afflict you, O hyena, with a viper").
   - تَدَاعَتِ الْحِيطَان — walls collapsing in succession, as if the first "called" the next; and دَاعَيْنَاهَا — we demolished it piece by piece.
   - دَوَاعِي الدَّهْر — the turns of fortune/Time, as though they draw events on.
   - adʿiya — riddles a tribe poses to one another (like the ughlūṭa), as if the poser "calls" the other to expose what is hidden (shāhid recited by Abū ʿUbayd from al-Aṣmaʿī).
   - مَا بِالدَّارِ دُعْوِيّ — "there is no one in the house," i.e. no one crying out.

6. Metaphorically, a place can be said to "call" someone (دَعَا فُلَانًا مَكَانُ كَذَا) when he sets out for it — praised by Ibn Fāris as eloquent Arabic, with a line of Dhū al-Rumma on the waters that "called Mayya away."

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
quran_words: يُدْحِضُ 2x "to refute"; مُدْحَضِين 1x "the losers"; دَاحِضَة 1x "(is) invalid"
poets_named: unnamed verse; Ṭarafa (pre-Islamic); al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Manẓūr's entry for the root د ح ض (d-ḥ-ḍ), Lisān al-ʿArab.

1. Core sense — slipping, losing one's footing. الدَّحْضُ (daḥḍ) is "slipping / a slippery footing." The verb دَحَضَتْ رِجْلُه (imperfect تَدْحَضُ; verbal nouns دَحْضاً, دُحُوضاً) = "his foot slipped." The example given is the camel's foot; al-Muḥkam gives it unrestricted, of any foot.

2. Causative. دَحَضَها and the form-IV أَدْحَضَها = "he made it slip"; الإِدْحاضُ = "causing to slip." A rain-description attributed to al-Ḥajjāj uses it of rain turning watercourses into slippery ground.

3. Active participle as a character-word. داحِض (dāḥiḍ), plural دُحَّض (duḥḥaḍ), is used of people who slip — glossed here as those with no steadiness and no resolve in affairs, from a report describing the Madhḥij delegation as "noble ones, not of the slipping-footed."

4. Slippery ground / slippery water. الدَّحْض also names the wet, muddy going itself, and specifically the water that makes a place slippery. A report about the Friday gathering pairs الطين (mud) with الدَّحْض (the slick); a report of Abū Dharr speaks of a road "having daḥḍ" before the bridge of Jahannam.

5. Place-nouns and vowelling. مكان دَحْضٌ (also دَحَضٌ with a vowelled middle radical) = a slippery spot where feet do not hold. مَزَلَّةٌ مِدْحاضٌ = a slippery place where slipping happens often. Ibn Manẓūr cites a rajaz verse describing a she-camel drinking a pool dry "until it becomes a slippery daḥaḍ" as the attestation for the vowelled form, and Ṭarafa's line — "he swerved as the camel swerves away from the slippery ground" — as the attestation for the sukūn form daḥḍ.

6. Metaphorical extension: an argument collapsing. دَحَضَتْ حُجَّتُه دُحُوضاً — "his argument slipped," i.e. it became void — is explicitly labelled here as a metaphor (على المثل) from the physical sense. أَدْحَضَ حُجَّتَه = he nullified it, and أَدْحَضَها اللّهُ of God. The Qur'anic attestation cited is حُجَّتهم داحِضة, "their argument is dāḥiḍa" (slipping / void).

7. Scraping with the foot. In a report of Muʿāwiya to Ibn ʿUmar, تَدْحَضُ is glossed "you slip"; a variant reading with ṣād (تَدْحَصُ) gives "you scrape about in it with your foot." Ibn Manẓūr notes دَحَضَ برجله and دَحَصَ برجله both mean scraping or scratching with the foot — a ḍād/ṣād pair.

8. Further senses. الدَّحْضُ also = الدفْع, pushing away or repelling. الدَّحِيضُ (daḥīḍ) = flesh, meat.

9. The sun's decline. دَحَضَتِ الشمسُ = the sun moved off the middle of the sky, i.e. past the zenith toward the west — "as though it had slipped." Ibn Manẓūr cites a report on the appointed times of ṣalāt: "until the sun tadḥaḍa."

10. Place-names. دَحِيضَة (Daḥīḍa), a water-source of Banū Tamīm; and, on Ibn Sīda's authority, دُحَيْضَة (Duḥayḍa), a place, attested in a line of al-Aʿshā recalling "days we had at Duḥayḍa … between al-Badiyy and Thahmad."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats د-ح-ر as having a single underlying sense: driving away and pushing off to a distance.

1. Core sense — to drive off, expel, and keep at a remove.

Shāhid: he cites Qurʾān 7:18, "Go out from it, disgraced and driven away (مَدْحُورًا)", where the passive participle مدحور names the one so driven off.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) on the root د ح و (d-ḥ-w):

**Core meaning:** one single idea — "spreading out" and "leveling/preparing a surface" (basṭ wa-tamhīd).

**1. Of God and the earth:** دَحَا اللَّهُ الْأَرْضَ (daḥā Allāhu al-arḍ) — "Allah spread the earth out" (verb: yadḥūhā, verbal noun: daḥwan).

**2. Of rain and pebbles:** دَحَا الْمَطَرُ الْحَصَى عَنْ وَجْهِ الْأَرْضِ — "the rain swept/spread the pebbles off the surface of the ground." Ibn Fāris explains the link to the core sense: doing this levels the ground.

**3. Of a horse's gait:** said of a horse that throws its forelegs out in a low, sweeping stride without lifting its hoof far off the ground — مَرَّ يَدْحُو دَحْوًا, "it went along sweeping/gliding low."

**4. Of the ostrich's nest-site (أُدْحِيّ, udḥiyy):** the place where an ostrich hatches its young is called udḥiyy — morphologically the pattern ufʿūl from the same verb daḥawtu — because the bird scrapes/levels the spot with its foot before laying its eggs there. Ibn Fāris notes as an aside that the ostrich has no ordinary nest (ʿushsh).

All four uses are tied by Ibn Fāris to the one underlying sense of spreading/flattening out a surface.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats d-b-b as one sound, regular root whose meaning is movement over the ground that is lighter than walking. He derives the rest of the entry from this, and sets a few words aside as anomalous, as arising from letter substitution, or as unfounded.

1. **Creeping.** The verb is dabba, and its verbal noun is dabīb. Everything that walks on the earth is a dābba.

2. **The talebearer.** Ibn Fāris cites a ḥadīth: "Neither a daybūb nor a qallāʿ will enter the Garden." He explains the daybūb as the talebearer who creeps among people spreading tales. The qallāʿ is the one who informs on a person to his ruler in order to uproot him (yaqlaʿ) from his standing with that ruler.

3. **Slow, heavy movement.** A she-camel is dabūb when she is so fleshy that she can only creep along.

4. **Anyone at all.** "There is no dibbī or dubbī in the house" means there is no one there who creeps about.

5. **A seeping wound.** A thrust is dabūb when blood creeps out of it. A line by al-Hudhalī is cited: "on his side a creeping wound that spills over."

6. **Following someone's way.** "He rode so-and-so's dubba" or "he took to his dubba" means he acts just as the other does, as if walking the way he walks.
