7. **The gourd (al-dubbāʾ).** Ibn Fāris says this word may be anomalous. It is also possible that the gourd was named for its smoothness, as though it moves lightly when rolled. He cites Imruʾ al-Qays: "When she comes forward, you would say: a green gourd dipped in the pools."

8. **Hairiness (al-dabab).** Ibn Fāris explains this as letter substitution: the d stands in for a z, so the word is a variant of z-b-b (hairiness). A camel that is adbab is azabb, meaning hairy. He cites a ḥadīth with the reservation "if it is sound": "Which of you is the rider of the hairy camel?"

9. **Rejected sense.** Some say al-dabūb is a cave with a very deep bottom. Ibn Fāris dismisses this as worthless.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: دُبُر 18x "their backs"; مُدْبِر 8x "(in) flight"; يَتَدَبَّرُ 4x "they ponder"; دَابِر 4x "(the) roots"; يُدَبِّرُ 4x "disposing"; أَدْبَرَ 4x "he turned back"; إِدْبَٰر 1x "and after"; مُدَبِّرَٰت 1x "and those who arrange"
text:
Ibn Fāris organizes the root د ب ر (d-b-r) under one governing idea: the back, rear, or end of a thing — the opposite of its front (qubul). Most usages reduce to this analogy; a few words stand apart, which he flags at the end.

Core sense — "back / rear / end," opposite of "front":
1. الدُّبُر — the hind or back part, opposite of the front.
2. الدَّبِير — thread twisted backward, away from the chest (per Ibn al-Sikkīt: qabīl is twisted toward the chest, dabīr away from it).
3. دَابِرَة — the rear part of things: a bird's back toe; the rear of a hoof at the pastern.
4. "I put his words دَبْر أُذُنِي (behind my ear)" — I ignored them and feigned deafness.
5. دَبَرَ / أَدْبَرَ النَّهار — the day drew to its end (its dubur).
6. دَبَّرْتُ الحديث عن فلان — I narrated a report on someone's authority; the later narrator "comes behind" the earlier one.
7. قَطَعَ اللهُ دَابِرَهُم (Qur'anic phrasing) — cut off the last remnant of them.
8. الدَّابِر (of arrows) — one that overshoots the target, as if it "turned its back" on the archer (verb dabara–dubūran).
9. الدَّبَرَان — a star, named because it follows behind the Pleiades.
10. دَابَرْتُ فلاناً — I was hostile to him; the ḥadīth «لا تدابروا» ("do not turn your backs on one another") — each stops facing the other.

Extended senses still tied to "outcome / rear":
11. التَّدْبِير (management) — to manage an affair by looking to how its end (dubur) will turn out.
12. التَّدْبِير (a second sense Ibn Fāris records) — freeing a slave "ʿan dubr," i.e. to take effect after the owner's death ("he is free after my death").
13. رجل مُقَابَل مُدَابَر — noble in lineage on both parents' sides (noble "from the front" and "from the back").
14. المُدَابَرَة — a ewe whose ear is slit from the nape side.
15. الدَّابِر (of gaming-arrows) — the losing arrow, opposite of the winner (fāʾiz); it "turned its back" on its owner.
16. الدَّابِر (the follower) — on this basis Ibn Fāris reads وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا دَبَرَ ("by the night when it dabara") as: the night followed after the day.
17. دَبَرَ بالقمار — won and carried off the stake.
18. "This affair has neither قِبْلَة nor دِبْرَة" — no front and no back by which it can be recognized.
19. رجل أُدَابِر — one who cuts off kin ties, turning his back on them.
20. الدَّبُور — the wind blowing from behind (the rear of) the Kaʿba.
21. الدَّابِرَة — a wrestling grip/throw.
22. Abū Zayd: praying الصلاة دَبَرِيًّا (traditionists: duburiyyan) — praying at the very end of the time, when the time has "turned away."

Words Ibn Fāris counts as deviating from the root:
- Doubtful: دُبَار as a Jāhilī name for Wednesday — he considers this questionable.
- Sound: الدِّبَار — furrows or plots of tilled land (with a verse of Bishr); and الدَّبْر — abundant wealth (māl dabr), the form unchanging for singular, dual, and plural.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root د ف أ (d-f-ʾ), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha — this entry actually covers two distinct roots grouped together (d-f-ʾ, hamzated, and d-f-w/y, weak-final)

**First root — dfʾ: warmth**
1. al-difʾ — the opposite of cold; dafuʾa yawmunā — our day grew warm (with a dialect variant noted, dafiʾ). Applied to people: dafiʾa → dafʾān (masc.)/dafʾā (fem.); a warm garment is dhū difʾ; "mā ʿalā fulānin difʾ" — nothing warms him; "uqʿud fī difʾi hādhā al-ḥāʾiṭ" — sit in this wall's warmth/shelter.
2. al-dafaʾiyy — summer rain; al-ibil al-mudfaʾah — a large camel-herd, so called because the animals warm one another with their breath.
3. The entry's central Qur'anic citation, al-Nahl 16:5: "lakum fīhā difʾun wa manāfiʿ" — "for you in them [livestock] is warmth and [other] benefits." Al-Umawī glosses difʾ here specifically as camels' offspring, milk, and general usefulness. A matching hadith citation uses the same word for "their warmth/wool and their harvest."
4. A further extension: al-dafaʾ as "a bending/stooping," applied in a hadith description of the Dajjāl ("there is a stoop in him") — Ibn Fāris notes that, if authentic, this fits the root's logic, since anything that warms something must envelop and lean over it.

**Second, related root — d-f-w/y: length with a slight bend**
5. al-dafā — the length of a bird's wing (ṭāʾir adfā); applied to mountain-goats with long horns, and to a long-necked, noble she-camel (dafwāʾ). al-dafwāʾ also names a great, tall tree, illustrated with a hadith about a tree called Dhāt Anwāṭ; the eagle is called dafwāʾ for its long, curved beak. tadāfā al-baʿīr — a camel walking with a leaning, uneven gait.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: دَفَعْ 5x "repel"; دَفْع 2x "(for the) repelling"; دَافِع 2x "preventer"; يُدَٰفِعُ 1x "defends"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats د-ف-ع as one well-known root whose core meaning is pushing a thing aside or removing it.

1. Basic sense — to push, repel, drive away: دَفَعْتُ الشَّيْءَ ("I pushed the thing away"). In the III form, دَافَعَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ السُّوءَ means "God warded off evil from him."

2. الْمُدَفَّعُ (al-mudaffaʿ) — "the pushed-away one," i.e. the poor man, because he is rebuffed when he begs. Ibn Fāris cites: "People are enemies to every rebuffed, empty-handed man, but brothers to the man of plenty," and a second line describing a man "struck who moans without a blow," tossed from hardship to hardship.

3. الدُّفْعَةُ (al-dufʿa) — a burst or gush, as of rain or blood. الدُّفَّاعُ (al-duffāʿ) — a mighty torrent or flood. He derives both from the image of one part pushing against another.

4. الْمُدَفَّعُ (al-mudaffaʿ) — a second, contrasting sense: the noble, prized camel, so called because whenever it is brought to be loaded it is set aside and another used instead, out of honor for it. Shāhid from Ḥumayd: "And they brought forward for departure every prized camel."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root د ف ق (d-f-q), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One sound, regular root: pushing something forward.

1. dafaqa al-māʾ — water gushed forth; māʾ dāfiq — gushing water; "hādhihi dufqatun min māʾ" — a gush of water. Extended idiom: "jāʾū dufqatan wāḥidatan" — "they came all at once, in a single gush," i.e. together, in one instance.
2. baʿīr adfaq — a camel whose elbows/forelegs stand out away from its sides — Ibn Fāris explains this fits the root's logic: standing out means, in effect, being "pushed away and gushing forth" from the body.
3. al-difaqq — a swift camel; "mashā fulānun al-difaqqā" — he walked with a hastening gait, glossed by Abū ʿUbaydah as the utmost, fastest neck-stretching pace — illustrated with a hadith of al-Zibriqān describing an ungainly woman's walk and manner of sitting.
4. sayl dufāq — a torrent that fills a valley.
5. Closing imprecation: "dafaqa Allāhu rūḥahu" — "may God dafaqa [expel] his soul," a curse invoking someone's death.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root د هـ م (d-h-m), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: something enveloping in darkness — which then branches out so that "darkness" and other extended senses become treated equally under the same root.

1. "marra dahmun min al-layl" — a portion of the night passed; al-duhmah — blackness; al-duhaymāʾ — the diminutive of al-dahmāʾ, itself a name for calamity (al-dāhiyah), named for its "darkness"/gloom.
2. al-dahm — a great number [of people], extending the root to abundance/multitude.
3. idhāmma al-zarʿ — a crop overtaken by blackness from being well-watered and lush. The entry's central Qur'anic citation, al-Rahman 55:64, describes the two Paradise-gardens as "mudhāmmatān" — "deep green [almost black]" — glossed as: appearing black to the eye on account of their lushness and verdant green.
4. dahamathum al-khaylu — cavalry "dahama"d them, i.e. descended upon and overwhelmed them.
5. Closing, unrelated sense: al-dahmāʾ — also a name for a cooking-pot.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يُدْهِنُ 2x "so they would compromise"; دُّهْن 1x "oil"; دِّهَان 1x "like murky oil"; مُّدْهِنُون 1x "(are) indifferent"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats d-h-n as one root whose core idea is softness, ease, and a small quantity. He derives every application from that.

1. Oil / anointing. الدُّهْن (duhn) is oil or grease; the verb دَهَنَ / يَدْهُن / دَهْنًا means to oil or anoint. الدِّهَان (dihān) is the substance used for anointing. He cites Q 55:37, "and it becomes rose-red like dihān," and reports the explanation that dihān here means the dregs of olive oil.

2. A light blow. دَهَنَهُ بِالْعَصَا — "he dahana him with the stick" — is used of striking someone lightly, fitting the root's sense of smallness/gentleness.

3. Ingratiation and duplicity. الْمُدَاهَنَة (mudāhana) is مُصَانَعَة, humouring or accommodating someone; دَاهَنْتُ الرَّجُلَ means to dissemble with a man, showing him the opposite of what one conceals. Ibn Fāris explicitly ties this to the root image: the dissembler is, as it were, oiling the other man down and quieting him. The fourth-form أَدْهَنَ / إِدْهَان he glosses as "I acted deceitfully," and cites Q 68:9, "they wished that you would be pliant, so they too would be pliant."

4. Oil-vessel, and morphological note. الْمُدْهُن (mudhun) is the container for oil. He flags it as a grammatical rarity: one of the few implement-nouns built on the pattern مُفْعُل with an initial mīm.

5. Rock-hollow (by likeness). By resemblance to the oil-vessel, mudhun also names a hollow in a mountain where water collects — with the saying attributed to al-Nahdī: "The rock-hollow dried up and the root-stock withered."

6. Scanty yield. الدَّهِين (dahīn) is a she-camel with little milk. And دَهَنَ الْمَطَرُ الْأَرْضَ means the rain only lightly wetted the ground — again the "small amount" sense.

7. Names. Banū Duhn is an Arab clan (ʿAmmār al-Duhnī is affiliated with them), and al-Dahnāʾ is a place named for its soft sand, with the relative form Dahnāwī.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root د-ه-ق (d-h-q), per Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha.

Core idea: fullness combined with a back-and-forth motion or agitation — not just "full," but full in a way that stirs, comes and goes, or churns.

1. Filling (to the brim): The verb is used as أَدْهَقْتُ الْكَأْسَ, "I filled the cup." Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'an's وَكَأْسًا دِهَاقًا (78:34), "a cup dihāqā" — i.e., a cup filled to the brim.

2. The agitation sense — الدَّهْدَقَة (dahdaqa): a reduplicated form describing a large piece of meat turning over in the cooking pot, bobbing up and sinking down again as it cooks. This illustrates the "coming and going, agitation" component of the root's core meaning alongside "fullness."

The entry links both senses (brimming fullness; churning/tumbling motion) under the same root idea.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root d-h-r — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris

Core meaning: a single root-idea — "overcoming, subduing" (al-ghalabah wal-qahr).

1. Why "time" (dahr) carries this root: dahr is named from this sense because it comes upon everything and overcomes it.

2. On the hadith "Do not curse al-dahr, for God is al-dahr": Ibn Fāris relays Abū ʿUbayd's explanation — pre-Islamic Arabs, when calamity struck, blamed "time" itself as the agent ("time destroyed us," "time came upon us"), as shown in verses he quotes (by ʿAmr al-Ḍubaʿī and an unnamed poet), which personify time as an archer that strikes without being struck back and that robs without restoring. The Prophet's statement corrects this: the true agent behind these events is God, not dahr — dahr itself performs no action. So cursing "time" as though it were the doer amounts to cursing God, who is far above what wrongdoers say.

3. An alternative grammatical analysis Ibn Fāris offers: dahr could instead be a noun built directly from the verb "to overcome," the way Arabic sometimes uses a verbal noun as a description of a person (e.g. calling a man "fasting" or "fast-breaking"). On this reading, "do not curse al-dahr" means "do not curse the Overpowering One who subdues you in your affairs" — still ultimately pointing to God, not to time as an independent force.

4. Related form: dahrun dahīr, an intensifying pair formed like abadun abīd ("ever-enduring").

5. From Kitāb al-ʿAyn: dahrahum amrun means "a misfortune befell them."

6. Idiom: mā dahrī kadhā ("that is not my dahr") is used to mean "that's not my concern." Ibn Fāris flags this as a loose extension of the word's meaning — strictly, "concern" is not what dahr denotes; the phrase literally means "I do not spend my time on it."

7. Separate derivative: al-dahwarah, meaning to gather something up and hurl it into a pit or chasm — which Ibn Fāris notes still fits the root's underlying sense of forceful subjection.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha gives the root د-ه-ي (with a weak final radical) a single core meaning: something striking or befalling a thing in a way that is unpleasant.

1. mā dahāhu ("what befell him") — used only for bad or distressing events, never for good ones.

2. dawāhī al-dahr ("the calamities of fate") — the great misfortunes and severe blows that strike a person over time.

3. al-dahy — shrewdness/cunning sharpness of mind and excellence of judgment. Ibn Fāris derives this from the same root: a shrewd person "strikes" or achieves what he wants through his judgment, just as misfortune "strikes" a person — the same underlying idea of forceful, effective impact, applied here to the mind rather than to fate.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: دَكّ 3x "pounded"; دُكَّتِ 2x "and crushed"; دَكَّاء 1x "level"; دَكَّة 1x "(with) a crushing"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats d-k-k as having two roots: one of lowness and flatness, and one of pounding, which he explains as close to letter-substitution, with the kāf standing in for the qāf of d-q-q ("to crush fine").

**Root 1: low, flat and spread out**

1. Al-dukkān, the familiar raised platform or bench. Al-ʿAbdī speaks of "the clay-plastered dukkān of the gatekeepers".
2. Al-arḍ al-dakkāʾ, broad, level ground. The entry cites Q 18:98, "He will make it level (dakkāʾ)".
3. Al-nāqa al-dakkāʾ, a she-camel with no hump.
4. Al-Kisāʾī: al-dukk (sing. adakk) are broad mountains; a horse adakk al-ẓahr is broad-backed.

**Root 2: pounding (like d-q-q)**

1. Dakaktu l-shayʾ, "I pounded the thing", equivalent to daqaqtuhu.
2. Dukka l-rajul, madkūk: said of a man who has fallen ill. Ibn Fāris allows that this may belong to the first root instead, as if illness had stretched him out flat, so it fits either.
3. Al-dakdāk, sand that seems pounded fine. The philologists define it as sand compacted onto the ground that does not rise. Jarīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh, asked by the Messenger of God about his home at Bīsha, answered: "soft plain and flat sand (dakdāk), salam and arāk trees."
4. Dakaktu l-turāb ʿalā l-mayyit, "I heaped earth over the dead man", and likewise of filling in a well, because the earth is like something pounded.

**Outliers**

Ibn Fāris lists two usages as standing apart from both roots: amatun midakka, a slave-woman strong for work (he adds "if it is sound"), and ḥawlan dakīkan, "a full year", as in "I stayed with him a full year".

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris's account of the root d-l-k (دلك):

Core meaning: the root signals something departing/moving away from something else, and — he stresses — always gently, not violently.

Senses recorded:
1. "Dalakati ash-shamsu" (the sun dalakat) — the sun declined [past its zenith]; also glossed as "it set/disappeared." Al-dalak is the name for this time of the sun's decline/setting.
2. "Dalaktu ash-shay'a" ("I rubbed the thing") — rubbing belongs to this root because in rubbing, the hand keeps moving, never settling in one spot — the same "gentle departure/motion" idea extended to a back-and-forth physical action.
3. Al-daluk — something (perfume, etc.) that a person rubs onto the body.
4. Al-dalik — a dish of butter and dates, similar to tharid (bread soaked in broth).
5. Al-madluk — a camel worn down and wearied by travel; alternatively, a camel with slack/loose knees (a milder fault than the stiffness called al-taraq).
6. "Farasun madlukul-hajaba" — a horse whose hip-bone doesn't protrude.
7. "Ardun madlukah" — land grazed bare, as if it had been rubbed smooth.
8. Al-dulaka — the last bit of milk left in the udder, said to be named this because the hand rubs the udder to draw it out.

Author's closing remark: Ibn Faris adds a personal reflection — that God places a subtlety in every root, and that throughout this whole chapter, wherever dal and lam combine with any third letter, the resulting word always carries the sense of motion, coming and going, and moving from one place to another. He closes with "God knows best."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris traces d-l-l to two root meanings: (1) making something clear by a sign that one learns, and (2) agitation or swaying in a thing.

**1. Showing by a sign; guidance.**
- Dalaltu fulānan ʿalā al-ṭarīq means "I guided so-and-so to the road".
- Al-dalīl is the sign or indicator in a thing.
- A thing that is bayyin al-dalāla (or al-dilāla) is clearly indicated.
- Ibn Fāris also places here a usage al-Farrāʾ reports from the Arabs: adalla, yudillu, "to put forward a kinship tie as one's claim".

**2. Agitation, swaying.** Tadaldala al-shayʾ means "the thing swayed or shook". Aws describes a tribe "wavering (daldāl) between al-qusūṭ and al-dīn". Ibn Fāris glosses al-qusūṭ as injustice and al-dīn as obedience.

Ibn Fāris puts two more usages under this second meaning:
- A woman's dalāl, or coquetry: her boldness with softness and airs, as if she were contrary when she is not. He says this comes only through swaying and restless movement.
- Yudillu ʿalā aqrānihi fī al-ḥarb, "he bears down on his peers in war", like a falcon swooping on its prey.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: أَدْلَىٰ 2x "and present"; دَلْو 1x "his bucket"; تَدَلَّىٰ 1x "and came down"
text:
Al-Rāghib's entry on the root د‑ل‑و:

1. Literal well-imagery. دَلَوْتُ الدَّلْوَ means to send the bucket down into the well; أَدْلَيْتُهَا means to draw it up. Al-Rāghib notes an alternative reported by Abū Manṣūr (in al-Shāmil) that أدلى can also mean "send it down." Qur'anic witness: "then he let down his bucket" (Yūsuf 12:19).

2. Figurative extension: gaining access to something. The bucket-in-the-well image is borrowed for reaching or obtaining a thing. Poetic witness: "Sustenance does not come by frantic seeking — rather, cast your bucket in among the buckets."

3. Related usage: the go-between. By the same imagery, the means or intermediary is called المائح — the man who descends into the well to fill the buckets. Poetic witness: "And I have a māʾiḥ before whom no one had brought people to water…"

4. Qur'anic application of the figurative sense: "and that you let it down / convey it to the judges" (al-Baqara 2:188).

5. Form V, التَّدَلِّي: drawing near, and letting oneself down or hanging low. Qur'anic witness: "then he drew near and let himself down" (al-Najm 53:8).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root د م ع (d-m-ʿ) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris states this root has a single underlying meaning: water, or a tear/weeping.

1. Tears (core sense). الدَّمْع (al-damʿ) = "the water of the eye," i.e. tears; a single drop is a دَمْعَة (damʿah). "To shed tears" is attested in three verb-patterns — دَمَعَتْ (damaʿat), دَمِعَتْ (damiʿat) — each with its own verbal noun (damʿ, damaʿ, dumūʿ). A weeping eye is عَيْنٌ دَامِعَةٌ. Plural of al-damʿ: دُمُوع (dumūʿ).

2. The corner of the eye. Citing al-Khalīl: الْمَدْمَع (al-madmaʿ) is the spot where tears collect at the corner of the eye, plural مَدَامِع (madāmiʿ).

3. A tearful woman. امْرَأَةٌ دَمِعَة (imraʾah damiʿah) — a woman who weeps easily and copiously.

4. A "weeping" wound — and a correction. Al-Khalīl's book calls a wound that flows with blood شَجَّة دَامِعَة (shajjah dāmiʿah). Ibn Fāris disagrees: the wound that flows with actual blood should be called الدَّامِيَة (al-dāmiyah, from the separate root d-m-y, "blood"); al-dāmiʿah names a lesser wound, one that seems to ooze only a thin, reddish, watery discharge rather than blood proper.

5. The tear-trace on the cheek. Al-Yazīdī glosses الدُّمَاع (al-dumāʿ) as the mark tears leave on the cheek, citing the line: "O for an eye that never stops pouring forth — the tears have left a dimāʿ [tear-trace] upon it" (also pronounced dumāʿan).

6. Sap of the vine. In both its light and doubled pronunciations (دُمَاع / دُمَّاع), al-dumāʿ also names the sap that exudes from grapevines in springtime — a secondary application of the same "water/exuding fluid" core sense, beyond human weeping.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root د م د م (d-m-d-m), al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān

1. Qur'anic citation, al-Shams 91:14: "fa-damdama ʿalayhim rabbuhum" — "so their Lord repeatedly crushed them" (the destruction of Thamūd) — glossed as: He destroyed them and struck them with terror.
2. A second, more mundane sense is noted: al-damdamah as the imitative sound of a cat's growl/purr, extended to damdama fulānun fī kalāmihi — so-and-so "damdama"d in his speech, i.e. mumbled or growled indistinctly.
3. A cluster of loosely related words sharing consonants rather than meaning: damamtu al-thawb — to coat a garment with dye; al-dimām — a coating/plaster substance; baʿīr madmūm bi-l-shaḥm — a camel coated with fat; al-dāmmāʾ/al-dumamah — a jerboa's burrow; al-daymūmah — a wasteland/desert.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris classifies the root d-m-gh (دمغ) as a "single word" root — one that carries only one core meaning, with no further senses branching off it, and on which no analogical derivation (qiyās) can be built.

1. Ad-dimāgh (الدماغ) — "the brain." Ibn Fāris calls this well known and offers no further gloss.
2. The verb damaghtuhu (دمغته) — "I struck him on his head until I reached the brain," i.e. to deliver a blow to the head hard/deep enough to reach the brain itself.
3. Such a blow (or the striking of this kind) is named ad-dāmighah (الدامغة).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats د-م-ر (d-m-r) as a single root whose core sense is entering into a house or the like.

1. Basic sense — entering. دَمَرَ الرَّجُلُ بَيْتَهُ means "the man entered his house."

2. A disputed legal restriction. Some distinguished entering with permission from entering without it. Abū ʿUbayd, glossing the Prophetic report "Whoever peers into a people's house without permission has done dumūr," took dumūr to mean entering, but only when done without permission — with permission it is not dumūr. Ibn Fāris notes this is a juristic (sharʿī) reading; the word's own linguistic analogy is simply "entering," as stated at the outset.

3. The hunter's blind. In a verse of Aws, the مُدَمِّر (mudammir) is, per al-Shaybānī and al-Aṣmaʿī, one who enters the قُتْرَة (a hunter's hide). Likewise دَمَرَ الْقُنْفُذُ = "the hedgehog entered its burrow." Others held mudammir meant a hunter who fumigates with camel-hair to mask his scent from the game, but Ibn Fāris rejects this: the term names the one who enters the hide (who may then fumigate once inside), not "one who fumigates" — the root's analogy does not support that reading.

4. Destruction. The Qur'an (Muḥammad 47:10) uses دَمَّرَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِمْ ("God brought destruction down upon them"), and الدَّمَار (al-damār) means destruction or perdition.

5. Etymological note. The تَدْمُرِيّ (tadmurī) is said to be a kind of jerboa; if so, it fits the root, since it burrows ("enters") into its holes.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: unnamed verse ×3; al-Ḥuṣayn b. al-Ḥumām al-Murrī (pre-Islamic); Jarīr (Umayyad); al-Laʿīn al-Minqarī (pre-Islamic); ʿAlī (undated)
text:
The Lisān treats d-m-y (listed here under dmw) as the article on al-dam, "blood". It sets out the grammarians' debate on the word's original form, then covers bleeding and wounds, blood-coloured things, the "bloodied" arrow, blood as solidarity and blood-claims, oaths by blood, and the related noun al-dumya, "image".

**1. al-dam, blood.** Al-dam is blood, one of the bodily humours. Abū l-Haytham calls it a two-letter noun, and al-Kisāʾī says he knows no one who pronounces it with a doubled m. A Hudhalī line that seems to end in al-damm is explained as a pausal doubling that the poet, under the pressure of the metre, carried into connected speech. Ibn Sīda argues from the scansion (the first ḍarb of the ṭawīl) that the doubled form is required there.
- Dual: damān and damayān, as in the line "were we slaughtered on one stone, the two bloods (al-damayān) would run with the certain news". The line rests on a belief of the Arabs that the bloods of two slaughtered enemies do not mix. Damawān is anomalous and rare.
- Plural: dimāʾ and dumiyy. Diminutive: dumayy. Relative adjective: damiyy or damawiyy.
- Al-dama is a single piece or clot of blood, more particular than al-dam (like bayāḍ and bayāḍa). Ibn Jinnī reports dam and dama as two dialect forms.

**2. The debate over its original form.** The grammarians reported here disagree on what the word's lost third radical was:
- Abū Isḥāq: originally damay. The yāʾ reappears in damiyat yaduhu ("his hand bled"), tadmā and the dual damayān, just as yad goes back to yaday.
- Sībawayh (via al-Jawharī): originally damy (pattern faʿl), because it is pluralised dimāʾ and dumiyy, like ẓaby and dalw. Ibn Barrī replies that the plural pattern fuʿūl also occurs for faʿal nouns (ʿaṣan, ʿuṣiyy), so this argument does not hold.
- Ibn Sīda reports a view that it was damy, and that the m took a vowel when the lost letter was restored, to show the word had been used in shortened form.
- Al-Jawharī: originally damaw, the yāʾ in damiya yadmā coming from the preceding kasra, as in raḍiya from al-riḍwān. Ibn Barrī counters that the final radical is yāʾ, citing damayān.
- Al-Mubarrad (via al-Jawharī): originally faʿal with a lost yāʾ. The evidence is the dual damayān and poets who restore the full form al-damā, as in al-Ḥuṣayn b. al-Ḥumām al-Murrī's "…on our heels the blood (al-damā) drips". The report calls this view the sounder one. Ibn Barrī adds parallel lines ending in yaqṭuru l-damā ("drips blood") from Jarīr, al-Laʿīn al-Minqarī and one attributed to ʿAlī.

**3. To bleed, to make bleed.** Damiya yadmā daman / dumiyyan, "to bleed", and the one bleeding is damin. All agree the verbal noun has a vowelled m. Admāhu and dammāhu (tadmiya) mean "to strike someone until blood comes out". Ruʾba's line, explained by Thaʿlab, and another poet's line allude to the wolf that turns on its companion to eat it once it sees blood on it. A proverb says: "Your child is the one who bloodied your heels." ʿUmar told Abū Maryam al-Ḥanafī, who is said to have killed "his brother Zayd" at al-Yamāma, "I hate you more than the earth hates blood". The explanation given is that the earth does not soak blood up, and its refusal is called hatred figuratively.

**4. Wounds and bleeding.**
- Al-dāmiya is a head-wound that has bled, or split the skin so blood shows, but not yet flowed. Once blood drips or flows it is a dāmiʿa. Zayd b. Thābit's ruling: "for a dāmiya, a camel".
- Istadmā: to lower one's head with blood dripping from it. Al-Aṣmaʿī says al-mustadmī is someone with a nosebleed who bows his head, and also a creditor who draws his debt out of a debtor gently.
- In the ʿaqīqa report ("his head is shaved and he is bloodied", or in another transmission "and he is named"), Qatāda described smearing the child's crown with the sacrificed animal's blood. Ibn al-Athīr reports that Abū Dāwūd called "bloodied" a mistake by Hammām, a practice of the Jāhiliyya that was abrogated, and preferred "named". Al-Khaṭṭābī objects that someone who ordered dry dirt removed from the child's head would hardly order it bloodied, since blood is heavily impure.
- A hare "bleeding" (tadmā) in a ḥadīth is explained as menstruating, since the hare menstruates as women do.

**5. al-mudammā, blood-coloured.** Used of a red garment and of an intense sorrel. In al-Tahdhīb it is a horse of deep red resembling blood. More generally it is anything whose colour mixes black and red, or anything intensely red. In Ṭufayl's line on "blood-tinged bays", the redness is said to tend toward duskiness rather than bright red. Abū ʿUbayda: a bay is mudammā when its dark coat is deep red down to the soft parts. A mudammā sorrel has yellowish tips like a yellow bay. Among colours, mudammā is one with black in it.

**6. al-mudammā, the "bloodied" arrow.** This is an arrow shot at the enemy and shot back again. A man would keep such an arrow, with blood on it, in his quiver for blessing. It is also any arrow the archers pass back and forth between them. Saʿd said he shot a man at Uḥud and the same arrow came back at him three times, so he called it "a blessed, mudammā arrow" and kept it until he died. Explanations given:
- blood stained it black-red;
- the name comes from al-dāmiyāʾ, "blessing";
- Shamir: it was as if bloodied on striking;
- dried blood darkened it;
- it reddened with blood.

**7. Blood as solidarity and as a claim.**
- At the ʿAqaba pledge, Abū l-Haytham b. al-Tayyihān feared the Prophet might return to his own people once victorious. The Prophet answered: "Nay: the blood is the blood and the hadm is the hadm; I make war on whom you make war on and peace with whom you make peace with." Some transmit it as al-ladamu l-ladamu wa-l-hadamu l-hadamu, a variant treated under its own roots. Ibn al-Aʿrābī cites the Arab saying "my blood is your blood, my hadm is your hadm", meaning "if you are wronged, I am wronged".
- Al-Farrāʾ explains the grammar: the article can stand for a possessive, as in "the Blaze is the refuge" (Q 79:39) and "the Garden is the refuge" (Q 79:41), meaning "his refuge". Al-Zajjāj glosses it as "the refuge for him". On al-Farrāʾ's view, "the blood is the blood" means "your blood is my blood": each side is pursued for the other's blood, and the two are one.
- Thumāma b. Uthāl: "if you kill, you kill one who has blood". This means someone pursued for blood, or whose own blood will be avenged. A variant reads dhā dhimm, "one who has a pact and standing among his people".
- At the killing of Kaʿb b. al-Ashraf: "a voice like the voice of blood", meaning one seeking blood-vengeance.

**8. Oaths by blood.** Al-Walīd b. al-Mughīra said of the Prophet, "By the blood, he is no poet". The entry calls this a Jāhiliyya oath by the blood of animals slaughtered on the nuṣub (standing stones). Similarly "No, by the bloods", meaning of slaughtered animals, which is also transmitted as "No, by the dumā", meaning images, that is, idols.

**9. Other uses of dam.**
- Al-dam: the cat, reported by al-Naḍr, with a verse recited by Kurāʿ: "thus the cat stalks the male jerboas".
- Dāmī l-shifa, "bleeding of lip": poor (from Abū l-ʿAmaythal).
- Dam al-ghizlān, "gazelles' blood": a herb with a beautiful flower.
- Banāt dam: a plant.
- Dam al-akhawayn, "blood of the two brothers": al-ʿandam.
- Sātī Damā: a mountain, said to be so named because blood is shed on it every day, two nouns made into one. It appears in verses of ʿAmr b. Qamīʾa (recited by Sībawayh) and al-Aʿshā, and Yazīd b. Mufarrigh shortens it to Sātī Dā.

**10. al-dumya, image.**
- An idol. It is also said to be an image decorated in ivory and the like, and Kurāʿ takes it to mean any image.
- A woman, used as a metonymy.
- Plural: dumā.
- A line about women "trailing in the dumā" is taken to mean garments with images on them. Ibn Barrī corrects the reading to "like the dumā" and explains its grammar from the preceding line.
- Dammā l-rāʿī l-māshiya: the herdsman grazed the flock so well that they fattened into "images".
- The Prophet's neck is described as "like the neck of a dumya", a carefully crafted and beautified image.
- Dumyat al-ghizlān (al-Layth): a flowering herb.
- Thaʿlab also gives dammā lahu, "it appeared to him" ("take what has appeared to you"), and "he came near" in some matter.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats d-n-r as a single-sense root: its only meaning is the word دِينَار (dīnār), a gold coin.

From this noun the Arabs formed a verb: دَنَّرَ وَجْهُهُ (dannara wajhuhu), "his face dannara" — used of a face that glittered and shone, i.e. it took on a dinar-like gleam. The verb is a denominal derived directly from the coin's shine, not an independent root-sense.

Entry closes with the standard formula "wa-Allāhu aʿlam" (God knows best).

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: دُّنْيَا 115x "(of) the world"; أَدْنَىٰ 12x "(is) more suitable"; دَانِيَة 3x "hanging near"; دَنَا 2x "he approached"; دَان 1x "(is) near"
text:
Al-Rāghib treats d-n-w as nearness (al-dunūw = al-qurb), whether nearness in essence or nearness in status and judgement, and applies it to place, time and rank.

**Nearness.** The palm tree's "clusters hanging near" (qinwān dāniya, Q 6:99) show the plain sense. "Then he drew near and came down" (thumma danā fa-tadallā, Q 53:8) he classes as nearness by status/judgement.

**The comparative adnā.** Al-Rāghib identifies four uses, each defined by the word it is paired against:

1. **Smaller**, against "greater": "nor fewer than that nor more" (Q 58:7).
2. **Baser, lower**, against "better": "would you exchange what is lower for what is better?" (Q 2:61).
3. **First**, against "last": al-dunyā against al-ākhira, as in "he has lost this world and the Hereafter" (Q 22:11) and "We gave him good in this world, and in the Hereafter he is among the righteous" (Q 16:122).
4. **Nearer**, against "farther": "when you were on the nearer side of the valley and they on the farther side" (Q 8:42).

The plural of dunyā is dunā, on the pattern kubrā/kubar and ṣughrā/ṣughar.

**Adnā as "more likely".** In "that is adnā that they will give the testimony" (Q 5:108), adnā means it is nearer, for their own souls, to aiming at justice in testifying. "That is adnā to their eyes being cooled" (Q 33:51) is read the same way.

**Al-dunyā and al-ākhira.** "That you may reflect on al-dunyā and al-ākhira" (Q 2:220) covers the conditions of the first coming-into-being and those of the last.

**Bringing near (verbs).** Dānaytu bayna al-amrayn means "I brought the two matters close together", and adnaytu one of them to the other means "I brought it near". So in Q 33:59 women "draw (yudnīna) some of their outer garments close over themselves". Adnati al-faras means that a mare's foaling is near.

**Danīʾ.** This word is reserved for what is mean or of little worth. One says danīʾ bayyin al-danāʾa, "base, plainly lowly". The text as it stands sets it against al-sayyiʾ.

**The report "fa-dannū".** In the saying "when you eat, fa-dannū", al-Rāghib derives the word from al-dūn ("what is near/below"), giving the sense "eat from what is next to you".

dictionary: ʿAyn — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786)
text:
Root د ر هـ م (d-r-h-m), al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad al-Farāhīdī, Kitāb al-ʿAyn

1. al-darham and al-dirhim — two dialectal pronunciations of the coin "dirham."
2. rajul mudarham — a man rich in dirhams.
3. adrahamma al-shaykh — an old man "adrahamma"d, i.e. grew aged and decrepit — a verb formed from the same root-letters, extending "dirham" (a small, round coin) to an image of a wizened, shrunken old age. Illustrated with a line of poetry vowing not to tire until the addressee does, or until old age overtakes the speaker.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: دَرَجَة 18x "(in) degrees"; نَسْتَدْرِجُ 2x "we will gradually lead them"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats د-ر-ج (d-r-j) as one core root meaning the passing-on of something and the moving-along within something. He also flags a possible second, separate root.

1. Passing on / going one's way: دَرَجَ الشَّيْءُ — "the thing passed on," went its way.

2. Retracing a path: رَجَعَ فُلَانٌ أَدْرَاجَهُ — someone "returned by his adrāj," i.e., went back along the very road he had come by.

3. A child's toddling walk: دَرَجَ الصَّبِيُّ — "the child darija-walked," walked with its toddling gait.

4. Dying without heirs (from al-Aṣmaʿī): دَرَجَ الرَّجُلُ — the man "passed on," died leaving no offspring.

5. Crosswise hill-paths: مَدَارِجُ الأَكَمَةِ — the tracks running across a hill. Cited verse: "Go crosswise along the tracks and range about, as Orion goes crosswise among the stars."

A possible SECOND root — covering / wrapping over — which Ibn Fāris admits only conditionally ("if it is sound"), tied to الدُّرْج (durj, a small casket or container):

6. Rolling or folding up: أَدْرَجْتُ الكِتَابَ ("I rolled up the writing"), أَدْرَجْتُ الحَبْلَ ("I coiled up the rope"). Cited verse: "tightly-twisted, wound up as the tether-rope is wound."

7. الدُّرْجَة (durja): rags placed in a she-camel's vulva and then withdrawn; smelling them, she takes them for her own young and shows it affection. Cited verse: "and the duraj of the fostering were not set for her."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَدْرَكَ 6x "grasp him"; ٱدَّٰرَكَ 3x "is arrested"; دَّرْك 1x "the depths"; دَرَك 1x "to be overtaken"; مُدْرَكُون 1x "(are) surely to be overtaken"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats د-ر-ك as a single root meaning one thing overtaking, catching up with, or reaching another.

1. Core sense — attaining/overtaking. أَدْرَكْتُ الشَّيْءَ ("I attained/overtook the thing"), verbal noun إِدْرَاك. A horse called دَرَكُ الطَّرِيدَةِ is one no quarry ever escapes.

2. Reaching maturity. أَدْرَكَ الْغُلَامُ وَالْجَارِيَةُ — the boy and girl "came of age," i.e. reached puberty/full growth.

3. Following on / catching up. تَدَارَكَ الْقَوْمُ — the last of a group catches up with the first. Likewise تَدَارَكَ الثَّرَيَانِ, when a second layer of soil-moisture reaches the first rainfall.

4. Qur'anic example. Ibn Fāris reads {ادَّارَكَ عِلْمُهُمْ فِي الْآخِرَةِ} (al-Naml 27:66) from this root: their knowledge "overtook" them in the Hereafter, at the point when it no longer benefited them.

5. الدَّرَك (the well-rope piece). A short length of rope tied at the end of the main rope to the bucket's cross-bar, protecting the rope from being worn away by the water; and it is the means by which the bucket is retrieved (tudrak).

6. الدَّرَك / دَرَكَات (levels of the Fire). The dwelling-stations of the people of the Fire. Ibn Fāris contrasts Paradise, which is دَرَجَات (ascending degrees), with the Fire, which is دَرَكَات (descending levels), citing {إِنَّ الْمُنَافِقِينَ فِي الدَّرْكِ الْأَسْفَلِ مِنَ النَّارِ} (al-Nisāʾ 4:145) — the stations the dwellers "reach" and are joined to. He closes: "We seek refuge in God from them."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris holds that doubled d-r points to two root meanings: one thing issuing from another, and agitation (unsteady movement) in a thing.

**First root meaning: one thing issuing from another**

1. **Milk and rain.** darr is the flow of milk; darra is the pouring of clouds, and clouds of abundant rain are midrār.

2. **A person's output.** In lillāhi darruhu, "to God belongs his darr", darr means the person's work, as though likened to the milk that comes from milk-giving animals. The curse lā darra darruhu means "may his good not be abundant".

3. **Revenue.** In "the milch-camel of the Muslims has flowed", the milch-camel stands for their revenue and tribute (fayʾ and kharāj).

4. **A brisk market.** A market has dirra when trade is brisk, as though it had flowed; the opposite is ghirār, slackness. A verse speaks of the market having both a dirra and a ghirār.

5. **Goats seeking the male.** Goats are said to istadarrat when they want the stud, as though wanting the stud's water to flow for them.

**Second root meaning: agitation**

6. **A swift mount.** darīr: a riding animal that runs hard and fast. A verse likens it to a boy's whirligig, which he sets whirling (adarra) on a string with the alternating strokes of his palms.

7. **Gums and quivering.** durdur: the places where a child's teeth grow. Ibn Fāris takes it from tadardarat al-luḥma, "the flesh quivered", and from dardara, said of a child chewing something.

8. **Wind and road.** darar al-rīḥ is the place where the wind blows; darar al-ṭarīq is the direct line of a road, so called because it is never empty of people coming and going.

9. **Pearls.** durr: large pearls, named, he says, for the movement seen in them because of their clearness, as if they were moving water. He cites al-Hudhalī's verse on a pearl over which "the sweet water lingers and surges", meaning that its clearness and beauty make it look as though water were surging inside it.

10. **The bright star.** al-kawkab al-durriyy: the piercing, shining star, likened to durr and named after it for its whiteness.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: دَرَسُ 5x "which they could study"; دِرَاسَت 1x "their study"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats د-ر-س as a single root meaning: something faint, low-lying, or worn away by use.

1. **Effaced trace / faint track.** الدَّرْس (dars) is a road so faint it is barely visible. دَرَسَ الْمَنْزِلُ — "the dwelling was darasa," i.e. its traces were rubbed out.

2. **Worn-out cloth.** الدَّرِيس (darīs) is a threadbare, thoroughly used garment.

3. **Menstruation.** دَرَسَتِ الْمَرْأَةُ — "the woman darasat," she menstruated. He notes the reported kunya أَبُو أَدْرَاس (Abū Adrās) for the female pudendum, derived from this same menstrual sense.

4. **Threshing grain.** دَرَسْتُ الْحِنْطَةَ — to thresh wheat still in the ear by treading it. Ibn Fāris explicitly refers this back to the root idea: the grain is put underfoot, just as a road is trodden and walked over. He cites the verse-fragment: سَمْرَاءَ مِمَّا دَرَسَ ابْنُ مِخْرَاقْ — "dark wheat of the kind Ibn Mikhrāq threshed."

5. **Light mange.** الدَّرْس also denotes a mild case of mange on a camel.

6. **Reciting/studying a text.** دَرَسْتُ الْقُرْآنَ وَغَيْرَهُ — "I darastu the Qurʾān and other things." His stated rationale: the دَارِس retraces what he had already read, exactly as a traveller follows an existing road along its course. On this account the "study" sense is not a separate meaning but the tracking-a-path image applied to speech.

**Outlier:** الدِّرْوَاس (dirwās) — thick-necked, of people and of animals — which Ibn Fāris marks as falling outside the root's organizing sense.

text:
Ibn Fāris analyzes the root د-ر-ي, treating both its weak-final form (دري) and its hamzated form (درأ). He finds three underlying senses: the un-hamzated form yields two roots — (1) aiming at / making for a thing in pursuit, and (2) sharpness in a thing — while the hamzated form yields a single root: repelling / pushing away.

Root 1 — aiming at / stalking a thing:
- ادَّرَى بَنُو فُلانٍ مَكانَ كَذا: "they made for such-and-such a place," i.e. headed for it on a raid (with a verse of shāhid).
- الدَّرِيَّة (dariyya): the animal a hunter hides behind to stalk his game; hence دَرَيْتُ / ادَّرَيْتُ, "to stalk under cover." A verse of al-Akhṭal plays on the hunter who "hunts without being detected" (yaṣīdu wa-lā yadrī).
- Per Ibn al-Aʿrābī, تَدَرَّيْتَ الصَّيْدَ = you scouted where the game was without yet seeing it; دَرَيْتُهُ = "I outwitted it."
- From this same idea of "knowing where the quarry is" comes دَرَى in the sense of knowing/perceiving: دَرَيْتُ الشَّيْءَ ("I knew the thing"), أَدْرانِيهِ اللهُ ("God made me know it"). Ibn Fāris cites Q 10:16, {…nor would He have made you know of it} (walā adrākum bihi), and حَسَنُ الدِّرْيَةِ = "of good acumen." He treats knowing as one continuous analogy with stalking, not a separate root.

Root 2 — sharpness:
- مِدْرًى (midran): a pointed comb/pin for combing and parting hair — so named because it is sharp-pointed.
- شاةٌ مُدْراةٌ: a sharp-horned ewe; تَدَرَّتِ المَرْأَةُ: a woman combed out her hair.
- The two مِدْرَيَان are said to be a ewe's (or she-camel's) teats — called so because their tips sharpen as they fill (verse of Ḥumayd).

Root 3 (hamzated) — repelling / pushing away:
- دَرَأْتُ الشَّيْءَ = "I pushed the thing away"; Ibn Fāris cites Q 24:8, {and it averts the punishment from her} (wa-yadraʾu ʿanhā l-ʿadhāb), with a supporting verse.
- الدَّرِيئَة: the practice-ring for spear-thrusting (verse of ʿAmr).
- جاءَ السَّيْلُ دَرْءًا: a flood that surges in from far off; ذُو تُدْرَإٍ: one strong at driving off his enemies (verse of shāhid).
- دَرَأَ = to appear suddenly (as if thrusting oneself forth); دارَأْتَ فُلانًا = to push back against someone.
- With the hamza softened, the form shifts to "outwitting / deceiving," which Ibn Fāris folds back into Root 1 (stalking) — with a verse: "what can the poets stalk of me?"
- الدَّرْء = crookedness, derived by analogy from "pushing," since a bending thing is pushed off straight; hence طَرِيقٌ ذُو دَرْءٍ (a broken, eroded road) and أَقَمْتُ مِنْ دَرْئِهِ ("I straightened its crookedness"), with a verse.
- Further extensions kept under "pushing/swelling": دَرَأَ الْبَعِيرُ (a camel's back swells up) and أَدْرَأَتِ النَّاقَةُ (a she-camel lets her udder droop at calving).

text:
Root د س ر (d-s-r), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: pushing/thrusting.

1. dasartu al-shayʾa — to push something with force. Two hadith citations: one on ambergris being exempt from zakah because "the sea has thrust it up" (i.e. it's found, not earned); one from ʿUmar warning that people might be "shoved about, as a slaughter-camel is shoved."
2. dasarahu bi-l-rumḥ — to thrust someone with a spear; rumḥ midsar — a thrusting spear, illustrated with a line of poetry about a warrior formidable enough to uproot a mountain with a single thrust. A huge, powerful camel is called dawsariyy; Dawsar is the name of a military unit, so called because it thrusts back the enemy.
3. Closing outlier, which Ibn Fāris flags as not fitting the "pushing" pattern but nonetheless sound: al-disār — the palm-fiber cord binding a ship's planks together (plural dusur). Qur'anic citation, al-Qamar 54:13: "wa ḥamalnāhu ʿalā dhāti alwāḥin wa dusur" — "and We carried him [Noah] on a vessel of planks and cords" — with a note that al-dusur may also mean the nails/rivets used in shipbuilding.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats d-s-s, in its doubled and matching forms, as one root meaning (aṣl wāḥid): a thing's entering under concealment and secrecy.

1. **Thrusting something in, out of sight.** dasastu l-shayʾa fī l-turāb, adussuhu dassan: "I thrust the thing into the earth". His Qur'anic example is Q 16:59: "Shall he keep it in humiliation, or thrust it (yadussuhu) into the dust?"

2. **A snake.** al-dassāsa is a deaf snake that lives under the soil.

3. **The camel.** For dussa l-baʿīr he records two explanations, each of which he says fits the root: either the camel has a slight touch of mange, which belongs here because such mange is like something slight tucked away; or tar is put on the camel's masāʿir (the armpits and groin, where mange sets in).

4. **Other words.** He also places al-dasīs here, without glossing it, and the saying al-ʿirqu dassās, "the strain steals in", explained by the strain's drawing in concealment and subtlety.

text:
The Lisān defines dasā as the opposite of zakā (to grow, to be pure) and gathers its authorities' views on dassāhā in Q 91:10, one of whom derives that word from the doubled root d-s-s.

1. **The opposite of zakā.** The article opens: dasā, imperfect yadsā, is the opposite of zakā. Al-Layth gives the verb as dasā, imperfect yadsū, verbal noun daswa, the opposite of zakā (imperfect yazkū, verbal noun zakāh). Such a man is dāsin ("one who dasā"), not zākin ("one who zakā"), and one says dassā nafsahu, "he made himself so". Al-Layth counts the imperfect yadsā as a dialect form and yadsū as more correct.

2. **Hiding oneself.** Ibn al-Aʿrābī: dasā is said of someone who has hidden himself.

3. **Abū Manṣūr: a doubled letter changed.** Abū Manṣūr finds Ibn al-Aʿrābī's gloss close to al-Layth's, and thinks both were going by the change of a doubled letter. Al-Layth, he says, took his account from Q 91:9–10, "he has succeeded who zakkāhā, and he has failed who dassāhā", where dassāhā means "hid it". Abū Manṣūr refers back to the earlier explanation that dassāhā is originally dassasahā: the s's came one after another and one of them was changed to y. A verb dassā that is not converted in this way from the doubled verb of al-dass (hiding) he says he neither knows nor has heard.

4. **The meaning of the verse.** The article gives the meaning as: he has failed who dassā'd his own soul, that is, made it obscure and debased its share. It is also said that the failed soul is one that God has dassā'd. Anything one hides and makes little, one has dasas-ed (dasastahu). A verse that Thaʿlab relates from Ibn al-Aʿrābī, "We visit a man who, as for God, is wary of Him, and as for the deeds of the righteous, follows their lead", is cited with the comment that the poet meant fa-yaʾtammu where he says fa-yaʾtamī.

5. **Hiding from guests.** Abū al-Haytham: dassā fulānun nafsahu is said of a man who hides himself and makes himself obscure out of meanness, for fear that he will be noticed and asked for hospitality.

6. **Inciting and corrupting.** The article also records dasā, with the verbal nouns daswan and dasyan, as the contrary of zakā (the subject here is al-layl, "the night", as the text reads). It lists dassā nafsahu and form V tadassā, and gives dassāhu as "he incited him and corrupted him". It cites Q 91:10 again, and a verse that Ibn al-Aʿrābī recited from a man of Ṭayyiʾ: "You are the one who dassayta ʿAmr, so that their women became widows of them, forsaken". The comment explains dassayta as "you led astray and corrupted", and ʿAmr as a tribe.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root د ث ر (d-th-r), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha — companion, more analytical entry to al-Khalīl's on the same root

One sound, regular root: the doubling/piling of a thing, one layer upon another.

1. al-dathr — abundant wealth; al-dithār — an outer wrap, worn over al-shiʿār (the garment worn against the skin) — hence "doubling/layering." A poetic variant, "al-ʿakar al-dathir," is explained as a metrically-shifted form of al-dathr, meaning "abundant."
2. Figurative extension: taddaththara al-faḥlu al-nāqata — a stallion camel mounting a she-camel, as though becoming a dithār (covering) over her; taddaththara al-rajulu farasahu — a man leaping onto and riding his horse — both images of "covering/layering over."
3. al-dathūr — a heavy sleeper, named because he wraps himself up (yataddaththaru) to sleep.
4. rasm dāthir — an effaced trace (of an abandoned encampment) — Ibn Fāris explains this fits the same root logic: the trace stays visible until wind and drifting sand accumulate over it, becoming like a dithār that conceals it.

text:
Root د و ل (dwl) — Tāj al-ʿArūs (al-Zabīdī)

**1. Core meaning: a turn, a rotation of fortune**
Al-dawlah is time turning from hardship and misery to a state of enviable joy. It is also "the turn" in wealth — one party's share or rotation in property, explained via nawbah ("turn") and badal ("exchange"). Lexicographers disagree over the vowel: some give ḍamm (dūlah) for wealth/property and fatḥ (dawlah) for war (Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ); others say ḍamm is for the thing itself that circulates and fatḥ is the act of circulating it (Abū ʿUbayd); others say ḍamm is for this-worldly rule/custom and fatḥ names a single occurrence; others (ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar) say the two forms are simply interchangeable for both wealth and war, and Yūnus admits he can't tell them apart. Zabīdī's own teacher notes it is used for a person's run of good luck ("so-and-so's dawlah has arrived"). Plural: duwal (vocalized three ways). Ibn Jinnī uses the odd plural pattern to argue the word was originally felt as dūlah, because wāw naturally follows a ḍammah — evidence, he says, of how unstable the "weak" letters (w/y/alif) are.

**2. In war**
Al-dawlah in war is that one side gets the upper hand/victory (tudāl) over the other — "we had the dawlah over them."

**3. The Qur'anic reading — Q59:7**
On "kay lā yakūna dūlatan bayna al-aghniyāʾ minkum" ("so that it not become a dūlah circulating among the rich among you"), al-Farrāʾ reports al-Sulamī read it with fatḥ (dawlatan) and argues dūlah (ḍamm) doesn't belong here at all: dawlah is what happens between two armies — one defeats the other, then the victor is later defeated in turn, so people say "the dawlah has come back around to these," almost meaning "one round/instance."

**4. Circulation, giving/receiving victory — the verbs**
Adāla (God) "gave someone the turn/victory": adālanā Allāhu min ʿaduwwinā, "God gave us victory over our enemy" — al-idālah = ghalabah, "victory" ("O God, give me the turn over so-and-so"). Al-Ḥajjāj's saying "the earth will be given its turn over us as we had our turn over it" is glossed as "it will consume us as we consumed it." Tadāwalū: "they took it in turns," passed it hand to hand. This is the sense of Q3:140, "those days We rotate (nudāwiluhā) among people" — i.e., turn them around, from dāla, "to revolve." Dālat al-ayyām, "the days turned."

**5. The idiom dawālayka**
Means "turn-taking upon the matter" — Sībawayh allows also "it happened in this state" or "turn after turn." It belongs to a small family of frozen dual-suffixed words (with ḥajāzayka, "intervene/restrain yourself," and hadhādhayka, "settle it decisively"). It comes from tadāwalū al-amra baynahum, each side taking a dawlah in turn — illustrated by a verse about a man tearing a woman's clothes to see her body, and her tearing his in return: "dawālayka, until none of us is left clothed." With the article added it can act as a noun (al-dawālayka), and also describes a forceful bracing gait, or a swaggering walk when the body sways.

**6. andāla — sagging, protruding, hanging**
Used of a stabbed man's guts spilling from his belly; of a belly gone slack and drooping toward the ground; and generally of anything that sways and dangles loosely (illustrated by an obscure verse about a sagging pack-load, cited from Ibn Durayd — the text here is partly unclear). Al-Sīrāfī explains the form mundāl as a metathesis of tadallī ("to hang down"), and notes that, being a metathesized form, it has no verbal noun of its own.

**7. Other, more concrete senses of the noun**
- al-duwalah: a name for calamity/disaster (like al-tuwalah).
- al-dawīl: dried-out, year-or-two-old plant growth with no nutritional value — illustrated by a verse of al-Rāʿī about camels reduced to eating it; or specifically dried naṣī/sabaṭ grass, or any withered, blackened plant.
- al-dawālī: a black Ṭāʾifī grape with a reddish tinge.
- al-dālah: fame/renown; dāla yadūlu = "he became famous."
- al-dawlah (anatomical/zoological): a bird's crop (from its sagging), a camel's inflatable throat-sac (shiqshiqah), a narrow-mouthed skin-bag, a bird's gizzard, or the side of the belly; dāla baṭnuhu repeats the "belly went slack" sense above.
- Dūlān: a place-name; "he brought dūlāhu wa-tūlāhu / dūlātihi wa-tūlātihi" = "he brought disaster."
- al-dawl: a metathesized dialect form of al-dalw, "bucket"; also, without the tāʾ, another word for "turn of fortune."
- al-dawal: arrows shared/circulated in common use among a group.

**8. Metaphorical extension**
Abū Zayd: dāla al-thawbu = the garment wore out; "his affection began to dūlu" = it faded — explicitly marked as a figurative (majāz) usage.

**9. Tribal and personal names**
Several early Arab lineages carry this root as a name: al-Dūl (a branch of Banū Ḥanīfah, and of Bakr ibn Wāʾil — whose Farwah ibn Nufāthah ruled Syria in pre-Islamic times — plus lines among the Azd and al-Ribāb); al-Dīl (a branch of ʿAbd al-Qays that produced the people of Oman, a Basran judge, and a companion of ʿAlī, among others; also lines among the Azd, Iyād, and Kinānah — kin of Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī — and among ʿAnazah); and Banū Dālān (a Hamdān subtribe in Kūfah, including a ḥadīth-narrator of disputed reliability, and a poet who wrote of a keen heart, a sharp sword, and a spirit that keeps wrongs away).

**10. Miscellany added by later compilers (mustadrak)**
- al-dawalāt = plural of dūlah, illustrated by verses of al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad (on friends who only wanted his "turns" of luck) and a satire of the governor al-Muhallab ("with turns of fortune you squandered people's blood").
- "mā aʿẓama dūlata baṭnihi" = idiom for "his navel."
- al-diwalah = calamity (another word for the same idea).
- indāla al-qawm = the people gathered together from place to place.
- Grammar note on the letter al-dāl itself: its articulation point, that it can be masculine or feminine, its plurals (adwāl or dālāt), and that it can stand in for tāʾ after a jīm, as in one anomalous (shādhdh) Qur'anic variant reading.
- al-Khalīl also records al-dāl as a word for "a plump woman," with an illustrative verse.
- al-duwāl: yet another small Arab subtribe carrying the root.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats د-و-م (d-w-m) as one root whose single idea is **stillness and staying put** — being motionless, and by extension continuing without break.

**1. To be still / motionless.** دَامَ / يَدُومُ (dāma / yadūmu) = to become still. الماء الدائم (al-māʾ al-dāʾim) is standing, unmoving water. Ibn Fāris supports this reading with a report forbidding urinating into "dāʾim water" and then washing from it, and argues the sense is confirmed because another wording of the same report says "الماء القائم" — standing water. His method here is textual: a parallel transmission fixes the meaning of the word.

**2. To quiet something that is boiling.** أَدَمْتُ القِدْرَ (adamtu al-qidr) = to still a pot's boiling by adding water. Shāhid from al-Jaʿdī: "Their pot boils over against us, and we still it (nudīmuhā) … and cool it away from us when its heat rises."

**3. Hovering — apparent motionlessness in the air.** تَدْوِيم الطائر (tadwīm al-ṭāʾir): a bird circling high, which at that point seems to hold a standstill.

**4. The sun at the meridian.** دَوَّمَتِ الشمس في كبد السماء — the sun "dawwamat" when it reaches mid-heaven; observers say it seems to pause there before declining. Dhū al-Rumma: "the sun is bewildered, having a tadwīm in the sky" — i.e. as though it is not moving on.

**5. A disputed line.** In a verse describing dogs — "until, when they dawwamat over the ground, pride came back to him, though flight could have saved him" — Ibn Fāris reports the judgement that the poet erred: he meant دَوَّتْ (dawwat) and said دَوَّمَتْ; the point is treated in that other root's chapter.

**6. Dissolving saffron.** دَوَّمْتُ الزعفران = I steeped/dissolved it. Ibn Fāris says this follows the root's analogy, because the saffron settles and comes to rest in the liquid.

**7. Form X: to proceed gently so a thing lasts.** اسْتَدَمْتُ الأمر (istadamtu al-amr) = to handle a matter gently. His explanation: gentleness, without harshness or haste, is what makes a thing endure. Shāhid: "Do not hasten your affair — take it slowly; none has warmed [and straightened] your staff like one who takes his time."

**8. "Hope keeps the covetous man's mouth moist."** On the line وقد يُدَوِّمُ ريقَ الطامعِ الأملُ, Ibn Fāris rejects the gloss "moistens" (yabullu) and holds that yudawwimu means "makes it last / keeps it going," reasoning that it is the man who despairs whose saliva dries up.

**9. دِيمَة (dīma):** rain that keeps on for a day and a night or more. Ibn Fāris places under this an answer of ʿĀʾisha, asked about the Prophet's practice: "his practice was a dīma" — i.e. continuous. He explains it as keeping something up steadily, little or much, without breaking off, and says she meant this of his devotional practice.

**10. Wine's effect.** دَوَّمَتْهُ الخمر — wine "dawwamat" him: on Ibn Fāris's account it belongs here because it makes him heavy until his movements come to rest.

**11. دَأْمَاء (daʾmāʾ), the sea.** He suggests it may belong to this root, since it is standing water that is never drained and never leaves. Shāhid: "and the night is like the daʾmāʾ, wearing beneath it a colour like that of sudūs (dark cloth)."

Throughout, the derivational argument is the same one: things called by this root either sit motionless (still water, the sea, the steeped saffron, the pot taken off the boil, the drinker) or seem to hold in place / carry on unbroken (the hovering bird, the sun at the meridian, the long rain, unhurried handling of an affair, sustained hope).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root d-w-n from a single core sense: nearness and proximity.

1. Core sense — nearness. هَذَا دُونَ ذَاكَ (hādhā dūna dhāka) means "this is nearer than that." The diminutive form is دُوَيْن (duwayn). Ibn Fāris notes that no verb is derived directly from this sense.

2. Use in urging. In the imperative of incitement (ighrāʾ), دُونَكَهُ (dūnaka-hu) means "take it — get near it and draw it close to you."

3. Extension to "low in value." أَمْرٌ دُونٌ (a dūn affair) and ثَوْبٌ دُونٌ (a dūn garment) mean something of low or slight value — literally "near/close" in worth, hence cheap.

4. A weakness-sense reported from al-Qutaybī. He gives the verb دَانَ / يَدُونُ / دَوْنًا (dāna, yadūnu, dawnan) meaning "to become weak," with the form udīnu / idānatan. Supporting verse: "and upon the herd of wild cows came a hardship that was not weakened (lam yudan / lam yuḍʿaf)." Al-Qutaybī links this to al-shayʾ al-dūn, "the paltry thing."

Ibn Fāris adds a caution: if al-Qutaybī's weakness-sense is correct, then it too traces back by analogy to the root's core meaning (nearness/lowness) that he has laid out.
