text:
Ibn Fāris treats د-و-ر (d-w-r) as a single root whose core idea is one thing encircling or surrounding another from its sides. The base verb is دَارَ / يَدُورُ (to turn, revolve), verbal noun دَوَرَان.

1. **Time as "the turner."** الدَّوَّارِيّ (the ever-turning) is a name for al-dahr (time/fate), because it turns people through one condition after another. Cited: "and time, with man, is ever-turning."

2. **al-duwār — a circled stone.** A stone once taken from the Ḥaram to a spot aside and circumambulated; said to belong to the precinct of the Kaʿba that is circled. Two shawāhid: "as the women circled about the duwār," and a verse on Banū al-Hujaym whose assembly "circles round" when it moves.

3. **al-duwār — dizziness.** Vertigo in the head, from the same turning sense. Forms: دِيرَ بِهِ / أُدِيرَ بِهِ (he was made giddy); the person is madūr bihi / mudār bihi.

4. **al-dāʾira.** The whorl of little turning hairs in a horse's throat — a known term.

5. **دَارَتْ بِهِمُ الدَّوَائِر** — "adverse turns of fortune encircled them," i.e., disliked conditions surrounded them.

6. **al-dār (root letter wāw) = the tribe.** Beyond "house," dār denotes a tribe. Ibn Fāris cites two prophetic ḥadīths using dūr/dār for tribes: "the best of the dūr of the Anṣār" (= the tribes), and "no dār remained but a mosque was built in it" (= no tribe).

7. **al-dārī = the perfumer.** A ḥadīth likens a good companion to the dārī whose scent clings to you even if he gives you no perfume; the sense intended is "perfumer." A verse describes the dārī musk-merchant. The word derives from dār (house): he is called dārī because he dwells in the house.

8. **al-dārī = a homebody.** Also the man who stays in his house and hardly leaves; supported by a verse contrasting the "stay-at-homes" with mounted travelers.

9. **al-dāra.** Level ground ringed by mountains; the Arabs have many such dārāt, and Ibn Fāris says the origin of dār is dāra. Two shawāhid illustrate the singular and the plural dārāt.

10. **Named dārāt.** The entry closes with a long list of about thirty-five famous Arabian dārāt (place-names), e.g., Dārat Juljul, Dārat al-Salam, Dārat Ṣulṣul, Dārat Māsal, Dārat al-Dūr, Dārat Rahbā, and many more.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: دَخَلَ 76x "enter"; أُدْخِلَ 42x "he will admit him"; مُّدْخَل 3x "(to) an entrance"; دَٰخِلُون 2x "those who enter"; دَخَل 2x "(as) a deception"; مُدَّخَل 1x "a place to enter"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats د-خ-ل (d-kh-l) as a single, regularly patterned root whose core sense is entering, going in, penetration (wulūj): دَخَلَ = "he entered."

From that core he derives a range of senses, each turning on something having "gone in":

1. Inner / hidden matter: al-dukhla is the concealed inner state of a person — "I know his inner state (dukhla)."

2. Defect in lineage: al-dakhal is a flaw in one's pedigree (ḥasab), as if something had "entered" and spoiled it. He links it to al-daghal (corruption/blight), which he says follows the same analogy.

3. Emaciation: al-madkhūl means the lean/wasted one — sound, he says, because the flesh is as though it had been eaten into ("entered").

4. Intimate associate: dakhīluka (also al-dukhlal) is one admitted deep into your affairs, a close confidant.

5. Interleaved watering: al-dikhāl at a watering-place is the practice of letting the camels drink, then returning them to the trough so any that had not yet drunk may do so — cited with a line of al-Hudhalī on "an interleaved drinking (shurb dikhāl)."

6. Lump of flesh / a bird's name: any compact lump of flesh is a dukhkhala; from this the wren-like bird is called dukhkhal.

7. Mental disturbance: dukhila fulān / he is madkhūl when there is a "dakhal" (flaw/disturbance) in his mind.

8. Adjoined lineage: to say a clan is dakhīl among another clan means they attach their genealogy to them as incomers.

9. Rotted core: a madkhūla palm-tree is one decayed on the inside.

10. Feathers: the dukhkhal of a bird's plumage is the layer between back- and belly-feathers — the finest feathers.

11. Inner edge of a garment: dākhilat al-izār is the waist-wrapper's edge that lies against the body.

12. In-grown herbage: the dukhkhal of pasturage is the growth that has pushed in among the roots of the trees — with a poetic line on "dusky dukhkhal and lush jamīm grass."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris (Maqayis al-Lugha) treats d-kh-n as a single root whose core sense is "what comes from fuel/kindling", i.e. smoke, from which everything resembling it, including enmity and rancor, is metaphorically named.

1. Smoke itself: al-dukhan is the ordinary word for smoke; its plural dawakhin is irregular (not formed by the usual pattern).

2. Verb forms distinguished by vowel pattern:
- dakhanat (fire) tadkhunu - the fire smoked, i.e. its smoke rose.
- dakhinat (fire) tadkhanu - a different pattern, meaning: you piled firewood on it and thereby ruined it, causing smoke to billow up.
- dakhina l-ta'am yadkhanu - food became smoke-tainted (spoiled by smoke) in the same way.
- dakhana l-ghubar - the dust rose (the same verb extended to dust, not just smoke).

3. The hadith phrase "hudnatun 'ala dakhan" ("a truce upon dakhan") - Ibn Faris glosses this as a settling or steadying upon matters that are disliked/detestable, i.e. an uneasy truce masking lingering resentment (the "smoke" sense carried into the abstract).

4. Color sense: al-dukhnah names a dusky color, a murkiness within black. This gives rise to a small cluster of color terms: a ewe called dakhna', a ram called adkhan, and a night called dakhnanah (all sharing that smoky-grey/overcast hue).

5. Character sense: a man is called dakhinu l-khuluq, literally "smoky of disposition", meaning ill-tempered or rancorous - the metaphorical extension to enmity that Ibn Faris flagged at the outset.

6. A tribal epithet: "the sons of Dukhan" (Abna'u Dukhan) refers to the groups Ghaniyy and Bahilah.

7. Incense: al-dukhnah also names an incense/fumigant used to perfume a house with smoke.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats د-خ-ر as having one base sense, plus one look-alike word he explicitly excludes.

1. Base sense — lowliness/abasement. The three letters point to ذُلّ (being brought low, humbled). دَخَرَ الرَّجُلُ = the man was abased; the active participle دَاخِرٌ = one who is abased/humbled.
2. Causative form. أَدْخَرَهُ (form IV, with another person as agent) = he abased him, brought him low.
3. Excluded homograph — دَخْدَار. This word means a fine garment that is kept carefully stored away. He cites the verse fragment "and he polishes the surface of a new dakhdār." Ibn Fāris states this belongs to no part of the first entry, since it is a loanword (muʿarrab): its origin is reported as Persian takht dār, i.e. something kept safe in a chest (takht).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: دِين 92x "the religion"; دَيْن 5x "any debt"; مَدِينِين 2x "surely be brought to judgment"; تَدَايَن 1x "you contract with one another"; يَدِينُ 1x "they acknowledge"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives all uses of the root d-y-n (دين) from one core idea: submission/compliance (inqiyād) and lowliness or abasement (dhull).

1. Dīn as obedience/submission. Al-dīn is "obedience." One says dāna lahu ("he submitted and obeyed him"); qawmun dīn means "an obedient, submissive people." Shāhid: "and mankind, except us, were submissive."

2. Related derivations of submission:
- Al-madīna ("city," pattern maf ʿala): so named because the obedience owed to authority is enforced in it.
- Al-madīna also = "slave-woman"; al-ʿabd is madīn ("a bondsman") — as if service had abased them. Shāhid: "...the son of a slave-woman who keeps pressing on his spade."
- The line "O, the abasement (dīn) of your heart because of Salmā, when it has been abased" means the heart was brought low (udhilla).

3. Dīn as habit/custom. Some hold a habit (ʿāda) is called dīn; if so, it is because the soul, once accustomed to something, goes along with and submits to it. Shāhid (from Imruʾ al-Qays): "like your wont (ka-dīnika) with Umm al-Ḥuwayrith..." — a variant reads ka-daʾbika ("your custom"), with a close meaning.

4. Qurʾānic usage (as Ibn Fāris explains it):
- {fī dīni l-malik} (Yūsuf 12:76): "under the king's ṭāʿa (authority/obedience)" or "under his ḥukm (judgment/rule)."
- {māliki yawmi l-dīn} (al-Fātiḥa 1:4): "Master of the Day of Judgment/Rule (ḥukm)"; some say it means "the Day of Reckoning and Requital." Either way, it is something one submits to.

5. A passive usage. Abū Zayd: dīna al-rajulu yudānu — "he was burdened with what he dislikes."

6. Al-dayn (debt) — same chapter. To deal on credit (giving or taking) is dāyana; dintu/iddantu = "I took on credit," adantu = "I lent." Shawāhid illustrate crediting and repayment. Debt fits the root's core because it carries "all abasement and lowliness"; hence the proverb: "Debt is humiliation by day and grief by night."

7. A disputed shāhid. The verse "...I task her with nothing but al-Marāna until she recognizes al-dīn": per al-Aṣmaʿī, al-Marāna is the poet's she-camel, who knew the road; here al-dīn means "the state/condition and the familiar matter" — the poet means he relies only on his camel to reach the abode.

Ibn Fāris closes by noting that hamzated and weak-alif forms may also belong here, treated in their own chapters.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
text:
Root f-sh-l (ف ش ل) — Tāj al-ʿArūs, al-Zabīdī

1. Core verb — فَشِلَ (fashila), noun فَشَل, adjective فَشِل: to grow sluggish, weak, slack, cowardly, and afraid. Al-Zabīdī cites two Qur'anic instances: "when two parties among you were about to lose heart" and "do not dispute, lest you lose heart and your strength depart." He quotes the grammarian al-Zajjāj's gloss: it means becoming cowardly before an enemy once disagreement sets in — disagreement weakens people, while unity increases their strength.

2. A weak, cowardly man — رجل خَشْل فَشْل, both words with fatḥ. Al-Zabīdī flags that al-Qāmūs (the base dictionary he is annotating) mis-transcribed this as فَشِل; the correct source text (al-Muḥkam) gives خَشْل فَشْل and خَسْل فَسْل — the same phrase with shīn or sīn, two dialect variants, not the vowel pattern al-Qāmūs's author assumed.

3. Plural فُشْل: supported by a line of poetry about spearheads that overtook the poet — "neither weak nor fushl" — also transmitted with sīn (fusl). A further plural, أَفْشَال, is reported from al-Jawharī.

4. الفِشْل (kasr): the curtain/cover of a woman's howdage, or an item of howdaj furnishing placed beneath her — sources differ on the vowel. Plural فُشُول.

5. A cluster of verbs about outfitting a howdaj — افْتَشَلَتْ / تَفَشَّلَتْ / فَشَّلَتْه: a woman hangs a garment over the howdaj, draws it inside, and ties its edges to the frame's base, protecting against the frame's curved bows, the pack-saddles, and the rope-knots (per Ibn Shumayl).

6. تَفَشَّلَ منهم: he married into them (Ibn al-Sikkīt). تَفَشَّلَ الماء: the water flowed.

7. الفَيْشَلَة: the glans/tip of the penis, or "the head of anything bulging." Al-Zabīdī works through a morphological debate (echoing Ibn Jinnī) over whether the lām or the yāʾ is the augmented (non-root) letter, comparing it to the pair ḍayyāṭ/ḍayṭār. Plural فياشل (also formed by dropping the final hāʾ). Illustrated with a mocking line by the poet Jarīr about a rival tribe's crude eating habits.

8. Al-Fayāshil, by extension, also names: a kind of tree; a spring belonging to Banū Ḥuṣayn; and red hillocks around that spring (named for their resemblance to sense 7), with a supporting verse by al-Qattāl al-Kilābī.

9. المِفْشَل: (a) the howdaj's covering (Ibn al-Aʿrābī); (b) a man who marries outside his close kin, so the child is not born frail.

10. Al-Farrāʾ: al-tafshīl / al-tamshīl — the milk left over in the udder [after milking].

11. فَشَال: a village near Zabīd on the road to Mecca. Al-Ufshūliyya: a village near Wāsiṭ, home town of the blind grammarian Ḥabashī ibn Muḥammad al-Ufshūlī.

12. Additional notes: two attested Qur'anic recitation variants of the verb (yafshulu vs. yafshilu, following different conjugation patterns — one read by al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī), transmitted by al-Ṣāghānī.

13. الفَشْل = "the weak one," illustrated by a rain-prayer verse about poor food (last season's colocynth, weak ʿilhiz plant) — al-Zabīdī compares this to the Qur'anic "cursed tree," where a quality is attributed to the thing itself though it really belongs to those who consume/depend on it.

14. Minor entries: al-mifshala (a vessel/implement, per Ibn Shumayl, not further defined here); فَنْشَلَ لحيته — he ruffled his beard; فَشْل — a village in Yemen.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ف-أ-د (f-ʾ-d) as a single sound root whose core idea is fever and intense heat. He derives its usages from that core:

1. Roasting/broiling by heat: فَأَدْتُ اللَّحْمَ (faʾadtu al-laḥma) = "I roasted the meat"; the passive result is فَئِيد (faʾīd) = "roasted."
2. Related instruments/places: المِفْأَد (mifʾad) = the roasting-spit or skewer (safūd); المُفْتَأَد (muftaʾad) = the place where roasting is done. He cites a verse of poetry picturing a forgotten roasting-spit left "at the roasting-place" (muftaʾad).
3. الفُؤَاد (fuʾād, the heart): in Ibn Fāris's judgment this fits the same root by analogy, the heart being named for its heat.
4. الفَأْد (faʾd): the verbal noun of فَأَدْتُهُ (faʾadtuhu) = "to strike someone's heart (fuʾād)."
5. Baking in embers: فَأَدْتُ الْمَلَّة (faʾadtu al-malla) = to bake bread in hot ashes.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: al-Namir b. Tawlab (lived into Islam); Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad)
text:
Ibn Manẓūr treats the root as ف-أ-و / ف-أ-ي, with wāw and yāʾ forms alongside each other. The core idea is splitting, cleaving, and parting apart, from which the other senses branch.

1. To strike or split. فَأَوْتُه بالعَصا = "I struck him with the staff" (from Ibn al-Aʿrābī). Al-Layth: فَأَوْتُ / فَأَيْتُ رأْسَه = "I split his head" with a sword — or, more precisely, struck the skull-bone until it opened away from the brain.

2. Cleaving / cracking generally. الفَأْو = a cleft or split. The verb is used of cracking a cup: فَأَيْتُ القَدَحَ فَتَفَأَى / انْفَأَى = "I cracked the cup and it split apart." The reflexive forms انْفَأَى / تَفَأَى mean "it split open."

3. The word فِئة (party/company of people) is said to derive from this root — a "party" being a portion split off from the whole.

4. Landscape senses (all from the idea of parting):
   - A fissure in a mountain (al-Liḥyānī).
   - The ground lying between two mountains; the low soft ground between two lava-fields; or a rounded sandy hollow. Shāhid from al-Namir b. Tawlab: an ungrazed fāʾw of land, its meadow concealed, "encircled by landmarks."
   - Al-Aṣmaʿī: a hollow of ground ringed by sands, long or otherwise — called fāʾw because the surrounding heights part away from it.

5. In Dhū al-Rumma's verse (the camels crossing until "انْفَأَى الفَأْوُ"), fāʾw means the tract they traversed and emerged from. One reported gloss takes al-fāʾw here as "the night" (Abū Laylā), which Ibn Sīda says he cannot vouch for; the Tahdhīb glosses انْفَأَى as "became uncovered / disclosed."

6. As a place-name: فَأْو الرَّيّان, a wide pass between two hillocks in the district of al-Daww; al-Azharī notes he passed by it.

7. الفَأْوى (shortened form): the glans of the penis (al-faysha), with a supporting verse.

8. فِئة (company/faction of people): plurals فِئات and فِئُون. The final hāʾ replaces a dropped weak letter. Ibn Manẓūr first says it stands for yāʾ; Ibn Barrī corrects this to wāw, since fiʾa is a group split off, from فَأَوْتُ ("I divided, split") — though he allows the yāʾ derivation too, since both فَأْواً and فَأْياً are transmitted. The Tahdhīb: fiʾa (pattern fiʿa) comes from فَأَيْتُ رأسه ("I split his head"); it was originally fiʾwa (fiʿla) and got shortened.

9. Usage note from a hadith: when Ibn ʿUmar's party returned from a raid he told them «أنا فِئتُكم» ("I am your fiʾa"). Here fiʾa means both the company of people in general and, specifically, the reserve detachment stationed behind an army, to which fighters fall back if they meet fear or defeat.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats f-ḍ-ḍ as a sound root pointing to separating and dividing into parts.

1. **Separating, dispersing.** Faḍaḍtu al-shayʾ means I separated the thing; infaḍḍa means it came apart. Infaḍḍa al-qawm means the people dispersed. The Qur'an has "had you been harsh, hard of heart, they would have dispersed (la-nfaḍḍū) from around you" (Q 3:159).

2. **Breaking a seal.** Faḍaḍtu ʿan al-kitāb khatmahu: I broke the seal off the letter.

3. **Silver (fiḍḍa), tentatively.** Ibn Fāris says it is possible that fiḍḍa belongs here, as though silver is broken up for the ornaments made from it.

4. **Fragments (fiḍāḍ).** What breaks off from a thing when it comes apart.

5. **Calamity (fāḍḍa, plural fawāḍḍ).** So called as though it breaks people apart and disperses them.

6. **Ampleness (faḍfaḍa), by analogy.** Among derivations he says may be drawn by analogy: faḍfaḍa is the wideness of a garment; a faḍfāḍ garment or a faḍfāḍa coat of mail is ample, because when it is wide its edges lie far apart.

7. **Sweet water (faḍīḍ).** Fresh sweet water, named for its faḍāḍa and the ease with which it passes down the throat.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) treats ف-ض-ح as carrying two related core meanings.

1. Exposure / uncovering (always of something shameful)
- افضح الصبح / فضّح — "the dawn broke/showed itself," used of first light appearing.
- الفضوح (al-fuḍūḥ) — the tearing-away of cover, i.e. disgrace, public exposure.
- افتضح الرجل (iftaḍaḥa) — "the man was disgraced," said when his faults or vices became uncovered.
Ibn Fāris notes this sense is almost never used except of something ugly/shameful — the root inherently marks a bad exposure, not a neutral one.

2. An unattractive color
- الفضح (al-faḍaḥ) — a dusty color mixed with an ashen/dun hue; he calls it "an ugly color."
- أفضح البسر — unripe dates are said to "become faḍaḥ-colored" when redness first shows in them.
- الأفضح (al-afḍaḥ) — an epithet for the lion, and likewise the camel, taken from this same faḍaḥ coloring.

Ibn Fāris presents these as two parallel senses of one root: uncovering something shameful, and an unpleasing dusty/ashen color — with the second explicitly linked back to the root by name (faḍaḥ al-lawn, "the faḍaḥ of color").

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: فَضْل 84x "his bounty"; فَضَّلَ 17x "and we preferred them"; تَفْضِيل 2x "(in) excellence"; يَتَفَضَّلَ 1x "assert (his) superiority"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root f-ḍ-l from a single core idea: an increase or excess in something.

1. الفَضْل (al-faḍl): surplus, extra — and, by extension, "good."

2. الإفْضال (al-ifḍāl): doing good, beneficence; a مُفْضِل (mufḍil) is a man who acts beneficently.

3. Verb: فَضَلَ … يَفْضُلُ (faḍala…yafḍulu) = "to be left over, remain in surplus." A variant فَضِلَ (faḍila) also occurs but is rare.

4. المُتَفَضِّل (al-mutafaḍḍil): one who claims superiority over his equals and peers. Ibn Fāris cites Qurʾān 23:24, where objectors say a man "wishes to exalt himself (yatafaḍḍala) over you."

5. A second sense of المُتَفَضِّل: someone draped or wrapped loosely in his garment. Related is الفُضُل (al-fuḍul): a person wearing only a shirt and a cloak, without a waist-wrapper or trousers — i.e., in undress. He supports this clothing sense with a line of Imruʾ al-Qays describing a woman who sleeps late "without girding herself," in loose morning attire (tafaḍḍul).

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib defines al-faḍāʾ as the wide place and derives the verb afḍā from it.

1. **Al-faḍāʾ.** The wide place.

2. **Afḍā, to reach.** From al-faḍāʾ come afḍā bi-yadihi ilā kadhā, "he reached out with his hand to such-and-such", and afḍā ilā imraʾatihi, "he reached his wife". Al-Rāghib notes that as an indirect expression the latter says more, and comes closer to plain statement, than the phrase khalā bihā, "he was alone with her". He cites Q 4:21, wa-qad afḍā baʿḍukum ilā baʿḍ, "and one of you has reached the other".

3. **Faḍan, open to all.** A poet's line, "their food is fawḍā faḍan in their abodes", is explained as meaning that the food is open to all (mubāḥ), as though it had been set down in a faḍāʾ, a wide place, into which whoever wants it pours.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: فَعَلَ 88x "does"; فَاعِل 9x "doers"; مَفْعُول 7x "to be fulfilled"; فَعَّال 2x "doer"; فِعْل 1x "(the) doing"; فَعْلَت 1x "your deed"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats f-ʿ-l as a single sound root whose core sense is bringing something about — an action (ʿamal) or otherwise.

1. Verb and verbal noun: faʿaltu kadhā afʿaluhu faʿlan — "I did such-a-thing, I do it," the verbal noun being faʿl.

2. faʿla (with the -a of a single instance): a discrete deed, which can be "fair or foul" — the word is neutral as to whether the act is good or bad.

3. Morphology: fiʿāl is given as the plural of fiʿl (a deed/act).

4. faʿāl (with fatḥa on the first letter) is a distinct word meaning generosity or nobility (al-karam) — the good that a person does.

5. The author adds one word he is uncertain about: some say fiʿāl also denotes the wooden haft of an axe. He explicitly flags that he does not know whether this usage is sound.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root F-Ḥ-Sh from a single core notion: ugliness or foulness in a thing, together with hideousness.

1. Core sense — foulness/ugliness. From this root come al-fuḥsh (obscenity, foulness), al-faḥshāʾ (indecency), and al-fāḥisha (a gross or indecent act).

2. Exceeding proper measure. Anything that goes beyond its due measure is called fāḥish (excessive, outrageous) — but the word is applied only to what is found abhorrent, not to excess in something desirable.

3. Speaking obscenity. The verb afḥasha (also faḥasha) means to utter obscene speech; the intensive form faḥḥāsh describes a habitually foul-mouthed person.

4. Extended sense — the miser. Al-fāḥish is also used for a miser. Ibn Fāris notes this is a figurative extension (ittisāʿ), on the reasoning that stinginess is the ugliest trait in a person. He cites Ṭarafa: "I see death picking off the noble and selecting out the wealth of the tight-fisted miser."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root f-ṣ-ḥ (فصح) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: purity/clarity in something, and being free of any admixture.

1. The "clear tongue/speech" sense. al-lisān al-faṣīḥ ("the faṣīḥ tongue") = the free, unimpeded tongue. al-kalām al-faṣīḥ ("faṣīḥ speech") = Arabic speech.

2. Etymological base: milk. The root usage is said to be afṣaḥa al-laban, "the milk's froth settled" — i.e. once the foam subsides/clears, the pure milk underneath is faṣīḥ. A related report: faṣuḥa al-laban fa-huwa faṣīḥ, "the milk became faṣīḥ once the froth was skimmed off it," with the note that "beneath the froth is the clear (faṣīḥ) milk."

3. Applied to human speech. afṣaḥa al-rajul = "the man spoke Arabic." faṣuḥa = his speech became sound/excellent, free of laḥn (grammatical lapses).

4. A disputed usage note. Ibn Durayd's book distinguishes: an Arab "afṣaḥa" (form IV) but a non-Arab "faṣuḥa" (form I), when each speaks Arabic. Ibn Fāris rejects this distinction as a mistake, holding that the earlier account (simply: to speak sound Arabic) is correct.

5. Extended to light/clarity generally. afṣaḥa al-ṣubḥ = "dawn broke," i.e. its light became clear/manifest. General principle stated: "everything clear is mufṣiḥ." Also: al-aʿjam is what does not articulate (speak clearly), while al-faṣīḥ is what does articulate.

6. Explicit exclusion. Ibn Fāris notes that al-fiṣḥ, "the feast of the Christians" (with the expression afṣaḥū, "their feast has come"), does NOT belong to this root's core meaning — i.e. he treats it as an unrelated, look-alike word rather than a derivative of the "purity/clarity" sense.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: فَصَّلَ 17x "we explain"; فَصْل 9x "(of) judgment"; فَصَلَ 5x "will judge"; تَفْصِيل 5x "and a detailed explanation"; فِصَال 3x "weaning"; فَٰصِلِين 1x "(of) the deciders"; مُفَصَّل 1x "explained in detail"; مُّفَصَّلَٰت 1x "manifest"; فَصِيلَت 1x "and his nearest kindred"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats فصل (f-ṣ-l) as a single sound root whose core meaning is distinguishing one thing from another and separating it off.

1. Basic verb: فَصَلَ / فَصَلْتُ الشَّيْءَ فَصْلًا — "to separate/divide" a thing (verbal noun faṣl).

2. الْفَيْصَل (al-fayṣal): the arbiter or judge — the one who decides a matter.

3. الْفَصِيل (al-faṣīl): a young camel that has been separated (weaned) from its mother.

4. الْمِفْصَل (al-mifṣal): the tongue — so called because matters are decided and distinguished by means of it. Cited: al-Akhṭal, "…and bones and the tongue have died."

5. الْمَفَاصِل (al-mafāṣil): the joints of the bones.

6. الْمَفْصِل (al-mafṣil): the gap or cleft between two mountains; plural mafāṣil. Cited: Abū Dhuʾayb, comparing a liquid to "the water of the mountain-clefts."

7. الْفَصِيل (al-faṣīl, second sense): an outer wall built below/short of a city's main rampart.

8. From a hadith: نَفَقَة فَاصِلَة (a "separating" expenditure) — glossed within the hadith itself as the spending that separated a person's belief (īmān) from his disbelief (kufr); i.e. a decisive act of giving. Ibn Fāris reports this as the hadith's own explanation.

Across all these senses the unifying idea is separation/decisive division: cutting apart, weaning, judging, or marking a boundary.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: ف ص م (f-ṣ-m). Source: Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha (d. 1004 CE).

Core meaning: This root denotes a thing cracking or fracturing without breaking fully into two separate pieces — a partial crack, not a full break.

1. al-faṣm — a thing cracks/splits without becoming fully detached.
2. Any bent or curved object — of wood or another material — is termed mafṣūm ("cracked/bent"), i.e., it bears this kind of crack at its bend.

Shāhid (poetic citation, poet unnamed in this entry): a verse likens a curved object to a silver bracelet (dumluj), described as notable/renowned, left in a playground where the tribe's young women used to play — the bent, cracked object is called mafṣūm.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: فَطَرَ 10x "created me"; فَاطِر 6x "creator"; فِطْرَت 1x "nature"; فُطُور 1x "flaw"; مُنفَطِر 1x "(will) break apart"; ٱنفَطَرَتْ 1x "(is) cleft asunder"
text:
Ibn Sīda's entry for the root ف ط ر (f-ṭ-r), whose base sense is "to split/cleave," branching into "to originate/create" and "to break a fast."

1. To split, cleave. فَطَرَ / فَطَّرَ = to split a thing. The noun الفَطْر = a cleft/split (plural فُطُور), as in Q al-Mulk 67:3, "do you see any rifts?" Thaʿlab cites a verse where love "split the heart" and then "the rifts closed up."

2. To be split / rent. Intransitive forms فَطَرَ, تَفَطَّرَ, انْفَطَرَ. Cited from Q al-Muzzammil 73:18, "the heaven is rent thereby," where منفطر takes a masculine form by grammatical relation (nasab), compared to دَجاجة مُعْضِل (a hen laboring to lay).

3. Related "cracked/split" uses:
- سَيْفٌ فُطَار = a sword with cracks in it (with a line of ʿAntara).
- فَطَرَ نابُ البعير = a camel's canine split the gum and emerged. In a line of Himyān, al-fuṭūr may mean the cracks (the she-camel being well-knit where others are disjoined), or she is firm and tightly bound at the point of her tooth's emergence.

4. Milking, and related fluids.
- فَطَرَ الناقةَ/الشاةَ = to milk with the fingertips (said to be milking as one counts "thirty" with thumbs and forefingers).
- الفُطْر = the small amount of milk drawn out; also المَذْي (pre-seminal fluid), likened to this milking because both come only in small amount by the fingertips — semen is not so.

5. Splitting open in nature (all from the "split" sense):
- الفُطْر = new plant growth that breaks open; also a kind of truffle/mushroom, since the earth splits over it (singular فُطْرة); also the grape when its tips appear, since the shoots split open.
- التَّفاطِير = the first spring-rain plants; grouped with three other pluralia tantum (التَّعاشِيب, التَّعاجِيب, تَباشِير الصُّبْح "the streaks of dawn") that have no singular.
- التَّفاطِير / النَّفاطِير = pustules on a youth's face (singular نُفْطُور), with a supporting verse.
- فَطَرَ أصابِعَه = he pressed/squeezed his fingers.

6. To originate, create. فَطَرَ اللهُ الخَلْقَ = God created and originated them; cited from Q "Originator (فاطر) of the heavens and the earth." Ibn ʿAbbās says he did not know the word's sense until he heard a bedouin, disputing over a well, say أنا فَطَرْتُها ("I originated/began it"). Related: فَطَرَ الشيءَ = to bring into being / to begin.
- الفِطْرة = (a) the created nature/constitution (with a verse contrasting a man of "a dog's nature" with religion and lineage); (b) per this author, the innate knowledge of God upon which He created mankind.

7. To break a fast. الفِطْر = the opposite of fasting; verbs أَفْطَرَ / فَطَرَ / أَفْطَرَه / فَطَّرَه. Sībawayh notes فَطَّرْتُه فأَفْطَرَ is anomalous. رَجُلٌ/قَومٌ فِطْرٌ = one/people breaking the fast (using the verbal noun as adjective); also مُفْطِر, plural مَفاطِير. الفَطُور = the meal one breaks the fast with (breakfast).

8. Unleavened / hastily made. فَطَرَ العَجِينَ → فَطِير = dough baked at once without leavening (plural فَطْرى); خُبزٌ فَطِيرٌ = unleavened bread; used of unleavened clay too. By extension anything rushed before it is ready is فَطِير, hence the saying "the worst counsel is the half-baked one." فَطَرَ جِلْدَه / أَفْطَرَه = to leave a hide insufficiently tanned (from Ibn al-Aʿrābī).

9. Proper name. فِطْر (Fiṭr) is a name — the traditionist Fiṭr ibn Khalīfa.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats f-ẓ-ẓ as a single word (kalima) that indicates repugnance and aversion.

1. **Paunch water.** al-faẓẓ is the water of the paunch (karish), and uftuẓẓa l-karish is said when the paunch is squeezed out. A poet likens a people to the lion's nose, which has never smelt humiliation, and says the lion does not get at the faẓẓ of its prey until it has rolled it in the dust.

2. **A man of repugnant character.** Ibn Fāris reports that some scholars of the language derive al-faẓāẓa from this. A man who is faẓẓ is one of repugnant character; the word is traced to paunch water because that is taken only under necessity and with repugnance.

3. **al-faẓīẓ.** They also say that al-faẓīẓ is the stallion's water (māʾ al-faḥl), its seminal fluid.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: ٱفْتَدَىٰ 7x "to ransom themselves"; فِدْيَة 3x "any ransom"; تُفَٰدُ 1x "you ransom them"; فَدَيْ 1x "and we ransomed him"; فِدَاء 1x "ransom"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ف-د-ي as two entirely separate words.

1. Ransom / shielding. The core idea is putting one thing in the place of another to protect it. فَدَيْتُهُ ("I ransomed him") means you shield someone with yourself or with something given in his stead. The noun has two forms: with kasra it is lengthened — فِدَاء (fidāʾ) — and with fatḥa it is shortened — فَدَى (fadā); hence both هُوَ فِدَاؤُكَ and هُوَ فَدَاكَ ("he is your ransom"). Poetic witnesses use both forms ("May my mother and aunt be a ransom for you two…"; "May all peoples be a ransom for you…").

From this comes تَفَادَى مِنَ الشَّيْءِ ("to ward oneself off from a thing," to shun it and pull away). Ibn Fāris makes al-tafādī the underlying sense: people shielding themselves by means of one another, each treating his companion as the ransom that spares himself — illustrated by the line of lions "shrinking back, warding themselves off."

2. A heap of food (a homonym, unrelated to sense 1). al-fadāʾ (lengthened form) is the floor on which dates are spread out (misṭaḥ al-tamr), in the dialect of ʿAbd al-Qays — reported by Ibn Durayd. Abū ʿAmr adds that al-fadāʾ is a gathered mass of grain such as barley and dates. A verse compares such a heap of threshed grain, with people gathered round it, to a lone orphaned young partridge.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: فَهَّمْ 1x "and we gave understanding of it"
text:
Root: fhm (فهم) — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (early 11th c. CE)

1. Core definition: al-fahm ("understanding") is a human faculty by which the meanings of what is perceived become established/verified in the mind. Usage: "fahimtu kadhā" — "I understood such-and-such."

2. Qur'anic citation — Q 21:79: "So We made Solomon understand it" (فَفَهَّمْنَاهَا سُلَيْمَانَ).

3. Al-Rāghib offers three possible explanations for how this God-given understanding worked:
   - God granted Solomon a superior natural capacity of understanding, and he arrived at the answer through that capacity himself; or
   - God directly cast the understanding into his mind (rawʿ), without Solomon working it out; or
   - God revealed it to him specifically, singling him out with it.

4. Related word — afhamtu-hu ("I made him understand"): used when you explain something to someone until he forms a clear mental picture of it.

5. Related word — al-istifhām ("inquiry," asking a question): requesting that someone else make you understand something.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats f-j-j as a sound root whose meaning is opening out and parting.

1. **Wide road.** Al-fajj is a wide road.

2. **Bow.** A bow is called fajjāʾ when its string stands well apart from the middle of the bow.

3. **Al-fajaj.** Al-fajaj is uglier than al-faḥaj (legs set wide apart).

4. **Domed hoof.** A hoof is mufijj when it is domed; such a hoof has something like a gap (fajwa) on its inner side.

Ibn Fāris lists two words as departing from this root:

5. **Unripe.** Al-fijj is something that has not yet ripened, of the things that ought to ripen.

6. **Hurrying.** Ibn al-Aʿrābī reports afajja, yufijju, "to hurry". From it comes rajul fajfāj, a man who talks a great deal.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: فَجْر 6x "by the dawn"; فُجِّرَتْ 6x "and we caused to gush forth"; فُجَّار 4x "the wicked ones"; يَفْجُرَ 2x "you cause to gush forth"; تَفْجِير 2x "abundantly"; ٱنفَجَرَتْ 1x "then gushed forth"; يَتَفَجَّرُ 1x "gush forth"; فَاجِر 1x "a wicked"; فُجُور 1x "(to distinguish) its wickedness"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ف-ج-ر (f-j-r) as a single root meaning an opening-up or bursting-open in something. He derives the other senses from that core image:

1. Dawn (al-fajr): the darkness "bursting open" to let the morning through.
2. Water bursting forth (infajara al-māʾ): water breaking open and flowing out; the fujra is the spot where water breaks through (its outlet).
3. Moral transgression (fujūr): by extension, a "bursting out" and breaking loose into acts of disobedience came to be called fujūr. Because of this, lying too was called fujūr.
4. The deviant person (fājir): the usage spread further, so anyone who swerves from the truth is called fājir. In Arab usage anything that leans or deviates is fājir. Ibn Fāris cites Labīd, using fājir of a part of a mount that "leans/deviates" aside (the rump swerving off when the rider holds back).
5. Generosity (al-fajar): also from this root — openhandedness, a "bursting forth" with bounty/good.
6. Valley outflows (mafājir al-wādī): the channels where a valley discharges; Ibn Fāris suggests they are named for the bursting-forth (infijār) of water in them, and quotes a verse placing the mafājir "beside the ʿalandā thorn-tree." Related: munfajar al-raml, a track running through the sand.
7. Yawm al-Fijār: an Arab battle-day named because the sacred truce/inviolability was violated on it.

The organizing method is etymological: one physical sense (bursting open) generates the moral senses (fujūr, fājir) by metaphorical extension, which Ibn Fāris marks with "then this became frequent."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ف-ج-و (f-j-w) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning (per Ibn Fāris's method of one governing sense per root): width or spaciousness in a thing.

1. فَجْوَة (fajwah) — the open, wide gap between two things.
2. قَوْس فَجْوَاء (qaws fajwāʾ) — a bow whose string stands away/apart from its kabid (the bow's central curved "belly"), i.e. a widely-strung bow.
3. فَجْوَةُ الدَّار (fajwat al-dār) — the open courtyard of a house.
4. الفَجَا (al-fajā) — the wide separation between a camel's two hocks (a splayed, bow-legged stance).

A closing note distinguishes a look-alike root: if the same consonants end in hamzah instead of wāw (i.e. ف-ج-أ), the meaning shifts entirely — "to surprise, catch unawares," as in fajiʾanī al-amr yafjaʾunī, "the matter took me by surprise." Ibn Fāris adds this to keep the two similar-sounding roots apart.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: فَٰكِهَة 11x "(are) fruits"; فَوَٰكِه 3x "(are) fruits"; فَٰكِهِين 3x "(in) amusement"; تَفَكَّهُ 1x "wondering"; فَكِهِين 1x "jesting"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ف-ك-ه (f-k-h) as a single sound root whose core meaning is pleasantness — finding something agreeable or delightful.

Senses grouped under it:

1. فَكِه (fakih) — of a person: pleasant and good-humored in disposition.

2. فَاكِهَة (fākiha) — "fruit," so named because it is found agreeable and delightful.

3. مُفَاكَهَة (mufākaha) — light-hearted jesting or banter; pleasant, enjoyable speech.

4. أَفْكَهَت (afkahat) — of a she-camel or ewe: to yield plentiful milk after grazing on spring pasture, the milk being slightly thick — which is reckoned the most agreeable milk.

A separate note on the Qur'an: Ibn Fāris holds that التَّفَكُّه (tafakkuh) in Q 56:65, {فَظَلْتُمْ تَفَكَّهُونَ}, does NOT belong to this root. He explains it as a case of letter-substitution (ibdāl): the original word was تَفَكَّنُونَ (tafakkanūn), from تَنَدُّم (tanaddum, "regret/remorse"), which he has already discussed under the root f-k-n.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: فَكّ 1x "(it is) freeing"; مُنفَكِّين 1x "to be abandoned"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats f-k-k as a sound root (aṣl ṣaḥīḥ) indicating an opening up and a parting (tafattuḥ, infirāj).

**1. Releasing a pledge.** Fakāk al-rahn is the release of a pledge, its "opening" from being locked (al-inghilāq). Al-Kisāʾī records the form fikāk, with i.

**2. Parting a thing.** Fakaktu l-shayʾa (imperfect afukku, verbal noun fakk): I parted the thing, opened it up.

**3. Dislocation.** Of someone who has fallen it is said infakkat qadamuhu, "his foot came apart," that is, it parted (infarajat). Al-fakk is the shoulder's parting from its joint through weakness.

**4. Not ceasing.** Lā yanfakku yafʿalu dhālika means the same as lā yazālu, "he keeps on doing that." Ibn Fāris explains that he and the action do not part from each other, so the idiom is in line with the root's analogy (al-qiyās).

**5. The jaws.** Al-fakkān are the meeting-place of the two sides of the mouth (al-shidqān). They are so named because of the parting.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris assigns the root f-k-r a single core sense: the heart's or mind's repeated turning-over of something — dwelling on a matter and revolving it in thought.

1. Core sense: the mind turning a thing over and over (taraddud al-qalb fī al-shayʾ).
2. Derived verb: tafakkara — "he reflected," used of one who turns something over in his heart to take heed of it or draw a lesson from it (muʿtabiran).
3. Derived form: rajul fikkīr — "a man of much thought," someone given to abundant reflection.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ف ل ح (f-l-ḥ) from two sound origins: (1) splitting/cleaving, and (2) winning and endurance.

1. Splitting (shaqq). فَلَحْتُ الْأَرْضَ (falaḥtu l-arḍ) = "I cleaved/plowed the earth." Proverb: الْحَدِيدُ بِالْحَدِيدِ يُفْلَحُ ("iron is cleaved by iron"). From this the plowman/cultivator is called فَلَّاح (fallāḥ). A person with a cleft lower lip is أَفْلَح (aflaḥ), the cleft itself being الفَلَحَة (falaḥa). The pre-Islamic poet ʿAntara al-ʿAbsī bore the nickname الفَلْحَاء (al-Falḥāʾ) because of such a cleft, cited in the verse likening him to "a black crag of Mount ʿAmāya."

2. Winning and endurance (fawz wa baqāʾ), yielding الفَلَاح (falāḥ). A man's saying to his wife, اسْتَفْلِحِي بِأَمْرِكِ (istafliḥī bi-amriki), means "prosper/win by your own affair." Falāḥ also names the pre-dawn meal (السَّحُور, saḥūr) — so called, they said, because through it one's strength to endure the fast persists. A ḥadīth uses it in this sense: they prayed with the Prophet until they feared missing al-falāḥ (the pre-dawn meal). A cited verse plays on the "endurance" sense: for every worry there is relief, yet as evening and morning pass "there is no falāḥ [abiding] with them."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats f-l-k as a single sound root whose core sense is roundness or circularity in a thing. From that one idea he derives every usage:

1. Roundness itself — the spindle-whorl (فَلْكَة), named for being round; likewise فَلَكَ is said of a woman's breast when it becomes rounded.

2. The celestial sphere / orbit (فَلَكُ السَّمَاء) — placed under the same analogy of circular form/rotation.

3. A verbal use: فَلَكْتُ الْجَدْيَ — to wind a twig or tuft of hair around a kid's tongue so it cannot suckle (i.e. to loop something round).

4. الْفَلَك for terrain: rounded patches of ground that rise above their surroundings.

5. فَلْكَةُ اللِّسَان — the hardened part at the base of the tongue.

6. The ship, فُلْك — with the note that its singular and plural forms are identical; Ibn Fāris suggests it may be called this because it is turned about (made to revolve) in the water, keeping it within the same root-sense of turning/roundness.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text: 1. The word fulan (so-and-so), given here by its root letters fa-la-nun, is an allusive placeholder (kinaya) standing for any person, used when the actual name is left unspecified, much like English so-and-so. 2. Ibn Faris cites a line of verse by the poet Abu al-Najm in which fulan is clipped to ful, an instance of tarkhim (poetic apocopation, or truncation, of the end of a word): In an uproar, hold so-and-so back from so-and-so. 3. This bare form, fulan (without the definite article), is used specifically for people. 4. For anything other than a person, e.g. an animal, the word instead takes the definite article: al-fulana / al-fulan, as in the example given: I rode the such-and-such mare and the such-and-such horse.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: فَالِق 2x "(he is the) cleaver"; ٱنفَلَقَ 1x "so it parted"; فَلَق 1x "(of) the dawn"
text:
Ibn Faris derives the root f-l-q from two core ideas: (1) splitting/cleaving something so it opens and separates, and (2) something being impressive or momentous in scale.

Sense 1, splitting/cleaving: falaqa = to split or cleave something. al-falaq = daybreak/dawn, because the darkness is split apart by it. al-falaq = a low hollow in the ground, as if split open; plural filqan. al-falaq = creation as a whole, pictured as something split open so that what was inside was brought out and made visible. infalaqa = it split open (said of a stone, etc.). The idiom "so-and-so spoke to me min filqin fihi" means he spoke to me plainly/openly, built on the same image of an opening. al-faliq = an open gap between two sand ridges. qawsun filq = a bow made from a piece of split wood, as opposed to a single unsplit branch. al-faliq (a related word) = a hollow in the underside of a camel's neck, illustrated with a line of verse describing it as smooth, like a bent spear.

Sense 2, magnitude/wonder: al-fulayqah = a great calamity or momentous event; Arabs exclaim "ya la-l-fulayqah!" for something astonishing. aflaqa = he did something extraordinary; a poet who produces brilliant verse is called sha'ir mufliq. This sense is illustrated with a verse by Suwayd describing camels achieving marvels (filqan) crossing a vast desert as their driver sang. al-faylaq likewise carries the sense of something astonishing.

Ibn Faris treats both senses as branches of one underlying image: a thing being forced open or apart, whether literally (dawn splitting the dark, a stone splitting, a bow of split wood) or figuratively (an event so large it "breaks open" the ordinary, or speech/poetry that is strikingly remarkable).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: تُفَنِّدُ 1x "you think me weakened in mind"
text:
Root ف ن د (f-n-d) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha (d. 1004 CE)

Ibn Fāris states the root's core sense is heaviness and severity/intensity, with its various senses derived from one another by analogy.

1. Find — a mountain's jagged peak/ridge; some say it means a great mountain itself. A man could be named Find after this.

2. Tafnīd — blame or censure. Ibn Fāris derives this from the core sense: reproachful speech is "heavy" and "intense" upon the one who hears it.

3. Fanad — senility, extreme old age. Also derived from the core sense. Crucially, he specifies it only applies when the old age comes with a decline of the mind — not old age alone. The related verb form is afnada ("to become fanad-afflicted"), and such a man is called mufnid. He notes a linguistic curiosity: an old woman is never called mufnida, because (in his reasoning) she is not said to have "lost" sound judgment in old age, since she is held not to have possessed it even in her youth.

4. Fanad also means lying/falsehood. Ibn Fāris offers two possible explanations for this sense, without preferring one: either it is named this way because a liar gets blamed (yufannad — linking back to sense 2), or because lying is a grave sin, i.e., a "severe burden" (linking back to the root's core sense of severity).

The entry cites no poetry or Qurʾānic verses.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats f-n-n as two separate sound roots.

1. **Wearying, driving hard.** The first is الفَنّ (al-fann): wearing someone out and driving him hard. One says فَنَنْتُهُ فَنًّا, "I drove him hard and wore him out".

2. **Kinds, and the branch.** The second denotes one kind among the kinds, in anything at all. الأَفَانِين (al-afānīn) are the kinds of a thing and its ways. From this root comes الفَنَن (al-fanan), a branch, plural أَفْنَان (afnān). A tree is called فَنْوَاء (fanwāʾ); Abū ʿUbayd says it is as though the word's underlying form were فَنَّاء (fannāʾ).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ف ن ي (f-n-y) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris opens by flagging this as an irregular chapter: its words don't reduce to one analogical core meaning the way his method usually finds; he simply lists what is attested.

1. **فَنِيَ يَفْنَى فَنَاءً** — to perish, come to an end. "Allah afnāhu" (caused it to perish) is used when something انْقَطَعَ (is cut off/ceases) — "Allah cut it off" meaning He took it away.

2. **الفَنَا** (written without hamza, distinct from fanā' "annihilation"): the "fox's grape," a plant name — a separate word that happens to look similar.

3. **الفِنَاء**: the courtyard or open ground running along the sides of a house; plural afniya. From this comes the idiom "he is of the afnā' al-ʿArab" — said of someone whose tribal origin is unknown/mixed.

4. **المُفَانَاة**: humoring or gently managing someone — tactful handling. Illustrated with a verse (poet not named in the source): the speaker makes his companion stand and sit by turns, "just as a leader humors a headstrong mount."

5. **الأَفَانِي**: a plant (singular afāniya).

6. **الفَنَاة**: the cow (wild cow), plural fanawāt.

7. A tree called **فَنْوَاء** is one whose branches (afnān) spread out on every side. Ibn Fāris notes the "regular" form should have been fannā' (with doubled nūn), since the word actually belongs to the root f-n-n ("bough"), not truly to f-n-y — he includes it here only because of its surface shape.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ف ق ع (f-q-ʿ), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris opens with an explicit disclaimer: this chapter's words are not built on a single unifying analogy — they are disparate, unrelated meanings sharing only the same three letters.

1. al-faqʿ — a kind of truffle-fungus, used as a comparison for a lowly, despised man: "he is more lowly than a faqʿ-truffle on a barren plain" (a well-known proverb).
2. al-faqʿ — also, separately, flatulence/wind, connected to "faqqaʿa bi-aṣābiʿihi," cracking one's knuckles (a cracking/popping sound).
3. An unrelated color-term: "aṣfaru fāqiʿ" — a vivid, pure yellow.
4. al-ifqāʿ — bad circumstance or poverty; afqaʿa — to fall into destitution. fawāqiʿ al-dahr — Time's sudden calamities (paired with the synonym bawāʾiq).
5. al-fuqqāʿ — a fermented beverage, noted as genuine Arabic; al-Khalīl explains the name comes from the froth rising to its surface, and describes al-faqāqīʿ (the bubbles) as resembling tiny glass vessels floating on water.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: تَفْقِدُ 2x "we are missing"; تَفَقَّدَ 1x "and he inspected"
text:
Ibn Faris identifies a single core sense for the root f-q-d: the departure or loss of something.

1. Basic sense - faqada / faqd: to lose a thing, for it to go away from one's possession.

2. al-faqid: specifically, a woman who has lost her child or her husband (plural: fawaqid).

3. Derived sense - tafaqqada, "to seek out / look for": Ibn Faris explains this as belonging to the same root, on the logic that one goes looking for a thing precisely because one has lost it (i.e., its absence is what triggers the search) - so "seeking" and "losing" are two faces of the same underlying idea.

Qur'anic citation given: Surat al-Naml 27:20 - "And he sought among the birds and said, 'What is with me that I do not see the hoopoe - or is he among the absent?'" - illustrating the tafaqqada ("sought out / looked for") sense.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَفْقَهُ 19x "understand"; يَتَفَقَّهُ 1x "that they may obtain understanding"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats f-q-h as a single sound root whose core meaning is grasping or perceiving a thing and having knowledge of it.

1. Core sense: to understand or comprehend. Example: فَقِهْتُ الْحَدِيثَ أَفْقَهُهُ ("I understood the speech, and I understand it"). Any knowledge of a thing is fiqh (understanding). A common saying, لَا يَفْقَهُ وَلَا يَنْقَهُ ("he neither understands nor comprehends"), pairs the root with its near-rhyme n-q-h.

2. Specialized sense: the word later became attached specifically to knowledge of the religious law (ʿilm al-sharīʿa), so that any scholar of what is lawful and forbidden came to be called a faqīh (jurist). Ibn Fāris presents this as a later narrowing of the general sense, not the original meaning.

3. Causative form: أَفْقَهْتُكَ الشَّيْءَ (afqahtuka al-shayʾ) means "I made the thing clear to you / explained it to you."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats f-q-r as one sound root meaning a splitting or cleaving-apart in something — a bodily part or otherwise. All the senses trace back to that.

1. Anatomical core: al-faqār = the vertebrae of the back (singular faqāra), named for the notches and divisions between them. al-faqīr = a man whose backbone is broken.

2. Poverty (derived): The language scholars derive the word for "poor man" (faqīr) from this — as though he were someone with a broken backbone, because of his lowliness and abjectness.

3. Calamity: al-fāqira = a disaster; "the fāqira struck them," as if it were a breaker of the backbone.

4. A dissenting definition: Some scholars hold that faqīr denotes one who has only a bare sufficiency of livelihood, citing a verse about a man whose one milking-camel was exactly matched to his dependents' needs, leaving no surplus.

5. Water-outlet: al-faqīr can also mean the water-outlet of an underground channel (qanāt); this fits the root, since such an outlet is "broken through" and cleft into the ground.

6. Hunting idiom: afqaraka al-ṣayd ("the game has offered you its faqār") = it has exposed its back/vertebrae so you can shoot it.

7. Camel-training: faqartu al-baʿīr = to notch a camel's muzzle and set the lead-rope on the notch to subdue and train it. afqartuka nāqatī = "I lent you my she-camel's back to ride."

8. A named well: In the line "The night of al-faqīr is nothing but a devil," al-faqīr is a particular well-known well (rakiyy).

9. Digging/boring: faqartu lil-fasīl = to dig a hole for a palm-shoot when planting it; faqartu al-kharaz = to bore/pierce a bead.

10. "Stopping up poverty": sadda llāhu mafāqirahu = "God closed off his avenues of poverty," i.e. made him rich — illustrated by a verse hoping in the Lord "for the stopping-up of my points of need."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: فِرَٰش 3x "couches"; فَرْش 1x "and (some for) meat"; فَرَشْ 1x "we have spread it"; فَرَاش 1x "like moths"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats f-r-sh as a single sound root whose core idea is smoothing something out and spreading it flat. He holds that every word in the section returns to that idea, except one he marks as anomalous.

1. Base sense — spreading. فَرَشْتُ الفِرَاشَ ("I spread the bedding"). الفَرْش is both the verbal noun (the act of spreading) and the thing spread out.

2. A bird "spreading" itself. تَفَرَّشَ الطَّائِرُ: the bird drops close to the ground and beats its wings. He cites a report that some Companions took two lark nestlings and the mother bird came fluttering in this way, and a line of Abū Duʾād describing a scout who "came running with the fluttering of the ostrich, at a sprint, the day already high."

3. الفَرْش of livestock — animals fit only for slaughter and eating.

4. فِرَاش as bedfellow. On the saying "the child belongs to the firāsh," he reports that some took firāsh to mean the husband, while arguing that strictly the firāsh is the woman, since she is the one bedded; the husband was lent her name because the two share spousehood and each is a "garment" to the other. Jarīr's line is cited, where a woman's firāsh (her man) lies slain in his worn cloak.

5. أَفْرَشَ = to backbite. Reported from Abū Zakariyyāʾ: to speak ill of one's companion. Ibn Fāris judges this a sound extension of the root — as if one trod the man down with ugly speech.

6. فَرَاشَة = a light, nimble man. By likeness to "the farāsha of water": according to some, the sheet of water lying on the ground just before it drains away, as though something spread out — and anything light is called farāsha. Others define the farāsha of land as ground the water has left, dried and flaking.

7. Further spreading idioms: افْتَرَشَ السَّبُعُ ذِرَاعَيْهِ (a predator stretches out its forelegs); افْتَرَشَ الرَّجُلُ لِسَانَهُ (a man "spreads out his tongue," i.e. talks as he pleases).

8. فَرَاش الرأس — the fine layers lying against the skull-bone.

9. الفَرْش — (a) thin firewood; (b) a wide open expanse.

10. From Ibn Durayd: كَرِيمُ الْمَفَارِش, said of a man who has married noble women; جَمَلٌ مُفَرَّشٌ, a humpless camel; أَكَمَةٌ مُفْتَرِشَةُ الظَّهْرِ, a hillock flattened along its back.

11. مَا أَفْرَشَ عَنْهُ = "he did not desist from it," with a poetic line ("it did no more than that the polishing left off from it"). Ibn Fāris notes this sits far from the root's logic and suspects a consonant substitution for أَفْرَجَ.

12. فَرَاشَة also denotes the tongue/plate of a lock; and فَرَاش is the flying insect (moth/butterfly), so named for its lightness.

13. Marked as outside the root: الفَرِيش, a mare seven days after foaling.

dictionary: Ṣiḥāḥ — al-Ṣiḥāḥ, al-Jawharī (d. 1003)
quran_words: فَرَضَ 9x "you have specified"; فَرِيضَة 6x "an obligation"; مَّفْرُوض 2x "obligatory"; فَارِض 1x "old"
poets_named: Labīd (lived into Islam); unnamed verse ×2; Ṣakhr al-Ghayy (pre-Islamic); ʿUbayd b. al-Abraṣ (pre-Islamic)
text:
al-Jawharī derives the root ف ر ض (f-r-ḍ) from the concrete idea of a notch or incision, and traces the many senses out from there.

1. Notch / cut. al-farḍ is a notch cut into something: "I notched the fire-stick and tooth-stick." farḍ al-zand is the spot on a fire-stick where fire is struck; farḍ al-qaws is the notch of a bow that holds the string (plural firāḍ). Related tools and forms: al-mifraḍ (the iron used for notching), al-farīḍ (an arrow notched at its top), al-tafrīḍ (the act of notching).

2. Opening / outlet. firāḍ is also the mouth of a river — cited from Labīd, "as the Euphrates flows over the outlet of the streamlet." Several furḍa forms follow: furḍat al-nahr (the breach from which water is drawn), furḍat al-baḥr (a harbor where ships put in), furḍat al-dawāt (the ink-hollow of an inkwell), furḍat al-bāb (a door's pivot-socket). The idiom mā ʿalayhi firāḍ means "not a stitch of clothing on him."

3. A kind of date. Per al-Aṣmaʿī, al-farḍ and al-balʿaq are the finest dates of Oman, with a poetic citation.

4. Shield, and gaming-arrow. al-farḍ can mean a shield (with a verse from Ṣakhr al-Ghayy, and the note that one must not read the word as qirṣ), and also the divining/gaming arrow al-qidḥ (with a verse from ʿUbayd b. al-Abraṣ on lightning).

5. Marked gift; allotment. al-farḍ is a designated gift: "I got from him neither gift (farḍ) nor loan (qarḍ)." faraḍtu / afraḍtu al-rajul = "I gave to him"; faraḍtu lahu fī al-ʿaṭāʾ / fī al-dīwān = "I assigned him a share in the stipend / entered him in the register."

6. Old age (of a cow). faraḍat / faruḍat al-baqara: the cow grew old and advanced in years — al-Jawharī connects this to the Qur'anic lā fāriḍun wa-lā bikr ("neither aged nor young").

7. Large / bulky. al-fāriḍ is the huge of anything; per al-Akhfash, liḥya fāriḍa is a great beard, with a verse using rijāl farḍ for "huge men."

8. Obligation, and its offshoots. al-farḍ is what God has made obligatory; al-Jawharī explains the name by saying such a thing "has landmarks and defined limits." He reads the Qur'anic naṣīban mafrūḍan as "an apportioned, delimited share," and cites the variant reading faraḍnāhā (with doubled ḍ), which Abū ʿAmr b. al-ʿAlāʾ glossed as "We set it out in detail." From the same sense: the verb aftaraḍa ("made obligatory"); the noun al-farīḍa; al-fāriḍ / al-faraḍī for one learned in farāʾiḍ (inheritance-shares), the science of dividing estates being called farāʾiḍ (ḥadīth: "the most versed of you in farāʾiḍ is Zayd"). al-farīḍa is also the ṣadaqa due on grazing livestock: livestock is said to "become liable to the farīḍa" once it reaches the niṣāb (taxable minimum); the two farīḍatān are the jadhaʿa among sheep and the ḥiqqa among camels.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ف ر ع (f-r-ʿ), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One sound root: elevation, rising, loftiness, and fullness/abundance.

1. al-farʿ — the top/highest part of a thing; farraʿtu al-shayʾ — to rise above something. afraʿa banū fulānin — a tribe seeking fresh pasture ahead of everyone else [i.e. "rising" to be first]. al-faraʿ — ample, prepared wealth.
2. al-afraʿ — a man full/complete in hair (feminine farʿāʾ, per Ibn Durayd); the entry notes a precise usage rule: afraʿ describes hair-fullness as a trait, opposite of aṣlaʿ (bald) — not simply "having a big head of hair" — and notes the Prophet himself was described as afraʿ. rajul mufraʿu al-katif — a man with a prominent (or broad) shoulder.
3. iftaraʿtu al-bikr — to deflower a virgin, explained via the same "rising over/overpowering" logic. afraʿtu al-arḍ — to traverse land thoroughly and come to know it. faraʿatu al-ṭarīq — a road's elevated stretch. tafarraʿtu banī fulānin — to marry into a tribe by taking their finest woman ["rising" to the top match]. faraʿtu raʾsahu bi-l-sayf — to strike someone's head with a sword ["rising over" it]; faraʿtu al-jabal — to reach a mountain's summit.
4. Two senses Ibn Fāris flags as close to, but not identical with, the core analogy: al-faraʿ as the firstborn offspring of camels/sheep; and, further outside the pattern, al-faraʿah (a small creature, diminutive furayʿah, source of a woman's name) and al-faraʿ, a pre-Islamic practice — dressing a newborn calf in a dead calf's skin so a bereaved mother-camel would accept it as a substitute — illustrated with a line of poetry by Aws comparing a dull-witted man to such a swaddled calf.
5. Closing grammatical note: "afraʿtu fī al-wādī" means "I descended into the valley" — the opposite sense from farʿ ("rising"), explained by the general Arabic pattern where the hamzated causative form (afʿala) can reverse a root's basic meaning; illustrated with the saying "laqītu fulānan fāriʿan mufriʿan" — "I met so-and-so, one of us ascending, the other descending."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives فرح (f-r-ḥ) from two distinct roots.

1. The opposite of grief — joy, gladness. The verb is فَرِحَ / يَفْرَحُ / فَرَحًا (fariḥa — to rejoice), giving the adjective فَرِحٌ (fariḥ — joyful). He cites Qurʾān 40:75, "That is because you used to rejoice on the earth without right, and because you used to exult." The form مِفْرَاح (mifrāḥ — one habitually joyful) is the counterpart of مِحْزَان (miḥzān — one habitually sorrowful).

2. Burdening / weighing down — the sense carried by إِفْرَاح (ifrāḥ). Ibn Fāris supports this with the Prophetic saying, "A mufraḥ is not to be left [unaided] in Islam," explained as the person whom debt has weighed down. He also cites a line of verse: "If you never cease discharging one trust and shouldering another, the deposits have burdened you" — where أَفْرَحَتْكَ (afraḥatka) means "have weighed you down."

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: فَرَّط 5x "we neglected"; مُّفْرَطُون 1x "(will) be abandoned"; فُرُط 1x "(in) excess"; يَفْرُطَ 1x "he will hasten"
poets_named: Thaʿlab (unnamed); unnamed verse ×2; Ibn Barrāqa (undated); Sāʿida b. Juʾayya (pre-Islamic); Abū Wajza (disputed date); Ṣakhr al-Ghayy (pre-Islamic); Labīd (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Sīda treats ف ر ط as one root turning on **going ahead / getting out in front**, and derives every other sense — excess, filling to overflow, forerunners, intervals of time, and finally neglect — from that.

**1. Going in front (the core sense).** فارِط (fāriṭ) is the one who precedes; the verb is فَرَطَ يَفْرُطُ فُروطاً. He cites a bedouin asking al-Ḥasan for "a middling dīn — not one racing ahead (furūṭan) and not one dropping behind": i.e. a middle course, neither pushed forward by excess nor trailing. Al-Ḥasan approved, quoting "the best of affairs are their middles." This exchange fixes furūṭ as one pole (going too far forward) and falling short as the other.

**2. Sending something forward.** فَرَّطَ عَيْرَه — he sent his mount ahead (Thaʿlab's verse: a horse sent out ahead "of the press of the horses"). فَرَّطَ إليه رسولَه — he sent his messenger ahead. فَرَّطَه — he pushed him forward in a quarrel and emboldened him.

**3. The water-scouts.** فَرَطَ القومَ (farṭan / firāṭatan) — he went ahead of the group to the watering-place to mend the well-ropes and buckets and clay-line the troughs. Such men are الفُرَّاط. A verse: "they hurried on ahead of us... as an advance water-man goes before those coming to drink." The one who does this is a فَرَط; hence the Prophet's reported words, "I am your faraṭ (forerunner) at the basin." One says rajulun faraṭ of one man and qawmun faraṭ of a group.

**4. Grammatical note on faraṭ.** faraṭ can be a collective noun (ism jamʿ). In the line "she has fawāris (horsemen) and faraṭ," faraṭ could be the form used for singular and plural alike, or the collective of fāriṭ — Ibn Sīda prefers the latter, because a plural (fawārisan) precedes it, and pairing a plural with a collective (which has the force of a plural) is the better match.

**5. Water and land that "come first."**
- الفَرَط: water lying ahead of other waters.
- الفُراطة: water held open among several clans — first to reach it owns it; a well on those terms is biʾr furāṭa.
- الفَرَط (fatḥa on the rāʾ): a small mountain, plural furuṭ (from Kurāʿ).
- الفُرُط: an upright landmark used for navigation; also the crest and outline of a hillock, plural afruṭ / afrāṭ (Ibn Barrāqa: "from the hill-tops crouching owls cried out"). Some read afrāṭ there as the streaks of dawn, since owls hoot then; Ibn Sīda prefers the hill-top reading.
- الفارِطان: two stars running in front of Banāt Naʿsh.
- أفراط الصبح: the first streaks of dawn — they run ahead and give warning of morning; singular faraṭ.

**6. What precedes you: reward, and children who die young.** الفَرَط is also whatever of reward and deed has gone ahead of you. فَرَطُ الوَلَد is one's small children not yet grown (plural afrāṭ; some say faraṭ covers singular and plural). In the prayer over a dead child, "O God, make him a faraṭ for us" — i.e. a recompense that goes on ahead until we reach it. Hence فَرَطَ فلان ولداً / افْتَرَطَهم (his children died young) and افْتُرِطَ الولد (his death was brought forward, per Thaʿlab) — all, he stresses, from the idea of precedence. Abū Dhuʾayb's furrāṭ likewise means those who go ahead to dig the grave.

**7. Overstepping and excess.** فَرَطَ منّي إليه كلام — words got out ahead of me to him. فَرَطَ عليه في القول — he overstepped and pressed forward against him in speech; cited for Q 20:45, "we fear that he will press excessively upon us or transgress." الفُرُط is wrongdoing and overstepping, cited for Q 18:28, "his affair was furuṭ." A فَرَس فُرُط is a mare that outstrips (Labīd). افْتَرَطَ إليه في هذا الأمر — he got ahead in the matter. الإفراط is hastening and going ahead; أفْرَطَ في الأمر — he went to excess. Ibn Sīda records three glosses for furuṭ here: the matter one goes to excess in; haste; or regret (nadam). A cloud تُفْرِط the water at the start of the first seasonal rains — it brings it early.

**8. A grammatical usage from Sībawayh.** فَرَطَكَ is said when warning someone of something in front of him, or telling him to move forward; it is one of the "nouns of verb" (asmāʾ al-fiʿl) and takes no object.

**9. Overwhelming and overfilling.** فَرْطُ الشهوة والحزن — desire and grief in their overmastering force. أفْرَطَ عليه — he loaded him past his capacity. أفْرَطَ الحوضَ والإناءَ — he filled the trough or vessel until it overflowed (Sāʿida b. Juʾayya: mixed with water from a brimming pool). In Abū Wajza's line, يُفْرِطُه means fills the animal with fright until it bolts.

**10. Neglect — letting slip what should have been kept.** فَرَّطَ في الشيء / فَرَّطَه — he let it go to waste and put shortcoming forward in it; cited for Q 39:56, "alas for my neglect regarding the side of God." Ibn Sīda's own gloss on that verse is that the neglect is of God's affair and of the road God called to, which he identifies as affirming God's oneness and acknowledging His messenger's prophethood — his reading, not something the wording states. Ṣakhr al-Ghayy's "that is my war-gear, and I shall not ufarriṭhu" he glosses as "I shall not squander it," noting an alternative: "I shall not send it ahead and lag behind it." فَرَّطَ في جنب الله — he wasted what he had and did no work for Him. تَفارَطَتِ الصلاةُ عن وقتها — it fell behind its time. فَرَّطَ اللهُ عنه ما يكره — He removed it from him.

**11. An interval of time.** الفَرْط is a stretch of time: "I only come to him al-farṭa / fī l-farṭ"; أتيتُه فَرْطَ أشهرٍ — after some months (Labīd: the soul is a loan that "comes to its owner farṭa ashhurin"). Some define farṭ as a gap of not fewer than three days and not more than fifteen. He records a bedouin who said "I went on farṭa sāʿatin and did not trust I would get away," and when asked what a farṭ of an hour is, answered "about since I began speaking" — a usage in which kāf is attached to mudh; and his ūmin means "I did not trust or credit it." تَفارَطَتْه الهموم — cares came on him at intervals.

**12. Leaving behind / forgetting.** فَرَّطَه — he held off from him and gave him respite. الفِراط is leaving/abandoning: ما أفْرَطَ منهم أحداً — he left none of them. أفْرَطَ الشيءَ — he forgot it; cited for Q 16:62, "and that they are left behind / forgotten."
