text:
Ibn Sīda's entry on the root ف ر د (f-r-d), organised by sense:

1. **fard = half of a pair.** The basic contrast is with zawj (a pair/even number).

2. **fard = the single, solitary one.** Plural firād. Ibn al-Aʿrābī cited a line about "the falcon's snatching of the firād (strays) of the flock."

3. **fard = that which has no counterpart, the unmatched one.** Plural afrād. Several parallel adjectival forms exist for the same idea: fard, farad, farid, farud, farūd, fārid.

4. **fārid / fārida = standing apart, isolated.** Of a tree: al-Musayyab b. ʿAlas, "in the shade of a solitary lote-tree." Of a doe (ẓabya fārid): one that keeps away from the herd. Of a she-camel: fārida or mifrād, one that grazes alone — of the male only fārid is used. Of camels generally, farūd: one that keeps apart at pasture and at water.

5. **A saying with fārida.** "Let your fārida not pilfer." Thaʿlab explained: whoever among you goes off alone — one man or two — and gets booty should hand it back to the group rather than keep it for himself.

6. **afrād of the stars:** the bright stars that rise in the open horizons, so called because they stand apart from the rest.

7. **Verbs.** farada bi-l-amr (yafrudu) — to be alone in a matter; also infarada and istafrada. Ibn Sīda notes, with some hesitation, that al-Liḥyānī reported the variants farida and faruda. istafrada someone = to get him alone; istafrada a thing = to take it out from among its fellows; afradahu = to make it single. jāʾū furādā / firādan = they came one after another. shāt mufrid = a ewe that bore a single lamb.

8. **fard = one of the two halves of the jawbone**, as though conceived of as a single piece; plural afrād. Ibn Sīda argues on grammatical grounds that this, not fard "opposite of a pair," is what Sībawayh meant when he gave "fard / afrād" as a plural pattern — because fard in the sense of "odd, unpaired" hardly ever takes a plural.

9. **Place-names from the root.** Fard: a dune standing apart from the others, the description having hardened into a proper name that keeps the article, like a personal name; a poet: "…who alights at the dune of Suwayqa or at Fard." Fardah: a well-known sandy tract (al-Rāʿī: "between Fardah and al-Raḥā"). Al-Furudāt: another place, cited from ʿAmr b. Qamīʾa. Al-Firindād: said to be a tree, or a place, or a high sand tract in the territory of Banū Tamīm where Dhū al-Rumma's grave is claimed to be; Dhū al-Rumma made it dual ("the two Firindāds") for metrical necessity, comparable to "the two Rāmahs" in another poet's line.

10. **Anatomical farīd / farāʾid** (singular farīda): the vertebrae that fall apart from the others, between the last of the six vertebrae next to the base of the neck and the six lying between the rump-bone and those — so named for standing apart. An alternative account: the farīda is the vertebra emerging from the saddle-place next to the hip joints, sometimes protruding in horses, named so because it sits between the backbone vertebrae and the joints of the rump.

11. **Jeweller's farīd / farāʾid:** the small beads that separate pearls from gold (singular farīda). Alternatively, farīd without the feminine ending is the precious solitary gem, as though unique in its kind. The maker is a farrād; mufarrad gold is gold set/spaced with farīd.

12. **al-furūd:** stars around Ḥaḍāri (itself a star, one of the two "oath-provokers"), cited by Thaʿlab: "…as though it were Ḥaḍāri when it shows itself, and its furūd."

13. **A prosodic note.** In the anonymous two-line piece quoted under "Fard," the poet supplied the ridf (the long vowel before the rhyme consonant) in one line but not the other — which Ibn Sīda calls rare, paralleling it with a passage of Abū Firʿawn. He also allows that "or Fard" may be a shortened (murakhkham) form of Fardah, clipped outside the vocative under metrical necessity, as Zuhayr said "O family of ʿIkrim" for ʿIkrima.

Throughout, the organising notion Ibn Sīda records is separateness — being one, standing apart from a group, or set off from what surrounds it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats f-r-gh as one sound root whose single idea is emptiness together with breadth of scope. From that core he derives:

1. **Being unoccupied.** الفَرَاغ (farāgh) is the opposite of being busy. The verb takes two verbal nouns, farāghan and furūghan, and also occurs in the form fariga (with a kasra on the middle radical).

2. **The pouring-outlet.** الفَرْغ (al-fargh) is the mouth of a water-bucket, the place the water pours from.

3. **Pouring out.** أَفْرَغَ (afragha) = to pour water out; افْتَرَغَ (iftaragha) = to pour water over oneself.

4. **Blood shed for nothing.** ذَهَبَ دَمُهُ فَرْغًا — "his blood went farghan," i.e. in vain, with no claim pressed for it.

5. **Ample gait.** فَرَسٌ فَرِيغٌ, a horse of wide stride. Ibn Fāris explains the naming: it is as if the horse were emptied of everything, so its running and walking became light.

6. **A wide stroke.** ضَرْبَةٌ فَرِيغٌ, a wide blow; likewise a wide spear-thrust.

7. **A cast ring.** حَلْقَةٌ مُفْرَغَةٌ — so called because it is something formed by pouring (casting).

8. **A wide road.** طَرِيقٌ فَرِيغٌ, supported by a verse (poet unnamed here) describing a track left by a blade that one would take for a clear path made plain "in a broad, well-trodden way."

**Qurʾānic note.** On {سَنَفْرُغُ لَكُمْ أَيُّهَا الثَّقَلَانِ} (55:31), Ibn Fāris states the usage is figurative, on the ground that God is not occupied by one matter to the exclusion of another. He reports that the exegetes glossed sa-nafrughu as نَعْمِدُ ("We shall set about / turn deliberately to"), citing the idiom فَرَغْتُ إِلَى أَمْرِ كَذَا, "I set about such-and-such a matter."

Method: the whole entry is organised by Ibn Fāris's characteristic procedure of tracing each attested usage back to one underlying sense — here "emptiness / breadth" — including the concrete senses of pouring and the derived sense of turning one's attention freely to something.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: unnamed verse ×2; ʿAdī ibn Zayd (pre-Islamic); al-Nābighah (pre-Islamic); Mālik ibn Jaʿdah al-Thaʿlabī (pre-Islamic); Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam)
text:
Root ف ر هـ (f-r-h), Ibn Manẓūr, Lisān al-ʿArab — the fullest of the two entries on this root, companion to al-Zamakhsharī's

1. fāriha bayyinu al-farāhah — excellent, spirited (of an animal), with a grammatical note from al-Jawharī on the word's irregular pattern (compared to ḥāmiḍ), illustrated with a line of poetry about lavish gifts including a fāriha slave.
2. The entry's central usage rule, developed at length: fārih is properly said of a pack-horse, mule, donkey, or dog — never of a thoroughbred horse, which instead takes jawād or rāʾiʿ. Several authorities are surveyed (Ibn Sīdah citing Sībawayh on the grammar of the plural furhah; al-Tahdhīb; a hadith of Jurayj using fārihah for a lively, strong mount) confirming this restriction — and two lines of poetry by ʿAdī ibn Zayd describing a horse as fārih are cited specifically as a documented grammatical error: Abū Ḥātim and al-Aṣmaʿī both judged ʿAdī to have lacked real expertise in horse-terminology, since he broke the very rule this entry establishes.
3. A citation from al-Nābighah uses al-fārihah for a singing-girl and the gifts accompanying her (per Ibn Sīdah's gloss), with a note on its irregular plural forms (fawāriḥ, furūḥ).
4. afraḥat fulānatu — a woman bore beautiful children (furrāhah); afraḥa al-rajulu — a man acquired a fārih (fine) slave-boy. al-Azharī reports Bedouin usage of jāriya farihah for a beautiful young woman; ghulām farih — a handsome young man (plural furḥ). Al-Shāfiʿī's legal ruling is cited by name: slaves possessing farāhah (beauty) are owed increased clothing and maintenance allowances.
5. afraḥat al-nāqah — a she-camel that habitually bears fine offspring (mufriḥ/mufriḥah/mufarriḥah), illustrated with a full citation from Mālik ibn Jaʿdah al-Thaʿlabī and, per Ibn Sīdah, a further line from Abū Dhuʾayb.
6. fārih used on its own: skilled/expert at a thing (al-ḥādhiq bi-l-shayʾ); al-furūhah, al-farāhah and al-farāhiyyah also carry the separate sense of liveliness (al-nashāṭ).
7. A distinct sense, fariha with kasra: insolent, reckless (ashira wa baṭira) — a man farih in this sense is "lively, insolent." The entry then turns to the Qurʾānic phrase "wa tanḥitūna min al-jibāli buyūtan fārihīn" (you carve houses out of the mountains, fārihīn): read with kasra the word is said to take this insolent/reckless sense; read fāriḥīn (from faruha, with ḍamma) it instead means skilled/excellent, per al-Farrāʾ's gloss ḥādhiqīn, supported by a further verse of poetry. Ibn Manẓūr adds that al-farih (spelled with ḥāʾ) means the same as al-ashir al-batir, and connects this to the separate Qurʾānic verse "lā tafraḥ inna Allāha lā yuḥibbu al-fariḥīn" — noting that the hāʾ in fariha/farih is here treated as standing in for the ḥāʾ of farih/faraḥ ("joy"), i.e. the two roots are presented as orthographic variants of one another in this sense, not identified doctrinally.
8. Closing: a man farih can also mean a voracious eater (shadīdu al-akl), reported from Ibn al-Aʿrābī via an anecdote of a slave telling a prospective buyer not to purchase him, "for I eat fārihan [voraciously] and walk kārihan [reluctantly]."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats f-r-j as one sound root whose single idea is **an opening-up in something**. His entry runs as follows.

1. **A gap or opening.** الفُرْجَة (furja) is the gap in a wall or in anything else — a cleft or split. Verb: فَرَجْتُهُ / فَرَّجْتُهُ, "I opened it."

2. **Relief from distress.** الفَرْجَة (farja, with fatḥa) is getting free of worry or grief. Ibn Fāris notes that the underlying analogy is the same as sense 1 — speakers simply mark the difference by the vowel (fatḥa vs. ḍamma). His witness-verse: "Often souls fret over a matter which has a farja (a way out) like the untying of a hobble-rope."

3. **The space between a horse's hind legs.** Cited from Imruʾ al-Qays: the mare "has a tail like a bride's train, with which she closes her farj from behind."

4. **Frontier openings.** الفُرُوج (furūj) are the frontier gaps (thughūr) lying between the danger points; so named, he explains, because they require watching and guarding. He reports the saying that the two farjs from which danger to Islam is feared are the Turks and the Sūdān. Generalizing: any place of danger is a farj.

5. **A splayed bow.** A bow is called فُرُج (furuj) when its curved tip (siya) has spread apart.

6. **Bodily description.** الْأَفْرَج (afraj), of a man whose buttocks do not meet; feminine فَرْجَاء.

7. **One who cannot hold a secret.** الفُرُج (furuj), and likewise الفِرْج (firj) — a person who does not keep a secret. Related: الفَرِج (farij), one whose private part is constantly getting uncovered.

8. **A slit robe.** الفَرُّوج (farrūj) is the qabāʾ (outer robe), named for the opening in it.

**Deviating from the root**, in his judgement, is الْمُفْرَج (mufraj), which he reports in two explanations: (a) a slain man whose killer is unknown; (b) the ḥamīl — an outsider with no clientage bond (walāʾ) and no lineage attaching him to anyone. He cites a report, "No mufraj is left [unattended] in Islam," noting the word is with jīm.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ف ر ق (f-r-q) as a single sound root whose core sense is distinguishing and separating between two things. He then lists its derivatives:

1. الفَرْق — parting the hair (faraqtuhu farqan, "I parted it").
2. الفِرْق — a flock or herd of sheep.
3. الفِرْق — a piece split off from something when it splits apart. He cites Qurʾān 26:63, "so it split, and each part (firq) was like a great mountain."
4. الفَرِيقَة — a flock of sheep, pictured as a portion that has broken away from the main body of the flock (with a poetic verse about a hyena falling on a "night-flock").
5. إِفْرَاق — a fevered man's recovery, because the fever has "departed" from him. He notes one view that the term applies only to a disease that strikes a person once, like smallpox or measles.
6. نَاقَة مُفْرِق — a she-camel parted from her young by its death.
7. الفُرْقَان (sense a) — the Book of God, so called because through it He distinguished truth from falsehood. Ibn Fāris gives only this "distinguishing" rationale; he does not gloss it as a technical creed or code.
8. الفُرْقَان (sense b) — the dawn, because by it night and day are told apart, or because darkness scatters away from it.
9. الأَفْرَق — a rooster with a forked (split) comb.
10. الفَرَق (in horses) — having one haunch higher than the other.
11. الفَرَق (in livestock) — a wide gap between a ram's two testicles, or between a ewe's two teats.
12. الفَارِق — a pregnant she-camel that bolts off across the land in labour-pain and gives birth where no one knows; plurals fawāriq, furraq. Named for separating from the other camels; a lone cloud drifting apart from the rest is likened to her and also called fāriq.
13. الفَارِق (of a person) — one who distinguishes between matters and decides them.
14. He notes that faraq and falaq of the dawn mean the same thing.

Ibn Fāris then marks a group as anomalous (shādhdh), i.e. not derivable from the "separation" sense:
- الفَرَق / الفَرْق — a measuring-vessel. Al-Qutaybī reads it faraq (with a vowelled rāʾ), the measure named in the ḥadīth "that of which a faraq intoxicates — a handful is forbidden," reckoned at sixteen raṭls; with a supporting verse from Khidāsh b. Zuhayr.
- الفَرِيقَة — dates cooked with fenugreek, used medicinally.
- الفَرُوقَة — kidney fat (with a poetic citation).
- الفَرُوق — a place-name.
All four, he states, fall outside the root's core sense.

quran_words: فَرَّتْ 6x "you flee"; فِرَار 4x "(in) flight"; مَفَرّ 1x "(is) the escape"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats f-r-r as having three separate root meanings: (1) laying bare or uncovering something, (2) a kind of animal, and (3) lightness and flightiness.

**1. Uncovering, laying bare.**
- The basic usage is فَرَّ عن أسنانه: drawing back the lips to lay bare an animal's teeth, as one does to judge its age. From this, افترّ is said of a person who smiles, showing the teeth. A verse contrasts someone whose smile reveals gleaming white teeth with another whose teeth are yellowed and crowded.
- A proverb says of a good horse, "the sight of him is his teeth-examination" (عينه فِراره): his looks tell you enough about his quality. Ibn Fāris explains that simply looking at him spares you from having to open his mouth and inspect his teeth.
- أفرّ المُهر: a colt has reached the age when its teeth would be examined as a jadhaʿ (a young animal at its first change of teeth). أفرّت الإبل للإثناء: camels have lost their milk teeth and reached the next stage (thaniyy).
- The same verb is used figuratively for probing a person or a matter: "sound out so-and-so about what is in him" (the copy is damaged at this word), "investigate the matter".
- Ibn Fāris also derives al-firār, "flight", from this root, while admitting that the two senses are far apart. He treats flight as a kind of breaking away and exposure (انكشاف). The verb is فرّ يفرّ, "to flee". Al-mafarr is both the verbal noun and the place one flees to. Al-farr means "people in flight", a plural of fārr ("one who flees") on the same pattern as ṣaḥb from ṣāḥib and sharb from shārib.

**2. An animal.** Al-farīr is a calf, the young of a cow. Al-furār is said to mean small-bodied young goats, with the singular farīr. Ibn Fāris compares this plural pattern with rakhl/rukhāl (ewe lamb) and ẓiʾr/ẓuʾār (wet-nurse).

**3. Lightness, flightiness.** Al-farfara means flightiness and levity. A flighty man is farfār and a flighty woman farfāra. Al-farfāra is also the name of a tree.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris records only one sense for the root f-r-t: it denotes sweet, fresh water — al-māʾ al-furāt, glossed simply as al-ʿadhb ("sweet/fresh," as opposed to salty or brackish water).

He notes the word furāt is used as an adjective for water in both grammatical numbers:
- singular: māʾun furātun — "fresh water"
- plural: miyāhun furātun — "fresh waters"

No further senses, derivations, or citations are given; this is a single-meaning root in his account.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ف-ر-ث (f-r-th) as a minor root whose core sense is "something crushed/broken into fragments."

1. Literal, concrete sense: faratha kabidahu, "he crushed/pulverized his liver," i.e. fattahā ("broke it into bits").

2. Noun al-farth: what is inside the karish (the stomach/rumen) — its contents, i.e., the pulverized/crushed matter found there.

3. Metaphorical extension: afratha fulānun aṣḥābahu — "so-and-so afratha'd his companions" — used when a man informed against / slandered his companions and thereby cast them into calamity. The image carries over from sense 1: just as farth is matter broken down and reduced to fragments, one who "afratha's" his companions breaks them down (ruins them) by exposing/betraying them into affliction.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: ٱفْتَرَىٰ 50x "invent"; ٱفْتِرَاء 2x "(as) an invention"; مُفْتَرُون 2x "the ones who invent (falsehood)"; مُّفْتَرًى 2x "invented"; مُفْتَرَيَٰت 1x "fabricated"; مُفْتَر 1x "(are) an inventor"; فَرِيّ 1x "an amazing thing"; يَفْتَرِي 1x "they invent it"
text:
Ibn Fāris organizes the root ف ر ي (f–r–y) around one core sense — cutting a thing (qaṭʿ) — with a second, disputed strand of "covering," plus one unrelated hamzated word.

Core sense — to cut:
1. فَرَيْتُ الشَّيْءَ (faraytu al-shayʾ), verbal noun فَرْي: to cut something in order to repair or shape it. Ibn al-Sikkīt adds that فَرَى can mean to stitch/sew leather (kharaza).
2. Contrast with the alif form: أَفْرَيْتُهُ (afraytuhu) = to cut something so as to spoil or ruin it — cutting toward destruction rather than toward repair. A verse cited contrasts one who "cuts through" (executes) what he has planned with one who only plans and never follows through.

Derived senses (still tied to "cutting"):
3. To do something marvellous: فُلَانٌ يَفْرِي الْفَرِيّ ("he cuts the marvellous cutting") — to produce something astonishing, as if performing a wondrous cut. A cited line uses تَفْرِينَ الْفَرِيّ for someone who "spoke much about a thing and magnified it."
4. To fabricate: فَرَى كَذِبًا (farā kadhiban) = to invent/concoct a lie (glossed with khalaqahu, "he shaped/made it up").
5. تَفَرَّتِ الْأَرْضُ بِالْعُيُونِ: the ground burst open with springs.
6. الْفَرَى (al-farā), the coward — named because he is "cut off" (furiya) from advancing/boldness.
7. الْفَرَى also = the marvellous/astonishing thing (same as al-fariyy).
8. الْفَرَى = astonishment, bewilderment, stupor; verb فَرِيَ يَفْرَى fariya/yafrā. A cited line: struck dumb with fright, unable to shoot.

Second (disputed) analogy — to cover:
9. الْفَرْوَة (al-farwa), the worn fur/pelt garment. Some derive it not from "cutting" but from a separate sense of covering (taghṭiya). On that reasoning: فَرْوَةُ الرَّأْس = the scalp (skin covering the head); al-farwa also = wealth/riches; and al-farwa = a mass of matted vegetation once dried. A ḥadīth is cited (al-Khaḍir sitting on a farwa of the earth, which then turned green). Ibn Fāris concludes that, if that report is sound, the chapter runs on two analogies — cutting, and covering/veiling with something thick.

Unrelated hamzated word:
10. الْفَرَأ (al-faraʾ, with hamza) = the wild ass. Ibn Fāris states it stands outside the above analogy and nothing else is measured on it. He cites the saying to Abū Sufyān, "All game is in the belly of the wild ass," and a line comparing sword-strokes to "the ears of wild asses."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text: Ibn Faris states that the root f-s-h has one single core meaning: spaciousness, width, openness. Al-fasih ("the spacious one, the wide one") is built directly from this root-sense. Tafassahtu fi al-majlis ("I made room for myself / spread out in the sitting-gathering") describes a person opening up space for themselves within a seated assembly. Fassahtu al-majlis ("I widened the gathering / made room in it") describes making a sitting-place more spacious, e.g. for others. No further senses, grammatical notes, or citations are given; the entry is a short, self-contained note tying the whole root to the single idea of wideness and room.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: مُفْسِد 21x "(of) the corrupters"; أَفْسَدُ 15x "spread corruption"; فَسَاد 11x "the corruption"; فَسَدَتِ 3x "surely they (would) have been ruined"
text:
Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī on the root فسد (f-s-d):

1. Core meaning: al-fasād is "corruption" — a thing's departure from its balanced or proper state (al-iʿtidāl), whether that departure is slight or great. Its opposite is al-ṣalāḥ (soundness / being in good order).

2. Range of use: the term applies to the soul, to the body, and to things generally that leave their upright, straight condition.

3. Grammar/derivation: the intransitive verb is fasada, with two verbal-noun forms, fasād and fusūd. The causative (Form IV) is afsada — "to corrupt / spoil something else."

4. Qurʾānic evidence he cites includes: the heavens and earth being "corrupted" had there been other gods (al-Anbiyāʾ 21:22; al-Muʾminūn 23:71); corruption appearing "on land and sea" (al-Rūm 30:41); God's not loving fasād (al-Baqara 2:205); the command "do not cause corruption in the land" and the label al-mufsidūn, "the corrupters" (al-Baqara 2:11–12); kings who "ruin" a town they enter (al-Naml 27:34); and the contrast God knows between al-mufsid (the corrupter) and al-muṣliḥ (the reformer) (al-Baqara 2:220) — the same ṣ-l-ḥ / f-s-d opposition noted in sense 1.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: فَاسِق 37x "the defiantly disobedient"; فَسَقَ 10x "defiantly disobeying"; فُسُوق 4x "(of) disobedience"; فِسْق 3x "grave disobedience"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats f-s-q as a single root with one core idea.

1. Core sense: al-fisq means "going out / departing from obedience." The whole root reduces to this one notion.

2. Concrete usage cited as evidence: the Arabs say a ripe date "fasaqat" from its skin — i.e. it came out of / broke free from it (reported from al-Farrāʼ). This shows the literal image of "coming out" underlying the word.

3. Derived form: the mouse is called a fuwaysiqa (a diminutive, "little transgressor"); Ibn Fāris notes this usage appears in the ḥadīth.

4. Note on attestation: Ibn Fāris reports Ibn al-Aʿrābī's observation that the active-participle form fāsiq is not attested anywhere in pre-Islamic (Jāhilī) speech, neither in poetry nor prose — which he found remarkable, since it is otherwise sound Arabic.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris derives the root f-s-r from a single core meaning: to make something clear, to explain or elucidate it.

1. General sense - clarification: the noun is al-fasr. Both fasartu (plain verb form) and fassartuhu (intensive/doubled verb form) are said for "I explained/clarified [something]."

2. Specialized medical sense: al-fasr and al-tafsira also denote a physician's inspection of a patient's urine and the diagnosis he makes from it - reading an outward sign to judge the hidden condition it points to.

Ibn Faris closes with the standard formula, "And God knows best what is correct."

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: unnamed verse ×5; Laylā al-Akhyaliyya (Umayyad); Sāʿida ibn Juʾayya (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Manẓūr's Lisān al-ʿArab groups two roots here: ف ت ي/و (fatā, "young/noble one," the main entry) and the separate hamzated root ف ت أ ("never to cease").

**فتا — fatā**

1. **Basic meaning: youth.** الفَتاء (al-fatāʾ) = youthfulness. الفَتى / الفَتاة = young man / young woman. Verb: fatuwa/fatiya — "to be young." "He was born children while [still] in the youth of his years." A cited verse plays on the same word scanned two ways: "if the young man lives two hundred years, pleasure and youth are gone." The word is also used of young animals.

2. **Plurals and the grammar behind them.** fatā → fityān, futuww, aftāʾ, fitya, fitwa, futiyy — several sources (al-Jawharī, Sībawayh, al-Azharī) are cited disagreeing over which plural is legitimate and why. A separate technical thread (al-Sīrāfī, Ibn Barrī) explains why the abstract noun futuwwa takes a wāw instead of the expected yāʾ, calling several of these forms grammatically "anomalous" (shādhdh) even though established in usage.

3. **A moral/social sense, not just "young."** Al-Qutaybī insists fatā often means not "youth" but "the complete, resolute man" — supported by verse: "the fatā is the one who bears every calamity, not [merely] a pampered youth," and by a line about a man attaining nobility despite a patched shirt. A longer illustrative narrative follows: a king sought a girl named Umm Kahf from the Banū Ḥanẓala in marriage; refused, he made war on them, drove them out, and killed them — recorded with the father's defiant verses refusing to marry his daughter to kings, and a note (from al-Jawharī) naming the family more precisely.

4. **Diminutives and dialect note.** futayya/futayy are the diminutives of fatāh/fatā. One authority (Yaʿqūb) records a dialect form fitwān for fityān, with a grammatical consequence for how futuwwa is analyzed.

5. **A girl "becoming secluded."** "The girl tafattat" = she started acting like the older girls while being the youngest; "she was futtiyat" = she was kept from playing/running with children and secluded in the house as she neared puberty. A ḥadīth compares war at its outset to a "futayya" (young girl).

6. **fatā/fatāh also meant "slave."** A ḥadīth has the Prophet preferring "my fatā / my fatāh" over "my slave," reportedly because he disliked applying the language of servitude to anyone but God. The Qurʾānic "Moses said to his fatā" (18:60) is read as "his servant/companion," on the strength of 18:62 ("bring us our meal"). In 4:25, "your fatayāt" is glossed as female slaves, contrasted with muḥṣanāt, free women. In 12:36, "two fatayān entered the prison with him" is noted as ambiguous in age, since the Arabs called a slave "fatā" whatever his years.

7. **fatā = generous, noble man** (al-Jawharī). Verbal forms tafattā/tafātā = "he showed himself chivalrous." Ibn Barrī traces this sense to the same root — originally an abstract noun used descriptively of a man — supported by a verse of Laylā al-Akhyaliyya.

8. **al-fatayān (the two fatās) = night and day**, an idiom meaning "forever," paralleled by other dual expressions for the same pair; illustrated by a verse about night and day as a pair that "carry a key for every lock."

9. **The fatwā family, and its own etymology.** aftāhu fī al-amr = he made the matter clear to him; istaftā/aftā = to seek/give a (legal-type) ruling; futyā/fatwā = the ruling itself. Illustrated with Qurʾān 37:11 ("ask them, whether they are a harder creation…") and 4:176 ("they ask you for a ruling; say, God rules for you"), plus a ḥadīth on ignoring a ruling that still nags at one's conscience. The author explicitly derives futyā from fatā itself: a ruling "strengthens" and clarifies a difficult point the way a youth grows into strength — so this legal-ruling sense is presented as rooted in the "young/growing" sense, not a separate origin. Note on regional pronunciation: Medinans favored fatḥa (fatwā).

10. **Minor technical entries.** al-muftī is also recorded as the name of a specific measuring-vessel (of Hishām ibn Hubayra), referenced in a report about Umm Salama displaying the Prophet's ablution vessel; al-futayy names a wine-drinker's cup, with "aftā" meaning "he drank from it"; al-Fityān is named as a clan of Bajīla.

**فتأ — a different root: "never to cease"**

"mā fatiʾtu" / "mā fataʾtu adhkuruhu" = "I did not cease to remember [it/him]" — two dialect pronunciations. This verb is used only in negative sentences, or with an understood-but-omitted negation (grouped grammatically with defective verbs like kāda). The Qurʾānic line "By God, you will not cease (tafta'u) remembering Joseph" (12:85) is cited as exactly this omitted-negation case. A poetic citation (Sāʿida ibn Juʾayya) uses the verb the same way, describing a beast that "never ceases" night-travel. A dialect note records Tamīm saying aftaytu against Qays's fatiʾtu, and a further sense — "fatiʾtu ʿan al-amr" — meaning "I forgot/gave up on the matter."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: فَتَحَ 16x "we opened"; فَتْح 12x "the victory"; ٱسْتَفْتَحُ 3x "you ask for victory"; مَفَاتِح 3x "its keys"; تُفَتَّحُ 1x "be opened"; فَٰتِحِين 1x "(of) those who decide"; فَتَّاح 1x "(is) the judge"; مُّفَتَّحَة 1x "(will be) opened"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ف ت ح (f-t-ḥ) as a single sound root whose core sense is the opposite of shutting or locking. The base usage is "I opened the door (or anything else)," and he treats every other word of this form as tracing back to that meaning of opening:

1. Judgment / adjudication — al-fatḥ and al-fitāḥa mean rendering a decision (ḥukm). On this basis he glosses the divine name al-Fātiḥ as "the Judge" (al-Ḥākim). Shāhid: a verse addressed to Banū ʿAwf declaring "I have no need of your arbitration (futāḥa)."

2. Flowing water — al-fatḥ is water that issues out from a spring or the like.

3. Victory / aid — al-fatḥ also means triumph and being granted the upper hand (naṣr, iẓfār); istaftaḥtu means "I sought victory/aid" (istanṣartu). He cites the ḥadīth that the Prophet used to seek victory through the poor among the Muhājirūn and Anṣār.

4. fawātiḥ al-Qurʾān — the "openings," i.e. the beginnings of the sūras.

5. bāb futuḥ — a wide, open doorway.

All five senses are presented as radiations from the single idea of "opening."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: فَتِيل 3x "(even as much as) a hair on a date-seed"
text:
Root ف ت ل (F-T-L) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: twisting something.

1. Basic verb sense: fataltu al-ḥabl — "I twisted the rope" (or similar things).

2. al-fatīl — the thin twisted fiber/thread found in the crevice of a date-stone, so named because it looks as if it has been twisted. Ibn Fāris cites a verse about a king who musters a huge army and campaigns, then deals the enemy only a trivial loss — the citation is defective/incomplete at this point in the source, so the exact wording of the comparison can't be fully recovered. A second opinion he records: al-fatīl is instead whatever one twists or rolls between two fingers.

3. al-fatal — the outward bowing of a camel's two forelegs away from its sides, as though they had been bent and twisted. Illustrated with a line by the poet Ṭarafa, describing a she-camel with such outward-bent forelegs.

4. A proverb: "So-and-so twists around the hump of so-and-so" — said of one who circles behind another person, scheming and deceiving him.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: فِتْنَة 34x "a trial"; فَتَنُ 23x "we tried"; فُتُون 1x "(with) a trial"; فَٰتِنِين 1x "can tempt away (anyone)"; مَفْتُون 1x "(is) the afflicted one"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ف ت ن (f-t-n) as a single sound root whose core meaning is trial and testing (ibtilāʾ, ikhtibār).

1. Core sense — testing/assaying. From this root comes fitna ("trial"), with the verb fatantu / aftinu / fatnan. A concrete example is fatantu al-dhahaba bi'l-nār, "I assayed the gold with fire," i.e. tested it. What is so tested is maftūn or fatīn.

2. Tempting/beguiling. Al-fattān ("the great tempter") is a name for the Satan. The verb appears in two forms, fatanahu and aftanahu ("he tempted / infatuated him") — though al-Aṣmaʿī rejected the fourth-form aftana. A verse is cited defending aftana ("If she has beguiled me, yesterday she beguiled Saʿīd…"). A "beguiled heart" is called qalb fātin (active form used with passive sense, = maftūn), supported by a further line of verse.

3. Burning. On the authority of al-Khalīl, fatn means burning (iḥrāq); something fatīn is "burnt," and a lava field (ḥarra) is called fatīn because its stones look scorched.

4. Deviant senses (outside the core). Ibn Fāris notes two usages that fall outside the root's main sense: fitān, the leather cover of a camel-saddle; and the phrase al-ʿaysh fitnān, "life is two colors/kinds." He suggests the second can still be reconciled with the root, citing the verse "life is of two kinds, sweet and bitter" — since a person may be tested (fitna) by either.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris's entry for the root ف-ت-ق (f-t-q):

**Core sense.** The three letters fāʾ, tāʾ, qāf form one coherent root meaning "to open" or "to split" something (fatḥ). The base verb: fataqtu al-shayʾa fatqan, "I split/rent the thing" — a fatq.

**Extended senses recorded:**
1. Al-fatq as an idiom — "splitting the staff of the community" (shaqq ʿaṣā al-jamāʿah) — meaning to break apart the group's unity/cohesion.
2. Al-fatq = "daybreak" (al-ṣubḥ) — the sky "splitting open" with light.
3. Aʿwām al-fataq = "years of abundance/fertility" (khiṣb). A line of verse is cited (source not named) using the phrase: "She did not hope for milk after the years of abundance" — risl ("milk," possibly also "ease") no longer expected once the good years passed.
4. Aftaqa al-qamar — said of the moon when it comes through a break/gap (fatq) in the clouds and appears.
5. Aftaqa al-qawm — said of a group of people when the clouds part and clear away from them.
6. Al-Aṣmaʿī's usage: jamalun fatīq, "a fatīq camel" — a camel so full-bodied it has "split open" with fatness (tafattaqa simanan). A parallel verb form, fatiqa yaftaqu fataqan, is given for the same idea.
7. Al-faytaq = "carpenter" — attested in a line of al-Aʿshā's poetry: "At the door is a faytaq" (a carpenter).

All senses trace back to the one root-idea: something opening up or splitting apart, whether literally (a rip, a break in cloud, daybreak) or figuratively (a rift in a group, or a body "splitting" with fatness/plenty).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: فَتْرَة 1x "(after) an interval (of cessation)"; يَفْتُرُ 1x "they slacken"; يُفَتَّرُ 1x "will it subside"
text:
Root ف‑ت‑ر (f-t-r), from Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha.

Core meaning: weakness or slackness in a thing.

1. Basic verb — fatara/yafturu/futūr: something "fatara-ed," i.e. it grew weak, slack, or faltered.

2. A languid gaze — al-ṭarf al-fātir describes a glance that is soft/languid rather than sharp and piercing (the opposite of a keen, sidelong look).

3. Causative forms — both fattara and aftara ("I weakened/enfeebled it") are used for weakening something, i.e. two verb-forms (Form II and Form IV) carry the same causative sense.

4. Qur'anic citation — Ibn Fāris quotes {lā yufattaru ʿanhum} ("it is not lightened/relaxed from them," Q43:75, al-Zukhruf), glossing it simply as "it is not weakened" (lā yuḍʿafu). No further exegesis is given.

5. An irregular offshoot — al-fitr, the span between the tips of an open thumb and forefinger (a hand-span unit of measure), which Ibn Fāris flags as not fitting the root's core "weakness" sense.

6. A proper name — Fitr, a woman's name, illustrated with a line of verse: "Have you cut the rope of affection that was from Fitr?" (poet not identified in this entry).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَسْتَفْتُ 6x "then ask them"; يُفْتِي 5x "explain to us"; فَتَىٰ 3x "to his boy"; فِتْيَة 3x "to his servants"; فَتَيَٰت 2x "your slave girls"; فَتَيَان 1x "two young men"; فَتًى 1x "a youth"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root f-t-y (fāʾ, tāʾ, plus a weak letter) as two distinct roots, plus a separate hamzated form:

1. Freshness and youth. al-fatiyy is the young/fresh animal among camels; al-fatā is a young man (plural al-fityān), and al-fatāʾ is youthfulness itself — one says "a youth clearly in his prime." A verse of poetry illustrates it: when a man has lived two hundred years, cheerfulness and youth are long gone.

2. Clarifying a ruling. From this comes al-futyā — giving an authoritative answer. aftā means a jurist stated the ruling on a question; istaftā means to ask for such a ruling. Ibn Fāris cites Q 4:176 ("They ask you for a ruling; say: God gives you the ruling concerning al-kalāla"). The nouns fatwā and futyā belong here.

3. The hamzated form (fatiʾa / fataʾa) falls outside both senses above. mā fatiʾtu / fataʾtu adhkuruhu means "I never ceased mentioning it" (equivalent to mā ziltu, "I kept on"). He cites Q 12:85 ("By God, you will not cease remembering Yūsuf"), glossing taftaʾu tadhkuru as "you will not stop remembering."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: f-w-D -- Ibn Faris, Maqayis al-Lugha

Core meaning: reliance on someone else in a matter -- handing a matter over to another and referring it to him. All other uses branch out from this core sense.

1. fawwada ilayhi amrahu -- "he entrusted/delegated his affair to him," i.e. he referred it to that person. Ibn Faris cites the Quran here: "wa-ufawwidu amri ila Llah" -- "and I commit my affair to Allah" (Ghafir 40:44), spoken by the figure in that surah's narrative.

2. batu fawda -- "they spent the night fawda," meaning intermingled/mixed together. Ibn Faris treats this as an extension of sense 1: each person had entrusted his affairs to the others, so nothing was kept separate. He supports this with a line of verse describing people whose food is held in common, scattered loose among their packs, who "cannot keep a secret except by calling out to one another" -- i.e. they hide nothing from each other.

3. maluhum fawda baynahum -- "their property is fawda between them," used when none of them disputes or opposes the other over it -- wealth held jointly, without contention.

4. tafawada sh-sharikani fi l-mal -- two business partners "engage in tafawud" over property: they form a partnership in which each entrusts his affair to the other, each satisfied with what the other does. Ibn Faris notes this arrangement is of the kind permitted by the sharia (the law) -- his own characterization, not elaborated further.

All four senses trace back to one root idea: handing a matter over to, or holding something in common with, another party.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ف-و-ه (f-w-h) as a single sound root whose core idea is an opening or gaping in something.

1. **Wideness of the mouth** — al-fawah is a wide mouth; the adjectives are afwah (of a man) and fawhāʾ (of a woman).

2. **Origin of the word "mouth"** — Arabic philologists hold that al-fam ("mouth") derives from fawah, which is why the adjective for a wide-mouthed man is afwah.

3. **To utter/speak** — fāha bi'l-kalām, yafūhu bihi means to give voice to something, to pronounce it. From this, al-mufawwah is one who is capable and eloquent in speech.

4. **Protruding front teeth** — some say al-fawah also denotes the length and outward projection of the upper front teeth (Ibn Fāris attributes this to unnamed others).

5. **Mouth of a river** — al-fuwwaha means a river's mouth; this special form was coined to distinguish the river's "mouth" from a human's.

6. **Aromatic spices** — al-fūh is the singular of afwāh al-ṭīb (aromatic spices), paralleling sūq/aswāq (market/markets). Ibn Fāris notes the underlying analogy is one: as if, when a spice's scent "spread out," it "spoke" — tying the sense back to the root's idea of an opening/emission from a mouth.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats f-w-j as a single semantic idea: gathering, coming together in a mass.

1. Core sense — assembling, a crowd forming. From this comes fawj, a group or band of people. Plural afwāj; the doubled ("plural of the plural") forms are afāwij and afāwīj.

2. Excluded from this root — the verb afāja al-rajul ("the man moved fast, hurried") does not belong here; Ibn Fāris assigns it to the root with yāʾ (f-y-j). The noun fayj (a runner/courier) derives from that yāʾ root, not from f-w-j.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: unnamed verse; Abū Miḥjan al-Thaqafī (lived into Islam); Umayyah (pre-Islamic)
text:
Root ف و م (f-w-m), Ibn Manẓūr, Lisān al-ʿArab

1. al-fūm — crop/grain or wheat generally; the Azd tribe of al-Sharāh used it specifically for an ear of grain (singular fūmah), illustrated with a line of poetry. Some hold al-fūm means chickpeas in a Levantine dialect, its seller called fāmiyy (altered from fūmiyy, by a pattern of nisbah-alteration also seen elsewhere).
2. al-fūm also means bread — "fawwimū lanā" ("bake bread for us") is cited as an old dialectal usage.
3. The entry's core dispute — Qur'anic citation al-Baqarah 2:61, "wa fūmihā wa ʿadasihā" — "and its grain/garlic and its lentils." A substantial scholarly debate is surveyed: some exegetes read fūm as "garlic," treating the fāʾ as a substitution for thāʾ (supported by a variant reading from Ibn Masʿūd, "wa thūmihā"); others — including al-Zajjāj, whom Ibn Manẓūr treats as decisive — insist al-fūm means wheat/grain, arguing it would be absurd for the Israelites to request food with no wheat, the basic staple, in it. Al-Farrāʾ, al-Liḥyānī, and Abū Manṣūr are all cited weighing in on the same debate, generally favoring the wheat/grain reading even when acknowledging the thāʾ variant.
4. A grammatical note on the word's plural, fumān, distinguishing its vowel patterns from the singular (via Ibn Jinnī).
5. Illustrative citations: a line of poetry by Abū Miḥjan al-Thaqafī about not needing to cultivate fūm; a line by Umayyah listing fūmān among garden produce (with a manuscript variant, and a gloss identifying a companion word as "onions"); Ibn Durayd's note that al-fūmah names a single ear of grain, and a guess (which Abū Manṣūr doubts is genuinely Arabic) about the sugar-seller's title.
6. Closing idiom: "qaṭṭaʿū al-shāta fūman fūman" — they cut up the sheep piece by piece.
7. Al-Fayyūm — a place in the land of Egypt, noted as where Marwān ibn Muḥammad, the last king of the Umayyads, was killed.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ف و ق as two distinct sound roots: (I) elevation/height, and (II) return/reversion.

Root I — height (fawq):
1. الفَوْق means loftiness. فاقَ أصحابَه = he surpassed/rose above his companions; أمرٌ فائق = an eminent, elevated matter.

Root II — return/reversion (fuwāq):
2. فُوَاق الناقة = the return of milk into a she-camel's udder after milking. Hence "he stayed only the span of a she-camel's fuwāq" (a brief interval). The gathered milk-flow is called فِيقَة (fīqa), whose original radical is wāw. Ibn Fāris cites al-Aʿshā: "until, when a fīqa had gathered in her udder, she came to suckle her heart's darling."
3. From this sense, a hadith about the Qur'an: "atafawwaquhu tafawwuqa al-laqūḥ" — reading one's portion not all at once but in successive draughts, likened to milk returning to the udder.
4. Both فُوَاق and فَوَاق are attested. On {mā lahā min fawāq} (Q. 38:15), Ibn Fāris glosses fawāq as: no returning, no relenting/repetition, no reversal. He reports another view: "no respite (naẓira)," and notes the two senses are close.
5. Also from "return": أفاقَ السكرانُ (the drunkard sobered up) — his reason returning to him. And الأفاويق = water gathering in the clouds.
6. Also here: الفُوق, the notch of an arrow — so called because the bowstring is set as though returned into it; plural أفواق. An inverted (metathesized) form فُقًى also occurs. سهمٌ أفوق = an arrow with a broken notch.

Anomalous (outside both roots):
7. هو يَفُوق بنفسِه (he is expiring). Ibn Fāris explains this as a case of letter-substitution (ibdāl): the original is يَسُوق (yasūq), with fāʾ replacing sīn, used of a person giving up his soul.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ف و ر (f-w-r), from Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha.

Core meaning: "boiling" (ghalayān) — a single root-idea, with everything else derived from it.

1. Al-fawr = boiling. Used of a cooking pot: "fārat al-qidru tafūru fawran" — the pot boiled/boils. Ibn Fāris cites a verse of poetry describing an enemy's "pot boiling over" against the speakers, who let it settle and skim it while it is still hot — a figure for hostility coming to a head.

2. By extension, "fāra ghaḍabuhu" — "his anger boiled over" — said when anger surges or seethes (jāsha), i.e. boiling applied metaphorically to rage.

3. From this same idea comes the common expression "faʿalahu min fawrihi" — "he did it fawrihi," meaning he did it right at the outset of the matter, immediately, before things had settled down (i.e., "on the spot," "at once," while the matter was still "boiling").

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats f-w-t as one sound root whose single idea is the opposite of catching up with something and reaching it — a thing getting past you, or staying out of reach.

1. Escaping / slipping past. فَاتَهُ الشَّيْءُ, verbal noun فَوْت — the thing got away from him, he failed to attain it.

2. Being at a remove from each other. تَفَاوَتَ الشَّيْئَانِ — the two things grew far apart, i.e. neither one reached the other. (Derived on the tafāʿul pattern of mutual action.)

3. Acting ahead of someone without consulting him. الِافْتِيَاتُ is an iftiʿāl-form built from fawt: getting to a matter first, without taking counsel. Hence فُلَانٌ لَا يُفْتَاتُ عَلَيْهِ — "no one gets ahead of him," i.e. nothing is done without his order.

4. A gap or interval. الْفَوْتُ is also the space between two things, as between two fingers; plural أَفْوَاتٌ. Ibn Fāris places this in the same chapter, the gap being what has not been closed.

5. Idioms built on the root:
   - مَاتَ مَوْتَ الْفَوَاتِ — "he died the death of fawāt," explained as dying such that what he had intended to do (make a bequest and the like) escaped him. (The clause describing the manner of death is defective in this text; the sense given is "suddenly.")
   - هُوَ مِنِّي فَوْتَ الرُّمْحِ — "he is a spear's remove from me."
   - A man's curse against another, cited here: "may God make his provision at the fawt of his mouth" — that is, where he can see it but cannot reach it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: فَوْز 19x "(is) the success"; فَائِزُون 4x "(are) the successful ones"; فَازَ 3x "has attained"; مَفَازَة 2x "to their place of salvation"; مَفَاز 1x "(is) success"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root f-w-z (فوز) as producing two opposite meanings: (1) deliverance/escape, and (2) destruction/dying.

Sense 1 — deliverance, success, carrying something off:
- فَازَ / يَفُوزُ (fāza/yafūzu): to escape safely, be delivered; the agent noun is fāʾiz.
- فَازَ بِالْأَمْرِ (fāza bi-l-amr): to make off with a matter, take it and get clear away with it — hence, of anyone who gains some good and carries it off.
- Idiom: on divorcing his wife a man would say فُوزِي بِأَمْرِكِ ("take charge of your own affair"), equivalent to "your affair is in your own hand."
- Qur'anic witness: Āl ʿImrān 3:185, "whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to the Garden has attained [fāza]."

Sense 2 — perishing/dying:
- فَوَّزَ الرَّجُلُ (fawwaza): the man died/perished. Ibn Fāris cites the poet al-Kumayt: "…and after him Jarwal perished [fawwaza]."

The desert (al-mafāza) — a disputed derivation:
- Some derive it from sense 1: it is called mafāza as a hopeful omen for the traveler, wishing him safety; so mafāza = "place of safety/deliverance." Qur'anic witness: Āl ʿImrān 3:188, "in a place of safety [mafāza] from the punishment."
- Others derive it from sense 2 (fawwaza = to perish, given the desert's deadliness); from this, fawwaza al-rajul means "he set out across the desert," as in the verse "he crossed the desert from Qurāqir to Suwā."

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: فَخُور 4x "boaster"; فَخَّار 1x "like the pottery"; تَفَاخُر 1x "and boasting"
text:
Ibn Sīda's account of the root ف خ ر (f-kh-r):

1. Core sense — boasting, self-praise. A cluster of nouns (fakhar, fikhr, fukhr, fakhār, fakhāra, fakhkhīrī, fikhkhīrāʾ) all mean "praising oneself by listing one's qualities." The verb is fakhara / yafkhar, verbal noun fakhr; al-Liḥyānī records the phrase "a fine instance of boasting." The doer is fākhir or fakhūr. The reflexive VIII form iftakhara means the same.

2. Competitive boasting. Tafākhara (VI): a group vaunt against one another. Fākhara (III): to match someone boast for boast — a contest, as in the verse recited by Thaʿlab about "the day of vaunting (yawm al-fikhār)," where a rival is silenced and blinded to both generosity and boasting. Your fakhīr is your opponent in such a contest; al-fakhīr also names the one who loses it. Fākharahu fa-fakharahu: he out-boasted him. Fakharahu / afkharahu ʿalayhi: he ranked one man above another in boasting.

3. Derived nouns and idioms. Mafkhara / mafkhura: the thing one boasts about, a title to glory. Fukhra: boasting attributed to a person — "he has fukhra over them"; "what is this thing's fukhra (glory) to you?" (al-Liḥyānī). Fakhara can also shade into arrogance: "the man grew haughty through boasting."

4. Extension to excellence in things. Al-fākhir means the choice, superior specimen of anything. Ibn Sīda derives this from sense 1 through Labīd's line about a valley adorned with fākhir herbage: the plant that has reached full, excellent growth, "as though it boasted over what was around it." Istafkhara l-shayʾ: to buy something of the superior grade.

5. Bulk without yield — a specialised animal sense. Al-fakhūr of a she-camel: big-uddered but poor in milk; alternatively, one that gives what milk she has with nothing held in reserve. An udder called fakhūr is thick, with narrow ducts and little milk; the abstract noun is fukhr / fukhur, as in the verse cited by Ibn al-Aʿrābī praising a camel "wide of teats, without fukhur."

6. Sheer size, in other bodies. A palm-tree is fakhūr when its trunk is massive and its fronds thick. A stallion is fakhūr when its member is large and long; faykhar describes a large male member, and a man in whom that part is large — sometimes pronounced with zāy (fayzar), rarely.

7. A disdain sense. In one cited line, "you see him yafkhar that his tents be pitched" beside a mean, short-reined man; Ibn al-Aʿrābī glossed the verb here as "he disdains, holds himself too high for it."

8. Pottery. Al-fakhkhāra: an earthen jar; plural fakhkhār. Ibn Sīda cites the Qur'an, "from dry clay like the fakhkhār (baked pottery)" (Q 55:14).

9. A plant name. Al-fākhūr: a fragrant plant; Abū Ḥanīfa identifies it as the broad-leaved marw (a marjoram).

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
**Root f-y-ʾ (فيأ)** — al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's account:

1. **Core sense — returning to a praiseworthy state.** The nouns *fayʾ* and *fayʾa* denote a return to a good or approved condition. Qur'anic evidence: "until it returns to the command of God; and if it returns" (49:9), and "and if they return" (2:226).

2. **Shade that turns back.** From the same sense: *fāʾa al-ẓill*, "the shade turned/came back." Al-Rāghib specifies that *fayʾ* is used only of the shade that returns — the afternoon shadow, not shade in general. Cited with "its shadows incline and turn about" (16:48).

3. **Spoil taken without hardship.** Property gained without effort or struggle was called *fayʾ*: "what God has given back as *fayʾ* to His messenger" (59:7); "of what God has given back to you as *fayʾ*" (33:50). He reports the view of some that this was named with the word for "shade" to signal that even the most prized worldly goods behave like a shadow that passes — supported by a poet's line, "I see wealth as the returning shadows of an evening," and the saying "this world is only a passing shade."

4. **fiʾa — a mutually supporting band.** A group that stands together, whose members "return to one another" in giving each other backing. Qur'anic evidence: "when you meet a band, stand firm" (8:45); "how many a small band has overcome a numerous band" (2:249); "two bands that met" (3:13); "two parties concerning the hypocrites" (4:88); "any band to help him" (28:81); "when the two bands came in sight of each other, he turned back on his heels" (8:48).

Method: al-Rāghib derives every branch — turning shade, unearned spoil, and the allied band — from the single idea of *returning*, and glosses each only through Qur'anic usage plus one poetic line.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ف ي ض (f-y-ḍ) as a single sound root whose core notion is a thing flowing or running easily; the remaining uses, on his method, are extensions measured analogically against that core.

1. Water overflowing — فَاضَ الْمَاءُ (fāḍa al-māʾ), "the water overflowed." This is the base image.

2. Filling to overflow — أَفَاضَ إِنَاءَهُ, "he filled his vessel," i.e. filled it until it ran over; likewise أَفَاضَ دُمُوعَهُ, "he poured out his tears."

3. A crowd surging away — أَفَاضَ الْقَوْمُ مِنْ عَرَفَةَ, "the people poured forth from ʿArafa," i.e. they pushed off in a body; Ibn Fāris explicitly likens it to the running of a flood. Cited proof-text: Q 2:199, "then pour forth from where the people pour forth."

4. Plunging into talk — أَفَاضَ الْقَوْمُ فِي الْحَدِيثِ, "they launched into the conversation," i.e. threw themselves into it. Cited proof-text: Q 10:61, "when you are pouring into it."

5. Casting the divining arrows — أَفَاضَ بِالْقِدَاحِ, "he threw the arrows," explained as though the caster made them run out of his hand. Supported by a verse describing arrows as if in their case (ribāba) while the caster casts and announces the outcome.

6. A camel bringing up its cud — أَفَاضَ الْبَعِيرُ بِجَرَّتِهِ, "the camel pushed up its cud from its chest," with a supporting verse: the camels brought up the cud after their silent abstention, having grazed at Dhū al-Abāṭiḥ on the plant ḥaqīl.

7. Land with surface water — أَرْضٌ ذَاتُ فُيُوضٍ, land in which there is water that overflows.

8. Proverbial contrast — أَعْطَاهُ غَيْضًا مِنْ فَيْضٍ, "he gave him a ghayḍ out of a fayḍ," glossed as "a little out of much."

9. A proper name — al-Aṣmaʿī is cited for the river of Basra being called, uniquely, al-Fayḍ.

10. Dying — فَاضَ الرَّجُلُ, "the man passed away," the soul being spoken of as flowing out. Two verses are given: "an eye was put out and a soul flowed away," and a line in which the speaker says his soul would nearly have poured out had a fixed term not been deferred. Ibn Fāris adds a dialect observation: eloquent elders of Rabīʿa b. Mālik pronounced فَاضَتْ نَفْسُهُ with ḍād (rather than the variant with ẓāʾ), one of them reciting the second verse.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ف ي ل (f-y-l), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: slackness/limpness and weakness.

1. rajul fīlu al-raʾy — a man of unsound, feeble judgment, illustrated with a line of poetry by al-Kumayt reproaching sons for being fīl (failing/weak) rather than worthy of their noble lineage.
2. Ibn Fāris speculatively connects this to al-fāʾil — the flesh over the hip-socket's hollow, possibly named for its softness — though he notes Abū ʿUbayd reports some considered al-fāʾil instead to be a blood-vessel, not flesh.
3. Closing outlier, explicitly flagged as not fitting the root's pattern: al-mufāyalah — a children's guessing-game where something is buried in sand divided into two portions, and players guess which portion hides it — illustrated with a line of poetry by Ṭarafah comparing a ship cleaving water to a player dividing sand by hand.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: فَزِعَ 3x "and will be terrified"; فَزَع 2x "the terror"; فُزِّعَ 1x "fear is removed"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats f-z-ʿ as two distinct sound roots: (1) fright/alarm, and (2) coming to someone's aid.

**Sense 1 — fright, alarm (al-fazaʿ / al-ḏuʿr)**
- Verb pattern: faziʿa / yafzaʿu / fazaʿan — "to be frightened"; causative afzaʿtuhu — "I frightened him."
- mafzaʿ al-qawm — the one people run to in fright when something suddenly overtakes them.
- Form II with the preposition ʿan, fazzaʿtu ʿanhu, reverses the sense: to remove the fright from someone. Ibn Fāris cites Q 34:23, "until, when fright is removed from their hearts" (ḥattā iḏā fuzziʿa ʿan qulūbihim), for this usage.
- mafzaʿa — the place a frightened one takes refuge in. Poetic witness: "Tall, his gaze raised high … toward the dog's place of refuge."

**Sense 2 — aid, rescue (al-ighātha)**
- Ibn Fāris cites a saying attributed to the Prophet, addressed to the Anṣār: "You are many at the call for aid, and few when there is gain to covet."
- He notes the same causative form carries both senses: afzaʿtuhu can mean "I terrified him" or "I came to his aid."
- faziʿtu ilayhi fa-afzaʿanī — "I took refuge with him in fright, and he aided me," combining both senses in one construction.
- Poetic witnesses for the "aid" sense: "So I said to Kās: bridle her — we alighted at the dune of Zarūd only to give aid"; and "Whenever a crying, frightened man came to us, his cry was answered by the striking of shin-bones" — i.e. by springing at once to action.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats f-z-z as a small root (uṣayl) that indicates lightness (khiffa) and what is close to it.

1. **To make light, to unsettle.** fazzahu and istafazzahu mean istakhaffahu, "he made him light", that is, unsettled him. Ibn Fāris cites Q 17:76, "And indeed they were near to unsettling you (la-yastafizzūnaka) from the land", and explains it as: they would bring you to move lightly away from it. One also says that a man's folly (jahl) has unsettled him (istafazzahu).

2. **To alarm.** afazzahu l-khawfu, "fear alarmed him", has the same meaning as afzaʿahu.

3. **Light.** A man described as fazz is light (khafīf).

4. **To turn aside.** People say fazza ʿan al-shayʾ, meaning he turned aside from the thing.

5. **The calf.** al-fazz is the young of the cow. Ibn Fāris suggests that it may be called this because its body is light. He cites a verse: "As the calf (fazz) of a ghayṭala cried for relief with the first milk (sayʾ): it feared the eyes, and the gathering of the milk (ḥashak) was not waited for on its behalf."

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: غَشِيَ 13x "it covers it"; أُغْشِيَتْ 4x "he covers"; غَٰشِيَة 3x "(of) the overwhelming"; غَشَّىٰ 3x "covered"; غِشَٰوَة 2x "(is) a veil"; ٱسْتَغْشَ 2x "they cover (themselves)"; تَغَشَّىٰ 1x "he covers her"; مَغْشِىّ 1x "(of) one fainting"
poets_named: Jaʿfar ibn ʿUlba al-Ḥārithī (Umayyad); unnamed verse
text:
Root غ-ش-و (gh-sh-w), as recorded by Ibn Sīda. The core idea running through the whole entry is covering / enveloping (taghṭiya).

1. Nouns for "a covering" of the sight or the heart: ghashw, ghashwa (also ghishwa, ghushwa), ghishāwa (also ghashāwa), ghāshiya, ghishya, and ghishāya/ghashāya — the last three cited from al-Liḥyānī. All mean "a covering" (ghiṭāʾ).

2. Verbs: ghashā / aghshā Allāhu ʿalā baṣarihi = God put a covering over his sight; ghashiyahu al-amr / taghashshāhu = the affair enveloped him; aghshaytuhu iyyāhu / ghashshaytuhu = I made it cover him.

3. Qur'anic usage of the verb "cover":
 - (yughshī al-layl al-nahār) "He covers the night with the day"; al-Liḥyānī notes a variant reading (yaghshā al-layl).
 - In al-Anfāl, three readings of the drowsiness verse: (yughshīkum), (wa-yughshīkum), and (yaghshākumu al-nuʿās) — "drowsiness covers you."
 - (hal atāka ḥadīthu al-ghāshiya): the al-ghāshiya is glossed either as the Resurrection (it envelops all creation) or as the Fire (it envelops the faces of the deniers).

4. ghishāʾ = the cover of anything: of the heart, saddle, mount, sword, etc.

5. Colour/marking senses: al-ghashwāʾ (she-goat) whose face is covered with white; al-aghshā (horse) whose blaze spreads over its face. al-Ghashwāʾ was also the name of Khassān ibn Salama's mare — a descriptive word turned proper name.

6. Sword and saddle terms: ghishāwat/ghāshiyat al-qalb = the heart's enveloping membrane ("shirt"); ghāshiyat al-raḥl = the iron piece above the saddle's cantle; al-ghāshiya = the leather sheathing a scabbard from below the "moustache" (near the hilt) to the "shoe" (the tip), or the leather covering on sword-hilts. Ibn Sīda cites Jaʿfar ibn ʿUlba al-Ḥārithī: "We share our swords with them in the worst division: ours the coverings, theirs the edges."

7. al-ghāshiya also = a disease that settles in the belly — again from the sense of "covering."

8. istaghshā thiyābahu = to wrap oneself in one's clothes so as not to be seen or heard; cited with the Qur'anic (wa-staghshaw thiyābahum) and (alā ḥīna yastaghshūna thiyābahum).

9. al-ghashwa = the sidr (lote-tree), with a poetic citation: "I went out at dawn toward a lote-tree on a mountain peak... and the trace of a ewe that had died of emaciation."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats gh-ḍ-ḍ as two sound roots: one indicates holding back and diminution, the other freshness.

1. **Holding back, and diminishing.**
   - The first instance is ghaḍḍ al-baṣar, lowering the eyes. More generally, anything you have held back, you have "ghaḍḍ-ed" (ghaḍaḍtahu).
   - From this comes the expression "a ghaḍāḍa attaches to him in that," meaning a matter that makes him lower his eyes.
   - al-ghaḍghaḍa is diminution. A ḥadīth says: "He has passed from this world with his fill, not diminished (lam yughaḍghaḍ)." People also say, "He is a sea that is not diminished." ghaḍghaḍtu al-siqāʾa means "I diminished the waterskin," and the verb is used the same way of a due (ḥaqq).

2. **Freshness.** al-ghaḍḍ is the fresh of anything, and the palm's spathe (ṭalʿ) is called ghaḍīḍ when it first emerges.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: غَضَب 14x "wrath"; غَضِبَ 6x "and allah's wrath (is)"; غَضْبَٰن 2x "angry"; مَغْضُوب 1x "those who earned (your) wrath"; مُغَٰضِب 1x "(while) angry"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats غ‑ض‑ب as a single sound root whose core sense is intensity and strength. His entry records:

1. Core notion — the root points to intensity (shidda) and strength (quwwa).

2. Concrete anchor — al-ghaḍba is said to mean a hard, solid rock, and Ibn Fāris reports that al-ghaḍab ("anger") was derived from this, since anger is an intensification of displeasure (sukht).

3. Verb and forms — ghaḍiba / yaghḍabu / ghaḍaban ("to become angry"); the agent nouns are ghaḍbān and ghaḍūb.

4. A usage distinction — ghaḍibtu li-fulān ("I grew angry for someone") is used when the person is living, whereas ghaḍibtu bihi is used when he is dead. Cited support: a line of Durayd, "annā ghiḍābun bi-Maʿbadi" ("that we are enraged over Maʿbad").

5. A further sense — al-ghaḍūb is also said to denote a great serpent.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
text:
Root: غصص (gh-ṣ-ṣ) — from the Tāj al-ʿArūs (Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī, d. 1791 CE)

1. Core sense — choking/obstruction in the throat.
al-ghuṣṣah (الغُصَّة) means ash-shajā, a lump or obstruction that catches in the throat (plural: ghuṣaṣ). The entry cites Qur'an 73:13, "wa-ṭaʿāman dhā ghuṣṣah" — "and food that chokes [the throat]."
- Ibn Durayd: al-ghuṣṣah is something that lodges crosswise in the throat and blocks it.
- Al-Layth: it is an obstruction one chokes on, located in the upper throat area (near what is popularly called the "Adam's apple").
- Al-Zabīdī's teacher (Shaykhunā) notes that the dictionary's own wording treats ghuṣṣah, shajā, and sharaq as synonyms.
- Some philologists distinguished finer usage by what one chokes on: ghaṣṣa (food), shariqa (drink), shajiya (a bone), jariḍa (saliva) — though writers often used these interchangeably.

2. As a personal byname — "Dhū l-Ghuṣṣah" ("the one with the choke/lump in his throat")
Used as a nickname for two different men, both apparently because something in their throat made their speech unclear:
- al-Ḥuṣayn ibn Yazīd al-Ḥārithī, a Companion of the Prophet (there is disagreement over whether he had a formal delegation-visit to the Prophet — Ibn Fahd says that claim is mistaken).
- ʿĀmir ibn Mālik al-Ḥarīshī, an Arab horseman/knight known for a boasting-contest with Zufar ibn al-Ḥārith at the court of the Umayyad caliph ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān. Also called "Dhū l-Quṣṣah" (with a qāf) in some sources.

3. Grammar and verb forms.
- "ghaṣiṣta" (you choked) is the standard form (kasr on the middle radical); "ghaṣaṣta" (fatḥ) is recorded as a rare/irregular dialectal variant, attributed by Abū ʿUbaydah to the tribe of al-Ribāb.
- Two imperfect/verbal-noun patterns are given: taghaṣṣu with maṣdar ghaṣaṣan, and tughaṣṣu with maṣdar ghaṣṣan (per the Lisān al-ʿArab). Al-Zabīdī flags that al-Jawharī misreported this verb under a different root (ʿ-ṣ-ḍ) and that al-Fīrūzābādī, the base author, uncritically repeated the same error.
- Active participle: ghāṣṣ ("choking," e.g. anta ghāṣṣun bi-l-ṭaʿām, "you are choking on food"); also ghaṣṣān with the same meaning, which some restrict to choking specifically on water. A citation from the poet ʿAdī ibn Zayd al-ʿIbādī uses ghaṣṣān of choking on water.

4. A plant name.
al-ghaṣghaṣ is reported (on Abū Mālik's authority, via Ibn Durayd) as the name of a plant — though the author notes his own colleagues did not recognize the word.

5. Extended/figurative sense — crowding, fullness.
A place can be described as ghāṣṣ bi-l-qawm — "packed/crowded with people." A saying is quoted: true sociability is found in the crowded gathering, not the exclusive private one. The causative aghaṣṣa is used of "cramming" land with people so that it becomes too narrow/crowded — illustrated with a satirical verse by al-Ṭirimmāḥ against al-Farazdaq, picturing the tribe of Qaḥṭān filling the land against him with spears, swords, and horses.

6. Further derived expressions (appended notes).
- aghaṣṣahu ighṣāṣan — "he made him choke."
- al-ghuṣṣah can also denote generally "what one has choked on," and ghuṣaṣ al-mawt ("the chokings of death") derives from this image.
- ghaṣṣa bi-rīqihi ("he choked on his own saliva") is used as a euphemism for dying.
- aghaṣṣahu bi-rīqihi — "he irritated/distressed him."
- ightaṣṣa l-majlisu bi-ahlihi — "the gathering was crowded with its people" — a synonym of ghaṣṣa in the crowding sense.

dictionary: ʿAyn — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786)
text:
Root: غصب (gh-ṣ-b), from Kitāb al-ʿAyn by al-Khalīl b. Aḥmad al-Farāhīdī (d. 786 CE).

Al-Khalīl's dictionary groups roots by their letter-set, so this entry opens by noting that of the three letters gh-ṣ-b, only two orderings are actually used as roots in Arabic: غصب (ghaṣb) and صبغ (ṣabgh). It then gives both.

**غصب (ghaṣb)** — one sense: taking something wrongfully and by force/coercion.

**صبغ (ṣabgh)** — several senses:
1. Dye/coloring matter used on garments (al-ṣibgh, al-ṣibāgh); the verbal noun is al-ṣabgh; dyeing as a trade is al-ṣibāgha, its practitioner al-ṣabbāgh.
2. The same words also denote a food relish or condiment — something dipped into food. The ʿAyn cites Qur'an 23:20, "wa-ṣibghin lil-ākilīn" ("and a relish for those who eat"), as its example.
3. The Qur'anic phrase ṣibghat Allāh ("God's dye," Q. 2:138) — the text glosses this as the milla, the creed/religious community that the Muslims adhere to as their religion. (This gloss is the book's interpretive statement, not a separate lexical citation.)
4. A bird called al-aṣbagh is one with a white tail; the abstract noun for this marking is al-ṣibgha.
5. Of a she-camel, ṣabaghat (a dialect variant of sabaghat) means she gave birth to fully-formed young.
6. Al-maṣbagh is both the place where dyeing happens and the verbal noun of the act; e.g. ṣabaghtuhu maṣbaghan, "I dyed it."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
**Root: غطش (gh-ṭ-sh) — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris**

Core meaning: Ibn Fāris treats gh-ṭ-sh as one sound, single-sense root meaning "darkness" and things that resemble it. Everything below branches from that one idea.

1. **Of the eye:** al-aghṭash is a man whose eye has a defect resembling ʿamash (weak, dim, blear sight) — a "darkness" of vision. The feminine form is ghaṭshāʾ.

2. **Of the desert:** a falāt (open desert plain) called ghaṭshā is one so obscure/confusing that no direction can be found across it — effectively "dark" in the sense of trackless. Ibn Fāris quotes a line of poetry (poet unnamed) describing a night crossing of a landmark-less desert (yahmāʾ), "dark-at-night" (ghaṭshā), where the only company is the cry of its fayyād — a nocturnal desert creature/phantom said to call out at night.

3. **Of the night:** ghaṭasha al-layl simply means "the night grew dark." Ibn Fāris then gives the causative: "Allāh taʿālā aghṭashahu" — God darkened it (i.e., made the night dark). This phrasing echoes the wording used of the night in the Qur'an, though Ibn Fāris states it here as his own gloss of the verb, not as a citation with a verse reference.

4. **Figurative — feigned obliviousness:** al-mutaghāṭish is one who feigns blindness to something, i.e. pretends not to see or notice it (glossed by the author as synonymous with al-mutaʿāmī). The reflexive verb yataghāṭash carries the same sense: "he acts as though he doesn't notice."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ghayn-ṭāʾ-wāw (ghtw) from a single core sense: covering and concealment.

1. Verb usage: ghaṭaytu al-shayʾ and ghaṭṭaytu-hu both mean "I covered the thing" -- the doubled form (ghaṭṭaytu) is simply the intensive variant of the same verb.

2. Noun: al-ghiṭāʾ ("the cover/covering") is defined as whatever a person covers himself with.

3. Extended usage, night: the phrase ghaṭā al-laylu yaghṭū ("the night ghaṭā-ed") is used when the night envelops things in its darkness -- i.e. night "covering" the world is treated as an instance of the same root meaning.

The entry gives no Qur'anic or poetic citations beyond these illustrative phrases, and records only this one semantic core for the root.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root غ ب ن (gh-b-n), from Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha.

Core meaning: the root conveys weakness and being wronged or diminished.

1. Commercial sense — "ghubina al-rajulu fī bay'ihi" = the man was cheated/shortchanged in his sale (he is "yughbanu," the loss is "ghabn"). This happens when he is wronged/diminished in the deal.

2. Sense in judgment — "ghabana fī ra'yihi" = he showed a deficiency in his opinion, i.e., his judgment was weak.

Ibn Fāris notes both senses trace to one and the same underlying idea: a diminishing or coming up short — whether in a transaction or in one's own reasoning.

Derived noun: al-ghabīnah (the instance/state of being cheated) is built from al-ghabn on the same pattern as al-shatīmah ("an insult") is built from al-shatm ("reviling") — a standard fa'īlah noun pattern.

Extended/body-part sense: al-maghābin = the groin-folds/armpit creases of the body, so called because these areas are soft and weak compared to the strength of the rest of the body.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: غَٰبِرِين 7x "those who remain behind"; غَبَرَة 1x "(will be) dust"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats غ-ب-ر (gh-b-r) as two sound, independent roots: (1) remaining or lasting, and (2) a colour — that of dust.

**Root 1 — remaining, being left over**
1. غَبَرَ (ghabara) = "he/it remained." He cites Qur'an 29:33, {إِلَّا امْرَأَتَكَ كَانَتْ مِنَ الْغَابِرِينَ} — "except your wife; she was among those who remained behind."
2. بِالنَّاقَةِ غُبْرٌ (bi-l-nāqati ghubr): the she-camel has a remainder left in her.
3. بِهِ غُبَّرٌ مِنْ مَرَضٍ (bihi ghubbar min maraḍ): a residue of illness is still in him. Shāhid, attributed to Ibn Muqbil (or another): "If Sulaymā asks after me, tell her — a remnant of his malady is in him, yet he is well."
4. عِرْقٌ غَبِرَ (ʿirq ghabir): a vein that keeps re-opening, as though some residue always remained in it.
5. تَغَبَّرَتِ الْمَرْأَةُ الشَّيْخَ: a woman took what remained of an old man's fluid.

**Root 2 — the colour of dust**
6. غُبَار (ghubār, dust) is named from its غُبْرَة (ghubra), i.e. its colour; and أَغْبَر (aghbar) is any colour that is dust-coloured.
7. Shāhid from Ṭarafa: "I saw that the Banū Ghabrāʾ do not disown me, nor do the folk of that outstretched pavilion." Ibn Fāris glosses بَنُو غَبْرَاء (Banū Ghabrāʾ) as the destitute poor — their colouring is dust-covered; they are "people of the dust" (ahl al-matraba).
8. الْغَبْرَاء (al-ghabrāʾ) = the earth.
9. الْغُبَيْرَاء (al-ghubayrāʾ) = nabīdh (a steeped/fermented drink) made from millet/sorghum; he suggests its colour may have a dustiness to it.
10. دَاهِيَةُ الْغَبَر (dāhiyat al-ghabar, a disaster of ghabar): he assigns this, as his own judgment, to the colour root — the calamity is "dusty," i.e. murky and bewildering, so that the way it comes at you cannot be seen.

**Outside both roots**
11. Reported from Ibn al-Sikkīt: أَغْبَرْتُ فِي طَلَبِ الْحَاجَةِ (aghbartu fī ṭalab al-ḥāja) — "I applied myself hard / was persistent in pursuing what I needed." Ibn Fāris marks this as anomalous to the two roots above.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root gh-d-q (غدق) from a single core sense: copiousness, abundance, and plenty/ease.

1. Core sense — al-ghadaq: something copious and abundant. Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'anic verse {la-asqaynāhum māʾan ghadaqan}, "We would have given them abundant water to drink" (al-Jinn 72:16), as the anchoring example — water so plentiful it overflows.

2. Extended sense — al-ghadaq / al-ghaydāq: "the soft/luxuriant of anything" — i.e. anything marked by richness or ease, not just water.

3. Verb usage: ghadiqat ʿaynu l-māʾi taghdaqu ghadaqan — "the spring became copious, flowing abundantly" — the standard verb form built on this root, describing a water-source that gushes plentifully.

4. Human character sense — al-ghaydāq: a man of generous, noble character — the idea of abundance extended metaphorically to generosity of disposition.

5. A reported (not asserted) usage — Ibn Fāris notes that some people call the ḍabb (a large lizard) ghaydāq, and offers his own guess that this is only because of the fatness and plumpness of the animal — i.e. another metaphorical extension of "abundance/plenty" onto physical bulk.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root غ‑د‑ر (gh-d-r) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris states the root has one sound core sense: leaving/abandoning something (tark al-shayʾ). Every sense below is presented as a branch of that core idea.

1. Breaking faith — al-ghadr: breaking a covenant and failing to keep one's word ("leaving" one's commitment unfulfilled). Verb: ghadara/yaghdiru/ghadran. As an insult: "yā ghudar!" ("you treacherous one!"), plural "yā la ghudar."

2. A pitch-dark night — laylatun ghadiratun, a night "manifestly ghadir," i.e. very dark — said to be called this because it "abandons" people shut up in their houses, unable to go out because of the darkness.

3. A pool of rainwater — al-ghadīr, a standing pool left by rain, named because the flood/torrent "left it behind" when it receded.

4. A straggling ewe — ghadirat al-shātu describes a ewe that falls behind and is separated from the flock; if the shepherd leaves her there, she is called ghadīrah.

5. Rocky, impassable ground — al-ghadar: a stony, rugged terrain, so called because it is barely passable — as if travelers had "left it alone." From this comes the expression rajulun thabtu l-ghadar, "a man firm on rough ground," meaning steadfast in speech and in battle — he doesn't shy from the difficult ground others avoid.

6. Braided hair — al-ghadā'ir: plaited locks of hair, called this because once plaited they are "left" bound up that way for a time. Ibn Fāris cites a line of verse (poet unnamed in the entry) describing a woman's braids rising firmly upward, the plaits scattering between doubled and loosened strands.

Throughout, Ibn Fāris derives every sense — treachery, a dark night, a rain-pool, a lagging ewe, rocky ground, even braided hair — from the single underlying idea of "leaving/abandoning" something.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: غُدُوّ 5x "in the mornings"; غَد 5x "tomorrow"; غَدَ 3x "you left early morning"; غَدَوٰة 2x "in the morning"; غَدَاء 1x "our morning meal"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives غ-د-و (gh-d-w) from three consonants — ghayn, dāl, and a weak final letter — treating it as a single sound root whose core notion is a time of day (the morning).

1. Core verb: الْغُدُوّ (al-ghuduww) — going forth in the morning. Verb form: غَدَا يَغْدُو (ghadā yaghdū), "he set out in the morning."

2. Nouns for the morning: الْغُدْوَة (al-ghudwa) and الْغَدَاة (al-ghadāt), both meaning morning/forenoon. Their plurals differ: ghudwa → غُدًى (ghudan); ghadāt → غَدَوَاتٌ (ghadawāt).

3. الْغَادِيَة (al-ghādiya): a cloud that forms in the morning.

4. غَدًا (ghadan, "tomorrow"): from the same root, its original form being غَدْوًا (ghadwan). Cited verse: "…where they had encamped — and by morning, empty wastes."

5. الْغَدَاء (al-ghadāʾ): the daytime meal, so called because it is eaten during that (morning) time.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: غَٰفِل 27x "unaware"; غَفْلَة 5x "heedlessness"; تَغْفُلُ 1x "you neglect"; أَغْفَلْ 1x "we have made heedless"; غَٰفِلَٰت 1x "the unaware women"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats غ-ف-ل (gh-f-l) as a single sound root whose core meaning is leaving a thing out of inadvertence or heedlessness — usually unintentionally, though he notes it can also be deliberate.

1. Basic verb: غَفَلَ عَنْ (ghafala ʿan), with the verbal nouns ghaflah and ghufūl — "to be heedless of / neglect" something, i.e. to leave it because you have forgotten it (sāhiyan).

2. Grammatical/derivational contrast: the form-IV verb أَغْفَلَ (aghfala) means to leave something while still remembering it — a pointed distinction from ghafala (leaving through forgetfulness).

3. Extended sense — ghufl (غُفْل): applied to anything with no distinguishing mark, as if it had been "overlooked." Ibn Fāris gives three usages:
   - أَرْضٌ غُفْلٌ — land with no landmark or sign;
   - نَاقَةٌ غُفْلٌ — a she-camel bearing no brand;
   - رَجُلٌ غُفْلٌ — a man untested and inexperienced in affairs.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: غَفُور 91x "(is) oft-forgiving"; غَفَرَ 65x "forgive"; ٱسْتَغْفَرَ 40x "and ask forgiveness"; مَّغْفِرَة 28x "(is) forgiveness"; غَفَّار 5x "the oft-forgiving"; غَافِر 2x "(of) forgivers"; غُفْرَان 1x "(grant) us your forgiveness"; مُسْتَغْفِرِين 1x "and those who seek forgiveness"; ٱسْتِغْفَار 1x "(the) asking of forgiveness"
text:
Ibn Fāris organizes this root around one core idea — السَّتْر (covering, concealing) — then lists several senses he treats as deviations from it.

Core sense — covering:
