1. غَفْر / غُفْرَان (ghafr / ghufrān): covering. Applied to God's action toward a sin — غَفَرَ اللَّهُ ذَنْبَهُ, "God covered/forgave his sin" (verbal nouns ghafr, maghfira, ghufrān). A verse of poetry uses مَالِك الغَفْر ("possessor of al-ghafr") as an epithet of a supreme king.
2. غَفِرَ الثَّوْبُ: a garment "ghafira-ed" when its nap or pile rises — placed here because the nap covers the surface of the cloth.
3. Related concrete items of covering: المِغْفَر (migfar), a known head/helmet guard; الغِفَارَة (ghifāra), a cloth an oiling person lays on the crown of the head; الغَفِير (ghafīr), hair hanging over the nape. An Arab woman told her daughter اغْفِرِي غَفِيرَكِ — "cover it."
4. الغَفِيرَة (ghafīra) also means forgiveness (ghufrān), attested in a line lamenting a people who have "no ghafīra among them."

Deviant senses (Ibn Fāris marks these as departing from the covering idea):
5. الغُفْر (ghufr): the offspring of the wild mountain goat / ibex; its mother is called مُغْفِر (mughfir).
6. الغَفْر (ghafr): a relapse of illness, cited in verse alongside a fevered or wounded man who relapses.
7. المَغْفُور (maghfūr): a gum-like substance that exudes from the ʿurfuṭ tree (an acacia).

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: غَلِيظ 9x "severe"; ٱغْلُظْ 2x "and be stern"; غِلْظَة 1x "harshness"; ٱسْتَغْلَظَ 1x "then it becomes thick"
text:
al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's account of the root GH-L-Ẓ (غلظ):

1. Core sense: al-ghilẓa means "thickness" or "coarseness," the opposite of riqqa ("thinness, fineness"). It can be vocalized either ghilẓa or ghulẓa.

2. Physical origin, metaphorical extension: The word originally describes physical bodies (thick, solid, coarse), but is borrowed for abstract meanings — the same way words like "great" (kabīr) and "much" (kathīr) extend from the concrete to the abstract.

3. Applied to persons as harshness/sternness:
   - "let them find in you a ghilẓa" [al-Tawba 9:123] — glossed here as khushūna, "harshness, roughness."
   - "be stern toward them (ughluẓ ʿalayhim)" [al-Tawba 9:73] — the imperative sense of acting harshly.

4. Applied to punishment as severity: In "a punishment ghalīẓ" [Luqmān 31:24; Hūd 11:58], ghalīẓ carries the sense of a harsh, severe punishment.

5. Verbal form istaghlaẓa: means "it made itself ready / became prepared for that," and is also used when something literally grows thick (ghaluẓa). Shāhid: "then it grew thick/stout and stood firm upon its stalks" [al-Fatḥ 48:29], describing a plant becoming sturdy.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: غَلَبُ 15x "they will overcome"; غَالِب 13x "(are) the victorious"; غَلَب 1x "their defeat"; مَغْلُوب 1x "one overpowered"; غُلْب 1x "(of) thick foliage"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats غ-ل-ب (gh-l-b) as one sound root whose core sense is strength, domination (qahr), and force.

1. Core verb: غَلَبَ (ghalaba) — to prevail over, overcome, get the upper hand. It takes three verbal nouns: ghalb, ghalab, ghalaba. He cites Qurʾān al-Rūm 3, "and after their being overcome (ghalab) they will overcome (sa-yaghlibūn)."

2. غِلَاب (ghilāb) = مُغَالَبَة — a mutual contest in which each side strives to overcome the other.

3. أَغْلَب (aghlab) = thick-necked; from a distinct verb form غَلِبَ / yaghlabu / ghalaban. Related descriptive uses: هَضْبَةٌ غَلْبَاءُ, a firm, imposing rocky hill, and عِزَّةٌ غَلْبَاءُ, overpowering, invincible might.

4. The tribe Taghlib was nicknamed al-Ghalbāʾ (the invincible one), evoked in a line of verse about inheriting "a new glory after their ancient glory."

5. اغْلَوْلَبَ الْعُشْبُ (ightlawlaba) — of herbage: to grow to its utmost, thick and luxuriant (the notion of overwhelming abundance).

6. مُغَلَّب (mughallab) carries two opposite senses: (a) among poets, the one repeatedly defeated in contests; (b) the one who defeated his opponent or peer — victory being assigned to him.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root غ-ل-ف (gh-l-f) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris gives this root a single core sense: a covering, or one thing enveloping/overspreading another.

1. Concrete use — ghilāf (غِلَاف): the sheath or case of a sword or knife.

2. Metaphorical use — qalbun aghlaf ("a sheathed/covered heart"): a heart described this way is as if wrapped in a case, so it takes nothing in — it does not comprehend.

3. Qur'anic citation, with a textual variant: {wa qālū qulūbunā ghulf} — "and they said, our hearts are ghulf" (Q 2:88).
   - Standard reading ghulf (غُلْف): "covered over" — i.e. their hearts have been sealed by something, so they do not comprehend.
   - A variant reading ghuluf (غُلُف): taken instead as "vessels/receptacles" (awʿiya) — i.e. containers already full of knowledge.
   Ibn Fāris notes both readings trace back to the same underlying sense of "enclosing/containing" — a case that shuts things out, or a vessel that holds things in.

4. Related usage: tughallafu bi'l-ghāliya, "anointed/enveloped with ghāliya" (a compound perfume) — again fitting the same root idea of being covered or wrapped.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats gh-l-l as a single sound root meaning a thing passing into or through something else and becoming fixed there, like something stuck in. He derives each of the words below from that idea.

1. **To insert, fix in.** غَلَلْتُ الشَّيْءَ فِي الشَّيْءِ, "I set the thing firmly into the thing," as if sticking it in. A verse describes an eye reaching up to a brow "in which the lashes have been set" (غُلَّ فِيهِ الشُّفُرْ).

2. **Thirst.** al-ghulla and al-ghalīl mean thirst, so called because it works its way into the inside with heat. A thirsty camel is ghallān.

3. **Water among trees.** al-ghalal is water running between trees.

4. **Hiding spoils (al-ghulūl).** In the case of booty, ghulūl means hiding an item so it is not returned for division, as though the person had slipped it in among his clothes.

5. **Rancour (al-ghill).** Resentment that works its way into the breast.

6. **Treachery (al-ighlāl).** In the Prophet's saying "no ighlāl and no islāl," ighlāl is treachery, and Ibn Fāris says the link to the root is clear. He cites al-Namir, who prays that God repay Jamra, daughter of Nawfal, "as one who betrays a trust (mughill) and lies" is repaid.
   The hadith "three things over which a believer's heart does not …" is read two ways. With yughillu it comes from ighlāl (treachery). With yaghillu it comes from ghill (rancour).

7. **Hidden valleys.** al-ghullān (singular ghāll) are hidden, deep-lying valleys, because whoever travels them disappears into them.

8. **Undergarment.** al-ghilāla is a garment worn under the outer clothes, and a lining worn under a coat of mail.

9. **Ewer stopper.** al-ghulla (plural ghulal) is the cloth stopper on the mouth of a ewer. Labīd describes ewers with stoppers of white linen and cotton, held by non-Arab servants who wait on the chiefs.

10. **Speed; a far-travelling message.** al-ghalghala is speed in travelling. A risāla mughalghala is a message carried from land to land. Ibn Fāris ties this to the root because the message passes through the lands and works its way into them. A cited verse begins "Convey to Abū Mālik from me a far-carried message; in reproach there is life between peoples."

11. **Fodder mix.** al-ghalīl is date-stones worked into dry fodder and fed to camels. A cited verse describes a lean she-camel for whom chewed date-stones were mixed in.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats gh–l–m as a sound root whose core idea is youthfulness together with the surging of (sexual) desire.

1. غُلام (ghulām): a youth or boy — specifically one whose moustache is just beginning to sprout. The abstract state "boyhood" is غُلومِيّة / غُلومة (ghulūmiyya / ghulūma). Plurals: غِلْمة and غِلْمان (ghilma / ghilmān).

2. From the same root: اغْتَلَمَ (ightalama), said of a stallion in rut — it surged with the desire to mate (غُلْمة, ghulma). This carries the "surge of desire" side of the root's meaning.

3. غَيْلَم (ghaylam) has three recorded senses: (a) a young girl; (b) a young man; (c) the male tortoise/turtle. Ibn Fāris notes it is plausible that this word too fits the root's general pattern (i.e. can be traced to the same core sense).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris identifies one core meaning for gh-l-q (غ ل ق): something getting caught/entangled/stuck fast within something else.

1. **Locking/shutting.** أَغْلَقْتُ الْبَابَ = "I locked/shut the door"; it is then mughlaq ("locked"). This is the base, literal sense — a door catching shut.

2. **A pledge becoming forfeited.** غَلِقَ الرَّهْنُ فِي يَدِ مُرْتَهِنِهِ = a pledge/collateral "becomes stuck/forfeited" in the hand of the person holding it, i.e. when its owner fails to redeem it (it effectively becomes locked in). Ibn Fāris cites a saying attributed to the Prophet: "The pledge does not become forfeited" (لَا يَغْلَقُ الرَّهْنُ). He explains, per the jurists, the practice this targeted: a debtor tells his creditor "I'll pay you by such-and-such date, or else the collateral is yours" — the Prophet forbade attaching that automatic-forfeiture condition to a pledge.

   He generalizes: anything not freed/extricated is called ghaliq. He quotes Zuhayr's line about a woman parting with an unredeemable pledge on the day of farewell, "so the pledge became ghaliqā [forfeited]."

3. **The seventh arrow in maysir (the pre-Islamic lot-casting/gambling game).** Called al-mighlaq, because it "locks in" a share/portion for its holder, however small. Labīd's verse describes a gambling group's slaughter-camel being marked for death "with locking arrows [maghāliq] of matching shape."

4. **A camel's chronic saddle-sore.** غَلِقَ ظَهْرُ الْبَعِيرِ = the camel's back becomes ghaliq, meaning it no longer heals from saddle-galls — the wound has "locked in."

5. **A palm tree whose fruit-bearing has stopped.** غَلِقَتِ النَّخْلَةُ = the bases of its fronds have withered, so it ceases to bear fruit.

Ibn Fāris closes with the standard disclaimer: "And God knows best what is correct."

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib defines al-ghuluww as exceeding the limit, and treats the boiling of a pot (al-ghaly) in the same article.

1. **Exceeding the limit.** Al-ghuluww is going beyond the limit. The noun changes with the domain: in price it is ghalāʾ ("dearness"); in worth and rank it is ghuluww; with an arrow it is ghalw. All of them share one verb, ghalā, yaghlū. He cites Q 4:171: "Do not go beyond the limit in your dīn."

2. **Boiling.** Al-ghaly and al-ghalayān are said of a cooking pot when it boils over. From this, he says, comes the metaphor in Q 44:44–46: "the food of the sinful one; like al-muhl, it boils in the bellies like the boiling of scalding water." The boiling of anger and of war is likened to it.

3. **A form that may belong to either sense.** Taghālā l-nabt, said of plants, may come either from al-ghaly (boiling) or from al-ghuluww (exceeding the limit).

4. **Al-ghalwāʾ.** This is exceeding the limit in restiveness (al-jimāḥ); the ghalwāʾ of youth is likened to it.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: unnamed verse ×5; Shabīb ibn al-Barṣāʾ (Umayyad); Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad) ×2; Ibn al-Ruqayyāt (Umayyad); Ṭufayl (pre-Islamic); Al-Ḥārith ibn Khālid (pre-Islamic); Abū Wajza al-Saʿdī (disputed date); Labīd (lived into Islam); Abū l-Aswad (Umayyad); ʿAdī ibn Zayd (pre-Islamic)
text:
The article under غلا gathers words of rising and going beyond measure (verbs with the imperfect yaghlū), words of boiling (imperfect taghlī), and the name of a perfume. It states that the basic sense (aṣl) of ghalāʾ is rising and going beyond the measure, in everything, and it traces several of the uses below to "rising and going beyond".

1. **High price.** Ghalāʾ, dearness, is the opposite of rukhṣ, cheapness. Ghalā al-siʿr (yaghlū, verbal noun ghalāʾ): the price, or anything else, became dear; what is dear is ghālin, or ghaliyy (the latter on Kurāʿ's authority). Aghlāhu Allāh: God made it dear. Ghālā bi-l-shayʾ: to buy a thing at a high price; ghālā bihi and ghallāhu: to bargain and go to excess. A poet says "we pay dear for meat for our guests while it is raw, and make it cheap once the pot is cooked", dropping the preposition bi- while intending it; Abū Mālik explains: we buy it dear, then give it away freely when it is cooked. Aghlā is also used, as in "a pearl the merchants priced high", and Ibn Barrī cites Shabīb ibn al-Barṣāʾ: "I pay dear for meat while it is raw". Al-Farrāʾ accepts both ghālaytu al-laḥm and ghālaytu bi-l-laḥm. Ghālaytu ṣadāq al-marʾa means "I set the woman's bridal gift high"; hence ʿUmar's saying "do not raise women's bridal gifts high" (reported in three wordings), i.e., do not go to excess in their amount. Ibn al-Aʿrābī gives biʿtuhu bi-l-ghalāʾ, bi-l-ghālī or bi-l-ghaliyy, "I sold it dear", with a verse saying that if Salmā's words were for sale "we would give a high price for them".

2. **Going beyond the bound (ghuluww).** Ghalā fī l-dīn wa-l-amr (yaghlū, ghuluww): to go beyond the proper limit in religion or in any matter. The Qurʾān has lā taghlū fī dīnikum, "do not go to excess in your religion". The Tahdhīb records further verbal nouns, ghalāniya and ghalāniyan, "going beyond the limit, overstepping all measure", and notes that the n is an addition. The form is illustrated by a half-line of al-Aʿshā recited by Ibn Barrī and by a verse of Dhū al-Rumma: repay love with love "and go on adding to it beyond all measure".
   A ḥadīth, "beware of ghuluww in religion", is explained as severity in religion and overstepping its bound, like the ḥadīth "this religion is firm, so go deep into it gently". Another explanation given is that it means probing the hidden sides of things, their causes, and the obscure points of their devotional observances. A further ḥadīth speaks of "the bearer of the Qurʾān who neither goes to excess in it nor keeps aloof from it"; this is explained by the moderation (qaṣd) it enjoins, since the best of affairs are the middle ones, and "both extremes of the middle course are blameworthy". Ghuluww is also glossed as iʿdāʾ (a making to run, or going beyond), and ghulawāʾ can simply mean ghuluww.

3. **Shooting for distance.** Ghalā bi-l-sahm (ghalw, ghuluww) and ghālā bihi (ghilāʾ): to raise the hand in shooting, aiming the arrow at the farthest limit, which the article counts as a kind of going beyond. Al-Layth glosses it simply as "to shoot it", citing al-Shammākh. The one who shoots so is al-ghālī or al-mughālī, and a man who shoots far is ghallāʾ (Ghaylān al-Rabaʿī, describing a race-meeting). Of the arrow itself, ghalā means it rose in flight and passed beyond the range; the same is said of a stone. One such shot is a ghalwa (plural ghalawāt and ghilāʾ), and "all of it", the article says, "is from rising and going beyond".
   Ghālaytuhu (mughālāt, ghilāʾ) is to vie with someone in shooting. Hence qitr al-ghilāʾ, the name given in a ḥadīth to an arrow among weapons presented by Yaksūm (qitr being the target-arrow). The term is also used for the extent of a horse's run or heat, but the shooting sense is called the original one.
   As a measure, a ghalwa is the distance of one arrow-shot ("between it and the road is a ghalwa", in the ḥadīth of Ibn ʿUmar); it is sometimes used in horse-racing, and it means a limit of that length. The Tahdhīb reckons a full farsakh (parasang) at twenty-five ghalwas. A proverb says "the running of mature horses is ghilāʾ". The mighlāt or mighlā is an arrow for vying at distance; Ibn Sīda describes it as an arrow with which the hand is raised high so that it passes the measure or comes near it. Sahm al-ghilāʾ is the arrow used to measure the length of miles, parasangs and race-courses.

4. **A fault of rhyme.** In prosody, ghuluww is giving a vowel to the quiescent rhyme-letter (rawiyy) after the metre is complete, and ghālī is an extra n after that vowel, as in a line ending al-mukhtaraqin in one recitation: the vowel on the q is the ghuluww, the n the ghālī. The term comes from ghuluww as overstepping what is due. It is held to be a more glaring fault than the one called taʿaddī, it is not counted in the metre because the metre has already ended, and it is treated as the line-end counterpart of khazm, an addition at the start of a line.

5. **A fast pace.** A riding-beast taghlū (ghalw) and taghtalī: it goes fast on light legs. Ibn Sīda: it rises in pace beyond an ordinary good gait. Ightilāʾ is going fast, as in a verse of al-Aʿshā on a camel-built she-camel that speeds on carrying riders behind, and in other verses. A she-camel called mighlāt al-wahaq is one whose feet stretch out in the pace (a verse of Ruʾba).

6. **Rapid growth; the rush of youth.** Ghalā bi-l-jāriya (or al-ghulām) ʿaẓm: a girl's (or boy's) frame shot up, i.e., they grew fast and outstripped their age-mates, which again is "from going beyond". Ghulwān and ghulawāʾ al-shabāb are the quickness and the beginning of youth; Abū ʿUbayd defines ghulawāʾ as the quickness of youth, and it is also glossed as youth's beginning and its fire (shirra). Poets use it of a woman who "went on in her ghulawāʾ", paying no heed to her age-mates (Ibn al-Ruqayyāt), of one pressing on "in his ghulawāʾ" like a star cleared of clouds, of warriors entering battle "at its height" (Ṭufayl), and of a bough "in its ghulawāʾ"; a report of ʿAlī speaks of "the haughty lift of his nose and the height of his ghulawāʾ".
   Al-Ḥārith ibn Khālid's line "her frame has shot up (ghalā bihā ʿaẓm)" is read by Ibn al-Sikkīt in this sense of youthful growth. Another authority says al-ghālī is fat flesh, so that the phrase means she has grown plump; a verse of Abū Wajza al-Saʿdī uses ghālin ʿatīq for the old fat in a pregnant she-camel's hump.

7. **Rising in general; plants.** Anything that rises is said to ghalā and taghālā, as when Dhū al-Rumma says his love for Mayya "kept rising" until nothing more could be added. Ghalā al-nabt: plants grew tall, large and dense (Labīd); taghālā and ighlawlā are used the same way (Dhū al-Rumma, of buhmā grass shooting up in summer). Aghlā al-karm: the vine grew dense in leaf, with many shoots, and long; aghlāhu: to thin its leaves so that it rises and thrives.

8. **Of flesh: rising, or shrinking away.** Taghālā laḥmuhu is glossed as the flesh shrinking away, which the article notes makes it look like a word of opposite meanings (ḍidd). The Tahdhīb: said of the flesh of a riding-beast or she-camel when it "rose and went", or, some say, when it shrank under lean-training (taḍmīr). In Labīd's line "when her flesh taghālā and she grew lean", it is explained as the flesh rising up to lie on the tops of the bones; Thaʿlab transmitted the word as taʿālā, with ʿayn.

9. **Boiling.** Ghalat al-qidr (taghlī, ghaly, ghalayān): the pot, or a jar, boiled; aghlāhā or ghallāhā: to make it boil. Ghaliyat is not correct: Abū l-Aswad boasts that he never says "qad ghaliyat" of a pot (nor maghlūq of a door), meaning that he speaks correctly. Ibn Sīda cites Ibn Durayd for a saying of the ancients, "… water, and bring it to the boil", also transmitted as "make water seethe, and bring it to the boil".

10. **The perfume al-ghāliya.** A well-known perfume. Taghallā bihā (Thaʿlab): to perfume oneself with it; ghallā: to perfume someone else. One also says taghallaltu, taghallaftu and taghallaytu, all from al-ghāliya; asked by Abū Naṣr, al-Aṣmaʿī allowed taghallaltu when it means working the perfume into one's beard or moustache. It is said that Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik first gave it this name. Al-ghalwā is the same perfume, in a verse of ʿAdī ibn Zayd. In a report, ʿĀʾisha says she used to daub the beard of the Messenger of God with ghāliya; it is described as a compound of musk, ambergris, aloeswood and oil, and taghalluf with it is smearing oneself with it.

11. **A name.** Ghalwā was the name of a famous mare.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root غ م ض (gh-m-ḍ), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One sound root: a lowering/dipping in a thing, combined with a sense of overlapping/enclosure.

1. al-ghamḍ — a low-lying dip in the land (plural ghumūḍ). Extended: ghamaḍa al-shayʾ min al-ʿilm — something (e.g. a point of knowledge) is "ghāmiḍ," obscure/unclear; dār ghāmiḍah — a house not exposed on a visible thoroughfare; nasab ghāmiḍ — an unknown lineage.
2. The literal, regular-analogy sense: ghammaḍa/aghmaḍa ʿaynahu — to close one's eye (two equivalent verb forms). Idiom: "mā dhuqtu ghumḍan min al-nawmi" — "I haven't tasted a wink of sleep," i.e. not even the time it takes to blink.
3. Figurative: "aghmiḍ lī fīmā biʿtanī" — "be lenient with me in what you sold me," an idiom for asking for an allowance/discount for a poor-quality good — explicitly tied back to "closing the eye," i.e. overlooking a flaw as though not seeing it.
4. al-mughammiḍāt — sins a person knowingly commits while "closing their eyes" to them, pretending not to have seen.
5. A specific idiom for camels: "ghummiḍat al-nāqah" — a she-camel driven back from a watering-trough charges at the one guarding it with eyes closed, forcing her way to the water anyway — illustrated with a line of poetry by Abū al-Najm.
6. Closing: "aghmaḍat ḥadda al-sayf" — she thinned a sword's edge, as though hiding its thinness from view — another figurative extension of "concealing/closing over" something.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: غَمّ 6x "the distress"; غَمَٰم 4x "with the clouds"; غُمَّة 1x "any doubt"
text:
Root غ م م (gh-m-m), as recorded by al-Zamakhsharī in Asās al-Balāgha. The organizing idea is covering / veiling, from which the other senses branch.

1. Distress and hardship. غمّ (ghamma) is to distress or oppress. al-Ghammāʾ is the severest kind of hardship — "one like you dispels al-ghammāʾ and wards off the solid calamity." To be فِي غمّة (fī ghumma) of one's affair is to be in a perplexity from which one sees no way out.

2. Concealment / obscuring. From غمّ الشيء = "he covered or veiled the thing." Hence غُمّ عليهم الهلال, "the crescent was hidden from them" (by cloud), and such a night is called laylat al-ghummā — the night of the obscured crescent (illustrated by a verse: "a night of obscured moon, its crescent effaced").

3. A low, hair-covered hairline. جبهة غمّاء is a forehead over which hair grows low; رجل أغمّ is a man with such a hairline; al-ghamam is the hair encroaching on the forehead, regarded as unattractive. It contrasts with al-nazaʿ (a receding/bare hairline at the temples), which was preferred: "they like the receding hairline and dislike the low one." Two illustrations: a verse warning a woman not to marry a man "hairy of nape and face, not receding at the temples"; and a woman's saying that poverty with a receding hairline brings only slight grief, but poverty combined with a low hairline doubles the distress (a play on al-ghamam / al-ghumam).

4. Clouds (al-ghamām). "She smiles showing teeth like ḥabb al-ghamām" — the "grains of the clouds," i.e. hail.

5. Figurative uses. سحاب أغمّ = clouds with no gap or break in them (cited from a verse by Abū Wajza describing gapless, thunderous rain-clouds). And "so-and-so protected the ghamāma of such-and-such valley" means he fenced off as a guarded reserve the herbage that the cloud's rain had made grow.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha on the root gh-m-r (غمر):

CORE MEANING: "covering / concealing," combined with a sense of intensity or hardship.

1. Al-ghamr — abundant, deep water; called this because it "covers" (yaghmuru) whatever lies beneath it.
   - Extended to a horse abundant in running (its speed likened to the covering flood).
   - Extended to a generous man: ghamru l-ridāʾ, "ample of cloak" — a man whose generosity is pictured as an overflowing garment. Illustrated with a line from the poet Kuthayyir describing such a man's smile.

2. Al-ghamra — total absorption in falsehood and idle amusement; so called because it "covers"/veils the truth from the person immersed in it. Related: ghamarātu l-mawt, "the death-throes/agonies," the crushing hardships that overwhelm (taghshā) the dying — every severe hardship can be called a ghamra for the same reason ("it covers"). A line of verse is cited: "the ghamarāt, then they clear away."

3. Al-ghamīr — green new growth still hidden under a layer of dry, withered plant matter — cited as confirming the same root-sense of "covering."

4. "He entered the ghimār of people" — the press/crowd of people, so called because in a crowd people cover/hide one another. From the same image: a mughāmir is someone who "throws himself" recklessly into affairs, as though plunging into things that conceal him so he cannot find a way out. Related: al-ghumr, an inexperienced person — one for whom worldly affairs are, as it were, still veiled. Illustrated with a verse contrasting a patient, tested man with "the weak untried one" (al-ḍaraʿ al-ghumr).

5. Al-ghimr — a grudge or rancor concealed in the chest, named because the chest "wraps around" (yanṭawī ʿalā) it; one says "his breast harbored rancor against him." By resemblance to this same word, al-ghimr also means thirst (plural: aghmār) — illustrated by a verse about camels' thirst being quenched.

6. Ghamaru l-laḥm — the smell of meat that clings to the hand, as if "covering" it.

7. Al-ghumar — a small drinking-cup. Ibn Fāris tentatively includes it under the same root-logic (the little water in it "covers"/fills it), but notes it may instead be an irregular (shādhdh) formation unrelated to the core sense. A verse about a man content with a small cut of meat and a small cup of drink is cited in illustration.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris (d. 1004 CE), Maqayis al-Lugha, root gh-m-z:

The root is a single, sound root. Its core, literal sense is "to poke or prick something with something" (like al-nakhs). From there the word is extended metaphorically to several related uses.

1. Physical pressing: ghamaztu ash-shay'a bi-yadi - "I pressed/squeezed the thing with my hand" (a ghamz).

2. Faultfinding / speaking ill: ghamaza is said of someone who found fault in another and spoke of him without decency - i.e., disparaged him. The plural noun al-maghamiz means "faults, blemishes."

3. A flaw or weak point: the phrase "in so-and-so's intellect there is a ghamizah" describes a flaw taken as a sign the person is regarded as weak or deficient.

4. A wink/gesture: metaphorically, ghamaza bi-jafnihi means "he winked" - he made a sign with his eyelid.

5. An animal's limp: ghamazat ad-dabbah min rijlihi - the mount limped/faltered in its leg, described as if the animal were "pressing" the ground with that leg - i.e., favoring it, treading gingerly because of injury.

Ibn Faris derives all these senses (physical pressing, faultfinding, a personal flaw, winking, and an animal's limp) from one underlying image: applying a light, pointed pressure against something.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مَغَانِم 4x "and spoils of war"; غَنَم 3x "my sheep"; غَنِمْ 2x "you obtain (as) spoils of war"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats gh-n-m as a single, sound root with one core idea, and derives the rest from it.

1. Core sense: acquiring something that one did not previously own — coming into possession of a thing as a gain.

2. Narrowed sense: the word then becomes specific to what is taken from the property of the mushrikūn (those who associate others with God) by force and conquest. His proof-text is Qur'an 8:41, "And know that whatever you take as spoil (ghanimtum) of a thing, a fifth of it belongs to God and to the Messenger."

3. Idiomatic usage: the expression غُنَامَاكَ أَنْ تَفْعَلَ كَذَا, "your ghunāmā is to do such-and-such," meaning your utmost aim — the thing you treat as your prize (from تَغَنَّمَ, to seize as gain).

4. Proper name: غَنْم (Ghanm) is the name of a tribe.

5. Suggested etymology: he proposes, tentatively, that الغَنَم (sheep and goats, small livestock) may derive from this same root — presented as a plausible conjecture rather than a settled fact ("that is not far-fetched").

poets_named: al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam) ×2; Qays (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse
text:
Ibn Fāris treats غ-ن-ي (with the weak final letter) as two sound roots: one meaning sufficiency, the other meaning a sound.

FIRST ROOT — sufficiency / freedom from need:
1. al-ghinā = wealth in property; verb غَنِيَ يَغْنَى غِنًى (to become rich).
2. al-ghanāʾ (with fatḥa and lengthening) = sufficiency. Example: "So-and-so does not suffice as So-and-so does" (i.e. does not fulfil his role).
3. غَنِيَ عَنْ (to have no need of something); the active participle is غَانٍ (one free of need).
4. غَنِيَ الْقَوْمُ فِي دَارِهِمْ = the people stayed/resided in their abode, as if they found sufficiency in it; their dwellings are called مَغَانٍ (maghānī).
5. al-ghāniya = a woman. Explanations offered: she is content with her parents' home; or content with her husband; or content with her own beauty so as to need no jewellery. Cited from al-Aʿshā.
6. al-ghunyān = wealth / self-sufficiency (cited from Qays).
7. Reflexive forms تَغَنَّيْتُ بِ / تَغَانَيْتُ بِ = to make oneself content or independent by means of something (i.e. to dispense with need of it). al-Aʿshā is cited; also the reciprocal al-taghānī (two parties each dispensing with the other), with a verse on brothers who need each other neither in life nor in death.

SECOND ROOT — sound:
8. al-ghināʾ = singing (a kind of sound). al-ughniya = a mode or type of song.

Method: the entry classifies the root into two "sound roots," gives the verb pattern (غَنِيَ يَغْنَى غِنًى), distinguishes the vocalisation of al-ghanāʾ (fatḥa + madd) from al-ghinā, notes the participle غَانٍ and the plural-of-place مَغَانٍ, and documents each sense with pre-Islamic poetic shawāhid.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مَغْرِب 10x "and the west"; غُرَاب 2x "[the] crow"; غَرَبَت 2x "setting"; غُرُوب 2x "its setting"; غَرْبِيَّة 1x "(of the) west"; غَرْبِىّ 1x "western"; غَرَابِيب 1x "and intensely black"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats غ-ر-ب as a genuine root whose senses cannot all be traced to one underlying idea, though they are of a related family; so he lists them as they stand rather than forcing them under a single meaning.

1. Edge / cutting-edge — الغَرْب: the edge of a thing, e.g. "the edge of the sword"; "I blunted his edge" = dulled its edge. He suggests استغرب ("to burst out laughing to excess") may belong here — as if reaching the furthest edge of laughter.

2. Large bucket — الغَرْب: a big well-bucket.

3. Corners of the eye — الغَرْبان: the inner and outer corners of the eye.

4. Lustre of teeth — غُروب الأسنان: the glisten/"water" of the teeth.

5. Tear-channels — الغُروب: the runnels of the eye; cited with a verse: "…your eyes have runnels flowing."

6. Stray arrow — الغَرْب (rāʾ silent): سهمٌ غَرْبٌ, an arrow whose shooter is unknown.

7. Water-skin — الغَرَب (rāʾ vowelled): said to be the large water-skin (rāwiya).

8. Spoiled well-water — الغَرَب: water spilt at a well whose smell turns; cited from Dhū al-Rumma.

9. A tree — الغَرْب: a kind of tree.

10. Gold/silver vessel — الغَرَب: reported (Ibn Fāris flags uncertainty: "God knows best its correctness") to mean a vessel of gold or silver; supported by a recited couplet.

11. Eye swelling — الغَرْب: a swelling in the inner corner of the eye; verb غَرِبَتِ العينُ.

12. Constant-flowing vein — الغَرْب: a vein that keeps running (weeping) and does not stop.

13. Distance from home — الغُرْبة: being far from one's homeland (غَرَبتِ الدار). Ibn Fāris groups here: غُروب الشمس (sunset), as the sun's going far from the earth's face; شأوٌ مُغَرَّبٌ (a far-off range/goal), with a verse; and هل من مُغَرِّبةِ خبرٍ ("any news brought from afar?"). He notes al-Khalīl's report that dogs "غَرَّبَتْ" when they range far after quarry, but marks it doubtful.

14. Withers — الغارِب: the top of the back and the hump; idiom ألقى حبلَه على غاربِه ("he threw his rope over its withers") = he let it loose / left it to itself.

15. Crow / raven — الغُراب (well known). Related: الغُرابان, two hollows by the horse's haunch-bones; الغُراب, the head of an axe; رِجل الغُراب ("crow's foot"), a type of tight knot (verse by al-Kumayt); الغِرْبِيب, deep black, seemingly from the crow's colour.

16. White-lashed — المُغْرَب: anything white in the eyelashes.

17. الغَرْبِيّ: (a) a fermented drink made from unripe dates; (b) a red dye.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: غُرْفَة 5x "lofty dwellings"; ٱغْتَرَفَ 1x "takes"; غُرُفَٰت 1x "the high dwellings"
text:
Root غ ر ف (gh-r-f), as treated by al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī:

1. Core sense — scooping up. الْغَرْف (al-gharf) is raising something and taking it up in the hand or a vessel: غَرَفْتُ الماءَ والمرقَ, "I scooped up the water and the broth."

2. Related forms built on that sense:
   - غُرْفَة (ghurfa, with u) — what is scooped up, a scoopful.
   - غَرْفَة (gharfa, with a) — the single act of scooping (noun of one instance).
   - مِغْرَفَة (mighrafa) — the tool used for scooping, a ladle.
   Qur'anic witness: 2:249, "except him who scoops up a scoopful with his hand."

3. Extended (borrowed) uses. From the sense of taking off/away: غَرَفْتُ عُرْفَ الفرس, "I clipped the horse's mane"; and غَرَفْتُ الشجرة, said of stripping a tree.

4. A separate lexical item spelled from the same letters: الْغَرَف (al-gharaf) is a known kind of tree, and غَرَفَتِ الإبل means the camels fell ill from eating it.

5. غُرْفَة also means an upper chamber or raised room of a building. On this basis, al-Rāghib notes, the dwellings of the Garden are called غُرَف (ghuraf, "upper chambers"), citing 25:75 ("those shall be recompensed with the upper chamber for their steadfastness"), 29:58 ("We shall settle them in upper chambers of the Garden"), and 34:37 ("and they, in the upper chambers, are secure").

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مَّغْرَم 3x "(as) a loss"; غَٰرِمِين 1x "and for those in debt"; غَرَام 1x "inseparable"; مُغْرَمُون 1x "surely are laden with debt"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats غ-ر-م (gh-r-m) as a single sound root whose core idea is clinging to and staying fastened upon something or someone — sticking close, holding on, pressing insistently.

1. غَرِيم (gharīm) — the party to a debt (creditor or debtor). Named from the root because of the way he sticks to the other party and presses his demand insistently.

2. غَرَام (gharām) — punishment that clings and will not let go. Ibn Fāris cites Qurʾān 25:65, "Truly its punishment is gharām," and reads the word there as this inseparable, unshakeable affliction. He supports the sense with a line of the pre-Islamic poet al-Aʿshā: if such a one punishes, the punishment is inescapable; if he gives, he gives lavishly without concern.

3. غُرْم (ghurm) of property — the sum owed and paid out. He derives it from the same root on the ground that it is the property belonging to the غَرِيم (gharīm).

The whole entry is built by derivation: one physical/relational idea (clinging, holding fast) explains all three usages, including the Qurʾānic one, without appeal to any later technical sense.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أُغْرِقُ 17x "and we drowned"; مُّغْرَقُون 4x "the drowned"; غَرَق 1x "the drowning"; غَرْق 1x "violently"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats غ-ر-ق (gh-r-q) as a single sound root whose core idea is reaching the extreme limit of something — arriving at its very utmost.

1. Core sense: الغَرَق, drowning in water (submersion carried to its limit).

2. الغَرِقَة (al-gharaqa): land soaked to the utmost — saturated in the extreme.

3. اغْرَوْرَقَت (ighrawraqat): the eye or the land brimming over — as if drowned in its own tears; derived from the same idea.

4. أَغْرَقْتُ في القَوْس: to draw a bow to the very limit of its pull — again the notion of taking something to its extreme.

5. اغْتَرَقَ الفَرَس في الخَيْل: said of a horse that mingles among the other horses and then outstrips them.

6. An outlier that Ibn Fāris marks as departing from the root's core: الغُرْقَة (plural غُرَق), a measure of milk equal to about a third of the vessel. He cites a verse describing a she-camel whose udders held such third-measures of milk, sweet-tasting and not drained dry.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
text:
Al-Zamakhsharī's Asās al-Balāgha treats the root غ ر ر (gh-r-r) in two blocks — literal usage, then figurative (majāz) — organised around the idea of a bright mark, and the linked ideas of being caught off guard, deception, risk, and scantness.

LITERAL:
1. ghurra — the white blaze on a horse's forehead; تغرّر الفرس = "the horse got its blaze" (with tahjīl, white on the legs).
2. Being heedless/off guard: صبّحهم الجيش وهم غارون = "the army struck them at dawn while they were unawares (ghārūn = heedless)." Proverb: "more heedless than a gazelle on a moonlit night" — it mistakes the moonlight for day, ventures out, and is eaten.
3. Being taken unawares: اغترّه الأمر = "the affair caught him off guard," with a verse where a raider strikes while the loved ones are still curtaining their litters.
4. ghirra as someone's unguarded moment: "he kept watching for his ghirra until he found it," then seized him.
5. Daring/being emboldened: ما غرّك به؟ = "what emboldened you against him?" — cited alongside the Qur'an, ما غرّك بربك الكريم (Q 82:6), "what emboldened/deceived you concerning your generous Lord."
6. Deceiving: من غرّك منه = "who deceived you about it, who led you into a blind spot."
7. gharīr = a warrant or surety of knowledge: "I am your gharīr in this" = ask me on the spot and I'll answer, so sure is my grasp of it.
8. Risk: taghirra = endangering oneself; غرّر بنفسه = "he risked himself"; على غرر = "in danger"; and the noted prohibition of بيع الغرر (a sale involving hazard/uncertainty).
9. ghurar = unreliable — a line of al-Namir uses a "bond that became ghurar," i.e. not to be trusted.
10. ghurūr (plural) = the natural creases of a thing: "fold it along its ghurūr."

FIGURATIVE (majāz):
11. A "blazed and stockinged" day = a bright, distinguished, famous day (Dhū al-Rumma on the day of Dhī Qār).
12. aghar also = fiercely hot: a "dazzling" (gharrāʾ) noon-heat, white like salt, so hot the gazelle hides and locusts leap — two Dhū al-Rumma citations.
13. ghurrat al-māl = the choicest wealth: camels, horses, slaves.
14. ʿaysh gharīr = a carefree, untroubled life.
15. Of the aged: "his gharīr (carefree vigour) has left and his harīr (decrepit snarl) has come."
16. gharrarat of a child's tooth = it first breaks through, showing white (a qurḥa/ghurra).
17. ghurrāt of a torrent = its bubbles and foam.
18. al-gharrāʾ "daughter of the churning" — a Bedouin's praise of a woman, likening her to fresh butter.
19. In trade: a market has durra and ghirār = brisk sale and stagnation; "its flow outran its ebb," like "your flood outran your rain."
20. ghirār = a short while / a shortfall: "I sat with him only briefly"; the saying "no ghirār in the ṣalāt" (no diminishing of it). Root image: a she-camel "ghārrat" when her milk ran short.
21. mughār al-kaff = tight-fisted, of a miser; "I taste sleep only in scant measure (ghirār)."
22. Wordplay on ghirār as a blade's edge: "paying out the ghirār is lighter to him than the fall of the ghirār [edge]"; and "sitting on thrones lies beneath the spear-points and the blade-edges."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris, Maqayis al-Lugha, root gh-r-w

Core meaning: admiration and wonder at the beauty of a thing.

1. Beauty/admiration sense
 - al-ghariyy = "the handsome/beautiful one"; "rajulun ghar" = "a handsome man."
 - From this same idea, "wonder/astonishment" itself came to be called gharw.

2. Gluing/sticking sense
 - aghraytuhu is explained through al-ghira' - the substance by which things are glued or stuck together (i.e. glue).

3. Eyes streaming with tears
 - "gharati l-'aynu bi-d-dam'i ghira'an" and "ghariyat bi-d-dam'i" both describe an eye that persists relentlessly in weeping (keeps streaming with tears).
 - Cited verse of poetry: whenever the speaker tries to console himself, his eye keeps pouring with weeping, and abundant tears swell it further.

Ibn Faris presents these together as one root, moving from admiration fixed on beauty, to a substance that fixes things together, to an eye fixed in weeping.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: تَغْتَسِلُ 1x "you have bathed"; ٱغْسِلُ 1x "then wash"; مُغْتَسَل 1x "(is a spring of) water to bathe"; غِسْلِين 1x "(the) discharge of wounds"
text:
Root غ-س-ل (gh-s-l), as treated by al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī:

1. Core sense — ghasaltu al-shayʾ ghaslan: to wash a thing, i.e. to pour water over it so that its grime (daran) is removed. Qur'anic citation: "so wash your faces and your hands" (al-Māʾida 5:6).

2. Vowelling distinguishes two nouns:
   - al-ghasl (fatḥa) — the noun of the act itself, the washing.
   - al-ghisl (kasra) — the thing one washes *with*, the washing-agent.

3. Form VIII, al-ightisāl — washing the body specifically. Citation: "until you wash yourselves" (al-Nisāʾ 4:43).

4. al-mughtasal — the noun of place/instrument, carrying two readings here: the place from which one washes, and the water with which one washes. Citation: "this is a cool mughtasal and a drink" (Ṣād 38:42).

5. al-ghislīn — glossed by this author as the ghusāla, the run-off water washed from the bodies of the deniers in the Fire. Citation: "nor any food except from ghislīn" (al-Ḥāqqa 69:36).

The entry's method throughout is to derive each Qur'anic form from the one act of pouring water to remove dirt, then to place the derived nouns by their pattern (verbal noun, instrument, noun of place) and anchor each with a verse.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: غَسَّاق 2x "and purulence"; غَسَق 1x "(the) darkness"; غَاسِق 1x "(of) darkness"
text:
Root ghayn-sīn-qāf (غسق) has one core meaning: darkness.

1. al-ghasaq (الغَسَق) = darkness itself.
2. al-ghāsiq (الغَاسِق) = the night (called this because of its darkness).
3. Used of the eye: "ghasaqat ʿaynuhu" = his eye darkened/dimmed.
4. Used of prayer timing: "aghsaqa al-muʾadhdhin" = the caller to prayer delayed the maghrib prayer until the ghasaq (darkness) of night had set in.
5. Regarding al-ghassāq, the word that appears in the Qur'an — Ibn Fāris does not derive its meaning himself here but reports that the commentators (mufassirūn) explained it as what drips from the skins of the people of the Fire.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib treats gh-th-w briefly, through the noun al-ghuthāʾ.

1. **al-ghuthāʾ: what a torrent or a pot throws up.** The ghuthāʾ of a torrent is the dry vegetation that rises to the surface and scatters; the ghuthāʾ of a cooking-pot is its froth.

2. **Proverbial use.** The word serves as a proverbial image for whatever is lost and goes away without being reckoned of any account.

3. **The verb for a valley.** One says ghathā l-wādī (verbal noun ghathw), of a valley carrying ghuthāʾ.

4. **Nausea.** ghathat nafsuhu (imperfect taghthī, verbal noun ghathayān), "he felt nauseous," which al-Rāghib glosses as "his soul became foul."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: gh-w-ṣ (غوص), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core sense: a single, unified meaning — plunging or descending down onto/into something that lies low or beneath a surface.

1. Literal sense: al-ghawṣ (الغوص) is entering beneath the water — diving. Someone who does this is a ghā'iṣ (غائص), "a diver," literally "one who plunges upon a thing."

2. Metaphorical extension: Ibn Fāris then applies the same image to the mind. He cites the expression ghāṣa ʿalā al-ʿilm al-ghāmiḍ ḥattā istanbaṭahu — "he dove into obscure/hidden knowledge until he drew it out (istanbaṭa)." Just as a diver goes down under water to bring something up, a person "dives" into knowledge that is concealed or difficult, in order to extract it.

The entry is short and self-contained: one root-sense (downward plunging into something low/hidden), realized concretely as diving underwater, and figuratively as probing hidden/obscure knowledge to draw out its meaning.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root gh-w-ṭ (غوط) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core sense: the letters ghayn-wāw-ṭāʾ form a sound root meaning settledness/lowness and depth — something that sinks or lies low.

1. al-ghāʾiṭ (الغائط) — a low-lying depression in the land (al-muṭmaʾinn min al-arḍ). Plurals: ghīṭān, aghwāṭ.
2. Ghūṭat Dimashq (the Damascus Ghouta) — reportedly named from this root, as if to say it is low-lying land.
3. inghāṭa al-ʿūd — said of a stick or branch when it bends/curves, since bending brings it lower. Ibn Fāris notes that the qiyās (derivational logic) tying this usage back to the core sense of "lowness" is sound.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) derives the root غ-و-ل (gh-w-l) from a single core sense: stealthy seizure or destruction — something taking or striking a person from a direction they cannot perceive.

1. Core verb: ghālahu yaghūluhu — "it took/destroyed him from where he did not perceive [it]."
2. al-ghawl = the remoteness of open desert land, because that very distance "destroys" (overtakes unnoticed) anyone who crosses it. He quotes an unattributed line of verse picturing a riding-mount stretching out over such remote distance, to illustrate this sense of ghawl as 'distance.'
3. al-ghūl — the demon-like desert creature (one of the saʿālī) — is named this way because it too preys on its victims stealthily.
4. al-ghīla = assassination / stealthy killing; he notes the ī here comes from an original w.
5. al-mighwal = a slender sword with a blunt, rounded spine on its back. Ibn Fāris offers this etymology as his own tentative guess ("I think... God knows best"): it may be called mighwal because it stays hidden inside its sheath, so its true nature is concealed from view.

All five senses trace back to the same thread: something acting on you, or encountered by you, from a hidden or unperceived angle.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
poets_named: unnamed verse ×2; Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); al-Akhṭal (Umayyad); Ṭufayl (pre-Islamic)
text:
Root غ-و-ر (gh-w-r) — Ibn Sīda, al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam (d. 1066 CE)

The root's core idea is going down / sinking / an inward depression, branching into geography, the body, raiding, and rest-time.

1. **Depth/bottom.** الغَوْر of anything is its bottom (قَعْر). "Ghawr Tihāma" names the lowland tract between Dhāt ʿIrq and the sea. "The people went to the Ghawr" (غار القوم / أغاروا / غوّروا) means they went down into this lowland — illustrated with lines by Jarīr, al-Aʿshā, and Jamīl contrasting highland (Najd) and lowland (Ghawr/Tihāma) people.

2. **Sinking/entering.** غَار في الشيء = it entered/sank in (Sībawayh). Applied to: a sunken eye (غارت عينه); water sinking into the ground or vanishing into its springs — with the Qurʾānic citation «إن أصبح ماؤكم غَوْرًا», "should your water sink away" (67:30); and the sun, moon, and stars "sinking" = setting (غارت الشمس).

3. **Cave/hollow.** الغَار is a cave-like hollow in a mountain (a house-like recess, per al-Liḥyānī; a depression, per Thaʿlab) — and by extension any low-lying stretch of ground, or a lair where wild animals shelter. Plural of paucity أغوار, plural of multitude غيران. المَغَارَة is a synonym, cited from the Qurʾān: «لو يجدون ملجأ أو مغارات أو مدخلا», "if they found a refuge, or caves, or a place to enter" (9:57).

4. **Mouth and body.** الغَار can denote the area at the back of the upper mouth/uvula, or the groove between the jaws, or the mouth's interior. الغَاران (dual) = the two eye-sockets; or, in another usage, a person's mouth and genitals (or, alternatively, belly and genitals) — with a supporting verse.

5. **A multitude of people.** الغَار can mean a large crowd, as in al-Aḥnaf's remark about al-Zubayr bringing together "two ghārs of people" and then deserting them.

6. **Plant senses.** الغَار is glossed by some as grapevine leaves (explaining a line of al-Akhṭal), but its main sense is the laurel/bay tree: long fragrant leaves used in perfume, a small blackish peeled fruit used medicinally (called الدهمشت), singular غَارة. Separately, الغَار is also given as "dust" (per Kurāʿ).

7. **Hastening/raiding.** أَغَار = hastened in something, or set off/departed into the land (noun: الغَارَة). "He ran the fox's run" (عدا غارة الثعلب) = ran swiftly like a fox (noun: الغُوَيْر). Most importantly: أَغَار على القوم = he raided them, drove horsemen against them — الإغارة is judged the correct term for the verbal action, الغَارة for the raiding party/event itself. تغاور القوم = they raided each other. A رجل مِغوار is a habitual raider; a فرس مِغوار a swift/hard-running horse (cited: Ṭufayl). المُغيرة/المِغيرة = raiding horses. The cry "ashriq Thabīru kaymā nughīr" ("shine, Thabīr, that we may hasten") is glossed as hurrying toward slaughter and driving toward the stones.

8. **Coming for aid; provisioning.** أغار فلان بني فلان = he came to a clan seeking their support. غارهم الله بخير = God favored them with fertility/rain; غارهم = he provisioned them.

9. **Asking for providence.** استغور الله = he asked God for الغِيرَة. Thaʿlab glosses a cited verse's "istaghwirā llāha" as "ask Him for provision (mīra)"; Ibn Sīda himself prefers "ask Him for abundance/fertility," reasoning that fertility is God's provision for His creation. He notes this root has both wāw and yāʾ forms, cross-referenced elsewhere.

10. **Midday rest.** الغائرة = noon, or the midday nap-time. غوّر القوم = they entered the noon-rest, or (in another usage) alighted for it, or traveled during it (with a verse of Imruʾ al-Qays about dogs and a wild bull); التغوير = sleeping at that hour.

11. **Twisting/tightness.** الإغارة also means tight twisting (of a rope): حبل مُغار = a tightly twisted rope; فرس مُغار = a horse with tightly-knit joints. استغار فيه الشحم = fat spread through it; استغارت الجرحة = a wound swelled.

12. **Proper names and places.** مُغيرة is a personal name; Ibn Sīda notes and explains an irregular vocalization مِغيرة some use for it, comparing it to other irregular forms. الغَار also names a place in Syria. الغَورة/الغُوَير names a watering place of the Kalb tribe near al-Samāwa — the site referenced in Queen al-Zabbāʾ's proverb "ʿasā l-ghuwayri abʾusan" ("perhaps al-Ghuwayr brings misfortunes"), with an anecdote about ʿUmar applying the same phrase to a foundling child to mean "the suspicion may lie with you" — though Ibn Sīda notes this application does not sit well with Sībawayh's grammatical account of the phrase.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
quran_words: ٱسْتَغَٰثَ 4x "they call for relief"; يُغَاثُ 1x "they will be relieved"
poets_named: ʿĀʾisha bint Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ (Umayyad); unnamed verse ×3; Zuhayr (pre-Islamic)
text:
**Root GH-W-TH (غوث) — al-Zabīdī's account in Tāj al-ʿArūs**

**1. The core: a cry for help.** غَوَّثَ / اسْتَغاثَ originally means to shout «وَاغَوْثاهُ» — "O for help!" Example: "So-and-so was struck and cried out for help." Al-Zabīdī reports his teacher as saying that grammarians state plainly this cry is the word's origin; only afterwards was it used generally for shouting and calling out in search of غَوْث (help, relief).

**2. The noun forms, and a grammatical anomaly.** The noun is غَوْث (ghawth) and غُوَاث (ghuwāth, with ḍamma) — the latter being the regular pattern. The variant غَوَاث with fatḥa is anomalous, breaking the rule: words for sounds take ḍamma (ṣurākh "shouting," nubāḥ "barking") or kasra (nidāʾ "calling," ṣiyāḥ "crying"), never fatḥa. This rule is credited to al-Farrāʾ via al-Jawharī.

**3. Poetic witness for غَوَاث.** A line ascribed to ʿĀʾisha bint Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ: "I sent you to fetch provisions and you stayed away a year — when does your help arrive, you who would help others?" Ibn Barrī corrects the first word: "I sent you to fetch a firebrand." The story: her client Find was sent for fire, went to Egypt instead, stayed a year, then ran back with it, tripped, scattered the embers and cursed haste. A second poet mocks the same figure: "We found no likeness for the crow we sent... except Find, sent for a firebrand, who lingered a year and cursed haste."

**4. Helping (Form IV).** اسْتَغَاثَنِي فُلانٌ فَأَغَثْتُهُ — "he sought my help and I helped him," with the verbal nouns إِغَاثَة (ighātha) and مَغُوثَة (maghūtha). Idiom: "I sought his help but got no maghūtha from him," i.e. no relief.

**5. What istighātha means, and how it is construed.** Al-Zabīdī's teacher: istighātha is the seeking of ghawth, defined here as deliverance from hardship and calamity, and aid in getting free of distress. In the Qurʾān the verb takes its object directly, without a preposition — «إِذْ تَسْتَغِيثُونَ رَبَّكُمْ» (Q 8:9, "when you call on your Lord for help"). But it can also take a preposition, as in the verse "until he sought relief at water that needed no well-rope, in the wadi-beds, waterfowl along its edges." Sībawayh used it that way too; on that basis al-Zabīdī (citing al-Shihāb) dismisses Ibn Mālik's objection to the grammarians' phrase "the one for whom / by whom help is sought."

**6. Everyday and ḥadīth usage.** A person in trouble says أَغِثْنِي — "help me," i.e. relieve me. A ḥadīth has «اللَّهُمَّ أَغِثْنَا» ("O God, give us relief"), with the hamza, from ighātha.

**7. Etymology and a disputed base form.** Ibn Durayd: the original verb was غَاثَهُ يَغُوثُهُ غَوْثاً, but it died out of use. Al-Azharī: he never heard anyone say it with the wāw. A variant غَاثَهُ يَغِيثُهُ is rare, and is said to belong to غَيْث (rain) rather than to ighātha. Ibn Sīda gives both أَغَاثَهُ اللهُ and غَاثَهُ غَوْثاً وغِيَاثاً, the first being better attested.

**8. The vocalisation of غياث.** Ibn al-Aʿrābī records غِيَاث with kasra; the first letter thus admits all three vowels. Al-Ṣiḥāḥ explains the wāw turning into yāʾ because of the preceding kasra. All three readings appear in manuscripts of al-Bukhārī: some lexicographers rejected the kasra (hence its absence from the dictionaries); the ḍamma comes via Abū Dharr; Ibn Ḥajar attributes the anomalous fatḥa to the majority, and Ibn al-Khashshāb fixed it so; the kasra is recorded by Ibn Qarqūl and by al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ, and is the reading given first in the Yūnīniyya recension, which the later jurists followed. Al-Tahdhīb defines غِيَاث as "that by which God gives you relief."

**9. Further derivatives.**
- المَغَاوِث (al-maghāwith): waters — said to be a plural with no singular.
- الغَوِيث (al-ghawīth): (a) great speed in running — "he is a man of ghawīth"; (b) what one relieves a person in distress with, whether food or armed aid (al-Ṣāghānī). A copy reading التَّغْوِيث here is an error.
- الغَوَاث (ghawāth, pattern saḥāb): provisions — a Yemeni usage.

**10. Names and places.** Ghawth, Ghiyāth and Mughīth are used as personal names (Ghawth standing in for the verbal noun of aghātha). Ghawth is a clan of Ṭayyiʾ; also a Yemeni tribe (Ghawth b. Udad b. Zayd b. Kahlān b. Sabaʾ); al-Tahdhīb makes it a clan of al-Azd, citing Zuhayr: "you fear the archers of Ghawth from every lookout." Other Ghawths are named among Muḍar and in Yemen, plus the Egyptian judge Ghawth b. Sulaymān al-Ḥaḍramī. **Yawm Aghwāth** was the second day of the battle of al-Qādisiyya, commemorated in a line by al-Qaʿqāʿ b. ʿAmr. Al-Zabīdī then lists many ḥadīth transmitters called Ghiyāth — most notably the judge Ḥafṣ b. Ghiyāth and his son ʿUmar, a teacher of al-Bukhārī and Muslim, and the poet al-Akhṭal, whose name was Ghiyāth b. Ghawth al-Taghlibī — along with two men named Ghayyāth (intensive pattern). **Al-Mughītha** names two waypoints on the pilgrim road (said to be two wells where pilgrims halt) and a college in eastern Baghdad.

**11. يَغُوث (Yaghūth):** an idol of the tribe of Madhḥij — reported by Ibn Sīda as al-Zajjāj's statement.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَغْوَيْ 8x "we led astray"; غَٰوِين 6x "to the deviators"; غَيّ 4x "(of) [the] error"; غَوَىٰ 3x "has he erred"; غَوِىّ 1x "(are) surely a deviator"
text:
Ibn Fāris (d. 1004 CE), *Maqāyīs al-Lugha*, on the root gh-w-y.

He splits the root into two independent bases:

**Base 1 — going astray / being overshadowed and darkened.**
1. **الغَيّ (al-ghayy)**: the opposite of *rushd* (right guidance) — ignorance of a matter and sinking into falsehood. Verb غَوَى / يَغْوِي (ghawā/yaghwī, "to go astray"). Illustrated by a line of verse contrasting the man praised for meeting good with the one who "goes astray" and never lacks a blamer.
2. **Etymology (Ibn Fāris's own view):** *ghayy* derives from الغَيَايَة (al-ghayāya), the haze of dust and darkness that covers things — the astray person being, as it were, so overspread that he can no longer see the path of truth. This "overshadowing" sense recurs across the base:
   - تَغَايَا القَوْم (taghāyā): a group massing over someone's head with swords, as if shading him.
   - أَغْوِيَّة (ughwiyya): a calamity, a "dark" affair one falls into.
   - التَّغَاوِي (al-taghāwī): gathering together — and never for a rightly-guided purpose.
   - المُغَوَّاة (al-mughawwāt), pl. مُغَوَّيَات: a hunter's trapping-pit. A ḥadīth ("they love to be *mughawwayāt*") is read as: they hoard wealth the way a hunter traps game.
3. **الغَايَة (al-ghāya)**: primarily a war-**banner**, so called because it shades those under it (with a verse mentioning a wine-merchant's raised banner). The familiar sense "end-point / limit" is, Ibn Fāris says, a secondary metaphorical extension: one halts *at* the ghāya just as troops rally back to their banner in battle.

**Base 2 — spoilage from over-drinking.**
4. **غَوِيَ الفَصِيل (ghawiya al-faṣīl)**: said of a young weaned camel that drinks too much milk and gets a spoiled/sick belly; verbal noun الغَوَى (al-ghawā). Supported by a verse describing a she-camel whose calf has neither drained her nor died of *ghawā*.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) treats gh-y-ḍ as a sound triliteral root with a single core meaning that branches into two senses: (1) a thing decreasing/diminishing, and (2) obscurity and denseness — with an added note of scarcity.

1. Decrease/diminishing: ghāḍa al-māʾu yaghīḍu means "the water diminished/receded" — the direct opposite of fāḍa, "it overflowed." The passive form ghīḍa is used specifically when the diminishing is caused by something else acting on it, not happening on its own. Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'an as an attestation of this passive usage: {wa ghīḍa al-māʾu} — "and the water was made to subside" (Hūd 11:44).

2. Obscurity/denseness: from this same root comes al-ghayḍah, meaning a thicket — a dense growth of trees or reeds. Ibn Fāris explains the naming: it is called ghayḍah because of its ghumūḍ (obscurity, denseness), and because someone walking inside it can barely be seen.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats غ-ي-ظ (gh-y-ẓ) as a small root with a single core meaning: a distress or anguish (karb) that a person suffers at the hands of another — that is, vexation or provocation.

Usage and morphology:
- Verb: غَاظَنِي / يَغِيظُنِي (he vexed me / he vexes me); also the second-person form قَدْ غِظْتَنِي يَا هَذَا (you have vexed me).
- Agent nouns: غَائِظ (ghāʾiẓ), one who vexes; and the intensive غَيَّاظ (ghayyāẓ), a habitual or intense vexer.

Poetic citation (shāhid): an unattributed line plays on the name Ghayyāẓ — "You were named Ghayyāẓ, yet you vex no enemy; it is your friend you vex" — illustrating the sense of causing another distress.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: غَيْب 49x "(of) the unseen"; غُيُوب 4x "(of) the unseen"; غَائِبِين 3x "absent"; غَيَٰبَت 2x "(the) bottom"; غَائِبَة 1x "hidden"; يَغْتَب 1x "backbite"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats غ ي ب (ghayn–yāʾ–bāʾ) as a single sound root whose core sense is the concealment of a thing from the eyes; the other meanings follow from it by analogical extension.

1. الغَيْب (al-ghayb): what is absent or hidden — specifically, in his phrasing, that which none knows except God.

2. Verbal usage of غاب: the sun "set/vanished" (ghābat al-shams, with the verbal nouns ghaybah, ghuyūb, ghayb); a man "was absent" from his town; and of a woman whose husband is away, aghābat, so she is called mughībah.

3. غَيْبة / غَيابة (ghaybah / ghayābah): a hollow or dip in the ground where something becomes hidden. He cites Qurʾān Yūsuf 12:10 — "cast him into the ghayābah [dark depth] of the well" — as an instance of this sense.

4. الغابة (al-ghābah): a thicket or dense woodland (plurals ghābāt, ghāb), so named because a person is hidden within it.

5. الغِيبة (al-ghībah): backbiting/slander of people — derived from the same root, since it is said only in a person's absence.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: غَيْر 147x "without"; يُغَيِّرُ 4x "they change"; مُغَيِّر 1x "one who changes"; يَتَغَيَّرْ 1x "changes"; مُغِيرَٰت 1x "and the chargers"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats غ-ي-ر (gh-y-r) as two sound roots with distinct meanings.

Root 1 — soundness, setting-right, benefit:
- al-ghīra means provision (mīra) that secures a household's welfare. غِرْتُ أَهْلِي = "I provided for my family" (verbal nouns ghīra, ghiyār). غَارَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِالْغَيْثِ (present yaghīr / yaghūr) = God gave them rain, i.e. set their affairs right and benefited them.
- مَا يَغِيرُكَ كَذَا = "such-and-such does not benefit you." A cited verse uses yaghīr in the sense of "avail."
- al-ghayra, a man's protective jealousy over his family (غِرْتُ عَلَى أَهْلِي), is placed here too, on the reasoning that such jealousy is itself a form of setting-right and benefit.

Root 2 — the difference/otherness of two things:
- هَذَا الشَّيْءُ غَيْرُ ذَاكَ = "this is other than / the opposite of that."
- ghayr used for exception: عَشَرَةٌ غَيْرَ وَاحِدٍ = "ten less one." Cited in Qur'an 1:7, {…غَيْرِ الْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ} ("not those against whom there is wrath").

A disputed case — blood-money (diya), called al-ghiyar:
Ibn Fāris cites a prophetic address to a man seeking retaliation, «أَلَا الْغِيَر» ("Will you not accept the blood-money?"). He notes it could derive from either root: from Root 1, since the diya sets things right for the killer and preserves his life; or from Root 2, since retaliation was changed (ghuyyira) into something other than (ghayr) itself. A supporting verse threatens the sons of Umayma if they refuse to accept al-ghiyar (blood-money).
