text:
Ibn Fāris treats gh-y-th as a single, sound root whose core meaning is al-ḥayā — the life-giving rain that comes down from the sky.

Usage he cites:
1. jādanā ghayth — "rain came generously upon us."
2. arḍ mughīthah / maghyūthah — "land that has been rained upon" (two equivalent passive-participle forms from the same root).
3. ghithnā — "we were rained upon / the rain struck us."

He supports this with a line from the poet Dhū al-Rummah, who reports asking a Bedouin woman about the rain in her land; she replied with notable eloquence, ghithnā mā shi'nā — "we were rained on as much as we wished."

No other senses, derivations, or Qur'anic material are given in this entry; it is a short, single-sense root centered entirely on rain.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
text:
Root غزل (gh-z-l) — from the Tāj al-ʿArūs of Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791 CE), a general Arabic dictionary entry (not specific to Qur'anic usage, though it cites one verse).

1. Core verb: a woman "spun" (غَزَلَتْ) cotton, flax, etc. — maṣdar غَزْل. The spun material/thread is called غَزِل or مَغْزُول, plural غُزُول. The dictionary cites Qur'an 16:92 — "like her who unravelled her spun thread" — as an example of the noun. Sībawayh reportedly also used غَزْل for what a spider spins.

2. "Spinning women" = نِسْوَةٌ غُزَّلٌ or غَوَازِل, illustrated with a line of pre-Islamic verse. Al-Zabīdī notes the same plural pattern can, grammatically, refer to men too.

3. المِغْزَل, "spindle" — pronounced with kasra (Tamīm), ḍamma (Qays, and the original/commonest form), or rarely fatḥa; grammarians disagree over which vowel is correct, and al-Farrāʾ is quoted at length deriving the word from a root sense of "twisting/rotating" (comparing it to مِصْحَف, "codex," from "gathering pages"). A citation from a Jewish legal letter uses رُبُع المِغْزَل, "a quarter of what your women have spun," which Ibn al-Athīr glosses three ways depending on vowel: the tool, the place of spinning, or the container for the spun thread.

4. المُغَيْزِل, diminutive form, means a thin rope — named for its resemblance to a spindle.

5. Courting/flirting with women: مُغَازَلَة, noun الغَزَل, verb غَازَلَ. Ibn Sīda defines الغَزَل simply as "dallying with women."

6. A long excursus (quoting several literary critics — Ibn Rashīq, and two commentators named ʿAbd al-Laṭīf and ʿAbd al-Qādir al-Baghdādī on Qudāma's poetics) works out how ghazal relates to the neighboring terms nasīb and tashbīb, used in classical love-poetry criticism:
 - Some critics treat the three as synonyms.
 - The finer distinction given: ghazal is the actual conduct and words passing between lover and beloved; tashbīb is publicly praising/naming the beloved's qualities; nasīb is the broadest term, covering the poet's own state, the beloved's, and what passes between them — so tashbīb sits inside nasīb, and nasīb includes ghazal.
 - Qudāma's definition: ghazal is infatuation and reckless preoccupation with women — a غَزِل man is one disposed to the tender feeling proper to relations with women, drawing them in through charm, grace, gentle manner, and pleasant talk.
 - Ghazal can describe either the underlying temperament for this or the actual state of being smitten by it (compared to how غَضْبَان covers both "irritable" and "now angry").
 - تَغَزُّل is either "performing/affecting ghazal" or simply "talking about ghazal" — in either case distinct from ghazal itself.

7. غَزِل (adjective) = a man given to courting/flirting with women; verb غَزِلَ, maṣdar غَزَلاً.

8. A second, separate sense of غَزِل: weak or listless in other matters — per Ibn al-Aʿrābī, a man is called غَزِل as a term for a womanizer precisely because he is incapable of anything else.

9. Proverbial phrase: "more attached than fever" (أَغْزَلُ مِنَ الحُمَّى) — fever recurs to a sick person so habitually it seems infatuated with him.

10. غَازَلَ الأَرْبَعِينَ = "he neared forty" (of age).

11. الغَزَال = the gazelle fawn, especially once past weaning, or specifically the young when it begins to move; poets liken a girl to it in praise-poetry (hence masculine grammatical forms even for a female subject, following the masculine noun ghazāl). Other accounts tie the term to specific growth stages. Plural غِزْلَان; feminine غَزَالَة. Al-Zabīdī's later commentator ("Shaykhunā") pushes back at length against the claim that ghazāl names only the male gazelle (with ẓabya for the female) — citing other lexicographers (al-Fayyūmī, etc.) that ghazāl/ghazāla is simply male/female.

12. ظَبْيَةٌ مُغْزِل = a doe with a fawn.

13. غَزِلَ الكَلْبُ = a hunting dog "flagged" — it chases the prey, but once the prey bleats in fear on being caught, the dog loses interest and turns away (two slightly different descriptions are given, from al-Ṣiḥāḥ and Ibn al-Aʿrābī). Idiom: "by God, your dog has flagged."

14. الغَزَالَة = the sun — explained as "spinning out" its rays like thread, or specifically the rising sun (one says the ghazāla "rose," never "set"), or the high midday sun, or simply "the sun's disc." Several conflicting explanations are given side by side.

15. الغَزَالَة is also the proper name of the wife of the rebel Shabīb al-Khārijī, famed for bravery — tradition holds she once raided Kūfa with thirty horsemen against thirty thousand troops, prayed dawn prayer there reciting Sūrat al-Baqara, and put al-Ḥajjāj to flight; verses about her are quoted (with a textual correction).

16. الغَزَالَة, per the botanist Abū Naṣr, also names a low, sweet, thornless ground-herb with a peelable edible stalk and yellow flowers, grazed by livestock.

17. Also the name of a particular horse.

18. غَزَالَةُ الضُّحَى = the early forenoon (with several fine explanations of exactly which part of the morning, and a grammatical/textual note on a line of Dhū al-Rummah).

19. غَزَالُ شَعْبَان = a small insect, a kind of grasshopper.

20. دَمُ الغَزَال ("gazelle's blood") = a pungent, edible, tarragon-like plant with a red root, whose juice girls used to draw red markings on their hands (per Abū Ḥanīfa the botanist).

21. غَزَال = the name of a mountain pass/road (grammatically a diptote), with a supporting verse.

22. الغُزَيِّل = a personal/tribal name (an ancestor of al-Makshūḥ) and a place-name (Dārat al-Ghuzayyil).

23. المَغَازِل = the axles/poles of a threshing-sledge.

24. Ghazāl and Ghazāla were also used simply as personal names.

25. A closing set of proverbs, idioms, and onomastic notes: sayings comparing someone unfavourably to a spider or to figures called "Furʿul" and "Imruʾ al-Qays" for excessive or feckless "spinning"; two place-names (Fayfā Ghazāl, Qarn Ghazāl); the saying "the spinner is more lost than a spindle-shaft — he clothes others while going naked himself"; metaphorical uses of "flirting" for a pleasant breeze or an easy life; and a roll-call of poets, Qurʾān-reciters, and hadith scholars who carried Ghazāl/Ghazzāl as a name or epithet — including a philological note that Imam Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī's nisba is correctly traced to "al-Ghazzāl" (yarn-seller), with doubled zāy, rather than to the village Ghazāla near Ṭūs that some had linked it to.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root غزو (gh-z-w) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris treats this root as covering two separate, unrelated original senses (not one sense derived from the other):

1. "To seek/pursue a thing" — the base for al-ghazw.
   - Verb: ghazawtu, aghzū — "I sought/raided; I seek/raid."
   - al-ghāzī = "the seeker" [of that pursuit]; plural ghuzāh or ghazīy — paralleling how the collective of pilgrims (ḥājj) is called ḥajīj.
   - al-mughziyah = a woman whose husband has gone off on a ghazw.
   - Relational adjective (nisba): ghazawī.

2. A term of animal husbandry, about conception:
   - aghzat al-nāqah — said of a she-camel when her insemination/conception has become difficult.
   - Some extended the same word to she-asses: al-atān al-mughziyah = a she-ass whose delivery is delayed before she finally gives birth.
   - Poetic citation (al-Hudhalī): a wild ass brays over the late-bearing females, roaming with them across the desolate tracts of al-ṣilāl [an obscure term, likely a terrain/place description].

Ibn Fāris gives no third sense and draws no link between the two roots beyond sharing the same three letters.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats h-sh-sh as a sound root (aṣl ṣaḥīḥ) that indicates looseness and softness, and places these words under it:

1. **Soft.** Anything loose and soft is hashsh.

2. **Bright of face.** A man who is hashsh is ṭalq al-muḥayyā, bright of countenance. One says hashishta, "you have become so", and such a man is dhū hashāsh.

3. **A horse that sweats.** A horse that is hashsh is one that sweats a great deal.

4. **A copious ewe.** A ewe that is hashūsh is tharra, yielding copiously.

5. **Beating leaves.** Hashashtu al-waraq means "I beat the leaves with a stick"; Ibn Fāris counts this as belonging to the same category.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root h-sh-m (هشم) from one core idea: breaking something, whether the thing is hollow or solid. The verb hashama means "to break/crush," and hashamtuhu hashman means "I broke/crushed it."

Senses recorded under this root:

1. Al-hāshimah — a wound to the head severe enough to crush/break the skull bone.

2. The name Hāshim — Ibn Fāris notes it is agreed that this ancestor (whose own given name was ʿAmr) was called Hāshim because he "hashama al-tharīd," i.e., he crumbled/broke bread into a communal broth dish (tharīd).

3. Al-hashīm, said of plant matter — dry, brittle vegetation that has crumbled or broken apart.

4. A man called hashīm — meaning physically weak/frail.

5. Tahashshama ʿalā (تهشّم على) — an idiom meaning "to show tenderness or affection toward" someone; Ibn Fāris classes this too as belonging to the same root, though he does not spell out the link to "breaking."

6. Ihtashama mā fī ḍarʿ al-nāqah — to milk out what is in a she-camel's udder. Ibn Fāris flags this sense explicitly as "what analogy would predict" (al-qiyās), i.e., a natural extension of the root's "breaking/releasing" idea rather than an irregular usage.

dictionary: Qāmūs — al-Qāmūs al-Muḥīṭ, al-Fīrūzābādī (d. 1415)
text:
This entry (al-Qāmūs al-Muḥīṭ, al-Fīrūzābādī) covers the root h-ā-t (هات) in a few short notes:

1. هاتِ يا رَجُلُ ("hāti, O man!") means أَعْطِ — "give!" It is used as a command meaning "hand [something] over."

2. المُهاتاة (al-muhātāh) is identified as the مُفَاعَلَة (Form III) verbal noun formed from this same word — the pattern used for reciprocal or back-and-forth action.

3. ما أُهاتِيكَ ("mā uhātīka") is explained as meaning ما أنا بِمُعْطِيكَ — "I am not going to give you [anything]."

4. هَتِيٌّ مِنَ الليل ("a hatiyy of the night") is glossed simply as هَتْء — the entry gives only this terse cognate-noun equivalent, without further explanation of what portion or aspect of the night it denotes.

No Qur'anic citation or morphological/iʿrāb discussion is given beyond these bare glosses; the entry is a brief note tying the imperative hāti to the sense "give."

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: Ziyād ibn Munqidh (Umayyad); al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); Ṭarafah (pre-Islamic); Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); Labīd (lived into Islam) ×2; ʿAntarah (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse
text:
Root h-ḍ-m (هضم) — Lisān al-ʿArab

The lexicographer notes the underlying idea is "breaking" (أصل الهضم الكسر); digestion, generosity, wronging, slenderness, low ground, and incense all branch from that core.

1. Digestion. haḍama al-dawāʾu al-ṭaʿāma — the medicine "digested" the food, i.e. wore it down. Al-haḍḍām / al-haḍūm / al-hāḍūm = any digestive medicine (compared to a jawārishn electuary). Food is "quick" or "slow to digest."

2. Wronging. haḍamahu / ihtaḍamahu / tahaḍḍamahu = he wronged, usurped from, or oppressed him; the noun is al-haḍīmah. A wronged man is haḍīm or muhtaḍam. haḍamahu ḥaqqahu = he diminished/withheld his right. But haḍama lahu min ḥaqqihi (note the added "lahu," for him) flips the sense to generosity: he left him part of it willingly — "I haḍamtu him a share of my portion" means I relinquished it to him.

3. Breaking / giving. haḍama al-shayʾa = he broke or crushed it (passive: mahḍūm, haḍīm). From this comes haḍama lahu min mālihi = he broke off and gave a share of his wealth. Al-haḍḍām / al-haḍūm = a lavish spender, plural huḍum — cited in a verse by Ziyād ibn Munqidh praising generous young men. A "haḍūm hand" likewise gives freely, holding nothing back — cited in a verse by al-Aʿshā.

4. Slenderness (waist/flank). ahḍam al-kashḥayn = a man whose two flanks are drawn in. Al-hadam = hollowness of the belly, fineness of the flank. Man: ahḍam; woman: haḍmāʾ or haḍīm; a belly can likewise be haḍīm/mahḍūm/ahḍam. Ṭarafah is cited praising a man's slender waist this way. Al-haḍīm alone also just means "fine, delicate" — and, separately, "well-ripened" (naḍīj). Applied to women, haḍīm al-kashḥ = slender-waisted; Imruʾ al-Qays's famous line ("she leaned toward me, slender of flank") is cited, as is a hadith describing Saʿd, governor of Kufa, the same way. In horses the same drawn-in build (al-hadam) is instead a defect — straight, sunken ribs; the sources say an ahḍam horse never wins a long race.

5. Qur'an 26:148 — "wa-nakhlin ṭalʿuhā haḍīm" ("palm-trees whose blossom-spathe is haḍīm"). Ibn Manẓūr records several explanations current among the philologists:
   - folded/compressed within its calyx-covering (the standard gloss);
   - al-Farrāʾ: called haḍīm only while still inside its calyx-coverings;
   - haḍīm = soft/tender; or (Ibn al-Aʿrābī) wholesome/palatable, or soft and delicate, or "folded-in and fully ripened";
   - al-Zajjāj: haḍīm = whose parts fold into one another — some said because its fresh dates have no pit, some said it means "that which crumbles apart easily";
   - the spathe is called haḍīm only before it emerges from its covering, its parts being folded one into another.

6. Funeral food. Al-Athram: the food prepared for a man's death is called al-haḍīmah, plural al-haḍāʾim.

7. Crushed/jointed reeds. Al-hāḍim = that which crushes something soft or supple. A thing haḍamahu ("he crushed it") becomes inhaḍam, like a "crushed reed." A reed made into a pipe (mizmār) is called mahḍūmah / muhaḍḍamah / haḍīm — said to be because such a pipe is built of broken pieces joined together. Cited in verses by Labīd (a donkey's bray likened to such pipes) and ʿAntarah ("crouching like a rough, crushed reed-pipe").

8. Low ground. Al-hadm/al-hidm (kasrah) = a depressed tract of land, a valley-bottom, or a hollow that sometimes bears vegetation; plural ahḍām, huḍūm. This underlies the proverbial warning against a hidden danger: "[Beware] the night, and the ahḍām of the valley" — you cannot know who may be lying in ambush there. A hadith likewise places "the enemy in ahḍām al-ghīṭān," glossed either as low ground or, via the "breaking" sense, as "breaking-points" in the terrain. Al-Muʾarrij glosses ahḍām as "hidden places" — whatever conceals something from view. Ibn Shumayl uses the same verb for the foot of a mountain nearing level ground, and for coming down on someone unexpectedly (haḍama ʿalayhi).

9. Submission. tahaḍḍamtu lil-qawm = I yielded to the people and made myself lesser before them.

10. Separate sense: rajulun ahḍam = a man with thick, coarse front teeth.

11. Livestock dentition. ahḍama al-muhru lil-irbāʿ = the colt neared the age of shedding its milk teeth for the rubāʿī stage; likewise said of young camels, she-camels, and lambs (for camels/lambs, covering both the irbāʿ and isdās stages). Al-Jawharī records the synonym set ahḍamat / adramat / afarrat for livestock reaching this milestone.

12. Perfume/incense. Al-mahḍūmah = a perfume blended with musk and bān (ben-oil). Al-ahḍām = perfume generally, or specifically incense, or (more narrowly) any incense besides ʿūd (agarwood) and lubnā (storax); singular hiḍm/hadm/hadmah. Cited in verses by an unnamed poet, al-Aʿshā, and al-ʿAjjāj, comparing pleasant or thick scent/smoke to ahḍām-incense; one commentator (Abū Manṣūr) suggests al-ʿAjjāj's verse actually describes a wild bull's lair, its dung-smell likened to perfume.

13. Place-names. Ahḍām Tabālah = the low-lying land among the mountains of Tabālah, a known fertile district (cited in a verse by Labīd). Banū Muhaḍḍamah = the name of a tribe.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: h-ṭ-ʿ (هطع)
Source: Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004 CE)

Ibn Fāris treats h-ṭ-ʿ as a small root carrying one core notion: turning/advancing toward something combined with submission — being led.

He records three usages:

1. haṭaʿa ('the man haṭaʿa toward the thing with his gaze') — he turned/fixed his gaze on it, advancing toward it.
2. ahṭaʿa (of a camel) — it lowered its neck, in a submissive, led manner.
3. ahṭaʿa (used absolutely, without an object) — he/it hastened.

So the entry links a directed, fixed advance-toward (especially of the gaze) with an accompanying sense of submissiveness/being led, and separately notes a related sense of hastening for the causative form ahṭaʿa.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats هبط (h-b-ṭ) as a single-idea root: the three letters hāʾ–bāʾ–ṭāʾ point to انحدار — going down, descent, a falling away of level.

1. Base verb: هَبَطَ, "to go down / descend" (with its verbal noun; the form is defective in the text and is ordinarily هُبُوطًا).

2. الْهَبُوط (al-habūṭ) — the downward slope itself, the declivity or descent (glossed by الحدور, sloping ground).

3. The verb works both ways without changing form: هَبَطْتُ أَنَا, "I went down," and هَبَطْتُ غَيْرِي, "I brought someone else down" — i.e. it is used intransitively of the one descending and transitively of causing another to descend.

4. Extended (non-spatial) use: هَبَطَ الْمَرَضُ لَحْمَ الْعَلِيلِ, "the illness brought down the flesh of the sick man" — the wasting or reduction of a body, the same notion of downward movement applied to bulk rather than place.

5. Derived adjective: الْهَبِيط (al-habīṭ) — a lean, wasted camel; the animal whose flesh has "gone down."

The entry is terse and gives no poetic or Qur'anic citations; the whole account rests on the single organising sense of downward movement, with the wasting of flesh presented as its natural extension.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root هبو (h-b-w) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core sense: dustiness, and a fineness/thinness associated with it.

1. al-habwa — dustiness. habā al-ghubār — the dust rose and spread (verb hābin, "rising").

2. al-habāʾ — fine, powdery dust, illustrated with a verse about a fatal blow that sent someone down to the dusty earth.

3. habā al-ramādu — ashes mixed with dust and died out (cooled and settled), extending the same "fine, scattered particles" image from dust to ash.

4. A specific, everyday usage: the fine motes you see scattered and floating in a beam of sunlight are called habāʾ.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats h-d as a sound root (aṣl ṣaḥīḥ) indicating breaking, crushing and demolishing (kasr, haḍm, hadm), and states that the whole chapter goes back to this analogy.

1. **Demolishing.** hadadtuhu haddan means "I demolished it."

2. **The weak man.** al-hadd among men is the weak one, "as though he had been demolished"; the plural is haddūn.

3. **A contrary report.** Ibn Fāris notes that al-Aṣmaʿī was contradicted here. Reports going back to Ibn al-Aʿrābī and to the father of ʿAmr ibn Abī ʿAmr say that al-hadd is the generous, noble man, while the coward is hidd, with the vowel i. They cited: "They are no weaklings (haddīn) in wars, when the belts are tied above the hip-bones." If that is so, Ibn Fāris says, the coward is hidd in the sense of mahdūd ("demolished"), just as dhibḥ is used for madhbūḥ ("slaughtered"), and the generous hadd is the man who "demolishes" his wealth.

4. **Sounds and rocking.** Among words that behave like sound-words (aṣwāt) is al-haddah, the sound of a wall falling. The hoopoe (hudhud) is well known. hadhada is said of doves making their call, and of a woman rocking her son so that he sleeps.

5. **An exception.** One usage departs from the chapter, and Ibn Fāris knows no analogy for it: "marartu bi-rajulin haddaka min rajulin", said like "ḥasbuka min rajulin" ("enough for you as a man"). It is, he says, simply an expression used in this form. A poet: "I have a companion in the cave, haddaka ṣāḥiban (enough of a companion for you)."

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
Root h-d-d (هدد) — Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr)

1. Violent demolition/crushing (al-hadd). To smash something — a wall — so it collapses at once (hadda yahuddu, verbal nouns hadd/hudūd). Kuthayyir ʿAzza's line pictures grief that would crush mountains. Al-Asmaʿī: to break and flatten a building; "I heard a hādd" = I heard it being demolished. By extension, an event or loss "hadda" (crushes/overwhelms) a person, or "breaks his supporting pillar (rukn)" — e.g. "the death of no one has crushed me like the death of my peers."

2. A violent crashing sound (al-hadda) — heard when a wall, pillar, or mountainside collapses (a different verb pattern: hadda yahiddu). A hadith has the Prophet seeking refuge from "al-hadd and al-hidda." In a rain-prayer hadith, "it hadda-t and poured" describes thunder and downpour (one variant reading gives "it grew calm" instead).

3. A camel's groan/bellow is also called its hadd (al-Liḥyānī). More generally, al-hadd/al-hadad names any thick, coarse sound.

4. al-hādd: an eerie rumbling that people on coasts hear coming from the sea, resonating in the ground and sometimes producing an earthquake. The same word is used for thunder ("we heard no hādda this year").

5. Of men, al-hadd = a physically weak man (plural haddūn), illustrated by a verse of al-ʿAbbās b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib; al-ahadd = a coward; "I am not a hadd" is a man's boast of strength when issuing a threat. The lexicographers disagree sharply on the vowel here: Ibn al-Aʿrābī says al-hadd (fatḥa) actually means the generous, noble, strong man, while al-hidd (kasra) is the coward — the reverse of al-Asmaʿī, who took al-hadd (fatḥa) as the weak man; Ibn al-Aʿrābī rejected al-Asmaʿī's usage. Shimr separately records hadd/hadāda/hadād for cowardice, backed by a verse of Umayya.

6. al-hadīd and al-fadīd both simply mean "noise." "istahdadtu fulānan" = I judged so-and-so weak (with a supporting verse of ʿAdī b. Zayd); al-Asmaʿī records a warning-idiom pairing al-fadīd and al-hadīd.

7. Topography: a hillock "hadūd" is one steep/hard to descend; al-hadūd also names a difficult mountain pass. Of a man, al-hadīd means tall.

8. An idiom of praise: "I passed a man — haddaka min rajulin," roughly "what a man!," or, per one gloss, "the account of his virtues would overwhelm you." Grammarians split on whether "haddaka" stays invariant (like a fixed noun) or is a fully inflected verb (haddatka for a woman, haddāka for two men, haddūka for a group, etc., paralleling kafāka/kafatka). One citation (from Ibn al-Aʿrābī) uses it admiringly of a wolf as a "companion." Related: in a hadith, Abū Lahab's exclamation "la-hadda mā yaḥarrukum ṣāḥibukum" uses la-hadda as an expression of astonished admiration ("how vigorous he is!"). Likewise "fulānun yuhaddu" and "innahu la-haddu l-rajuli" both mean a man is being praised for vigor and strength — Ibn Sīdah compares it directly to the standard praise-formula "niʿma l-rajulu" ("what a fine man"). A separate phrase, "mahlan hadādayka," means "ease off — that's enough for you."

9. The ordinary abstract sense: al-tahaddud, al-tahdīd, al-tahdād = threatening, menacing, intimidation.

10. Proper names built on the root: Hudad, a king of Ḥimyar (said to have been married by Solomon to Bilqīs) — one source gives his father's name as Hammāl, another as Badad. A verse of al-ʿAjjāj applies the "hadda l-rajulu" praise-idiom to a protector: "what a fine protector for one who seeks refuge." Hudāhid and Hadād are recorded as Yemeni clans, Hadhād as a personal name.

11. A separate note (from al-Nawādir) strings together near-synonymous passive verbs (yuhadhadu, yuhaddā, yusawwalu, yuhdā, yuhawwalu, yuwaswasu, yukhayyalu, yukhālu) all describing an unconfirmed notion a person merely imagines about himself by conjecture or resemblance — closer to "it is suggested/fancied to me" than to demolition or noise.

12. Bird sense: "hadhada" of a bird = it cooed/made a low rumbling call; any cooing bird can be called hudhud or hudāhid. The dictionary catalogues real disagreement over which bird hudāhid actually is — al-Azharī says one resembling al-khamān; al-Asmaʿī offers several candidates (ring-dove, dubsī, warashān, hudhud, dukhkhal, ayk) and denies (against al-Kisāʾī) that it is simply a diminutive of hudhud, arguing instead it applies to any bird that coos and rumbles; Ibn Sīdah sides with al-Asmaʿī on morphological grounds. Abū Ḥanīfa extends hudhud/hudāhid to a pigeon that coos a great deal, and to a stud-camel that hums among the herd without mating (with its own verbal noun, hudāhida/hadhada, per al-Jawharī). al-hudhud proper is the well-known bird (the hoopoe); its call is hadhada or hadīl. One poetic image compares a broken-winged hudhud to a man whose baggage-camels were seized by a tax-collector. In a transmitted verse the same word is read either as "hudhud" (the bird) or "hadhad," which elsewhere is glossed as "the voices of the jinn" (a word with no singular).

13. Rocking sense: "hadhada" something from above downward = to let it down. "hadhadahu" = to rock or jostle something, especially a mother rocking her child to sleep (the act itself is called al-hadhada). A hadith likens a devil rocking the sleeping Bilāl — so that he missed waking the people for prayer — to a mother rocking her child.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root هـ د م (h-d-m), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: the bringing-down of a structure; further senses are measured against it.

1. hadamtu al-ḥāʾiṭa — I demolished the wall; al-hadam (fatḥ on the dāl) — what has collapsed/been demolished.
2. al-hidm — a worn-out garment (plural aḥdām).
3. "dimāʾuhum hadam" — their blood is forfeit/unavenged, likened to a demolished structure for which no one seeks redress; a hadith formula, "al-damu al-damu, wa al-hadamu al-hadam," is cited and glossed as a treaty pledge of shared life and shared death.
4. nāqah hadimah — a she-camel intensely in heat, as though she "collapses" toward the stud; al-hadmah — a sudden downpour of rain, as though it "collapses" in its onrush.
5. Closing exception, explicitly flagged by Ibn Fāris as anomalous and NOT derived from the root's core "demolition" sense: al-mahdūm, said of milk, meaning al-rathīʾah — soured, curdled milk.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: هَدَى 144x "guide"; هُدًى 85x "the guidance"; ٱهْتَدَىٰ 40x "(be) guided"; مُّهْتَدُون 17x "the guided ones"; هَدْي 7x "the sacrificial animal"; أَهْدَىٰ 7x "better guided"; هَاد 7x "guide"; مُّهْتَد 3x "(is) a guided one"; هَادِي 2x "(as) a guide"; هَدِيَّة 2x "a gift"; مُهْتَدِى 1x "(is) the guided one"; هَٰدِى 1x "guide"
text:
Ibn Fāris analyzes the root h-d-y (with a weak final letter) as having two base meanings, and treats the hamzated form h-d-ʾ separately as belonging to a different analogy.

FIRST BASE MEANING — going ahead in order to guide.
1. هَدَيْتُهُ الطَّرِيقَ ("I guided him on the road") = I went ahead to direct him; anyone who leads this way is a هَادٍ (guide). A verse of poetry illustrates a spear-point as a man's "guide" through the land.
2. From this branch: الْهُدَى (right guidance) as the opposite of الضَّلَالَة (going astray) — هَدَيْتُهُ هُدًى.
3. Extended physical uses, all sharing "what goes in front": هَوَادِي الْخَيْل = horses' necks; هَادِيهَا = the lead troop of horses; الْهَادِيَة = a walking-staff, since it goes before its holder as if directing him.
4. Further idioms of "direction/course": نَظَرَ هَدْيَ أَمْرِهِ = he considered the direction of his affair; مَا أَحْسَنَ هِدْيَتَهُ = how good his manner/way; يُهَادِي بَيْنَ اثْنَيْنِ = he walks between two people leaning on them; a second arrow shot هُدَيَّاهُ = in the same aim as the first. Ibn Fāris notes the underlying analogy is one throughout.

SECOND BASE MEANING — sending a kindness.
5. الْهَدِيَّة (a gift) = a kindness sent to someone one loves; verb أَهْدَى / إِهْدَاء. الْمِهْدَى = the tray a gift is carried on.
6. الْهَدِيّ = a bride, who is "conducted" (هُدِيَتْ ... هِدَاءً) to her husband; a cited verse says every chaste woman deserves such conducting.
7. الْهَدْي / الْهَدِيّ = livestock offered/led to the Sanctuary as a means of nearness to God; a verse of poetry uses هَدِيّ of a man led to slaughter. It is also said that الْهَدِيّ can mean "a captive."

SEPARATE FORM — h-d-ʾ (hamzated), a different analogy, mostly denoting stillness.
8. هَدَأَ هُدُوًّا = became calm/settled; هَدَأَتِ الرِّجْل = grew quiet once people sleep; أَهْدَأَتِ الْمَرْأَةُ صَبِيَّهَا = the woman soothed her infant to sleep; هُدْءٌ مِنَ اللَّيْل = a stretch of night after people first settle; الْهَدَأَة = a kind of easy running.
9. An outlier of this group: الْهَدَأ = a shoulder inclining toward the chest (compared to الْجَنَأ).

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
poets_named: Zuhayr b. Abī Sulmā (pre-Islamic); Abū Qays b. al-Aslat (pre-Islamic); Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad); Suwayd al-Yashkurī (pre-Islamic); ʿAmr b. Maʿdī Karib (pre-Islamic)
text:
Root h-j-ʿ (هجع) — Tāj al-ʿArūs, al-Zabīdī

1. Core meaning: sleep. Al-hujūʿ and al-tahjāʿ mean "sleep" in general. Some restrict it to night-sleep specifically, citing Q 51:17: "they used to sleep [yahjaʿūn] but little of the night."

2. A refinement — "resting," not necessarily sleeping. Al-hujūʿ can describe lying down/resting even without actually being asleep. Zuhayr b. Abī Sulmā: he "hajaʿa" in a desolate place, using a couched camel's neck as a pillow, "though I was not asleep."

3. An alternative split some lexicographers draw: al-tahjāʿ = a light nap; al-hujūʿ (unqualified) = sleep proper. Illustrated by Abū Qays b. al-Aslat, who says his shaved-bare head lets him taste "no sleep but a light nap [tahjāʿ]."

4. Verb conjugation and derived forms. hajaʿa/yahjaʿu (verbal nouns hajʿ, hujūʿ; active participle hājiʿ, "sleeping/asleep"), plural hujjaʿ or hujūʿ ("sleepers") — with citations from Dhū al-Rumma (a dream-visit while "hājiʿ"; birds "hujjaʿ" [roosting] while travelers press on by night), Suwayd al-Yashkurī (the eye "hajaʿa," fell asleep, prompting a fleeting dream-visit), and ʿAmr b. Maʿdī Karib (a caller keeps me awake "while my companions are hujūʿ").

5. Al-hajīʿ = a watch/portion of the night (synonym: al-hazīʿ), per al-Jawharī and Thaʿlab.

6. Figurative sense: "the fool." Several nominal forms — al-hijʿ, al-hijʿa, hujaʿ, hajiʿ, al-mihjaʿ — denote a person heedless of schemes against him, i.e. a simpleton (Ibn al-Aʿrābī). Al-Zabīdī notes this is a metaphorical extension of "sleep" (someone "asleep" to danger), glossed further as one too quick to trust anyone (al-Zamakhsharī's Asās al-Balāgha: "a hujaʿ man trusts everyone").

7. Proper names and a source-critical note. Two men are listed as Companions bearing names from this root: Mihjaʿ b. Ṣāliḥ (client of ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb, said to be an early martyr of Badr) and Hujayʿ b. Qays. Al-Zabīdī personally disputes this entry on two grounds: (a) other hadith-authorities (al-Dhahabī, Ibn Fahd) vocalize the second name differently, as Hajannaʿ, calling the Qāmūs author's spelling a copying error; (b) hadith scholars (Abū Ḥātim) hold this man's report to be mursal (chain-broken) with no actual companionship of the Prophet established.

8. An unrelated homonymous use: "hunger blunted." hajaʿa al-ṭaʿāmu jūʿahu / ahjaʿahu = the food blunted/broke his hunger (without full satiety); a hamza-variant hajaʾa/ahjaʾa exists too. Grammarians differ on whether the verb is intransitive only (al-Jawharī) or also transitive (Ibn Shumayl, via ahjaʿa).

9. Minor extended uses:
 - ṭarīq tahjaʿ = a wide road (Ibn ʿAbbād).
 - rakiba... hajāʿi (or corrected: hajāji) = "rode his own head," i.e. acted rashly/headstrong — with a supporting verse whose correct reading al-Ṣāghānī corrects from a scribal error.
 - Plural forms for women: hujjaʿ, hujūʿ, hawājiʿ, hawājiʿāt (the last two are "plurals of plurals").
 - hajjaʿa (form II) = "they went to sleep."
 - hajʿ/hajʿa of the night = a portion/stretch of the night; "came to him after a hajʿa" = after a light nap early in the night.
 - al-hijʿa relates to al-hujūʿ the way "a sitting" (jilsa) relates to "sitting" (julūs) — i.e., one instance of the act.
 - rajulun hujaʿa(tun) = a heedless fool (al-Jawharī).
 - hajaʿtu ilayhi fa-khadaʿanī = "I let my guard down / trusted him, and he deceived me" — marked as metaphorical, extending the same "sleep = inattention" logic.

text:
Ibn Fāris (d. 1004 CE), *Maqāyīs al-Lugha*, root ه‑ج‑د (h‑j‑d)

**Core meaning:** the root is a genuine (aṣīl) triliteral signifying "stillness — settling down in one place."

1. **هَجَدَ (hajada)** — "he slept." The verbal noun is هُجُود (hujūd, "sleeping"), and the doer-noun هَاجِد (hājid) means "sleeper."

2. **مُتَهَجِّد (mutahajjid)** — the word used for one who prays at night. Ibn Fāris flags this as a seeming paradox, since the same root (hajada) means "to sleep." His explanation: mutahajjid works by an *applied analogy* pattern also seen in Arabic word-formation — the same pattern that turns آثِم (āthim, "a sinning man") into مُتَأَثِّم (mutaʾaththim, "one who strives to avoid sin, disavows sin"). In both cases, the مُتَفَعِّل (mutafaʿʿil) form doesn't mean "doing X" but "casting X off / working against X." So mutahajjid is literally "one who has shed sleep [hujūd] from himself" by staying up to pray — not "one who sleeps," but the opposite, reached through the same derivational logic that produces mutaʾaththim from āthim.

3. **أَهْجَدَ الْبَعِير (ahjada al-baʿīr)** — said of a camel: it means the camel laid its جِران (jirān, the underside of the neck/throat) down on the ground — i.e., it settled/lay down, tying back to the root's core sense of stillness.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives h-j-r from two base meanings: (1) severance and cutting-off, and (2) binding/tying a thing.

FIRST BASE — severance:
1. al-hajr (and al-hijrān): the opposite of union or connection.
2. hājara (to emigrate): to leave one abode for another — as the Muhājirūn did in moving from Mecca to Medina. To tahajjara / tamahjara is to make oneself resemble the emigrants; the ḥadīth "Emigrate, and do not merely play at emigrating" urges being truly one of them. Ibn Fāris judges tahajjarū the correct form over tamahjarū.
3. al-hajr / al-hajīr / al-hājira: midday at peak heat; hajjarū = they traveled then. Named hājira because people shut themselves indoors, as if shunning one another.
4. al-hajīr: dried-out herbage broken by livestock, so called because the herdsman shuns it (cited with a verse about al-Khalṣāʾ).
5. al-hujr: (a) raving/delirium — hajara al-rajul, "the man raved"; (b) foul or obscene speech — ahjara, "he spoke foully" (cited with a verse). ramāhu bil-hājirāt = he assailed him with scandals. All of this traces to al-mahjūr, "the shunned thing with no good in it."
6. By an inverse twist, hajr also marks the peerless: hādhā shayʾun hajr = "a thing without equal," as though its very excellence set it apart from all else; ahjaru min = "more excellent/noble than" (cited with a verse on incomparable Yemeni water/a day's march).

SECOND BASE — binding/tying:
7. al-hajīr: the great watering-trough — explained as something set apart for water — cited with two verses.

Note: the entry develops the "severance" base fully; the "binding" base is represented only by the great trough, whose stated rationale ("set apart for water") itself leans on the cutting sense.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root h-l-ʿ from one core meaning: speed combined with sharpness/intensity.

1. In animals: a she-camel called hilwāʿ is "keen and swift." An ostrich called hāliʿ carries the same sense of swiftness.

2. In humans - al-halaʿ: from that root sense comes al-halaʿ, glossed as "something resembling greed/covetousness." A man with this trait is called haliʿ or halūʿ.

3. Ibn al-Sikkīt's citation: he describes such a man (hulʿa) as one who becomes agitated and panics quickly - a fast, intense reaction, tying back to the root's "speed" meaning.

4. An idiom: "he has neither hillaʿ nor hillaʿa" means "he has neither a male nor a female kid-goat" (i.e. nothing at all). Ibn Fāris notes young goats got this name because of their nazaq - their skittish, flighty quickness - again linking back to the root's basic sense of speed/agitation.

text:
Ibn Fāris's account of the root h-l-k:

Core sense: the root points to "breaking and falling."

1. halāk — a falling/collapse, hence "destruction, perishing." A dead person is said to have "perished" (halaka).

2. ihtalaka (VIII) — to fling oneself into danger: a sandgrouse fleeing a falcon "ihtalakat," i.e. hurled itself into places of destruction (mahālik).

3. halūk — a woman languorous and wanton in her coquetry, carrying herself in a "broken"/languid way. Ibn Fāris notes the form is used only of women, never of a man. (A cited Hudhalī verse uses the plural huluk of such women, and there negates it.)

4. muhtalik — one who perpetually throws himself on whoever will support or provide for him; such people are called muhtalikūn or hullāk.

5. In al-Ḥuṭayʾa's line, mustahlik (of one pressing on to the watering-place) was glossed by some as "earnest, diligent" (jādd); Ibn Fāris holds that the root's analogy really only supports the "hurling oneself forward" sense seen in the sandgrouse image.

6. al-arḍ al-halakīn — barren, drought-stricken land.

7. halak — (a) a perishing thing; (b) the chasm/abyss between two mountains, illustrated by a line of Dhū al-Rumma picturing an earring overhanging an empty gorge.

8. al-Hālikī — a blacksmith. Reportedly traced to a man named al-Hālik b. ʿAmr (of Asad b. Khuzayma) who worked iron, which is also why the Banū Asad were nicknamed al-quyūn ("the smiths").

text:
Ibn Fāris treats h-l-l as a single sound root meaning "raising the voice". In his account the meaning widens in two steps: a thing at which people raise their voices is named from the root, and then other things that resemble that thing take the same name.

1. **Raising the voice (the base sense).** ahalla bi-l-ḥajj: he raised his voice in the talbiya. istahalla l-ṣabiyy: the newborn cried out at birth. Ibn Aḥmar speaks of riders who "raise their voices at al-Farqad, as the mounted muʿtamir raises his." Rain inhalla when it pours down hard and loud.

2. **The new moon, named from the voice.** The hilāl is so called because people raise their voices on seeing it, proclaiming God's greatness and calling out in prayer. It is hilāl for the first three nights and qamar (moon) after that. One says ahalla l-hilāl ("the new moon appeared") and ustuhilla ("it was hailed").

3. **Glittering, by likeness to the new moon.** A cloud tahallala with its lightning: it glittered, the lightning being likened to the new moon.

4. **A two-pronged spearhead** is also called hilāl, by the same likening.

5. **Water at the bottom of a well.** hilāl is the little water left at the bottom of a well.

6. **A snake.** hilāl is a kind of snake; Dhū l-Rumma pictures a hilāl appearing on scorching ground, writhing. Some say hilāl is a snake's cast-off skin.

7. **A broken millstone edge.** hilāl is the rim of a millstone when it breaks off.

8. **Flimsy and fine.** A halhal garment is flimsily woven, as thin as the new moon's light; halhal poetry is fine and thin.

9. **Muhalhil.** Imruʾ al-Qays ibn Rabīʿa was called Muhalhil either because he was the first to make poetry fine, or, according to others, from his line "I halhaltu, seeking vengeance for Jābir or Ṣinbil", where the word means he shouted as he pressed on to overtake his quarry.

10. **Water with a voice.** al-hulāhil is abundant water, named for the sound it makes as it runs; the word was originally hurāhir.

11. **A saddle-piece.** hilāl (plural ahilla) is also what holds together the two curved frame-pieces of a camel-saddle.

12. **An exception.** Ibn Fāris lists "he charged at his opponent, then hallala", meaning he held back, as a use that departs from the root.

13. **A call to horses.** halā is a sound made to horses, meaning "be still".

The article also quotes a verse about a night-traveller in sultry heat who "yuhillu and yanqaʿu", but the explanation that should follow it is missing from this copy.

text:
Ibn Fāris's entry for the root H-M-D (هَمَدَ):

Core meaning: the root points to something dying down or going out — khumūd, "extinguishing/subsiding."

Senses he lists:
1. hamadat al-nār — "the fire hamada-ed" = it went out completely, all the way extinguished.
2. arḍun hāmidah — "a hāmid land" = land bare of any vegetation.
3. nabātun hāmid — "hāmid plant-growth" = vegetation that has dried up and withered.
4. al-ihmād — staying put, remaining in one place.

He then flags one outlier usage that breaks from this pattern: some say al-ihmād instead means swiftness in walking, and cites a line of verse — "it was nothing but the swift pace (ṭalaq) of al-ihmād" — as evidence, though without naming the poet in this excerpt. Ibn Fāris marks this sense explicitly as anomalous (shādhdh) relative to the root's main thread of "dying down / going still."

text:
Ibn Fāris treats h-m-m as a single sound root indicating melting, flowing and creeping, and similar notions, from which the other senses are drawn by analogy. After tracing grief and resolve back to it, he states that "the analogy is one".

**1. Melting.** "Hammanī al-shayʾ" means "the thing melted me", and "inhamma al-shaḥm" means "the fat melted". Al-hāmūm is fat that yields much grease.

**2. Flowing water and rain.** A hāmūm cloud is one that pours abundantly; a hamūm well is one with plenty of water (cited verse: "she has a deep well, abundant in water"). Al-hamīma is a light shower. The text also glosses al-rīḥ al-raydāna as the gently blowing wind.

**3. Creeping.** Al-hawāmm, the small crawling creatures of the ground, are named for their hamīm, their creeping; a verse likens a mark on someone's sides to the track of creeping creatures. "Hammama fī raʾsihi" is said of someone who runs his fingers back and forth through his hair to fall asleep, as though they crept through it.

**4. Old age.** Al-himm is an aged man and himma an aged woman, as though both had melted away with age.

**5. Grief.** Ibn Fāris holds that al-hamm in the sense of grief belongs to the same analogy: grief, by its intensity, seems to melt a person.

**6. Intention and resolve.** Al-hamm is also what one resolves on doing, as is al-himma. From al-himma comes al-humām, the king of great resolve. Muhimm al-amr is the grave part of an affair, and "ahammanī" means "it disquieted me".

**7. Al-Kumayt's "lā hamāmi".** In a verse of al-Kumayt, "lā hamāmi lī" means "I will not intend it and I will not do it".

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris rules that h-m-n (هـ-م-ن) is not a real root at all — it carries no established meaning of its own.

He raises this specifically to correct a possible misreading of al-muhaymin (المهيمن), "the witness" (al-shāhid): despite its surface form, this word is not built on h-m-n. He derives it instead from the root ʾ-m-n (أمن, "security, trust, safety"), explaining that its initial hāʾ stands in for an original hamza — i.e., al-muhaymin is etymologically a form of amina/āmin, not a separate h-m-n word.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives all uses of h-m-r (همر) from one core idea: pouring out / gushing forth.

1. Physical pouring/flowing — hamara damʿahu, "he poured out his tears"; hamara al-damʿu / inhamara, "the tears poured out, gushed forth" — both meaning simply "it flowed."

2. Taking something up in bulk — yuhāmiru al-shayʾa, said of someone who scoops something up wholesale, in one sweeping take (jarfan) — extending "pouring" to a sweeping, wholesale seizing.

3. Talking at length — hamara fī kalāmihi, "he poured forth in his speech," meaning he talked excessively. Someone habitually like this is called a mihmār, "one who talks a great deal" — speech flowing out like poured liquid.

4. Giving generously — hamara lahu min mālihi, "he poured out for him from his wealth," i.e. gave to him abundantly, as though pouring the wealth out for him.

All four senses — tears, seizing in bulk, torrential speech, lavish giving — are presented by Ibn Fāris as branches of the same image: something poured out in a continuous outflow.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root هـ م س (h-m-s), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha — companion, shorter entry to al-Khalīl's on the same root

One core meaning: the faintness of a sound or sensation.

1. al-hams — a faint sound; hams al-aqdām — the faintest possible tread of a footstep.
2. al-hammās — the fierce lion — Ibn Fāris argues this word, too, belongs to the same root: what is meant by it is the lion's "hams," whether in its stealthy tread or in the faint-but-deadly grip of its bite — illustrated with a line of poetry describing its fierce, biting nature.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ه-م-ز (h-m-z) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: pressing, squeezing (al-ḍaghṭ wa-l-ʿaṣr).

1. Literal: hamaztu al-shayʾa fī kaffī — "I pressed/squeezed the thing in my palm."

2. Linguistic extension: al-hamz — the glottal-stop sound in speech — is explained as an extension of this pressing sense, as though the letter itself is being squeezed/compressed.

3. hamaza bihi al-arḍ — "he threw him down forcefully to the ground."

4. qaws hamzā — a bow with a powerful, forceful release of the arrow.

5. Figurative — slander: al-hammāz and al-humaza both mean "the faultfinder, the slanderer" — one who "presses" others with backbiting. A cited verse: "You show me affection to my face, deceitfully — but when I'm absent, you're the one who slanders and backbites."

6. Religious extension: "the hamz [whispered prompting] of Satan is like a fainting-fit that overtakes a person's heart and carries him away" — Satan's whisper described with the same root-image of a forceful, overpowering pressure on the heart.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats h-n plus a weak letter as a root without a single governing principle: he states outright that it holds problematic words and items with no analogy (qiyās) to reduce them to. He then records the following:

1. هُنَا (hunā) — a word indicating nearness ("here"); the extended form هَاهُنَا (hāhunā) he assigns to distancing.

2. The disputed line of Imruʾ al-Qays: "and the talk of the riding party on the day of hunā … and what talk it was, for all its brevity." Ibn Fāris reports three readings of يَوْمَ هُنَا in it, without deciding between them:
   - it means the past day, taken as an instance of the "nearness" sense — i.e. "my last acquaintance with them was on that day";
   - it means play or sport (al-laʿib);
   - hunā is a place-name.

3. هَنٌ (han) — a word of allusion (kināya), a stand-in for something left unnamed: أَتَاهُ هَنٌ, "such-and-such a thing came to him." Its plural appears in فِي فُلَانٍ هَنَاتٌ, which he glosses as traits of evil; he notes the expression is not used of good qualities.

text:
ROOT ه-ر-ع (h-r-ʿ) — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311 CE)

Core sense: urgent, driven, often trembling haste — of people, animals, wind, spears, or flowing liquid.

1. **al-haraʿ / al-hurāʿ / al-ihrāʿ** — intensity of driving on; speed of running. A poet: laden camels following one another are like a troop "hurrying" (yuhraʿūn) toward another troop. Passive forms: huriʿū / uhriʿū, "they were driven/hurried."

2. **istuhriʿati l-ibil** — the camels hastened to the watering-trough.

3. **uhriʿa r-rajul** (passive) — a man moves swiftly and trembles, from speed, fear, eagerness, anger, or fever.

4. **Qur'anic citation (11:78)**: "and his people came to him, yuhraʿūn ilayhi" ("hurrying to him"). Abū ʿUbaydah: they were being urged on toward him, as though spurring one another.

5. **taharraʿa ilayhi** — he hastened toward him.

6. Abū al-ʿAbbās: al-ihrāʿ is "hastening in calm composure"; pressed on whether it instead means "hastening in fright," he agreed it can mean that too.

7. Al-Kisāʾī: al-ihrāʿ is "hastening while trembling." Al-Muhalhil's verse: captives came "hurrying" (yuhraʿūn), led along in forced humiliation.

8. Al-Layth: yuhraʿūn — captives being driven and hurried along; the forms are huriʿū / uhriʿū.

9. Abū ʿUbayd: uhriʿa r-rajul describes someone arriving trembling from cold; a man can also be "muhraʿ" from fever or anger, at the moment of trembling — and muhraʿ can also mean simply "eager/covetous." (Abū ʿUbayd treats this under words of passive-participle form used with active meaning.)

10. **Qur'anic citation (37:70)**: "and they, in the footsteps of their fathers, are yuhraʿūn" — meaning they run along hastily.

11. Standard usage: uhriʿū / huriʿū → muhraʿūn / mahrūʿūn. Ibn Aḥmar's wind poem is quoted describing a fierce, wide-blowing, gusting wind (using the adjective hayraʿ for "swift/violent") that brings a downpour — the poet uses "wird" (watering) to mean rain.

12. **Hariʿ** (of a man): quick-walking; also: quick to weep. **Al-hariʿ**: flowing (of liquid).

13. **hariʿa / haraʿan**, and its synonym hamaʿa — to flow, or to flow in continuous succession. Al-Shammākh's verse compares a camel's sweat to tar oozing from a flowing source.

14. **Dam hariʿ** — clearly flowing blood.

15. **Al-hariʿah** (of a woman) — one who reaches climax as soon as intercourse begins, ahead of the man, out of lust and eagerness for men.

16. **Al-mahrūʿ** — a madman seized by fits (synonyms: makhfūʿ, mamsūs). Abū ʿAmr: also used for someone collapsed from exhaustion.

17. **Al-hayraʿ** — one who cannot control himself; also the cowardly, weak, easily-distressed type. Ibn Aḥmar's verse: "I am not a hayraʿ... who flies off when the wind stirs him."

18. **Al-hayraʿ / al-haylaʿ** — the weak one.

19. When men level their spears and advance, this is harraʿū bihā; spears coming forward leveled is taharraʿat. A cited half-verse: "the spears coming leveled forward" at a sudden clash.

20. **Al-hayraʿah** — the ghoul (a desert-demon), like al-ʿayharah.

21. **Rīḥ hayraʿ** — a fast-blowing wind, or one that whips up dust; **rīḥ hayraʿah** — a violent dust-bearing gust.

22. **Al-hayraʿah** (separately) — the shepherd's reed pipe, also called yarāʿah.

23. **Al-harʿah / al-farʿah** — the small louse (or, some say, the large one); al-hurnūʿ is the commoner term; farʿah, harʿah, hayraʿah, and khayḍaʿah are said to be synonyms.

24. **Al-hiryāʿ** — fallen tree leaves.

25. **Al-harīʿah** — a small, fine-branched shrub.

26. **Yahraʿ** — a place-name.

text:
Root h-r-b (هرب) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha (d. 1004 CE)

Ibn Fāris states that the three root letters h-r-b express a single, unified meaning: haraba (هَرَبَ), "he fled" — i.e., he ran away or escaped.

He then cites the fixed idiom mā lahu hāribun wa-lā qāribun (مَا لَهُ هَارِبٌ وَلَا قَارِبٌ), literally "he has neither a hārib nor a qārib." He glosses hārib here as one going out from water and qārib as one coming to it (terms tied to livestock going to or returning from a watering place). The idiom as a whole means: he has nothing at all — no livestock going to water and none coming from it, hence no possessions whatsoever.

So the entry records two things: the core sense "to flee," and a proverbial expression built on a (different) sense of the same letters relating to coming to/from water, used idiomatically to mean total destitution.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root h-w-d from a single core sense: gentleness/deliberateness and stillness or quiet.

From this he lists:
1. **al-tahwīd** — walking softly and slowly.
2. **hawwada** — to sleep; also used of drink: "the drink hawwada the drinker's self," i.e. it made his self sluggish and heavy.
3. **al-hawāda** — a state of things in which peace and safety between people can be hoped for.
4. **al-muhāwada** — making a truce, mutual peace-making.

On the word **al-Yahūd** ("the Jews"): Ibn Fāris takes it from hāda / yahūdu, "to repent, turn back," the verbal noun being hawd. In his account they were given the name because they turned back (repented) from worshipping the calf. He cites the Qurʾān: "Indeed, we have turned [back] to You" (al-Aʿrāf 7:156). He connects this to his core sense by noting that in turning-back/repentance there is a gentleness of state and a safety — tying the name back to the root's underlying idea of calm and reconciliation.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مُّهِين 14x "humiliating"; هُون 4x "humiliating"; هَيِّن 3x "(was) insignificant"; أَهَٰنَ 2x "(has) humiliated me"; هَوْن 1x "(in) humbleness"; مُهَان 1x "humiliated"; أَهْوَن 1x "(is) easier"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats h-w-n as a small root pointing to one field: stillness, calm/tranquillity, or lowliness and abasement.

1. al-hawn — calm, composure, dignified gravity (sakīna and waqār). Cited from Q al-Furqān 25:63, {yamshūna ʿalā al-arḍ hawnan} ("who walk upon the earth gently").

2. al-hūn — abasement, humiliation (hawān). Cited from Q al-Naḥl 16:59, {ayumsikuhu ʿalā hūn} ("shall he keep it in humiliation").

3. al-hāwūn — a mortar (the implement with which something is pounded). He judges it sound, genuine Arabic, apparently of the pattern fāʿūl derived from al-hawn.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: هَار 1x "(about to) collapse"; ٱنْهَارَ 1x "so it collapsed"
text:
Root h-w-r (هور) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha (d. 1004 CE)

Core meaning: something falling down or collapsing.

1. Physical collapse — تَهَوَّرَ الْبِنَاءُ ("the building tahawwara") = it collapsed, was demolished (انْهَدَمَ).

2. Applied to time, by extension — the same verb form is used metaphorically for a period "collapsing" or passing:
 - تَهَوَّرَ اللَّيْلُ ("the night tahawwara") = its darkness broke up, as though it had collapsed and gone by.
 - تَهَوَّرَ الشِّتَاءُ ("winter tahawwara") = its harshest phase had passed.

3. A flock of sheep is called هَوْرٌ (hawr). Ibn Fāris judges this a sound extension of the same root: because of their large numbers, the sheep tumble/fall over one another — the same "falling" sense as in senses 1–2.

4. An irregular offshoot, not fitting the root's core pattern: هُرْتُ فُلَانًا بِكَذَا أَهُورُهُ ("I hurtu so-and-so with such a thing") = I suspected/accused him of it (أَزْنَنْتُهُ بِهِ). Ibn Fāris flags this explicitly as anomalous (شَذَّ عَنِ الْبَابِ) — it does not derive transparently from the "falling/collapsing" sense.

5. He supports sense 4 with an unattributed line of verse: "He saw that I do not accuse him of much" (لَا بِالْكَثِيرِ أَهُورُهُ) — using the same verb in the "suspect/accuse" meaning.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَهْوَاء 17x "their desires"; هَوَاء 11x "the desire"; هَوَىٰ 8x "desire"; ٱسْتَهْوَتْ 1x "whom (has been) enticed"; هَاوِيَة 1x "(will be the) pit"
poets_named: Zuhayr (pre-Islamic) ×2; Hudhalī poet (lived into Islam); unnamed verse
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root ه‑و‑ي as a single sound root carrying two joined ideas: emptiness (khuluww) and falling/dropping (suqūṭ).

1. Core origin — al-hawāʾ, the air or open space between earth and sky, so called because it is empty. Hence anything empty is hawāʾ. He cites Q 14:43, "their hearts are hawāʾ" (void, comprehending nothing), and a line of Zuhayr describing an ostrich whose breast is hollow (hawāʾ).

2. Falling — hawā / yahwī = to fall. From this: Hāwiya as a name for Hell, because the disbeliever falls into it; al-hāwiya = any abyss; al-huwwa = a deep pit; tahāwā al-qawm = people tumbling into a pit one after another.

3. ahwā bi-yadihi — to reach/stretch out the hand toward something to take it, as if casting the hand toward it.

4. Direction distinguished by vowel: al-hawiyy (fatḥa) = movement downward in descent; al-huwiyy (ḍamma) = movement upward in ascent. He backs each with a verse — Zuhayr for descent (like a well-bucket dropping) and a Hudhalī poet for ascent (like a falcon soaring).

5. Extended senses from "emptiness": hawat al-ṭaʿna = a stab-wound gaping open (from hawāʾ, void); hawat ummuhu = a curse, "may his mother fall and perish," and ummuhu hāwiya parallels thākila (a mother bereaved of her child); al-mahwā = the gap between two upright things, even used of the span between the shoulders.

6. al-hawā (desire, the inclination of the soul) — Ibn Fāris derives it from both senses at once: it is empty of all good, and it drops its owner into what he should not do. He cites Q 53:3, "nor does he speak from hawā," describing the Prophet; the verb is hawiya / ahwā / hawan.

7. al-muhāwāt — two reported meanings: Abū ʿAmr, "mutual obstinacy/contentious persistence" (mulājja); Abū ʿUbayd, "hard, intense travelling," with a supporting verse. Ibn Fāris finds both apt: mulājja because each party loves the other's hawā (desire), and travel because of the hurling of bodies along the way.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: هَيْـَة 2x "like the shape"; يُهَيِّئْ 2x "and will facilitate"
text:
Al-Rāghib's entry for the root h-y-ʾ has three parts.

1. هَيْئَة (hayʾa) — the condition or form in which a thing exists. He notes it covers both what is perceived by the senses and what is grasped abstractly, but says the sensible use is the more frequent one. Qur'anic witness: Q 3:49, "I create for you out of clay something like the hayʾa (form) of a bird."

2. مُهَايَأَة (muhāyaʾa) — the verbal-noun form of the reciprocal pattern: something a group prepares for itself and then settles on by mutual agreement, arrived at by estimation rather than exact measure. Under this heading he places the causative verb هَيَّأَ / يُهَيِّئ (to make ready, put in order): Q 18:10, "make ready for us right direction in our affair," and Q 18:16, "He will make ready for you ease in your affair."

3. هَيَّاكَ (hayyāka) — a warning particle, "beware," used in the construction hayyāka an tafʿala kadhā ("beware of doing such-and-such"), which he identifies as equivalent in sense to إِيَّاكَ (iyyāka). Poetic witness: "hayyāka hayyāka wa-ḥanwāʾa l-ʿunuq" — "Beware, beware, of the curve-necked one." The poet is unnamed in the entry.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives two distinct senses from the root h-y-j (هيج):

1. Stirring / arousal — the core sense applied to animals, blood, and conflict:
   - hāja al-faḥl ("the stallion became excited/aroused"), with verbal nouns hayj and hiyāj; the same verb is used of blood becoming agitated.
   - al-hayjā' ("war, battle") — attested in both a lengthened form (hayjā') and a shortened one (hayjā).
   - hijtu al-sharr / hayyajtuhu — "I stirred up trouble," using either the simple (Form I) or intensive (Form II) verb.
   - hayyajtu al-nāqa fa-inba'athat — "I roused the she-camel and she got up and went."
   - A she-camel pining for her home territory is termed mihyāj.

2. Dryness of plants — a separate, unrelated sense:
   - hāja al-baql — said of herbage turning yellow just before it dries out.
   - arḍun hā'ija — "land whose herbage has dried up."
   - ahyajtu al-arḍ — "I found its plant growth already withered and dried out."
   - Cited verse, by the poet Ru'ba: he describes finding the place called al-Khalṣā' (near Dhāt al-Buraq) dried up — illustrating this sense in use.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: h-y-l (هيل), from Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha.

Ibn Fāris gives this root a single core meaning: to pour or tip out something measurable, letting it flow out freely rather than measuring it with a proper measure.

1. Core sense (verb): "hiltu al-ṭaʿām uhīluhu haylan" — "I poured out the food" — meaning I let it stream out/released it, without using a measuring vessel.

2. Qur'anic citation: the passive participle mahīl (مَهِيل, "poured/tipped out") appears in the Qur'an describing the mountains on the Last Day: "and the mountains will be as a heap of poured-out sand" (73:14) — i.e., loose sand-heaps that pour and collapse, the way grain pours out when tipped rather than carefully measured.

3. Idiom derived from the root: "jāʾa bi-l-hayli wa-l-haylumān" ("he came with hayl and haylumān") — an expression meaning he came with a great abundance of something, extending the sense of freely poured-out quantity to "a lot of something."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَهِيمُ 1x "[they] roam"; هِيم 1x "(of) the thirsty camels"
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) treats h-y-m as a single-idea root: "intense thirst."

1. al-hayamān — thirst itself.
2. al-hīm — thirsty camels.
3. al-hīm (same word, second sense) — sands that soak up/swallow water, i.e. ground so thirsty it drinks up whatever water reaches it.
4. al-huyām — a disease that strikes thirsty camels, making them wander the land restlessly, unable to settle or check themselves.
5. From sense 4 comes the description of an infatuated lover as al-haymān: he is imagined as driven mad by love and wandering aimlessly, with no direction or purpose — the same restless, thirst-crazed wandering seen in the afflicted camel.
6. al-haymā' — a waterless desert tract (a place matching the root's "thirst" idea).

So the entry derives every sense — thirst, thirsty camels, water-absorbing sand, the camel-wandering disease, the love-crazed wanderer, and the waterless desert — from one core image of intense, restless thirst.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: h-y-t (هيت) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: the three letters hāʾ-yāʾ-tāʾ form a word denoting a shout or loud call.

1. Usage: Arabs say hayyata bihi ("he called out to him") when someone shouts (ṣāḥa).

2. A citation (only half a line given, poet unnamed): "had he been meant by it, he would have called out" (law kāna maʿniyyan bihā la-hayyatā) — offered simply to illustrate the verb's use.

3. The phrase hayta laka: Ibn Fāris glosses it as equivalent to halumma, i.e. "come" / "come here" — a call summoning someone.

The entry is brief and gives no further senses beyond this: the root is about calling/shouting, and hayta laka is explained as a summons ("come here").

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: ٱسْتُهْزِئَ 21x "mock"; هُزُو 11x "(in) ridicule"; مُسْتَهْزِءُون 2x "(against) the mockers"
text:
al-Zamakhsharī's entry for the root ه ز أ (h-z-ʾ), "to mock / scoff."

1. Literal sense — mockery. The verb appears as هزئ به (haziʾa bihi, "he mocked him"), with the derived forms هزأ, تهزّأ, and استهزأ (hazaʾa, tahazzaʾa, istahzaʾa), all meaning to deride. Related idioms: اتخذه هزؤاً (huzuʾ) — "he made him an object of mockery"; and فعل ذلك استهزاءً به — "he did it in derision of him."

2. Person-nouns. رجل هزاء / هزأة (hazzāʾ, huzaʾa) — a habitual mocker. By contrast هو هزأة بين الناس (huzʾa) — one who is himself mocked, a laughing-stock among people.

3. Figurative usage (majāz), where the entry classes the following:
   - مفازة هازئة بالرّكب — a desert that "mocks" its riders, meaning one that holds a mirage (سراب); it is called هزّاءة, "endlessly mocking" of them, because the mirage deceives the traveler.
   - A cold dawn — غداة هازئة — an intensely cold morning, described as if it "mocks" people when they are seized by huddling, shivering, and the chattering of teeth.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris derives the root h-z-l from a single underlying sense: weakness.

From this one root, two distinct senses branch off:

1. Al-hazl - "jesting," the opposite of al-jidd ("seriousness"). It denotes frivolous or joking speech, as opposed to earnest speech.

2. Al-huzal - "emaciation" or leanness, the opposite of fatness (al-siman).

He supports this with usage examples: "hazaltu dabbati wa-qad huzilat" - "I made my mount emaciated, and it became emaciated" (used of a riding animal losing condition); "hazala fi mantiqihi" - "he jested in his speech"; and "ahzala" (form IV), said when huzal (leanness/depletion) befalls a person's property or livestock, i.e. his wealth or herd grows thin.

Ibn Faris's analytical point is that both branches - verbal frivolity and physical leanness - trace back to the same core notion of weakness: jesting is speech drained of seriousness, just as an emaciated body is drained of substance.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: هَزَمُ 2x "soon will be defeated"; مَهْزُوم 1x "(they will be) defeated"
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) states that the root h-z-m (هزم) has one sound core meaning: "pressing/pinching" and "breaking."

Senses grouped under that core meaning:

1. **al-hazm** — pressing something with the hand so it gives way and caves inward, the way a cucumber or a melon dents when squeezed.
2. **al-hazīma** ("rout, defeat") in war — derived from sense 1 (the enemy line "gives way/caves in").
3. **ghayth hazīm** — a rain that gushes/bursts forth copiously (mutabaʿʿiq).
4. **hazīm al-raʿd** — the sound of thunder, likened to something cracking/breaking apart; related to the phrase tahazzama al-siqāʾ, "the waterskin dried out and cracked."
5. **ihtazamtu al-shāh** — "I slaughtered the sheep" (also grouped under this root's meaning).
6. **al-hazma** — a low, depressed patch of ground.

Separately, Ibn Fāris notes one word he considers etymologically unrelated to this "press/break" core:
- **al-mihzām** — a fire-tipped stick that Bedouin children play with, illustrated with a single (incomplete) line of poetry attributed to Jarīr: "...and she plays with the mihzām."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats h-z-z as a root meaning agitation and motion in a thing, and he closes by stating that one principle runs through all of its uses.

1. **Shaking and quivering.** hazaztu l-qanāt: I shook the spear-shaft, and it quivered (ihtazzat).

2. **Plants and wind.** Plants ihtazza (stir), and the wind hazza them (shakes them).

3. **Camels and the driving-song.** The camel-driver hazza the camels with his driving-song, and they are stirred (ihtazzat) as they go.

4. **The wind's rush.** hazīz al-rīḥ is the wind's motion and its sound.

5. **Upheavals.** al-hazāhiz are the turmoils (fitan) in which people are shaken.

6. **A quivering sword.** A sword that is hazhāz or huzhuz is bright and quivers well.

7. **Running water.** Water that is huzahiz quivers as it runs.

8. **A falling star.** A star quivers (yahtazzu) as it swoops down.

9. **A light man.** al-huzahiz is a man who is light (khafīf).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats j-dh-dh as one root meaning (aṣl wāḥid) with two sides: breaking, or cutting.

1. **Breaking.** jadhadhtu al-shayʾa, "I broke the thing". He cites Q 21:58, "so he made them judhādh, except a great one of theirs", and explains it as "he broke them to pieces".

2. **Cutting.** jadhadhtuhu, "I cut it". From this he takes Q 11:108, ʿaṭāʾan ghayra majdhūdhin, "a gift not cut off".

3. **A scrap of clothing.** mā ʿalayhi judhdha, "there is not a judhdha on him", means he has nothing of clothing to cover him; Ibn Fāris suggests the speaker has in mind a rag or the like.

4. **Crushed grain.** al-jadhīdha is grain that is broken and made into sawīq, a meal of parched grain.

5. **Gold ore.** The stones that gold comes from are called judhādh, because they are broken up and dissolved. A verse of al-Hudhalī speaks of "the masāḥin grating over the judhādh"; the masāḥin (singular misḥana) are the implements used to pound such stones.

6. **Fixed on the saddle (offered tentatively).** Ibn Fāris thinks it "not far-fetched" that al-mujdhawdhī belongs to this root: the rider who keeps to his camel-saddle, never leaving it, sitting upright on it (the verb is ijdhawdhā). His reasoning is that such a rider has, as it were, cut himself off from everything and set himself upright on his saddle for the journey. A verse asks: "Are you not forever mujdhawdh on the saddle? Yet you have no share but what you have been granted."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha lists three unrelated base meanings for the root j-dh-ʿ.

1. Newness/freshness of age. A jadhaʿ animal is a young one — two years old for sheep or goats, five years old for a camel. By extension, Time/Fate (al-dahr) is sometimes called by the epithet "al-azlam al-jadhaʿ," because it is perpetually new/fresh; a poet uses this phrase for the fate that "cast its hands upon" him despite his standing among his people, and some said the poet actually meant "the lion" by the phrase. The same word describes a person newly engaged in something: "he is jadhaʿ in this matter" means he has only just taken it up.

2. Jiḏʿ of a tree — its trunk or stem.

3. The verb jadhaʿa, "to rub or knead something" (jadhaʿtu al-shayʾ, "I rubbed/kneaded the thing"), illustrated by a single half-line of verse about something worn down "from the length of the rubbing of struggle" — the citation is a fragment, and its full sense is not recoverable from what's quoted.

Ibn Fāris closes by noting the proverb "Take from Jidhʿ whatever he gives you," explaining that Jidhʿ here is simply a man's proper name and has nothing to do with the three senses above.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ج ذ و (j-dh-w), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: uprightness/standing erect.

1. jadhawtu ʿalā aṭrāfi aṣābiʿī — I stood up on my fingertips, illustrated with a line of poetry about a singer poised upright while performing. Al-Khalīl is cited comparing jadhā yajdhū to jathā yajthū ("to kneel"), but notes jadhā more strongly implies remaining fixed in place — Ibn Fāris endorses al-Khalīl's authority on this point explicitly.
2. jadhā al-qurādu fī janbi al-baʿīr — a tick clinging fixedly to a camel's flank; jadhat ẓalifatu al-ikāfi fī janbi al-ḥimār — a packsaddle's edge stuck fast in a donkey's side — both illustrating firm, unmoving attachment.
3. A hadith is cited: "the likeness of the hypocrite is like the cedar standing fixed on the ground, until its uprooting comes all at once" — al-mujdhiyah glossed as "the firmly-standing one."
4. tajādhā al-qawmu al-ḥajar — people competing to hoist/lift a stone between them, sharing the root's sense of upward effort.
5. A disputed extension, flagged by Ibn Fāris as his own judgment ("in my view"): rajul jādhin — a man "short of reach" (i.e., stingy or of limited generosity) — connected to the root because a short, non-extended reach resembles something stunted and upright rather than long and outstretched, illustrated with a line of poetry contrasting the caliphate with a miserly, short-reached man.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Note: This dictionary entry actually bundles two separate root-shapes under one heading: جأر jaʾara (with hamza — "to cry out") and جار/جور jāra/jawr (without hamza — "neighbor," "to be near," "to deviate/be unjust"). Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (early 11th c. CE) treats them together.

**1. جأر (jaʾara) — to cry out in supplication**
Cited at Q16:53 (فَإِلَيْهِ تَجْئَرُونَ, "to Him you cry out"), Q23:64 (يَجْأَرُونَ, "they cry out"), and Q23:65 (لَا تَجْأَرُوا, "do not cry out"). Al-Rāghib defines jaʾara as going to excess in duʿāʾ (supplication/calling out) and taḍarruʿ (pleading, self-abasing entreaty) — he likens the sound to the juʾār, the bellowing cry of wild animals such as gazelles.

**2. جار al-jār — the neighbor (a reciprocal term)**
Al-jār is one whose dwelling is near yours. Grammatically/conceptually it is one of the "reciprocal nouns" (al-asmāʾ al-mutaḍāyifa): someone is only a jār if the other party is a jār to him in return — the same logic as akh ("brother") or ṣadīq ("friend"), which only make sense as a pair.

Because the right of the neighbor was treated as weighty — both by reason and by the sharʿ (the revealed/legal order) — the word jār was extended to anyone whose right is treated as weighty, or who treats another's right as weighty. Cited: Q4:36, "the neighbor who is near of kin, and the neighbor who is a stranger" (dhī l-qurbā vs. al-junub).

**3. جار as "protector, one who grants safe-conduct"**
From the same root: istajartuhu fa-ajāranī, "I sought his protection, and he granted me protection." On this usage: Q8:48, "and indeed I am a jār [protector/guarantor] to you," and Q23:88, "He grants protection, and none can be protected against Him."

**4. جاور / تجاور — nearness, adjacency**
The core idea of qurb (nearness) generalized further: jāra/jāwara/tajāwara all describe two things being near or neighboring one another. Cited: Q33:60 ("they will not remain near you there except a little") and Q13:4 ("adjoining tracts of land").

**5. جور jawr — deviation, injustice**
From the same idea of "nearness/proximity to a path," Arabic also says jāra ʿan al-ṭarīq, "he swerved off the road." Al-Rāghib treats this as the root-sense from which jawr (wrongdoing, deviation, tyranny) is built: departing from any ḥaqq (right/truth), not only a literal road. Cited: Q16:9, "and among them [the paths] is one that deviates" — glossed by the author as one that turns away from al-maḥajja, the right course.

Al-Rāghib closes by reporting an opinion of others (not asserted in his own voice): "al-jāʾir among people is the one who prevents [others] from adhering to what the sharʿ commands."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root j-ḥ-d from a single core notion: scarcity of good, a shortfall of benefit.

1. Scarcity / dearth (the base sense). A "jaḥid year" (عَامٌ جَحِدٌ) is a year of little rain; a "jaḥid man" is a poor man, with the verbs جَحِدَ / أَجْحَدَ used of him. Ibn Durayd is cited: al-jaḥd of anything at all means paucity. A poetic line illustrates it: "as long as he lives he will see nothing but scarcity." Al-Shaybānī adds that a man "ajḥada" or "jaḥada" when he was stripped of everything and lost his wealth, quoting al-Farazdaq's verse mentioning "the pack-beasts of a destitute man (mujḥid)."

2. Denial / repudiation (juḥūd) — treated as belonging to the same category. It is the opposite of acknowledgment (iqrār), and, on Ibn Fāris's account, it occurs only when the denier actually knows that what he denies is true. He cites Qur'an al-Naml 27:14: "And they repudiated them, though their own selves were convinced of them."

He closes with the remark that "no denier (jāḥid) ever came with any good" — tying the sense of denial back to the root's core idea of lack of good.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ج-ح-م from a single core idea: heat and its intensity.

1. Heat / blazing. الْجَاحِم (al-jāḥim) is a place of intense heat. He cites al-Aʿshā's line describing a battle-morning in which "death blazes (jāḥim)." From this sense الْجَحِيم (al-jaḥīm, the blazing fire) takes its name.

2. The eye. الْجَحْمَة (al-jaḥma) means "eye," reported to be a Yemeni usage. Ibn Fāris links it to the same root of heat, reasoning that the two eyes are like two kindled lamps. He cites a verse of lament addressed to "my eye (jaḥma)," and the saying that the lion's two eyes are called jaḥmatān "in all the dialects" — sound, he holds, because a lion's eyes are always ablaze.

3. Related eye-terms:
   - جَحَّمَ (jaḥḥama): to open the eyes wide in a fixed stare; such an eye is called jāḥima.
   - الْجُحَام (al-juḥām): an eye disease that makes a person's eyes swell.
   - الْأَجْحَم (al-ajḥam): one whose eye is intensely red and wide; feminine jaḥmāʾ.
   - جَحَّمَنِي بِعَيْنِهِ (jaḥḥamanī bi-ʿaynihi): he fixed a sharp gaze on me.

4. An excluded form. The expression أَجْحَمَ عَنِ الشَّيْء (ajḥama ʿani l-shayʾ, "he shrank / held back from the thing") does NOT belong to this root: Ibn Fāris judges it a metathesis (letter-transposition) of أَحْجَم (aḥjama), treated under its own entry.
