text:
Ibn Fāris treats j-b-b, in its doubled form, as resting on two root meanings: cutting, and the drawing-together of a thing.

**1. Cutting**

1. al-jabb is cutting: jababtuhu, ajubbuhu, jabban, "I cut it". A eunuch who has been cut is majbūb.
2. jabbahu is said when one person outdoes another, in beauty or in anything else. Ibn Fāris reads it as though the winner cut the other off from rivalry and boasting. His example is a verse about a woman who "outdid (jabbat) the women of all the world with the cord": she had measured her hips with a rope and sent word to the other women asking whether any of them had the like; none had, and she beat them. He compares another verse in which Ḥabāba bint Jazʾ sends "a long rope" as a gift to the people of Julājil.
3. al-jabab is the cutting-off of a camel's hump. Such a camel is ajabb; a she-camel, jabbāʾ.

**2. Drawing together**

1. al-jubba, the familiar robe, belongs here, he says, because it encloses the body and gathers it within itself. The same word names the socket of a spearhead, into which the end of the shaft goes.
2. al-jubjuba is a leather basket in which earth is gathered for carrying. It is also a stomach into which meat is put; this is al-khalʿ.
3. jabba al-nakhl is said of people pollinating date-palms, and pollination time is "the season of al-jibāb".
4. al-jabūb is hard, rough ground, named for its compactness. Abū Khirāsh, describing an eagle that lifts its prey and then lets it drop, says the prey "struck the hard ground (al-jabūb) with the place between its eyes".
5. al-majabba is the main track of a road, where it comes together.
6. al-jubb is a well.
7. jabbaba (verbal noun tajbīb) means to flee, because the one who flees gathers himself together and girds himself for flight.
8. al-jubāb is something like butter that gathers from camels' milk, although, he notes, camels have no butter. A rajaz poet likens spittle caking around a mouth to jubāb caking on the lips of a milk-skin.

He closes by quoting Ibn Durayd: al-jibjāb, and likewise al-jubājib, is abundant water.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ج ب هـ (j-b-h), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core word from which further senses are drawn by likeness/metaphor.

1. al-jabhah — horses, collectively (a name applied to the whole class, not a single horse); al-jabhah, of people — a company/group; al-jabhah — a star, namely "jabhat al-asad," the Lion's Forehead constellation.
2. jabahnā al-māʾ — an idiom for arriving at water with no rope-and-bucket apparatus or measuring device to draw it, so one simply "faces" the water directly with nothing to assist. From this, a recorded Arab proverb: "every one who comes to face the water [jābih] gets one draught [jawzah], then he is turned away" — al-jābih being the one who arrives thus, al-jawzah being the single measured turn he is allotted before being excluded.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats j-b-l as a single regular, analogizable root whose core sense is the massing of a thing in height (elevation). From this he derives:

1. الْجَبَل (al-jabal) — "the mountain," the well-known sense.

2. الْجَبَل also — a great, numerous multitude of people. He cites a verse praising Quraysh as "the jabal of God" that other mountains fall short of.

3. جَبَلَة / جَبْلَة (jabala / jablah) — a she-camel with a huge hump; some apply jablah to the hump itself. امْرَأَة جَبْلَة (imraʾa jablah) is a woman of massive build. He quotes a line describing a tall hump rising "upon a jablah."

4. الْجِبِلَّة (al-jibillah) — created nature, the creatures (al-khalīqa).

5. الْجِبِلّ (al-jibill) — a numerous multitude. He cites Qurʾān 36:62, "He has led astray a great jibill (multitude) of you," noting the variant reading jubull.

6. أَجْبَلُوا (ajbalū) — of people digging, "they struck hard, solid ground."

All six senses hang on the one image: something gathered and rising up — a mass with height, whether of rock, of people, of a camel's hump, or of created stock.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) treats the root ج-ب-ن (j-b-n) as covering three separate words that happen to share the same three letters but are not derived from one another:

1. al-jubn (الجُبن) — "that which is eaten," i.e. cheese. He notes an alternate pronunciation with a geminated (doubled) nūn and ḍamma on the bā': jubunn (جُبُنّ).

2. al-jubn (الجُبن) — also the abstract quality of al-jabān (الجَبان), "the cowardly one," i.e. cowardice.

3. al-jabīnān (الجَبِينان) — the dual form naming the two areas flanking the forehead (al-jabha), one on the right and one on the left; each single side is called a jabīn (temple).

Ibn Fāris's method here is to flag these as three unrelated lexical items that merely coincide in their root letters, rather than as one word branching into related senses.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ج-ب-ر (j-b-r) as one root meaning greatness, loftiness, and setting-straight. From this core he derives several senses:

1. Tall / beyond reach — الجَبَّار (al-jabbār) is what has grown tall and passed beyond the hand's grasp: a towering horse (فرس جبار), a date-palm too tall to reach (نخلة جبارة).

2. Might and dominion (used of God) — ذو الجَبُّورة / ذو الجَبَروت (dhū al-jabbūra / al-jabarūt) denotes God. He cites a line of verse pairing this with "the loftily supreme one." Related forms for this quality of might: جَبْرِيّة، جَبَروّة، جَبَروت، جَبُّورة.

3. To mend / set right — جَبَرْتُ العظمَ فجُبِرَ, "I set the bone and it was set." Cited verse: "God has restored the [dīn / order], so it was restored." A splint used to bind a broken bone is a جِبارة (jibāra), plural جبائر (jabāʾir); by likeness, a bracelet is also called جِبارة (cited in a verse about a henna-dyed hand and a wrist filling its bracelet).

4. An outlier from the root — الجُبار (al-jubār): loss that goes unrequited, with no compensation (hadar). He quotes the Prophet's saying "the well is jubār and the mine is jubār": an ancient ownerless well someone falls into brings no liability, and a mine that collapses on hired diggers is likewise uncompensated — because they worked for wages.

5. To compel — أَجْبَرْتُ فلاناً على الأمر, "I forced him to do the thing"; per Ibn Fāris this happens only through coercion (qahr) and a kind of overbearing dominance over the person.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root: ج ب ت (jbt). Dictionary: al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (early 11th c. CE).

Qur'anic anchor: the word occurs paired with al-ṭāghūt in Q4:51 — "They believe in al-jibt and al-ṭāghūt."

1. Core sense: al-jibt is given as synonymous with al-jibs — a worthless, base person, "one in whom there is no good."

2. Philological note: al-Rāghib records the view that jibt is a phonetic variant of jibs, with tāʾ standing in for sīn. He treats this substitution as a device that intensifies the sense of baseness. He illustrates the general pattern of using an epithet to intensify blame with a line of (unnamed) poetry: "ʿAmr ibn Yarbūʿ are the shirār al-nās (worst of people)," glossed as meaning khisās al-nās (the basest of people).

3. Extended usage recorded by al-Rāghib: jibt is applied to anything worshipped besides Allah.

4. Extended usage recorded by al-Rāghib: jibt was also used as a name for the sorcerer (al-sāḥir) and the soothsayer/diviner (al-kāhin).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats jīm–bāʾ + a weak letter as one root meaning the gathering of a thing and coming-together.

1. Collecting/gathering: جَبَيْتُ الْمَالَ ("I collected the wealth") — verb jabā/yajbī, verbal noun jibāya; likewise جَبَيْتُ الْمَاءَ فِي الْحَوْضِ ("I gathered the water in the trough").

2. The container of gathered water: a basin or cistern is called جَابِيَة (jābiya). Cited shāhid — al-Aʿshā: a great feast-bowl reaching al-Muḥallaq's family is likened to "the cistern of the Iraqi elder, brimming over."

3. Related forms:
   - الْجَبَا (al-jabā, shortened alif): the margin/rim around a well.
   - الْجِبَا (al-jibā, with kasra): the water that has collected in a basin or elsewhere; also called جِبْوَة (jibwa) or جِبَاوَة (jibāwa). Al-Kisāʾī records جَبَيْتُ الْمَاءَ فِي الْحَوْضِ جِبًى.

4. جَبَّى / يُجَبِّي (jabbā): to prostrate oneself — which Ibn Fāris explains as an instance of the same idea, the body drawing/gathering itself together.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats j-d-d as having three separate root meanings: greatness, fortune and cutting. He then traces most of the root's other words back to the third, cutting.

**1. Greatness.** He cites "exalted is the jadd of our Lord" (Q 72:3) for this sense. People say a man "became jadd in my eye", meaning he grew great in my estimation. Anas ibn Mālik said that a man who had recited Sūrat al-Baqara and Āl ʿImrān "became jadd among us", meaning he grew great in their hearts.

**2. Wealth and fortune.** Ibn Fāris cites the Prophet's supplication, "the jadd of the one who has jadd does not avail him against You". He explains it as: a man's wealth does not help him before God; only acting in obedience to God helps him. "More jadd" and "more fortunate" mean the same.

**3. Cutting.** Jadadtu al-shayʾ means "I cut the thing". What is cut is majdūd or jadīd, as in the verse where a lover's rope (their bond) has become "worn out and cut" (khalaqan jadīdan). Ibn Fāris derives the following from this sense:

- **Earnestness.** He thinks it likely that jidd, earnestness in a matter, belongs here, because one cuts the matter off decisively and resolves on it. The question ajiddaka ("in earnest?") means "is this a firm decision on your part?". Two verses of al-Aʿshā use it.
- **The well (judd).** The same idea, with a different vowel, because the ground is cut out for a well. A verse of al-Aʿshā speaks of "the doubtful well" that no rain has reached.
- **Level ground.** Jadjad and jadad mean level ground. Proverbs: "whoever travels the level ground is safe from stumbling" and "gently, they are coming up onto the level ground". Ajadda al-qawm means the people have reached level ground. Jadīd is "the face of the earth".
- **Streaks and tracks.** A judda is a streak or track, and also the stripe on a donkey's back. The side or edge of anything is its judda, such as the edge of a water-skin, where it was cut.
- **Waterless land and dried milk.** Jaddāʾ is land without water, as if the water had been cut off from it. Jadūd and jaddāʾ are ewes whose milk has dried and whose udders have withered.
- **Harvesting palms.** Jidād or jadād is cutting the date crop.
- **The highway.** Jāddat al-ṭarīq is the level middle of a road, as if it were cut off from what is around it. It is also the part that is travelled, or "cut through".
- **Tent cords.** Some say juddād in a verse of al-Aʿshā is a Nabataean word for the cords tied to a tent. Ibn Fāris rejects this: he holds it is sound Arabic from jadd, "cutting", because the cords are cut into equal lengths. He explains juddād in a verse of al-Ṭirimmāḥ the same way, as a comparison with tent cords. Others give it a different meaning, but that explanation breaks off in this copy.
- **Newness.** A jadīd garment is one its weaver has "just cut". Ibn Fāris calls this the original sense. Later, anything that time has not yet worn was called jadīd. So night and day are al-jadīdān and al-ajaddān, since each is new when it comes. On his account, newness (jidda) comes from cutting.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib's account of the root ج-د-ل (j-d-l):

1. Core sense — al-Jidāl (disputation): an exchange or negotiation carried on through contention, each side trying to overcome the other.

2. Etymology (firm twisting): The word derives from جَدَلْتُ الحبل (jadaltu al-ḥabl), "I twisted the rope tightly / made its twisting firm." From the same root come: al-jadīl (a firmly plaited cord), jadaltu al-bināʾ ("I made the building solid"), dirʿ majdūla (a tightly woven coat of mail), al-ajdal (the falcon, so called for its firm/solid build), and al-mijdal (a solidly built palace or fortress). On this basis, disputation is pictured as each disputant "twisting" the other away from his opinion.

3. Alternative etymology (wrestling): It is also said that the root's origin is al-ṣirāʿ (wrestling) — throwing one's opponent down onto the jadāla, meaning the hard, firm ground.

4. Qurʾānic usage: The verb (jādala / yujādilu) and noun (jidāl / jadal) recur throughout the Qurʾān in the sense of disputing or arguing — e.g. "dispute with them by that which is better" (16:125); "those who dispute concerning the signs of God" (40:35); "you have disputed with us and multiplied dispute with us" (11:32, where a variant reading jadalanā is noted); "they cited it to you only in dispute" (43:58); "man is, of all things, most given to dispute" (18:54); "and no disputing during the ḥajj" (2:197); and "O Noah, you have disputed with us" (11:32), among others.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: جِدَار 2x "the wall"; أَجْدَر 1x "and more likely"; جُدُر 1x "walls"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats j-d-r as two independent roots.

ROOT 1 — a wall and its base, and what is built on it
1. جِدَار (jidār) = a wall; plurals جُدُر (judur) and جُدْرَان (judrān).
2. جَدْر (jadr) = the foundation or lower base of a wall. He cites the report: "Water [your land], O Zubayr, then let the water return to the jadr" — i.e. up to the base of the wall.
3. Related names: الجَدَرَة (al-Jadara), a clan of al-Azd who built the wall of the Kaʿba; and جَدَر (Jadar), a village, whose wine is called جَدَرِيَّة (jadariyya) in the verse he quotes ("pour us a morning cup of Jadar wine…").
4. جَدِيرَة (jadīra) = a pen or enclosure built for sheep — a built structure, so from the same idea.
5. From this same root he derives هو جَدِيرٌ بكذا (huwa jadīrun bi-kadhā), "he is fit/worthy of it," equivalent to حَرِيّ (ḥariyy). His reasoning: it is a matter one ought to make firm and build one's affair upon — i.e. worthiness is pictured as something founded, like a wall on its base.
6. He also records جَدِيرَة (jadīra) used for طَبِيعَة (ṭabīʿa), innate nature or disposition.

ROOT 2 — something coming out or breaking to the surface (plants and otherwise)
1. جُدَرِيّ / جَدَرِيّ (judarī / jadarī) = smallpox, the eruption on the skin; a ewe afflicted with it is شاة جَدْرَاء (shāt jadrāʾ).
2. جَدَر (jadar) = a lump or swelling that appears on the body.
3. جَدْر (jadr) = vegetation as it comes up; the verbs أَجْدَرَ المكان (ajdara al-makān) and جَدَرَ (jadara) mean a place's plants have broken through. Shāhid from al-Jaʿdī: "At the sprouting time you take pleasure in having uncles from the family of Jaʿda."
4. جَدْر (jadr) also = the welt or chafe-mark on a donkey's neck. Shāhid from Ruʾba: "or one with welted sides of the neck, lean of flank."
5. He justifies placing (4) under this root by analogy (qiyās): the skin there rises in a protrusion, so it resembles the eruption of smallpox.

The organizing idea, in his account: sense-group 1 is building and its foundation (hence "worthy of" = well-founded), and sense-group 2 is anything that pushes up and shows itself on a surface — shoots, pustules, swellings, welts.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib's entry on جدث (j-d-th) is short:

1. Core sense: al-jadath (جَدَث) means "grave." Its plural is al-ajdāth (الأجداث).

2. Qur'anic citations, both describing the resurrection — people coming out of their graves:
   - Q70:43 (al-Maʿārij): "The Day they emerge from the graves, rushing" (يَوْمَ يَخْرُجُونَ مِنَ الْأَجْدَاثِ سِرَاعًا).
   - Q36:51 (Yā-Sīn): "Then behold, from the graves they hasten forth to their Lord" (فَإِذَا هُمْ مِنَ الْأَجْدَاثِ إِلَى رَبِّهِمْ يَنسِلُونَ).

3. Lexical note: al-Rāghib records a variant form — the same word is also said as جَدَف (jadaf), with ف in place of ث.

No further senses, etymology, or grammatical discussion is given; the entry is limited to defining the word, giving its plural, noting the ث/ف variant, and citing its two Qur'anic occurrences.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's entry on ج ف أ (root of jufāʾ) — al-Mufradāt.

**1. The Qur'anic word: jufāʾ.**
He cites 13:17 — "But as for the scum, it goes away as jufāʾ" — and glosses jufāʾ as what a flood-torrent (wādī) or a cooking-pot throws off to its sides: the floating scum/debris (ghuthāʾ) that gets cast aside as worthless.

**2. Related verb: ajfaʾa (to cast off).**
- ajfaʾati l-qidru zabadahā — "the pot cast off its froth," i.e. threw it out; the verbal noun is ijfāʾ.
- ajfaʾati l-arḍu — "the land became ajfaʾa," i.e. it turned into something like jufāʾ by losing its goodness/produce — used metaphorically of land stripped of its fertility.
- A variant is noted: jaffati l-qidru / ajfat, parallel forms for the pot casting off its froth.

**3. A root-origin note.**
Al-Rāghib flags that some hold the true root letter here is wāw, not hamza — i.e. this word is actually connected to ج ف و (jafā), not a separate ج ف أ root.

**4. The wāw-root sense: al-jafāʾ (estrangement).**
From that connection comes al-jafāʾ — harsh treatment, estrangement, unkindness. He gives the verb: qad jafawtuhu ajfūhu jafwatan wa-jafāʾan — "I estranged/treated him harshly," with both jafwa and jafāʾ as verbal nouns.

**5. A further extension: "lifting off."**
From the same root is also derived jafā l-sarju ʿan ẓahri l-dābbati — "the saddle jafā off the mount's back," meaning it rose up and separated from it.

So the entry threads one underlying idea — matter (froth, produce, goodness, or a saddle) being cast off, separated, or lifted away from something — through the Qur'anic jufāʾ (worthless scum flung aside), the everyday ajfaʾa (a pot ejecting its froth, land losing its fertility), and the parallel root jafā/jafāʾ (a person being kept at a distance, treated with estrangement; or an object lifting clear of its base).

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
poets_named: unnamed verse ×3; al-Akhṭal (Umayyad); Ḥassān (lived into Islam) ×2
text:
ROOT ج ف ن (jafana) — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791 CE)

Al-Zabīdī records a cluster of distinct senses under this root, each supported by citation:

1. **Eyelid.** الجَفْن = the covering of the eye, upper and lower. Plurals: ajfun, ajfān, jufūn. He quotes a line of wordplay his own teacher had been taught, punning ajfān "eyelids" against ajfān "scabbards," and ghirār "sleep" against ghirār "a sword's edge."

2. **Sword-scabbard.** Also pronounced with a short i (jifn); Ibn Durayd doubted that variant's validity.

3. **The grapevine's root-stock** (or, per other reports, its shoots/branches — singular jafnah — or a particular variety of grape). Al-Rāghib explains the name: the vine was called jafn because it was pictured as a "vessel" holding the grapes. A Yemeni dialect use is noted where jafn means the vine's very substance. "The water of al-jafn" is recorded as an expression for the vine's produce (i.e. its juice).

4. **Self-restraint from impurity/filth** — jafana nafsahu ʿan al-shayʾ, "he held himself back from the thing," with a supporting verse. Two authorities, al-Aṣmaʿī and Abū Zayd, are quoted saying they did not know this sense.

5. **A sweet-smelling tree/shrub**, per the botanist Abū Ḥanīfa, who used this meaning to explain a verse of al-Akhṭal about a wine-jar sealed with "jafn and laurel." Al-Zabīdī notes this jafn is a separate plant from the vine's jafn — it is what the vine-shoot becomes once it climbs up into that tree, named for its "settling in" (tajaffun) there.

6. **A place name**, a locality/district near al-Ṭāʾif — sources differ on whether it is vocalized Jafn or Jufn.

7. **Figurative use: "the shining jafnah [bowl]"** as a way of calling a man generous and hospitable — he is likened to the bowl he feeds guests from, "shining" for the rich fat glistening in it. Al-Zabīdī notes this usage appears in a ḥadīth about ʿAbdallāh ibn al-Shikhkhīr.

8. **A small well** — by comparison to a food-bowl (al-Rāghib).

9. **A large bowl/platter (qaṣʿah).** Al-Muḥkam calls it the largest size of bowl; al-Rāghib specifies it as a food-vessel. Plural jifān is attested in the Qur'an (34:13, "basins like reservoirs"). A separate counted plural, jafanāt, is explained grammatically (the medial consonant of the faʿlah pattern takes a vowel in this plural unless it is wāw/yāʾ). A verse of Ḥassān is cited for "the gleaming bowls."

10. **Jafnah, a Yemeni tribe** (of al-Azd). Elsewhere: Āl Jafnah were kings from Yemen who settled in Syria — this is the Ghassānid dynasty — with a verse of Ḥassān praising them as dwelling in their fathers' inherited lands. Al-Zabīdī adds their genealogy: descendants of Jafnah ibn ʿAmr (personal name ʿAlaba), branching into three clans — Kaʿb, Rifāʿah, al-Ḥārith.

11. **Verb: jafana al-nāqata** — to slaughter a she-camel and distribute its meat to people in bowls. Illustrated with a report about ʿUmar doing this with an injured camel from the alms-herd.

12. **Verbs jaffana / ajfana** — to have frequent intercourse, with a Bedouin's complaint that this practice had worn him out.

13. **The proverb "with Jufaynah/Juhaynah is the sure news."** Sources disagree whether the name is Jufaynah (said to be a wine-merchant, per Ibn al-Sikkīt) or Juhaynah (the well-known form). Al-Zabīdī relays the backstory as given by Ibn al-Kalbī: a man of Banū Juhaynah killed his travelling companion Ḥuṣayn ibn ʿAmr and took his goods; when the dead man's kinswoman Ṣakhrah wept for him publicly, a poet quipped that the "sure news" of what happened to Ḥuṣayn could be had precisely from Juhaynah — since it was one of their own who did it. Ibn Barrī judges Ibn al-Kalbī the more reliable source on this story than al-Aṣmaʿī.

**Additional notes appended by the author** (marked as supplementary, "wa-mimmā yustadraku ʿalayhi"):
- jifan (on the pattern of ʿinab) is also given as a plural of jafnah "bowl" (Sībawayh's analogy: haḍbah/hiḍab).
- jafnah can also mean "the grapevine" itself (Ibn al-Aʿrābī) or "the leaf of the grapevine" (Ibn Sīdah).
- jafn is also a low-spreading tender herb that curls up when dry, with a seed like fenugreek (Abū Ḥanīfa).
- jafana/tajaffana said of a vine means it grew a proper root-stock.
- Ibn al-Aʿrābī: jafn is the grape's skin holding its juice; wine itself is called "the water of jafn," and a cloud can be called "jafn of water" — illustrated with a verse likening a woman's saliva to snow-chilled wine.
- jaffanū: "they made bowls."
- tajaffana: "he claimed descent from [the tribe] Jafnah."
- Al-Laḥyānī: the soft crumb of bread is what lies between its two "jafn" — meaning the loaf's top and bottom crust/face.
- jafnah is also recorded as a word for wine itself (Ibn al-Aʿrābī).
- Mujaffinah ibn al-Nuʿmān al-ʿAtakī is noted as an Azdī poet spanning the pre-Islamic/Islamic transition.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
text:
Root: ج ف و (j-f-w). Source: al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066 CE).

**1. Core sense — not staying fixed in place.** jafā l-shayʾ / tajāfā: a thing failed to stay attached to its place; ajfaytuhu = "I removed it from its place." A poet is cited describing something (an animal, straining) that stretches or twists its neck, "complaining" of the touch of its innards, which are rarely relieved/shifted (nujfīhā) — illustrating the sense of not settling in position.

**2. A body's side drawing away from a bed.** jafā janbuhu ʿan al-firāsh / tajāfā: his side pulled away from the bed, recoiled, did not rest on it. This is the sense used in the Qur'an, "their sides draw away from their beds" (32:16). Ibn Sīda records three exegetical views on what this describes: (a) they used to pray at night; (b) they did not sleep through the ʿatamah (late-night) prayer; (c) they used to pray voluntarily between maghrib and the later ʿishāʾ. He adds al-Zajjāj's argument: the next verse, "no soul knows what delight is kept hidden for them" (32:17), shows this is prayer in the depth of night, since that is something a person keeps concealed.

**3. Weighing heavily on someone.** jafā l-shayʾ ʿalayhi = it weighed on him (thaqula). Ibn Sīda notes a grammatical point: because jafā here means the same as thaqula ("to be heavy"), and thaqula takes the preposition ʿalā, jafā was likewise made to take ʿalā by analogy — a common pattern.

**4. Jafāʾ as the opposite of ṣilah (severing ties vs. maintaining them).** al-jafāʾ = the antonym of ṣilah (connection/keeping ties). Verb: jafāhu, verbal nouns jafw and jafāʾ.

**5. A grammatical note on the form majfiyy.** In the line "I am neither the jāfī [one who shuns] nor the majfiyy [one shunned]," al-Farrāʾ explains that majfiyy was coined as though the root were jafiya (ending in yāʾ) rather than jafā (ending in wāw) — paralleling maʿdiyy from ʿadā in a verse Sībawayh cites ("I am the lion, both preyed-upon and preying").

**6. Neglecting property.** jafā mālahu = he did not stay close to / attend to his property (livestock).

**7. Personal harshness (jafwah/jifwah).** A man can have jafwah/jifwah (coarseness, harsh manner) in him; "he is plainly jifwah-marked" means his harshness is obvious. If instead he is the one on the receiving end of harsh treatment (majfuww), the idiom is "bihi jafwah."

**8. The goat's proverb.** Asked what she will do on a rainy night, the she-goat answers: her wool is fine, her hide thin, and her tail is jafāʾ (too scant/inadequate to shelter her) — so she cannot bear to stay away from home. Al-Liḥyānī left the word jafāʾ here unexplained; Ibn Sīda gives his own view that it belongs with the senses of recoiling (nubūw), distancing (tabāʿud), and lack of adherence (qillat al-luzūq) — i.e., the tail is too "detached/inadequate" to cover her.

**9. Causative form (ajfā).** ajfā l-māshiyah = he exhausted the livestock by not letting it graze and not having foddered it beforehand.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: جَٰهَدَ 27x "strive"; جَهْد 5x "strongest"; مُجَٰهِدِين 4x "the ones who strive"; جِهَاد 4x "and striving"; جُهْد 1x "their effort"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ج-ه-د (j-h-d) from a single core sense — الْمَشَقَّة, hardship or toil — onto which the related meanings are built.

1. Effort / capacity. جَهَدْتُ نَفْسِي and أَجْهَدْتُ mean "I exerted or wore myself out." The noun الْجُهْد means الطَّاقَة, one's capacity or utmost effort. He cites Qurʾān 9:79, {those who find nothing but their juhd}, i.e. their utmost capacity.

2. Extracted milk (مَجْهُود). Milk from which the butter has been drawn off is called majhūd, since that is achieved only through hard labor. Ibn Fāris quotes al-Shammākh, describing udders full of sweet milk "not drained of its butter" (ghayr majhūd).

3. Related extensions of the root:
   - الْجَهَاد: hard, firm ground.
   - يَجْهَدُ الطَّعَامَ: to set upon food and eat a great deal of it vigorously.
   - الْجَاهِد: the greedy or craving person (al-shahwān).
   - مَرْعًى جَهِيدٌ: a pasture that livestock have grazed hard and eaten up because it was good.

The unifying idea throughout is straining or being worked to the utmost.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: جَاهِل 10x "the ignorant"; يَجْهَلُ 5x "ignorant"; جَهَٰلَة 4x "in ignorance"; جَٰهِلِيَّة 3x "(of the time of) ignorance"; جَٰهِلِيَّة 1x "(of) [the] ignorance"; جَهُول 1x "ignorant"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ج-ه-ل from two distinct roots:

1. The opposite of knowledge. Al-jahl is the antithesis of al-ʿilm (knowledge). From this: a majhal — a trackless desert waste with no landmark to steer by.

2. Lightness/levity, the opposite of settled steadiness. From this: a mijhal — the stick used to stir up embers; and istajhalat al-rīḥ al-ghuṣn, "the wind set the branch shaking and tossing." He cites al-Nābigha ("Passion called you, and the ruined dwellings stirred you to folly...") as belonging here, because the meaning is that the dwellings "made you frivolous and provoked you." Also al-majhala: the matter or thing that drives one to jahl — here in the sense of rash, agitated behaviour rather than mere not-knowing.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: جَهْر 7x "the loudness"; جَهَرَ 5x "be loud"; جَهْرَة 3x "manifestly"; جِهَار 1x "publicly"
text:
Al-Rāghib treats جَهْر (jahr) as denoting a thing's appearing to a conspicuous, excessive degree — and he splits it by the sense involved: sight or hearing.

1. Of SIGHT — being openly/plainly visible. Example: رأيته جِهَارا ("I saw it in plain view"). Qurʾānic citations: حَتَّى نَرَى اللَّهَ جَهْرَةً [2:55] and أَرِنَا اللَّهَ جَهْرَةً [4:153] — "to see God openly." From this: جَهَرَ / اجْتَهَرَ the well = to bring its water into view. Also ما في القوم أحد يجهر عيني — no one whom the eye finds striking to look at.

2. Etymological note: al-jawhar ("substance/essence; gem") is morphologically فَوْعَل (fawʿal) from this root — that which, if it ceases, whatever it carries ceases too — so named because it is what is manifest to the senses.

3. Of HEARING — uttering aloud (as opposed to keeping secret). Citations: أَسَرَّ الْقَوْلَ / جَهَرَ بِهِ [13:10] (secret vs. aloud); تَجْهَرْ بِالْقَوْلِ [20:7]; الْجَهْرَ مِنَ الْقَوْلِ [21:110]; أَسِرُّوا / اجْهَرُوا [67:13]; لا تَجْهَرْ بِصَلاتِكَ [17:110] (not loud in your ṣalāt); لا تَجْهَرُوا لَهُ بِالْقَوْلِ [49:2] (not loud in speech to him). In these the contrast is consistently loud/audible vs. secret/hushed.

4. Derived usage: كلام جوهري and جَهِير; a رجل جهير is one loud of voice — or one who stands out conspicuously for his beauty.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: جَهَّزَ 2x "he had furnished them"; جَهَاز 2x "with their supplies"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ج-ه-ز as having a single underlying sense: a set of things gathered together, held, and kept for use.

1. Core sense — outfit, gear, equipment. The noun جَِهاز (jahāz / jihāz, pronounceable with fatḥa or kasra on the first letter) is the goods and equipment of a household.

2. Verbal use — to outfit or provision. جَهَّزْتُ فُلانًا means to take on oneself the outfitting of someone's journey, i.e. to supply the traveller with what he needs.

3. Proverbial extension. Of a camel that bolts, the Arabs say ضَرَبَ فِي جَهَازِهِ — literally "it struck out into its own gear," i.e. it carried its own baggage off and went. Ibn Fāris cites Abū ʿUbayda: the same proverb said of a person (ضَرَبَ فلانٌ في جهازه) is applied to estrangement and to putting distance between oneself and others.

Ibn Fāris closes by noting that the base meaning remains the one stated at the outset: gathered, kept equipment.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) treats ج-ل-ب as having two distinct base meanings.

Sense 1 — Bringing a thing from one place to another
- جَلَبْتُ الشيءَ جَلْبًا = "I brought/imported the thing." A quoted verse fragment illustrates it: "It was granted to him, from his land and his sky ..." (the citation is given incomplete). The word الْجَوَالِب names the things/causes that "bring" something distant near.
- الْجَلَب is a specific practice condemned in a hadith. Ibn Fāris gives two competing explanations of what it refers to: (1) a zakat-collector should go himself to livestock-owners at their watering places to collect the sadaqa, rather than staying put and ordering them to drive (جَلَب) their animals to him; or (2) it describes a horse-racing trick — a man positions someone to shout at / urge on his horse during the race, making it run faster than the horse it is racing against.

Sense 2 — A covering that coats something (الْجُلْبَة)
- الْجُلْبَة: a piece of hide fitted onto a pack-saddle; also the scab/crust that forms over a healing wound (verb: جَلَبَ / أَجْلَبَ الجرح, "the wound scabbed over").
- جُِلْبُ الرَّحْل: the wooden frame of a camel-saddle — named this, Ibn Fāris suggests, by association with the "covering" sense.
- الْجُِلْب: a thin, rainless cloud crossing the sky. Abū ʿAmr adds that الْجُلْبَة/الْجُِلْب can also describe a cloud shaped like a mountain, citing a verse where a man says he is not "a jilb of mere wind and cold," nor a hard rock cut off from doing good — i.e., not all bluster and no substance.
- From this covering-sense comes الْجِلْبَاب, "the shirt/wrap" (plural جَلَابِيب). A cited verse compares vultures walking calmly in an open, threat-free space to young women walking about wrapped in their jalālīb — safe and unhurried, with nothing to startle them.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: جُلُود 9x "their skins"; ٱجْلِدُ 2x "then flog them"; جَلْدَة 2x "lashe(s)"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ج ل د (j-l-d) as a single root whose core sense is strength and firmness/hardness. From that he lists:

1. جِلْد (jild) — "skin": well known, and stronger and firmer than the flesh beneath it.
2. جَلَد (jalad) — the firmness of the skin itself.
3. أجلاد (ajlād) — the body; a man's frame is called his ajlād or tajālīd.
4. مِجْلَد (mijlad) — a piece of leather a mourning-woman holds and beats her face with at a funeral lament (cited with a line of verse describing wailing women displaying it).
5. جَلَد (jalad) as a hide, with two explanations: (a) the flayed skin of a camel or other animal put onto a different beast (with a supporting verse); or (b) the skin of a dead young camel stuffed with grass and presented to its bereaved mother so she takes to it with affection. A line of al-ʿAjjāj uses this image: women grow fond of him as a she-camel grows fond of the stuffed hide.
6. A disagreement: Ibn al-Aʿrābī held jild and jalad to be one and the same word (like the pair shibh / shabah); Ibn al-Sikkīt rejected this as unrecognized.
7. جَلَّدَ (jallada) — "he skinned his slaughter-camel"; Ibn Fāris notes the idiom uses jallada, not salakha, for a camel.
8. مُجَلَّد (mujallad) — a horse that does not flinch from the whip.
9. ذَاتُ مَجْلُودٍ (dhāt majlūd) — said of a strong she-camel (with a verse: even when her spirit softens with fatigue, her bulk and strength remain).
10. جَلَد (jalad) of camels — the large, full-grown ones, with no young among them.
11. جَلَد (jalad) — rough, hard ground.
12. جِلَاد (jilād) — camels that give less milk than the abundant-milk khūr; singular جِلْدَة (jildah).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris says that j-l-l has three root meanings (uṣūl): greatness, one thing enveloping another, and sound. He sets two words apart as standing outside this pattern.

1. **Greatness (the first root).** jalla al-shayʾ: the thing was great; the jull of a thing is its greater part. The jalāl of God is His greatness, and He is dhū al-jalāl wa-l-ikrām, "Possessor of greatness and honour". al-jalal is a great matter. The expression faʿaltu dhāka min jalālika, "I did that out of your jalāl", is explained as "out of your greatness in my breast", and Kuthayyir says "and my honouring of the enemies is out of her jalāl".

2. **Large and small, much and little (within the first root).** Ibn Fāris lists several livestock terms here:
al-jillah are the full-grown, aged camels, as in the line "…or that my camels should one day take up their weapons against me, neither the full-grown among them nor the young".
al-julālah is a large she-camel.
al-jalīlah is the opposite of al-daqīqah, so mā lahu daqīqah wa-lā jalīlah means "he has neither a sheep nor a she-camel".
mā ajallanī wa-lā aḥshānī means "he gave me nothing, small or large, neither from the full-grown camels (jillah) nor from the small ones (ḥāshiyah)".
adaqqa wa-ajalla means to give little and much. A poet says of an eye that weeps whenever it sees the summits of al-Ḥimā and the mountain of al-Rayyān that it "gave little and much" in its weeping, that is, it wept both a little and a great deal.

3. **One thing enveloping another (the second root).** The examples are the jull of a horse, and al-mujallil, rain that covers the earth with water and vegetation. From this comes al-julūl, singular jull, the sails of ships, cited from al-Quṭāmī: "in a vessel with sails, whose occupant goes through death, when the mariner cries out in supplication at its terrors".

4. **Sound (the third root).** A cloud is called mujaljil when it makes a sound, and al-juljul (bell) is derived from this. Of the same group is jaljaltu al-shayʾ fī yadī, said when you mix a thing together in your hand and then strike it, as in the line "He shook it twice, then let it go …".

5. **Words Ibn Fāris links to sound, some tentatively.** He considers it possible that juljulān al-simsim, sesame seed, belongs here, because it rattles in its pod when it dries; the saying aṣabtu juljulāna qalbihi, "I hit the grain of his heart", is referred to the same. al-jull (or al-jill; both vowels are printed), the stalks of the crop, belongs here because the wind rattles them when it falls upon them, though he allows that it may belong to the first root because of its thickness. al-jalīl is thumām, a grass, cited in the line "Would that I knew whether I shall spend a night in a valley with idhkhir and jalīl around me".

6. **Exceptions.** al-majallah, a written sheet (ṣaḥīfah), stands outside the pattern, unless it is attached to the first root because of the great weight and dignity of knowledge. Abū ʿUbayd says that among the Arabs every piece of writing is a majallah. al-jullah, dung, also stands outside the pattern.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: al-Hudhalī and others (lived into Islam); al-Farazdaq (Umayyad); al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha derives every sense of the root ج-ل-س (j-l-s) from one core meaning: rising/elevation (al-irtifāʿ).

1. The verb "jalasa" (to sit). He specifies its precise sense: jalasa describes the transition from lying down or sleep into a sitting position — i.e., a rise. This is distinguished from qaʿada ("to sit down"), which describes the opposite transition, from standing down into sitting — i.e., a descent. So Arabic pairs "qāma wa-qaʿada" (he stood, then sat down) as the standard opposite-motion pair, while jalasa is properly the upward move. (The following note on al-muqīm/al-muqʿid is terse in the source and left as given.)

2. Derived nouns. Al-jilsah = the manner or posture of a person's sitting ("he sat in a good sitting-posture"). Al-jalsah = a single instance of sitting.

3. Geographic sense: Najd. "Jalasa al-rajulu" can also mean "the man went up to Najd" (the highland region of Arabia), and Ibn Fāris says this fits the root's core logic perfectly, since Najd is the elevated counterpart to al-Ghawr, the lowland. Najd itself is accordingly nicknamed "al-Jals." He cites a hadith referring to mines in both the lowland and highland parts of al-Qabaliyyah, and several lines of poetry (al-Hudhalī and others) using jalasa/al-jālis in this "went up to Najd" sense — including a line addressed to the poet al-Farazdaq telling him, if he dislikes the order given him, to "fajlis" (go up to Najd), which Ibn Fāris glosses plainly as "go to Najd," not "sit."

4. A bird sense. Umm al-Haytham (cited via Abū Ḥātim) reports that "jalasat al-rakhamah" (a vulture 'sat') is said when it crouches/settles on the ground.

5. Al-jals = rugged terrain. The word also names coarse, rugged ground, and by extension a "jals she-camel" is a tough, hardy she-camel.

Ibn Fāris then remarks that this root behaves consistently (muṭṭarid) — every sense traces back to the one idea of elevation.

Finally, he addresses a line of al-Aʿshā's poetry mentioning "jullasān" alongside violets and other flowers, and notes that this word is actually Persian in origin (from "julshān," meaning scattered rose-petals).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: تَجَلَّىٰ 2x "it shines in brightness"; جَلَّىٰ 2x "can reveal [it]"; جَلَاء 1x "the exile"
poets_named: Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam); unnamed verse
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ج-ل-و as a single root with one consistent analogy: a thing being uncovered and coming into open view.

1. **Displaying, burnishing.** جَلَوْتُ الْعَرُوسَ (jalwa / jalāʾ) — to show the bride unveiled; جَلَوْتُ السَّيْفَ (jalāʾ) — to polish a sword so it shines.

2. **A clear sky.** Al-Kisāʾī is cited for السَّمَاءُ جَلْوَاءُ — the sky is cloudless, unclouded.

3. **Becoming manifest.** تَجَلَّى الشَّيْءُ — a thing becomes manifest, i.e. is uncovered.

4. **Bared forehead.** رَجُلٌ أَجْلَى — a man whose hair has receded from the front of his head; the noun is الْجَلَا. Supported by an unattributed half-line pairing this baldness with "the gleam of grey hairs showing."

5. **Departure and expulsion.** Within the same field: جَلَا الْقَوْمُ عَنْ مَنَازِلِهِمْ (jalāʾ) — a people quit their dwellings; and the causative أَجْلَيْتُهُمْ (ijlāʾ), also جَلَوْتُهُمْ — I drove them out. Abū Dhuʾayb's line is cited: when he drove them out with smoke (the bees), they scattered in groups, "upon them their abasement and their dejection."

6. **ابْنُ جَلَا — the man whose affair is not hidden**, i.e. one so well known nothing about him is concealed. Cited with the famous verse: "I am ibn jalā, a scaler of the mountain passes; whenever I lay aside the turban you will know me."

The organising idea across all of these, in Ibn Fāris's presentation, is exposure: something veiled — a bride, a blade's surface, the sky, a forehead, a man's reputation, a people's settled place — is stripped of its cover and laid open.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ج-م-ع (j-m-ʿ) from a single core sense: the drawing-together or joining of a thing. From this he lists:

1. Basic verb: جَمَعْتُ الشَّيْءَ — "I gathered the thing."

2. جُمَّاع (jummāʿ): a motley crowd made up of people from various tribes. A verse of Abū Qays contrasts a proper جَمْع (assembly) with a جُمَّاع (rabble).

3. مَاتَتْ بِجُمْعٍ — said of a woman who dies while pregnant. It is also given the sense of a woman who dies untouched by any man (a virgin), with a saying of al-Dahnāʾ cited: "I am, as regards him, bi-jumʿ (untouched)."

4. جَامِع (jāmiʿ): a she-ass at her first pregnancy.

5. قِدْر جِمَاع / جَامِعَة: a very large cooking-pot.

6. جَمْع (jamʿ): any un-named variety of date-palm, especially palms grown up wild from date-stones.

7. جُمْع / جِمْع الكَفّ: the closed fist — "I struck him with my fist."

8. نَهْب مُجْمَع: plunder gathered/driven together, with a supporting verse of Abū Dhuʾayb.

9. اسْتَجْمَعَ الفَرَسُ جَرْيًا: a horse gathering itself for a run, running at full stretch.

10. Jamʿ as a place-name: Mecca, so called because people gather there; and likewise يوم الجُمُعة (Friday) is named from the same gathering.

11. أَجْمَعْتُ على الأمر (also أَجْمَعْتُه): to resolve or settle firmly on a course of action, with a verse of al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza ("they resolved their affair by night…").

12. فلاة مُجْمِعة: a desert waste in which travellers stay together and do not split up, for fear of getting lost.

13. جَوَامِع (jawāmiʿ): shackles or fetters.

14. جَمْعَاء (jamʿāʾ): said of an animal (or other creature) that is whole and intact, having lost no part of its body.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ج-م-ح (j-m-ḥ) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: a single, consistent root — something going forward headlong, overpowering restraint by sheer force.

1. A riding animal that jamaḥa (verbal noun jimāḥ) has overpowered its rider and bolted out of control. A horse prone to this is called jamūḥ ("headstrong/bolting"). A cited verse describes a swift horse as "sabūḥ jamūḥ," its gallop "like the crackling of kindled palm-fronds."

2. In a children's game, a boy "jamaḥa" a knucklebone (kaʿb) with another knucklebone, meaning he threw it and knocked the target piece out of its place. Ibn Fāris flags this sense as doubtful, noting the action is more properly named with a different word, treated elsewhere in the dictionary.

3. Al-jummāḥ is an arrow tipped with a pellet of clay, shot by boys at play. A cited verse compares a young ostrich's head to a jummāḥ.

4. Some philologists extend the word figuratively: al-jamūḥ is "one who rides his own whim" — a person headlong and unrestrained in following his own desire.

5. On the Qur'anic verse "they would turn to it while yajmaḥūn" (9:57), the sense given is yasʿawna, "they run/rush [toward it]" — the same headlong-motion meaning as the rest of the root.

6. A cited verse: "I cast off my rein, headlong — no rebuke turns me back from fair women like statues" — illustrating jāmiḥ as unrestrained, headlong pursuit.

7. A woman who "jamaḥat" to her family went to them without permission — again, a headlong departure that overrides normal restraint.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris derives the whole root j-m-d from one core idea: jumud, the solidifying or congealing of something that was liquid - caused by cold or by anything else.

1. Core/literal sense - freezing or solidifying a liquid: jamada al-ma'u yajmudu, "the water froze/solidified."

2. Extended sense - a dry year: sanatun jamadun, "a jamad year," means a year with little rain. Ibn Faris explains this as derived by analogy from the first sense: it is as if the year's rain itself had "frozen" (i.e., stopped). In the same vein, al-Shaybani defined al-jamad as land that has gone unrained-upon.

3. Idiomatic curse against a miser - the Arabs would say to a stingy man, "jamadi lahu," meaning "may his state stay frozen [i.e., never improve]." This is the opposite of hamadi, a word of praise/commendation.

4. Poetic citation - al-Mutalammis uses the contrast directly: "Say 'jamadi' to her, 'jamadi' - never say 'hamadi' for her, whenever she is mentioned." I.e., wish her stagnation, not praise.

So the root's throughline is solidification/stasis of what was fluid or flowing - applied literally to water, then metaphorically to a rainless year and to a person's fortunes standing still.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: جَمِيل 7x "good"; جَمَل 1x "the camel"; جَمَال 1x "(is) beauty"; جُمْلَة 1x "all at once"; جِمَٰلَت 1x "camels"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ج-م-ل (j-m-l) from two distinct base senses: (1) gathering-together and largeness of build, and (2) beauty.

BASE 1 — Aggregation / bulk:
1. أَجْمَلْتُ الشَّيْءَ = "I totalled / summed the thing up"; جُمْلَة = the aggregate or whole of something. أَجْمَلْتُهُ can also mean "I collected/obtained it."
2. He cites Qur'an 25:32, where the disbelievers ask why the Qur'an was not sent down "as a single whole" (jumlatan wāḥidatan) — i.e. all at once.
3. He suggests the جَمَل (camel) may belong here, named for the largeness of its build. Likewise جُمَّل, a thick rope; جُمَالِيّ, a man of massive build (as if likened to a camel), and نَاقَة جُمَالِيَّة, a similarly bulky she-camel.
4. أَجْمَلَ الْقَوْمُ = a people whose camels grew numerous.
5. On authority of al-Farrāʾ: جِمَالَات is the plural of جَمَل (camel); it also denotes bundles of ropes and cables (qulūs).

BASE 2 — Beauty:
1. الْجَمَال = beauty, the opposite of ugliness; a handsome man is jamīl or jumāl.
2. Ibn Qutayba traces this to الْجَمِيل, the grease of melted fat — the image being that a healthy sheen ("the water of fatness") runs over the face.
3. جَمَالَكَ أَنْ تَفْعَلَ كَذَا is an idiom meaning "act gracefully / hold back, and do not do such a thing." Ibn Fāris quotes Abū Dhuʾayb: "Restrain yourself, O wounded heart — you shall meet the one you love and find rest."
4. He records a mother's saying to her daughter, لَا تَجَمَّلِي وَتَعَفَّفِي, glossed as "eat the jamīl (the melted fat) and drink the ʿufāfa (the last remnant of milk)."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: unnamed verse ×4; al-Namir ibn Tawlab (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the doubled root j-m-m as having two root meanings (aṣlān): first, the abundance of a thing and its gathering together; second, the lack of weapons.

**1. Abundance and gathering together**

Quantity and fullness. al-jamm means "much, abundant", as in Q 89:20, "and you love wealth with an abundant love (ḥubban jammā)". al-jimām is fullness, a container's full measure: a vessel is called jammān when it has reached its jimām. A cited verse compares something to "the water of a drained well after it was full (jimām)".

Wells. The jamma of a well is the spot where its water collects. A jamūm well is one with abundant water; of it one says jammat, verbal noun jumūm, and a line of rajaz says the churning of the buckets adds to its jumūm. A jamjama is a well dug in salt ground (sabakha).

Horses. A horse "in its jamām" is at rest. Ibn Fāris explains that at rest the horse is collected, its limbs still, so the word keeps to the root's analogy (qiyās). A horse is said to jamma or ajamma when it is left unridden, and he places this in the root too, because its strength comes back to it and gathers. A jamūm horse is one that, whenever one burst of running is spent, has another come to it. He says these usages point to abundance and gathering, and cites al-Namir ibn Tawlab on a mare "jamūm in her running, her tail raised; you would take the white of her blaze for a lamp".

People. al-jumma is a group of people who ask for help toward a blood-money (diya), so named because they band together for it; a line of verse says "many a jumma asking of me, I have given". jamājim al-ʿArab, "the skulls of the Arabs", are the tribes that gather many clans, so that a person's lineage is traced to the tribe rather than to a clan: calling a man "Kalbī", after Kalb ibn Wabra, makes it unnecessary to name any of its clans. al-jammāʾ al-ghafīr is a gathered company of people; some said it is the iron helmet (bayḍa), because it gathers the hair of the head.

Body and plants. The jumma of a person is the gathered hair of his forelock. al-jumjuma, the human skull, is so called because it gathers together the sections (qabāʾil) of the head. al-jamīm is a thick mass of the plant buhmā, illustrated by a verse on an animal grazing the buhmā when it was jamīm.

Drawing near. Ibn Fāris also puts here ajamma al-shayʾ, "the thing drew near".

**2. Lacking a weapon**

al-ajamm is a man who has no spear with him in battle, and a jammāʾ sheep or goat is one without horns. A ḥadīth says "We were commanded to build the masājid (places of prostration) jumman", which is explained as meaning that their walls should have no crenellations (shuraf).

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: جُنَاح 25x "blame"; جَنَاح 7x "your wing"; جَنَحُ 2x "then you (also) incline"
text:
Zamakhsharī's entry for the root ج ن ح (j-n-ḥ) treats it under the core idea of "leaning / inclining," then the noun jināḥ ("wing"), then a set of figurative uses.

Literal senses:
1. To incline or lean toward something: "they inclined toward peace"; "they inclined to it"; "the sun inclined toward setting." Of night: it "inclined," i.e. leaned toward coming or going. Of the late afternoon (al-aṣīl): janaḥa, "declined" — with a verse of al-Namir on hastening a she-camel "when the late afternoon declined."
2. Of a ship: janaḥat = it reached shallow water and ran aground, stuck fast and unable to move on.
3. Of a bird: janaḥa = it folded its wings to swoop down and alight; jawāniḥ = swooping birds (two verses of al-Nābigha, one on carrion-birds trailing an army, sure of victory).
4. Of mountains: junūḥ ʿalā l-arḍ = leaning/inclining upon the earth (verse of al-Nābigha).
5. al-jawāniḥ = the ribs of the chest: "a matter from which the ribs crack."
6. ijtanaḥa ʿalā = to bend or stoop over something. Cited: Ibn al-Riqāʿ on a wild bull "bent over" as it digs the ground at night; al-Quṭāmī on a tar-coated ship that "leaned over" as its wave-crests plunged in. Also "I came to him at the leaning of the late afternoon."
7. janāḥ = blame/fault: "there is no janāḥ upon you" (no blame on you). [Zamakhsharī records this only as attested usage, without further definition.]

Figurative uses (min al-majāz), all built on janāḥ = "wing":
- "He lowered his wing to him" — gentleness/humility.
- "Clipped of wing" (maqṣūṣ al-janāḥ) — said of the powerless or incapable.
- "The two wings of the valley flowed" — i.e. its two sides.
- "They broke the two wings [flanks] of the army."
- "He rode the two wings of an ostrich" — he threw himself earnestly and hastily into an affair.
- "I am in so-and-so's wing" — under his shelter and protection.
- "He is on a bird's wing" — said of someone anxious and bewildered.
- A tharīda (sopped-bread dish) served "with two wings of bones," i.e. flanked/garnished with bones.

dictionary: Ṣiḥāḥ — al-Ṣiḥāḥ, al-Jawharī (d. 1003)
quran_words: ٱجْتَنَبُ 9x "avoid"; جَانِب 9x "side"; جَنب 8x "their sides"; جُنُب 4x "(who is) farther away"; ٱجْنُبْ 1x "and keep me away"; يَتَجَنَّبُ 1x "and will avoid it"; يُجَنَّبُ 1x "but will be removed from it"
poets_named: al-Muhalhil (pre-Islamic); al-Akhfash (unnamed); al-Jumayḥ b. Munqidh (pre-Islamic); Abū Duʾād (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse; ʿAlqama b. ʿAbada (pre-Islamic); Sāʿida b. Juʾayya (pre-Islamic); al-Kumayt (Umayyad); Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad)
text:
al-Jawharī groups the root ج-ن-ب around the idea of the "side," and radiating from it, notions of nearness, being led at one's side, and being set apart / foreign.

1. al-Janb — the side (of the body). "I sat at his janb" = "at his jānib," same sense.

2. Janb — a tribe of Yemen (with a shāhid from al-Muhalhil).

3. al-Janb / al-jānib / al-janaba — a direction, region, quarter. al-Akhfash's line contrasts "the people on one side, the ruler on another." al-ṣāḥib bi-l-janb = the companion at your side, i.e. your travelling companion.

4. Nearness that shades into strangeness: al-jār al-junub = a neighbour who belongs to another people (a stranger-neighbour).

5. Avoidance/keeping apart: jānabahu, tajānabahu, tajannabahu, ijtanabahu all mean to keep away from. A person termed ajnabī / ajnab / janab / jānib = foreign, unrelated.

6. Physical senses of the verb: janabahu (struck and broke his side); janaba a beast or a captive = led it at one's side, hence khayl mujannaba (led horses). jannaba/janaba a thing from someone = removed it far off — cited with Q 14:35, "keep me and my sons from worshipping idols."

7. al-Janāb (fatḥa) — the courtyard or ground near a people's dwellings; plural ajniba. Used in phrases for a fertile or barren "precinct." Also "they travelled along its two janābān" = its two flanks. A horse ṭawʿ al-jināb (kasra) = easy to lead. "He persisted in an ugly jināb" = in estranging himself from his family.

8. jannaba al-qawm — a people whose camels' milk ran short (shāhid from al-Jumayḥ b. Munqidh: "every year to her a year of tajnīb").

9. al-Tajnīb — an admired curve and tautness in a horse's hind leg (shāhid from Abū Duʾād).

10. Being led vs. unled: al-janība = a led beast; anything docile is janīb; al-ajnab = one that won't be led. al-janība also = the ʿalīqa, a she-camel lent to others to bring back provisions on it (with a rājiz line where such mounts are "strays," i.e. wasted by a poor manager).

11. Foreignness: al-janīb = the stranger. janaba fī banī fulān = settled among a people as a stranger; he is jānib, pl. junnāb. "the neighbour of janāba" = the neighbour who is a foreigner (shāhid from ʿAlqama b. ʿAbada, where janāba = remoteness).

12. al-Janba — (a) a strip of hide from a camel's side, used to make a milking-bowl; (b) "he encamped janba" = off to one side, apart from people; (c) a name for any plant that grows lush in summer.

13. Ritual impurity: a man junub (from janāba); the form is invariable for singular, plural, feminine, though plurals ajnāb / junubūn occur. Verbs: ajnaba, januba. (al-Jawharī gives no further definition of janāba here beyond the state itself.)

14. Winds and the "side": al-janūb = the south wind, opposite the north (shamāl); janabat al-rīḥ = it turned southerly; a cloud majnūba is one the south wind drives; a people janaba/ajnaba (entered the south wind) or were junibū (struck by it), so majnūbūn — and the like is said of the east, west and north winds. al-majnūb also = one afflicted with dhāt al-janb (pleurisy), a sore inside the side.

15. al-Mijnab (kasra) — (a) a shield (shāhid from Sāʿida b. Juʾayya); (b) the frontier zone where Arab and non-Arab lands meet (shāhid from al-Kumayt).

16. al-Majnab (fatḥa) — abundance: "abundant good and abundant evil" = much.

17. al-Janab (a-a) — (a) the forbidden racing trick: leading a second horse beside one's own at a race to switch onto it if outrun; (b) verbal noun of janiba (kasra): a camel limping from its side — per al-Aṣmaʿī, its lung sticking to its side from thirst; per Ibn al-Sikkīt (from the Bedouin), writhing from thirst (two shawāhid from Dhū al-Rumma on a wild ass).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root j-n-d from two linked ideas: gathering together and giving aid or support.

1. Core sense: helpers, supporters. One says "they are his jund," i.e. his aides and supporters (a group banded together to back someone).

2. al-ajnād as regions: the ajnād of Syria (al-Shām), five military districts each called a jund — Damascus, Ḥimṣ, Qinnasrīn, the Jordan district (al-Urdunn), and Palestine.

3. Janad (proper noun): the name of a town.

4. al-janad: rugged ground strewn with white stones. Ibn Fāris notes this sense may either belong to the same root or arise by letter-substitution (ibdāl) from an original al-jalad (hard, firm ground).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) gives the root j-n-f a single underlying meaning: al-mayl, "leaning/inclining/deviating."

1. Core verb — janifa: to swerve and act wrongfully (ʿadala wa jāra), i.e., to deviate from the straight/correct course, with an implication of injustice. Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 2:182: "But whoever fears from a testator janafan [an unjust deviation]" — janaf here names an unjust bias or deviation in how a bequest is made.

2. Physical sense — ajnaf: a man is called ajnaf when there is a mayl ("tilt/leaning") in his bodily build. Ibn Fāris notes this bodily usage applies specifically to height/stature and to bending or stooping — i.e., a tall man who leans or stoops.

3. Derived form — tajānafa ʿan: "to lean/turn away from" something, glossed simply as māla, "he inclined/deviated." Ibn Fāris supports this with a line of poetry in which a she-camel "turns away" (tajānafat) from the bulk of al-Yamāma, yet never swerves from her own people toward anyone else — illustrating tajānafa as a directional turning-away.

In short: the root's single semantic core is inclination/deviation, expressed (a) morally, as an unjust swerve from what is right (as in the Qur'anic janaf of 2:182), (b) physically, as a bodily lean or stoop, and (c) as the derived verb tajānafa, "to turn away from."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: جَنَّة 147x "gardens"; جِنّ 22x "the jinn"; مَجْنُون 11x "a madman"; جِنَّة 10x "the jinn"; جَانّ 7x "any jinn"; جُنَّة 2x "(as) a cover"; جَنَّ 1x "covered"; أَجِنَّة 1x "fetuses"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats j-n-n as a single root (aṣl wāḥid) whose meaning is covering and concealment, and he explains each derived word by that idea.

1. **The Garden of the next world.** al-janna is what the Muslims come to in the next world; he explains it as a reward concealed from them today.

2. **Orchard.** al-janna is also an orchard, because trees conceal with their leaves. Some say that for the Arabs al-janna meant tall date palms, citing Zuhayr's verse comparing his weeping eyes to the buckets of a water-drawing camel "watering a janna of tall palms".

3. **Foetus and the buried.** al-janīn is the child in its mother's belly; al-janīn is also the one buried in the grave.

4. **Heart.** al-janān is the heart.

5. **Shield and protective arms.** al-mijann is a shield, and any weapon one is concealed behind is a junna. Abū ʿUbayda distinguishes: al-silāḥ is what one fights with, al-junna what one protects oneself with. A verse pictures horses "rising up with Indian swords and junan".

6. **Madness.** al-jinna is madness, because it covers the mind; al-majanna also means madness.

7. **Night.** janān al-layl is the night's blackness and its hiding of things, as in the verse "had it not been for the janān of the night, our galloping would have overtaken ʿIyāḍ ibn Nāshib". junūn al-layl means the same.

8. **Plants.** junna al-nabtu junūnan: the plant grew strong and came into flower. Ibn Fāris suggests this may be a metaphor from madness, as a person is made mad and becomes agitated, with madness itself going back to covering; he judges the analogy sound.

9. **The mass of people.** janān al-nās is the bulk of the people, also called al-sawād.

10. **The snake.** The snake called al-jānn is so named by comparison with one of the jānn.

11. **Jinn.** The jinn are so named because they are hidden from the eyes of created beings, as in Q 7:27: "He sees you, he and his tribe, from where you do not see them."

12. **Chest bones.** al-janājin are the bones of the chest.

dictionary: Lane — Arabic-English Lexicon, Edward William Lane (d. 1876)
text:
Lane's Arabic-English Lexicon, entry for the root ج ن ي (jny)

Core verb: جَنَى (yajnī), "to gather/pluck fruit." The base meaning is to gather, pluck, or pick fruit from a tree (equivalent verbs: اجتنى, تجنّى). It extends to anything fruit-like — one can "gather" truffles (جَنَيْتُكَ أَكْمُؤًا, "I gathered truffles for thee") or even gold collected from its mine (جَنَى ذَهَبًا). The poet Abū Dhu'ayb uses it figuratively — جَنَى العُلَى, "he gathered/acquired eminence, or nobility."

Extended (metaphorical) sense — committing an offence. From the image of "gathering," lexicographers (notably al-Rāghib) say the verb was extended metaphorically to جَنَى عَلَيْهِ / عَلَى قَوْمِهِ — "he committed a crime or offence against him/his people," with the noun جِنَايَةٌ for the offence itself. A ḥadīth is cited: "No wrongdoer shall bring injury save upon himself" (one isn't punished for a relative's crime). A well-known proverb, جَانِيكَ مَنْ يَجْنِي عَلَيْكَ, plays on the same root ("your true offender is the one who wrongs you") — Lane records two rival explanations of it (A'Obeyd's and AHeyth's), turning on whether it warns against relatives sharing blame, or against suspecting even benefactors.

Form III — جَانَى: to accuse someone of a جِنَايَة (crime).

Form IV — أَجْنَى (said of a tree/palm, or of land): to have ripening or ripe fruit ready for gathering, to reach fruit-bearing maturity; of land, to abound in جَنًى (produce — herbage, truffles, etc.).

Form V — تَجَنَّى: same as the base verb ("to gather"), but also, importantly, "to falsely accuse someone of a crime he did not commit" — to fabricate a charge against an innocent person. Cited saying: "He accuses us of what we did not do."

Form VIII — اجْتَنَى: same as the base verb, "to gather/pluck." A separate recorded phrase, اِجْتَنَيْنَا مَاءَ مَطَرٍ ("we came upon rainwater and drank it"), is noted without explanation by Ibn al-A'rābī, though Ibn Sīdah takes it to mean this.

Noun جَنًى — whatever is gathered/plucked, especially from trees while still fresh. Applied broadly to: fruit ready for picking (the word used in Qur'an 55:54), fresh ripe dates, grapes, truffles, cotton, herbage, gold (mined), cowrie shells (as if "gathered" from the sea), and honey once collected. Plural: أَجْنَاء. Related forms: جَنَاة (a single "gathering" or a fresh-picked item, same class as جَنًى), جَنِيّ (an adjective for fruit "freshly picked," also used for dates cut straight from the tree), and مَجْنًى (fruit that has been gathered, pl. مَجَانٍ).

A proverb is recorded here: "This is my gathering, and its best part is in it — when every other gatherer has his hand at his own mouth [eating as he picks]." Lane traces its origin to a story about Jadhīmah ordering his men to gather truffles: most ate the best ones themselves, but 'Amr ibn 'Adī brought Jadhīmah the best and said these words — later echoed by 'Alī on entering the public treasury, meaning he had taken nothing of the Muslims' revenue for himself.

Noun جِنَايَة — traces a semantic ladder: (1) literally, the act of picking fruit; (2) then, metaphorically, bringing about something evil; (3) then, evil itself; (4) then, doing a forbidden act. In ordinary and legal usage it settles as "a crime, offence, or injurious act warranting punishment" — in law specifically a wounding, amputation, or maiming. Plural: جنايات (rarely جَنَايَا). A separate homonym, جَنِيَّة, denotes a round cloak made of خَزّ (a silk-blend fabric) — an unrelated sense of the same form.

Noun جَانٍ — "one who gathers" (fruit), and by the same metaphor, "one who commits a جِنَايَة" (an offender). Plurals: جُنَاة, جُنَّاء, and the irregular/doubtful أَجْنَاء (giving the proverb أَجْنَاؤُهَا أَبْنَاؤُهَا). Separately, الجَانِي is recorded as a name for "the wolf," and جَانٍ can also mean a date-palm pollinator (لَقَّاح), per Ibn al-A'rābī and al-Azharī.

Other: الجَوَانِي = "the sides" (an irregular plural pattern parallel to الجَانِب); مُجْتَنًى = a place where fruit is gathered/picked.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ج ر ع (j-r-ʿ), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: the smallness/scantiness of what is drunk (a sip).

1. jariʿa al-shāribu al-māʾ / jaraʿa yajraʿu — to sip water, two attested verb forms.
2. al-jarʿāʾ — a sandy tract that grows nothing, explained as belonging to this root because even rainfall only "sips" at it, so it is as though never fully watered/quenched — illustrated with a line of poetry by Dhū al-Rummah about an abandoned campsite at a place called Jarʿāʾ Mālik.
3. The idiom "aflata fulānun bi-jurayʿati al-dhaqan" ("so-and-so escaped by the mere last sip of the chin") — glossed, per al-Farrāʾ, as an escape by the narrowest margin, the last gasp of breath.
4. nūq majārīʿ — she-camels scant of milk, as though their udders held only sips.
5. Closing exception, explicitly flagged by Ibn Fāris as anomalous and NOT derived from the "sip" sense: al-jaraʿ — a twist/kink standing out in one strand of a rope, more prominent than the rest.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: جَوَارِح 1x "(your) hunting animals"; جُرُوح 1x "and (for) wounds"; جَرَحْ 1x "you committed"; ٱجْتَرَحُ 1x "commit"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ج-ر-ح from two distinct roots:

1. Earning or acquiring (al-kasb). The form اجْتَرَحَ (ijtaraḥa) means to work and to earn. He cites Qur'an 45:21, "Or do those who ijtaraḥū evil deeds suppose…", i.e. those who acquire/commit them. He explains the name ijtirāḥ as derived from the جَوَارِح (jawāriḥ), the limbs that do the acquiring — action carried out with the body's earning-organs. From the same sense, الجوارح among birds and beasts of prey means those that hunt.

2. Splitting the skin — wounding. جَرَحَهُ بِحَدِيدَةٍ (jaraḥahu bi-ḥadīdatin) is "he wounded him with an iron blade"; the noun is الجُرْح (al-jurḥ), "the wound."

Extended uses of the second sense:
- جَرَحَ الشَّاهِدَ (jaraḥa al-shāhid): to reject a witness's testimony by reporting something discreditable about him.
- اسْتَجْرَحَ (istajraḥa): to do something that makes one liable to be impugned.

Disputed shāhid: Ibn Fāris discusses the saying attributed to ʿAbd al-Malik — "I have admonished you, and you have gained from the admonition nothing but istijrāḥ." Abū ʿUbayd glossed istijrāḥ as "a decrease in good." Ibn Fāris accepts that the resulting sense is correct but holds that the wording does not support it; on his reading, ʿAbd al-Malik meant that his hearers only earned themselves grounds for being impugned and censured — the way ḥadīth reports are impugned. Where Abū ʿUbayd took a related remark to mean that such reports are numerous while few are sound, Ibn Fāris again reads it through his own derivation: the reports grew so numerous that scholars were obliged to impugn some of them as unsound.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: ج-ر-د (J-R-D) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core sense: the exposure or bareness of a thing's outer surface, with nothing covering it. Every other usage below is treated by Ibn Fāris as an extension of this one idea of "being laid bare / uncovered."

1. Tajarrada (تَجَرَّدَ) — a man "stripped himself" of his clothes; undressed, laid bare.

2. Al-jarīd (الجريد) — palm-frond stalks (singular jarīdah), so called because the leaflets have been stripped off them.

3. Al-arḍ al-jarad (الأرض الجرد) — a wide open plain, named for lying exposed with nothing covering it.

4. Faras ajrad (فرس أجرد) — a horse with a thin, smooth coat; also praised as "fine in its jurdah/mutajarrad" (its bare sleekness).

5. Rajul jārūd (رجل جارود) — an ill-omened man, as if he strips and scrapes everything bare.

6. Sanah jārūdah (سنة جارودة) — a barren, drought year, from the same idea of being stripped bare.

7. Al-jarād (الجراد) — locusts (well known). Arḍ majrūdah (أرض مجرودة) — land locusts have struck. Some scholars said locusts are named jarād because they strip the land bare of whatever grows on it.

8. Al-jarad (الجرد) — the skin breaking out/itching from eating locusts.

9. By the same recurring analogy: ʿām jarīd (عام جريد) — a "complete" year, i.e. one that ran its full course with nothing lacking. Likewise the expression "I have not seen him for ajradān wa-jarīdān [two days]" means two full, complete days.

10. Injarada binā al-sayr (انجرد بنا السير) — "the journey stretched on/extended" with us.

11. A proverb for something that vanishes untraceably: "I don't know which locust-swarm carried it off" (مَا أَدْرِي أَيُّ الْجَرَادِ عَارَهُ) — here jarād keeps its plain, literal sense of locusts.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ج ر ف (j-r-f) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris derives every sense of this root from one single core idea: taking or carrying off a thing wholesale — sweeping the whole of it away at once.

1. Basic verb — jaraftu al-shay' jarfan, "I swept/carried the thing off entirely," said of taking all of something away.
2. sayfun jurāf — "a sweeping sword," one that destroys or cuts through everything in its path.
3. al-jurf — a bank or stretch of ground that a flash-flood (sayl) eats away/erodes: land carried off wholesale by water.
4. Figurative use — jarrafa al-dahru mālahu, "time swept away his wealth," meaning it wiped it out completely; wealth ruined this way is called mālun mujarraf.
5. A man given to excessive intercourse is called jurāf (nukaḥa) — as if he "sweeps" at it, the same image of taking the whole of something at once applied here to sexual excess.
6. Related sense — al-jurfa: cutting a strip of skin from a camel's thigh and gathering/rolling it up on the thigh — again the idea of removing or gathering something in one wholesale motion.

Ibn Fāris ties all six usages back to the single image of sweeping something away or taking it entirely, in one motion.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مُجْرِم 52x "the criminals"; أَجْرَمُ 5x "committed crimes"; جَرَم 5x "doubt"; يَجْرِمَ 3x "prevent you"; إِجْرَام 1x "(is) my crime"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ج-ر-م (j-r-m) as a single root whose branches all return to one core idea: cutting or severing (al-qaṭʿ).

1. Core sense — cutting/harvesting. الجِرْم (jirm) is cutting. Hence الجَِرام (jarām) is the harvesting of date-palms ("the season of al-jarām has come"), and jaramtu means to shear a sheep's wool and take it. الجُرامة (jurāma) is what drops from dates when they are picked (or what is gathered from the palm-stalks after harvest).

2. Extensions of "cut off." سنة مُجَرَّمة (mujarrama) is a complete year — as if cut off at its full term; compare تَجَرَّمَ الليل, "the night passed away." الجَرام / الجَريم are dry dates. Ibn Fāris notes all these agree in form, meaning, and analogy.

3. Earning/acquiring. جَرَمَ (jarama) = "to earn, acquire" — because what one gains is, in effect, cut off and taken for oneself. جَريمة الأهل is a family's provider; a cited verse describes a mother eagle as the "earner" feeding her chick.

4. Sin/offense. الجُرم and الجَريمة mean a sin (dhanb). Ibn Fāris derives this from sense 3: a sin is something "earned," and earning is itself a cutting-off. He explains the expression لا جَرَمَ (lā jarama) likewise as coming from jaramtu ("I earned"), citing a verse where a spear-thrust "earned" the tribe Fazāra their anger.

5. Body/mass. الجِرْم (jirm) is the physical body, because it has measurable size and articulation. "Elders great of jarīm" means elders of large physique. Of a good singing voice one says ḥasanu l-jirm; Ibn Fāris prefers Ibn Durayd's reading — that it refers to the fine way the voice issues from the body — over the view that jirm itself means "voice."

6. Names. Banū Jārim are an Arab group; al-jārim means "the earner." The tribe Jarm is named from jarm ("earning") and comprises two clans, one within Quḍāʿa and one within Ṭayyi.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats j-r-r as one root meaning (aṣl wāḥid): drawing a thing out and dragging it, as in jarartu al-ḥabl, "I dragged the rope". He ties word after word back to that sense ("it belongs to this root").

1. **Dragging.** jarartu al-ḥabl, "I dragged the rope". Laqīṭ's line: "she has trailed the rope of a skittish mount over what is between us, so that we see from her neither plain despair nor hope".

2. **The foot of a mountain.** al-jarr, as though it were something dragged out: "I have crossed a valley and a jarr."

3. **A horse that will not be led.** al-jarūr, explained two ways: as the pattern faʿūl with a passive sense (it always has to be dragged), or in its own active sense (it drags the one leading it toward itself).

4. **A great army.** al-jarrār, because it drags its followers along and is itself drawn along: "a huge, jarrār host, its neighing horses many".

5. **A great herd of camels.** al-jurjūr, by the same analogy: "a hundred of their bounty, a jurjūr".

6. **A rope.** al-jarīr is a leather rope on a she-camel's neck; the man's name Jarīr comes from it.

7. **An offence.** al-jarīra is the offence a person "drags" onto himself.

8. **The cud.** al-jirra, the cud of livestock, because it is drawn up.

9. **The Milky Way.** majarrat al-samāʾ is so called because it looks like the track left by something dragged.

10. **Pinning a foal's tongue (al-ijrār).** The weaned foal's tongue is drawn out and pinned through so that it cannot suckle; some say it is drawn out and then slit. The line of ʿAmr is explained this way: "Had my people's spears made me speak, I would have spoken; but the spears ajarrat [my tongue]." Had they fought, he would have boasted of it in his poetry; as it is, their spears have in effect cut off his tongue from boasting of them.

11. **A spear left in the enemy.** ajarrahu al-rumḥ: he stabbed him and left the spear in him to drag along. Two verses illustrate it, one describing Naḍla left on a field of battle "dragging the spearheads like a gatherer of firewood". Ibn Fāris calls this a figurative use (mathal) whose base is the dragging of a thing.

12. **An overdue she-camel.** jarrat al-nāqa: she passes her due time and gives birth only some days later, having "dragged out" her pregnancy.

13. **Camels that are led.** The ḥadīth "no ṣadaqa on al-ibil al-jārra" refers to camels drawn by their reins and led, as though pack camels were meant; others say they are the people's riding camels.

14. **Deferring a debt.** ajrartu fulānan al-dayn: letting someone's debt run on, which is compared to letting a spear or a halter trail.

15. **Songs in succession.** ajarra fulānun fulānan aghāniyya: giving someone song after song, as in a verse about being given "songs the crooner does not tire of".

16. **Continuity.** "It was so in the first times, wa-halumma jarran up to today" means that it has been drawn on to the present without breaking off.

17. **Grazing on the move.** al-jarr in camels is grazing while travelling, dragging their loads.

18. **A channel.** al-jārūr, reportedly, is a channel cut by a torrent.

19. **A gazelle trap.** al-jurra is a stick about a cubit long with a noose at its head and a rope at its middle, buried for gazelles. A caught gazelle and the trap drag each other back and forth until the trap wins and the gazelle stays caught. Hence the proverb for someone who opposes the group's opinion and then comes round to it: "he struggled with the jurra, then made peace with it".

20. **The earthenware jar.** al-jarra, because it is always being drawn up to fetch water.

21. **A dangling skin bag.** al-jarr is made from the skin stripped off a camel's hock; a woman keeps preserved meat in it and, when travelling, hangs it from the back of her load, so it always swings. A verse says of a husband who gave out: "we hung him where the jarr is hung".

22. **A deep well.** rakiyy jarūr is a very deep well worked with draught-camels, whose water has to be hauled up.

23. **A loaf.** al-jarra is a loaf drawn out of the hot ashes, as in a verse about treating an ailing companion "with a jarra like a stallion lying down".

24. **Rumbling.** al-jarjara, the sound a camel sends back and forth in its throat, belongs here too: it is a sound drawn out, and because it repeats, the verb is doubled to jarjara, as ṣalla becomes ṣalṣala. Al-Aghlab has "it rumbled in a throat like a great water-jar", and a ḥadīth says that whoever drinks from silver vessels "only gulps (yujarjiru) the fire of Jahannam into his belly".

Ibn Fāris concludes that the root has run on as one consistent analogy along a single line.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: جَرَيْ 57x "flow"; جَوَار 3x "(are) the ships"; جَارِيَة 2x "flowing"; مَجْرىٰ 1x "(is) its course"; جَٰرِيَٰت 1x "and those sailing"
poets_named: Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam); Ruʾba (Umayyad); unnamed verse; Labīd (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Sīda's account of the root ج‑ر‑ي (j‑r‑y), whose core idea is "to flow / to run / to move onward."

1. Of water, blood and the like: to flow. Verbal nouns jary, jirya, jarayān. "It flows beautifully." The causative ajrā = to make (it) flow.

2. Of a horse and the like: to run (jary, jirāʾ, jarāʾa). Ibn Sīda notes that in a verse of Abū Dhuʾayb the "running" is a man's charge into battle, not a horse's gallop — since the tribe of Hudhayl were foot-soldiers. Causative ajrā = to make (it) run.

3. al-ijriyy: a particular manner of running, cited from two poetic shawāhid (including Ruʾba, where sinkh is pronounced with ḥāʾ for khāʾ).

4. Of the sun and stars: to travel from east to west. Hence al-jāriya = the sun, "the runner," moving from one quarter of the sky to another. Ibn Sīda reads the Qurʾanic "al-jawārī" (Q 81) as the stars.

5. Of a ship: to sail. Hence al-jāriya = a ship — a descriptive term that became a fixed name for it — citing the Qurʾanic "in the jāriya" and "the jawārī raised up on the sea."

6. Grammatical/prosodic sense — al-majrā, al-majārī (the "running" of word-endings):
