   - Al-Akhfash: in poetry, al-majrā is the vowel on the rhyme-letter (fatḥa, ḍamma, or kasra). A consonant-final rhyme has no majrā because it has no vowel. It is called majrā because inflectional and structural vowels "run" there. al-majārī then = the ends of words, where those vowels occur.
   - Ibn Jinnī: so named because the sound begins to flow through the letters of prolongation; he illustrates with three verse-openings where the ending vowel launches the sound into the following alif, yāʾ, or wāw.
   - On Sībawayh's "the majārī of word-endings … running along eight channels": Ibn Jinnī argues Sībawayh did not mean vowels alone (as the prosodists narrowly did) but the states, rulings, and forms that word-endings take — so a quiescent ending (sukūn) is one such "state" just as a vowel is. He therefore dismisses a critic who accused Sībawayh of inconsistency for mentioning pause and quiescence among the majārī, calling the objection a failure to grasp Sībawayh's meaning; and cites common usage — "you run the course of so-and-so," "this runs the course of that" — where "run" plainly means "resembles / stands in the same case," not literal motion.

7. al-ijriyyāʾ / al-ijriyyā: the course or way one takes and runs along (Labīd's line on the wild ox). Also idiomatic: "generosity is from his ijriyyā" = from his innate nature (from al-Liḥyānī) — because what belongs to one's nature "runs" toward and upon one.

8. al-jariyy: (a) an agent or proxy (wakīl) — one form for masculine, feminine, singular and plural; verbal noun jarāya/jirāya; jarrā = to appoint as proxy (Abū Ḥātim allows a rare feminine jariyya); (b) a messenger (one "dispatched," ajrāhu, on an errand); (c) a hired worker (ajīr, from Kurāʿ).

9. al-jāriya: a young/youthful woman, with evident jarāya (youthfulness); several verbal-noun forms, one from Ibn al-Aʿrābī.

10. al-jirriyy: a kind of fish. al-jirriyya: a bird's crop/gizzard. If treated as biliteral, these follow the patterns fuʿlā and fuʿliyya (handled under the biliteral roots).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
ROOT ج ر ز (j-r-z) — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004 CE)

Ibn Fāris states the root has one core meaning: cutting (al-qaṭʿ). "Jarazttu ash-shay'a" = "I cut the thing."

From this core sense, the entry traces several derived uses:

1. Sharpness/cutting power: a sayf jurāz ("cutting sword") is one that cuts very well.

2. Barren land: arḍ juruz is land with no vegetation, as if growth had been cut off from it. Al-Kisā'ī and al-Aṣma'ī are cited on the related form arḍ majrūzah: it means land that rain never reached, or (alternate gloss) land whose plant growth has been eaten away entirely.

3. A voracious eater: al-jarūz describes a man (or, in the feminine, a woman or she-camel) who leaves nothing behind when eating — everything is "cut away" / consumed. A verse is quoted describing an old woman as "cunning and voracious" (jarūzā).

4. Total destruction (proverb): "A hating woman will not be satisfied except with a jarzah" — i.e., out of the intensity of her hatred and envy, nothing short of complete uprooting/annihilation of those she hates will satisfy her. Jarzah here carries the sense of a total cutting-off.

5. A rasping cough: al-jāriz is severe coughing, explained as "cutting" the throat. Ash-Shammākh's line is cited describing a rasp in the nasal passage and nostrils.

6. Harsh terrain: arḍ jārizah is dry, hard, rugged land ringed by sand.

7. Barrenness (of a woman): imra'ah jāriz means a barren woman.

8. Ibn Fāris's own analogical note: the expression dhū jaraz, used of something thick and hard (and applied to a camel in the same way), is — in his judgment — derived by analogy from sense 6, the "rugged hard land" (al-arḍ al-jārizah al-ghalīẓah), rather than being an independent sense.

Throughout, Ibn Fāris ties every branch back to the single idea of "cutting": cutting with a blade, land cut off from rain/growth, a person who cuts food down to nothing, a proverbial cutting-off of mercy, a cough that cuts the throat, and hard terrain/objects understood by extension from that cut, unyielding land.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ج-س-د as one core notion with a short list of derived uses.

1. Core sense. The three letters point to a thing's gathering/coalescing together, and to its hardening or becoming compact. (He marks this as "likewise," i.e. sharing the notion of the preceding root entry.)

2. جَسَد (jasad) — the human body: given as the primary instance of that notion of a mass gathered and firm.

3. مِجْسَد (mijsad) — the piece of clothing worn next to the body.

4. Dried blood. جَسَد / جَسِد used of blood means blood that has dried; the participle is جَاسِد. Citation: the poet al-Ṭirimmāḥ — "of it [there is] congealed [blood] and fresh gore" — contrasting clotted blood with still-flowing blood. Ibn Fāris also reports an alternative distribution held by some: جَسَد = the blood itself, while جَسِد = specifically the dried blood.

5. An outlier. جَسَاد (jasād) meaning saffron is flagged by him as departing from (شَذَّ عَن) the chapter's governing sense — he does not force it back into the "gathering/hardening" idea.

6. Grammatical/school dispute over vowelling. With kasra on the mīm, مِجْسَد is the garment next to the body — a usage he attributes to the Kufan grammarians. The Basrans, he reports, recognise only مُجْسَد (ḍamma on the mīm), which for them means a garment steeped/saturated with dye.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: j-s-m (ج-س-م), from Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha.

Core idea: the jīm-sīn-mīm root signals the gathering or coming-together of a thing into one mass.

1. al-jism (الجِسْم) — "body, physical form." Citing Ibn Duraid, defined as "every perceptible individual" (كل شخص مدرك) — i.e., any discrete thing that can be perceived by the senses.
2. al-jasīm (الجَسِيم), also al-jusām (الجُسَام) — an adjective describing something "great/large in body": bulky, large-bodied.
3. al-jusmān (الجُسْمَان) — a synonym for "the individual" or "the person/body" (الشَّخْص).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats j-s-s as a single root meaning (aṣl wāḥid): coming to know a thing through a light, gentle touch.

1. **Feeling with the hand.** One says jasastu al-ʿirq, "I felt the vein," and the same is said of other things; the verbal noun is jass.

2. **The spy.** al-jāsūs, "spy," is formed from this root on the pattern fāʿūl, because a spy finds out what he wants in secret and with subtlety.

3. **The senses.** al-Khalīl is reported as saying that the senses (ḥawāss), a person's faculties of perception, were sometimes called jawāss.

4. **Feeling out with the eye.** Ibn Durayd says jass can also be done with the eye, and the entry takes this as confirming al-Khalīl's report. The verse cited: "They banded together, then felt him out with their eyes."

dictionary: Lane — Arabic-English Lexicon, Edward William Lane (d. 1876)
text:
Lane's article on ج-ث-م (with the related ج-ث-و / ج-ث-ى appended).

CORE VERB — جَثَمَ / جَثُمَ (verbal nouns جُثُوم, جَثْم)

1. Of a bird — and of a hare, sometimes a gazelle or a fawn (خِشْف), also a camel, a jerboa, or a man: to cleave to the ground; or to stay put, not leaving one's place; or to fall upon the breast. Lane records the lexicographers' calibration: جُثُوم for a bird or hare is what بُرُوك (couching) is for a camel; or, per the Mughrib, what جُلُوس (sitting) is for a man — i.e. the bird simply "sat."
2. Of standing crops: to rise a little above the ground.
3. Of a palm's fruit-cluster (Abū Ḥanīfa al-Dīnawarī): its unripe dates grew somewhat large; or (Tahdhīb) it grew large and stayed in place.
4. Of the night (Thaʿlab), figuratively: it became half spent.
5. Separately: to collect together clay or mould, earth or dust, and ashes.

DERIVED FORMS
- Form II جثّم: to pin a bird or hare to the ground so it can then be shot or pelted to death; to keep a bird confined until it dies. (Golius adds: to turn an animal on its side for slaughter — a sense Lane could not find in his own copy of the source.)
- Form V تجثّم: of a bird, to mount the female.

NOUNS FROM THE "CLINGING/SETTLING" SENSE
- جَثْم / جَثَم: crops just risen above the ground; also a date-cluster whose fruit has grown somewhat large.
- جُثْمَة: clay, earth and ashes gathered in a heap.
- جُثُوم: (a) plural of جَاثِم; (b) a low hill (أَكَمَة) — likewise جَثَمَة, جَثْمَة.
- مَجْثَم / مَجْثِم (pl. مَجَاثِم): the spot where a bird or the like settles; specifically a hare's form or lair.
- مُجَثَّمَة: an animal pinned or propped up as a target and then shot or pelted until dead. Lane records that this way of killing was forbidden; variant definitions: any animal set up and pelted to death (Abū ʿUbayd); a sheep or goat shot with arrows (ʿIkrima); a sheep or goat stoned to death and then eaten (Shammar).

THE BODY SENSE
- جُثْمَان: the body with its limbs (جِسْم), and also شَخْص, a person. The lexicographers differ: al-Aṣmaʿī assigns "person" to جُثْمَان and "body" to جُسْمَان; Abū Zayd treats the two as synonyms. Idiom: مَا أَحْسَنَ جُثْمَانَ الرَّجُلِ, "how fine the man's body/person is!" Poetic evidence: al-Jawharī cites Bishr — "a hump, long-necked, like the جُثْمَان of the بَنِيَّة," glossing بَنِيَّة as the Kaʿba; Ibn Barrī corrects the reading to البَلِيَّة, the she-camel tethered at a dead man's grave and left to die, so the sense is "a hump like that camel's body." Also the proverb-like phrase "he brought us broth-soaked bread heaped up like the body of a sand-grouse."
- جُثْمَانِيَّة المَاء, in a line of al-Farazdaq (misattributed in Qāmūs copies): the water itself, or its middle, or the place where it pooled. Lane flags an unresolved difficulty in the line's phrase إلى ذات رحل, and notes printing errors in the Cairo Qāmūs.

THE NIGHTMARE / IMMOBILITY SENSE
- جُثَام — with synonyms جَاثُوم, جَثَّامَة, جُثَم, جُثَمَة — the incubus or night-pressing that comes on a sleeper; per Ibn al-Aʿrābī, what comes on a man at night and stops him speaking (= نَيْدُلَان).

ACTIVE PARTICIPLE AND INTENSIVES
- جَاثِم: a bird, hare, gazelle, camel, jerboa, or man clinging to the ground, staying put, or fallen on its breast; also sitting on its legs like a bird. Plural جُثُوم. Intensives: جَثُوم and جَثَّام (doing this often), جَثَّامَة (very often). جَثُوم by extension is also a name for the hare.
- Qurʾānic evidence: فَأَصْبَحُوا فِى دَارِهِمْ جَاثِمِينَ (7:78 and parallels) — Lane's gloss: "bodies cast upon the ground"; al-Bayḍāwī: extinct or motionless, and dead.
- Astronomical use, figurative: الجُثُوم, the stars of Scorpio, also called البُرُك.
- جَثَّامَة, figuratively: a man who sticks to settled country and does not travel; one who sleeps much and does not travel (so too جُثَمَة, جُثَم, جَاثُوم); also dull or ineffective in affairs; and, in another direction, a forbearing chief or man of rank.
- جَاثِمَة (al-Layth): one who never leaves his house or tent.

APPENDED ROOT ج-ث-و / ج-ث-ى — kneeling and heaping

1. جَثَا / جَثَى على ركبتيه (جُثُوّ, جُثِيّ): to sit on the knees, characteristically in contention or disputation; Abū Zayd: to kneel, the posture of a disputant; elsewhere described as putting the knees down and raising the buttocks, or the sitting posture of one reciting the tashahhud. Alternative sense: to stand on the tips of the toes — Abū ʿUbayda derives this from جَذَا by substituting ث for ذ, while Ibn Jinnī treats the two as parallel dialect forms. Shāhid: Abū Thumāma — "I dispute with them standing one time, and drop to my knees when they drop to theirs."
2. Same root, separate sense: جَثَوْتُ / جَثَيْتُ — I gathered camels and sheep or goats.
3. Form III جَاثَيْتُهُ: to sit knee-to-knee with someone in dispute. Form VI تَجَاثَوْا على الرُّكَب: to sit together on the knees in contention; also التَّجَاثِى فِى إِشَالَةِ الحَجَرِ, competing at lifting a stone for strength.
4. جُثْوَة (also جِثْوَة, جَثْوَة): stones heaped together; earth-stones heaped like a grave-mound; a hillock or heap of earth; and hence a grave (tradition: "I saw the martyrs' tombs as heaps of earth"). Also, per Ibn al-Aʿrābī, the middle of a thing; per Shammar, the body (جَسَد); per Ibn Shumayl, a big man. Yaʿqūb holds that in the sense of a live coal it is جَذْوَة with ث substituted for ذ.
5. جُثَى الحَرَم: the Ṣiḥāḥ says these are the collected pebbles of the jimār at Minā; the Qāmūs (following al-Ṣaghānī) calls that an error and defines them as stones heaped at the boundaries of the sacred territory, or the أَنْصَاب on which victims were slaughtered.
6. جُثًا also = a company or congregated body of people, and its plural. Traditions: people "shall become جُثًا on the day of resurrection, each community following its prophet"; and "so-and-so is of the جُثَى of Jahannam" (variant: of those kneeling therein). Lane notes a report that الجُثَا was also the name of an idol to which sacrifices were made.
7. جَثَاء / جُثَاء: a person or body (شَخْص) — and perhaps hence, the nightmare; also requital (جَزَاء); also quantity, size, bulk, or number, e.g. of a company of men.
8. جَاثٍ: kneeling — or standing on the toe-tips; plurals جُثِيّ, جِثِيّ (al-Rāghib allows these to be verbal nouns used adjectivally). Qurʾānic evidence: 19:72 وَنَذَرُ الظَّالِمِينَ فِيهَا جُثِيًّا, "we shall leave the wrongdoers in it, kneeling"; 45:28 وَتَرَى كُلَّ أُمَّةٍ جَاثِيَةً, "you shall see every community kneeling" — al-Bayḍāwī: upright and ill at ease; or, alternatively, "gathered in a body," from جَثْوَة "company." Hence the name of Sūrat al-Jāthiya, the 45th sūra. الجَاثِى (على ركبتيه) also names the constellation Hercules.
9. مَجْثًى: a place of kneeling.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris holds that j-th indicates the gathering together of a thing, and calls this a sound derivation (qiyās ṣaḥīḥ).

1. **The body.** al-juththa is a person's body when he is sitting or asleep.

2. **A mound.** al-juthth is a raised, gathered mass of ground, like a hillock. Ibn Durayd reckons that a man's juththa comes from this.

3. **Debris in honey; wax.** al-jathth is said to be the debris that mixes with honey, as in a verse by al-Hudhalī: "The ropes did not stop until they had set him down beside the swarm, clearing away its jathth and smoking it out." It is also said that al-jathth is wax; the derivation, Ibn Fāris says, is the same.

4. **Abundant growth.** nabt juthājith is abundant vegetation, and Ibn Fāris suggests that al-jathjāth may come from this.

5. **Fright.** juthithtu min al-rajul, "I was frightened of the man," because a frightened person draws himself together.

6. **Uprooting.** Ibn Fāris imagines someone asking how the following fit this principle: jathathtu al-shayʾ and ijtathathtuhu, "I pulled the thing up by the roots," al-jathīth, "a palm offshoot," and al-mijaththa, "the iron tool for pulling things out." He answers that they follow the same derivation, since a thing counts as majthūth, "uprooted," only when it has been pulled out with all its roots and rootlets, so that nothing of it is left; in this way, he says, they go back to the principle he laid down.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
text:
Root ج ث و (j-th-w) — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144 CE)

1. Core verb — "to kneel." جثا على ركبتيه جثواً: "he knelt on his knees." The active participle is جاثٍ (jāthin, "kneeling"): "I saw him kneeling before him" (رأيته جاثياً بين يديه). The entry quotes the Qur'anic phrase وترى كل أمة جاثية, "and you will see every community kneeling." The plural جُثِيّ (juthiyy) appears in "I saw them kneeling at his place" (رأيتهم جثياً عنده).

2. Kneeling before a judge/litigant. A ḥadīth is cited: "I am the first to kneel for the litigation, before God — Exalted is He — on the Day of Resurrection" (أنا أول من يجثو للخصومة بين يدي الله تعالى يوم القيامة). This sense is extended in two derived forms:
   - تجاثوا على الركب — "they knelt together, on their knees" (reciprocal, Form VI).
   - جاثى خصمه مجاثاة — "he knelt facing his adversary" (Form III, verbal noun مجاثاة, mujāthāh) — i.e. two disputants kneeling opposite one another in confrontation.

3. Noun جَثْوَة (jathwa) — "a mound/heap [of earth]," extended to mean a grave-mound: وصار فلان جثوة من تراب, "so-and-so became a mound of dust" (i.e. died, and his grave became a heap of earth). This is supported by a line of poetry attributed to Ṭarafa: "You see two mounds of dust, upon which are solid slabs of arranged flagstone" (ترى جثوتين من تراب عليهما صفائح صم من صفيح منضد) — describing two grave-mounds capped with flat stones.

In sum: the root's basic sense is physical kneeling (on the knees), specialized for kneeling before a judge or opponent in a dispute, and extended by metaphor to a heaped mound of earth, as over a grave.

dictionary: Lane — Arabic-English Lexicon, Edward William Lane (d. 1876)
text:
**Root ج و ع (j-w-ʿ) — Lane's Lexicon**

Lane's article treats this root as denoting hunger — emptiness of the belly — and its extension to intense longing.

**1. جَاعَ (Form I) — to be or become hungry, empty in the belly.** Verbal nouns جَوْعٌ and مَجَاعَةٌ; جُوعٌ is either a verbal noun or, as some hold, a simple noun. Lane defines it by its opposite: it is the contrary of شَبِعَ, "to be satiated."

**2. Figurative extension — to hunger *for* something.** جَاعَ إِلَيْهِ / جَاعَ إِلَى لِقَائِهِ: to desire and long to meet someone, as though hungering for him; Lane marks this as tropical and compares عَطِشَ, "to thirst." Likewise جَاعَ إِلَى مَالِهِ, "he longed for his property" (attributed to Abū Zayd).

**3. أَجَاعَهُ / جَوَّعَهُ (Forms IV and II) — to make someone hungry.** Either to constrain him to hunger, or (per al-Miṣbāḥ) to debar him from food and drink. Illustrated by the proverb أَجِعْ كَلْبَكَ يَتْبَعْكَ, "Make your dog hungry and he will follow you" — glossed as: keep the base man in need of you so that he stays with you, since a man who needs nothing from you will leave.

**4. تَجَوَّعَ (Form V) — to make oneself hungry deliberately.** Used of fasting the stomach before taking medicine: تَجَوَّعْ لِلدَّوَآءِ, i.e. empty the stomach, or eat less than a full meal, before treatment.

**5. اِسْتَجَاعَ (Form X) — to show hunger.** Extended figuratively in اِسْتِجَاعَةُ العِلْمِ, being insatiable for knowledge.

**6. The nouns of hunger: جُوعٌ, مَجَاعَةٌ, مَجْوَعَةٌ, مَجُوعَةٌ.** All signify hunger or emptiness of the belly, the contrary of شِبَعٌ (satiety). Usages Lane records:
- جُوعًا لَهُ وَنُوعًا — an imprecation, "hunger to him"; Sībawayh explains the accusative as governed by an understood verb, and the order is fixed because نُوعًا merely corroborates. Some take نُوعٌ to mean "thirst."
- عَامُ مَجَاعَةٍ / عَامُ المَجَاعَةِ — "a (the) year of famine"; plurals مَجَائِعُ and مَجَاوِعُ, as in "famines befell them."
- الرَّضَاعَةُ مِنَ المَجَاعَةِ — cited from al-Mughrib: the suckling that creates the marriage bar is the one that answers an infant's hunger with milk, not the stage when only solid food would satisfy the child. (Lane reports this as a juristic gloss of the phrase, from that source.)
- سَمَنُ كَلْبٍ بِجُوعِ أَهْلِهِ — "the dog grows fat by its owners' hunger," said of a household reduced to want by cattle-plague; alternatively explained as referring to a man named Kalb who pledged his family, then made off with the pledgees' cattle. Also related as سَمِنَ كَلْبٌ بِبُؤْسِ أَهْلِهِ.

**7. جَوْعَةٌ** — a single, passing pang of hunger; also the destitution and hunger of a whole tribe.

**8. The participles: جَائِعٌ and جَوْعَانُ — "hungry."** Lane notes the colloquial جَيْعَانُ is an error. Feminines جَائِعَةٌ and جَوْعَى; plurals جُوَّعٌ, جُيَّعٌ (with و shifting to ى), جِيَاعٌ, جَاعَةٌ, and جَيَاعَى (this last irregular, possibly a copyist's error for جِيَاعٌ). The phrase جَائِعٌ نَائِعٌ pairs the word with a rhyming echo-word, which some instead take to mean "thirsty."
Two tropical idioms: رَجُلٌ جَائِعُ القِدْرِ, "a man whose cooking-pot goes unfilled," and اِمْرَأَةٌ جَائِعَةُ الوِشَاحِ, "a woman hungry of the girdle," i.e. slender-waisted.

**9. مَجَاعٌ — hunger as a measure of distance.** هُوَ مِنِّى عَلَى قَدْرِ مَجَاعِ الشَّبْعَانِ: "he is as far from me as the distance in which a well-fed man grows hungry," with the parallel expression for a man's growing thirsty after drinking his fill.

**10. مُسْتَجِيعٌ** — one who always appears hungry; or, on Abū Saʿīd's account, one perpetually eating one thing after another.

Note on method: Lane's entry is a compilation, and each sense carries a source-tag (al-Ṣiḥāḥ, al-Qāmūs, al-Miṣbāḥ, the Lisān, al-Zamakhsharī, and others), so competing definitions are set side by side rather than reconciled.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: ٱسْتَجَابَ 28x "respond"; أُجِيبَت 8x "respond"; جَوَاب 4x "(the) answer"; مُّجِيب 2x "(are we as) responders"; جَابُ 1x "carved out"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives root ج و ب (j-w-b) from two origins.

FIRST ORIGIN — "to pierce / cut through a thing" (خرق).
1. Traversing ground: جُبْتُ الأرضَ = "I cut across the land"; the agent is جائب / جوّاب, a great traverser. He cites al-Jaʿdī: one who "cuts through the gloom of night, a sturdy traverser of the wilderness."
2. Extended idiom: جائبةُ خبرٍ = a piece of news that "travels through" the lands.
3. Derivatives from the piercing sense: the جَوْبة, a hollow / low patch of ground, counted here because it is like a hole cut in the earth; the جَوْب, a woman's coat of mail, called مَجوب ("worked/pierced"), named from the verbal noun; and the مِجْوَب, an iron tool used for stitching leather.

SECOND ORIGIN — "the exchange / returning of speech," i.e. answering.
4. كلّمه فأجابه جوابًا = "he spoke to him and he answered him"; تجاوبا = they answered one another. The مُجابة is the answer.
5. Proverb: أساء سمعًا فأساء جابةً — "he heard wrong, so he answered wrong" (jābah = a verbal noun for answering).
6. Poetic shāhid, al-Kumayt (rebuking Quḍāʿa for shifting allegiance to Yemen): the one you call on for help "is no quicker to answer you than the hadīl [cooing]."
7. Ibn Fāris appends the lore behind hadīl: a chick in Noah's ark flew out, fell into the water and drowned, and the birds are said to weep for it; hence the closing verse mourning "Hadīl, who perished before Tubbaʿ ever existed."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ج و د (j-w-d), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: generosity with a thing, and abundance of giving.

1. rajul jawād — a manifestly generous man; qawm ajwād — a generous people.
2. al-jawd — heavy, abundant rain.
3. al-jawād — the swift, fleet-footed horse (plural jiyād), tied to the Qur'anic citation Sad 38:31, "idh ʿuriḍa ʿalayhi bi-l-ʿashiyyi al-ṣāfinātu al-jiyād" — "when there were displayed before him in the evening the standing, swift-footed horses." The verbal noun is al-jawdah.
4. Closing idiom: "fulānun yujādu ilā kadhā" — so-and-so is "driven/urged" toward something — as though he were being led toward it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ج-و-ف (j-w-f) as expressing a single underlying idea: the interior, hollow, or cavity of a thing.

1. Core sense — jawf (جَوْف): the inside/cavity of something. Examples given: jawf al-insān, "the interior of a person" (i.e. the body's cavity), and jawf kulli shayʾ, "the interior of anything [at all]" — i.e. the word applies generally, not just to the body.

2. Derived usage — ṭaʿnah jāʾifah (طَعْنَةٌ جَائِفَةٌ): a stab-wound is called jāʾifah specifically when it penetrates through to the jawf, the body's interior cavity.

3. Derived usage — qidr jawfāʾ (قِدْرٌ جَوْفَاءُ): a cooking-pot described as jawfāʾ is one that is wide/spacious inside (wāsiʿat al-jawf).

4. A place-name — Jawf ʿAyr: a locale that a man named Ḥimār kept as his own protected preserve (ḥimā).

5. A proverb built on this place-name: "أَخْلَى مِنْ جَوْفِ عَيْرٍ" — "Emptier than the jawf of ʿAyr." Ibn Fāris explains its origin as a man who used to guard a valley belonging to him [so effectively that it stood empty of others]. He notes the fuller account of this story is given in al-Khalīl's Kitāb al-ʿAyn.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يُجِيرُ 6x "then grant him protection"; جَار 3x "and the neighbor"; ٱسْتَجَارَ 1x "seek your protection"; مُّتَجَٰوِرَٰت 1x "neighboring"; جَائِر 1x "(are) crooked"; يُجَاوِرُ 1x "they will remain your neighbors"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ج و ر (j-w-r) as having a single core meaning: **swerving or deviation from the road**. The verb is jāra / jawr.

1. **Core sense — swerving off the path.** jāra, jawran = "to deviate from the way."

2. **A related use — felling.** ṭaʿanahu fa-jawwarahu = "he thrust at him and knocked him down (felled him)." Ibn Fāris suggests this may actually be a case of letter-substitution (ibdāl), with the jīm standing in for a kāf (i.e. borrowed from the root k-w-r).

3. **An anomalous form.** al-ghayth al-jiwarr = "copious/heavy rain." He notes this does not fit the core root and is exceptional (shādhdh). He proposes it may instead belong to a different root, ج ء ر (j-ʾ-r): Ibn al-Sikkīt reported the variant juʾar (pattern fuʿal). On that reading it would come from juʾār ("a cry / roar"), as if the rain "roars" when it strikes the ground. He cites a line of verse as evidence: "Do not give it to drink the downpour of a rumbling, roaring [cloud]."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris gives the root ج-و-س (j-w-s) a single core meaning: to interpenetrate or move back and forth through something (takhallul al-shayʾ).

1. Core sense — ranging/passing through: The Arabs say jāsū khilāla l-diyāri yajūsūna, 'they ranged/moved back and forth through the dwellings.' Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'anic verse {fa-jāsū khilāla l-diyār}, 'so they ranged through the houses' (al-Isrāʾ 17:5), as the exemplar of this usage.

2. A look-alike word that is NOT part of this root: al-jūs (الجُوس). Ibn Fāris explicitly excludes it from the root's meaning, explaining it is merely an itbāʿ — a rhyming echo-word tacked onto al-jūʿ ('hunger') for emphasis, with no independent meaning of its own. This is shown by the expression jūʿan lahū wa-jūsan lahū ('hunger to him, and jūsan to him'), where jūsan simply rhymes with and intensifies jūʿan and carries no separate sense.

So, per this entry, the root's one true meaning is 'to pass/range through' something, as in the Qur'anic phrase about ranging through houses; the similar-sounding al-jūs is a false lead the author flags and sets aside.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats j-w-w (the jīm and the wāw) as a single meaning: something that encloses something else from its sides.

1. **al-jaww, the jaww of the sky**: what arches over the earth on its sides.
2. **jaww al-bayt, the jaww of a house**, belongs to the same meaning.
3. **al-juʾjuʾ, the chest**, has a hamza, but Ibn Fāris allows that it may be taken with this meaning.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: جَاوَزَ 4x "he crossed it"; نَتَجَاوَزُ 1x "and we will overlook"
poets_named: Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); Aws ibn Maghrāʾ (pre-Islamic); al-Quṭāmī (Umayyad)
text:
Ibn Fāris traces ج و ز (j-w-z) to two distinct base ideas: (1) cutting through or crossing something, and (2) the middle of something.

Sense 1 — the middle:
- جَوْز (jawz) of anything = its middle part.
- الْجَوْزَاء (al-jawzāʾ) = a ewe whose middle is white.
- الْجَوْزَاء is also a star/constellation (Orion/Gemini). Ibn Fāris reports two explanations: some held it was named so because it crosses the jawz of the sky, i.e. its middle; others because of the three stars in its middle.

Sense 2 — crossing / passing through:
- جُزْتُ الْمَوْضِع = I travelled through a place.
- أَجَزْتُهُ = I passed it, left it behind, cut across it; also, I carried it through / made it go through.
- Poetic witness (Imruʾ al-Qays): "when we had passed beyond the open ground of the encampment," a lowland with sand ridges and a heaped dune drew them on.
- Poetic witness (Aws ibn Maghrāʾ): "until it is said: let the family of Ṣafwān pass" — praise for their granting passage to pilgrims (ḥājj), i.e. the causative form ijāza = enabling others to cross.

Derived sense within Sense 2 — a granted watering:
- الْجَوَاز (al-jawāz) = the water given to livestock and cultivated land.
- اسْتَجَزْتُ فُلَانًا فَأَجَازَنِي = I asked someone for such water and he gave it to me, for my land or my animals.
- Poetic witness (al-Quṭāmī): Fuqaym holds the water, so ask ʿUbāda for a turn; "the one who asks for water is on a qutr" — glossed by Ibn Fāris as a side or edge.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root ج-ي-أ (jīm–yāʾ–hamza) as covering two senses that are not derivable from one another:

1. "Coming." جَاءَ / يَجِيءُ / مَجِيئًا (jāʾa / yajīʾu / majīʾan) — to come, with its imperfect and verbal noun. He notes the construction جَاءَانِي فَجِئْتُهُ (jāʾānī fa-jiʾtuhu): "he outdid me in frequency of coming [and I outdid him]" — a competitive form built on repeated coming. The verbal noun (maṣdar) of جَاءَ is الْجَيْئَةُ (al-jayʾa).

2. Gathered water. الْجِئَةُ (al-jiʾa) is a place where water collects around a fortress or the like; a variant form is جِيِّئَةٌ (jiyyiʾa), with a kasra and a doubled letter.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ج ي ب (j-y-b) as a substitution-variant (ibdāl) of another root — its yā' standing in for an original wāw, meaning the 'true' root is ج و ب (j-w-b).

1. Core noun: al-jayb is the jayb of a shirt/garment — the opening (e.g. at the neck or bosom).

2. Verb jibtu al-qamīṣa — 'I cut/hollowed out the shirt's opening' (qawwartu jaybahu).

3. Verb jayyabtuhu — 'I made an opening (jayb) for it' (a garment).

4. Etymological note: because the root's true radical is wāw (not yā'), the underlying sense of the verb is kharaqtu — 'I tore/pierced/cut through' — i.e. jayb as 'opening' derives from the idea of piercing or cutting a garment open.

Ibn Fāris cross-references his earlier, fuller discussion of the root ج و ب (j-w-b) for more on this sense.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives jīm-yāʾ-dāl from a single core meaning: the neck.

1. Core sense — jīd = "neck"; plural ajyād.
2. Derived terms — al-jayd = length of the neck (i.e. having a long neck as a trait); al-jaydāʾ = a woman who is long-necked.
3. A poetic exception — in a line by the poet al-Aʿshā, "the men of Iyād bi-ajyādihā," the word ajyād is said NOT to mean "necks" here. Ibn Fāris notes it is instead an arabicized foreign word, and that the poet meant "cloaks/garments" by it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ج-ز-أ (j-z-ʾ) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: "being content with / made sufficient by a thing" (al-iktifāʾ bi-sh-shayʾ).

1. Verb forms built on this idea:
   - اجتزأ بـ (ijtazaʾa bi-) — "to content oneself with" something.
   - أجزأ (ajzaʾa) — "to be sufficient for someone" ("the thing sufficed me").
   Ibn Fāris cites a line of poetry where a man swears he will never betray his people even in a year of drought and even if offered valuable she-camels, "for the free/noble man makes do (يَجْزَأُ) with mere livestock" — i.e., he is content with little rather than betray anyone.

2. الجُزْء (al-juzʾ) as a verbal noun: a grazing animal's not needing to drink water, because the moist, fresh pasture it eats already gives it enough moisture.

3. On Qurʾan 43:15 — "And they assigned to Him a juzʾ (portion/share) from among His servants": Ibn Fāris reports that some scholars connected this juzʾ to the present root's sense, since it was the polytheists' way of saying God had "made do with" giving Himself daughters rather than sons, i.e., taken a "portion" for Himself from His creation. He follows this immediately with the standard exalting formula, declaring God far above what the polytheists said. He attributes the etymological link to "some people" (nās), not stating it as his own conclusion.

4. الجُزْء (al-juzʾ) in the ordinary sense: "a part or portion of a thing."

5. An irregular derivative not fitting the root's usual pattern: الجُزْأَة (al-juzʾah), "the handle of a knife." The verb أجزأتُها (ajzaʾtuhā) means "I fitted it with a handle." Ibn Fāris suggests it may have been named this because a handle is a part/portion of the tool as a whole — linking it back, loosely, to sense 4.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) identifies two unrelated base meanings for the root ج-ز-ع (j-z-ʿ):

**1. "Cutting across / breaking off"**

- جَزَعْتُ الرَّمْلَةَ — "I crossed the sand-tract," i.e. cut across it.
- From this: جِزْعُ الْوَادِي (jizʿ al-wādī) — the spot in a valley where one crosses from one side to the other. It is also said to mean the valley's bend or turn — explained as the valley having departed from a straight course and curved.
- الْجَزَعُ (al-jazaʿ, "impatience/distress") is the opposite of ṣabr (endurance). It denotes the *cutting-off of one's strength* to bear what has struck one — i.e. one's capacity to endure "breaks off."
- الْجِزْعَة (al-jizʿa) — a small remaining quantity of water. Ibn Fāris notes this fits the same underlying pattern (something reduced/cut short).

**2. A type of gemstone**

- الْجَزْع (al-jazʿ) is the well-known banded bead/gem (agate-like, onyx).
- Expression: بُسْرَةٌ مُجَزَّعَةٌ (busra mujazzaʿa) — an unripe date whose ripening has reached the halfway point, so it shows two colors/bands, resembling the mottled jazʿ stone.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: جَزَىٰ 73x "we recompense"; جَزَاء 42x "a reward"; جِزْيَة 1x "the jizyah"; جَاز 1x "(can) avail"; نُجَٰزِى 1x "we recompense"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root j-z-y from a single core notion: one thing standing in the place of another and requiting or compensating it.

1. Requiting/recompensing. جَزَيْتُ فُلَانًا (I requited so-and-so), verbal noun جَزَاء; and the form-III جَازَيْتُهُ مُجَازَاةً (I recompensed him).

2. Sufficing / standing in for all. هَذَا رَجُلٌ جَازِيكَ مِنْ رَجُلٍ means "this man suffices you" — he stands in the stead of everyone. Ibn Fāris compares the parallel forms كَافِيكَ ("your sufficer") and نَاهِيكَ ("your deterrer"), the latter as if it forbids you to look for anyone besides him.

3. Discharging / settling a matter. جَزَى عَنِّي هَذَا الْأَمْرَ ("this matter discharged [the obligation] on my behalf"), paralleling قَضَى / يَقْضِي (to settle, discharge).

4. Exacting a debt. تَجَازَيْتُ دَيْنِي عَلَى فُلَانٍ = "I collected my debt from him." He notes a regional usage: the people of Medina call the one exacting payment (al-mutaqāḍī) al-mutajāzī.

Qurʾānic witness: Q 2:48, "…a day when no soul shall jazī for another soul in anything" — which Ibn Fāris glosses as lā taqḍī, "shall not discharge [anything on its behalf]," tying the verse to sense 3.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
text:
Root: k-sh-ṭ (كشط) — from the Tāj al-ʿArūs of Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791 CE)

1. **Core sense — stripping a covering off:** al-kashṭ is "lifting/removing a thing from [another] thing that had covered it" — e.g. stripping hide off a camel's hump or a flayed carcass (per Kitāb al-ʿAyn).

2. **Qur'anic citation, 81:11** — «إِذَا السَّمَاءُ كُشِطَتْ» ("when the sky is kushiṭat"). Al-Zajjāj: torn/uprooted away, like a roof torn off (a dialectal spelling qushiṭat, with qāf, carries the same sense). Al-Farrāʾ: removed, then rolled/folded up.

3. **Dialect note:** Quraysh say kashaṭa; Tamīm and Asad say qashaṭa — two independent tribal pronunciations, not one derived from the other (per Yaʿqūb).

4. **Ordinary usage:** to kashaṭa a covering off something, a hide off a slaughtered camel, or a saddle-cloth off a horse's back — meaning to tear it off, pull it away, and uncover what's beneath.

5. **The noun al-kishāṭ** (pattern of kitāb; qāf-form also used) names the removed covering itself — i.e. the stripped-off hide.

6. **Figurative sense:** al-kishāṭ / al-inkishāṭ also means "becoming uncovered." "His fright was kushiṭa" or inkashaṭa means his fear lifted — marked explicitly as a metaphorical (majāz) extension of the literal stripping sense.

7. **Al-Layth's note:** the stripped hide (kishāṭ) is sometimes draped back over the carcass; one then says "lift the kishāṭ off it so I can see the meat." He says this word is used specifically for the slaughtered camel.

8. **Al-Jawharī (al-Ṣiḥāḥ):** for a camel one says kashaṭtu (stripped its hide), not the generic salakhtu used for other animals — Arabs only say kashaṭtuhu or jaladtuhu of a camel.

9. **Al-kashaṭah:** the owners/co-sharers of a skinned camel.

10. **Illustrative anecdote(s):** A Bedouin finds people who have skinned a camel and covered it back with its kishāṭ; he asks "who are the kashaṭah?" hoping for a share, and they answer him in riddling nicknames rather than plain names — he decodes them ("O Kinānah, O Asad, O Bakr, feed us the meat!"). A parallel version (from Ibn Sīdah's al-Muḥkam) has a man ask the names of "the two strippers" (al-kāshiṭayn) — Kinānah and Asad — again answered with riddling epithets ("concealer of the splitting-blows" = Kinānah/quiver; "crusher of rivals" = Asad/lion), with some variant transmissions swapping in "O baldy" for "O Asad." These citations simply document kashaṭa/kāshiṭ being used for stripping a camel's hide.

11. **inkashaṭa al-rawʿ:** "the fright inkashaṭa" = it went away (al-Jawharī; figurative).

12. **Additional notes (mustadrak):**
   - Clouds that takashshaṭa in the sky: they broke apart and scattered.
   - Al-kashshāṭ = the butcher/slaughterer (same as al-kāshiṭ).
   - kashaṭa al-ḥarf = he removed/erased a letter from its place.
   - Ibn al-Makshūṭ is simply the name of a ḥadīth-transmitter, not a separate lexical sense.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: كَشَفَ 14x "we removed"; كَاشِف 3x "remover"; كَشْف 1x "(to) remove"; كَٰشِفَٰت 1x "removers"; كَاشِفَة 1x "any remover"
text:
Ibn Sīda's al-Muḥkam on the root ك-ش-ف (k-sh-f).

Core sense: kashf is raising a thing off whatever conceals or covers it — uncovering, laying bare. Verb kashafa/yakshifu (kashf); intensive kashshafa; reflexive/passive forms inkashafa and takashshafa (to be uncovered).

1. Uncovering / laying bare (physical). rayṭ kashīf = a thin garment that is uncovered or laid open. Poetic witness — Ṣakhr al-Ghayy describes a thundering cloud that "raises a cloak laid bare" for the distant lightning; Abū Ḥanīfa explains that a lightning-flash lights the cloud white, as if it had uncovered a garment.

2. Prosody. In the sarīʿ metre, "al-makshūf" ("the uncovered") is the foot mafʿūlun, derived from original mafʿūlāt: the tāʾ is dropped, leaving mafʿūlā, then converted in sarīʿ to mafʿūlun.

3. Disclosing a matter. kashafa al-amr = made it manifest, disclosed it. kashafahu ʿan al-amr = compelled him to disclose it.

4. al-kāshifa — a verbal noun (like ʿāfiya, khātima). On the Qur'anic phrase "laysa lahā min dūni-llāhi kāshifa," Ibn Sīda records three explanations: (a) it means kashf, an uncovering (none but God can uncover/remove it); (b) the hāʾ was added only to rhyme with "azifat al-āzifa" in the preceding verse; (c) the hāʾ is intensive (mubālagha). Thaʿlab reads it as: none uncovers the Hour but the Lord of the worlds — with the hāʾ intensive.

5. Hairline/forehead terms. kashfa = a turning-back of hair at the hairline (a noun like nazʿa); verb kashifa (kashaf), adjective akshaf. In the forehead, kashaf = the forelock receding without true baldness; or the forelock's hair going back before the crown (yāfūkh). kashfa also = a whorl at the front hairline, or upward-growing hairs forming no circle — held to be an ill omen.

6. Of land: takashshafat al-arḍ = patches of it dried out and withered.

7. Battle senses. al-akshaf = one carrying no shield, or one who does not stand firm in war. al-kushf = men who do not fight in earnest (no known singular). kashafa al-qawm = the people were routed (Ibn al-Aʿrābī, with a verse of praise: "nor did they break when a shouter alarmed the company").

8. al-kishāf (of camels). A she-camel conceiving out of her normal mating season; variously defined as the stallion covering her while she is not pregnant, or her being bred two (or more) consecutive years, or bred one year then rested two or three. Verb kashafat (kishāf); she is kashūf, plural kushuf; also akshafat, and akshafa al-qawm = their camels conceived thus. Used figuratively of war "conceiving out of season" (Zuhayr's verse of the war-mill that grinds, conceives, bears, and bears twins). Also akshafa al-kabsh al-naʿja = the ram mounted the ewe.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: كَذَّبَ 176x "denied"; كَذِب 33x "a lie"; كَٰذِب 32x "the liars"; مُّكَذِّبِين 21x "to the deniers"; كَذَبَ 11x "lied"; كَذَّاب 5x "a liar"; كِذَّاب 2x "(with) denial"; مَكْذُوب 1x "(to) be belied"; تَكْذِيب 1x "denial"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats k-dh-b (ك ذ ب) as a single sound root meaning the opposite of truthfulness. He defines its core precisely: speech that "falls short of the utmost limit of veracity."

1. Core sense — falsehood. al-kadhib is the opposite of al-ṣidq (truthfulness): kadhaba kadhiban ("he lied"). Derived verbs: kadhdhabtu fulānan = I accused him of lying / gave him the lie; akdhabtuhu = I found him to be a liar. Intensive forms for a habitual liar: kadhdhāb and kudhaba.

2. Extended sense — failing to make good on something. Of a warrior: ḥamala thumma kadhaba/kadhdhaba, "he charged, then 'lied'" — i.e., did not press the attack home. Ibn Fāris cites Abū Duʾād on a wild ass that "lied" (held back) even though it did rush.

3. Of a she-camel's milk. kadhaba labanu al-nāqa is reported to mean the milk "lied" = went away / dried up. Ibn Fāris flags this as doubtful (fīhi naẓar) but grants that it fits the root's logic.

4. Not tarrying. mā kadhdhaba fulān an faʿala kadhā = he did not delay in doing it. He counts all these as branches of the one root.

5. A separate idiom — incitement (ighrāʾ). The Arabs say kadhaba ʿalayka kadhā / kadhdhabaka kadhā to urge someone on: "take to it!" or "it has become incumbent on you." He quotes the ḥadīth "kadhaba ʿalaykumu al-ḥajj" as meaning "it has become obligatory," reported as attested Arab usage (attributed here to the ḥadīth and to the Arabs, not asserted as a legal definition). Two lines of verse illustrate it: a Dhubyānī woman urging her sons that "the coverlets and milk-vessels have 'lied'" (go seize them), and another poet's "I 'lied' upon you — threaten me…"

Ibn Fāris closes with a personal caveat: he thinks this incitement usage belongs to archaic speech that has died out along with the people who spoke and understood it.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: Al-Akhṭal (Umayyad); Umayya b. Abī al-Ṣalt (pre-Islamic) ×2; al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); ʿAlqama (pre-Islamic); Umayya (pre-Islamic); Sībawayh (unnamed); Muhalhil (pre-Islamic); al-Jaʿdī (disputed date); al-Khansāʾ (lived into Islam); Jarīr (Umayyad); Abū Duʾād al-Iyādī (pre-Islamic)
text:
Root: ك أ س (k-ʾ-s), the word kaʾs, "cup." Ibn Manẓūr's account.

Form and gender
- Ibn al-Sikkīt groups kaʾs with faʾs (axe) and raʾs (head) as words properly written with hamza; the hamza is sometimes dropped in speech for ease.
- kaʾs is grammatically feminine; the proof cited is the Qur'anic phrase "with a cup from a flowing spring, white (bayḍāʾ)," where the adjective is feminine.
- Plurals: akʾus, kuʾūs, kiʾās. Al-Akhṭal: "moist with cups (kiʾās)…". Abū Ḥanīfa also reported a hamza-less plural kiyās; Ibn Manẓūr explains it, if sound, as a substitution: hamza → alif giving kās (pattern of nār), pluralised as kiwās, the wāw becoming yāʾ after the kasra.

Senses
1. The glass vessel, so long as there is drink in it.
2. The drink itself. Abū Ḥātim and al-Aṣmaʿī held this. Because of it al-Aṣmaʿī rejected the reading "death has a cup (li-l-mawti kaʾs)" in Umayya b. Abī al-Ṣalt's line, reading instead "death is a cup (al-mawt kaʾs)," cutting the conjunctive alif since it opens the second hemistich — a licence he allowed.
3. Wine itself, as a name for it (Ibn Sīda). Cited: Qur'an, "they are served with a cup from a flowing spring, white, a delight to the drinkers"; al-Aʿshā, "a cup like the eye of a cock…"; ʿAlqama, "a cup, prized, of the grapes, aged by a tavern-woman for one of its lords."
4. The vessel when wine is in it. Some restrict it: a glass with wine in it is a kaʾs; empty, it is a qadaḥ. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: it is not called kaʾs unless there is drink in it. Others say the word serves for one and for many alike. More broadly, kaʾs covers any vessel taken together with its drink. Ibn Manẓūr notes the word occurs in ḥadīth.
5. Metaphorical: a "cup" of any hardship — "he gave him a cup of humiliation," a cup of love, of separation, of death.

Grammatical notes
- On Umayya's "whoever does not die in the freshness of youth (ʿabṭa) dies in old age (haram)": Ibn Barrī explains ʿabṭa as "young, in his prime," and takes both accusatives either as verbal nouns with an elided governing noun ("a death of youth," "a death of old age"), or as circumstantial qualifiers ("possessing youth," "possessing old age"), again with elision.
- On ʿAlqama's line, Ibn Sīda notes two readings: kaʾsun ʿazīzun as adjective ("a prized cup," a wine grudged to any but kings and lords), versus the more familiar kaʾsu ʿazīzin by annexation, "the cup of a mighty owner/claimant" — the reading Sībawayh gives.
- Cutting the conjunctive alif at the start of a hemistich is common, that being a place of beginning; Sībawayh's example is "al-qidra yunziluhā bi-ghayri jiʿāl."

The "cup of death" citations
Against al-Aṣmaʿī, Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī defended annexing kaʾs to death, citing Muhalhil, "…given to drink from the cup of Ḥalāqi" (Ḥalāq being a name for death/fate). Ibn Manẓūr adds parallels: al-Jaʿdī, of a wild cow that killed a hunter's dogs, "until she gave him the cup of death and he was felled"; al-Khansāʾ, "he gives to drink, when the spear-shafts clash, the cup of death"; Jarīr, "we gave him the cup of death till he was gorged"; Abū Duʾād al-Iyādī, "given to drink from the cups of death in draughts."

Etymology suggested
Ibn Buzurj records kāṣa (with ṣād) "to take much of food and drink," and kaʾṣ (pattern of kaʿṣ) of a man persistent in his eating and drinking. Al-Azharī reckons kaʾs to be derived from that, since ṣād and sīn interchange in many words because their points of articulation are close.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: كَعْبَة 2x "the kabah"; كَعْبَيْن 1x "the ankles"; كَوَاعِب 1x "and splendid companions"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats k-ʿ-b as a single sound root whose core sense is protrusion and rising up in something. All the applications he lists are instances of that one idea:

1. **kaʿb — the ankle-bone.** The bone at the ends of the shank where foot and shank meet (i.e. the projecting knob there).

2. **al-Kaʿba — the House of God.** He reports that it is said to be so named for its protrusion and its four-sided (squared) shape.

3. **Dhū al-Kaʿabāt.** A house belonging to the tribe of Rabīʿa, which they used to circle in procession.

4. **kaʿba = an upper chamber/room.** Given as a reported alternative sense.

5. **kaʿabat al-marʾa (verbal noun kaʿāba), and she is kāʿib.** Said of a girl/woman when her breast becomes prominent.

6. **thawb mukaʿʿab** — a garment folded and tightly rolled up.

7. **burd mukaʿʿab** — a cloak with a square-patterned decorative figuring.

8. **kaʿb of a reed** — the internode, the segment of tube between two joints; and likewise the kuʿūb of a spear-shaft (its nodes). Poetic witness, ʿAntara: "So I thrust with the spear whose joints are solid — the noble man is not forbidden to the lances."

9. **kaʿb of clarified butter (samn)** — a lump of it.

Method: Ibn Fāris derives each usage — anatomical, architectural, textile, botanical, and of a measured lump of fat — from the single physical notion of a raised, projecting, or knot-like part, rather than treating them as unrelated homonyms. His note on the Kaʿba's name is given as a report ("it is said"), attached to shape (protruding, squared), not to any ritual definition.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: كَظِيم 3x "(is) filled with grief"; كَٰظِمِين 2x "choked"; مَكْظُوم 1x "(was) distressed"
text:
Root ك ظ م (k-ẓ-m), as al-Zamakhsharī presents it: a literal core of "swallowing down / stopping up / holding in," then a figurative extension to holding in one's breath and one's feelings. He marks the second group explicitly as majāz (figurative usage).

Literal senses
1. Of a camel: kaẓama l-baʿīru jirratahu — it swallowed its cud back down and stopped chewing it. Hence camels that pass the night not chewing the cud are kuẓūm / kawāẓim.
2. kaẓāma / kaẓīma (pl. kaẓāʾim) — a dug water-conduit: a shaft running from well to well, and also a watering-place or trough. He cites a ḥadīth: "he came to a people's kaẓāma and performed ablution," and a line of Ṭarafa comparing drinking the dregs of wine to drinkers gulping the water of a kaẓīma (the line is partly broken in the text). He notes al-shurb, "drinkers," is the plural of sharūb.
3. The irrigation channels of a vineyard are likewise called kaẓāʾim.
4. kaẓāmatā l-mīzān — the two rings at the ends of a balance-beam, to which the cords are tied.
5. kaẓama l-qirba — he filled the waterskin and stopped its mouth. kaẓama l-bāb — he blocked the door; kiẓām al-bāb is the thing that stops it up.

Figurative senses (his own heading: "and among the figurative")
6. kaẓama l-ghayẓ / kaẓama ʿalā l-ghayẓ — to hold in rage; the agent is kāẓim.
7. Reversed, with the emotion as subject: rage or grief "kaẓama" a man, i.e. seized his breath; he is then makẓūm or kaẓīm. Al-Zamakhsharī quotes two Qur'anic phrases as examples of exactly this: "when he called out while he was makẓūm," and "his face becomes darkened and he is kaẓīm" — that is, choked with suppressed feeling, on the physical image of the breath being caught.
8. mā kaẓama fulānun ʿalā jirratihi — literally "he did not keep his cud down": said of someone who cannot stay silent about what is inside him until he has blurted it out (the clause that follows is unclear in the text).
9. akhadha bi-kaẓamī — "he seized my kaẓam," the outlet of the breath (throat/windpipe); plural akẓām.
10. akhadhtu bi-kiẓām al-amr — to take hold of a matter by its secure, reliable grip.
11. Of a woman's anklet: kaẓīm, or she is kaẓīmat al-khalkhāl — the anklet is packed tight by the fullness of the leg. He cites a Hudhalī poet: "tight of anklet, bright of face, matched in beauty of form, complete."
12. jāʾa fa-kaẓama l-bāb — he came and stood in the doorway, blocking it with his own body.

The organising image throughout the entry is a passage held shut: cud kept down, a skin or door stopped up, a channel confining water, an anklet filled tight, and breath — and with it anger or grief — caught and held in.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats k-b as a sound root which, he says, indicates gathering and being gathered together, and he states that nothing in it departs from this.

1. **Gathered sand.** Sand that has gathered together is called kubāb; a verse speaks of "stirring up the clumped kubāb".

2. **Throwing face-down.** From this comes kababtu al-shayʾa li-wajhihi, "I threw the thing down on its face" (imperfect akubbu, verbal noun kabb).

3. **Bending over a task.** akabba ʿalā al-amr: a man "bends over" a matter he is doing.

4. **Camels collapsing.** Camels are said to takabbabat when they collapse from emaciation or disease.

5. **Tumbling down (kabkabah).** al-kabkabah is a thing's tumbling down when it is thrown into a pit, until it comes to rest. Ibn Fāris reads the doubled form as the throwing down repeated: "as though it went over and over in the kabb".

6. **Bundled up.** jāʾa mutakabkiban fī thiyābihi means "he came bundled up in his clothes".

7. **A ball of yarn.** al-kubbah is a ball of spun yarn.

8. **The main body of water.** Ibn Fāris places kawkab al-māʾ, the main body of the water, in this chapter.

9. **A troop of horses.** al-kabkabah is also a troop of horses.

10. **Star (kawkab).** The star is called kawkab, Ibn Fāris says, by this same analogy. Abū ʿUbaydah reports the saying "the people went off under every star" for people who have scattered.

11. **A boy near adolescence.** A boy nearing adolescence is called kawkab, because his frame has come together.

12. **Crowding.** al-kabbah is crowding.

13. **Uses by likening.** Calling a meadow's blossoms kawkab is, Ibn Fāris says, a likening that belongs under the heading of light. Al-Aʿshā describes a glistening blossom (kawkab) that "smiles back at the sun", wrapped about with luxuriant growth. The gleam of a squadron is likewise called kawkab.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root k-b-d (ك ب د) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: Ibn Fāris states that kāf-bāʾ-dāl is a sound root pointing to intensity (shidda) and strength (quwwa) in a thing. Every sense below is traced back to that core.

1. Hardship/toil — al-kabad (كَبَد) means mashaqqa, "toil, hardship." Usage: "so-and-so met kabad from this matter" = met hardship. The verb kābada means to endure something with hardship (kābadtu al-amra — "I bore the matter through hardship"). Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'an here: "We have certainly created man in kabad [toil/hardship]" (90:4).

2. The liver (al-kabid) — the organ, "well-known." He derives its name from the same root sense: it is called kabid because of its takabbud — its density/firmness/hardening, i.e., the same notion of intensity/solidity that underlies sense 1. Related forms:
   - al-akbad: someone whose liver-region protrudes.
   - kabadtu al-rajula: "I struck the man's liver," i.e., hit him there.
   - al-kubād: pain of the liver.

3. The "liver" of a bow (kabid al-qaws) — a metaphor borrowed from the human liver, naming the bow's grip/handle. A "liver-ed bow" (qaws kabdāʾ) is one whose grip fills the hand.

4. The "liver" of the sky (kabid al-samāʾ) — a further metaphor for the middle of the sky. A diminutive form, kubaydāʾ al-samāʾ (plural kubaydāt), is also used. From this comes the expression takabbadat al-shams — "the sun reached the kabid [middle/zenith] of the sky," i.e., it stood at its highest point.

5. Milk thickening — takabbada al-labanu means the milk grew thick and curdled, again the underlying sense of density/solidity.

Ibn Fāris thus treats "liver," "hardship," "bow-grip," "zenith of the sky," and "curdled milk" as branches of one core idea: something becoming dense, firm, or intensified.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
Root k-b-b (كبب) — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr

**1. Core sense — to overturn / throw face-down.** kabba (Form I) means to tip something over or throw it down on its face: kabba the vessel, kabba the bowl (turned it onto its rim), kabbahu li-wajhihi fa-nkabba ("he threw him face-down and he fell prone"). A horse or hunter kabba a donkey/prey means "threw it down on its face"; kabba a camel means to hamstring/slaughter it.

**Grammatical oddity the author flags:** normally in Arabic the derived Form IV (afʿala) is the causative and the base Form I is what happens to the subject itself. Here it's reversed: Form I kabba/kababtu is "I threw someone else down"; Form IV akabba/akbabtu is "I [myself] fell down / bent down." So "kabba Allāhu ʿaduwwa l-Muslimīn" (may God cast the enemy down) is correct, but akabba is never used that way. A disputed ḥadīth reading (Ibn Ziml) turns on exactly this point: akabbū vs. the likely-correct kabbū ("they kept the camels firmly to the road").

**2. akabba ʿalā / li- — to apply oneself, bend/lean over.** To be bent over something doing it persistently (akabba ʿalā ʿamalin = stuck to a task); to bow the head (nakkasa); to lean over (tajānaʾa); to press someone for payment (akabba ʿalā fulānin yuṭālibuhu). A man mukibb/mikbāb is one who habitually stares at the ground. Cited in the Qur'an: "Is he who walks face-down (mukibban) on his face..." (Q 67:22). The poet Labīd uses mukibban of a craftsman bent over his work, scrutinizing arrowheads.

**3. kabba/kabbat — intensity, onslaught, crush.** al-kabba (fatḥa) = the thick/intensity of a thing, a charge in war, a surge in battle or a race, the crush of a crowd, winter's onset. kabbat al-nār = the Fire's onslaught (in a ḥadīth of Muʿāwiya). A ḥadīth of Abū Qatāda uses the Form VI verb takābbū ʿalayhā for people crowding around a water-vessel. Ibn Masʿūd warns against "the kubba of the market, [which] is the kubba of Satan" — its crush/crowd.

**4. al-kubba (ḍamma) — a mass or group.** A troop of horses; a large herd of camels (also kubāb, "naʿamun kubāb" = teeming livestock piled together from sheer numbers, illustrated by a verse of al-Farazdaq); a group of people generally. Related forms kabkaba and kabkab carry the same "group" sense (a ḥadīth speaks of "a kabkaba of the Children of Israel"). A proverb — "like the one who sells the kubba for the hubba [wind]" — plays on kubba (a fading fire, in a variant reading) versus hubba (blowing dust); it is also used idiomatically for "having dependents to support" (ʿalayhi kubbatun wa-baqaratun).

**5. kubbat al-ghazl — a ball of yarn.** The wound-up ball of thread/yarn; the verb kabba l-ghazla = to wind it into a ball. This sense connects to takabbaba, said of sand or earth clumping together when damp — Dhū l-Rumma pictures a bull's hooves stirring up "curled, clumped earth," and Umayya's verse about Noah's dove has her return with a twig bearing mud and "clumped clay" (al-kubāb). Related uses of kubāb: dust, sticky clay, moist earth.

**6. al-kabāb — the roasted-meat dish.** kabba l-kabāba = he prepared the kabāb; the verbal noun is al-takbīb. (Full description of the dish is given under a separate entry.)

**7. al-kubb — a desert fodder-shrub.** A ḥamḍ-plant used for treating horses' tails (makes them fuller, longer); has thorny joints, grows on soft ground; also the name of good firewood in another usage recorded by Abū ʿAmr. A related agricultural note: al-mukabbaba is a dust-grey wheat variety with thick sparrow-sized ears and coarse straw that livestock don't relish.

**8. Qur'anic and other citations of kabkaba — to tumble/hurl down.** "fa-kubkibū fīhā hum wa-l-ghāwūn" — "and they were hurled/tumbled into it, they and those who went astray" (Q 26:94–95). The lexicographers gloss kubkibū as "rolled/toppled headlong and gathered up, then flung into the pit of the Fire" — its literal sense, they note, is repeated inkibāb: falling face-first over and over until coming to rest at the bottom. An alternative gloss ties it instead to the "gathered/massed together" sense of kabkaba (§4).

**9. Physical build and other derived words.** kubākib / kubakib: a man of compact, solid, powerful build (also used of abundant livestock). mutakabkib: wrapped up in one's garments. kabkāba/bakbāka: a plump young woman.

**10. Proper names.** Kabkab — a mountain (or mountain-pass) near Mecca, cited in verses of Imruʾ al-Qays (who declines it as fully inflected) and al-Aʿshā (who leaves it undeclined) as a marker of shame ("what he did wrong becomes like a fire on Kabkab's summit"). Kabāb/Kubāb/Kibāb — a particular water-source or well, in a verse of al-Rāʿī. Qays Kubba — a clan of Banū Bajīla, satirized by al-Rāʿī for baseness and poverty.

**11. Nawādir note.** A cluster of near-synonymous verbs (kamhala, ḥabkara, dabkala, ḥabḥaba, zamzama, ṣarṣara, karkara, and kabkaba) are all recorded meaning "to gather scattered livestock/property back together."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: ٱسْتَكْبَرَ 40x "were arrogant"; كَبِير 40x "great"; أَكْبَر 24x "(is) greater"; كَبُرَ 8x "difficult"; كَبِيرَة 7x "(the) greater"; مُتَكَبِّر 7x "(of) the arrogant"; كُبْرَىٰ 7x "the greatest"; كِبَر 6x "the old age"; مُسْتَكْبِر 6x "(are) arrogant"; كَبِّرْ 4x "magnify"; يَتَكَبَّرُ 2x "are arrogant"; كِبْرِيَاء 2x "the greatness"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats k-b-r as a single sound root whose core sense is "the opposite of smallness" — greatness or largeness. From it he draws several distinct senses:

1. Great / large: كبير (kabīr), with the intensive forms كُبَار and كُبَّار ("very great"). He cites Q 71:22, "they plotted a mighty (kubbār) plot."

2. كِبْر (kibr) as the greater or main part of something. He cites Q 24:11, "he who took upon himself the greater part (kibr) of it," glossing it as "the main part of the affair," and the idiom "the chief part of managing a people lies in wealth."

3. كُبْر (kubr, with a different vowel) as al-quʿdud — closeness in lineage to the common ancestor. In the legal saying "clientage (walāʾ) belongs to the kubr," it means the most senior kinsman, the one nearest to the eldest forefather.

4. كِبَر (kibar): old age, decrepitude.

5. كِبْر (kibr): greatness or pride; and likewise كِبْرِياء (kibriyāʾ), grandeur or majesty.

He adds usage notes: "they inherited glory great-one-after-great-one" (kābiran ʿan kābirin), meaning one eminent man after another in nobility and might; "old age came over him" (ʿalat-hu kabra) when someone ages; and أكبرتُ الشيء (akbartu l-shayʾ), "I deemed the thing great / momentous."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats k-b-t (كبت) as a single unified sense: humiliation combined with being turned away / repelled from something.

He gives the usage kabata Llāhu l-ʿaduwwa yakbituhu — "God kabata the enemy" — glossing it as: God turns him away (ṣarafahu) and humiliates him (adhallahu). So the verb carries both ideas at once — not just disgrace, but disgrace that comes with being repelled or driven back.

His shāhid (citation) is Qur'an 58:5 (al-Mujādila): "those who oppose God and His Messenger are kubitū, just as those before them were kubita" — i.e., they are turned back and humbled, as earlier opponents were.

That is the entry's entire content — one root-sense, one supporting citation, no further branches.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris gives the root k-d-ḥ a single core sense: making a mark or effect on something.

1. Literal — to scratch or score: kadaḥahu / kaddaḥahu (كدحه، كدّحه) = "he scratched/scored it." A mukaddaḥ (مُكَدَّح) donkey is one bitten by other donkeys, i.e. marked by their bites.

2. Figurative, by the same analogy — kadaḥa (كدح) = "to strive, labor, toil to earn a living": yakduḥu kadḥan, so the doer is a kādiḥ (كادح, "one who toils/labors"). Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'an, {إِنَّكَ كَادِحٌ} "Indeed you are kādiḥ" (al-Inshiqāq 84:6), and glosses kādiḥ there simply as kāsib (كاسب), "one who earns/strives" — i.e. the Qur'anic use is read as continuous with the everyday sense of laboring/earning, not given any separate technical meaning by this entry.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris's *Maqāyīs al-Lugha* on the root K-D-R (ك-د-ر):

The root has two separate core meanings.

**1. Turbidity — the opposite of clear/pure**
- كَدِرَ / كَدُرَ الْمَاء (kadira/kadura al-māʾ) — "the water became muddy/turbid." Both verb forms are attested.
- A proverb: "Take what is clear and leave what is turbid."
- Used metaphorically for non-liquids too: كَدِرَ عَيْشُهُ (kadira ʿayshuhu) — "his life became clouded/troubled."
- الكُدْرِيّ (al-kudriyy) is a name for the qaṭā (sandgrouse), because most of these birds are كُدْر (kudr, "dusky/ash-grey") — the same "murkiness" idea applied to color.
- الكُدَيْرَاء (al-kudayrāʾ) — fresh milk with dates soaked in it, again named for its clouded look.
- بَنَات أَكْدَر (Banāt Akdar) — a breed of wild ass named after a stallion called Akdar, likely because of its dusky color.

**2. Swift motion**
- انْكَدَرَ (inkadara) means "to move fast, to rush/plunge." Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'an: "And when the stars inkadarat" (Q81:2), i.e., when the stars fall/scatter headlong.

Ibn Fāris treats these as two unrelated primitive senses of the same three-letter root — "turbid/dingy" (extending from water to color to a troubled life) and "swift, headlong motion" (the Qur'anic usage of the stars).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ك د ي (k-d-y), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: hardness in a thing, from which further senses are measured.

1. al-kudyah — a hard, rocky layer in the ground; "ḥafara fa-akdā" — he dug until he struck this hard layer.
2. From this, figuratively: a man who gives a little then stops giving is said to have "akdā" — likened to the digger who hits rock and must cease digging. The entry's central Qur'anic citation is al-Najm 53:34: "wa aʿṭā qalīlan wa akdā" — "and gave a little, then withheld [further giving]".
3. "arḍun kādiyah" — land slow to yield produce, belonging to the same root; Ibn Fāris notes this word is sometimes spelled with a hamzah, though its true origin is not hamzated.
4. A separate report from al-Khalīl: "aṣābat zurūʿahum kādiʾah" — frost/cold damage struck their crops; kaddaʾa al-zarʿ — frost beating a crop back down into the ground.
5. Per al-Farrāʾ: kadiya al-kalbu — a dog's insides became upset from drinking milk. akdaytuhu — I turned someone back from a thing. Ibn Fāris notes that the underlying analogy across everything mentioned in the entry is a single one — being stopped or blocked by hardness or resistance.
6. Closing: Kadāʾ, a place-name, possibly derived from al-kudyah.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ك-ف-و/ي (kafā) from a single core idea: sufficiency — a measure that is enough, with nothing further needed or sought beyond it.

1. Basic verb use: kafāka al-shayʾu yakfīka — "the thing was/is sufficient for you." The thing meets the need completely.

2. Sense of "undertaking/discharging a matter": qad kafā kifāyatan is said of someone when he takes charge of and carries out a task (qāma bi-l-amr) — i.e., he "sufficed" by seeing to it himself.

3. Noun al-kufyah: sufficient food/provision (al-qūt al-kāfī), with the plural kufan.

4. Idiomatic sufficiency-expressions: ḥasbuka Zaydun min rajulin — "Zayd is enough of a man for you" (i.e., he's all the man you need) — and kāfīka, "he is your sufficer," said of someone who takes care of what you need.

All four uses trace back to the same root sense: something or someone that meets a need fully, so nothing more is required.

poets_named: Ibn Muqbil (lived into Islam); Ḥumayd (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats k-f-f as a single sound root meaning grasping and contracting, and says that the different words drawn from it vary somewhat in meaning while sharing one underlying analogy.

1. **The hand.** al-kaff is the human hand, named so because it grasps things.

2. **Holding back.** kafaftu fulānan ʿan al-amr, and the doubled kafkaftuhu, mean "I held him back from the matter".

3. **Begging with the palm.** A man who begs from people is said to yastakiffu or yatakaffafu.

4. **kuffa and kiffa (al-Aṣmaʿī's distinction).** Al-Aṣmaʿī held that anything elongated is a kuffa (with u): the border of a garment, so called because it is hemmed (makfūfa), and likewise a strip of sand. Anything round is a kiffa (with i): the pan of a balance, or the hunter's snare. Ibn Fāris adds that although the two words differ as al-Aṣmaʿī describes, their underlying analogy is the same.

5. **Blindness.** al-makfūf is a blind man.

6. **Circles in tattooing.** al-kifaf are circular marks in a tattoo.

7. **Surrounding and gazing.** istakaffa al-qawm ḥawla al-shayʾ: people gather round a thing, looking at it. Ibn Muqbil speaks of "the surrounding (mustakiffa) eyes glancing". In Ḥumayd's line "to mustakiffāt that have ghurūb", some take the mustakiffāt to be eyes and others camels gathered together; ghurūb here means shades.

8. **Shading the eyes.** istikfāf is putting the hand over the eyebrows, as someone shading himself from the sun does, to see whether he can make out something. It is named for placing the palm (kaff) on the brow.

9. **Sudden meeting.** laqītuhu kaffatan kaffatan: "I came upon him suddenly", as though palm touched palm.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives k-f-l from a single sound root meaning one thing containing or enveloping another.

1. الكِفْل (kifl) — a cloth wrapped around a camel's hump, or one knotted at both ends over the camel's rump so a second rider can mount behind. A ḥadīth applies the word to the broken notch of a vessel, calling it "Satan's kifl." The naming reflects the root: the thing wraps around and is, as it were, contained by the animal. Plural: أَكْفَال (akfāl).

2. By extension, كِفْل is used for a coward — the man who lags at the rear of battle, intent only on holding back. He is likened to the wrapped bundle: carried, unable to walk or move on his own. Ibn Fāris cites a verse ("He grew exhausted, so we slung him… and bound him fast above") and notes poets use the image often; al-Aʿshā pairs such "borne-at-the-rear" men with the weaponless.

3. الكَفِيل (kafīl) — a guarantor or surety (ḍāmin); verb كَفَلَ بِهِ (to stand surety), verbal noun كَفَالَة. Ibn Fāris says this confirms the "containing" sense.

4. الكافِل (kāfil) — one who takes charge of and maintains a person. He cites the Qur'anic وَكَفَّلَهَا زَكَرِيَّا (Āl ʿImrān 37), "He put her in Zakariyyā's charge." Also أَكْفَلْتُهُ المالَ, "I made him responsible/guarantor for the wealth."

5. الكَفَل (kafal) — the rump/buttocks, so named for the flesh gathered there.

6. الكِفْل — in some dialects, a double share of reward; its origin, per Ibn Fāris, is sense 1 — a load one carries as on the camel's kifl. The same usage applies to a double share of sin.

7. A further, separately noted كافِل — one who does not eat, said also to mean one who fasts continuously. Ibn Fāris judges this remote from the other senses and admits he does not know its origin, though he affirms it is sound Arabic; he cites al-Quṭāmī's verse comparing wild cattle at the water's edge to fasting Christian women (كُفَّل).
