The entry's organising idea, as al-Jawharī presents it, is a single sense of turning/inclining off a straight line, applied in three directions: swerving from a dīn, offending inside the sanctuary, and physically cutting a side-recess in a grave — with "refuge" derived from the same inclining motion.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris derives the root l-h-f from a single core idea: enveloping/wrapping something around oneself, and by extension, sticking closely and persistently to something.

1. Wrapping/covering - iltahafa bi-l-lihaf means "he wrapped himself in the lihaf," a covering or wrap one draws over oneself.

2. Clinging/staying attached - lahafahu means "he stayed constantly close to him, clung to him" (lazamahu) - the covering-sense extended to a person keeping fast to another.

3. Persistent asking - alhafa al-sa'il means the one who asks or begs "pressed insistently, would not let up" (alahha) - again the same underlying notion of clinging, applied to insistence in a request.

All three uses trace back to one image: wrapping around something so as not to let go of it, whether literally (a covering) or figuratively (persistence in company or in demand).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats l-ḥ-m as a single sound root whose core sense is interpenetration — parts entering into and interlocking with one another — the image being لحم (flesh), whose fibers interlock.

1. Flesh / meat (اللحم): the base sense from which the root's image is drawn.

2. War = ملحمة (a fierce battle), for two reasons: (a) the combatants press and merge into one another (تلاحم); (b) the slain lie strewn like discarded flesh. Related: اللحيم = the slain man (with a supporting line from the Hudhalī poet).

3. لحمة of the falcon: the food it is given when it hunts. لُحمة / لَحمة of cloth: the weft (the crosswise threads) — both vowellings attested.

4. Persons described by flesh: لحيم = fleshy, having much flesh; لاحم = one who has meat on hand (formed like تامر, "one who has dates"); لَحِم = one who craves meat; مُلْحِم = one who feeds meat to others.

5. Figurative: ألحمتك عرض فلان = "I put so-and-so's honor at your mercy" by letting you revile him — as if handing you a piece of flesh to eat.

6. Joining: لَحَمْتُ بين الشيئين = لاءَمْتُ — to join or make congruous between two things.

7. Other applications of the "flesh/joining" image: المتلاحمة = a head-wound that has cut down to the flesh; a crop is called مُلْحِم when the grain has formed in it; لَحَمْتُ اللحمَ عن العظم = to scrape flesh off the bone; a حبل مُلاحَم = a tightly twisted rope.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ل-ح-ن (l-ḥ-n) from two distinct bases:

1. **Deviation/tilting of speech from its correct course.** Al-laḥn (with a quiescent ḥāʾ) means speech that has been tilted away from its correct Arabic form — i.e., a grammatical error (laḥana laḥnan = "he erred in speech"). Ibn Fāris notes this is, in his judgment, a later ("generated," muwallad) usage — not found among the original, linguistically pure Arabs who spoke by unspoiled natural instinct.

 From the same root-idea:
 - "He has a pleasant *laḥn*" / "he recites *bi-l-alḥān*" (with melodic modulation) — because melodic recitation likewise shifts speech away from its plain form, through the reciter's added or omitted vocal ornamentation (tarannum).
 - *Al-laḥn* also means the underlying drift or gist of speech (its implied sense rather than its plain wording). Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 47:30, *wa-la-taʿrifannahum fī laḥni l-qawl* ("you will surely know them by the drift of their speech"), glossing this as speech conveyed allusively/indirectly (al-kalām al-muwarrā bihi) — turned away from being straightforward and openly stated.

2. **Perspicacity / quickness of understanding.** Al-laḥan means sharp-wittedness. One says laḥina yalḥanu laḥnan ("he grasped something quickly"); such a person is called laḥin or lāḥin. Ibn Fāris cites a ḥadīth: "Perhaps some of you is more skillful (alḥan) in arguing his case than another" — i.e., quicker and sharper in making his point.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats l-ḥ-q as a single root whose core idea is catching up with something and reaching it — one thing coming up to another.

1. Basic verb: laḥiqa fulānun fulānan — "so-and-so overtook / caught up with so-and-so"; the active participle is lāḥiq, "one who catches up." The form-IV verb alḥaqa is given as carrying the same meaning.

2. Shāhid: the supplication wording "inna ʿadhābaka bi-l-kuffāri mulḥiq" ("Your punishment is mulḥiq upon the deniers"). Ibn Fāris reports that its meaning was explained as lāḥiq — punishment that catches up with them.

3. A reported finer distinction: laḥiqtuhu can mean "I followed after him," while alḥaqtuhu means "I reached him / arrived at him."

4. Derived noun al-mulḥaq: someone attached to a lineage — the daʿī, a person claimed as a son and affixed to a family he does not belong to by birth. The sense of "made to catch up / joined on" is the link to the root idea.

5. Al-laḥaq used of dates (tamr): [a disease that afflicts them] — the phrase stands in the edition's brackets.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ل-ح-ي (laḥiya). Ibn Fāris treats it as covering two separate, internally coherent senses.

1. A body part. Al-laḥy is the jawbone — the bone on which the beard grows, in humans and in animals alike. Its relational adjective is laḥawiyy. Al-liḥya is the beard-hair itself, plural liḥan; the plural of laḥy (the jawbone) is alḥin.

2. Bark / peel. Al-liḥāʾ is the bark of a tree. Laḥaytu l-ʿaṣā ("I stripped the stick") or laḥawtuhā means you peeled its bark off. From the same idea, laḥḥaytu (an intensified verb form) means "I reproached/rebuked [someone]" — Ibn Fāris explains this by the same analogy as bark-stripping, as if rebuke strips away a person's outer covering and exposes them. Al-mulāḥāh ("mutual reproaching") is equated here with al-mushātama ("mutual reviling").

Citation: the poet Aws illustrates the bark-sense with a line of verse — "We stripped them as one strips a stick, and drove them out... into a year whose ticks had not [yet] grown fat" — using the stripping-image for harsh treatment and expulsion, paired with the image of a lean year (fattened ticks being a sign of good grazing/rain).

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: لَطِيف 7x "the all-subtle"; يَتَلَطَّفْ 1x "and let him be cautious"
poets_named: Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam) ×2; al-Farazdaq (Umayyad); Abū ʿUmāra b. Abī Ṭarafa (undated)
text:
Ibn Sīda's entry for the root ل ط ف (l-ṭ-f):

1. Core sense. **luṭf / laṭaf** = kindness or benevolence (*birr*), combined with subtlety — literally "going unperceived" (*takhaffī*). Verb: *laṭufa bihi* (verbal nouns *laṭaf*, *laṭāfa*), and the form-IV *alṭafahu*, both meaning to act kindly/gently toward someone. The noun proper is *luṭf*.

2. To give a gift. *alṭaftuhu* = "I presented him with a gift" (*atḥaftuhu*) — kindness expressed as a material favour.

3. Concrete plural sense: intimates. *hāʾulāʾi laṭafu fulān* = "these are so-and-so's *laṭaf*", meaning his companions and household, the people who show him kindness (reported from al-Liḥyānī). Shāhid — Abū Dhuʾayb: *"nor an intimate, sincere, weeping over me."* Ibn Sīda's grammatical analysis of the line offers three options: (a) the singular adjective *naṣīḥ* agrees with the *form* of *laṭaf*, which is singular in shape though collective in sense — hence a plural may be qualified by a singular; (b) *laṭaf* here simply means one person; (c) *laṭaf* is read as a verbal noun, so the sense is "nor one possessed of *laṭaf*."

4. Deftness in handling a matter. *huwa laṭīf bi-l-amr* = he is *rafīq* — gentle, adroit in dealing with it; verb *laṭafa bihi*.

5. As a divine attribute. *al-Laṭīf* is listed among the attributes of God. Ibn Sīda cites two Qur'anic proof-texts without further gloss: Q 42:19 ("God is *laṭīf* toward His servants; He provides for whom He wills, and He is the Strong, the Mighty") and Q 6:103 ("and He is the *Laṭīf*, the Aware").

6. Fineness of substance or of speech. Applied to physical bodies (*ajrām*) and to speech, *laṭīf* = that which has no coarseness or roughness (*jafāʾ*) in it; verb *laṭufa*, verbal noun *laṭāfa*.

7. Slenderness of body. Shāhid — Abū Dhuʾayb: *"seven of them, like the upper shafts of spears, white of face, slender at the waist-wrappers."* Ibn Sīda explains: it means only that they were lean-bellied, slim where the *izār* is tied.

8. Subtlety as closeness of attachment. Shāhid — al-Farazdaq: *"God is nearer to me than my jugular vein, and more* laṭīf*."* Ibn Sīda glosses *alṭaf* here as *alṭafu ittiṣālan* — finer/subtler in its connection.

9. Falling short. *laṭufa ʿanhu* is used exactly like *ṣaghura ʿanhu* — "he/it was too small for it."

10. Technical animal-husbandry usage. *alṭafa al-baʿīra*, and *alṭafa lahu*, of a camel covering a she-camel; the second construction is credited to Ibn al-Aʿrābī. The form-X *istalṭafa* is used when the animal does this of its own initiative.

11. Onomastics. *Abū Laṭīf* is attested as a kunya among the Arabs, with a line from [Abū] ʿUmāra b. Abī Ṭarafa: *"so join my wing to Abū Laṭīf."*

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
Root ل ظ ي (l-ẓ-y) — Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr)

1. **Core sense — fire/flame.** *al-laẓā* means fire; some say specifically pure, smokeless flame. A verse of al-Afwah is cited using it this way ("...as though the men were upon glowing coals and al-laẓā").

2. **A name for Hell.** *Laẓā* is also a proper name of Jahannam (Hell). Grammatically it is a diptote — a definite proper noun that takes no tanwīn and isn't fully inflected, because it combines being a proper name with feminine gender. Ibn Manẓūr says it was given this name because it is the fiercest of all fires. He cites the Qur'an: "Nay! It is indeed Laẓā, a stripper of the extremities" (Q 70:15–16).

3. **Verb forms — "to blaze."** From the same root: *iltiẓāʾ* (blazing/kindling) and *talaẓẓī* (flaming up) are near-synonyms. Verbs *laẓiyat*, *iltaẓat*, *talaẓẓat* all mean "it (the fire) blazed." A verse by Ibn Jinnī uses *iltiẓāʾ* metaphorically for the "blazing" heat of romantic passion (with a note that the poet shortened the word for the metre).

4. **Qur'anic citation.** Q 92:14, "a fire that *talaẓẓā*" — glossed as short for *tatalaẓẓā* (the initial tāʾ dropped), meaning it glows and flares.

5. **Idiom for anger.** "So-and-so *yatalaẓẓā* against so-and-so" means he flares up in intense anger at him.

6. **Extended to heat generally.** The poet Dhū al-Rumma applies *al-laẓā* to fierce heat itself (a day so hot the [ostrich] eggs in their nest nearly crack open from it). Likewise a common saying uses *yatalaẓẓā* of heat, "as if it blazes like fire" — and *talaẓẓati l-mafāzah* means a desert's heat intensified.

7. **Extended to war/death.** A hadith about Khayfān visiting ʿUthmān describes a tough clan as men "on whose spears death *tatalaẓẓā*" (blazes) — i.e., flames and rages. Similarly *iltaẓati l-ḥirāb* ("the spears blazed") is cited from Ibn al-Aʿrābī as a metaphorical usage for weapons flashing in battle.

8. Also: *talaẓẓā ghaḍaban* / *iltaẓā* — "he flared up" (with anger). Morphological note: the word's final alif is written as yāʾ because the root's last radical is yāʾ (hence root l-ẓ-y, not l-ẓ-w).

9. **A related but distinct root noted for contrast.** Al-Azharī, writing under the separate root l-ẓ-ẓ, records a cheek described as "*tatalaẓẓā* [glowing] from its warmth and beauty" — Ibn Manẓūr notes this actually derives from *tatalaẓẓaẓu* (root l-ẓ-ẓ), not from *laẓā* itself, though the two forms look alike.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats l-b(-b) as a sound root with two meanings: keeping close and staying fixed, and purity and excellence. A few words, he says, fall outside both.

**1. Keeping close, staying fixed**

- Alabba bi-l-makān (verbal noun ilbāb) means to stay in a place. A man who is labb in a matter keeps to it constantly.
- Al-Farrāʾ reports imraʾa labba, "a woman loving toward her husband." Ibn Fāris explains that she stays fixed in her affection for him forever.
- The talbiya, the saying labbayka, belongs here. It is explained as "I remain steadfast in obedience to you." It is an accusative verbal noun, and it is put in the dual to mean one answer after another.
- Labīb can mean one who says labbayka. A verse has the speaker say he is ḥarām and labīb, which Ibn Fāris glosses as "a muḥrim saying labbayka."
- Lablaba min al-shayʾ means to be solicitous and anxious over something; such a person is mulablib ("among us are the solicitous and the tender"). Ibn Fāris derives this from staying fixed in affection.

**2. Purity, the choice part**

- Lubb of anything is its pure part, what is picked out of it. For this reason, he says, the intellect is called lubb. A labīb is an intelligent man; the verb is labba, yalubbu. The pure part of anything is its lubāb.
- Labba is the place on the chest where a necklace lies, and Ibn Fāris counts that spot as "pure." Labab is the same. Labibtu al-rajula means "I struck him on the labba."
- One who girds himself is mutalabbib, as though he had tucked his garment up to his labba, ready for action. The labab of a horse is, he says, well known.
- By likeness, labab of sand is sand near a mountain that joins onto level ground. A verse likens a woman "gleaming of neck and upper breast" to a gazelle that such sand has brought into view.

**3. Anomalous words**

Labāb is said to mean pasture herbage, and lablāb is a plant. Ibn Fāris says these depart from the root's pattern.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root l-b-d: the core sense is things matting or piling up, layer upon layer, into a compacted mass.

1. Al-libd — "felt" (matted wool/hair cloth), a familiar object; its name comes directly from this matting sense.

2. The ground "talabbadat" — became matted/compacted (e.g. by rain: "labbadahā al-maṭar"). People who crowd together on/around something are said to become "lubad" — a compacted mass. Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'an: "when the servant of God stood calling upon Him, they almost became a compact mass (libadan) upon him" (al-Jinn 72:19) — i.e. they crowded densely around him.

3. The same word lubad, on a different grammatical pattern (fuʿal), also derives from "albada bi'l-makān" — to settle down and stay in a place — so it can carry the sense of people clustering/staying put.

4. The lion is called "dhū libda" — possessor of a libda (mane) — because its thick coat mats together from the blood it laps up. A verse of al-Aʿshā is quoted describing an animal whose coat "mats together" wherever it's touched, and the proverb "more unassailable than the lion's mane" is given.

5. By the same logic: "albada bi'l-makān" = to settle/remain in a place; "al-lubad" = a man who never leaves his home. Ibn Fāris notes all these usages are analogically derived from the base sense of matting.

6. "Labada bi'l-arḍ labūdan" — to cling/stick to the ground.

7. "Albada al-baʿīr" — said of a camel that swats its tail onto its own dung-soiled rump, so the mess mats there like a libda.

8. "Albadati al-ibil" — said of camels when they show signs of being ready to fatten up, the visible change being likened to a forming libda.

9. "Al-labīd" is given as another word for a large sack (al-juwāliq); "albadtu al-qirba" means to have stuffed something into a waterskin/sack.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root l-b-n (لبن) -- Ibn Faris, Maqayis al-Lugha

Ibn Faris classes l-b-n as a sound root whose core meaning is al-laban, "milk" (the drink). Everything below either derives regularly from that core, or is flagged by him as an outlier that doesn't fit the pattern.

Regular derivatives (from "milk"):
1. labintuhu albinuhu -- "I gave him milk to drink."
2. labin -- "having milk [on hand]," parallel to tamir, "having dates." A short unattributed verse illustrates the pair: someone falsely claimed to be labin in summer and tamir with dates.
3. mulbin -- someone with abundant milk.
4. naqah labinah -- a she-camel copious in milk.
5. For a she-camel: mulbin describes her once her milk has come down into the udder; labun simply means she has milk at all, whether her yield is large or small.
6. malbun (of a man) -- dazed or foolish from drinking too much milk.
7. malbun (of a horse) -- a horse given special preference and fed milk.
8. "How much is the lubn/libn of your flock?" -- asking how many of the animals are milk-producing.

An anomalous branch (shadhdh -- Ibn Faris explicitly says these don't fit the milk-root pattern):
9. al-laban can also mean neck pain caused by a pillow; a man with that pain is called labin.
10. From the same odd branch: al-labinah, the sun-dried mud brick.

A grammatical/etymological dispute he settles:
11. Ibn al-Sikkit held that the idiom "he is his brother by shared milk-nursing" must use the form bi-libani ummihi, never bi-labani ummihi, because laban strictly names the drunk substance, not the act of nursing. Ibn Faris agrees with the usage but disputes the reasoning: he argues liban is still derived from laban -- the two foster-siblings can be said to have "shared a milk-suckling" (talabana liban-an), on the same pattern as taqatala qital-an ("they had a fight"). So the word is from laban after all; it's simply that idiomatically one only ever says bi-libani ummihi, not bi-labani ummihi.

Related but separate words, close to the root but not squarely inside it:
12. al-laban (different vowel pattern, labaan) -- the chest/breast.
13. al-luban -- frankincense, described as though it were a milk-like resin that "oozes" from a tree; Ibn Faris says its derivation here is coherent and single.
14. al-lubanah -- "a need" or "a want." He allows this could be brought under the root by a stretch of analogy, but judges it closer to being an unrelated, anomalous item.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: لَبَسْ 11x "mix"; لِبَاس 10x "(are) garments"; لَبُوس 1x "(of) coats of armor"; لَبْس 1x "doubt"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ل-ب-س (l-b-s) as one sound root whose core idea is mixing together and interpenetration.

1. Base sense — wearing. لَبِسْتُ الثَّوْبَ ("I put on the garment") is the root meaning, and everything else branches from it, since a garment interpenetrates with the body.

2. Confusion / obscuring an affair. اللَّبْس is the entanglement of a matter. With the causative form, لَبَسْتُ عَلَيْهِ الْأَمْرَ ("I made the matter obscure to him"). Ibn Fāris cites Q 6:9, {وَلَلَبَسْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ مَا يَلْبِسُونَ} ("We would have confused for them what they [already] make obscure"). To say an affair has a لَبْسَة is to say it is not clear. The same word also denotes the mingling of darkness (dusk blurring together).

3. Involvement. لَابَسْتُ الْأَمْرَ — to involve oneself in, mix with, an affair.

4. Spouse as "garment." From this root, لِبَاس is used for a man's wife, and the husband is her libās — each clothes the other. Shāhid: al-Jaʿdī — "When the bedfellow bends her neck, she yields and becomes a garment upon him."

5. اللَّبُوس — anything worn, whether ordinary clothing or a coat of mail (dirʿ).

6. Close acquaintance. لَابَسْتُ الرَّجُلَ حَتَّى عَرَفْتُ بَاطِنَهُ — "I kept close company with the man until I knew his inner character."

7. Metaphorical extension — something left to enjoy. فِيهِ مَلْبَس means there is in it something still to be benefited from, a remainder. Shāhid: "after destitution a man may still gain an acquisition, and after grey hair, long life and a malbas [something yet to enjoy]."

8. Covering of the howdah and the Kaʿba. لِبْس (with kasra) denotes the drapery/covering placed over them.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: لَبِثَ 30x "you remained"; لَّٰبِثِين 1x "(they will) be remaining"
text:
Root ل-ب-ث (l-b-th). Ibn Fāris gives it a single core meaning: to tarry, linger, or stay put in one place (تَمَكُّث).

1. لَبِثَ بِالْمَكَانِ (labitha bi-l-makān) — "he stayed / remained in the place," i.e. he abided there.

As a Qur'anic attestation he cites al-Aḥqāf 46:35: {لَمْ يَلْبَثُوا إِلَّا سَاعَةً مِنْ نَهَارٍ} — "They did not tarry save an hour of a day."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: Ibn Aḥmar (lived into Islam); unnamed verse
text:
Ibn Fāris treats l-d-d as two sound roots: one meaning disputation, the other a side or flank.

1. **Fierce disputing.** al-ladad is intense contentiousness. A man is aladd and a people are ludd, "fiercely contentious", as in "that you may warn with it a contentious people (ludd)" (Q 19:97).

2. **Side, flank.**
   - al-ladīdān are the two sides of the neck, its two flat surfaces; the ladīdān of a valley are its two sides.
   - taladdada is said of someone who turns right and left in bewilderment.
   - al-ladūd is medicine given to a person to drink in one of the two sides of his face. One says ludda, "he was given ladūd", and iltadadtu, "I took it myself". Ibn Aḥmar: "I drank the shukāʿā and took doses of ladūd, and brought the cautery-irons to the mouths of the veins."
   - The saying "short of this matter I find no muḥtadd and no multadd" means "I find no way of turning aside from it"; Ibn Fāris adds that whoever turns aside from a thing comes to be at one side of it.
   - mā ziltu ulāddu ʿanka means "I have kept defending you", as though turning evil aside from the person.

3. **An outlier.** al-ladd, which "they say" means a sack (juwāliq), is listed by Ibn Fāris among the words that depart from the root; a verse runs "as though its two sacks were on the flank of a mountain". He adds that it could be counted in after all, since, as one of a pair of balanced loads, it lies on the flank of the animal that carries it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root l-d-n as carrying a single core meaning, with two applications:

1. لَدْن (ladn) — describing a twig or branch that is soft, supple, and pliant.

2. لَدُنْ (ladun) — used with the sense of لَدَى (ladā), i.e. عِنْد (ʿind): "at," "with," or "in the presence of."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root ل-ف-ح (l-f-ḥ) as expressing one single, unified meaning.

1. Core sense — heat striking the face: The verb is used of fire "scorching" someone with its heat (لفحته النار بحرها), and likewise of the samūm — the hot, scorching wind — when its heat strikes a person and visibly changes the colour of his face.

2. A look-alike expression set aside: The phrase لفحه بالسيف لفحة ("he struck him with the sword a light blow") is sometimes said with this same root-form, but Ibn Fāris explains that this usage does not really belong to ل-ف-ح at all — its true origin is the letter nūn, i.e. it is properly نفحه (nafaḥahu), from the separate root ن-ف-ح. He excludes it from this entry's core meaning as a case of formal resemblance rather than shared root-sense.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ل ف ظ (l-f-ẓ), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: the casting-off of a thing, most often from the mouth.

1. lafaẓa bi-l-kalām — to utter speech, i.e. to "cast it out" [of the mouth]; lafaẓtu al-shayʾa min famī — I cast a thing out of my mouth.
2. al-lāfiẓah — used as a name for the rooster, or, alternatively, for the millstone, or for the sea — all sharing the sense of "casting out" what they hold. This usage is illustrated with a line of poetry praising a generous man as more openhanded even than al-lāfiẓah.
3. Closing: something cast out is called malfūẓ or lafīẓ.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: لَفِيف 1x "(as) a mixed crowd"; ٱلْتَفَّتِ 1x "and is wound"; أَلْفَاف 1x "(of) thick foliage"
text:
Ibn Fāris calls lām–fāʾ a sound root that indicates one thing winding around another.

1. **Wrapping, winding.** lafaftu al-shayʾa bi-l-shayʾ (verbal noun laff): I wrapped one thing with another. lafaftu ʿimāmatī ʿalā raʾsī: I wound my turban around my head.

2. **Those who join a group.** "The people came, and whoever wrapped in with them (man laffa laffahum)" means whoever attached himself to them, as though he had become entwined with them. Al-Aʿshā uses the phrase: "Qays, and whoever wrapped in with them, have filled Nubāk, then Qaww, then al-Rajā, then al-Nawāʿiṣ." The entry also gives al-lafīf: people gathered together from various tribes.

3. **Tongue-tied.** A man who is halting in speech is called alaff, as though his tongue had become twisted; there is lafaf in his tongue.

4. **Intertwined trees.** al-alfāf are trees intertwined with one another, as in the Qur'an's "and gardens alfāf" (Q 78:16).

5. **Close thighs; heaviness.** al-alaff is one whose thighs come close together from fatness, as though they were entwined, and that condition is al-lafaf. An unattributed verse speaks of those "broad of rump, the fleshy parts of their thighs pressed together", and says that the thick-thighed (al-luff) leave no one his reason. A heavy, slow man is also called alaff.

6. **Wrapping the head.** alaffa: a man wraps his head in his clothes; a bird tucks its head under its wing.

7. **Tangled herbage.** Someone reports the expression "in the land there are tangles (talāfīf) of herbage".

8. **Withholding.** lafaftuhu ḥaqqahu: I withheld his right from him.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَلْتَفِتْ 2x "let look back"; تَلْفِتَ 1x "to turn us away"
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) treats l-f-t as one root with a single core sense: twisting something, or turning it away from its straight course.

1. Basic verb — lafata al-shay' ("he lafata'd the thing") = he twisted/wrung it (lawā).
2. lafata fulānan ʿan ra'yihi = he turned someone away from their opinion (ṣarafa, "diverted").
3. al-alfat = a left-handed man. Ibn Fāris says this fits the root's underlying pattern — the sense being that the left-handed person acts/turns toward the "twisted," reversed side.
4. al-lafītah = a thick porridge (ʿaṣīdah), named this because it is tulfat — twisted/stirred vigorously — in its making.
5. A lafūt woman = one who has a husband but also a child by another man; she is called this because she keeps turning/glancing (talfitu) back toward that child.
6. al-iltifāt and al-talaffut (turning one's face aside, glancing back) both derive from the same root idea of turning away from straight-ahead.
7. Abū Bakr (a transmitter Ibn Fāris cites) adds one more sense: lafata al-liḥā' min al-shajarah = to peel/strip the bark off a tree.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats l-f-w (lafā) as a sound root (aṣl ṣaḥīḥ) that indicates a thing's becoming uncovered and the uncovering of it. Its words occur both with hamza (lafaʾa) and without it (lafā).

1. **Stripping something off.** One says that the wind lafaʾat the clouds from the face of the sky, stripping them away. Of meat: lafaʾtu the flesh from the bone, I scraped it off; lafawtu, without hamza, means the same. Abū Bakr reports both forms.

2. **al-laffāʾ**: the dust and rubbish lying on the surface of the ground. A proverb says "he was content, in place of full payment, with al-laffāʾ": he accepted a little in place of the full amount he was owed.

3. **alfaytuhu**: I met him, found him. The verbal noun is ilfāʾ.

4. **talāfaytuhu**: the same as tadāraktuhu, I caught up with it in time.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root لغب (l-gh-b) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core sense: weakness and fatigue.

1. Basic definition: a man described as laghb is marked by evident feebleness.

2. An anecdote (via al-Aṣmaʿī and Abū ʿAmr): a Bedouin was heard calling someone laghūb because he disregarded a letter sent to him; when asked what laghūb means, he said simply "the fool" — showing the word's extension from physical weakness to weakness of judgment.

3. Poor arrow-fletching: a verse of Taʾabbaṭa Sharran boasts that his own "feather" was not made from inferior tail-feathers or laghb (defective plumage). Abū Bakr explains: an arrow is called laghb when its feathers are cut from the belly rather than the wing — a mark of poor-quality fletching. Illustrated further with a verse about a failed man being sent off equipped with a laghb arrow, i.e. poorly outfitted for his task.

4. Core meaning restated: al-lughūb is fatigue, exhaustion, hardship. "He arrived hungry and exhausted" pairs the two states. Cited: Q50:38, "and no weariness (lughūb) touched Us" — describing God's creation of the heavens and earth without fatigue.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: لَغْو 9x "vain talk"; ٱلْغَ 1x "and make noise"; لَٰغِيَة 1x "vain talk"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives لغو (l-gh-w) from two sound roots:

1. Something not reckoned with / of no account.
- laghw: that which is not counted. Used of camel-offspring not reckoned in blood-money (diya); a verse of al-ʿAbdī is cited ("a hundred whose offspring are made laghw... the flank of the hundred like solid rock"). The verb is لَغَا / يَلْغُو / لَغْوًا (laghā/yalghū/laghwan). laghā is an exact synonym of laghw.
- This underlies laghw al-aymān, the "idle" element in oaths. Ibn Fāris cites Q 2:225, "God will not take you to task for the laghw in your oaths," glossing it as an oath you did not resolve upon with your heart (did not truly intend). He records two further explanations from others, attributed not as his own definition: the jurists say it is heedlessly saying "No, by God" or "Yes, by God"; others say it is swearing that an approaching figure is a certain person, believing it, when it turns out otherwise — the oath counts as laghw because the swearer did not deliberately lie.

2. Being fond of / persistent in something.
- laghiya bi-l-amr means to be absorbed in or keen on a matter (lahija bihi). Ibn Fāris notes it is said that lugha ("language, tongue") derives from this sense — a speaker being continually occupied with his tongue.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ل-ه-ب (l-h-b) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha (d. 1004 CE)

Core meaning: Ibn Fāris identifies the root's core sense as "the rising of a tongue of fire" — everything else in the entry is treated as an extension or metaphor from that image.

1. Flame itself — اللَّهَب (al-lahab) is the blaze/flame of a fire. The verb اِلْتَهَبَ (iltahaba) means "it blazed up." By extension, anything whose light rises and glitters intensely can be described this way. An unnamed poet is cited using the image for a crown "blazing" with royal splendor.

2. Thirst (metaphor) — A thirsty person is called لَهْبَان (lahbān), Ibn Fāris explicitly flags this as metaphorical usage (istiʿāra) — as if the heat inside the thirsty person were itself ablaze. Likewise اللُّهَاب (al-luhāb), "blazing," is also applied to thirst.

3. Rising dust (metaphor) — اللَّهَب is also reported to mean "gleaming/rising dust," which Ibn Fāris again calls metaphorical, if the usage is even sound. From this comes فَرَسٌ مُلْهِب (faras mulhib), "a horse that kicks up dust," and أُلْهُوب (ulhūb), a term for a horse's burst of speed — all derived, in his account, from the original fire-image. He quotes Imruʾ al-Qays' line pairing ulhūb (a shout-driven burst of speed) with dirra (leg-vigor) and a well-timed whip-strike that brings out a trained horse's best.

4. A look-alike that is NOT from this root — اللِّهْب (al-lihb), "a narrow mountain pass/defile," looks similar but Ibn Fāris says it does not derive from l-h-b at all: its true root has ṣād (لِصْب, liṣb), with the ṣād later replaced by hāʾ.

5. Tribal name — بَنُو لِهْب (Banū Lihb) is noted as the name of an Arab subtribe.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ل هـ م (l-h-m), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: the swallowing-down of a thing, from which further senses are measured.

1. iltahama al-shayʾa — to swallow a thing whole, to engulf it.
2. From this same image: al-ilhām — inspiration, as though something is cast into the mind and then "swallowed" (absorbed) by it. The entry's central Qur'anic citation is al-Shams 91:8: "fa-alhamahā" — "then He inspired it [the soul]" — with its wickedness and its God-consciousness.
3. iltahama al-faṣīlu mā fī ḍarʿi ummihi — a weaned young camel swallowing everything in its mother's udder, taking it in fully.
4. faras lahimm — an outstripping, champion racehorse, as though it "swallows" the ground it runs over.
5. al-luhaym / "Umm al-Luhaym" — words for calamity/death, both named for their vastness, as though disaster "swallows" whatever it meets.
6. al-lihamm — said of a great, capable/sufficient person; al-luhmūm — a generous man — both extensions of the same underlying sense of vastness and breadth.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ل-ه-ث (l-h-th) as a single unified root with one core meaning.

1. Core sense: a dog letting its tongue loll out from thirst — the panting motion of a thirsty dog.

2. Qur'anic citation: he quotes {If you load it, it pants, or if you leave it, it [still] pants} (al-Aʿrāf 7:176), where the verb yalhath describes this panting — notably, the dog pants either way, whether burdened or not.

3. Related noun: al-luhāth is defined as "the heat/burning of thirst."

4. Method note: Ibn Fāris explicitly states that all uses of this root are measured/derived (maqīs) from the base image of the dog's panting behavior — i.e., the dog scenario is the semantic anchor for the whole root, not a secondary application of some more abstract sense.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: لَهْو 10x "and amusement"; أَلْهَىٰ 4x "and diverted them"; لَاهِيَة 1x "distracted"; تَلَهَّىٰ 1x "(are) distracted"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root l-h-w from two sound (original) meanings: (1) being occupied and turned away from one thing by another, and (2) casting something from the hand.

FIRST ROOT — distraction / diversion (al-lahw):
- al-lahw is anything that occupies you and diverts you from something else; such a thing "has distracted you" (alhāka).
- Related forms: lahawtu ("I diverted/amused myself"), and lahitu ʿan al-shayʾ ("I left a thing for the sake of another"). Ibn Fāris notes the underlying analogy is a single one, though the vowelling shifts slightly.
- Usage of the imperative: when God reserves something for Himself, one says falha ʿanhu — "leave it alone, do not busy yourself with it." He cites a ḥadīth on moisture left after ablution ("leave it be"), and reports that Ibn al-Zubayr, on hearing thunder, would break off (lahā) whatever he was saying and turn away from it.
- Euphemistic use: al-lahw can stand in for something else. On {Had We wished to take a lahw} (Qurʾān 21:17), Ibn Fāris reports two early interpretations — al-Ḥasan and Qatāda glossed lahw here as "a woman/wife," while others glossed it as "a child/offspring." (These are attributed opinions, not the word's base sense.)

SECOND ROOT — throwing from the hand (al-luhwa):
- al-luhwa is the grain the miller throws by hand into the hole of the millstone; plural luhan.
- By extension a gift is called luhwa, and a generous man is said to be kathīr al-luhā ("abundant in gifts").
- al-lahāt (the uvula, the furthest part of the mouth) is named from this image — likened to the millstone's hole — because food is thrown down into it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: ل-ج-أ (l-j-ʾ) — لجأ
Source: Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004 CE)

Ibn Fāris treats the three letters as expressing one single underlying idea: al-lajaʾ / al-malja' — "the place one takes refuge in." That is, the root's core sense is a place of shelter or refuge sought out for protection.

Verb forms: lajaʾat and iltajaʾat — both meaning "she/it sought refuge" or "took shelter," used interchangeably.

Citation (shāhid): Ibn Fāris quotes an unnamed poet using lajaʾ in this literal sense:

"Winter has come, and I had not yet made myself a lajaʾ [refuge/shelter] ... O the burning of my two palms from digging the qarāmīṣ [pits/burrows dug for winter shelter]!"

The line depicts someone caught by the onset of winter without shelter prepared, forced to dig a makeshift burrow (qarāmīṣ) by hand — illustrating lajaʾ concretely as a physical refuge from harsh conditions, which is also the sense behind the related word malja' ("place of refuge").

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: لَّجُّ 2x "they persist"; لُّجِّىّ 1x "deep"; لُجَّة 1x "(was) a pool"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats l-j-j as a sound root (aṣl ṣaḥīḥ) indicating a thing's going back and forth, part of it over part, and the repeating of a thing. Under it he places:

1. **Persistence (al-lajāj).** The verb is lajja, yalajju, with the first-person form lajijtu, "I persisted" (pattern faʿiltu); the verbal nouns are lajaj and lajāj.

2. **The deep of the sea (lujj, lujja).** The lujj of the sea, or its lujja, is its deepest part (qāmūs), so called, he says, because it rolls back and forth upon itself. Of the sea one says iltajja, "it surged" (verbal noun iltijāj). A ḥadīth: whoever puts to sea when it is surging is no longer covered by any guarantee of protection.

3. **The sword (lujj).** He says the name is only a comparison: as if to make the sword grand, it is likened to the deep of the sea. His example is the ḥadīth of Ṭalḥa: "They came forward and put the lujj on the back of my neck."

4. **Turning food over in the mouth (lajlaja).** To keep moving a morsel about in the mouth without swallowing it. Zuhayr: "He turns over and over a morsel with half-cooked meat in it; it has gone rank, and beneath the flank it is a malady."

5. **Faltering speech (al-lajlāj).** One who stumbles over his words and does not speak clearly.

6. **Clamour (al-lajja).** An uproar, as in Abū al-Najm's line: "In an uproar: 'Hold so-and-so back from so-and-so!'"

7. **A restless heart (lajāja).** "There is lajāja in his heart" means the heart flutters and will not settle, from hunger. He derives this from al-lajāj.

8. **Darkness and a black eye.** The lajāj of darkness is its commingling, likened to the surging of the sea. Used figuratively, an eye is called multajja when it is intensely black.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ل-م-ح (l-m-ḥ), from Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha:

**Core meaning:** the flashing or gleaming (lamʿ) of something — a brief, bright appearance.

1. **Basic usage:** لَمَحَ (lamaḥa) is used of lightning and of a star that "lamaḥa" — i.e., flashed or gleamed (lamaʿa).

2. **Poetic citation:** a verse describes watching for "a lamḥ [flash/glimpse] of Suhayl [the star Canopus]," comparing its appearance at the end of the night to a blink (yaṭrif) — the star's light catching the eye for an instant, like an eye blinking.

3. **Further usage:** "I saw the lamḥah of the lightning" — lamḥah being a single instance of that flash.

4. **Idiom:** the expression لَأُرِيَنَّكَ لَمْحًا بَاصِرًا ("I will surely show you a lamḥan bāṣiran") is explained as meaning "a clear, evident matter" (amran wāḍiḥan) — i.e., something shown so plainly it is unmistakable, like a bright flash catching the eye.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
al-Rāghib's short entry on l-m-m covers the verb lamma, the noun al-lamam and its source alamma, and the particles lam and lammā, each with a Qur'anic example.

1. **Gathering and setting right.** lamamtu l-shayʾ means "I gathered the thing together and set it right", as in lamamtu shaʿathahu, "I set right what was scattered of it". He cites "and you eat up the inheritance with a gathering eating (aklan lammā)" (Q 89:19).
2. **al-lamam: coming near to wrongdoing.** al-lamam is coming near to disobedience, and the word is used for a small offence. "So-and-so does such-and-such lamaman" means he does it from time to time. Likewise the verse "those who avoid the major wrongs and the gross deeds, except al-lamam" (Q 53:32).
3. **Its source: alamma, to come near.** al-lamam comes from almamtu bi-kadhā, "I alighted at it and came near to it without actually engaging in it". A visit called ilmām is an infrequent one.
4. **lam.** lam negates the past, although it stands before the future form of the verb. With the interrogative alif (a-lam) it draws out an acknowledgement: "did we not raise you among us as a child?" (Q 26:18); "did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?" (Q 93:6).
5. **lammā.** It has two uses. It negates the past while bringing the action near: "while God has not yet known those who strove" (Q 3:142). It also marks time: "then when the bearer of good news came" (Q 12:96), meaning at the time of his coming. al-Rāghib notes that examples are many.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats l-m-s as one root with a single core idea: seeking something out, and also making contact with it.

1. Groping / seeking by hand. تَلَمَّسْتُ الشَّيْءَ means to feel about for a thing with your hand in order to find it. Ibn Fāris cites Ibn Durayd: lams originally means using the hand so that the feel of a thing can be known; the usage then spread so widely that any seeker at all came to be called mullamis/multamis ("one groping after" something).

2. Touching. لَمَسْتُ means simply "I touched," equivalent to مَسِسْتُ; and, as he reports the lexicographers saying, anyone who touches (māss) is a lāmis.

3. Disputed application in Q 4:43. On {أَوْ لَامَسْتُمُ النِّسَاءَ} ("or you have touched the women"), Ibn Fāris records two positions without endorsing either: one group took it to mean sexual intercourse; another took it as ordinary contact, holding that lams and mulāmasa can occur without intercourse. The second group cited a line of verse — "I touched his palm with my palm, seeking wealth; I did not know that generosity is contagious from his palm" — but Ibn Fāris notes this verse does not count as a valid proof-text.

4. اللَّمَاسَة (lamāsa): a thing sought after; a need or want. This is the "seeking" side of the root as a noun.

5. Idiom of defencelessness. "لَا يَمْنَعُ يَدَ لَامِسٍ" — "he does not fend off the hand of a groper" — is said of someone in whom there is no benefit and who has no capacity to defend. A cited half-line runs: "were it not for them, you would not have repelled the hand of one who reaches out."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ل-م-ز as yielding a single meaning, with no competing branches.

1. Core sense: اللَّمْز (al-lamz) = fault-finding, disparaging or pointing out defects in someone.

2. Verb pattern: لَمَزَ / يَلْمِزُ / لَمْزًا (lamaza / yalmizu / lamzan) — a form-I verb with an i-vowel imperfect and the verbal noun lamz.

3. Qurʾānic witness cited: Q 9:58, "And among them is he who finds fault with you concerning the ṣadaqāt" — the verb used of people criticising the addressee over the distribution of ṣadaqāt.

4. Intensive personal forms: رَجُلٌ لَمَّازٌ (lammāz) and لُمَزَة (lumaza), both meaning عَيَّاب — a habitual, persistent fault-finder.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ل ق ح (l-q-ḥ), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: a male impregnating a female, from which further senses are measured by analogy.

1. liqāḥ al-naʿam wa-l-shajar — the impregnation of livestock (by their males) and of trees (by the wind). riyāḥ lawāqiḥ — fecundating winds, that impregnate clouds with rain and impregnate trees. Ibn Fāris adds a grammatical note (also held by Qur'anic commentators): the form lawāqiḥ looks like it should mean "impregnating," but properly the winds only impregnate because they are themselves already laqiḥ ("having conceived") — singular laqiḥah.
2. laqiḥat al-nāqah — a she-camel conceived (several verb-forms); nāqah laqiḥ/laqūḥ — a conceiving/pregnant she-camel. al-laqḥah — a milk-giving she-camel (plural liqāḥ/luquḥ).
3. al-malāqiḥ — female animals carrying young in the womb; Abū Bakr notes the term has no attested singular, and applies to the unborn young themselves as much as to the pregnant mothers.
4. Closing exception, explicitly flagged by Ibn Fāris as anomalous and outside this root's regular pattern: qawm laqāḥ (fatḥah on the lām) — a people who owe allegiance to no king and are ruled by no sultan.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root لقط (l-q-ṭ) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core sense: picking something up off the ground, typically encountered by chance rather than deliberately sought — though Ibn Fāris notes it can also happen intentionally.

1. Basic usage: laqṭ al-ḥaṣā — gathering pebbles; al-luqṭa — lost property someone picks up. al-laqīṭ — an abandoned infant, named for being "picked up."

2. A tribal-origin story: Banū al-Laqīṭa were named after their ancestress, a captive woman rescued from famine-stricken circumstances by Ḥudhayfa ibn Badr, who took her in, was pleased by her, and married her — the clan's name preserving the memory of her being "found" this way.

3. al-laqaṭ — anything you've picked up; al-iltiqāṭ — happening upon something by chance, illustrated with a verse about stumbling upon a watering-place unexpectedly.

4. Figurative and idiomatic extensions: a lowly, despised man is compared to al-laqīṭa (a foundling). The proverb "for every stray word there's a picker-up" means any notable remark finds someone to hear and spread it. al-alqāṭ describes people who are few and scattered. A well come upon unexpectedly is biʾr laqīṭ.

5. Mining and harvest: al-laqaṭ also names nuggets of gold or silver found in a mine. luqāṭat al-zarʿ — the gleanings, grain picked up from a field after harvest.

6. An obscure idiom is also noted: the lung is called "the pebble-picker" — its precise logic unexplained in the entry.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ل-ق-ب (l-q-b) — Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha)

Ibn Fāris opens by noting that this root expresses a single, unified meaning (not multiple branching senses, as he does for some other roots).

1. Core sense — al-laqab: a nickname or epithet. Ibn Fāris defines it simply by equating it with the synonym al-nabz ("one [and the same]").
2. Verb — laqqabtuhu talqīban: "I nicknamed him / gave him a nickname" (Form II verb laqqaba, verbal noun talqīb).
3. Qur'anic citation (shāhid) — {وَلَا تَنَابَزُوا بِالْأَلْقَابِ}, "And do not taunt one another with nicknames" (al-Ḥujurāt 49:11), given as the attested Qur'anic occurrence of the word.

The entry is brief and self-contained: no etymological branching, no additional morphological detail (plural pattern, iʿrāb, etc.) beyond the Form II verb, and only the one Qur'anic shāhid.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: al-ʿAjjāj (Umayyad); Abū Dhu'ayb (lived into Islam); Abū Khirāsh al-Hudhalī (lived into Islam); unnamed verse
text:
Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr) on the root l-q-f (لقف)

1. Core sense — "to catch/snatch what is thrown": al-laqf is taking hold of something thrown at you, and specifically doing so swiftly, whether the thing is thrown by hand or "thrown" as speech (i.e. words directed at you). Verb forms: laqifahu/yalqafuhu (laqfan, laqafan), also iltaqafahu and talaqqafahu, all meaning "he snatched/caught it quickly." A line of poetry by al-ʿAjjāj uses it of a wild bull catching and flinging away the loose earth/twigs that crumble on it as it digs its den.

2. Grasping speech quickly: a Ḥajj-related report has someone say "I caught (talaqqaftu) the talbiya-formula from the Prophet's own mouth," meaning he picked it up and memorized it on the spot.

3. Adjective for a sharp, capable person: "thaqifun laqifun" (also thaqfun laqfun, thaqīfun laqīfun) describes someone light/agile and adept — variously glossed as: quick to grasp what is said to him and quick to take what is handed to him; or someone who firmly masters and holds onto whatever he takes up; or simply someone skilled at his craft. "Laqif" alone can carry the same sense. A report about al-Ḥajjāj has him call a woman "laqūf, ṣayūd" — al-laqūf being a woman whose hand closes on/seizes anything the moment a man touches her.

4. "Gulping down food": Ibn Shumayl records that "yulaqqifūna aṭ-ṭaʿām" (they laqqif the food) simply means they eat it — one does not use the reflexive talaqqafa here. A cited verse tells people, when called to a meal, to "laqqifū" (gulp it down) the way lean Syrian wolves gulp down food.

5. Swallowing: Ibn al-Sikkīt gives al-laqf as the verbal noun of "I laqaftu a thing," meaning I took it and ate or swallowed it; talaqquf likewise means swallowing. This is the sense the entry ties to the Qur'an: "fa-idhā hiya talaqqafu mā ya'fikūn" — "then it swallows up what they had fabricated" — with a variant reading "talqaf." Al-Farrā' is cited as glossing the verb here, in this context, as "it swallows."

6. A trough or cistern (ḥawḍ): "laqif/laqīf" applied to a trough has two competing glosses recorded here — (a) simply "full [of water]," and (b) an unlined trough (never coated with clay) whose water seeps or gushes out at the sides because its bottom has hollowed out and caved in (al-Aṣmaʿī explains this hollowing, talajjuf, as the water eating away at its walls until it collapses/widens). Two verses by Abū Dhu'ayb are cited using laqīf of a trough that "crumbles" and "gushes forth." Opinion is divided in the entry itself: Abū al-Haytham thought "full" the better fit, while al-Jawharī states the "collapsed/hollowed-out" sense is the correct one. Related: al-laqaf (with fatḥa) is separately given by al-Jawharī as "the collapse of a wall." A verse (by Abū Khirāsh al-Hudhalī, per Ibn Barrī's correction of an earlier attribution to Khuwaylid) compares a generous host's cooking-bowl in winter to such a trough.

7. Motion of horses and camels: talqīf is used of a she-camel raising her foreleg vigorously as if stretching it out, or of striking her chest with her forelegs as she moves. Abū ʿUbayda separately describes talqīf in a horse as pawing/striking with the forelegs while running without drawing them up toward the belly (the entry adds a comparison to "al-karw," a term/reading that is unclear as transmitted). A camel called "mutalaqqif" swings its forefeet outward to its off side as it walks.

8. Sides of a well or trough: al-alqāf (singular laqaf) names the sides/edges of a well or trough — a synonym set with al-aljāf (singular lajaf).

9. Place-name: "Laqf" or "Liqf" is recorded as a place, illustrated with a verse (via Thaʿlab) cursing its watercourse as barren and its water as scanty.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) treats l-q-m as a single, coherent root whose core sense is: taking food by hand to the mouth. All other uses are extensions of this by analogy.

1. Core verb — laqimtu l-ṭaʿām / alqamuhu: "I took the food as a mouthful / put it in my mouth."
   - talaqqamtuhu (reflexive/intensive form) and iltaqamtuhu (another derived form): both mean "I took it in / swallowed it [as a mouthful]."

2. Descriptive noun — a man called tilqāmah is one who takes large or frequent mouthfuls (a big eater, in the sense of mouthfuls); the word-pattern itself (tifʿālah) marks someone who does this habitually.

3. Extended, metaphorical sense — al-laqam is the main, well-trodden track of a road. Ibn Fāris explains the image: the road is pictured as if it "swallows" or takes in as a mouthful whoever travels along it — the same metaphor he notes he already used when discussing the word al-sirāṭ ("path/road") elsewhere in the dictionary.
