poets_named: unnamed verse ×2; Ibn Aḥmar (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris analyzes the root l-q-y (lām, qāf, and a weak final letter) as three unrelated base meanings: (1) crookedness, (2) the meeting of two things, and (3) casting something off.

1. Crookedness / bending. From this comes laqwa, a facial disease that leaves the face twisted; a man afflicted by it is malqūw, and one says the person was "struck" (luqiya). The same word laqwa names the well-bucket that swings and catches on another bucket rising past it as it is lowered — a poet calls it "the worst of buckets, the clinging laqwa." It also names the eagle (ʿuqāb), from the crookedness of its beak, and the she-camel that conceives quickly.

2. Meeting / encounter. This is liqāʾ — meeting and the coming-together of two who face each other. Usage: laqītuhu laqwatan ("I met him a single time"), also liqāʾatan, luqyan, and luqyānan. The noun luqya (pattern fuʿla) has the plural luqan. A cited verse: "Truly I long for sleep though not drowsy — perhaps a meeting with you may come in the dream."

3. Casting off. Alqaytuhu means "I flung it away" (verbal noun ilqāʾ), and a discarded thing is a laqan. Ibn Fāris explains the term's origin: some Arabs, on coming to the Sacred House to circumambulate, refused to do so in garments they had sinned in, so they threw them off — and the cast-off garment was called a laqan. A verse of Ibn Aḥmar, describing a sandgrouse chick, uses the word: "It shelters a cast-off thing flung on a barren flat, scorched by the sun yet not melting."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ل-س-ن as a single sound root whose core sense is "a slight, non-prominent length" — in a bodily limb or in anything else. He derives the following from it:

1. لِسَان (lisān), "the tongue" — the familiar organ. Grammatically masculine; plural أَلْسُن (alsun), and for a large number الْأَلْسِنَة (al-alsina).

2. لَسَنْتُهُ (lasantuhu) — "I assailed him with my tongue," i.e. attacked him verbally. Shāhid: Ṭarafa, "when their tongues assail me, I am not a feeble, callow weakling."

3. lisān used for "a message/dispatch" (risāla) — in this sense the word is treated as feminine. Shāhid: "a message [lisān] came to me by which I am not gladdened, from ʿAlwā."

4. لَسَن (lasan) — excellence of tongue, eloquence.

5. لِسْن (lisn) — a people's language: "every people has a lisn." Ibn Fāris cites a variant recitation of the verse "We sent no messenger except in the lisn of his people" (with lisn in place of lisān).

6. نَعْل مُلَسَّنَة (naʿl mulassana) — a sandal shaped like a tongue. Shāhid: Kuthayyir, on treading tongue-shaped Ḥaḍramī sandals underfoot.

7. مَلْسُون (malsūn) — a liar. He explains it as derived from lisān: once a man is known for lying he is lusina, i.e. tongues talk about him.

8. تَلْسِين (talsīn) — the practice of a man lending another his young camel (faṣīl) so that his she-camel will let down her milk to it; once she does, the young camel is taken away. The link to the root: the animal "tasted" the milk with its tongue.

9. قَدَم مُلَسَّنَة (qadam mulassana) — a foot marked by delicacy and slight length (illustrating the root's core sense of gentle elongation).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: ل-و-ذ (l-w-dh)
Source: Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004 CE)

Ibn Fāris gives this as a single, sound root whose core meaning is: a person going around / circling close to something, seeking shelter in it and using it as cover.

1. Basic usage — لَاذَ بِهِ (lāḏa bihi), "he took refuge in / clung to it," with verbal nouns lawdh and liyādh. This is used when someone shelters behind or beside a thing out of fear, or out of hope of gaining something from it.

2. Form III — لَاوَذَ (lāwadha), verbal noun liwādh, "to take shelter one behind another." Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 24:63: "Allah indeed knows those of you who slip away, sheltering one behind another (liwāḍan)." He explains this described the hypocrites: when one of them wanted to leave the Prophet's gathering, he would duck behind someone else to hide himself before slipping off.

3. A grammatical note: the Qur'an's spelling لِوَاذًا (liwāḍan, with wāw) rather than لِيَاذًا (liyāḍan, with yā') is explained morphologically — this word is the verbal noun of the Form III verb lāwadha, whose verbal noun keeps its wāw intact ("sound"). Had the word instead derived from the plain Form I verb lāḏa, the wāw would have shifted to yā' after the preceding kasra, giving liyāḍan instead. So the spelling itself signals which verb form is meant.

4. A related noun sense: al-lawdh is the land that skirts or encircles the base of a mountain (its surrounding foothills). Plural: alwāḍ.

[Note: the manuscript's opening word for the core sense is transmitted as إطاقة ("empowering/enabling"), which does not fit the entry's actual content; it is almost certainly a copying/OCR slip for إطافة ("circling/going around"), the sense the rest of the entry — including the closing gloss "that which encircles the mountain" (يُطِيفُ) — consistently supports.]

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats L–W–Ḥ as a single sound root whose main body sits close to the semantic field of gleaming and flashing.

1. Core sense — to gleam, glint, show up brightly. لَاحَ / يَلُوحُ (lāḥa / yalūḥu): a thing glinted and gleamed; its verbal noun is لَوْح (lawḥ). A line of verse illustrates it: "I watch for a gleam of Suhayl [Canopus], as though, when it appears late in the night, it were blinking."

2. Causative/fourth-form uses of flashing. أَلَاحَ بِسَيْفِهِ (alāḥa bi-sayfihi) — he made his sword flash. أَلَاحَ الْبَرْقُ (alāḥa al-barq) — the lightning flashed. Related to brightness: اللِّيَاح (al-liyāḥ), the white one.

3. Weaponry as "the gleaming things." On the line "At evening she is like the alwāḥ of weaponry, and in the forenoon like a wild-cow on the morning after rain," Ibn Durayd is cited as explaining أَلْوَاح (alwāḥ) as whatever gleams among weapons — most often swords.

4. Scorching that makes a thing conspicuous. لَوَّحَهُ الْحُرّ (lawwaḥahu al-ḥarr) — the heat burned and blackened him, so that he stood out visibly from a distance. Ibn Fāris keeps this inside the "gleaming/showing" family.

5. Board, plank, broad bone. لَوْح (lawḥ) is the shoulder-blade; also a single plank of a ship's boards (alwāḥ al-safīna); and by extension any broad bone. His stated derivation: it is called lawḥ because it يَلُوحُ — it shows/gleams.

6. The open air. لُوح (lūḥ), with u-vowel, is the air between sky and earth.

Two senses he marks as deviating from the root's main line:
7. لَوْح (lawḥ) meaning thirst; and a mount described as مِلْوَاح (milwāḥ) — one that grows thirsty quickly.
8. أَلَاحَ مِنَ الشَّيْءِ (alāḥa mina l-shayʾ) — to be wary of something, to guard against it.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: مَلُوم 5x "blameworthy"; لُمْ 3x "you blamed me"; مُلِيم 2x "(was) blameworthy"; لَوْمَة 1x "the blame"; لَائِم 1x "(of) a critic"; يَتَلَٰوَمُ 1x "blaming each other"; لَّوَّامَة 1x "self-accusing"
text:
Root ل-و-م (l-w-m), from al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's Mufradāt.

1. اللَّوْم (al-lawm) — core sense: to censure someone by attributing to him something blameworthy. لُمْتُهُ = "I blamed him"; the one blamed is مَلُوم (malūm). Qur'anic examples: "do not blame me, but blame yourselves" (14:22); "that is the one about whom you blamed me" (12:32); "they do not fear the blame of any blamer" (5:54); "they are not to be blamed" (23:6). On this last verse al-Rāghib notes that mentioning blame signals that, since they incur no blame, nothing worse than blame befalls them either.

2. أَلَامَ (alāma), Form IV — to deserve or become liable to blame. Example: "and he was blameworthy" (مُلِيم, 51:40).

3. التَّلاوُم (al-talāwum), Form VI — mutual blaming, people blaming one another. Example: "they turned to one another blaming each other" (68:30).

4. النَّفْس اللَّوَّامَة (al-nafs al-lawwāma), "the self-reproaching soul" (75:2). Two readings reported: (a) the soul that has gained some virtue and so reproaches its owner when he does wrong — ranking below the tranquil soul (al-nafs al-muṭmaʾinna); or (b) the soul settled in itself and fit to discipline others — ranking above the tranquil soul.

5. Agent/patient forms on the سُخَرة/سُخْرة pattern: لُوَمَة (lūʾama) = one who blames people; لُومَة (lūma) = one whom people blame.

6. Related nouns: اللَّوْمَة (al-lawma) = blame, censure (synonym of al-malāma); اللَّائِمَة (al-lāʾima) = the thing for which a person is blamed.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats L–W–N as having a single underlying sense: the outward look or complexion of a thing (سَحْنَة).

1. **Colour.** لَوْن (lawn) is the colour of a thing — for example redness or blackness.

2. **Changeableness of character.** تَلَوَّنَ فُلَان, literally "he became many-coloured," is used of a person whose traits and dispositions keep varying — i.e. he is inconstant.

3. **A variety of dates.** لَوْن also names a kind of date-fruit.

4. **The palm tree, with an etymological note.** لِينَة (līna) means a palm tree, and Ibn Fāris derives it from this same root: the yāʾ in لِينَة stands in place of an original wāw (so līna traces back to l–w–n). He cites Q 59:5, "whatever līna you cut down."

He closes with the standard formula that God knows best what is correct.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris opens this entry unusually by rejecting the root itself: he states he cannot vouch for the soundness of lām–wāw–tāʾ, and in his own judgment it is not genuine Arabic speech at all.

He nonetheless records two claims made by others about it, without endorsing them:

1. Some say لَاتَ يَلُوتُ (lāta yalūtu) is used of a person who answers with something other than what he was actually asked — i.e., gives an evasive or off-point reply.
2. Others say اللَّوْت (al-lawt) means "concealment" (al-kitmān).

He closes by noting that both of these claims are doubtful (fīhimā naẓar) — he is skeptical not just of the root's authenticity but of the specific senses reported for it.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: يَلْ 3x "casting a glance"; لَيّ 1x "twisting"; لَوَّ 1x "they turn aside"
poets_named: unnamed verse ×5; Al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); Al-Jaʿdī (disputed date)
text:
Al-Zamakhsharī organises ل و ي (l-w-y) around one physical act — twisting, bending, winding — and then lists the figurative extensions separately.

LITERAL SENSES

1. To twist or twine. لوى الحبل — he twisted the rope. لوى الشيء فالتوى — he twisted a thing and it became twisted. Also of body parts: he twisted his hand, his finger.

2. A bend or curve in terrain. ملتوى الوادي — the valley's bend. Related: الملاوي, the winding roads, cited in a verse about riders taking the twisting ways at evening. Also لوى الرمل (plural ألواء), the curving tract of sand — with a verse: "I saw the liwā, O Juml, gone grey since our time, altered by the storming winds."

3. To turn the head aside. كلّمته فلوّى رأسه — I spoke to him and he turned his head away. Zamakhsharī cites the Qur'anic phrase لوّوا رءوسهم (they turned their heads aside), noting it is also recited in the un-doubled reading (lawaw).

4. To writhe or coil. يتلوّى من الجوع — he writhes from hunger; تلوّت الحية — the snake coiled; and لاوت الحية الحية (verbal noun ملاواة) — one snake wound itself against another.

5. لويّة (lawiyya): food set aside as a store or provision; the verb التويت لويّةً means to lay such a store by. Two verses attest it — one of a gaunt man who gets a share of the lawiyyāt of the pack-loads, and one asking a woman to serve breakfast "from the lawiyya." (In the second, النقبة is glossed as the skin of the face.)

6. ألوى of a person: hard-going, one who twists against his opponent — as in the proverb "you will surely find so-and-so alwā, hard to bring round."

7. To stall over a debt. لواه دينه, verbal nouns ليّ and ليّان: to defer payment. Al-Aʿshā: "They put me off over my debt by day, while I press my claim when drowsiness fells the sleepers."

8. أَلْوَى forms: ألوت به العقاب — the eagle carried it off; ألوى بيده وبثوبه — he waved/flashed a signal with hand or garment; ألوت الناقة بذنبها — the she-camel flourished her tail (with a verse likening the tail to a dyed palm-spray).

9. لوًى in the belly — a twisting pain.

10. لواء — a banner; ألوى الأمير له لواء means the commander bound a banner for him.

FIGURATIVE USES (Zamakhsharī's own heading, ومن المجاز)

11. Of strength: "his back is not twisted"; of one thrown down: "no one ever twisted his back."

12. Of grief: لوى الحزن قلبه — grief twisted his heart.

13. Of concealment: لوى سرّه — he twisted, i.e. hid, his secret; لويت عنه الحديث — I folded the talk away from him. Al-Jaʿdī's verse on God withholding His knowledge from all but Himself is cited here.

14. Of ageing: لوت الليالي كفّه على العصا — the nights bent his hand over a staff, i.e. made him decrepit, with a supporting verse.

15. Of a bird tucking its eggs into an inaccessible place — cited with a verse on the vulture (al-anūq).

16. Of intractability: التوى عليه الأمر — the matter twisted against him, became impossible; التوت عليّ حاجتي; and causatively لوّى عليه الأمر تلويةً — he made the matter difficult for him.

17. Of passing by without stopping: مر لا يلوي على أحد — he went on without turning toward anyone, neither halting for him nor waiting; with a verse on horsemen turning back in fear of a mailed lion.

18. Of being carried off by force or fate: ألوت الحرب بالسّوام — war swept off the grazing herds; ألوى بهم الدهر واستلوى بهم — time carried them away.

19. Of winning an argument: يلوي أعناق الرجال في الجدال — he twists men's necks in disputation, i.e. overcomes them.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
poets_named: unnamed verse; ʿAmr b. Shaʾs (pre-Islamic); al-Farazdaq (Umayyad); al-Nābigha (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Sīda's account of the root ل ي ل (layl, "night"):

1. Core sense: al-layl is what follows the day, beginning at sunset. Sībawayh noted the idiom sīra ʿalayhi laylun ("a night was travelled through") used to mean "a long night" — the adjective ṭawīl ("long") is dropped because the context supplies it.

2. Morphology of number: the unit-noun is laylah ("a night"); the plural layālin is irregular, formed as if the singular were laylāh. Its diminutive luyayliyah is likewise anomalous — Sībawayh treats both the broken plural and the diminutive as exceptions. Ibn al-Aʿrābī did record the singular laylāh (with a verse of shāhid), and al-Kisāʾī recorded a rare plural layāyil.

3. Variant form al-layn: Yaʿqūb reported layn as a substitution-form (badal) for layl ("night"), citing a verse ("…upon the cheek of the night…"); others transmit the same verse with layl.

4. Adjectival intensives (a dark/hard night): laylah laylāʾ or laylā = a long, severe, hard night; said to be the darkest night of the month — the source of the woman's name Laylā — or specifically the thirtieth night. Parallel adjectives for a dark/deep night: alyal, lāʾil, mulayyal (this last possibly meaning "abundant [in nights]," as if intensified), with a shāhid from ʿAmr b. Shaʾs.

5. Verbs: alāla al-qawmu and alyalū = "the people entered upon the night." lāyaltuhu = "I hired him by the night" (al-Liḥyānī); ʿāmalahu mulāyalatan = "he contracted with him night-by-night."

6. Bird sense: al-layl is also the bustard (ḥubārā), male and female alike, or its chick — and likewise the chick of the stone-curlew (karawān). On al-Farazdaq's line (grey hair as a "layl" flanked by a crying "nahār"), some read layl and nahār as the chicks of these birds, but Yūnus rejected this: "the layl is this night of yours, the nahār this day of yours."

7. Other named senses: umm Laylā = dark/black wine (from Abū Ḥanīfa). Layl and Laylā are also place-names; al-Nābigha's line is transmitted with both min Laylin and min Laylā.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: لِن 2x "you dealt gently"; لَّيِّن 1x "gentle"; أَلَ 1x "and we made pliable"; لِّينَة 1x "(the) palm-trees"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats L-Y-N as having one single meaning, with no competing branches.

1. Core sense — softness, pliancy: al-līn is the opposite of roughness or coarseness (khushūna).

2. Extended to living conditions: هو في لَيَانٍ من عَيْشٍ ("he is in a soft manner of life") means he is in ease and comfort (niʿma).

3. Extended to character: calling someone مَلْيَنَة (malyana) means he is layyin al-jānib — "soft-sided," i.e. gentle and easy to deal with.

4. Morphological note: in words from this root the long alif may be a transformation of an original yāʾ or wāw, and it can also stand for a hamza.

dictionary: Lane — Arabic-English Lexicon, Edward William Lane (d. 1876)
text:
Lane's entry (drawn from Sībawayh, the Ṣiḥāḥ, the Muḥkam, the Miṣbāḥ, the Mughnī, etc.) for لَيْسَ (laysa):

1. Core meaning. لَيْسَ is a word of negation — "is not / are not." It typically denies a predicate at the present time (a particular, not a universal, negation): لَيْسَ زَيْدٌ قَائِمًا = "Zeyd is not standing."

2. It is a verb, not a particle. Despite the claim (Ibn al-Sarrāj and others) that it merely stands in for مَا, the grammarians treat it as a defective preterite (past-tense) verb: it inflects for person like a verb — لَسْتَ, لَسْتُمَا, لَسْتُمْ, لَيْسَا, لَيْسُوا, لَيْسَتْ — paralleling ضَرَبْتَ, etc. But it is "imperfectly inflected": it has no present/future, no participle, no verbal noun, and no derivatives, so in some ways it behaves like a non-verb (compare لَيْتَ).

3. Form and etymology. Its measure is فَعِلَ, originally لَيِسَ, contracted to لَيْسَ because the fuller form was awkward to pronounce (compare عَلْمَ for عَلِمَ). The medial ى is not turned into ا precisely because the verb is defective. A dialectal form لُسْتُ / لُسْنَا (Banū Ḍabba), and even لِسْتُ, is reported. A separate view (attributed to al-Farrāʾ and al-Khalīl) derives لَيْسَ from لَا أَيْسَ ("not-existing"), citing the expression جِئْ بِهِ مِنْ أَيْسَ وَلَيْسَ ("bring it from where it is and is not"); on this reading أَيْسَ = "existing," لَا أَيْسَ = "not existing," contracted to لَيْسَ. Lane notes this etymological gloss likely derives from the saying مَا يَعْرِفُ أَيْسَ مِنْ لَيْسَ ("he cannot tell a thing that exists from one that does not").

4. Grammatical government. Like كَانَ and its sisters, it puts its subject in the nominative and its predicate in the accusative. Two peculiarities: (a) the preposition بِ may be added to its predicate for emphasis — لَيْسَ زَيْدٌ بِمُنْطَلِقٍ ("Zeyd is not going away"); this is optional. (b) Its predicate may not (per the Baṣrans) be fronted before it: مُحْسِنًا كَانَ زَيْدٌ is allowed, but مُحْسِنًا لَيْسَ زَيْدٌ is disputed (some permit it, some forbid it).

5. As an exceptive ("except"). It can replace إِلَّا: جَآءَنِى القَوْمُ لَيْسَ زَيْدًا ("the people came to me, except Zeyd"), understood as لَيْسَ الجَائِى زَيْدًا. One may even say لَيْسَكَ ("except thee"), though the free pronoun إِيَّاكَ is preferred.

6. Dialectal / Tamīmī usage. When إِلَّا follows, Banū Tamīm may put the following noun in the nominative: لَيْسَ الطِّيبُ إِلَّا المِسْكُ ("nothing is perfume except musk"). This construction has several proposed analyses; some take it as ليس used as a mere particle.

7. As a general (total) negation. It can carry the force of لَا التَّبْرِئَة (absolute/universal "no"). Lane's example is Qur'an 2:194, لَيْسَ عَلَيْكُمْ جُنَاحٌ, equivalent to لَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْكُمْ ("there is no blame/sin upon you") — the same wording as 2:235.

8. As a connective particle. In the sense of لا: e.g. the verse … وَالأَشْرَمُ المَغْلُوبُ لَيْسَ الغَالِبُ ("… and al-Ashram [Abraha] the vanquished, not the victor"); analyzed as ليس with الغالب as subject and a suppressed predicate.

9. Treated as a noun. In one poetic line the very word ليس is inflected as a noun (بِلَيْسِ), the poet mocking someone "addicted to using the word laysa."

(Note on 2:194: Lane gives the theological/moral gloss "no crime or sin chargeable upon you" as his rendering of جُنَاح; the entry's own grammatical point is only that laysa here functions as a total negation equivalent to لَا.)

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ل ي ت (l-y-t), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris explicitly notes this root does not follow a single extendable pattern (lā tanqāsān) — it consists of two unrelated words sharing the same letters.

1. al-līt — the side/surface of the neck (dual lītān).
2. al-layt — deficiency/diminishment; lātahu yalītuhu — he diminished him. The entry's central Qur'anic citation is al-Hujurat 49:14: "lā yalitkum min aʿmālikum shayʾan" — "He will not diminish you anything of your deeds."
3. A separate, homonymous sense of the same verb-form: al-layt as "turning away/deflection" — lātahu yalītuhu (he turned him aside), illustrated with a line of poetry about traveling through a dark night with nothing turning the traveler back.
4. Closing note: layta — the Arabic particle of wishing ("would that..."), recorded here simply as sharing these letters, without further comment on its relation to the other two senses.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ل-ز-ب (l-z-b), per Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha.

Core sense: fixedness and clinging persistence — something firmly attached and hard to remove.

1. Lāzib is given as equivalent to lāzim ("persistent/necessary/inseparable") — the two words are used for the same idea of something that sticks fast.

2. The phrase "ḍarbata lāzib" (lit. "a fixed/clinging sort") describes something that has become permanent, that scarcely ever departs or separates.

   Ibn Fāris cites al-Nābigha's line: people do not assume that good, once it comes, will never be followed by evil, nor do they assume evil is "ḍarbata lāzib" — a permanent, unshakeable condition. The phrase is used here for something one assumes has become a fixed state of affairs.

3. Al-lazba means a severe or hard year (i.e. a year of drought/hardship), plural lazbāt — named this way as if the drought itself "lazaba" (became fixed, took firm hold) in that year.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
quran_words: أَلْزَمَ 3x "should we compel you (to accept) it"; لِزَام 2x "the inevitable (punishment)"
poets_named: Ṣakhr al-Ghayy (pre-Islamic); Ibn Barrī (unnamed); Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam); Kuthayyir (Umayyad)
text:
Ibn Manẓūr's entry for the root L-Z-M (لزم) records the following.

1. Core sense: adhering, sticking fast, not parting. اللُّزوم (al-luzūm) is described as a well-known word. Verb لَزِمَ / يَلْزَمُ (lazima/yalzamu); active participle لازم (lāzim, "cleaving, inseparable"), object ملزوم (malzūm, "made to cleave"). Verbal nouns lazm and luzūm. A man called لُزَمَة (luzamah) is one who sticks to a thing and never leaves it.

2. Derived forms and what each adds:
   - لازَمَ (lāzama, III), verbal nouns mulāzamah / lizām: to keep close company with, stay constantly at.
   - التَزَمَ (iltazama, VIII): to take upon oneself; also to embrace, clasp — الالتزام is glossed as al-iʿtināq ("embracing").
   - أَلزَمَه إياه (alzamahu, IV): to impose something on someone, so that he then takes it on (fa-iltazamahu).
   - Al-Jawharī's usage: لَزِمْتُ به ولازَمْتُه ("I clung to it, I kept close to it").

3. A second, apparently opposite sense: decisive separation. اللِّزام (al-lizām) is glossed as al-fayṣal — that which decides/cuts off — "emphatically so." Ibn Manẓūr notes that since the word also means constancy and persistence, it is treated as though it belonged to the aḍdād (words carrying two contrary senses). اللَّزَم (al-lazam) is likewise given as "the separating of a thing," on the fayṣal reading, though he reports that others derive it instead from luzūm ("adhering").

4. The Qur'anic evidence and the two readings. On «فسوف يكون لِزاماً» (Q 25:77): the entry glosses it as a punishment that cleaves inseparably to the addressees. Al-Zajjāj reports Abū ʿUbayda's gloss fayṣalan ("a decisive severance"), and reports that the exegetes as a body took it to mean the Day of Badr and what befell them there — a "separation made" among the slain. On the variant reading لَزاماً (lazāman): the denial will cling to them and the penalty with it, with no repentance granted; Badr and other punishments fall under this.
   Grammatical point: لِزام (with i) is the verbal noun of form III lāzama, hence equivalent to مُلازِم ("one keeping close"); لَزام (with a) is the verbal noun of lazima, parallel to salām from salima, hence equivalent to لازِم ("cleaving"). Both readings are attested.

5. Further senses of لِزام: death (al-mawt) and the reckoning (al-ḥisāb). A ḥadīth on the portents of the Hour mentions al-lizām, explained there as the Day of Badr, while linguistically the word means keeping constantly to a thing and persisting in it — and also decisive settlement of a case.
   On «ولولا كلمةٌ سبقت من ربك لكان لِزاماً» (Q 20:129): the punishment would have cleaved to them, but they were deferred to the Day of Resurrection.

6. Poetic evidence:
   - Ṣakhr al-Ghayy: though they escape the death of one land, they have met their deaths lizāman — glossed as: decreed death is inescapable; escape it in one place and it meets you in another.
   - Ibn Barrī's line: may you never cease bearing rancour against me until death be, from you, an inseparable thing.
   - Abū Dhuʾayb: "he saw nothing but a charging band, lizāman" — here lizām means mulāzim, pressing close; the ʿādiyah are men charging on foot, their onslaught clinging so that they will not leave the state they are in. (laqīf = a cistern collapsed from below.)
   - Kuthayyir, on Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya imprisoned by Ibn al-Zubayr, includes the line "the severity of affliction is no ḍarbat lāzim" — i.e. not a permanent blow. The idiom صار الشيء ضربةَ لازِم is noted as a variant of ضربة لازِب, and Ibn Manẓūr says the form with bāʾ is the better attested.

7. Concrete/technical uses: المِلْزَم (al-milzam) is a clamp — two pieces of wood bound at the middle with an iron band and tightened by a wedge, gripping whatever is inside it firmly; used by blade-polishers and needle-makers. المُلازِم is also glossed as al-mughāliq ("the one who locks fast"). Idiomatic emphatic forms on the qaṭāmi pattern: سَبَبْتُه سُبّة تكون لَزامِ (al-Kisāʾī) and لأضربنّك ضربةً تكون لَزامِ (Thaʿlab) — a reviling or blow that clings and is remembered, on the pattern of darāki, naẓāri.

8. Proper name: لازِم (Lāzim) was a horse of Wuthayl ibn ʿAwf.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha gives m-sh-j (م ش ج) a single, sound root meaning "mixing."

1. Core sense: mixing/blending.

2. Key expression: nuṭfatun amshāj ("a mixed drop") — glossed here as the mingling of fluid (al-māʾ) with blood (al-dam).

3. Grammar note: the plural amshāj has three attested singular forms — mashaj, mashij, and mashīj.

4. Supporting citation (poetry): a verse describing an arrow, where the arrowhead and its two nock-ends carry a blended/mottled colouring (mashīj) distinct from the shaft — illustrating the same core idea of something "mixed" or "blended together."

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
Root M-SH-Y (مشي), from Ibn Manẓūr's Lisān al-ʿArab.

1. Walking (the core sense). al-mashy, "walking" (verb mashā yamshī), well known; the noun of manner is al-mishya. Forms: tamashshā ("to walk about"), the causative amshāhu / mashshāhu ("to make walk"). Illustrated by verses of al-Ḥuṭayʾa, al-Shammākh (ostriches walking "as Christians walk in leather boots"), and others. Figuratively, tamashshat fīhi ḥumayyā al-kaʾs — the wine's intoxication "walked"/crept through him.

2. A manner of walking. al-mishya is a particular gait. Sībawayh notes ataytuhu mashyan ("I came walking"), an idiom heard only in fixed usage. Al-Liḥyānī records timshāʾ ("walking") from a women's charm-formula; Ibn Sīda holds it is used only there.

3. Extended sense — to proceed. Anything continuous is said to "walk," even if not an animal: mashā hādhā al-amr, "this affair went on." A ḥadīth about a man who vowed to perform the ḥajj on foot but tired: "he walks what he rode and rides what he walked" — he returns the next year to cover on foot the stretch he had ridden.

4. Tale-bearing. al-mashshāʾ is one who goes about among people spreading calumny (namīma); al-mushāt, the slanderers. Also mashā yamshī bil-namāʾim, "he goes about with slanders."

5. Livestock — al-māshiya. Camels and sheep (plural al-mawāshī, covering camels, cattle, and sheep; per Ibn al-Athīr, most often sheep). Any grazing beast kept for breeding and property is māshiya.

6. The underlying sense: growth and increase. al-mashāʾ means growth, abundance, procreation (al-namāʾ) — the very reason livestock is called māshiya, since it multiplies. mashat al-māshiya, "its young multiplied"; amshā al-rajul, "his livestock grew numerous." Applied to people: athrā wa-amshā, "he grew rich and livestock-rich" (as in verses of al-Nābigha and a ḥadīth of Ismāʿīl and Isḥāq, where amshaytu = "your livestock multiplied"). Also afshā / amshā / awshā, all "his wealth grew." Extended even to childbearing: imraʾa māshiya, "a woman of many children"; nāqa māshiya, "a she-camel of many young." Grammarians cited include Ibn al-Sikkīt, al-Layth, Abū al-Haytham, Abū Ḥanīfa.

7. Loose bowels and the purgative. mashā baṭnuhu, "his bowels ran loose." al-mashiyy / al-mashiyya (also mashuww, mashw, mashāʾ, with a noted yāʾ↔wāw morphological alternation) is the purgative medicine. Verb istamshā, "to take the purge"; the drug yumshīhi, "makes him go." A ḥadīth of Asmāʾ: bima tastamshīn, "with what do you loosen your bowels?"; another: "the best remedy is al-mashiyy." It is so named because it drives the drinker to walk repeatedly to the privy. Ibn Barrī distinguishes al-mashiyy (doubled yāʾ = the medicine) from al-mashy (single yāʾ = what the drinker passes). Ibn Durayd deemed al-mashy for the medicine an error, though Abū ʿUbayd transmitted it.

8. A plant. al-mashā (singular mashāt), a plant resembling the carrot; per Ibn al-Aʿrābī, the edible carrot itself (al-iṣṭaflīn). Dhāt al-Mashā is a place-name, cited from a verse of al-Akhṭal.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-أ-ي (m-ʾ-y) as a single word cluster with two connected uses:

1. **Talebearing / sowing discord.** al-maʾy (المأي) is slander and stirring up trouble among people (النميمة، الإفساد بين القوم). The verb is مَأَيْتُ بَيْنَهُمْ (maʾaytu baynahum), "I sowed discord between them." A cited verse fragment gives: "and slander among them, a companion of foul deeds" (وَمَأْيٌ بَيْنَهُمْ أَخُو نُكُرَاتٍ).

2. **Making a hundred.** From the same letters comes al-miʾa (المائة), "a hundred." The verb أَمْأَيْتُ الدَّرَاهِمَ (amʾaytu al-darāhim) means "I made the dirhams up to a hundred."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: م-ض-غ (m-ḍ-gh) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris states that mīm-ḍād-ghayn is a sound root whose core meaning is "chewing food" (al-maḍgh).

1. Verb: maḍagha / yamḍughu — "he chewed / he chews."

2. Al-maḍāgh — food that is (being) chewed.

3. Al-muḍāghah — the residue left in the mouth from something chewed.

4. Al-maḍghah — a piece (morsel) of flesh; named this because it resembles a piece taken up in order to be chewed.

5. Al-māḍighān (dual) — the two parts of the mouth's sides that draw/contract together, i.e. the jaw muscles at the corners of the mouth used in chewing.

6. An irregular outlier under this same word-pattern family: al-ʿaqabāt, the sinew bindings wrapped around the two tips (nocks) of a bow. Ibn Fāris flags this as a "shādhdh" (anomalous) case — a word that shares the pattern of the maḍgh-group but is not semantically about chewing. The singular form he gives for this word is corrupted/illegible in the source text (only the ending "-ghah" survives), so it cannot be reliably reconstructed here.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-ض-ي (with a weak third radical) as one sound root whose core idea is passing through and going by — both "passing" in time or motion and "penetrating" so as to get through something.

1. The verb مَضَى / يَمْضِي, verbal noun مُضِيّ — to pass, go on, go by.
2. الْمَضَاء (al-maḍāʾ) — effectiveness in a matter: carrying something through to completion, following it through rather than stalling.
3. الْمُضَوَاء (al-muḍawāʾ) — moving forward, advancing ahead.

For the third sense he cites the poet al-Qaṭāmī: "and when they hung back, he pressed on in his forward course" — the others fall behind while the subject keeps advancing.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root م ع ن (m-ʿ-n), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: ease in flowing, or in running, or otherwise.

1. maʿana al-māʾ — water flowed; māʾ maʿīn — flowing/running water; majārī al-māʾ fī al-wādī muʿnān — a valley's water-channels (per Abū Bakr); al-maʿnah — a small flowing stream.
2. amʿana al-farasu fī ʿadwihi — a horse ran freely/at ease (or far) in its running; "amʿana bi-ḥaqqī" — he made off with what was rightfully mine. rajul maʿn fī ḥājatihi — an easy-going man, for whom things go smoothly. amʿanati al-arḍu — land became well-watered/saturated; kalaʾ mamʿūn — pasture that water has flowed through.
3. A line of poetry by al-Namir is cited using "ghayr maʿn" to mean "not easy [to bear]," describing the neglect of wealth as no light matter.
4. The idiom "mā lahu saʿnatun wa lā maʿnatun" ("he has neither much nor little") is noted as an echo-word pairing (itbāʿ), though Ibn Fāris allows it may also genuinely belong to this root's sense of "ease," meaning he has nothing of even negligible, easy worth.
5. A resting-place/stopover on a journey is called maʿān (plural muʿun) — the entry's closing note. maʿana al-wādī — a valley filled with abundant flowing water.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
text:
Root م ع ي (m-ʿ-y), al-Zamakhsharī, Asās al-Balāgha

1. "hum mithlu al-maʿā wa-l-kirsh" — "they are like the intestine and the paunch" — an idiom describing a prosperous, well-fed people, illustrated with a line of poetry contrasting an idle sleeper with a people who set their affairs in order and thereby grew full and content ("like the intestine and paunch" — i.e. well-nourished).

Figurative sense (majāz)
2. "jarā al-māʾu fī amʿāʾi al-wādī" — "the water flowed in the 'intestines' of the valley," meaning its channels/runnels — extending the anatomical image of intestines to the winding water-channels of a valley, illustrated with a further line of poetry describing something's "intestines" creeping toward its firm base.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
text:
Root m-ʿ-z (معز) — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144 CE)

**Literal senses — "goat"**
1. maʿz / miʿz / maʿzā / muʿayz — collective nouns for "goats" (as a herd/species).
2. amʿaza — verb: "his goats became numerous," said in a paired construction with aḍʾana ("his sheep became numerous").
3. maʿʿāz — "a goat-owner."
4. māʿiz / māʿiza — the singular "he-goat"/"she-goat" picked out of the collective maʿz.
5. amʿūz — a herd of wild mountain-goats (ibex).

**Figurative senses (majāz)** — built on the contrast between goats (lean, firm, sure-footed on rock) and sheep (fat, soft, at ease on sand):
6. Of people: "Zayd is ḍāʾin, ʿAmr is māʿiz" — Zayd is fat-fleshed (sheep-like), ʿAmr is lean and firmly/tightly built (goat-like).
7. Exclamatory idiom: "How amʿaza he is!" (of a man or of his opinion) — meaning "how firm/hard/unyielding," glossed by the author as "how solid he is."
8. Of sand dunes: ḍawāʾin al-raml ("sheep" of the sand) = the soft, large dunes; mawāʿiz ("goats" of the sand) = the firm, fine sand.
9. al-amʿaz / al-maʿzāʾ — rough, stony ground.
10. A verse of al-Shammākh, cited via Sībawayh, illustrating al-maʿzāʾ: a man with a head-wound, the crown of his skull lying bared, and the stony ground having further disfigured the mark/scar on him. (The line is difficult; one word in the second hemistich, rendered here as "scar/mole," is uncertain.)
11. istamʿaza fī amrihi — "he grew firm and earnest/diligent in his affair."

Running theme: every figurative use — a man's hard character, a firm opinion, a lean physique, rough stony terrain, firm sand — extends the base opposition between the goat (firm, hardy) and the sheep (soft, fat), which al-Zamakhsharī treats as the productive image behind this root's non-literal meanings.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) gives the root م-ح-ص (m-ḥ-ṣ) a single core meaning: to clear a thing and refine/purify it.

1. Basic sense: maḥaṣa-hu = he freed it from every defect.

2. Moral/religious use: "God maḥaṣa the servant from sin" means He purified and cleansed him of it (also said with the doubled form maḥḥaṣa). Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'an — "that God may purify/sift those who believe" (3:141) — as an instance of this doubled form.

3. Metallurgical use: "I maḥḥaṣtu gold with fire" = I purified it, removing the dross/alloy.

4. "A mumaḥḥaṣ horse": popularly said to mean a horse of strong, sound build. Ibn Fāris adds his own reasoning here — by analogy with the core sense, he takes it to really mean a horse free of defects, rather than simply "strong-built."

5. Craft use: al-maḥiṣ, applied to ropes and bowstrings, is a rope/string that has been worked until its fuzzy nap is gone and it has become smooth and supple.

He supports this last sense with a line of Hudhali poetry describing such a rope/bowstring as smooth and not stiff-stranded, creaking when drawn taut at a bent or curving point — a line whose closing image is compressed enough that the exact physical detail it pictures is not further explained in the entry itself.

Overall, every sense in this entry — physical purification (gold), moral purification (the believer, per the Qur'anic citation), and physical smoothing/refining (a rope, a horse's build) — traces back to Ibn Fāris's single core idea: clearing something of what does not belong to it, until only the sound, refined substance remains.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) treats م-ح-ل (m-ḥ-l) as a sound root carrying two distinct meanings, plus one usage that fits neither.

**1. Scarcity/drought (qillat al-khayr).**
- al-maḥl = the cutting-off of rain and the drying-up of land, i.e. loss of pasturage.
- arḍun muḥūl — "drought-stricken land" (muḥūl here is a plural-pattern word, fuʿūl).
- Al-Khalīl [ibn Aḥmad] notes the term gets applied to places generally.
- amḥalat → land "became drought-stricken" (mumḥil); amḥala l-qawm → "the people were hit by drought"; zamānun māḥil → "a time/year of drought."

**2. Slander / malicious informing (al-wishāya wa-l-siʿāya).**
- maḥala bihi = he slandered him / informed against him maliciously (saʿā bihi).
- Cited in a supplication: "Do not make the Qur'an a māḥil against us" — i.e., do not let the Qur'an testify against us [before God] for having abandoned following it; rather, make us people who follow it and act on it. (Ibn Fāris glosses the supplication this way himself.)

**3. An outlying usage, unrelated to both senses above.**
- labanun mumaḥḥal, and maḥḥalahu l-qawm — "the people muḥaḥḥal'd it [the milk]," meaning they stored/preserved it (ḥaqanūhu), i.e., kept it in a skin to let it thicken or sour. Ibn Fāris flags this explicitly as diverging from the root's two core meanings.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris states that m-ḥ-n (مَحَنَ) yields three words, and unusually for his method, he does not derive them from one shared core meaning — he flags them explicitly as "not following a single pattern."

1. Testing/trial — al-maḥn (المَحْنُ) = al-ikhtibār ("testing"). Both maḥanahu and imtaḥanahu are used for "he put him to the test."

2. Giving — from the idiom "I came to him but mā maḥananī shayʾan" ("he mā maḥana-ed me anything"), which means "he gave me nothing" (mā aʿṭānī).

3. Striking with a whip — maḥanahu sawṭan means "he struck/lashed him with a whip."

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
poets_named: unnamed verse; al-Mufaḍḍal al-Nukrī (pre-Islamic); Sāʿida ibn Juʾayya al-Hudhalī (pre-Islamic); Sabra ibn ʿAmr al-Asadī (pre-Islamic); Ruʾba (Umayyad) ×2
text:
Root: م ح ق (m-ḥ-q) — Tāj al-ʿArūs (al-Zabīdī, d. 1791 CE)

1. Core meaning — to nullify, efface completely. maḥaqahu (yamḥaquhu, maḥq) = he abolished it and effaced it until nothing of it remained. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: "al-maḥq is for a thing to vanish entirely so that none of it is seen." Cited as scripture: "wa yamḥaqa l-kāfirīn" (Q 3:141), which the author glosses as "He uproots them and nullifies their deeds."

2. Intensive form. maḥḥaqa (Form II, tamḥīq) is the same verb intensified. The author notes it appears in a variant recitation attributed to ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zubayr of the ribā/charity verse: "God effaces (yumaḥḥiqu) usury and makes charity grow (yurabbī)." The passive/reflexive forms tamaḥḥaqa, imtaḥaqa, immaḥaqa all mean "it diminished, became void."

3. Loss of blessing. Abū Zayd: "God effaced (maḥaqa) the thing" means He removed its blessing, its good, and its yield. A rival form amḥaqahu is called an inferior dialect variant; al-Aṣmaʿī accepted only maḥaqahu.

4. A minor botanical sense. Ibn Sīdah records al-maḥq also meaning palm trees planted too close together.

5. Heat destroying things. "The heat maḥaqa the thing" = burned and destroyed it; the thing "imtaḥaqa" (was consumed).

6. The moon's waning (al-maḥāq / muḥāq / miḥāq) — the entry's longest discussion, with several competing definitions from different grammarians, all describing the end of the lunar month when the crescent is invisible:
   - The night(s) when the waned crescent simply isn't seen (Ibn Sīdah), illustrated with two poetic citations about a month "becoming muḥāq."
   - The last three nights of the month, called al-sirār (Abū ʿUbayd, Ibn al-Aʿrābī; also preferred by al-Zamakhsharī and al-Ṣāghānī).
   - Two nights when the moon is hidden, seen neither morning nor evening (Ibn al-Aʿrābī).
   - Specifically nights 25, 26, and 27, after which the moon becomes visible again before dawn (al-Aṣmaʿī, Ibn Shumayl, Abū al-Haytham, al-Mubarrad, al-Riyāshī) — al-Azharī states this is, in his own judgment, the sounder of the two main views.
   - Etymology per Ibn al-Aʿrābī: the moon is named this way because it rises together with the sun, and the sun "effaces" it so no one can see it.

7. Figurative/metaphorical extensions:
   - naṣl maḥīq — a blade thinned and sharpened until it seems "worn away."
   - qarn maḥīq — a horn rubbed/polished smooth, its edge gone (illustrated with a line of poetry by al-Mufaḍḍal al-Nukrī).
   - Morphological note: al-Jawharī classifies maḥīq as the pattern faʿīl (from maḥaqahu); he rejects Ibn Durayd's claim that it is instead the pattern mafʿūl, calling it far-fetched.

8. Intense heat. yawm māḥiq al-ḥarr / māḥiq al-ṣayf = a day, or the peak, of fierce heat, "because it effaces and burns up everything" (al-Aṣmaʿī). Illustrated with a verse by Sāʿida ibn Juʾayya al-Hudhalī describing wild asses standing exhausted in the blazing summer heat.

9. To perish. amḥaqa = it perished, compared to the moon's waning. Abū ʿAmr: al-imḥāq is said of wealth or anything that perishes, like the crescent's muḥāq. Illustrated with a satirical verse by Sabra ibn ʿAmr al-Asadī (one word in the line, أَنَسّ, is textually uncertain).

10. A pre-Islamic (Jāhiliyya) custom, called al-maḥīq. When it was the "miḥāq day" of the month, a man could take over another man's water source in the owner's absence, use it to water his own livestock, and remain its custodian for that month; when the month ended, the original owner regained the greater right to it. The author attributes this social practice specifically to pre-Islamic custom, not to any later legal institution.

11. Supplementary entries (mustadrak):
    - al-amḥāq = plural of al-maḥq (with a citation from the poet Ruʾba; one word in the line, نَخْسات, is uncertain).
    - shayʾ maḥīq = mamḥūq, "effaced."
    - "this thing is a mamḥaqa for blessing" = it tends to make blessing disappear.
    - imtiḥāq al-qamar = the moon's "burning up" — it rises just ahead of the sun for two nights near month's end and so goes unseen.
    - muḥiqa l-rajulu / immaḥaqa = a man came close to death.
    - A line of Ruʾba's poetry about a thin crescent is glossed as referring to the moon at the point of miḥāq, when it has become small and faint.
    - imtaḥaqa l-nabātu = a plant dried up, scorched by intense heat.
    - al-inmiḥāq = synonym for effacement/attrition.
    - amḥaqa l-qamaru = the moon entered its miḥāq phase.
    - al-maḥaqa = destruction, perishing.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris (Maqayis al-Lugha) gives the root m-h-w a single core sense: going away with a thing, that is, removal or erasure.

1. Wind and clouds: "The wind went away with the clouds" means it carried them off, dispersed them.

2. The north wind's name: The north wind is called mahwah, precisely because it erases (tamhu) the clouds - the name derives directly from this root's core sense.

3. Erasing writing: The basic verb is mahawtu l-kitaba amhuhu mahwan, "I erased the writing," with mahw as the verbal noun for the act of erasing.

4. Becoming erased (intransitive): Something "became erased" (immmaha l-shay'u) means its trace or mark disappeared. Ibn Faris notes a second form with the identical meaning, imtaha.

So the entry traces one thread from a literal sense (wind erasing/dispersing clouds, hence the wind's own name) to the general verb for erasing written text, to the passive/reflexive sense of a mark vanishing.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-ص-ر as one sound root with three meanings: a kind of milking, the setting of a limit, and a bodily organ.

1. Milking with the fingertips. maṣr is drawing milk out with the tips of the fingers. A nāqa maṣūr is a she-camel whose milk comes slowly and can only be got out this way. Ibn al-Sikkīt is cited for maṣr as milking out whatever the udder holds; tamaṣṣur is said to be the milking of the last remnants left in the udder, and the leftover milk itself is called maṣr. From the same idea, maṣṣartu ʿalayhi al-shayʾ means "I gave it to him little by little" — doling out in small amounts.

2. A limit or boundary. miṣr is a boundary-line. Ibn Fāris reports that the people of Hajar wrote in their contracts "so-and-so bought the house bi-muṣūrihā," meaning with its boundaries. He cites the poet ʿAdī: the One who made the sun a miṣr — an unmistakable boundary — between day and night, dividing them. He also gives miṣr as any administrative district (kūra) in which the fayʾ and the ṣadaqāt are apportioned.

3. An organ: the intestine. maṣīr is the intestine; its plural is muṣrān, and the plural of that in turn is maṣārīn. The compound muṣrān al-faʾra ("mouse-guts") names a variety of inferior dates.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مَّطَر 7x "a rain"; أُمْطِرَتْ 7x "and we rained"; مُّمْطِر 1x "bringing us rain"
text:
Ibn Fāris identifies م-ط-ر as a sound root with two core meanings.

1. Rain falling from the sky. The noun is مَطَر (maṭar, rain); one says muṭirnā maṭaran ("we were rained upon"). Ibn Fāris notes that some hold the form IV verb umṭira ("to be rained upon") is used only in the context of punishment, citing the Qur'an: "it was rained upon with the rain of evil" (al-Furqān 25:40). The verb tamaṭṭara means to expose oneself to rain; from it comes al-mustamṭir, "one who seeks rain" — used figuratively for a seeker of good or bounty.

2. A kind of running or swift movement. Tamaṭṭara fī al-arḍ means "he went off / departed." Al-mutamaṭṭir is a rider urging his horse to run, and tamaṭṭarat bihi farasuhu means "his mare galloped with him."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root م ط و (m-ṭ-w), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: extension in a thing, and stretching-out.

1. maṭawtu bi-l-qawmi — I drove/stretched the people onward in their travel, illustrated with a line of poetry by Imruʾ al-Qays about driving mounts until exhausted, even outrunning the need for reins.
2. al-maṭiyyah — the riding-mount, derived from this same idea of extension/stretching-out; alternatively, said to be named because one rides its maṭā, its back — and the back itself is called al-maṭā for the "extension" found in it (i.e. its length).
3. al-miṭw — a companion, because he "stretches along"/travels the distance together with you, illustrated with a line of poetry about calling out to a travel-companion as day declined.
4. Ibn al-Aʿrābī derives the word from imtaṭaytu al-baʿīra, "I mounted the camel."
5. Closing extension: the palm-tree's frond-cluster (ʿadhq al-nakhlah) may be measured against this same root, for its own length/extension.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مَدَّ 13x "extend"; أَمَدَّ 10x "we extend"; مَدّ 2x "extensively"; مَّمْدُود 2x "extended"; مُمِدّ 1x "going to reinforce you"; مُدَّت 1x "their term"; مِدَاد 1x "ink"; مَدَد 1x "(as) a supplement"; مُّمَدَّدَة 1x "extended"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats m-d-d as a single root meaning: drawing something out in length, and joining one thing to another so that it extends.

1. **Drawing out.** madadtu al-shayʾ, amudduhu, maddan: "I drew the thing out" (verbal noun madd).

2. **A river swelling and being fed.** madda al-nahr: the river rose. maddahu nahrun ākhar: another river fed it, meaning it added to it and joined on to it, so lengthening its extent (muddah).

3. **Reinforcement.** amdadtu al-jaysh bi-madad: "I reinforced the army with a reinforcement (madad)."

4. **Pus.** amadda al-jurḥ: the wound suppurated, that is, pus (midda), the matter that comes out, formed in it. Ibn Fāris derives this from the same root sense.

5. **A mixed drink for camels.** To give camels water with flour, or with something else mixed into it to extend it, is expressed with the verb from this root (verbal noun madd); the drink itself is called al-madīd.

6. **The day's advance.** madd al-nahār is the rising of the day as it lengthens.

7. **Ink.** al-midād is what one writes with, so called because it is extended with water. Of the inkwell one says both madadtu al-dawāh and amdadtuhā. al-madda is one dip of the pen into the inkwell to take ink.

8. **A dry measure.** al-mudd, one of the measures of capacity, also belongs here, because it extends one measured amount by another of the same size.

Ibn Fāris lists one word as an exception that does not fit the root meaning: māʾ imiddān, extremely salty water.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م د ن (m-d-n) as a root with essentially a single sense.

1. Its only content is مدينة (madīna), "city, town" — taken on the morphological pattern faʿīla (فَعِيلَة).

2. Morphology: the plural is مُدُن (mudun, "cities"); and the denominal verb مَدَّنْتُ مَدِينَةً (maddantu madīnatan) means "I built/founded a city."

(The received text is slightly damaged where the head-word "madīna" appears, but the sense is recoverable from the plural and verb Ibn Fāris cites.)

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مِهَٰد 7x "[the] resting place"; مَهْد 5x "the cradle"; يَمْهَدُ 1x "they are preparing"; مَٰهِدُون 1x "(are) the spreaders"; مَهَّد 1x "and i spread"; تَمْهِيد 1x "ease"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root م-ه-د from a single core notion: smoothing, levelling, and making a thing easy or well-prepared.

1. Core sense: to make smooth/level and easy. From it comes al-mahd, the cradle or bed.

2. Verbal uses: mahhadtu al-amr — "I made the matter smooth / prepared it," i.e. waṭṭaʾtuhu. Tamahhada — "it became smoothed out / settled level."

3. al-mihād: the soft, level bedding or ground of anything (equivalent to al-wiṭāʾ). Its plural is muhud.

4. An extended physical sense: imtahada, said of a camel's hump and the like, means it rose up and swelled. Ibn Fāris cites the poet Abū al-Najm ("and the withers swelled up as a boil does"), glossing it as rising, evening out, and becoming like a level mihād.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مُهْل 3x "like molten brass"; مَهِّلِ 2x "so give respite"; أَمْهِلْ 1x "give respite to them"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-ه-ل as two sound (unrelated) roots: one for unhurriedness, one for a molten substance.

1. Deliberateness, going slowly (تُؤَدَة).
   - مَهْلًا ("gently", "slow down") is used as an address: مَهْلًا يَا رَجُلُ, and the same form serves for two people or many — it does not inflect for number.
   - It can be rebuffed: to someone saying مَهْلًا one answers لَا مَهْلَ وَاللَّهِ ("no going easy, by God"), or مَا مَهْلٌ بِمُغْنِيَةٍ عَنْكَ شَيْئًا ("going easy will do nothing for you"). A verse cited: "and 'go easy' is no admonisher of the ignorant."
   - أَمْهَلَهُ اللَّهُ — God gave him respite, i.e. did not move against him hastily.
   - مَشَى عَلَى مُهْلَتِهِ — he walked at his own unhurried pace (عَلَى رِسْلِهِ).

2. A contrary usage. Abū ʿUbayd is quoted as glossing التَّمَهُّل as التَّقَدُّم (going forward, advancing). Ibn Fāris notes this runs against sense 1 and suggests the word may belong to the أَضْداد — terms carrying two opposite meanings.

3. الْمُهْل — the second, separate root: reported either as the sediment/dregs of oil, or as molten copper. Ibn Fāris records both reports without deciding between them.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-ه-ن (m-h-n) as one sound root whose core idea is contempt and lowness — a thing being slight or of little worth.

1. **Low, of little worth.** مَهِين (mahīn) means حَقِير — contemptible, paltry. The noun مَهَانَة (mahāna) is that quality of lowliness, as in the phrase "he is mahīn, manifestly of low estate."

2. **Service / menial work.** Ibn Fāris places مَهْن (mahn) — service, menial labour — and the noun مِهْنة / مَهْنة (mihna / mahna, vowelled either way) in this same root-chapter, i.e. he derives the idea of serving from the same notion of lowliness. The agent noun مَاهِن (māhin) is the servant.

3. **Pulling at a garment.** مَهَنْتُ الثَّوْبَ (mahantu al-thawb) = I tugged/pulled the garment; the garment so handled is مَمْهُون (mamhūn).

4. **Milking camels** (reported with reservation). He adds "perhaps they said" مَهَنْتُ الْإِبِلَ (mahantu al-ibil) for "I milked the camels" — marked by him as a less certain usage.

Method note: the entry follows Ibn Fāris's usual procedure of positing a single semantic origin (here: contempt/lowness) and then showing the other attested uses — service, tugging a garment, milking — as branches of that one chapter.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-ج-د (m-j-d) as one sound root whose single idea is reaching the furthest point — and, he specifies, only in something praiseworthy.

1. **majd (glory)** — reaching the utmost limit in karam (generosity, noble open-handedness). This is the core noun of the root.

2. **Divine names** — al-Mājid and al-Majīd are applied to God on this basis: no generosity stands above His.

3. **mājada (III form)** — "so-and-so mājada so-and-so": to contend or vie with another in glory, to boast against him.

4. **Shāhid — a proverb**: "In every tree there is fire, but the markh and the ʿafār took the fullest share of it." Ibn Fāris explains istamjada here as the two trees having taken fire in abundance, as much as sufficed them — going to the limit in it, so much so that fire is struck from them. This is his evidence that the root means reaching a maximum.

5. **majadat al-ibil (verbal noun mujūd)** — said of camels: reported by others to mean that they got nearly their fill of fresh pasture and the like.

6. **amjadtu al-dābba** — "I foddered the animal with what sufficed it." Ibn Fāris judges this second usage the better fit with the root's governing analogy (sufficiency to the full measure), rather than the camel-form in point 5.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root m-j-s (مجس) as an outlier: unlike most Arabic roots he catalogues, he says it has no recognizable Arabic derivational pattern (qiyās) linking it to a core meaning.

His judgment: it is likely a loanword from Persian.

Its one attested Arabic use, per this entry, is the name al-Majūs — the Magians (Zoroastrians). From this noun, Arabic speakers formed a verb: tamajjasa ("he tamajjasa-ed") — meaning a man became a Majūsī, i.e., joined their number/became one of them.

So the entry records not an inherited Arabic root-meaning but a borrowed ethnonym that was then naturalized into an Arabic verbal pattern (tafaʿʿala, denoting "became [one of]").

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
quran_words: مَكَّ 13x "we established"; مَّكِين 4x "firm"; أَمْكَنَ 1x "so he gave (you) power"
poets_named: Abū al-Hindī (Umayyad); Banū ʿUqayl (undated); Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad); Ibn al-Aʿrābī and Abū Wajza (later (Abbasid or after))
text:
Root م ك ن (m-k-n), as recorded in al-Zabīdī's Tāj al-ʿArūs. The entry sets out two originally distinct clusters — one about lizard/locust eggs, one about place, position, and capability — plus a plant name and some proper names.

**1. al-makn / makin — eggs of the ḍabba (spiny-tailed lizard) and the locust.** Singular makna / makina. A cited verse (Abū al-Hindī) makes it a bedouin delicacy that non-Arabs find unappetizing.

**2. The verb of egg-bearing.** makinat (the lizard) → it is makūn; amkanat → it is mumkin: it has gathered its eggs inside; the locust likewise (al-Kisāʾī). A verse of Banū ʿUqayl praises the egg-bearing (makūn) ḍabba as the best. Alternatively, makūn is a lizard sitting on its eggs. al-Ṣiḥāḥ gives makina (kasra) as singular of makin/makināt.

**3. The ḥadīth "leave the birds upon their makunāt."** al-Zabīdī records several readings:
- (a) makunāt/makināt = eggs, the word borrowed for birds from the lizard, since eggs (makin) are not really a bird word. Abū ʿUbayd notes bedouins rejected makināt for birds (a bird's is a wukna, a nest), confirming makināt = lizard eggs, but allows the metaphorical transfer (compare calling Ethiopians' lips mashāfir, properly a camel word).
- (b) = the birds' places/perches: leave them where God set them; they neither harm nor benefit — do not take omens.
- (c) Shamir: makina here = tamakkun, an established position (as in "he has makina with the ruler"); so, "leave the birds in whatever position you find them and drop augury." Ibn Barrī agrees makina means "being established," and a place is only called makina by extension.
- (d) al-Zamakhsharī notes a variant mukunāt (plural of mukun, itself plural of makān).
- (e) al-Shāfiʿī (via Yūnus) explains the practical background: pre-Islamic men startled a settled bird — flight to the right meant "go ahead," to the left "turn back"; the Prophet forbade this. al-Azharī endorses al-Shāfiʿī's reading and faults the base dictionary's author for missing it.

**4. makāna = an unhurried, measured pace** (synonym makīna). "He went at his makāna"; "walk at your makīna/makāna/hīna" (Abū Zayd). The Qur'anic {iʿmalū ʿalā makānatikum} is glossed as "according to your side/quarter," or "according to the footing you are established upon." al-Farrāʾ pairs makāna with mawqiʿa and maḥilla (a standing in the heart).

**5. makāna = rank/standing with a king** (manzila); plural makānāt, with no broken plural.

**6. makuna → makīn = a person of established standing;** plural mukanāʾ. Grammatical use of the derived term al-mutamakkin (al-Jawharī): a noun is mutamakkin if it is declinable (e.g. ʿUmar, Ibrāhīm); if also fully triptote it is mutamakkin amkan (Zayd, ʿAmr, taking all three cases -u/-a/-i); the non-mutamakkin is the indeclinable (kayfa, ayna). Of an adverb, mutamakkin means it can also serve as an ordinary noun.

**7. al-makān = the place that contains something.** al-Rāghib notes that some theologians define it instead as an "accident" — the containing relation between an enclosing body and what it encloses — but observes this is not the ordinary linguistic sense. Plurals amkina and amākin. Thaʿlab argues the mīm is really an added prefix (the word deriving from kāna), and the plural amkina arises by treating that added mīm as if it were a root letter — a known assimilation (compare manāra → manāʾir, masīl → amsila).

**8. al-maknān = a spring plant** with dense endive-like leaves and a yellow flower, slow-growing because of its softness; livestock that graze it give richer, thicker milk (Abū Ḥanīfa). Illustrated by verses of Dhū al-Rumma (its flowering bed like patterned carpets) and, under **wādin mumkin** ("a valley that grows maknān"), by Ibn al-Aʿrābī and Abū Wajza.

**9. Proper name — Abū Makīn:** Nūḥ ibn Rabīʿa al-Baṣrī, called a tābiʿī in the manuscripts but, al-Zabīdī corrects, really of the generation after; graded trustworthy (thiqa), with the transmission links given from al-Dhahabī, Ibn al-Muhandis, and Ibn Ḥibbān.

**10. The "enable/make possible" sense.** makkana / amkana someone min al-shayʾ = to give him power over it; so tamakkana / istamkana = he gained mastery. al-Azharī's usage note: you say amkananī al-amr ("the matter became possible for me") and lā yumkinuka al-ṣuʿūd ("you cannot ascend"), but not anā umkinuhu / anta tumkinu al-ṣuʿūd — i.e. "possible" is predicated of the matter, not of the person as agent.

**Further notes.** mikān = another plural of makūn (egg-bearing lizards). makān is also pluralized mukun (al-Zamakhsharī). "People upon their sakināt, nazilāt, and makināt" = their dwelling-places (Ibn al-Aʿrābī; al-Zamakhsharī calls this metaphor-upon-metaphor). "mā amkanahu ʿinda al-amīr" (how favored he is) is anomalous per al-Jawharī, though Ibn Barrī cites makuna yamkunu ("to settle," of water) to make it regular. tamakkana bi-l-makān / tamakkanahu (with the preposition dropped); a Sībawayh citation. "makānak!" is said to warn someone of danger behind him. al-mukna (ḍamma) = power, capability. Among the Sufis, al-tamkīn is the station of being firmly rooted and settled in uprightness. Banū al-Makīn are ʿAlawids in Yemen; Mākiyān and Mākīna are ancestors of two named transmitters.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مَكَرَ 22x "plotted"; مَكْر 19x "a plot"; مَٰكِرِين 2x "(of) the planners"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م ك ر (m-k-r) as two unrelated words:

1. **al-makr** — contrivance and deception (al-iḥtiyāl wa-l-khidāʿ); the verb is makara bihi, yamkuru ("he plotted/schemed against him").

2. **al-makr** — plumpness and roundness of the lower leg. Hence the phrase imraʾatun mamkūratu al-sāqayn, "a woman with full, rounded shins."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مَكَثَ 4x "stay here"; مَّٰكِثِين 2x "(they will) abide"; مُكْث 1x "intervals"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-ك-ث as a single semantic root with one core idea, then lists its forms.

1. Core sense: the root points to coming to a stop and waiting — halting in place rather than moving on.

2. Verb and verbal nouns: مَكَثَ (makatha, "he stayed/tarried"), with two attested verbal nouns, مَكْث (makth) and مُكْث (mukth). He also records a second vowelling of the perfect, مَكُثَ (makutha) — the pattern typical of an inherent quality rather than a one-off act.

3. Applied to a person: رَجُلٌ مَكِيثٌ (rajul makīth) describes someone weighty and deliberate, not hasty — the trait of not rushing.

4. Derived form: التَّمَكُّث (tamakkuth, form V) is glossed simply as waiting.

The entry is terse: no poetic citations, Qur'anic verses, or grammatical apparatus beyond the vowellings and derived forms noted above.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats m-k-w (headed مكا) as a sound root with three meanings: a kind of sound, roughness in a thing, and a third that this copy states as "a kind of honey", although everything he gives under it concerns washing.

1. **A sound: whistling.** makā yamkū, verbal noun mukāʾ, is to whistle into one's hand held gathered together. ʿAntara uses it of a spear-wound: the flesh of the man's shoulder "whistles" like the mouth-corner of a split-lipped man, that is, the wound makes a sound as it opens and closes. The bird al-mukkāʾ is named for its whistling; a poet says that when it sings somewhere that is not a meadow, woe to the owners of sheep and donkeys. The same verb is said of a man breaking wind.

   Set off within this section ("as for"): al-makā and al-makw are the hare's lair, the spot where it crouches. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ speaks of a place holding many lairs of wild creatures.

2. **Roughness.** makiyat yaduhu tamkā makan: his hand became thick and rough.

3. **tamakkā: washing oneself.** tamakkā means to wash oneself (tawaḍḍaʾa), as in the verse "like one who washes himself with the blood of the slain". Ibn Fāris says the word's origin is tamakkā said of a horse that rubs its eye with its knee.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: مَلَأ 30x "the chiefs"; مُلِئَتْ 6x "surely i will fill"; مَالِـُون 2x "and fill"; مِّلْء 1x "full"; ٱمْتَلَأْ 1x "you filled"
text:
al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī treats two related roots under this heading: ملا (m-l-w/y) and ملأ (m-l-ʾ, with hamza).

ملا (m-l-w/y) — extension in time and space, and dictation:
1. al-imlāʾ basically means "extending/granting" (imdād). From it, a long stretch of time is called malāwa or maliyy — hence وَاهْجُرْنِي مَلِيًّا [Maryam 19:46], "shun me for a long while." Related verbs: tamallaytu dahran ("I endured for an age"), tamallaytu al-thawb ("I got long use out of the garment"), tamallā bi-kadhā ("he long enjoyed something"); malāka llāh (no hamza) = "may God grant you long life"; ʿishta maliyyan = "may you live long."
2. al-malā (short final) = the wide open desert — the spatial counterpart of extension.
3. al-malawān is said to be "night and day," but al-Rāghib argues its real sense is their recurrence and continual extension. His proof: a poet annexes malwā to "day and night" ("Day and night, whose malwā is unceasing…"), which would be redundant if malawān just meant night and day.
4. Another branch is "granting respite": وَأُمْلِي لَهُمْ [al-Aʿrāf 7:183] and وَأَمْلى لَهُمْ [Muḥammad 47:25] = "I/he grant(s) them respite"; likewise نُمْلِي لَهُمْ [Āl ʿImrān 3:178].
5. And "dictation": from amlaytu al-kitāb ("I dictated the book"). Grammatical note: amlaytu originally was amlaltu (from the root l-l), with the doubled lām transposed for ease — hence the two Qurʾanic forms فَهِيَ تُمْلى عَلَيْهِ [al-Furqān 25:5] and فَلْيُمْلِلْ وَلِيُّهُ [al-Baqara 2:282] ("let his guardian dictate justly") sit side by side.

ملأ (m-l-ʾ, with hamza) — fullness:
1. al-malaʾ = a council/company united on one opinion, who "fill the eyes" with splendour and the souls with awe — hence the Qurʾanic "chiefs/notables": البقرة 2:246, الأعراف 7:60, القصص 28:20, النمل 27:29, etc.
2. Idioms of "filling the eye": fulān milʾ al-ʿuyūn = greatly esteemed by onlookers, as if he fills their eye; shābb māliʾ al-ʿayn = an impressive youth. al-malaʾ can also mean a nature "filled with beauty" (poetic shāhid: "Do well in disposition, Juhayna!").
3. mālaʾtuhu = "I backed him, became one of his company" — parallel to shāyaʿtuhu ("I became one of his partisans"). huwa malīʾ bi-kadhā = "he is competent/solvent in it."
4. al-malāʾa = a head-cold that "fills" the brain; muliʾa / umliʾa fulān = he caught it.
5. al-milʾ = the capacity of a full vessel: aʿṭinī milʾahu wa-milʾayhi wa-thalāthata amlāʾihi ("give me its fill, twice, three times its fill").

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
ROOT m-l-ḥ (ملح) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris treats m-l-ḥ as one sound root whose various branches all trace back to a single core idea — whiteness — even though some of them look unrelated on the surface.

1. Core meaning — whiteness. Al-milḥ ("salt") is named for its white color. Supported by a verse describing a blade as "white like salt."

2. Salty water. Māʾ milḥ and (per Ibn al-Aʿrābī, with a supporting verse about the water of Qaww) māʾ māliḥ are both attested for "salty water." The verb maluḥa l-māʾu means "the water became salty."

3. Salted/cured fish: samak mamlūḥ or malīḥ.

4. Amlaḥa/amlaḥnā (form IV) — "to find salty water" or "[of water] to turn salty." Illustrated with a verse by Nuṣayb lamenting that his once-sweet drinking water had turned salty, adding to his suffering.

5. Malaḥtu l-qidra — "I put the right/measured amount of salt in the pot" (form I, a positive, careful act).

6. Amlaḥtuhā — "I ruined it with [too much] salt" (same form-IV verb, but here meaning to spoil by over-salting — the opposite nuance of sense 5).

7. Mallaḥtu l-nāqata (form II) — a veterinary usage: "I treated the she-camel with salt," said of a barren she-camel whose womb was treated with something salty as a remedy.

8. Maluḥa l-shayʾu (malāḥa, milḥ) — "the thing became comely/charming/witty." The taste sense of "pleasant/salty" is extended metaphorically to beauty and charm.

9. Al-mumālaḥa = al-muwākala, "eating together," i.e., commensality.

10. Metaphor — milḥ = wet-nursing/suckling. Ibn Fāris cites the tribe of Hawāzin telling the Prophet: "Had we nursed [malaḥnā] al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Shamir or al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Mundhir, he would have honored that bond for us" — meaning the Prophet had been wet-nursed among them. The shared milk-bond is called milḥ by extension.

11. Metaphor — milḥ = fat. Amlaḥtu l-qidra can also mean "I put fat in the pot." On this basis a verse praising a plump woman — whose "milḥ" (fat) sits above her knees — is explained as being about her fleshiness, not salt.

12. Color term. Al-mulḥa describes a whiteness sometimes mixed with black — i.e., a grey/pied color; kabsh amlaḥ = "a grey ram." One of the winter months is called Milḥān for the whiteness of its snow.

13. Al-Malḥāʾ — the name of a cavalry unit that belonged to the House of al-Mundhir.

14. Al-mallāḥ — "ship's master/sailor." Ibn Fāris derives this from milḥ, since sea water is salty; he notes others instead trace it to al-malḥ, "the rapid flapping of a bird's wings" (supported by a verse about falcons flapping beneath a storm cloud).

15. Outlier not cleanly fitting the root: al-mullāḥ, a name for a certain ḥamḍ (salt-tolerant desert) plant — unless its taste is in fact somewhat salty, which would tie it back after all.

16. Two further specialized nouns: al-malḥāʾ, the slope of an animal's back below the withers and spine (anatomy); and al-malaḥ, a swelling in a horse's hock.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)

poets_named: Ibn Aḥmar (lived into Islam); Abū Wajza (disputed date); Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam); Qays b. al-Khaṭīm (pre-Islamic); Aws b. Ḥajar (pre-Islamic); Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad)
text:
Ibn Sīda's al-Muḥkam entry for the root م ل ك (m-l-k).

Core sense: to possess or contain a thing and to have the power of sole disposal over it. The verb malaka / yamlik carries several verbal-noun forms — malk, milk, mulk (the last transmitted only by al-Liḥyānī) — plus malaka, mamlaka, mamluka.

1. Ownership and property. "He has no malk/milk/mulk" = he owns nothing. "I have malk in this valley" = pasture, a watering-place, property and the like that one owns; also specifically a well one digs and holds alone. amlaka / mallaka someone a thing = to make him its owner (e.g. "entrust wealth to its owner even if he is a fool").

2. Water as a source of control. al-māʾu malaku amr — "water rules an affair": a people who hold water control their situation. A verse of Abū Wajza and a note from Thaʿlab tie "having no milk/malk/mulk" to having no water. malaknā al-māʾ = the water strengthened us to manage our affair.

3. Marital authority and captivity. mulk al-walī over a woman = a guardian's keeping and authority over her. ʿabd mamlaka = a slave taken captive himself (his parents not owned), as opposed to qinn (a born slave). ṭāla mulkuhu = his servitude lasted long; ḥasan al-milka = well-treated in servitude.

4. Dominion / kingship (al-mulk). Well known; grammatically both masculine and feminine, like sulṭān. mulk Allāh / malakūt = His dominion and greatness; malakūt of a place = its glory and power. The possessor of dominion is called malk, malik, malīk, or mālik (plurals: mulūk, amlāk, mulakāʾ, mullak/mullāk; umlūk is a collective). mallaka / amlaka a man = to make him king. Some hold malik and malīk apply to God and others, but malk only to other than God. By extension, mulūk al-naḥl = the "kings" (leaders) of a bee-swarm (Abū Dhuʾayb cited).

5. A poetic crux. Ibn Aḥmar's line "bannat ʿalayhi al-mulk(a) aṭnābahā... kaʾs" is analysed two ways: (a) Ibn al-Aʿrābī reads al-mulk as = the wine-cup, a substitution (badal); (b) others read al-malk in the accusative as a verbal noun standing for a circumstantial qualifier (= "made king"), comparable to arsalahā al-ʿirāk. Variant readings (Thaʿlab's lightened nūn; "maddat") are noted. All trace back to milk; mulk merely takes a ḍamma on the mīm for magnification.

6. Self-mastery. tamālaka ʿan al-shayʾ = to restrain oneself; laysa lahu malāk = one who cannot restrain himself. milāk / malāk al-amr = the mainstay by which a matter is held together. Proverb: "either I perish (hulk) or I gain mastery (mulk)."

7. Marriage contract. imlāk / milāk / malāk = a man's marriage-contract. amlaka someone a woman = to marry her to him; umlika = to be given in marriage. One does not say malaka bihā. umlikat amrahā (of a woman) = she was divorced (given charge of her own affair).

8. Working / mastering physically. malaka / amlaka al-ʿajīn = to knead dough well (ʿUmar's ḥadīth: "knead the dough well, for it is one of the two increases"). malaka al-khishf ummahu = the fawn grew strong enough to follow its mother; nāqa milāk al-ibil = a she-camel the herd follows. In two verses (Qays b. al-Khaṭīm on a spear-thrust; Aws b. Ḥajar on a bow), mallaka / malaka = to brace or strengthen firmly.

9. "Middle / edge" senses. malk/mulk/milk of a road or valley = its middle and main part, or (per al-Liḥyānī) its edge/limit. mulk al-dābba = a beast's legs and guiding fore-part. Ibn Sīda uses this last sense to correct al-Liḥyānī: the Bedouin's "an old man who has no mulk and no sight" means no hands, feet, or sight — a metaphor from a beast's limbs — not "who has nothing."

10. Miscellaneous. al-mulayka = a small scroll. al-umlūk = (a) a Ḥimyarite Arab tribe (the Prophet wrote "To the Umlūk of Radmān"); (b) a small sand-lizard-like creature. Mulayk, Mulayka, Mālik, Muwaylik, Mumallak, Milkān = proper names; Mālik also names a tract of sand (Dhū al-Rumma cited). Ibn Sīda flags mālik al-mawt (for malak al-mawt, "angel of death") in one verse as an error, since malak is contracted from malʾak.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
poets_named: Firās al-Fazārī (pre-Islamic); al-Rāʿī (Umayyad); unnamed verse; Suwayd (undated); Ibn Muqbil (lived into Islam)
text:
Al-Zamakhsharī groups the root m-l-l into literal uses and figurative (majāz) extensions.

LITERAL
1. Weariness / boredom. مللته / مللت منه, استمللته = to grow weary or vexed of something (تبرّم). The verbal nouns are malal, malāl, malāla. One prone to it is malūl(a); a person who is himself tiresome is dhū amālīl (wearisome). amallanī / amalla ʿalayya = "it bore hard on me." Shāhid: Firās al-Fazārī — a camel yearns when the shackles wore hard on her forelegs.

2. Ash-baked bread. milla = hot ashes/embers; khubz milla / khubza malīl = bread baked in them; malla / imtalla l-khubza = to set the loaf in the hot ash.

3. Sewing. al-mall = the first running/tacking stitch; the tailor malla the garment, then hemmed it (kaffa). (mamlūl vs makfūf are glossed by a Persian phrase, apparently "one seam vs two seams.")

FIGURATIVE (majāz)
4. Inner fever. milla / malīla = a fever felt within the body.

5. A worn-out mount. mumall (m.) / mumalla (f.) = a much-ridden, wearied camel. Shawāhid from al-Rāʿī and another poet (mounts that had "amallat wa kallat" — wearied and spent).

6. A well-trodden road. ṭarīq mumall = much-used, long traversed back and forth. From this: amalla ʿalayhi al-malawān — day and night (al-malawān) long alternate over a place. Shawāhid: Suwayd (odes wearing a road smooth) and Ibn Muqbil (the two time-spans passing over ruins, wearing them with decay).

7. A way / path of life. al-milla = a trodden way, extended to "religion/way." Al-Zamakhsharī cites millat Ibrāhīm ("the way of Abraham," which he calls the best of ways) and imtalla fulān millat al-islām (following the way of Islam). He treats this religious sense as figuratively derived from the underlying image of a trodden path — not as a separate primary meaning.

8. Dictation. amalla ʿalayhi al-kitāb = to dictate a text to someone (from the sense of going over it repeatedly).

9. Restlessness. malmalahu al-maraḍ fa-tamalmala = illness made him toss and turn.

10. Kohl-stick. milmāl = the applicator rod (mikḥāl) used to apply kohl.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris's Maqayis al-Lugha states that the root m-l-q has one consistent underlying sense: something being stripped/denuded, together with a notion of softness or smoothness. All the derived words below are traced back to this one idea.

1. Flattery: Ibn al-Sikkit says malaq/tamalluq ("flattery, fawning") derives from talyin, "softening" -- i.e., smoothing one's manner or speech toward someone.

2. Smooth rock: malaqah names a smooth, flat rock (safah malsa').

3. Ruin/poverty: imlaq means squandering one's wealth until one is reduced to want. Ibn Faris ties this to the same root idea -- the person is, as it were, "stripped bare" of his wealth.

4. Worn/chafed limb: the phrase "inmalaqa sa'idu al-rajul" describes a man's forearm becoming chafed and worn from carrying loads -- again a "wearing away/stripping" sense. A verse is quoted describing an aged or enfeebled man (hawqal) whose forearm has become worn this way, scowling and saying it would be good "if he strikes" (salaqa); the line is cited without attribution and its full sense is somewhat obscure in isolation.

5. Trackless ground: malaqah also names land so smooth/hard that footprints barely show on it; plural malaq or malaqat.

6. Washing a garment: "malaqtu al-thawb" means "I washed the garment" -- explained as stripping it of dirt, again the root sense of denuding/removing.

Ibn Faris presents all these senses -- flattery, a smooth rock, financial ruin, a worn limb, trackless ground, and washing -- as variations on one core idea: stripping something bare, joined with softness/smoothness.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
quran_words: أَمْلَىٰ 9x "and i will give respite"; مَلِيّ 1x "(for) a prolonged time"
poets_named: unnamed verse ×3; Ibn Muqbil (lived into Islam); Taʾabbaṭa Sharran (pre-Islamic)
text:
