Al-Zabīdī's Tāj al-ʿArūs on the root م ل و (m-l-w). The senses fall into two broad clusters: (a) swift motion, and (b) long duration / prolonging.

**A. Motion**
1. مَلاَ (of a camel), imperf. يَمْلُو, verbal noun مَلْو — to travel at a hard, vigorous pace. Cited from Mulayḥ al-Hudhalī.
2. Same verb = to run / gallop (عَدَا), used in a Hudhalī report of a man who "ran off" (i.e. escaped, still breathing).

**B. Long enjoyment / long life**
3. مَلَّى … تَملِية — of God: to let someone long enjoy a loved one and live long with him (مَلاَّكَ اللَّهُ حَبِيبَكَ; from al-Jawharī). Related: تَمَلَّى عُمْرَهُ / مَلِيَّهُ = to enjoy one's lifespan; the well-wish to one wearing new clothes, أَبْلَيْتَ جَديداً وتَمَلَّيْتَ حَبِيباً ("wear out the new, long enjoy a loved one"). Also أَمْلاهُ اللَّهُ / مَلاَّهُ. A verse elegizing Yazīd b. Mizyad is cited.

**C. A span of time**
4. مَلاوة / مَلْوة (each attested with all three vowel patterns) — a while, a stretch of time: أَقَمْتُ عنده مَلاوةً من الدهر ("I stayed with him a while").
5. المَلِيّ (pattern of غَنِيّ) — (i) a long stretch of time; the entry reads Qurʾānic "وَاهْجُرْنِي مَلِيًّا" as "shun me a long time." (ii) A long hour of the day: مَضَى مَلِيٌّ من النهار.

**D. المَلا — open ground**
6. المَلا (written with alif by the Basrans, with yāʾ by others) — the open desert, wide expanse; al-Rāghib: a far-extending wilderness. Al-Aṣmaʿī: a white bareland, neither sand nor hard ground. A shāhid on the "plain" widening the distance is cited.
7. المَلَوان (dual of al-malā) — night and day, i.e. their alternation: لَا أَفْعَله ما اختلف المَلَوان ("never, so long as night and day alternate"). Al-Rāghib argues the core sense is their recurrence and extension, since a poet annexes "day and night" to them; alternatively it means the two ends of day and night. Cited from Ibn Muqbil.

**E. أَمْلَى (form IV) — to prolong, dictate, give respite**
8. أَمْلَيْتُ له في غَيِّه — to give long rein to someone in his error, i.e. prolong it.
9. أَمْلَيْتُ البعيرَ — to loosen/widen a camel's hobble.
10. أَمْلَيْتُ الكِتابَ ("I dictated the writing"), variant أَمْلَلْتُه — two good, equally valid forms, both occurring in the Qurʾān (per al-Jawharī).
11. أَمْلَى اللَّهُ الكافِرَ — God granted the unbeliever respite (amhala), deferred and prolonged for him; the entry links Qurʾānic "وَأُمْلِي لَهُمْ إِنَّ كَيْدِي مَتِينٌ."

**F. اسْتَمْلَى**
12. اسْتَمْلاهُ — to ask someone to dictate. Hence al-mustamlī, one who seeks the dictation of ḥadīth from a shaykh; the ḥadīth-scholar Abū Bakr al-Balkhī earned this title by taking dictation from Wakīʿ.

**G. Further forms**
13. المَلاة (pattern of قَناة) — a heat-and-mirage wasteland; plural مَلاً. Cited from Taʾabbaṭa Sharran.

**Supplementary notes:** المَلاوة / المَلا / المَلِيّ all denote the duration of life (تَمَلَّى العَيْشَ = to long enjoy life). مَلِيّ / مَلاً of the night = the span from nightfall to the first third (or an undefined portion); pl. أَمْلاء. Al-Aṣmaʿī: أَمْلَى عليه الزَّمنُ = time grew long on him. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: al-mulā = hot ashes, and also an era of time. al-Malā is also several place-names (verses of Qays b. Dharīḥ, Dhū al-Rumma, Kuthayyir, ʿAdī b. al-Riqāʿ cited) — variously a village near Mount Ajaʾ or watercourses of Ṭayyiʾ. المَلْوة — a dialectal Egyptian unit, half of a quarter.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
quran_words: مَّنَعَ 12x "prevented you"; مَّنَّاع 2x "forbidder"; مَمْنُوعَة 1x "forbidden"; مَّانِعَت 1x "would defend them"; مَنُوع 1x "withholding"
text:
Zabīdī's Tāj al-ʿArūs on the root م-ن-ع (m-n-ʿ), on withholding, preventing, and protecting.

1. Core sense — to withhold / prevent. مَنَعَهُ (manaʿahu, imperfect yamnaʿu) is the opposite of "he gave." It is defined as standing between a man and the thing he wants, or "fencing off" a thing. One says "he withheld it from him," "he withheld his right from him." The sense carries both interposing-between and protecting; Zabīdī (citing al-Khafājī) insists there is no letter-transposition in the phrasing, contrary to some. Form II مَنَّعَ intensifies it; the reflexive is امْتَنَعَ / تَمَنَّعَ ("to refrain, hold back"). Agent nouns: مانِع (māniʿ), مَنّاع (mannāʿ, intensive), مَنُوع (manūʿ).

2. Withholding as stinginess. The root can specifically mean being grudging. Zabīdī cites Qurʾānic usage: "they withhold small kindnesses" (māʿūn), "a withholder of good" (mannāʿ li-l-khayr), and "when good touches him, grudging" (manūʿ).

3. The divine name al-Māniʿ. Explained two ways: the One who withholds from whoever deserves to be denied; or the One who protects the people of His religion — guarding and aiding them. Its plural (of māniʿ) is مَنَعَة (manaʿa).

4. مَنَعَة / مَنْعَة — protective force. In "he is in might and manaʿa": vowelled manaʿa may (a) be a plural of māniʿ — i.e. clansmen who protect him from oppression (al-Jawharī; "min" here explanatory, not a verb-object) — or (b) per Zamakhsharī, a verbal noun like anafa/ʿaẓama, equal in sense to the sukūn form manʿa, meaning "a strength that repels aggressors." The ḥadīth "a people will seek refuge in this religion who have no manaʿa" is transmitted with both vowellings.

5. A rare concrete sense. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: al-manʿ (with fatḥa) can mean the crab (saraṭān), plural munūʿ; and al-manʿiyy is one who eats crabs.

6. Derived forms and grammar.
 • المَنْعَى (manʿā): refusal, abstention.
 • مَناعِ (manāʿi): a deflected imperative form = "withhold!"; illustrated by a rajaz line ("Withhold them! from the camels…") attributed variously to Bakr b. Wāʾil or Banū Tamīm. Banū Asad reportedly vowel it with fatḥa, but the kasr is more standard.
 • Noun forms: manaʿa, manʿa, minʿa; verbal noun manāʿa. مَنُعَ … مَناعَةً = "became mighty and hard to reach."
 • Ibn Jinnī: manāʿa may be faʿāla from manʿ, or mafʿala (origin manwaʿa) from "jāʾiʿ nāʾiʿ" (hungry), paralleling maqāma (< maqwama).

7. Place names. مَناعِ / al-Manāʿān: a hill or two mountains in the territory of Ṭayyiʾ — where the Prophet, per Ibn Durayd, told Zayd al-Khayl he was "better for you than Manāʿ and than the black stone you worship," meaning a black-stone idol. المَناعَة (al-Manāʿa): a town or mountain of Hudhayl, cited in a line of Sāʿida b. Juʾayya.

8. Figurative uses (labeled majāz by Zabīdī).
 • المُمْتَنِع = the lion: strong, self-mighty, untouchable by what he dislikes.
 • مانَعَ / تَمَنَّعَ: to repulse or desist; mumānaʿa can shade into "defending."
 • Al-Kilābī's المُتَمَنِّعان: a young she-camel and she-goat that "resist" a drought year, staying fat while older beasts weaken — or that fight the hard season to survive.
 • Chastity: امْرأة مَنِعَة, a woman who withholds herself from lewdness.
 • Protection/strength: حِصْن مَنيع / مُمَنَّع, an unassailable fortress; تَمَنَّعَ به, to take shelter in something; قَوْس مَنْعَة, a stiff, refractory bow; رَجُل مَنيع, a robust man; ناقَة مانِع, a she-camel that withholds her milk.

9. Further supplements (mustadrak). al-māniʿ = the niggardly withholder; قَوْم مَنَعات = unreachable people; Ibn al-Aʿrābī distinguishes مَنُوع (withholds from others) from مَنِع (protects himself); "he protects the neighbor from being wronged"; المَنَعات = strongholds and refuges; المَوانِع = plural of māniʿ; تَمانَعا = they mutually refused / defended themselves; al-Liḥyānī's "lā manʿa ʿan dhāk" = an emphatic "there is no denying you did that." Poetic witnesses are cited from ʿAmr b. Maʿdīkarib, Usāma al-Hudhalī, and ʿAmr b. Barrāʾ.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: مَنَّ 16x "bestows his grace"; مَنّ 6x "the manna"; مَمْنُون 4x "ending"; مَنُون 1x "a misfortune of time"
text:
al-Zamakhsharī groups the senses of م ن ن (m-n-n) around a core idea of "cutting off a portion," which runs through favor, strength, wearing-out, and death.

1. To confer a favor / grace. منّ الله على عباده — God bestowed favor on His servants; He is al-Mannān (the great Bestower). A favor is a minnah (pl. minan): "he has a favor over me"; "he favored me by what he did"; imtanna (he bestowed or laid claim to the favor). To receive one: "I incurred a great favor from you by what you did" — i.e. took on an obligation.

2. Strength / vigor (minnah). "He is of weak minnah" = of little strength; "his heart has no minnah" = no power; "they are weak in their minan." Travel's minnah = it saps a person's strength.

3. To wear out; a worn thing (al-manīn). The verb mananna = to wear down: Ibn Mayyāda — "We wore the she-camels down with night-travel until their backs were like ḍāl-tree staffs." al-manīn is a frayed, worn-out rope or garment whose nap is rubbed away, illustrated by shawāhid: a poet hopes "the knot of the worn rope does not fail me" while drawing water; another speaks of the "joined manīn" (the well-rope) by which he draws; Aws praises a rope "tightly twisted, not worn out (ghayr manīn)."

4. Death / fate that cuts off (al-manūn). mannat-hu al-manūn = death cut him off; al-manūn is "the cutter," equated with al-maniyyah (death). Poet: "as though he had never dwelt a day in ease, once death has cut a man off." The Qurʾānic phrase ajr ghayr mamnūn is placed here — "a reward not cut off / undiminished."

5. To reproach with a favor. mannahā = to spoil a favor by reminding of it: "how great a favor he conferred — were it not that he threw it back in reproach."

6. Colloquial usage: to a man seeking redress, "wa-man bik?" — "and who has worn you down / wronged you?"

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أُمْنِيَّت 6x "by your desire"; يَتَمَنَّ 6x "then wish"; تَمَنَّىٰ 3x "he wishes"; يُمْنَىٰ 3x "it is emitted"; يُمَنِّي 2x "and arouses desires in them"; مَّنِىّ 1x "semen"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-ن-ي as one sound root whose core sense is measuring-out / apportioning something (taqdīr) and the carrying-through of a decree (qaḍāʾ) upon it. From this single idea he derives every branch:

1. Apportioning/decreeing: مَنَى لَهُ الْمَانِي — "the apportioner apportioned for him," i.e. the determiner determined. Shāhid: a Hudhalī verse — feel no security even in a sanctuary "until you meet what the apportioner apportions for you."

2. الْمَنَا = destiny, fate (al-qadar). Shāhid: a poet driving his camels hard until stopped by "wealth of property or the manā [apportioned fate] of misfortunes."

3. مَنِيّ (semen) — the human fluid, so called because a person's formation is measured out from it.

4. الْمَنِيَّة = death, because it is decreed (apportioned) upon everyone.

5. تَمَنِّي (wishing, longing): a hope a person measures out for himself; some say it is the thing hoped for itself. The noun أُمْنِيَّة (wish) is of the pattern ufʿūla from this root.

6. مِنَى (the place near Mecca): some say it is named from what was decreed (quddira) to be sacrificed there — from مَنَاهُ اللَّهُ, "God apportioned it for him."

7. الْمَنَا (a weight-measure used in weighing): also from this root, since it is a fixed measure worked upon.

8. تَمَنَّى الْكِتَابَ = "he recited/read the scripture." Ibn Fāris reads Q 22:52 — {إِلَّا إِذَا تَمَنَّى أَلْقَى الشَّيْطَانُ فِي أُمْنِيَّتِهِ} — as "when he recited, Satan cast into his recitation," glossing tamannā as "recited." He ties this back to the core sense: reciting is itself a measuring-out, placing each verse in its proper place. Shāhid: a verse — "He recited God's Book at the start of his night, and by its end met the death of the decrees."

9. مَانَى / يُمَانِي / مُمَانَاة = to vie with, rival another. Shāhid from Ibn al-Ṭathriyya (the drinking-companion urging him to "rival the people in generosity"). This too is taqdīr: one measures one's own act against another's, seeking to equal it.

10. مُنْيَة (of a she-camel): the days during which one ascertains whether she has conceived or is carrying.

Method: Ibn Fāris opens with the phonetic root-analysis (three-letter sound root, weak final letter), fixes a single semantic origin (measuring/decree), then subsumes each attested usage — including the Qur'anic "recited" — under that origin by explicit analogy, supporting the derivations with poetic shawāhid.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-ق-ت as having a single root-meaning, with no competing branches.

1. Core idea: loathing and foulness — detestation (shanāʾa) combined with ugliness or repulsiveness (qubḥ). The root names something found hateful because it is regarded as vile.

2. Verb and derived forms: maqatahu, verbal noun maqt ("he loathed/detested him"). The one loathed is called maqīt or mamqūt — two passive-sense adjectives from the same root.

3. Attested usage: the phrase nikāḥ al-maqt ("the marriage of loathing") was a pre-Islamic (Jāhilī) term for a man marrying his father's wife. Ibn Fāris cites this as an established usage of the period, illustrating the sense of a union regarded as repugnant.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: ٱمْرَأَت 26x "his wife"; ٱمْرِئ 5x "person"; مَرْء 4x "a man"; مَّرِيـ 1x "(and) ease"; ٱمْرُؤٌا 1x "a man"; ٱمْرَأ 1x "an evil man"
poets_named: Abū Khirāsh (lived into Islam); Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad) ×2
text:
Ibn Sīda's al-Muḥkam entry for the root م ر أ records the following senses:

1. Moral worth / manliness. مَرُؤَ الرَّجُلُ ("the man had murūʾa") — he possessed manly virtue or moral worth; such a man is مَرِئ, and the verb تَمَرَّأَ is also used.

2. Wholesomeness (of food, pasture, land). طَعامٌ مَرِئٌ is "wholesome, agreeable food" of good consequence (pattern like تَمْرَة); the verbs are مَرُؤَ / مَرَأَ, and اسْتَمْرَأَه means "he found it wholesome." The idiom هَنَأَنِي ومَرَأَنِي ("it agreed with and nourished me") pairs the two verbs by phonetic assimilation, but used alone the second becomes أَمْرَانِى. Extended to كلأٌ مَرِئٌ ("wholesome, non-noxious pasture") and مَرُؤَت الأَرْضُ ("the land became wholesome — its air is good"), giving مَرِيئَة.

3. Anatomical: the gullet. المَرِئُ is the passage for food and drink — the top of the stomach and rumen where it meets the throat. Plurals: أمْرِئَة, مُرُوء.

4. Man / human being (مَرْء). The standard (analogical) inflection keeps a fatḥa on the mīm in all cases: هذا مَرْءٌ. A variant harmonizes the mīm's vowel to the case ending (ḍamma nominative, fatḥa accusative, kasra genitive), which parallels the vowel-harmony seen when the conjunctive alif is prefixed to give امْرُؤٌ. A verse of Abū Khirāsh (praising a man's gathered virtues — forbearance, kindness, noble lineage) is transmitted by al-Sukkarī with a kasra (al-mirʾ), said to be the dialect of Hudhayl.

Grammatical note: مَرْء takes no plural of any kind — not broken (أَمْراء, أَمْرُؤ, أَمارِئ) nor sound (مَرْؤُونَ, امْرُؤُون).

5. Woman (feminine forms). The feminine is مَرْأَة, regularly lightened to مَرَة; Sībawayh notes a form مَرَاة, later lightened likewise. With the conjunctive alif it becomes امْرَأَة, definite المَرْأَة (Abū ʿAlī also reports الإمْرَأَة). Ibn al-Aʿrābī records the rare usage of the masculine-based phrase for a woman: إِنّها لامْرُؤُ صِدْقٍ ("she is a person of true worth").

6. Proper names and nisba. امْرُؤُ القَيْسِ (Imruʾ al-Qays) is a personal name that came to stand for the whole tribe. Its relative adjective is امْرِئِيّ — nisba formed to the first element, because امْرَأ is annexed to a proper noun only in this one name. The alternative form مَرَئيّ (attested in a verse of Dhū al-Rumma) treats it as a nisba to مَرْء (which would regularly give مَرْئِيّ); مَرَئيّ is thus irregular.

7. Place-name. مَرْأَة is also a village, cited in a verse of Dhū al-Rumma; it is said to be the village of Hishām al-Maraʾī.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مَّرَض 13x "(is) a disease"; مَّرِيض 10x "sick"; مَرِضْ 1x "i am ill"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م ر ض (m-r-ḍ) as a single sound root whose core idea is: whatever takes a human being out of the state of health — in any respect at all.

1. Core sense — illness. From this root comes الْعِلَّة (ailment). The verb is مَرِضَ / يَمْرَضُ (to be/fall ill); the plural of مَرِيض (sick person) is مَرْضَى.

2. Derived verb forms.
 • أَمْرَضَهُ — "he made him ill."
 • مَرَّضَهُ — "he nursed him well through his illness."

3. Extended (metaphorical) use. شَمْسٌ مَرِيضَةٌ, a "sick sun," describes the sun when it is not bright — dimmed by a haze over its face.

4. Sickness of the heart. Ibn Fāris notes that hypocrisy (نِفَاق) is called a maraḍ, citing the Qur'anic فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ مَرَضٌ ("in their hearts is a sickness") and فَيَطْمَعَ الَّذِي فِي قَلْبِهِ مَرَضٌ ("so that he in whose heart is a sickness may covet"). He reports that some glossed the intended meaning here as القَهْر (subjugation/domination). He then reaffirms his general rule: maraḍ is anything by which a person leaves the bound of health, and the root's analogy holds consistently.

5. A near-related sense. مَرَّضَ فِي الْحَاجَة means "he fell short in the matter, his resolve not being firm."

6. An anomaly he flags as unresolved. Against the root's regular pattern, they say أَمْرَضَ of a man who has come close to attaining his need. He cites a verse of poetry: "But beneath that grey hair is firm resolve — when he forms a judgement, he either comes near the mark or strikes it." Ibn Fāris marks this usage as problematic and deviating from the root's otherwise consistent logic.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: م ر ح (m-r-ḥ) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: a gladness so intense that one can hardly stay still — exuberant, restless delight (ṭarab). The verb is mariḥa – yamraḥu, "to be/become exuberantly glad."

1. A lively horse is called mimrāḥ or marūḥ (spirited, frisky).

2. Qur'anic citation (40:75): "wa-bi-mā kuntum tamraḥūn" — "and for your exultant/insolent gladness."

3. Related word al-mirāḥ (treated by the author elsewhere), illustrated by a line of verse: an aging man asks whether his grey hair now bars him from his mirāḥ — his old high spirits.

4. A bow can be called marūḥ, either because onlookers marvel (yamraḥ) at it, or because its skillful shot makes it seem to possess marah, liveliness.

5. An eye called mimrāḥ is one that runs with abundant tears — Ibn Fāris notes this still fits the root's sense of not settling still.

6. The verb marraḥtu al-mazādata means "I filled the water-skin until it seeps and flows."

7. mariḥat al-ʿaynu (marahān) describes an eye becoming irritated/watering, illustrated by a verse about a mote of dust irritating one eye while asking why the other eye should suffer the same.

8. marḥā is an exclamation of admiration — said to an archer who hits the mark ("bravo!"). Ibn Durayd adds that barḥā is said instead when he misses. A closing verse: "marḥā and ayḥā, when he keeps scoring one hit after another."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مَّرِيد 2x "rebellious"; مَرَدُ 1x "they persist"; مُّمَرَّد 1x "made smooth"; مَّارِد 1x "rebellious"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-ر-د (m-r-d) as one sound root whose core idea is stripping a thing of its outer covering — its rind or the hair growing over it. He then derives the senses from that core, and separates out a group he considers a phonetic substitution.

1. Beardless youth: الأمرد (al-amrad) is a young man whose beard has not yet come in; verb مَرِدَ / يَمْرَدُ. تَمَرَّدَ فلان زماناً means he remained beardless for a period.

2. Stripped plant: مَرَّدَ الغصن (marrada l-ghuṣn) is to strip a branch of its bark, leaving it bare — hence شجرة مرداء, a bare/leafless tree.

3. Bare ground: المرداء (al-mardāʾ) is a flat, low-lying sandy tract with no vegetation; plural مَرادى.

4. Insolent, overbearing: المارد (al-mārid) and المريد (al-marīd) denote the defiant, overbearing one — explained by Ibn Fāris as though such a person had been stripped bare of good.

5. Of horses: an أمرد horse is one with no hair on the fetlock tuft (ثُنّة).

6. Tall building: الممرَّد (al-mumarrad) is a tall structure. Ibn Fāris says this fits the root's analogy because it stands as if stripped bare, like the leafless tree.

7. Reported sense: some say المراد (al-marād) means the neck; he accepts it as consistent with the root's logic "if it is sound" — flagging it as unverified.

8. Softening by soaking — a substitution, not a true member of the root: مَرَدَ الطعامَ, to soak or work food until it softens; likewise a child working at his mother's breast; and المريد, dates steeped in milk. Ibn Fāris judges all of these to be ibdāl (letter-substitution), the original word being مَرَسَ (marasa) with sīn, the dāl standing in for the sīn. All three carry the same sense, and the original letter is sīn.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مَرَجَ 2x "he released"; مَرْجَان 2x "and coral"; مَّرِيج 1x "confused"; مَّارِج 1x "a smokeless flame"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-ر-ج as a single sound root whose core idea is movement back and forth — coming and going — together with unsteadiness or agitation.

1. Being loose / unsteady: مَرِجَ الْخَاتَمُ فِي الْإِصْبَعِ — "the ring wobbled on the finger," i.e. it sat loosely and shifted about. Ibn Fāris states explicitly that the analogy governing the entire chapter is drawn from this image.

2. Becoming disordered and jumbled: مَرِجَتْ أَمَانَاتُ الْقَوْمِ وَعُهُودُهُمْ — "the people's trusts and covenants became unsettled," i.e. thrown into disorder and mixed together.

3. المَرْج (marj), a meadow: land covered with growth over which livestock roam freely — the noun is tied back to the same idea of moving about without restraint.

4. Qur'anic usage: on {مَرَجَ الْبَحْرَيْنِ يَلْتَقِيَانِ} (55:19), Ibn Fāris explains the verb as God having released or let loose the two bodies of water, so that they were set free to run — and he cites the parallel phrase "He it is who let the two seas flow."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مَرَّة 19x "time"; مَرَّ 10x "they pass"; مُّسْتَمِرّ 2x "continuous"; مَرَّٰت 1x "times"; مَرّ 1x "(as the) passing"; مِرَّة 1x "possessor of soundness"; أَمَرّ 1x "and more bitter"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats m-r-r as having two sound root meanings: the passing on of something, and the opposite of sweetness and pleasantness.

**1. Passing, going by.** marra, yamurru: a thing passed, went on its way. The marr of clouds is their trailing along and moving past. The word marra ("a time", as in "I met him once, twice") is, he explains, just a way of referring to a stretch of time that has gone by. People also say "I met him one time out of the marr," treating marr as a plural of marra.

**2. Bitterness, and from it hardship.** amarra (also marra), yumirru: a thing became murr, bitter. From this:
- al-amarrān, "the two bitterest things": hardships that are not pleasant; specifically, worry and illness ("I suffered the two bitter things from him").
- al-amarr: the intestines in which the stomach contents collect. A verse advises: "Do not give al-amarr and what lies next to it as a gift, and never give bones stripped of meat." Ibn Fāris says it got this name because it is unpleasant, and that afterwards every hardship and every severe thing came to be named with this word-form.
- Firm twisting: amrartu al-ḥabl, "I twisted the rope tight," and the rope is mumarr. al-marr is tightness of twist; al-marīr is a twisted rope; al-marīra is one strand of it, and also firmness and dignity of spirit. Ibn Fāris states that all of these share one analogical basis.
- al-murār: a bitter tree.

**Other words.** al-marmar is a kind of white, clear stone. al-marmara also means plumpness of the body and its quivering; a woman is called marmāra when she quivers from her plumpness. Ibn Fāris introduces these with "as for" and does not assign them to either of the two root meanings.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: يَمْتَرُ 5x "doubt"; مِرْيَة 5x "doubt"; مُمْتَرِين 4x "the doubters"; تَمَارَ 4x "then will you dispute with him"; تُمَارِ 1x "argue"; مِرَاء 1x "(with) an argument"
text:
Root م-ر-ي, as treated by al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī in his Qur'anic glossary.

1. al-miryah — wavering or hesitation about a matter. Al-Rāghib marks it as narrower than shakk (general doubt): a specific, unsettled going-back-and-forth. He cites its Qur'anic uses, all in the phrase "in miryah about" something: about "it" (al-Ḥajj 22:55), about what others worship (Hūd 11:109), about meeting Him (al-Sajda 32:23), and about the meeting with their Lord (Fuṣṣilat 41:54).

2. al-imtirāʾ / al-mumārāh (verbal forms yamtarūna, tumārī) — to dispute or wrangle over something that is itself subject to such wavering. Shawāhid: "the word of truth about which they dispute" (Maryam 19:34); "what they used to dispute about" (al-Ḥijr 15:63); "Do you dispute with him over what he sees?" (al-Najm 53:12); "do not dispute concerning them except with an evident dispute" (al-Kahf 18:22).

3. Etymology — al-Rāghib traces the root to maraytu al-nāqata, "I stroked the she-camel's udder to draw out her milk." The sense of drawing something out by persistent stroking underlies both the wavering of miryah and the drawing-out contention of disputation.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: ٱمْسَحُ 3x "and wipe (with it)"; مَسْح 1x "(to) pass (his hand)"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-س-ح as a single sound root whose core idea is passing one thing over another with a flat, spreading motion — wiping, stroking, smoothing. From that base he derives the rest, marking most of the derived uses explicitly as metaphor.

1. Core sense: to pass the hand (or something) flat over a surface — "I wiped/stroked it with my hand" (masaḥtuhu bi-yadī, verbal noun masḥ).

2. Metaphorical extension to sexual intercourse: masaḥahā, "he wiped her," i.e. he lay with her.

3. al-masīḥ as "wiped smooth/featureless": a man one side of whose face is mamsūḥ — flat, with no eye and no eyebrow on it. On this basis, Ibn Fāris says, the Dajjāl was called masīḥ, because he is "wiped" of an eye.

4. al-masīḥ = sweat, so called because it gets wiped away.

5. al-masīḥ = a worn, blank dirham, as if its stamped design had been wiped off.

6. al-amsaḥ = flat, level ground, as though it had been wiped smooth.

7. Metaphor with the sword: masaḥa yadahu bi-l-sayf, "he wiped his arm with the sword," meaning he severed it.

8. Metaphor of travel: masaḥat al-ibil yawmahā, "the camels wiped their day," meaning they journeyed through it.

9. al-masḥāʾ = a woman who is rasḥāʾ, lean and lacking flesh in the hindquarters, as if the flesh had been wiped off her.

10. Touch/trace sense: "upon so-and-so is a masḥa of beauty," as if his face had been wiped over with beauty; likewise "as though upon him were the masḥa of an angel/king." Ibn Fāris gives this as the reason Jesus was called al-Masīḥ — as though a touch of beauty lay upon him. (He thus offers two distinct explanations of the name masīḥ within one entry: sense 3, "wiped featureless," and this one, "brushed with beauty.")

11. al-masāʾiḥ (singular masīḥa) = the side-locks of hair, because they are smoothed with oil.

12. al-masāʾiḥ (singular masīḥa) also = bows, because they are rubbed/wiped while being softened. Supported by an unattributed verse describing bows curved aslant, supple at the shooting-place, with no weakness or thinness in them.

13. Anomaly: he flags rajul timsaḥ, "a rebellious, malicious man," as falling outside the root's core sense, and suggests it may instead be a comparison to the animal called timsāḥ (crocodile).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha entry for the root m-s-d (مسد):

Core meaning: the sound triliteral root m-s-d denotes plaiting/twisting something and twining it together.

1. Palm fibre: al-masad names the fibre stripped from palm-tree fronds (līf min jarīd al-nakhl).

2. Camel-hair rope: al-masad also names a rope made from twisted camel hair/wool. A poetic citation is quoted showing this rope-sense — "a masad-rope twisted from young she-camels" — though the poet is not named in this entry.

3. Metaphorical use for a firm physique: a woman called "mamsūdah" is one whose bodily build is described as "plaited" (majdūlat al-khalq) — tightly-knit and taut like a well-twisted rope, not slack or loose. This is a figurative extension of the rope sense onto physical constitution.

4. Underlying sense — twisting: some lexicographers state that the root's basic meaning is simply al-fatl, "twisting/spinning."

5. Circling back: al-masad is equally used for palm fibre precisely because such fibre is normally spun/twisted to make rope — tying senses 1 and 2 together under the single idea of twisting.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَمْسَكَ 18x "then retain them"; ٱسْتَمْسَكَ 3x "so hold fast"; إِمْسَاك 1x "then to retain"; يُمَسِّكُ 1x "hold fast"; مُمْسِك 1x "(can) withhold"; مُمْسِكَٰت 1x "withholders"; مُسْتَمْسِكُون 1x "(are) holding fast"; مِسْك 1x "(will be of) musk"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-س-ك (m-s-k) as one sound root meaning holding something back, or a thing holding fast.

1. Withholding / stinginess. A miser is a مُمْسِك (one who withholds); إمْسَاك (imsāk) is stinginess itself, and المَسَاك / المِسَاك / المَسِيك likewise name a miser. A رَجُل مُسَكَة is a man who, once he grips something, cannot be shaken loose from it.

2. Bracelet — المَسَك: a bracelet made of tortoise-shell or horn (ذَبْل), named for the way it clings to the arm; singular مَسَكَة. Ibn Fāris cites a verse describing a woman wearing such bracelets "made neither of ivory nor of tortoise-shell."

3. The firm part of a well — the مَسَكَة is the hard section of a well-shaft that needs no lining, fitting the root because it is self-cohering (mutamāsik).

4. Hide / waterskin — المَسْك is a skin or hide, so called because things are held inside it once it is made into a waterskin.

5. Anomalous sense — المِسْك (musk, the perfume) Ibn Fāris marks as deviating from this root rather than derived from its core meaning.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
quran_words: مَسَّ 56x "touches him"; مَسّ 2x "(his) touch"; يَتَمَاسَّ 2x "they both touch each other"; مِسَاس 1x "touch"
poets_named: unnamed verse; Dhū al-Iṣbaʿ al-ʿAdwānī (pre-Islamic); Kuthayyir (Umayyad); Ruʾba (Umayyad) ×2
text:
Root م س س (m-s-s), from al-Zabīdī's Tāj al-ʿArūs.

1. Core sense — to touch. مَسِسْتُه "I touched it with my hand" (imperfect أَمَسُّه; verbal nouns مَسّ, مَسِيس, مِسِّيسَي). The form following ʿalima (مَسِسْتُ) is judged the most eloquent; a variant مَسَسْتُ (like naṣartu) is reported by Abū ʿUbayda, and a contracted colloquial مِسْتُ (dropping the first sīn) by Sībawayh, who calls it anomalous.

2. Distinguished from lams. al-Rāghib: mass is like lams (touching), but mass is used for reaching after / seeking a thing even if it is not attained, while lams implies actual perception by the sense of touch.

3. A phonetic note (al-Jawharī): some readers leave the mīm with fatḥa rather than shifting the sīn's vowel to it, paralleling the Qurʾanic ظَلْتُم / فَظَلْتُم (originally ẓaliltum) — an instance of "lightening" (takhfīf). Cited verse (via al-Akhfash) attests both مِسْنا and مَسْنا.

4. Figurative: madness. mass = insanity (like als and lamam); Q "like one whom Satan has prostrated by [his] mass." A person so afflicted is mamsūs, "as though the jinn touched him"; Abū ʿAmr gives maʾsūs / mamsūs / maʾlūs all = madman.

5. Figurative: the first onset of something felt. Q "Taste the mass of Saqar" = the first of the Fire that reaches you; compare "he felt the mass of fever" — its first touch before it takes hold (al-Lisān: its onset before it manifests).

6. Kinship and need. رَحِمٌ ماسَّة (also مَسَّاسَة) = close kinship; مَسَّتْ بِكَ رَحِمُ فلان = his kinship has come near you. حَاجَةٌ ماسَّة = a pressing need; مَسِيسُ الحاجة = urgency of need. (Figurative.)

7. al-masūs (of water). Several reported senses: (a) water between sweet and salty (al-Jawharī); (b) water that hands have handled (so a passive sense, "touched when taken"); (c) wholesome water that "touches" thirst and removes it — Shamir and Ibn al-Aʿrābī: anything that quenches burning thirst; (d) sweet, clear water (al-Aṣmaʿī); (e) conversely, brackish water that burns with saltiness — hence al-Zabīdī notes it is treated as a contronym (ḍidd), though he questions the author's handling. Shawāhid from Dhū al-Iṣbaʿ al-ʿAdwānī.

8. Other lexical items. al-masūs also = theriac/antidote (fādhazahr), with a verse of Kuthayyir; also a village near Marw. al-masmās = thin/light, as قَتَامٌ مَسْمَاسٌ "thin dust" (verse of Ruʾba). Proper names: the traditionist Bushrā ibn Masīs; مُسَّة, a woman's name (incl. Mussa al-Azdiyya, a Successor).

9. لَا مَسَاسِ (al-Ṣiḥāḥ). Built on kasra (like qaṭāmi) as a form diverted from the verbal noun = "do not touch"; an anomalous Qurʾanic reading (Abū Ḥaywa, Abū ʿAmr). The standard Q form لَا مِسَاسَ (Moses to the Samaritan) = "do not touch me" / "no contact," imposed as a punishment of social isolation. al-Zabīdī remarks the author could have stated this more concisely.

10. tamāss / mumāssa = mutual touching, and used euphemistically for sexual intercourse: Q "before the two touch each other (yatamāssā)." Likewise mass itself is a euphemism for marital relations — Q "before you touch them (tamassūhunna)," variant tamāssūhunna; the meaning is the same. Thaʿlab notes some preferred the form without alif, taking such usage as "the act of the man" in coitus.

11. al-mismās / al-masmasa = the confusion or entanglement of an affair (verse of Ruʾba). al-Azharī disputes reading al-māsī here as a "lightened" form of mass, insisting al-māsī properly = one who inserts his hand to extract a stuck fetus (root m-s-y, مَسَيْتُها), which is unrelated to mass.

12. Extended and idiomatic uses. From "touching with the hand" mass was borrowed for taking, striking, coition, and madness. Hadith: "he found no mass of fatigue" = the first sense of weariness; and generally any harm that reaches a person — Q "the Fire will not touch us," "hardship touched them," "harm has touched me," "Satan has touched me." Hadith massūhā minhā = "take water from it [and do ablution]"; massahu bi-ʿadhāb = "He punished him." Also: a horse مُمَسّ / أَمَسّ = marked with leg-whiteness short of full taḥjīl; مَسَّتْه مَوَاسُّ الخير والشر = occasions of good and ill befell him; رِيقَة مَسُوس = thirst-quenching saliva; كَلأ مَسُوس = thriving pasture; al-massa = a children's grabbing/tag game; al-miss (kasra) = copper (Ibn Durayd unsure if Arabic — al-Zabīdī: Persian); حَسَنُ المَسِّ فِي ماله = "he has a fine touch/effect in managing his property" (figurative).

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: Ruʾba (Umayyad); Ibn Barrī (unnamed); Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad) ×2; Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt (pre-Islamic); Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); Al-Aḍbaṭ ibn Qurayʿ al-Saʿdī (pre-Islamic); Mirdās (undated)
text:
This article on m-s-w (headed مسا) covers clearing a female animal's womb by hand, a character turning bad, delay after a promise, evening and its many expressions, calamities, pulling a thing out, helping, the middle of the road, mocking, and a man who ignores advice or is light.

1. **Clearing a womb by hand.** masawtu ʿalā al-nāqa or masawtu raḥimahā (amsūhā maswan): to put one's hand into a she-camel's vulva and clean it out. Al-Jawharī defines al-masy as taking the sperm out of the womb (referring to masaṭa). The same act is masaytu al-nāqa, masy being a dialect form of masw: one puts a hand into the womb of a she-camel or a mare and draws out the stallion's semen and the young. One account gives the reason: the stallion is judged base, and she is not wanted to conceive by him. Al-Liḥyānī describes it as cleaning out the womb and says he did not know whether of sperm or of something else. The entry adds that every drawing-out (istilāl) is masy.
   - A verse of Ruʾba uses the image as an insult, "he assails your mother as the māsī assails"; Ibn Barrī corrects it to "then assail your mother", because it follows "if you are in a muddle (masmās) over your affair". al-masmās is the confusion and obscurity of an affair.
   - A verse of Dhū al-Rumma, quoted next, says the days of crossing and the long pounding of the waymarks on shod, bleeding feet "masathunna", drained them.

2. **A character turning bad.** Ibn al-Aʿrābī: masā yamsī masyan, a man's character turned bad after being good.

3. **Delay after a promise.** masā, amsā and massā: to promise something and then be slow to deliver it.

4. **Evening.** al-masāʾ is the opposite of morning (al-ṣabāḥ), and al-imsāʾ, entering the evening, the opposite of al-iṣbāḥ. It runs from after midday until the sunset ṣalāt; some say until midnight. The plural is amsiya (Ibn al-Aʿrābī).
   - Sībawayh pairs ṣabāḥ and masāʾ with bayāḍ and sawād (whiteness and blackness). laqītuhu ṣabāḥa masāʾa, "morning and evening", is an indeclinable compound; ṣabāḥa masāʾin is an annexation.
   - Related nouns: al-musy and al-misy are like al-masāʾ; musy is to masāʾ as ṣubḥ is to ṣabāḥ. al-mumsā, like al-muṣbaḥ, is both a verbal noun (amsaynā mumsan, "we came into the evening") and a noun of place. Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt praises God "at our evening and at our morning". In a line of Imruʾ al-Qays a young woman lights the dark like the lamp at a secluded monk's mumsā, meaning the cell where he spends the evening. Al-Aḍbaṭ ibn Qurayʿ al-Saʿdī: every care has some relief, but with evening and morning there is no falāḥ, no lasting.
   - Time expressions: li-musyi khāmisatin (on the evening of the fifth; also li-misyi); musayyānan, the diminutive of masāʾ (at early evening); uṣbūḥata kulli yawmin wa-umsiyyata kulli yawmin (every morning and every evening); musiyya amsi, or in Ibn Sīda masāʾa amsi, musyahu, misyahu and amsiyyatahu (yesterday evening). Ibn Sīda also gives jiʾtuhu musayyānātin, like mughayribānātin, as rare and used only adverbially.
   - Greetings and verbs: kayfa amsayta? means "how are you this evening?"; massaytu fulānan is to say that to someone; amsaynā, we came into the evening. Al-Liḥyānī reports that on taking an ill omen from someone, people say masāʾu Allāhi lā masāʾuka, "God's evening, not yours" (the accusative is also allowed).
   - A point of grammar: a poet wrote amsajat and amsajā for amsat and amsā, putting jīm, a sturdy letter resembling yāʾ, in its place to save his rhyme and metre. Ibn Jinnī takes this as one of the proofs for the claimed underlying forms (ramayat for ramat, ghazawat for ghazat, amsayat for amsat, and so on): jīm, unlike yāʾ and wāw, is not subject to change, so the poet kept it sound, which shows that ghazā goes back to ghazawa.

5. **Calamities.** Abū ʿAmr: laqītu min fulānin al-tamāsī, "I met with calamities from so-and-so"; its singular is not known. A verse by Mirdās: "I work round her so that she may soften, yet whatever the case I meet calamities from her."

6. **Pulling out.** masaytu al-shayʾa masyan: I pulled the thing out. Dhū al-Rumma: brisk friskiness all but pulls out their girths.

7. **Helping.** Ibn al-Aʿrābī: amsā fulānun fulānan, he helped him with something.

8. **The middle of the road.** Abū Zayd: rakiba masāʾa al-ṭarīq, he rode in the middle of the road.

9. **Mocking.** māsā fulānun fulānan: he mocked him (set beside sāmāhu, he vied with him in boasting).

10. **A man deaf to advice.** rajul māsin (like māshin) pays no heed to anyone's admonition and does not accept what he says. Abū ʿUbayd gives it as māsun (like mālun), which the text calls a mistake. One says mā amsāhu. Al-Azharī sees the form as if metathesized, like hārin, hārun and hāʾirun, or shākī al-silāḥ and shākun; Abū Manṣūr suggests that al-mās (the form māsun) may originally have been māsiyan, and hamzated in origin.

11. **Light.** rajul māsun also means light (khafīf), and mā amsāhu, "how light he is!"

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris says the root m-s-kh (مسخ) covers two separate, unrelated words.

1. al-maskh - disfigurement / loss of taste

The core sense is disfiguring something, or a thing being flavourless.
- "God masakha him" = God changed his form from good/beautiful into ugly.
- A man called masikh = a man with no charm or comeliness.
- Food called masikh = food with no salt, no taste.
- A verse illustrates the "neither one thing nor the other" sense: "You are masikh like the meat of a young weaned camel... neither sweet nor bitter."
- Arabs also say "I masakhtu the she-camel," meaning: I wore her down / drove her hard through relentless riding.

2. al-qisiyy al-masikhiyyah - the "masikhi" bows

A distinct word: certain bows called masikhiyyah, named after a man called Masikhah from the tribe of Asad. A cited verse describes a poet bringing a well-trimmed arrow-shaft whose curves resemble those of the strung masikhi bows.

Ibn Faris treats these two uses (disfigurement/tastelessness vs. the named bow-type) as unrelated words that merely happen to share the same three root letters.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مَتَٰع 35x "an enjoyment"; مَّتَّعْ 18x "we will grant enjoyment"; تَمَتَّعَ 11x "enjoy"; ٱسْتَمْتَعَ 6x "enjoyed"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-ت-ع (m-t-ʿ) as a single sound root meaning "a benefit, and the extension of a good period of time." From it comes istamtaʿtu bi-l-shayʾ ("I got benefit/enjoyment out of the thing").

1. Benefit / provision (mutʿa, matāʿ). This is the core sense, "benefit." He cites Q 24:29, "uninhabited houses in which there is matāʿ [benefit] for you." Related: a divorced woman is "provided" (muttiʿat) with something because she benefits from it; and amtaʿtu bi-mālī = tamattaʿtu ("I benefited from my wealth").

- A cited verse describes two companions from different tribes whose only shared "benefit" (mutʿa) turned out to be their parting; al-Aṣmaʿī gives a variant wording.
- Idiom: "if you buy this boy you'll get the benefit of a fine servant."

2. Lasting / extending in duration. A "fine rope" (ḥabl mātiʿ) is so called because it lasts. mataʿa al-nahār = "the day grew long"; mataʿa al-nabāt = "the plant grew tall/flourished"; mataʿa al-sarāb = "the mirage stretched out early in the day."

3. Preponderant / surpassing. In a line of al-Nābigha, mātiʿ (of a "balance") is glossed as rājiḥ zāʾid — "outweighing, surpassing."

4. Enjoyment and preservation. Abū Bakr defines mutʿa as "what you have enjoyed," and supposes the disapproved nikāḥ al-mutʿa (temporary marriage) derives from this root. Household matāʿ is the goods a person uses for his needs. mattaʿa/amtaʿa Allāhu bihi fulānan = God kept someone alive so as to benefit from him in joys and advantages.

Two etymological views Ibn Fāris reports from the "verifiers": (a) the root's origin is pleasure-taking (taladhdhudh) — one "enjoys" daylight, matāʿ is enjoying something with immediate pleasure; (b) the origin is extension and elevation (imtidād, irtifāʿ) — matāʿ being a benefit drawn out over time. Finally, sharāb mātiʿ is a red drink enjoyed for its fine quality.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: m-t-n (م ت ن) - from Ibn Faris's Maqayis al-Lugha.

Core meaning Ibn Faris identifies: firmness/hardness combined with extension and length - something solid that also runs on or reaches far.

1. Physical ground sense. Al-matn is a firm ridge of raised, hard ground that runs in a continuous line; plural mitan.

2. The human back. By analogy, al-matnan (the two matns) names the two muscular strips flanking the spine (sinew and flesh). From this:
   - matantuhu = I struck his matn/back.
   - matna(tun) = the flesh of that region (singular usage).
   - Imru' al-Qays is cited describing two matnas, firm and plump, as the leopard leans on its forearms - praising a firm, muscled back.
   - matana qawsahu = he strung his bow, using sinew taken from that back-sinew.
   - matana yawmahu = he traveled the whole day through without stopping - Ibn Faris flags this as a metaphorical extension of the root's length sense.
   - matantuhu bi-s-sawt = I struck him with a whip; Ibn Faris personally holds that this specifically means striking him on the matn (the back), not just anywhere.

3. Going the distance / going far. Al-mumatana means pushing on toward a distant goal. He traveled a mumatin journey = an intense, long journey. matanahu = he stalled/procrastinated with him. Ibn Faris also places under this same root the mumatanat ash-sha'irayn - a poetic contest where two poets trade verses back and forth, each line extending further, as though reaching toward a goal they intend.

4. One irregular item. Ibn Faris notes that matantu d-dabbata does not fit the root's core pattern: it means I gelded the animal (split its scrotum and removed the testicle).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مَثَل 88x "an example"; مِثْل 75x "like"; تَّمَاثِيل 2x "[the] statues"; مَثُلَٰت 1x "[the] similar punishments"; تَمَثَّلَ 1x "then he assumed for her the likeness"; مُثْلَىٰ 1x "the exemplary"; أَمْثَل 1x "(the) best of them"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-ث-ل (m-th-l) as a single sound root whose core sense is the correspondence or matching of one thing to another.

1. Likeness. هَذَا مِثْلُ هَذَا means "this is the counterpart (naẓīr) of this." The forms mithl and mithāl carry one meaning; a further variant mathīl is sometimes used, parallel to shabīh ("resembling"). Likewise mathal is a variant of mithl ("the like"), just as shabah/shibh are variants.

2. Retaliation. أَمْثَلَ السُّلْطَانُ فُلَانًا — "the ruler executed him in retaliation (qawad)" — because he did to him the like (mithl) of what the man had done.

3. The proverb/parable (al-mathal al-maḍrūb). Derived from the root's core sense, because a proverb is cited allusively to stand in place of something it resembles in meaning.

4. Exemplary punishment / mutilation. مَثَّلَ بِهِ = to inflict exemplary punishment (nakkala); the logic is that the punished person is made a "model" (mithāl) warning everyone who did, or meant to do, the same deed. مَثَّلَ بِالقَتِيلِ = to mutilate a slain man (jadaʿahu).

5. al-Mathulāt. From the same idea. Ibn Fāris cites Q 13:6, {وَقَدْ خَلَتْ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمُ المَثُلَاتُ}, glossing al-mathulāt as "the punishments that deter from the like of what caused them." Singular mathula (pattern of samura, ṣaduqa). Alternatively, they may be the calamities that befall a person and become a model/example (mithāl) by which others are restrained.

6. Standing erect. مَثَلَ الرَّجُلُ قَائِمًا = the man drew himself up straight (intaṣaba) — as though he were a figure/model (mithāl) set upright. Plural of mithāl here is amthila.

7. Bed/mattress. mithāl also denotes a bed (al-firāsh), plural muthul — a thing that corresponds to (matches) what lies beneath or above it.

8. Excellence. فُلَانٌ أَمْثَلُ بَنِي فُلَانٍ = "so-and-so is the nearest of his people to good," i.e. he most resembles the people of righteousness. هَؤُلَاءِ أَمَاثِلُ القَوْمِ = "these are the best/choicest of the people."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م و ه (m-w-h) as one sound, single root, all of whose vocabulary branches from a core notion of "water."

1. Core form. al-mawh is the underlying base of the noun الماء ("water"); its diminutive is muwayh. Ibn Fāris cites this diminutive as evidence that the hamza in māʾ (الماء) is a substitute for an original hāʾ.

2. mawwaha (to give water / to plate). mawwahtu l-shayʾ means literally "I gave the thing water to drink," and by extension "I plated/coated it with silver or gold" — the plating pictured as a coating the object is "made to drink."

3. Sheen of youth. mā aḥsana mūhata wajhihi — "how beautiful the sheen of his face" — i.e. the shimmering "water of youth" glistening in it.

4. māwiyya. From the same root: al-māwiyya means rock-crystal, and also a mirror. Shāhid: a line of Ṭarafa likening two eyes to "two māwiyyatān" (mirrors/crystals) set in the hollows of a rock at a watering-place.

5. Water entering / emerging. māhat al-safīna — "the ship took in water." amāhat al-arḍ — ground-seepage (nazz) appeared in the land. amāha l-faḥl — the stallion cast his "water" (semen) into the female's womb.

6. "Water of the heart." rajulun māhu l-qalb — a man with abundant "water of the heart." Shāhid: a rajaz line, "truly you, O Jahḍam, are watery of heart." Ibn Fāris notes such a person is reckoned dull/stupid, and that the form māh is built on the pattern of māl.

7. Tempering / nisba forms. amahtu / amhaytu l-sikkīn — "I watered (tempered) the knife." The relative adjectives: from māh → māhī and māʾī; from māʾ → māʾī and māwī.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-و-ج as a single root whose core idea is agitation or turbulence in something.

1. Of people: مَاجَ النَّاسُ يَمُوجُونَ — people "surge," i.e. are thrown into commotion and move confusedly.
2. Of an affair or situation: مَاجَ أَمْرُهُمْ ("their affair surged"), paired with مَرِجَ ("became disordered") — it was thrown into turmoil.
3. الْمَوْج (mawj) is the waves of the sea; the entry derives the name from that same agitation.

Morphology: the verb is مَاجَ / يَمُوجُ, with two verbal nouns, مَوْجًا (mawj) and مَوَجَانًا (mawajān).

General rule stated: anything whatever that becomes agitated may be described with مَاجَ.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
According to Ibn Fāris, the root م و ل (m-w-l) carries a single notion, tied to wealth or property (māl):

1. Wealth and its acquisition — تَمَوَّلَ (tamawwala) means "the man acquired wealth/property," and مَالَ يَمَالُ (māla yamālu) means "his wealth grew abundant."

2. A disputed byform — He notes a line of verse, "brimming with water like the spring of al-mūlah," in which some take al-mūlah (المُولَة) to mean "the spider." Ibn Fāris flags this reading as questionable (fīhi naẓar).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: م و ر (m-w-r) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: this root is classed as a "sound" (unreduced) triliteral whose single unifying idea is taraddud — repeated back-and-forth motion, surging or wavering movement.

Ibn Fāris gathers this sense across several usages:

1. Flowing/surging blood — "māra al-damu ... yamūru": blood poured out and surged to and fro on the ground. The causative "amartu damahu" means "I made his blood flow." A ḥadīth is cited using this verb ("let the blood flow as you wish"), with a variant transmission from a different root (m-r-y), which Ibn Fāris says he will address separately.

2. Swirling dust — "al-mūr" is dust that the wind whips and stirs about.

3. A swift, supple gait — a she-camel "tamūru" (sways/surges) as she moves, and is called "mawwāra," swift. Ṭarafa's ode is quoted describing such a camel: tawny-tufted, firm-backed, long-striding, with a free, surging swing to her foreleg ("mawwārat al-yad"). A horse with a supple, swift back is likewise "mawwārat al-ẓahr."

4. A proverb of uncertainty — "I don't know whether he went to the Ghawr [lowland] or māra [turned back toward Najd]," used for not knowing which way someone went.

5. The shed birth-coat of a wild donkey — in spring the young donkey's first coat falls off in patches; each patch is a "muwāra," a term explained by the same root sense: it is so named because, as it falls, it flutters/moves to and fro. A line of verse is quoted using the plural "muwārāt al-ʿiqaq" for these falling patches.

6. "Al-mawr" as road — a path is called "mawr" because people move back and forth along it.

7. "Al-mawr" as wave — the surging swell of water.

8. A saying distinguishing "sāʾir" from "māʾir" — someone who "doesn't know sāʾir from māʾir" cannot distinguish: al-māʾir, a cutting sword that darts to and fro inside the thing it strikes, from al-sāʾir, poetry that is well known and widely transmitted (from a different root, meaning "current/circulating").

All senses in this entry — flowing blood, blowing dust, a camel's swaying gait, shed skin-patches, a road, a wave, a darting sword-blade — are presented by Ibn Fāris as expressions of one underlying idea: repeated to-and-fro motion.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مَوْت 50x "[the] death"; مَّاتَ 39x "die"; مَّيِّت 38x "the dead"; أَمَاتَ 21x "and causes death"; مَيْتَة 6x "the dead animals"; مَّيْت 5x "dead"; مَمَات 3x "(after) the death"; مَوْتَت 3x "our death"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-و-ت (m-w-t) as a single sound root whose core sense is the departure of strength or vigor from a thing.

1. الْمَوْت (al-mawt) — death, the opposite of life. Ibn Fāris grounds his "departure of strength" reading in a Prophetic saying about the pungent plant (garlic/onion): if you must eat it, "kill it" (amītūhā) by cooking — i.e. deaden or weaken it — showing the root's underlying idea of draining a thing's potency.

2. الْمَوَتَان / الْمَوَات (al-mawatān / al-mawāt) — land not yet "brought to life" by cultivation or improvement; inert, unused ground. Al-Aṣmaʿī cites the saying: "Buy of the inert property (mawatān), not of the living stock (ḥayawān)."

3. الْمُوتَان (al-mūtān, with ḍamma on the mīm) — death as a widespread event; an epidemic. "A mūtān fell among the people."

4. نَاقَةٌ مُمِيت / مُمِيتَة (nāqa mumīt/mumīta) — a she-camel whose young dies.

5. مَوْتَانُ الْفُؤَاد (mawtān al-fuʾād) — a man with a dead/lifeless heart (feminine: mawtāna).

6. أُمِيتَتِ الْخَمْر (umītat al-khamr) — the wine was "deadened," i.e. cooked.

7. الْمُسْتَمِيت (al-mustamīt) — one who gives himself over completely to a matter.

8. الْمُوتَة (al-mūta) — a condition resembling madness that overcomes a person.

9. الْمَوْتَة (al-mawta) — a single instance of dying.

10. الْمِيتَة (al-mīta) — the manner or state in which one dies, good or ugly; e.g. "he died a Jāhiliyya death."

11. الْمَيْتَة (al-mayta) — an animal (of a normally edible kind) that has died [rather than being ritually slaughtered].

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives everything in this root from one physical image: something liquid being agitated/churned inside the container that holds it. From that core sense, the root is then extended metaphorically to several usages:

1. **The literal verb** — makhaḍtu al-laban, amkhuḍuhu, makhḍan: "I churned the milk" (e.g., in a churn, to separate butter).

2. **A camel's bellow (al-makhḍ)** — also used for the rumbling/groaning sound a male camel makes. Ibn Fāris explains this as a simile: it is as if the camel is "churning" something inside his shiqshiqa, the inflatable throat-sac he displays when bellowing.

3. **A woman/female in labor (al-māḫiḍ)** — the term for a pregnant female overtaken by labor pains (al-ṭalq). Again explained by simile: it is as though what is in her belly is a liquid substance being churned/convulsed (yatamakhkhaḍu).

4. **Pregnant she-camels collectively (al-makhāḍ)** — the plural noun for pregnant she-camels; the singular is khalifa (a different root/word).

5. **"Ibn makhāḍ" (a camel-age term)** — the name given to a she-camel's offspring once the breeding stallion is again introduced into the herd that contains its mother — regardless of whether the mother has actually conceived again by that point. So the term marks an age-stage by the herd's breeding cycle, not literally by the mother's pregnancy status.

Ibn Fāris's method throughout is to trace sense 2–5 back to sense 1 (physical churning of a liquid) as similes/metaphorical extensions, rather than treating them as separate roots.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) gives the root m-kh-r (مخر) one core meaning: splitting/rending open (shaqq, fatḥ).

1. Ships cutting water. The primary usage: makharat al-safīnatu al-māʾa — "the ship makhara'd [cleaved through] the water." A cited rajaz verse applies the same image to women racing in a swim, helping themselves along with their hands "like a swimmer does" — described as "the hands of the mawākhir," the ones that cleave the water. (Mawākhir is the plural form later used in the Qur'an for ships that cut through the sea.)

2. Channeling water into land. makhartu al-arḍa — "I makhara'd the land," said of releasing/sending water into it, i.e. irrigating or channeling water in — the same underlying image of opening a way for something to pass through.

3. Facing the wind. istamkhartu al-rīḥa — "I istamkhara'd the wind," said of turning to face the wind with your nose. Ibn Fāris notes the derivation is sound here too: it is as if you are cutting/splitting the wind with your nose.

4. Picking out the best people. imtakhartu al-qawma — "I imtakhara'd the people," said of selecting the best among them — as if one cut a path through the crowd toward the chosen one and singled him out. A verse is cited using the same word for "the elect he had picked out."

Outlier: al-yamkhūr ("a tall man") is noted as irregular — it doesn't fit the root's core sense of splitting/opening.

Not actually from this root: banāt makhr ("daughters of makhr"), the term for clouds that form in summer, is explicitly excluded by Ibn Fāris. He explains it as a case of letter-substitution (ibdāl) — its true root is bāʾ-khāʾ-rāʾ ("bakhr"), covered elsewhere in the dictionary, not mīm-khāʾ-rāʾ.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: Ibn Aḥmar (lived into Islam); unnamed verse
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-ي-د (m-y-d) as two sound (genuine) roots: (1) motion in a thing, and (2) benefit and giving.

FIRST ROOT — motion
1. mayd = movement; the verb māda / yamīdu (to move, sway).
2. Of branches: mādat al-aghṣān = they swayed back and forth.
3. maydān, on the morphological pattern faʿlān: soft, well-watered, abundant living. Shāhid — Ibn Aḥmar: "…and it met with ease and a green maydān of living."

SECOND ROOT — giving and provisioning
4. māda / yamīdu = he fed, he benefited (someone).
5. mādanī / yamīdunī = he lifted me up, relieved me.
6. From this, Ibn Fāris reports, the māʾida (the food-table) got its name, and by the same analogy māʾid = one who provides. Shāhid (poet unnamed): "and I was a provider (māʾid) to those who came seeking bounty."
7. Abū Bakr is cited for: aṣābahu mayd = dizziness/vertigo struck him from sea travel.
8. Related verb forms: midtuhu = I gave to him; amadtuhu bi-khayr = I supplied him with good; imtadtuhu = I sought his bounty.

A COMPETING DERIVATION
9. Ibn Fāris notes that some exacting scholars traced mayd wholly back to motion, and on that account explained māʾida (the eating-table, khiwān) as so called because it "sways" with what is set on it — moving the food and shifting it out of its arranged order. Related: mādahum = he fed them at the table.

A DIALECTAL PARTICLE
10. On the prophetic report "mayda annā ūtīnā al-kitāba min baʿdihim" ("… that we were given the Book after them"), the sense given is "except that we…" or "given that we…"; mayda is treated as a dialect variant of the particle bayda.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: يَمِيلُ 3x "incline"; مَيْل 2x "the inclination"; مَّيْلَة 1x "(in) an attack"
text:
**Root م ي ل (m-y-l)** — al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's account:

1. **Core sense.** *Mayl* is deviation from the middle toward one side or the other — going off-centre.

2. **Extended to wrongdoing.** The word is also used for injustice (*jawr*), i.e. a lopsided departure from the balanced middle.

3. **Grammatical distinction in physical bodies.** When the tilt is inborn and constitutional, the vowelling is *mayal* (مَيَل); when it is an accidental, passing condition, it is *mayl* (مَيْل).

4. **مِلْتُ إلى (miltu ilā, "I inclined toward") = to side with, support, assist someone.** Citation: Qur'an 4:129, فَلَا تَمِيلُوا كُلَّ الْمَيْلِ — "do not incline with the whole of inclining."

5. **مِلْتُ عليه (miltu ʿalayhi, "I inclined against") = to bear down hard on someone, press against him.** Citation: Qur'an 4:102, فَيَمِيلُونَ عَلَيْكُمْ مَيْلَةً وَاحِدَةً — "so they fall upon you in a single onslaught." The change of preposition flips the sense from siding with to attacking.

6. **Etymology of مَال (māl, "wealth").** Al-Rāghib derives it from this root: wealth is so named because it is perpetually *inclining away* (*māʾil*) and *passing off* (*zāʾil*). For the same reason it is termed *ʿaraḍ* — a transient accident rather than something stable.

7. **Supporting saying.** He cites the proverb: "Wealth is a whore — one day in a perfumer's house, the next in a farrier's house," as evidence of the same idea of wealth's constant shifting.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م‑ي‑ر (m-y-r) as one coherent root, centered on a single core sense: fetching or supplying provisions (food).

1. The verbal noun is al-mayr, from the verb pattern mirtu mayran — "I went and fetched provisions [for someone]."

2. The related noun al-mīra names the thing itself: food carried/brought to a person, to his town — i.e., provisions imported or brought in from elsewhere for someone's locality.

3. He cites a set phrase used by the Arabs: mā ʿindahu khayrun wa lā mayrun — "he has neither good nor provision" — noted as a fixed pairing of khayr and mayr (a rhyming/assonant expression, not a separate sense of the root).

No further senses, derivations, or Qur'anic shawāhid are given in this entry — it is a short root article limited to the mayr/mīra sense.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَمِيزَ 2x "he separates"; ٱمْتَٰزُ 1x "but stand apart"; تَمَيَّزُ 1x "bursts"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-ي-ز (m-y-z) as a single sound root with one core idea: one thing coming apart from another, being set apart or held distinct.

1. Core sense — separation / setting apart. The root denotes the detaching of a thing from a thing and its being kept distinct.

2. Verb forms recorded:
   - مِزْتُهُ مَيْزًا (mizt-hu mayzan), form I: "I separated it," verbal noun mayz.
   - مَيَّزْتُهُ تَمْيِيزًا (mayyaztu-hu tamyīzan), form II: "I distinguished/separated it," verbal noun tamyīz.
   - امْتَازُوا (imtāzū), form VIII: "they became separated" — i.e. they became distinct from one another.
   - انْمَازَ (inmāza), form VII: a thing came detached, split off from another.

3. Idiomatic use — يَكَادُ يَتَمَيَّزُ غَيْظًا, "he almost comes apart with rage." Ibn Fāris glosses the verb here as يَتَقَطَّعُ, "he is all but torn to pieces": the same physical idea of splitting apart, applied to a person consumed by fury.

4. Poetic witness (shāhid) — an unnamed poet describing a snake: "It hoarded up venom until the skin of its head came away (انْمَازَ) from the bone — a deadly serpent, lethal of sting, refractory." The line illustrates انماز in its concrete sense: one layer physically parting from another.

The entry is short and stays within this one semantic field; Ibn Fāris records no further or figurative senses for the root here.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: م-ز-ج (m-z-j)
Dictionary: Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004 CE)

Core meaning: mixing one thing into another.

1. Verb — مَزَجَ يَمْزُجُ مَزْجًا (mazaja / yamzuju / mazjan): to mix, as in mixing a drink.

2. مَزْج (al-mazj) as a name for honey: philologists reportedly called honey "al-mazj" because every drink used to be mixed with it.

3. Poetic citation (Abū Dhu'ayb al-Hudhalī): he describes a mazj-mixture "the like of which people had never seen ... it is al-ḍaḥik [brightness/'laughter'], except that it is the bees' work" — describing honey as a bright mixture that is nonetheless the product of bees' labor.

4. مِزَاج (mizāj): when two kinds or substances are combined, each one is termed the "mizāj" (mixing-counterpart) of the other.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris treats the root m-z-n as a sound triliteral root with three senses he regards as diverging from one another in derivation:

1. al-muzn - "rain-cloud"; a single cloud-mass is a muznah. He quotes a verse (which he suspects is not genuine) in which "the son of the cloud" (ibn al-muznah), leaning low near the horizon, is likened to a nail-paring cut from a little finger - a poetic image identified as meaning the crescent moon (al-hilal).

2. al-mazin - "ant eggs."

3. mazana qirbatahu - "he filled his waterskin." From this comes the expression yatamazzanu ala ashabihi, "he exalts/shows himself superior over his companions," as if he were likening himself to the rain-cloud's generosity.

Ibn Faris concludes by suggesting that al-muzn (the cloud) is probably the root sense of the entry, with the other two meanings (ant eggs; filling a waterskin/boasting of generosity) branching off from it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats م-ز-ق as a single sound root whose core notion is a tearing or rending in something. From that one idea he derives:

1. To tear — مَزَقَ / يَمْزِقُ, with the doubled (intensive) form مَزَّقَ / يُمَزِّقُ for tearing to shreds.

2. المِزَق (al-mizaq) — the torn-off strips or pieces of a garment that has been rent.

3. نَاقَةٌ مِزَاقٌ — a she-camel of extreme speed, described as one whose hide almost tears off her as she runs (the tearing image applied to velocity).

4. مَزَقَ الطَّائِرُ بِذَرْقِهِ — said of a bird expelling its droppings: it shot or cast them out.

5. مَزَّقْتُ القَوْمَ — "I tore the people apart," i.e. scattered them; the reflexive تَمَزَّقُوا means they were dispersed. Social scattering is thus presented as the same tearing applied to a group rather than to cloth.

The entry cites no poetic or scriptural witnesses; it is a brief derivational sketch typical of Ibn Fāris's method of tracing every usage back to one governing sense.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: أَنشَأَ 20x "produced"; نَّشْأَة 3x "the creation"; يُنَشَّؤُا 1x "is brought up"; مُنشَـَات 1x "elevated"; إِنشَاء 1x "(into) a creation"; مُنشِـُون 1x "(are) the producers"; نَاشِئَة 1x "(the) rising"
poets_named: al-Shammākh (lived into Islam); Abū Qudāma al-Ṭāʾī (undated); ʿAbd al-Wāsiʿ al-Khuzāmī (pre-Islamic); Bishr b. Abī Ḥāzim (pre-Islamic); Nuṣayb (Umayyad)
text:
Al-Zamakhsharī's Asās al-Balāgha entry for the root ن ش أ (n-sh-ʾ), which turns on "coming into being / being brought forth" and, from that, "growing up." The dictionary is organized around ordinary and figurative usage.

1. To originate / bring into being. "God brought creation forth (anshaʾa), so it came to be (nashaʾū)." He cites "وننشئهم النّشأة الأخرى" ("We bring them forth in the other/second bringing-forth"). Extended to producing things one makes: to compose (anshaʾa) a discourse, poetry, or a building. "I asked him for an ascetic ode (istanshaʾtu), and he composed it (anshaʾa) for me."

2. To set about / begin. "He set about doing such-and-such." "From where did you nashaʾta / anshaʾta?" glossed as نهضت — "you rose up, set out."

3. Of clouds and raised objects. A cloud "arose" (nashaʾat), and God "raised it up" (anshaʾa). A nashʾ is the first wisp of cloud as it appears. One "raises up" (anshaʾa / istanshaʾa) a desert landmark or a sail. Qur'anic phrase "الجوار المنشآت" — the running ships with sails hoisted. A verse of al-Shammākh uses mustanshaʾāt ("raised-up things") of howdah-like shapes; with lexical glosses (dujya = a hunter's blind; jazīza = a tuft of wool).

4. Of tending camels. "He yanshaʾ toward so-and-so's camels" — he attends to and eyes them, presents himself to them.

5. To grow up / be reared. "I grew up (nashaʾtu) among Banū so-and-so; my birthplace and upbringing (manshaʾ) are among them." "He grew up with a good upbringing (nashʾa / nashāʾa)." Passive: to be reared in comfort (unshiʾa / nushshiʾa), with the Qur'anic phrase "من ينشّؤا في الحلية" ("one reared amid ornament").

6. The young one (nāshiʾ, pl. nawāshiʾ; nashʾ, collective). Used of an adolescent youth or girl. Shawāhid illustrating a young girl come of age: Abū Qudāma al-Ṭāʾī ("an adolescent of plump limbs"); ʿAbd al-Wāsiʿ al-Khuzāmī ("when she was a young girl, wrapped in a waist-cloth, hunting the one who does not hunt her"). The phrase nashʾ sūʾ = "bad young stock." Bishr b. Abī Ḥāzim speaks of "a pampered one of the young stock of Aslam, a maiden come of age (muʿṣir)"; Nuṣayb, of amusing himself with "the little young ones (al-nashʾ al-ṣighār)."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَّٰشِطَٰت 1x "and those who draw out"; نَشْط 1x "gently"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives everything under this root (n-sh-ṭ) from one core meaning: **vibration and motion** (اهتزاز وحركة).

1. **Liveliness / briskness.** الْنَّشَاط (an-nashāṭ), "energy, vigor," gets its name from exactly this — motion, quivering, an openness or brightness about it. Verb: نَشِطَ يَنْشَطُ, "to become lively/brisk." If a people's riding animals grew frisky, one said أَنْشَطَ الْقَوْم.

2. **A roaming/migrating wild bull.** الثَّوْر النَّاشِط is the wild bull, so called because it migrates (يَنْشِط) from one territory to another. Ibn Fāris cites a line of the poet Dhū al-Rumma describing such a bull — dappled-legged, dark-cheeked, a leader of its kind, a roaming young bull (نَاشِطٌ شَبَبُ) — as illustration.

3. **To peel/strip something** (نَشَطْتُ الشَّيْءَ = قَشَرْتُهُ), the idea being that peeling draws the thing out from its own skin.

4. **A road that veers off.** طَرِيقٌ نَاشِط is a side-track branching right or left off a main road — again a sense of movement/departure.

5. **A she-camel quickening her pace** — نَشَطَت in her stride when she tightens up and speeds up.

6. **The slip-knot (الأُنشوطة)** — a loose, easily-pulled knot like the drawstring-knot of trousers. From this: أَنْشَطْتُ الْعِقَال, "I released a hobble-rope," by pulling its slip-knot undone. Ibn Fāris notes some authorities reversed the technical pair: for them الإنشاط means *untying* and التنشيط means *tying*.

7. **A shallow well** (بئر أَنْشَاط) — one so shallow that the bucket comes up in a single pull; and نَشَطْتُ الدَّلْو, drawing the bucket up without needing a pulley-rope.

8. **النَّشِيطَة — an incidental prize of a raid.** Camels that are simply come upon and driven off, without having been the deliberate target of the raid. Some say specifically: livestock the raiding party encounters and seizes *before* reaching the settlement it actually meant to raid — the chief takes this portion for himself, separate from the main division of spoils. Ibn Fāris quotes a verse listing a chief's customary shares of war-spoil: the one-fourth share, the pick of the booty, his own judgment/discretion, the nashīṭa, and the surplus.

All eight senses trace back, in Ibn Fāris's account, to the single underlying idea of motion, quivering, and release/departure — whether it is a body's vigor, an animal's migration, a knot coming loose, a bucket pulled up, or a portion of booty peeled off before the rest.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نُشُور 5x "resurrection"; نُشِرَتْ 3x "will spread"; أَنشَرَ 3x "he will resurrect him"; تَنتَشِرُ 3x "then disperse"; مَنشُور 2x "unrolled"; مُنشَرِين 1x "(will be) raised again"; مُّنتَشِر 1x "spreading"; مُّنَشَّرَة 1x "spread out"; نَّٰشِرَٰت 1x "and the ones that scatter"; نَشْر 1x "far and wide"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats N-Sh-R (نشر) as a sound root whose core sense is the opening out of something and its spreading or branching apart. From that core he lists:

1. Sawing: نَشَرْتُ الْخَشَبَةَ بِالْمِنْشَارِ — "I sawed the wood with a saw" (verbal noun nashr).

2. A fragrant breeze: النَّشْر — the sweet-smelling wind.

3. Spreading out (of feathers): a falcon that "put on feathers nasharan" means feathers spread wide, broad and long.

4. Unrolling a scroll: نَشَرْتُ الْكِتَابَ — "I spread open the book," the opposite of folding/rolling it up (طَوَيْتُهُ).

5. Reviving the dead: نَشَرَ اللَّهُ الْمَوْتَى فَنَشَرُوا — "God brought the dead back to life and they revived"; the form-IV verb أَنْشَرَ carries the same sense. Shawāhid: the Qur'an, ثُمَّ إِذَا شَاءَ أَنْشَرَهُ ("then, when He wills, He revives him," Q 80:22); and a verse of al-Aʿshā marveling at "the dead man come back to life (al-nāshir)."

6. Land bursting into growth: نَشَرَتِ الْأَرْضُ — spring rain reaches the earth and it puts forth vegetation; such land is nāshira and the growth itself is al-nashr. Ibn Fāris notes this growth is said to be harmful for grazing animals; an alternative account makes al-nashr dried herbage that, struck by rain, produces something resembling ticks — a plant disease.

7. Forearm veins: النَّوَاشِر — the veins of the inner forearm, so named for their spreading out (intishār).

8. Swollen sinew: الِانْتِشَار — the swelling of a beast's tendon from fatigue.

9. Scattering flocks: النَّشَر — sheep scattering to graze at night. From this comes the idiom for someone who has put his affairs in order: قَدْ ضَمَّ نَشَرَهُ ("he has gathered up his scattered [affairs]").

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: نُشُوز 2x "ill-conduct"; ٱنشُزُ 2x "rise up"; نُنشِزُ 1x "we raise them"
text:
Root ن ش ز (n-sh-z) — Ibn Sīda's account. The organising idea running through the entry is raised, standing up above a level.

1. Raised ground. النَّشْز / النَّشَز (nashz, nashaz): a raised back or ridge of ground; also the land that rises up out of a valley, provided it is not rough or rugged. Plurals: anshāz and nushūz. Some hold that nashz pluralises as nushūz and nashaz as anshāz. النَّشاز (nashāz) is an equivalent form.

2. To come up onto high ground. نَشَزَ / يَنْشُزُ / نُشوزاً — to reach or overlook a raised patch of ground.

3. To rise, be elevated (of a thing). تَلٌّ ناشِزٌ — a hill that stands up high.

4. To rise up where one is sitting. نَشَزَ في مَجْلِسِه — to lift oneself up slightly in one's seat. Ibn Sīda cites the Qur'an here: "and when it is said, rise up, then rise up."

5. Bodily protrusion. رَكَبٌ ناشِزٌ — a pubic mound that juts out. عِرْقٌ ناشِزٌ — a swollen, raised vein that keeps on throbbing, whether from illness or some other cause.

6. Poetic evidence for the bodily sense (recited by Ibn al-Aʿrābī): "Laylā is not one whose short rib juts out, nor short-necked…" Ibn Sīda's gloss: nāshizat al-quṣayrā describes a woman heavy in the flanks, the short rib standing out because of the flesh piled on it — which the poet denies of Laylā.

7. Causative: to raise something up. أَنْشَزَ الشيءَ — to lift a thing from its place. Ibn Sīda cites the Qur'an, "look at the bones, how We raise them up," and glosses: We raise some of them up onto others.

8. Rising up against a spouse. نَشَزَت المرأةُ بِزَوجِها (she is ناشِز) — she rose up against him and came to detest him; and the same verb is used of the husband rising up against the wife, نَشَزَ هو عليها. Ibn Sīda cites the Qur'anic phrase about a woman who "fears from her husband nushūz or turning away." He supplies a verse of poetry using nāshiz of a female who travels by night toward the poorest corner of a tent.

9. A bulky man. رَجُلٌ نَشَزٌ — thick-set and stout. Al-Aʿshā: "if you test my utmost mettle you will find in me a stout one, already grey, no weakling twin." Ibn Sīda notes the poet's intent was magnification, and that this is why he made the figure grey-haired.

10. To rouse people for a dispute. نَشَزَ بالقَومِ في الخُصومةِ — to rise up with them / stir them for the quarrel.

11. To throw an opponent. نَشَزَ بِقِرْنِه — to lift his adversary and hurl him down.

12. A restive mount. دابَّةٌ نَشيزَةٌ — a beast on which rider and saddle can hardly stay settled.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَذِير 58x "a warner"; أَنذَرَ 44x "and warn"; مُنذِر 15x "a warner"; مُنذَرِين 5x "(of) those who were warned"; نَذَرْ 4x "[i] have vowed"; نَّذْر 2x "the vows"; نُذُور 1x "their vows"; نُذْر 1x "warning"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the whole root n-dh-r from a single core idea: frightening someone, or being afraid oneself.

1. Warning (inḏār): to convey or deliver a message — but almost always a message meant to instill fear. The form tanāḏarū means "they frightened one another."

2. The vow (naḏr): tied to the same core sense because the one who vows fears the consequence of breaking it.

3. Grammatical/usage note from Thaʿlab: naḏirtu bihim means "I grew aware/wary of them, so I prepared for them and was on my guard against them."

4. The warner (naḏīr) = one who warns (munḏir); its plural is nuḏur.

5. A second sense of naḏr: something that becomes obligatory — as if it had been "vowed," i.e. made binding. Ibn Fāris cites the legal phrase naḏr al-mūḍiḥa (the fixed compensation set for the head-wound that exposes the bone) as an instance of this.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives two related senses from the root n-'-y (نأي):

1. Al-nu'y — a drainage trench dug around a tent to keep rainwater from reaching it. The verb is "an'aytu nu'yan" ("I dug a nu'y-trench"). Al-munta'á in this sense is simply the spot where such a trench is dug.
   - Shāhid (cited by al-Khalīl): a verse describing tears at a parting as "showers whose flow is diverted [yun'á] with the fingers" — the image is of fingers wiping/damming tears the way a nu'y-trench diverts rainwater.

2. Al-na'y — distance, remoteness. The verb is "na'á yan'á na'yan" ("he became distant/went far away"), with the derived form "inta'á." Al-munta'á in this sense means "the distant place."
   - Shāhid: a verse addressing someone as being like the night that always catches up with the speaker, "even though I thought the distant place [munta'á] from you was wide" — i.e., even distance couldn't shake him off.

Ibn Fāris notes a variant form: speakers sometimes shift the hamza later in the word, saying "nā'in" instead of the more original "na'á" — same root, same meaning of turning/going away.
   - Shāhid: a verse contrasting how a person treats you when rich versus poor — friendly ("softens his side") when you're wealthy, but "turns away [nā'a] and grows estranged" when you're poor.

The entry closes with the standard formula, "God knows best what is correct."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ن ض د (n-ḍ-d) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: joining one thing to another in an orderly, gathered arrangement — stacking or ranging things together, either upright or spread flat. The verb naḍadtu means "I stacked/arranged [a thing] part upon part," either in neat order or one layer on top of another.

Senses recorded:

1. Al-naḍad = piled/stacked clothing (al-manḍūd min al-thiyāb). Illustrated by a line of al-Nābigha describing a stream let loose, its water rising up to the tent-curtains and then to the naḍad, the stacked pile of furnishings/goods.

2. Al-naḍad = a bed or couch on which goods/furnishings are stacked (a raised platform for piling one's belongings).

3. Anḍād al-jibāl = the boulders/rock-slabs of mountains lying stacked one on top of another.

4. Al-naḍad (of clouds) = banked, piled cloud (like ṣabīr), where one mass adjoins another; plural anḍād.

5. Anḍād al-qawm = a people's assembled groups and their numbers/muster.

6. Naḍad al-rajul = a man's paternal and maternal uncles, i.e. the kin who rally together to support him.

7. Al-naḍad = eminence, high standing/nobility.
