8. Naḍā'id al-dībāj (plural of naḍīdah) = cushions/pillows, and more broadly any furnishing stuffed with padding.

Ibn Durayd's gloss, cited approvingly: anything stacked part upon part is called naḍīd.

In short, every sense in this entry — piled cloth, a couch for piled goods, stacked mountain rock, banked cloud, a mustered group of people, a man's rallying kinsmen, stuffed cushions, and even "eminence" — traces back to the single image of things set or piled one upon or beside another in orderly fashion.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ن ض ج (n-ḍ-j), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: reaching completion in the cooking of a thing; then figuratively borrowed for anything that has reached the utmost degree of soundness.

1. naḍija al-tamru wa-l-laḥmu — dates and meat became fully ripe/cooked (nuḍj); andajtuhu — I brought it to that state; andajathu al-shamsu — the sun ripened it.
2. Figurative extension: "huwa nadīju al-raʾy" — he is one of mature, well-considered judgment — sound opinion likened to fully-cooked food.
3. A distinct, technical use: a she-camel that has passed her due date without giving birth is described as naddajat (munaddaj), illustrated with a line of poetry about camels historically overdue by nearly a month — an idiom built on the same root, though its exact connection to "ripeness" is left implicit by the entry.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root n-ḍ-r (ن ض ر) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: this root is a sound one, and it points to beauty, comeliness, and purity/clarity.

1. Freshness of color. Al-naḍra means "beauty of color" — a fresh, glowing complexion or hue. The verb is naḍara/yanḍuru, "to be radiant/fresh" (the text preserves more than one attested vowel-pattern for this verb).

2. "May God make his face radiant." The expression naḍḍara Allāhu wajhahu means "made his face beautiful and luminous." Ibn Fāris cites the well-known hadith: "May God make radiant a man who heard my words and preserved them" — using naḍḍara as a prayer for someone who transmits knowledge faithfully.

3. "Green and radiant." Akhḍar nāḍir ("green, radiant") is a standard word-pair. More generally, the author says this root's word is used for anything that shines and is beautiful — not restricted to color.

4. Qur'anic usage. Ibn Fāris cites Q75:22: "Faces, that day, radiant" (wujūhun yawma'idhin nāḍira), as the model instance of this sense — a face lit up with radiant beauty.

5. Gold. Al-naḍīr is a name for gold, because of its beauty and purity. He supports this with a line of poetry (unnamed poet) describing something stripped bare and compared to a striped woollen wrap (khamīṣa) touched with the glossy flush of radiant gold — the poem's exact color-word (jiryāl) is a little ambiguous on its own, roughly "gleam" or "red tint."

6. A wooden cup called nuḍār. Qadaḥ nuḍār names a drinking-bowl carved from athl (tamarisk) wood found in the lowland region (al-Ghawr). Ibn Fāris only tentatively links the name to this root, adding: "perhaps it is so called because it is beautiful" — he does not assert this derivation confidently.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives naḍakha (ن-ض-خ) as a root close to, and alongside, naḍaḥa (ن-ض-ح) — the two are near-synonyms in his system, but naḍakha denotes a greater degree/intensity than naḍaḥa.

1. Core sense: al-naḍkh is like al-laṭkh — a smearing or staining action by some substance that leaves a visible trace or mark behind.

2. Usage example: naḍakha thawbahu bi'l-ṭīb — "he dabbed/sprinkled his garment with perfume," i.e. applied it so a trace of scent remained.

3. Extended usage — the intensive adjective form "naḍḍākh" applied to abundance:
   - ghayth naḍḍākh — a copious, abundant rain.
   - ʿayn naḍḍākha — a spring abundant/plentiful in water.

So the root's throughline, per this entry, is an action of daubing/spraying that leaves a lasting mark, with the intensive form extended to mean "profuse" or "abundant" when applied to rain or water sources.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ن-ع-ج as a single sound root whose core idea is a colour.

1. Colour proper. النَّعَج (naʿaj) is pure whiteness. A جَمَل نَاعِج is a camel of fine colour and good breeding. A woman described as نَاعِجَة is one of fine colouring.

2. The ewe and comparable females. From the colour sense comes النَّعْجَة (naʿja), the ewe of the domestic flock — a word also applied to the female of the wild cow and of the mountain sheep/goat. The plural for the females of all these kinds is نِعَاج. The phrase نِعَاجُ الرَّمْل ("ewes of the sand") denotes wild cattle.

3. A verb from the meat. نَعِجَ الرَّجُل means a man ate ewe-flesh and was made ill by it. Ibn Fāris cites a verse: as though the people had been fed mutton at supper, "so they are naʿijūn, their necks already drooping."

4. A verb from the flock. أَنْعَجُوا — their ewes became fat.

5. A disputed case. Of نَوَاعِج الْإِبِل (a class of camels), others say these are the swift camels; Ibn Fāris holds instead that they are the choice, noble ones, because that fits the root's colour-and-excellence analogy he has set out. This is his methodological signature: an outlying sense is re-read so it stays under the one root idea.

6. Land. النَّاعِجَة of ground is soft, level terrain, valued for growth: it brings forth the rimth shrub and the choicest herbage.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ن ع ل (n-ʿ-l), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris notes this is a small (uṣayl) root indicating settledness in a thing, and lowness/being-underneath.

1. al-naʿl — the well-known sandal, named for being beneath the foot. rajul nāʿil/muntaʿil — a man wearing a sandal; anʿaltu al-dābbah — I shod the riding-animal (only the causative Form IV is correct here, not the bare verb). ḥimār al-waḥsh nāʿil — the wild donkey, described this way for the hardness of its hoof.
2. al-naʿl, of a sword — the iron or silver fitting at the bottom of its scabbard, illustrated with a line of poetry about a scabbard-tip not reaching halfway up the shin despite long carrying-straps. faras munʿal — a horse whose white marking sits low on the fetlock, at the hair-fringe, without extending further.
3. al-naʿl, of a bow — sinew fitted over the back of its curved tip.
4. al-naʿl, of land — a place-name, said to denote volcanic rocky terrain (al-ḥarrah) that grows nothing.
5. Closing, figurative sense (per al-Khalīl): al-naʿl also names an abased man — one trodden upon, just as a sandal is trodden underfoot.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نِعْمَة 50x "(the) favor"; نَّعَم 33x "the cattle"; نِعْمَ 18x "and an excellent"; أَنْعَمَ 17x "i bestowed"; نَعِيم 17x "(of) delight"; نَّعْمَة 2x "(of) the ease"; نَعْمَاء 1x "(of) favor"; نَّاعِمَة 1x "(will be) joyful"; نَعَّمَ 1x "and favors him"
text:
Ibn Fāris holds that although the root n-ʿ-m has many branches, they all trace back to one core sense: ease, pleasant living, and wellbeing.

1. النِّعْمَة (niʿma) — a benefit God bestows on His servant, such as wealth and livelihood ("God has a niʿma upon him"). It also means a favour or grace (minna), as does النَّعْماء (naʿmāʾ).

2. النَّعْمَة (naʿma) — luxuriating and pleasant living, cited from Q 44:27 (al-Dukhān): "and a comfort in which they took delight."

3. النُّعامَى (nuʿāmā) — a gentle, soft wind.

4. النَّعَم (naʿam) — camels, so called for the good/blessing in them. Ibn Fāris cites al-Farrāʾ: the word is masculine, not made feminine (هذا نَعَمٌ واردٌ), and its plural is أنعام (anʿām). By the same logic الأنعام (anʿām) means livestock/beasts.

5. النَّعامة (naʿāma) — (a) the ostrich, named for the softness of its feathers; (b) by likeness, a shade-canopy set on a mountain-top for shelter (supported by a poetic citation).

6. Set expressions of delight — نُعْمَى عَيْنٍ / نُعْمَةَ عَيْنٍ, meaning "coolness/delight of the eye" (qurrat ʿayn).

7. Verbal forms — نَعِمَ الشيءُ, "the thing became pleasant/soft"; نَعَّمَ أولادَهُ, "he pampered/indulged his children."

8. ابن النَّعامة (ibn al-naʿāma) — the ball/front of the foot, said to be named for being a soft, smooth spot (with a poetic citation). Related: تَنَعَّمَ, "he walked barefoot."

9. النَّعامة for a group — شالَتْ نَعامَتُهُم ("their ostrich took flight") means they scattered; a metaphor from the ostrich flying off.

10. تنعَّمَتْني الأرضُ — "the land suited/agreed with me."

11. نِعْمَ (niʿma) — the verb of praise, opposite of بِئْسَ (biʾsa, dispraise); also the idiom فبها ونِعْمَتْ, "excellent is that trait." Ibn Fāris counts even نَعَمْ (naʿam, "yes," the affirmative answer opposite لا) as belonging to this root, deriving it from niʿma.

12. النَّعائِم (naʿāʾim) — (a) by likeness, a constellation/star; (b) wooden posts set over a well to hang the pulley-beam, when the well lacks a frame.

13. شقائق النُّعمان (anemones) — said to be ascribed to Ibn al-Mundhir, who kept it as a preserve; another view takes al-nuʿmān to mean blood, but Ibn Fāris judges the first more fitting.

14. Ibn Durayd's usage — تنعَّمْتُ زيداً, "I sought out Zayd," as if directing the sole (naʿāma) of one's foot toward him. Also نَعِمَ اللهُ بكَ عَيْناً, "may God gladden your eye," in the same vein.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ن-ع-ق (n-ʿ-q) from a single core idea: a sound or cry (ṣawt).

He illustrates it with one usage: naʿaqa al-rāʿī bi-l-ghanam — "the shepherd naʿaqa at the sheep" — meaning the shepherd shouted or cried out at the flock to drive/herd them. He notes the imperfect is attested in two forms, yanʿaqu and yanʿiqu, with the verbal noun naʿīq (a shouting/crying-out).

No further senses, citations, or grammatical notes are given; this is the entry's entirety.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ن-ع-س (n-ʿ-s) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

1. Core sense: drowsiness, dozing (wasan). The verb naʿasa – yanʿusu – nuʿāsan means "he dozed / drowsed."

2. Applied to a she-camel: nāqatun naʿūs ("a drowsy she-camel") is a term of praise, used for a camel that is generous with her milk. She is called "drowsy" because when she lets her milk flow freely she stands calm and still, as if dozing off.

3. Supporting verse (quoted as a fragment, ellipsis in the source, poet unnamed): "naʿūsun idhā darrat, jarūzun idhā shatat … buwayzilu ʿāmin aw sadīsun ka-bāzil" — "she is drowsy [docile] when she gives her milk, hardy/voracious when winter scarcity comes … whether a little yearling or a six-year-old as sturdy as a fully mature camel."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) derives the root ن-ح-ب (n-ḥ-b) from two basic senses.

**Sense 1 — Vow, wager, all-out effort, and (by extension) death**
- al-naḥb (النَّحْب) = "the vow" (al-nadhr).
- "So-and-so travelled ʿalā naḥb" describes someone straining and exerting himself hard, as if he had staked something on the outcome and so gave it everything.
- A quoted verse-fragment glosses al-munaḥḥib as "the one who wagers/risks" (al-mukhāṭir).
- al-tanḥīb was an old Arab custom resembling a wager: "If such-and-such happens, you owe me X; if not, I owe you X." Ibn Fāris notes that Islam prohibited this practice.
- From the same idea: nāḥabtuhu ilā fulān means "I brought him before so-and-so to have the matter judged" — i.e. submitted a dispute to arbitration/litigation. Ibn Fāris says the same underlying logic connects the wager-sense and this litigation-sense.
- By extension, al-naḥb can also mean death itself — as if death were a vow every person has made, one he must fulfill and cannot escape.

**Sense 2 — A sound**
- al-naḥīb = the sound of someone weeping loudly, with wailing and lament.
- al-nuḥāb = the coughing sound camels make; naḥaba al-baʿīru yanḥabu describes a camel making this sound.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ن-ح-ل (n-ḥ-l) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris says this root covers three unrelated senses:

1. Thinness / emaciation (دِقَّة وهُزَال)
- نَحَلَ جِسْمُهُ نُحُولًا, "his body became emaciated" → نَاحِلٌ, "emaciated (person)."
- أَنْحَلَهُ الْهَمُّ, "worry wasted him away."
- النَّوَاحِل, "al-nawāḥil" — swords whose blade-edges have grown thin from repeated use in battle.

2. Giving (عَطَاء)
- نَحَلْتُهُ كَذَا = "I gave him such-and-such." The noun is النُّحْل (al-nuḥl).
- Abū Bakr: the thing given is called النُّحْلَان (al-nuḥlān).
- Some define النُّحْل as giving something without expecting anything back in return.
- نَحَلْتُ الْمَرْأَةَ مَهْرَهَا نِحْلَةً, "I gave the woman her dower as a niḥla" — i.e. willingly, with no counter-demand.
- Ibn Fāris notes the exegetes explained the Qur'anic phrase {وَآتُوا النِّسَاءَ صَدُقَاتِهِنَّ نِحْلَةً} ("give the women their dowers as a niḥla," 4:4) this same way — as a free, willing gift, not something extracted under compulsion.

3. Claiming / appropriating as one's own (ادِّعَاء)
- انْتَحَلَ كَذَا, "he claimed such-and-such" — he took it up and asserted it as his own.
- Some grammarians tried to split this into two: انْتَحَلَ for a *true* claim, تَنَحَّلَ for a *false* one.
- Ibn Fāris rejects that distinction outright ("this is nothing, in our view") and holds the two verbs are simply synonyms.
- He backs this with a line of the poet al-Aʿshā, who uses انْتِحَال for composing/claiming authorship of verse in old age, calling it a disgrace — showing the word carries no built-in judgment of truth or falsehood.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
poets_named: al-Kumayt (Umayyad); unnamed verse ×2; 'Alqama (pre-Islamic); Abu Wajza (disputed date); al-Ra'i and Ibn Mayyada (Umayyad)
text:
Root n-h-r (نحر) — Asas al-Balagha, al-Zamakhshari (d. 1144 CE)

Base/literal sense: nahr, plural nuhur, is the upper chest — the point at the base of the throat where the collarbones meet. "He struck his nahr / their nuhur" is given as an example of the word's use.

From this comes nahara, "to slaughter [a camel]" — properly, to stab it at the nahr (distinct from dhabh, cutting the throat). An animal so slaughtered is manhura; the place of slaughter is a manhar (plural manahir); professional slaughterers are nahharun. People who "slaughter one another" (tanaharu) in war are killing each other.

Al-Zamakhshari then marks eight extended (figurative) uses, each built on the image of the nahr as the body's foremost, confronting point:

1. The start of a time-period. "The nahr of the day" or "the nahr of the month" means its very beginning. Related plurals (nuhur, naha'ir, nawahir) applied to months all denote month-onsets. A verse of al-Kumayt links rain with crescent moons at the "nawahir" — glossed by the author as meaning: rain right at a month's start signals abundance.

2. Facing/confronting. "He sat in the nahr of so-and-so" = he sat facing him; "I nahara'd him" = I faced him. Neighboring dwellings that "face each other" are described the same way, as are abodes that "face" a road. A verse praises a chief as "lord of the people of al-Abtah, facing [others]."

3. Getting to the very core of a subject through knowledge — "he nahara'd matters" means he penetrated straight to their essence. From this comes nihrir, "an expert, a master of his craft" (plural naharir). A folk-saying holds that a north wind meeting a new crescent moon foretells a drought month. A verse of 'Alqama pictures dawn "confronted" by a bright star. In a well-known anecdote, the poet Jarir, asked who the best poets of Islam were, credited al-Farazdaq with "the choice wood of poetry," then said of himself: "I have gotten to the very heart of poetry."

4. Competing jealously for something — people who are "grudging rivals" over a matter. A proverb, "the thief stole, then intahara," describes someone compounding a wrong with a further drastic act.

5. A wide, clear road is described as muntahir. A verse of Abu Wajza pictures a rider following such a well-trodden night track.

6. Clouds "bursting" with rain — intahara al-sahab, clouds breaking open and pouring down. Verses of al-Ra'i and Ibn Mayyada picture clouds "bursting" over abodes and watering the land so plants like khuzama flourish.

7. People "following one after another" onto a road or in an attack. A cited verse (partly obscure in its closing line) complains of a tribe, 'Amir, coming against the speaker one after another unjustly.

8. The opposite sense — turning away from a road: they "turned away from it."

Throughout, al-Zamakhshari treats these extended senses as genuine metaphor rooted in the literal image of the nahr as the body's foremost, confronting part — not as separate, unrelated meanings.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَّحِسَات 1x "(of) misfortune"; نَحْس 1x "(of) misfortune"; نُحَاس 1x "and smoke"
text:
ROOT: n-h-s (نحس) - Ibn Faris, Maqayis al-Lugha (d. 1004 CE)

Ibn Faris identifies a single core meaning for n-h-s: the opposite of good fortune - misfortune, ill omen. Nuhisa huwa means "he was afflicted with bad luck," and such a person is manhus, "ill-fated."

1. Al-nuhas as smoke: he first glosses al-nuhas as smoke without flame, quoting a line of poetry - "devils, whose accursed one is pelted with al-nuhas" - describing devils being struck with this smoke/vapor.

2. Al-nuhas as a metal: he also notes al-nuhas is used for a metal (brass/copper), and offers a speculative etymology: it may have been so named because it falls short of, or differs from, the noble metals (gold, silver) - he flags this explicitly as conjecture, not certain.

3. "Ill-omened day": the everyday expression is yawmun nahsun or yawmun nahisun, "an unlucky day" - he notes both forms occur, matching the two Qur'anic qira'ah variants at Fussilat 41:16, nahisat and nahsat, describing the days of the storm sent upon 'Ad.

4. Alternative derivation - "base/origin": he then offers a second possible account (attributed to other scholars): that nuhas itself may mean "the base/origin" (al-asl) of a thing, and because the metal nuhas (copper) served as the underlying base material for many other alloys/substances, the word came to denote the fundamental substrate or essence of anything.

So the entry records two distinct, tentatively connected strands under this root: (a) ill fortune/ill-omened, and (b) nuhas as smoke, as a base metal, and - possibly - as "origin/base substance" generally.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
Root نحت (n-ḥ-t) — Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr, d. 1311 CE)

1. Core sense: cutting away, paring, hewing. Ibn Manẓūr opens with naḥt = sawing/cutting up and stripping off the surface, then specifies it as what a carpenter does to wood. The verb naḥata takes the imperfect with either kasra or fatḥa (yanḥitu / yanḥatu), verbal noun naḥt; the form VIII intaḥatat means the wood "came to be shaped." Nuḥāta is the material hewn off — the shavings.

2. Hewing rock. naḥata al-jabal = he cut into the mountain, treated as the same sense. The entry's Qur'anic citation: "and you hew houses out of the mountains, secure." Related to this: al-Naḥāʾit, a set of well-known wells, named by a description that stuck because they were hewn (cut) out — cited from Zuhayr's verse locating a desolate waste "at the outflow of al-Naḥāʾit" (a variant reading of the place-name is noted).

3. Figurative wearing down. Ibn Manẓūr marks this explicitly as tashbīh (likeness/figure): travel "hews" a camel or a man, i.e. reduces him and makes him thin. Hence a naḥīt camel is one whose footpads are worn away (with a verse: worn out from weariness), and a naḥīt hoof is one whose edges have worn off.

4. Hewn objects. al-naḥīta: a tree-trunk hewn and hollowed into a jar-shaped hive for bees; plural nuḥut.

5. Grammatical/derivational notes (from al-Jawharī): naḥatahu yanḥituhu, with kasra, = barāhu (whittled it); nuḥāta = burāya (parings); and the instrument-noun al-minḥat, "the thing one hews with" (pattern mifʿal).

6. The outsider grafted on. al-naḥīt = the incomer among a people, one not of their own stock. Shāhid from al-Khirniq, sister of Ṭarafa, praising her people as those who "mingle their naḥīt with their nuḍār" (their adopted outsider with their pure-blooded), and their rich with their poor. Ibn Manẓūr glosses nuḍār as those of pure lineage, notes Ibn Barrī's textual correction (read wa-l-khāliṭīn, with wāw), and explains the closing line — "when I perish, my grave will cover me" — as putting the cause (her death) in place of the effect (her praise ceasing). He records that this shāhid is also attributed to Ḥātim Ṭayyiʾ.

7. Innate nature as "what one was cut from." al-naḥīta is the disposition a person was hewn upon; al-Liḥyānī glosses it as both nature (ṭabīʿa) and origin (aṣl). "Generosity is of his naḥt" means: of the stock he was cut from. Abū Zayd treats ṭabīʿa, naḥīta and gharīza as one meaning. Al-Liḥyānī also pairs naḥt with niḥās (stock) and gives "he was hewn upon generosity and moulded upon it."

8. Further extended senses:
   - naḥatahu bi-lisānihi (both imperfect vowellings): he blamed and abused him — "hewing" with the tongue.
   - al-naḥīt: the worthless or bad specimen of anything.
   - naḥatahu bi-l-ʿaṣā: he beat him with a stick.
   - naḥata … naḥītan: he groaned.
   - naḥata al-marʾa: had intercourse with her — with Ibn Manẓūr noting that laḥata is the better-known form here.

Method worth noting: the entry moves from the concrete craft sense (cutting wood and rock) outward, flags the figurative step where it occurs, and grounds the extended senses in poetry and in named earlier lexicographers (al-Jawharī, al-Liḥyānī, Abū Zayd, Ibn Barrī).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَاصِح 6x "the sincere advisors"; نَصَحُ 5x "and [i] advise"; نُصْح 1x "my advice"; نَّصُوح 1x "sincere"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives نصح (n-ṣ-ḥ) from a single core idea: the fitting-together of two things and the setting of them right.

1. Root sense — sewing/joining. The primary referent is النَّاصِح (al-nāṣiḥ), the tailor, and النِّصَاح (al-niṣāḥ), the thread used to sew (plural نِصَاحَات niṣāḥāt). Stretched hides laid out on the ground for tanning are likened to these threads/stretched things. A verse of poetry is cited: "You see the people, all of them drunk, just as the stretched hides (niṣāḥāt) of the young ape are spread out."

2. Sincere counsel / good faith. From this root come النُّصْح and النَّصِيحَة, meaning sincere advice or good faith — the opposite of غِشّ (ghishsh, deceit or adulteration); with the verb نَصَحْتُهُ أَنْصَحُهُ. The expression نَاصِحُ الْجَيْب ("sincere of bosom") is used proverbially of someone pure in deed. التَّوْبَةُ النَّصُوح ("sincere repentance") belongs here too, pictured as sound (ṣaḥīḥa), with no tear or breach in it.

3. Watering camels to the full. أَنْصَحْتُ الْإِبِل means to water camels until they are fully satisfied, so that نَصَحَت = they are watered/sated — which Ibn Fāris links back to the same underlying analogy.

4. Purity. نَاصِحُ الْعَسَل is pure clear honey, as though it were unmixed with any adulterant.

Two further usages: نَصَحْتُ لَهُ and نَصَحْتُهُ carry the same meaning; and قَمِيصٌ مَنْصُوحٌ means a sewn shirt — closing the circle back to the sewing sense.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَصِيب 21x "a portion"; نَصَب 4x "fatigue"; نُصُب 3x "the stone altars"; نُصِبَتْ 2x "then labor hard"; نُصْب 1x "with distress"; نَّاصِبَة 1x "exhausted"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ن-ص-ب (n-ṣ-b) as a single sound root whose core idea is setting something up and making it stand out, prominent and upright.

1. Erecting: naṣabtu al-rumḥa — "I planted the spear" (and similar objects). Related: a he-goat is anṣab and a she-goat naṣbāʾ when its horns stand erect; a she-camel is naṣbāʾ when high-chested.

2. al-naṣb / al-nuṣub: a stone that was set up and worshipped — specifically a stone set before an idol on which the blood of animals sacrificed to the idols was poured (attributed to this author's account of usage).

3. al-naṣāʾib: stones set up around a well's rim to serve as supports.

4. al-naṣab: toil, weariness — because a person keeps standing upright (muntaṣib) until worn out. Likewise "rising dust" (ghubār muntaṣib) is dust raised up.

5. al-naṣīb (one sense): a stone-built water-trough.

6. niṣāb of a thing: its base or origin — as the handle (niṣāb) of a knife, into which the blade is raised and mounted.

7. al-naṣīb (another sense): one's share or lot ("this is my naṣīb" = my share) — from the same root, as if it is what has been raised up and set out for you.

8. al-naṣb: a genre of song — perhaps because the voice is raised (yunṣab) with it.

9. niṣāb as a threshold: wealth "reaching the niṣāb at which zakāt is due," i.e. rising to that amount (Ibn Fāris names it as the amount at which zakāt becomes obligatory).

10. Grammatical term: Arabic grammarians call the fatḥa vowel al-naṣb, as though the word stands upright in the mouth.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-ṣ-f as two sound roots: (1) the half of a thing, and (2) a kind of service and being put to use. Only the first is developed in this entry.

1. **Half.** نِصْف (niṣf) and نَصِيف (naṣīf) both mean the half of something. He cites the ḥadīth «مَا بَلَغَ مُدَّ أَحَدِهِمْ وَلَا نَصِيفَهُ» ("it did not reach the mudd of one of them, nor half of it"), and notes the morphological parallel: niṣf/naṣīf pattern together like ثُمْن/ثَمِين. A verse of poetry: "No mudd fed her, nor half a mudd, nor little dates, nor going hungry."

2. **Half-full.** إِنَاءٌ نَصْفَانُ (ināʾ naṣfān) — a vessel whose water has reached its halfway mark.

3. **Middle-aged (of a woman).** النَّصَف (al-naṣaf) is the woman between old and young — one who has reached the half of her lifespan.

4. **Fair dealing.** الإنصاف (inṣāf) in dealings with others — as though it were being content with [just] the half. النِّصْف (al-niṣf) likewise carries this sense of equitable dealing.

5. **Reaching the midpoint (verb).** نَصَفَ النَّهَارُ / يَنْصُفُ — the day reached its middle (equivalent to انتصف). Shāhid: "The day reached its midpoint, the water covering him, while his companion, out of sight, does not know."

6. **Reaching halfway up something.** نَصَفَ الْإِزَارُ سَاقَهُ (yanṣufuhā) — the waist-wrapper came halfway up his shank. Shāhid: "You see his sword — its tip does not reach halfway up the shank; indeed not, even if its carrying-straps are long."

Method: Ibn Fāris derives every sense from the single core notion of "half" — halved quantity, half-filled vessel, half a lifetime, half the day, half a limb's height — and explains the ethical sense (fairness) as accepting one's half rather than more.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَصَرَ 59x "will be helped"; نَصِير 35x "any helper"; نَصْر 22x "with his help"; نَصْرَانِيّ 15x "and the christians"; نَاصِر 11x "helpers"; ٱنتَصَرَ 7x "you will (be able to) defend yourselves"; مُّنتَصِر 4x "(he) supported"; ٱسْتَنصَرَ 2x "sought his help"; مَنصُور 2x "helped"; تَنَاصَرُ 1x "you help one another"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-ṣ-r as a single sound root whose core meaning is bringing good and bestowing it. From this he draws the following senses:

1. Granting victory / triumph. "God nasara the Muslims" = He gave them triumph (ẓafar) over their enemy (imperfect yanṣuru, verbal noun naṣr).

2. Taking retribution / avenging oneself — the form intaṣara, which he treats as belonging to the same root.

3. Coming to / arriving at a place. The Arabs say "I nasartu such-and-such a land" meaning "I came to it." Shāhid: a verse advising, when the sacred month begins, to leave the lands of Tamīm and "come to" (wa-nṣurī) the land of ʿĀmir.

4. Rain, by extension of sense 3: rain is called naṣr; "the land was nusirat" means it was given rain, and such land is manṣūra ("rained upon").

5. Giving / a gift (ʿaṭāʾ). Shāhid (rajaz): "…I am one who says: O Naṣr, a gift, a gift!"

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text: Root n-s-t (نصت), from Ibn Faris's Maqayis al-Lugha. A short entry with a single core meaning: silence. The idea behind this root is falling silent. Anṣata (Form IV) means to fall silent specifically in order to listen to speech. Naṣata / yanṣitu (Form I, past and present tense) carries the same basic sense of being or becoming silent. Ibn Faris notes the word's occurrence in the Qur'an, wa-anṣitu (and be silent, attend silently), as an example of this root's use in scripture, without further commentary on it. No other senses, morphological notes, or citations are given in this entry.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-ṣ-w/y (nūn, ṣād and a weak letter that is, he notes, mostly wāw) as a sound root whose meaning he gives as selection, eminence in a thing, and elevation.

1. **The choice part.** al-naṣiyya of a people, or of anything, is its choicest part. intaṣaytu al-shayʾ means "I picked the thing out", and "this is my naṣiyya" means "this is my choice".

2. **The forelock.** al-nāṣiya, the forelock, belongs here, according to Ibn Fāris, because the hair grows from a high place. al-nāṣiya is also defined as the hairline.

3. **Verbs made from the forelock.** naṣawtu someone: I seized him by the forelock. nāṣaytuhu: we each seized the other by the forelock. By comparison, one desert is said to tunāṣī another when it joins onto it, as if holding it by the forelock; Ibn Fāris marks this use as a figure of comparison.

4. **Long hair.** intaṣā al-shaʿr: the hair grew long.

5. **A saying of ʿĀʾisha.** "Why do you tanṣūn your dead?" Ibn Fāris explains that she meant stretching out the dead person's forelock, and takes it that she disliked combing a dead person's head.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَّطِيحَة 1x "and that which is gored by horns"
text:
Root n-t-h (nataha) -- Ibn Faris, Maqayis al-Lugha

Ibn Faris treats this root as built on one basic idea: to butt (nataha) -- as when a ram butts with its horns (nataha al-kabshu yantihu, "the ram butts").

Senses recorded:

1. Core meaning: butting/goring. Said of a ram: yantihu, "it butts."

2. Extended to a wild animal: one that comes straight at you, facing you head-on, is called natih ("a butter," one that confronts you). Such an animal was regarded as a bad omen, and for that reason an ill-fated person could likewise be called natih.

3. Applied to a horse: natih also describes a horse with white markings on both sides (temples) of its head.

4. Figurative use for hardship: nawatih al-dahr, "the butting-blows of time," means the hardships of fate; asabahu natih, "a natih struck him," means a severe misfortune befell him. Ibn Faris notes both follow the same analogical pattern as the core sense.

5. Astronomical use: the twin stars called al-Sharatan are also named using this root (al-natih forms).

6. Proverbial idiom: "the night is dark and the rams are butting each other" -- used figuratively for warriors clashing in battle, heroes fighting one another.

7. The related verb tanataha ("to butt against one another") is extended to waves, floodwaters, and men clashing together in war.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris traces the root N-Ṭ-F (نطف) to two base meanings: (1) a kind of jewellery, and (2) moisture and wetness, which then gets extended figuratively.

1. Jewellery sense — النَّطَف (al-naṭaf): said to mean pearl, with the singular نَطَفَة (naṭafa) being a single pearl. An alternative view holds that it means ear-rings or pendants.

2. Moisture sense — النُّطْفَة (al-nuṭfa): clear, pure water. Related forms: a night called نَطُوف (naṭūf) is one that rained until morning, and النِّطَاف (al-niṭāf) means sweat.

3. Figurative extension of the moisture sense: النَّطَف (al-naṭaf) can mean being smeared or besmirched. This use is almost always negative — applied to something ugly or to a fault. Hence نَطِفٌ (naṭif) means defective or blemished, and نَطِفَ الشَّيْءُ (naṭifa al-shayʾ) means the thing became corrupted or spoiled.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَنطِقُ 9x "speak"; أَنطَقَ 2x "allah made us speak"; مَنطِق 1x "(the) language"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives نطق (n-ṭ-q) from two sound roots.

1. Speech or something like it. The noun is al-manṭiq (articulate speech); the verb naṭaqa / yanṭiqu / nuṭqan ("to speak"). This can also cover utterance we do not ourselves understand — as in the Qurʾān's account of Sulaymān: "We have been taught the speech (manṭiq) of the birds" (al-Naml 16).

2. A kind of garment — al-niṭāq, a waist-wrapper with a drawstring. Related forms all cluster around the waist:
- al-nāṭiqa: the flank/waist, so named because it is where the girdle sits.
- munaṭṭaqa: a ewe marked with red at the waist (girdle-line).
- Dhāt al-Niṭāq: a hillock (a place-name).
- al-minṭaq: anything you tie your waist with; al-minṭaqa: a specific named belt.
- The phrase jāʾa muntaṭiqan farasahu ("he came leading his horse at his side") — keeping the horse alongside, unridden, as if at one's girdle.

Ibn Fāris notes a disputed verse ("...against the enemies muntaṭiqan mujīdan"): some read muntaṭiq under sense 2 (a man who keeps a noble horse led at his side), others under sense 1 (a man who speaks, uttering praise of his people).

He closes with a proverb belonging to sense 2: "Whoever's father has a long train girds himself with it" — i.e. a man with many brothers (his father's many sons) is supported by them.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَّظَرَ 87x "see"; يُنظَرُ 12x "give me respite"; يَنتَظِرُ 8x "and wait"; مُنتَظِرُون 6x "the ones who wait"; مُنظَرُون 6x "given respite"; نَٰظِرِين 5x "for the observers"; نَاظِرَة 2x "and see"; نَظِرَة 1x "then postponement"; نَظْرَة 1x "a glance"; نَظَر 1x "a look"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-ẓ-r as a single sound root, all of whose branches trace back to one core sense: to contemplate and behold a thing. From that base the root is then extended metaphorically.

1. Literal sense — to look at, behold: نَظَرْتُ إِلَى الشَّيْءِ ("I looked at the thing") = you beheld it. Related: حَيٌّ حِلَالٌ نَظَرٌ, of neighbouring people who dwell close and look upon one another.

2. To wait for: نَظَرْتُهُ means "I waited for him" (= انْتَظَرْتُهُ). Ibn Fāris ties this to the core sense — the one waiting is as if looking toward the moment of arrival. He cites a line of verse: "if you two wait for me a single night… it will profit me at Umm Jundab's."

3. Figurative extensions of "looking":
 - نَظَرَتِ الْأَرْضُ ("the land looked") = it put forth / displayed its vegetation; also نَظَرَتْ بِعَيْنٍ ("it looked with an eye").
 - نَظَرَ الدَّهْرُ إِلَى بَنِي فُلَانٍ فَأَهْلَكَهُمْ ("time looked upon so-and-so's people and destroyed them").

4. نَظِير (counterpart): هَذَا نَظِيرُ هَذَا ("this is the counterpart of this") derives from the same idea — when a thing and its like are set side by side and looked at, the two prove equal.

5. نَظْرَة as pallor: بِهِ نَظْرَةٌ means he has a wan, faded look — as though he were something that had been looked at until its colour drained away.

Ibn Fāris closes with the formula "and God knows best."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَبَذَ 10x "and we threw them"; ٱنتَبَذَتْ 2x "and she withdrew"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ن-ب-ذ as a single sound root whose core meaning is throwing or casting away.

1. Base verb: نَبَذَ (nabadha), imperfect anbidhu, verbal noun nabdh — to throw something, to cast it from one's hand.

2. النَّبِيذ (nabīdh): dates put ("thrown") into a vessel with water poured over them (a steeped date-drink), from the same act of casting in.

3. الصَّبِيُّ الْمَنْبُوذ (manbūdh): a "cast-off" child — one abandoned by its mother.

4. Extended sense of a small amount: a nabdh of property means a scant, trifling quantity; a nabdh of grey hair on the head means just a little — as though it were so slight it had been tossed aside. The same word is used of a light sprinkling of rain.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَّبِىّ 75x "the prophets"; نَبَّأَ 46x "then he will inform you"; نَبَأ 29x "(the) news"; نُّبُوَّة 5x "and the prophethood"; أَنبَأَ 4x "he had informed them"; يَسْتَنبِـُ 1x "and they ask you to inform"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the whole root n-b-ʾ from a single core idea: "coming from one place to another."

1. Movement / arrival. نَابِئ (nābiʾ) is one who comes across from one land to another. It is used of a torrent (سَيْل نَابِئ) that has flowed from one town to the next, and of a man likewise. A cited verse speaks of a "disheveled incomer" whom the fates brought "from where we know not."

2. Report / news. النَّبَأ (al-nabaʾ, "report, tiding") flows from the same idea, because a piece of news travels from one place to another. The one who conveys it is المُنْبِئ (the informer), and the verbs أَنْبَأَ / نَبَّأَ mean "to inform, announce."

3. A missed shot. "The archer shot and anbaʾa" describes an arrow that failed to tear or pierce — as if it swerved off the graze and landed elsewhere (again, moving from its place).

4. Sound. النَّبْأَة (al-nabʾa) is a sound or voice, fitting the same principle since sound carries from one place to another. A line of Dhū al-Rumma pictures a keen-eared creature catching a faint stir by such a sound.

5. The word نَبِيّ. Those who pronounce it with a hamza (nabīʾ) do so on the grounds that a prophet أَنْبَأَ — "gave tidings" — from God. Ibn Fāris closes with "God knows best what is correct."

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: ʿAntara (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse; Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam) ×2; al-Shammākh, al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); Durayd b. al-Ṣimma (pre-Islamic); Kuthayyir (Umayyad); al-Marrār (pre-Islamic)
text:
Root n-b-ʿ (نبع) — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr

1. Core verb — to gush/spring forth. نَبَعَ الماء (water نَبَعَ, or نبِعَ, or نَبْعَ — variants recorded from al-Laḥyānī), imperfect ينبِعُ/ينبَعُ/ينبُعُ, maṣdar نَبْعاً/نُبُوعاً: to burst open/gush, i.e. "it came out from the spring." This is why a spring is called يَنْبُوع (yanbūʿ, "spring/wellspring") — al-Azharī explains it as a يَفْعُول-pattern noun from the same verb, plural يَنابِيع. He notes a real spring of this name (يَنْبُع) in the Ḥijāz, between Mecca and Medina, which irrigated palm groves belonging to the family of ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib.

2. يَنْباعُ — a grammatical digression. A line of ʿAntara uses the form يَنْباعُ; the grammarians explain this as يَنْبَعُ with the vowel after the bāʾ lengthened into an extra alif for metrical necessity. A long technical discussion follows on whether, if used as a man's name, يَنْباعُ would be a declinable or non-declinable (diptote) noun — the majority view treats it as resembling the pattern يَنْفَعِلُ (like يَنْقاد, يَنْحاز) and therefore non-declinable, though the reasoning behind the resemblance is disputed. Al-Aṣmaʿī held that يَنْباعُ actually is of the pattern يَنْفَعِلُ, citing انْباعَ الشجاعُ يَنْباعُ انْبِياعاً, "the brave man surged forward from the battle line," with a supporting verse.

3. Spring/gushing-place. يَنْبُوعُه = "the place it is made to gush from"; اليَنْبُوعُ = a rivulet or spring abundant in water, plural ينابيع. Cited here is the Qur'anic phrase "حتى تَفْجُرَ لنا من الأَرض يَنْبُوعاً" — "until you make a spring gush forth for us from the earth" (cf. Q. 17:90) — plus a line of Abū Dhuʾayb using يَتَنَبَّعُ for a fate that "wells up"/draws near.

4. النَّبْعُ — the tree and its wood. A mountain tree (al-Azharī: used to make bows). A ḥadīth mentions it as a tree that used to grow very tall, until the Prophet ﷺ said of it, "God not lengthen you further, O wood" — after which, it is said, it stopped growing tall. Verses (al-Shammākh, al-Aʿshā) describe bow-staves cut from it and use it proverbially: nabʿ-wood was reputed to strike little or no fire, so "even he could strike fire from nabʿ-wood" became a compliment for a person of exceptional skill or sound judgment. Abū Ḥanīfa describes it further: yellow, dense, heavy wood that reddens with age; the finest of all bows because it uniquely combines firmness and suppleness; arrows were also cut from its branches (verse of Durayd b. al-Ṣimma). Al-Mubarrid adds: النبع, الشريان, and الشوحط are actually the same species of tree — the name changes only with where it grows (mountain-top, slope, or lowland respectively) — and repeats the "no fire in nabʿ" proverb, glossed as praise for good judgment.

5. النَّبَّاعة (1) — the soft spot on a baby's skull before it hardens (after which it is called اليافوخ).

6. Place names. يَنْبُع — a place between Mecca and Medina (cited in a verse of Kuthayyir). نُبايِعُ — a place, mountain, or valley in Hudhayl's territory (cited from Abū Dhuʾayb), plural نُبايِعات, with variant forms and spellings discussed at length by later grammarians (Ibn Barrī, Kurāʿ, Abū Bakr ibn al-Anbārī, Ibn Jinnī) — including a technical dispute over whether the pattern نُفاعِل/يَفاعِل was recognized by Sībawayh. The substance of this is philological classification of place-name morphology, not meaning.

7. نَوابِعُ البعير — the spots on a camel's body from which its sweat runs. Ibn Barrī adds that النَّبِيع itself can simply mean "sweat," with a supporting verse from al-Marrār.

8. انْباعَ — "to burst out" (speaking). Al-Jawharī, from al-Aṣmaʿī: "so-and-so انْباعَ at us with speech," meaning انْبَعَثَ, "burst out." Proverb: "مُخْرَنْبِقٌ ليَنْباعَ" — "silent [now], so as to burst forth [later]," paired with "مُطْرِقٌ ليَنْثالَ." Ibn Barrī notes that, strictly, this انباع belongs to a different root (ب-و-ع, from باعَ الفرسُ "the horse stretched out its stride"), and is cross-referenced there rather than truly belonging under n-b-ʿ.

9. النَّبَّاعة (2) — a separate, coarser sense: the buttocks/anus. Idiom: "كَذَبَتْ نَبّاعَتُك" ("your nabbāʿa lied"), said of someone who lets out a loud fart; also spelled with غ (نَبّاغة).

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
poets_named: Dhū al-Rummah (Umayyad); Kaʿb al-Ghanawī (lived into Islam)
text:
Root ن ب ط (n-b-ṭ), al-Zamakhsharī, Asās al-Balāgha

Literal senses
1. huwa min al-nabaṭ/al-nabīṭ/al-anbāṭ — descended from the Nabataeans (nabaṭiyy/nabāṭiyy/anbāṭiyy); illustrated with an anecdote about Khālid ibn al-Walīd asking ʿAbd al-Masīḥ ibn Buqaylah whether his people are Arabs or Nabataeans, and receiving the reply, "Arabs who became settled/agrarian, and Nabataeans who became Arabized" — a wordplay connecting the tribal name Nabaṭ to the root's core sense of "drawing/extracting [water]." A further citation (Abū al-ʿAlāʾ al-Maʿarrī) plays on the same pun, and mentions al-kamāy (truffle-derived resin) used by Nabataeans as a wound-plaster.
2. "kayfa nabṭu biʾrikum" — "how is your well's nabṭ," meaning its drawn-out water; nabaṭa al-māʾu min al-biʾr — water was drawn from a well (causatives anbaṭahu/istanbaṭahu). faras anbaṭ — a white-bellied horse, illustrated with a line of poetry by Dhū al-Rummah.

Figurative senses (majāz)
3. "fulānun lā yanālu nabṭahu" — "none can reach his nabṭ [his depths]," said of a mighty, inaccessible man, illustrated with a line of poetry by Kaʿb al-Ghanawī. A threatening idiom: "I will empty your quiver and draw out your nabṭ [your hidden secret]."
4. istanbaṭa maʿnan ḥasanan / raʾyan ṣāʾiban — to deduce/draw forth a fine meaning or sound opinion (the origin of the modern sense "to deduce, infer"), attributed to one's learning from those capable of such extraction; istanbaṭtu min fulānin khabaran — to draw a piece of news out of someone — the entry's closing example, extending "drawing water from a well" to "drawing information/insight from a person."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَنبَتَ 16x "then we caused to grow"; نَبَات 9x "vegetation"; تَنبُتُ 1x "(which) produces"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-b-t as a single root meaning growth in something planted or cultivated, which is then extended metaphorically.

1. Core sense — plant-growth: النَّبْت (nabt) is the familiar word for vegetation; the verb نَبَتَ means "it grew/sprouted." أَنْبَتَتِ الْأَرْضُ means the land brought forth growth. نَبَّتُّ الشَّجَرَ means "I planted the tree" (i.e., set it in the ground).

2. Metaphorical extension to human "growth": إِنَّ فِي بَنِي فُلَانٍ لَنَابِتَةَ شَرٍّ — "among so-and-so's people there is an outgrowth of evil." نَبَتَتْ لِبَنِي فُلَانٍ نَابِتَةٌ — "a new growth has sprung up for them," said when a fresh generation of small children has come up.

3. Related forms and usages: النَّبِيت (al-Nabīt) is a tribe of Yemen. مَا أَحْسَنَ نِبْتَةَ هَذَا الشَّجَرِ — "how fine the growth-form (nibta) of this tree is." هُوَ فِي مَنْبِتِ صِدْقٍ — "he is of noble stock," literally "of a true growing-place (manbit)."

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
Root: n-b-z (نبز) — from Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr, d. 1311 CE)

1. Core noun. al-nabaz (fatḥa) = "a nickname/epithet"; plural al-anbāz. With sukūn, al-nabz is the verbal noun of the same idea ("the act of nicknaming").

2. Verb. nabazahu yanbizuhu nabzan = "he gave him a nickname" (laqqabahu). [The dictionary's own footnote adds a grammatical note on the verb's conjugation pattern, and separately notes that al-nibz — a different vowel pattern of the same letters — is used elsewhere for "a person base in lineage and character."]

3. Related/variant form. The noun al-nabaz is paired with al-nazab, its letters transposed — apparently treated as a doublet of the same meaning.

4. Intensive form. yunabbizu (doubled middle radical) = "he nicknames [people] repeatedly/habitually," e.g. of someone who keeps giving nicknames to boys.

5. Reciprocal form. tanābazū bi-l-alqāb = "they nicknamed one another." al-tanābuz = calling one another out by nicknames — and Ibn Manẓūr notes this word is mostly used where the nicknames are insulting.

6. Ḥadīth citation. A man was nicknamed (yunbazu) "Qurqūr" (a type of ship) — cited simply as an example of the usage.

7. Qur'anic citation and exegesis (Q49:11): "And do not tanābazū one another with nicknames," followed by "wretched is the name of transgression after faith."
   - Thaʿlab's view: this addressed Muslims calling converts "O Jew!" or "O Christian!" after their conversion — though Ibn Manẓūr records Thaʿlab himself calling this explanation weak ("this is nothing").
   - Al-Zajjāj's view: the verse means a Muslim must not taunt a former Jew or Christian, now Muslim, with a nickname recalling his former religion; the follow-on phrase ("wretched is the name of transgression after faith") reinforces that calling him "O Jew!" after he has believed is a bad practice. Al-Zajjāj adds that the ruling may extend more broadly to any nickname a person dislikes, since a believer is obliged to address his brother by the name he loves best.

8. Al-Khalīl's classification of names. Names are of two types: "nabaz-names" — personal names like Zayd or ʿAmr — versus "general names" — common nouns like "horse" or "man."

9. Near-synonym. al-nabz is likened to al-lamz (fault-finding, defaming).

10. Unrelated homograph. al-nibz (kasra) also denotes the husks/peelings of al-jidām, i.e. palm-frond stalks (al-saʿaf) — noted as a separate sense sharing the same root letters.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-d-d as a sound root whose sense is running off and parting.

1. **Bolting.** nadda al-baʿīr: the camel bolted, going off headlong and straying. The verbal nouns are nadd and nudūd.

2. **An opponent.** From the same root come al-nidd and al-nadīd, the one who takes the opposing side in a matter (yunāddu): someone who puts forward an opinion other than his companion's. A verse shows the word: "lest al-Sandarī be my rival (nadīdatī), and I revile uncles, whole throngs of them."

3. **A high hill.** According to Ibn Durayd, al-nadd is a hill rising high into the sky. Ibn Fāris remarks that this would be close to the root's regular pattern of meaning (qiyās).

4. **A perfume.** al-nidd as the name of a perfume is, Ibn Fāris says, not an Arabic word.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
**Root ن د م (n-d-m) — al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī**

1. **Core sense.** *Nadm* and *nadāma* mean regret: the grieving distress a person feels when his view of something changes after the matter is already past and cannot be undone. Al-Rāghib's definition thus ties regret to two elements — a reversal of judgement, and an event beyond recall.

2. **Qur'anic evidence.** He cites two passages, both using the participle *nādimīn* with the verb *aṣbaḥa* ("came to be"): al-Māʾida 5:31, "so he became one of the regretful," and al-Muʾminūn 23:40, "in a little while they will surely become regretful."

3. **Derivation.** He derives the sense from *munādama* — the relation of a drinking- or boon-companion — the image being that grief "keeps company" with the person who regrets.

4. **Related forms.** *Nadīm*, *nadmān* and *munādim*, all denoting a companion (especially a drinking-companion), are close in meaning to one another.

5. **A reported alternative derivation.** Some, he notes, connect *mundāma* with *mudāwama* (constancy, persistent keeping-together) — i.e. the companion is the one who stays constantly alongside.

6. **A second reported explanation.** Others held that two drinking-partners are called *nadīmān* ("two boon-companions") precisely because of what follows their sessions: the regret each comes to feel over what they did.

Al-Rāghib reports points 5 and 6 as the views of unnamed others, without adjudicating between them.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: نَادَىٰ 44x "he called"; نِدَاء 2x "a call"; نَادِي 2x "his associates"; مُنَادِي 1x "a caller"; نَدِيّ 1x "(in) assembly"; تَّنَاد 1x "(of) calling"; مُنَاد 1x "the caller"; تَنَادَ 1x "and they called one another"
text:
Al-Rāghib treats n-d-w starting from al-nidāʾ, "calling", which he traces back to al-nadā, "moisture".

1. **al-nidāʾ as raised voice.** Nidāʾ is raising the voice so that it becomes manifest.
   - It can mean bare sound without meaning: in "one who shouts to what hears nothing but a call and a cry (nidāʾ)" (Q 2:171), the hearer grasps only the sound, not the meaning that composed speech carries.
   - It can also mean meaningful speech: "when your Lord called Moses" (Q 26:10).

2. **Calling to prayer.** "When you call to the prayer" (Q 5:58) means "when you summon"; likewise "when the call is made to the prayer on the day of gathering" (Q 62:9). Al-Rāghib notes that in the Law the call to prayer is restricted to its well-known wording.

3. **Calling and distance.** "Those are called from a far place" (Q 41:44): using nidāʾ of them signals their remoteness from the truth. He sets beside this "the day the caller calls from a near place" (Q 50:41), "We called him from the right side of the Mount" (Q 19:52) and "when he came to it, he was called" (Q 27:8).

4. **The hidden call.** In "when he called to his Lord a hidden calling" (Q 19:3), the word nidāʾ is used because he pictured himself as far from God through his sins and bad states, as one who fears His punishment does.

5. **The caller to faith.** In "we have heard a caller calling to faith" (Q 3:193), the caller stands for the intellect, the revealed Book, the Messenger, and all the signs showing that faith in God is obligatory. They are called a "caller" because they are as manifest as a call and urge people on as a caller does.

6. **Origin in moisture (al-nadā).** Nidāʾ comes from nadā, moisture. A "nadiyy voice" is a high voice. The voice is called nidāʾ because someone with a moist mouth speaks well, and so the eloquent are described as having plenty of saliva. Nadā has the plurals andāʾ and andiya. Trees are called nadā because they come from it: the effect is named after its cause.

7. **Appearing.** A poet says of the vine that it "called out from the kāfūr", meaning it appeared as a caller's voice appears.

8. **Assembly.** Sitting together came to be called nidāʾ, so a place of assembly is al-nādī, al-muntadā or al-nadiyy, and the words are also used for the people one sits with: "then let him call his assembly (nādiyahu)" (Q 96:17). Dār al-Nadwa in Mecca, the place where they used to gather, is named from this.

9. **Generosity.** Nadā also means generosity: "so-and-so is moister of hand than so-and-so" means more generous; "he is moist toward his companions" means he is generous to them; "I was not moistened by anything from him" means he gave me nothing.

10. **mundiyāt al-kalim.** Shameful words that become known.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text: Ibn Faris (Maqayis al-Lugha) treats the root n-f-sh as a sound root whose core meaning is "spreading out / dispersal" (intishar). He gives three illustrations of this one idea. First, wool (nafsh al-suf): carding wool means beating it until it fluffs out and spreads apart. Second, a bird's wings: "the bird spread/ruffled its two wings" (nafasha al-ta'iru janahayhi). Third, camels (nafashat al-ibil): camels "scattering," meaning they wander back and forth and disperse at night without a shepherd watching them; he gives the verbal noun al-nafsh for this straying, and the plural forms nuffash and nawafish for camels in this untended, scattered state. All three senses - wool being beaten apart, a bird's wings opening out, and unshepherded camels straying loose - are presented as expressions of the same single root-idea of things spreading out or dispersing.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root n-f-dh - Ibn Faris, Maqayis al-Lugha

Core meaning Ibn Faris gives: passing all the way through something, or acting decisively and effectively in a matter.

1. He states this is a single, sound root whose meaning is "going/passing decisively through" - whether physically (piercing through an object) or figuratively (carrying an affair through to effect).

2. Physical sense (the arrow): "nafadha as-sahmu ar-ramiyyata" - the arrow passed clean through the game/target it was shot at. The verbal noun is nafadh ("penetration, passing-through"). Causative form: anfadhtuhu, "I made it pass through."

3. Figurative sense (a person): "huwa nafidh" - "he is nafidh" - is glossed by Ibn Faris as madin fi amrihi, "one who goes forward decisively in his affair," i.e. someone whose word or action is effective and carries through.

The entry is brief: a single core sense (decisive passing-through), illustrated with one physical shahid (the arrow) and one derived adjectival usage (nafidh, of a person).

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī defines the root نفع (n-f-ʿ) as follows:

Sense: al-nafʿ ("benefit") is that by which one attains good things (al-khayrāt). His reasoning: since anything that leads to good is itself good, benefit is therefore a species of good. Its opposite is al-ḍurr ("harm").

He supports this with a series of Qur'anic citations pairing benefit against harm or denying its possession: "they possess for themselves neither harm nor benefit" [25:3]; "I have no power over benefit or harm for myself" [7:188]; "Your kinship-ties will not benefit you, nor your children" [60:3]; "nor does intercession benefit" [34:23]; "nor will my counsel benefit you" [11:34]; noting that further verses beyond these could be added.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) gives the root ن ف ح (n-f-ḥ) one core sense: something surging or bursting forth, or being raised/lifted.

1. Scent: "the fragrance of perfume nafaḥat" — it spread out, burst forth. A nafḥah is a single waft or whiff of that scent.

2. Giving/generosity (an analogical extension of sense 1): "he nafaḥa with wealth" — he gave it out, as if releasing it from his hand in one release. A person who keeps giving is said to have continual nafaḥāt ("outpourings") of good/kindness.

3. Wind: nafaḥat al-rīḥ — the wind blew.

4. A bow described as nafūḥ is one that shoots the arrow far — it has a strong, far-reaching propulsion.

5. A riding animal that nafaḥat kicked out with its hoof and struck with it. By the same image, "he nafaḥahu with the sword" means he struck/reached him with it.

6. A she-camel called al-nafūḥ is one whose milk flows out of her teats by itself, without being milked — the milk "bursts forth" on its own.

All six senses trace back to the one idea: a sudden outward surge, release, or lift — whether of scent, wealth, wind, an arrow's flight, a kick/sword-strike, or milk.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-f-d as one sound root whose core idea is a thing being cut off and running out.

1. Basic sense — exhaustion. نَفِدَ / يَنْفَدُ, verbal noun نَفَاد: a thing is used up, runs out, comes to an end.

2. Fourth-form use of supplies. أَنْفَدُوا (anfadū): they exhausted their provisions — said of travellers whose stores are finished.

3. Third-form use in disputation. An opponent in an argument is a مُنَافِد (munāfid): two men contend, each trying to use up — exhaust — the other's argument (ḥujja). The disputation sense is thus derived from the core sense of running something out.

4. Citation. Ibn Fāris cites a ḥadīth, «إِنْ نَافَدْتَهُمْ نَافَدُوكَ», and glosses it: if you speak (contend) with them, they will speak (contend) back at you.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَنفَال 2x "the spoils of war"; نَافِلَة 2x "(in) addition"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-f-l as a single sound root whose core notion is a gift and the act of giving.

1. **نَافِلَة (nāfila)** — a gift made voluntarily, in a situation where it is not owed or required. Ibn Fāris adds, as an instance of this, نَافِلَةُ الصَّلَاة — the voluntary (non-obligatory) portion of ṣalāt.

2. **نَوْفَل (nawfal)** — a man who gives abundantly. He cites the line: "the munificent, open-handed man in him refuses wrongdoing."

3. **نَفَل (nafal), pl. أَنْفَال (anfāl)** — what is gained or taken as spoil. Ibn Fāris derives this from the same giving-sense: the one in command *grants* (yunaffilu) the fighters what they have gained. Hence the verb نَفَّلْتُكَ — "I gave you a nafal."

4. **Etymological note (letter-substitution).** The expression انْتَفَلَ مِنَ الشَّيْءِ, "he disavowed/disclaimed something," does not belong to the giving-sense: Ibn Fāris classes it under ibdāl (consonant substitution), with the lām standing in for an original yāʾ — i.e. it goes back to n-f-y (to deny, disown). His witness is al-Mutalammis: "Did you suppose me one who disavows the support of Buhtha? Indeed I am of them, wherever I may be."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَنفَقَ 68x "they spend"; مُنَٰفِقُون 27x "the hypocrites"; مُنَٰفِقَٰت 5x "and the hypocrite women"; نِفَاق 3x "and hypocrisy"; نَفَقَة 2x "any spending"; نَافَقُ 2x "(are) hypocrites"; مُنفِقِين 1x "and those who spend"; نَفَق 1x "a tunnel"; نَفَقَٰت 1x "their contributions"; إِنفَاق 1x "(of) spending"
text:
Ibn Fāris analyzes the root n-f-q (نفق) as two sound roots that, on close inspection, converge.

Sense 1 — passing away, expiring, being used up:
- نَفَقَتِ الدَّابَّةُ (nafaqat al-dābba): a beast died.
- نَفَقَ السِّعْرُ (nafaqa al-siʿr): a price/market moved briskly and did not stagnate; likewise أَنْفَقُوا means their market became active.
- نَفَقَة (nafaqa, expenditure) is named because it "goes forth on its way."
- نَفَقَ الشَّيْءُ: a thing ran out/came to an end (e.g. "the people's provision has run out").
- أَنْفَقَ الرَّجُلُ: a man became poor — what he had went away. Ibn al-Aʿrābī connects this to the Qur'anic phrase "then you would withhold for fear of spending" (khashyat al-infāq).
- فَرَسٌ نَفِقُ الْجَرْيِ: a horse whose gallop soon gives out.

Sense 2 — concealment and a hidden way out:
- نَفَق (nafaq): a tunnel or burrow with an outlet to another place.
- نَافِقَاء (nāfiqāʾ): the thin-crusted escape spot of a jerboa's burrow; attacked from the front entrance (qāṣiʿāʾ), the animal butts through the nāfiqāʾ and escapes (fa-ntafaqa, "it went out").
- From this Ibn Fāris derives نِفَاق (nifāq): the one so described conceals the opposite of what he shows — as if faith (īmān) slips out of him, or he slips out of faith in secret. (This creedal application is Ibn Fāris's own derivation, given as etymology.)

Unifying note: Ibn Fāris suggests the whole root may reduce to a single idea — going out (khurūj); a nafaq is precisely a through-passage one can exit by.

Loanword note: نَيْفَق (nayfaq), the gusset of trousers, is reported by Abū Bakr to be an arabicized Persian word.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَفَرَ 8x "go forth"; نُفُور 5x "(in) aversion"; نَفَر 3x "(in) men"; نَفِير 1x "numerous"; مُّسْتَنفِرَة 1x "frightened"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ن-ف-ر (n-f-r) from a single core idea: shying away, recoiling, and moving apart.

1. Bolting / shying. نَفَرَ (nafara), verbal noun نِفَار (nifār): an animal (or anything else) shies and bolts — recoils and withdraws from its place and resting-spot.

2. Swelling. نَفَرَ جِلْدُهُ ("his skin nafara") = it swelled. Cited from a ḥadīth: a man picked his teeth with a reed and his mouth "nafara," i.e. swelled. Abū ʿUbayd explains this as still the core sense — the skin "recoils" away from the flesh because of an ailment that arises between them.

3. يَوْمُ النَّفْرِ ("the day of nafr"): the day people depart/withdraw from Minā.

4. Idiom: لَقِيتُهُ قَبْلَ صَيْحٍ وَنَفْرٍ ("I met him before any cry or bolting") = very early, before anyone cries out or stirs.

5. المُنَافَرَة (munāfara): taking a dispute before a judge for adjudication between two parties. The point sought is to rank one nafar (man/group) above another; أَنْفَرْتُ أَحَدَهُمَا = I ruled for one over the other.

6. النَّفَر (nafar): a band/company of men — also from the same core, because they "rally forth" (yanfirūn) to give aid. النَّفِير (nafīr), النَّفْر (nafr), and النَّفْرَة (nafra) all carry this same underlying sense. Shāhid (via al-Farrāʾ) for nafra: "She greeted you, then said: 'Our band today, O ʿUrwa, are all preoccupied.'"

7. نَفَّرْتُ عَنِ الصَّبِيِّ ("I naffartu about the boy") = I gave the child a nickname (laqab) — understood as "scaring off" the jinn and the evil eye from him. A bedouin reports that at his birth his father was told, "Ward off (naffir) from your son!", so his father named him Qunfudh ("hedgehog") with the kunya Abū al-ʿAddāʾ.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَفْس 295x "themselves"; تَنَفَّسَ 1x "it breathes"; يَتَنَافَسِ 1x "let aspire"; مُتَنَٰفِسُون 1x "the aspirers"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives all of n-f-s from a single core idea: the going-out of breath or breeze (however it occurs, from wind or anything else). Every branch of the root traces back to this.

1. Breath and relief. تَنَفُّس (tanaffus) is breathing — breath leaving the body's inner cavity. Because exhaling brings رَوْح (relief) and rest, نَفَّسَ means to relieve distress ("God relieved his distress"), and نَفَس (nafas) comes to mean anything that eases a person in distress. Ibn Fāris cites two ḥadīths for this sense: "Do not curse the wind, for it is from the nafas of the Merciful" (a relief breathed onto the distressed), and, of the Anṣār, "I find the nafas of your Lord from the direction of Yemen" (relief coming through them to believers persecuted at Mecca).

2. The (evil) eye. نَفَس can denote the eye; one says "a nafs struck him."

3. Blood. نَفْس also means blood — soundly so, he argues, since losing one's blood is losing one's nafs (life). Related: a woman in childbirth-bleeding is نُفَسَاء (nufasāʾ), and نِفَاس (nifās) is childbirth; being born is expressed with يُنْفَس (yunfas), and a newborn is مَنْفُوس (manfūs). نِفَاس is also the plural of nufasāʾ.

4. A draught (of water). One sips "a nafas or two" from a vessel, and water is said to have a nafas — a transferred usage, since life (nafs) is sustained by water just as it is sustained by breath (nafas). A verse is quoted of camels passing the night at "a draught of the sweet water of Māwiyya."

5. Metaphorical extensions. تَنَفَّسَتِ الْقَوْسُ — "the bow breathed," i.e. cracked. A prized thing is نَفِيس (nafīs): it has نَفْس (worth/consequence) and is competed for; hence تَنَافُس (rivalry), where each contender brings out the strength of his nafs.

6. Tanning. Calling a small measure of tanning agent a نَفَس fits the pattern: the little needed to tan a hide once is likened, in its smallness, to a single breath. Ibn Fāris concludes that the root's analogy is uniform across all these senses.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text: Ibn Faris treats n-f-th as one root meaning: something coming out of a mouth or opening with the faintest sound or puff of breath. He gives four illustrations. First, a charm-reciter blows out his spittle while reciting, a lighter action than ordinary spitting. Second, a sorceress blows out poison. Third, a proverb holds that a person with an afflicted chest must expel breath, i.e. cough or breathe it out. Fourth, a saying about refusing to give someone even the leftover bits stuck in one's teeth after chewing a tooth-stick (nufatha), illustrating extreme stinginess. He closes by noting that blood a wound expels and brings to the surface is called nafith. The common thread across all four is a mild, breath-carried expulsion of something from an opening.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-f-kh (نفخ) as a single sound root whose core meaning is swelling/inflation combined with rising or elevation.

1. Basic sense — to swell up: انْتَفَخَ الشَّيْءُ (the thing swelled), verbal noun intifāḫ.

2. Extended to "rising high": انْتَفَخَ النَّهَارُ (the day "swelled") means the day rose high, i.e. climbed toward its peak.

3. Seasonal usage: نَفْخَةُ الرَّبِيعِ ("the swelling of spring") = spring's putting forth of greenery, so called because the earth rises and swells up in springtime.

4. Applied to a person: الْمَنْفُوخُ ("the puffed-up one") = a fat man.

5. Of terrain: النَّفْخَاءُ (a swollen/raised patch of ground) is equivalent to النَّبْخَاءُ, which he says he has already covered under its own root.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-f-y as a small root (uṣayl) that means stripping one thing away from another and putting it at a distance.

1. **Driving away.** nafaytu al-shayʾa anfīhi nafyan: I drove the thing away; intafā: it was driven away. al-nufāya is the worthless part that gets thrown out.

2. **What is thrown off (nafiyy).** nafiyy al-rīḥ is the dust the wind drives along until it gathers at the foot of walls. nafiyy al-maṭar is rain the wind drives off or sprays. nafiyy al-māʾ is the water that flies off the well-rope onto the back of the man filling the bucket inside the well; a verse speaks of the spray on "those wells".

3. **The form with hamza.** It has one word only: al-nufaʾ (singular nufaʾa), scattered patches of pasture apart from its main body. A verse tells of night clouds that rained generously and of patches of al-ṣafrāʾ and al-zubbād that reinforced the growth.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris gives the core sense of n-gh-ḍ as "shaking, setting in motion." Six attested uses branch from it:

1. **al-naghaḍān** — the looseness/wobbling of the teeth (teeth that shake in the gum).

2. **al-ingāḍ** — a person shaking his head at someone, as a gesture of astonishment. Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 17:51, {فَسَيُنْغِضُونَ إِلَيْكَ رُءُوسَهُمْ}, "then they will shake their heads at you," as the Qur'anic instance of this verb form.

3. **al-naghḍ** — the male ostrich, named for the unsteady bobbing of its head as it walks. An unnamed authority is quoted comparing it to "the mangy, tar-smeared [camel]" (al-ajrab al-mudajjal) — the entry gives this comparison without further explanation of context or source.

4. **al-nāghiḍ / al-nughḍ** — the cartilage of the shoulder, named for its mobility; the same term is also applied to the cartilage of the ear.

5. **al-naghūḍ** — a she-camel with a very large hump, the reasoning being that a hump grown large wobbles as she moves.

6. **naghaḍa al-ghaym** — said of a cloud: "it moved, travelled."

All six senses trace back to the single idea of shaking or unsteady motion.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris, in Maqayis al-Lugha, holds that the root n-h-j carries two separate, unrelated core meanings.

1. Road / path -- and by extension, clarity or method.
- al-nahj = "the road, the path."
- "nahaja li al-amr" = he made the matter plain/clear to me (laid it out like an open path).
- "huwa mustaqim al-minhaj" = he/it is straight-pathed -- i.e., follows a straight method.
- al-manhaj = also "road, path"; plural al-manahij.

2. Being cut off / short of breath.
- "fulanun yanhaju" = so-and-so comes gasping, breathless, his breath cut short.
- "darabtuhu hatta unhija" = I struck him until he collapsed/fell.
- Extended from this: a garment said to have "nahaja" or "anhaja" has become worn thin -- though not yet actually torn -- as if worn through; "anhajahu l-bala" = wear/age wore it threadbare.

A closing note: the grammarian Abu Ubayd is cited as saying one does not say "nahaja" in that garment sense -- i.e., he disputes that particular wording as correct usage.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَهَار 57x "and the day"; نَهَر 54x "the rivers"; تَنْهَرْ 2x "repel"
poets_named: Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam); unnamed verse
text:
Ibn Fāris analyzes the root نهر (n-h-r) as a single sound root whose core idea is the opening-up or splitting-open of something.

1. Opening/making flow: أَنْهَرْتُ الدَّمَ means "I opened the blood and let it run."

2. River (نَهْر): named from this root because a watercourse "cleaves" the earth — it splits the ground open. Its plurals are أنهار (anhār) and نُهُر (nuhur).

3. Related derivatives:
   - المَنْهَرَة (manhara): an open clearing between a community's houses where they dump their refuse.
   - اسْتَنْهَرَ النَّهْرُ: the river settled into / took its channel.
   - أَنْهَرَ الماءُ: the water flowed.
   - نَهْرٌ نَهِرٌ (nahir): a stream abounding in water — cited from a verse by Abū Dhuʾayb describing a tent pitched by reeds and a sweet, water-rich stream.

4. Daytime (نَهار): Ibn Fāris traces this to the same root — daytime is "the opening-up of darkness into light," the span from daybreak to sunset. He notes it is said to take the plural نُهُر (nuhur). From it also رَجُلٌ نَهِرٌ (nahir), "a daytime man," one who does not stir by night — supported by a line: "I am no night-man; rather I am a day-man."

5. A rejected sense: he records that some claim نَهار also means the chick of a certain bird, but dismisses it as not worth considering and as carrying no real meaning.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: نَهَىٰ 32x "and forbid"; ٱنتَهَىٰ 16x "you desist"; مُنتَهَىٰ 3x "(of) the utmost boundary"; نُّهَىٰ 2x "(of) intelligence"; يَتَنَاهَ 1x "forbidding each other"; مُّنتَهُون 1x "(be) the ones who abstain"; نَّاهُون 1x "and those who forbid"
poets_named: unnamed verse ×3; Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Sīda's account of the root ن هـ ي (n-h-y).

1. Core sense — forbidding/restraining. النَّهْي (al-nahy) is the opposite of "command": to forbid. نَهاه (he forbade him); the one forbidden انْتَهى / تَناهى (desisted, stopped). A cited line: "When my knowledge reaches its limit, I stop there."

2. Mutual forbidding. تَناهَوْا عَن الشَّيْء: they forbade one another. Cited from the Revelation: "they did not forbid one another from a wrong they committed" — where the sense may also be "they used to desist."

3. Grammar of "nāhiyā." On the line "grey hair and Islam suffice a man as a restrainer (nāhiyan)," ناهيا is either the active participle of nahaytu (like sāʿ, shār), or a verbal noun (maṣdar) on the fāʿil pattern (as with fālij) — i.e. "as restraint," "as a possessor of restraint," with the annexed noun dropped.

4. Related nouns and forms. النُّهْيَة (al-nuhya) is the noun of the act. فلان نَهِيُّ فلان: one who forbids another. نفس نَهاة: a soul that desists.

5. End / utmost limit. النُّهْيَة، النِّهاية، النِّهاء: the furthest point and end of a thing — because its end "forbids" one from going further. انْتَهى / تَناهى / نَهَّى: reached its end. A line of Abū Dhuʾayb uses "my sight ended away from them" (with ʿan) to mean it was cut off from them. Al-Kisāʾī (via al-Liḥyānī) lists several forms for "it reached": nahhā, anhā, intahā, etc.; the light unstressed nahā is rare — Abū Jaʿfar says he never heard it used.

6. Concrete "end-point" senses.
 - النِّهاية: the tip of the nose-cord in a camel's nose (where it terminates).
 - النَّهْي / النِّهْي: a place with a barrier that stops water from overflowing; also a pool (ghadīr). Plurals: anhin, anhāʾ, nuhiyy, nihāʾ. النِّهاء also means the smallest rain-catchments.
 - التَّنْهاة / التَّنْهِية: where water ends in a valley (unusually built on the tafʿila pattern, normally reserved for verbal nouns).
 - نُهْيَة الوتد: the notch at a peg's head that keeps the rope from slipping off.

7. "Reaching the utmost." أنهى الشيء: conveyed/made it arrive. ناقة نَهِيَّة: a she-camel at the peak of fatness (originally of she-camels, then any fat animal, but only livestock).

8. Intellect. النُّهَى (both singular and plural), النُّهْيَة، النِّهاية، المَنْهاة all = the intellect/reason. From the Revelation: "signs for those possessed of intellect (uli al-nuhā)." Al-Liḥyānī holds al-nuhā to be the plural of nuhya. A man of intellect: مَنْهاة, نَهِيّ (pl. anhiyāʾ), نَهٍ / نِهٍ — of consummate reason. Ibn Jinnī notes the vowel-shifting (nah/nih) follows the grammarians' rule for guttural letters (like fakhidh > fakhdh).

9. "Sufficiency." نَهْيُك / ناهيكَ / نَهاكَ من رجل: all mean "enough of a man," i.e. he suffices.

10. Quantity / height. نِهاء النهار: the day's height. نُهاء مائة: "about a hundred" (like zuhāʾ miʾa).

11. النُّهاء — several material senses:
 - glass vials, or glass generally (said to have no singular, or singular nahāʾa); heard in only one cited verse comparing crushed pebbles to shattering glass.
 - a white stone softer than marble, found in the desert or brought from the sea (sg. nuhāʾa).
 - a desert medicine that is drunk as a remedy.

12. Beads and a name. النَّهَى: a kind of bead (sg. nahāt); also the cowrie-shell. نَهاة: the name of a mare (of Lāḥiq b. Jarīr).

13. Etymological note. Ibn Sīda judges the final weak radical throughout to be yāʾ (not wāw), since a final yāʾ is the more common case.

14. Further idioms.
 - أنهى / نَهِيَ عنها: he gave up (abandoned) a need he was pursuing, whether or not he attained it.
 - نُهْيَة of sounds around him = a preoccupation/distraction.
 - "Tamīm went and is neither... nor mentioned (tunhā)" = not spoken of.
 - نِهْيا / نَهَيا: the name of a water-source; discussion of whether the hāʾ is vowelled (only for the guttural) or silent, settled by the meter of a cited line, "to the people of Nahyā."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ن ج د (n-j-d), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: elevation, strength, and prominence.

1. al-najd — the courageous man; najuda al-rajulu — he became courageous; najd/najud/najid/najīd — near-synonymous adjectives for "brave." al-munājid — the combatant. "laqiya fulānun najdatan" — so-and-so encountered a hardship, illustrated with a line of poetry by Ṭarafah about a glance at a woman striking the onlooker with an overwhelming affliction (i.e. awe at her beauty).
2. al-najad — sweat; najida najadan — to sweat from exertion or distress, illustrated with a line of poetry about an exhausted sailor. The variant "nujida" (manjūd, "the distressed one") is illustrated with a further citation. "istanjadtuhu fa-anjadanī" — I sought his aid and he aided me — Ibn Fāris notes this sense carries an underlying idea of prevailing/overcoming an adversary.
3. al-najūd — a tall, prominent wild donkey; istanjada — to grow strong after weakness; "najadtu al-rajula" — I overcame the man (per Ibn al-Sikkīt).
4. al-najd — elevated land, highlands; anjada — to ascend from lowland to highland (the origin of the region-name Najd).
5. "huwa najd fī al-ḥājah" — he is swift/deft at a task; al-nijād — a sword's baldric/carrying-strap, because it rises over the shoulder; al-najd — the furnishings that deck out a tent or house (al-tanjīd, adornment/decoration); al-najd — an elevated road.
6. Closing: al-munajjad — one whom Time has "seasoned," i.e. made experienced and knowledgeable, as though Time had emboldened and strengthened him — Ibn Fāris notes each of these senses follows the same underlying analogy of elevation and strength.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-j-m (ن-ج-م) as a single sound root whose core meaning is rising up and appearing / becoming visible. He derives every sense from that idea:

1. To rise or come up: نَجَمَ النَّجْمُ ("the star/najm rose"); likewise a tooth or a horn "najama" when it comes up or sprouts.

2. al-najm as the Pleiades (al-Thurayyā): this is used as a proper name for that cluster, so the phrase "the najm has risen" is understood to mean the Pleiades specifically.

3. Figurative "origin": the saying "this report has no najm" means it has no root (aṣl) and no point of emergence (maṭlaʿ) — no traceable source.

4. al-najm as a plant type: a stemless, stalkless ground-plant, so called from najama (to spring up / emerge).

5. al-minjam in a balance/scale: the transverse iron bar that holds the pointer-tongue — which Ibn Fāris notes fits the same underlying analogy of rising/standing up.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ن-ج-س (n-j-s) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha (d. 1004 CE)

Core sense: the opposite of ṭahāra (purity/cleanness) — i.e. impurity, filth.

1. Plain sense: something najis or najas [two forms of the same adjective] is qadhir — filthy, dirty. Al-najas as a noun simply means "filth."

2. Extended sense — "incurable": Ibn Fāris proposes, cautiously ("it is not unlikely"), that from this comes the expression al-nājis for "a disease with no cure." As evidence he cites the poet Sāʿida al-Hudhalī, who calls grey hair/old age an "incurable disease" (dāʾ najīs lā dawāʾa lahū) afflicting a man once healthy and bold in his undertakings — as though, the longer it stays with a person, the more it "najisa/najjasa" him, i.e. makes him filthy.

3. A separate derived practice — al-tanjīs: an old Arab custom of hanging an object (possibly a bone or similar item) on a child as a protective charm against the jinn; this practice was named tanjīs for that reason. A verse is cited: "the munajjis [the one who performs tanjīs] hung anjās [the charm-objects] upon me" — anjās being the plural of the thing hung.
