Grammatical note: the entry marks the root as a "sound root" (aṣl ṣaḥīḥ), meaning Ibn Fāris treats all these senses as branching from one unified core idea (impurity), rather than being coincidental homonyms.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: نَجَّىٰ 37x "we saved"; أَنجَىٰ 23x "so we saved him"; نَجْوَىٰ 11x "your private consultation"; تَنَٰجَيْ 4x "hold secret counsel"; نَجَا 2x "you have escaped"; نَجِيّ 2x "(for) conversation"; مُنَجُّو 2x "(will) save you"; نَاج 1x "(would be) saved"; نَّجَوٰة 1x "the salvation"; نَٰجَيْ 1x "you privately consult"
poets_named: unnamed verse ×5; al-Muthaqqib (pre-Islamic); ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Ḥassān (pre-Islamic)
text:
Root ن ج و (n-j-w), as recorded by Ibn Sīda.

1. Deliverance / escape (al-najāʾ). To be saved from something: najā (verbal nouns najw, najāʾ, najāt); the forms najjā and istanjā carry the same sense. Attested in verses of al-Rāʿī and Abū Zubayd al-Ṭāʾī.

2. Causative "to deliver": najjā and anjā. Qurʾānic: "and thus We deliver the believers" (21:88). Ibn Sīda discusses the variant reading nujjiya al-muʾminīn: he holds it is not a passive with the verbal noun standing in for the agent, but a case of dropping one of the two nūns of nunajjī — parallel to tadhakkarūn (for tatadhakkarūn). Evidence: the lām of nujjī keeps its sukūn, whereas a true past tense would carry fatḥa (except under poetic license); compare al-Muthaqqib's taṭṭāliʿu for tataṭālaʿu.

3. najawtu bihi / najawtuhu — to carry someone/something off to safety. In a Hudhalī verse the poet drops the preposition ("saved nothing but [by] a scabbard and a wrapper") and links the verb directly to the noun.

4. To extract or draw out: istanjā ḥājatahu minhu (extracted his need from him — Ibn al-Aʿrābī); intajā matāʿahu (drew out and stripped away his goods — Thaʿlab).

5. High ground / refuge (al-najwa, al-nijāt, plural najāʾ): raised land the flood does not reach; hence "I took it for your refuge." The Qurʾānic "today We deliver you with your body" (10:92) is glossed: We set you on, or cast you upon, a height of ground so you may be recognized. Abū Ḥanīfa: al-manjā = a place beyond the flood's reach.

6. Speed in travel (al-najāʾ): najā najāʾan. Idioms of urging: al-najāʾa al-najāʾa and al-najā al-najā ("Quick! Quick!"), used both lengthened and shortened; also al-najāka, where the kāf marks the addressee and has no grammatical case (parallel to the kāf of dhālika). A swift she-camel is nājiya or najāt — one that "cuts through the land"; a male camel is not so described.

7. Passing cloud (al-najw, plural nijāʾ, nujuww): a cloud that has emptied its rain and moved on — or, per another view, a cloud as it first forms. Related verbs: anjatat al-saḥāba (the cloud veered away); "where did the sky rain on you?" (Abū ʿUbayda); anjaynāhā bi-makān kadhā (we made it rain there).

8. Bodily discharge (al-najw): wind or excrement from the belly; najā al-insān wa-l-kalb (the person/dog relieved itself). al-istinjāʾ: cleansing this with water, or wiping with stones; Kurāʿ: removing the filth by either.

9. Cutting (a central thread — Ibn Sīda notes several senses "all from cutting"):
 - najā / anjā / istanjā the branches of a tree = cut them; al-najā = branches (sing. najāt, per Abū Ḥanīfa) or a staff/stick; a tree "of good najā" = of good wood.
 - istanjā al-jāzir watara l-matn = the butcher cut the back-sinew (verse of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Ḥassān).
 - najā / anjā the hide of a camel = flayed it off; al-najw / al-najā = the flayed piece itself. Al-Zajjājī: al-najā = what is flayed off a sheep or camel, and also clothing cast off a man.

10. Confiding / secret talk (a major sense). najā / nājā / intajā / tanājā = to speak secretly, whisper, confer privately. al-najwā and al-najī mean both "the secret" and "those conferring in secret." Qurʾānic: "when they are in secret counsel" (17:47); "no secret conclave of three…" (58:7, which Ibn Sīda says can be parsed as adjective or genitive construct); "they withdrew in private counsel" (12:80). Plural anjiya. intajāhu = singled him out for private talk. In one cited verse najī is glossed as "voice" (of a singing camel-driver).

11. najāhu = smelled someone's breath (illustrated by a jesting verse).

12. Date-harvest senses: anjatat al-nakhla = the palm bore ripe dates (like ajnat, per Abū Ḥanīfa). istanjā al-nās = people obtained (or ate) fresh dates; al-Aṣmaʿī: istanjā al-rajul = the man got fresh dates. Others extend it: any fruit-gathering is istinjāʾ, e.g. najawtuka iyyāhu ("I gathered it for you") — though the better-known reading of the cited truffle verse is janaytuka ("I plucked for you").

13. Proper names: Nājiya (a personal name); Banū Nājiya (a tribe, per Sībawayh).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَكَحَ 14x "marry"; نِكَاح 5x "(of) the marriage"; تُنكِحُ 3x "and marry"; يَسْتَنكِحَ 1x "marry her"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ن-ك-ح as a single root whose core meaning is al-biḍāʿ (sexual union).

1. Base verb: نَكَحَ / يَنْكِحُ (nakaḥa / yankiḥu).

2. Usage: امْرَأَةٌ نَاكِحٌ فِي بَنِي فُلَانٍ — "a woman who is nākiḥ among the Banū so-and-so" means a woman who has a husband from among them.

3. Sense-distinction: النِّكَاح (al-nikāḥ) can refer to the marriage contract itself (al-ʿaqd), separate from the act of coitus (al-waṭʾ).

4. Related forms: نَكَحْتُ (nakaḥtu) is used to mean "I married" (= tazawwajtu); the causative أَنْكَحْتُ غَيْرِي (ankaḥtu ghayrī) means "I gave another in marriage / married someone else off."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ن‑ك‑ص (n-k-ṣ) as a single-sense root.

1. Core sense: the phrase نَكَصَ عَلَى عَقِبَيْهِ, literally "he turned back on his two heels," describes someone shrinking back (أَحْجَمَ) from something out of fear and cowardice — i.e., recoiling or retreating.

2. Ibn Duraid's refinement: he glosses the same phrase, "turned back on his heels," as reverting from some good he had been doing. He adds a usage restriction: this expression is specifically used for turning back *from good* — not for reverting from just anything.

So the root denotes a fearful, cowardly retreat, and by Ibn Duraid's account its idiomatic use is narrowed to abandoning or backsliding from good conduct one had been engaged in.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: n-k-b, from Ibn Faris, Maqayis al-Lugha.

Core meaning: a leaning, tilting, or deviation to one side in something.

1. Verb, nakaba an al-shay, yankubu: "to turn away / swerve from a thing." The entry cites the Quran: {ani al-sirati la-nakibun}, "swerving away from the path" (23:74).

2. Al-nakbaa: a wind that blows off the line of the four cardinal wind-directions, i.e. a slanting or veering wind. A line of verse is quoted, partially, describing a cold nakbaa wind striking travelers among the tent-dwellers.

3. Al-ankab: someone who walks as though leaning to one side.

4. Al-mankib: the shoulder, the point where the upper arm joins the shoulder-blade. It takes the dual form mankiban ("two shoulders") because a person has one on each side of the body.

5. Al-nakab: a disease that strikes camels in their shoulders and makes them limp.

6. Al-mankib (a second, distinct sense): the deputy/assistant of the arif (an overseer or head of a group). He is called by this name because he is compared to a person's shoulder: he props up the arif's authority the way a shoulder supports and strengthens a person.

All six senses are traced by the author to one underlying idea: leaning or deviating away from a straight line.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ن ك د (n-k-d) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha.

Core sense: something coming out to the one seeking/asking for it only with difficulty or harshness — a grudging, hard-won emergence.

1. مَطْلَبٌ نَكِدٌ ("a nakid quest") — a pursuit or request whose object is obtained only with difficulty.
2. رَجُلٌ نَكِدٌ / نَكَدٌ ("a nakid/nakad man") — a man from whom good or benefit comes only grudgingly — i.e. a hard, stingy, or ill-natured person.
3. نَكَدَ الْغُرَابُ ("the crow nakada") — said of a crow that strains itself to the utmost in its cawing, as though it were retching or vomiting — the same "forced, difficult emergence" idea applied to a sound being pushed out.
4. نَاقَةٌ نَكْدَاءُ ("a nakdāʾ she-camel") — a she-camel that gives no milk at all — here the sought thing (milk) fails to come out.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ن‑ك‑ف (n-k-f) from two distinct bases.

**1. Cutting off / pushing away**
- Al-nakf is the act of wiping tears off your cheek with a finger — a physical "cutting away."
- Extended to time and distance: an Arab saying describes a rainstorm so persistent that "no one could nakafahu" (cut it short) even over a day or two — i.e., no one could bring it to an end.
- A sea described as "lā yunkafu" (cannot be nukifa) means it cannot be exhausted or drained, paralleling the expression "lā yunzaḥ" (cannot be drained).
- From the same idea comes al-intikāf — leaving one place for another, or abandoning one course of action for a different one. Example: "He intended this, then intakafa and intended that instead" — as if he had cut off his original resolve.
- A related idiom, "intakafa al-athar," means he tracked down and found a trace or footprint.

**2. A bodily organ, and what is reasoned from it**
- Al-nakaf (plural of nakafah) names the gland at the base of the jaw. Camels whose jaw-glands are visibly swollen are called "munakkifah."
- From this physical sense, the lexicographers reasoned analogically to a moral one: "nakifa min al-amr" and "istankafa minhu" mean he disdained something — regarded it as beneath him.
- Ibn Fāris explains the logic of the analogy: disdaining something makes a person turn away and present only the base of his jaw to it — just as "aʿraḍa" ("he turned aside") describes someone who shows his cheek/side to something rather than facing it.
- He adds, as a parallel (not a shared root), that "al-ānif" — one who scorns something, from anf, "nose" — works the same way: as if he lifted his nose in disdain against it.

He closes by noting that this single analogical logic runs through the whole entry, with the standard closing formula that God knows best.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَكَٰل 3x "(as) an exemplary (punishment)"; تَنكِيل 1x "(in) punishment"; أَنكَال 1x "(are) shackles"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-k-l as one sound root whose core idea is prevention and holding back, with every derived form traced back to that.

1. Holding back / shrinking from something — نَكَلَ عَنْهُ, verbal noun نُكُول, imperfect يَنْكِل: to hold off or draw back from a thing. Related: نَاكِلٌ عَنِ الْأُمُورِ, a man who hangs back from affairs, i.e. too weak for them.

2. The concrete origin: النِّكْل, a fetter or shackle (plural أَنْكَال). Ibn Fāris derives the whole root from this, since a fetter "prevents" — the physical restraint gives the abstract sense. النِّكْل also names the iron bit of a bridle, another restraining device.

3. Being struck with what checks one — Ibn Durayd's phrase رَمَاهُ اللَّهُ بِنُكْلِهِ / بِنُكْلَةٍ: may God strike him with what checks or punishes him.

4. Making an example of someone — نَكَّلَ بِهِ, verbal nouns تَنْكِيل and نَكَال. Ibn Fāris says this follows the same analogy as the rest of the root: to do to a person something that prevents him from repeating the act and prevents others from doing the like. He judges this the better of the two available explanations. Related noun: الْمَنْكَل, the thing with which a person is thus checked, with the poetic line "and hurl at the backs of their necks a mankal" (something that will check them).

5. A reported exception — the ḥadīth "God loves the nakal upon the nakal" is glossed within the report itself as the strong, experienced man on the strong, experienced horse. Ibn Fāris notes that this meaning depends on the interpretation transmitted with the report and does not belong to the prevention-sense he has established for the root.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مُنكَر 18x "the wrong"; نَكِير 4x "my rejection"; مُنكِرُون 3x "(are) rejecting him"; يُنكِرُ 3x "will you deny"; نُّكْر 3x "terrible"; نَكِرَ 1x "he felt unfamiliar of them"; مُّنكِرَة 1x "refuse"; نَكِّرُ 1x "disguise"; أَنكَر 1x "(the) harshest"; نَّكِير 1x "denial"; نُّكُر 1x "terrible"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ن-ك-ر (n-k-r) as one sound root with a single core meaning: the opposite of recognition (maʿrifa) — that settled knowing in which the heart is at rest. He states that every derivative of the root traces back to this one idea.

1. Core sense: نَكِرَ / أنكرَ a thing = one's heart does not accept it and one's tongue does not acknowledge it — failure to recognize, rejection. He cites a verse of poetry: a woman fails to recognize the speaker, though the only change in him was graying hair and baldness.

2. النُّكْر (nukr): cunning or shrewdness.

3. النَّكْرَاء (nakrāʾ): a difficult, hard, severe matter; and the verb نَكُرَ (with verbal noun نَكَارَة, nakāra) = a matter turns difficult/severe.

4. الإنكار (inkār): the opposite of acknowledging or avowing something (denial).

5. التَّنَكُّر (tanakkur): a change from a pleasing state into a disliked one.

6. A specialized usage: نَكِرَة (nakira) is the name given to blood and the like discharged from the fetal membrane / afterbirth (al-ḥuwalāʾ).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نُكِسُ 1x "they were turned"; نَاكِسُوا 1x "(will) hang"; نُنَكِّسْ 1x "we reverse him"
text:
Ibn Faris, Maqayis al-Lugha, root n-k-s (نكس)

Core sense: the nun-kaf-sin root signals turning something upside-down (inverting it).

1. Al-naks - the basic verbal noun: turning a thing over onto its head.

2. Al-wilad al-mankus ("inverted/breech birth") - a birth in which the legs emerge before the head.

3. Al-niks - an arrow whose notch (fuq, where the bowstring sits) has broken, so its top end is turned into its bottom end and it is used reversed. By analogy, a foolish or dull person is also called niks, likened to that reversed, damaged arrow.

4. Al-munakkis, said of a horse - a horse that, from weakness, cannot raise its head or neck (its hadi, leading part) while running.

All four senses trace back to one image: something flipped from its proper upright orientation to the opposite one - literally (a body position, an arrow) or figuratively (a person's dullness, a horse's drooping weakness).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-k-th as a single sound root whose core idea is undoing something that had been made or bound.

1. Breaking an agreement: nakatha al-ʿahd, yankuthu, verbal noun nakth — to undo a covenant.
2. Reflexive/passive: intakatha al-shayʾ — the thing came undone, unravelled.
3. Of speech: "he said a word with no nakītha in it" means there is no going back on it, no failure to keep it.
4. Undoing a resolve: "he sought one need, then intakatha toward another" — he unravelled his first intention.
5. Concrete/textile sense: al-nikth is the unravelling of the worn fibres of cloaks so that they can be spun again; a man was given the name Nikth from this.
6. Al-nakītha: a hard, difficult situation in which people come apart. Ibn Fāris cites Ṭarafa: "Whenever there is a matter of the nakītha, I am present."

The entry thus links the abstract sense (breaking a pact, reversing a resolve) to the physical image of unpicking spun cloth and respinning it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَّمْل 2x "(of) the ants"; أَنَامِل 1x "the finger tips"; نَمْلَة 1x "an ant"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats N-M-L under his usual method: a root has one governing idea, and words are sorted by whether they fit it or deviate from it. The compound and augmented forms at the end come from his separate chapter for the whole letter nūn on words of more than three letters, which our source runs into this root.

**Governing sense of N-M-L:** gathering together in a thing, plus smallness and lightness (nimbleness).

1. **Ants.** نَمْل (naml) is the plural of نَمْلَة (namla), "an ant." طَعَامٌ مَنْمُولٌ — food that ants have got into.
2. **Nimbleness.** فَرَسٌ نَمِلُ الْقَوَائِم — a horse light and quick on its legs; Ibn Fāris takes this as a likeness drawn from the ant.
3. **A spreading sore.** نَمْلَة is also an ulcer breaking out on the side of the body; he explains the name by its spreading and diffusion, likened to an ant and its creeping.
4. **Fingertips.** أُنْمُلَة (unmula), plural أَنَامِل (anāmil) — the tips of the fingers.
5. **Reported but not from this sense.** Some say نَمْلَة is a crack in a horse's hoof, running from the hairline (الأَشْعَر) to the المَقَطّ. Ibn Fāris flags it as not belonging to the root's idea.
6. **Outside the chapter.** With a different vowelling — نُمْلَة (numla), ḍamma on the nūn, sukūn on the mīm — the word means talebearing/slander (نَمِيمَة); and نَمَلَ is used for "he carried tales." He lists this as a deviation from the governing sense, not an instance of it.

**Compound and augmented words from the letter nūn's chapter on longer words** (Ibn Fāris's naḥt, "carving," where he derives a four-letter word from two three-letter ones, or identifies an added letter):

7. **نَهْشَل (nahshal)** — the wolf, or (it is said) the falcon. Carved from نَشَلَ "snatch out" + نَهَشَ "tear with the teeth": it snatches flesh and tears at it.
8. **نَهَابِر (nahābir)** — deathtraps, places of ruin. Carved from نَهَبَ "plunder" + نَهَرَ (from the widening of a tear): something that plundered, tore open, and destroyed. Related: نَهْبَرَ فِي كَلَامِهِ — a man who speaks off the proper track, as though plundering speech (نهب) and sprawling out in it (نهر).
9. **نَهْبَلَة / نَهْبَل** — a huge she-camel; also an old woman (nahbala) and an old man (nahbal). Here Ibn Fāris judges the nūn to be an addition: the real root is H-B-L, since an old man is هِبِلّ and an old woman هِبِلَّة.
10. **نَقْرَشَة (naqrasha)** — a faint scratching sound, like that of a mouse or jerboa. Shāhid: "O you scrabbling rat." Carved from three verbs: نَقَرَ "peck/bore," قَرَشَ "gather," نَقَشَ "pick out" (as with tweezers, مِنْقَاش).
11. **نِقْرِس (niqris)** — a formidably shrewd guide; also دَلِيلٌ نِقْرِس (a keen guide) and طَبِيبٌ نِقْرِس / نِقْرِيس (a skilful physician). The sīn is an addition; the base is نَقْر "boring, probing" — he probes into matters, i.e. investigates them.
12. **نَقْثَلَة (naqthala)** — a walk that kicks up dust. Shāhid: "and at times I scuff up dust with the scuffing of the naqthala." Carved from نَقَثَ (hastening in walking) + نَقَلَ (shifting of the legs).
13. **نُمْرُقَة (numruqa)** — a cushion. The qāf is an addition; the word really derives from نَمِرَة (namira), the striped cloak.

The entry closes with "and God knows best what is right."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-m-m as a sound root with two meanings: first, making a thing apparent and bringing it into the open; second, "a colour, one of the colours".

**First meaning: bringing into the open**

1. Al-Farrāʾ reports that camels are called namma when no water remains in their bellies. Ibn Fāris derives al-nammām, the tale-bearer, from this, because he keeps no speech inside him; a tale-bearing man is rajul nammām.

2. The saying "May God silence his nāmma" refers to whatever movement of a person gives him away.

3. Al-namīma is sound and whispering, because both give a person away.

4. Al-nammām is also an aromatic plant, whose scent points to it.

5. The phrase mā bihā nummiyy means "there is no one there", as though a nummiyy were someone whose movement points to him.

6. The use of nummiyy for a coin (fals) is, he says, not Arabic.

**Second meaning: a colour**

7. Al-namnama is the setting of lines close to one another.

8. Al-nimnim (also vowelled numnum) is the whiteness that appears on the fingernails; the singular is nimnima (or numnuma).

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
quran_words: أَنقَذَ 4x "would be saved"; يَسْتَنقِذُ 1x "they (could) take it back"
poets_named: Luqaym b. Aws al-Shaybānī (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse; Yazīd b. al-Ṣaʿiq (pre-Islamic)
text:
Root ن ق ذ (n-q-dh) — as recorded by al-Zabīdī in Tāj al-ʿArūs.

1. Core sense: getting someone or something free. النَّقْذ (al-naqdh) is extrication, rescue, saving. The same idea runs through the derived forms إِنْقاذ (inqādh), تَنْقِيذ (tanqīdh), اسْتِنْقاذ (istinqādh) and تَنَقُّذ (tanaqqudh). Al-Zabīdī cites al-Ṣiḥāḥ (and al-Tahdhīb for the same): أنقذه من فلان, استنقذه منه and تنقّذه all mean one thing — he saved him and got him clear.

Grammatical note on the shāhid: in Luqaym b. Aws al-Shaybānī's line — "Or was your thanks that, out of grudging, you made light of my rescuing you yesterday; would that I had not been there" — the form نَقْذِيك (naqdhīka) is a verbal noun with an attached object pronoun, exactly parallel to ضَرْبِيك (ḍarbīka): "my rescuing of you," "my striking of you."

2. Safety, coming off unhurt. النَّقْذ also means safety and escape. Hence the exclamation نَقْذاً لَك (naqdhan laka), a wish of safety called out to someone who stumbles; al-Zabīdī cites al-Asās for it, and notes from al-Takmila that this is how the people of Yemen say it.

3. النَّقَذ (al-naqadh, both consonants vowelled) — the thing rescued. Morphologically a فَعَل (faʿal) form carrying a passive sense ("what has been rescued"), on the analogy of نَفَض (nafaḍ) and قَبَض (qabaḍ).

4. النَّقَذ as a verbal noun. From نَقِذَ (naqidha), of the fariḥa class: he escaped, he came through safe. The proverb ما له نَقَذ ("he has no naqadh") is cross-referenced to the root ش ق ذ.

5. الأَنْقَذ (al-anqadh) — the hedgehog, i.e. القُنْفُذ; al-Zabīdī notes he treated it under the undotted dāl (root n-q-d). The proverb بات بليلة أَنْقَذ ("he spent a night like anqadh's night"), transmitted with two vocalizations, is said of someone who stays awake the whole night.

6. النَّقِيذَة / النَّقِيذ — a mount recovered from the enemy. A horse you rescued and took back from an enemy; plural نَقائِذ (naqāʾidh). Al-Tahdhīb gives the singular of الخيل النقائذ as نَقِيذ without the feminine tāʾ. Al-Muḥkam: فَرَس نَقَذ is a horse taken from another people, and خيل نقائذ are horses recovered from people's or the enemy's hands (singular نَقِيذ, on Ibn al-Aʿrābī's authority), with the verse: "she was led off to another people as though she were a naqīdh, won by the spear from beneath a rider whose thrust kills." Al-Asās extends the usage to a camel or any beast: what an enemy seized and made his own, then you took back out of his hand — it is a نَقِيذَة, نَقِيذ, or نَقَذ.

7. النَّقِيذَة — the coat of mail. On al-Mufaḍḍal's authority: so called because it rescues its wearer from the swords. Shāhid from Yazīd b. al-Ṣaʿiq: "I have made ready against fate's blows every naqīdha — untouched, like the shimmer of the mirage, long-trailing." Al-Zabīdī glosses أُنُف here as "long," and لائحة المُضِلّ as the mirage: the mail is made to gleam like a mirage because of its brightness. Al-Azharī reports a variant reading in Shamir's hand — that النَّقِيذَة is specifically a coat of mail rescued from an enemy — and takes أُنُف to mean that no one else has worn it.

8. النَّقِيذَة — a woman who has previously had a husband.

9. Proper names. مُنْقِذ (Munqidh), on the pattern of muḥsin, is a man's name; نَقَذَة (Naqadha) is a place, mentioned by Ibn Durayd in al-Jamhara.

10. Additions by al-Zabīdī: النَّقِيذ, whatever has been rescued; رجل نَقَذ, a man who has been rescued; and the idiom هو نقيذة بؤس / هم نقائذ بؤس, "he is / they are rescued-ones of misery," i.e. people delivered out of hardship.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-q-ḍ as one sound root meaning the undoing or unravelling of something (nakth), with a secondary branch covering a type of sound.

1. Undoing, unmaking. نَقَضْتُ الْحَبْلَ وَالْبِنَاءَ — "I untwisted the rope and pulled down the building." النَّقِيضُ (naqīḍ) simply means "the thing undone."

2. A worn-out camel: نِقْضٌ (niqḍ), plural أَنْقَاضٌ — so called, he says, as though long travel had unravelled it.

3. Poetic rebuttal: مُنَاقَضَةٌ (munāqaḍa), a counter-poem, belongs here — the poet aims to undo what his rival had knotted tight.

4. Breaking a compact: نَقْضُ الْعَهْدِ is from the same sense of undoing.

5. النِّقْضُ also names the spot where a truffle breaks up out of the ground when it is being dug out; the verb is نَقَضْتُهَا نَقْضًا.

6. انْتَقَضَتِ الْقَرْحَةُ — a sore that had closed up breaks open again.

7. Sound sense. The cracking of the joints is called نَقِيضُهَا. Ibn Fāris links this back to sense 1: the joints seem to come apart, and a sound is heard at that moment.

8. أَنْقَضَتِ الدَّجَاجَةُ — the hen gave its cry.

9. الْإِنْقَاضُ is the cry used to urge on a young camel (qaʿūd). Cited verse: "Many an aged old woman of some folk — I taught her the inqāḍ-cry after the qarqara-rumble." The explanation given: the speaker stole the woman's full-grown she-camel, which she used to call with the deep qarqara rumble, and left her only a young camel, which is urged with the lighter inqāḍ cry.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ن ق ع (n-q-ʿ), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Two distinct sound roots: (1) the settling of a liquid in its resting-place, and (2) a kind of sound/outcry.

**Root 1 — settling, steeping, standing water**
1. naqaʿa al-māʾu — water came to rest/settled; istanqaʿa al-shayʾu fī al-māʾ — a thing was steeped in water. al-naqūʿ — what is steeped (medicine, a raisin drink); al-minqaʿ — the vessel for this, including a small stone pot used to feed a child milk (minqaʿ al-burum). al-naqīʿ — a raisin-based drink, or the trough in which dates are steeped, or standing/settled water that slakes thirst (like al-nājiʿ). al-naqīʿ — also a well with abundant water; "naqʿ al-biʾr," cited from a hadith, is a well's pooled water. al-unquʿah — the fat-pooled hollow in a bowl of sopped bread.
2. The proverb "huwa sharrābun bi-anquʿ" — "he is a drinker at [hidden] pools" — describes someone who repeats a matter over and over, explained by the image of a wary bird avoiding open watering-places for hidden, safer pools, just as a cautious man only takes risks where safety lies.
3. al-naqīʿah — pure, unmixed milk. A separate, disputed sense of al-naqīʿah (a sacrificial/customary meal): Ibn Fāris weighs two competing explanations — meat set aside from plunder before division (illustrated with a line of poetry), or food prepared for a returning traveler — judging these two, together, the best and most analogically sound accounts given — and notes a further usage: a camel slaughtered communally on behalf of several camel-owners, paralleling al-faraʿah for sheep-owners.

**Root 2 — sound/outcry**
4. al-naqīʿ/al-naqʿ — a shout/outcry; naqaʿa al-ṣawt — a sound rose up, illustrated with a line of poetry about a war-cry gathering people for battle. al-naqʿ is also said to describe the ostrich's cry. al-naqqāʿ — a boastful man who exaggerates what he doesn't truly have, as though "crying it out."
5. Closing note: the phrase "intuqiʿa lawnuhu" ("his color drained") is explained as a letter-substitution from the more original "imtuqiʿa," discussed elsewhere by Ibn Fāris.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root n-q-ṣ as expressing a single idea: naqṣ, "diminution / decrease," the opposite of ziyāda ("increase, addition").

1. Core sense — to decrease or become less. The verb is used both intransitively (naqaṣa l-shayʾ, "the thing decreased") and transitively (naqaṣtuhu, "I diminished it"); the passive participle is manqūṣ ("diminished, deficient").

2. Derived sense — naqīṣa: a fault or defect (ʿayb). The idiom mā bihi naqīṣa ("there is no naqīṣa in him") means there is nothing that diminishes him.

He states that every use in the root traces back to this one meaning of diminution.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَقِيب 1x "leaders"; نَقْب 1x "(to do) any penetration"; نَقَّبُ 1x "so they explored"
text:
Root n-q-b (نقب) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: "an opening made in something" — piercing, perforating, breaching.

1. Physical piercing/breaching
   - naqaba al-ḥāʾiṭ — to breach/pierce a wall (naqb = a breach or hole).
   - A farrier lances (yanqubu) the swollen navel of a working animal to drain fluid; the lancing tool is a minqab.
   - kalb naqīb — a dog whose throat has been deliberately pierced to weaken its bark, done by mean people so a guest's arrival won't be given away by barking.
   - al-nāqiba — an ulcer on the side of the body that breaks through into the abdominal cavity.
   - A worn-through hole in a camel's foot-pad is also called a naqab.

2. Mange spots (al-nuqba)
   - al-nuqba = the first spot of mange to appear on the skin (pl. nuqab). A verse describes someone dabbing tar on these spots. Ibn Fāris says the link to the core meaning is sound: mange "pierces the skin."

3. "The learned/investigative one" (al-naqqāb / al-niqāb)
   - Someone versed in affairs is called al-naqqāb because he "probes" into matters and extracts (deduces) knowledge from them — the same image as physically boring into something to get at what's inside. A verse calls such a man a niqāb who "reports the unseen," i.e., uncovers what others can't see.
   - al-naqīb — the appointed representative of a group: their witness and their guarantor. Ibn Fāris treats this as the same word as al-niqāb ("the learned one") — the naqīb is one who probes into people's affairs, the way one probes to uncover secrets.

4. Mountain paths and travel
   - al-naqb and al-manqaba both mean a pass/path through a mountain — again, an "opening" cut through something solid.
   - naqqabū fī l-bilād, "they traveled through the land," derives from traveling along these mountain-passes (al-nuqūb).

5. A noble deed (al-manqaba)
   - A generous or admirable act is a manqaba, because it is something good that becomes famous — as if it had been "dug out" and brought to light.

6. Items the author flags as outliers
   - niqāb al-marʾa, a woman's face-veil, is explicitly noted by Ibn Fāris as not fitting this root's derivational logic.
   - nāqabtu fulānan — "I ran into so-and-so unexpectedly."
   - A second, unrelated-looking al-nuqba is a waist-garment with a drawstring (distinct from a niṭāq).
   - Colour itself can be called al-nuqba (ḥasan al-nuqba = "of good colour"). Ibn Fāris speculates this too may tie back to the root's core sense — colour as something that "comes to light" once uncovered.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-q-m as one small, genuine root whose core sense is disapproving of something and finding fault with it.

1. Core verb: نَقَمَ (naqama ʿalā, imperfect anqimu) — to condemn or reject someone's action, to hold it against him. Ibn Fāris glosses نقمت عليه as "I found fault with what he did."

2. Derived noun نِقْمَة (niqma) — punishment and retribution (intiqām). He explains the link: it is as if the agent, having disapproved of the person, then penalized him — so the sense of "punishment" grows out of the root's core sense of condemnation.

3. A note on نَقِيمَة (naqīma), as in the phrase "he is of blessed naqīma" [said of a person's inner self/temperament]: Ibn Fāris judges this not to belong to n-q-m at all, but to be a phonetic substitution (ibdāl) — the original form being نَقِيبَة (naqība, from the root n-q-b), with b replaced by m.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-q-r as a single sound root whose core sense is: striking something until a dent or hollow is beaten into it. Everything else in the entry is presented as an extension of that image.

1. Pecking / striking. The bird's beak is called a minqār because it pecks at a thing until it marks it. The same word names the iron tool used to dress a millstone (naqartu al-raḥā bi-l-minqār).

2. Probing, investigating. naqqartu ʿan al-amr = "I dug into the matter until I knew it" — inquiry pictured as pecking into a thing. (Ibn Fāris repeats this sense later in the entry.)

3. Faulting a person. naqartu al-rajul = "I found fault with him," as though you struck him and left a mark. He cites a woman's saying to her husband: take me past the men of naẓarā (who look) but not past the women of naqarā (who backbite) — i.e. past those who gaze, not those who pick at me.

4. Hollows and hollowed things (the dent itself):
   - nuqra: a hollow where floodwater collects, as if it had been beaten out.
   - minqar (pl. manāqir): small wells with narrow mouths, as if hollowed into the ground.
   - nuqrat al-qafā: the hollow at the nape of the neck.
   - naqīr: the small speck on the back of a date-stone.
   - naqīr: a hollowed-out tree-trunk used as a steeping vessel — the one, he notes, that a prohibition was issued about.
   - naqīr also = origin/stock: "so-and-so is of noble naqīr," the place he was dug out of and emerged from.

5. Selective invitation. daʿāhum al-naqarā: inviting some and meanly leaving others out. Ibn Fāris judges this a sound analogy: the man does not summon everyone aloud but comes to the gathering and signals or nudges (yanqur) one person with his hand to get up and come along.

6. al-nāqūr. Per Ibn Fāris, the horn the angel blows on the Day of Resurrection, so called because its striking "pecks" the worlds.

7. An outlier from the base sense: anqara ʿan al-shayʾ = to desist, leave off. He supports it with a ḥadīth — God would not leave off from the slayer of a believer, i.e. not desist from punishing him — and a verse: "and I am not one to desist from the enemies of my people."

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root ن س أ (n-s-'), al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qur'ān

Core sense: delay, deferral in time.

1. nusi'at al-mar'ah — a woman's menstrual period being delayed, taken as a hopeful sign of pregnancy; such a woman is called nasū'.
2. Idiom: nasa'a Allāhu fī ajalika / nasa'a Allāhu ajalaka — "may God extend your appointed term."
3. al-nasī'ah — selling on deferred payment, i.e. credit.
4. al-nasī' — the pre-Islamic Arab practice of postponing one of the sacred months to another month, condemned in the Qur'an: "the postponing [of sacred months] is only an increase in disbelief" (al-Tawbah 9:37).
5. A Qur'anic recitation variant of 2:106, "mā nansakh min āyatin aw nansa'hā," is glossed here as "whatever verse We defer" — either by causing it to be deferred, or by nullifying its ruling.
6. al-minsa' — a staff, so called because it is used to push/move something away (nasa'a); this is the word used for the staff eaten by an insect in Sabaʾ 34:14.
7. nasa'at al-ibil fī ẓamaʾihā — camels delaying their drinking a day or two. Illustrated with a line of poetry describing a sturdy she-camel driven across a bare track.
8. al-nasūʾ — milk whose drinking is delayed until it sours, then is diluted with water.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root n-s-b (نسب) from one core meaning: the connection or joining of one thing to another (ittiṣāl shayʾin bi-shayʾin).

Three senses given, all tied to that core:

1. al-nasab (النَّسَب) — lineage/kinship. Named this because it is itself a connection, and it connects a person to what came before him (his ancestry). Verb: nasabtu ansubu ("I traced/attributed lineage"). A related person is called nasīb fulān — "the kinsman of so-and-so," one connected to him by descent.

2. al-nasīb (النَّسِيب) in poetry — the amatory verses (nasīb/ghazal) addressed to a woman. Ibn Fāris explains the name the same way: it is as if the poet's words form a discourse that attaches itself to her. He notes this term is used only for women, never men. Same verb again: nasabtu ansubu.

3. al-nasīb (النَّسِيب) also names a straight road, because its parts are joined continuously to one another.

All three senses — genealogical connection, the poetic address to a woman, and a continuous road — are presented by Ibn Fāris as expressions of the same underlying idea of things being linked or joined in sequence.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats N–S–F as a single sound root whose core notion is uncovering a thing and stripping it away.

1. Of wind: intasafat al-rīḥ al-shayʾ — the wind carries something off, such as dust or dry chaff, as if it had laid it bare from the surface of the ground and taken it away.

2. Of a building: nasf al-bināʾ is demolishing it to the foundations, cutting it out completely.

3. Nusāfa is the froth or scum on milk, so called because it is skimmed off the surface.

4. Related to this: intusifa lawnuhu — his colour was drained from him.

5. Of an animal: a baʿīr nasūf is a camel that tears up plants from the ground with the front of its mouth.

6. A reported usage: humā yatanāsafān, said of two people whispering confidences to each other. Ibn Fāris holds that the same underlying analogy applies — each one is, as it were, stripping off what the other has.

text:
Ibn Fāris's account of the root n-s-k (نسك):

1. Core sense. He classes n-s-k as a "sound" root — one with a single coherent origin — whose meaning is devotion/worship (ʿibāda) and drawing near to God. From this comes نَاسِك (nāsik), used of a man, i.e. one who is devout or given to worship.

2. The offering. An animal slaughtered as a means of drawing near to God is a نَسِيكَة (nasīka), plural نَسَائِك (nasāʾik).

3. The place. الْمَنْسَك (mansak, also vocalised mansik) is the place where such offerings are slaughtered. Ibn Fāris restricts this: the word is used only in connection with the قُرْبَان (qurbān), the offering brought near to God.

4. A rejected alternative. He notes that some have claimed mansak means simply "a place someone frequents or is attached to", and he marks this as doubtful (fīhi naẓar) rather than endorsing it.

The entry gives no poetic or Qur'anic citations and no further morphological detail beyond the plural nasāʾik and the two vocalisations of mansak.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-s-l as one sound root whose core idea is a thing being drawn out and slipping away.

1. Core sense — drawing out, slipping loose (سَلّ / انسلال).

2. Offspring: نَسْل (nasl) is a child or progeny, so named because it is drawn out from its mother. تَنَاسَلُوا (tanāsalū) = they were born one from another.

3. Rapid movement: نَسَلَان (nasalān) is the wolf's gait when it thrusts its neck forward and speeds up; a walker يَنْسِل (yansil) when he moves fast. Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 21:96 — {وهم من كل حدب ينسلون}, "from every height they come hurrying."

4. Shed hair and feathers: نُسَالَة (nusāla) is an animal's hair when it drops off its body in patches; نُسَال الطير is the down or feathers birds shed. He quotes the poetic line "وتجلو سبيخ جفال النسال" (clearing away the loosened tufts of shed down). Related: أَنْسَلَتِ الإبل — the camels have reached the season for shedding their coat.

5. Things slipping off: نَسَلَ الثوبُ عن الرجل — the garment slipped off the man.

6. نَسِيل (nasīl): honey once melted, as if it had slipped free of its wax and separated from it.

7. أَنْسَلْتُ القومَ — I got ahead of the people, outstripped them.

The thread through all of these, on his analysis, is separation by slipping out: the newborn from the mother, the hair from the hide, the honey from the comb, the garment from the body, and the fast walker from the group.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris treats the root n-s-r as a sound root whose core meaning is a furtive snatching or seizing (ikhtilas / istilab) - taking something quickly and making off with it.

1. Basic sense: al-nasr = taking a bit of food; "nasarahu" = he snatched a small thing away.

2. The bird: al-nasr, the eagle/vulture, is named from this root because it "yansuru" - snatches at / tears at - its prey.

3. al-minsar (a raiding troop of 100-200 horsemen) is named by the same analogy: it "comes only to snatch and plunder something." Alternatively, some say it is so called because it does not pass anything without tearing it up/uprooting it.

4. By resemblance, al-nasr also names two stars: al-nasr al-ta'ir ("the Flying Eagle," i.e. Altair) and al-nasr al-waqi' ("the Falling Eagle," i.e. Vega) - named after the bird by likeness.

5. nasr al-hafir: the part on the underside of a horse's hoof, described as resembling date-stones and pebbles.

All senses trace back to the one idea of snatching/plundering - the bird for its predatory snatching, the raiding troop for its plundering, and the hoof-part apparently for its pebble-like appearance.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam); unnamed verse ×6
text:
Lisān al-ʿArab gathers several word-families under n-s-w/n-s-y: "women", the sciatic vein (al-nasā), forgetting and leaving, the discarded thing (al-nisy), a few words it traces to a hamzated root, and a milk drink.

**1. Women.** Niswa / nuswa, nisāʾ, niswān / nuswān (and nisūn) serve as the plural of imraʾa (woman), though they are formed from a different word than the singular, as with "that / those". Ibn Sīda says nisāʾ is the plural of niswa when the women are many; for that reason Sībawayh formed the relative adjective of nisāʾ as niswī, going back to its singular. The diminutive is nusayya, plural nusayyāt, a diminutive of the plural.

**2. The sciatic vein (al-nasā).** Al-nasā is a vein running from the hip to the ankle. Its final alif goes back to a wāw (dual nasawān), though a dual nasayān with yāʾ is also recorded. Al-Aṣmaʿī describes it in a beast (dābba): it runs from the hip along the inside of the thighs, past the hock, down to the hoof. In a fat animal the thigh muscles separate and the vein shows in the groove between them; in a lean one it is hidden. The hadith of Saʿd has "I shot Suhayl ibn ʿAmr on the day of Badr and cut his nasā."

- Plural ansāʾ. Abū Dhuʾayb speaks of a fat female beast whose "nasā veins part", which the entry explains as the thighs parting at the place of the vein. Ibn Barrī compares the construction of his "remnant not sucked" (meaning there is no remnant at all) with "they do not ask people importunately" (Q 2:273): they do not ask at all.
- Verbs: nasaytuhu, "I struck him on the nasā" (he is mansī); nasiya, yansā, nasan, "he suffered pain in his nasā" (he is nasin; according to al-Muḥkam ansā, feminine nasʾāʾ; according to al-Tahdhīb nasyāʾ).
- The dispute over ʿirq al-nasā ("the vein of the nasā"). Al-Aṣmaʿī and Ibn Sīda reject the phrase: the Arabs say simply al-nasā, as they say al-akḥal and al-abjal, and Ibn Sīda says Thaʿlab erred in using it. Ibn al-Sikkīt, al-Kisāʾī and others accept it. Ibn Barrī defends it: the commentary from Ibn ʿAbbās on Q 3:93 ("except what Israel forbade to himself") says Israel gave up camel meat because he suffered from ʿirq al-nasā. He explains the phrase as a thing annexed to its own name, like ḥabl al-warīd, and cites further examples, including lines of al-Kumayt, Farwa ibn Musayk and Himyān.

**3. Forgetting.** Al-nisyān is the opposite of remembering and retaining. Verbal nouns: nisyān, nasy, nisy, niswa, nisāwa, nasāwa. Ibn Khālawayh cites a line with "nor forgetful (niswa) of a pledge". Related forms: tanāsāhu, "he made a show of having forgotten it"; ansāhu iyyāhu and nassāhu, "he made him forget it"; nasyān, nasiyy and nāsin, "very forgetful". Thaʿlab compares nāsin / nasiyy to ʿālim / ʿalīm and similar pairs. The Lisān also argues that nasiyy is more likely faʿīl than faʿūl. Al-Farrāʾ says the Arabs say nisyānan and nisyan but not nasayānan, since nasayān is only the dual of the vein.

**4. Forgetting as leaving (tark).** The entry states outright that "al-nisyān: leaving", and several scholars read Qur'anic uses this way:

- Q 9:67 "they forgot God, so He forgot them": Thaʿlab says God does not forget; it means they left Him and He left them, because forgetting is a kind of leaving. Al-Tahdhīb: they left God's command, so He left them out of His mercy. Q 20:126 "so today you are forgotten": you are left in the Fire.
- Q 20:115, Adam "forgot": this too is glossed as "left", since one who truly forgets is not held to account. The entry adds that "the first is more regular by analogy". Elsewhere it says Adam was held to account for his forgetting and came down from the Garden. It cites a hadith praising Adam's forbearance and resolve, alongside "We found in him no resolve".
- Q 2:106 "whatever sign We abrogate or nunsi-hā". One gloss is "We command you to leave it" (ansaytuhu, "I ordered it left"; nasītuhu, "I left it"). Al-Farrāʾ gives two senses: leaving it unabrogated (compare Q 9:67 and Q 2:237 "do not neglect generosity between you"), or actual forgetting (compare Q 18:24 "remember your Lord when you forget"). Al-Zajjāj reports three readings: nunsihā, nunassihā and nansaʾhā. Some take the verse as actual forgetting, citing Q 87:6–7 ("you will not forget, except what God wills"). Al-Zajjāj rejects this because of Q 17:86. He reads Q 87 as "you will not leave anything except what God wills". He also allows that it may mean the ordinary lapses of human nature, later remembered, and not the loss of any wisdom given to the Prophet. He also rejects "or We leave it", since unsītu is not used for "I left". His own reading is "or We have it left", i.e. We command you to leave it.
- Al-Azharī supports this with a verse recited by Ibn al-Aʿrābī, "I am not nāsī-hā nor munsī-hā", glossed as "not leaving it nor postponing it". Al-Azharī suggests that Ibn al-Aʿrābī took munsī here as the hamza-less form of ansaʾtu, "I deferred (a debt)".
- Niswa also means leaving off work. Q 59:19 "He made them forget themselves": He made them forget to work for their own selves.
- Q 6:41 "you forget what you associate [with Him]", Q 7:51 "today We forget them as they forgot the meeting of this day", and "when they forgot what they had been reminded of". Al-Zajjāj and the entry allow either "leave" or "act like one who has forgotten". In Q 7:51 the sense is that they are left without mercy, as they left off working for that day.

**5. Hadith on saying "I forgot".** The Prophet disliked someone saying "I forgot (nasītu) such-and-such a verse"; he should say "I was made to forget (nussiya)". The Lisān gives two reasons. God is the one who causes forgetting, since He decrees all things. And the root sense of forgetting is leaving, so the phrase would sound like "I abandoned the Qur'an", when it was not by choice. Nusiya without the doubled s would mean "he was left out of good, deprived". Abū ʿUbayd's version ("he did not forget but was made to forget") is called clearer, and he takes it as leaving. The saying "I am only made to forget so that I may set a practice" is explained as showing people what one must do on forgetting part of worship. Another hadith says some "are left in al-mansā beneath the foot of the All-Merciful", i.e. forgotten in the Fire. "Beneath the foot" is called a metaphor: God makes creatures forget them so no one intercedes. The entry compares the Prophet's words at the Conquest, that every inherited glory of the Jāhiliyya is "beneath my two feet". Nasiyy is also one not counted among the people, because forgotten.

**6. The discarded thing (al-nisy / al-nasy).** Al-nisy is a forgotten, disregarded thing. Specifically it is:
- a menstrual rag thrown away (plural ansāʾ);
- the worthless odds and ends left behind at a camp. When moving off, the Arabs say "look to your ansāʾ", meaning check small things such as a staff, a cup or a tent-peg so they are not forgotten.
Al-Akhfash defines it as a paltry thing overlooked; al-Zajjāj as a thing thrown aside and not heeded. On Maryam's words "and I had been nisyan mansiyyan" (Q 19:23), Thaʿlab explains nisy as menstrual rags thrown away and forgotten. With kasra (nisyan) it means a discarded rag; with fatḥa (nasyan) it means a forgotten thing, "I would not be known". ʿĀʾisha's wish to be "nisyan mansiyyan" is glossed as a paltry, discarded thing no one turns to. Al-Farrāʾ calls nisy and nasy two dialect forms, like witr and watr, and says nisy may also be taken as a verbal noun of forgetting. Poetic witnesses are cited from Dukayn al-Fuqaymī and al-Shanfarā.

**7. God is not forgetful.** On Q 19:64 "your Lord is not nasiyy": He forgets nothing. Al-Zajjāj also allows the reading "your Lord has not forgotten you, O Muḥammad, though revelation is delayed". This is tied to the report that Jibrīl was slow in coming and said "We descend only by your Lord's command."

**8. Grammar of wa-lā tansawu (Q 2:237).** Al-Jawharī notes that some allowed a hamza on the plural wāw. Al-Mubarrad says any wāw with ḍamma may take hamza except this plural wāw, where they differ; hamza is rare and leaving it is preferred. He derives the form from tansayū, whose yāʾ was dropped and whose ḍamma passed to the wāw. Ibn Barrī corrects the derivation: the yāʾ turned into alif after fatḥa and was then elided when two quiescent letters met.

**9. Words from the hamzated root.** Ibn al-Aʿrābī gives nāsāhu, "he put him far off", without hamza though its base has one. Al-Jawharī gives al-minsāh, "the staff", also properly hamzated, and cites a line on creeping along on a staff in old age.

**10. A milk drink.** Al-nasy (no hamza) is anything that makes the mind forget. In a line recited by Ibn al-Aʿrābī it is fresh milk with water poured on it. Shamir reports another form, nasiyy, with a line warning against drinking sour milk or nasiyy on a day of coming to water, lest one come back sluggish. Ibn al-Aʿrābī also gives naswa as "a gulp of milk".

text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-s-kh as one root, but notes that lexicographers disagree about the single principle underlying it:

- View 1: the principle is removing one thing and putting another in its place.
- View 2: the principle is transferring or converting one thing into another.

Senses he records:

1. Copying a text — نَسْخُ الكِتَاب, transcribing a book.
2. Superseding a prior ruling — a command that was formerly acted upon and is then cancelled by a new one; his example is a verse containing a command that is then abrogated by another verse.
3. General displacement/succession — anything that takes the place of another thing has "superseded" it: the sun displaces the shade; grey hair displaces youth.
4. تَنَاسُخ, successive turnover — of heirs, when heirs die one after another while the estate still stands undivided; and by extension the succession of eras and generations.

Etymological note he cites from al-Sijistānī: nasḫ originally means transferring the honey and bees of one hive into another — and, on that account, the copying of a book derives from this sense of transfer.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats نسي (n-s-y) as two sound base-meanings, then adds a related hamzated branch (نسأ) and a few outliers.

Two base senses:
1. Being unmindful of / neglecting a thing — نَسِيتُ الشَّيْءَ ("I forgot it," when you fail to remember it), verbal noun نِسْيان.
2. Leaving / abandoning a thing.

Related to sense 1: النِّسْي — the worthless goods travellers drop and leave at a campsite; hence تَتَبَّعُوا أَنَسَاءَكُمْ ("go track down your discarded things"). Cited with a line of al-Shanfarā using نِسْي for a dropped/left object.

Qur'anic application: On this basis Ibn Fāris reads نَسُوا اللَّهَ فَنَسِيَهُمْ (al-Tawba 67) and فَنَسِيَ (of Adam, Ṭāhā 115) as "leaving/abandoning" — Adam "left the covenant" (فترك العهد) — i.e. the "forgetting" here is glossed as abandonment, not mere memory-loss.

Outlier under n-s-y: النَّسَا, the sciatic vein (plural أَنْسَاء, dual نَسَيَانِ); عِرْقُ النَّسَا is the same. One view: the true root-sense is النِّسْيان, "a thing slipping from the mind after being present," and the thigh-vein is named النَّسَا because it lies set back toward the thigh — likened to what is "put back and left."

Hamzated branch نسأ = deferring / delaying:
- نُسِئَتِ الْمَرْأَة: her menses is late (so pregnancy is hoped).
- النَّسِيئَة: a deferred-payment sale; أَنْسَأْتُ = I deferred.
- نَسَأَ / أَنْسَأَ اللَّهُ أَجَلَكَ: God postponed your term.
- انْتَسَؤُوا: they drew back / grew distant; نَسَأْتُهُمْ: I set them back.
- نَسَأْتُ نَاقَتِي: either "I went gently with my camel," or (Ibn Fāris judges this more fitting) "I drove her with the مِنْسَأَة (staff)," since a staff pushes a thing away.
- النَّسْء: new camel-fur grown after the old has fallen (i.e. "late" fur).
- Abū Zayd: نَسَأْتُ الْإِبِلَ فِي ظِمْئِهَا = lengthen the camels' watering-interval by a day or two.

Qur'anic النَّسِيء (al-Tawba 37, إِنَّمَا النَّسِيءُ زِيَادَةٌ فِي الْكُفْرِ): "postponement." Ibn Fāris explains the pre-Islamic practice — on leaving Minā a man of Kināna would proclaim his decree binding, and people would ask him to "postpone a month" (أَنْسِئْنَا شَهْرًا), shifting the sanctity of al-Muḥarram onto Ṣafar, because three straight sacred months without raiding hurt a raiding economy; so al-Muḥarram was declared permissible.

Further outliers: النَّسْء also = the first onset of fatness in animals (with a line of Abū Dhuʾayb); and النَّسِيء = milk diluted with water (verb نَسَأْتُ), attested in verse by ʿUrwa.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
text:
Root ن ت ق (n-t-q) — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144 CE)

Core (literal) sense: to shake or jolt something violently, typically so as to dislodge, empty, or extract what it holds.

1. natq al-baʿīr al-raḥl — the camel shakes/jolts its saddle-pack loose (zaʿzaʿa, "to jolt, dislodge").
2. natq al-zubd — to extract butter by churning.
3. God "nataqa" the mountain — He raised it up, shaking it, above them.
4. natq al-jirāb — to shake out a bag until everything in it falls out; used of giving to a beggar: "shake out for him what you can spare."

Figurative (majāz) extensions:

5. imraʾa nātiq, "a nātiq woman" — one who has "shaken out" her belly, meaning she has borne many children. A verse calls a certain lineage "Banū Nātiq," sons of such a prolific mother, saying they could never be made to know disgrace.
6. zand nātiq, "a nātiq fire-stick" — one that strikes/kindles fire readily.
7. A verse about a mare: taken while full-bellied and distended, later grown lean-bellied and fluttering — al-Zamakhsharī notes the poet likens her, in the fullness and stoutness of her belly, to pregnant females.
8. A battle verse names a place or moment "Nātiq," where the horsemen of Khathʿam were routed. Al-Zamakhsharī explains the poet actually meant Ramaḍān: it "wrings out" (yantuqu) those who fast just as it "scorches" (yarmuḍuhum) them — a wordplay tying natq to the meaning behind Ramaḍān's own name.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris states that the root n-th-r has one sound underlying sense: "casting/scattering something that is dispersed."

1. Core sense - scattering: nathara al-darahim = "he scattered the dirhams" (coins) and similar things.

2. Extended to the nose: nathurat al-shah - a ewe "nathura-s" when it expels irritant matter from its nose. From this the nose itself came to be called al-nathra, "because it expels what is harmful in it." A hadith uses the related verb: "When you perform ablution, then intathir/fanthir" - meaning put water into your nostril (nathra).

3. A star name: al-Nathra also denotes an asterism called "the nose of the Lion [Leo]," one of the moon's lunar mansions - likely named by the same nose-association.

4. Throwing down/unhorsing: ta'anahu fa-antharahu - "he speared him and cast him down on his nasal cavity (khayshum)." Ibn Faris notes this fits the root's regular pattern. He cites a verse of poetry: a rider "worth ten" who, whenever he sees an enemy horseman, anthara-s him - flings him down. The same verb, anthara, is also used for "made him bleed from the nose."

5. Armor: al-Nathra can also mean "coat of mail." Ibn Faris flags this sense as possibly irregular (shadhdh) - not clearly derivable from the "scattering" root he has set out.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ن و ش (n-w-sh), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: the reaching-for/taking of a thing.

1. nushtuhu nawshan — I reached for and took it; tanāwashtu — I reached for/took something. Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'an as an example of this usage: Saba' 34:52, "wa annā lahumu al-tanāwushu min makānin baʿīd" — "and how could they attain [it] from so distant a place?"
2. A secondary construction: nushtuhu khayran (without the alif) means "I granted him good" — extending "reaching/taking" to "reaching out to give." Ibn Fāris closes with a line of poetry using the intensive form (intiyāsh) for a reaching/plucking motion.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib's short entry on nāʾa gives its forms, a gloss from Abū ʿUbayda, and one Qur'anic use.

1. **Forms.** One says nāʾa bi-jānibihi ("nāʾa with his side"), imperfect yanūʾu or yanāʾu.

2. **Rising.** Abū ʿUbayda: nāʾa is like nāʿa, meaning "he rose". Anaʾtuhu means "I made him rise".

3. **Qur'an.** He cites Q 28:76: "that of which the mafātiḥ would weigh heavily on the band (al-ʿuṣba)".

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ن و ص (n-w-ṣ) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: back-and-forth motion — wavering, coming and going.

1. Verb — nāṣa ʿan qarnihi ("he swerved away from his adversary"): to shy away or recoil from one's opponent/equal in a contest.

2. Noun al-manāṣ: the verbal noun of that action, and separately used to mean "refuge" or "a place/moment of escape." Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'an: "wa-lāta ḥīna manāṣ" — "and it was not a time for escape" (38:3).

3. Al-nawṣ as a name for the wild donkey: given this name because it is constantly nā'iṣ — raising its head and wavering back and forth, like a headstrong, bolting animal (al-jāmiḥ).

4. Nāwaṣa al-jarra ("he nāwaṣa the jar") = "he grappled with / worked at it." Ibn Fāris notes he already explained this expression under the letter jīm (i.e., in the entry for root j-r-r), and does not repeat it here.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root n-w-b as a single idea: habitually frequenting a place and returning to it.

1. Core sense — returning to / regularly resorting to a place. Verb forms: نَابَ / يَنُوبُ (nāba/yanūbu) and انْتَابَ / يَنْتَابُ (intāba/yantābu, "to keep coming back").

2. النُّوَب (al-nuwab) — reported to mean "bees," said to be named from their pasturing and their returning (nawb) to their place. An alternative view takes the word as the plural of نَائِب (nāʾib, "one that recurs/returns").

Attesting citation: a line of Abū Dhuʾayb using نَوْب (nawb) in the sense of a recurring cause — "I lay sleepless at his memory, with no recurring cause (nawb), as a striped, freshly-sloughed snake is stirred up."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-w-m as a single sound root whose core idea is inertness and the stilling of movement — something that has ceased to stir.

1. Sleep. نَوْم (nawm) is the primary derivative: نَامَ / يَنَامُ (nāma / yanāmu, "to sleep"), with the verbal nouns نَوْمًا (nawman) and مَنَامًا (manāman).

2. Intensive forms for a heavy sleeper. نَؤُوم (naʾūm) and نُوَمَة (nuwama) both describe someone who sleeps a great deal.

3. Extended to a person's standing. رَجُلٌ نَوْمَةٌ (rajul nawma) is a man who is inert and unnoticed — obscure, of no account to anyone. The root's idea of stillness is applied here to social presence rather than to sleep itself.

4. Form X — settling into ease. اسْتَنَامَ لِي فُلَانٌ (istanāma lī fulān) is said when someone comes to feel at ease and settles down with another; Ibn Fāris glosses it as اطْمَأَنَّ (became tranquil) and سَكَنَ (grew still) — the same stilling, now of unease.

5. A noun of place/instrument. مَنَامَة (manāma) is the plush napped cloak or coverlet, so named because one sleeps in it.

6. Acknowledged metaphorical uses. Ibn Fāris marks the following explicitly as borrowings (استعارة) from the root's literal sense:
   - نَامَتِ السُّوقُ ("the market slept") — trade went slack, sales stagnated.
   - نَامَ الثَّوْبُ ("the garment slept") — the cloth wore out and became threadbare, its nap gone flat.

The entry is brief and offers no poetic or Qur'anic citations; it records only the derivations above.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-w-n (نون) as a single, unitary root — meaning it does not branch into multiple unrelated senses; everything under it traces to one core idea.

He gives two attested applications:

1. **al-nūn (النُّون)** — "the fish" / "the whale."
2. **Dhū al-Nūn (ذُو النُّون)** — the name of a sword belonging to a particular Arab man, said to be so called because it was likened to (compared in shape to) the nūn, i.e. the fish.

No further senses, grammatical notes, or Qur'anic/poetic citations are given in this entry.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats N-W-Q as a single root whose core idea is height and elevation.

1. Core sense — loftiness, rising high. This is the meaning he assigns to the root as a whole.

2. نِيق (nīq) — the highest point of a mountain, a peak. Morphological note: the middle radical is originally wāw; it turned into yāʾ because of the kasra that precedes it.

3. نَاقَة (nāqa) — the she-camel. He offers this as a possible member of the same pattern, the connection being the animal's tall build. Plural: نُوق (nūq).

4. اسْتَنْوَقَ الْجَمَلُ — "the male camel became like a she-camel." A comparison drawn from the she-camel, used as a proverb for someone brought low after having enjoyed standing and honour.

5. النَّاقَة as a star-name — a group of stars whose arrangement resembles a she-camel.

6. تَنَوَّقَ فِي الْأَمْرِ — to be exacting or take great pains over something. Ibn Fāris explicitly assigns this to the same root, reasoning that Arabs liken a thing to whatever they consider fine, and that this verb is formed by analogy on the noun nāqa, the she-camel being among the most prized of their possessions. He rejects the view of those who call the form تَنَوَّقَ a mistake, holding that the analogy he has given justifies it.

7. النِّيقَة (nīqa) — fastidiousness, refined taste. He states it can derive only from تَنَوُّق.

8. Proverb: "خَرْقَاءُ ذَاتُ نِيقَةٍ" — "a clumsy woman with fastidious taste." Applied to a person who is ignorant of something yet claims expertise in it.

Method note: the entry is etymological rather than doctrinal — Ibn Fāris derives each usage from one underlying image (height/eminence) and defends a disputed verb form on that analogical basis.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَار 145x "the fire"; نُور 43x "the light"; مُّنِير 6x "[the] enlightening"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root ن-و-ر from a single sound origin carrying three linked ideas: giving light, turbulent motion, and instability.

1. Light and fire. النُّور (light) and النَّار (fire) both belong here — named for their illumination, and because fire is restless and quick-moving. The verb تَنَوَّرْتُ النَّارَ means "I looked out for / made out the fire," illustrated by a line of Imruʾ al-Qays about sighting a distant fire from Adhriʿāt.

2. Blossom. النَّوْر (and its plural نُوَّار) is the blossom of trees; أَنَارَتِ الشَّجَرَةُ = "the tree put forth blossom."

3. Morphology of "lighthouse." المَنَارَة is a مَفْعَلَة form from الاسْتِنَارَة (seeking light); its underlying form is مَنْوَرَة.

4. Landmarks. مَنَار الأَرْض = the boundaries and boundary-markers of land, so called because they are clear and conspicuous.

5. Recoiling / instability. From the "instability" sense: امْرَأَةٌ نَوَارٌ is a chaste woman who recoils from what is base (plural نُور); نَارَتْ = "she shied away, took flight" (verbal noun نَوْرًا), with a poetic citation ("Recoiling so quickly, O Farūq?"); نُرْتُ فُلَانًا = "I made him flee"; and النِّوَار/النَّوَار = aversion, flight.

6. An outlier. Ibn Fāris flags النَّؤُور — lampblack/soot used as kohl and for tattooing — as deviating from the root's core sense; related is نَوَّرْتُ اللِّثَةَ, pricking the gum with a needle and setting antimony into it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ن-و-س as a single root whose core sense is agitation and swinging back and forth.

1. Core sense: to swing, dangle, or oscillate. نَاسَ الشَّيْءُ (a thing swung to and fro), imperfect يَنُوسُ.

2. Illustrative name: the poet Abū Nuwās was called this because of two locks of hair that used to swing.

3. A related transitive use: نُسْتُ الْإِبِلَ ("I drove the camels on"), glossed as سُقْتُهَا (I drove them).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ن و ي (n-w-y) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris says this root carries two core meanings: (1) aiming/purposing toward something, and (2) the stone/pit of something.

1. Aim, intention, purpose (النَّوَى / النِّيَّة)
The base sense the philologists give for al-nawā is "moving from one dwelling to another" — i.e. departure or migration. From this base, the whole family of derivatives grew: nawā al-amr means "he set his purpose on/intended the matter."

Supporting this, the phrase nawāhu Allāh ("may God nawā him") is explained as God "directing His aim" toward someone with preservation and care — as in a cited verse asking God to grant someone good nawā "with right guidance."

From the same sense: al-niyyah ("intention") is defined as "the direction you have your aim set on." And nawiyyuka ("your nawiyy") means a companion whose intent matches yours — a fellow traveler heading the same way.

2. The date-stone, and a unit of weight (النَّوَى)
The second, separate root-sense is al-nawā meaning "the pit of a date." This word was also sometimes extended to describe a specific weight: a nawāh was said to equal five dirhams — e.g. "he married her for a nawāh of gold," meaning gold weighing five dirhams.

Appended note: the hamzated word ن-و-ء ("rising")
Ibn Fāris adds — as a separate, hamza-final word — nā'a yanū'u naw'an, "he rose/stood up," illustrated by a verse describing warriors left slain, "their rising feeble." From this:
- al-naw' (a rain-bringing star's rising/setting) is named because it "rises bearing" the rain.
- Anyone straining upward under a heavy load "nā'a" — e.g. a camel rising under its burden.
- Two mirror-image expressions about a woman: her hindquarters "weigh her down" (tanū'u bihā), versus she herself "rises up bearing them" (tanū'u bihā) — same wording, opposite roles (burdened vs. bearing).
- Al-munāwa'ah, "mutual hostility/opposition" between people (nāwa'ahu = "he opposed him"), is explained by the same logic: each side "rises up against" the other, like two people straining against each other's weight.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَخْل 11x "and date-palms"; نَّخِيل 7x "date-palms"; نَّخْلَة 2x "(of) the date-palm"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root n-kh-l from a single core idea: picking a thing out and selecting it.

1. Selecting the best. The verb انتخل (intakhala) means to examine something thoroughly until one takes the finest part of it.

2. The date-palm (نَخْل, singular نَخْلَة). On this author's own reasoning, it is called by this root because it is the noblest of trees that have a trunk — i.e. the "select" or choicest of such trees.

3. Sifting flour. النَّخْل also means sieving flour through a sieve (مُنْخُل); what falls through as residue is نُخَالَة (bran).

4. Palm-shaped ornament. النَّخْل is likewise a type of jewellery fashioned in the shape of a palm-tree, cited with the verse: "she has clothed herself with [ornaments of] arnab and nakhl."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ن خ ر (n-kh-r), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: a kind of sound, from which further senses branch.

1. al-nakhīr — the sound that emerges from the nostrils; the nostrils themselves (al-munkharān) are named for the nakhīr that comes from them; further derived, the two openings of the nose are called al-nukhratān. al-nakhūr — a she-camel that won't yield milk until a finger is inserted into her nostril to provoke her. al-nukhrah — also used simply for "the nose"; and for the sound of wind blowing.
2. Extended to non-anatomical things: shajarah nakhirah (a decayed tree) and ʿaẓm nakhir (a decayed bone) belong to the same root, Ibn Fāris explains, because such things become hollow and wind passing through them produces the same nakhīr-like sound. al-nakhir — anything crumbling/decayed; al-nākhir — anything wind enters and exits, producing a nakhīr — Ibn Fāris affirms all these senses share one underlying analogy.
3. "mā bihā nākhir" — "there is no one [there]" — an idiom using nākhir to mean "anyone who makes a sound."
4. Closing, related word: al-nakhwariyy — a man wide of urethral opening, likened to something wind can enter and pass through with a nukhrah-sound.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib's account of the root n-y-l (نيل):

1. Core sense — النَّيْل (al-nayl): what a person attains or reaches with his hand. Verb: نِلْتُهُ أَنَالُهُ نَيْلًا ("I attained it"). Qur'anic citations: "You will never attain piety" (3:92); "nor do they attain from an enemy any attainment" (9:120); "they did not attain any good" (33:25).

2. Related form النَّوْل (al-nawl): the act of taking or reaching for something. Verb نِلْتُ ... أَنُولُ نَوْلًا. The causative أَنَلْتُهُ means "I made [him] attain it" = "I bestowed it on him." Al-Rāghib draws a parallel pair: عَطَا / تَنَاوَل (to reach for, take) corresponds to أَعْطَى / أَنَال (to give, to make attain).

3. Morphology: نِلْتُ derives from an original نَوِلْتُ (pattern faʿiltu), which was then contracted to filtu.

4. Idiom مَا كَانَ نَوْلُكَ أَنْ تَفْعَلَ كذا ("it was not your nawl to do such") means: doing so holds no نَوَال (benefit) for your welfare or rightness. A poet's line — "I grew anxious, and that is not the nawāl" — is glossed as "not the right course." Al-Rāghib defines the true sense of النَّوَال (al-nawāl) as what one attains by way of a gift or connection (ṣila), and explains the idiom as: this is not conduct from which you attain what you desire.

5. Qur'anic capstone: "Their flesh will not reach God, nor their blood, but the God-consciousness (taqwā) from you reaches Him" (22:37) — using يَنَال in the sense of what reaches or attains to God.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
