text:
Al-Zamakhsharī's Asās al-Balāgha treats the root ن ز ع (n-z-ʿ) in his characteristic way: literal senses first, then a separately flagged figurative (majāz) section. The core physical idea is pulling, drawing, or wresting something out.

LITERAL SENSES:
1. To pull/wrest a thing from someone's hand; to draw it away. A "minzaʿ" is a man strong at drawing.
2. Drawing water: نزع الدلو من البئر (he drew the bucket from the well). A "manzaʿa" is the spot from which one draws (illustrated by a rajaz verse of a man slipping at the drawing-place); a well of "far manzaʿ" has deep water, while a بئر نزوع is drawn by hand because its water is near. To "nāzaʿa" someone at a well is to draw water alongside him.
3. Plucking/pulling up plants: thumām that has been pulled up; "we plucked the herbage for the beast with our hands."
4. Tugging: نازعه الثوب (he tugged the garment against him).
5. Archery: انتزع السهم من الكنانة (he drew the arrow from the quiver); to draw (an arrow) at game; to draw (pull) at one's bow; نوازع = drawing hands. A wordplay pairs nazʿ (drawing bows) with nazw (vaulting onto horses). A bow "twangs like a drawing bow."
6. Horses pulling at the reins — with a verse of al-Nābigha comparing reined horses straining forward to birds fleeing a hailstorm.
7. To desist: نزع عن الأمر (he desisted from the matter). To "istanzaʿa" someone bent on evil is to ask him to desist.
8. A "minzaʿ" is also the far-shooting arrow (with a verse likening a galloping wild ass to such an arrow).
9. أنزع: a man whose temples have gone bald and shiny (the two bald temple-spots are the nazaʿatān); the verb نزع is used of becoming so.

FIGURATIVE SENSES (min al-majāz):
10. Removal from office: نزع الأمير العامل (the emir dismissed the official).
11. Dying: the dying man is "in the nazʿ" — the drawing-out of the soul, the death-throes.
12. Yearning/longing: the soul "nazaʿa" toward a thing (nizāʿ, nuzūʿ); a camel that longs for its home-pastures is nāziʿ / nazūʿ.
13. Being drawn away from one's origin: خيل نزائع (horses that are strangers from another people); نساء نزائع (women married outside their kin); a نزيع / نزيعة is a noble creature of stock from outside one's land; رياح نزائع are cross-winds pulling between two cardinal directions (with a verse of al-Buʿayth).
14. Family resemblance: of a man who takes after his uncles it is said "he drew toward them," "they drew him," "the maternal-uncle vein drew him" — with al-Farazdaq's line to Jarīr that his mother "drew" him to her likeness.
15. Adducing/citing: to "draw forth" a Qur'anic verse for someone; to "draw" with one's proof (bring it forth). Zamakhsharī cites Qur'an "And We drew forth from every community a witness."
16. Withdrawing allegiance: نزع يده من الطاعة (he withdrew his hand from obedience); a rebel is نازع يدٍ (one who withdraws the hand) — with a line of Ibn Muqbil.
17. Disputing/contending: نازعه / تنازعوا (to quarrel, munāzaʿa, nizāʿ); a horse "contends" with its rider for the rein.
18. Passing/handing across: نازعني بنانه (he gave me his fingertips — shook hands), with a verse of al-Rāʿī; تنازعوا الكأس (they passed the cup round); "the cup of slumber" was passed, i.e. drowsiness came on (verse of al-Shammākh).
19. Idioms of finish and outcome: قريب المنزعة = of low (not lofty) ambition; "the matter returned to the nazaʿa" = a right returned to its rightful owner (like "give the bow to its maker"); a drink of good "manzaʿa" = of pleasant aftertaste (maqṭaʿ); a فلاة نزوع = a far-off desert (verse of al-Buʿayth).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root n-z-f, Ibn Faris, Maqayis al-Lugha

Core sense: something running out or being used up entirely, and thereby being cut off.

1. Blood: "his blood was nuzifa" - it all drained out of him.

2. Drunkenness: a drunk man is called nazif, because his reason (aql) has been "drained." A verse of poetry is cited comparing a woman's gait to that of the nazif, the man drained of sense, whom breathlessness fells on a sand dune.

3. Drawing water: al-nazf is drawing water out of a well little by little.

4. Anzafu - two distinct uses: (a) their well's water ran out; (b) their supply of drink ran out.

5. Quranic citation, Surat al-Waqi'ah 56:19: those given the drink described in that passage will not be headached by it, nor will they be yunzifun - will not have their reason drained by it, unlike ordinary wine.

6. Al-nuzfah: a scoop or single draught of water.

7. Idiom: "a sea that is not drained" - said of something inexhaustible.

8. Figurative use in disputation: a man is said to be nuzifa in an argument when his case or evidence has run out - he has nothing left to argue with.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: نَّزَغَ 4x "had caused discord"; نَزْغ 2x "[an evil suggestion]"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-z-gh as carrying one meaning:

1. Core sense: causing spoilage or corruption between two parties — that is, damaging the relationship that holds between them.

2. Attested usage he cites: نَزَغَ بَيْنَ الْقَوْمِ, "he nazagha among the people," glossed as أَفْسَدَ ذَاتَ بَيْنِهِمْ — he ruined the bond or standing that existed between them.

The entry records no further senses, no morphological notes, and no poetic or Qur'anic citations.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَنزَلَ 183x "has been revealed"; نَزَّلَ 62x "sends down"; تَنزِيل 15x "(the) revelation"; نُزُل 8x "(as) a lodging"; تَنَزَّلَتْ 7x "descend"; نَزَلَ 6x "descends"; مُنزِلِين 5x "(of) those who cause to land.'"; مُنزَل 2x "(at) a landing place"; مَنَازِل 2x "phases"; مُنَزِّل 1x "(will) send it down"; مُنَزَّل 1x "(is) sent down"; نَزْلَة 1x "(in) descent"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats n-z-l as a sound root with a single core idea: the descending of a thing and its coming down or settling into place. All the following are branches of that idea:

1. Basic act of coming down: نَزَلَ عَنْ دَابَّتِهِ ("he dismounted from his mount"); نَزَلَ الْمَطَرُ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ نُزُولًا ("the rain came down from the sky").

2. النَّازِلَة (al-nāzila): a severe misfortune of Time that "comes down" upon one — a calamity that befalls.

3. النِّزَال (al-nizāl) in war: the two sides coming down to close with each other in combat.

4. نَزَالِ (nazāli): a fixed word standing in for the imperative "come down! / dismount!"

5. مَكَانٌ نَزِلٌ: a place where people alight or halt often. Related: وَجَدْتُ الْقَوْمَ عَلَى نَزَلَاتِهِمْ = "I found the people at their halting-places (manāzil)" — attributed to Ibn al-Aʿrābī.

6. النُّزُل (al-nuzul): provisions prepared for a lodger/guest. Hence طَعَامٌ ذُو نُزْلٍ وَنَزَلٍ = food of abundance or increase.

7. Applied to pilgrimage: the Arabs express al-Ḥajj by al-nuzūl ("alighting"), and use نَزَلَ to mean "performed the Ḥajj." Two poetic citations illustrate this — one asking whether Asmāʾ is "coming down" (to the pilgrimage), and one where "we alighted" is glossed by the poet himself as "we came to Minā."

8. النُّزَالَة (al-nuzāla): a man's seminal fluid.

9. النَّزِيل (al-nazīl): the guest — with a line of verse making the guest's rights the weightiest, bound up with God's due.

10. التَّنْزِيل (al-tanzīl): arranging a thing and setting it in its proper place/rank (manzila).

Note: Ibn Fāris links Ḥajj to this root only as an Arab idiom of usage ("they express Ḥajj by nuzūl"), not as a doctrinal definition.

dictionary: ʿAyn — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786)
text:
Root ق ش ع ر (Q-SH-ʿ-R) — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786 CE)

1. **A dialect word for "cucumbers."** القُشْعُر (al-qushʿur) is what the people of al-Jawf in Yemen call cucumbers (القِثّاء). The singular is made by adding a tāʾ marbūṭa (one cucumber).

2. **Shuddering of the skin from fear.** القُشَعْريرة (al-qushaʿrīrah) — noted as pronounced with the ʿayn vowelless — names the shivering/goosebumps that come over the skin from fright (fazaʿ) or similar.

3. **General sense: "changed/altered."** Anything that has changed is called مُقْشَعِرّ (muqshaʿirr) — the shuddered, altered thing.

4. **Extended figurative uses of the verb اقشَعَرَّ (iqshaʿarra):**
   - A year "shudders" (اقشَعَرَّتْ) when drought is severe.
   - The earth likewise "shudders" from drought.
   - Skin "shudders" from mange/scabies.
   - A plant "shudders" when it lacks enough water.
   All of these extend the core sense of a surface bristling, contracting, or turning harsh/altered under stress.

5. **A near-synonym given.** القُشَعريرة (al-qushaʿrīrah) is stated to mean the same as الإقشعرار (al-iqshiʿrār) — the shivering/shuddering itself.

**Poetic citation** (poet unnamed in this entry): a verse describes a tent — "the tent of the family of Bayān" — as having become مُقْشَعِرّاً (muqshaʿirran, shriveled/desolate) one morning, with its encampment left empty (ḥayy khalūf) — using the root to picture a dwelling gone barren and abandoned once its people departed.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ق-ذ-ف as a single root whose core idea is throwing and flinging away.

1. Basic verb: قَذَفَ / يَقْذِفُ / قَذْفًا — to throw or hurl something.

2. Applied to distance: بَلْدَةٌ قَذُوفٌ, a "far-flinging" town — remote, so that the journey to it keeps hurling the traveller onward. Likewise مَنْزِلٌ قَذَفٌ / قَذِيفٌ, a distant halting-place.

3. Of a camel: نَاقَةٌ مَقْذُوفَةٌ بِاللَّحْمِ — a she-camel well covered with flesh, as if the flesh had been thrown onto her.

4. Of speed: الْقِذَافُ is swiftness of pace in travelling; a فَرَسٌ مُتَقَاذِفٌ is a fast-running horse, as though it flings itself forward as it runs.

5. Of terrain (placed by him under the same head): أَقْذَافُ الْجَبَلِ, the flanks or sides of a mountain; singular قَذَفٌ.

6. The noun of the thing thrown: الْقَذِيفَةُ, a projectile. He cites an unattributed line: "A missile of a driven-off shayṭān, which he hurled — and it became a growth in the jaw-glands of an aged she-camel," glossing ضَوَاة as a wen or swelling and ضِرْزِم as an old she-camel.

7. Of the body: قَذَفَ also means "he vomited" — as though he threw the matter out.

The method throughout is Ibn Fāris's usual one: assert a single semantic origin (throwing/casting), then show each usage — distance, bulk, speed, mountain flanks, projectile, vomiting — as an extension of that one act, each justified by a "as though it were thrown" paraphrase.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris says qāf and ḍād form three root meanings: the falling of a thing, roughness in a thing, and a perforation in a thing.

1. **Falling.** Inqaḍḍa is said of a wall that comes down, and inqiḍāḍ of a bird dropping down in its flight.

2. **Roughness.** A dirʿ qaḍḍāʾ is a coat of mail rough to the touch, not yet worn smooth. Ibn Fāris traces this sense to al-qiḍḍa, low-lying ground with sandy soil beside a stretch of hard ground. To the same group belong al-qaḍaḍ, broken fragments of stone, and from it al-qaḍqaḍa, the breaking of bones (a bone-crunching lion is asad qaḍqāḍ). Here too is al-qaḍḍ, earth or grit lying on bedding: aqaḍḍa ʿalayhi maḍjaʿuhu means "his bed turned gritty under him", as in Abū Dhuʾayb's line, "What ails your body, that it rests easy in no bed, but that bed turns gritty under you?" Laḥm qaḍḍ is meat that has got earth on it while roasting.

Ibn Fāris adds, as his own view, that the phrase jāʾū bi-qaḍḍihim wa-qaḍīḍihim belongs to this group as well: "they came with a large, rough company". He cites Aws: "Jiḥāsh came, the whole of them, as numerous as they had ever been."

3. **Perforation.** Qaḍaḍtu al-luʾluʾa means "I pierced the pearl", and from this comes iqtiḍāḍ al-bikr, the deflowering of a virgin. He reports this from al-Shaybānī.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ق ض ب (q-ḍ-b), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: cutting/removing a thing.

1. qaḍabtu al-shayʾa — I cut something off. A report describes the Prophet cutting a cross-pattern out of any garment he saw it woven into. inqaḍaba al-najmu — a star "cut away"/shot from its place, illustrated with a line of poetry by Dhū al-Rummah about a streaking star.
2. al-qaḍīb — a branch/twig; al-qaḍb — green fodder (lucerne), named because it is regularly cut (quḍiba); al-maqāḍib — lands that grow this fodder. qaḍabtu al-karma — I trimmed a vine's branches in spring. sayf qāḍib/qaḍīb — a sharp-cutting sword; rajul qaḍḍābah — a decisive man, capable of "cutting through" matters. quḍābat al-karm — the trimmings that fall away when a vine is pruned.
3. Figurative extension: iqtaḍaba fulānun al-ḥadīth — to improvise speech on the spot, as though "cutting it off" without prior deliberation. Also borrowed for: nāqah qaḍīb — a she-camel ridden before being broken in/trained ("cut into" premature use); iqtaḍabtuhā — I so rode her.
4. Closing: Qaḍīb — the name of a valley. Ibn Fāris ends with "and God knows best."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: قَضَىٰ 59x "he decrees"; مَّقْضِيّ 2x "decreed.'"; قَاض 1x "(are) decreeing"; قَاضِيَة 1x "the end"
poets_named: Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam); al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ق-ض-ي (qāf, ḍād, weak final letter) as one sound root whose core sense is settling a matter firmly, perfecting it, and carrying it through to its proper end. From this single core he derives the following:

1. To complete / perfect. Citing Qur'an 41:12, "So He completed them as seven heavens in two days," he glosses qaḍāhunna as "He made firm / perfected their creation." A verse of Abū Dhuʾayb uses qaḍāhumā of two coats of mail "fashioned" by David or by the armourer Tubbaʿ — here the sense is "made/wrought."

2. Judgement (al-qaḍāʾ = al-ḥukm). He cites the Qur'anic phrase "So decree what you would decree," glossing it as "do and judge." From this he explains why the qāḍī (judge) bears that title: because he settles rulings and puts them into effect — the same core notion of firmly carrying a matter through.

3. Death (al-maniyya) called qaḍāʾ. Death is named qaḍāʾ because it is a decree executed upon humankind and the rest of creation. He cites al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza, where spears whose points are "al-qaḍāʾ" means death.

Method note: Ibn Fāris states that every word in this section follows the analogy (qiyās) he has laid out — all trace back to the one core sense.

Hamzated variant (meaning shift): when the root is hamzated, the sense changes entirely. al-quḍʾa then means a defect or blemish — as in "there is no fault upon you from it" and "in his eye there is a quḍʾa," i.e. corruption/damage.

dictionary: Ṣiḥāḥ — al-Ṣiḥāḥ, al-Jawharī (d. 1003)
quran_words: قَعَدَ 12x "sit"; قَاعِد 7x "the ones who sit"; مَقْعَد 4x "in their staying"; قُعُود 4x "and sitting"; قَوَاعِد 3x "the foundations"; قَعِيد 1x "seated"
poets_named: al-Kumayt (Umayyad); Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam); ʿAbdallāh b. Awfā al-Khuzāʿī (Umayyad); Durayd; al-Aʿshā (pre-Islamic); al-Nābigha (pre-Islamic)
text:
Root ق ع د (q-ʿ-d), from al-Jawharī's al-Ṣiḥāḥ. Core meaning: to sit.

1. Verb: qaʿada (verbal nouns quʿūd, maqʿad) = "he sat"; aqʿada = to seat/make another sit. al-qaʿda = a single act of sitting; al-qiʿda (with kasra) = a mode or manner of sitting. al-maqʿada = the posterior/buttocks. Dhū al-Qaʿda = a month-name (plural dhawāt al-qaʿda).

2. Extended "settling/being seated" senses: a vulture "sits" = roosts (qaʿadat al-rakhma); a palm-shoot "sits" = grows a trunk; a "sitting" palm-tree is one low enough for the hand to reach.

3. Of women, al-qāʿid = one past childbearing and menstruation (plural al-qawāʿid). Of the Khārijites, al-qāʿid = those who hold back from fighting (plural al-qaʿad, like ḥāris/ḥaras); also said of people with no place on the stipend-register (dīwān). al-qaʿad also = slackness/lowness in a camel's pastern.

4. Architectural/structural: qawāʿid al-bayt = a building's foundations; qawāʿid al-hawdaj = the four crosspieces at the base of a camel-litter.

5. "Holding back / hindering" forms: taqaʿʿada ʿan al-amr = to fail to pursue a matter; taqāʿada bihi = to withhold someone's due; taqaʿʿadtuhu = I held him back and hindered him ("nothing kept me from you but being occupied"). A quʿada ḍujaʿa man = one much given to sitting and lying about.

6. al-qaʿūd (camel): a young male (bakr) grown ridable — from about age two until it becomes thanī, after which it is a jamal; a young female is not qaʿūd but qalūṣ. Abū ʿUbayda: the qaʿūd is the herdsman's all-purpose errand-camel (Persian "rakht"). Hence the proverb "they made him qaʿīd al-ḥājāt" (their errand-drudge). Variant qudʿa (with ḍamma) for the mount, as in "what an excellent mount." Cited: al-Kumayt (describing his she-camel).

7. al-maqāʿid = sitting-places in markets etc. "He is to me at the midwife's seat" = extremely close (clinging from the front).

8. al-qaʿīd: (a) saddles/camel-saddles (qaʿīdāt); (b) one who sits with you, a companion — as in Qur'an 50:17, "on the right and on the left a qaʿīd (seated one)," where the two are called qaʿīds. al-Jawharī notes that faʿīl and faʿūl patterns take one form for singular, dual, and plural (comparing Qur'an 26:16 "we are the messenger of your Lord" and 66:4 "the angels are supporters"). (c) locusts with wings not yet grown; (d) qaʿīda = a sack (ghirāra; cited: Abū Dhuʾayb); (e) qaʿīda of sand = a dune that is not elongated; (f) qaʿīdat al-rajul (also qiʿād) = a man's wife (cited: ʿAbdallāh b. Awfā al-Khuzāʿī); (g) qaʿīd of game = quarry that comes from behind you, opposite of naṭīḥ which comes head-on (cited: Abū ʿUbayda).

9. Oath formula: qaʿīdaka / qaʿīdaka llāh / qaʿdaka llāh "lā ātīka" — an Arab oath, accusative verbal nouns governed by an implied verb, meaning "by your companion, the companion of every private converse," parallel to nashadtuka llāh ("I adjure you by God").

10. Disease/defect senses: al-iqʿād / al-quʿād = an ailment in camels' haunches that tips them earthward; al-iqʿād in a horse's leg = extreme bowing that won't straighten; al-muqʿad = a lame man (verb uqʿida); al-muqʿad of a breast = firm and swelling, not yet drooping (cited: al-Nābigha).

11. Genealogy: quʿdud = a man few generations removed from the great ancestor (close in descent). ʿAbd al-Ṣamad b. ʿAlī was called "the quʿdud of Banū Hāshim." The term cuts both ways: praise, since seniority-right (walāʾ) attaches to the eldest line; and dispraise, since it implies descent from the aged and hence weakness (cited: Durayd; al-Aʿshā).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) treats ق-ع-ر (q-ʿ-r) as a single sound root whose core meaning is a hollow going downward — depth, a bottom, a low-lying cavity in something.

1. **Physical depth/bottom.** The base sense: qaʿr = the bottom of a thing.
   - qaʿru al-biʾr — the bottom (depth) of a well
   - qaʿru al-ināʾ — the bottom of a vessel
   - qaṣʿah qaʿīrah — a deep bowl/dish

2. **Affected, "deep" speech (form II, qaʿʿara).** Said of a man who "qaʿʿara" in his talk: he stretched/distended his jaws (shaddaqa) — i.e., he spoke in an affected, pompous, mouth-filling manner, reaching for deep or ostentatious words.

3. **A term of censure for a woman (imraʾah qaʿirah).** The entry records this as "a bad description relating to intercourse" — a critical/deficient designation, without further elaboration of the physical referent.

4. **Uprooting (form VII, inqaʿara).** A tree that "inqaʿarat min arūmatihā" was torn out from its root-stock — synonymous with inqalaʿat ("it was uprooted").

The entry cites no Qurʾānic or poetic shawāhid; all four uses are given simply as attested idiomatic sayings (yuqālu).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris's Maqayis al-Lugha derives the root q-h-m from a single core meaning: entering or plunging into something abruptly, with roughness and rash boldness.

1. The verb qahama - qahama fi l-umuri (he plunged into affairs) means he threw himself into matters with no prior experience or training.

2. Quham al-tariq - the hardships or rough stretches of a road.

3. Al-maqahim (camels) - stud camels that force their own way into a herd of she-camels on their own initiative, rather than being deliberately let in by their owner. The underlying image is the same: barging in uninvited.

4. Al-qahm - a camel whose dental age-stages come too close together, shedding its second and third sets of teeth within a single year, so that one stage plunges prematurely upon the next - again, things arriving out of proper sequence, forced together.

5. Qahhama (of a horse) - a horse that throws its rider face-first to the ground is said to qahhama him.

6. A saying about disputes - litigation has its quham, meaning a quarrel can force a person headlong into outcomes he never wanted.

7. Al-quhmah - a drought year severe enough to force the Bedouin off the open steppe and into the settled, cultivated lands (al-rif).

Across all these uses the common thread is the same: something or someone being driven or thrown abruptly into a state, place, or situation it did not choose gradually or willingly.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: قَصَّ 20x "we relate"; قَصَص 6x "the story"; قِصَاص 4x "(is) retribution"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-ṣ-ṣ as a sound root with one core meaning: following something step by step, tracking it.

1. **Tracking a trail.** اقْتَصَصْتُ الْأَثَرَ, "I followed the track," is his first illustration of the core meaning.

2. **Retaliation (al-qiṣāṣ).** The term for retaliation in cases of wounding comes from the same idea: the offender has done to him exactly what he did to the first person, so the retaliation "follows his track."

3. **Story and narrative (al-qiṣṣa, al-qaṣaṣ).** A story or narration is something followed point by point and then told.

4. **The breast (al-qaṣṣ).** Ibn Fāris holds that this word also fits the root, because the breastbone's bones are evenly matched, each seeming to follow the next.

5. **Clipping hair (qaṣaṣtu al-shaʿr).** Cutting hair evens each strand with its neighbour, so each seems to follow the other along the same line. Related terms: quṣāṣ al-shaʿr, the front edge of the hairline, which he says fits the root; and al-quṣṣa, the forelock.

6. **A trailing camel (al-qaṣīṣiyya).** A camel that follows in the track of the riding-camels.

7. **Bringing near to death (aqaṣṣahu).** "He struck him and aqaṣṣahu" means he brought him close to death, explained as the victim now "following the track" of death.

8. **Granting retaliation.** When the ruler has an offender killed in retaliation (qawad) on someone's behalf, one says the ruler aqaṣṣa that person from the offender.

**Words he treats as outside the root.** Ibn Fāris lists several words as anomalous, not fitting the core meaning: aqaṣṣat al-shāt, "the ewe's pregnancy became visible"; al-qaṣqāṣ, which people say means the lion; al-quṣquṣa, a short man; and al-qaṣīṣ, a kind of plant.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)

text:
Ibn Sīda's entry on the root q-ṣ-d (ق ص د) in al-Muḥkam. He gathers the material under several distinct heads.

1. Straightness of a road. al-qaṣd is "the straightness of the road." He reads the Qur'anic phrase "and upon God is the qaṣd of the road" as meaning that it is upon God to make the straight road to Him plain by proofs and demonstrations. A ṭarīq qāṣid is an easy, straight road; a safar qāṣid is an easy, short journey — as in the verse "had it been a near gain and an easy journey (safaran qāṣidan) they would have followed you."

2. Purposing, heading for. qaṣada / yaqṣidu / qaṣdan: to aim at, make for, rely on; also qaṣada lahu. aqṣadanī ilayhi l-amr = "the matter directed me toward him." huwa qaṣdaka (or quṣdaka) = "he is facing you"; Ibn Sīda notes the word is used as a noun more often than otherwise.

3. Moderation. qaṣd in a matter is "the opposite of excess." Verb iqtaṣada. He cites the ḥadīth "no moderate man (muqtaṣid) has become poor, nor will he." A man is described as qaṣd or muqtaṣid; the well-attested form maqṣid describes someone neither bulky nor slight of build.

4. Of bodies. al-qaṣda of women: the tall, fully formed woman whom no one sees without admiring. al-maqṣada: one tending to shortness. A laylatun qāṣida of travel is a night's stage with neither fatigue nor delay.

5. The qaṣīda (formal poem). qaṣīd is poetry whose lines are metrically complete — named for its completeness and sound metre. Ibn Jinnī's explanation: it is called qaṣīd because it was "aimed at and relied upon," even though shorter, less regular forms such as ramal and rajaz are also deliberately composed; the point is that complete, full verse ranked higher with the Arabs, so they reserved the name "intended, aimed-at" for the long and full sort. Plural qaṣāʾid; the form qaṣīda also occurs, plural qaṣāʾid and qaṣīd. When a single poem is called al-qaṣīd without the feminine -a, Ibn Jinnī explains it as a generic noun applied to an individual by extension, like saying "I went out, and there was the lion," or "I ate the bread."

6. Composing poems. qaṣṣada l-shāʿir / aqṣada: to compose at length, to keep making qaṣīdas. A rajaz citation ends "…they defeated our muqaṣṣid and our rajjāz." Grammatical note: the form here written as mufʿil is to be understood as mufaʿʿil, the doubled form marking repeated action — proved by its being paired with rajjāz, which is faʿʿāl, a pattern set for frequency (unlike muḥsin, mujmil and the like, which have no doubled middle radical and no sense of multiplicity).

7. How long is a qaṣīda? Al-Akhfash held there is no qaṣīda of fewer than three lines, thus making three lines sufficient. Ibn Jinnī considered this a licence: customarily a piece of three, ten, or fifteen lines is called a qiṭʿa, and only what exceeds that do the Arabs call a qaṣīda. Al-Akhfash elsewhere identified qaṣīd with ṭawīl and the complete forms of basīṭ, kāmil, madīd, wāfir and rajaz — meaning the fullest forms actually in use (the first two ḍarbs of each), since their theoretical forms in the metrical circles are not used.

8. The root's core sense. Ibn Jinnī: the underlying sense of q-ṣ-d in Arabic is resolve, turning toward, setting out and rising toward something — whether the aim is even or deviant. That is its reality, even though in some contexts it is specialised to aiming at straightness rather than swerving. One may aim at wrongdoing (jawr) just as one aims at justice (ʿadl); "resolve and turning toward" covers both.

9. Breaking. A separate sense: qaṣd is breaking, in any manner; some say breaking in half. qaṣadtuhu; intensive qaṣṣadtuhu, with the reflexives inqaṣada and taqaṣṣada. A citation from Thaʿlab compares a kneeling she-camel's leg-bones to "broken reed-pipes," likening her sound to reed-pipes. qiṣda: a broken-off piece; a rumḥ qaṣid or qaṣīd is a broken spear. A qiṣda of bone is a third or quarter of the thigh, forearm, shank or shoulder-blade. qaṣada / qaṣṣada l-mukhkh: to break marrow-bone and divide it up (inqaṣadat, taqaṣṣadat).

10. Marrow and fat. qaṣīd (singulative qaṣīda) is thick, fat marrow; a bone that has marrow is ʿaẓm qaṣīd — with Thaʿlab's line, "the bone before was qaṣīd," i.e. full of marrow (or, alternatively, "possessing marrow"). A she-camel that is fat and has niqy (marrow) is nāqa qaṣīd or qaṣīda, with a citation from Ibn al-Aʿrābī. qaṣīd also means dried meat — al-Akhṭal: "your provision there will be the dried flesh of the camels."

11. Neck. al-qaṣada = the neck, plural aqṣād, on Kurāʿ's authority; Ibn Sīda flags the plural as anomalous (afʿāl as plural of faʿala works only by discarding an augment) and notes that the usual word is al-qaṣara.

12. Plant growth. al-qaṣd, al-qiṣd and al-quṣd (the last from Abū Ḥanīfa) all denote the fresh shoots of ʿiḍāh (thorn-trees) — their buds and tender growth before it hardens. Verbs aqṣadat / qaṣṣadat al-ʿiḍāh. Abū Ḥanīfa: this growth appears in autumn when the nights turn cold, without rain. qaṣīd likewise means such fresh shoots (Abū Ḥanīfa), with a verse on "shady thickets whose fresh growth glistens."

13. Sudden death. al-iqtiṣād: to strike or shoot something so that it dies on the spot. al-muqṣad: one who falls ill and then dies quickly.

14. Compelling. qaṣadahu qaṣdan: he compelled him (qasarahu).

15. A staff. al-qaṣīd is the staff, so called because a person is directed by it — it guides and aims him; cited with al-Aʿshā's line about a man whose guide in the land is the butt of a spear-shaft.

16. A plant name. al-qaṣad = the ʿawsaj (boxthorn), in Yemeni usage.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
text:
Root ق ص ف (q-ṣ-f) — from Asās al-Balāgha by al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144 CE)

**Core sense — breaking, snapping.**
1. *qaṣafa l-qanāta wa-l-ʿūd* — "he broke" a reed or a wood-stick (kasarahu). It can also be said intransitively (*fa-qaṣafa*, "it broke") or with the reflexive form *inqaṣafa*, "it snapped/broke apart."
2. *qaṣafa ẓahrahu* — "his back was broken"; a *maqṣūf al-ẓahr* is a "broken-backed man."
3. A violent wind (*ʿaṣafat*) is said to have "broken/wrecked" a ship (*qaṣafat al-safīnah*).
4. *ʿūd qaṣif* — a stick that is brittle, quick to break. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ is cited using this image of Tamīm: they talk boldly of war but, when it comes, are "brittle as canes," their weakness showing.
5. Intensive form: *qaṣṣafahu* — "he shattered it," *taqaṣṣafa* — "it shattered/broke apart." A *ramḥ muqaṣṣaf* is a splintered spear. An anonymous verse is cited contrasting the hard *nabʿ*-wood, used for bows, with the castor plant (*kharwaʿ*), which shatters easily — illustrating strong vs. brittle wood.
6. *qaṣīf al-shajar* — the dead, broken-off wood/twigs (*hashīm*) of a tree.

**Figurative extension (majāz).**
7. A *rajul qaṣif* — figuratively, "a man who breaks quickly" — describes someone whose courage/resolve gives way fast, i.e. not steadfast under pressure.
8. *thawb qaṣīf* — a narrow-width garment; al-Zamakhsharī notes this usage is known only from what was heard directly from the Arabs (*samāʿī*), not derived by analogy.
9. Said of a group who abandon something out of poverty and helplessness: "they have *inqaṣafū* [broken away] from it."

**Crowd-surge / rush.**
10. *qaṣfat al-nās* — "the crowd-push of people," their surging press. Al-ʿAjjāj is cited using the phrase for the crowd surging — the author explains the poet means the crowd pouring forth from ʿArafah [i.e., the mass departure at the end of the standing there].
11. *inqaṣafū ʿalaynā inqiṣāfan* — "they surged/rushed upon us." *inqaṣafa l-ziḥām ʿalā l-bāb* — "the crush surged at the door."

**Loud, crashing sound.**
12. *qaṣafa al-raʿd* — thunder's loud crashing sound, as if the sky itself were breaking apart.
13. *qaṣafa al-baʿīr al-hādir* — a roaring camel's crashing bellow; a *faḥl qaṣṣāf al-hadīr* is a stallion camel with a thunderous roar. Al-ʿAjjāj is cited describing dread of such a beast's silencing roar, adding that this stallion is one that passes through two stages of dental maturity (*thanniya*, *irbāʿ*) within a single year — i.e., matures unusually fast.
14. From the same idea of sticks cracking/snapping (*qaṣafat al-ʿīdān*) comes *al-qaṣf*: dancing accompanied by noisy clamor — revelry. "I saw them *yaqṣifūna wa-yalʿabūn*" — reveling and playing.
15. *taqaṣṣafa al-qawm* — a group made an uproar/clamored, in a dispute or a threat. Al-Kumayt is cited: a rabble of lowly folk clamored around "us," as though we were from the tribes Juhayna or Jasr — tribes of low standing, so the line conveys the contempt of the jeering crowd.
16. *rajul qaṣṣāf* — a loud-voiced man.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs entry for the root ق-ص-م (q-ṣ-m):

1. Core sense: the root is a single, sound (unweakened) root meaning "breaking" (al-kasr). Verb: qaṣamtu al-shay' qaṣman — "I broke the thing."

2. Derived noun: al-quṣam — a man who smashes/breaks whatever he comes across (an intensive or habitual-agent noun pattern).

3. Qur'anic citation (his sole shāhid): Q21:11, wa-kam qaṣamnā min qaryatin kānat ẓālimatan — "How many a wrongdoing town We qaṣamnā [broke]." Ibn Fāris explains — qualifying it with "God knows best" — that God's actual intent here is destruction (ihlāk), but the verse expresses that destruction through the vocabulary of breaking (al-kasr). In other words, qaṣm functions as the verse's chosen expression for ihlāk, not a separate sense.

4. Unrelated look-alikes: al-qaṣīmah and al-qayṣūm are simply the names of two plants, noted in passing with no further explanation.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: قَصْر 4x "palaces"; قَٰصِرَٰت 3x "(will be) companions of modest gaze"; تَقْصُرُ 1x "you shorten"; يُقْصِرُ 1x "they cease"; مُقَصِّرِين 1x "and shortened"; مَّقْصُورَٰت 1x "restrained"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives قصر (q-ṣ-r) from two sound roots that lie close together: (1) a thing's falling short of its full extent, and (2) confinement or restraint.

FIRST ROOT — falling short:
1. al-qiṣar = shortness, the opposite of length ("he is short, of evident shortness").
2. Transitive: qaṣṣara — "I shortened the garment or the rope."
3. qaṣr al-ṣalāt = shortening the prayer, i.e. not completing it because of travel; cited from Q "there is no blame upon you that you shorten of the prayer."
4. al-quṣayrā = the lowest rib (also called the "frail one"); and, separately, a viper — so named for its shortness.
5. aqṣarat al-shāt = the ewe aged until its teeth-tips grew short; aqṣarat al-marʾa = a woman bore short children.
6. Figurative "falling short": qaṣṣara fī l-amr = to be remiss/slack; qaṣara ʿanhu = to be unable to reach it; aqṣara ʿanhu = to desist from something one is still capable of doing (with a verse of poetry on the heart "desisting").
All of these share one logic: not reaching a thing's limit and end.

SECOND ROOT — confinement (ḥabs):
1. qaṣartuhu = "I confined/imprisoned him"; maqṣūr = confined; cited from Q "houris confined (maqṣūrāt) in the pavilions" [55:72].
2. qāṣirat al-ṭarf = a woman who restrains her gaze, not extending it beyond her husband, as if confining the gaze; cited from Q "in them are those restraining the gaze."
3. quṣārāka / qaṣruka = the utmost you limit yourself to — i.e. what you confine yourself upon.
4. maqṣūra (pl. maqāṣir) = a walled-off quarter of a large house (Ibn Fāris notes this could belong to the first root instead).
5. farasun qaṣīr = a mare kept close and not let out to graze freely because she is prized (with a supporting verse); likewise jāriya qaṣīra / qaṣūra = a secluded girl.
6. al-tiqṣār = a choker-like necklace, as though "confined" at the neck (with a supporting verse).
7. qaṣr al-ẓalām = the gathering of darkness at evening (maqāṣir al-ẓalām); the time is called al-maqṣara (pl. maqāṣir). This too can be read under the "confinement" logic: darkness confines one from moving about.

DEVIATING FROM BOTH:
al-qaṣar (sing. qaṣara) = the base of the neck, and the base/thick part of a tree; cited with the variant reading "it throws up sparks like the qaṣar [trunks]" [77:32]. Also a disease affecting the neck-base. "And God knows best."

dictionary: ʿAyn — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786)
quran_words: أَقْصَا 3x "(the) farthest end"; قُصْوَىٰ 1x "the farther"; قَصِيّ 1x "remote"
text:
Kitāb al-ʿAyn treats this under the chapter of qāf and ṣād with the weak letters, listing four permutations in use: q-ṣ-w, w-q-ṣ, q-y-ṣ, ṣ-y-q.

**قصو (q-ṣ-w)**

1. **Cropping a camel's ear.** al-qaṣw is cutting a camel's ear; a she-camel so marked is قَصْواء (qaṣwāʾ), a male camel مَقْصُوّ (maqṣūw). The entry notes that by analogy the masculine should have been أَقْصَى (aqṣā), but Arabs did not in fact use that form. The verb قَصَوْتُ الأذن means to cut a piece off the ear's tip.

2. **Withdrawing / being far off.** قَصَا – يَقْصُو – قُصُوّاً is to move away or stand apart, said of anything. القاصية (al-qāṣiya) describes both people and places that are remote and set apart. The participle is قاصٍ (qāṣin), "far off."

3. **Grammatical note on the superlative and the wāw/yāʾ shift.** The forms القُصْوَى (fem.) and الأَقْصَى (masc.) pair like الكُبْرَى / الأَكْبَر. Normally a fuʿlā form built from a wāw-final root turns its wāw into yāʾ — as الدنيا from دنوت ("draw near") — but القُصْوَى is the exception, keeping the wāw, with القُصْيَا existing only as an alternative dialectal usage. The text offers a parallel: الفُتْيَا beside الفُتْوَى, which it attributes specifically to the people of Medina.

4. **The forecourt of a house.** القَصَا (short final alif; some lengthen it, القَصَاء) is the open space in front of a dwelling. Cited verse: "They circled about us at a distance, though they had seen us close by, where whispered speech can be overheard."

**وقص (w-q-ṣ)**

1. Shortness of neck, as if the neck were sunk back into the chest cavity: a man is أَوْقَص, a woman وَقْصاء.
2. وَقَصْتُ رأسه — to press or squeeze a head hard, sometimes hard enough to break the neck.
3. Used of animals: a beast "waqṣ-es" flies off itself with its tail, striking and killing them; and beasts break the tops of hillocks with their hooves.

**قيص (q-y-ṣ)** — قاصَتِ السنُّ (or انقاصَتْ): a tooth works loose.

**صيق (ṣ-y-q)** — الصِّيق (also صِيقَة) is dust swirling in the air. Ruʾba: "it leaves the soil of the deserts with its dust-clouds driven wild." Another line: "as an ʿuwwār swoops down beneath the dust-cloud" — the ʿAyn glosses ʿuwwār here as the bat.

poets_named: al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); al-Hudhalī (lived into Islam); unnamed verse ×2
text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-ṭ-ʿ as a single sound root meaning severing and separating one thing from another. From this core he derives:

1. Basic act: قَطَعَ / قَطْع — to cut something.

2. Cutting social ties: الْقَطِيعَة is estrangement; تَقَاطَعَ الرَّجُلَانِ = two men break off relations. An أُقْطُوعَة is a token one woman sends another to signal a rupture.

3. A "piece" of time: الْقِطْع (kasra) is a portion of the night.

4. Migration: قَطَعَتِ الطَّيْرُ = birds migrate, moving from cold lands to hot or vice versa.

5. الْقَطِيع (one sense): a whip — cited from al-Aʿshā.

6. Granting land: أَقْطَعَ = to grant someone a fief, seen as a portion "cut off" from a territory.

7. Despair: قُطِعَ بِهِ is said of one who despairs, as if his hope were severed.

8. Crossing: قَطَعَ النَّهْرَ = to cross a river.

9. Cutting plants/wood: أَقْطَعَ = to permit cutting vine-shoots; الْقَضِيب is a tree-piece from which arrows are whittled (plural aqṭuʿ), with a shāhid from al-Hudhalī.

10. Sufficiency for cutting: هَذَا الثَّوْبُ يُقْطِعُكَ قَمِيصًا = this cloth is enough to cut you a shirt.

11. مُقَطِّعَةُ النِّيَاطِ ("cutter of heart-strings"): said to be the hare, because it "cuts the heart-strings" of the pursuing birds of prey; alternatively al-niyāṭ = the vast stretch of desert.

12. Outstripping: قَطَّعَ الْفَرَسُ الْخَيْلَ = a horse leaves the others behind — Ibn Fāris links this to the hare's name above. The augmented form مُقْطَوْطِعَات = horses coming swiftly.

13. Being "cut off from" an act: جَارِيَةٌ قَطِيعُ الْقِيَامِ = a girl too plump to rise easily. مُنْقَطِعُ الْقَرِينِ = peerless (in generosity, etc.).

14. Qurʾānic note: on {ثُمَّ لِيَقْطَعْ} [al-Ḥajj 15], he reports an exegesis reading it as self-strangulation (al-ikhtināq), and judges the analogy to the root sound.

15. Where something ends: مُنْقَطَعُ/مَقْطَعُ الرَّمْلِ = where sand ends; مَقَاطِعُ الْأَوْدِيَة = the lower ends of valleys.

16. A "portion" of livestock: الْقَطِيع = part of a flock of sheep.

17. Short garments: الْمُقَطَّعَات = short clothes (with a ḥadīth citation); also used of short pieces of verse.

18. الْقُطْع = shortness of breath/panting.

19. Diminished well: قُطْع striking a well = its water dropping.

20. الْقِطَع (kasra) = a saddle-rug, named because the weaver "cuts it off" when finished (compared to calling a garment jadīd, "new," as if just made); plural quṭūʿ, with a shāhid.

21. الْقِطْع = the broad arrowhead, as if "cut" when whittled.

Outlier: Ibn Fāris flags الْقُطَيْعَاء, a kind of date, as deviating from the root's meaning, with a supporting verse.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-ṭ as a sound root (aṣl ṣaḥīḥ) meaning "cutting a thing quickly, crosswise". He fits most of its words to that idea, sets the word for a cat aside as an exception, and holds that qaṭ "enough" does not belong to the root at all.

1. **Cutting across.** Qaṭaṭtu l-shayʾa aquṭṭuhu qaṭṭan means "I cut the thing across". The qaṭṭāṭ is the turner (kharrāṭ) who makes small boxes (ḥuqaq), as though he cuts them; a quoted half-line speaks of "the cutting (taqṭīṭ) of boxes".

2. **al-qiṭqiṭ, drizzle.** Al-qiṭqiṭ is drizzle (radhādh). Ibn Fāris ties it to the root because rain this slight seems broken into pieces.

3. **qaṭaṭ hair.** Hair that is qaṭaṭ contracts and draws in on itself, the opposite of sabṭ (lank, straight hair), as though it had been cut. One says of a man that his hair is qaṭiṭ; this form, with its two ṭs kept apart rather than merged, is one of the rare words that show their doubling.

4. **al-qiṭṭ, a written deed.** Al-qiṭṭ is said to be the written deed (ṣakk) for a gift (jāʾiza). Ibn Fāris is tentative here: if the word belongs to the root's pattern, it is perhaps because the material written on is cut. Al-Aʿshā uses the plural, quṭūṭ, in a line on King al-Nuʿmān "giving out the quṭūṭ" on the day the poet met him. Q 38:16, "Our Lord, hasten to us our qiṭṭ before the Day of Reckoning", is explained by this sense: those who said it meant, as it were, the documents of reward they are given in the Hereafter.

5. **al-qiṭṭa, the cat (an exception).** Al-qiṭṭa, the cat (sinnawra), is listed among the words that stand apart from the root's meaning. The word is said to apply to the female, not the male.

6. **qaṭ, "enough", from another word.** Qaṭ in the sense of ḥasb, "enough", is not from this root in Ibn Fāris's view: it is qad with the d replaced by ṭ. He cites Ṭarafa for qad ("when 'Gently!' is said, his companion says qadi, 'enough'"). With the ṭ one says qaṭī, qaṭka and qaṭnī, as in the recited line "The basin filled up and said: qaṭnī, enough for me; gently, you have filled my belly." Speakers also say qaṭāṭi, "enough for me".

7. **qaṭṭu, "never".** In mā raʾaytu mithlahu qaṭṭu, "I have never seen the like of him", Ibn Fāris explains qaṭṭu as "I cut off the talk on this", adding that it is said ʿalā jihat al-imkān, "by way of possibility". The word is used only of the past.

text:
Root: q-ṭ-f (ق ط ف) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core sense: taking/picking fruit off a tree.

1. Basic verb: qaṭafa = "he picked (fruit)." Example: qaṭaftu ath-thamarata aqṭifuhā qaṭfan, "I picked the fruit, I pick it — a picking."

2. Noun qiṭf = a cluster or bunch (e.g. of grapes).

3. aqṭafa al-karmu = "the vine's picking-time drew near" — i.e. the vine became ready for harvest.

4. quṭāfah = the gleanings — what falls or drops from what has already been picked.

5. Extended sense (animal gait): applied to a riding beast, qaṭafa describes a short, stumbling stride; such an animal is called qaṭūf. The image is that, moving its legs quickly, it seems to "pluck" at the ground with each step.

6. Extended sense (scratching): qaṭf can also mean a scratch or scrape — Ibn Fāris judges the sense "close" to the root's core meaning. He illustrates this with a line of verse: "but your patron's face scratches" (walākinna wajha mawlāka taqṭifu).

text:
Root: q-t-m-r (qitmir)
Dictionary: al-Mufradat fi Gharib al-Qur'an, al-Raghib al-Isfahani (early 11th c. CE)

Al-Raghib's entire discussion of this root is built around a single Qur'anic citation: "And those you call upon besides Him do not possess so much as a qitmir" (Fatir 35:13).

He glosses qitmir as: the thin streak or mark on the back of a date-stone (al-nawah) - the faint groove visible on the pit of a date.

He then states the function of the word in the verse: it is used as a mathal, a figure/similitude, for something paltry or negligible (al-shay' al-tafif) - i.e., the verse uses "not even the mark on a date-pit" to express that the things called upon besides God possess nothing at all, however small.

No other senses, derivations, or citations are given for this root in the entry.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-b-ḍ as one sound root with a single core idea: something taken/seized, and a drawing-together or gathering-in within a thing. From that core he arranges the following:

1. **Taking possession.** قَبَضْتُ الشَّيْءَ (qabaḍtu al-shayʾ) — "I took/received the thing," said of property and of other things alike; verbal noun qabḍ.

2. **Grip-point.** مَقْبِض / مَقْبَض السَّيْف (maqbiḍ / maqbaḍ al-sayf), given in both vowellings: the part of a sword where the hand closes on it.

3. **Collected spoil.** الْقَبَض (al-qabaḍ), with a fatḥa on the bāʾ: what has been gathered in and amassed from war-spoil. Idiom cited: "Throw this into the qabaḍ" — i.e. in with the rest of what has been collected.

4. **Speed/haste.** Ibn Fāris derives qabḍ in the sense of moving fast from the same core, reasoning that one who hurries pulls himself and his limbs in together. His Qurʾānic shāhid is Q 67:19, on the birds overhead "spreading [their wings] and drawing them in"; he reports that "they said" this means they move swiftly in flight.

5. **Keeping a flock bunched.** He links the previous sense to رَاعٍ قُبَضَة (rāʿin qubaḍah), a herdsman who does not let his flock spread out over the pasture, and to the pairing قُبَضَة رُفَضَة (qubaḍah rufaḍah): he holds them tightly together on the way, then releases them to scatter once he reaches his destination.

6. **Driving hard.** A rough driver is called قَبَّاضَة (qabbāḍah) or قَابِض (qābiḍ). Poetic witness from Ruʾbah: "a brisk driver, between the rough-handed and the deft."

7. **Drawing back / recoiling.** Also of this root: انْقَبَضَ عَنِ الْأَمْر (inqabaḍa ʿan al-amr) and تَقَبَّضَ (taqabbaḍa) — to shrink back from a matter in distaste.

Method: throughout, Ibn Fāris argues by tracing each usage back to the one physical image of closing the hand / drawing in, rather than listing senses as unrelated.

text:
Root ق ب ح (q-b-ḥ), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: the opposite of beauty — ugliness (al-qubḥ).

1. "qabbaḥahu Allāh" — "may God disgrace/make him ugly"; hādhā maqbūḥ wa qabīḥ — "this is ugly/disgraced" (near-synonymous forms). Some authorities held that qabbaḥahu properly means "he removed him and cast him far away" — connecting it to the entry's central Qur'anic citation, al-Qasas 28:42: "wa yawma al-qiyāmati hum mina al-maqbūḥīn" — "and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the maqbūḥīn [the disgraced/cast-away]" (of Pharaoh and his people).
2. Closing exception, which Ibn Fāris explicitly flags as anomalous — likely a term whose original underlying logic has been lost even to those who once used it correctly: "kisr qabīḥ" — a specific term for the half of the forearm-bone nearer the elbow, illustrated with a line of poetry contrasting a humiliated donkey with a broken bone-fragment.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats ق ب ل (q-b-l) as a single sound root whose core meaning is one thing facing or confronting another (muwājaha); every derived word branches from this.

1. Front vs. back: al-qubul is the front of anything, opposite its dubur (back), since the front "faces" (yuqbil) toward things. Related: al-qabīl is the forward-twisted strand of a woman's yarn, al-dabīr the backward strand — hence the proverb "he doesn't know qabīl from dabīr" (front from back).

2. Turning toward: al-qiblah is so called because people turn toward it in prayer (ṣalāt) while it faces them. qibalan means "face-to-face"; min qibali fulān means "from so-and-so's side," as if he brought the thing forward to you.

3. Paired straps: al-qibāl is a camel's nose-rein or a sandal-thong; qābaltuhā = I gave it two qibāls, each facing the other. A sheep whose ear is nicked at the front (piece left hanging) is muqābalah; nicked at the back, mudābarah.

4. What is coming: al-qābilah = the coming night; al-ʿām al-qābil = the coming year (no verb is formed from it). Separately, al-qābilah is the midwife who "receives" (tuqabbil) the newborn.

5. Facing winds: al-qabūl is the east wind (ṣabā), because it faces the west wind (dabbūr) or the House. Also qabiltu al-shayʾa qabūlan = "I accepted the thing."

6. Eye and terrain: al-qabal in the eye is the iris's black turning toward the inner corner (or, it is said, toward the nose) — a squint. al-qabal is also rising ground that faces you ("I saw a figure on that rise").

7. Standing surety: al-qabīl is a guarantor (kafīl); qabila bihi qabālatan = he stood surety, because he "faces" the matter he guarantees.

8. Time to come: ilā ʿashrin min dhī qabalin = within the time newly begun/ahead.

9. Watering camels: aqbalnā ʿalā al-ibil = we drew water at the camels' heads as they drank (this act is al-qabal). al-qābil is also the man who receives the bucket from the watering-camel (with a verse illustrating him singing as the water gushes).

10. Fresh youth: muqtabal al-shabāb describes someone showing no mark of age, his youth undiminished (cited with a verse contrasting an aged man with fresh-hued Uthayla).

11. Ibn Durayd's additions: al-qabalah = a whorl-like bead hung on horses' necks; also a charm a sorceress uses to turn one person's face toward another.

12. Joined sections → tribes: qabāʾil al-raʾs are the skull-plates joined by the sutures, named because each faces the next; from this the Arab qabāʾil (tribes) take their name.

13. Tribal overseer: qabīl al-qawm is their chief/overseer (ʿarīf), so called because he faces them to learn their affairs (cited with a verse). Being under someone's qabālah = under his overseeing. mā li-fulānin qiblah = he has no direction to face.

14. Group vs. lineage: some say al-qabīl is a mix of several tribes and al-qabīlah is the sons of one father. Ibn Fāris regards this as merely a reported distinction, noting that a single lineage can also be called qubayl (Labīd cited).

15. Incapacity: lā qibala lī bihi ("I have no power for it") belongs here too — one cannot "face"/advance upon it.

16. "Before": qablu (opposite of baʿdu, "after") may be anomalous to this root; one could strain to link it as "facing upon time," but Ibn Fāris judges it closer to being an exception.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: قَبْر 6x "the graves"; أَقْبَرَ 1x "and provides a grave for him"; مَقَابِر 1x "the graves"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-b-r as one sound root whose core idea is **something obscured or hidden, together with lowness / sinking down**. Everything in the entry is derived from that single semantic core.

1. **The grave.** القَبْر (al-qabr) is the grave of a dead person — an instance of the "sunken and concealed" idea. The base verb is قَبَرَ / يَقْبُرُ ("to bury"). He cites al-Aʿshā as the poetic witness: had she leaned a dead man against her breast, he would have revived and never been carried off to a قابِر ("one who buries").

2. **The causative form: providing a grave.** If you assign someone a place in which he is to be buried, the verb shifts to the fourth form أَقْبَرَ (aqbara). Ibn Fāris marks this as a distinct sense from plain qabara, and gives the Qur'anic shāhid: "then He caused him to die and أَقْبَرَهُ (gave him a grave)" (80:21).

3. **An interpreters' gloss on 80:21.** He reports that some exegetes read فَأَقْبَرَهُ in that verse as meaning that man was *inspired/taught how burial is done* — reported as their view, not endorsed as the lexical sense.

4. **A methodological aside.** Ibn Fāris pauses to note his unease at placing God's words and a line of poetry together in a single book — let alone on one page — and says he does so only because earlier scholars permitted it, asking forgiveness for himself and them. This is a remark about lexicographic method (using poetic shawāhid alongside Qur'anic ones), not about the meaning of the root.

5. **Non-burial uses, from Ibn Durayd.** These show the root's underlying sense outside the death context:
   - أَرْضٌ قَبُورٌ — ground that is sunken and hidden from view.
   - نَخْلَةٌ قَبُورٌ (also كَبُوس) — a palm tree that carries its fruit down inside its fronds, i.e. concealed among them.

6. **Place-noun.** The place of graves is مَقْبَرَة or مَقْبُرَة (maqbara / maqbura), attested with either vowel on the middle radical.

text:
Ibn Fāris on the root ق-ب-س (q-b-s):

1. **Core sense.** The three letters qāf-bāʾ-sīn form one sound root pointing to a property of fire, which then gets carried over metaphorically to other things.

2. **al-qabas** = a flame or firebrand of fire. Cited proof: the Qur'an, in the story of Moses — "Perhaps I will bring you from it a firebrand (qabas)" (Ṭāhā 20:10).

3. **Verb usage — literal and metaphorical fire:**
   - aqbastu al-rajula ʿilman — "I gave the man knowledge" (literally, kindled him with knowledge, using the fire-image metaphorically).
   - qabastuhu nāran — "I gave him fire" (literal).

4. **Ibn Durayd's finer distinctions** (three related but different verbs):
   - qabastu min fulānin nāran — "I took fire from so-and-so."
   - iqtabastu minhu ʿilman — "I acquired/borrowed knowledge from him" (the metaphorical, knowledge-transfer sense — this is the verb form behind the later term iqtibās, "quotation/borrowing").
   - aqbasanī qabasan — "he gave me a firebrand."

5. **Extended metaphor — animal husbandry.** faḥlun qabīsun, "a stallion quick to impregnate," is built on the same image: he is likened to a leaping flame of fire. A line of verse is quoted illustrating the usage: "a mother swift to conceive, and a father quick to impregnate."

6. **A related but distinct word.** al-qibs (different vowel pattern from al-qabas) is said by some to mean simply "the origin" or "the root" (al-aṣl) of a thing — Ibn Fāris notes this without elaborating further.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ق-د-ح (q-d-ḥ) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris finds two distinct core meanings in this root:

A. Striking / hollowing out / decay

1. Qadaḥa, in its basic sense, means to strike or gouge into something — the raw verb behind the noun al-qadḥ.
2. Al-qadḥ also names a kind of corrosive decay that occurs in trees and in teeth (like rot or corrosion). Al-qādiḥa is specifically the worm that eats away at a tree.
3. From the decay-sense comes the idiom qadaḥa fī nasabihi, he struck at his lineage — meaning he slandered or cast aspersions on it.
4. A cited verse curses a woman named Buthayna: may grit fill her eyes and decay-worms (qawādiḥ) eat into her white canine teeth — illustrating the tooth-decay sense.
5. Al-qidḥ is an arrow-shaft with no head and no feathers — plain wood. Ibn Fāris suggests it is named this either because one strikes fire with it, or because striking is simply possible with such a shaft.
6. By extension/metaphor, al-qidḥ also names one of the gambling-arrows used in maysir (the pre-Islamic game of chance).
7. A horse that has been trained down lean is described as quddiḥa — made slender like a qadḥ (a shaft).
8. An eye that has sunk into its socket is described with the same verb: qaddaḥat/qadaḥat al-ʿayn.
9. The verb also covers striking fire (qadaḥtu l-nār) and lancing/draining a diseased eye of its bad fluid (qadaḥtu l-ʿayn).

B. Scooping / ladling

10. Al-qadīḥ is the residue left at the bottom of a cooking-pot, retrievable only by scooping hard.
11. A cited verse pictures slave-women racing each other to scoop out the qadīḥ, compared to the tribe of Kalb racing for the waters of Qurāqir.
12. Qadaḥtu l-qidra means I ladled out the contents of the pot.
13. A well that can be drawn from by hand is called rakiyyun qadūḥ.
14. Finally, al-qadaḥ, the ordinary drinking-cup or bowl, gets its name from this same scooping sense — it is the vessel used to scoop things out.

Ibn Fāris keeps the two senses separate throughout: everything to do with striking, hollowing, or eating-away (fire-strikers, arrow-shafts, gambling-lots, sunken eyes, tooth decay, slander) belongs to the first root; everything to do with ladling out liquid or dregs (pot residue, wells, the drinking-cup) belongs to the second.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-d-d as a sound root (aṣl ṣaḥīḥ) that indicates cutting a thing lengthwise, and says it is then used by borrowing.

1. **Cutting lengthwise.** qadadtu al-shayʾa qaddan (imperfect aquddu) means "I cut the thing lengthwise".

2. **Figure.** A man "of fine qadd" is finely "cut" in the length of his stature.

3. **Thong.** al-qidd is a thong cut from untanned hide; the word al-qadīd is derived from it.

4. **Way, faction.** al-qidda is a way, and a faction of people, used when each one's inclination differs from his fellow's.

5. **Borrowed uses.** From this they say iqtadda al-umūr, "he managed affairs and sorted them out". Also qadda al-musāfiru al-mafāza, "the traveller cut through the desert".

6. **al-qaydūd.** A she-camel long in the back, over the ground.

7. **al-qadd, a kid's skin.** The skin of a young goat. The proverb says: "what brings your qadd up to your adīm (hide)?"

8. **al-qudād.** A pain in the belly.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-d-m as a single sound root whose core sense is precedence and forward motion; the other meanings branch off from that.

1. Antiquity: الْقِدَم is the opposite of coming-newly-into-being (حُدوث). A قَدِيم thing is one whose time is past. He traces this to the phrase مَضَى قُدُمًا, "he went straight ahead" — without turning aside or bending back.

2. Diminutives of قُدَّام ("front") are قُدَيْدِيم / قُدَيْدِيمَة, illustrated by a line of al-Quṭāmī.

3. Front/foremost parts: رَكِبَ مَقَادِيمَهُ = fell forward on his face; قَادِمَة of a saddle is its front board (vs. the rear); the قَادِمَة teat of a she-camel is the front one, near the navel. قَدَمُ صِدْقٍ ("a foot of truth") means a prior record of good repute.

4. Verbs: قَدِمَ (to arrive home from travel) and أَقْدَمَ / إِقْدَام (to advance boldly on something).

5. From Ibn Durayd: قَادِم of a person = his head (pl. قَوَادِم, singular rarely used); قَوَادِم of a bird = the ten foremost flight-feathers per wing (sing. قَادِمَة, also called قُدَامَى).

6. Military/motion senses: مُقَدِّمَة of an army = its vanguard; أَقْدِمْ = a cry urging a horse forward; الْيَقْدُمِيَّة = advancing/pressing ahead in battle (with a supporting verse); قَيْدُوم of a mountain = a forward-jutting prominence.

7. A cited verse ("...as the butcher strikes the slaughtered camel of the قُدَّام") prompts two readings of الْقُدَّام: (a) "the king," which Ibn Fāris calls a sound analogy since the king is the one put foremost (الْمُقَدَّم); (b) "those returning from a journey."

8. قَدَم (the human foot) is well known; he suggests it may be named for being the instrument of advancing and going ahead.

9. Outliers from the root: الْقَدُوم = an adze (a hewing tool); الْقَدُوم = also a place-name. He notes the hadith that Abraham circumcised himself "with the qadūm" (understood as either the tool or the place).

text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-d-r as one sound root meaning the extent, essence, and limit of a thing; the various senses radiate from that core of "measure."

1. Core sense — measure/extent. al-qadr = the extent or amount of anything (qadruhu kadhā = "its measure is such"); al-qadar carries the same. The verb qadara/yaqdiru (also yaqduru) and the intensive qaddara belong here, from taqdīr ("determining a measure").

2. Divine decree. al-qadr / al-qadar is also God's decreeing of things according to the extents and ends He willed for them. Ibn Fāris cites a verse using al-qadar (with fatḥa) for compelling "fate," and another using al-qadr (with sukūn) in the same sense. Note the two vocalisations sit under the one sense.

3. al-aqdar (of a horse): one whose hind hooves land exactly where the forehooves did — as if precisely "measured out"; supported by a poetic line describing a high-backed, long-striding bay.

4. Qur'anic usage. In Q 6:91 (mā qadarū llāha ḥaqqa qadrihi) the exegetes gloss "they did not magnify God with His true greatness"; Ibn Fāris accepts this, explaining it as their failing to describe Him fitly. In Q 65:7 (man qudira ʿalayhi rizquhu) qudira means qutira, "was straitened" — given provision in scant measure.

5. Power (qudra). God's qudra over creation is His bringing them to the extent He wills — by the same analogy of "measure" as the previous sense.

6. Affluence. A man dhū qudra / dhū maqdira is one of means: by his wealth he reaches the extent of what he wills.

7. al-aqdar (of a man): short-necked — fitting the root, as if the neck had been "measured/cut short."

Anomalous senses (which Ibn Fāris flags as deviating from the root's analogy): al-qidr, the cooking-pot; al-qadīr, meat cooked in it; al-qudār, the butcher (or, he thinks more aptly, the cook); and, more doubtfully, al-qudār as a great serpent — of which he says "there is doubt."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: قُدُس 4x "the holy spirit"; مُقَدَّس 2x "the sacred"; قُدُّوس 2x "the holy"; نُقَدِّسُ 1x "and we sanctify"; مُقَدَّسَة 1x "the holy"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ق-د-س (q-d-s) as one sound root. He suspects it belongs to Islamic religious vocabulary, and holds that its core meaning is purity (ṭuhr).

1. Purity — the base sense. He derives several usages from it, all carrying the same meaning:
   - الأرض المقدّسة (the "holy/sanctified land") = the purified land.
   - حظيرة القُدْس ("the enclosure of quds"), a name for Paradise = the enclosure of purity.
   - روح القُدُس ("the spirit of al-qudus"), which he identifies with Gabriel.

2. As a divine attribute — القُدُّوس (al-Quddūs) carries this same sense: God is declared free of opposites, rivals, a consort, or a child.

3. Proper names and other usages:
   - al-Qādisiyya is said to take its name from this root; Ibn Fāris reports that Abraham prayed for it with "quds" (holiness) and that it be a lodging-place for pilgrims.
   - قُدْس (Quds) is also the name of a mountain.
   - القُداس (al-qudās) is said to be a small silver bead, like a pearl. He cites a verse: "like a string of qudās-beads whose thread is broken."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) on the root ق د و (q-d-w/y):

The root has one coherent core meaning: taking guidance or a "kindled light" from something (iqtibās/ihtidāʾ), combined with the idea of measuring or proportioning a thing so as to match it against another (muqādarah).

1. Measuring/matching. "Hādhā qidā rumḥin" — "this is the qidā of a spear" — means its exact length (qays). The same idea of matching underlies qudwah: an exemplar, someone who is followed or imitated (the text gives this word with two possible vowelings, qidwah/qudwah). Ibn Fāris also notes people call the origin-stock from which branches split off al-qadw — again, the fixed reference-point that other things are measured/derived against.

2. Steady, even pace. A horse that "yaqdū bihi" keeps an even, regular gait — called qadw precisely because it is a "measuring" (taqdīr) of the pace. Likewise taqaddā ʿalā dābbatihi means he rode his mount along a straight, steady course.

3. The first arrivals. A qādiyah is a group of people — specifically the first wave to turn up somewhere; the verb qadat taqdī is used of them. Ibn Fāris files this too under the general sense of "reckoning/measuring of travel."

4. An unrelated (anomalous) sense. Separately, qadā l-laḥmu yaqdū/yaqdī (verbal noun qadw/qady) means the meat gave off a pleasant smell — Ibn Fāris flags this explicitly as not fitting the root's core meaning.

5. A further aside: qindaʾw is given as a word for a man who is strong-backed and short-necked.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) treats ق-ف-ل (q-f-l) as one sound root carrying two distinct underlying senses:

1. **Returning from a journey.** The verbal noun al-qufūl means "returning from travel." Ibn Fāris notes a usage point: travelers who are still on their way out are not called a qāfila (caravan) — that label only applies once they are on the return leg.

2. **Hardness / toughness / dryness in a thing.** The base word here is al-qafīl, "dry wood." From this same sense comes al-qufl, "a lock" — so called, he says, because a lock involves both binding (shadd) and toughness (shidda). Related usages he cites:
   - aqfaltu l-bāb, "I locked the door" → the door is muqfal, "locked."
   - A miser is described as muqfalu l-yadayn, "one whose two hands are locked shut" (i.e., closed-fisted, withholding).
   - qafila l-shayʾ, "the thing dried up/withered."
   - khaylun qawāfil, "gaunt, lean horses."
   - aqfalahu l-ṣawm, "fasting left him gaunt/dried out."

So the entry derives "lock" from the idea of hard, tight binding, and links a separate cluster of "dryness/leanness" usages (dry wood, gaunt horses, a body wasted by fasting) to that same core sense of hardness.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib starts q-f-w from al-qafā, the back of the neck, a word he calls well known.

1. **Striking the nape.** qafawtuhu means "I struck him on the back of the neck."

2. **Following.** qafawtu atharahu means "I followed his track", and iqtafaytuhu, literally "I followed his nape", means following behind someone. He defines the verbal noun al-iqtifāʾ as "following the nape", just as al-irtidāf is "following the rump" (ridf).

3. **Backbiting.** The expression is also used by allusion (kināya) for backbiting and for searching out faults.

4. **Q 17:36.** He explains "do not follow (lā taqfu) that of which you have no knowledge" as: do not judge by qiyāfa (tracking, reading traces) and conjecture. Qiyāfa is described as a craft, and he reports the view that the word is iqtifāʾ with its letters transposed, as with jadhaba and jabadha ("to pull").

5. **Placing behind.** The doubled form qaffaytuhu means "I placed him behind another", as in Q 2:87: "and We made messengers follow after him".

6. **Rhyme.** al-qāfiya is the name for the last part of a line of verse, whose wording is to be kept and repeated in every line.

7. **Food.** al-qafāwa is food with which someone who is cared for is looked after, so that he is "followed" with it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: قَهَّار 6x "the irresistible"; قَاهِر 3x "(is) the subjugator"; تَقْهَرْ 1x "oppress"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ق-ه-ر (q-h-r) as a sound root with one core idea: overcoming/domination and superiority (being above).

1. Core sense — to overcome, subdue, dominate: qahara-hu yaqharu-hu qahran. The active participle al-qāhir means "the victor, the one who prevails."

2. Passive uqhira ("was subdued"): to be reduced to a state of humiliation and abasement. Cited verse (of Ḥuṣayn): he aspired to lord it over his kinsfolk but ended up "abased and put in a subdued state." The plain passive quhira means simply "he was overcome/defeated."

3. An extended, same-category usage: quhira al-laḥm — "the meat was cooked until its juices ran out" (heat overpowering the meat).

4. Two words Ibn Fāris connects, tentatively, to the root:
   - al-qahqar: reportedly "the billy-goat"; if the report is sound, he suggests it may fit the overcoming/dominating sense.
   - al-qahqar: also "hard, solid rock" — which he judges not far from the root's core idea (solidity/prevailing).

5. An outlier he marks as deviating from the root's sense: rajaʿa al-qahqarā — "he retreated, moved backward."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ق ل ع (q-l-ʿ) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

CORE MEANING: A sound triliteral root meaning to wrench or tear a thing loose from a thing. Everything below is presented by Ibn Fāris as branching from this one idea of forcible detachment.

1. Basic verb — qalaʿtu al-shayʾa ("I pulled/tore it out"); the doer is qāliʿ, the thing removed is maqlūʿ.

2. Being dislodged / unsettled (figurative extensions of "torn loose"):
   - A rider thrown from his saddle by poor horsemanship: qulʿa.
   - A dwelling that isn't a permanent home: manzil qulʿa.
   - A group about to depart/journey: they are ʿalā qulʿa.
   - A ruler removed from office: al-maqlūʿ.

3. Rock and cloud imagery: al-qilaʿa is a lone boulder broken off a mountain, hard to reach. Because of this image, a great cloud-mass is likewise called qilaʿa (plural qalaʿ). A poetic line is quoted describing such night-travelling cloud-masses bursting open, with a creature or plant called al-khāzibāz (the term's exact referent is disputed among lexicographers) going wild at the sound.

4. Cracked clay: al-qulāʿ is mud that cracks and flakes apart once water has drained from it — named for the way it "comes away."

5. Desisting / letting up: aqlaʿa ʿan al-amr = he held back from a matter. The same verb is used of illness: aqlaʿat ʿanhu al-ḥummā, "the fever released him"; one also says taraktuhu fī qalaʿin min ḥummā, "I left him in a remission of fever."

6. Throwing clods: ramāhu bi-qulāʿa — to tear up a clump of earth and hurl it at someone. Related: al-miqlāʿ, the sling (a well-known term, no further comment).

7. The slanderer (al-qalāʿ): glossed as "the guard/watchman" in common usage, but the entry's main discussion comes via a ḥadīth: "Neither a daybūb nor a qalāʿ enters the Garden." Al-daybūb is explained as one who spreads gossip to split people apart; al-qalāʿ is explained as one who, seeing a man's standing rise with someone else, keeps slandering between them until he "uproots" him from that favor — the same root-sense of forcible removal applied to social standing.

8. The ship's sail (al-qilʿ): so named because raising it "pulls" (pulls loose / propels) the ship from its place.

9. Two unrelated homonyms Ibn Fāris flags as NOT belonging to this root's meaning-family:
   - al-qalʿ = a leather pouch/bag (kinf). Cited proverb: "My fat is in my bag" (i.e., my resource is close at hand, within my own keeping).
   - al-qilʿ = a small garment worn over the chest, per a cited verse describing a man carrying a knife tucked in it under his arm.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: قَلْب 132x "their hearts"; ٱنقَلَبَ 17x "turns back"; قَلَّبُ 6x "and had upset"; تَقَلُّب 5x "(the) movement"; مُنقَلِبُون 3x "(will) return"; مُنقَلَب 2x "(as) a return"; تَتَقَلَّبُ 1x "will turn about"; تُقْلَبُ 1x "you will be returned"; مُتَقَلَّب 1x "your movement"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root q-l-b (قلب) from two sound origins: (a) the pure, noble core of a thing, and (b) turning something from one side to another.

FIRST ORIGIN — the pure core:
1. al-qalb = the heart (of a human or animal), named because it is the purest and highest thing in the body. By extension the "heart" of anything is its purest, noblest part; hence ʿarabiyy qulb/qalb = a thoroughbred, pure-blooded Arab (with a poetic citation of a "pure-bred Zubayrī mare").
2. al-qulāb = a disease that strikes a camel in its heart.
3. al-qulb = a plain single-loop bracelet, likened to qalb al-nakhla, the pith/heart of the palm; the same word was then applied to a snake, likened to that bangle.
4. al-qalb = the star Qalb al-ʿAqrab, "the Heart of the Scorpion" (Antares).
5. qalabtu al-nakhla = I removed the palm's pith (qalb).

SECOND ORIGIN — turning/overturning:
6. qalabtu al-thawb = I turned a garment inside out.
7. al-qalab = a turned-over/everted lip; such a woman is qalbāʾ, such a man aqlab.
8. qalabtu al-shayʾ = I overturned it; qallabtu (with intensive form) = I turned it over repeatedly by hand.
9. aqlabat al-khubza = the loaf is ready to be flipped.
10. mā bihi qalba(tun) = "there is nothing wrong with it": glossed as an animal having no ailment for which it would be turned over and examined (with a poetic line: no farrier turned over its legs for any defect).
11. al-qalīb = a well before it is stone-lined, so called because its dug-up earth is "turned over"; once lined it is called al-ṭawiyy. The word is grammatically masculine.
12. al-ḥuwwal al-qulb = a resourceful man who "turns matters over" and contrives schemes for them.

Ibn Fāris notes the underlying analogy is uniform across all these senses. He adds a marginal item: al-qillīb / al-qillawb is said to mean "the wolf," which he suggests may fit the same "turning" analogy — the wolf named for its roaming about (taqallub) in search of food (with a poetic citation naming the hyena as a wolf's prey).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: قَلَٰئِد 2x "and the garlands"; مَقَالِيد 2x "(are the) keys"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ق-ل-د as two sound roots.

ROOT ONE — hanging something on something so that it stays attached to it.

1. taqlīd — putting a mark on the neck. taqlīd al-badana is hanging something on the neck of the sacrificial camel so it is known to be a hady (an animal brought forward as an offering).
2. The underlying sense of qald is twisting: qaladtu l-ḥabla ("I twisted the rope"); a twisted rope is qalīd or maqlūd.
3. taqalladtu l-sayf — "I slung the sword over my shoulder." A man's muqallad is the spot on his shoulder where the sword-belt (nijād) rests.
4. Figurative: qallada fulānun fulānan qilādata sawʾin, "he hung an evil necklace on him" — i.e. lampooned him with something whose mark stays on him. Intensified: qalladahu ṭawqa l-ḥamāma, "he collared him with the dove's ring-collar," meaning the stigma never leaves him, as the ring never leaves the dove's neck. Ibn Fāris cites the poet Bishr: "Your patron bestowed it on you out of rancour — and Jaʿfar was collared with it as with a dove's ring-collar."
5. miqlad — a staff crooked at the tip, used to twist up herbage, as fodder (qatt) is twisted when made into ropes.
6. qild — a bracelet. Ibn Fāris judges this a sound analogy, since the arm is as though wearing it as a collar.
7. iqlīd — reported as the nose-ring by which a she-camel's halter is fastened.

ROOT TWO — a share, a portion.

8. qild — a share of water: saqaynā arḍanā qildahā, "we watered our land with its share"; saqatnā l-samāʾu qildan, "the sky watered us with a share." He cites a ḥadīth: "the sky gave us a qild every week."
9. maqālīd — said to mean treasuries or storehouses. He quotes Q 39:63, "To Him belong the maqālīd of the heavens and the earth," and offers the tentative explanation that they are so called because they secure things — guard them and hold them fast. He supports this with the Arab usage aqlada l-baḥru ʿalā khalqin kathīr, "the sea closed over a great many creatures," i.e. shut them inside itself.

OUTSIDE THE PATTERN.

10. qildah (also qishdah) — dates and parched-barley meal (sawīq) mixed with clarified butter. Ibn Fāris marks this as anomalous, not derivable from either root sense.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: قَلِيل 70x "a little"; أَقَلّ 2x "lesser"; قَلِيلَة 1x "small"; قَلَّ 1x "(is) little"; أَقَلَّتْ 1x "they have carried"; يُقَلِّلُ 1x "and he made you (appear) as few"
text:
Ibn Sīda's entry treats the root ق ل ل (fewness/smallness) together with the reduplicated ق ل ق ل (movement/rattling).

1. Core sense — fewness/scarcity. قِلَّة (qilla) is the opposite of abundance, قُلّ the opposite of muchness. Verb قَلَّ يَقِلُّ ("to be few/little"); participle قَلِيل, also قُلال and قَلال (the latter with fatḥa, per Ibn Jinnī).

2. Causative and related verbs. قَلَّلَ / أَقَلَّ = make little; أَقَلَّ also = bring little, or find something scarce; اسْتَقَلَّ = deem little; اقْتَلَّ منه = make little of it (Ibn Jinnī).

3. Applied to persons/things. قَليل of a man = short and slight of build (a woman likewise). Abū Ḥanīfa used qilla for narrowness: a pickaxe (miʿwal) is a long blade "of little width." A group is قَليلون / أَقِلّاء / قُلُل, covering both small number and slight build.

4. Grammatical excursus on قَلَّما ("seldom"). The particle "mā" attaches to qalla so a verb can follow. Some grammarians treat qall here as a verb with no subject, because "mā" reclassifies it as a verb-demanding particle (like لولا, هلّا, conditional إِنْ, the interrogative). On this basis Sībawayh analyzed a verse (صددت فأطولت الصدود وقلما / وصالٌ ... يدوم) as raising "union" by an implied verb signaled by yadūm ("endures"). He compares رُبَّمَا in the Qur'an (رُبَّمَا يَوَدُّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا): "mā" lets rubba take a verb. Just as rubba shifts its behavior once compounded with "mā," so do ṭāla and qalla — and composition can create a wholly new meaning: إِنَّ alone affirms, but إنّما ("I am but…") restricts/belittles. They also said أَقَلُّ امرأتين يقولان ذلك; Ibn Jinnī explains it as resembling a subject with a negating particle and no predicate.

5. Poverty. الإِقلال = scarcity of means; قَلَّ مالُه = his wealth dwindled; a مُقِلّ / أَقَلّ = a poor man. "He did it من بين أثرى وأقلّ" = among all people, rich and poor. قالَلْتُ له الماءَ = to ration one's water for fear of thirst.

6. Idioms of obscurity/quantity. هو قُلُّ بن قُلّ (paired with ضُلّ بن ضُلّ) = neither he nor his father is known. Per Sībawayh, قَلَّ رجلٌ يقول ذلك إلا زيدٌ = "no man says that except Zayd." قُلَل من الناس = people from scattered tribes who, once gathered, form qulal.

7. القُلَّة as a noun. (a) A large cistern or jar — variously the great well-pit, the great jar, a jar generally, or a small mug; plural قُلَل / قِلال. (b) The top/summit of anything (some restrict it to the crown of the head, a camel's hump, a mountain-peak). (c) قُلَّة of a sword = its pommel.

8. Verbs of lifting/rising. أَقَلَّ / اسْتَقَلَّ الشيءَ = carry and raise it; اسْتَقَلَّ الطائرُ = the bird took off and climbed; اسْتَقَلَّ النباتُ = the plant grew tall; اسْتَقَلَّ القومُ = the people set off/departed.

9. Trembling. القُلَّة / القُلّ = a shudder — specifically the shiver of anger, greed, and the like; أَقَلَّتْهُ / اسْتَقَلَّتْهُ الرِّعدةُ = a tremor seized him (with a supporting verse).

10. Miscellaneous. القِلال = wood set up to trellis vines (Abū Ḥanīfa, with a verse). ارتحلوا بقِلِّيَّتِهم = they left nothing behind. أكل الضبُّ بقِلِّيَّتِه = ate it bones, skin and all. بنو وَقْل = a clan.

Reduplicated ق ل ق ل:

11. Movement. قَلْقَلَ (nouns قِلْقال / قَلْقال, the latter rare, per Kurāʿ) = to shake/move; per al-Liḥyānī also = to travel/roam a land; تَقَلْقَلَ likewise. قُلْقُل / قُلاقِل = nimble and quick in travel; of a horse = swift. القَلْقَلة = loud shouting. Abū Isḥāq classed qulqul/ṣulṣul as pattern فُعْفُل.

12. Plants. القُلْقُل = a tree with black seed, or a plant of soft/rough lowland (not mountains) with a flattish pod of lentil-like seeds that rattle like a bell when dry and wind-blown; grey reed-like leaves. القُلاقِل / القُلْقُلان = two plants — Abū Ḥanīfa says qulqul, qulāqil and qulqulān are all one: a green stalked tree of the hillocks, seed like cowpea, eaten and craved by livestock. Its seed is a sexual stimulant, eaten for that purpose (cited with rajaz attributed to Laylā, and a line of Dhū al-Rumma on the hot wind).

13. Bird. القُلْقُلاني = a bird resembling the dove.

14. Phonetics. The "letters of qalqala" — ج ط د ق ب — so named by Sībawayh for the audible burst they produce at a pause, since one cannot stop on them without it, owing to the strong compression of the letter.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-l-m as one sound root whose core idea is trimming something even — paring it down and putting it right.
