1. Clipping. قَلَمْتُ الظُّفُرَ / قَلَّمْتُهُ = "I clipped the nail" (simple and intensive forms both used). A weak man is described as مَقْلُومُ الْأَظْفَار, "with his nails clipped." قُلَامَة (qulāma) is the clipping itself — what falls off the nail.

2. Pen. The قَلَم (qalam, pen) belongs here, he reports, because it is named from the paring done to it, exactly as a nail is pared.

3. Arrow-shaft. The قِدْح (arrow-shaft used for casting lots) was then likened to the pen and also called qalam. Ibn Fāris notes it may equally have earned the name directly from the same idea — its being evened and pared. He cites Q 3:44, "when they cast their aqlām," under this heading, without deciding between the two senses.

4. Extended physical uses. الْمِقْلَم is the tip of a camel's sheath, as though pared; and مَقَالِم الرُّمْح is said to mean the nodes (raised joints) of a spear-shaft.

5. Outlier. He marks قُلَام (qulām), a plant, as falling outside the root's core idea, quoting a verse of complaint: they served the speaker qulām and told him to dine on it — "and does anything eat qulām but camels?"

Method note: the entry works by positing a single semantic core (evening/paring), deriving each form from it, and explicitly flagging the one item it cannot so derive.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: قَالِين 1x "those who detest"; قَلَىٰ 1x "he is displeased"
text:
Root: q-l-y (قلي) — al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān

Core meaning: al-qilā = intense hatred, aversion. The verb is qalāhu, "he hated him." Al-Rāghib notes its imperfect form is attested two ways — yaqlīhi and yaqlūhu — and builds his whole entry around that ambiguity: is the weak final letter of the root a wāw or a yāʾ?

Qur'anic citations:
- 93:3 — mā waddaʿaka rabbuka wa-mā qalā, "your Lord has not forsaken you, nor is He displeased [with you]."
- 26:168 — innī liʿamalikum min al-qālīn, "I am, toward your deeds, among those who hate [you]."

Two proposed derivations, depending on the reading of the weak letter:

1. From wāw → al-qalw, "throwing, casting off." Support: a she-camel is said to "throw" its rider (qalat... bi-rākibihā qalwan), and qalawtu bi'l-qullah means to throw/play with a qullah (a stick or piece used in a children's throwing-game). On this reading, "the hated one" (al-maqlūw) is someone the heart casts out — throws away — in its aversion, refusing to take him in. Hatred, in other words, is a kind of inner expulsion.

2. From yāʾ → the verb of roasting: qalaytu al-busra wa'l-sawīq, "I roasted unripe dates and parched barley-meal," done on a miqlāh (roasting pan). On this reading the word for "hatred" is homonymous with, and possibly derived from, the word for roasting/frying.

Al-Rāghib does not decide between the two; he simply lays out both etymological routes side by side.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha, on ق-م-ع (q-m-ʿ)

He sets out three genuine base-meanings for this root:

1. A liquid descending into a vessel made for it
The clearest case is al-qimaʿ, "the well-known thing" — a funnel (pronounced either qimaʿ or qimʿ). A ḥadīth calls certain people "the funnels of speech" (aqmāʿ al-qawl): those who hear but retain nothing, as if their ears were funnels that hold nothing back. Related to this: iqtamaʿtu mā fī l-siqāʾ, "I funneled what was in the waterskin," said of someone who drinks a container completely dry — you became, in effect, its funnel.

2. Humbling / overpowering
Qamaʿtuhu means "I humbled/subdued him" (adhlaltuhu). The same verb also means "I struck him with al-miqmaʿ," a mace or club — and Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 22:21, "wa-lahum maqāmiʿu min ḥadīd" ("for them are maces of iron"). He explains the name Qamaʿah ibn Ilyās this way too: his father ordered him to do something and he inqamaʿa — shrank back and withdrew into his house — hence the name. Ibn Fāris himself notes the two base-meanings (1) and (2) are close in logic: both involve something "entering in," whether water subsiding into a funnel or a person retreating into his house. He also gives aqmaʿtu l-rajula ʿannī, "I drove the man off," as belonging to this sense of repelling/overpowering.

3. A kind of animal
Al-qamaʿ is the large blue fly. "We left him yataqammaʿu the flies out of boredom" means swatting them away, "as a donkey does." He quotes the pre-Islamic/early poet Aws (ibn Ḥajar): God sent down His help, while the dust-colored gazelles in their lairs go on warding off flies (taqammaʿu). A further derived use, aqmaʿtu l-rajula ʿannī ("I repelled the man from me"), is folded back into sense (2).

Extended by resemblance to these: al-qamaʿ also names the ridge above the vertebrae at the top of a camel's hump, a callus-like thickening in a horse's knee, and a pustule of excess flesh at the inner corner of the eye — all, in Ibn Fāris's view, modeled on the same underlying images.

One usage he flags as not fitting any of the three roots: qamʿat māl al-qawm means "the choicest part of a people's wealth."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) treats ق-م-ح (q-m-ḥ) as a genuine single-meaning root: it denotes a drinker raising his head at the moment of drinking water.

1. **al-qāmiḥ (القَامِحُ)** — a camel that raises its head while drinking, refusing to drink; plural qimāḥ. Illustrated with a verse of poetry comparing lowered gazes to qimāḥ camels.
2. **"rawiyat ḥattā inqamaḥat"** — "it drank until it inqamaḥat" — an idiom meaning the animal stopped drinking because it was already sated.
3. **"Shahrā qimāḥ"** ("the two months of qimāḥ") — an Arabic expression for the harshest stretch of winter cold. Ibn Fāris explains the name: camels coming to water in that cold would recoil from the water's coldness and raise their heads (qāmaḥat) rather than drink — the same root-image as sense 1.

He then flags one word as falling outside this root's core sense (shādhdh, "anomalous"):

4. **al-qamḥ (القَمْحُ)** = wheat, grain — explicitly noted as not derived from the "raising the head while drinking" meaning.

Two further usage notes, which he introduces cautiously ("perhaps it is correct"):

5. **iqtamaḥtu al-sawīq / qamaḥtuhu** — said of scooping parched barley-meal into one's mouth with the palm of the hand.
6. Citing Ibn Durayd: **al-qumḥah** of water = a mouthful, i.e., enough to fill the mouth.
7. **al-qummaḥāt** — reported (with all three glosses given as alternatives) to mean either wars (a yellow dye-plant), saffron, or dharīrah (a fragrant powder).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-m-ṣ as having two separate root-senses:

1. Putting something on and slipping into it. From this comes قميص (qamīṣ), a person's shirt or tunic — a familiar word. The verb تَقَمَّصَ (taqammaṣa) means "he put it on." The usage is then extended metaphorically to anything a person enters into or takes on: تَقَمَّصَ الإمارة ("he donned the command") and تَقَمَّصَ الولاية ("he donned the governorship"). Plurals of qamīṣ: أقمصة (aqmiṣah) and قُمُص (qumuṣ).

2. Leaping and movement. From this comes القَمْص (al-qamṣ): قَمَصَ البعير, imperfect يَقْمُصُ, verbal nouns قَمْصًا and قِماصًا — said of a camel that raises its forelegs, throws them down together, and "kneads" with its hind legs, i.e. bucks. Ibn Fāris notes that القامصة (al-qāmiṣah), mentioned in a ḥadīth, belongs here. The same verb is used of the sea: قَمَصَ البحرُ بالسفينة, when the waves toss a ship about — as though the ship were a bucking camel.

dictionary: ʿAyn — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786)
poets_named: Ḥumayd (lived into Islam); Abū Ṭālib (pre-Islamic); al-Khansāʾ (lived into Islam)
text:
Root ق-م-ط-ر (qmṭr) — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786 CE)

1. **A huge camel.** Al-qimaṭr is a massive, bulky camel. A verse by Ḥumayd is cited: the cowrie-shells on its breast-strap gleam, and a low rumbling comes from the wind beneath it.

2. **"A qamṭarīr day."** Describes a day on which evil is widespread/rife (fāshī l-sharr).

3. **Severe, overwhelming evil.** "Evil" (sharr) described with the related forms qumāṭir, qimṭar, or muqmaṭirr — i.e. harsh, all-encompassing evil. Illustrated with a verse by Abū Ṭālib about returning a blow measure for measure, using this same word for something "severe" — though the exact wording of that verse's central image is obscure/hard to construe as transmitted.

4. **To pile up, to loom.** The verb aqmaṭarrat is used of stones "piling up" on someone. More generally, aqmiṭrār of a thing is its casting of shadow (looming) and its accumulating. A verse by al-Khansāʾ is cited describing stones piled up (muqmiṭirrāt) over a grave-niche.

5. **Al-qimṭīr** — the small stalk/attachment by which a date-stone stays joined to its calyx-cap when the stone is pulled out of the fruit. Alternatively, it is said to be the thin membrane between the stone and the flesh of the date.

6. **Also of a she-camel.** Al-qimaṭr can likewise describe a she-camel noted for speed and strength.

7. **Al-qimaṭrah** — a woven container resembling a chest or case, made from reed/cane.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root q-m-l (قمل) from a core sense of meanness and vileness (ḥaqāra, qamāʾa).

1. From this sense: a "qamalī" man (رجل قملي) means a mean, contemptible man.

2. Al-qummal (القمّل) is defined here as the small, young locusts (ṣighār al-dabā).

3. The verb "aqmala" is used of the rimth shrub (a desert plant) when its leaves first appear small — the sprouting is described as being likened in appearance to al-qummal (the small locusts of sense 2).

Ibn Fāris ties all three uses back to the same root idea of smallness/lowliness.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-m-r as a sound root whose core meaning is "whiteness in a thing," with the other senses branching from it.

1. Whiteness / the moon: al-qamar (the moon) is named for its whiteness; ḥimār aqmar = a white donkey. The diminutive is qumayr, cited in a verse describing a young crescent-moon at twenty-five nights.

2. Moonlight-related verbs: al-qamrāʾ = moonlight / a moonlit night. taqammartuhu = "I came to him in the moonlight." taqammara al-asad = the lion went out to hunt by moonlight (with a supporting verse). qamara al-qawm al-ṭayr = they caught birds by blinding them at night.

3. Cold-damaged dates: qamira al-tamr / aqmara = the dates were hit by cold so their sweetness was lost before ripening.

4. On al-Aʿshā's line taqammarahā ("an old man taqammara-ed her at night…"): two readings are reported — either "as a lion hunts by moonlight," or "he deceived her, as a bird is blinded at night and caught."

5. Impaired sight from glare: qamira al-rajul = the man could not see in the snow; compare qamirat al-qirba, a waterskin affected by a scorching-like damage from the qamar (glare).

6. Gambling: qamara yaqmiru qamran and al-qimār (gambling, from muqāmara). Ibn Fāris reports two views: some hold it anomalous and outside the root; others link it to the root, since a gambler's wealth increases and never stays fixed (matching the "does not stay in one state" idea). He notes he only heard this and defers on its correctness ("God knows best"). Ibn Durayd adds taqammara al-rajul = he sought someone to gamble with; and qamartu al-rajul (aqmuruhu / aqmiruhu) = I won from the man at gambling.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مُقْنِعِى 1x "raised up"; قَانِع 1x "the needy who do not ask"
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) analyzes ق ن ع as containing two distinct core ideas, plus a possible third.

**Core idea 1: turning/facing toward something**

- iqnāʿ = turning one's face toward a thing (aqnaʿa lahu yuqniʿu iqnāʿan); also used for stretching out the hand in supplication (named for turning toward the direction one reaches toward), and for tilting a vessel so water pours out.
- From here: qanaʿa yaqnaʿu qunūʿan = to beg/ask. He cites Q22:36, "feed the qāniʿ and the muʿtarr" — al-qāniʿ being "the one who begs," so called because he turns toward the person he's asking. A supporting verse contrasts a man's well-managed wealth, which spares him need, as more honorable than begging (qunūʿ).
- By contrast, qaniʿa qanāʿatan = to be content/satisfied — explained the same way, as "turning toward" and accepting what is one's own. Ibn Fāris flags this as the same root sense producing near-opposite outcomes (begging vs. contentment) depending on the verb pattern.
- iqnāʿ is also used of a camel stretching its head toward water to drink, and (per Ibn al-Sikkīt) of camels/sheep inclining toward pasture.
- A "muqnaʿ witness" (shāhid muqnaʿ, pl. maqāniʿ) is one one is satisfied/content with, from qaniʿtu bi'l-shayʾ ("I was content with it"). A verse is cited about witnesses who were not "satisfactory" (maqāniʿ) in a secret pact made with a woman named Laylā.

**Core idea 2: roundness**

- al-qinʿ = a rounded sand formation.
- al-qinʿ / al-qināʿ = a tray-like object on which a gift is presented.
- qināʿ = a woman's veil/head-covering, named for the way she winds it around her head.
- From this comes the expression "he struck (qannaʿa) his head repeatedly with the whip," as if the blows formed a covering (qināʿ) over it.

**A possible third sense**

Ibn Fāris notes one usage that doesn't fit either core idea: iqnāʿ meaning "raising something up with no downward dip." He suggests this might warrant its own (third) root, citing Q14:43, "muhṭiʿīna muqniʿī ruʾūsihim" (hastening forward, heads raised), which the exegetes explained as "raising their heads."

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root q-n-ṭ, as al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī presents it:

1. Core sense — al-qunūṭ is despair of good, i.e. giving up hope that good will come.

2. Grammatical note — the verb is attested in two patterns: qanaṭa / yaqniṭu (verbal noun qunūṭan), and qaniṭa / yaqnaṭu.

3. Qur'anic evidence cited for this one sense:
   - "So do not be among the despairing" (al-Ḥijr 15:55) — active participle al-qāniṭīn.
   - "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except those gone astray?" (al-Ḥijr 15:56).
   - "O My servants who have been excessive against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God" (al-Zumar 39:53).
   - "But if evil touches him, he is despondent (yaʾūs), given to despair (qanūṭ)" (Fuṣṣilat 41:49) — the intensive form qanūṭ paired with yaʾūs.
   - "behold, they despair" (al-Rūm 30:36).

The entry records no further senses; in every citation the object of the despair is good or divine mercy.

dictionary: Lane — Arabic-English Lexicon, Edward William Lane (d. 1876)
text:
Lane's entry for the quadriliteral root ق-ن-ط-ر (q-n-ṭ-r).

1. Core verbal sense — to knit firmly / to arch. قَنْطَرَ الشَّىْءَ is glossed by az-Zajjāj as عَقَدَهُ وَأَحْكَمَهُ: he tied or knit the thing together and made it firm and strong; in later usage, he arched or vaulted it. Lane suggests "he compacted the thing." From this, a قَنْطَرَة (bridge) is said to be named for the firmness of its knitting or arching.

2. Second verbal sense — to aggregate. The verb also means to collect something into a single mass (see the participle in point 6).

3. Third verbal sense — to be rich by the qinṭār. Of a man: he came to possess property measured by the qinṭār; Ibn Sīdah: he possessed large wealth, as though it were weighed out by the qinṭār.

4. A related form: تَقَنْطَرَ بِهِ فَرَسُهُ is used in place of تَقَطَّرَ بِهِ (of a horse throwing its rider) — cross-referenced to the root قطر.

5. قَنْطَرَةٌ (qanṭara) — a bridge: a structure built over water to cross on. Azharī specifies an arched or vaulted oblong structure of baked brick or stone spanning water. Some equate it with جِسْر (jisr); others hold jisr to be the broader word, covering both built and unbuilt crossings. The Qāmūs adds the sense of a lofty structure. Plural قَنَاطِر.

   Morphology note: the Miṣbāḥ treats qanṭara as pattern فَنْعَلَة from the root قطر, with an added ن — and the placement of the word in the Ṣiḥāḥ and some other lexicons may imply the same; the Qāmūs, by contrast, treats the ن as an original radical.

6. قِنْطَارٌ (qinṭār) — a large measure of wealth. Described broadly as a standard of weight or measure; or an indeterminate quantity; or simply a large, unspecified mass of property, heaped up. The transmitted valuations vary enormously, and Lane lists them side by side without resolving them: 4,000 dinars (Thaʿlab reports this as what most Arabs held); 4,000 dirhams; 1,200 ūqiyyahs (Abū ʿUbayd, attributed to Muʿādh ibn Jabal); 100 raṭls — equated with the preceding, and equal to the hundredweight of Lane's own day — or 100 raṭls of gold or silver (as-Suddī); 120 raṭls; 1,000 ūqiyyahs of gold or silver; 12,000 ūqiyyahs (attributed to Abū Hurayrah from the Prophet); 100 ūqiyyahs of gold or silver; 100 mithqāls, a mithqāl being 20 qīrāṭs (Ibn ʿAbbās); 40 ūqiyyahs of gold; 1,200 dinars; 1,100 dinars; 70,000 dinars; in Berber, 1,000 mithqāls of gold or silver; 80,000 dirhams (Ibn ʿAbbās); 100 dirhams; 100 manns; or enough gold (or silver) to fill a bull's hide — reported by as-Suddī as the Syriac sense. Lane notes further definitions exist. Plural قَنَاطِير.

   Morphology note: the Miṣbāḥ takes qinṭār as pattern فِنْعَال from قطر with an augmentative ن; the Qāmūs takes the ن as radical.

7. مُقَنْطَرٌ (muqanṭar) — gathered into one aggregate; heaped up, made complete (synonym مُكَمَّل). The phrase قَنَاطِيرُ مُقَنْطَرَةٌ is explained as "much wealth heaped together" (Jalālayn at Q 3:14), where al-Bayḍāwī treats the participle as intensifying rather than adding a new idea.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: قَانِت 8x "and the obedient"; قَٰنِتَٰت 3x "and the obedient women"; يَقْنُتْ 2x "be obedient"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-n-t as a single sound root whose meaning centers on obedience and religious good; in his account nothing falls outside that field.

1. Core sense: obedience/devotion (الطاعة). The verb is قَنَتَ / يَقْنُتُ, verbal noun قُنُوت (qunūt).

2. By extension, any steadfast uprightness on the path of religion is called qunūt.

3. Two further applications named qunūt, per this author: prolonged standing in prayer (طول القيام في الصلاة); and keeping silent during prayer while attending to it (السكوت في الصلاة والإقبال عليها).

Qur'anic witness cited: {وَقُومُوا لِلَّهِ قَانِتِينَ} — "And stand before God, qānitīn" (al-Baqara 2:238), the active participle carrying the sense of devout obedience.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-n with a weak third letter (the article headed qanā) as having two root meanings: keeping close to something and mingling with it, and a rising in something. Forms with hamza, he adds, fall outside this scheme.

**1. Keeping close and mingling**

1. To mingle. Qānāhu means "it mingled with it", as one colour mingles (yuqānī) with a different one; al-Aṣmaʿī records qānaytu al-shayʾa, "I mixed the thing." Imruʾ al-Qays speaks of "the first (bikr) of al-muqānāt, whiteness mingled with yellow, nourished by wholesome water."

2. Not agreeing. A saying meaning "this does not agree with me" (printed mā yuʿānīnī hādhā, apparently for yuqānīnī) he explains as the thing shying away from the speaker, so that it does not mingle with him.

3. To keep for oneself. Qanā a thing, or iqtanāhu, is said when it is kept ready for oneself and not for trade. Māl qunyān is property taken as a qunya (or qinya), a holding kept for oneself.

4. To hold fast. Qanaytu ḥayāʾī means "I held fast to my modesty"; he derives it from qunya. A poet says: "So hold fast to your modesty (fa-qnay ḥayāʾaki) — no father to you! — and know that I am a man who will die if I am not killed."

5. The date-cluster. Al-qinw is the date-cluster (ʿidhq) with what is on it, so called because it keeps close to its tree.

6. The shaded spot. Al-maqnāt, for those who say it without hamza, is a place the sun does not strike, named so because the shade keeps to it and hardly ever leaves. Those learned in the Qur'an say that the cave of the Companions of the Cave lies in such a spot on a mountain.

**2. Rising**

1. The nose. Al-qanā is a hump in the nose; the verb is qaniya, verbal noun qanan.

2. The shaft. Al-qanāt, the shaft (as of a spear), may belong here, he suggests, because it is set upright and raised. Its alif stands for an original wāw, as the plurals qanan and qanawāt show.

3. The water channel. If qanāt al-māʾ, "water channel", is an Arabic word, he takes it to be named after the shaft: not for height, but because such a channel consists of underground conduits (kaẓāʾim) and wells, like a shaft made of joints and hollow sections.

**Forms with hamza**

With hamza the word leaves this pattern: qanaʾa means "its redness became intense", and qāniʾ is "deep red". The shaded spot is sometimes pronounced with hamza, maqnaʾat al-ẓill, but he judges the form without hamza closer to his analysis.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root ق ن ي (qny) — al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt

Anchor verse: Q53:48 (al-Najm), "aghnā wa-aqnā" — "He enriched and aqnā."

1. Core gloss: aqnā means God gave a person that which brings ghinā (sufficiency/wealth) and that which brings qinya — i.e. stored, saved-up wealth (al-māl al-muddakhar).

2. A second reported reading: some say aqnā here instead means "He satisfied/pleased [him]" (arḍā).

3. Al-Rāghib's own reconciling explanation: what God actually gave was a qinya — a lasting possession — made up of contentment (riḍā) and obedience (ṭāʿa). He calls this "the greater of the two enrichments," i.e. more significant than the enrichment of mere material wealth.

4. Morphology: the plural of al-qinya is qinyāt.

5. Related verb usage: qanaytu kadhā and iqtanaytu-hu both mean "I acquired/laid up such-and-such [to keep as a lasting possession]" — the same root behind the modern word for "acquiring" something.

6. Figurative extension (cited as an example of this usage): qanītu ḥayāʾī ʿiffatan wa-takarruman, "I held on to my modesty, [treating it] as chastity and nobility" — i.e. treating one's own sense of shame/modesty itself as a possession kept and preserved, here for the sake of chastity and generosity.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: قُرْءَان 70x "the quran"; قَرَأَ 16x "read"; قُرُوء 1x "monthly periods"; نُقْرِئُ 1x "we will make you recite"
text:
Al-Rāghib's entry for the root q-r-ʾ (قرأ) covers two connected fields of meaning: menstrual cycles (qurʾ) and reciting/gathering (qirāʾa, Qurʾān).

1. The verb of menstruation. قَرَأَتِ المرأة = "the woman menstruated (saw blood)"; أَقْرَأَتْ = "she came to have a qurʾ"; قَرَأْتُ الجاريةَ = "I verified (by a qurʾ) that she was not pregnant."

2. What al-qurʾ really names. Al-Rāghib argues that qurʾ is, strictly, the transition from a state of purity (ṭuhr) into menstruation (ḥayḍ). Because it jointly names two linked things — the purity and the menstruation that follows it — it then gets applied to either one alone. He compares al-māʾida, which names both the table and the food on it, then each separately.

3. Neither purity nor menstruation by itself. Evidence that qurʾ is not simply "purity" or simply "menstruation": a pure woman who has seen no blood is not called ذات قُرْء ("having a qurʾ"), and neither is a woman whose bleeding is continuous or a woman bleeding after childbirth (nufasāʾ).

4. Qurʾ in scripture and hadith. Q 2:228, "they shall wait three qurūʾ," is read as three transitions from purity into menstruation. The Prophetic saying "refrain from prayer during the days of your aqrāʾ" means the days of menstruation — a whole period named after the event within it, as one says "do X during the days of so-and-so's arrival" though the arrival is momentary.

5. Etymology (gathering). The lexicographers derive qurʾ from qaraʾa = "to gather/collect," seeing a "gathering" of purity-time and menstruation-time, and physically the gathering of blood in the womb.

6. Qirāʾa (recitation). Al-qirāʾa is the joining of letters and words to one another in measured recitation (tartīl). Al-Rāghib notes it does not mean gathering in general: one cannot say qaraʾtu of gathering a crowd, and a single uttered letter is not called a qirāʾa.

7. Al-Qurʾān as a word. Originally a verbal noun (maṣdar) on the pattern of kufrān and rujḥān. He cites Q 75:17–18 ("Upon Us is its gathering and its qurʾān…"), with Ibn ʿAbbās glossing: "when We have gathered it and fixed it in your heart, act by it."

8. Qurʾān as a name for the Book. The term became a proper name for the Book revealed to Muhammad, as "Torah" and "Gospel" are for the books of Moses and Jesus. Some scholars, al-Rāghib reports, held it is called Qurʾān because it gathers the fruit of the earlier books — indeed the fruit of all the sciences — citing verses on the Book as "a detailing of everything" (Q 12:111), "an exposition of everything" (Q 16:89), and others (Q 39:28; 17:106; 30:58; 56:77). In Q 17:78, "the qurʾān of dawn" means its recitation.

9. Further derived forms. أَقْرَأْتُ فلاناً = "I made someone recite" (cf. Q 87:6, "We shall make you recite, so you will not forget"); تَقَرَّأْتُ = "I understood/grasped"; قَارَأْتُهُ = "I studied it together with him."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَقْرَضُ 6x "and who lend"; قَرْض 6x "a loan"; تَّقْرِضُ 1x "passing away from them"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-r-ḍ as a single sound root whose core meaning is cutting (al-qaṭʿ). He derives its several uses from that one idea:

1. Literal cutting: قَرَضْتُ الشَّيْءَ بِالْمِقْرَاضِ — "I cut the thing with shears (miqrāḍ)."

2. Qarḍ (a loan): wealth you give to someone to be repaid — as though it were a piece "cut off" from your own property.

3. Qirāḍ (a commercial profit-sharing partnership): from the same idea — the capital-owner "cuts off" a portion of his wealth and hands it to his partner (muqāriḍ) to trade with.

4. Qarīḍ: reported to mean the cud/regurgitated matter (jirra), used in the proverb "ḥāla al-jarīḍ dūna al-qarīḍ" ("the choking swallowed matter came between [him] and the qarīḍ"). Ibn Fāris judges that here qarīḍ more correctly means poetry (shiʿr).

5. Mutual exchange of praise: yataqāraḍāni al-thanāʾ — when two people each praise the other, as though each "lent" the other praise the way one lends money. Ibn Fāris folds this back into the root's basic sense of cutting.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
**Root ق ر ع (q-r-ʿ) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha**

Ibn Fāris gives the root a single governing idea: **striking a thing**. Most of the section is derived from it, with two items marked as deviating.

**1. Core sense — to strike.** قَرَعْتُ الشَّيْءَ (I struck the thing) = "I beat it." مُقَارَعَة between champions is their striking one another. The stud-male is القَرِيع because he "strikes" the she-camel.

**2. Casting lots.** الإِقْرَاع / المُقَارَعَة = drawing lots for shares — so called, he says, because the lot is a thing that is, as it were, struck. قَارَعْتُ فُلَانًا فَقَرَعْتُهُ = "I drew lots against him and beat him," i.e. the lot (القُرْعَة) fell to me and not to him.

**3. القَارِعَة — the striking calamity.** A severe stroke of fortune, so named because it strikes people with its severity. Ibn Fāris also glosses القَارِعَة as القِيَامَة (the Rising), because it strikes and befalls people. On his account, قَوَارِع القُرْآن are those verses that leave the reciter untouched by terror; he adds tentatively ("God knows best") that the name is because they strike the jinn.

**4. Concrete idioms of striking.** A drinker "strikes his forehead with the cup" when he drains it. أَقْرَعَ الدَّابَّةَ بِلِجَامِهِ = he reined in the beast with its bit.

**5. Being open to counsel.** رَجُلٌ قَرِعٌ — a man who accepts advice; the explanation is that he was "struck" with words and took them. One who does not accept is فُلَانٌ لَا يُقْرَع ("he cannot be struck"). Related: أَقْرَعْتُ إِلَى الحَقِّ = I returned to the truth.

**6. Chief / best portion.** القَرِيع also means the lord or chief, because people rely on him in affairs — as though he is "struck" by the sheer number of requests made of him; Ibn Fāris cites as proof that he is also called مَقْرُوع ("struck"). Extended metaphorically: أَقْرَعَ فُلَانٌ فُلَانًا = he gave him the best of his property; the best of property is its قُرْعَة, again because it is what one falls back on in hardship. Widened further: القَرِيعَة, the best room in a dwelling — the warmest shelter in cold, the best shade in heat.

**7. Outside the root idea.** Ibn Fāris marks القَرَع and فَصِيل مُقَرَّع (a scab-afflicted weanling camel) as anomalous, citing Aws: at every trench they leave an armoured man "dragged as the scab-ridden weanling is dragged." He adds that القَرَع also means loss of the hair of the head (baldness).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) on ق ر ح (q-r-ḥ): three distinct underlying senses.

1. Pain / wound. Qarḥ is a sore or wound on the skin, or the sores (qurūḥ) that break out on the body and hurt. Qaraḥahu = "he wounded him." Al-qarīḥ = the wounded person; al-qariḥ = one covered in sores. Cited: Qur'an 3:140, "If a wound touches you, a similar wound has already touched the [other] people" — used of both sides suffering harm in battle.

2. Admixture / purity. Al-māʾ al-qarāḥ is water with nothing else mixed into it — pure water (illustrated with an anonymous verse about drinking plain water in the wild). Al-arḍ al-qarāḥ is land whose soil is likewise unmixed/pure. From the same idea: a man untouched by smallpox or disease is called qurḥān, a people qurḥānūn — "unmixed" with illness. A related word, qirwāḥ, means the same as qarāḥ, or else "wide open land" — a sense Ibn Fāris treats as close to this one, differing only in that some roughness of terrain is mixed in.

3. Extraction / eliciting. Al-qarīḥa is the first water drawn from a newly-dug well, which is why a person of sharp insight is called "good of qarīḥa" — the term for eliciting knowledge. From here: iqtaraḥtu al-jamal, "I rode the camel before anyone else had," and iqtaraḥtu al-shayʾ, "I worked the thing out myself, without hearing it from anyone" (independent derivation).

Outliers that don't fit the three roots:
- Al-qāriḥ describes a riding animal whose teeth have finished coming in (full dental maturity); al-Farrāʾ gives the verb qaraḥa yaqruḥu qurūḥan for horses at this stage, noting it's the one such age-term that doesn't take the usual alif-pattern (unlike athnā, arbaʿa).
- Al-qurḥa is a white facial marking on a horse smaller than a full blaze (ghurra); a "qarḥāʾ meadow" has white blossoms at its center — illustrated with a line from the poet Dhū al-Rumma describing a dark-green meadow with a white patch, tied to the seasonal rain-star (ashraṭ), kept going by light showers and fringed with buds.
- The expression qaraḥa fulānun fulānan bi-l-ḥaqq ("he confronted him directly with the truth") Ibn Fāris suggests is either a sound-substitution of qaraʿahu ("he struck him with it"), or an extension of the "wounding" sense (jaraḥahu).

Note: this is a purely philological entry — no doctrinal or ritual meaning is attached to the root; qarḥ throughout denotes physical wound/sore, and the extended senses (purity, extraction, dental age, markings) are traced as separate lexical branches, not derivations from a religious concept.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's entry for qrṭs is brief and consists of one definition plus two Qur'anic citations:

1. Definition — al-qirṭās is the physical writing surface itself: what a text is written upon (paper, parchment, or a scroll), not the writing or its content.

2. Qur'anic evidence — he grounds this with two verses from Sūrat al-Anʿām that use the word in its singular and plural forms:
   - 6:7, where God speaks of sending down "a written text on parchment (qirṭās)" — the singular, referring to a physical inscribed sheet.
   - 6:91, where the disbelievers are said to render the revelation Moses brought into "qarāṭīs" — the plural of qirṭās, i.e., separate sheets or scrolls — the point being they broke the unified Book up into scattered leaves.

No further senses, grammatical notes, or poetic shawāhid are given; the entry is limited to this single definition supported by the two Qur'anic occurrences of the root.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: قَرِيب 26x "near"; أَقْرَب 19x "(is) nearer"; قُرْبَىٰ 16x "the relatives"; يَقْرَبُ 11x "go near"; مُقَرَّبُون 8x "those brought near"; قَرَّبَ 5x "will bring you close"; ٱقْتَرَبَ 5x "has come near"; قُرْبَان 3x "a sacrifice"; قُرُبَٰت 1x "(as) means of nearness"; قُرْبَة 1x "(is) a means of nearness"; مَقْرَبَة 1x "near relationship"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-r-b as one sound root whose core meaning is the opposite of remoteness — nearness.

1. Nearness in general: قَرُبَ / يَقْرُبُ / قُرْبًا, "to be or become near."

2. Kinship: someone "of my qarāba" is a near blood-relative (raḥim). قَرِيب means "relative"; qurba and qurbā both mean kinship.

3. Approaching a matter: al-qirāb is the near-approach of an affair. "I have not gone near this matter, nor do I" means one has not touched or become entangled in it.

4. Watering camels (al-qarab): the night when camels come down to water. Herders drive the camels toward water as they graze; when only one evening's distance remains they hasten on, and that night is laylat al-qarab. The al-qārib is one who seeks water by night — al-Khalīl notes it is not used of a daytime seeker. The verb is conjugated قَرَبْتُ الْمَاءَ أَقْرُبُهُ قَرَبًا, on the pattern of "to seek" (ṭalaba) and "to milk" (ḥalaba).

5. Small boat (al-qārib): a light dinghy kept with seagoing ships for the crew's needs, seemingly named for its nearness to them.

6. Offering (al-qurbān): what is brought near to God, whether a sacrificial victim (nasīka) or otherwise. Ibn Fāris keeps this under the root's core sense of "bringing near," not defining a specific rite. Related: a king's qurbān / qarābīn are his close ministers and companions.

7. The kept-near mare (faras muqraba): a mare kept close rather than left to roam. Ibn Durayd: this is done with mares so that no base stallion mates with them.

8. A horse's gait (taqrīb): a pace below full gallop (ḥuḍr); called taqrīb because a full gallop covers a longer stretch. A horse is said to have two taqrībs, lower and higher.

9. A ewe: أَقْرَبَتِ الشَّاةُ — its lambing time drew near.

10. A "middling" garment (thawb muqārib): per Ibn al-Sikkīt, a garment that is not of high quality — i.e. moderate in price, neither costly nor remote from affordability. Others gloss muqārib as simply "poor" or "cheap"; the underlying analogy is the same.

11. The flank (al-qurb = al-khāṣira): named for its nearness to the side. Some derive it instead from likening it to a waterskin (qirba) — a second analogy, based on enclosing/containing a thing. From that containing-sense also comes qirāb, a sword's sheath (plural qurub).

Ibn Fāris cites two poetic witnesses: one using al-quruba for sword-sheaths ("gather the people's saddle-gear and the sheaths"), and one using al-aqrāb for the flanks of a firm she-camel ("close-knit in its flanks, not slight, as though a spare water-skin").

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
poets_named: unnamed verse ×4; al-Ḥuṭayʾa (lived into Islam); al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); Ibn Mayyāda (Umayyad)
text:
Root ق ر د (q-r-d), from al-Zamakhsharī's Asās al-Balāgha ("Foundations of Eloquence").

The entry is built around two creatures — al-qird (the monkey) and al-qurād (the tick) — and develops both a literal cluster (about ticks, camels, and rugged terrain) and a wide metaphorical cluster (stillness, abasement, deception, matting/clumping) said by Zamakhshari to derive from them.

LITERAL SENSES

- A proverb of contempt: "So-and-so is more abject than the monkey and the tick — lower than the tick."
- qarrada his camel = he picked the ticks off it. A crow qarradahu = it landed on the camel pecking off ticks.
- A camel aqrada = it went still [while being picked at]. A quoted line compares a submissive, motionless group of people to a camel sitting still under a crow doing this.
- qarūd (of a camel) = one that stays still for this tick-picking.
- qardad = raised ground beside a hollow, contrasted in verse with qarqara (smooth flat ground) and other terrain words (sabsab, fadfad, ghāʾiṭ) in a line about a long journey.

METAPHORICAL SENSES (marked by Zamakhshari as majāz)

1. "I plucked so-and-so's tick" — an idiom for getting the better of someone unawares (the word for "tick" here may be a copying error for qurād, but the sense follows the next entry).
2. qarradtuhu = "I deceived him" — extending the tick-removal image to trickery. Two verses illustrate it: al-Ḥuṭayʾa says even Banū Kulayb's "tick" is hard to draw out and manage; al-Aʿshā praises a people as trustworthy ("ghee with spice, no deceit in them") who protect their neighbor from being tricked (yuqarrada).
3. qarūd (of a man) = still, quiet. aqrada = he pressed himself to the ground out of humiliation. "I spoke to him and he aqrada" = he fell silent, unable to answer.
4. qarid al-fam = small-toothed (teeth small and close-set).
5. Matted/clumped things are all called qarid: matted wool, a curled/matted camel-hump, stacked-up clouds, and spoiled, gummy chewing-gum (qarida l-ʿilk when its chewed mass goes bad).
6. faras qarid al-khaṣīl = a horse with firm, compact thigh-muscle — illustrated by a verse praising a horse's compact build, with bones still showing signs of earlier careful breeding/training.
7. aqrada (of a camel, a second, distinct sense) = it moved with a smooth, gentle gait that doesn't jolt its rider — illustrated by a verse imagining an ever-pleasant, unjolting ride through life.
8. qurād al-ṣadr = the nipple. One can speak of a "fine" or "ugly" qurād al-ṣadr. A verse by Ibn Mayyāda likens a man's two nipples to seals stamped in clay from al-Jawlān by foreign scribes.
9. Finally, an anecdote from an Arab speaker: when speech turned difficult ("hardened") and wouldn't flow easily, he says "I took a qirdīda from it and rode it, never swerving right or left" — meaning he found and held to one clear path/approach through it. Zamakhshari traces this back to qirdīdat al-ẓahr, the ridge-line running along the middle of the back — the literal source of the metaphor.

Note: this is a rhetorician's (balāgha) dictionary entry, organized around literal usage versus Zamakhshari's own labeled metaphorical extensions — it records classical poetic and idiomatic usage, not doctrinal or technical vocabulary.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: ٱقْتَرَفْ 4x "and so that they may commit"; مُّقْتَرِفُون 1x "(are) committing"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-r-f as one sound root whose single idea is: mingling with a thing, getting entangled in it, and putting it on like a garment.

1. Core image — peel, rind, covering. The base is قَرْف (qarf), any rind or peel, e.g. قِرْف الخُبْز, the crust of bread. Ibn Fāris explains the naming: the peel is "the clothing" of whatever lies under it.

2. A leather container. قَرْف also denotes a vessel made of hides used for خَلْع (khalʿ) — meat cooked with spices and then poured into it. He cites a line about a Dhubyānī woman urging her sons on, mentioning "the velvet cloaks and the leather bags (al-qurūf)."

3. To acquire, earn. اقْتَرَفَ (iqtarafa) = to acquire or gain something — derived, on his account, from the person having mingled with it and clothed himself in it.

4. To be accused. يُقْرَف بكذا = to have something cast at one, i.e. to be accused of it.

5. قِرْفَة (qirfa) — the suspect, or the party where information lies. When a man loses something he says "So-and-so is my qirfa," meaning the one he suspects — as though he had dressed him in suspicion. Also "the sons of so-and-so are my qirfa," i.e. the ones he thinks have what he is looking for; and "Ask them about your she-camel, for they are qirfa" — i.e. news of it will be found with them. Ibn Fāris notes this all follows the same analogy of the root.

6. مُقْرِف (muqrif) of a horse — one bordering on mixed breeding; specifically, per what "they say," a horse whose sire is of non-Arab stock and whose dam is an Arab mare. Verse cited: if she foals a noble colt, so much the better; if there is iqrāf, the taint comes from the stallion's side.

7. قَارَفَ (qārafa) — to mingle with, be involved in. قارف الخطيئة = he mixed himself up with the offence. قارف امرأته = he lay with his wife; Ibn Fāris grounds this in the root's image, since each spouse is "the garment" of the other.

8. قَرَف (qaraf) — an epidemic afflicting a locality, explained as something that clings to its people like clothing and becomes disease. He cites a ḥadīth: a people complained of the pestilence of their land and were told, "Move away, for from al-qaraf comes destruction."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: قَرْن 23x "the generations"; قَرِين 8x "a companion"; مُّقَرَّنِين 3x "bound in chains"; مُقْرِنِين 1x "capable"; مُقْتَرِنِين 1x "accompanying (him)"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ق‑ر‑ن from two sound roots: (1) joining one thing to another, and (2) something protruding with strength. He then lists a set of forms that fall outside both.

FIRST ROOT — joining/coupling:
1. قَارَنَ — to couple two things; قِرَان and قَرَن both = the rope that couples two things (with a verse of Jarīr: "bound at the door as if in a qaran").
2. قَرَن — a small quiver attached to a large one; also the meeting-point of the eyebrows (a man مَقْرُون الحاجبين has joined eyebrows).
3. قِرْن (kasra) = your match in courage; قَرْن (fatḥa) = your equal in age. Ibn Fāris notes the underlying sense is one — the vowel difference marks the two different attributes.
4. قِرَان — pairing two dates eaten together; also joining a ḥajj to an ʿumra.
5. قَرُون (of a she-camel) — one whose front and rear teats are paired; or one that puts fore- and hind-legs down together when running.
6. مُقْرِن لكذا = equal to / able for something. He reads Q 43:13 (مُقْرِنِين) this way — "we were not able/equal for it" — tying it to qirn (a match), which he calls the analogy.
7. قَرِينَة — one's own self/soul (as if paired with the person); also, of a man, his wife. Variants قَرِينة / قَرُونة / قَرُون all = the self.
8. قَارِن — a man carrying both sword and arrows.

SECOND ROOT — protrusion:
1. قَرْن — the horn of a sheep etc., protruding and strong. By likeness, tresses of hair are قُرُون; hence Abū Sufyān's phrase for the Byzantines "those of the qurūn," which al-Aṣmaʿī explained as their long hair (with a verse of Muraqqish).
2. قَرْن — a fleshy growth in a ewe; also a small isolated hillock.
3. أَقْرَنَ الرمح — to raise the spear.

ANOMALOUS (outside both roots):
1. قَرْن — a generation/nation of people; plural قُرُون. Cites Q 25:38 ("many generations between that").
2. قَرْن — a burst of sweat; plural قُرُون (with a verse of Zuhayr).
3. قَرْنُوَة — a tanning plant; مُقَرْنَى hide = hide tanned with it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مُسْتَقَرّ 10x "abode"; قَرَار 9x "a resting place"; تَقَرَّ 5x "may be cooled"; أَقْرَرْ 4x "and we cause to remain"; قُرَّة 3x "comfort"; مُّسْتَقِرّ 3x "placed"; قَوَارِيرَا 3x "glass"; ٱسْتَقَرَّ 1x "it remains"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-r-r as having two sound root meanings: cold, and firm establishment (settling in place).

**1. Cold.**
- Al-qurr is cold. A day is qārr or qarr, a night qarra or qārra, and "our day has turned cold" is qarra yawmunā. Imruʾ al-Qays: "when they mount the horses and put on their mail, the earth burns, though the day is cold (qarr)."
- Al-qirra is the chill of fever, felt with languor and aching. A saying pairs it with thirst: "ḥirra (thirst) beneath qirra (fever-chill)."
- Al-qarūr is cold water for washing; iqtarartu means "I washed with cold water."
- Some people, Ibn Fāris reports, place aqarra Allāhu ʿaynahu ("may God cool his eye") under this meaning, reasoning that joy has a cold tear and grief a hot one; hence the curse askhana Allāhu ʿaynahu, "may God make his eye hot."

**2. Firm establishment.**
- Qarra and istaqarra: to settle, to become settled.
- Al-qarr is a kind of litter on which women ride, as in the verse "on a bier like a woman's litter, my shrouds flapping."
- Al-qarr is also pouring water into something (qarartu al-māʾ), and pouring speech into someone's ear.
- Al-qarqar is smooth level ground; al-qurāra is the residue stuck to the bottom of a pot, "as though it had settled in the pot."
- Al-iqrār, acknowledgement, the opposite of denial, belongs here by what Ibn Fāris calls a sound analogy: to acknowledge a right is to set it firmly in its place.
- Others explain aqarra Allāhu ʿaynahu from this meaning: may God give him enough that his eye rests and does not look longingly to anyone above him.
- Yawm al-qarr is the day the people stay settled at Minā, the morning after the Day of Sacrifice.

**His method.** Ibn Fāris says these analogies are sound in both branches, but he refuses to stretch them. He rejects the claim, reported to him from someone, that the qārūra (flask) is named for the settling of water in it. In his view some Arabic words follow analogy and others were simply assigned, and he records both kinds.

**Sounds.** Sound-words can occasionally be analogical, but most are imitations, such as qarqarat al-ḥamāma, "the dove cooed" (qarqara, qarqarīr).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris's account of the root ق-ر-ي / ق-ر-و / ق-ر-أ (he treats the weak-final and the hamzated forms as one root). Core meaning: gathering and assembling.

1. Town/village (قَرْية) — so named because people gather in it. Plural قُرًى, on the pattern kiswa → kusan.

2. Gathering water — قَرَيْتُ الماءَ = "I collected the water" (in a trough, مِقْراة); the collected water is قَرِيّ. The مِقْراة is also a large serving-bowl, named either for the guests who gather at it or for the food gathered in it.

3. القَرْو (a): a press or press-basin (like a miʿṣara); and a long watering-basin beside the great trough where camels drink. A cited verse places the poet "between the qarw and the presser."

4. القَرْو (b): a single uniform manner or course — "I saw the people upon one qarw" (all on one path). Related: قَرَوْتُ / قَرَيْتُ = to traverse/follow a route; al-Nābigha's line about a beast "traversing the low dunes and hillocks." Ibn Fāris files this under the first sense — as though following the land town by town.

5. القَرَا: the back, so named for the bones gathered in it. A strong-backed she-camel is قَرْواء (with a supporting verse); the term is not used of a male camel.

6. Hamzated form (قرأ), treated as the same root: ما قَرَأَتِ الناقةُ سَلًى = a she-camel that "never gathered a membrane," i.e. never carried a fetus (supported by a verse: "that has never carried a fetus").

7. القُرآن — Ibn Fāris reports (attributing it to others, "they said") that the name comes from this root, as though named for its gathering together of rulings, narratives, and the like.

8. أَقْرَأَتِ المرأة (a woman's qurʾ / menses) is said to belong here too, with two views recorded: (a) it refers to her state of purity, as though she has gathered her blood within and not released it; (b) it is her transition from purity to menstruation or vice versa. القُرْء is thus a period that can denote either purity or menstruation. Related usage: هَبَّتِ الرياحُ لِقارِئِها = "the winds blew at their appointed time" (with a verse). Ibn Fāris notes the whole word is problematic (mushkila); some jurists held it applies only to purity — their statement is lost to a gap in the text.

9. القارِئة = a witness (from the first sense). "People are God's qawārī on earth" = His witnesses. Explained on the same "gathering" logic: they gather things as knowledge, then testify to them.

10. القِرَة: wealth or livestock (camels and sheep); also dependents/family. A verse praises a king with "more livestock (قِرة) and dignity" than any other.

11. Deviating from the root's core sense: القارِّيّة = the tip of a spear-head; and the قارِية of anything = its edge or blade.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: قِسْط 15x "in justice"; تُقْسِطُ 3x "and act justly"; مُقْسِطِين 3x "those who act justly"; أَقْسَط 2x "(is) more just"; قَٰسِطُون 2x "the unjust"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-s-ṭ as one sound root that carries two opposite meanings from a single form.

1. Justice / equity — al-qisṭ (with kasra) is "justice, fairness" (al-ʿadl). The verb form is aqsaṭa / yuqsiṭu ("to act justly"). He cites Q 5:42, {God loves the just} (al-muqsiṭīn), noting the same phrase recurs at 49:9 and 60:8.

2. Injustice — al-qasṭ (with fatḥa) is the opposite: "wrong-doing, injustice" (al-jawr). Related is al-qusūṭ, "turning away from the truth," from the verb qasaṭa ("to act unjustly"; yaqsiṭu, verbal noun qasṭan). Thus the root yields two contrary senses distinguished partly by vowelling.

3. A bodily sense — al-qasaṭ is a "crookedness in the legs," the opposite of faḥaj (an outward splay/bow-leggedness).

Grouped under the first (justice) sense:
4. Share / portion — al-qisṭ also means "a share, allotment" (al-naṣīb); the verb taqassaṭnā means "we divided a thing into fair shares among ourselves."
5. The balance / scales — al-qisṭās means "scales, balance" (al-mīzān). He cites the Qurʾanic {weigh with the upright balance}.

Set apart from the root entirely:
6. Incense — al-qusṭ (with ḍamma) is a substance used for fumigation/incense; Ibn Fāris notes it is an authentic Arabic word, not derived from the above senses.

dictionary: ʿAyn — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786)
text:
Kitab al-Ayn on the root q-s-t-s -- al-Khalil b. Ahmad al-Farahidi

1. al-qistas / al-qustas -- two dialectal pronunciations of the same word -- mean "the most exact/most just of scales/balances." An alternative gloss given is that it means al-shahin, the pointer or tongue of a balance (the part that shows true equilibrium).

2. al-qarastun -- a related word, said to be Levantine (Syrian) dialect, meaning the steelyard balance (qabban), a hanging weighing device with a sliding counterweight.

3. al-qustunas -- a different sense from the same root-letters cluster: a flat stone slab used for grinding/crushing perfume and aromatic substances.

4. As evidence, the entry cites a line by the pre-Islamic poet Imru al-Qays, describing a bay-red, pure wine and comparing its colour to a qustunas perfume-grinding stone stained with wars (a yellow dye-plant) and jasad (a red pigment) -- i.e., a mottled reddish-yellow hue.

Kitab al-Ayn thus records this root primarily as vocabulary for weighing instruments (the "most accurate balance," and related terms for a steelyard), with a secondary, likely homonymous or loosely associated sense (qustunas) naming a perfume-grinding stone, attested only through the Imru al-Qays citation.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: أَقْسَمُ 20x "i swear"; قِسْمَة 3x "(at) the (time of) division"; قَسَمْ 2x "[we] distribute"; قَسَم 2x "(is) surely an oath"; تَسْتَقْسِمُ 1x "you seek division"; قَاسَمَ 1x "and he swore (to) both of them"; مَّقْسُوم 1x "assigned"; مُقْتَسِمِين 1x "those who divided"; تَقَاسَمُ 1x "swear to each other"; مُقَسِّمَٰت 1x "and those distributing"
poets_named: Labīd (lived into Islam); unnamed verse ×2; al-Quṭāmī (Umayyad); Ruʾba (Umayyad); ʿAntara (pre-Islamic); Zuhayr (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Sīda's account of the root q-s-m (ق س م):

1. Core sense — dividing/apportioning. Qasama (and intensive qassama) = to divide a thing into parts. Verbal noun qisma (division). Al-qism = a share/portion (plural aqsām); also qasīm (plurals aqsimāʾ, aqāsīm), and maqsam/miqsam in the same sense.

2. Sharing among people. Reflexive/reciprocal forms taqassama, iqtasama, taqāsama = they divided a thing among themselves. Istaqsama bi-l-qidāḥ = to apportion a slaughtered camel by lots using divining arrows. Qāsamtuhu al-māl = I divided the property with him. Qasīm = one's co-sharer in land, house, or property; "this is the qasīm of that" = its counterpart/half.

3. Ḥaṣāt al-qism (the "pebble of division"): a desert water-rationing device — a pebble is dropped in a vessel, water poured just to cover it, and travellers short of water take turns by it.

4. The apportioner. Al-qassām = one who divides things among people. Labīd applies it to God: "Be content with what the Sovereign apportioned; its Divider has apportioned our livelihood." A qism can also mean a gift one distributes (uncountable), from the same root.

5. Scattering. Qasama/qassama al-dahr = time split people apart, a portion here and there. Nawan qasūm = a parting that divides and separates (with a shāhid from Ibn al-Aʿrābī).

6. Pondering / mental division. Al-qism = opinion; or doubt; or measure/destiny. Qasama amrahu = he weighed his affair — or, alternatively, was at a loss how to act. A man muqassam = one whose mind is divided among cares.

7. Oath. Al-qasam = an oath (plural aqsām). Aqsama bi-llāh = he swore by God. Taqāsama al-qawm = they bound each other by mutual oath — as in Q 27:49, "They said, swear a mutual oath by God." Al-qasāma = a group who jointly swear or testify; the oath of qasāma is named for them.

8. Beauty. Al-qasām = beauty; a man is muqassam or qasīm (handsome), fem. qasīma, verb qasuma (became beautiful). The phrase "the muqassam trace" is glossed as the Maqām of Ibrāhīm, as though "made beautiful." Qasāmī = attributed to such beauty; al-Quṭāmī uses it (shortened, like tihām/shām) paired with hijān ("comely and pure-white") of noble ancestry and religion. Al-qisma likewise = beauty.

9. Features of the face. Al-qisma = the face, or the part facing you; variously the hairless part, the nose and its sides, its middle, the top of the cheek, or the tear-channel. A shāhid ("as if dinars upon their qasamāt") is explained either as the features generally or, per Ibn al-Aʿrābī, as the space between the eyes; also said to be the area above the eyebrow. Opening the sīn (qasama) is a variant throughout.

10. Folding cloth. Al-qasāmī = one who folds garments along their original creases (shāhid from Ruʾba).

11. Horse dentition. A horse is qasāmī when it cuts its mature (qāriḥ) tooth on one side only, at the end of its rabāʿ stage (with a shāhid).

12. Perfumer's casket. Qisma and qasīma = a perfumer's box. In ʿAntara's line, qasīma is read as either "daybreak" or "the perfumer's casket"; Ibn al-Aʿrābī's known form is qisma, so the poet may have lengthened the vowel metrically. Ibn al-Aʿrābī also gives qasīma = market, which Ibn Sīda thinks could equally fit ʿAntara's line.

13. Names. Al-Qusūmiyyāt = place-names (shāhid from Zuhayr). Qāsim, Qasīm/Qusaym, Qassām, Miqsam, Maqsam = personal names. Al-Qism = a known place.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives every word from this root (q-s-r) from one core idea: overpowering something, subduing it by force or severity.

1. al-qasr — the act of overpowering/subduing (ghalabah + qahr). Verb: qasartuhu qasran ("I overpowered him"); intensified Form VIII: iqtasartuhu iqtisāran ("I forcibly subdued him").
2. qaysariyy — said of a camel that is solid, hard, tough — the same underlying sense of being unyielding/hard to overcome extended to physical toughness.
3. al-qaswarah — "the lion." Ibn Fāris explains the naming: the lion is called this specifically because of its strength and its capacity to overpower/dominate (quwwah + ghalabah) — i.e., the animal is named directly from the root meaning "to overpower by force."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris holds that most words of q-s-s concern following something up, tracking it (tatabbuʿ al-shayʾ), and that some words close to it in form stand apart from that idea.

1. **Tracking and seeking.** The scholars he cites define al-qass as following a thing up and seeking it. One also says taqassastu aṣwāt al-qawm bi-l-layl, "I tracked the people's voices by night."

2. **Tale-bearing.** al-qass also means tale-bearing (namīma). On his scholars' account this belongs to the same idea: the tale-bearer tracks down what is said and then carries it to others. The gloss of qasastu l-qawm as "I hurt the people with ugly words" Ibn Fāris calls loosely worded; in his view it means only tale-bearing.

3. **The guide.** al-qasqās is the guide who shows the way, named for knowing the road and for seeking it out and following it well. The verb is qassa, yaqussu.

4. **Unremitting travel.** qurb qasqās and sayr qasīs describe travel kept up without let-up. Ibn Fāris ties this to the same principle, since such travel tracks the land and follows it.

5. **Dark night, cold night.** These he lists among what departs from the chapter: a layla qasqāsa is a dark night, and a cold night is sometimes called qasiyya.

6. **Qusās.** A place to which the Qusāsī swords are attributed.

7. **Hunger (doubted).** Some report from al-Shaybānī that al-qasqās means hunger, with the verse: "The qasqās brought him to us by night, though in his way lay mounds of sand with chasms between them." Ibn Fāris answers that if this is sound it is an anomaly, and if it fits the rule the poet simply meant the guide; he does not know what "hunger" would mean in the line.

8. **Inferior coin.** A dirham qasiyy is an inferior dirham; some say qasiyy is the Arabicised form of the Persian word qāss.

9. **Qassī cloth.** al-thiyāb al-qassiyya are said to be garments brought from Yemen.

10. **Calling to a dog.** qasqastu bi-l-kalb means "I shouted at the dog."

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root q-s-w, as al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī records it:

1. Core sense: qaswa is hardness of the heart. He derives it from the concrete image of ḥajar qāsin, "a hard stone" — the physical hardness is the origin of the moral usage.

2. Related form: muqāsāt is the coping with, or enduring of, that hardness.

3. Qur'anic attestations he cites for the verb and participle: "then your hearts hardened" (2:74); "woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of God" (39:22); "those whose hearts are hardened" (22:53); "and We made their hearts hard" (5:13).

4. Variant reading: the same word is also read qasiyya, which he glosses not as "hard" but as "not pure, not unalloyed." He grounds this in the coinage idiom dirham qasiyy — a dirham of adulterated silver. Such a coin has qasāwa in it, i.e. a hard, unyielding solidity (as against pure soft silver).

5. Poetic evidence for that coinage sense: "the adulterated coins rang out in the hands of the money-changers" — the ringing being how a debased coin betrays itself when handled.

The entry thus links two strands under one root: hardness (stone, hard heart) and adulteration/impurity (debased silver), the second reached through the variant reading of the Qur'anic word.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: قَتَلَ 83x "kill"; قَٰتَلَ 54x "fight"; قِتَال 13x "the fighting"; قَتْل 10x "[the] killing"; ٱقْتَتَلَ 4x "they (would have) fought each other"; قُتِّلُ 4x "they were killing"; قَتْلَى 1x "(the matter of) the murdered"; تَقْتِيل 1x "and massacred completely"
poets_named: unnamed verse ×3; Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ق-ت-ل from a single sound root meaning debasement and putting to death.

1. Core sense — killing. قَتَلَهُ قَتْلًا (he killed him). Related forms: القِتْلَة (kasra) = the manner/state in which one is killed, as in قَتَلَهُ قِتْلَةَ سُوءٍ (he killed him in an evil manner); القَتْلَة (fatḥa) = a single instance of killing; مَقَاتِل = a person's vital spots, which kill if struck.

2. Extended sense — to master/know thoroughly. قَتَلْتُ الشيءَ خُبْرًا وعِلْمًا = I came to know a thing exhaustively. He cites Q 4:157 {وما قتلوه يقينًا} in this sense — "they did not attain sure knowledge of it."

3. The imagery of love. تَقَتَّلَتِ الجاريةُ = a woman made herself alluring (as if yielding herself) until the man loved her, illustrated by a verse contrasting a woman's seduction with her later feigned piety. أَقْتَلْتُ فلانًا = I exposed him to being killed. A "slain heart" (قلب مُقَتَّل) is one killed by passion — with Imruʾ al-Qays's line about arrows striking "the pieces of a slain heart."

4. A grammatical distinction from the linguists: قُتِلَ = the man was killed generally, but اقْتُتِلَ is used specifically when the cause is passionate love — or when the jinn have slain him (with a line from Dhū al-Rumma).

5. A metaphor for diluting wine: قُتِلَتِ الخمرُ بالماءِ = the wine was "killed" (diluted), which Ibn Fāris calls a fine usage, with a verse punning on قُتِلَت / قُتِلْتَ.

6. Outliers he brings under the root by analogy:
- القِتْل = enemy (plural أقتال), reasoned as "the one who fights," on the pattern of سِبّ; with a supporting verse.
- هما قِتْلانِ = two equals/likes.
- القَتَال = vitality or firmness of body — ناقة ذات قتال is a sturdy she-camel. Some hold this is a phonetic substitution for original الكَتَال (bodily compactness, from تَكَتَّلَ "to cluster together"), a view he considers sound.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مُقْتِر 1x "the poor"; قَتَر 1x "dust"; قَتُور 1x "stingy"; يَقْتُرُ 1x "and are not stingy"; قَتَرَة 1x "darkness"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-t-r as a genuine root whose core idea is gathering together and narrowing/restricting, then derives the individual senses from that core.

1. **qutra** — the hunter's hide or blind. So called because it is cramped and because the hunter huddles together inside it. Plural: qutar.

2. **iqtār** — restricting, straitening. Verb forms: qatara ʿalā ahlihi / yaqturu, aqtara, qattara — to be tight-fisted with one's household. He cites the Qur'anic phrase describing those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor grudging (25:67).

3. **qatar** — what overspreads a face out of distress; he cites Yūnus 10:26, "no qatar nor abasement shall overcast their faces." Also: dust.

4. **qātir** (of a saddle) — one that sits well on the camel's back. He assigns it to this root because a well-seated saddle draws the hump together.

5. **qutār** — the smell of roasting meat. Ibn Fāris offers an etymology: a lion-hunter would burn meat in his hide (qutra), the lion would catch the scent and come to the pit-trap; from there any smell of roasted meat was called qutār. Shāhid: Ṭarafa's line in which people in their assembly ask whether what they smell is roasting meat (qutār) or the scent of burning aloes-wood (quṭr). Related: qattarat li-l-asad, to set out meat whose qutār a lion will catch. Ibn al-Sikkīt is quoted for qatara al-laḥm — the meat sent up smoke — the participle being qātir.

6. **qatīr** — the protruding heads of the rings in chain-mail work. Grey hair is also called qatīr, likened to nail-heads for its whiteness and glint.

**Excluded by Ibn Fāris:** qutr meaning "side" does not belong here; it is a consonant-substitution variant of quṭr, treated under that root.

**Anomalous:** ibn qitra, a malignant, rather small snake — reported from al-Farrāʾ, who suggests it is named after the qitra, an arrow with no iron head (plural qitr).

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
text:
Root ق ث أ (q-th-ʾ) — "cucumber," per al-Zamakhsharī's Asās al-Balāgha

This is a short, purely lexical entry (no figurative/metaphorical extension is marked) listing agricultural vocabulary built on this root, paired throughout with the parallel root for "melon" (ب ط خ):

1. Verb usage: one says أقثأتِ الأرض ("the land aqthaʾat") and أبطخت ("...and abṭakhat") to mean that cucumbers and melons, respectively, grew abundant in it.

2. Nouns for the growing-ground: a person's cucumber-patch is his مقثأة (maqthaʾa), his melon-patch his مبطخة (mabṭakha); the plurals are مقاثي (maqāthī) and مباطخ (mabāṭikh).

3. Set phrases: "with him is القثاء (cucumbers) and القثد (a related word/small-cucumber variety)," and "the melon with him is رثد (rathad)" — i.e. heaped up in abundant layers.

Note: the word given here as القثاء is garbled in the source text (القّاء, missing the ث) but is restored with confidence from context, since the whole entry concerns cucumbers.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
text:
Root ق و ع (q-w-ʿ) — Taj al-Arus, al-Zabidi (d. 1791 CE)

VERBS
1. A male animal covering/mounting a female (qaAEa al-faHlu ... al-naAqata) — treated as the letter-reversal of qaEaA, same meaning.
2. qaAEa al-kalbu (Abu Amr) — a dog limped.
3. qaAEa fulaAnun — he shrank back, recoiled.
4. iqtaAEa al-faHlu (al-Jawhari) — a male animal went into rut; in al-Lisan the same verb, and taqawwaEa, mean "it covered her." A cited verse (Thalab) pictures young camels mounting a she-camel once they've grown tall enough.
5. taqawwaEa al-insaAnu (Abu Amr) — a person staggers/leans while walking, as on thorny or rough ground.
6. taqawwaEa al-Hirbaau al-shajarata (al-Layth) — "the chameleon climbed the tree," used figuratively, borrowed from the mounting-sense above.

NOUN: al-qawE
7. al-qawE (Ibn Duraid) — a flat spread where dates or wheat are laid out to dry; a dialectal term. Plural aqwaAE. Ibn Barri equates it with three other words for "threshing floor."

NOUN: al-qaAE — the central sense
8. al-qaAE — a level, low-lying, spacious, firm stretch of ground: no roughness, no rise or dip; the surrounding hills/mountains stand back from it; no pebbles or stones; no trees grow there; its surroundings are higher, and it is where water drains and collects. Two alternative glosses are also recorded: a spot where water pools on hard clay, or simply level, bare, hard ground.
   - Plurals: qiyE, qiyEah, qiyEaAn, aqwaAE, aqwuE. Al-Zabidi notes qiyEah as a plural-pattern is almost unmatched elsewhere — only jaAr/jiyrah, and (his own addition) naAr/niyrah from a poem of al-Aswad, share the pattern. The root letter waw becomes yaA in qiyEah/qiyEaAn because of the vowel before it.
   - Qur'an citations: "then He will leave it a level plain" (Q20:106) and "like a mirage in a lowland" (Q24:39). Abu Ubayd argued qiyEah can itself be a singular, not only a plural — comparable to diymah ("steady rain"), which behaves the same way.
   - Hadith: "they are but lowlands that retained the water."
   - Each form (qiyEaAn, al-qaAE, al-qiyE, al-aqwaAE, al-aqwuE) is backed by an old Arabic verse or saying illustrating its use — describing camel-foam on lowlands, a she-camel's hooves on flat ground, camels trotting over firm terrain, and a farewell to withered flatlands.
   - al-quwayEah is the diminutive (feminine usage); masculine usage has al-quwayE.
   - A rare Qur'an reading variant, qiyEaAh, is reported from a reciter named Maslamah; Ibn Jinni treats it as equivalent to qiyEah (comparing the pattern pair Eizh/EizhaAh, "a man who shuns women and amusement"), while allowing it might instead be a distinct plural of qiyEah.

PLACE NAMES built on al-qaAE / al-qaAEah
9. A fortress (uTum) in Medina, called Utum al-Balawiyyin.
10. A place near Zubalah, a day's journey off.
11. yawm al-qaAE — a battle-day of the Arabs, on which Bistam ibn Qays captured the poet Aws ibn Hajar.
12. Further place-names: qaAEu al-Baqiy (Sulaym's territory), qaAEu MawHuwsh (al-Yamamah, cross-referenced elsewhere), a spot before Yabrin (Zayd Manat ibn Tamim's territory), a place in Yemen a day from Ghumdan, qaAEu al-Hubaab (Sinhan's territory), and qaAEu al-Bazwah (between Badr and Rabigh).
13. taquoEu — a village near Jerusalem known for good honey, popularly mispronounced "Daquoo."

RELATED NOUN: al-qaAEah
14. qaAEatu al-daAr — a house's courtyard (also called baAHah, SarHah), illustrated by a verse about women kindling fires there. Plural qawaEaAt.
15. al-qaAEah — the top point of a well-irrigation rig where the bucket's pull ends.
16. al-qaAEah — in Meccan (and, al-Zabidi adds, Egyptian) usage, the ground floor of a house, contrasted with the Eilliyyah (upper floor) — per al-Zamakhshari. Plural qaAEaAt.

OTHER DERIVED NOUNS
17. al-quwaAE (Ibn al-Arabi, via al-Layth) — the male hare (female form takes taA marbuTah); al-Saghani flags this masculine usage as an irregular formation.
18. al-qawwaAE (Abu Zayd) — the loud-howling wolf.

Al-Saghani's summary of the root's underlying sense: "a spreading/flattening out in a place."

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
text:
Root ق و ب (q-w-b), from Tāj al-ʿArūs by Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī. Al-Zabīdī gathers the following senses, citations, and scholarly disagreements around this root.

1. Digging a hollow. Al-qawb = digging the earth into a rounded pit (like taqwīr, "hollowing out"). Verb: qāba/qawwaba the ground = to dig such a pit; the ground itself "became hollowed" is inqābat/taqawwabat.

2. A bird cracking its egg. Al-qawb also names a bird's splitting open its own egg.

3. The chick. Al-qūb = a chick/fledgling, also called al-qā'iba or al-qāba; plural aqwāb.

4. The "egg-and-chick" proverb — with a real dispute about which word means what. A well-known proverb runs "qā'iba (freed) from qūb" or "qāba from quwab." Ibn Durayd and other sources (al-Ṣiḥāḥ, Majmaʿ al-Amthāl, al-Ḥarīrī's Maqāmāt) gloss it as "an egg, from a chick" — i.e. qā'iba/qāba = egg. But the grammarian Abū al-Haytham states the opposite: al-qāba is the chick and al-qūb is the egg. The entry preserves both without fully reconciling them. Its meaning: separation once and for all — used of someone who has parted ways with a companion. A Bedouin of Banū Asad tells a merchant hiring his escort: once I get you to such-and-such a place, "an egg is freed from its chick" — meaning, my duty to you ends there, and just as a hatched chick never returns to its shell, there's no going back. A tribal-rebuke verse uses the same image for a clan that shifted its claimed lineage to Yemen: if they don't return to their true lineage, the split is as final as chick from egg. A verse of al-Kumayt applies it to women fleeing old, greying men, as a chick flees its egg and a beautiful young woman does not return to it. A ḥadīth of ʿUmar uses the same proverb: he forbade combining ʿumra with ḥajj on the grounds that people would then treat ʿumra as sufficing for ḥajj, leaving Mecca empty of pilgrims the rest of the year — "like an egg parted from its chick." Al-Azharī adds: the egg is also called qā'iba (as "having-a-chick," maqūba) and, once the chick is out, qāwiba; the hatchling itself is qūb or qūbiyy. Against this whole picture, Abū ʿAlī al-Qālī records a common oath, "by Him who brought forth a qā'iba from a qūb," meaning "a chick from an egg" — reversing the sense again; Abū ʿUbayd al-Bakrī judged this a scribal/linguistic inversion (qalb), i.e. an error.

5. Peeling / molting. Al-mutaqawwib = something that peels or sloughs: a black snake that has shed its skin, or a man whose skin has peeled from mange. Al-Layth notes that mange strips a camel's hide bare of fur in patches, and those bald patches are called al-qūba or al-quwaba, and (with a long vowel) al-qūbāʾ/al-quwabāʾ. Ibn al-Aʿrābī and Ibn Sīdah are quoted disagreeing over the exact singular/plural relationship between these forms.

6. The skin disease qūbāʾ, and related grammar. Qawwaba = to uproot something from its base; taqawwaba = to come uprooted, to peel. From this comes al-qūbāʾ/al-quwabāʾ, a skin eruption that peels and spreads (something like ringworm) — al-Jawharī calls it a well-known disease, feminine and indeclinable, plural quwab, and quotes a verse marveling that mere saliva can defeat it (said to work especially with a fasting or hungry person's saliva). A long grammatical excursus follows on how the word is declined, its gender, and its rare morphological pattern (fuʿlāʾ with a quiescent middle radical) — shared, per Ibn al-Sikkīt, by only one other word in the language, al-khushshāʾ (the mastoid bone behind the ear) — with a comparison to al-muzzāʾ ("a kind of wine," cited from a verse of al-Akhṭal).

7. A chick-eater. Al-qūbiyy = someone greedy for eating chicks.

8. A name for disaster. Umm Qūb is one of the names given to calamity.

9. Eggshells. Per Ibn Hāniʾ, al-quwab means eggshells; al-Kumayt uses it describing ostrich eggs cracking open.

10. A homebody. A man described as "malīʾ quwaba" is one settled firmly in place, who never leaves home.

11. Qāb — the bow term, and the Qur'anic phrase. Al-qāb is the section of a bow between the hand-grip and the curved tip; every bow has two qābs. On the Qur'anic phrase "qāba qawsayn" (Q. 53:9, al-Najm), the entry notes that some scholars read it as short for "qābay qaws" — two qābs of a single bow, with the wording inverted — a reading al-Jawharī pointed to (attributed to those exegetes, not stated as settled fact). Separately, qāb/qīb also just means "a measure" or "amount" — as in phrases like "the measure of a bow" — and "qāba qawsayn" is glossed elsewhere as simply "the length of two bows." A ḥadīth is quoted: "the qāb of one of your bows is better than the world and everything in it." Ibn al-Athīr derives qāb/qīb from a root sense of "leaving a mark," per the phrase "they left marks (qawwabū) in the ground."

12. A contronym: to flee, or to draw near. Qāba (yaqūbu, qawban) can mean either "he fled" or "he drew near" — the two opposite senses are both attested, per al-Ṣāghānī.

13. To choose. Iqtābahu = he chose it.

14. Leaving tracks on the ground. Qawwabtu al-arḍ = I left marks on the ground by treading on it, and set markers along its irrigation channels — with two supporting verses about a tribe's encampment leaving its trace on the land.

15. The egg splitting (repeated). Taqawwabat al-bayḍa and inqābat al-bayḍa are given as synonyms: the egg split open and released its chick.

16. Extra material al-Zabīdī adds beyond his base text: a place can "inqāba" or "taqawwaba" when its trees and pasture are stripped away in patches; qawiba min al-ghubār means it became covered in dust (per Thaʿlab); al-muqawwaba describes land hit by rain where old trees still stand in patches (per Abū Ḥanīfa); al-Zamakhsharī's al-Asās has "the settlers qawwabū the land," meaning they left their mark on it; "quwab" on a person's head or skin means pits or hollows; and figuratively, "their egg split open (inqābat) regarding their affair" means their situation became clear — comparable to the idiom "their egg hatched" (afrakhat bayḍatuhum).

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: قَالَ 1618x "say"; قَوْل 92x "the word"; قَائِل 5x "a speaker"; قِيل 4x "and his saying"; تَقَوَّلَ 2x "he has made it up"; أَقَاوِيل 1x "sayings"
text:
Ibn Sīda al-Mursī's al-Muḥkam, root ق و ل (q-w-l):

1. Core sense — "saying, speech." Loosely, qawl is kalām (connected speech). More precisely (per the exacting grammarian), it is any utterance the tongue produces, complete or incomplete.

2. Qawl vs. kalām. In Arab usage, "I said" (qultu) reports kalām — a full sentence (e.g. "Zayd is departing," "Zayd stood"). Qawl proper is the single word out of which a sentence is built (e.g. "Zayd," "ʿAmr" taken alone).

3. Why beliefs and opinions are called qawl. A belief (iʿtiqād) or opinion (raʾy) is hidden and becomes known only through speech — or through the circumstantial evidence (shāhid al-ḥāl) that stands in for speech. Because speech is the means by which the belief shows itself and the sign pointing to it, the belief itself came to be called "qawl" (a thing named for what it is bound up with). Ibn Sīda's argument for why qawl rather than kalām: qawl resembles belief more closely, because a belief is grasped only through an outward expression, just as an incomplete qawl (e.g. the bare verb qāma, "he stood," stripped of its subject) has no complete meaning until joined to what it needs. Kalām, by contrast, was coined to stand on its own; so qawl — which can be dependent — is the better fit for belief, which must be spelled out.

4. Qawl of non-humans (figurative "saying" = making a sound, or displaying a state). Shawāhid: Abū al-Najm — the birds "said" to him, "Go forward, you will return praising"; another — the two eyes "said, 'Hearing and obedience,'" shedding tears like unpierced pearls; a rajaz line — the trough filled and "said: enough for me" (qaṭnī); another — the rain-clouds "said: iniyah iniyah" (iniyah = the rumble of cloud and moan of thunder); and "the saddle-girths said to the belly: draw tight." The reasoning: if opinion and belief (no sound at all) can be called qawl, actual noises the more so — birds coo, the trough gurgles, girths creak, clouds rumble. The "eyes said" case is by state, not sound: had they an organ of speech, the situation itself says they would have spoken. Ibn Jinnī cites ʿAntara making the same point: had his horse known speech, it would have addressed him.

5. Plurals and verbal nouns. Plural aqwāl; plural-of-plural aqāwīl. Verb qāla / yaqūlu, with verbal nouns qawl, qīl, qawla, maqāl, maqāla. A reported distinction: qawl covers good and evil, but qāl and qīl are for evil speech specifically.

6. A Qur'anic reading. Ibn Masʿūd read faqulā lahu qawlan layyinan ("speak, you two, gently to him") for faqūlā — treating the fixed vowel on the lām like the movable connecting-vowel seen in qul[i] llāhumma mālika l-mulk and qum[i] l-layl. (Cited as a grammatical point about the vowel, not for content.)

7. Agent nouns and "eloquent speaker." qāʾil (speaker), plurals quwwal, qiyyal, qālah (Thaʿlab: "they are qālah — speakers — of the truth"); intensive/expressive forms qaʾūl, qawūl, qawwāl, qawwāla, qūla, tiqwala, tiqwāla; and (Sībawayh) miqwal / miqwāl — feminine without the -a ending, not pluralized in -ūna. All mean "articulate, eloquent." Related nouns: qāla, qāl, qīl. "Son of aqwāl / son of qawwāl" = a fine, fluent speaker (faṣīḥ).

8. Ascribing words falsely. aqwalahu / qawwalahu / (al-Liḥyānī) aqālahu mā lam yaqul = to attribute to someone what he did not say. qawl maqūl / maqʾūl (al-Liḥyānī; the hamza-form is Abū al-Jarrāḥ's dialect) = a saying that is said. taqawwala qawlan = to fabricate a saying as a lie. A kalima maqūla = one said over and over.

9. al-Miqwal = the tongue.

10. Qayl / miqwal / maqūl = a king among the kings of Ḥimyar, "who says what he wills and it is carried out"; origin qayyil; said to rank below the paramount king. Plural aqwāl (Sībawayh: broken on the afʿāl pattern by analogy to fāʿil); also maqāwil, maqāwila.

11. iqtāla qawlan = to draw speech to oneself; iqtāla ʿalayhim = to arbitrate / give a ruling over them.

12. al-Qāl = the qulla, the little stick of the tip-cat game (a metathesized form); plural qīlān. Cited in verse: "and I am at the striking of the qīlān of the qulla."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: قَوْم 383x "for a people"; قِيَٰمَة 70x "(of) the resurrection"; أَقَامَ 54x "and establish"; مُّسْتَقِيم 37x "straight"; قَامَ 33x "stand"; قَائِم 17x "standing"; مَقَام 14x "standing"; مُّقِيم 10x "lasting"; ٱسْتَقَٰمُ 10x "they had remained"; قَائِمَة 5x "standing"; قَيِّم 5x "straight"; أَقْوَم 4x "and more suitable"
text:
