Ibn Fāris derives the root q-w-m from two sound base-meanings:

1. A group of people. القَوْم (qawm) denotes a people or group; he reports it is treated as the plural of "man" (imriʾ) and, in his account, applies specifically to men. Evidence: Q 49:11, "let no qawm mock a qawm," which then separately adds "nor women [mock] women" — marking qawm off from the women. Also Zuhayr's line asking whether the House of Ḥiṣn "are men (qawm) or women." Plurals: qawm, aqwām, and aqāwim (a plural of a plural).
   - Borrowed extension: qawm can be applied beyond people. A poet calls a rooster's flock at dawn "an unarmed qawm" — grouping them and naming them a qawm.

2. Standing erect, or resolve. قَامَ / قِيَام (qāma / qiyām) is to stand; al-qawma is a single act of standing up. The same verb also means to resolve upon or undertake something: قَامَ بِهَذَا الأَمْرِ = "he took on / stood by this affair." Ibn Fāris labels the two: qiyām ḥatm (a standing of necessity) versus qiyām ʿazm (a standing of resolve).

Derived items he places under this second sense:
   - قَوَّمَ / تَقْوِيم (qawwama): to set straight or appraise. القِيمَة (value/price) traces to the wāw, its underlying idea being that you set one thing up in place of another. He notes the Meccans' usage istaqamtu al-matāʿ = "I priced the goods."
   - قِوَام (qiwām): the mainstay or support of a thing — "this is the qiwām of religion and truth," i.e. that by which it stands.
   - القَوَام (qawām): goodly height/tallness; and القُومِيَّة (qūmiyya): stature and height — cited with a verse, "in the days when I was of comely stature."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root q-w-s — Ibn Faris, Maqayis al-Lugha

Core meaning: measuring or estimating one thing against another. (The root's waw sometimes shifts to ya in derived forms, but the underlying sense stays the same.)

1. Al-qaws = the dhira', a forearm-length unit of measurement — named this because it is the standard by which something is measured. The same word names the qaws, the archer's bow. Cited: Qur'an 53:9, "he was at the distance of two bow-lengths (qaba qawsayni) or nearer" — the exegetes gloss this as "two forearm-lengths."

2. Al-aqwas = someone whose back is bent/curved; qawwasa al-shaykh = "the old man grew bent, like a bow." Cited: a verse of Imru' al-Qays on women not loving a poor or grey-haired, stooped man.

3. With the waw shifted to ya: qisu rumhin = "a spear's length" (as a measure of distance). From here comes al-qiyas — measuring/comparing one thing against another — and miqyas, an instrument of measurement. Verb form: qayastu ("I compared/measured [two things]"). A cited verse plays on the image "count the pebbles, then measure them out."

4. Plurals of qaws (bow): qisiyy, aqwas, qiyas. A verse mentions warriors ("the Asawira") stringing their bows.

5. A secondary account Ibn Faris reports (without adopting it as primary): qaws can instead mean "outstripping/precedence" (sabq), and some derive qiyas from that sense — qasahum = "he outstripped them." A verse is cited about a father who outstripped everyone. Ibn Faris adds that even this sense ultimately traces back to the same waw-based root already discussed.

Anomalous items — the author explicitly marks these as NOT derived from the core "measuring" sense:
- Al-qaws — dates left over in a large storage basket.
- Al-qaws — a star/constellation.
- Al-miqwas — a horse-racing ground: a rope is held across the horses' chests to line them up evenly before release.
- Al-qus (different vocalization) — a monk's cell. Ibn Faris says he doubts this is a genuine Arabic word, though it appears in poetry — he cites a fragment comparing something to a monastery-priest's smooth, straight staff, and a verse by Jarir referencing a monastery (both citations are partial/incomplete in the source).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ق و ت (q-w-t), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

A sound root with one core meaning: holding/preserving something, and having power or capacity over it.

1. Qur'anic citation, al-Nisā' 4:85: "wa kāna Allāhu ʿalā kulli shayʾin muqītan" — glossed here as: a preserver of every thing, a witness over it, and capable of whatever He wills.
2. A line of poetry uses muqīt the same way of a person: holding back from someone who bore him rancor, though he had the power to answer the wrong done to him.
3. From the same root: al-qūt, one's sustenance (what keeps the last breath of life going) — called qūt because it is the body's mainstay and its strength.
4. al-qawt is given as a synonym of al-ʿawl (provision); quttuhu qawtan means "I provided for him."
5. A distinct idiom from the same letters: aqtatta li-nārika qītatan, "feed your fire firewood," illustrated with a line of poetry by Dhū al-Rumma about reviving a dying fire.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: قُوَّة 30x "(in) strength"; قَوِىّ 11x "(is) all-strong"; مُقْوِين 1x "for the wayfarers in the desert"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats q-w-y as two distinct roots — one for strength, one for emptiness/barrenness — plus one anomalous usage.

Root 1 — strength (opposite of weakness):
1. القُوَّة (quwwa) = strength; القَوِيّ = the strong, opposite of the weak. He derives this from القُوَى (quwā), the plural of quwwa, originally the individual strands or twists of a rope (قُوَى الحَبْل) — many strands making one strong cord.
2. المُقْوِي = a man whose companions and camels are strong.
3. المُقْوِي also = one who strengthens his bowstring, when he twists it so its strands lie doubled/overlapping.
4. رجل شديد القُوَى = a man of powerful strength, i.e. firmly knit in physical build.
5. Poetic term: أقوى (iqwāʾ) in verse = a metrical fault in which the poet falls short in his metre "by a quwwa." Cited line (attribution not named): "Is it, after the slaying of Mālik ibn Zuhayr, that women hope for the outcomes of their pure periods?"

Root 2 — emptiness / barrenness:
6. القَوَاء (qawāʾ) = uninhabited land; أقوت الدار = the dwelling stood empty.
7. أقوى القوم = the people came to be in the empty barren waste (القَوَاء / القِيّ).
8. بات القَوَاءَ / بات القَفْرَ = spent the night in the waste, i.e. spent the night without food.
9. المُقْوِي (in this sense) = a man carrying no provisions — grouped here as if he had halted in barren land.

Anomalous usage (fits neither root):
10. اقتَوَوْه (iqtawaw) — of partners who jointly bought something and then bid it up against one another until it reached its highest price.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root ق-ي-ض (qyḍ).

Al-Rāghib explains the verb qayyaḍa ("to assign/appoint [someone or something to a person]") through two Qur'anic citations:

1. Fuṣṣilat 41:25 — "wa-qayyaḍnā lahum quranāʾa" ("We appointed/assigned them companions").
2. al-Zukhruf 43:36 — "wa-man yaʿshu ʿan dhikri l-Raḥmāni nuqayyiḍ lahu shayṭānan" ("Whoever turns a blind eye to the remembrance of the All-Merciful, We appoint for him a satan").

He glosses qayyaḍa as nutīḥ — "We cause [it] to happen to him / We ordain [it] for him" — meaning the thing appointed (here, the satan) is set upon the person so as to take hold of him.

Etymological note: the image behind the word is that this taking-hold is like the grip of al-qayḍ — the outer eggshell — over al-bayḍ, the egg. Qayḍ, he specifies, is the topmost/outer shell.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
poets_named: unnamed verse ×5; Umm Taʾabbaṭa Sharran (pre-Islamic); Ibn Rawāḥah (lived into Islam)
text:
Root ق ي ل (q-y-l), from Tāj al-ʿArūs (al-Zabīdī). Two main senses run through the root: (I) midday — resting, sleeping, drinking, or milking at noon — and (II) undoing a bargain / being let off a fault. A cluster of proper names (mostly Ḥimyarite/tribal) rounds out the entry.

1. Al-qāʾilah = midday itself, or the noontime heat (so in al-Muḥkam, al-Ṣiḥāḥ, al-ʿAyn): 'he came to us at qāʾilat al-nahār.' It also shifts to mean al-qaylūlah, the midday nap. Al-Layth defines qaylūlah as sleep at midday, also called al-qāʾilah.

2. The verb: qāla – yaqīlu, with several verbal nouns (qaylan, qāʾilatan, qaylūlatan, maqālan, and maqīlan — this last flagged by al-Jawharī as an irregular form). Taqayyala = he slept at midday. Al-Azharī stresses that qaylūlah/maqīl really means resting at midday, not necessarily sleeping — proof: there is no sleep in Paradise, yet the Qur'an calls Paradise 'a better maqīl' (Q 25:24). Several ḥadīths use the root this way: 'Take your midday rest, for devils do not' (i.e. rest); a saying contrasting the one who travels in the noon heat with the one who stays home resting; in the report about Umm Maʿbad, two men 'qālā' (rested) at her tent; and a funeral report where 'qāʾil' means simply 'at home resting at noon.'

3. Plurals of qāʾil (one who takes the midday rest): quyyal, quyyāl, and the collective qayl — al-Jawharī quotes a line using two of these; some say qayl is itself just the plural of qāʾil.

4. Al-qayl / al-qayūl: the midday milk-drink, paired with ṣabūḥ (morning) and ghabūq (evening) — or simply 'drinking at midday.' Supported by verse citations (a watering-song; a line from Umm Taʾabbaṭa Sharran contrasting qayl with secret nursing). By extension al-qayl/al-qaylah can also mean the she-camel milked at that hour ('qaylātī' = 'my midday-milkers'), and al-qayl can mean a person sleeping at home at midday.

5. Related verbs: taqyīl = giving someone their midday drink (qayyalahu); taqayyala = to drink at midday, or (another reading) to milk the camel at midday — both senses backed by verse citations. 'The camels drank qāʾilatan' = drank at midday, paralleling 'drank ẓāhiratan' = at noon-heat. Aqaltuhā / qayyaltuhā = I brought the animals to water at that hour.

6. Second sense-cluster — commercial and moral 'release.' Qiltuhu / aqaltuhu l-bayʿa = I annulled a sale for someone (the bare qiltu form is rare/weak per al-Liḥyānī). Istaqālahu = he asked to be released from a deal; aqālahu = he released him. Taqāyala l-bayyiʿān = both parties to a sale mutually cancelled it, goods and price reverting. From here the meaning extends to moral pardon: 'aqāla llāhu ʿathrataka' = God overlooked your stumble; a ḥadīth promises that whoever releases someone who regrets a deal, God will release him from Hell; another urges overlooking the lapses of people of good standing.

7. Figurative extension: taqayyala abāhu = he took after / resembled his father (Abū Zayd; also used of following someone's way); and, of water, taqayyala l-māʾu = it pooled/collected in a low spot.

8. Named entities: Qayl, a man of ʿĀd (said to be their envoy to Mecca, identified by some as Qayl ibn ʿAyr); Qaylah bint Kāhil (or bint Jafnah), the eponymous mother of the Medinan tribes al-Aws and al-Khazraj; a Yemeni fortress called Qaylah; a desert mountain called Qiyāl.

9. A few unrelated homonyms attached to the same root-letters: al-qaylah/al-qīlah = a hernia or testicular swelling (with a ḥadīth reference and a colloquial variant 'al-qaylītah'); al-qayūlah = a she-camel kept for her own midday milk; al-iqtiyāl = bartering/exchanging one thing for another; al-muqāyalah = the same as muqāyaḍah, barter.

10. Appendix of further usages the author gathers: al-maqīl (also al-maqāl) = the resting-place itself, with a supporting verse; a ḥadīth praises someone for never holding onto money overnight or past noon before giving it away; 'maqīl al-raʾs' extends metaphorically to mean the place where the head sits (used in a battle-verse by Ibn Rawāḥah); Sībawayh notes the exclamative 'mā aqyalahu' is simply not said, Arabs using 'mā anwamahu' instead; regional variants are recorded — 'qayyālah' for qāʾilah in Egyptian usage, 'qaylah' for qaylūlah in Meccan usage; 'qayyāl' describes a man fond of the midday drink, and a related idiom describes a thirsty, slender-waisted person as 'sharūb li-l-qayl'; al-miqyal is a large midday milking-vessel (with a supporting verse about an abundant goat); al-qayl is also explained as a royal title among the kings of Ḥimyar, on the notion that each 'resembles' (yataqayyalu) his predecessors, with al-qiyālah as the rulership itself; a few more incidental senses (a shade-tree called miqyāl, 'the maqīl of his rancour' = his chest, and even a type of comb called qaylah) are noted as figurative or marginal usages; and the entry closes with a short roster of women named Qaylah among the Companions, plus two men, Abū Qāʾilah (a Successor) and Qayl ibn ʿAmr al-Tamīmī.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: رُشْد 6x "(of) the righteousness"; رَشَد 5x "(in the) right way"; رَّشِيد 3x "right-minded"; رَّشَاد 2x "the right"; يَرْشُدُ 1x "(be) led aright"; مُّرْشِد 1x "a guide"; رَّٰشِدُون 1x "the guided ones"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ر ش د (r-sh-d) as one root whose core idea is a road's being straight and sound.

1. Core sense: straightness of a path or way (istiqāma al-ṭarīq).

2. al-marāshid — the destinations or aims that roads lead to.

3. al-rushd / al-rashad — two forms meaning right direction or sound course, defined here as the opposite of al-ghayy (straying, error).

4. Idiom of attaining it: "So-and-so attained rushd (or rashad, or rishda) in his affair," i.e., he found the right course. Ibn Fāris notes the three variant nouns rushd, rashad, and rishda.

5. Applied to birth: "he is li-rishda" means of legitimate birth, the opposite of li-ghayya (of illegitimate birth) — the same right-versus-astray contrast carried into lineage.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root r-dh-l, as treated by al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī:

1. Core sense. The forms al-radhl and al-rudhāl denote something turned away from — rejected or held undesirable — because of its poor quality or inferiority (radāʾa). The entry gives a single sense, defined by the reaction the thing provokes rather than by a physical property.

2. Qur'anic evidence cited:
- 16:70, "returned to the ardhal of age" — the most reduced or worst stage of a lifespan.
- 11:27, "those who are our arādhil" — the people a community regards as its lowest.
- 26:111, "the ardhalūn have followed you" — the same dismissive social judgement.

3. Grammatical note. al-ardhalūn in 26:111 is given as the plural of the elative form al-ardhal. (arādhil in 11:27 is the other plural form the citations display.)

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
In Ibn Fāris's account, the root ر-أ-ف (r-ʾ-f) carries a single core notion: tenderness and mercy. The noun is al-raʾfa (compassion).

1. Verb and verbal nouns: raʾufa / yarʾufu ("to be compassionate"), with two verbal-noun forms — raʾfa (pattern faʿla) and raʾāfa (pattern faʿāla).

2. Qur'anic witness: Q 24:2, "let no compassion for the two take hold of you in God's religion/judgement." Ibn Fāris notes a variant reading raʾāfa alongside raʾfa.

3. Adjective: a person is called raʾūf ("compassionate"), on the pattern faʿūl; the stative verb is raʾufa (pattern faʿula).

4. Poetic witnesses: for raʾūf — "He is the Merciful; He has ever been compassionate toward us"; and for al-raʾūf — "He holds that the Muslims have a right upon him, like the act of the compassionate, merciful father."

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); al-Kumayt (Umayyad); al-Mukhabbal (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Manẓūr's Lisān al-ʿArab entry for the root ر-أ-س (r-ʾ-s), organised by sense.

1. Core meaning — "head / topmost part." رَأْس is the head of anything, hence its highest point. Plurals: paucal أَرْؤُس and آراس (by metathesis); plural of abundance رُؤوس, also رؤْس (by elision). Poetic witness (Imruʾ al-Qays): driving horses "down from the tops of the mountains." Figuratively, some grammarians called the rhyme "the head of the verse."

2. Striking or ailing the head. رَأَسَه: he struck his head; رُئِسَ: he had a headache. مَرْؤوس / رَئيس: one struck in the head, or (per al-Tahdhīb) one whose head brain-fever (sirsām) has struck; مَرْؤوس also of one afflicted with pleurisy/delirium (birsām). Labīd's رَئيس is glossed as one whose head is bound up. A ḥadīth about "taking from the head while fasting" is explained as referring to kissing.

3. To mount / seize by the head. ارْتَأَسَ الشيءَ: to ride on its head. Of a camel, المُرائِس / الرَّؤوس (al-Farrāʾ): one with no fat left except in its head. ارْتَأَسَني فلان: he preoccupied me — originally "took me by the neck and pulled it down."

4. Big-headedness (descriptive adjectives). فحل أَرْأَس: a big-headed stallion; الرُّؤاس / الرُّؤاسِيّ / الأَرْأَس: great-headed, fem. رَأْساء. A شاة رأْساء / نعجة رأْساء: a ewe black of head (and face), body white — contrasted (Abū ʿUbayd) with رَخْماء / مُخَمَّرَة (white-headed on a dark body). شاة رَئيس: struck in the head (pl. رَآسَى). رَأْآس: a seller of heads (colloquial رَوّاس).

5. "Head" as the upper end / leading edge of things. الرَّائِس: the head of a valley; any projecting height is رائِس. رَأَسَ السَّيْلُ الغُثاءَ: the torrent gathered the scum (then carried it off); Dhū al-Rumma's الرَّوائِس = the gathering floods. Of clouds, سحابة رائِسة / مُرائِس (pl. رَوائِس): the foremost cloud. A رَأْس of garlic = a bulb.

6. "Head" as a numerous, mighty people. الرَّأْس: a host of people when many and strong (ʿAmr b. Kulthūm). Al-Jawharī suggests the poet actually meant "the chief" (raʾīs), since he wrote "with it" not "with them."

7. Leadership — the dominant sense-cluster. رَأَسَ القومَ: he became their chief; رَآسَة / رِياسَة = chieftaincy. Verb-forms: رَأَسَ عليهم, تَرَأَّسَ (like taʾammara), رَأَّسُوه ("they made him chief," like ammarūhu); a disputed رَوَّسُوه (al-Azharī: analogy requires رَأَّسوه). الرَّئيس: the lord/chief of a people (pl. رُؤَساء; colloquial رُيَساء); variant رَيِّس (like qayyim). Poetic witness (al-Kumayt): "the flock is rightly guided so long as the chief (rayyis) stands upright" — a figure for a just ruler under whom wolf and sheep share one water. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: to رَأَسَ is to vie and jostle for leadership; a saying holds that leadership "descends from heaven and is bound onto the head of one who does not seek it." Ḥadīth witnesses: "Did I not leave you to rule (tarʾas) and prosper?"; and "the raʾs (head) of unbelief is from the east" (taken as a pointer to the Dajjāl or eastern leaders of misguidance).

8. "Head" / leader among hunting dogs. رَئيس الكلاب / رائِسها: the lead dog none outstrips in the chase, as a raʾīs among people. كلبة رائِسة: a bitch that takes the quarry by the head; كلبة رَؤوس: one that lunges at the quarry's head. رائِس / رَوائِس of a river or valley: its upper reaches.

9. Idioms of "leading with the head." Of the lizard (ḍabb) provoked by a viper: خرج مُرَئِّساً, it emerged head-first (vs. مُذَنِّباً, tail-first). وَلَدَتْ … على رَأْسٍ واحدٍ / رأْساً على رأْس: she bore (children) one after another.

10. Place-names and proper nouns. رَأْسُ عَين / رَأْس العَين: a place — Ibn Barrī notes the definite form (Raʾs al-ʿAyn) is used only of the town in the Jazīra, the indefinite (Raʾs ʿAyn) of any spring; illustrated by satirical verses of al-Mukhabbal against al-Zibriqān (over Hazzāl's marriage and killing) and a "Day of Raʾs al-ʿAyn." رائِس: a mountain in the sea (Umayya al-Hudhalī). بَيت رأْس: a wine-selling village in Syria (Ḥassān b. Thābit). بنو رُؤاس: a clan of ʿĀmir b. Ṣaʿṣaʿa — Abū ʿUmar al-Zāhid held the correct nisba to be al-Rawāsī (unhamzated, from Rawās of Sulaym), rejecting the traditionists' al-Ruʾāsī.

11. Further idioms. أَنت على رأْسِ / رِئاسِ أَمرك: at the height or the outset of your affair (al-Jawharī prefers rīʾās). رِئاس السيف: the sword's hilt or pommel, as if derived from raʾs (Ibn Muqbil; Shamir heard the word only here; Ibn Sīda found the unhamzated kiryās and was unsure of its derivation). رُمِيَ فلان منه في الرأْس: he was disregarded and found burdensome ("he raised no head for him"). أَعِدْ عليّ كلامَك من رأْسٍ / من الرأْسِ: "say it to me again from the start" — the second (definite) form being the rarer and disputed.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: رَءَا 271x "you see"; أَرَيْ 40x "we show you"; رُّءْيَا 7x "the vision"; رِئَاء 3x "and showing off"; رَأْى 2x "immature in opinion"; يُرَاءُ 2x "make show"; تَرَاءَتِ 2x "came in sight"; رِءْي 1x "and appearance"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root r-ʾ-y (rāʾ, hamza, yāʾ) from a single core sense: looking and seeing — whether physically with the eye or inwardly with insight (baṣīra). From this he lists:

1. الرَّأْي (al-raʾy): what a person "sees" in a matter, i.e. his opinion or view; plural الآراء (al-ārāʾ).

2. The verb: رَأَى (raʾā, "he saw"). The form رَاءَ (rāʾa) is the same verb with the letters transposed (metathesis).

3. الرِّئْي (al-riʾy): a fair or pleasing condition/appearance that the eye takes in.

4. Dialectal/contracted forms and reciprocals: رَيْتُهُ (raytuhu) used to mean رَأَيْتُهُ ("I saw him"); تَرَاءَى القومُ ("the people saw one another").

5. رَاءَى / يُرَائِي (rāʾā/yurāʾī): to make a show of oneself. The phrase رِئَاء الناس (riʾāʾ al-nās) means doing something specifically so that people will see it (acting for display).

6. الرُّوَاء (al-ruwāʾ): beauty or goodliness of outward appearance.

7. المِرْآة (al-mirʾāt): the mirror (noted as a well-known term).

8. التَّرْئِيَة (al-tarʾiya) — or, softening the hamza, التَّرِيَّة (al-tariyya): the yellowish discharge a menstruating woman sees after the menstrual blood, or her noticing the early signs of menstruation beforehand.

9. الرُّؤْيَا (al-ruʾyā): the dream/vision (noted as well known); plural رُؤًى (ruʾan).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَرْضَعَتْ 5x "then may suckle"; رَّضَاعَة 2x "the nursing"; يُرْضِعْ 1x "shall suckle"; تَسْتَرْضِعُ 1x "ask another women to suckle"; مُرْضِعَة 1x "nursing mother"; مَرَاضِع 1x "the wet nurses"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-ḍ-ʿ as one root with a single core meaning: drinking milk from an udder or a breast.

1. Basic verb: رَضِعَ / يَرْضَعُ — "(an infant) suckled / suckles."

2. Idiom لَئِيمٌ رَاضِعٌ ("a base 'suckler'"): a stingy man so mean that he suckles his own she-camels himself, so the sound of his milking will not be heard (and no one will come to ask for milk).

3. Grammatical distinction between two participles: امْرَأَةٌ مُرْضِعٌ describes a woman who has a nursing child (a status), while مُرْضِعَةٌ describes her in the very act of nursing. Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 22:2 — "every مُرْضِعَة (nursing mother) will be distracted from what she nursed" — where the act-form is used.

4. الرَّاضِعَتَانِ: the two front teeth, so called because one drinks upon them.

5. Dialectal note: the people of Najd inflect it رَضَعَ / يَرْضِعُ (pattern faʿala/yafʿilu), cited with a verse of poetry that pictures people "suckling" at the world draught by draught until its teat runs dry.

6. Milk-kinship / derived nouns:
   - أَخٌ مِنَ الرَّضَاعَة (raḍāʿa, with fatḥa) — a foster-brother by suckling.
   - الرِّضَاع — the verbal noun of رَاضَعْتُهُ (to be suckled alongside / share suckling).
   - رَضِيع — one's milk-companion, formed like رَسِيل (travel-companion) and أَكِيل (messmate).
   - الرَّضُوعَة — a ewe that suckles its young.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
quran_words: رَّضِىَ 38x "and they are pleased"; رِضْوَٰن 13x "and pleasure"; مَرْضَات 5x "pleasure"; رَاضِيَة 4x "pleasant"; يُرْضُ 3x "they should please him"; ٱرْتَضَىٰ 3x "he has approved"; تَرَٰضَ 2x "they agree"; تَرَاض 2x "mutual consent"; رَضِيّ 1x "pleasing"; مَرْضِيّ 1x "pleasing"; مَّرْضِيَّة 1x "and pleasing"
poets_named: al-Quḥayf al-ʿUqaylī (undated); Zuhayr (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse ×2; al-Akhṭal (Umayyad)
text:
In Lisān al-ʿArab, r-ḍ-w (entered under رضي) centres on al-riḍā, being pleased or content, defined as the opposite of al-sakhaṭ, displeasure. The article gathers grammatical notes from earlier authorities and ends with proper names from the root.

1. **Pleasure, contentment (al-riḍā).** The opposite of displeasure. A ḥadīth of supplication is quoted: "O God, I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your displeasure, and in Your pardon from Your punishment; I seek refuge in You from You; I cannot count the praise due to You; You are as You have praised Yourself." One version puts pardon before pleasure. Ibn al-Athīr explains that order as a rising sequence: pardon is an attribute of acts, lower in rank than attributes of the essence, so the speaker moves from acts to attributes to the essence itself, then from seeking refuge to praise, and finally admits that his praise falls short. On the other version, he says pleasure comes first because pardon follows from it; pardon is then named outright because the first phrase only implied it, and because one who is pleased may still punish for some benefit or to settle another's right.

2. **Verb and verbal nouns.** raḍiya, yarḍā (to be pleased). Verbal nouns: riḍan, ruḍan, riḍwān, ruḍwān (Sībawayh, comparing shukrān and rujḥān) and marḍāh. Al-Ṣiḥāḥ treats riḍwān, ruḍwān and marḍāh as equal to riḍā. All the Qur'an readers read riḍwān with i, except a report that ʿĀṣim read ruḍwān. Al-Akhfash gives the noun (as distinct from the pure verbal noun riḍan) as al-riḍāʾ, with a long final vowel.

3. **Short or long riḍā.** Abū Manṣūr: as the verbal noun of raḍiya it is short (riḍā); in the sense of murāḍāh, mutual pleasing, it is long (riḍāʾ). Al-Muḥkam also says the long form is used only in that sense.

4. **A wāw root with a yāʾ surface.** The root is originally wāw-final. Al-Jawharī says the proper form would be raḍuwa, but raḍiya is said because of the kasra, as with shabiʿa shibaʿan. The same explains the passive participle: usually marḍiyy, but some say marḍuww "according to the original". Dual of riḍā: riḍawān (original wāw) and riḍayān (wāw alternating with yāʾ), perhaps dualised with the genus in mind. Al-Kisāʾī heard riḍawān and ḥimawān; al-Jawharī reports that the proper forms are riḍayān and ḥimayān, that some Arabs use yāʾ, and that wāw is more common. Sībawayh notes the rare form raḍyū (they were pleased), with the middle letter made quiescent, compared with ghazyā.

5. **Participles and plurals.** rāḍin (pleased), plural ruḍāh; raḍiyy, plural arḍiyāʾ and ruḍāh (the latter from al-Liḥyānī, which Ibn Sīda calls rare and would assign only to rāḍin); raḍin, plural raḍīn (al-Liḥyānī).

6. **Pleased "with": ʿan, ʿalā, bi-.** One says raḍītu ʿanka and also raḍītu ʿalayka. A verse of al-Quḥayf al-ʿUqaylī has "when Banū Qushayr are pleased with me (ʿalayya)". This is explained in two ways: being pleased with someone means loving and turning toward (aqbala ʿalā) him; or, the view of al-Kisāʾī that Abū ʿAlī approved (reported by Ibn Jinnī), the verb borrows the preposition of its opposite, sakhiṭa ʿalā (to be angry with). Ibn Jinnī adds that Sībawayh often reasons this way. raḍītu bihi ṣāḥiban means "I was content with him as a companion", and raḍītu ʿalayhi is sometimes used in the sense of bihi and ʿanhu.

7. **The Qur'anic phrase.** "God is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him" (raḍiya llāhu ʿanhum wa-raḍū ʿanhu) is interpreted as: God was pleased with their deeds, and they were pleased with what He recompensed them with.

8. **Approved, acceptable (al-raḍiyy, al-marḍiyy).** al-raḍiyy is the one approved. Ibn al-Aʿrābī adds two further senses of al-raḍiyy: the obedient one, and the guarantor. raḍītu l-shayʾa and irtaḍaytuhu: I approved the thing, so it is marḍiyy. irtaḍāhu: he judged him fit for something. Ibn Sīda: raḍiyahu li-dhālika l-amr, "he approved him for that matter".

9. **riḍan as an adjective.** "A man who is riḍan, of a people who are riḍan" means an accepted arbiter (qunʿān) who is approved. The verbal noun is used as an adjective with a passive sense, as ʿadl (just) and khaṣm (adversary) are used with an active sense. Zuhayr: "They are between us, and they are acceptable (riḍan), and they are just (ʿadl)."

10. **A pleasing life (ʿīsha rāḍiya).** Qur'anic fī ʿīshatin rāḍiya is explained as marḍiyya, "pleasing", that is, possessed of satisfaction, like hamm nāṣib ("a wearying care"). Sībawayh calls it a form of relation (nasab). One says ruḍiyat maʿīshatuhu in the passive ("his livelihood was found pleasing"), never raḍiyat in the active.

11. **Causing and seeking pleasure.**
   - arḍāhu: to give someone what will please him. arḍaytuhu ʿannī and raḍḍaytuhu: I made him pleased with me.
   - taraḍḍāhu: to seek someone's pleasure. taraḍḍaytuhu: I pleased him after effort.
   - istarḍaytuhu fa-arḍānī: I asked him to be pleased, and he pleased me.
   - A verse: "If the old woman grows angry, divorce her, and do not placate her (lā taraḍḍāhā) nor flatter." The alif is kept in a jussive position, as a yāʾ is kept in "Has it not reached you (a-lam yaʾtīka) … what the milch camels of Banū Ziyād met with?" Ibn Sīda says this avoided a metrical defect (khabn); some transmit the regular lā taraḍḍahā and accept the defect.

12. **Competing in contentment.** rāḍānī murāḍātan wa-riḍāʾan fa-raḍawtuhu arḍūhu: he vied with me in being pleased and I outdid him (the wāw shows here). Al-Muḥkam: "I was more strongly pleased than he."

13. **Names.**
   - Raḍwā is a mountain at Medina (adjective raḍawī). Ibn Sīda calls it a particular mountain after which women were named. He will not derive it the way taqwā is derived, because the language has no r-ḍ-y from which it could come.
   - Al-Tahdhīb gives Raḍwā as a woman's name, citing al-Akhṭal: "Wāsiṭ has been effaced of Raḍwā's people … so patience is more fitting."
   - Ruḍayyā is a woman's name, patterned like al-Thurayyā; the non-diminutive forms are Raḍwā and Tharwā.
   - Raḍwā was also the name of Saʿd ibn Shujāʿ's horse.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-ʿ-b as three separate root-meanings: (1) fear, (2) filling, (3) cutting.

1. Fear. الرَّعْب (raʿb) is fear; the verb رَعَبْتُهُ ("I frightened him") takes the verbal noun رَعْبًا, while the noun proper is الرُّعْب (ruʿb). He also reports a further use: الرَّعْب as an incantation — people claim to "raʿb" a practitioner of sorcery by means of certain words, i.e. to terrify him. The agent-nouns are رَاعِب (rāʿib) and the intensive رَعَّاب (raʿʿāb).

2. Filling. سَيْلٌ رَاعِبٌ is a torrent that fills the valley; رَعَبْتُ الْحَوْضَ means "I filled the watering-trough."

3. Cutting. Something cut into pieces is مُرَعَّب (muraʿʿab). A piece cut from a camel's hump is a رُعْبُوبَة (ruʿbūba); a slender, well-formed woman is likewise called رُعْبُوبَة, by comparison with that piece of hump. A hump that drips with fat is described as مَرْعُوب (marʿūb).

The entry cites no poetry and no Qur'anic verses; the method is Ibn Fāris's usual one of reducing the letter-set to a small number of independent semantic origins and listing the derived forms under each.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris (Maqayis al-Lugha) treats r-'-d as a single root meaning motion and agitation/trembling.

1. Core sense -- trembling/shaking. Anything that shakes is said to "irta'ada." From this: ri'didah/ri'did, "a coward," and the phrase for a man's shoulder-muscles trembling from fright. Ri'didah is also used for "a soft, tender woman" (plural ra'adid).

2. Thunder. Al-ra'd ("thunder") belongs to the same root -- Ibn Faris describes it as the mas' ("driving motion," itself meaning "coming and going") of an angel who drives the clouds; the same word mas' is used of an animal flicking its tail.

3. Verbal usage. "The sky thundered and lightninged." Applied to a person, "he thundered and lightninged" means he threatened and menaced -- with the hamza-forms ar'ada/abraqa also allowed in the same sense. He cites a line of verse: "Thunder and bluster, O Yazid -- your threat does not harm me," illustrating the metaphorical "threatening" sense.

4. Proverbs cited:
   - "Bluster beneath the thundering [cloud]" -- said of a man who talks a great deal but has no substance to him (salaf is glossed as "scantiness of yield/benefit").
   - "We had thunder and lightning" -- said when thunder was heard and lightning seen.
   - "He came with that of thunder and clanging" -- said when news [of good fortune] and a raiding expedition arrived together; the phrase "that of thunder and clanging" is said to denote war itself.
   - "That of the thunderers" -- a name for calamity/disaster.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: رَٰعِ 2x "raina"; رَعَ 2x "they observed it"; رَٰعُون 2x "(are) observers"; مَرْعَىٰ 2x "the pasture"; رِّعَاء 1x "the shepherds"; رِعَايَت 1x "observance"
poets_named: Abū Qays (pre-Islamic); al-Khansāʾ (lived into Islam); Dhū al-Iṣbaʿ (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse
text:
Ibn Fāris derives رعي from two base meanings: (1) watching/guarding, and (2) turning back.

Root 1 — watching over and safeguarding:
- رَعَيْتُ الشيءَ = to watch over or keep an eye on something; رَعَيْتُهُ = to attend to / regard it.
- الرَّاعِي ("shepherd") also denotes the governor or ruler. A line of Abū Qays contrasts the one shepherded (المَرْعِيّ) with the shepherd (الرَّاعِي). Plurals: رِعَاء (on the rare pattern فِعَال) and رُعَاة.
- رَاعَيْتُ الأمرَ = to watch and see what an affair will come to. رَعَيْتُ النُّجُومَ = to watch/observe the stars, illustrated by a verse of al-Khansāʾ ("I watch the stars though not charged to").
- الإِرْعَاء = keeping/sparing/preserving — placed here because to spare is to safeguard. A verse of Dhū al-Iṣbaʿ uses فلم يُرْعُوا ("they did not spare one another").
- رجلٌ تُرْعِيَةٌ / تِرْعَايَةٌ = a man skilled at tending camels.
- Also from this sense: أَرْعَيْتُهُ سَمْعِي = to listen attentively; أَرْعِنِي سَمْعَكَ (with kasra on the ʿayn) = "lend me your ear," i.e. let your hearing attend to my words.

Root 2 — turning back / desisting:
- ارْعَوَى عن القبيح = to desist and turn away from an ugly deed. Related nouns: الرَّعْو / الرِّعْو / الرَّعْوَى (good sense in desisting).

Anomalous (fitting neither root cleanly): الرَّعَاوَى / الرُّعَاوَى = the camels used for labour. A woman's verse likens a worn-out man to "the worn beast of the work-camels." Ibn Fāris suggests this could still belong to Root 1, since such camels grow old and are reduced to a poor state — comparable to the Qurʾanic phrase "returned to the most abject age" [al-Naḥl 70].

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-ḥ-b as one consistent root meaning breadth or spaciousness, and derives every listed usage from it.

1. Core sense — spaciousness: الرُّحْب (roominess); مَكَانٌ رَحْبٌ (a spacious place).
2. As a greeting: مَرْحَبًا, which he explains as "you have come to ample space" — i.e. the word of welcome is literally an offer of room.
3. Anatomical: الرُّحْبَى, the broadest of the ribs in the chest.
4. Of a person: الرَّحِيب, a big eater — explained by the capaciousness of his belly, so the sense is still "wide/roomy inside."
5. Verbal forms: رَحُبَتِ الدَّارُ and أَرْحَبَتْ, both for a house being spacious.
6. Grammatical note (from al-Khalīl's book): Naṣr b. Sayyār's line "أَرَحُبَكُمُ الدُّخُولُ فِي طَاعَةِ الْكِرْمَانِيِّ" — "did entering into obedience to al-Kirmānī give you room enough?", glossed as أَوَسِعَكُمْ. Ibn Fāris flags this as anomalous (شاذّ) because the pattern فَعُلَ, normally intransitive, is here used with a direct object.
7. Of land: الرَّحْبَة, ground much alighted upon and abundantly productive.
8. Driving horses: the call "أَرْحِبِي", meaning "spread out, make room."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-ḥ-l as a single root whose core idea is setting out and going forward on a journey. Everything else in the entry he derives from that one notion.

1. Journeying. رَحَلَ / يَرْحَلُ / رِحْلَة — to travel, a journeying. رِحْلَة is equivalent to الارتحال, departure or setting out. A جَمَل رَحِيل is a camel "possessed of journeying," i.e. strong enough for travel.

2. رَحْل — travel-gear, then dwelling. In "this is the man's raḥl," meaning his lodging and shelter, Ibn Fāris says the word still belongs to this root: properly it names the traveller's equipment that goes with him, which he loads up when he moves on and returns to when he halts. That is the original sense; only afterwards was رَحْل extended to a man's dwelling when he is settled rather than travelling.

3. أَرْحَل — a beast with a white back. Also derived here: such an animal looks like a mount with a رِحَالَة on its back. رِحَالَة = the saddle.

4. Metaphorical use. "So-and-so yarḥalu so-and-so with what he dislikes" — i.e. loads/saddles him with something unwelcome.

5. المُرَحَّل — a type of Yemeni striped cloth patterned with figures of saddles (رِحَال).

6. أَرْحَلَتِ الإِبِل — the camels grew fat after being lean and so became capable of the journey.

7. الرِّحَال — also the carpets of al-Ḥīra (الطنافس الحيرية). Cited verse: "She spread over him her striped cloaks and her carpets."

8. الرَّاحِلَة — a riding-mount from among camels, male or female alike.

9. Verb forms. رَاحَلَهُ: helped him on his journey. رَحَّلَهُ: made him depart from his place. أَرْحَلَهُ: gave him a riding-camel. مُرْحِل (of a man): owning many riding-camels.

10. An insult. "O son of the spot where the riders' saddles are thrown down" — used as an aspersion, pointing (Ibn Fāris says) to something shameful.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: رَّحِيم 116x "most merciful"; رَحْمَة 114x "and mercy"; رَّحْمَٰن 57x "the most gracious"; رَّحِمَ 28x "receive mercy"; أَرْحَام 12x "the wombs"; رَّٰحِمِين 6x "(of) those who show mercy"; أَرْحَم 4x "(are) the most merciful"; رُحْم 1x "(in) affection"; مَرْحَمَة 1x "to compassion"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the three letters r–ḥ–m as one root with a single core meaning: tenderness, affectionate inclination, and compassion.

1. Core sense — mercy/compassion. رَحِمَهُ يَرْحَمُهُ means to have mercy on someone, i.e. to feel tenderness and incline toward him with affection. The nouns الرُّحْم, الْمَرْحَمَة, and الرَّحْمَة are given as synonyms, all meaning "mercy/compassion."

2. Kinship and womb. الرَّحِم (al-raḥim) is the bond of kinship. From this same sense the female's womb is called raḥim, because from it comes the child — the very thing that is shown mercy and tenderness. (Ibn Fāris derives "womb" from the compassion sense, not the reverse.)

3. Applied to animals. A ewe is called رَحُوم (raḥūm) when she suffers pain in her womb after lambing; the related verb forms are رَحُمَتْ / رُحِمَتْ (to be afflicted in the womb).

4. A rare form — al-ruḥum. Via al-Aṣmaʿī, the reader Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ is cited reciting a line of the poet Zuhayr in which "God and al-ruḥum" protect a pious man from stumbling. Al-Aṣmaʿī notes he never heard this particular form except in that one verse. Abū ʿAmr also read Qur'ān 18:81 as رُحْمًا (ruḥman), apparently taking al-ruḥum to mean simply "mercy" (al-raḥma).

5. A place-name. It is reported that Mecca used to be called أُمَّ رِحْمٍ (Umm Riḥm).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-ḥ-q as a "single-meaning" root — under his method, its letters do not branch into multiple senses but converge on one idea.

That one sense is al-raḥīq (الرحيق): a name for wine (khamr). He adds that some say the word specifically denotes the finest / choicest wine, not wine in general.

No further senses, derivations, or citations are given in this entry.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-ṣ-ṣ as a single root meaning (aṣl wāḥid): one thing joined to another with force, so that the two enter into one another.

1. **Pressing a structure together.** raṣaṣtu al-bunyān means "I pressed the building together, one part against another". He cites Q 61:4: "as though they were a building pressed tightly together (bunyān marṣūṣ)".

2. **Lead as the origin.** He suggests that this usage appears to be derived from al-raṣāṣ, "lead", and states that lead is the origin of the whole group of words.

3. **Standing close in a row.** tarāṣṣa al-qawmu fī al-ṣaff: the people pressed close together in the row.

4. **Stones set close.** Reported from al-Khalīl: al-raṣrāṣ is stones set close together around a spring.

5. **Close face-veiling.** al-tarṣīṣ, also called al-tawṣīṣ, is a woman's veiling her face so that only her eyes are seen.

6. **Hard ground.** al-raṣrāṣa is hard ground.

He closes by saying that the whole group is regular and consistent (munqās muṭṭarid).

dictionary: Lane — Arabic-English Lexicon, Edward William Lane (d. 1876)
quran_words: رَصَد 2x "a guard"; مِرْصَاد 2x "lying in wait"; مَرْصَد 1x "place of ambush"; إِرْصَاد 1x "and (as) a station"
text:
**Root ر ص د (r-ṣ-d) — Lane's Lexicon**

**1. The base verb: to watch for, to lie in wait.**
رَصَدَهُ (raṣadahu, imperfect yarṣudu; verbal nouns رَصْد and رَصَد) means he sat or lay in wait for someone in the road, or he watched and waited for him. Lane records the same sense for the reflexive/reciprocal stems: ارتصدهُ (VIII), ترصّدهُ / ترصّد لَهُ (V), راصدهُ (III), and ارصد لَهُ (IV).

The verb is neutral as to intent: one says رَصَدَهُ بِالخَيْرِ وَغَيْرِهِ — "he watched for him with what was good, and otherwise" — and رَصَدَهُ بِالمُكَافَأَةِ, "he watched for him with requital." Some authorities restrict the "prepare" sense to the alif form (see 3 below), reserving رَصَدَهُ for plain watching; on that view اِرْتِصَاد is a synonym of رَصْد.

Concrete uses cited:
- a snake تَرْصُدُ المَارَّةَ عَلَى الطَّرِيقِ لِتَلْسَعَ — lies in wait for passers-by on the road, to bite;
- a predator or wolf يَرْصُدُ لِيَثِبَ — watches for its moment to spring;
- a she-camel تَرْصُدُ شُرْبَ الإِبِلِ ثُمَّ تَشْرَبُ — waits for the other camels to drink, then drinks.

**2. Rain sense of the passive.** رُصِدَتِ الأَرْضُ: the land received the kind of rain called رَصْدَة / رَصَد (see 6).

**3. Form IV: to charge with watching; to prepare.**
- ارصدهُ عَلَى كَذَا — he put him in charge of watching or guarding something.
- ارصد لَهُ (marked by Lane as figurative) — he prepared or made ready something for someone: an army for battle, a horse for a charge, money for a debt. أَرْصَدْتُ لَهُ العُقُوبَةَ, "I prepared punishment for him," literally means "I placed punishment in his road" — the metaphor runs straight back to the ambush sense. Likewise أَرْصَدْتُ لَهُ خَيْرًا / شَرًّا. A tradition has إِلَّا أَنْ أُرْصِدَهُ لِدَيْنٍ عَلَىَّ, "unless I set it aside for a debt I owe."
- From this Lane cites يُرْصِدُ الزَّكَاةَ فِى صِلَةِ إِخْوَانِهِ — he puts الزكاة into kind and considerate treatment of his brethren, i.e. he counts such treatment as الزكاة and so lays up its recompense for himself (parallel to يَحْتَسِبُ عَمَلَهُ = "he reckons on the recompense of his deed").
- ارصدهُ also = he requited him — with good, which Lane reports as the original application, or, on some authorities' usage, with evil.
- ارصد الحِسَابَ — he cast up or produced the reckoning.

**4. رَصَد as "road / place of ambush."**
رَصَد, and the nouns of place مَرْصَد, مِرْصَاد and مُرْتَصَد, denote a road or way, and specifically a place where one lies in wait for an enemy. Plurals: أَرْصَاد (of رَصَد), مَرَاصِد (of مَرْصَد), the latter also used of the lurking-holes of snakes. Idioms: قَعَدَ لَهُ بِالمَرْصَدِ / بِالمِرْصَادِ / بِالرَّصَدِ, "he lay in wait for him in the road"; أَنَا لَكَ بِالمِرْصَادِ, "I hold the ambush-post against you" — i.e. you cannot escape me. ʿAdī's verse: وَإِنَّ المَنَايَا لِلرِّجَالِ بِمِرْصَدِ — "deaths lie in ambush for men," so that men cannot slip past them.

**5. Qurʾānic citations Lane gives under this head.**
- Q 9:5 وَاقْعُدُوا لَهُمْ كُلَّ مَرْصَدٍ — "lie in wait for them on every road"; al-Farrāʾ specifies the road to the Sacred House.
- Q 89:14 إِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَبِالْمِرْصَادِ — "your Lord is in the way," i.e. on the road you travel, so that no act of yours escapes Him (Msb); al-Zajjāj: He watches to punish the one who denies Him and turns away; Ibn ʿArafa: He watches every man in order to recompense his deeds; al-Aʿmash reported as taking المرصاد here as a name of three bridges behind the ṣirāṭ — on one security, on another mercy, on the third the Lord.
- Q 72:27 رَصَدًا — explained as watchers set over an angel bearing a revelation, so that no jinnī could overhear it and pass it to diviners, who would then relay it to men and so rival the prophets.

**6. رَصَد / رَصْد as light rain, and derived herbage.**
A small quantity of rain: بِهَا رَصَدٌ مِنْ حَيًا, "there is a little rain on it (the land)." Other accounts: rain following earlier rain; or rain falling first, ahead of rain to come; or simply the first of the rain. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: the sort called عِهَاد, after which more rain is expected — and if more follows, herbage comes up. A single shower is رَصَدَة or رَصْدَة; رَصْدَة is also given as "a downpour at one go." Plurals: أَرْصَاد and رِصَاد. رَصَد likewise means a small quantity of herbage on land where the spring (الرَّبِيع) rain is hoped for.

**7. Other derived nouns.**
- رَصْدَة: noun of unity of the verb; pl. رَصَدَات — لَا يُخْطِئُكَ مِنِّى رَصَدَاتُ خَيْرٍ / شَرٍّ, "my watchings, for good or ill, will not miss you," i.e. I will repay your deeds.
- رُصْدَة: a pitfall dug for a lion (زُبْيَة); also a brass or silver ring in the sword-hanger's thongs.
- رَصَدِىّ (and رَصَّاد): one who waylays travellers to take their property unjustly; equated with Persian rāhdār.
- رَصُود: a she-camel that waits for the others to drink before drinking.
- رَصِيد: a predator or wolf lying in wait to spring; also a snake lying in wait to bite travellers.
- رَصَائِد (also وَصَائِد): snares set for beasts of prey.

**8. The active participle and its plurals.**
رَاصِد: one lying in wait in the road, or watching for something, or posted in a watch-place for the purpose of guarding. Plural رَاصِدُونَ; رَصَد functions as a quasi-plural noun of the same meaning, formed like حَرَس from حَارِس and خَدَم from خَادِم, and used unchanged for singular and plural, masculine and feminine; أَرْصَاد, رَصَدَة and رُصَّد are also reported as plurals. Example: فُلَانٌ يَخَافُ رَصَدًا مِنْ قُدَّامِهِ وَطَلَبًا مِنْ وَرَائِهِ — he fears an ambush ahead and pursuers behind. From the watching sense, الرَّاصِد is used as a name for the lion.
- مُرْصِد = رَاصِد: أَنَا لَكَ مُرْصِدٌ بِإِحْسَانِكَ حَتَّى أُكَافِئَكَ بِهِ, "I am on watch for you on account of your kindness, that I may repay it."
- أَرْضٌ مُرْصِدَة (also مَرْصُودَة): land holding a little herbage; or land rained on and expected to produce herbage; or land that has had a رَصْدَة shower. Some grammarians reject both adjectives and prefer the phrase أَصَابَهَا رَصْدٌ / رَصَدٌ.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris states that the root r-ṭ-b (ر-ط-ب) has one core meaning: the opposite of dryness — that is, moistness or freshness.

He lists these derived usages:

1. al-raṭb and al-raṭīb — both simply mean "moist, fresh."
2. al-ruṭb (vocalized with ḍamma on the rāʾ) — "pasture, pastureland."
3. al-ruṭab — the well-known word for fresh, ripe dates (as opposed to dried dates). The verb arṭaba is used of a palm tree "ripening into" fresh dates, and rattabtu al-qawm means "I fed the people fresh dates."
4. al-riṭāb — a term for fresh green plants/herbage; correspondingly, raṭabtu al-faras means "I fed the horse fresh green fodder."
5. al-raṭbah — the specific name for freshly-cut alfalfa/lucerne (qaḍb), used only while it is still moist.
6. rīshun raṭīb — "a moist feather," meaning soft or supple.
7. A usage transmitted from Abū Zayd: raṭiba al-rajulu bi-mā ʿindahu — said of a man who spoke out whatever he had to say, right or wrong, without restraint or filtering — i.e., loose, unguarded speech.

Ibn Fāris closes with the standard formula "wa-Allāhu aʿlam" ("and God knows best").

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: أَرْبَعَة 9x "four"; أَرْبَع 7x "forty"; رُبَٰع 2x "or four"; رُّبُع 2x "(is) the fourth"; رَابِع 2x "the forth of them"
text:
Al-Rāghib treats the root ر ب ع (r-b-ʿ) as one family built on the number "four" and its derivatives: أربعة (four), أربعون (forty), رُبع (a quarter), رُباع (four at a time).

1. Qurʾānic attestations of the numeral family: "the fourth of them their dog" (18:22); "forty years... wandering" (5:26); "forty nights" (2:51); "theirs is the quarter of what you leave" (4:12); "two, three, and four" (4:3).

2. Verbal uses from "four": رَبَعْتُ القومَ — I was the fourth of a group, or took a quarter of their wealth; رَبَعْتُ الحبلَ — I made a rope of four strands.

3. الرِّبْع — a camel-watering interval (watering every fourth day); also the quartan fever. أَرْبَعَ إبلَه — he watered his camels on that interval. A man called مربوع / مُرْبَع is one gripped by the quartan fever.

4. Time-words from "four": الأربعاء (Wednesday, the fourth day from Sunday) and الربيع (spring, the fourth season). From "spring" comes رَبَعَ / ارْتَبَعَ (to reside during spring), then figuratively any residing at any time — so much so that any dwelling came to be called رَبْع, though the word was originally specific to spring.

5. Spring-born offspring: الرُّبَع / الرُّبَعِيّ — young born in spring; because spring is the earliest and most favored birthing time, this was extended to any child born in the parents' youth, hence the saying "prosperous is he who has spring-born offspring." المِرْباع — spring-born young; غيث مُرْبِع — rain arriving in spring.

6. "Taking by the four sides": رَبَعَ الحَجَرَ / الحملَ — to grasp a stone or load by its four sides. المِرْبَع — a lever-wood used to lift something; the lifted stone is a رَبِيعة. The proverb ارْبَعْ على ظَلْعِكَ ("go easy / mind your limit") is read either from "staying" (stay within your lameness) or from lifting the stone (lift only what your lameness allows).

7. Leadership sense: المِرْباع — the quarter of spoils the chief takes (from رَبَعْتُ القومَ). From this الرِّبَاعة was borrowed for chieftaincy, by analogy with taking that share: "none but So-and-so can uphold the leadership of the people."

8. Other "four"-derived nouns: الرَّبْعَة — a chest/box, named for its four tiers or four legs; الرَّبَاعِيتان — a pair of teeth, said to be named for the four teeth between them; اليَرْبوع (jerboa) — a mouse whose burrow has four openings; and أرض مَرْبَعة — land full of jerboas (parallel to مَضَبّة, land of lizards).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ر ب ح (r-b-ḥ), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: a surplus/margin gained in a transaction.

1. rabiḥa fulānun fī bayʿihi — so-and-so gained a profit in his sale; tijārah rābiḥah — a profitable trade. Ibn Fāris notes ribḥ and rabaḥ are equally valid noun-forms, comparing the pattern to mithl/mathal.
2. al-rabaḥ — horses and camels brought/driven for sale and profit-seeking, illustrated with a citation from al-Aʿshā (with a dispute among authorities over the precise meaning of al-nisāḥāt in that verse) and a further citation whose exact sense Ibn Fāris leaves unresolved, noting only that Ibn Durayd discussed it.
3. Closing exception, flagged as anomalous and outside this root's regular pattern: al-rubbāḥ, said to mean the monkey/ape.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: تَرَبَّصْ 13x "so wait"; مُّتَرَبِّص 3x "those who wait"; تَرَبُّص 1x "(is a) waiting (of)"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ر-ب-ص (r-b-ṣ) as a single root whose core meaning is waiting and expectation.

1. Base sense — waiting/awaiting. The derived form التَّرَبُّص (tarabbuṣ) means "awaiting," as in تَرَبَّصْتُ بِهِ ("I waited for him").

2. Noun of waiting — رُبْصَة (rubṣa). Ibn Fāris cites al-Sijistānī for the phrases لِي بِالْبَصْرَةِ رُبْصَةٌ ("I have a rubṣa at Basra") and لِي فِي مَتَاعِي رُبْصَةٌ ("I have a rubṣa in my goods"), glossed as "I have in it a period of waiting or tarrying."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: رَّبَطْ 3x "and to strengthen"; رَابِطُ 1x "and [be] constant"; رِّبَاط 1x "tethered"
poets_named: Labīd (lived into Islam); Ibn Aḥmar (lived into Islam); Laylā al-Akhyaliyya (Umayyad)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ر-ب-ط as one root with a single core idea: **binding/fastening, and the firmness that results from it**.

1. **To tie, to bind.** رَبَطَ / يَرْبِطُ / رَبْط — to tie a thing. The instrument or cord used is a رِبَاط (tether, tie, band).

2. **Holding station at a frontier post.** رِبَاط also names staying put at the outpost facing an enemy — Ibn Fāris explains it as though such men had been *tethered* there, so they stood fast and did not leave. He derives the sense from the physical tying, not from any institutional definition.

3. **Firmness of heart.** رَابِطُ الْجَأْشِ = a man firm of heart and self-command. Two pre-Islamic/early witnesses:
   - Labīd: "steadfast of heart at the gap in their line, I wheel the dark horse with a middle-gripped, felling spear."
   - Ibn Aḥmar: "firmer of heart in defence of his people's notables, when the waist-wraps are drawn up" (i.e. in the crisis of battle).

4. **Keeping horses tied up ready.** ارْتَبَطَ الفَرَسَ لِلرِّبَاطِ — to tether a horse for standing readiness.

5. **A stock of horses.** رِبَاط is said to be five or more mounts; "such a family has a ribāṭ of horses" parallels تِلَاد (long-held, inherited stock) — the base holding of horses a household owns. Laylā al-Akhyaliyya: "a people whose tethered horses stand among their tents, and blue spearheads that look like stars."

6. **A snare.** قَطَعَ الظَّبْيُ رِبَاطَهُ — "the gazelle broke its ribāṭ," i.e. the net/snare that held it.

7. **Perennial water.** From al-Shaybānī: مَاءٌ مُتَرَابِطٌ — water that stays, that never leaves (the "fixity" side of the root).

8. **A proper name.** الرَّبِيط was the byname of al-Ghawth ibn Murr.

9. **A doubtful item.** رَبِيط used of dates — said to mean dried dates over which water is poured. Ibn Fāris flags this as probably a loanword (دَخِيل), notes a variant reading with dāl (رَبِيد), and judges it not genuinely part of this root.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: رَبّ 975x "your lord"; رَبَّٰنِيِّن 3x "and the rabbis"; رِبِّيُّون 1x "(were) religious scholars"; رَبَٰئِب 1x "and your step daughters"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-b-b as pointing to three root meanings, which he considers related to one another. He adds that, looked at closely, the whole article reduces to a single analogy.

**1. Setting a thing right and taking charge of it**

- **Rabb.** The rabb is the owner, the creator and the master, and also the one who sets a thing right. Rabba fulān ḍayʿatahu means "he tended his estate," taking charge of keeping it in good order. Ibn Fāris says God is al-rabb because He sets right the conditions of His creatures.
- **Ribbiyy.** One who knows the Lord.
- **Rubb.** A waterskin is marbūb when it is treated with rubb, a preparation made from grapes and other things, called so because things are treated (yurabbu) with it. A well-tended horse is also marbūb; Salāma describes a horse "given to drink as a remedy the choice portion kept back from the household, well-tended (marbūb)."
- **Rearing.** Rababtu al-ṣabiyy (or rabbabtuhu) means "I reared the boy." Al-rabība is the nurse who fosters a child.
- **Step-relations.** A man's rabīb is his wife's son, and the rābb is the one who takes charge of the rabīb's affairs. A ḥadīth says it is disliked for a man to marry the wife of his rābb.

**2. Keeping to a thing and staying with it (akin to the first)**

- **Lasting rain and clouds.** Arabbat al-saḥāba is said when a cloud stays over a land, and a land where rain never ceases is marabb. That is why clouds are called rabāb. Others say rabāb is the cloud hanging below the main clouds, white or black (singular rabāba).
- **The ewe kept at home.** Al-rubbā is the ewe kept in the house for her milk, and arabbat is said when she keeps to the house. Others say al-rubbā is a ewe that has just given birth. In that case, Ibn Fāris says, she is the one rearing her young, and the word belongs to the first meaning.
- **Drawing near.** Al-irbāb is said to be drawing near to a thing. Arabbat al-nāqa is said when a she-camel keeps close to the stallion and loves him; she is muribb.

**3. Joining a thing to a thing (also akin to the preceding)**

- **The arrow-rag.** Ribāba is the rag in which the gaming arrows are gathered. A Hudhalī verse runs: "as though they were a ribāba, and he an arrow-player who casts the gaming arrows and calls out."
- **The pact.** Ribāba also means a pact (ʿahd), and people bound by a pact are aribba. Ibn Fāris explains the name: a pact gathers and binds people together. A verse says: "Bahz were their pact-partners (aribba), and the knot of protection deceived them." In ʿAlqama's line "my ribāba passed to you; before you, lords (rubūb) had charge of me, and I was lost," ribāba is the pact, and rubūb, the plural of rabb, belongs to the first meaning.
- **Tithes.** Abū ʿUbayd says al-ribāb are the tithes, citing Abū Dhuʾayb. Ibn Fāris suggests this may be called ribāb because, once paid, it becomes like a pact of protection.
- **Abundant water.** Al-rabab is abundant water, named for its gathering together; a verse pairs "brown wheat and abundant water."

**Irregular and underived words**

- **Rabrab.** A herd of wild cattle. Ibn Fāris first lists it as irregular, then allows that it may belong to the third meaning, named for its gathering together.
- **Rubba.** A particle used to express the fewness of a thing, as in rubba rajulin jāʾanī, "a man (and few like him) came to me." Ibn Fāris says no derivation of it is known.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: رِّبَوٰا 7x "[the] usury"; رَبَتْ 4x "and grows"; رَبْوَة 2x "a high ground"; أَرْبَىٰ 2x "more numerous"; رَبَّيَ 2x "they brought me up"; رَّابِي 1x "rising"; رِّب 1x "usury"; رَّابِيَة 1x "exceeding"
text:
al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī derives the root ربو (r-b-w) from a single core idea — swelling, rising, increasing — and traces its Qurʾanic uses to that idea.

1. Elevated ground. رَبْوَة (also vocalized ribwa, rubwa, ribāwa, rubāwa) is high ground, as in Q 23:50, "to a rabwa possessed of a resting-place and flowing water." He reports Abū al-Ḥasan's view that the fatḥa form رَبْوَة is best, since one says رَبَى; رَبَا فلان means "he came to be on high ground." Such a rise is called رَابِية as though it had swelled up (rabat) by itself.

2. To increase and rise. From the same core, رَبَا means "to increase, rise high." Q 22:5: the earth "stirs and swells (rabat)" when water descends — i.e. it increases as a growing thing does. Also رابٍ (swelling) of the torrent's foam in Q 13:17, and رابية (a mounting, overwhelming seizure) in Q 69:10. أَرْبَى عَلَيْهِ means "he overtopped/surpassed him." Rearing a child, رَبَيْتُ الولد فَرَبَا ("I raised him so he grew"), belongs here too. He notes a view that the root is originally a doubled root later lightened to a weak-final one — comparable to تَظَنَّيْتُ for تَظَنَّنْتُ.

3. ribā. الرِّبَا is, at root, "increase over the capital." al-Rāghib states that in the Law (sharʿ) the term was narrowed to increase of a specific kind. For the general sense he cites Q 30:39 ("whatever you give of ribā to increase within people's wealth increases not with God"). From Q 2:276 ("God effaces ribā and makes charities grow") he draws that the meaningful increase — the one called "blessing" (baraka) — stands above ribā; hence its counterpart in Q 30:39, zakāt given for God's face, whose givers "multiply" their reward.

4. Anatomical sense. الأُرْبِيَّتَان: the two protruding fleshy parts at the inner roots of the thighs (the groin).

5. Breathing. الرَّبْوُ: panting or breathlessness, named by picturing the breath "rising up"; hence the expression "he draws deep, heaving breaths."

6. A caution: الرَّبِيئَة, "the scout," is spelled with hamza and does not belong to this root.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
**Root: ردأ (r-d-ʔ)** — al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt

1. **الرِّدْء (al-ridʾ)** — "one who follows another as a helper/supporter." Cited: "Send him with me as a *ridʾ* (helper) to confirm me" (Qur'an 28:34). The related verb أَرْدَأَهُ (ardaʾahu) means "he gave him a helper" / "he supported him."

2. **الرَّدِيء (al-radīʾ)** — originally from the same root-sense (a "supporter/companion"), but later usage narrowed it to mean "bad, defective, of poor quality" — the blameworthy sense. Verbal form: رَدُأَ رَدَاءَةً (raduʾa radāʾatan), "it became bad/defective," giving radīʾ, "bad, defective."

3. **الرَّدَى (al-radā)** — destruction, perdition.

4. **التَّرَدِّي (al-taraddī)** — exposing oneself to destruction, falling to ruin. Three Qur'anic citations given:
   - 92:11 — his wealth will not avail him "when he falls to ruin" (taraddā).
   - 20:16 — one who follows his own desire "so that he goes to ruin" (fa-tardā).
   - 37:56 — "you nearly destroyed/ruined me" (la-turdīni).

5. **المِرْداة (al-mirdāh)** — a [heavy] stone used to break other stones, so-named because it "destroys" (turdīhā) them.

The entry traces one root across two directions of sense: a positive "helper/companion" branch (ridʾ, ardaʾa) and a "ruin/destruction" branch (radīʾ as bad/defective, radā, taraddā, mirdāh) — the latter, per the author, a later semantic narrowing of an originally neutral root-idea.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: رَدَّ 36x "returned"; ٱرْتَدَّ 8x "so they returned"; مَرَدّ 6x "return"; رَادّ 3x "(will) surely take you back"; رَدّ 2x "to take them back"; مَرْدُود 2x "indeed be returned"; يَتَرَدَّدُ 1x "they waver"; رَادِّى 1x "would hand over"
poets_named: Malīḥ (undated); Kuthayyir ʿAzza (Umayyad); al-Akhṭal (Umayyad); unnamed verse; Abū Khirāsh (lived into Islam); Abū al-Najm (Umayyad); Abū Ṣakhr al-Hudhalī (Umayyad); Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Sīda's account of the root ر د د (r-d-d):

1. Core sense — al-radd: turning a thing away and sending it back (verb raddahu / yarudduhu). The verbal noun tirdād is an intensive form denoting repetition. On this Sībawayh is cited: verbal nouns on the pattern tifʿāl (tirdād, tilʿāb, tihdhār, etc.) are not the maṣdar of the doubled verb faʿʿaltu; they are simply the maṣdar rebuilt on this pattern to convey frequency, paralleling how faʿaltu is intensified to faʿʿaltu.

2. al-maradd = al-radd; irtaddahu = raddahu (turned/repelled it back). Shāhid from the poet Malīḥ (resolve like a sword's fall that no censurer can turn back). Qurʾānic citation: al-Shūrā 47, "a day for which there is no maradd (turning-back) from God" — Thaʿlab: the Day of Resurrection, since it cannot be turned back.

3. radīd = mardūd, "returned/rejected" (shāhid on radīd al-gharāʾib, the rejected offspring of distant women).

4. irtadda / irtadda ʿanhu: to turn away or change from something. Qurʾānic citation: al-Māʾida 54, "whoever of you turns back (yartadd) from his dīn." The noun is al-ridda; from it comes ridda "from Islam," i.e. the turning-back (rujūʿ) from it. (Ibn Sīda gives this as the derived usage, glossed simply as "turning back.")

5. istaradda / irtaddahu: to seek the return of something (shāhid from Kuthayyir ʿAzza; a loan that the lender reclaims). Its noun is radād / ridād, both vowellings attested (shāhid from al-Akhṭal).

6. rudūd al-darāhim: returned coins (sing. radd); anything given back after being taken is a radd.

7. al-ridd: a prop or support that pushes a thing back and repels it (shāhid: "be for us a ridd against calamities," i.e. a stronghold that wards off calamity).

8. al-ridd: a cave (from Kurāʿ). On this basis the reading riddan at al-Qaṣaṣ 34 ("send him with me as a ridd") could mean "support" or "cave"; alternatively it reflects geminating the word in pausal position after softening the hamza of ridʾan.

9. al-mardūda: a divorced woman — all senses trace back to al-radd. Ḥadīth citation: the Prophet tells Surāqa b. Juʿshum that supporting "your daughter returned to you (mardūda), with no earner but you," is the best charity.

10. taraddada / tarādda: to go back and forth. mā fīhi riddīdā: no holding-back nor going to and fro.

11. Bodily/compactness senses: a man mutaraddid is stocky and short, not of elongated build; a limb radīd is firm and dense (shāhid from Abū Khirāsh).

12. Camel senses (swelling/return of milk): al-radad / al-ridda — camels take a second draught of water so the milk returns (tartadd) into the udder; a pregnant female near delivery, with enlarged belly and udder, is muridd; al-ridda is the swelling of a she-camel's udder as milk settles in it (verb araddat, adj. muridd); araddat al-nāqa also = swelling of the udder and vulva from kneeling on dew, or from being in heat, or from drinking water; al-radad / al-ridda is likewise a swelling in the teats from accumulated milk (shāhid from Abū al-Najm).

13. aradda al-rajul: to swell up with anger (from the author of al-Alfāẓ; Abū al-Ḥasan notes some copies read arbadda).

14. al-ridda: a remnant, a lingering remainder (shāhid from Abū Ṣakhr al-Hudhalī: when nothing remains between two lovers but a memory of the past, the memory fades).

15. al-ridda: a recession in the chin — a face carrying some ugliness yet touched by some beauty. Ibn Durayd: radda in a face = ugliness (qubḥ); ridda = a defect (ʿayb).

16. aradda al-baḥr: the sea's waves grew many and it raged.

17. Proper name Raddād; anecdote from the Day of al-Kulāb (a warrior calling himself "Abū Shaddād" then, wheeling back, "Abū Raddād").

18. A man miradd: much given to repelling and to renewed charging (shāhid from Abū Dhuʾayb).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مُرْدِفِين 1x "one after another"; رَدِفَ 1x "close behind"; رَّادِفَة 1x "the subsequent"
text:
Root ر-د-ف (r-d-f) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris gives this root a single, consistent core meaning: al-ittibāʿ, "the following of a thing" — one thing coming after another.

1. Basic vocabulary of following: al-tarāduf — succession, one thing after another. al-radīf — one who follows/rides behind you. From this same idea, al-ʿajīza (the rump) is called ridf, since it is the "following" part of the body. "A matter befell them, then something greater ridifa [followed] it" — the second event outweighing the first. al-ridāf — the seat where the rider-behind sits; "this pack-horse does not yurādif" — it doesn't carry a second rider.

2. Astronomy: ardāf al-nujūm — stars in succession; al-radīf specifically names a star that rises in the east just as its paired counterpart sets in the west.

3. Political/social usage: ardāf al-mulūk in pre-Islamic Arabia — those designated to succeed kings, i.e. heirs. al-ridfān — night and day, a pair each "following" the other. In Labīd's poetry, al-ridf names a ship's steersman.

4. Idiom: "a matter with no ridf" — one with no consequence or follow-up.

5. Cooperation: al-Aṣmaʿī cites tarādafū and tarāfadū as synonyms meaning "they helped one another."

6. Mating (of locusts): rādafa al-jarād — locusts paired/mounted; al-murādafa names the male mounting the female.

7. Gambling terminology (Abū Ḥātim): al-radīf, in the pre-Islamic maysir game, is a latecomer who joins after one or two partners have already won, asking to add his arrow-lot to theirs.

8. al-rudāfā (al-Aṣmaʿī): camel-drivers/chanters, so called because when one tires, another takes over — illustrated with a verse describing their antiphonal chanting.

9. A closing line names al-rawāfid as the offshoots of a palm tree — included in the source without further explanation of its connection to the main root.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ر د م (r-d-m), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: closing up a gap or breach.

1. radamtu al-bāba/al-thulmah — I blocked up the door, or a breach; al-radm — both the verbal noun for this action and a noun for the resulting barrier/rampart itself. thawb muraddam — an old, patched-up garment. A citation of poetry ("has the [array of] poets left anything unpatched-over...") is glossed, per one transmission, as meaning speech pieced together, one part stuck to another.
2. Extended figuratively: "ardamat ʿalayhi al-ḥummā" — fever "closed in" persistently upon him, without break; "wird mudrim" — a persistent recurring fever; "saḥāb mudrim" — an unbroken, continuous cloud-cover — both extending the sense of "sealing a gap" to "leaving no gap/break at all."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَرْدَىٰ 3x "it has ruined you"; مُتَرَدِّيَة 1x "and that which has a fatal fall"; تَرْدَىٰ 1x "lest you perish"; تَرَدَّىٰ 1x "he falls"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-d-y as a single root whose core idea is throwing, pelting, or flinging — and things resembling that.

1. Throwing / pelting. رَدَيْتُهُ بِالْحِجَارَةِ = "I pelted him with stones," equivalent to رَمَيْتُهُ ("I threw at him"). The stone used is a مِرْدَاة.

2. Three uses of الرَّدْي, all traced back to that same core sense:
   - رَدَى الْحَجَرَ — he threw the stone;
   - رَدَى الْفَرَسُ — the horse went fast, rushed;
   - رَدَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ — the girl hopped, raising one leg and skipping on the other.
   All three reduce to تَرَامٍ, flinging/hurling.

3. الرَّدَيَان — a donkey's trot back and forth between its tethering-place and its rolling-spot.

4. Perishing. الرَّدَى is destruction; رَدِيَ يَرْدَى = "he perished"; أَرْدَاهُ اللَّهُ = "God destroyed him." Ibn Fāris keeps this inside the same root-idea rather than treating it as separate.

5. Falling headlong. التَّرَدِّي is plunging into a chasm; رَدِيَ فِي الْبِئْرِ ("he fell into the well") is used like تَرَدَّى — a usage he credits to Abū Zayd.

6. Disappearing. مَا أَدْرِي أَيْنَ رَدَى = "I don't know where he went" — which he explains, within the root-logic, as "where he flung himself."

7. Rock. الرَّدَاة is a boulder, plural الرَّدَى, with the poetic witness: فَحْلُ مَخَاضٍ كَالرَّدَى الْمُنْقَضِّ ("a rutting stud-camel like hurtling boulders"). Calling a she-camel مِرْدَاة is a comparison to a boulder.

8. Shooting on someone's behalf. رَادَيْتُ عَنِ الْقَوْمِ = to exchange shots in defence of a group.

Excluded case. Ṭufayl's line يُرَادَى عَلَى فَأْسِ اللِّجَامِ… he rules out of this root: the form is metathesised and actually belongs to r-w-d (يُرَاوَد, "to be coaxed"), discussed elsewhere.

Outliers he acknowledges:
- الرِّدَاء, the worn cloak — he states plainly that he does not know its derivation or which analogy it falls under. Related usage: فُلَانٌ حَسَنُ الرِّدْيَةِ ("he wears the cloak well").
- أَرْدَى عَلَى الْخَمْسِينَ — "he went past fifty," i.e. exceeded it.

The hamzated root (r-d-ʾ), which he calls two sharply distinct words:
- أَرْدَأْتُ = "I spoiled/corrupted"; رَدُؤَ الشَّيْءُ فَهُوَ رَدِيءٌ — the thing became bad, hence "defective, poor."
- أَرْدَأْتُ = "you aided"; فُلَانٌ رِدْءُ فُلَانٍ = his helper/backer. His Qur'anic witness is Q 28:34, on Moses: "So send him with me as a رِدْء (support), confirming me."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: رَفَعَ 22x "and we raised"; مَّرْفُوعَة 3x "exalted"; رَافِع 1x "and raise you"; رَفِيع 1x "possessor of the highest ranks"; مَرْفُوع 1x "raised high"; رَّافِعَة 1x "raising up"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-f-ʿ (رفع) as a single root whose core sense is the opposite of setting-down or lowering — raising, lifting up.

1. To raise / lift. رَفَعْتُ الشَّيْءَ ("I raised the thing"), the opposite of khafḍ (lowering). Applied to a she-camel's gait, مَرْفُوع is her quick, "raised" pace as opposed to مَوْضُوع, her lowered one — cited from the poet Ṭarafa, who likens her raised pace to a loud burst of rain driven on the wind. One says the camel "raised" its pace (رَفَعَ البَعِيرُ), and causatively "I made it raise its pace" (رَفَّعْتُهُ).

2. To bring near. A sub-sense: rafʿ as drawing a thing close. Ibn Fāris cites Qurʾān 56:34, وَفُرُشٍ مَرْفُوعَةٍ, glossing مرفوعة as "brought near to them."

3. To refer / submit to authority. رَفَعْتُهُ لِلسُّلْطَان ("I referred him/the matter to the ruler"); its verbal noun is rufʿān (also vocalized rifʿān). Related: a she-camel is called rāfiʿ when she holds up (withholds) the colostrum in her udder.

4. To broadcast / make public. rafʿ can mean divulging a thing and bringing it to light. Ibn Fāris cites a ḥadīth — "Every conveying group that conveys from us of the message, I have declared it [Medina] forbidden" — glossing it as: every group that transmits from the Prophet should pass on that he made Medina a sanctuary. Comparable is رَفَعَ فُلَانٌ عَلَى الْعَامِل ("So-and-so raised a report against the tax-official"), i.e. spread news about him.

5. Carrying in the harvest. رَفْع الزَّرْع is transporting the crop after reaping to the threshing-floor; the season of doing so is called ayyām ar-rifāʿ ("the days of carrying-in").

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: رِّفْد 1x "(is) the gift"; مَرْفُود 1x "which (will) be given"
text:
Root ر ف د (r-f-d) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris states this root has one single, regular meaning: assisting and backing someone by giving — a gift or other support.

1. Core sense — giving/aiding: الرَّفْد (al-rafd) is the verbal noun of "rafadahu" — he gave him [something]; the related noun is الرِّفْد (al-rifd). A ḥadīth uses it: "the fayʾ [war-gained wealth] becomes rifd" — meaning it turns into loose gifts handed out rather than placed where they properly belong.

2. Related forms: "irtafadtu min fulān" — I gained from so-and-so's earnings. "Urfidtu al-māl" — I was given/granted the wealth (glossed as "you earned it").

3. Agent nouns: الرَّافِد (al-rāfid) and المُرْفِد (al-murfid) both mean "the helper." When a tribe "rafada" a man, it meant they made him their chief and honored him; he is then called مُرَفَّد (murafad, "one made chief").

4. الرَّافِدَان (al-Rāfidān), dual — "the two Rāfids": a name for the Tigris and Euphrates. Ibn Fāris cites a line of al-Farazdaq mentioning "Iraq and its two Rāfids."

5. Cooperation: تَرَافَدُوا (tarāfadū) — they helped one another in something. الرِّفَادَة (al-rifāda) names a pre-Islamic Quraysh custom: each person contributed something, and the pooled money was used to buy food, raisins, and drink for the pilgrims (al-ḥājj) — this is Ibn Fāris's own description of a Jāhiliyya-era practice, not a ritual-law term.

6. Physical supports: الرَّوَافِد (al-rawāfid) are roof-timbers/beams, so called because they "rafad" (prop up) the roof. A cited poetic line praises a generous man by comparing his roof-beams to "the noblest of supports," likening him to a vast, overflowing sea.

7. Other, more marginal senses under the same root: 
   - المَرْفَد (al-marfad) — a padded bustle worn by a flat-buttocked woman to enlarge her rear.
   - الرِّفْد/الرَّفْد/المِرْفَد (al-rifd/al-rafd/al-mirfad) — a large drinking-bowl; المِرْفَد is also said to be the vessel used for hosting guests.
   - الرَّفُود (al-rafūd) — a she-camel that fills that large bowl in a single milking.
   - الرُّفَيْدَات (al-Rufaydāt) — the name of an Arab tribe/group.

Ibn Fāris ties all these back to the one root idea of support/assistance-by-giving: propping a roof, filling a guest-bowl, backing a chief, or watering the land (the two great rivers) are all variations on "rafada" — to aid by supplying something.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مُرْتَفَق 2x "(is) the resting place"; رَفِيق 1x "companion(s)"; مَرَافِق 1x "the elbows"; مِّرْفَق 1x "(in) ease"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-f-q as one root meaning accord, coming alongside, and closeness without harshness.

1. Core sense — gentleness. رِفْق (rifq) is the opposite of ʿunf (roughness, harshness); the verb is رَفَقَ / يَرْفُقُ. He cites a ḥadīth: God "loves gentleness in every matter." Everything else in the root, he says, derives from this: whatever brings ease and accord.

2. Elbow. مِرْفَق / مَرْفِق (mirfaq / marfiq) — the elbow, so called because one rests by leaning on it. Both vowellings are reported from Thaʿlab. The verb ارْتَفَقَ (irtafaqa) = to prop oneself on the elbow while seated; he cites a ḥadīth in which the Prophet is identified to a bedouin as "that ruddy-white one, the one leaning" (al-murtafiq), i.e. resting on his elbow. A further use: ارْتَفَقَ سَاهِرًا = to pass the night propped on the elbow, sleepless.

3. Travelling company. رُفْقَة / رِفْقَة (rufqa) — the group you travel with. Ibn Fāris links it to the root twice over: through accord, and because walking side by side puts their elbows level. Quoting al-Khalīl: the name rufqa applies only while the group is together and lapses when they separate; but رَفِيق (rafīq), the individual companion — one who shares a rufqa with you — keeps the name even after you part.

4. An accommodating affair. مُرْفِق (murfiq) — a matter that is easy or obliging toward you.

5. Camel-tether. رِفَاق (rifāq) — a rope tying a camel's elbow to its pastern, illustrated by the verse fragment: "like the resentful [she-camel] walking in the rifāq-tether."

6. Privy. مِرْفَق also denotes the latrine (mirḥāḍ); plural مَرَافِق (marāfiq).

7. Markings. شَاةٌ مُرَفَّقَة — a ewe with forelegs white as far as the elbows.

8. Outward turn of the limb. رَفَق (rafaq) — a turning-out away from the side, in a camel: نَاقَةٌ رَفْقَاء (female), جَمَلٌ أَرْفَق (male).

9. Easily obtained. مَاءٌ رَفَقٌ (water) and مَرْتَعٌ رَفَقٌ (pasture) — easy to reach or come by.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
The article is headed r-f-f and gathers the simple verb raffa together with the reduplicated forms rafraf, rafrafa and rafrāf.

Several authorities quoted in it separate two verbs by the vowel of the imperfect. Abū ʿUbayda says raffa yaruffu (with u) is sucking and sipping, while raffa yariffu (with i), "to gleam", comes from something else. Thaʿlab lists raffa yaruffu "he ate", raffa yariffu "it gleamed" and warafa yarifu "it spread wide". Ibn Barrī reports Ibn Ḥamza's claim that al-raff has ten meanings; the ones named are sucking, a camel nibbling herbage without filling its mouth, and earning (all yaruffu), and gleaming (yariffu). The article nonetheless records both vowels for an eye twitching and, from Abū Ḥanīfa, for camels eating.

**1. Gleaming and flashing.** Raffa lawnuhu yariffu (verbal nouns raff, rafīf): his colour shone and glistened. The same is said of teeth and of lightning: raff al-barq is lightning's flash, and a raffa is a single flash. When al-Nābigha al-Jaʿdī recited two verses to the Messenger of God (there is no good in forbearance without flashes of temper to keep its clear water from being muddied, nor in rashness without a forbearing man who, having led the matter down to water, can lead it back), the Messenger of God said to him, "May God not break your mouth"; the narrator says al-Nābigha's teeth went on gleaming (tariffu) until he died. al-Nihāya words it: "as if his mouth were hail, his teeth gleaming".

Another ḥadīth has "his ghurūb gleam", the ghurūb being the teeth. al-Aʿshā, on a woman's mouth: "crystal whose ghurūb gleam, giving drink to the love-enslaved man who burns with thirst". Ibn Barrī sets beside it a line of Bishr: "it gleams as though, deep in the night, it were wine".
