**2. An unexplained gloss.** Raffa yariffu is also glossed bariḥa wa-takhayyala and illustrated with the half-line "and Umm ʿAmmār on al-qird tariffu". The article explains neither, and the sense is unclear.

**3. Quivering with freshness.** Raffa l-nabātu yariffu rafīfan: plants sway and grow lush; Abū Ḥanīfa says it means that their moisture glistens and shines. A garment or trees are rafīf when moist. Anything so full of sap from lushness and freshness that it almost sways is said to raffa. Ibn Ziml's ḥadīth: "my eye never saw anything like it, quivering with freshness, its dew dripping". A woman said to Muʿāwiya: "I commend you to God against alighting in a valley and leaving its first part lush (yariffu) and its last part dried up (yaqiffu)".

Rafīf and warīf are two dialect forms, used of plants that sway green and glistening. al-Aʿshā's phrase "al-Shām, dhāt al-rafīf" is explained as orchards that quiver with freshness and swaying or, on another view, as two or three boats lashed together for the king, on which people crossed.

**4. Twitching.** Raffat ʿaynuhu taruffu or tariffu: his eye twitched, and the same is said of any part of the body; a raffa is one twitch. A verse recited by Abū l-ʿAlāʾ: "I could only guess, as one who is absent guesses: was it for you or for the unseen that my eyebrow twitched?"

**5. Ample good fortune.** Raffat ʿalayhi l-niʿma: good fortune spread amply over him.

**6. A man who yariffu.** "A man yariffu when he is ... like swaying with freshness": the copy has a gap in the middle of this definition.

**7. Sucking, sipping, kissing.** Raffa l-shayʾa yaruffuhu (raff, rafīf): he sucked it or, some say, ate it; a raffa is one suck, and raff is sucking and sipping (rafaftu aruffu). Raffa l-marʾata yaruffuhā: he kissed her with the tips of his lips. Ibn Barrī recites: "By God, were it not for my fear of your father, my lips would have sipped at your mouth as the gazelle nibbles arāk leaves".

Abū Hurayra, asked about kissing while fasting, said: "I do sip at her lips while fasting"; Abū ʿUbayd explains this as drinking and sipping the saliva. ʿAbīda al-Salmānī, asked by Ibn Sīrīn what makes janāba binding, answered "al-raff and al-istimlāq", explained as sucking and intercourse, sucking being one of its preliminaries.

**8. Eating.** A raffa is a solid, thorough meal. Abū Ḥanīfa: raffat al-ibil, the camels ate. In the ḥadīth of Umm Zarʿ, "my husband, if he eats, raffa", which Ibn al-Athīr explains as eating a great deal. In Ibn Ḥamza's list, a camel yaruffu herbage when it eats without filling its mouth.

**9. Doing good and looking after.** Raffa l-rajula yaruffuhu: he treated the man well and did him a kindness. Fulān yaruffunā: he protects us and is kind to us; "he has neither ḥāff nor rāff" means no one looks after him. Yaḥuffunā wa-yaruffunā: he gives to us and provisions us (al-Tahdhīb: shelters and feeds us). Abū ʿUbayd took yaruffunā as a mere echo (itbāʿ) of yaḥuffunā; the first view is said to be better known. al-Aṣmaʿī explains yaḥiffu wa-yariffu as busying oneself on someone's behalf, advising him sincerely and caring for him, yaḥiffu referring to the rustle one hears.

The proverb "whoever ḥaffanā or raffanā, let him hold back" (al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "let him be moderate") refers to praise and flattery. Related uses: rafrafa ʿalā l-qawm, he bent over the people with tender care; raff, provisions (mīra); and Ibn Ḥamza's "he yaruffu for him", he earns.

**10. Beating the wings.** Rafrafa is a bird's moving its wings in the air while keeping its place; Ibn Sīda gives both raffa and rafrafa for moving the wings in the air. It is also said of a bird beating its wings around something it wants to land on, spreading them as it comes down and circles. A ḥadīth says "mercy hovered (rafrafat) over his head".

Al-rafrāf is the male ostrich, which beats its wings and then runs; the wing of an ostrich or a bird; and a bird called "snatcher of its own shadow" (from Abū Salama, who adds that the ostrich is sometimes given that name). Umm al-Sāʾib, shaking with fever, was asked "why are you turafrifīna?", that is, trembling; the word is also transmitted with z.

**11. Hanging edges, screens and coverings.** Rafraf (unit noun rafrafa) is the lower edge of a tent's side and the like, and the sides of a coat of mail with what hangs from them; also a strip of cloth sewn along the bottom of a large tent or pavilion. The raff of a house is described in the same way (plural rufūf), and raffa l-bayta is to make one for it. Ibn Sīda: the rafīf of a fusṭāṭ (tent) is its roof. A ḥadīth tells of a visit to ʿUthmān, encamped at al-Abṭaḥ, where a tent was pitched with a sword hanging from its rafīf; Shamir says this is the roof, and it is also said to be what hangs down from it.

In Anas's account of the death of the Messenger of God: "he lifted the rafraf, and we saw his face as though it were a rustling leaf". Ibn al-Aʿrābī: here the rafraf is the edge of the tent, while in the ḥadīth of the miʿrāj it is a spread (bisāṭ). Ibn al-Athīr: a spread or a curtain, meaning something that screened between them and him. The passage goes on: anything left over from a thing and folded back is a rafraf; and in another use a rafraf is the shelf on which a house's choice objects are placed.

Ibn al-Athīr reports Ibn Masʿūd on Q 53:18 ("he truly saw, of the signs of his Lord, the greatest"): "he saw a green rafraf that blocked the horizon", glossed as a spread, or a bed-covering. The rafraf of a coat of mail is mail fastened to the helmet and let fall over the back; according to another authority, the surplus of the coat's skirt. Rafraf and rafīf are both also glossed rawshan (a projecting window or ledge).

**12. Shelves.** Raff (with a): a board raised off the ground along a wall to protect what is placed on it; plurals rufūf and rifāf; also something like a niche (ṭāq). A woman who asked her husband to take her on the ḥajj, and heard that he had nothing, answered: "sell the dates on your shelf". Kaʿb b. al-Ashraf says his shelves are "cracking with ʿajwa dates the molar sinks into".

**13. Drooping branches.** The rafraf of a thicket is its loosely hanging branches. al-Muʿaṭṭal al-Hudhalī, of a lion: "he has a thicket whose hidden depths people do not feel safe from; he has made a preserve of its trailing growth, long and lank, and of castor plants". al-Aṣmaʿī: rafraf here is a trailing tree that grows in Yemen; elsewhere it is defined as soft, trailing trees.

**14. Fine cloth, green furnishings and Q 55:76.** Raffa l-thawbu rafafan: the garment grew thin, a usage noted as not firmly established; Ibn Barrī gives the adjective rafīf and says the verb's underlying pattern is faʿila. Rafraf is thin brocade, and green cloths made into furnishings for sitting-places (al-Muḥkam: spread out), unit noun rafrafa.

Q 55:76 has "reclining on green rafraf", also read rafārif. al-Farrāʾ reports that some took these to be the meadows of the Garden and others beds and spreads; its plural is rafārif. On form and origin, the passage that reports Ibn Masʿūd adds that some treat rafraf as a plural whose singular is rafrafa, with rafārif as the plural of rafraf; and that, on one view, rafraf was originally fine, well-made brocade and the like, the word later being extended.

**15. Herds and groups.** Raff is a great herd of camels; al-Liḥyānī extends it to a flock of small livestock, sheep or goats alike. It is also a group of sheep, and a pen for sheep and goats; al-Farrāʾ speaks of "a raff of people". A ḥadīth says "after al-riff and al-waqīr", riff (with i) being great herds of camels and waqīr many sheep and goats, meaning after wealth and affluence.

**16. Other senses.** Every thinning stretch of sand is a raff. Rafraf is also a kind of sea fish and, from al-Liḥyānī, the clitoris. Ruffa (printed once as rufa) is straw and its fragments; raffahu, he fed it this straw. Rufāf is what is chipped off straw and dried samur (Ibn al-Aʿrābī). Dārat Rafraf is a place.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris traces the root r-f-t (رفت) to a single core meaning: crumbling/crushing (fatt) combined with twisting (layy).

1. Crumbling: rafattu al-shayʾa bi-yadī — "I crushed/crumbled the thing with my hand," until it became rufāt, i.e. crumbled fragments or dust.

2. Fraying: irfatta al-ḥablu — "the rope frayed and gave way," said when it snapped or was severed.

3. Derived sense: rafata ʿunuqahu — "he wrenched his neck," meaning he crushed it and twisted/wrung it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives r-f-th from a single core idea: speech one would be ashamed to say openly.

1. Primary/original sense — sexual intercourse (al-nikāḥ). He supports this with Qur'an 2:187: "Lawful for you, on the night of the fast, is al-rafath to your wives" — i.e., intercourse with one's wives is permitted at night during Ramadan.

2. Secondary sense — obscene or lewd speech (al-fuḥsh fī al-kalām), extending the "shameful to voice" core to indecent talk generally, not only the sexual act itself.

3. Grammar note — the verb is used in two forms, arfatha and rafatha, both meaning "to engage in/utter rafath."

text:
**Root رغب (r-gh-b) — al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī**

**1. Core sense: breadth, capaciousness.** He takes the root's basic meaning to be width or spaciousness in a thing. Usage he cites: رَغُبَ الشيء — "the thing was ample," i.e. it widened; حوض رَغِيب — a capacious watering-trough; رَغِيب الجوف — wide of belly; فرس رَغِيب العدو — a horse with an ample stride.

**2. Extension to the will: breadth of wanting.** The nouns رَغْبَة / رَغَب / رَغْبَى all denote breadth in what one wants — desire understood as an expansive reaching-out, not a separate idea from sense 1. Shāhid: Q 21:90, "they call upon Us in *raghab* and *rahab*" — eager wanting paired with dread.

**3. Construction determines direction.** He makes the preposition the deciding factor:
 - رَغِبَ فيه / رَغِبَ إليه ("desire *in*" / "*toward*") = eagerness, keen wanting for the thing. Shāhid: Q 9:59, "we are, toward God, ones who desire."
 - رَغِبَ عنه ("desire *away from*") = the reverse — desire turned away, disinclination, abstaining. Shawāhid: Q 2:130, "who turns away from the *milla* of Abraham"; Q 19:46, "are you one turning away from my gods?"

**4. رَغِيبَة (raghība): an abundant gift.** He offers two possible derivations rather than choosing one: either from *raghba* as "desire" — because such a gift is a thing desired (*marghūb fīhi*) — or from the root's original sense of breadth, because the gift is ample. Shāhid (unnamed poet): "he gives the *raghāʾib* to whom he will, and withholds."

**Method:** the entry moves from a concrete physical sense (width) to a psychological one (wanting), then uses Qur'anic constructions with *fī* / *ilā* versus *ʿan* to separate two opposite meanings of the same verb, and closes by tracing a derived noun back to either layer.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root r-gh-d (ر غ د) from two distinct base senses.

1. Pleasant, ample living. A "raghad" or "raghīd" life (عيش رَغَد / رَغِيد) is one that is pleasant and abundant. The verb form arghada l-qawm ("the people arghada'd") is used when a people came into abundance or fertile pasture. In some dialects, al-raghīdah is said to mean simply "butter." And arghada l-rajulu māshiyatahu ("the man arghada'd his livestock") describes turning livestock loose to graze freely and unattended (sawm).

2. The opposite sense: weakened/uncertain condition. Al-murghādd describes someone whose bodily state has changed for the worse through weakness. From this same idea, the word is also used for someone who is unsure of his own opinion — doubting it and unable to settle on it or bring it out decisively.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ر غ م (r-gh-m), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Two distinct roots: (1) dust, and (2) a way/course/escape-route.

**Root 1 — dust**
1. al-ragham — dust; "arghama Allāhu anfahu" — "may God press his nose into the dust" (an imprecation for humiliation/defeat), and a hadith of ʿĀʾishah on hair-dye using the same verb ("cast it into the dust"). Ibn Fāris notes this physical sense is the origin, later extended by analogy: al-Khalīl glosses al-raghm as "doing what one is loathe to do"; raghama fulānun — so-and-so was unable to obtain satisfaction/redress. al-ragham — also the name of a specific sand-tract. rāghama fulānun qawmahu — so-and-so broke with and abandoned his people.

**Root 2 — way/refuge**
2. al-murāgham — a way out, an escape/refuge. The entry's central Qur'anic citation is al-Nisa' 4:100: "yajid fī al-arḍi murāghaman kathīran wa saʿah" — "he will find in the earth many a refuge, and abundance" (part of a verse about those who emigrate for God's sake), illustrated with a line of poetry by al-Jaʿdī. "mā lī ʿan dhālika al-amri murāgham" — "I have no escape from that matter."

**Closing exception, flagged as anomalous to both roots**
3. al-rughāmā — variously glossed as the nose, or the appendage of the liver, illustrated with a line of poetry by al-Shammākh.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives everything under ر-ه-ط from a single core idea: **a coming-together**, of people or of other things.

1. **A small band of men (three to ten).** Al-rahṭ names a group of men numbering from three up to ten. Al-Khalīl adds that a group smaller than seven, down to three, is separately called a nafar. The lighter pronunciation (rahṭ, with a silent hāʾ) is preferred over the fuller-vowelled form.

2. **Kinsmen.** By extension, when speaking of one's clan (ʿashīra), Arabic allows either plural form — rahṭuka or arhuṭuka — for "your kinsmen," meaning the men of one's clan. A verse of poetry laments a war that "laid low bands of men (arāhiṭ), and so they found rest" — meaning it killed them, releasing them from this world.

3. **Tarhīṭ — gulping food.** A related form, al-tarhīṭ, describes rolling a mouthful of food together and gathering it into the mouth — i.e., eating in large, hasty bites. A line of verse addresses "the eater given to tarhīṭ."

4. **Al-rāhiṭāʾ — a jerboa's burrow-chamber.** This is one of the named chambers in a jerboa's burrow system (alongside the nāfiqāʾ and qāṣiʿāʾ), where it hides its young. This chamber is also called ruhaṭa.

5. **Al-rihāṭ — a leather strap-skirt.** This is a piece of tanned leather cut to reach from the waist to the knee and then slit into thong-like strips, worn by a young girl. One strip on its own is called a rahṭ; the garment as a whole (rihāṭ) is grammatically singular, with plural arhiṭa. Two verses are cited using rihāṭ/rahṭ in this material sense — one comparing the tearing sound of a sword-thrust to the rending of this garment, another using rahṭ figuratively of something placed "upon menstruating women."

All these senses — a knot of men, a bundle of food in the mouth, a chamber tucked in a burrow, strips gathered into a garment — trace back, in Ibn Fāris's method, to the same root sense of things drawn or gathered together.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَرْهَبُ 3x "(are) fearful"; رُهْبَٰن 3x "and the monks"; ٱسْتَرْهَبُ 1x "and terrified them"; تُرْهِبُ 1x "(to) terrify"; رَهَب 1x "and fear"; رَّهْب 1x "fear"; رَهْبَانِيَّة 1x "but monasticism"; رَهْبَة 1x "(in) fear"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ر ه ب from two distinct roots: one meaning fear, the other meaning fineness/thinness and lightness.

1. Fear. الرَّهْبَة is fear or dread. The verb رَهِبَ (to fear something) takes the verbal nouns ruhb, rahab, and rahba. Under this same sense he places:
 - التَّرَهُّب — devotion / ascetic worship (glossed as al-taʿabbud, "devoting oneself in worship"); i.e. becoming a monk.
 - الإِرْهَاب — driving camels away from the watering-trough and repelling them.

2. Fineness / thinness / lightness. Under the second root:
 - الرَّهْب — an emaciated (lean) she-camel.
 - الرِّهَاب — thin arrowheads or blades; singular rahb.
 - الرَّهَاب — a tongue-shaped bone in the chest that overlooks the belly.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: رِهَٰن 1x "then pledge"; رَهِين 1x "(is) pledged"; رَهِينَة 1x "(is) pledged"
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) derives root r-h-n (رهن) from one core idea: the fixedness or permanence of a thing that is held or retained, whether by legal right or otherwise.

1. al-rahn — "the pledge": a thing given/held as security. Verb: rahantu (I pledged), verbal noun rahn. He notes explicitly that arhantu is NOT used for this ordinary sense of pledging.

2. al-rāhin ("fixed") describes anything firmly established, permanent, and enduring.

3. rahana laka al-shayʾu — "the thing stayed/remained for you" (it stayed put). Its causative is arhantuhu laka — "I made it stay for you."

4. Abū Zayd's usage: arhantu fī al-silʿa — "I bid up / overpaid for the merchandise," which he ties specifically to the sense of costliness (ghalāʾ), supported by a poetic line about a she-camel for which dinars were bid up. Ibn Fāris flags Abū ʿUbayd's wording here as irregular, and instead endorses Ibn al-Sikkīt's view: urhinat means "was paid in advance" (uslifat) — this he calls the correct reading.

5. arahantu waladī irhānan — "I staked/wagered my children," i.e., put them up as the stake in a wager (akhṭartuhum).

6. rāhin is also the word for an emaciated person or camel — explained as an extension of the same "fixedness" idea: from leanness, the creature stays put and doesn't move. Illustrated with a line of poetry: "If you see my body grown lean and fixed from emaciation — the glory of men is not in fatness."

7. The corresponding verbal noun for this "becoming fixed" sense is ruhūn (from rahana ruhūnan).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَرْهَقُ 5x "will cover them"; يُرْهِقَ 3x "he would overburden them"; رَهَق 2x "any burden"
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) treats the root ر-ه-ق as having two closely related core meanings: (1) one thing overtaking or enveloping another, and (2) haste and delay.

Sense 1 — overtaking / enveloping:
- رَهِقَهُ الأمرُ = the affair overtook and covered him (equated with غَشِيَهُ).
- رَهُوق (of a she-camel): a swift, wide-strider that "catches up to / overtakes" you when urged on, because of her long stride.
- Qur'anic citation, Yūnus 10:26: "no gloom nor abasement overtakes (يَرْهَق) their faces."
- مُرَاهِق: a boy who has drawn near to puberty.
- مُرَهَّق (of a man): one upon whom guests constantly alight — much visited by guests.
- أَرْهَقَ القومُ الصلاةَ: they delayed the prayer until the time of the next prayer drew near.

Sense 2 — haste (and delay), extending to wrongdoing:
- الرَّهَق = haste and wrongdoing/oppression. Qur'anic citation, al-Jinn 72:13: "he fears neither loss (بَخْس) nor رَهَق (oppression/burden)."
- الرَّهَق also = haste in lying and in fault. Poetic fragment: سَلِيمُ جَنَبِ الرَّهَقَا ("sound of flank as to rahaq" — free from the fault of impetuosity).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris finds two base meanings under ر-ه-و (rahawa):

1) Ease, lowering, stillness
- al-rahw = the calm, still sea.
- ʿayshun rāhin = a tranquil, easy life.
- arhi ʿalā nafsika = go easy on yourself, be gentle with yourself.
- Ibn al-Aʿrābī: yarhū, said of travelling at a gentle, unhurried pace.
- al-faras al-mirhā' = a horse with a loose, easy gait (like al-mirkhā') — fast, yet calm and unagitated.

2) A place that is either low or high (a disputed, two-sided term)
- al-rahw = low-lying ground, according to one view.
- According to the opposing view, it means elevated ground — supported by two lines of poetry: one about nursing women retreating to a rahwa out of fear (i.e., to high ground), another describing a bird perched atop a rahwa.
- al-Khalīl: al-rahwa = a pool where standing water collects.
- A hadith about the tribe Ghaṭafān calls it "a rahwa that gushes forth water" — Ibn Fāris explains this as meaning a lofty mountain, used as a metaphor for the tribe. A second hadith calls it "a rough hillock that repels people."
- al-Qutaybī states outright that rahwa is one of the aḍdād — a single word carrying two opposite meanings, both low ground and high ground.
- Related word: al-rahā' = a flat, level desert plain, rarely without a mirage.

Outside both bases (anomalous uses):
- al-rahw = a kind of bird.
- al-rahw = a disparaging term applied to a woman.
- the horses came rahwan = they came one after another, in succession.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: رَجَعَ 79x "you will be returned"; مَرْجِع 16x "(is) your return"; رَٰجِعُون 4x "will return"; رَجْع 3x "(is) a return"; يَتَرَاجَعَ 1x "they return to each other"; رُّجْعَىٰ 1x "(is) the return"
poets_named: unnamed verse ×4; Ḥumayd (lived into Islam); al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root r-j-ʿ (رجع) as a large, regular root whose core sense is returning / sending back (radd) and repetition (takrār). From this one idea he derives:

1. To return, come back — رَجَعَ / يَرْجِعُ / رُجُوعًا (to go back, come back). الرُّجْعَى (al-rujʿā) is a noun meaning the returning.

2. Taking a wife back — رَاجَعَ a man "returned to"/took back his wife; the act is al-rajʿa / al-rijʿa.

3. Exchange-taking (of livestock) — الرَّاجِعَةُ (al-rājiʿa) is a she-camel sold so that another like her is bought with the price; the replacement is al-rājiʿa, and she is said to be ارْتُجِعَتْ (taken in exchange). Cited: a ḥadīth in which a ṣadaqa-collector says he "took [a fine she-camel] in exchange (irtajaʿtuhā) for other camels"; the verbal noun is al-rijʿa. A verse of poetry uses رِجْعَة for such exchange-taking (paired with jalab, "driving to market").

4. Taking back what one gave — أَعْطَيْتُهُ ثُمَّ ارْتَجَعْتُهُ (I gave it, then took it back); and استرجع (istarjaʿa) = to reclaim, illustrated by a verse where "the towns reclaimed their far-wanderers."

5. A widow returned home — امْرَأَةٌ رَاجِعٌ (rājiʿ): a woman whose husband has died and who has gone back to her own family.

6. Reiteration in the voice — التَّرْجِيعُ (al-tarjīʿ): repeating/modulating a sound.

7. الرَّجْعُ (al-rajʿ): a beast drawing its forelegs back in its gait.

8. A reply / thing returned — الْمَرْجُوعُ (al-marjūʿ): that to which something is returned; also the answer to a message. Illustrated by Ḥumayd's line imagining a dwelling that might "return an answer" to one who questions it.

9. Putting the hand back — أَرْجَعَ يَدَهُ فِي كِنَانَتِهِ (he returned his hand into his quiver) to draw an arrow; supported by a Hudhalī verse.

10. Birds' return — الرِّجَاعُ (al-rijāʿ): birds returning after migrating away.

11. The cud — الرَّجِيعُ (al-rajīʿ): the cud, so named because its chewing is repeated (cited from al-Aʿshā). Also الرَّجِيعُ of a mount = one brought back from one journey to another.

12. Camels regaining condition — أَرْجَعَتِ الْإِبِلُ: lean camels that grew fat again, i.e. returned to their former state.

13. Rain — الرَّجْعُ also means the beneficial rain (al-ghayth). Ibn Fāris reads the Qurʾānic {وَالسَّمَاءِ ذَاتِ الرَّجْعِ} (al-Ṭāriq 86:11) this way: the sky "returns" — it pours rain, then comes back and rains again. A closing verse contrasts a famine year with "no rajʿ (rain) and no ṣadʿ (sprouting)."

text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-j-f as a single root whose core idea is iḍṭirāb — shaking, agitation, unsteady motion.

1. Literal trembling. Used of the earth quaking (رَجَفَتِ الأَرْضُ) and of the heart trembling (رَجَفَ القَلْبُ).

2. The sea as rajjāf. The intensive form رَجَّاف is applied to the sea — the heaving, restless one — precisely because of its constant agitation.

3. Form IV: arjafa. أَرْجَفَ النَّاسُ فِي الشَّيْءِ describes people plunging into talk about some matter and being thrown into commotion over it — the agitation being social rather than physical.

The entry is brief and gives no poetic citations; all three usages are presented as branches of the one sense of agitation.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-j-j as a root indicating agitation or unsteady motion (al-iḍṭirāb), and he calls it consistent and regular across the words built on it.

1. **To shake, to heave.** Al-rajj is setting a thing in motion: rajajtu al-ḥāʾiṭ, "I shook the wall". Of the sea one says irtajja al-baḥr, "the sea heaved".

2. **Things that quiver or heave.** Rajraj is a descriptive word for anything that quivers, as in the verse "and she clothed the wrap in a quivering rump". A katība rajrāja is an army troop that churns and can scarcely move forward. A jāriya rajrāja is a girl whose buttocks quiver. A nāqa rajjāʾ is a she-camel with a large hump; Ibn Fāris explains that a hump, once it grows large, shakes and wobbles.

3. **Confused speech.** Irtajja al-kalām means that speech has become confused. He explains the expression: speech that turns murky is like the heaving sea.

4. **Weakness.** Al-rajāj is a word for weak men. A verse describes a company worn out by travelling at night: "they are rajāj, and upon rajāj", that is, weak, and upon weak ones. He also reports that al-rajāja is said to mean an emaciated ewe, and accepts it only conditionally: if the report is correct, it fits because an emaciated animal is unsteady.

5. **Rijrija and rijrij.** Al-rijrija is the water remaining in a basin; the same word also names a soft tharīda, bread broken into broth. In the verse "and rijrij between her two jawbones, in scattered clumps", the rijrij is said to be saliva.

text:
Ibn Fāris organizes the root ر-ج-ل (r-j-l) around one central image — the leg/foot (rijl) of any creature that has one — with a handful of words he treats as deviations from it.

Core sense (the leg/foot and what walks on it):
1. الرِّجْل (al-rijl) — the leg/foot of a human or animal.
2. الرَّجْل (al-rajl) — foot-soldiers/infantry (al-rajjāla), so named because they travel on their feet; related plurals for "men on foot" include الرُّجَّال, الرُّجَالَى, and رَجْلَان (a footman), plural رَجْلَى. Cited verse: a vow to visit "the House of God, on foot and barefoot."
3. Verbal and idiomatic uses: رَجَلْتُ الشَّاةَ — to hang a sheep up by its leg; كَانَ ذَاكَ عَلَى رِجْلِ فُلَانٍ — "that happened on so-and-so's leg," i.e. in his lifetime/era.
4. Descriptions of legs: الأَرْجَل — a beast with one white leg among otherwise black legs (thought undesirable), or an animal/person with a large foot; رَجُلٌ رَجِيلٌ / ذُو رُجْلَةٍ — a strong walker.
5. Further verbs: تَرَجَّلْتُ فِي الْبِئْرِ — to climb down into a well unaided (not lowered by rope); ارْتَجَلَ الْفَرَسُ — a horse blending a stretching gait with an amble; أَرْجَلْتُ الْفَصِيلَ — to let a young camel walk with its mother and nurse at will; ارْتَجَلْتُ الرَّجُلَ — to grab a man by his leg.
6. Al-Khalīl's specialized "leg/foot" terms: رِجْلُ الْقَوْسِ (the bow's upper curved tip), رِجْلُ الطَّائِرِ ("bird's foot," a type of branding-iron), رِجْلُ الْغُرَابِ ("crow's foot," a way of tying a she-camel's teats), and حَرَّةٌ رَجْلَاءُ (a lava-field hard to walk across). Ibn Fāris folds all of these back into the core "leg" sense.

Words he marks as deviating from the core:
7. الرَّجُل (al-rajul) — a "man," a single adult male; occasionally الرَّجُلَة was used for a woman.
8. الرِّجْلَة (al-rijla) — purslane, "the foolish herb" (al-baqla al-ḥamqāʾ), reportedly so named because it grows only in a watercourse; on a related view, الرِّجَل (sing. رِجْلَة) means watercourses themselves.

Metaphorical extensions he traces back to "leg":
9. تَرَجَّلَ النَّهَارُ — "the day rose high," as if it stood up on its leg; رَجَّلْتُ الشَّعْرَ — combing/dressing hair, as if strengthening it; المِرْجَل — a cauldron, since when set up it is as though propped on a leg.
10. A further outlier, reported by al-Umawī: وَلَّدْتُهَا الرُّجَيْلَاءَ, said when sheep give birth one after another.

text:
**Root رجم (r-j-m), from al-Zabīdī's Tāj al-ʿArūs.**

The article treats stone-pelting as the root's original, concrete sense, from which a family of figurative meanings was borrowed.

**Verbal senses of al-rajm:**
1. **Killing** — specifically stoning the married adulterer to death. Al-Zabīdī reads the Qurʾanic {لتكونن من المرجومين} as "those killed in the ugliest way."
2. **Casting an accusation (qadhf)** of fault or suspicion.
3. **Conjecture / guessing at the unseen.** Al-Zamakhsharī: "rajama bi-l-ẓann" originally = "he flung out a guess," then became so common it simply meant "to conjecture" (قاله رجماً = "he said it as a guess"). The Ṣiḥāḥ ties this to {رجماً بالغيب} (guessing at the unseen). A verse of Abū al-ʿIyāl al-Hudhalī uses "the conjecturing of doubts." {لأرجمنك} is read here as "I will say behind your back what you hate." Al-Rāghib: rajm is borrowed for hurling out an imagined guess.
4. **Cursing (laʿn)** — hence al-shayṭān al-rajīm, "the accursed, pelted with the curse" (noted as figurative).
5. **Reviling / abuse** — another reading of {لأرجمنك} as "I will insult you."
6. **Shunning; and driving away/expulsion.** The epithet rajīm for Satan is explained by any of three: cursed, reviled, or driven off.

**Etymology.** Al-Zabīdī states plainly that the root's original meaning is **pelting with stones**, later extended to all the above. From it: rajamahu → marjūm and rajīm. One explanation of Satan as rajīm is that he is pelted with the shooting stars.

**Nouns:**
- **al-rajm** = a missile/thing thrown; pl. rujūm. This underlies {وجعلناها رجوماً للشياطين}: the *shuhub* (meteors) are missiles against the demons. Note on the astronomy: the demons are pelted by the darting meteors detached from the stars' fire, not by the fixed stars themselves — as a firebrand is taken from a fire that stays in place. An alternative reading: rujūm = the guesses of astrologers, and "demons" = the demons among humankind.
- **al-rajam** (fatḥa) = a well; an oven; a wide round pit (or "ditch," ḥafra, in other texts). Also a mountain in Ajaʾ (of Ṭayyiʾ).
- **al-rajam** = a **grave** — originally the stones set on a grave, then the grave itself (verse of Kaʿb b. Zuhayr; "arjām ʿĀd" = the graves of ʿĀd). Variant al-rajma.
- **al-rujum / al-rujma** (ḍamma) = raised stones set on a grave; or simply the grave-**marker**.
- **al-rajam** = brethren/companions — but Ibn Sīdah admits "I do not know how it is."

**Verb of grave-marking.** rajama/rajjama al-qabr = to mark it or set the stones on it. In Ibn Mughaffal's will "lā tarjumū qabrī": most read it "do not heap stones on my grave" (level it, don't raise it); Abū Bakr reads it "do not wail (utter ugly speech) at my grave," from rajm = abuse.

**Other derived words:**
- **al-rujma** = a hyena's den; also (dialectally) the prop a palm-tree leans on (elsewhere rujba).
- **al-marājim** = foul speech.
- **rājama ʿan** (fig.) = to contend/defend on someone's behalf; **rājama** in speech, running, or war = to compete to the utmost.
- **al-mirjām** = a strong or long-necked camel (as if pelting pebbles with its hooves); also a **stone-hurler / sling**, pl. marājīm.
- **rajul mirjam** (fig.) = a strong man, "as if the enemy is pelted with him" / who defends his honor (verse of Jarīr); **faras mirjam** = a horse that "pelts the ground" with its hooves.
- **ḥadīth murajjam** (fig.) = a conjectured report whose truth cannot be pinned down (verse of Zuhayr).
- **al-rijām** (kitāb pattern) = (a) a weighted stone lowered to churn a deep well's slime for cleaning (= al-mirjās); (b) the structure built over a well with a beam laid across for the bucket; **al-rijāmān** = the two uprights carrying the pulley.

**Grammatical note on "dragoman."** al-turjumān is analyzed as the pattern tafʿulān from this root (per al-Jawharī); al-Rāghib's Mufradāt derives it from murājama = "mutual reviling." Al-Zabīdī argues it belongs under r-j-m here, not under t-r-j-m.

**Proper names / places:** Marjūm al-ʿAṣrī, a Jāhilī noble of ʿAbd al-Qays (al-Zabīdī corrects and reconciles the genealogies, and the anecdote of a chief named "Marjūm" after a king told him "I have out-honored [rajamtuka] you"; a verse of Labīd is cited, the "Marjūḥ" reading called an error). Also: al-Arjām and Rijām (mountains/places, with verses of Jubayhāʾ and Labīd's muʿallaqa), Rajmān (a village on the Khābūr), and the traditionists Murājim b. al-ʿAwwām and Murājim b. Sulaymān.

**Supplement.** tarājamū / irtajamū bi-l-ḥijāra = they pelted each other with stones; tarājamū bi-l-kalām = they traded insults (fig.). rujūm can also be a verbal noun. al-rijām = crags/hills (Abū ʿAmr). al-rajma = a tower once circumambulated. lisān mirjam = a forceful, eloquent tongue. al-rajāʾim = stone-throwing mountains. A woman "came to ask the Prophet to stone (tastarjim)" = to request the rajm.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root r-j-s as having a single core sense: mixing or commingling (ikhtilāṭ). He derives its uses from this:

1. Confusion / intermixing. The expression هم في مَرْجُوسَة من أمرهم means "they are in a muddle about their affair."

2. Reverberating sound. الرَّجْس is the sound of thunder, so named because it rolls back and forth (yataraddad). By extension, the rumbling growl of a camel (hadīr) is rijs; a thundering cloud is called رَجَّاس and a much-growling camel رَجَّاس. Ibn al-Aʿrābī cited هذا راجسٌ حسنٌ — "this is a fine thundering cloud."

3. Filth. الرِّجْس means dirt or filth (qadhar), which Ibn Fāris ties back to the core sense because filth is a smearing and mixing together (laṭkh wa-khalṭ).

text:
al-Rāghib treats r-j-w through two strands, "side" and "hope", and ties further derivatives to hope.

1. **Side.** rajā is the side of a well, of the sky and of other things; plural arjāʾ. Q 69:17: "and the angels will be upon its sides (arjāʾihā)."

2. **Hope.** al-rajāʾ is defined as a supposition that entails the coming about of something that brings gladness.

3. **Hope in the sense of fear.** On Q 71:13, "What is the matter with you that you do not *tarjūna* for God any dignity?", it has been said that the meaning is "do not fear". A line of verse is cited in support: "When the bees stung him, he did not *yarju* their sting", i.e. he did not fear it, "and he kept close to them in a house of working bees." al-Rāghib's explanation is that hope and fear are inseparable companions. He also cites Q 4:104, "and you hope from God what they do not hope."

4. **Deferred.** He cites Q 9:106, "and others are *murjawna* (deferred) to the command of God," within this entry.

5. **A she-camel near birth.** arjati al-nāqa means her delivery drew near. al-Rāghib explains the underlying sense as: she gave her owner hope in herself because her birth was close.

6. **Purple-red.** al-urjuwān is a red colour which, he says, gladdens the way hope gladdens.

text:
Ibn Sīda's account of the root ر ج ز (r-j-z):

**1. Trembling in camels (the base image).** al-Rajaz is the quivering of a camel's leg when it tries to rise before it straightens out; also a shaking that seizes a male or female camel in the thighs and hindquarters as it gets up. Verb rajiza; the male is arjaz, the female rajzāʾ. A nāqa rajzāʾ is also a she-camel weak in the hindquarters that needs two or three tries to stand.

**2. Rajaz as a poetic metre.** A metre whose foot begins with two "causes" then a "peg"; easy on the ear, so it tolerates shortened forms — the mashṭūr (half a line dropped) and the manhūk (reduced to two feet), e.g. "Would that in it I were a young colt, trotting and galloping." Some held it was not true poetry but closer to rhymed prose (sajʿ); al-Khalīl held it sound poetry, robust enough to stand even on a single foot.
- Why called "rajaz": Abū Isḥāq (al-Zajjāj) — because vowel-then-quiescent alternate through its feet, like the twitching of a camel's leg (move, still, move, still). Others: for the unsettled, close-packed feet; or because it is "fore-parts without hind-parts."
- Ibn Jinnī: anything built on the rajaz pattern is called rajaz. al-Akhfash: among the Arabs rajaz is whatever runs on three feet — the chant used at work, in markets, and for driving camels — reportedly also al-Khalīl's view. Ibn Jinnī notes al-Akhfash ignored two-foot rajaz (as in "…jadhaʿ") only because it is rare, not because it fails the definition; indeed, being named for its "disturbance," two-foot rajaz shows that disturbance even more strongly.

**3. Composing and reciting.** An urjūza is a rajaz-poem; rajaza / irtajaza = to compose one; rajaza bihi / rajjazahu = to recite one to someone; tarājazū / irtajazū = to trade rajaz back and forth.

**4. Thunder and sound (irtijāz).** al-Irtijāz is the rolling sound of thunder; a rain-cloud with thunder is murtajiz or mutarajjiz (with a poetic citation from Abū Ṣakhr on a roaring sea-swell). al-Murtajiz was the name of the Prophet's horse, for its loud, fine neighing. tarājaza al-qawm = the people quarrelled.

**5. al-Rijz / al-Rujz (Qur'anic sense).** (a) punishment, torment; (b) the worship of idols, and it is said, shirk of any kind — the reasoning being that one who worships other than God is in doubt and inner disturbance, compared to Q "and among people is he who worships God on an edge," i.e. on doubt, without firm assurance. On Q "and the rujz — forsake it," some said the rujz here is an idol; Ibn Sīda adds "and God knows best." (The "disturbance/unsteadiness" idea links this sense back to the root's core image.)

**6. al-Rijāza (litter gear).** A stone-filled cloak hung on one side of a camel-litter to counterbalance a tilting load — named for its swaying; also a woman's mount smaller than a litter; also litter-adornment of wool and red hair (with a line by al-Shammākh, which al-Aṣmaʿī judged a misreading of jazāʾir/jazīra).

**7. al-Rajjāz.** A known valley, cited in a line by Badr b. ʿĀmir al-Hudhalī (also read al-Rujjāz).

text:
ROOT: ركض (r-k-ḍ) — Tāj al-ʿArūs, al-Zabīdī (d. 1791 CE)

According to this entry, al-rakḍ is a cluster of senses built on the core image of striking or driving with the foot/leg.

1. Core sense — moving/striking with the leg. Al-Jawharī (al-Ṣiḥāḥ) glosses rakḍ as "moving the leg," citing Q38:42, where Job is told, "Strike (urkuḍ) with your foot — here is a cool bathing place and drink." Al-Ṣāghānī takes this as striking and treading the ground; Ibn al-Athīr says the root sense is hitting with the foot, as a mount is struck. The entry extends this literal "kicking" to a locust kicking hot pebbles, and (figuratively) to ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz "kicking" in the grave-niche he dug for al-Walīd.

2. A push or thrust (al-dafʿ) — the sense behind "rakḍat al-shayṭān" ("Satan's thrust"), a name for the blood of istiḥāḍa, taken up again in sense 7.

3. Urging a horse on with the foot, driving it to run. Al-Jawharī notes usage broadened so people said "the horse rakaḍa" (ran) without mentioning the rider's kick — which he judges loose usage; strictly the passive "rukiḍa" (was driven to run) is correct (see sense 8).

4. (Figurative) A bird's wingbeat: "it rakaḍa with its wings" = flapped them. Illustrated with verses on ravens' wing-beats and a debated line about old age "overtaking" someone, where the key term (al-yaʿāqīb) could mean either partridges in flight or galloping horses — grammarians disagreed, and al-Aṣmaʿī called the line unique.

5. Fleeing/being routed. Ibn Shumayl: "he rakaḍa" = he fled. This is the sense given for Q21:12–13: when they felt the punishment coming, "behold, they were fleeing (yarkuḍūn) from it," followed by the taunt "Flee not (lā tarkuḍū), and return [to your comforts]." Al-Zajjāj and al-Farrāʾ both read it as fleeing/being routed from the punishment.

6. Running/galloping — a horse striking the ground with its hooves at a gallop (figurative).

7. رَكْضَة (a single thrust/movement). Used in a ḥadīth of Ibn ʿAbbās describing the blood of istiḥāḍa as either "a persistent vein" or "a rakḍa from Satan." Ibn al-Athīr explains this as Satan figuratively "striking" the woman — confusing her about her ritual purity and prayer until she loses track of her normal cycle. A related idiom, "he does not rakuḍu the crook-stick," means he does not stand up for himself.

8. A live grammatical dispute the entry records at length: several authorities (al-Aṣmaʿī, al-Jawharī) insist the "correct" form is the passive rukiḍa al-farasu ("the horse was driven to run"), not the active rakaḍa al-farasu ("the horse ran"), even though the active use became common and is attested in verse (Ibn Durayd) and in expressions for animals' or birds' swift motion (e.g. a line by Ruʾba on a soaring vulture, and one on birds/gazelle-like creatures "running a mile and drawing back a mile"). Al-Zabīdī treats the active/intransitive use as a secondary, figurative extension rather than the base pattern.

9. (Figurative) The marākiḍ of a water-trough = its sides, struck by the water.

10. (Figurative) al-mirkaḍ = a fire-poker/iron rod for stirring embers (illustrated by a verse of ʿĀmir b. al-ʿAjlān al-Hudhalī).

11. (Figurative) al-mirkaḍa = the tip/end of a bow (dual mirkaḍā per Ibn Barrī; combined by al-Zamakhsharī as the two curved bow-tips, plural marākiḍ). A separate verse (attributed to Aws b. Ghalfāʾ) uses the same word-shape to describe a thoroughbred mare that kicks the ground galloping (rakkāḍa) — figurative.

12. (Figurative) arkaḍat, properly said of a mare — the entry flags al-Qāmūs's wording "the woman" as an outright error, since al-Ṣiḥāḥ, al-ʿUbāb, Lisān al-ʿArab, and Abū ʿUbayd all have "the mare": her foal grew large and stirred in the womb; such a mare is murkiḍa.

13. (Figurative) irtakaḍa = to be agitated/stirred — of a person disturbed in his affairs, a child stirring in the womb, water churning in a well, a fetus moving in a she-camel (murtakiḍa). murtakaḍ al-māʾ = the pool where water collects.

14. rākaḍahu = he raced him, each spurring his horse against the other's.

15. Two rare adverbial nouns, tarkaḍā/tirkiḍāʾ (short and extended forms), which grammarians cite as examples without explaining. Al-Fīrūzābādī (author of al-Qāmūs) guessed they just mean "the rakḍ"; al-Zabīdī, following Abū Ḥayyān, corrects this — they actually name a swaggering, strutting gait, unrelated to running.

Additional items noted as supplementary: al-markaḍān = where a rider's heels rest on the mount's flanks; a camel, like a horse, can "kick" (rakaḍa) — but the near-synonym ramaḥa is not used of a camel; rakaḍa al-arḍ/al-thawb = struck the ground or a garment with the foot; al-rakḍ can mean an ordinary person's gait (walking with both legs together), and, of a woman, the swish of her skirts and anklet against her legs as she walks (illustrated by al-Nābigha) — figurative; related verbs for racing/competing (tarākaḍū, irtakaḍū fī l-ḥalba); "I came to him rakḍan" (at a run, Sībawayh) — figurative; an anecdote from Abū al-Duqaysh has a young bride "kicking" her poor elderly husband in the chest; figurative extensions include stars "coursing" (rakaḍat) across the sky, and a bow "driving" (rakaḍat) an arrow forcefully — hence qawsun rakūḍ/murkiḍa, illustrated by a verse of Kaʿb b. Zuhayr; a dying man "kicking/convulsing" (yarkuḍu/yartakiḍu) in his death-throes; two names built on the root (Rakkāḍ b. Abbāq al-Dubayrī, a poet, and Murakkiḍ); and "Rakḍat Jibrāʾīl" (Gabriel's rakḍa) recorded as one of the names of the well of Zamzam.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-k-ʿ as a single root meaning "to bend or stoop," in humans or anything else.

1. Core sense — bending / stooping. رَكَعَ الرَّجُل means "the man stooped," and anything that bends over is رَاكِع (rākiʿ, "stooping"). He cites a verse of Labīd: "I recount the tidings of ages past; I creep along, as though each time I stand I am stooping." From the ḥadīth he cites الْمَشَايِخ الرُّكَّع ("the stooping old men"), meaning men bent over with age.

2. Extension to prayer. The رُكُوع (rukūʿ, the bowing) in the ṣalāt derives from this bending sense. The usage then broadened so that a person performing the prayer was called rākiʿ, and one who prostrated in thanksgiving was likewise called rākiʿ.

3. Qurʾānic citations. Of David: "he sought his Lord's forgiveness and fell down bowing (rākiʿan) and turned in repentance." And Āl ʿImrān 3:43: "prostrate and bow (wa-rkaʿī) with those who bow." Ibn Fāris notes some read the two verbs here as "pray" and "give thanks along with the thankful (al-shākirīn)" rather than physical postures.

4. Dialectal sense (per Ibn Durayd). الرُّكْعَة (al-rukʿa) means "a pit or hollow in the ground" — a Yemeni usage.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: رَكِبَ 9x "embark"; رُكْبَان 1x "riding"; مُّتَرَاكِب 1x "thick clustered"; رَّكْب 1x "and the caravan"; رَكُوب 1x "they ride them"; رِكَاب 1x "camels"; رَكَّبَ 1x "he assembled you"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ر ك ب (r-k-b) as one consistent root with a single core sense: one thing rising or mounting upon another. From this he derives:

1. Riding/mounting — رَكِبَ (rakiba, "he rode/mounted"), verbal noun رُكُوب (rukūb).

2. Mounts and transport — الرِّكَاب (al-rikāb): riding-camels, singular رَاحِلَة (rāḥila). "Rikāb-oil" (زَيْت رِكَابِيّ) is oil brought from Syria on such pack-camels. رَكُوبَة / حَمُولَة (rakūba / ḥamūla): an animal to ride versus one to carry loads. أَرْكَبَ الْمُهْر: a colt has reached rideable age. نَاقَة رَكْبَانَة: a she-camel fit for riding.

3. Groups of riders — الرَّكْب (al-rakb) and الْأُرْكُوب (al-urkūb): a riding party. Al-Khalīl distinguished these (riders of beasts) from الرُّكَّاب (al-rukkāb), a ship's passengers.

4. رَجُل مُرَكَّب (rajul murakkab) — a man who borrows a horse to fight on, splitting the spoils half-and-half with the horse's owner.

5. Layered things — رَوَاكِب الشَّحْم (rawākib al-shaḥm): folds of fat stacked at the front of the camel's hump (singular رَاكِبَة); the rear ones are الرَّوَادِف (rawādif). الرَّكَّابَة (al-rakkāba): a palm-shoot near the crown of a palm, sometimes fruiting alongside the parent tree.

6. Origin/stock — الْمُرَكَّب (al-murakkab): one's root and place of growth, as in هُوَ كَرِيمُ الْمُرَكَّب ("he is of noble stock").

7. The knee — رُكْبَة (rukba), so named because it sits raised above what is below it; الْأَرْكَب (al-arkab) is one with a large knee. رَكَبْتُ الرَّجُل means to strike someone's knee, or to strike him with one's knee.

8. Raised ridge — الرَّكِيب (al-rakīb): the elevated back between two water-channels of a vineyard.

9. الرَّاكِب (al-rākib): a disease affecting sheep in their backs.

10. الرَّكَب (al-rakab): the pubic mound. Al-Khalīl restricted the word to women; al-Farrāʾ applied it to the pubic region of both sexes, citing a verse ending "...without the arkāb meeting."

The unifying method throughout is Ibn Fāris's signature move: each usage — mount, hump-fat, knee, vineyard-ridge — is traced back to the one image of something elevated upon or above something else.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ر ك د (r-k-d), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: stillness.

1. rakada al-māʾ — water grew still; rakadati al-rīḥ — the wind died down; rakada al-mīzān — a scale balanced/settled; rakada al-qawm — people grew still and calm. jafnah rakūd — a bowl so full it stays motionless (unsloshing).
2. Closing exception, flagged by Ibn Fāris as departing from the root's core pattern (if genuinely attested): "tarākada al-jawārī" — a children's game in which one girl, seated on her feet, leaps in that position toward her companion.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَرْكُمَ 1x "and heap them"; رُكَام 1x "(into) a mass"; مَّرْكُوم 1x "heaped up"
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) gives the root r-k-m (ركم) a single core meaning: things gathering or piling up on one another.

1. Verb — rakamtu al-shayʾa, "I heaped the thing up": to throw or pile part of something on top of another part, so it accumulates in a mass.

2. Clouds — saḥābun murtakim / rukām: clouds described this way are piled-up, massed clouds (heaped one bank upon another).

3. Noun — al-rukmah: a heap of gathered clay or mud.

4. Idiom — murtakam al-ṭarīq: the well-trodden track/beaten path of a road — so called because travelers tread on it so heavily and repeatedly that they "pile up" (tartakimu) on it.

All four uses trace back to the one idea of accumulation — things laid or trodden one upon another.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-k-n as one root whose single idea is strength.

1. Core sense — strength. The rukn of a thing is its strongest side. Hence the expression "he takes shelter at a strong rukn," i.e. at might and protection that cannot be breached.

2. Extended to persons and mountains. A man described as rakīn is grave and steady. A mountain is called rakīn when it has lofty arkān — high corner-masses or buttresses.

3. رَكَنَ إِلَيْهِ — "to incline toward / rely on." Ibn Fāris explicitly derives this from the same core: the person "became settled toward him and steady with him." The leaning is, on his account, a leaning onto something solid, not mere inclination.

4. Morphological note. رَكَنْتُ أَرْكَنُ is a rare verb on the pattern faʿaltu / afʿalu (perfect in a, imperfect in a) even though the root contains no guttural consonant — normally the condition for that vowel pattern.

5. Reported conjugations. Al-Khalīl gives rakana / yarkanu, verbal noun raknan. The dialect of the lower Muḍar has rakina / yarkanu. A form rakina / yarkunu is also reported, but Ibn Fāris flags it as questionable. Abū Zayd reports rakina / yarkanu.

6. Concrete derivatives. Al-mirkan is a large washing-tub or basin. A she-camel is called murakkanat al-ḍarʿ when her udder is swollen and distended — as though it were a rukn, a solid corner-mass.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ر ك س (r-k-s), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One sound root, one core meaning: turning a thing on its head, returning its beginning to its end — i.e., reversal.

1. Qur'anic citation, al-Nisāʾ 4:88, "wa Allāhu arkasahum bimā kasabū" — glossed as: God returned them to their disbelief [because of what they had done].
2. irtakasa fulānun fī amrin — "so-and-so relapsed into a matter he had [already] escaped," the general sense of the root applied to backsliding.
3. al-Rakūsiyyah — named here as a religious group whose beliefs fell somewhere between Christianity and Sabianism (mentioned as a named derivative of the root, not otherwise explained).
4. A hadith citation: the Prophet, brought stones for ritual cleansing, found a piece of dung among them, threw it away, and said "it is riks" — explained as: it had been "turned back" (irtakasat) from being usable as food into something unclean, unfit for the purpose at hand.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) identifies two basic senses for the root ر-ك-ز (r-k-z):

1. **Fixing/driving something into something else so it goes downward** — i.e., planting or embedding something firmly in the ground.
2. **A sound.** (Named as the second sense, but this entry gives no example or citation developing it further.)

Sense 1 is illustrated as follows:
- *rakaztu al-rumḥa rakzan* — "I planted/drove the spear firmly [into the ground]."
- *markaz al-jund* — "the post of the troops," the fixed station they are assigned to and required to hold (the source of the later word *markaz*, "center/post").
- *irtakaza ʿalā qawsihi* — "he braced himself on his bow": setting the bow's curved tip on the ground and leaning his weight on it.
- *al-rikāz* — property/treasure buried in the Jāhiliyya (the pre-Islamic era). Ibn Fāris derives this directly from the root's core sense, since the owner "*rakazahu*" — fixed/buried it in the ground. Some authorities instead said *al-rikāz* means a mineral deposit or ore (*al-maʿdin*), with *arkaza al-rajulu* meaning "the man found ore." Ibn Fāris notes that if this second usage is correct, it is a metaphorical extension (*mustaʿār*) of the root's literal, primary sense — not the base meaning itself.
- *al-murtakiz* — dry grass whose leaves have crumbled and blown away, leaving what remains standing firm. Ibn Fāris glosses this as: what was lost from it is lost, and what remains "*irtakaza*," i.e., became firmly fixed/settled in place.

Sense 2 (a sound) is only stated, not elaborated, in this entry.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: ر م ح (r-m-ḥ) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris treats r-m-ḥ as a single root-idea from which everything below is derived.

1. Core word: al-rumḥ (الرمح) = "the spear/lance" — the ordinary, well-known weapon. Plurals: rimāḥ, armāḥ.

2. Star name: al-Simāk al-Rāmiḥ ("the Lancer Simāk") — a star so called because a smaller star travels ahead of it, as if it were its spear.

3. Extended/figurative use — "kicking":
   - ramaḥat-hu al-dābbah = "the riding-beast kicked him" — the beast's leg-strike is likened to a spearman's thrust, hence it too is called ramḥ.
   - ramaḥa al-jundub = said of a locust when it strikes the ground/pebbles with its foreleg — same image of a striking "spear."

4. Trade term: al-rammāḥ = a spear-maker; his craft is al-rimāḥah (spear-making).

5. Agent nouns: al-rāmiḥ can mean either (a) one who thrusts/stabs with a spear, or (b) simply one who carries one.

6. Figurative use in pasture description: of al-buhmā (a spiny grass) once its awns harden and it becomes too sharp for grazing animals to eat, it is said "it has taken up its spears (rimāḥ)." Ibn Fāris supports this with a line of poetry describing a time when the poet's she-camels — young and old alike — had not yet had "weapons" (silāḥ) turned against them by the pasture, i.e. before the grass had hardened into spines.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ر م د (r-m-d), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Three distinct roots: (1) a disease, (2) a color, (3) a kind of running.

**Root 1 — eye disease**
1. al-ramad — ophthalmia (eye inflammation); ramida yarmadu ramadan — to suffer from it; ramid/armad — afflicted with it. From this: al-ramd — destruction/ruin, illustrated with a line of poetry about the ancient tribe of ʿĀd being enveloped by ruin. "ramadnā al-qawma" — we overwhelmed/destroyed a people.

**Root 2 — the color/substance ash**
2. al-ramād — ash (the well-known substance); rimdid — the finest, most powdery grade. rammadati al-nāqah — a she-camel leaving little milk at birthing time, named for a discoloration on her udder. al-armad — anything ash-gray with a dusky tinge; from this, a gray-colored mosquito is called rumd, illustrated with a line of poetry by Abū Wajzah about a hunter's nighttime companions. al-armidāʾ — a further word for ash. al-murammad, of roasted meat — meat buried in embers to cook, illustrated with a proverb about ruining one's own good work at the last moment ("your brother roasted it, then buried it in ash").
3. ʿĀm al-Ramādah — "the Year of Ashes" (a historical famine year) — Ibn Fāris records two competing explanations: either named for the ruin/destruction (ramd) it brought, or because drought turned the land ash-colored. Abū Ḥātim's closing note: māʾ ramid — stagnant, discolored water.

**Root 3 — intense running**
4. al-irmidād — intensity of running; "irmadda al-ẓalīm" — the male ostrich sped up.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris assigns r-m-m four root meanings (uṣūl), arranged as two opposed pairs: gathering a thing together and mending it, against its wearing out; and silence, against its opposite.

1. **Mending (first root).** Al-ramm is mending a thing: ramamtuhu arummuhu, "I mended it, I mend it". He places here:
   - aramma, said of a camel or other animal that grows fat (yurimmu irmāman), with a verse about one who "satirized them when his bones had grown fat", though among the Bedouin he would have died of leanness;
   - al-murimm, which Abū Zayd defines as a she-camel with some marrow in her, the marrow itself being al-rimm;
   - al-rimm, moist earth, so called because its parts cling together, as in the saying "he has the ṭimm and the rimm", where al-ṭimm is the sea and al-rimm the moist earth.

2. **Wearing out (second root, the opposite of the first).** Ramma al-shayʾ: a thing wore out.
   - Al-ramīm is decayed bones, as in Q 36:78: "Who will give life to the bones when they are ramīm?" Al-rimma means the same; a ḥadīth reports that the Messenger of God forbade cleaning oneself after relieving nature with dung or with rimma.
   - Al-rumma is worn-out rope, illustrated by a line of Dhū al-Rumma.
   - Hence "hand it over bi-rummatihi", said to go back to a man who sold a camel with a rope on its neck and was told to hand it over "with its rumma". The phrase became common for handing over anything whole. They say al-Aʿshā meant this when he offered a wine-seller a she-camel, still on her lead-rope, for his wine.

3. **Picking up herbage.** Also in this group: a sheep tarummu the herbage from the ground with its maramma, and a ḥadīth says cattle tarummu from every tree.

4. **Silence (third root).** Al-irmām is silence: aramma irmāman, "he fell silent".

5. **The opposite of silence (fourth root).** Mā taramrama means "he did not move his mouth to speak". In a verse of Aws, a man who marvels at the poet's people would, had war buffeted him, not have stirred his lips (lam yataramram).

6. **Not a root sense.** In the saying "there is neither ḥumm nor rumm from that matter", meaning nothing stands in its way, rumm is not a root meaning, Ibn Fāris says, because it is like an itbāʿ, an echo word following another.

7. **An anomaly.** Naʿja rammāʾ, "a white ewe", is reported with the caution "if it is sound", and Ibn Fāris calls it anomalous, outside his four roots.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
Root r-m-n (رمن) — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr

1. Basic sense: رُمَّان (rummān) is the pomegranate, the fruit of a well-known fruit tree; singular رُمَّانة (rummāna).

2. Grammatical debate over the word's pattern (is the nūn part of the root, or added?):
   - Sībawayh reports that al-Khalīl treated rummān, when used as a proper name, as belonging to the "majority pattern" in which the alif and nūn are extra letters, not root radicals — because its derivation is simply not known.
   - Al-Akhfash disagreed, holding the nūn to be an original root letter, comparing rummān to words like qurrāṣ and ḥummāḍ, and describing the pattern fuʿʿāl as more common [in this connection] than fuʿlān.
   - Ibn Barrī corrects this: al-Akhfash did not claim fuʿʿāl is generally commoner than fuʿlān — he said only that fuʿʿāl is a common pattern specifically among plant-names (e.g. murrān, ḥummāḍ, ʿullām), which is why he classed rummān that way.

3. A ḥadīth usage: in the ḥadīth of Umm Zarʿ, a woman is described as having "two children playing beneath her waist with two pomegranates." This is explained as picturing a woman with very large hips: lying on her back, her flesh protrudes enough to leave a hollow beneath her waist where something round could roll — and separately, that her two sons literally each held a pomegranate and tossed them to one another beneath her waist.

4. رُمَّانة الفرس (rummānat al-faras) is a part of a horse['s gear] that holds its fodder. Ibn Sīdah notes he places this word under r-m-n because al-Akhfash treats it as a three-letter root here, though al-Khalīl and Sībawayh placed it under root r-m-m instead; al-Azharī lists it under r-m-n too.

5. Qur'anic point (Q 55:68): "In them is fruit, and date-palm and pomegranate." Some argued the "and" shows that date-palm and pomegranate are not kinds of "fruit," since "and" joins separate things. Abū Manṣūr (al-Azharī) rejects this as a misunderstanding of Arabic: the "and" here marks singling-out (ikhtiṣāṣ), not exclusion — Arabic speech commonly names something in general, then picks out one part of it again for special mention, precisely to highlight that part's excellence, without removing it from the general category. He compares two other verses on the same pattern:
   - Q 2:238, "Guard the prayers, and the middle prayer" — prayer is commanded generally, then "the middle prayer" is repeated for emphasis, not because it is a different thing from "the prayers."
   - Q 2:98 (as cited here), "...an enemy to God, His angels, His books, His messengers, Gibrīl and Mīkāl" — Gibrīl and Mīkāl are already included among "His angels," but are named again to mark their excellence and nearness to God.

6. مَرْمَنة (marmana) — the name for a place where pomegranate trees grow thickly.

7. The diminutive of rummāna is رُمَيْمينة (rumaymīna).

8. رَمَّان (Rammān, with fatḥa) — a place-name; per al-Ṣiḥāḥ, a mountain belonging to the tribe of Ṭayyiʾ.

9. إِرْمينِيَّة (Irminiyya, with kasra) — a province in Byzantine territory (Armenia); its adjectival form is أَرْمَنِيّ (Armanī). Ibn Barrī cites a line of poetry by Sayyāra ibn Qaṣīr mentioning "the horsemen of al-Armanī" fought at a place called Marʿash.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-m-y (rāʾ, mīm, and a weak third letter) as a single root with one core idea: **flinging or casting a thing away**. Everything else in the entry, he says, is carried onto that core either by regular derivation or by metaphor.

1. **Throwing / shooting (the base sense).** رَمَيْتُ الشَّيْءَ أَرْمِيهِ — "I threw (or shot at) the thing, I throw it."

2. **Mutual pelting.** رِمِّيَّا (rimmiyyā), on the morphological pattern فِعِّيلَى (fiʿʿīlā): "there was a rimmiyyā between them," i.e. an exchange of shooting at one another.

3. **Exceeding a number.** أَرْمَيْتُ عَلَى الْمِائَةِ — "I went past the hundred," i.e. exceeded it. Ibn Fāris raises the objection himself — how does this fit the root? — and answers: when something exceeds a limit it has *shot itself onward* (تَرَامَى) to the point it reached. He notes the plain form رَمَيْتُ can carry this same sense as the form-IV أَرْمَيْتُ.

4. **مِرْمَاة (mirmāt) — the rounded arrowhead.** Named from the root because it is the thing one shoots with.

5. **مَِرْمَاة (marmāt / mirmāt, vowelled either way) — a sheep's cloven hoof.** Cited with the ḥadīth phrase: "If one of them were invited to two marmātayn…" (quoted only as a lexical witness for the word).

6. **رَمِيَّة (ramiyya) — the quarry**, i.e. the game animal that is shot at.

7. **رَمِيّ (ramiyy) — a cloud with large raindrops.** The explanation offered: such a cloud forms and then has pieces of cloud "flung" at it from here and there until they gather into one mass.

8. **Verbal nouns.** Al-Khalīl: رَمَى / يَرْمِي with the maṣdars رِمَايَة (rimāya), رَمْي (ramy) and رِمَاء (rimāʾ).

9. **Practising at targets.** Ibn al-Sikkīt: خَرَجْتُ أَتَرَمَّى — "I went out shooting," said of going out to shoot at butts or targets (aghrāḍ). Also أَرْمَيْتُ الْحَجَرَ مِنْ يَدِي — "I flung the stone from my hand."

10. **An idiom of divine aid.** Abū ʿUbayda: أَرَمَى اللَّهُ لَكَ, glossed as "He helped you and acted in your favour."

11. **رَمَّاء (rammāʾ) — increase, surplus.** Ibn Fāris ties this back to the root on the same reasoning as sense 3: it is something that "shoots itself upward" beyond its limit.

Method note: the entry's organising claim is etymological — one primitive sense (casting) plus derivation and metaphor accounts for arrowheads, hooves, clouds, quarry, and numerical excess alike.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Faris (Maqayis al-Lugha) gives the root r-m-z a single core meaning: motion and agitation/commotion.

He supports this with four usages.

1. A surging battalion (katiba rammaza) is a troop of soldiers that ripples or undulates along its flanks, i.e. is in constant motion.

2. The idiom he struck him, and he did not irma'azz (darabahu fa-ma irma'azza) means the person struck did not budge or stir at all. The verb irma'azza is glossed simply as moved.

3. The verb irtamaza is given as a plain synonym: he moved, he stirred.

4. A separate, reported usage: al-ramuz is said by the Arabs to mean the sea, consistent with the root's core sense of motion/agitation. Ibn Faris notes this cautiously, adding that he believes he has encountered the word in the poetry of the Hudhayl tribe, though he does not cite the actual verse.

Note: this entry records only the motion/agitation sense of the root; it does not address the separate, better-known sense of ramz as a silent gesture or sign (the sense behind the Quranic illa ramzan, Q3:41) — that sense simply does not appear in this particular dictionary entry.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: رَقَبَة 9x "(of) a slave"; رَقِيب 5x "an observer"; ٱرْتَقِبْ 4x "so watch"; يَرْقُبُ 3x "you respect"; يَتَرَقَّبُ 2x "(and) was vigilant"; مُّرْتَقِبُون 1x "(too are) watching"
text:
Zamakhsharī's entry for the root ر ق ب (r-q-b) organizes the material around watching/waiting, then moves to the neck (raqaba), then to figurative extensions.

1. Watching and waiting for something. يرقب / يرتقب / يترقّب = to watch for, await and expect. Examples: sitting to watch for a companion; awaiting an event; "so-and-so watches for his father's death in order to inherit."

2. The raqbā gift. أرقبته داري = "I gave him my house as a raqbā" — a conditional gift where ownership turns on whichever party dies first; named from مراقبة (mutual watching), since each party watches for the other's death.

3. Watcher / overseer / scout. رقيب = watcher of a people; مرقب / مرقبة = a high lookout or watchtower; رقيب الجيش = the army's scout or forward watch; "I will keep watch for you tonight." Also ترقب ذمّة فلان = to observe/heed someone's covenant of protection.

4. The neck (raqaba). أرقب / رقبانيّ = a man with a large neck.

5. Figurative uses (labeled majāz by Zamakhsharī):
 - Responsibility "on the neck": هذا الأمر في رقابكم = this affair is your responsibility; الموت في الرقاب = death is upon the necks.
 - "Necks of the provision-bags" (رقاب المزاود) as a mocking epithet for non-Arabs (ʿajam), on account of their ruddy complexion; cited with a verse (via al-Aṣmaʿī) contrasting "the Bedouin/Arabs" with this epithet.
 - The person as "neck": أعتق الله رقبته = may God free his neck (person from bondage); "he bequeathed his wealth for [freeing] necks (raqāb)," i.e. slaves.

6. Wariness / fear of consequences. رقبه / راقبه = to be wary of, on guard against — because the fearful person watches for and expects punishment. Hence "he does not heed God (lā yurāqib Allāh) in his affairs" = he disregards God's punishment and plunges recklessly into disobedience.

7. Watching the stars. بات يرقب النجوم = he passed the night watching the stars, parallel to يرعاها (watching over / attending to them).

8. The raqūb woman: one whose children do not survive, so she perpetually watches in dread for her child's death.

9. Astronomical raqīb: al-Dabarān (Aldebaran) is "the raqīb of the Pleiades," because it forever follows and watches for their rising, never parting from them. Proverb of impossibility: "I will not come until the Pleiades meet their watcher" (i.e. never); with the verse of Jamīl on never meeting Buthayna.

10. Successor / heir. ورث المجد عن رقبة = to inherit glory by collateral succession (kalāla), where possession is feared insecure because of obscure lineage; and "what an excellent raqīb (successor) you are to your father and forebears," likening the heir to al-Dabarān following the Pleiades. Closing shāhid from ʿAdī, describing a horse trailing the dust of wild asses (raqīb al-naqʿ = the trailing edge of the dust).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) holds that the root ر-ق-د (r-q-d) has a single core meaning — sleep — from which its derivatives branch.

1. **Core sense — sleep.** الرُّقَاد (al-ruqād) = sleep. Verb: رَقَدَ رُقُودًا (raqada ruqūdan), "he slept."

2. **Derived sense — settling/staying in a place.** أَرْقَدَ الرَّجُلُ بِالْأَرْضِ (arqada al-rajulu bi'l-arḍ) is said of a man who "arqada" in a land, meaning he took up residence/stayed there — an extension from lying down to sleep toward remaining fixed in one place.

3. **Anomalous usage — moving fast.** أَرْقَدَ الظَّلِيمُ وَغَيْرُهُ (arqada al-ẓalīm wa-ghayruh), said of the male ostrich and other creatures, means it hastened/sped up in its going. Ibn Fāris explicitly flags this sense as شَذَّ عَنِ الْأَصْلِ — a deviation from the root's core meaning — since it denotes swift motion rather than sleep or stillness.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ر-ق-م (r-q-m) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core sense: a line/mark, writing, and anything resembling these.

1. al-raqm = "the line" / a mark.
2. al-raqīm = "the writing" / an inscription.
3. Idiom: "he inscribes upon water" (yarqumu fī l-māʾ), said of someone extremely skilled at his craft — illustrated with an anonymous line of verse: "I shall inscribe upon the clear water to you… despite your distance, if there be an inscriber in water."
4. Any embroidered or patterned garment is called raqm.
5. al-arqam = a kind of snake, so named because its back bears markings like an engraving.
6. Al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad's definition: al-raqm is the diacritical dotting of a text. A "marqūm" document is one whose letters have been made clear by dots/signs.
7. raqmatā l-faras wa-l-ḥimār = the two marks on the inner side of a horse's or donkey's forelegs.
8. A meadow (rawḍa) is called raqma because it resembles a "raqm" (a marking) laid upon the ground.
9. Land with sparse vegetation is called marqūma.
10. Irregular usage, noted as outside the core pattern: a calamity is called al-raqim. Ibn Fāris suggests it may still fit the root's logic, since a calamity, when it befalls someone, "leaves its mark."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-q-q as two roots (aṣlān): a quality that is the contrary of coarseness (jafāʾ), and the quivering of something fluid.

1. **Thinness, fineness.** The first root is al-riqqa, thinness or fineness: raqqa, yariqqu, "to be or become thin, fine", and what has the quality is raqīq. From it come al-raqāq, soft ground, which is also called al-raqq and al-riqq; and al-raqaq, weakness in the bones, as in a poet's line: "neither feebleness nor weakness was found in her bone." According to al-Farrāʾ, "there is raqaq in his wealth" means that it is scant. Ibn Fāris also lists here al-riqqa, a place from which the water sinks away; al-riqq, the well-known thing on which one writes; and al-ruqāq, thin bread.

2. **The quivering of a fluid; gleaming.** The second root appears in taraqraqa, said of a thing that gleams. Tears taraqraqa when they circle within the rim of the eye; the mirage taraqraqa, and the sun taraqraqat when it looks as though it were turning round. A raqrāqa is a woman in whose face water seems to flow. The same root gives raqraqtu al-thawb bi-l-ṭīb, "I moistened the garment with perfume", and raqraqat al-tharīda bi-l-dasam, "the tharīda (bread sopped in broth) ran with fat". Al-Aʿshā uses it of perfume: "she is cool with the coolness of a bride's mantle in summer, into which she has made the ʿabīr perfume run."

3. **Outside both roots.** al-raqq, the male tortoise, which Ibn Fāris records with the reservation "if that is sound."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: تَرْقَىٰ 1x "you ascend"; رُقِيّ 1x "in your ascension"; يَرْتَقُ 1x "then let them ascend"; رَاق 1x "(will) cure"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-q-y (the letters rāʾ, qāf, plus a weak final letter) as three separate, unrelated roots rather than one core idea.

1. Ascending. From رَقِيتُ فِي السُّلَّمِ ("I climbed the ladder"), imperfect أَرْقَى, verbal noun رُقِيّ (a climbing/ascent). He cites Qur'an 17:93 — "or you ascend into the sky; and we will not believe in your ascent" — where the noun رُقِيّ is the act of going up. He also cites the proverb ارْقَ عَلَى ظَلْعِكَ, literally "climb according to your lameness," glossed as: ascend only so far as you have the strength for.

2. A protective charm. رَقَيْتُ الْإِنْسَانَ, "I recited a charm over the person," from رُقْيَة — a formula by which protection is sought.

3. A feature of terrain. الرَّقْوَة is the ground lying just above a دِعْص, a hillock or drift of sand; the form رَقْو, without the final hāʾ, is also used. Ibn Fāris notes it is most typically found beside a valley (wādī).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: رَسُول 332x "a messenger"; أَرْسَلَ 130x "we sent"; مُّرْسَل 35x "the messengers"; رِسَٰلَٰت 6x "(the) messages"; رِسَالَة 4x "his message"; مُرْسِل 4x "(can) release"; مُرْسِلَة 1x "going to send"; مُرْسَلَٰت 1x "by the ones sent forth"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats R-S-L as a single, regular root whose core sense is springing/sending forth (inbiʿāth) and extension (imtidād). All the usages he lists trace back to this idea of something going forth freely or stretching out.

Senses and usages:
1. al-rasl — an easy, gentle gait; hence a she-camel (rasla) that needs no driving, and also one that is supple-jointed; and hair (rasl) that hangs loose and flowing.
2. al-rasl — sheep/goats sent out to pasture; and al-rasal — a flock or herd.
3. al-risl — milk, because it flows (lets down) from the udder. Ibn Fāris cites Ṭahfa al-Nahdī's report "a flock many in rasal, little in risl," i.e. many in number but little in milk. From this, arsala al-qawm means "they came to have milk."
4. rasīl — a man's partner in a shooting-match, so called because he releases (irsāl) his arrow together with the other's release.
5. arsālan — "in successive groups," of people coming one after another (singular rasal).
6. al-rasūl — the messenger; noted as well known, needing no gloss.
7. marāsīl — swift camels.
8. al-murāsil — a widow, because suitors send to / correspond with her (yurāsilūnahā).
9. ʿalā rislik — "take your ease / your time," because the action proceeds freely (mursal) without strain.
10. On the phrase "except one who gives in her hardship (najda) and her ease (risl)": najda = hardship (with a supporting verse by Ṭarafa), and risl = ease/prosperity; the sense is giving from one's wealth in both hard and easy times.
11. istarsaltu ilā (something) — one's soul springs forth toward it and grows at ease with it.
12. al-mursalāt — the winds.
13. al-rāsilān — a pair of veins (anatomical).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-s-s as a single root (aṣl wāḥid) whose meaning is firmness and fixity (thabāt), and places the following uses under it.

1. **Being fixed.** rassa al-shayʾ: the thing became firmly fixed. al-rasīs: what is firmly fixed.

2. **A camel getting up.** rasrasa al-baʿīr: said of a camel shifting its knee about on the ground as it tries to rise.

3. **Talk turned over inwardly.** yarussu al-ḥadītha fī nafsihi: someone turns the talk over within himself.

4. **The first of a report.** "I heard a rass of news" means its beginning. Ibn Fāris explains the word by the fact that this first part becomes fixed in the ears.

5. **Burial.** russa al-mayyit: the dead man was buried.

He says these make up the greater part of the root.

6. **Two valleys.** al-Rass and al-Rusays are well-known valleys. He cites Zuhayr for both, including the line "Effaced of it are al-Rass, then al-Rusays, then its ʿĀqil."

7. **Making peace, or making trouble.** It is said that al-rass is one of the words with two opposite meanings (aḍdād): reconciling people, and setting them against one another. Ibn Fāris holds that either way it means establishing something firmly, whether enmity or affection, so it follows the root's analogy.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: رَوَٰسِى 10x "firm mountains"; مُرْسَىٰ 3x "its appointed time"; أَرْسَىٰ 1x "he made them firm"
text:
al-Rāghib treats r-s-w as the idea of becoming firm and fixed (thabata), and reads its Qur'anic uses in that sense.

1. **Basic verb.** rasā, yarsū: a thing became firm, fixed in place. Form IV arsāhu: someone else made it firm.

2. **Firmly fixed things in the Qur'an.**
- "cauldrons rāsiyāt" (Q 34:13): cauldrons fixed in place.
- "lofty rawāsī" (Q 77:27): firmly fixed mountains.
- "and the mountains, He set them firm (arsāhā)" (Q 79:32). al-Rāghib links this to "and the mountains as pegs" (Q 78:7). A poet: "and there are no mountains when the pegs do not hold firm."

3. **A cloud.** "The cloud cast down its marāsī (anchors)", like "it cast down its tent-ropes".

4. **majrā and mursā.** "Embark in it; in the name of God is its majrā and its mursā" (Q 11:41). The words come from ajraytu (I made it run) and arsaytu (I made it fixed). The form mursā can serve as verbal noun, place, time, or the thing acted upon. A variant reading is mujrīhā wa-mursīhā.

5. **mursā of the Hour.** "They ask you about the Hour: when is its mursā?" (Q 7:187): the time when it becomes fixed.

6. **Making peace firm.** rasawtu bayna al-qawm: I made the settling of peace firm between the people.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) gives the root r-s-kh a single core meaning: firmness, being firmly fixed or established.

- رَسَخَ (rasakha) is glossed simply as ثَبَتَ (thabata) — "it was/became firm, fixed, established."
- Anything called رَاسِخ (rāsikh, "deeply-rooted, firmly fixed") is, by definition, ثَابِت (thābit) — "firm."

The entry is very short: it states the one-sense root meaning and gives the defining synonym pair (rasakha = thabata), without further branches, morphological notes, or citations.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-t-ʿ (رتع) as expressing a single unified idea: abundance or freedom in eating.

1. Core sense — rataʿa/yartaʿu (رَتَعَ يَرْتَعُ) means to eat as much as one wants, without restriction. Ibn Fāris notes this can only happen where there is abundance/fertility (khiṣb) — the free eating presupposes plenty.

2. Derived noun — al-marātiʿ (المراتع) are the places where this free eating happens — grazing-grounds/pastures, i.e. the location-noun from al-ratʿah ("free eating/pasturing").

3. He adds that this is a "station" (manzilah) — a place where a person settles and comes to rest, tying the word to a sense of ease and settledness alongside the abundance of food.

The entry is a short, single-sense root note typical of Maqāyīs al-Lugha's method (deriving one core meaning from the letters), with no shawāhid (Qur'anic or poetic citations) attached.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: رَتَّلْ 2x "and recite"; تَرْتِيل 2x "(with) measured rhythmic recitation"
text:
Root ر-ت-ل (r-t-l), as treated by al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī:

1. Base sense — الرَّتَل (ratal): a thing's being evenly ordered and regularly arranged in a straight line. His illustration is physical: رجل رَتَلُ الأسنان, "a man with evenly set teeth" — spaced regularly, not crowded or crooked.

2. Derived verbal noun — التَّرْتِيل (tartīl): applying that same evenness to speech, i.e. letting the word issue from the mouth easily and straightly (without hurry or distortion).

3. Qur'anic evidence he cites for sense 2: وَرَتِّلِ الْقُرْآنَ تَرْتِيلًا (73:4) and وَرَتَّلْنَاهُ تَرْتِيلًا (25:32) — the second applying the same verb to God's own sending down of the recitation.

The entry is brief: it gives no plural patterns, no poetic citations, and no further senses.
