dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root: r-t-q (ر ت ق) — al-Mufradat fi Gharib al-Qur'an, al-Raghib al-Isfahani (early 11th c. CE)

1. Core sense — al-ratq: to join, bind together, or fuse (al-damm wa-l-iltiham). Al-Raghib notes this joining can be natural, as in something created already fused, or man-made, as in something joined by craft/work.

2. Qur'anic citation (21:30): 'kanata ratqan fa-fataqnahuma' — 'the two of them were a ratq [joined mass], then We split them apart.' Al-Raghib glosses ratqan as mundammatayn, 'the two [heavens and earth] joined/fused together' — i.e. the verse describes an original fused state that was then separated (fataqna).

3. Al-ratqa': a term for a girl/young woman whose two labia are fused together — an anatomical description of a closed/unopened genital opening.

4. Idiom: 'so-and-so is ratiq and fatiq in such a matter' — meaning he both ties and unties it, binds and undoes it. Al-Raghib explains this as describing someone who has full command over a matter, capable of both joining it together and taking it apart.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ر و ض (r-w-ḍ), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris identifies two closely related but distinct senses under this root.

First sense — spaciousness:
1. istarāḍa al-makān — the place became spacious; illustrated with the idiom "do such-and-such as long as the breath remains unstrained" (i.e., ample, not constricted) and a line of poetry offering to compose in either of two poetic metres with equal ease.
2. From this same sense comes al-rawḍah, the meadow.
3. arāḍa al-wādī / istarāḍa — a valley (or basin) "arāḍa" when water pooled and collected in it; standing, spread-out water is itself called a rawḍah, illustrated with a line of poetry about watering a tired mount at such a pool.
4. atānā bi-ināʾin yurīdu kadhā — he brought us a vessel providing such-and-such abundantly; arāḍahum — he gave them plenty to drink.

Second sense — softening/training:
5. rudtu al-nāqata arūḍuhā riyāḍatan — I trained/broke in the she-camel — the origin of the common sense "to train, discipline."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ر و ع (r-w-ʿ), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: fright, or the seat/locus of fright.

1. al-rawʿ — fright; rawwaʿtu/ruʿtu fulānan — I frightened so-and-so.
2. al-arwaʿ, of men — one of imposing bodily stature and bearing, so named because he "strikes fright/awe" into onlookers; al-rawʿāʾ, of camels — a keen, alert-hearted she-camel, as though prone to startle; the same term is applied to women who similarly command awe.
3. A distinct sense, "the seat of fright": al-ruʿ — the mind/inner awareness. Ibn Fāris illustrates with the well-known hadith: "the Holy Spirit breathed into my inner mind (rūʿī): no soul will die until it has received its full provision — so fear God and be measured in your seeking."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: رِيح 29x "the wind"; رُوح 21x "our spirit"; رَّوْح 3x "(the) mercy of allah"; رَّيْحَان 2x "and bounty"; تُرِيحُ 1x "you bring them in"; رَوَاح 1x "and its afternoon course"
poets_named: al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam) ×3; ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (Umayyad); Abū Kabīr (pre-Islamic); ʿUbayd (undated); al-ʿAjjāj (Umayyad)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-w-ḥ as one large, regular root whose core sense is breadth, open space, and steady movement. He traces the whole family back to الرِّيح (al-rīḥ, "wind") — noting that the yāʾ of رِيح was originally a wāw, shifted by the preceding kasra.

Senses and usages he records:

1. الرُّوح (rūḥ) — the human spirit, which he explicitly derives from رِيح (wind); the entire root, he says, works this way.

2. الرَّوْح (rawḥ) — a gentle breath of wind. أَرَاحَ (arāḥa) = to breathe (attested in Imruʾ al-Qays). أَرْوَحَ الماءُ = water (etc.) whose smell has turned.

3. الرُّوح as Gabriel (Jibrīl) — cited from Qurʾān 26:193, {the trustworthy Spirit brought it down upon your heart}.

4. الرَّوَاح (rawāḥ) — late afternoon/evening, named from the wind (rawḥ) that usually rises after midday; رَاحُوا = they set out in that span (from the sun's decline to night). أَرَحْنَا إِبِلَنَا = we brought the camels back then. A line of al-Aʿshā using الرَّوَح of birds is read either as "scattered birds" or "birds returning to their nests."

5. المُرَاوَحَة — alternating between two tasks, doing each in turn.

6. الأَرْوَح — someone with splayed feet (fronts spread apart, heels close), a state called رَوَح (رَوِحَ يَرْوَحُ رَوْحًا); also قَصْعَة رَوْحَاء, a shallow bowl.

7. Idioms of ease and relief: يَرَاحُ لِلْمَعْرُوف = moved by cheerful eagerness (أَرْيَحِيَّة) to do good; of the dead, قَدْ أَرَاحَ = "he has found rest"; أَرَاحَ الرجلُ = his breath returned after exhaustion; أَرَحْتُ حَقَّهُ = I returned his due; في سَرَاحٍ ورَوَاحٍ = with ease.

8. Wind/scent uses: رِيحَ الغَدِيرُ = the pool was struck by wind; أَرَاحَ القَوْمُ = they went into the wind; أَرْوَحَ الصَّيْدُ = the game caught a human's scent; "no trace [scent] of blood on his face."

9. المَرَاح — the night shelter of livestock; الدُّهْن المُرَوَّح — perfumed oil.

10. تَرَوَّحَ الشَّجَرُ / رَاحَ يَرَاحُ — a tree bursting into leaf (with a supporting verse).

11. Abū Zayd's material: أَرْوَحَنِي الصَّيْدُ = the game caught my scent; أَرْوَحْتُ طِيبًا = I smelled something pleasant; camels رَاحَتْ (came home) and أَرَحْتُهَا (I brought them home), tied to Qurʾān 16:6 {when you bring them home}. Al-Kisāʾī derives «لَمْ يُرِحْ رَائِحَةَ الجَنَّةِ» ("did not smell Paradise's scent") from أَرَحْتُ, while «لَمْ يَرَحْ» comes from رَاحَ يَرَاحُ (to smell the wind).

12. رَاحَ الفَرَسُ = the horse grew strong/spirited. المَرْوَحَة — a wind-swept place (with a verse associated with ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb).

13. Weather adjectives: يَوْمٌ رَيِّحٌ = a pleasant day; يَوْمٌ رَاحٌ = a day of strong wind (formed like كَبْشٌ صَافٌ, "a woolly ram"). A verse of Abū Kabīr uses يَرَاحُ for feeling the cold breeze. The Ramadan تَرْوِيحَة is named from the congregation's resting (istirāḥa) after every four rakʿas.

14. الرَّاح — (a) the plural of رَاحَة, the palm of the hand (verse of ʿUbayd); (b) wine/khamr (verse of al-Aʿshā).

15. ارْتَاحَ of God — "a calamity struck a man, then God showed him mercy (irtāḥa) and saved him"; a verse of al-ʿAjjāj, glossed as "He looked upon me and had mercy."

16. الأَرْيَحِيّ — the openhanded, magnanimous man (verse of al-Aʿshā). Ibn Fāris cites al-Khalīl: anything spacious is أَرْيَح (e.g. a roomy camel-litter); the variant مَحْمِل أَرْوَح would instead be dispraise, since رَوَح (splaying) is a defect in a litter. Al-Khalīl derives al-aryaḥī from رَاحَ يَرَاحُ.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَرَادَ 139x "desires"; رَٰوَدُ 8x "we will try to get permission"; رُوَيْد 1x "little"
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) on the root ر و د (r-w-d). He states that almost the whole family turns on one idea: a coming and going — setting out in a single direction, moving back and forth.

Senses and derivatives he records:

1. رَاوَدْتُهُ (rāwadtuhu) — to press or coax someone toward doing something; to urge him to it.

2. الرَّوْد / الرَّائِد (al-rawd / al-rāʾid) — the act, and agent, of scouting. "We sent a rāʾid to scout the pasture" = to look out and seek it.

3. الرِّيَاد (al-riyād) — camels' to-and-fro in a grazing-ground, advancing and retreating (verb رَادَ يَرُودُ).

4. الْمَرَاد (al-marād) — the place where grazing animals roam.

5. Of a woman, رَادَتْ تَرُودُ — she goes back and forth visiting her neighbors' houses.

6. الرَّادَة (al-rādah) — a gentle wind, so named because it "roams" rather than blowing hard.

7. رَائِدُ الْعَيْنِ (rāʾidu l-ʿayn) — the eye's watering/discharge that moves about within it.

8. Etymological note: some hold that إِرَادَة (irādah, "wanting/will") derives from the wāw of this root, the evidence being the form رَاوَدْتُهُ.

9. الرَّائِد (al-rāʾid) — also the wooden bar used to turn a millstone.

10. From أَرْوَدَ / إِرْوَاد (arwada / irwād) — to go gently and unhurriedly in travel; hence a horse called "swift both when urged and when at an easy gait" (جَوَادَ الْمَحَثَّةِ وَالْمُرْوَدِ), with variants murwad/marwad. The sense is gentleness (rifq) in movement.

11. رَادَ وِسَادُهُ (rāda wisāduh) — his cushion will not stay put, as if it "comes and goes."

12. الْإِرْوَاد / رُوَيْدًا (irwād / ruwaydan) — doing an action gently, slowly. Ibn Fāris notes رُود (rūd) as the non-diminutive base of the diminutive رُوَيْد.

13. جَارِيَةٌ رُودٌ (jāriyatun rūd) — a young woman; illustrated by a verse comparing her to "one who walks at an easy pace."

14. الْمِرْوَد (al-mirwad) — a probe or kohl-stick (a mīl).

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
poets_named: Khālid ibn Jaʿfar ibn Kilāb (pre-Islamic); ʿAdī ibn Zayd al-ʿIbādī (pre-Islamic); Ṭarafah ibn al-ʿAbd (pre-Islamic)
text:
Root: r-w-gh (روغ) — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī

Core sense: "he inclined and turned away from something" (māla wa-ḥāda ʿan al-shay'). A man or a fox rāgha, yarūghu — noun-forms rawgh and rawaghān.

1. To turn aside secretly / swerve in concealment. "Rāgha fulānun ilā fulānin" = he inclined toward someone covertly. The entry cites two Qur'anic instances of this verb: "fa-rāgha ilā ahlihi fa-jā'a bi-ʿijlin samīn" (Q51:26, "he turned secretly to his household and brought a fat calf") and "fa-rāgha ʿalayhim ḍarban bil-yamīn" (Q37:93, "he turned upon them, striking with the right hand"). Both are glossed as "a swerving in concealment," though a variant reading takes it simply as "he came forward." Al-Farrā' adds nuance: "rāgha ilā ahlihi" specifically means returning while hiding that one is returning — you would not call an ordinary return "rāgha" unless it is done furtively; and "rāgha ʿalayhim" means he turned/inclined against them, as if manufacturing a pretext before acting. Al-Rāghib gives the underlying image: leaning to one side in order to deceive someone positioned behind you.

2. As a noun: al-rawāgh (pattern of saḥāb). Al-rawwāgh (intensive pattern) = "the fox," from its proverbial dodging — illustrated by Muʿāwiya calling ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr "a dodging fox, every time you leave one den you burrow into another." [A cluster of men nicknamed al-Rawwāgh, and their genealogies/transmission chains, are listed as attestations of the name; the author notes he had already given this same passage under a different root (r-w-ʿ) and repeated it here without flagging the duplication.]

3. Riwāghatuhum / riyāghatuhum (kasra forms): their wrestling-ground — the place where people wrestle (with a wāw→yā' shift noted as irregular, not a fixed rule).

4. Al-riyāgh: fertility, abundance. Al-ruwayghah (diminutive): trickery, stratagem — "akhadhtanī bil-ruwayghah," "you got me by a ruse."

5. Arāgha / irtāgha: to want and to seek (arāda, ṭalaba) — "arightu al-ṣayd," I sought the game; "mādhā turīgh?", what are you after? Illustrated with a verse by Khālid ibn Jaʿfar ibn Kilāb about his horse Ḥadhfah ("seek me as you'd seek your due — Ḥadhfah and I are like a lump stuck beneath the throat") and a line cited by al-Layth. "Yurīghunī ʿalā/ʿan amrin" = he tries to draw me into/out of a matter (yurāwidunī). A ḥadīth of Qays uses it for tracking down a strayed camel "by every means." The fox's characteristic dodging (rawaghān al-thaʿlab) is linked to this same sense of restless seeking/evading.

6. Rawwagha (Ibn al-Aʿrābī): to grease and soak food (e.g., a bread-and-broth dish) with fat — a figurative extension; used in a ḥadīth about soaking a morsel in fat for someone.

7. Al-murāwaghah: (a) wrestling/grappling — "yurāwighu fulānan," to dodge and elude an opponent's moves, illustrated by a verse of ʿAdī ibn Zayd al-ʿIbādī ("a day when dodging avails nothing except the resolute, discerning man"); the reciprocal is al-tarāwugh, "they dodged each other." (b) Separately, al-murāwaghah = al-murāwadah, enticement/persuasion — trying to talk someone into or out of something, "he would not incline to it" (mā rāgha ilayhi). Ibn Durayd corrects a copying error: the verb for an animal rolling about is tarawwaghat, not tarawwagha.

8. Supplementary notes (mustadrakāt): arāgha/rāwagha = to deceive. "Rāgha al-ṣaydu" (figurative) = the game ran here and there. Proverb "arwaghu min thaʿlab," "more evasive than a fox" — quoted from Ṭarafah ibn al-ʿAbd's complaint about disloyal friends ("all of them more evasive than a fox — how alike tonight and last night"). Another proverb addresses the hyena by her name Jaʿārī: "dodge, and watch for your escape route" (the feminine imperative rūghī is used only for females). "Rāgha ḥājatan ilā fulānin" = he sought a favor from someone promptly. "Khayrun ruwāghā'" = abundant good. Figuratively, "yarūghu ʿan al-ḥaqq" = he swerves from the truth, and a byway/side-path is called rā'igh/zā'igh — illustrated by a ḥadīth of al-Aḥnaf turning down a Medina side-lane that veers off the main road.

9. Place-names: Rā'ighah — a pilgrim way-station for Basra's Ḥajj caravan (also said to be a water source of Banū al-Ḥulayf, and a mountain belonging to the Ghanī tribe).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ر خ و (r-kh-w), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: softness/looseness, and feebleness of mind.

1. shayʾ rikhw/rakhw — something soft, slack, loose (two attested dialectal vocalizations, per al-Khalīl); rakhiya/rakhuwa — to become slack. arkhat al-nāqah — a she-camel's hip-joint grew slack. faras rikhw — an easy-gaited, free-flowing horse, illustrated with a line of poetry by Abū Dhuʾayb.
2. "istarkhā bihi al-amr" / "istarkhat bihi ḥāluhu" — an idiom for falling into a good, untroubled state; tarākhā ʿani al-amr — to hold back from and delay a matter.
3. al-rukhāʾ — a gentle wind. The entry's central Qur'anic citation is Sad 38:36: "fa-sakhkharnā lahu al-rīḥa tajrī bi-amrihi rukhāʾan ḥaythu aṣāb" — "so We subjected the wind to him, blowing gently by his command wherever he directed" (of Solomon).
4. al-irkhāʾ, of a horse's running — not the intense, blazing gallop, but a pace beyond a moderate trot (taqrīb); faras mirkhāʾ — such a horse. Abū ʿUbayd glosses al-irkhāʾ as letting a horse run at its own pace without exhausting it. Closing: urkhiyyah — a name for anything one has "let loose" (arkhā).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ر ي ش (r-y-sh), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: good fortune/condition, and what a person acquires of good.

1. al-rīsh — good; al-riyāsh — wealth; rishtu fulānan — I saw to the good management of so-and-so's affairs, illustrated with a line of poetry contrasting a patron who "rishes" (builds up) a client with one who wears him down (barā).
2. Ibn Fāris discusses the hadith term al-rāʾish ("the intermediary," in "the bribe-giver, bribe-taker, and intermediary"): some held it names the go-between for the same reason as the general sense of "managing another's affairs," but Ibn Fāris prefers a second reading — rishtu fulānan meaning "I granted him good" — as the sounder view, supported by the same line of poetry, plus two further citations about riyāsh (favor/attachment) and being restored to one's rish (standing/wing-feathers, figuratively one's fortune).
3. From the same root: rīsh al-ṭāʾir — a bird's feathers; rishtu al-sahma — I fletched/feathered an arrow. irtāsha fulānun — so-and-so's condition improved. al-aryash — one especially abundant in ear-hair (a further, more literal derivative).
4. Closing figurative extension: a weak, flimsy spear is called rāsh, likened in its weakness to feathers (rīsh); from this, a she-camel described as "rāshshatu al-ẓahr" means a weak one.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ر ي ع (r-y-ʿ) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris treats this root as covering two distinct underlying senses: (1) elevation/height, and (2) return.

**Sense 1: Elevation, height, and growth**

- **al-rīʿ** — a rise or elevated part of the land. (Some say the word is itself a plural, with singular *rīʿah* and plural *riyāʿ*.) Cited in a line of poetry by Dhū al-Rummah describing feathers rising above a *rīʿah* (a hillock).
- From the same sense, **al-rīʿ** also means "road/path." Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 26:128, "Do you build on every *rīʿ* a landmark, amusing yourselves?" — noting that commentators took *rīʿ* here either as "road" or as "elevated ground."
- **al-rayʿ** — growth and increase. Examples given:
  - *rayʿ al-durūʿ* — the surplus/excess length of a coat of mail's sleeves.
  - *arāʿati al-ibil* — the camels multiplied and their young increased.
  - *rāʿati al-ḥinṭah* — the wheat throve/increased in yield.
  - *rayʿ al-bi'r* — the mound of earth raised up around a well.
  - *rayʿān* of anything — its best and earliest part.

**Sense 2: Return**

- **al-rayʿ** here means returning to something. Ibn Fāris cites a ḥadīth in which al-Ḥasan is asked about a fasting person who vomits, and answers "hal rāʿa minhu shay'?" ("did any of it come back?"), glossed as meaning "return."
- He also cites a line of poetry: "You hoped Laylā would return [to you] — but it is [only] cravings/greed that sever men's necks," using *tarīʿa* ("[she] returns") from this same sense.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: رَيْب 18x "doubt"; ٱرْتَابَ 9x "you doubt"; مُرِيب 7x "disquieting"; رِيبَة 1x "a (cause of) doubt"; مُّرْتَاب 1x "a doubter"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-y-b as a single small root pointing to doubt, or to doubt mixed with fear.

1. Doubt (al-shakk). This is the core sense. He cites Q 2:1–2, "that is the Book, in which there is no rayb," glossing rayb as "no doubt," and a line of verse in which "there is no rayb that there was slaughter there" carries the same meaning of certainty-through-negated-doubt.

2. That which disquiets or unsettles you. Al-rayb is also whatever troubles you about a matter. One says rābanī hādhā al-amr — "this affair disquieted me" — when it puts doubt and fear into you. The form-IV verb arāba means to become a person of suspicion/disquiet (dhū rībah), and one says "his affair disquieted me."

3. Rayb al-dahr — the turns and blows of fate/time. Ibn Fāris notes this still reduces to the one base sense (qiyās wāḥid), and quotes the line, "Is it over death and its vicissitude (rayb) that you grieve? — time gives no solace to the anxious."

4. A reported sense: need/want (al-ḥāja). In the verse "We settled from Tihāma every rayb, and Mecca," some take rayb to mean "need." Ibn Fāris finds this plausible, reasoning that one seeking a need is in doubt because of his fear of missing it — so even this ties back to the root idea of doubt.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ر ي ن (r-y-n), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: a covering and a concealment.

1. al-rayn — a covering over something; "qad rīna ʿalayhi" — it has been covered/he has been overwhelmed by it. Ibn Fāris illustrates with a hadith of ʿUmar about a man of Juhaynah who ran recklessly into debt and "was rīna bihi" by morning — glossed as: he died.
2. rāna al-nuʿāsu — drowsiness overcame [him]; rānat al-khamru ʿalā qalbihi — wine overpowered his heart/mind.
3. From the same chapter: "rānat nafsī tarīn" — my soul grew nauseated. "arāna al-qawm, fa-hum murīnūn" — a people whose livestock have perished, this too following the same underlying image, since being overtaken by such loss is itself a kind of being "covered over" (rīna) by calamity.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: رَزَقَ 61x "we have provided them"; رِزْق 55x "the provision"; رَّٰزِقِين 6x "(of) the providers"; رَّزَّاق 1x "(is) the all-provider"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats r-z-q (رزق) as a single small root whose core idea is a giving at an appointed time (عطاء لوقت); from there the sense is extended to giving that is not time-bound.

1. Provision/gift: الرِّزْق (al-rizq) is God's gift. One says رَزَقَهُ اللَّهُ رِزْقًا ("God provided him a provision"), with al-rizq as the noun form.

2. A dialectal sense — thanks: In the speech of the tribe of Azd Shanūʾa, al-rizq means "thanks, gratitude" (al-shukr). Ibn Fāris supports this with Qurʾān 56:82, {وَتَجْعَلُونَ رِزْقَكُمْ} ("and you make your rizq…"), read as referring to gratitude, and with the phrase فَعَلْتُ ذَلِكَ لَمَّا رَزَقْتَنِي, glossed as "I did that because you thanked me."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سَأَلَ 106x "you ask them"; يَتَسَاءَلُ 9x "questioning one another"; سَائِل 7x "for those who ask"; مَسْـُول 5x "questioned"; سُؤْل 1x "your request"; سُؤَال 1x "by demanding"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats s-'-l as having a single core meaning.

1. Core sense: to ask, to question. The verb is سَأَلَ / يَسْأَلُ (sa'ala / yas'alu), with the verbal nouns سُؤَال (su'āl) and مَسْأَلَة (mas'ala).

2. Derived form: a man described as سُؤَلَة (su'ala) is one who asks a great deal — an inveterate questioner.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī gives two separate entries here, sawm (س و م) and sa'ama (س أ م).

**سوم — sawm**

1. Core sense: "going in search of something" — a compound notion combining *going* and *seeking*.
 - The "going" side shows in sāmat al-ibil, "the camels went out to graze," so a grazing camel is a sā'ima.
 - The "seeking" side shows in sumtu kadhā, "I sought/demanded such-and-such" — which is how al-Rāghib reads the Qur'anic yasūmūnakum sū'a l-'adhāb, "they inflict evil torment on you" (Ibrāhīm 14:6): they actively pursue you with torment.
2. From the "seeking/imposing" sense: sīma fulānun al-khasf, "so-and-so was made to suffer abasement" — he has abasement imposed/sought upon him.
3. From the same root: al-sawm as commercial bargaining/haggling over price — hence the saying "the owner of the goods has the better right to set the price."
4. Also from the "going out to graze" sense: sumtu / asamtu / sawwamtu al-ibil — all mean "I turned the camels out to pasture," as in the Qur'anic wa-minhu shajarun fīhi tusīmūn, "and of it are trees among which you graze [your cattle]" (al-Naḥl 16:10).
5. A related but distinct pair of words, al-sīmā' / al-sīmiyā', mean "mark, sign" — illustrated by a line of poetry ("he has a mark not hard on the eye to see") and by the Qur'anic sīmāhum fī wujūhihim, "their mark is on their faces" (al-Fatḥ 48:29).
6. From that: sawwamtuhu, "I marked/branded him." Applied to the Qur'anic word musawwimīn (of the angels), al-Rāghib gives two possible readings: (a) passive — "marked, bearing a sign"; (b) active — "marking themselves or their horses," or "sending [the horses] forth." He supports this with a hadith: "Mark yourselves, for the angels have marked themselves."

**سأم — sa'āma**

1. Al-sa'āma is weariness/tedium that comes from something continuing too long — whether that "something" is an action the person does or a state they undergo.
2. Qur'anic citations: wa-hum lā yas'amūn, "and they do not grow weary" (Fuṣṣilat 41:38); lā yas'amu l-insānu min du'ā'i l-khayr, "man does not grow weary of praying for good" (Fuṣṣilat 41:49).
3. Supporting verse of poetry: "I have grown weary of life's burdens; whoever lives eighty years grows weary" — illustrating that even the most patient person eventually tires.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root س ع د (s-ʿ-d), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: good and joy, the opposite of ill-omen (naḥs).

1. al-saʿd — good fortune in a matter.
2. al-saʿdān — a plant counted among the very best pasturage, source of the proverb "no pasture like al-saʿdān."
3. The ten "fortunate" lunar mansions/stars (suʿūd al-najm) — e.g. Saʿd Bulaʿ, Saʿd al-Dhābiḥ — named suʿūd for their auspicious character.
4. From this root's core sense, Ibn Fāris derives sāʿid, the forearm — named because a person draws strength from it; hence sāʿadahu ʿalā amrihi, "he aided him," pictured as joining one's forearm to another's.
5. A distinction some scholars draw: al-musāʿadah is aid in general, while al-isʿād is reserved specifically for joining someone in weeping.
6. al-saʿdānah — the camel's knee-pad, named for resembling how the saʿdān plant spreads over the ground; the same word, al-saʿdānah, is also used for the knot nearest the ground on a sandal-strap, and al-saʿdānāt for the knots on a scale's pan.
7. Saʿd — also a place-name, illustrated with a line of poetry by Jarīr addressing its ruins out of love for a woman named Fāṭimah.
8. A closing note: some say al-saʿdānah (the female dove) is likewise derived from al-saʿd.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سَعِير 16x "(of) the blaze"; سُعُر 2x "and madness"; سُعِّرَتْ 1x "is set ablaze"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats س-ع-ر (s-ʿ-r) as a single root meaning the blazing or kindling of a thing, its catching fire, and its rising up. He groups the derivatives around these ideas:

1. Fire and burning: السَّعِير (al-saʿīr) is the blaze of a fire; اسْتِعَار (istiʿār) is its flaring into flame. المِسْعَر (al-misʿar) is the stoking-stick used to stir a fire. السُّعَار (al-suʿār) is fire's heat. The verbs سَعَرَ / أَسْعَرَ mean "to kindle," yielding مُسْعَرَة / مَسْعُورَة for a kindled fire.

2. Extensions of "burning": سُعِرَ الرَّجُل is said of a man struck by the samūm, the scorching desert wind. السِّعْرَارَة is the fine dust-motes one sees shimmering in sunlight.

3. Figurative "flaring up/spreading": اسْتَعَرَ اللُّصُوص — thieves becoming rampant, "as though they caught fire"; اسْتَعَرَ الجَرَب — mange breaking out and spreading in a camel. The poet Al-Asʿar al-Juʿfī took his name from a verse boasting that he would "blaze" (asʿar) against his enemies. Ibn al-Sikkīt notes the idiom سَعَرَهُمْ شَرًّا ("he kindled evil against them"), while أَسْعَرَهُمْ is not used.

4. Madness/frenzy: السُّعْر is madness, so called because it "blazes up" within a person; a نَاقَة مَسْعُورَة is a frenzied she-camel, named for its fierce sharpness, as if maddened.

5. Price: سِعْر الطَّعَام, the price of food, belongs here too — because a price "rises and climbs."

6. مَسَاعِر البَعِير: the camel's tender spots (its "sensory points," mashāʿir) — its armpits, groin-folds, and tail-base where the fur is thin — so named because mange first breaks out and rages there.

7. A poetic crux: in a line by ʿUrwa b. al-Ward, "they flew off into the lands of al-yastaʿūr," some said he meant al-saʿīr (the blaze); others that al-yastaʿūr is a place-name, or a tree used as a toothstick.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats س-ح-ب (s-ḥ-b) as a single sound root meaning to drag and stretch out something that is spread flat.

1. Core sense: dragging/trailing. Example: "I dragged my hem along the ground" (saḥabtu dhaylī bi-l-arḍ).

2. Derived noun: saḥāb ("cloud") is named from this, pictured as dragging itself across the sky (yansaḥib).

3. Figurative use: tasaḥḥaba ʿalā fulān — to grow bold or presume against someone, imagined as stretching oneself out over him. Ibn Fāris regards this as the correct extension of the root.

4. A rejected sense: some report al-saḥb to mean eating greedily. Ibn Fāris judges this a scribal error (taṣḥīf), since it fits no analogy of the root; the intended word, he says, is al-saḥt (with tāʾ).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) derives three distinct core meanings for the root س-ح-ل (s-ḥ-l), plus one outlying usage and one plant name that he says fall outside all three.

1. Stripping / scraping away
- "The winds saḥala-ed the earth" = they stripped its top surface off.
- Ibn Durayd's etymology: sāḥil ("shore," literally an active-participle shape, "one that strips") actually means masḥūl, "a thing stripped" — because the water strips/scours it. So "shore" is passive in sense though active in form.
- Base usage: saḥaltu al-ḥadīdata, "I filed the iron" (with a rasp); the filings are al-suḥāla.
- Al-saḥl = white cloth, as if scraped clean of its dirt; plural al-suḥul. A verse is quoted describing white suḥul-cloths brightened by rain, illustrating this sense.

2. A sound
- Al-saḥīl / al-suḥāl = the braying of a donkey — hence the donkey is called misḥal.
- By extension, al-misḥal is also used for an eloquent orator's tongue, and for the orator himself.

3. Hastening / facilitating something
- Saḥalahu miʾatan = he paid him a hundred promptly, in ready cash.
- The same phrase is used metaphorically for striking someone: "he gave him a hundred [lashes/blows]" swiftly.
- Also from this sense: al-saḥīl is cord twisted loosely (opposite: mubram/barīm, tightly twisted) — cited from a line of Zuhayr's poetry, "of loosely-twisted and tightly-twisted [strands]."

Outside the three roots:
- Al-misḥalān = the two rings at either end of a bridle's bit-shackle.
- Al-isḥil = a type of tree.

Ibn Fāris presents this purely as classical Arabic lexical usage (filing metal, a donkey's bray, prompt cash payment, cord-twisting, shore erosion) — no Qur'anic or doctrinal sense is attached to the root in this entry.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root س ح ق (s-ḥ-q), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Two distinct senses under this root:

First — distance:
1. al-suḥq — distance/remoteness. Qur'anic citation, al-Mulk 67:11: "fa-suḥqan li-aṣḥābi al-saʿīr" — [far] removal for the companions of the Blaze.
2. al-saḥūq — the tall palm tree, named for how far its crown stands from the ground.

Second — wearing down to decay:
3. saḥaqtu al-shayʾ — I ground/pulverized something; al-saḥq — a worn-out garment; saḥaqahu al-bilā fa-nsaḥaqa — wear-and-tear ground it down until it decayed.
4. Metaphorical extension: the eye is said to "grind out" (tasḥaqu) tears.
5. usḥiqa al-shayʾ — something shrank and contracted; asḥaqa al-ḍarʿ — an udder's milk dried up and it wasted away.

dictionary: Ṣiḥāḥ — al-Ṣiḥāḥ, al-Jawharī (d. 1003)
quran_words: سِحْر 28x "magic"; سَٰحِر 22x "the magicians"; مَّسْحُور 4x "bewitched"; سَحَر 3x "and in the hours before dawn"; سَحَرُ 3x "are you deluded"; مُسَحَّرِين 2x "those bewitched"; سَحَّار 1x "magician"
text:
al-Jawharī's al-Ṣiḥāḥ entry for the root س-ح-ر records several connected senses:

1. suḥr / saḥr / saḥar (السُحْر) = the lung. Plurals: asḥār and suḥūr. The vowel on the middle letter can shift (saḥar) because of the guttural ḥ. Of a coward one says "his lung has swelled up." The hare is nicknamed "she whose lungs (or heart-strings, niyāṭ) are cut up" — as a good-omen expression; later scholars also read it as an active participle ("the cutter-up"), i.e. she runs so hard she seems to tear her own lungs and heart-strings.

2. saḥar (السَحَر) = the period just before dawn. Grammatical notes: when it means one specific night's pre-dawn ("this saḥar of ours"), it is a diptote — it does not take full declension, because it is a "diverted" (maʿdūl) form and is treated as definite without either annexation or the article (compared to how "Ibn al-Zubayr" became a fixed name). As an adverb ("ride at saḥar") it stays in the accusative, since it is a non-fixed time-adverb. But when saḥar is meant indefinitely it declines fully — as in Q 54:34, "We saved them bi-saḥarin (at dawn)." It also declines if used as a man's name or in the diminutive (suḥayr), though the diminutive still functions adverbially, not in the nominative.

3. suḥra (السُحْرة) = the last/uppermost part of that pre-dawn time. One can say "I came to him at saḥar" or "at suḥra."

4. Derived verbs of time: asḥarnā = we travelled at the saḥar hour, or came to be in the saḥar; istaḥara al-dīk = the cock crowed at that hour.

5. saḥūr (السَحور) = the food with which the pre-dawn meal is taken.

6. siḥr (السِحْر) = a spell/enchantment (ukhdha). Al-Jawharī's defining principle: anything whose way of taking hold is subtle and fine is called siḥr. Verb: saḥarahu (he bewitched him).

7. sāḥir (الساحر) = one who has knowledge ("the knowing one"). The verb saḥarahu can also mean he deceived him, or beguiled/diverted him (ʿallalahu); tasḥīr carries the same sense. Shāhid: Labīd's line calling mankind "sparrows of this musaḥḥar people."

8. On Q 26:153, "you are only one of the musaḥḥarīn": al-Jawharī gives two readings — (a) musaḥḥar = one created with a lung (siḥr), i.e. a mortal like others; (b) one of the "beguiled / sustained with food." He cites a line attributed to Imru' al-Qays where humans are "fed (nusḥar) with food and drink — sparrows, flies and worms," reinforcing the "sustained/beguiled" sense.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سُّحْت 3x "the forbidden"; يُسْحِتَ 1x "lest he will destroy you"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats s-ḥ-t as a single sound root with one consistent idea: uprooting, so that nothing is left.

1. Core sense — to uproot, extirpate. سُحِتَ الشَّيْءُ (suḥita al-shayʾ) = the thing was pulled up by the roots; the fourth-form passive أُسْحِتَ (usḥita) is used the same way. Example given: سَحَتَ اللَّهُ الْكَافِرَ بِعَذَابٍ — God wiped out the denier with a punishment, i.e. removed him root and branch.

2. Of wealth — مَسْحُوت / مُسْحَت (masḥūt / musḥat): property swept away or destroyed. Cited shāhid, al-Farazdaq: "the biting of a time, O son of Marwān, that left of wealth nothing but what was swept away (musḥat) or pared down (mujallaf)."

3. Extended to appetite — رَجُلٌ مَسْحُوتُ الْجَوْفِ, a man who is never full: as if whatever he swallows is uprooted out of his belly, so nothing stays there.

4. السُّحْت (al-suḥt) as a noun for property: Ibn Fāris defines it as anything forbidden that brings disgrace on the one who consumes it — and he derives the name directly from the root idea, saying it is called suḥt because it does not last.

5. Derived verb — أَسْحَتَ فِي تِجَارَتِهِ (asḥata fī tijāratihi): he earned suḥt in his trade. أَسْحَتَ مَالَهُ (asḥata mālahu): he ruined his property.

The method is visible throughout: each usage, including the moral one in sense 4, is explained back to the single physical image of being uprooted and leaving no remainder.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) derives the root s-ṭ-ḥ (سطح) from a single core idea: spreading and extending something flat.

1. al-saṭḥ (السَّطْح) — "roof/flat surface," the well-known sense. More generally, the saṭḥ of any object is its upper surface, the part that extends along with the whole thing.

2. insaṭaḥa (انسطح) — to stretch out flat on one's back, unmoving. From this, someone permanently lying flat on his back because of a chronic illness is called saṭīḥ ("one stretched flat").

3. Saṭīḥ (سطيح), the name of a particular soothsayer/diviner (kāhin) — Ibn Fāris explains the name by saying he was created without bones, so his body lay flat.

4. al-masṭaḥ (المَسْطَح), with fatḥa — the place where dates are laid out to spread and dry.

5. al-misṭaḥ (المِسْطَح), with kasra — a tent-cloth or canopy (plural: masāṭiḥ). Ibn Fāris cites an anonymous line of poetry mocking clumsy men of the tribe of Khuzāʿah who "turn over" (fumble with) a tent-cloth. He explains the name: the tent is stretched taut by means of it — the same "stretching" idea as the root.

6. al-saṭīḥa (السَّطِيحة) — a large leather water-skin, named because when it falls it flattens/spreads out on the ground.

7. al-suṭṭāḥ (السُّطَّاح) — a ground-creeping plant, named because it spreads out flat over the earth.

Every sense Ibn Fāris lists — roof, lying flat, the diviner's name, the date-drying yard, the tent-cloth, the water-skin, the creeping plant — is tied back to the one root meaning: something spread out and extended flat.

dictionary: Ṣiḥāḥ — al-Ṣiḥāḥ, al-Jawharī (d. 1003)
quran_words: أَسَٰطِير 9x "tales"; مَسْطُور 3x "written"; مُصَيْطِر 2x "the controllers"; مُّسْتَطَر 1x "(is) written down"; يَسْطُرُ 1x "they write"
text:
al-Jawharī's entry for the root س-ط-ر (s-ṭ-r):

1. السَّطْر (saṭr) — a row or line of things. Used concretely: "he built a row (course of a wall)," "he planted a row." The variant سَطَر (saṭar) is the same.

2. By extension, saṭr means a written line, and writing itself (khaṭṭ, kitāba); grammatically it is originally a verbal noun. A verse of Jarīr uses it of a line in a register/ديوان.

3. Plurals: the plural asṭār (like sabab → asbāb), attested in a verse of Ruʾba; and asṭār is itself further pluralized as asāṭīr. saṭr also pluralizes as asṭur and suṭūr (like aflus / fulūs).

4. الأَساطير (asāṭīr) — falsehoods, baseless tales. Singular usṭūra (with ḍamma) or isṭāra (with kasra).

5. Verb: سَطَرَ / يَسْطُرُ (saṭara/yasṭuru) — "he wrote"; the form istaṭara means the same.

6. المُسَيْطِر / المُصَيْطِر (musayṭir/muṣayṭir, spelled with sīn or ṣād) — one placed in authority over something to oversee it, tend its affairs, and record its work. al-Jawharī derives this from saṭr: because a record is "written down" (musaṭṭar), the one keeping it is a musaṭṭir / musayṭir. Hence "you have gained mastery over us," and the Qur'anic لَسْتَ عليهِم بمُسَيْطِرٍ ("you are not a controller over them").

7. سَطَرَهُ (saṭarahu) — a separate sense: "he floored him / threw him down" (ṣaraʿahu).

8. المِسْطار (misṭār, mīm with kasra) — a kind of drink/wine with a tart sourness; also spelled with ṣād (miṣṭār).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats s-ṭ-w as a root (aṣl) that indicates overpowering and rising above.

1. **Overpowering by force.** Saṭā ʿalayhi, yasṭū: he overpowered him with violent force.

2. **Of animals.** A faras sāṭin is a horse that overpowers the other horses. A stallion is said to yasṭū upon the female he covers. When a ewe's young has died in her belly, the shepherd is said to saṭā upon her: he goes at her and brings it out.

3. **Of water.** Saṭā al-māʾ: the water became abundant.

4. **Other explanations of sāṭī.** Some scholars of language say the sāṭī horse is one that raises its tail in the gallop. Al-Shaybānī says the sāṭī is a camel in rut that goes out from one herd to another, and a line of verse follows: "its head is like the sāṭī stallion-camel."

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: سَبْع 23x "seven"; سَبْعَة 4x "(they were) seven"; سَّبُع 1x "the wild animal"
text:
Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī derives this root from the number seven and traces its extensions.

1. Core sense — the number seven. He lists Qurʾānic examples: "seven heavens" (2:29), "seven mighty ones" i.e. the seven heavens (78:16), "seven ears of grain" (12:46), "seven nights" (69:7), "seven, and their eighth their dog" (18:22), "seventy cubits" (69:32), "seventy times" (9:80), and "seven of the mathānī" (15:87).

2. On "seven of the mathānī" (15:87). One view: it means Sūrat al-Fātiḥa, since it has seven verses. The "seven long sūras" (al-sabʿ al-ṭiwāl) run from al-Baqara to al-Aʿrāf. The Qurʾān's sūras are called al-mathānī ("the repeated") because the narratives are repeated within them.

3. Watering terms. The forms al-sabʿ, al-sabīʿ, and al-sibʿ relate to watering intervals (coming to water).

4. Week / circuit — al-usbūʿ, plural asābīʿ. Used for a round of seven: "I circumambulated the House one usbūʿ (round of seven)." Verb forms: sabaʿtu al-qawm ("I was the seventh of the group"); akhadhtu subʿa amwālihim ("I took a seventh of their wealth").

5. Beast of prey — al-sabuʿ. Said to be named for the completeness of its strength, seven being one of the "perfect numbers."

6. Poetic citation. A verse by a Hudhalī poet ("as though he were a slave of Abū Rabīʿa's family, musbiʿ") is read two ways: (a) musbiʿ = one whose flock a beast of prey has struck; (b) a flock left abandoned among the beasts. A variant vowelling musbaʿ is also figuratively used for the foundling/adopted claimant whose father is unknown.

7. Verb of slander — sabaʿa fulānun fulānan: he backbit someone and "ate his flesh" as the beasts of prey do.

8. Al-masbaʿ — the haunt/lair of the beast of prey.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سَبَّحَ 42x "and glorify"; سُبْحَٰن 41x "glory be to him"; تَسْبِيح 2x "their glorification"; يَسْبَحُ 2x "floating"; مُسَبِّحُون 2x "those who glorify"; سَبْح 2x "(is) occupation"; سَّٰبِحَٰت 1x "and those who glide"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives سبح (s-b-ḥ) from two distinct roots: one denoting a kind of worship, the other a kind of physical exertion or movement.

Sense 1 — worship / declaring God far removed:
- السُّبْحَة (al-subḥa): Ibn Fāris glosses this as prayer (ṣalāt), and specifies that it refers to voluntary (nafl) prayer, not the obligatory kind. He cites the jurists' usage: a traveler joins two prayers and does not "tusabbiḥ" between them — i.e. offers no voluntary prayer in between.
- التَّسْبِيح (al-tasbīḥ): declaring God to be far removed (tanzīh) from every evil. He defines tanzīh itself as "putting far away."
- Idiomatic usage: the Arabs say سُبْحَانَ مِنْ كَذَا, meaning "how far removed / how astonishing is such-and-such." Shāhid: a line of al-Aʿshā using subḥāna of the boaster ʿAlqama. Ibn Fāris notes an alternative reading of the idiom as "amazement at him," and treats it as close in sense, since amazement here amounts to distancing him from the boast.
- سُبُّوح (subbūḥ): a divine attribute, derived from the same idea — that God is held far above all that is unbefitting.
- السُّبُحَات (al-subuḥāt): from a ḥadīth, meaning God's majesty and greatness.

Sense 2 — swimming / swift movement:
- السَّبْح / السِّبَاحَة: swimming in water.
- السَّابِح (of a horse): one that extends its forelegs well when galloping. Shāhid: a verse describing a rider carried off by such a horse, where the base of the rider's neck had come level with the horse's ears — explained as the rider having turned back in fear of a spear-thrust.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
poets_named: unnamed verse ×4; Abū Ḥunduj (undated); Ḥassān (lived into Islam); al-Quṭāmī (Umayyad); Ibn Harma (Umayyad); Al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); al-Mutanakhkhil al-Hudhalī (pre-Islamic)
text:
ROOT س ب ط (s-b-ṭ) — as recorded by al-Zabīdī in Tāj al-ʿArūs (d. 1791 CE)

**1. Lank, straight hair (sabṭ / sabaṭ / sabiṭ).** The opposite of jaʿd ("curly"): hair that hangs down loose with no crimp. The Ḥijāzī form is sabiṭ. Al-Zabīdī records the report that the Prophet's hair was neither curly nor lank but midway between. Verbs: sabuṭa (of the man), sabiṭa (of his hair), with several verbal nouns (sabṭ / sabaṭ, subūṭ, subūṭa, sabāṭa) — al-Zabīdī notes the author lists verbs and verbal nouns in unmatched order. Plural of sabṭ (hair) is sibāṭ; Sībawayh notes this is the usual plural for adjectives of the pattern faʿl. Sibāṭ also means "people with lank hair." A line of verse is cited in which a woman rejects both "the curly-haired" and "the lank-haired."

**2. Lank hair as an ethnic byword.** Sabiṭ came to stand for the non-Arab as jaʿd stood for the Arab; a verse contrasts "two water-drawers, one lank-haired and one curly-haired."

**3. Long-limbed, well-proportioned build.** Sabiṭ (or sabṭ) of a man: long in the frame and evenly built. A verse glosses this as being exactly as God formed him, with no excess length. Sabiṭ al-jism: of good stature; plural of such men, sibāṭ. Cited: "She bore him long-boned, as though his turban among men were a banner" (Abū Ḥunduj). In the Prophet's physical description, sabiṭ al-qaṣab = his forearms and shins extended smoothly, without knots or protrusions. In the liʿān ḥadīth, a child born sabṭ is one with extended limbs, complete in form. Of a man with long fingers: sabṭ al-banān (figurative).

**4. Open-handedness (figurative).** Sabṭ / sabiṭ al-yadayn: generous, free-handed; the quality is subūṭa. Ḥassān's line: "Many a maternal uncle of mine — open-handed on the bitterly cold day." Likewise sabṭ bi-l-maʿrūf: easy and obliging in doing good. Related: sabaṭa ʿalayhi al-ʿaṭāʾ, "he made the giving continuous and copious"; some derive sabāṭa from this. Of a woman, sabṭat al-khalq means soft and supple of body (from al-Zamakhsharī).

**5. Steady, pouring rain.** Maṭar sabṭ / sabiṭ — rain falling in unbroken succession (Shamir); its sabāṭa is its abundance and breadth. A verse of al-Quṭāmī is cited for sabiṭ = wide, plentiful rain.

**6. Sabaṭ, a sand-plant.** Al-Layth: like couch-grass but taller, growing in sands; singular sabaṭa. Abū ʿUbayd: the fresh state of naṣiyy grass (when dry it is ḥaliyy); Ibn Sīda similarly. Abū Ḥanīfa, from a bedouin of ʿAnaza: it resembles large millet, with seed like flax-seed that must be pounded from its husks; people extract and eat it as bread or cooked; good pasture. A saying: "ṣilliyān is the camels' bread and sabaṭ their sweetmeat." Abū Ziyād: a bare, tall, thin-stemmed shrub of the sands, eaten by sheep and camels, cut and sold as fodder along the roads, with no blossom or thorn and thin leaves like young leek. Al-Ṣāghānī: it whitens when dry and resembles grey hair — hence Ibn Harma's line comparing greying hair to "year-old sabaṭ." Plural asbāṭ (Dhū al-Rumma). Arḍ masbaṭa: land abounding in it.

**7. Etymology of asbāṭ.** Al-Azharī: sabaṭ is a tree with many branches but one root, and from this the word asbāṭ is derived — the parent standing as the tree, the offspring as its branches.

**8. Sibṭ = grandchild / descendant-group.** Sibṭ: the child of one's child; in al-Muḥkam, the child of either son or daughter. The ḥadīth: "al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn are the two sibṭs of the Messenger of God." Ibn al-Aʿrābī, asked what sibṭ means in Arabic speech, answered: sibṭ, sibṭān and asbāṭ are the innermost of one's offspring, their choicest stock. Others said asbāṭ are children's children, or specifically daughters' children. Al-Zabīdī comments that this last is the popular view, used to distinguish asbāṭ from aḥfād, but that the leading lexicographers explicitly include both son's and daughter's child, as Ibn Sīda states.

**9. Sibṭ = a tribal division of the Israelites.** Those tracing to one father; called sibṭ, the entry says, to distinguish the offspring of Isḥāq from those of Ismāʿīl. Plural asbāṭ. Al-Azharī: the asbāṭ among Banū Isḥāq correspond to the qabāʾil among Banū Ismāʿīl. He adds the terminological point: qabīla means a group from one father and mother; qabīl (without the tāʾ) is any gathering from various fathers. Quṭrub: the singular of asbāṭ is sibṭ, used invariably for one, one female, and a plural group, and it means "group" (firqa). A ḥadīth transmitted from Yaʿlā b. Murra (via al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Māja, al-Baghawī) has "Ḥusayn is a sibṭ among the asbāṭ"; Abū Bakr glosses this as "a community among communities in good," the word applying to the community and the community to him. Also cited: "God was angry with a sibṭ of the Children of Israel and transformed them into beasts."

**10. The grammar of Q 7:160.** On "wa-qaṭṭaʿnāhum ithnatay ʿashrata asbāṭan umaman": asbāṭan is a substitute (badal) for "twelve," not a specifier (tamyīz), since a specifier must be singular. Al-Zajjāj: the sense is "we divided them into twelve groups (firqa), asbāṭ," making asbāṭan an attribute of firqa — as though "we made them asbāṭ"; he calls this the sound analysis. Al-Ṣiḥāḥ (reporting, al-Zabīdī notes, al-Akhfash): the feminine "ithnatay" is because "twelve firqa" was intended, then the groups were described as asbāṭ; asbāṭ is a substitute, not a specifier, because a specifier must be singular and indefinite (one says "twelve dirhaman," not "darāhima"). Al-Akhfash added that the number does not fall on asbāṭ; Abū al-ʿAbbās calls that an error, holding rather that firaq is understood before "twelve," which is why the number is feminine.

**11. Sabbaṭat — to miscarry.** Of a she-camel or ewe: to cast her young before term (she is musabbiṭ). Al-Ṣiḥāḥ likens it to rijāʿ; Abū Zayd's Nawādir: of a camel that casts her young before its form is distinct one says sabbaṭat, ajhaḍat, rajaʿat rijāʿan. Al-Aṣmaʿī's wording: sabbaṭat (or sabbaghat, with ghayn) when she casts it after its fur has grown, before term. Al-Zabīdī notes al-Ṣāghānī entered this as a supplement to al-Jawharī although al-Jawharī's phrase already pointed to it.

**12. Asbaṭa — to go slack, stretch out, fall silent.** To fall silent (out of fright); in al-ʿUbāb, to lower the gaze and go still. Asbaṭa bi-l-arḍ: to cling to the ground. Abū Zayd: to fall to the ground and lie stretched flat from a beating, from illness, or from drinking medicine. Hence "why do I see you musbiṭ?" — head hanging, body slack; and "I left the sick man musbiṭ" — motionless and speechless. In a ḥadīth of ʿĀʾisha she struck an orphan in her care "until he stretched out on the ground." The form isbaṭarra ("to stretch out") is said to derive from this. A verse describing a woman who "stretched out, and what a stretching" after intercourse is cited to show that the author's restriction of isbāṭ to "from a beating" is too narrow. Also: asbaṭa fī nawmihi, to shut the eyes in sleep; asbaṭa ʿan al-amr, to feign obliviousness of a matter.

**13. Sabaṭāna — blowpipe.** Al-Layth: a hollow reed bound with sinew used to shoot birds; or through which small darts are blown, scarcely missing. Also treated under z-b-ṭ.

**14. Sābāṭ — a covered passage.** A roofed way between two houses (al-Muḥkam) or two walls, with a through road beneath (al-Ṣiḥāḥ); plurals sawābīṭ, sābāṭāt. As a place-name: a town beyond the Oxus; and Sābāṭ at al-Madāʾin belonging to Kisrā Abarwīz, which al-Aṣmaʿī says is arabised from Persian Balās Ābād ("Balās" being a man's name). Al-Aʿshā's line on al-Nuʿmān b. al-Mundhir, whom Abarwīz imprisoned at Sābāṭ and then threw beneath the elephants, is quoted with textual variants. Hence the proverb "more idle than the cupper of Sābāṭ": either because he once cupped Kisrā on a journey and was made rich enough never to work again, or because he stationed himself at the Sābāṭ of al-Madāʾin cupping passing soldiers on credit for a single dāniq, and in the idle weeks would bring out his own mother and cup her so as not to look unemployed — until he drained her blood and she died. A verse on the proverb is cited.

**15. Sabāṭi — a name of fever.** Indeclinable, on the pattern of qaṭāmi; cited from al-Mutanakhkhil al-Hudhalī. Al-Sukkarī: so named because it makes the person it seizes stretch out and go limp — linking it to sense 12. Al-Ṣāghānī: also said to be a fever with shivering. Verb: subiṭa (passive), "he was fevered."

**16. Subāṭ — a month name.** "So-and-so was born in Subāṭ" (also with shīn) — described as figurative usage. Abū ʿUmar al-Zāhid: a Byzantine month-name, before Ādhār, between winter and spring, variously declined. Al-Azharī: a winter division, in which falls the completion of the day whose fractions accumulate over the years; when that day completes, the people of Syria call that year the leap year (ʿām al-kabīs), held auspicious for a child born or a traveller arriving in it.

**17. Subāṭa — sweepings / refuse heap.** The rubbish thrown out daily in the forecourts of houses; or the place where refuse and house-sweepings are dumped, as in the ḥadīth of al-Mughīra where the Prophet "came to a people's subāṭa and urinated standing." Al-Zabīdī notes: attributing it to "a people" specifies, not owns, since such ground was ownerless; and the standing posture is variously explained — no level place to squat, an ailment (one report: in the back of the knee), or a remedy for back pain as they used to treat it — and the report is taken to show that holding back urine is disliked. Subāṭa also: hair that falls when combed; and, in Egyptian usage, the date-cluster of a palm with its stalks and dates.

**18. Further senses and names.**
- Sibṭ: the generation following a generation (al-Zajjāj, from some).
- Al-sibṭ al-ribʿī: a palm ripening at the end of the hot season.
- Sabaṭa ʿalā dhālika al-amr yamīnan (also with mīm, samaṭa): he swore an oath on it.
- Naʿja masbūṭa: a ewe scalded and shorn.
- Sābūṭ: a sea creature (from al-Lisān).
- Ibn Durayd held that al-ʿAjjāj — or Ruʾba — erred in saying "as though he were a sibṭ among the asbāṭ," meaning a man; al-Ṣāghānī identifies the two poets' urjūzas and assigns the disputed half-line to al-ʿAjjāj's.
- Proper names: Sābiṭ b. Abī Ḥumayḍa al-Jumaḥī (a Companion) and his son ʿAbd al-Raḥmān; ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Sābiṭ al-Shāmī (a Successor); Sabṭa b. al-Mundhir al-Salīḥī; Suwaybiṭ b. Ḥarmala al-ʿAbdarī, a Badr veteran who emigrated to Abyssinia; al-Mundhir b. Sabīṭ; Jarād b. Sabīṭ b. Ṭāriq; and a group of ḥadīth-transmitters known as "al-Sibṭ."
- Sabsaṭiyya (also Sabaṭya): a town in the district of Nābulus in Palestine, containing the grave of Zakariyyā and Yaḥyā.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: unnamed verse ×4; al-Hudhalī (lived into Islam); Abū Duʾād (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Fāris reports and accepts a definition by a lexicographer he thinks is Ibn Durayd: the root meaning of s-b is cutting, and reviling was derived from it. He says most of the chapter rests on this. He then allows that "rope" may be an exception or a second root meaning length and extension.

**First root sense: cutting**

1. **Head-veil.** al-sibb is the woman's head-veil (khimār), so called because it is cut from the loom.

2. **Hamstringing.** The root sense proper is al-sabb, hamstringing: sababtu l-nāqa, "I hamstrung the she-camel". A verse plays on both senses: "What fault was it of Banū Mālik that a youth of theirs was reviled (subba), and so he hamstrung (sabba)?" Ibn Fāris says it refers to the hamstringing contest between Ghālib ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa and Suḥaym.

3. **Reviling.** al-sabb is reviling, which he explains as a cutting: "there is no severance more severing than reviling". A person's sibb is the one who exchanges insults with him, as in the verse "Do not revile me, for you are no match for me; my sibb among men is the noble one."
   - A saying forbids cursing camels, "for in them is what stanches blood". Calling camels musabbaba ("much-cursed") comes from the praise formula "God fight her, what a noble possession!", like "God fight him!" said in wonder at a person. Ibn Fāris notes that this is an imprecation not meant to take effect.
   - rajul subaba is a man who reviles people a great deal; rajul subba is one who is reviled a great deal. An usbūba is a matter people revile each other with.

4. **Portion of time.** sabba min al-dahr is a portion of time, as in the half-verse "your being recalled to me at times (sabbāt) is a wonder".

**Second possible root: length and extension**

5. **Rope.** al-sabab, the rope, is either an irregular departure from the first root or a separate root meaning length and extension. Under it he places al-sabab; al-sibb as head-veil (the same word listed above under cutting) and as turban; and al-sibb as rope, citing al-Hudhalī: "he let himself down to it between a rope (sibb) and a cord".

6. **Desert.** al-sabsab is the wide, waterless desert, cited from Abū Duʾād: "many a wide, empty wasteland (sabsab), over which its blowing dust runs".

**Of uncertain derivation**

7. **al-sabāsib** is a feast-day of theirs. Ibn Fāris says he does not know what it derives from, and cites: "they are greeted with sweet basil on the day of al-sabāsib".

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
quran_words: أَسْبَغَ 1x "and amply bestowed"; سَٰبِغَٰت 1x "full coats of mail"
poets_named: ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zubayr al-Asadī (Umayyad); unnamed verse ×3; ʿAmr ibn Maʿdī Karib (pre-Islamic); Abū Dhuʾayb al-Hudhalī (lived into Islam); Abū Wajza (disputed date); Muzarrid (lived into Islam); Ibn Aḥmar (lived into Islam)
text:
ROOT s-b-gh (سبغ) — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791 CE)

Core sense: something growing long enough to reach all the way down/around — used literally of a garment, hair, or a coat of mail that trails to the ground, and figuratively of anything "complete, ample, full."

1. Literal root sense: sabagha — a garment, head of hair, or coat of mail "grew long, reaching the ground" (al-Layth).

2. Figurative — of favor/blessing: "the niʿma became ample/extensive" (sabaghat), as in "praise be to God for the fullness of His favor."

3. Of a place: "he inclined toward, and reached, his town" (sabagha li-baladihi) — attested for Baghdad and Kūfa in Abū ʿAmr's Nawādir; glossed as both "inclined toward" and "arrived at."

4–5. Figurative uses of the adjective sābigh(a), "full/ample/complete": a she-camel full in the ribs; ample buttocks; a full fatty haunch; an ample favor (one variant reading has "a full turban" instead); a copious rain-shower; a complete coat of mail. Al-Zabīdī notes these five phrases map one-for-one onto the four glosses "complete, abundant, long, wide" (a distributive listing), and that all are figurative except the coat-of-mail sense, which is literal.

6. Qur'anic citation: "make coats of mail" (Q34:11, an ʿamal sābighāt). He defines dirʿ sābigha as a coat of mail long and wide enough to drag on the ground, or reaching to the ankles.

7–10. Four poetic citations illustrating sābigha as "a full/long coat of mail" and sawābigh as its plural: verses by ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zubayr al-Asadī (a mail-shirt covering the fingertips, likened to a pool of shallow water), an unnamed poet on sābigh rain, ʿAmr ibn Maʿdī Karib addressing his father's widow in a pre-Islamic Jāhiliyya poem (his "adornment" is his sword, hers is a sābigha), and Abū Dhuʾayb al-Hudhalī (armor made by Dāwūd or by the legendary king Tubbaʿ).

11. Figurative, negative sense: lithatun sābigha — "unsightly gums" (al-Layth).

12. Figurative, of a stallion: sābigh — "long [in the penis]"; opposite kamīsh, "short/compact."

13. Technical military sense (al-Aṣmaʿī): a helmet "with a sābigh" means it has a tasbigha — a mail flap/aventail attached to the helmet's rim that covers the neck, so that the helmet becomes "complete" (sābigh); without it there is a gap exposing the neck between helmet and coat of mail. Also called mighfar. The word tasbigha is derived from the same root, from sound "fullness/comprehensiveness."

14–15. Two further verses (Abū Wajza; Muzarrid) illustrating tasbigha as an aventail attributed to Dāwūd's craftsmanship, and one made of smooth Ḥimyarite mail that deflects stones.

16. Al-Zabīdī adds his own critical note: Abū ʿUbayda's Kitāb al-Dirʿ wa-l-Bayḍa distinguishes a helmet's rafraf (an encircling ring-guard reaching the eye-sockets) from its tasbigha, though elsewhere Abū ʿUbayda calls a ring-mail (not solid-plate) neck-guard both mighfar/ghifāra and tasbigha — al-Zabīdī flags the tension for the reader to weigh.

17. Noun sabgha — "ampleness, ease of living" (figurative): "they are in sabgha of life," i.e. living comfortably.

18. A philological dispute over the word for "a man wearing a sābigha coat of mail": Ibn al-Aʿrābī/al-Ṣāghānī give rajulun subugh; al-Zabīdī, checking Lisān al-ʿArab and al-Asās, finds musbigh instead, and concludes subugh is a copyist's error that the Qāmūs author repeated uncritically.

19. Figurative, of God and favor: asbagha Allāhu ʿalayhi al-niʿma — "God made the favor complete/full for him." Qur'anic citation: "and He has lavished upon you His favors, outward and inward" (Q31:20).

20. Figurative, ritual-washing sense: asbagha al-wuḍūʾ — "he performed the ablution thoroughly," reaching every required spot and giving each limb its due. Supported by a ḥadīth addressed to Anas: "Perfect your ablution and your life will be lengthened."

21. Of pregnant animals: sabbaghat — "she miscarried/cast her young before term" (also given as ajhaḍat in al-Tahdhīb); specifically, per al-Aṣmaʿī, said of a she-camel that loses a fetus after it has already grown hair. Abū ʿAmr and al-Layth extend this to pregnant females generally.

22. A closing miscellany of shorter attestations (marked "to be added" by the author): sābigh as simply "complete, full" (al-Jawharī); asbagha shaʿrahu, "let his hair grow long"; asbagha thawbahu, "made his garment ample"; a "full/deep bucket" (dalw sābigha, with an illustrative verse); a "full tail"; a man with "large buttocks" (sābigh al-alyatayn); a horse's rib described as sābigha, "filled out" (with Ibn Aḥmar's verse); Dhū al-Subūgh as the name of one of the Prophet's coats of mail; a prosodic term musabbagh for a poetic foot lengthened beyond the "complete" (sābigh) measure, illustrated from a verse and compared to the fāḍil/faḍḍāl analogy; misbāgh, "a she-camel that miscarries" (Ibn Durayd, who calls the word itself not well-attested); musabbagh (per Kurāʿ) for a fetus miscarried after ensoulment; the comparative asbagh, "more complete," used in a ḥadīth wishing a coat of mail had been more ample than it was; and asbagha lahu fī l-nafaqa, "he spent on him the full amount he needed."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root s-b-l (سبل) from a single core idea with two branches: (a) letting something down from a high place to a low one, and (b) something extending or stretching out.

1. Letting-down (branch a): from أَسْبَلْتُ السِّتْرَ (I let down the curtain) and أَسْبَلَتِ السَّحَابَةُ مَاءَهَا (the cloud let down its water). Hence السَّبَل (al-sabal) = abundant, generous rain. Related to this are: a man's سِبَال (sibāl, moustache / loosely hanging hair), because it hangs down; and أَسْبَال (asbāl), the upper edges of a bucket, likened to that hanging hair. He cites a verse of a water-drawer who filled the buckets "up to their asbāl (upper edges)."

2. Extending lengthwise (branch b): السَّبِيل (al-sabīl) = the road or way, so named because it stretches out. From the same idea, السَّابِلَة (al-sābila) = travelers going to and fro along the roads (subul). Likewise the ear of grain is called سُنْبُل (sunbul) for its extending; one says أَسْبَلَ الزَّرْعُ (the crop put forth its ears) when the ear appears. Ibn Fāris notes on the authority of Abū ʿUbayd that sabal and sunbul of a crop mean the same, and that both سَبَلَ (sabala) and أَسْبَلَ (asbala) are used.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: سَبَقَ 20x "(that) preceded"; سَابِق 7x "(are) foremost"; ٱسْتَبَقَ 5x "so race"; مَسْبُوقِين 2x "(are) outrun"; سَابِقُ 1x "race"; سَّٰبِقَٰت 1x "and those who race each other"; سَبْق 1x "(in) a race"
text:
Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's account of the root س ب ق (s-b-q):

1. Core sense — physical precedence. The base meaning of al-sabq is going ahead or taking the lead in movement or travel: "and those that outstrip, outstripping" [79:4]. The form al-istibāq means racing one another (al-tasābuq): "we went off racing" [12:17]; "and they raced to the door" [12:25].

2. Extended sense — precedence in general. The word is then used figuratively for other kinds of "coming before": "they did not precede us to it" [46:11]; and "[a word] has gone forth from your Lord" [20:129], i.e. it has already issued and run ahead.

3. Borrowed sense — excelling / winning merit. Al-sabq is also used for attaining distinction and pre-eminence. On this basis, "and the foremost, the foremost" [56:10] means those who press ahead toward God's reward and Garden through righteous deeds — comparable to "they hasten to good works" [3:114] — and likewise "and they are foremost to it" [23:61].

4. Related nuance — not being outstripped / not escaping. From the same root: "and We are not to be outstripped" [56:60], i.e. they cannot elude Us; "let not those who disbelieve suppose they have got ahead" [8:59]; and "they were not able to outstrip [Us]" [29:39] — signalling that they do not escape Him.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سَّبْت 6x "the sabbath"; سُبَات 2x "a rest"; يَسْبِتُ 1x "they had sabbath"
text:
Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha — root س ب ت (s-b-t)

Core claim: the three letters s-b-t form a single root whose idea is rest and stillness. Ibn Fāris then derives each attested use from that one idea.

1. Easy, gentle motion. A soft, unhurried gait is called سَبْت (sabt). His witness is a verse describing a lean-flanked she-camel: her daytime travel is sabt (an easy pace), her night travel dhamīl (an ambling trot).

2. Shaving the head — سَبْت (sabt). He presents this as "carried upon" sense 1, i.e. derived from it rather than separate. He cites a line — "he rises in the morning drunk and comes to evening sabtan" — as confirming the analogy: by day's end the man is torpid and barely moving. From the same idea, someone dazed or stupefied is called مَسْبُوت (masbūt).

3. The day after Friday — السَّبْت (al-sabt, with a on the s). Ibn Fāris reports this as something said (يُقَال), not as his own assertion: the name is explained by creation having been finished and completed on Friday, so that the following day was not one on which anything was created. He closes the point with "God knows best."

4. السِّبْت (al-sibt, with i on the s) — a different vowelling, a different meaning: hides tanned with qaraẓ (acacia tanning material). He links this to the root idea by saying such leather has had its treatment brought to completion — it has come to rest at its finished state. He supports this by a parallel usage: a date is called مُنْسَبِتَة (munsabita) when ripening has fully run through it.

Method note: the entry works throughout by qiyās — showing that each usage can be reduced to the single underlying notion of rest/stillness — and it marks the Saturday explanation as reported opinion rather than established fact.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats s-d-d as a single root meaning (aṣl wāḥid): by his account it denotes filling in a thing and making it fit close.

1. **Stopping up; a barrier.** sadadtu l-thulma, "I stopped up the breach". Every barrier between two things is called a sadd.

2. **Straightness and rightness (sadād).** al-sadīd is one who has sadād, straightness, "as though there were no breach in him". What is right is also sadād: qultu sadādan, "I said what was right". saddadahu llāh, "God set him aright". asadda l-rajul, "the man said what was right". istadda l-shayʾ, "the thing had sadād".

3. **sidād: a stopgap.** fīhi sidādun min ʿawaz, "in it is a stopgap against want", with i in sidād (the copy is damaged where it names the vowel). Likewise the sidād of a breach or of a frontier gap (thaghr), as in the verse: "They let me go to waste, and what a young man they wasted, for a day of dire trouble and for stopping a frontier gap."

4. **al-sudda: the yard; the door.** al-sudda is like the open yard around a house. It is also said to be the door, which Ibn Fāris explains as "because it is shut" (yusaddu). A poet: "You see the delegations standing at his sudda, thronging the door of a man who is visited, not one who goes visiting." A ḥadīth mentioning the destitute (al-ṣaʿālīk) speaks of "those with dishevelled heads, for whom the doors (al-sudad) are not opened".

5. **al-sudād: a disease of the nose.** A disease that takes hold in the nose and keeps out the air.

6. **al-sadd and al-sudd: locusts.** Locusts that fill the horizon.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats س-د-ر (s-d-r) as one root whose single idea is something akin to bewilderment and unsettled judgement.

1. **Bewilderment.** السَّادِر (al-sādir) is a person who is bewildered or at a loss.

2. **Dazzled sight.** سَدِرَ بَصَرُهُ (sadira baṣaruhu) is said of the eye when it becomes dazed or glazed over and cannot fix on anything.

3. **Heedlessness.** السَّادِر also denotes one who does not care what he does and takes nothing seriously. Ibn Fāris cites the pre-Islamic poet Ṭarafa: "heedless (sādiran), I reckoned my straying to be right guidance — then I stopped short, once disaster had already struck."

4. **Letting hang loose — by letter-substitution, not from this root's core sense.** سَدَرَتِ الْمَرْأَةُ شَعْرَهَا ("the woman let her hair down") he classes under ibdāl (substitution of one consonant for a near one): it stands for سَدَلَتْ (sadalat, "let hang down"), r replacing l.

5. Similarly the idiom "جَاءَ يَضْرِبُ أَسْدَرَيْهِ" ("he came striking his two sides") is a substituted form; the original has ṣād (أَصْدَرَيْهِ), and Ibn Fāris refers the reader to his entry on that root.

Method note: the entry works by positing one governing sense for the root, then setting aside as borrowed-by-substitution any usage that does not fit it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سُّدُس 3x "(is) the sixth"; سَادِس 2x "(the) sixth of them"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats s-d-s as a root whose single organising sense is the number six.

1. **A sixth part.** السُّدْس (al-suds) is one part out of six.

2. **Six-fold.** إِزَارٌ سَدِيسٌ (izār sadīs) — a waist-wrapper described as sadīs, meaning سُدَاسِيّ (sudāsī), "of six".

3. **The six-day watering interval.** In the vocabulary of camel drinking-intervals, السِّدْس is when camels are kept from water for five days and brought to water on the sixth.

4. **A camel's dental age.** أَسْدَسَ الْبَعِيرُ — said of a camel when it sheds the tooth that follows the rubāʿiyya (the four-year tooth); this happens in its eighth year.

5. **Etymology of "six".** Ibn Fāris derives سِتَّة (sitta, "six") from this same root, explaining the form as the result of assimilation: originally, as it were, سِدْسَة (sidsa).

6. **The outlier.** He marks السُّدُوس (al-sudūs), a ṭaylasān (an outer shawl/cloak), as departing from the numerical sense. He also notes the personal name سَدُوس, citing Ibn al-Kalbī: among Shaybān it is vocalised with fatḥa (Sadūs), among Ṭayyiʾ with ḍamma (Sudūs).

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
poets_named: ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿah (Umayyad) ×2; unnamed verse
text:
Root س د ي (s-d-y), al-Zamakhsharī, Asās al-Balāgha

Literal senses
1. jamal siddiyy / ibil sadā — a stray/untended camel or camels left to roam; qawm sadā — an unsupervised, aimless people; arḍ sadā — uncultivated land. "waqaʿa al-nadā wa-l-sadā" — dew fell, al-sadā being what falls at night (a distinct homonymous sense: night-dew).
2. "hādhā al-thawbu sadāhu ḥarīr" — this garment's warp is silk; asdaytuhu / asdā al-ḥāʾiku al-thawba — the weaver set the garment's warp — the root's core technical, weaving sense.

Figurative senses (majāz) — the entry's larger cluster, all built on the weaving image
3. "qad asdaytu fa-alḥim, wa asrajtu fa-aljim" — a proverb urging one to finish what's begun ("I've set the warp, now weave the weft; I've saddled, now bridle"). asdā ilayhi maʿrūfan — he extended a kindness to him; sadā manṭiqan ḥasanan — he wove/composed fine speech; "sadā ʿalayhi al-wushāh" — slanderers "wove" intrigue against him, illustrated with a line of poetry by ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿah about false tales stitched together against him.
4. "amrun mubram, musdan mulḥam" — a matter fully "warp-set and weft-woven," i.e. firmly settled, illustrated with a further citation. asdā bayna al-qawm — he made peace between people. "mā anta bi-laḥmatin wa lā sadāh" — "you are neither weft nor warp," an idiom for someone who neither helps nor harms.
5. "al-rīḥu tusdī al-maʿālima wa tunīruhā" — the wind "weaves" and illuminates a place's landmarks (i.e. traces/restores them, sweeping away obscuring sand), illustrated with a line of poetry by ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿah comparing wind-traced landmarks to lines of writing.
6. tasaddāhu — to mount/overcome and seize something from above, compared to how "the warp of night" (sadā al-layl, night's darkness) envelops — illustrated with a line of poetry about a man seized by the forelock while mounted, alluding to al-Ḥakam ibn Marwān being captured this way.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root س ف ع (s-f-ʿ), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Two distinct roots: (1) a color, and (2) taking hold of something with the hand.

**Root 1 — the color sufʿah (blackness/duskiness)**
1. al-sufʿah — blackness; the hearth-stones under a cooking-pot are called sufʿ for their dark color. "arā bihi sufʿatan min ghaḍab" — "I see a sufʿah of anger in him," i.e. his complexion darkens with rage. al-safʿāʾ — a wan, pale woman; every falcon is called asfaʿ. al-safʿāʾ — the rock-dove, its sufʿah being the dark patch on its neck below the head. al-sufʿah, in the traces of an abandoned dwelling — the ash-mark that differs in color from the surrounding ground. Al-Khalīl held that sufʿah, as a color, is specifically a blackness shot through with red.

**Root 2 — seizing/taking hold**
2. "safaʿtu al-farasa" — to take hold of a horse's forelock. The entry's central Qur'anic citation is al-ʿAlaq 96:15: "la-nasfaʿan bi-l-nāṣiyah" — "We will surely seize by the forelock," illustrated further with a line of poetry about bridling or seizing a colt.
3. safaʿa al-ṭāʾiru ḍarībatahu — a bird of prey struck its quarry. "safaʿtu raʾsa fulānin bi-l-ʿaṣā" — I struck so-and-so's head with a staff, which Ibn Fāris notes is understood by analogy to "taking hold with the hand." Closing anecdote: a judge of Basra was fond of the phrase "isfaʿ bi-yadihi fa-aqimahu" — "take hold of his hand and set him upright" — illustrating the same "seizing" sense in everyday judicial usage.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مُسَٰفِحِين 2x "(to be) lustful"; مُسَٰفِحَٰت 1x "those who commit immorality"; مَّسْفُوح 1x "poured forth"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats s-f-ḥ as one root whose single core idea is pouring something out or spilling it.

1. Core sense — to pour out, spill. سَفَحَ الدَّمَ (safaḥa al-dam) = he poured out / shed the blood.

2. السِّفَاح (al-sifāḥ) — on this author's account, the pouring out of the fluid with no marriage contract; he explains the word as an instance of the core sense, something poured out and thereby wasted.

3. السَّفَّاح (al-Saffāḥ) — a proper name: a chief among the Arabs who poured out water on a raid he led, and was named Saffāḥ from that act.

4. سَفْح الْجَبَل (safḥ al-jabal), the foot or lower slope of a mountain — Ibn Fāris does not derive this from the pouring sense. He classes it as letter-substitution (ibdāl), its original form being صَفْح (ṣafḥ, "side, flank"), treated under that entry.

5. السَّفِيح (al-safīḥ) — one of the three arrows that carry no shares. He marks this as anomalous (shādhdh), i.e. not reducible to the root-meaning he has stated.

Method note: the entry is built on Ibn Fāris's usual procedure — assert one core idea, derive the usages from it, and explicitly set aside as ibdāl or as shādhdh whatever will not reduce to it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سَفِيه 7x "the foolish"; سَفَاهَة 2x "foolishness"; سَفِهَ 1x "fooled"; سَفَه 1x "(in) foolishness"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root س-ف-ه (s-f-h) from a single core idea: lightness and flimsiness/thinness. He treats this as a regular, predictable pattern across the root's uses.

1. Safah = folly / light-mindedness, the opposite of ḥilm (forbearance and steadiness of mind).

2. Extended to physical flimsiness: a thawb safīh is a garment of poor, loose weave.

3. Of wind: tasaffahat al-rīḥ means the wind swayed or bent things — cited from Dhū al-Rumma ("as swaying winds bend their tops"). The same poet uses safīh of a camel's plaited nose-rope, describing its restless shaking.

4. Of deception: tasaffahtu fulānan ʿan mālihi = I cheated him out of his property — as if you tilted him away from it and made his judgment "light." A verse illustrates cheating a naive youth "like the swaying bough of the ban-tree."

5. A reported (less certain) sense: safah as drinking much water without being quenched. Ibn Fāris notes that if genuine, it still fits the core idea of lightness/insatiable thinness.

6. Related form from Abū Zayd: sāfahtu al-waṭb aw al-dann = I sat by a waterskin or wine-jar and sipped from it hour after hour — supported by a cited verse contrasting a spear with such a waterskin sipped through the late afternoon.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris states that the root s-f-k has a single core meaning.

1. Core sense: to make a liquid flow/pour out — the verb-noun pattern is safaka / yasfiku / safkan.
2. Primary usage: safaka damahu — "he shed/poured out his blood," i.e., caused it to flow.
3. Extension: the same verb is likewise applied to tears (al-dam'), i.e., "to shed tears," by the same core idea of a liquid being made to flow.

Ibn Fāris gives no further senses, morphological detail, or citations for this root beyond the above.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَسْفَل 6x "the lowest"; سَافِل 3x "its lowest"; سُّفْلَىٰ 1x "the lowest"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats س-ف-ل (s-f-l) as having one single root idea: whatever is the opposite of height or elevation (ʿuluww). Everything else in the entry is that one idea applied in different registers.

1. Physical lowness — al-sufl (the text carries the vowelling both sufl and sifl) is the lower part of a house, or of anything else; al-sufūl is simply the contrary of height.

2. Low social standing — al-safila is the base, lowly sort of people. Ibn Fāris adds a usage restriction: the word is said in the partitive construction, "he is of the safila of the people" (huwa min safilati l-nās), and is not used as a bare standing form (safila) on its own.

3. Low condition or fortune — al-safāl is the opposite of al-ʿalāʾ, "loftiness". His example sentence: "their affair is indeed in safāl" — that is, in a low or declining state.

4. A technical directional use, with wind — one says that a man "sat at the sufāla of the wind and at its ʿulāwa." Ibn Fāris glosses the pair: the ʿulāwa is the side the wind blows from (upwind), and the sufāla is the side opposite to it (downwind). Here the height/lowness contrast is transferred to windward versus leeward position.

The entry is brief and cites no poetry or scripture; the illustrative phrases are Ibn Fāris's own idiomatic examples.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats س-ف-ن (s-f-n) as one root with a single core idea: taking something off the surface of something else — scraping, peeling, planing away.

1. Core sense — scraping/peeling. The base noun is السَّفْن (safn), "peeling, scraping." Verb: سَفَنْتُ الْعُودَ ("I planed/scraped the piece of wood"). Shāhid, Imruʾ al-Qays: an animal comes stealthily "its belly scraping the ground," dust clinging to it yet not stuck fast.

2. Wind scouring a surface. سَفَنَتِ الرِّيحُ التُّرَابَ عَنْ وَجْهِ الْأَرْضِ — "the wind swept/scoured the dust off the face of the earth." The same removal-from-a-surface idea applied to wind.

3. The tool — السَّفَن (safan): the iron implement used for planing or scraping down. Shāhid, al-Aʿshā: a yearly raid that "chafes the hoof-heels as the safan chafes."

4. Derivation of "ship" — السَّفِينَة (safīna). Ibn Fāris cites Ibn Durayd: the word is of the pattern faʿīla but carries an active sense (fāʿila), because the ship "scrapes" the water, as though peeling it. So the ship is named as the thing doing the scraping, not the thing scraped.

5. Related agent noun — السَّفَّان (saffān): the ship's sailor or pilot.

Method note: the entry is built the way Ibn Fāris typically builds one — assert a single semantic origin, then show that the concrete tool, the verb, the wind usage and the derived noun "ship" all reduce to it, with a poetic citation anchoring the concrete uses.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
