quran_words: سَفَر 7x "a journey"; أَسْفَار 2x "our journeys"; أَسْفَرَ 1x "it brightens"; سَفَرَة 1x "(of) scribes"; مُّسْفِرَة 1x "(will be) bright"
poets_named: unnamed verse ×2; al-Namir b. Tawlab (lived into Islam); al-Akhṭal (Umayyad); Zuhayr (pre-Islamic); Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad); Labīd (lived into Islam)
text:
Root س ف ر (s-f-r), as recorded by Ibn Sīda in al-Muḥkam. The senses radiate from a core idea of sweeping/clearing away, which then yields "uncovering," "travel," and "making plain."

1. Sweeping and stripping. سَفَرَ البيتَ = "he swept the house." A broom is مِسْفَرَة, and the sweepings are سُفارَة. سَفَرَهُ also = "he peeled/stripped it off." Of wind: سَفَرَتِ الريحُ الغَيْمَ = "the wind scattered the clouds" (intransitive انْسَفَر, "they dispersed"); سَفَرَتِ الريحُ التُّرابَ والوَرَقَ = "the wind swept away the dust and leaves," or carried them off in all directions. السَّفير = the leaves the wind sweeps up.

2. Travel (السَّفَر), the opposite of staying home (الحَضَر). Ibn Sīda derives it from sense 1: travel involves going and coming, as the wind carries swept leaves away and back. Plural أسْفَار. A traveler is سافِر (called ذو سَفَر, "one having a journey"; Ibn Sīda notes there is no attested verb for the participle). Group terms: سافِرة, سَفْر, أسْفَار, سُفَّار; سَفْر can also be singular ("...for I am a traveler," poetic citation). مُسافِر = the same. مِسْفَر = one who travels much and endures it well (of a person). Of animals: بعير مِسْفَر / ناقة مِسْفَرة / مِسْفَار = a camel or she-camel strong for travel (citations from al-Namir b. Tawlab and al-Akhṭal). Zuhayr called a wild cow مُسافِرة, "roaming."

3. Related nouns. السُّفْرة = the traveler's provisions; the leather eating-mat (سُفْرة) is named after it. السِّفَار = an iron piece or rope on a camel's nose (al-Liḥyānī: like a bridle-bit); plurals أَسْفِرَة, سَفائر, سُفْر; the verb سَفَرَهُ به = "he fitted it on." انْسَفَرتِ الإبل = the camels dispersed.

4. Daylight and shining. السَّفَر = the whiteness of day (with a Dhū al-Rumma citation, where سَفَراً also means "morning" and, separately, "travelers"). سَفَرَ / أسْفَرَ الصُّبْح = "dawn grew light"; أسْفَرَ القومُ = "they reached morning"; أسْفَرَ القمرُ = "the moon shone before rising"; أسْفَرَ وجهُهُ = "his face beamed." لَقِيتُهُ سَفَراً / في سَفَرٍ = at the reddening of the sun toward sunset.

5. Uncovering. سَفَرتِ المرأةُ نِقَابَها (verbal noun سُفور), "the woman uncovered her veil"; she is then سافِر ("unveiled").

6. Mediating. السَّفير = one who reconciles disputing parties; plural سُفَراء; سَفَرَ بينهم = "he mediated among them" (verbal nouns سِفارة / سَفارة).

7. Writing (the Qur'anic cluster). السَّفْر = a book — said to be specifically a large book, or a portion of the Torah; plural أسْفَار. السَّفَرَة = scribes (singular سافِر; said to be Nabataean سافرا), and specifically the recording angels who tally deeds. al-Zajjāj ties this back to the root's core: a writer is سافِر and a book سِفْر because writing "makes a thing clear and plain" — like أسْفَرَ الصُّبْح ("dawn lit up"), like a woman uncovering her face, and like سَفَرْتُ بين القوم ("I laid bare what was in each heart to reconcile them"). Qur'anic citation: بأيدي سفرة كرام بررة, "by the hands of scribes, noble and pious" (ʿAbasa 15–16). Ibn Jinnī, on a Hudhalī verse where سَفْر means effaced traces, links it instead to "sweeping" — as if the writing had been swept off the parchment.

8. Proper names / miscellaneous. السافرة = a nation of the Romans (cited via a saying of Saʿīd b. al-Musayyab about hearing "the thud of the sun"). سَفَارِ = the name of a water source (feminine, indeclinable). سُفَيْرَة = a known hill (Labīd citation).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root s-gh-b (سغب) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: this root points to a single idea — hunger.

1. Al-masghabah (مَسْغَبَة) = famine, starvation.
2. Verb: سَغِبَ يَسْغَبُ سُغُوبًا — "to hunger / to be hungry." Adjectives: sāghib (سَاغِب) and saghbān (سَغْبَان), both meaning "hungry."
3. Ibn Fāris cites Ibn Duraid, who reports that some language authorities restricted as-saghab specifically to hunger accompanied by fatigue/exhaustion — not hunger alone.
4. Ibn Duraid adds that saghab has occasionally been used for thirst as well, but notes this is not the standard usage of the word.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root s-h-l (سهل) from a single core sense: softness or pliancy, the opposite of ruggedness.

1. **Sahl (سَهْل)** — level, soft ground; the opposite of ḥazn (حَزْن), rugged/rough terrain.
2. **Suhlī (سُهْلِيّ)** — the relational adjective ("nisbah") used for someone or something belonging to "the level land."
3. **Asḥala l-qawm (أَسْهَلَ القوم)** — said of a group when they went out onto, or traveled over, level/easy ground.
4. **Nahr sahil (نَهْرٌ سَهِلٌ)** — a river is called this when it contains sihlah (سِهْلَة), a coarse (not fine/powdery) sand.
5. **Suhayl (سُهَيْل)** — the proper name of a star (Canopus), given as a related derivative with no further explanation of the semantic link offered in this entry.

All senses trace back to the same core idea of smoothness, ease, and lack of roughness.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) derives the root س-ه-م (s-h-m) from two distinct origins.

**1. Share, portion, lot (the more developed sense)**
- Al-suhmah = "a portion/share" (naṣīb).
- To "asham" (asḥama) means to draw lots with someone, so each party wins whatever falls to him.
- Ibn Fāris cites Q37:141, on the prophet Jonah: fa-sāhama fa-kāna min al-mudḥaḍīn — "he cast lots (sāhama), and was among those who lost the draw (al-mudḥaḍīn)."
- From this, the single arrow (sahm, plural sihām — the lot-casting arrow) got its name: as if each arrow were one portion or share among several.
- The same root gives suhmah = "kinship" (qarābah), reasoned as a "share" in the bond of the womb, i.e. blood relation.
- It also explains burd musahham, a "striped" cloak, because each stripe in the cloth resembles an arrow (sahm).

**2. Change of color (heat-caused)**
- Sahuma wajh al-rajul = "the man's face changed [color]" — this verb comes from suhām, the effect of summer's heat/blaze on a person that alters his complexion.
- Sahama al-rajul = "the man was struck by suhām" (i.e., changed color from heat).
- Suhām is also the name of a wasting, thirst-like disease that afflicts camels.
- Sawāhim describes camels whose condition/color has been altered by travel.

Ibn Fāris closes with "wa-Llāhu aʿlam" ("and God knows best").

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: Umayyah ibn Abī al-Ṣalt (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse; al-Shammākh (lived into Islam)
text:
Root: س-ه-ر (s-h-r). Source: Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha.

Core sense: wakefulness — the loss/absence of sleep. Verb: sahara/yasharu/saharan, "he stayed awake."

1. Extended to "the earth" (al-sāhirah): the ground is called "the wakeful one" because its work of growing plants goes on continuously, day and night. Ibn Fāris quotes a saying praising a spring that "stays awake when you sleep, and is present when you're away" — i.e. it flows unceasingly.

2. Poetic citations: Umayyah ibn Abī al-Ṣalt uses sāhirah for open ground (paired with "sea"); another poet uses it for the open plain where wild donkeys roam at night. From this, sāhirah broadened into a general word for open, bare land.

3. Qur'anic citation: this general sense of sāhirah ("the [open] ground") is what Ibn Fāris cites for al-Nāziʿāt 79:13 — "It is but a single blast, and behold, they are upon al-sāhirah." He gives no gloss beyond "land" here; he does not attach an afterlife-specific technical meaning to the word itself, only notes it as an instance of the root's land-sense.

4. Al-asharān: a distinct anatomical term — the two veins inside the nose. Ibn Fāris notes they discharge fluid when a male donkey is in rut, cites al-Shammākh's line describing this, and reasons that the veins get this name because, like the wakeful spring and the wakeful earth, they "flow by night as they flow by day" — continuous action, tying back to the core sense.

5. suharah: an adjective for a person who sleeps little.

6. al-sāhūr: disputed term for either the moon's covering/halo or the moon itself. Ibn Fāris says either way it belongs to this root, since the moon travels its orbit continuously, night and day — again the root idea of unceasing, round-the-clock activity.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root س-ه-و (s-h-w) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris states that most uses of this root trace to two core ideas: heedlessness/inattention (ghaflah) and stillness (sukūn).

1. Heedlessness (سَهْو, sahw). The base verb sahawtu means "I was heedless/inattentive" — the example given is sahawtu fī l-ṣalāh, "I was inattentive during the ṣalāh [prayer-act]."

2. Overlooking others' faults (المُسَاهَاة, al-musāhāh). Also from this root: good-natured ease in dealing with people — described as being "inattentive to" (i.e. overlooking) a lapse when it was someone else's fault, not one's own.

3. Calm stillness. Sahw can also mean stillness/calm, as in the phrase jā'a sahwan rahwan, "he came calmly, unhurriedly."

4. An unrelated homograph: al-sahwah, a raised platform or portico standing in front of a house — Ibn Fāris flags this as not fitting the root's core pattern.

5. An even more remote usage: the expression "she conceived her child sahwan" — meaning conception occurred while menstruation was still ongoing. Ibn Fāris treats this as outside the root's normal derivational logic.

6. Possible link — al-suhā: the name of a very faint star (identified with Alcor, near the Great Bear). Ibn Fāris suggests it may belong to sense 1 after all, since its faintness means the eye "is inattentive to" it — one looks without noticing it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: Ḥumayd (lived into Islam); unnamed verse ×2; al-Aswad (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats س ج د (s-j-d) as a single, consistent root meaning to lower oneself down (taṭāmun) and to be brought low / humbled (dhull).

1. Core sense: سَجَدَ (sajada) is to lower or humble oneself. On his principle, anything that is brought low can be said to have "prostrated."

2. Bowing the head (physical stooping): On the authority of Abū ʿAmr, أَسْجَدَ (asjada) is said of a man who bows his head and stoops. He cites two poetic witnesses of animals lowering their heads: Ḥumayd's line comparing camels bowing under slack reins to "the prostration of the Christians to their lords," and an Asadī bedouin's line (via Abū ʿUbayda), "they said to it, 'Bow to Laylā,' and it bowed," said of a camel lowering its head.

3. Fixing / lowering the gaze: أَسْجَدَ إِسْجَادًا (asjada isjādan) is used for holding or prolonging the gaze, which Ibn Fāris accepts — but he insists the root's logic requires it to mean a downcast, languid gaze, not a wide fixed stare (shākhiṣ) or a sidelong glare (shazr). His witness is a love-verse describing "the isjād of your two hunting eyes."

4. "Isjād-dirhams" (دَرَاهِمُ الْإِسْجَادِ): coins stamped with images of kings — a Persian practice — before which people would prostrate; hence the name. He cites a line of al-Aswad mentioning wine bought "for the isjād-dirhams."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats s-j-l as a single root whose core idea is: something pours out after it has been filled.

1. **Sajl — the large bucket.** The concrete base sense. From it the verb: "I poured out the water and it poured forth" (sajaltu al-māʾ fa-nsajala). A full udder is likewise called sajl. Ibn Fāris also cites al-Khalīl's dictionary, where sajl is "the filling of the bucket."

2. **Musājala — vying, contesting.** Boasting against a rival. Ibn Fāris says the image comes from the buckets: two men "take turns drawing/pouring" against each other, each trying to outdo the other.

3. **Musjal — made freely available, unrestricted.** Something released to everyone, "as though it had been poured out." Two witnesses: Muḥammad b. ʿAlī, on "Is the recompense of good other than good?" (55:60), said the statement is musjala — applying without restriction to the dutiful and the wicked alike; and a poet's line, "my kindness to my people became musjal" (open to all).

4. **Sijill — a written record.** Ibn Fāris derives it from sajl and musājala on two grounds: it is a document that gathers other documents and meanings together (the "filling/pouring" image), and it also carries the contest sense, since it arises out of dispute and litigation.

5. **Al-ḥarb sijāl — "war goes by turns."** A contest that swings one way, then the other; the same bucket-by-turns image.

6. **Sijjīl.** Ibn Fāris derives it from sijill, while allowing it may instead come from some other part of the material above. He also reports the reported gloss: sijjīl means al-shadīd, "hard/severe."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سِّجْن 6x "the prison"; يُسْجَنَ 3x "he be imprisoned"; سِجِّين 2x "sijjin"; مَسْجُونِين 1x "those imprisoned"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats s–j–n (سجن) as a single root whose core meaning is confinement / imprisonment (al-ḥabs).

1. The verb: سَجَنْتُهُ سَجْنًا (sajantuhu sajnan) — "I imprisoned him," with the verbal noun sajn.

2. The noun السِّجْن (al-sijn) — the place in which a person is confined. He cites the story of Yūsuf, Q 12:33: "My Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they call me to." He notes a reading distinction: read with fatḥa (al-sajn) it is the verbal noun (the act of imprisoning); read with kasra (al-sijn) it denotes the place.

3. A related poetic usage: in a line by Ibn Muqbil, "a striking the champions enjoined on one another, sijjīnan," it is said the poet actually meant sijjīlan ("severe, hard"), substituting an n for the l. Ibn Fāris explains that the word still fits the root's core sense of confinement: a severe blow holds its victim fast, as though it had imprisoned him.

quran_words: يُسْجَرُ 1x "they will be burned"; مَسْجُور 1x "filled"; سُجِّرَتْ 1x "are made to overflow"
text:
Root س-ج-ر (s-j-r) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris identifies three distinct underlying senses for this root: filling, mixing/close association, and kindling.

1. **Filling.** al-baḥr al-masjūr — a "filled" sea. A place a flood passes over and fills is called sājir (illustrated with a line from al-Shammākh listing natural water-catchments). From the same idea: al-shaʿr al-munsajir — hair so abundant it hangs loose and flows down, "filling" out and trailing.

2. **Mixing/close association.** al-sajīr — an intimate companion, the opposite of al-shajīr (an outsider). From the same sense: ʿayn sajrāʾ — an eye whose white has redness mixed into it (a bloodshot or reddish-tinged eye).

3. **Kindling.** sajjartu al-tannūra — I kindled the oven; al-sajūr (also called al-sijār) is the fuel used to kindle it — illustrated with a verse about maidservants stoking an oven until it blazes.

Ibn Fāris then notes two usages close to this third sense: istajarati al-ibilu — camels pressing hard in swift travel, as though "ablaze" in their pace; and sajarati al-nāqatu — a she-camel moaning with intense yearning, as if that longing itself were a kind of kindled fire.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
**Root: س ج و (s-j-w)** — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: stillness combined with a sense of closing-over or covering.

1. **Of the night**: sajā al-layl — the night "sajā'd" when it grew intensely dark and settled into stillness.

2. **Poetic citation** (poet unnamed in the entry): "Oh how lovely the moonlit night, and the still night... and paths like the weavers' cloth" — the night is called sāj (still), and the paths are likened to smooth woven cloth.

3. **Of a glance/eye**: ṭarfun sājin — a still, steady glance, i.e. sākin (calm, unmoving).

All three uses trace back to the one core sense: a settling into quiet, unmoving stillness.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: s-k-b (سكب), from Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha.

Core sense: pouring something out. The paradigm example is سَكَبَ الْمَاءَ (sakaba al-mā'a) — "he poured the water."

Extended/figurative sense: a horse called سَكْب (sakb) means a swift, fleet-running horse. Ibn Fāris explains the image: the horse is said to "pour out" its running (يَسْكُبُ عَدْوَهُ سَكْبًا) — its gallop flows like poured water. He notes this is the same kind of figurative naming as calling a fast horse بَحْر (baḥr, "a sea"): both names liken the horse's speed to the abundant, flowing motion of water.

So the entry records one underlying idea — pouring/flowing — applied literally to liquids and figuratively to a horse's swift running.

dictionary: Miṣbāḥ — al-Miṣbāḥ al-Munīr, al-Fayyūmī (d. 1368)
quran_words: مِسْكِين 23x "and the needy"; سَكَنَ 15x "dwell"; مَسْكَن 12x "their dwellings"; سَكِينَة 6x "his tranquility"; أَسْكَن 5x "lodge them"; سَكَن 3x "(for) rest"; مَسْكَنَة 2x "and the misery"; سِكِّين 1x "a knife"; مَسْكُونَة 1x "inhabited"; سَاكِن 1x "stationary"
text:
Root س ك ن (s-k-n), as recorded by al-Fayyūmī.

1. سِكِّين (knife). Named from the root's sense of "stilling," because it stills the movement of a slaughtered animal. Its gender was disputed: Ibn al-Anbārī reported it as both masculine and feminine; al-Sijistānī said Abū Zayd al-Anṣārī, al-Aṣmaʿī and others held it masculine and rejected the feminine, which appears only in poetry (on the sense of شَفْرَة, "blade") — al-Farrāʾ cited a line with feminine agreement. Al-Zajjāj's verdict: masculine, feminine use being anomalous and non-preferred. Morphology: if the nūn is a root letter, the pattern is فِعِّيل from التَّسْكِين (stilling); if the nūn is augmentative, the pattern is فِعْلِين (like غِسْلِين), putting it under the doubled root.

2. سَكَنَ الدَّارَ (to dwell in a place); verb of the طَلَبَ class (past fatḥa, imperfect ḍamma). Verbal noun السُّكْنَى; active participle سَاكِن (dweller), plural سُكَّان. Causative with the alif: أَسْكَنَ (to house someone). مَسْكَن (readable as maskan or miskan) = a dwelling, plural مَسَاكِن. سَكَن = that which one turns to for rest — family, wealth, and the like — the verbal noun of سَكَنَ إِلَى (to incline toward / find repose in), also of the طَلَبَ class.

3. سَكِينَة (unshaded form) = awe/dignity (مَهَابَة), gravity (رَزَانَة), and solemn dignity (وَقَار). A variant with a doubled kāf is reported in al-Nawādir, with the note that the pattern فُعَيْلَة with doubled middle radical is otherwise unknown in Arabic — an anomaly.

4. سَكَنَ (سُكُونًا): a moving thing coming to rest, its motion departing; causative by doubling, سَكَّنَ (to still). مِسْكِين derives from this — from a person's "stilling"/leaning upon others. Pronounced with fatḥa on the mīm in the Banū Asad dialect, kasra elsewhere. On its meaning relative to فَقِير:
   - Ibn al-Sikkīt and Yūnus: the miskīn has nothing, the faqīr has some subsistence — so the faqīr is better off. Yūnus cites a bedouin who called himself miskīn, not faqīr.
   - Al-Aṣmaʿī (which al-Fayyūmī calls the sounder view): the miskīn is better off than the faqīr, arguing from Qurʾānic usage — 18:79 assigns a valuable ship to masākīn, whereas 2:273 describes the fuqarāʾ as unable to travel and mistaken for rich only through their restraint.
   - Ibn al-Aʿrābī: the two are equivalent, both meaning one who has nothing.
   - miskīn also denotes the abased and subdued, even a wealthy person; cf. 2:61, where "abasement and مَسْكَنَة (wretchedness)" are stamped on a people.
   - Feminine مِسْكِينَة: strict analogy would omit the hāʾ (the مِفْعِيل / مِفْعَال feminine patterns don't take it, e.g. مِعْطِير, مِكْسَال), but it was formed by analogy with فَقِيرَة, so the hāʾ appears.

5. اسْتَكَنَ = to submit and become lowly (خَضَعَ وَذَلَّ); lengthened form اسْتَكَانَ, which Ibn al-Qaṭṭāʿ notes is common. Two derivations with two corresponding measures: from سُكُون (stillness), giving the pattern افْتَعَلَ; or from الكِينَة (a bad/wretched state), giving the pattern اسْتَفْعَلَ.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سُكَٰرَىٰ 3x "(are) intoxicated"; سَكْرَة 2x "(the) stupor"; سُكِّرَتْ 1x "have been dazzled"; سَكَر 1x "intoxicant"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats س-ك-ر (s-k-r) as one root whose single underlying idea is bewilderment or disorientation (ḥayra). From that he derives the following senses:

1. Intoxication. سُكْر (sukr) is the drunkenness produced by drink: سَكِرَ سُكْرًا ("he became drunk"). A سِكِّير (sikkīr) is a habitual drunkard — the intensive pattern marking "much given to" the state.

2. Causing bewilderment. The form-II verbal noun تَسْكِير (taskīr) means تَحْيِير (taḥyīr), "to throw into confusion / daze". He cites Qur'an 15:15, {إِنَّمَا سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا} — "our eyes have merely been sukkirat", i.e. dazed. He notes a variant reading with the light (undoubled) form, سُكِرَتْ (sukirat), which those who read it that way glossed as سُحِرَتْ, "were bewitched".

3. Damming water. سِكْر (sikr, with i) is the stretch of ground where water is held back; سَكْر (sakr, with a) is the act of holding water back. He connects this explicitly to the root idea: dammed water "becomes bewildered" — it is checked and mills about instead of running on.

4. Stillness. لَيْلَةٌ سَاكِرَةٌ (laylatun sākira) is a calm, mild night with nothing hurtful in it. Shāhid: a line of Aws — "My nights are made yet longer in their length; they are neither mild (ṭalq) nor still (sākira)." Likewise سَكَرَتِ الرِّيحُ, "the wind died down".

5. Drink. سَكَر (sakar, with two a-vowels) is simply "drink" (al-sharāb) — given as a bare gloss, with no further specification.

6. Throttling — reported with reserve. Some transmit سَكَرَهُ in the sense "he choked him". Ibn Fāris does not vouch for it: "if that is sound, then it belongs to this chapter", i.e. it would still fall under the one root. He adds the usage of a camel pinning (yusakkir) another with its foreleg until it nearly kills it, with an unattributed poetic fragment describing a lean young camel being so pressed.

Method note: the entry is built on Ibn Fāris's standard procedure of reducing all attested uses to one semantic origin — here ḥayra — and he flags a doubtful sense as conditional rather than asserting it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha): the root s-k-t (سكت) marks "the opposite of speech" — that is, silence. He records the following usages:

1. The base verb: sakata / yaskutu / sukūt (سَكَتَ يَسْكُتُ سُكُوتًا) — "to fall silent, to be silent."
2. sikkīt (سِكِّيتٌ) — an intensive form describing a habitually silent, taciturn man.
3. The expression "ramāhu bi-sukātah" (رَمَاهُ بِسُكَاتَةٍ), "he threw at him a sukātah" — meaning something that made him fall silent.
4. An extended, non-literal use: "sakata al-ghaḍab" (سَكَتَ الْغَضَبُ), "the anger fell silent," used to mean it subsided or calmed down (= sakana).
5. sukta (السُّكْتَةُ) — whatever is used to quiet a crying child.
6. A technical term explained via the same root: al-sukayt (السُّكَيْتُ), a diminutive-pattern noun, is the name for the horse that finishes tenth in a race. Ibn Fāris proposes this may derive from silence because such a horse's owner "falls silent" about boasting — having nothing to boast of — and compares it to the phrase "ajarrahu kadhā" (أَجَرَّهُ كَذَا), said of something that stops a man from boasting, as if it had dragged his tongue into silence.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root s-l-ḥ in two connected notices.

1. السِّلَاح (silāḥ) — weaponry: that with which fighting is carried out. He reports that Abū ʿUbayda drew a line between silāḥ and الجُنَّة (junna): silāḥ is what one fights *with*, while junna is what one shields oneself *behind*. Abū ʿUbayda's evidence is a line of verse describing horses scowling as they bear the champions, "rising with the Indian blades and the shields" — the point being that the poet lists the shields (junan) separately from the swords, so the two are not the same category.

2. الإسْلِيح (islīḥ) — a plant on which camels grow rich in milk. Ibn Fāris quotes a Bedouin woman's saying in praise of it: al-islīḥ means froth on the milk, milk flowing freely, and a hump — a towering one.

The entry is brief: it gives no further senses, no morphological or grammatical notes, and the poet of the cited line is not named.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root س-ل-ط (s-l-ṭ) from a single core idea: strength and overpowering domination (qahr).

1. Core sense — power and domination. From it comes salāṭa (forcefulness), from tasalluṭ (gaining mastery over), which is domination. On this basis the sulṭān is named sulṭān.

2. sulṭān also means ḥujja — a conclusive proof or authoritative argument.

3. salīṭ (of a man) — one who is eloquent, sharp, and fluent of tongue.

4. salīṭa (of a woman) — one who is loud and clamorous.

5. A branch Ibn Fāris marks as departing from the root's main sense: salīṭ meaning oil — olive oil in the dialect of Yemen, and sesame oil in the usage of others.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root س ل ب (s-l-b) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: taking something swiftly and by snatching it away.

1. Basic sense — stripping/snatching: salabtuhu thawbahu ("I stripped/snatched his garment from him"). Al-salab = "that which is stripped" (a spoil, a plundered thing); al-salīb is a synonym for it. A hadith is cited: "Whoever kills a [combatant] in battle, the salab [the slain man's weapons and gear] belongs to him."

2. Camels: a she-camel called salūb (pl. sulub) is one whose young has died or been taken from her; she is said to aslabat when in that state — the "taking away" sense extended to loss of offspring.

3. Tree bark: al-salab also names tree-bark, because bark is peeled/stripped off the tree — the tree is, as it were, "despoiled" of it. Ibn Fāris cites a line of poetry by Ibn Maḥkān describing hide stripped from a slaughtered animal "as the two hands of a qātil/fātil strip the salab (bark)." Two transmitters read the disputed word differently — Ibn al-A'rābī as qātil ("killer"), al-Aṣma'ī as fātil ("twister," i.e. one who twists bark into rope, tying it to Medina's bark-strippers' market). Ibn Fāris reports that later scholars judged al-Aṣma'ī's reading correct.

4. Mourning dress: tasallabat al-mar'ah, "a woman put on salab (mourning attire)," parallel to aḥaddat ("she mourned [her husband]"). Some traced this to al-sulub, "black garments," and Ibn Fāris links it back to sense 3 — such garments are likened to stripped tree-bark. He quotes Labīd's line mentioning "the black sulub-garments... and the amsāḥ [coarse cloth]." A distinction some scholars drew: iḥdād (mourning) applies specifically to a husband's death, while tasallub can be worn in mourning for others too.

5. faras salīb ("a salīb horse"): one view says this means long-legged; another says it means light and swift-footed — comparable to rajul salīb al-yadayn bi-l-ṭa'n ("swift-handed in striking") and thawr salīb al-qarn bi-l-ṭa'n ("swift-horned in goring"). Ibn Fāris judges the second view (swiftness) the sounder one, since such a creature seems to "snatch away" the blow/thrust instantaneously — tying the sense back to the root's core meaning of swift snatching.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سَلَفَ 5x "passed before"; أَسْلَفَتْ 2x "it did previously"; سَلَف 1x "a precedent"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats س-ل-ف (s-l-f) as one core notion — going before, preceding, coming first — plus two items he judges to fall outside it.

Core sense: precedence, priority in time or place.
1. السَّلَف (salaf) — those who have gone before, predecessors.
2. الْقَوْمُ السُّلَّاف (al-qawm al-sullāf) — the people out in front, those who go ahead.
3. السُّلَاف (sulāf) — the liquid that runs off grape juice before the grapes are pressed, i.e. what comes first of its own accord.
4. السُّلْفَة (sulfa) — food taken early, in advance of the midday meal.
5. السُّلُوف (sulūf) — the she-camel at the head of the herd when the camels come down to water.

Extension into transactions (Ibn Fāris explicitly keeps these under the same core):
6. السَّلَف (salaf) in a sale — money handed over in advance for goods to be delivered later.
7. Some people use سَلَف (salaf) for a loan (قَرْض, qarḍ). Ibn Fāris accepts this as the same reasoning: something given in advance against a return that comes afterwards.

A separate analogy (not "precedence"):
8. السِّلْف (silf) — two men related by each marrying a sister of the other's wife. Ibn Fāris explains this by the pattern of السَّالِفَتَان (al-sālifatān), the two sides of the neck: two matching things set opposite each other, i.e. pairing rather than priority.

Falling outside both patterns:
9. السَّلْف (salf) — a leather bag or satchel (jirāb); and, he reports, the foreskin (qulfa) is said to be called salf.
10. أَسْلَفْتُ الْأَرْضَ لِلزَّرْعِ (aslaftu al-arḍ li-l-zarʿ) — "I prepared the ground for sowing," i.e. levelled it. Ibn Fāris allows that this may after all belong to the first core sense, since it is work done in advance to put the land right.

Method note: Ibn Fāris's procedure here is to state one governing sense, list the usages that follow from it, and then flag which items he cannot derive from it — offering a competing analogy (paired neck-sides) for one, and admitting uncertainty about another.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
poets_named: ʿAdī b. Zayd (pre-Islamic); Sāʿidah b. al-ʿAjlān (pre-Islamic); Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse ×2; Qays b. ʿAyzārah (pre-Islamic); Zuhayr (pre-Islamic)
text:
Root س ل ك (s-l-k). Al-Ṣāghānī sums up the root: it denotes one thing penetrating or passing into another.

CORE VERB
1. سَلَكَ (salaka) — to traverse a place or road (verbal nouns salk and sulūk). Transitively it means to make someone/something traverse or pass into a thing. Two forms exist side by side, salaka and aslaka, and lexicographers treat them as equivalent (Abū ʿUbayd; Ibn al-Aʿrābī allows both "salaktuhu ghayrī" and "aslaktuhu ghayrī" for "I made another travel it").
   - Qurʾānic witnesses of the transitive sense: كذلك سلكناه في قلوب المجرمين ("thus We made it pass into the hearts of the criminals") and فسلكه ينابيع في الأرض ("then He caused it to flow as springs in the earth").
   - Poetic witnesses: ʿAdī b. Zayd ("they routed you into a grievous affair") for salaka; Sāʿidah b. al-ʿAjlān ("they barred the road and drove them onto a lofty peak") for aslaka.
2. سَلَكَ يَدَهُ في الجيب / السِّقاء — to insert one's hand into a pocket, waterskin, etc.; also aslaka (same sense).

NOUNS
3. السِّلْكَة / سِلْك (silkah / silk) — the thread used to sew a garment; plurals aslāk and sulūk.
4. السُّلْكَى (sulkā, with ḍamm) — (a) a straight thrust delivered straight at the face, contrasted with makhlūjah (a slanting thrust), from a line of Imruʾ al-Qays. That line was famously obscure: various early authorities (Ruʾba, Abū ʿAmr b. al-ʿAlāʾ, Ibn Durayd, Abū ʿUbaydah) disputed its meaning; Imruʾ al-Qays himself reportedly said he modelled the image on watching a fletcher at Babylon feather arrows, while Abū ʿAmr declared the wording "obsolete speech" no one could explain. (b) By extension, a straight/firm course: "the opinion is wavering, not straight (sulkā)"; "their affair is sulkā" = on one single course (Ibn al-Sikkīt). Qays b. ʿAyzārah likewise uses sulkā for an undivided, firm resolve.
5. السُّلَك (sulak, pattern ṣurad) — the chick of the sandgrouse (or partridge); fem. sulakah / silkānah (rare); pl. silkān (Al-Layth's shāhid). Note: al-salakah, the female partridge-chick, is said to fall outside the root's core meaning.
6. المُسَلَّك (musallak) — slender/thin: a slim man or a lean horse (Ibn Durayd).
7. السَّلَكُوت (salakūt) — a [kind of] bird.
8. المَسْلَكَة (maslakah) — a strip slit from a garment's edge, named for its length, resembling a thread.
9. السِّلْك (silk, with kasr; Ibn ʿAbbād) — the first milk that bursts from a she-camel's udder, preceding the colostrum.

FROM THE SUPPLEMENT
10. الانْسِلَاك (insilāk) — the reflexive of salaka: to enter/thread one's way in (Zuhayr's line: "see where you are heading").
11. المَسْلَك (maslak) — a road; pl. masālik.
12. Figurative usage (majāz): "take to the paths (masālik) of truth"; and of refined speech, "fine of thread, subtle of path."

PROPER NAMES (personal, tribal, place)
- Sulayk (dimin.): several bearers — a Companion Sulayk b. ʿAmr (or b. Hudbah) al-Ghaṭafānī; the celebrated brigand-poet and runner Sulayk b. al-Sulakah (named for his mother Sulakah), proverbial in "swifter than Sulayk," also called Sulayk al-Maqānib; plus the poets Sulayk al-ʿUqaylī and Shaqīq b. Sulayk al-Azdī; and transmitters Sulayk b. Mishal and al-Aghar b. Sulayk al-Kūfī (al-Zabīdī corrects the manuscripts' fuller pedigree here).
- Silkān: the Companion Abū Nāʾilah Silkān b. Salāmah (real name Saʿd), foster-brother of Kaʿb b. al-Ashraf; and Silkān b. Mālik.
- Salakā (pattern jamazā): a village in al-Gharbiyya, Egypt, which al-Zabīdī says he visited.
- Idioms of anatomy: musallak / musamlak al-dhakar — sharp-headed (Abū ʿAmr). sallakahu taslīkan = aslakahu.

poets_named: Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr (lived into Islam); Zuhayr (pre-Islamic)
text:
Root س ل ل (s-l-l) — from Tāj al-ʿArūs by Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791 CE).

**Core meaning — "to draw out gently."** السَّلّ is defined as extracting something and bringing it out with gentleness (رِفْق) — سَلَّهُ يَسُلُّهُ سَلاًّ, same as الاسْتِلال. A ḥadīth about Ḥassān [ibn Thābit] uses the image: "I will draw you out from among them the way a hair is drawn out of dough."

1. **Drawing a sword.** سَيْفٌ سَلِيل = "a drawn sword" (= مَسْلُول). Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr's famous line calls the Prophet "a sword of God, drawn" (سُيُوفِ اللهِ مَسْلُولُ). The phrase "we met them at the salla" means "at the drawing of swords," i.e. when fighting began — illustrated with a verse of a Meccan arming against the Prophet.

2. **Slipping away.** انْسَلَّ / تَسَلَّلَ = to slip out of a crowd, to leave stealthily and unnoticed. ʿĀʾisha's ḥadīth "فانسللت من بين يديه" is glossed as "I left, gently and gradually." Sībawayh notes this انسلّ is not a reflexive/passive form but behaves as a plain verb like فَعَلْتُ. The author connects the Qur'anic يَتَسَلَّلُونَ مِنكُمْ لِوَاذًا [24:63] to this sense, citing al-Layth that يتسللون and ينسلّون mean the same thing.

3. **سُلَالَة — "what is drawn out."** Defined as whatever is extracted from something; a drop of seed is called man's sulāla. The entry cites Qur'an 23:12 ("We created man from a sulāla of clay") and reports the scholarly disputes over what exactly sulāla refers to: al-Farrāʾ says "what is drawn from any soil"; Abū al-Haytham says "what is drawn from a man's loins and a woman's chest," comparing it to how anything is "drawn out"; a report from ʿIkrima glosses it as the fluid drawn from the back, supported by Qur'an 32:7–8, where God moves from "clay" to "a sulāla of despised water" — taken as God's own gloss of the term. Qatāda and al-Farrāʾ instead take it as "Adam was drawn out of clay, hence named sulāla." Al-Akhfash gives yet another sense: the newborn child at the moment of birth, also called سَلِيل for the same reason.

4. **Other "drawn/extracted" senses of سليل/سليلة:**
 - السليلة = "daughter" (poetic usage, Abū ʿAmr).
 - السليلة = a long strip of flesh or sinew along the back, with visible striations; السَّلائِل = long muscle-strips running along the spine (also the name of a long-beaked fish).
 - السليل = a newborn foal at the instant of birth, before its sex is known; also specifically one "born without caul or membrane" (otherwise called بَقِير).
 - السليل = the horse's brain; also a clear, pure drink (a ḥadīth asks God for "the salīl of Paradise," i.e. its clear drink — variously read as sweet/cold/pure or easy-swallowing; variant wordings give سلسبيل / سلسال); also the camel's hump; the watercourse (or its central, fullest-flowing part) in a valley; the spinal marrow.
 - السليل/السالّ = a wide, low-lying valley bearing certain named shrubs (salam, ḍaʿa, yanama, ḥalama, samur); plural السُّلاّن — grammarians differ on whether this plurals سليل or سالّ, and on the exact shape of the terrain.

5. **Names.** المِسَلَّة = a large needle/awl (pl. المَسالّ). السُّلاَّءة = a palm-thorn (pl. سُلاَّء). Several tribal/place names built on the root are recorded briefly: Salūl (a Hawāzin sub-clan, named for their mother — the mother of the "hypocrite" ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy is also called Salūl), Sulayy and al-Sullān (places/valleys, each with a supporting verse), and Sallā/Sillā (a Quḍāʿa clan and two place-names, one the site of a battle between al-Muhallab and the Khārijite Azāriqa). A handful of transmitters and companions bore the name al-Salīl or Abū al-Salīl.

6. **Craft/technical senses of السَّلَّة:** stitching two leather thongs into one seam; a flaw or gap in a water-trough's lining (with a supporting verse); the bread-basket (Ibn Durayd doubts this word is genuine Arabic; its plural سَلّ is treated as irregular since a basket is a made object, not a natural kind); an old she-camel whose teeth have fallen out; a horse's decisive burst of speed ahead of the field (metaphorical); cracks in the ground that "steal" water away.

7. **Supplementary notes (appended matter):**
 - أَسْلَلْتُ is a dialect variant of سَلَلْتُ ("I drew [the sword]"), used (along with السَّرِقَة "secret theft" and الرِّشْوَة "bribery") to explain the ḥadīth "no إغلال and no إسلال" — though الإسلال is also glossed oppositely as "open, undisguised raiding," so the ḥadīth was read both ways.
 - "اللهم اسلل سخيمة قلبي" ("draw the rancor from my heart") is flagged as metaphorical use of the root, echoed in the saying "gifts draw out rancor and loosen resentment."
 - A ḥadīth simile, "his bed was like the masall of a shaṭba," is glossed as "what is stripped from its rind" (a green frond, or, some say, a sword).
 - السليلة also names carded, bound hair from which a woman spins thread bit by bit — described in some technical detail (rolled strands about a forearm long).
 - سُلَّ المُهر = the foal "was drawn forth" i.e. born; سلائل السنام = strips cut from a camel's hump; سليل اللحم = its choice-cut flesh; السلائل = elongated worms/larvae in the nose; and an idiom, "a salīl of samur-acacia," parallel to other plant-thicket idioms.
 - A line of Zuhayr, سال السليل بهم, is explained by Ibn Barrī as "they traveled swiftly."
 - استلّ بكذا = to make off with something furtively; السالّ/السلاّل/الأسَلّ = "the thief"; أسَلّ = to become a habitual secret thief, or to abet one; المُسَلِّل = one adept at the trick of theft.
 - تسلّل الشيء = "it quivered" — al-Rāghib suggests the doubled form of the word itself mimics a repeated slipping motion.
 - The proverb "she pinned her own fault on me and slipped away" (رمتني بدائها وانسلت) is traced to a specific pre-Islamic anecdote about co-wives.
 - استلّ النهر جدولاً = a channel branched off from a river (metaphorical); السليلة also names a specific water-place in upper Thādiq.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سَلَٰم 42x "peace"; مُسْلِم 39x "muslims"; أَسْلَمَ 22x "submits"; إِسْلَٰم 8x "[the] islam"; سَلَّمَ 6x "and submit"; سَلَم 5x "[the] peace"; مُّسَلَّمَة 3x "(is to be) paid"; تَسْلِيم 3x "(in full) submission"; سُلَّم 2x "a ladder"; سَّلْم 2x "to peace"; سَلِيم 2x "sound"; مُسْلِمَٰت 2x "submissive"
text:
Ibn Fāris organizes the root س ل م around one core idea — soundness and well-being (ṣiḥḥa, ʿāfiya) — with a few outlying senses he flags as anomalous.

1. Core sense — safety (salāma): that a person be free from blight and harm.

2. Al-Salām as a divine name: Ibn Fāris reports that "the people of knowledge" call God al-Salām because He is free from the defect, deficiency, and perishing that affect created things. He cites {God calls to the Abode of Peace} [Yūnus 10:25], glossing al-Salām as God and "His Abode" as the Garden. (Attributed to the scholars, not stated as an independent fact.)

3. Al-Islām: submission/compliance (inqiyād) — so called because the one who submits becomes free of refusal and resistance. The sense is derived from the root's core meaning, not from a codified religious definition.

4. Al-silām: making peace with one another (musālama). Ibn Fāris notes the morphology: the fiʿāl pattern often carries the reciprocal (mufāʿala) sense, comparing qitāl / muqātala (fighting / mutual combat).

5. Al-salam (= al-salaf): a forward/advance payment. Linked to the ideas of accompanying and complying — as if it is property that is handed over willingly and does not withhold itself.

6. Silām (stones): possibly named thus, he suggests, because stones are the least perishable thing in the earth, given their hardness — so tied to the "enduring/sound" idea.

7. Al-salīm (a snake-bitten/stung person): two proposed explanations — (a) he has been "given over" to his affliction, or (b) it is a hopeful euphemism (tafāʾul) invoking safety. Ibn Fāris notes Arabs sometimes name things by good omen or ill omen.

8. Al-sullam (ladder): also traced to salāma, because someone climbing down is hoped to reach safety.

9. Al-salāma (a tree): plural salām.

Outlying senses he marks as deviating from the core:
- al-salm: a bucket with a single handle.
- al-salam: a species of tree (singular salama).
- al-salamān: a tree.

10. Al-silm / al-salm (reconciliation, ṣulḥ): usable as masculine or feminine. Cited with {And if they incline to peace, then incline to it} [al-Anfāl 8:61].

11. Al-salima: a stone, evidenced by a verse of poetry ("...who casts behind me with the arrow and the stone").

Proper names: Banū Salima, an Anṣārī clan unique among the Arabs; Salmā (a woman's name; also a mountain); and Abū Sulmā (father of the poet Zuhayr), with ḍamma on the sīn — a form he says is otherwise unique among the Arabs.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris opens by flagging this root (s-l-q) as an exception to his usual method: normally he seeks one unifying core meaning (qiyās) for a root's letters, but here he states outright that the senses are too disparate — scarcely two of them share one pattern — and attributes this diversity of speech simply to God shaping His creation's language however He willed.

He then lists the senses as separate, unconnected items:

1. Ground — as-salaq: a low-lying, sunken stretch of land.
2. Animal — as-silqah: a she-wolf.
3. Sound — salaqa: to cry out, shout.
4. Character — as-saliqah: one's natural disposition/innate nature.
5. Camel-gear mark — as-saliqah (same word-form, different sense): the mark a girth-strap leaves on a camel's side.
6. Place-name — Saluq: a town.
7. Wall-climbing — at-tasalluq 'alā al-ḥā'iṭ: scaling a wall to get over it into a house.
8. Dead wood — as-saliq: matter/wood that has fallen and crumbled off trees. He quotes an anonymous rajaz-verse describing a crackling sound heard from "the ashen-grey fallen brushwood, like blazing kindled fire."
9. Tongue condition — as-sulāq: the skin of the tongue peeling/flaking.
10. Greasing a water-skin — salaqtu al-mazādah: to oil/grease a leather water-skin. He quotes Imru' al-Qays comparing two things to "the two water-skins of one in haste — freshly made, not yet greased with oil."
11. A sack-tying technique — as-salq: inserting one of a sack's two loop-handles through the other, then folding it over again — a way of closing a sack (al-juwāliq).

Ibn Fāris draws no single thread between these; he presents the root explicitly as a set of unrelated homonyms.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: Abū Kabīr (pre-Islamic); Labīd (lived into Islam); Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam); Aws (pre-Islamic); Ḥassān (lived into Islam); Ibn Rawāḥa (lived into Islam); al-Akhṭal (Umayyad); unnamed verse ×2
text:
Ibn Manẓūr's Lisān al-ʿArab, root s-l-s-l:

1. Core sense — smooth, sweet water: salsal, salsāl, and sulāsil all describe sweet water that goes down the throat easily because of its clarity and sweetness (some also say it means cold). Cited in verse by Abū Kabīr (salsal wine, i.e. smooth wine, sweeter than the memory of youth), Labīd (sulāsil water among luxury goods in saddle-bags), and Abū Dhuʾayb (water from a mountain-cleft). A related idea: when such water flows or the wind ripples it, it comes to look like a silsila (chain) — illustrated by Aws's image of wind rippling a pool's surface.

2. Smooth wine: khamr described as salsal/salsāl means soft, smooth wine (Ḥassān cites the Baradā river mixed with such wine).

3. The verb: al-Layth says salsal is sweet, clear water that, when drunk, "tasalsala" — ripples/flows — down the throat (khalq). Tasalsala al-māʾ = the water flowed; salsaltuhu = I poured it in.

4. Salsabīl (Qur'anic term, Q76:18, "a spring therein called Salsabīl"): Ibn Rawāḥa's verse pairs raḥīq (choice wine) with salsabīl, glossed as "easy of entry into the throat." Ibn al-Aʿrābī says he never heard the word except in the Qur'an. Al-Zajjāj takes it as the proper name of the Paradise spring, meaning something at the height of smoothness. Others (via Sībawayh/al-Sīrāfī) treat it grammatically as a descriptive adjective rather than a proper name. Abū Bakr ibn al-Anbārī discusses the grammar in detail: if a proper name, its nunation in the verse is explained as matching the Qur'an's rhymed verse-endings even though a definite feminine noun would normally not take full declension; if a descriptive adjective, full declension is expected regardless. Al-Akhfash instead explains the added alif (salsabīlā) as a verse-end convention, comparable to qawārīrā elsewhere in the Qur'an. Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it as "it slides down their throats"; Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī as "soft, between the larynx and the throat." Ibn Manẓūr flags as an outright error the reading that splits the word into an imperative sentence, "Ask your Lord a way to this spring." A spring or drink called salsal/salsāl/salsabīl all carry the same sense: sweet and easy to swallow. Plurals given: salāsib/salāsīb (of salsabīl), salsabīlāt (of salsabīla).

5. Flowing/rippling more broadly: tasalsala al-māʾ also covers water running down a slope (cited from al-Akhṭal, a rivulet trickling to relieve thirst). Salsabīl by extension can describe anything soft and free of roughness, occasionally applied to water generally.

6. Worn cloth and a sword's pattern: a threadbare, poorly-woven garment is musalsal/mutasalsil (al-Liḥyānī: cloth "tasalsala" as it wears thin). Tasalsul separately names the gleam and shimmer of a sword blade's watered pattern (firind); a striped sword or garment is called musalsal or mulaslas (sources disagree on which word goes with which noun). A Hudhalī verse uses musallas for a blade whose ridges show a chain-like glitter in its pattern.

7. Silsila = a physical chain: al-salsala at root means "the joining of one thing to another"; silsila is the familiar linked ring of iron or similar material, derived from that root sense. A ḥadīth speaks of people "led to Paradise in chains" — explained as captives brought to Islam under compulsion, whose eventual entry into Paradise this describes figuratively, not a literal chain; the phrase is read to cover anyone driven toward good by outside pressure.

8. Extended/figurative "chain" uses: streaks of lightning across a cloud, and the winding ridge-lines of sand dunes, are both called salāsil (singular silsila or silsil), because of their chain-like, linked appearance — with supporting verse and a ḥadīth of Ibn ʿAmr comparing serpents in the "fifth earth" to sand-dune chains. Ibn al-Aʿrābī adds that lightning which streaks this way in its upper reaches is a reliable sign of coming rain. A draft-horse with chain-like markings on its legs is also "dhū salāsil."

9. Proper names and idioms: Ghazwat al-Sulāsil, a military expedition, is named for a water-source of that name in the land of Judhām — linguistically the same word as salsāl ("smooth") water. An agile, light-spirited boy can be called lu-slus or su-lsul. Al-Silsilān is a place in the territory of Banū Asad (also read as the name of two separate places in a cited verse). Salsal is also the name of a sand-ridge in the al-Dahnāʾ desert, illustrated with a verse about a bow-stave cut from its ridges.

dictionary: Lane — Arabic-English Lexicon, Edward William Lane (d. 1876)
text:
Root s-l-w (سلو), William Edward Lane, Arabic-English Lexicon

1. sala 'anhu / saliya — to become forgetful of, or find comfort/contentment without, someone or something; several verb-forms and verbal nouns are surveyed, with al-Azhari specifying the sense as a familiar's contentment in separation. sallahu/aslahu 'anhu (causative) — to console or comfort someone, illustrated with the idiom "he relieved me of my anxiety."
2. tasalla/insala (Forms V/VII) — to be made forgetful/comforted, or to feign such forgetfulness; salwah/sulwah — the resulting state of contentment-in-loss, illustrated with set phrases ("you have made me content without you"; "he is in an ample, pleasant life").
3. al-salwa — a bird identified with quail (al-suman), described physically and noted by al-Akhfash as having no clearly attested distinct singular form (comparing it to dafla); [this is the bird traditionally associated with the Israelites' wilderness provision, though Lane's entry itself does not cite the Qur'anic verses]. A second, unrelated sense of salwa is honey — attested in one poet's usage (which al-Zajjaj considered an error) and explained by Abu 'Ali al-Farisi as fitting the broader sense "whatever brings comfort," since honey comforts through sweetness.
4. sulwan — a drink or object used to induce forgetfulness in a lovesick person, with an unusually rich array of competing folk-explanations recorded: a special drink for the lovelorn; grave-dust in water to "kill" love; rainwater poured over a specific bead; a physician's mood-lifting medicine (mufarrih); a charm-bead used by women to bind men's affection; or a color-changing buried bead. Illustrated with a line of poetry by Ru'bah and an anecdote recording a scholarly disagreement (Nusayr ibn Abi Nusayr vs. al-Asma'i) over whether "sulwan" names a literal bead-potion or is simply the abstract noun for "forgetting."
5. Closing: sulla — a quality inducing forgetfulness of loved ones; sali — one whose heart is free of attachment; the idiom "fihi maslatun 'an al-kurab" (a source of forgetting one's troubles); al-musalli — the third-place horse in a ten-horse race, so named for consoling its owner; mutasalla — a means or place of consolation.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root: s-l-kh (سلخ)
Source: al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (early 11th c. CE)

1. Core sense — al-salkh is stripping the skin off an animal, i.e. flaying. Idiom: "salakhtuhu fa-nsalakha" — "I flayed it, so it came/peeled off." (Form I sallakha = to strip/flay; Form VII insalakha = to come off, be stripped off — the passive/reflexive counterpart.)

2. Metaphorical extension to clothing/armor — from the flaying sense, the word is borrowed for removing a coat of mail: "salakhtu dir'ahu" = "I stripped off his coat of mail," meaning simply "I removed it."

3. Extension to time — a month is said to "salakha" or "insalakha," i.e. to pass/slip away, as though it were being stripped off like a skin. Al-Raghib cites two Qur'anic instances:
- Q9:5 (al-Tawbah): "fa-idha insalakha al-ashhur al-hurum" — "So when the sacred months have passed [lit. been stripped off]..."
- Q36:37 (Ya-Sin): "naslakhu minhu al-nahar" — "We strip the day away from it [the night]," which he glosses simply as "We remove/pull it away" (nanzi'u).

4. Idiom "aswad salikh" — "a sloughing black [serpent]," so named because it sheds (salakha) its own skin, i.e., removes it.

5. Idiom "nakhla mislakh" — a palm tree "of the mislakh type," one whose green, unripe dates scatter and fall off (shed), by the same image of something coming loose/stripped away.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سَمِعَ 78x "we heard"; سَمِيع 47x "(is) all-hearing"; سَمْع 22x "the hearing"; ٱسْتَمَعَ 16x "listen"; أَسْمَعَ 13x "cause to hear"; سَمَّٰعُون 4x "who would have listened"; مُسْتَمِع 2x "their listener"; مُسْمَع 1x "to be heard"; مُسْمِع 1x "can make hear"; يَسَّمَّعُ 1x "they may listen"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats س-م-ع (s-m-ʿ) as one root whose core meaning is apprehending something with the ear — said of humans and of any creature that has an ear. The base verb: samiʿtu al-shayʾa samʿan ("I heard the thing").

Senses he records:
1. Hearing / perceiving by the ear — the primary sense.
2. al-simʿ / al-samʿ = a good reputation, fine repute. Example: "his simʿ has spread among the people" = his renown has spread.
3. samāʿi = an imperative form meaning "listen!"
4. samiʿtu bi-l-shayʾ = to put something about / broadcast it so that people will talk of it.
5. al-musmiʿa = a female singer.
6. al-mismaʿ = a loop set in the middle of the large leather draw-bucket (gharb), acting "like an ear" for it, through which a rope is threaded to balance the bucket. He cites a verse of poetry: "And we straighten the crooked one, should he assail us, as the draw-bucket is balanced by the mismaʿ."

Anomalous sense (departing from the root): al-simʿ = the crossbred offspring of a wolf and a hyena.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
ROOT s-m-d (سمد) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core idea: pressing straight forward, without turning aside or pausing.

1. Literal/physical sense: Said of camels — samadat al-ibilu fī sayrihā, "the camels samadat in their travel," meaning they pushed on hard, heads forward, without deviating. A cited rajaz verse calls them sawāmid al-layl khifāf al-azwād, "night-pressers, light of provisions" — i.e. they travel on without stopping to graze, empty-bellied.

2. Extended/figurative sense: From the same root comes al-sumūd = lahw ("diversion, idle amusement"), and al-sāmid = al-lāhī, "one absorbed/heedless in amusement." Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 53:61, wa-antum sāmidūn, glossing it as lāhūn, "diverted/heedless in amusement."

Ibn Fāris explains why this figurative sense still fits the root's core meaning: someone lost in diversion (lāhī) likewise "presses straight on" in what he is doing, without turning aside or lingering — heedless absorption is itself a kind of unbroken, unswerving forward motion.

A cited verse of poetry uses sumūd this way: "It was said, 'Rise and look at them'... then leave aside your sumūd" (i.e., stop being diverted/heedless).

Note on a look-alike expression: The phrase sammada raʾsahu ("he sammada his head," meaning he shaved all its hair off) is NOT treated as part of this root. Ibn Fāris explains it as a case of consonant substitution (ibdāl) — its true original is sabbada (with bāʾ), discussed separately elsewhere in his dictionary.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root س م ك (s-m-k), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: elevation/height.

1. samaka — to rise up; al-masmūkāt — the heavens (named for their elevated position). "samaka fī al-daraj" — he rose in rank; "usmuk" — an imperative, "rise/climb higher." sanām sāmik — a raised, prominent hump.
2. al-mismāk — a support-pole used to raise a tent-house, illustrated with a line of poetry by Dhū al-Rummah comparing a camel's legs to two sturdy, unpeeled poles. al-Simāk — a star (or pair of stars — Arcturus and Spica), named from the same root of elevation.
3. Closing exception, flagged as anomalous and outside this root's core pattern: al-samak — fish (an unrelated homonym).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سَمُوم 3x "(of) the scorching fire"; سَمّ 1x "(the) eye"
text:
Ibn Fāris gives s-m-m a consistent root meaning, a way in or opening into a thing, such as a hole, from which further words are derived.

1. **Hole, opening.** al-samm or al-summ is a hole in something, as in the Qur'an's "until the camel passes into the eye (samm) of the needle" (Q 7:40).

2. **Poison.** Deadly poison is al-samm or al-summ. He explains the name by its penetrating the body, unlike other things that are merely tasted.

3. **Intimates.** al-sāmma are one's intimates (al-khāṣṣa), so called because they enter in with a familiarity that others do not have. The Arabs ask, "How are the sāmma and the ʿāmma?", that is, the intimates and the people at large.

4. **Hot wind.** al-samūm is the hot wind, because it too penetrates bodies with force.

5. **Reconciliation.** al-summ is setting things right between people: people at odds stand apart and do not mingle, and once things are set right between them they mingle.

6. **Anomalous words.** Outside this root meaning he lists: al-samm, something like cowries that comes out of the sea; al-samsām, a bird; al-samsam, the fox; al-sumsumānī, a light man; al-samāsim, red ants (singular سُِمْسِمة); and al-simsim, sesame, a grain. He suggests these could be taken as a second root meaning: lightness.

7. **Outside both.** The saying mā lahu samm (or summ) wa-lā ḥamm (or ḥumm) ghayruka means "he has no concern (hamm) other than you"; he counts it as anomalous to both root meanings.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root س م ن (s-m-n), as treated by al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī in al-Mufradāt.

1. Core sense — fatness. السِّمَن (simanu) is the opposite of leanness. The adjective is سَمِين (samīn, "fat"), plural سِمَان (simān). Qur'anic witness: "seven fat cows" (Yūsuf 12:46).

2. Causative — to make fat. Both أَسْمَنَ (asmana, form IV) and سَمَّنَ (sammana, form II) mean "to make something fat." Qur'anic witness: "it does not fatten, nor does it avail against hunger" (al-Ghāshiya 88:7).

3. Further senses of the form-IV verb. أَسْمَنْتُهُ can also mean "I bought it fat," or "I gave him such [a fat animal]."

4. Form X — to find fat. اسْتَسْمَنْتُهُ (istasmantuhu): "I found it to be fat" (i.e. judged it fat).

5. Derived noun: سُمْنَة (sumna) — a drug or remedy used to induce fatness.

6. Derived noun: سَمْن (samn, clarified butter). Al-Rāghib derives the name from the root's core sense: it belongs to the category of fat and is produced out of it.

7. Derived noun: سُمَانَى (sumānā) — a bird. (The entry gives no further identification.)

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats س-م-ر (s-m-r) as one root whose core idea is colour that is *not* white — darkness or dusk of hue.

1. **السُّمْرَة (sumra) — brownness / dusky colour.** The base sense among colours. He derives it from the idiom "lā ātīka al-samar wa-l-qamar" ("I will not come to you [as long as there is] al-samar and al-qamar"): al-qamar is the moon, and **al-samar is the blackness of night**. The colour-term sumra is named from that night-darkness.

2. **السَّامِر (sāmir) — (a) people talking by night**, i.e. those who "samurūn" (converse in the dark); **(b) the place where they gather for such night talk.** Cited verse: "wa-sāmirin ṭāla lahum fīhi al-samar" — "and many a night-gathering in which their talk ran long."

3. **السَّمْرَاء (samrāʾ) — wheat**, so called from its (brown) colour.

4. **الأَسْمَر (asmar) — the spear**; also **water**.

5. **السَّمَار (samār) — thin, watery milk**, named so because in that state its colour is altered.

6. **السَّمُر (samur) — a species of ṭalḥ (acacia) tree**, singulative سَمُرَة (samura); Ibn Fāris suggests, tentatively, that it too is named for its colour.

7. **السَّمَار (al-Samār) — a place-name**, evidenced by the line: "If he comes down to al-Samār we shall surely kill him — but no, by your father, he never came down to al-Samār."

Method to note: he anchors the abstract sense (non-white colour) in an attested idiom about night, then reads the concrete nouns — wheat, spear, water, milk, acacia — as named from their hue, marking the acacia case as a possibility rather than a certainty.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root s-m-w from a single core notion: elevation or height (al-ʿuluww). He documents the following:

1. Verb of rising: samawtu = "I rose/ascended." Extended to the gaze — samā baṣaruhu, "his sight rose up" — and to a shape looming into view — samā lī shakhṣun, a figure "rose up to me until I could make it out."

2. samā al-faḥlu: of a stallion mounting its she-camels; the verbal noun is samāwa.

3. samāwa: the outline or visible shape (shakhṣ) of the crescent moon, or of anything; plural samāw.

4. samāʾ (sky/heaven) as a usage of this root: the Arabs call cloud samāʾ and rain samāʾ; when rain specifically is meant, the plural is sumiyy. Related form al-samāʾa = the visible figure.

5. Broadened senses of samāʾ, all keyed to "high / overlooking": the roof or ceiling of a house; then anything elevated and overhanging — even a horse's back is called its samāʾ; and by further extension, vegetation (because it comes down from the rain-bearing samāʾ). He cites a verse — "When the samāʾ descends on a people's land, we graze it even if they are enraged" — and the saying "We kept treading the samāʾ until we reached you," where samāʾ means the herbage and rain.

6. Etymology of ism ("name"): Ibn Fāris reports the view that its origin is simw, from the same root of elevation, since a name raises up and points to the meaning (a tanwīh, a making-known).

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
**Root س ن ب ل (s-n-b-l) — Ibn Manẓūr, Lisān al-ʿArab**

1. **Ear of grain.** سُنْبُل (sunbul) is the ear or head of a standing crop; plural سَنابِل, singulative سُنْبُلَة (one ear). Ibn Sīda is cited for this. The verb سَنْبَلَ الزرعُ means the crop put forth its ears. The word covers the ears of wheat, barley, and millet/sorghum.

2. **Constellation.** السُّنْبُلَة is also a sign in the sky (Virgo).

3. **A perfume.** السُّنْبُل is likewise the name of a fragrant substance.

4. **Long, trailing garment (سُنْبُلانيّ).** Reported of Salmān, seen at Kūfa wearing a قميص سُنْبُلانيّ. Explanations given:
   - Abū ʿAbd al-Wahhāb al-Ghanawī (via Shamir): a سُنْبُلانيّ garment is one that is full and long, let hang down (أُسْبِل).
   - Khālid ibn Janba: سَنْبَلَ الرجلُ ثوبَه = he trailed a "tail" of the garment behind him; that trailing portion is the سَنْبَلَة.
   - Khālid's brother: whatever hangs long both behind and in front has been "sanbala-ed" — that is the سُنْبُلانيّ shirt.
   - Shamir and others allow an alternative: سُنْبُلانيّ may simply be an adjective of relation to a place-name.
   A second report, of ʿUthmān sending a woman a شُقَيْقَة سُنْبُلانيّة, is glossed as "ample in length."

5. **Morphology.** The nūn in this word is augmentative (زائدة) — both in the garment sense and in سُنْبُل الطعام, "ear of grain." Ibn al-Athīr notes that lexicographers nonetheless all filed the word under sīn–nūn, following its surface form rather than its derivation.

6. **Proper names.**
   - ابن سِنْبِل, a man of Baṣra: Jāriya ibn Qudāma, a companion of ʿAlī, burned fifty Baṣrans in his house. The name is also transmitted as ابن صِنْبِل, treated again under ṣād.
   - السُّنْبُلة, an old well at Mecca dug by the Banū Jumaḥ, with their poet's line as witness: "It is we who dug Sunbula for the pilgrims."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root س ن د (s-n-d), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: the joining of one thing to another.

1. sanadtu ilā al-shayʾ — I leaned upon a thing; istanadtu — likewise; asnadtu ghayrī — I leaned/propped another (causative). al-sinād — a strong she-camel, as though her back were braced against something firm. al-musnad — Time itself, because its parts are joined together in sequence. "fulānun sanad" — so-and-so is someone relied upon.
2. al-sanad — the rising face of a mountain confronting you, above the foothill.
3. al-isnād, in hadith scholarship — tracing a report back to its original speaker (the chain of transmission), which Ibn Fāris notes follows exactly the same underlying analogy of "joining/attaching."
4. A distinct technical term in poetry, al-sinād — a discrepancy between the vowel-endings of the rhyme-support letters (a recognized prosodic flaw), illustrated via Abū ʿUbaydah with two mismatched lines of poetry. Ibn Fāris connects this to the idiom "kharaja al-qawmu mutasānidīn" — people going out under separate banners, each group having "attached itself" to its own standard — the same underlying sense of partial, uneven joining.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: س-ن-ه (s-n-h)
Source: Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004 CE)

Ibn Fāris states that these three letters form one root meaning "time" (zamān).

1. Etymology of "year": as-sanah ("the year") is built on this root, but with its final hāʾ elided in the ordinary form. He proves the hāʾ is original by pointing to the diminutive form sunayhah, where the hāʾ reappears.

2. Verb use — "sanahat an-nakhlah": said of a palm tree when years have passed over it (i.e., it has aged through repeated seasons).

3. Qur'anic citation: he cites Q2:259, {So look at your food and your drink — it has not yatasannah}, glossing yatasannah as "it did not become like something over which the years pass and so change/spoil it" — i.e., the root here carries the sense of being altered or aged by the passage of time.

4. Related form: an-nakhlah as-sanhāʾ — a palm tree so termed with reference to this same notion of years/time acting upon it.

The whole entry is organized around one core idea: this root denotes "time" in the sense of years passing and the change/aging that comes with their passage.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
**Root س-ن-م (s-n-m)** — Ibn Fāris, *Maqāyīs al-Lugha*

Ibn Fāris states this root has a single core meaning: **height, being raised up / elevation** (al-ʿuluww wa-l-irtifāʿ).

He supports this with four derived words, all built on the "raised" idea:

1. **السَّنَام (al-sanām)** — "the hump" (of a camel). He calls this a well-known word — its sense follows directly from the root's meaning of height, since the hump is the camel's raised part.
2. **تَسَنَّمْتُ (tasannamtu)** — "I mounted / climbed up onto [something]," glossed simply as ʿalawtu, "I rose above."
3. **نَاقَةٌ سَنِمَةٌ (nāqatun sanimah)** — "a she-camel with a large hump" (literally, great in the sanām).
4. **أَسْنَمْتُ النَّار (asnamtu al-nār)** — "I made the fire's flame rise/leap high" — the causative sense of the same root applied to flame instead of a camel's back.

He also notes **أَسْنُمَة (Asnumah)** as a place-name, without further comment.

No Qur'anic citation or shawāhid (poetic proof-text) is given in this entry; it is a short root-survey confined to the core sense and its immediate derivatives.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سُنَّة 16x "in (the) way"; مَّسْنُون 3x "altered"; سِّنّ 2x "and the tooth"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats s-n-n as one consistent root meaning: the flowing of a thing and its running on with ease. He derives every other use from this.

1. **Pouring, letting flow.** The base usage is sanantu al-māʾ ʿalā wajhī, "I poured the water over my face", letting it run freely.

2. **Smoothly formed.** A man masnūn al-wajh has a face on which the flesh seems to have been poured smoothly. al-ḥamaʾ al-masnūn (black mud that is masnūn) belongs here too: mud that seems to have been poured out.

3. **Sunna: a way of conduct.** al-sunna is al-sīra, a way of conduct or course followed; the sunna of the Messenger of God is his way of conduct. Ibn Fāris cites al-Hudhalī: "do not be distressed at a sunna you yourself set going; the first to accept a sunna is the one who sets it going." He says it is called sunna because it runs on.

4. **Course, direction.** "Go on along your sanan / sunan" means along your course. The wind comes sanāʾin when it blows along a single path.

5. **Whetting.** Carried over from this: sanantu al-ḥadīda, "I whetted the blade", by passing it over the sinān, here meaning the whetstone (al-misann). A poet's half-line is cited: "a sinān like the edge of the pared ṣullabī." The spearhead (sinān) is named from this because it is masnūn, drawn out and sharpened. The sanāsin, the ends of the back's vertebrae, are named as if they had been whetted.

6. **Tooth and tooth-cleaning.** The sinn (tooth) of a person or animal is likened to a spearhead. al-sanūn is what one cleans the teeth with, because the teeth are rubbed (sunna) with it.

7. **Pasturing camels.** sanna ibilahu, "he pastured his camels", means he grazed them until their skin grew fine, as if polished like a whetted blade. Ibn Fāris says this too goes back to the root meaning.

The text also begins a remark on "the bull" that breaks off unfinished.

text:
Ibn Sīda's entry for the root س-ن-و (s-n-w).

1. Light and blazing. سَنَتِ النار (sanat al-nār) — a fire's light rose and blazed high (imperfect tasnū, verbal noun sanāʾ). السَّنَا (al-sanā, shortened form) is the light of fire and of lightning; cited from Qur'an 24:43, "the sanā of its lightning almost takes away sight," and from a verse by Sībawayh about two distant fires "whose light rises high." سَنَا البَرْق means the lightning gave light (with a verse of Tamīm ibn Muqbil).

2. Related derived verbs. أَسْنَى النار = raised a fire's light; أَسْنَى البَرْق = the lightning shone forth; اسْتَنَى (istanā) = looked toward a fire's light (from Ibn al-Aʿrābī, with a verse about a benighted traveler who spots a fire and it flashes).

3. Rising in rank (figurative). سَنَا إلى معالي الأمور = he rose to noble affairs; سَنُوَ في حَسَبِه = he rose high in lineage/honor, so he is سَنِيّ (saniyy, "exalted").

4. A note on a variant Qur'anic reading. For the reading سَنَاءُ برقه with a long ending, Ibn Sīda holds the lengthened sanāʾ is NOT simply a dialect variant of the short sanā; it conveys the lightning's rising and flashing upward — compare the expression بَرْق رافع ("rising lightning").

5. سَنَّى الشيء = he mounted or rose over something (with a verse of Ibn Aḥmar).

6. Watering / drawing water (a distinct sense-cluster). سَنَا (verbal nouns sunuw, sināya, sināwa) = to draw or supply water. Derived nouns: السانِيَة (al-sāniya) = the large leather draw-bucket and its rigging, and also the she-camel used to draw water; المَسْنَوِيَّة = the well drawn from. سَنَتِ السحابةُ بالمطر = the cloud watered with rain. أرضٌ مَسْنُوَّة / مَسِنْيَّة = irrigated land. A grammatical note: Sībawayh did not recognize the form sanaytuhā; he derived masniyya from yasnūhā, the wāw shifting to yāʾ for lightness near the word's end (paralleled by ghiṭāʾa/ghiṭāʾ).

7. سَاناه = he sought to please or appease someone.

8. "Year" (سَنَة). The word for a year traces to both a wāw and a hāʾ origin (its full morphology is under the letter hāʾ). Plurals: سَنَوات and سِنُون. By extension السَّنَة means a drought-year: "the sana struck them" = the year of famine; hence the verb أَسْنَتُوا (asnatū, "they were hit by drought"), where a tāʾ replaces the underlying wāw/yāʾ — used only of drought, the opposite of plenty. أرضٌ سَنَة = barren land (by analogy to the drought-year); plural سِنُون, and al-Liḥyānī reports سُنُون. Further: أَسْنَى القوم = the drought-year came upon them; سَاناه (musānāt / sināʾ) = he hired someone by the year (parallel form musānaha with hāʾ); السَّنَة السَّنْواء = the severe drought-year.

9. The plant senna (السَّنَا / السَّنَاء). A plant used as an eye-application; the word occurs both short and long, singular سَناة (and by analogy سَناءة, not actually heard). In al-Nābigha al-Jaʿdī's line comparing a woman's smile to "the sanā of musk," Ibn Sīda notes sanā could mean this plant (mingled with musk) OR "light," since scent, like light, spreads (compare "its scent shone" = wafted) — though he judges the variant reading tanassumuhā ("her breath") the correct one. Abū Ḥanīfa (al-Dīnawarī) describes senna as a small shrub of the tanning/dye plants, mixed with henna to brighten and darken its color, bearing a dry pod that rattles in the wind (with a verse of Ḥumayd). Its dual is سَنَوان (also سَنَيان, mentioned earlier).

poets_named: unnamed verse ×3; al-Nābigha al-Jaʿdī (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Sīda (d. 1066 CE), al-Muḥkam, on the root س ق ط (s-q-ṭ). His whole entry works outward from one physical action — falling — and shows the derived senses as extensions of it.

**1. Falling, the base sense.** السَّقْطة (saqṭa) is a hard fall. The verb is سَقَطَ / يَسْقُطُ / سُقُوطاً; the participle is سَاقِط, and سُقُوط itself is used adjectivally, with no separate feminine form. A verse describes a woman as سُقوط البُرقُع, "whose veil slips down," and Ibn Sīda glosses the accompanying phrase "neither guarded nor let go" as meaning she needed no guarding against suspicion, and her parents did not neglect her.

**2. Place of falling.** مَسْقَط (and the anomalous variant مَسْقِط) is where something falls. Hence the idiom البصرة مَسْقَطُ رأسي — "Baṣra is where my head fell," i.e. my birthplace.

**3. Causative and iterative forms.** أَسْقَطَ = to make something fall. تَسَاقَطَ = to fall in continuous succession. سَاقَطَ (verbal nouns مُسَاقَطة, سِقَاط) = to let something drop piece after piece; a verse compares an antler being made to drop to sparks flying off the blacksmith's iron, "scattered bit by bit."

**4. Miscarriage.** أَسْقَطَتِ المرأةُ ولدَها: a woman cast out her child before term; she is مُسْقِط, and the child is سِقْط / سَقْط / سُقْط (three vocalisations). Ibn Sīda derives this directly from "falling."

**5. What falls off, drops, or sheds.** A cluster of concrete items, all explicitly traced to سُقُوط:
- سَقَط النار (also سِقَط, سُقَط): the sparks that fall between the two fire-sticks before the fire properly catches — also used proverbially.
- سَقَط الرمل (also مَسْقِط): where the bulk of a sand-mass ends and thins out; here مَسْقِط is one of the anomalous forms, with the regular مَسْقَط also attested.
- سُقَاطة النخل: unripe dates that drop from the palm.
- سَقِيط السحاب: hail. السَّقِيط: hoar-frost — a Ṭayyiʾ dialect word.
- سَقِيط الندى: dew fallen onto the ground.
- السَّقَط / السُّقَاطة: whatever has dropped off a thing.

**6. Low-value things (fallen in worth).** سَقَط البيت is household junk and oddments, so called because it ranks beneath the good furnishings (plural أَسْقَاط). By metaphor, أَسْقَاط الناس (reported from al-Liḥyānī) means the rabble. سَقَط الطعام is the worthless part of food — or, on another view, what falls from it. السَّقَط is also small retail goods such as spices, because their value is "fallen"; the dealer is a سَقَّاط.

**7. Passing back and forth, arriving.** سَاقَطَه الحديثَ: talk falls from you to him and from him to you — an exchange of conversation. سَقَطَ إلى قوم is to drop in on people; in the account of the Negus and Abū Simāl, "Abū Simāl فسَقَطَ إلى جيران له" means he came to some neighbours, who sheltered and hid him. Of heat, سَقَطَ الحرُّ is a euphemism for the heat coming down and settling, illustrated by a verse of al-Nābigha al-Jaʿdī about wild animals huddling in the shade. Ibn Sīda notes, on Ibn al-Aʿrābī's authority, that سَقَطَ عنك الحرُّ means the opposite — the heat lifted — "as if" the word were a contronym.

**8. Error and slipping in speech.** السَّقَط and السِّقَاط denote a mistake in speaking, in arithmetic, and in writing. سَقَطَ في كلامه = he erred in what he said; "he spoke and did not let a single word fall wrong" is the idiom for flawless speech. تَسَقَّطَه / اسْتَسْقَطَه = to work on someone so he slips into error, or lies, or blurts out what he is holding back; a verse has slanderers trying to trip the speaker into revealing a secret and finding him tight-lipped.

**9. The Qur'anic idiom سُقِطَ في أيديهم.** Ibn Sīda first gives the general sense "he slipped and erred," then cites Q 7:149, "and when it was made to fall into their hands, and they saw that they had gone astray." He reports two accounts: (a) al-Fārisī takes it as striking one's palms on one's hands out of regret — and adds that if that reading is sound, the expression does come from "falling"; (b) an alternative reading with the active verb سَقَطَ, i.e. regret fell into their hands. On this second view the idiom is a figure: just as one says of a person who acquires something intangible "something hateful has come into his hand," so what arises in the heart and soul is likened to what is held in the hand and seen with the eye.

**10. Deficiency in persons.** السَّقَط can mean public disgrace. السَّاقِطة and السَّقِيط (the latter form from al-Zajjājī; feminine سَقِيطة) mean weak-minded, deficient in intellect. السَّاقِط is the man who lags behind others.

**11. Specialised usages.**
- سَاقَطَ الفرسُ العَدْوَ: the horse ran slackly, loose-limbed.
- السَّوَاقِط: people who come down to al-Yamāma to obtain dates; السِّقَاط is the dates they carry off.
- سيفٌ سَقَّاطٌ وراء الضريبة: a sword that carries through past what it strikes; Ibn al-Aʿrābī describes it as one that keeps cutting until it reaches the ground.

**12. Edges and extremities.** سَقْط السحاب is the fringe of a cloud; سَقْطا الخِباء are the two sides of a tent; and a bird's two wings are its سَقْطان, سِقَاطان, or مَسْقَطان.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats s-q-f as a single root whose core idea is height that overlooks something, together with a bending or arching over it.

1. **saqf** — the roof of a house. He derives the name from the core idea: it is high and overhangs what lies below.

2. **saqīfa** — (a) a roofed portico or covered shelter (ṣuffa); (b) more generally, any broad plank or board in a building that projects out from a wall.

3. **The sky as a "roof."** He applies the same word to the sky, citing Q 21:32, "And We made the sky a guarded roof."

4. **asqaf** — used of a man: tall and stooping/bent over, i.e. height combined with a curve, matching the root idea. He gives the idiom asqafu bayyinu al-saqaf ("clearly stooped-tall"), where al-saqaf is the abstract noun for that quality.

The entry closes with the customary formula "and God knows best what is correct."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris states that the root s-q-m has a single core meaning: illness/sickness (al-maraḍ).

He notes that the noun for this is said in three dialectal forms, all synonymous: suqm, saqam, and saqām.
