quran_words: سَقَىٰ 12x "watered"; أَسْقَيْ 8x "surely we (would) have given them to drink"; ٱسْتَسْقَىٰ 2x "asked (for) water"; سِقَايَة 2x "the providing of water"; سُقْيَٰ 1x "and her drink"
poets_named: Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); Ibn Aḥmar (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root s-q-y (sīn + qāf + weak final letter) as a single core idea: giving a thing water — or the like — to drink.

1. Core verb: سَقَى / أَسْقَى = "to give (someone) drink" or "to appoint someone a supply of water." The verbal noun is السُّقْي. Idiom: كَمْ سِقْيُ أَرْضِكَ = "how much is your land's watering," i.e. its share of water.

2. أَسْقَيْتُكَ هَذَا الْجِلْدَ = "I gave you this hide" — specifically, gifted so you can make a waterskin from it.

3. سَقَيْتُ عَلَى فُلَانٍ = to invoke over someone the blessing سَقَاهُ اللَّهُ ("may God give him rain/drink"); reported from al-Akhfash.

4. السِّقَايَة: (a) the place at the pilgrimage season where drink is dispensed; (b) الصُّوَاع, the drinking-cup — as in Q 12:70, "he placed the siqāya in his brother's saddlebag," the king's own drinking vessel.

5. سَقَى بَطْنُ فُلَانٍ = the belly became dropsical, filling with a yellow fluid.

6. سَقَى عَلَى فُلَانٍ بِمَا يَكْرَهُ = to ply/pester someone with what he dislikes, by repeating it on him.

7. السَّقِيّ (pattern faʿīl): (a) papyrus/reed — cited from Imruʾ al-Qays, "a shank like the tube of the well-tended papyrus reed"; (b) a cloud of large raindrops.

8. السِّقَاء = the (well-known) waterskin. Figuratively أَسْقَيْتُ الرَّجُلَ = "I backbit the man" — cited from Ibn Aḥmar: "nor do I 'water my waterskin' against any whom I have opposed."

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: سَرِيع 10x "(is) swift"; يُسَٰرِعُ 9x "hasten"; أَسْرَع 2x "(is) swiftest"; سِرَاع 2x "rapidly"
poets_named: unnamed verse ×2; Mālik b. Zaghba al-Bāhilī (pre-Islamic); Bishr (pre-Islamic); ʿUmar b. Abī Rabīʿa (Umayyad)
text:
Root س ر ع (s-r-ʿ), also cross-listed under سير. Al-Zamakhsharī, arranging by literal then figurative usage, records:

1. Core sense — swiftness. سريع = "swift": "he came swiftly"; "a swift horse," plural "swift horses" (سراع). Proverb: "How are the slow to overtake the swift, the short-paced the wide-striding?"

2. The verb and its forms. سرُع إلى الأمر = "he was quick to a matter," with the verbal nouns saraʿa / surʿan / surʿa ("swiftness"). أسرع المشي = "he hastened his walking"; "he was quick to see to what mattered." Form III/VI: يسارعون / يتسارعون = "they vie and race toward the good" — cited with the Qur'ānic wording «أولئك يسارعون في الخيرات» ("those race in good deeds"). Form V يتسرّع can carry a negative edge: "he rushes headlong into evil."

3. The exclamative سرعان ("how quickly!"). "How quickly you came!" — paired with the synonyms لوشكان and لعجلان. Al-Kisāʾī reports three vowellings (sarʿān / surʿān / sirʿān). Proverb of ill-considered haste: "How quickly this [turned] to dripping-fat!" A cited verse: "Do you make oration among them after slaying their men? How swift is this, while the blood still streams!" A shorter form سرُع (without the -ān) also occurs, the base being سرُع — with a verse by Mālik b. Zaghba al-Bāhilī on aversion arriving "so soon" while the bond of union frays.

4. سُرعان الناس = "the vanguard of the people": their foremost, those who race ahead to a thing.

5. أُسروع, plural أساريع — sand-grubs/larvae, used as a beauty-image for slender fingers: "as though her fingers were grubs"; with a verse (recited to him by his father) likening a woman's fingers to "the grubs of the shifting dunes," and the phrase "her neck a gazelle's neck, her fingers a gazelle's grubs."

6. Figurative extensions of أساريع (streaks/lines, from the grub's markings):
 - Of a bow: قوس ذات أساريع = a bow with streaks and lines along it (verse of Bishr on a nabʿ-wood bow with a yellow tinge in its streaks).
 - Of teeth/mouth: ثغر ذو أساريع = a mouth with ẓalm, the water-like lustre on teeth (verse of ʿUmar b. Abī Rabīʿa) — where asārīʿ means the glistening enamel-streaks.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سَرِّحُ 3x "release them"; سَرَاح 2x "(with) a release"; تَسْرِيح 1x "to release (her)"; تَسْرَحُ 1x "you take them out"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats س-ر-ح (s-r-ḥ) as a single consistent root whose core idea is going forth freely, moving off without being held back (al-inṭilāq). He then arranges the vocabulary under that core:

1. Unimpeded action — أَمْرٌ سَرِيحٌ (amr sarīḥ): a matter with no obstruction and no stalling in it.

2. Releasing a wife — السَّرَاح (al-sarāḥ) is glossed by him as ṭalāq (divorce); سَرَّحْتُ الْمَرْأَةَ = "I let the woman go." He cites Q 2:231, {أَوْ سَرِّحُوهُنَّ بِمَعْرُوفٍ} ("or release them in a fitting manner"). He presents this sense as carried over from the base idea of letting go / setting free.

3. Speed — السُّرُح (al-suruḥ): the fast she-camel.

4. Stripped bare — الْمُنْسَرِح (al-munsariḥ): one who is naked, having come out of his clothes.

5. Grazing herds — السَّرْح (al-sarḥ): livestock turned out to pasture. السَّارِح (al-sāriḥ): the herdsman — or, on another report he mentions, the man who owns such pasturing stock.

6. The great tree — السَّرْحَة (al-sarḥah). Ibn Fāris flags this as possibly anomalous (shādhdh) to the root, but offers a way to keep it inside: the tree may be so called because its branches spread and run off in every direction (inṣirāḥ). He supports the word with a line of ʿAntara describing a champion whose garments hang as if on a sarḥah-tree, shod in sandals of tanned hairless leather, "no twin" — i.e. unmatched.

7. The wolf — السِّرْحَان (al-sirḥān), so named because it ranges freely after what it hunts; the lion too, when called sirḥān.

8. A cut of cloth — السَّرِيحَة (al-sarīḥah): a strip or piece of fabric.

Method note: the entry is built on Ibn Fāris's usual procedure of positing one semantic core and then showing each derivative as an application of it, explicitly marking the one item (the tree) that resists the scheme and proposing a motivated bridge for it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سَرَاب 2x "(are) like a mirage"; سَارِب 1x "or goes freely"; سَرَب 1x "slipping away"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats س-ر-ب as a single consistent root meaning breadth/spaciousness and moving out freely across the land. He then derives each usage from that one sense.

1. سِرْب / سُرْبَة (sirb, surba) — a herd of gazelles or sheep, so named because it spreads out over the ground grazing. By extension, sirb is used of a group of women.

2. سَرْب (sarb, with fatḥa) — originally used of camels. Hence the Arabs' formula to a divorced woman: "Go; I will not drive back your sarb" — i.e. I will not turn your camels back; let them go where they will. Here sirb means grazing livestock/property.

3. Path or way. Abū Zayd: khalli sirbahu, "leave him his road," let him go where he wishes. Also vocalised sirb with kasra. Shāhid: Dhū al-Rumma, "He left free for her the sirb of her foremost ones," where sirb is glossed as the road. Also: the wild animal "went off along its track" (insaraba... fī sirbihi).

4. سَرَب / سَرِب (sarab, sarib) — water leaking or flowing from a water-skin; verb sariba, sarab-an. Shāhid: Dhū al-Rumma, "What ails your eye that water pours from it, as though it were a leak from the split seams of a water-skin" — the word is read both with fatḥa and with kasra on the rāʾ.

5. سَرَّبْتُ الْقِرْبَةَ — to fill a water-skin until the stitching swells and closes. Related: سَرْب (sarb) = the stitch-hole, because water seeps out through it.

6. سَارِب (sārib) — one going forth openly in the land; verb sarabа, surūb-an. Qur'anic citation: "and one going forth by day" (13:10). Poetic shāhid: "How is it you went forth, when you were not one to go forth — and dreams bring near what is not near."

7. مَسْرَبَة (masraba) — the line of hair down the middle of the chest, so called because it seems to flow and run down the chest.

8. Idioms: آمِنٌ فِي سِرْبِهِ (with kasra) is explained by others as "secure in himself"; Ibn Fāris accepts this but notes an ellipsis — his self is secure wherever he goes about. Likewise وَاسِعُ السِّرْبِ, "wide of sirb," i.e. wide of chest, said of someone slow to anger. He ties this back to his root-sense: anger does not seize such a man so that he grows agitated and his outlets are blocked.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text: Root: s-r-b-l (سربل). 1. Core meaning: sirbal is defined simply as qamis, a shirt or garment/tunic, and al-Raghib notes this applies to any kind or material of garment. 2. Quranic citations: 14:50 (Ibrahim), their garments are of tar/pitch, describing the covering of the wrongdoers in the Fire. 16:81 (al-Nahl), garments that protect you from heat, and garments that protect you from your violence - al-Raghib glosses the second phrase specifically as garments that protect some of you from the violence/harm of others, i.e. armor worn in conflict, distinct from ordinary clothing worn against heat.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root س ر د (s-r-d), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One regular, analogically-sound core meaning: the succession of many things, each connected to the next.

1. al-sard — a collective term for chainmail and similar ring-linked work. The entry's central Qur'anic citation is Saba' 34:11, regarding David: "wa qaddir fī al-sard" — "and measure precisely in the link-work" — glossed as ensuring the proportion between rivet and hole is exact, neither too tight nor too loose. al-zarrād (armorer) is explained as properly al-sarrād, with a recognized sound-shift between rā' and zāy. al-misrad — the awl, its derivation from this root judged sound.
2. Our source then runs in Ibn Fāris's separate chapter for the whole letter sīn on words of more than three letters, where he surveys a long series of words he analyzes as "blends" (naḥt) or augmented forms built from this and other roots, each explicitly marked as a derived/compound formation rather than a core sense: al-musmaqirr (a scorchingly hot day, from saqarāt); al-saḥbal (a wide valley or waterskin, blended from saḥala/sabala/saḥaba); al-samādīr (weak eyesight, from al-sadar with an added mīm); a horse called surḥūb (swift, blended from saraḥa/saraba); a she-camel called sirdāḥ (swift, excellent, from saraḥat with an added dāl); islanṭaḥa (to spread out widely, from saṭaḥa with added lām/nūn); ismahadda (a hump grown full and soft, blended from mahada, illustrated with a line of poetry); al-samharīyyah (hard spears, from al-sumrah with an added hāʾ); al-muslahibb (a tall person, from al-salib with an added hāʾ); islahamma (a change of color, from suhām with an added lām); al-samlaq (an ill-natured old woman, from al-silqah with an added mīm); al-sirṭim (wide-throated, from saraṭa with an added mīm); al-sarmad (perpetual/eternal, from sarada "to connect" with an added mīm — as though time were linked together, one part joined to the next); and isbaghalla (to become soaked, from al-subūgh with an added lām).
3. Closing: words Ibn Fāris identifies as simply coined, with no clear derivational logic — al-sinnawr (the cat), al-sanawwar (worn armor/weaponry), al-salqaʿ (rugged terrain), and al-salfaʿ (a loud, clamorous woman, or, of men, a bold and daring one) — illustrated with two lines of poetry, one describing a bold warrior, one describing a bold woman.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
text:
Root srdq (سردق), Murtada al-Zabidi, Taj al-'Arus fi Jawahir al-Qamus

1. al-suradiq (السرادق) -- the entry's central noun: a covering/awning stretched over a house's courtyard, or more broadly (per Ibn al-Athir) anything -- wall, enclosure, or tent -- that surrounds something. Identified as an Arabicized Persian loanword (from saradar/saratag), per al-Jawaliqi.
2. Central Qur'anic citation: Qur'an 18:29 -- {أَحَاطَ بِهِمْ سُرَادِقُهَا}, describing the Fire prepared for wrongdoers, "whose pavilion/walls will encompass them." Al-Zajjaj glosses this as a punishment that will come to enclose them on every side.
3. Also attested (per al-Jawhari): a tent made of cotton (kursuf), illustrated by a verse addressed to Hakam ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Jarud ("the pavilion of glory is stretched over you").
4. Secondary senses (tropical): rising dust, or towering encircling smoke, illustrated by a verse of Labid describing wild asses kicking up dust.
5. baytun musardaqun -- a tent fully secured/bound top and bottom, illustrated by verses on the Persian king's killing of al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir under elephants.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مُسْرِف 15x "the transgressors"; أَسْرَفَ 6x "be extravagant"; إِسْرَاف 2x "and our excesses"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives س-ر-ف from a single core idea: exceeding the limit, and also neglecting/overlooking a thing.

1. Going beyond the due measure. فِي الْأَمْرِ سَرَفٌ = "there is excess in the matter," i.e. going past the proper amount. Cited: a ḥadīth that the third washing in ablution is "honor" (sharaf) but the fourth is "excess" (sarаf).

2. Heedlessness / overlooking. سَرِفْتُكُمْ = "I passed by you and took no notice of you." Verse of Jarīr: praising givers whose gift carries "neither reproach nor sarаf" (no heedless neglect).

3. Ignorance. السَّرَف can mean ignorance, and السَّرِف the ignorant man — proven by Ṭarafa's line about "a man ignorant of heart (sarif al-fuʾād)" who mistakes insults for sweetness. Ibn Fāris notes this reduces to the earlier senses; the root's logic is one.

4. Avid craving / addiction (ḍarāwa). السَّرَف can also mean a compulsive craving, as in the ḥadīth that "meat has a sarаf like the sarаf of wine." He observes this too is not far from the primary sense.

Anomalous (outside the main root-logic): السُّرْفَة (al-surfa) is a small wood-eating creature; سَرَفَتِ الشَّجَرَةَ = "it gnawed the tree's leaves," leaving the tree masrūfa (gnawed). It is said to build itself a fine little house, whence the proverb أَصْنَعُ مِنْ سُرْفَةٍ ("a more skillful maker than a surfa").

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats س-ر-ج as one sound root whose core idea is beauty, adornment and comeliness.

1. السِّرَاج (sirāj), a lamp — named from this root because of its light and its beauty.
2. السَّرْج (sarj), a saddle placed on a mount — because it is the animal's adornment.
3. The verb سَرَّجَ وَجْهَهُ — "he beautified his face," as though he made it like a lamp for him. He cites the poetic line: "and [hair] jet-black, and a nose-bridge made lamp-like" (وفاحماً ومَرْسِناً مُسَرَّجاً), where مُسَرَّج describes a nose given a lamp-like gleam or fineness.
4. Marked as an anomaly (shādhdh) outside this sense: سُرْجُوجَةٌ, used for a way or manner of doing something.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī glosses سَرْمَد (sarmad) simply as "the continuous/unceasing" (al-dāʾim) — something that goes on without end or interruption.

He supports this with the two Qur'anic occurrences of the word, both in Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ, where God asks what people would do if He made the night unceasing (28:71) and, in the very next verse, if He made the day unceasing (28:72) — night or day continuing without the relief of its opposite.

The entry is very brief: one gloss plus its two Qur'anic citations, with no further grammatical or etymological discussion given.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سَرَقَ 4x "has stolen"; سَّارِق 3x "thieves"; سَّارِقَة 1x "and the female thief"; ٱسْتَرَقَ 1x "steals"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats س-ر-ق as a single root whose core sense is: taking something in concealment and under cover.

1. **Core sense — taking by stealth.** The verb runs سَرَقَ / يَسْرِقُ with the verbal noun سَرِقَة (sariqa): to take a thing secretly. The defining element in his gloss is not the taking as such but that it is done hidden and covered over.

2. **The thing taken.** What is taken in this way (المسروق) is itself called سَرَق (saraq).

3. **Extension to listening — استرق السمع.** The idiom "to steal hearing" is used of someone who listens in while keeping himself out of sight. This shows the root applied beyond property: the concealment of the listener is what makes it a "stealing."

4. **An outlier sense.** Ibn Fāris flags one usage as anomalous to (not derivable from) this root-meaning: سَرَق as the plural of سَرَقَة, meaning a piece of silk. He records it without attempting to tie it back to the sense of concealed taking.

Method note: this is Ibn Fāris's characteristic procedure — state one governing sense for the letter-set, list the derivations that follow from it, then explicitly separate out any usage that does not.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَسَرَّ 18x "they conceal"; سِرّ 11x "secretly"; سُرُر 6x "thrones"; سَّرَّاء 2x "[the] ease"; إِسْرَار 2x "their secrets"; مَسْرُور 2x "happy"; تَسُرُّ 1x "pleasing"; سُرُور 1x "and happiness"; سَّرَائِر 1x "the secrets"
poets_named: Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse ×4; Al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); Dhū l-Iṣbaʿ (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats s-r-r as gathering its branches under the concealing of a thing, and under a thing's pure part and settled place. He says nothing in the root falls outside these. He arranges the article under three headings: concealment, purity, and settling.

**1. Concealment**

- **Secret.** Al-sirr is the opposite of open declaration. Asrartu al-shayʾ means "I kept the thing secret," the opposite of aʿlantuhu, "I declared it."
- **Sexual union.** Al-sirr also means al-nikāḥ, sexual union, so called because it is not done openly.
- **The hidden moon.** Al-sirār or al-sarār is the night the new moon is hidden: one night, or two when the month is complete. A ḥadīth has a man asked whether he fasted anything of "the sirār of the month," and being told to fast two days after Ramaḍān. A raiding verse speaks of attacking "on the evening of the new moon or its sirār."
- **The knowing man.** Al-sursūr is a learned, astute man. Ibn Fāris derives it from al-sirr, "as though he had seen into the secrets of affairs."

**The disputed "disclose" sense.** Abū ʿUbayda held that asrartu can mean both "I concealed" and "I made public." He read "and they asarrū their remorse when they saw the punishment" (Q 10:54; Ibn Fāris gives the reference as Yūnus 54) as "they showed it." He cited a half-line of Imruʾ al-Qays, "if they would yusirrūna my killing," as "make it public." Ibn Fāris then reports al-Farrāʾ's rebuttal. Al-Farrāʾ says Abū ʿUbayda got the interpretation wrong: asarrū al-nadāma means they concealed their remorse, for fear of gloating. He also says Abū ʿUbayda misread the verse: Imruʾ al-Qays wrote yushirrūna, with shīn, from ashrartu, "to lay out in the open," as in spreading meat out in the sun. Ibn Fāris says this word is treated under its own root.

**2. The pure or best part of a thing**

- Al-sirr is the pure part of a thing. From it comes **al-surūr, gladness**, "because it is a state free of sorrow."
- **Navel.** Al-surra is the navel, the pure and soft part of the body. Of a newborn, the sarar or sirar is the part that is cut off and the surra is what remains; the plural is asirra.
- **Best of a valley.** Sarārat al-wādī and sirr al-wādī are the best part of a valley. A verse mocks horsemen as shrubs swaying in the sarāra of a valley. Ibn Fāris explains the image: they look impressive but have nothing within.
- **Hollowness.** Al-sarar is an ailment in a camel's navel (such a camel is asarr). Al-sarr is repairing a fire-stick that has become asarr, "hollow": "repair your fire-stick, for it is hollow." A qanāt sarrāʾ is a hollow spear-shaft. Ibn Fāris traces all of these to the navel.
- **Lines and creases.** Al-asārīr, the creases of the forehead, are named by analogy with the creases of the navel. A ḥadīth describes the Prophet coming in to ʿĀʾisha "with the lines of his face shining." Al-asrār (singular sirr) are the lines on the inside of the palm. Abū Zayd names one such line al-sirar. Al-Aʿshā has "look at a hand and its lines." Ibn Fāris says the origin of all these is one.
- **Plant tips.** The tips of sweet basil may be called surūr "because they are the moistest and most tender thing in it," as in the verse about papyrus "when the water has mingled with its surūr."
- **Best of lineage.** Sirr al-nasab is the purest and best of lineage. Dhū l-Iṣbaʿ speaks of noble offspring "through the unmixed sirr of lineage."

**3. Settling**

- **Couch.** Al-sarīr is a couch, plural surur and asirra.
- **Ease.** Al-sarīr is also ease of life, "because a person settles in it and in its comfort."
- **Seat of the head.** Sarīr al-raʾs is where the head rests: "a blow that removes the head from its sarīr." Some read al-Aʿshā's papyrus verse with sarīr, which then means the plant's base on which it rests. Another verse speaks of an ample life whose sarīr "would pass away."
- **Sand on a hillock.** Al-sarīr is also the sand lying on a hillock.

**Al-surriyya**

Ibn Fāris reports several authorities on this word. According to al-Khalīl, it has the pattern fuʿliyya. Both yutasarraru and yatasarrā are said, but al-Khalīl calls yatasarrā an error; Ibn Fāris notes that al-Khalīl said no more than this. Al-Aṣmaʿī derives al-surriyya from al-sirr in the sense of sexual union, "because her owner chose her for union and not for trading in her," and Ibn al-Sikkīt records the same in his book. Ibn Fāris explains the u-vowel on the sīn as a common change in relative adjectives: sahl (soft ground) gives suhlī, and dahr (long time) gives duhrī.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
quran_words: أَسْرَىٰ 6x "travel by night"; سَرِيّ 1x "a stream"; يَسْرِ 1x "it passes"
poets_named: Labīd (lived into Islam) ×2; Ḥassān b. Thābit (lived into Islam); Nābigha (pre-Islamic); Kaʿb (lived into Islam); al-Farazdaq (Umayyad); Zuhayr (pre-Islamic); al-Ḥārith b. Waʿla (pre-Islamic)
text:
**Root س ر ي (s-r-y) — Tāj al-ʿArūs of al-Zabīdī (d. 1791 CE)**

**1. Core sense: travelling by night.** السُّرَى (al-surā), formed like الهُدَى, is night-travel. Al-Zabīdī's headword says it covers the *whole* night, not part of it — correcting al-Fanārī — but he then reports Abū Zayd (via al-Miṣbāḥ) that it may fall at the night's beginning, middle or end, and al-Muḥkam's looser "travelling by night generally," and concludes that al-Fanārī's view is defensible after all. The word is normally feminine; al-Liḥyānī knew only the feminine. Labīd's line "the night-journey has grown long" uses a masculine verb, evidence for masculine treatment; Ibn Sīdah suggests instead that the feminine ending was simply dropped because the word is not truly feminine.

**2. Verb forms.** سَرَى / يَسْرِي, with verbal nouns سُرًى, مَسْرًى, سَرْيَة (also سُرْيَة with ḍamma) and سِرايَة. Al-Fayyūmī notes the fatḥa form is the more specific; al-Ṣiḥāḥ gives "we made one night-journey" and treats سِرايَة as a verbal noun on an unusually plural-looking pattern — which, al-Ṣiḥāḥ adds, is why Banū Asad wrongly feminize السُّرَى and الهُدَى, taking them for plurals.

**3. أَسْرَى / اسْتَرَى.** أَسْرَى (verbal noun إسْراء) means the same as سَرَى; the alif-form is Ḥijāzī, and the Qurʾān uses both: "travel by night with your family," "and the night when it travels on," "glory to Him who made [him] travel by night." Ḥassān b. Thābit's verse pairs both forms of the verb. اسْتَرَى is a further equivalent, attested in a Hudhalī verse and one by Kuthayyir. All are made transitive with the preposition بـ: سَرَى بِهِ / أَسْراهُ / أَسْرَى بِهِ.

**4. The phrase "asrā bi-ʿabdihi laylan" (Q 17:1).** Since night-travel is by definition nocturnal, al-Zabīdī records three explanations of the added word "by night": (a) al-Ṣiḥāḥ — it is emphasis, like saying "I travelled yesterday, by day"; (b) al-Tahdhīb — the verb here means simply "He made him travel"; (c) ʿAlam al-Dīn al-Sakhāwī, in his tafsīr — the distance would ordinarily take at least forty days, so "in a night" is the point of wonder; and the indefinite لَيْل rather than لَيْلَة was used because "he travelled a night" usually implies the whole night was consumed by travel. Al-Rāghib derived أَسْرَى instead from السَّراة, "broad open land" (originally wāw-rooted), on the pattern of أَجْبَل / أَتْهَم — "he took him into a broad tract"; al-Zabīdī calls this derivation odd.

**5. Derivatives of night-travel.**
- السَّرَّاء (intensive pattern): one who travels much by night (from al-Azharī).
- السَّارِيَة: a cloud that moves by night (Nābigha's verse); said also to be the cloud between the morning and evening cloud; al-Liḥyānī: the rain that falls at night (Kaʿb's verse). Plural سَوارٍ.
- السُّراة / السَّراة: plural of السَّارِي, night-travellers — "they said, 'the night-travellers of the jinn.'"
- السارِيات: wild asses, because they graze at night (a line of al-Farazdaq lampooning Jarīr).
- السَّارِي, المُسارِي, المُسْتَرِي: the lion, from its travelling by night. السَّارِي is also a place-name.
- Proverbs of extreme night-travel: "a greater night-traveller than a hedgehog," since the hedgehog travels all night without sleep.

**6. السَّارِيَة, "pillar."** A column or pier — of stone or baked brick, per the author of al-Bāriʿ; plural السَّوارِي. (Given without an explicit link to the travel sense.)

**7. السَّرِيَّة, a raiding detachment.** Pattern faʿīlah with active sense, so named because it moves stealthily by night so the enemy is not alerted. Size: five men up to three hundred, or of cavalry about four hundred; al-Nihāya caps it at four hundred; al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "the best detachment is four hundred men." Fatḥ al-Bārī grades: 100–500 = sariyyah; more = مِنْسَر; over 800 = جَيْش; over 4,000 = جَيْش جَرَّار. Plurals سَرايا, سَرِيَّات. Al-Nihāya gives an alternative etymology — from السَّرِيّ, "precious," since they are the pick of the troops — and rejects derivation from سِرّ ("secretly") on the formal ground that سِرّ ends in rāʾ, not yāʾ. Related: سَرَّى (تَسْرِيَة), of a commander dispatching such a detachment against the enemy by night; المُتَسَرِّي, one who goes out in it (Ibn al-Athīr); and figuratively سارَ بالسَّرِيَّة, "he followed a noble course of conduct."

**8. A textual correction.** The dictionary lists "a small, short, rounded arrowhead without breadth, sometimes lying under the ground" as though it were another sense of سَرِيَّة. Al-Zabīdī says this is an error: the correct form is السِّرْية with kasra and light yāʾ (per al-Muḥkam), whose yāʾ may originally be wāw, since السِّرْوة is also said; al-Aṣmaʿī, in al-Takmila, gives السِّرْية as a variant of السِّرْوة among arrowheads. He judges the author's wording defective.

**9. Sense of creeping / spreading.** سَرَى عِرْقُ الشَّجَرِ — a tree-root creeps along under the ground (Ibn Sīdah, al-Azharī). سَرَى مَتاعَهُ — he threw his baggage onto his mount's back (Ibn Sīdah).

**10. السَّرِيّ, a watercourse.** Thaʿlab: a river. Ibn ʿAbbās and the lexicographers: a rivulet — a small stream running to palm trees (Labīd's verse describing palms on a stream). By this Q 19:24 is explained, "your Lord has placed beneath you a sariyy." Plurals أَسْرِيَة and سُرْيان; al-Jawharī notes أَسْرِياء is not attested.

**11. السَّراء**: a tree whose wood is used for bows; singulative سَراءة; Zuhayr's line likens wild she-asses to "bows of sarāʾ-wood."

**12. السَّراة, "the highest part."** Of anything — hence سَراةُ النَّهار (the day's height) and سَراةُ الجَبَل (a mountain's crest). Copies of al-Ṣiḥāḥ read "the middle of the day," which al-Zabīdī reports has been corrected to "the highest part." As a proper name, al-Sarāt is a mountain chain beginning near ʿArafāt and running to Najrān in Yemen (al-Fayyūmī) — the mountain of Azd — with many named stretches: the Sarāt of Bajīla, Zahrān, ʿAnz, al-Ḥijr, Banū al-Qarn, Banū Shabāna, al-Maʿāfir, al-Kurāʿ, Banū Sayf, Khatlān, Alhān, al-Maṣāniʿ, Qudum, Hatūm, and of al-Ṭāʾif (whose lowland is Mecca and whose highland is Hawāzin country). The nisba is سَرَوِيّ; al-Dīnawarī often cites "the Sarawīs" in his Book of Plants. From this: أَسْرَى, "he went to al-Sarāt," on the model of أَنْجَد, أَتْهَم. Al-Sarāt is also a city in Adharbayjān settled by people of Kinda, and السَّرا is a gate of Herat.

**13. Metaphorical extension (via al-Miṣbāḥ).** The Arabs applied سرى to non-physical things by likening them to bodies: poison or wine "courses" through a man (al-Fārābī); a bad hereditary strain "runs" in a person (al-Sarqusṭī); anxiety "comes upon" someone by night, or "departs" (Ibn al-Qaṭṭāʿ). Jurists say سَرَى الجُرْحُ إلى النَّفْسِ — the wound's effect continued until death resulted; a severed hand whose injury "spreads" to the forearm; and سَرَى التَّحْرِيم / سَرَى العِتْق for a ruling extending beyond its immediate object. Al-Miṣbāḥ notes these juristic usages are not in the famous lexica but are consistent with the attested pattern. Al-Muḥkam adds that السُّرَى itself was borrowed for calamities, wars and anxieties — al-Ḥārith b. Waʿla on war: "it travels by night while its people sleep, and comes upon what does not occur to the imagination." The prevailing verbal nouns for these extended uses are السِّرايَة and السَّرَيان.

**14. Sense of uncovering / stripping.** سَرَى عَنِّي الثَّوْبَ, "he removed the garment from me" — the wāw-rooted form is more standard (al-Muḥkam); al-Tahdhīb gives سَرَيْتُ / سَرَّيْتُ الثَّوْبَ, "you stripped it off." Also سُرِّي عنه, "it was lifted and removed from him," the doubled form being intensive; and سَرَّى العَرَقَ عن بَدَنِهِ, made sweat exude from the body.

**15. Miscellaneous.** السِّرْية (kasra) is also the locust grub (al-Jawharī). "He came the morning after a sāriyah" means after a rainy night. السارِيَة is likewise a mountain in Fārs, and (per al-Rāghib) a company travelling by night.

**16. Names and places recorded under the root.** Sāriya, a town in Ṭabaristān (Sārī of Māzandarān), whence Bundār b. al-Khalīl al-Sarawī. Sāriya b. Zunaym al-Kinānī — the man ʿUmar is reported to have called to from the pulpit ("O Sāriya, the mountain!") while he was campaigning at Nahāwand, who heard him and withdrew to the mountain; al-Zabīdī notes Ibn Saʿd and Abū Mūsā record no evidence he was a Companion, while Ibn Ḥibbān lists him among trustworthy Successors, and that the manuscripts' description of him (حَصْراً, "most constrained") is probably حَضْراً, "swiftest runner." Others omitted by the author: Sāriya b. Awfā, Sāriya b. ʿAmr al-Ḥanafī (Khālid b. al-Walīd's companion), Sāriya b. Maslama al-Ḥanafī, and the Successor Sāriya b. ʿAbd Allāh. Al-Sarī al-Saqaṭī (al-Sarī b. al-Mughallis), the ascetic, associate of Maʿrūf al-Karkhī and uncle of al-Junayd, plus other men named al-Sarī. Ghanm b. Suray in Khazraj lineage, ancestor of the Companion Ṭalḥa b. al-Barāʾ; another Suray in Banū Ḥanīfa, ancestor of the poet al-Baʿīth. The Suwayriyyāt / al-Sawārī, i.e. Banū ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Bakr b. Kilāb, mentioned by Labīd — Ibn Sīdah assigns the name to yāʾ because the letter is a final radical. The poet Ibn Isrāʾīl, Najm al-Dīn Muḥammad b. Sawwār al-Dimashqī (b. 603, d. 677). Places: Siryā near Basra (proverbial for its gnats) and another Siryā in eastern Egypt; Siryāqūs in Egypt's Sharqiyya with a famous khānqāh — which al-Zabīdī argues is not سِرْيا + قُوس but سِرْ (imperative of سارَ) + قَوْس, and belongs in the sīn chapter; and al-Surayyah, a village in the Syrian lowlands.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: س-ت-ر (s-t-r), from Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha (d. 1004 CE).

Core sense: the three letters s-t-r point to one idea — covering. Ibn Fāris gives the base verb: satartu al-shayʾa satran, "I covered the thing."

1. سُتْرَة (sutrah) — anything at all that you conceal or screen yourself with; a covering/screen of whatever kind.
2. سِتَار (sitār) — used the same way, i.e. a curtain or veil.
3. إِسْتَار (istār), as in the phrase "istār al-Kaʿbah" — here Ibn Fāris records two competing explanations:
   - His own preferred view: it still comes from sitr/"covering" — meaning the cloth drapery that covers the Kaʿbah.
   - A view he attributes to "some people": the word here has nothing to do with clothing, but instead means "the number four" — they claim Arabs used al-istār as a word for a group of four. As evidence they cite two lines of poetry that use istār to mean a disreputable foursome of people: one by al-Akhṭal (about himself, two sons of Juʿayl, and their mother) and one by Jarīr (mocking al-Farazdaq, al-Baʿīth, and their parents).
   - On that reading, the asṭār (pl.) of the Kaʿbah are said to be its four walls/sides.

Ibn Fāris does not adjudicate between the two explanations decisively — he ends the entry with a hedge: "this is something that has been said, and God knows best its soundness," signaling he is reporting, not certifying, the numerical explanation.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib treats s-t briefly, through two Qur'anic uses of the number six.

1. **Six.** "In six days" (fī sittati ayyām), Q 7:54.

2. **Sixty.** "Sixty poor persons" (sittīna miskīnan), Q 58:4.

3. **Origin.** Al-Rāghib says these words go back to سُدُس (sudus), and he leaves the full treatment to that root's chapter.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats s-w-ʾ as unrelated to the root discussed just before it and assigns it to a single field: ugliness (al-qubḥ).

1. **Ugly.** A man who is aswaʾ, or a woman who is sawʾāʾ, is ugly. He cites the Messenger of God: "An ugly woman who bears children is better than a beautiful woman who is barren."

2. **The bad deed.** This, he says, is why a bad deed is called a sayyiʾah.

3. **The Fire.** The Fire is called al-suwʾā because of its ugly appearance. He cites Q 30:10: "Then the outcome of those who did evil was al-suwʾā."

4. **al-sawʾah al-sawʾāʾ.** A verse of Abū Zubayd, about a man who showed no regard for the sacred right of his drinking-companion, cries out: "O my people, for the foul disgrace (al-sawʾah al-sawʾāʾ)!"

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root س و ع (s-w-ʿ) from a single core idea: the continuance of something and its passing/running on.

1. Core sense — continuous passing. The three letters signify a thing that goes on and moves along.

2. السَّاعَة (al-sāʿa), "the hour," is named from this core idea — a stretch of time that passes and runs on. He cites the usage "he came to us after a sawʿ / suwāʿ of the night," i.e. after a spell of stillness in it.

3. Derived time-expression. Because al-sāʿa means an hour, one says عَامَلْتُهُ مُسَاوَعَةً ("I dealt with him by the hour"), parallel to مُيَاوَمَةً ("by the day").

4. Extension to wandering/straying. From the notion of "passing along," أَسَعْتُ الْإِبِلَ ("I let the camels roam") means leaving them untended to wander off on their own; سَاعَتْ / تَسُوعُ describes that roaming. Hence هُوَ ضَائِعٌ سَائِعٌ ("he is lost and straying"), and نَاقَةٌ مِسْيَاعٌ is a she-camel that strays off in the pasture.

5. Separate concrete sense. السِّيَاع (al-siyāʿ) is clay or mud mixed with straw.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib's short article under ساح moves from open space, to water running across it, to people moving through the land, and then to the Qur'anic word al-sāʾiḥūn.

1. **Open space.** al-sāḥah is a wide, open place, and the courtyard of a house (sāḥat al-dār) is named from it. Q 37:177: "and when it comes down into their courtyard".

2. **Flowing water.** al-sāʾiḥ is water that keeps flowing across an open space.

3. **Roaming the land.** sāḥa fī al-arḍ means to go through the land the way such flowing water goes. Q 9:2: "so move freely about the land for four months". A man who roams the land is sāʾiḥ, or sayyāḥ (a great roamer).

4. **Those who fast.** Al-Rāghib glosses al-sāʾiḥūn (Q 9:112) as al-ṣāʾimūn, "those who fast", and sāʾiḥāt (Q 66:5) as ṣāʾimāt, "women who fast". He then reports one scholar's view that fasting is of two kinds: fasting by legal ruling, which is abstaining from food and sexual relations, and real fasting, which is guarding the bodily organs (hearing, sight, tongue) from acts of disobedience. On this view the sāʾiḥ is the one who keeps the real fast rather than the first kind.

5. **Travelling to reflect.** A further view, introduced with "it was said", takes al-sāʾiḥūn to be those who aim at what Q 22:46 calls for: "Have they not travelled through the land, so that they might have hearts to understand with, or ears to hear with?"

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root س و ط (s-w-ṭ) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: mixing/intermixing one thing with another.

1. Basic sense — to mix. سُطْتُ الشَّيْءَ ("I mixed the thing") = I blended part of it into another part. Similarly سَوَّطَ أَمْرَهُ ("he confounded/mixed up his affair") = he muddled it together. An (unnamed) poet is cited using this sense for someone who "stirs together" a bad, ill-fated plan they can't see through.

2. ال_سَوْط_ (al-sawṭ, "the whip") — derived from the same root because a whip comes into contact with / mingles against the skin when striking. Hence سُطْتُهُ بِالسَّوْطِ, "I struck him with the whip."

3. سَوْط as "a share/portion" (نَصِيب) — Ibn Fāris says this usage also derives from the same root. He cites Qur'an 89:13, {فَصَبَّ عَلَيْهِمْ رَبُّكَ سَوْطَ عَذَابٍ} ("your Lord poured upon them a sawṭ of punishment"), glossing sawṭ here as نَصِيبًا — a share/portion (of the punishment).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سَيِّد 3x "and a noble"; ٱسْوَدَّتْ 2x "turn black"; مُسْوَدّ 2x "dark"; أَسْوَد 1x "[the] black"; سُود 1x "and intensely black"; مُّسْوَدَّة 1x "(will be) blackened"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats س-و-د as having a single origin: blackness, i.e. the opposite of whiteness in colour. Everything else in the chapter, in his account, is carried back to that one sense by extension or derivation. He closes by restating this: "the analogy throughout the whole chapter is one."

1. Colour — blackness. سَوَاد (sawād) as a colour term is, he says, too well known to need explaining. He records a wider view held by some: any colour that is not white counts as falling within the domain of sawād. Verb forms: اسْوَدَّ / سَوَادَّ, "it became black."

2. Bulk, visible form. سَوَادُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ is its شَخْص (shakhṣ) — the body or figure of a thing as it appears. This is the pivot on which several later senses in the entry turn.

3. Secret converse. السِّوَاد (al-siwād) means السِّرَار, confidential talk; سَاوَدَهُ (verbal nouns مُسَاوَدَة and سِوَاد) is "he whispered to him in confidence." Abū ʿUbayd is cited for the derivation: it comes from bringing your sawād (your person) close up against his sawād — i.e. sense 2, two bodies drawn near for private speech. A line of verse is quoted as evidence for this sense: "Whoever may be, in siwād [secret converse], in dad and in ighrām, a zīr — I am no zīr." (The entry cites the line only for siwād and does not gloss its other terms.)

4. Snakes. الْأَسَاوِد is the plural of الْأَسْوَد, meaning snakes. Ibn Fāris then blocks that reading in one attested case: when Abū Dharr said "these asāwid are around me," he did not mean snakes but the visible shapes (sense 2) of the few utensils he owned — a water vessel, a tub and a large bowl, and nothing else.

5. A great multitude. السَّوَاد also denotes a large number of people. His etymology holds it to sense 1: the ground turns black under such a crowd.

6. Lordship (سِيَادَة). He reports two competing accounts and adjudicates between them. Some said سَيِّد (sayyid) means الْحَلِيم, the forbearing man. Others rejected any link with forbearance and derived it instead from sense 2: a man is called sayyid because people take refuge in his sawād, his person. Ibn Fāris judges the second "more consistent with the analogy of the root, and sounder" — consistent with his own governing claim that the whole chapter reduces to one sense. Comparative usage follows: فُلَانٌ أَسْوَدُ مِنْ فُلَانٍ, "so-and-so is more aswad than so-and-so," i.e. higher in lordship.

7. Fixed expressions.
- الْأَسْوَدَانِ, "the two black things": dates and water.
- سَوَادُ الْقَلْبِ / سُوَيْدَاؤُه: the heart's حَبَّة, its kernel or core.

8. Deliberate overlap of the two branches. سَاوَدَنِي فُلَانٌ فَسُدْتُهُ ("he contended with me and I outdid him") is noted as working from sawād of colour and from سُؤْدُد, lordship, at the same time — the two senses being, on his analysis, the same root sense.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib treats s-w-gh as the easy going-down of a drink.

1. **Going down easily.** When a drink sāgha in the throat, it went down easily; asāgha is to make it go down easily. The Qur'an has "easy to swallow (sāʾigh) for those who drink" (Q 16:66) and "he can hardly get it down (yusīghuhu)" (Q 14:17).

2. **Letting someone have something.** Sawwaghtuhu mālan, "I let him have wealth", is a borrowed use of this sense.

3. **Born soon after.** A man is called his brother's سوغ when he is born quickly after him, by the same likeness.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats س-و-ل as one root whose core idea is slackness or sagging in something.

1. Basic sense: to hang loose, sag, droop — سَوِلَ / يَسْوَلُ / سَوَل (sawila / yaswalu / sawal).

2. Poetic witness (a Hudhalī poet): white garments whose colour is brightened by rain pouring from "the sagging-bellied cloud" (al-ḥamal al-aswal) — al-aswal being the adjective from this root, describing something that hangs down slackly.

3. Derived usage: سَوَّلَ لَهُ الشَّيْءَ (sawwala lahu al-shayʾ), "to make a thing look attractive to someone," i.e. to embellish or adorn it in his eyes.

4. Ibn Fāris's proposal for that derived usage: it may not belong to the "slackness" idea at all, but rather to سُؤْل (suʾl, "a request, what one asks for") — so that "sawwala it to him" originally meant "gave him what he asked for," with the hamza of suʾl softened into a wāw. He gives this as a possibility (fa-mumkin), not as a settled derivation.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سِيمَٰ 6x "by their marks"; يَسُومُ 4x "would afflict them"; مُّسَوَّمَة 3x "marked"; مُسَوِّمِين 1x "[the ones] having marks"; تُسِيمُ 1x "you pasture your cattle"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root س-و-م (s-w-m) from a single core idea: seeking or pursuing a thing.

1. Seeking / pursuit — the base sense: سُمْتُ الشَّيْءَ (I sought the thing), verbal noun sawm.

2. Bargaining — from this comes al-sawm, haggling over price in buying and selling.

3. Pasturing — also from the base: سَامَتِ الرَّاعِيَة (the animal grazed/pastured), and the causative أَسَمْتُهَا (I put it out to graze). He cites Qur'an 16:10 {فِيهِ تُسِيمُونَ}, glossing tusīmūn as "you pasture (your flocks)."

4. Granting free rein — سَوَّمْتُ فُلَانًا فِي مَالِي: to give someone full authority over one's property; and سَوَّمْتُ غُلَامِي: to leave one's servant to do as he wishes.

5. Horses turned loose — al-khayl al-musawwama: horses let go with their riders on them.

Ibn Fāris states all of the above trace back to one origin.

He then flags one sense as an outlier from the base:
6. Mark / sign — al-sūma is a token placed on a thing. Al-sīmā is a shortened (maqṣūr) form of this, as in Qur'an 48:29 {سِيمَاهُمْ فِي وُجُوهِهِمْ مِنْ أَثَرِ السُّجُودِ} ("their mark is on their faces from the trace of prostration"). Lengthened, the word is al-sīmāʾ.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سِيقَ 7x "and (will) be driven"; سُّوق 4x "the markets"; سَاق 4x "about the leg"; سَائِق 1x "a driver"; مَسَاق 1x "(will be) the driving"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats س-و-ق (s-w-q) as a single root whose core meaning is driving something along.

1. Driving: سَاقَ / يَسُوقُ / سَوْقًا — to drive (e.g. animals forward). السَّيِّقَة is livestock that has been driven off.

2. Conveying a bridal gift: سُقْتُ إِلَى امْرَأَتِي صَدَاقَهَا (also أَسَقْتُهُ) — "I conveyed her bridal gift to my wife," an extension of the driving/sending sense.

3. Market (سُوق, pl. أَسْوَاق): derived from the same root, so called because goods of every kind are "driven"/brought to it.

4. Leg or shank (سَاق, pl. سُوق): named from this root because the walker is propelled along on it. Related forms: a large-legged woman is سَوْقَاء, a large-legged man أَسْوَق, with the verbal noun سَوَق. Ibn Fāris cites Ruʾba: "lean of belly from running, long-backed, [firm] in the shank."

5. سُوق الحَرْب — the "market" of war, i.e. the thick/heat of battle, which he also derives from the first sense of driving.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سُورَة 10x "a surah"; أَسَاوِر 5x "bracelets"; تَسَوَّرُ 1x "they climbed over the wall"; سُور 1x "a wall"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root s-w-r (سور) from a single core idea: **height and elevation**.

1. **To flare up in anger.** سَارَ / يَسُورُ (sāra / yasūru): to become angry and rise up. Hence سَوْرَة (sawra) = the surge or onset of anger ("his anger has a sawra").

2. **A tier of a building; a wall.** سُورَة (sūra), plural سُوَر (suwar): every level or story of a structure. A cited verse uses السُّور (al-sūr) for the top of a wall/rampart, which the speaker climbs to reach someone behind a guarded pavilion.

3. **A drinker's temperament — disputed reading.** In a line describing a wine-companion who is "neither abstemious nor a sawwār," Ibn Fāris takes سَوَّار (sawwār) to mean one who does not fly into a temper; others took it to mean one in whose head the drink quickly "surges" (yasūru).

4. **Foreign words (judged non-Arabic).** سِوَار (siwār, a woman's bracelet) and الإِسْوَار (al-iswār), from the Persian أَسَاوِرَة (asāwira) — meaning their commanders/leaders — he considers to be of non-Arabic origin.

5. **Potency of wine.** سَوْرَة الْخَمْر (sawrat al-khamr): the sharpness/potency of wine and its effervescence.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: ٱسْتَوَىٰ 35x "equal"; سَوَاء 27x "(it is) same"; سَوَّىٰ 13x "we equated you"; سَوِيّ 5x "even"; تُسَوَّىٰ 1x "was leveled"; سَاوَىٰ 1x "he (had) leveled"; سُوًى 1x "even"
poets_named: unnamed verse ×2; al-Ḥuṭayʾa (lived into Islam); al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root س و ي (s-w-y) from a single core sense: straightness/uprightness and balance or equilibrium between two things. From this he groups several usages:

1. Equality in value. هذا لا يساوي كذا = "this does not equal that" (does not match its worth); على سوية من هذا الأمر = being "on an equal footing" in some matter.

2. A marked, level place. مكان سوى = a recognized landmark that people know how to enter and leave.

3. Soundness/well-formedness. أسوى الرجل = his offspring and children turned out sound (sawiyy). He cites an idiom: in reply to "How are you this evening?" one says mustawūn ṣāliḥūn, meaning "our children and livestock are sound and thriving."

4. السِّيّ (al-siyy), two branches:
   a. An open expanse of land — with a poetic citation ("as though the ostriches of the open plain had laid eggs upon them").
   b. The like / equal (al-mithl). Hence سِيّان = "two of a kind," and لا سيّما (lā siyyamā) = "not the like of what." He proves siyy = "equal" with al-Ḥuṭayʾa's line about a serpent that is "no equal (bi-siyy) to you."

5. السَّواء (al-sawāʾ) = the middle (of a house, etc.), so called because it is level/even. Qurʾānic witness: "then he saw him in the midst (sawāʾ) of the Hellfire" (al-Ṣāffāt 37:55).

6. سِوى (siwā) = "other than." Ibn Fāris ties this back to the core sense: if one thing is "other than" another, each stands in its own domain on equal footing. Proof: the lengthened form سِواء (siwāʾ) used with the same meaning (al-Aʿshā's line: "nor did she turn... to any other than you"). He also notes قصدت سِوى فلان = "I headed toward so-and-so," parallel to qaṣadtu qaṣdahu, citing a line recited by al-Farrāʾ.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
**Root s-kh-ṭ (سخط)** — al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt

1. **Core sense.** The nouns *sakhaṭ* and *sukhṭ* (two vocalisations of the same word) denote intense anger — specifically the kind of anger that calls for punishment to follow. Al-Rāghib cites the Qurʾānic verb form: "then at once they are angered" (9:58).

2. **When the subject is God.** Used of God, al-Rāghib glosses the term not as an emotion but by its effect: the sending down of punishment. He supports this with three citations:
   - "that is because they followed what angered God" (47:28)
   - "that God was angered against them" (5:80)
   - "like one who has drawn upon himself anger from God" (3:162)

The entry is brief and offers no further derivations, plural patterns, or non-Qurʾānic poetic evidence.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سَخَّرَ 22x "and subjected"; سَخِرَ 11x "you ridicule"; مُسَخَّرَٰت 3x "subjected"; سِخْرِيّ 2x "(in) mockery"; مُسَخَّر 1x "[the] controlled"; يَسْتَسْخِرُ 1x "they mock"; سَّٰخِرِين 1x "the mockers"; سُخْرِيّ 1x "(for) service"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats س-خ-ر (s-kh-r) as a single sound root carrying two linked ideas: contempt/derision and subjugation/humbling.

1. Subjugation. سَخَّرَ (form II, sakhkhara) means to make something subservient by subduing it to one's command and will. Ibn Fāris cites God "subjecting" (sakhkhara) to humankind what is in the heavens and the earth (Q 45:13).

2. Compelled service vs. being mocked (a vowelling distinction).
- رَجُلٌ سُخْرَة (rajul sukhra) = a man put to forced/compelled labour; also سُخْرَة = one who is mocked.
- But if he is the one who mocks others, the form is سُخَرَة (sukhara), with fatḥa on the khāʾ and rāʾ.

3. Ships. The phrase سُفُنٌ سَوَاخِرُ مَوَاخِرُ describes ships: sawākhir = obedient/submissive ones with a fair wind; mawākhir = those that plough and cleave through the water.

4. Derision. سَخِرْتُ مِنْهُ (sakhirtu minhu) = I mocked/derided him. The idiom is also used with the preposition bi- (سَخِرْتُ بِهِ). Ibn Fāris cites Q 11:38, "then we mock you as you mock."

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: سِيحُ 1x "so move about"; سَّٰئِحُون 1x "those who go out"; سَٰئِحَٰت 1x "who fast"
text:
Root: s-y-h (سيح) — al-Zamakhshari, Asas al-Balagha

Core sense — water flowing:
1. sāḥa al-māʾ describes water flowing/streaming over the ground; the verbal noun is sayḥ. Flowing water is itself called sāʾiḥ or sayḥ. The causative asāḥa means to make a river flow — to channel or set it running. Al-Farazdaq's verse is quoted as evidence, boasting of the many rivers/canals "I made flow" (asaḥtu) for the Muslims by God's permission.

Related literal sense:
2. A masīḥ garment is a striped one (kisāʾ masīḥ = striped cloak) — presumably from the streak-like lines the root's "flowing" sense evokes.

Figurative sense (explicitly marked by the author as majaz) — traveling/roaming:
3. sāḥa fī al-arḍ means to travel or roam through the land (siyāḥa); a wanderer is sāʾiḥ or siyāḥ. Al-Zamakhshari cites the Qur'anic phrase "so travel/roam through the land" as the model usage. He notes that the person fasting is likened to such a roamer, which is why the faster is also called sāʾiḥ — the analogy being to the wanderer's usage. A verse attributed to Abu Talib is quoted about the sāʾiḥīn tasting no drop for their Lord's sake (the second half of the line is textually uncertain).

Further extended/figurative senses:
4. Said of a stallion: asāḥa/sayyaḥa its member — meaning it extended or let it protrude.
5. A wild ass with a whitish mark on its rump is called masīḥ al-ʿajīza ("streaked-rumped"), because of that white patch. Dhu al-Rumma's verse is cited, describing a lean she-camel racing through the dark as if her rump-edges were similarly streaked and tawny.
6. Said of a person: sayyaḥa tasyīḥan kathīran, "he sayyaḥa a great deal," used when someone embellished or ornamented his speech.

In short: the root's base meaning is water flowing/streaming (and, causatively, making it flow/channeling it); from this the author derives a literal sense of "striped" (masīḥ), a well-attested figurative sense of "roaming/traveling the land" (whence the fasting person's epithet sāʾiḥ, and the Qur'anic command to roam the land), and further extended usages for a stallion's member protruding, a streak-marked rump, and ornamented speech.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root s-y-b (سيب) from one core idea: something continuing on while also passing away/flowing off — i.e., ongoing motion of departure.

1. Flowing water: sayb al-mā' (سَيْبُ الْمَاءِ) is the channel/course a water flows along.

2. Gliding motion: a snake is said to "insāba" (glide/slither away) — the same continuous, departing motion applied to a creature's movement.

3. Setting loose: "sayyabtu d-dābbata" — to turn an animal loose, letting it go wherever it wants, unrestrained.

4. As-sā'ibah: a slave who is released without any walā' (bond of clientship/patronage) — he is set loose in the sense of #3, and is free to dispose of his own property as he wishes.

5. Gift/bestowal: as-sayb (السَّيْبُ) means a gift or bestowal — Ibn Fāris explains this by the same core image: a gift is "something made to flow" toward the recipient, i.e. sent his way like a current.

6. Found/buried treasure: as-suyūb (السُّيُوبُ, plural) means treasure found in the ground (rikāz). Again explained via the "gift" sense: it is as if God caused this to flow to whoever happens to find it.

7. An outlier: as-sayāb (السَّيَابُ), meaning unripe dates (singular: sayābah), does not fit the root's core meaning — Ibn Fāris explicitly flags it as anomalous rather than derived from the "continuing/flowing away" sense.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
quran_words: سَيْل 2x "the torrent"; سَالَتْ 1x "and flows"; أَسَلْ 1x "and we caused to flow"
poets_named: al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam) ×2; al-Mutanakhkhil al-Hudhalī (pre-Islamic); al-Zibriqān b. Badr (lived into Islam); Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad); unnamed verse; Abū Ḥayya al-Numayrī (pre-Islamic); al-Akhṭal (Umayyad); Ibn Hāniʾ al-Andalusī (later (Abbasid or after))
text:
Root س ي ل (s-y-l) as treated by al-Zabīdī in Tāj al-ʿArūs (d. 1791 CE).

1. Core sense — to flow, to run. sāla / yasīlu, verbal nouns sayl and sayalān, said of water or of a thing: it flowed. The causative asāla means "to make flow"; sayyala (form II) is a synonym of it. Al-Zabīdī cites the Qur'anic "and We made a spring of molten copper flow for him," glossing asalnā as "We made it run," and adds that "causing to flow" (isāla) in the case of molten metal is really a state that arises in it after melting. Also attested: sāla … masīlan / masālan as further verbal nouns.

2. sayl as a noun — a torrent. One may say māʾ sayl meaning "flowing water," the verbal noun standing in for the adjective; or sayl is specifically abundant flowing water. Thaʿlab records a pasture-scout's report: "I found herbage and small herbage, and shallow water, sayl" — i.e. abundant flowing water (the two words for herbage marking what had matured and what had not). Al-Zabīdī concludes that sayl is originally a verbal noun that became a name for water that reaches you although its rain did not fall where you are. Qur'anic evidence: "the torrent bore a swelling foam," and "We sent upon them the sayl of the ʿarim." Plural suyūl. Related: sīla (with i), the running or course of water; sawāʾil, plural of sāʾila used in the sense of "torrents," as in al-Aʿshā's line about a castaway with the floods running over him.

3. Applied to markings on a horse. A blaze (ghurra) is called sāʾila when it runs evenly down the bridge of the nose; or when it runs down to the nose-tip and covers it; or when it spreads wide across forehead and nose-ridge. sālat al-ghurra = the blaze ran long and broad; if narrow, it is called shimrākh instead.

4. Extension to length/drawing-out. asāla ghirār al-naṣl: he drew out and completed the edge of a blade — with a verse of al-Mutanakhkhil al-Hudhalī on keen arrowheads "with drawn-out edges and points." Similarly, in a description of the Prophet, sāʾil al-aṭrāf means having elongated extremities (some transmit the word with n instead of l, to the same effect).

5. sīlān — the tang. With kasra, sīlān is the tang of a sword- or knife-hilt: the tail-piece that goes into the haft (so al-Asās; al-Ṣiḥāḥ similarly). Abū ʿUbayd remarked that he had heard the word but not from a scholar. A verse of al-Zibriqān b. Badr is cited: "I will never make peace with you while I have a horse and my thumb grips hard on the sword-tang."

6. As a personal name. Sīlān names a group of people: Ibn Sīlān, a Kufan Companion named ʿAbd Allāh; ʿĪsā b. Sīlān and Jābir b. Sīlān, listed as two Successors by al-Dhahabī, though al-Ḥāfiẓ held them to be one man (a transmitter from Abū Hurayra) whose name was disputed — which is why al-Ṣaghānī mentioned only ʿĪsā; and the traditionist Ibrāhīm b. ʿĪsā b. Sīlān.

7. sayāl / sayāla — a thorn tree. A plant with a long white thorn that exudes milk when pulled up (Abū ʿAmr). Al-Asās compares a woman's teeth to "the thorns of the sayāl," and identifies it with the willow in Yemeni usage. Others describe it as a supple-branched tree with white thorns whose stems resemble maidens' front teeth; al-Aʿshā mentions wine flowing "among the thorns of the sayāl." Al-Muḥkam: a white-thorned tree of the ʿiḍāh class, or the tall variety of the samur (Abū Ḥanīfa from Abū Ziyād). Plural sayāl, with a line of Dhū al-Rumma likening camels to thirsty palms and sayāl trees.

8. masīl — watercourse, and its irregular plurals. masīl al-māʾ is the place where water flows; Ibn Sīda also gives the form masal. Al-Zabīdī's teacher called masal anomalous almost beyond parallel; al-Zabīdī answers that Ibn Sīda transmits it and it appears in Ibn Jinnī's Kitāb al-Shawādhdh. The regular plural is masāyil (without hamza), but musul, amsila and muslān are also used against analogy: masīl is of the pattern mafʿil, which is not pluralised that way, but speakers assimilated it to the pattern faʿīl — compare raghīf with its plurals rughuf, arghifa, rughfān. Al-Azharī's explanation: they took the mīm to be a root letter and the word to be faʿīl rather than mafʿil, as they made amkina the plural of makān; the phenomenon has parallels.

9. Other lexical items. sayyāl (pattern faʿʿāl) is named as a kind of reckoning (al-Ṣaghānī); it is also the name of the traditionist Sayyāl b. Sammāl al-Yamāmī. sayyāla with doubled y is a bend in the sea where it curves.

10. Figurative usages. "The torrent swept them away, and the sea surged with us" — a proverb meaning they met a hard trial and the speakers a harder one, since the sea's surge is worse than the torrent's sweep. tasāyalat al-katāʾib: squadrons streamed in from every side (marked as figurative), as does sālat ʿalayhi al-khayl. sāʾila or sayāla of people = a group streaming in from one quarter. A valley may be described as having swaying plants and freely flowing (sayyāl) water. Also figurative: musāl al-khaddayn, and musālā al-rajul, the two sides of a man's beard (with an anonymous verse), or his two flanks (verse of Abū Ḥayya al-Numayrī, the word there being accusative as an adverb of place).

11. Place and proper names. Sayāl, a place in the Ḥijāz (Naṣr). Al-Sayāla, a station near Medina, one stage out and the first stage for Medinans travelling to Mecca, lying between Malal and al-Rawḥāʾ. Al-Sayālā, a water-source in Syria, cited from al-Akhṭal. Saylūn, a village near Nablus; Sayla, a village in the Fayyūm; Sīlā, a frontier post; Ḥabs Sayal, between the lava-tract of Banū Sulaym and al-Sawāriqiyya. Sayl is given, on Naṣr's authority, as a name of Mecca, and Sayl b. al-Asal al-Naṣrī is identified as the subject of a (metrically defective) verse. Sayal is a mountain. Fāṭima bt. Saʿd b. Sayl was the mother of Quṣayy and of Zuhra b. Kilāb. Sīlān is given as a name for the Sea of China, and Sīlīn as a district in eastern Upper Egypt. Masīla (also transmitted Masīlā) is a well-known town in the Maghrib; al-Zabīdī's teacher judged Masīla the better-known form and rejected as a clear error the claim that the Fāṭimids built it, attributing its founding instead to the amīr Abū ʿAlī Jaʿfar b. ʿAlī b. Ḥamdān al-Andalusī, praised by Ibn Hāniʾ al-Andalusī in verses naming him a third luminary beside sun and moon. Scholars ascribed to the town include Aḥmad b. Muḥammad b. Ḥarb al-Masīlī and ʿAbd Allāh al-Masīlī, a commentator on Ibn al-Ḥājib's Mukhtaṣar.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: سَارَ 16x "travel"; سُيِّرَتْ 5x "could be moved"; سَيَّارَة 3x "a caravan"; سَيْر 2x "the journey"; سِيرَت 1x "(to) its state"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root s-y-r from a single core idea: going forth and flowing/running onward. From it:

1. سَارَ يَسِيرُ سَيْرًا (sāra) — to journey or travel; this can happen by night or by day.

2. السِّيرَة (al-sīra) — the way or manner one follows in something, and an established practice (sunna). Ibn Fāris links this to the core sense because such a practice "travels" and "runs on." The verb is used both intransitively (سَارَتْ, "it ran its course") and transitively (سِرْتُهَا, "I set it in motion"). He cites a verse: "Do not be distressed at a practice you yourself set going, for the first to be pleased with a practice is the one who puts it into course."

3. السَّيْر (al-sayr) — a leather strap or thong (a well-known sense), which he traces to the same root because of its extended, drawn-out shape, as though it "runs" along.

4. سَيَّرْتُ الْجُلَّ عَنِ الدَّابَّة — to cast/throw the saddle-cloth off a riding-animal.

5. الْمُسَيَّر (al-musayyar) of cloth — striped garments, whose lines resemble straps (suyūr).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root ت‑ع‑س (t-ʿ-s) as expressing a single core idea: al-kabb, "throwing down" or "toppling" (specifically, casting something face-down).

Usage he records:
- taʿasahu Allāh — "may God throw him down / topple him" (a curse/imprecation).
- atʿasahu — the causative form (Form IV) of the same verb, with the same meaning.

He supports this with a line of poetry: the poet describes routing an enemy host at a place called Mutāliʿ, after which the defeated "returned in downfall (iṭtiʿās), under the worst omen-bird" — i.e., they went home defeated and disgraced, marked by an ill omen (the reference to a "bird" reflects the old Arab practice of reading omens from birds).

The whole entry is a single, tightly-focused sense: physical/figurative overthrow or ruin, with no separate branches of meaning given.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root ت-ح-ت (t-ḥ-t) as expressing a single idea, with two related usages:

1. **taḥta (تَحْتَ)** — "beneath / underneath," as in taḥta al-shayʾ, "under the thing." This is the core spatial sense.

2. **al-tuḥūt (التُّحُوت)** — figuratively, the low or base sort of people. He cites a ḥadīth as evidence: "The wuʿūl perish and the tuḥūt come to prominence," and glosses al-wuʿūl (literally mountain-goats) as "the great and high-ranking people." The contrast pairs the lofty (wuʿūl) against the lowly (tuḥūt), extending the root's basic "below" sense to social rank.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: ٱتَّبَعَ 136x "follow"; أَتْبَعَ 15x "he followed"; تَبِعَ 9x "follows"; تَابِع 3x "(are) followers"; ٱتِّبَاع 2x "then follows up"; مُتَتَابِعَيْن 2x "consecutively"; تَبَع 2x "followers"; مُّتَّبَعُون 2x "(will be) followed"; تَبِيع 1x "an avenger"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats t-b-ʿ as one root with a single meaning: following-after, coming behind (al-tuluww, al-qafw). Nothing in the chapter departs from it.

1. Core verb. تَبِعْتُ فُلانًا ("I followed him") = came behind and followed him. A slightly altered form, أَتْبَعْتُهُ, adds the nuance of catching up with / overtaking him. The root is one; the Arabs marked the difference between plain following (qafw) and catching-up (luḥūq) by a minimal change of form.

2. Qur'anic evidence. In {fa-atbaʿa sababan} (18:85) and {thumma atbaʿa sababan} (18:89), on this reading the sense is catching-up / reaching a means. Some grammarians treat both forms as identical in meaning.

3. تُبَّع (tubbaʿ) = the shadow, cited from a line of poetry ("...as the sandgrouse comes to water when the tubbaʿ has shrunk"). It is called this because the shadow perpetually follows the person. Ibn Fāris judges "shadow" a truer reading of the verse than taking the word as qaṭāt (sandgrouse).

4. تَبِيع (tabīʿ) = a cow's calf once it follows its mother; it is the prescribed levy on thirty head of cattle. Some jurists defined it as the calf whose horns and ears have grown even — but Ibn Fāris notes this is a legal-ruling definition, not one drawn from linguistic analogy.

5. تَبَع (tabaʿ) = the legs of a riding-beast, so named because they follow one after another.

6. تَبِيع (tabīʿ) also = a helper/supporter, because his help follows [the one he aids].

7. تَبِيع also = a person who owes you money, whom you therefore pursue.

Supporting ḥadīth: "The rich man's delaying [of payment] is injustice; when one of you is referred to a solvent man [for his debt], let him follow [accept it]" — i.e., when the debt is transferred to him, let him accept the transfer.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats t-b-b as a single word meaning loss, and reports with reservation a second word of opposite sense.

**1. Loss.** The tāʾ and bāʾ, he says, form a single word, al-tibāb, meaning loss (al-khusrān). The phrase tabban li-l-kāfir, "ruin to the kāfir", means "perdition to him". In Q 11:101, "they added to them nothing but tatbīb", tatbīb means causing loss.

**2. Being set in order (reported with doubt).** Opposite to these, a word is reported: istatabba al-amr, said when a matter has become ready. Ibn Fāris accepts it only conditionally: if it is sound, the root has two aspects, loss and being set straight (al-istiqāma).

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
quran_words: تَبَّرْ 2x "and to destroy"; تَتْبِير 2x "(with) destruction"; مُتَبَّر 1x "destroyed"; تَبَار 1x "(in) destruction"
text:
Root t-b-r, as treated by Ibn Manẓūr in Lisān al-ʿArab.

1. tibr — unwrought metal, chiefly gold.
Definitions vary in scope: (a) gold in all its forms; (b) gold, silver, and any mineral dug from the earth — copper, brass, alloy, glass and so on — while still raw, i.e. before being fashioned and put to use; (c) broken-up gold specifically. A verse of poetry plays on the contrast: other clans are cast from mere ore (tibr), while the Banū ʿAbd Manāf are gold.

2. Refinements of that sense reported from earlier authorities.
- Ibn al-Aʿrābī: tibr is the fragments or filings of gold and silver before they are worked; once worked they are simply called "gold" and "silver."
- Al-Jawharī: tibr is gold not yet struck as coin; struck into dinars it becomes ʿayn (minted specie). Strictly the word is used of gold, though some extend it to silver. A ḥadīth cited here pairs the terms: gold for gold, "its tibr and its ʿayn," and likewise silver.
- The word can be extended to other metals (copper, iron, lead), but its dominant application is gold; some hold gold to be the original sense and the rest derivative or figurative.
- Ibn Jinnī: nothing is called tibr unless it is still in the soil of its ore-bed, or is in a broken state.
- Al-Zajjāj: on the same principle, broken glass is also called tibr.

3. tabār — destruction, perishing; and the verb tabbara — to shatter and destroy.
The two senses are linked by the idea of breaking: to tabbara something is to smash it to pieces and so annihilate it. Examples given: "these — what they are engaged in is mutabbar," i.e. shattered and ruined; and a saying of ʿAlī describing "an opinion that is mutabbar," i.e. ruinous.

4. Qur'anic citations, with al-Zajjāj's comments.
- "and increase not the wrongdoers save in tabār" — al-Zajjāj: "save in destruction"; and it is precisely because of this breaking-sense that anything shattered is called tibr.
- "and each We tabbarnā with a thorough tatbīr" — al-Zajjāj: tatbīr is demolition; anything you have broken and crumbled to pieces you have tabbara-ed.

5. Grammatical and morphological notes.
The intransitive verb is tabira / yatbaru, verbal noun tabār (an editorial footnote records disagreement among later lexicons over which conjugational class it belongs to). Ibn al-Aʿrābī distinguishes two similar-looking passive participles: al-matbūr = the one destroyed, al-mabtūr = the one cut short or made deficient. He also records al-tabrāʾ, a she-camel of fine colour.

6. Two idiomatic residues.
- "I got not a tabrīr out of him" = not a thing; used only in negative constructions (cited by Sībawayh, explained by al-Sīrāfī).
- tibriya, in the phrase "in his head is tibriya": per Abū ʿUbayda a dialectal variant of hibriya, the bran-like scurf that forms at the roots of the hair.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root: ت ف ث (t-f-th)
Dictionary: al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (early 11th c. CE)

1. Qur'anic anchor — Q22:29: "Then let them complete/finish their tafath." Al-Rāghib glosses tafath here as "their dirt" (wasakh) — so the verse means: let them remove it.

2. Grammatical support — He backs the sense of "complete, finish" (qaḍā) in the verse by citing the ordinary usage qaḍā al-shayʾ yaqḍī, said of cutting something off and getting rid of it.

3. Core meaning of tafath — al-Rāghib gives its root sense as the dirt/grime that collects under a trimmed nail and similar residue: generally, whatever accumulated matter is meant to be removed from the body (bodily grooming grime).

4. Supporting citation — He quotes a Bedouin's saying, mā atfathaka wa-adranaka ("How grimy and filthy you are!"), where atfatha is used as a verb from this root, paired with the near-synonym adrana ("to be grimy").

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
text:
Root ت ج ر (t-j-r) — al-Zamakhsharī, Asās al-Balāgha

Literal senses

1. To trade, to deal in merchandise. Both the form I verb تَجَرَ (tajara) and the form VIII اتَّجَرَ (ittajara) are used, e.g. "he deals in cloth." One says تَجَرَ تِجارةً رابحة — "he did a profitable trade."
2. Form III تاجَرَ = to trade *with* someone: "I dealt with so-and-so, and it was the most profitable dealing."
3. The exclamatory form: ما أَتْجَرَ فلاناً — "what a merchant so-and-so is!"
4. Plurals of تاجِر (merchant): تَجْر and تِجار — "the merchants of Iraq are many."
5. The place-noun مَتْجَر, plural مَتاجِر — a land one carries trade to, a trading destination.

Metaphorical usage (al-Zamakhsharī marks this section explicitly as majāz)

6. Commerce as an image for the hereafter and for reputation: "hold to the commerce of the hereafter"; "his bargain in the market of praise is profitable." The vocabulary of buying, bargaining and profit is transferred to non-commercial gain.

7. تاجِرة of a she-camel: fine and readily saleable — one that finds a buyer. Plural تَواجِر. This is grounded in three poetic citations:
 - an unattributed line: lined up, young she-camels filled the gaps between them, "like the palms of al-Khazrajī," described as tawājir (in demand);
 - an unattributed line describing a she-camel of Buzākha tossing fibre, likened to the shed coat of tawājir young camels;
 - al-Afwah al-Awdī: when Kaḥl (the drought year) cried out over the people, "the tawājir took shelter at the sheltered sides of the tents" — the valuable, saleable beasts being the ones brought in close.

8. A following line (of the same citation) mentions that every abundant milch-camel of the uplands was made a تِيمة — wealth was held cheap for its sake while honour stayed intact. Al-Zamakhsharī glosses الاتِّيام as "taking a tīma," a milch-animal kept at home for its milk.

9. The same adjective extends beyond camels to goods generally: تاجِرة is said of any commodity that sells well. "Keep to the marketable goods" (عليك بالسِّلع التواجر).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats t-l-l, the doubled form of tāʾ and lām, as a sound root that indicates standing upright and also the opposite of standing upright.

1. **Standing upright (intiṣāb).** Under this side he lists al-tall, the well-known word for a hill or mound; al-talīl, the neck; and the expression talaltu al-shayʾa fī yadihi, "I put the thing into his hand". He also places here al-taltala, agitating or making restless (iqlāq), and says it belongs to the same analogy (qiyās).

2. **The opposite: throwing down.** Tallahu means "he threw him down" (ṣaraʿahu). This, he says, is a kind of muqābala, the setting of a thing against its opposite. Al-mitall is the spear with which someone is thrown down. He cites the Qur'an, wa-tallahu li-l-jabīn, "and he threw him down on his forehead" (Q 37:103), and a verse of Labīd: "Firm of heart at their gap, I turn the dark one about with a middle-sized, felling [spear]." He explains the line as: I turn it about, having a felling spear (rumḥ mitall) with me.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: تَلَىٰ 61x "are recited"; تِلَاوَت 1x "(of) its recitation"; تَّٰلِيَٰت 1x "and those who recite"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root t-l-w from a single core idea: following / succession (al-ittibāʿ).

1. Basic sense: تَلَوْتُهُ = "I followed him." From this comes تِلَاوَة for reciting the Qurʼān, because the reciter takes one verse after another in sequence.

2. A reported sense "to forsake/abandon" (تَلَوْتُ الرَّجُلَ = I let a man down and left him). Ibn Fāris notes this only if it is authentically attested; if so, it still fits the root, since a companion who breaks away ends up behind the other, i.e. in the position of a "follower" (tālī).

3. التَّلِيَّة / التُّلَاوَة = "a remainder, remnant," because it comes after (follows) what preceded it. Shāhid: a line of Ibn Muqbil on "the remnants of youth" now gone without sight or trace. Also supported by al-Aṣmaʿī's report بَقِيَتْ لِي حَاجَةٌ فَأَنَا أَتَتَلَّاهَا ("a need of mine remained, and I follow up on it").

4. التَّلَاء = a covenant/guarantee of protection (dhimma), so called because it is pursued and sought after; hence أَتْلَيْتُهُ ذِمَّةً ("I extended him a guarantee").

5. al-mutālī = a singer who answers his partner back in song, since each one "follows" the other. Shāhid: al-Akhṭal, أَوْ غِنَاءُ مُتَالِ ("or the song of one who answers back").

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَتَمَّ 16x "and complete"; تَمَّ 4x "and was fulfilled"; تَمَام 1x "completing (our favor)"; مُتِمّ 1x "will perfect"
poets_named: Al-Nābigha (pre-Islamic); Abū Duwād (disputed date); unnamed verse
text:
Ibn Fāris treats t-m-m as a single, regular root meaning: completeness or perfection. tamma al-shayʾ means the thing became complete; atmamtuhu means "I completed it".

1. **Amulet (al-tamīma).** He places the amulet in this root, explaining that people seem to have meant it as the completion of the remedy and cure they sought. He cites the ḥadīth: "Whoever hangs up an amulet, may God not bring [his affair] to completion for him."
2. **Hard (al-tamīm).** A solid, hard thing.
3. **Full term.** A pregnant woman at full term is mutimm; she gives birth li-tamām, at full term. In the phrase layl al-timām only the form timām is used.
4. **Giving partners their full share (tatmīm al-aysār).** In the game of arrows, feeding your partners the whole of your arrow's winnings without holding any back. Al-Nābigha boasts: "I give my partners at the arrows their full share, grant them favours twice over, and cover the great bowl with fat."
5. **Asking for the last of the material (al-mustatimm).** One who asks for some wool or camel-hair to finish weaving his garment. Abū Duwād describes things "like eggs in ostrich nests; not even a tie-string of them is given to one seeking to complete his weaving." What is given this way is called timma or tumma.
6. **Broken (al-mutatammim).** A word glossed as "broken". Ibn Fāris says it may belong here, since a thing reaches its limit and then breaks, but he prefers the view that the t replaces a th (mutathammim). The verse cited is "like the re-breaking of an overtaxed, shattered [bone]."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris identifies two distinct, unrelated senses for the root ت-ق-ن (t-q-n):

1. Perfecting / making firm (iḥkām). The verb "atqantu al-shay'" means "I made the thing firm/sound" — i.e., I perfected or mastered it. From this comes the adjective "tiqn" (تِقْنٌ), applied to a skilled, adept man. The name "Ibn Tiqn" belonged to a man famed for excellent archery, proverbial enough that a poet praised someone's shooting as "more accurate than Ibn Tiqn's."

2. Mud / black mire (ṭīn, ḥam'ah). Here the verb "taqqanū arḍahum" describes people treating or improving their land by applying this substance to it. The substance itself is called "at-tiqn."

Ibn Fāris treats these as two separate original meanings under the same three-letter root, not as one meaning derived from the other.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: تُرَاب 17x "dust"; أَتْرَاب 3x "well-matched"; تَّرَائِب 1x "and the ribs"; مَتْرَبَة 1x "misery"
text:
Root ت-ر-ب (t-r-b), per Ibn Fāris, has two base meanings: (1) dust/earth and its derivatives, and (2) the equality or matching of two things.

Sense 1 — dust/earth:
- التراب (turāb) means dust or earth; variant forms are التَّيْرَب (tayrab) and التَّوْرَاب (tawrāb).
- تَرِبَ الرجل ("the man became poor") — literally as if he clung to the dust; its opposite أَتْرَبَ ("he became rich") — as if he gained wealth as plentiful as dust.
- التَّرْبَاء (tarbāʾ) is the earth/ground itself.
- رِيحٌ تَرِبَة is a wind that arrives carrying dust. A cited verse describes a worn-down dwelling visited "now by a rain-cloud, now by a dust-bearing hot wind."

Sense 2 — equality/matching:
- التِّرْب (tirb) is a companion or age-mate (someone of equal age); plural أَتْرَاب (atrāb).
- From this comes التَّرِيب (tarīb), the chest — named for the point where the heads of the bones lie level with one another; a cited verse: "her two breasts rose above the chest."
- Also from this sense: التَّرِبَات (taribāt), the fingertips (singular تَرِبَة).

Anomalous (falling outside the chapter): التُّرْبَة (turba), which Ibn Fāris notes is a plant.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مُتْرَفِين 5x "its wealthy ones"; أُتْرِفُ 3x "while we had given them luxury"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats t–r–f as having a single meaning, centred on التُّرْفَة (turfa): indulgence — a choice or special thing given to someone as a favour.

1. Core sense — being pampered / kept in plenty. A رَجُل مُتْرَف (mutraf) is a man who is indulged and kept in ease and comfort. The verb form تَرَّفَهُ أَهْلُهُ ("his family tarrafa'd him") means they pampered him: they gave him fine food and things reserved for him alone. The idea joining the derivatives is preferential provision, not mere wealth in the abstract.
