2. A rejected sense. Ibn Fāris notes that al-Khalīl's dictionary gives turfa a second meaning — the small protuberance or notch in the upper lip — and states flatly that this is a mistake: the word for that is تِفْرَة / تُفْرَة (tifra/tufra), with the rāʾ and fāʾ in the other order, which he has already dealt with under its own root.

The entry is brief and records no poetic or scriptural citations.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); Labīd (lived into Islam); unnamed verse
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root t-r-k (ت ر ك) from a single organizing sense: al-tark, "leaving off / relinquishing a thing." He treats this as the root's governing principle (qiyās), from which the other usages follow.

1. Core sense — leaving / abandoning. Everything else is built on this.

2. tarīka — an egg left lying on bare, open ground (from being "left behind"). He cites al-Aʿshā: in a trackless desert one finds ostrich eggs left abandoned (tarāʾik).

3. tarkat al-silāḥ / the helmet (al-bayḍa, literally "the egg" of armour) — derived by likeness to the abandoned egg; plural tark. He cites Labīd, describing a coat of mail with helmets "like onions."

4. tarāki — a poetic imperative meaning "leave it!" (equivalent to itruk), illustrated by a verse urging one to leave the camels alone in the face of death.

5. tarikat al-mayyit — a deceased person's estate: what he leaves behind of his inheritance (turāth).

6. al-tarīka — a meadow that people neglect and leave ungrazed.

7. A reported usage — taraktu al-ḥabla shadīdan, "I left the rope taut," i.e. "I made it taut" — attributed to the book ascribed to al-Khalīl. Ibn Fāris explicitly doubts this is genuinely al-Khalīl's.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris states that the root t-r-q yields only a single word: tarquwa, "collarbone" (clavicle).

- He notes that the grammarian al-Khalīl [ibn Aḥmad] analyzed tarquwa as built on the pattern fa'luwa (فَعْلُوَة).
- He defines the bone itself: it runs between the hollow of the throat (thughrat al-naḥr) and the shoulder/upper-back area ('ātiq) — i.e., the bone connecting the base of the neck to the shoulder.

Ibn Fāris explicitly flags that this root has no other attested sense in his system beyond this one anatomical term.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats t-s-ʿ as having only one meaning: the number nine (تِسْعَة). From it he records:

1. تَسَعْتُ الْقَوْمَ — "I became the ninth of the group," i.e. made their count nine by joining them.
2. أَتْسَعْتُ الشَّيْءَ (Form IV) — "I made a thing nine": it stood at eight and one completed it to nine.
3. التِّسْع — a term for three nights of the lunar month, the last of which is the ninth night.
4. تَسَعْتُ الْقَوْمَ, imperfect أَتْسَعُهُمْ — with a second application: to take a ninth (تُسْع) of people's property.

He closes by noting that the remaining arrangement of these three letters is مُهْمَل — unused in the language.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: تَابَ 63x "they repent"; تَوَّاب 12x "(is) the acceptor of repentance"; تَوْبَة 7x "the repentance"; مَتَاب 2x "(with) repentance"; تَّٰئِبُون 1x "those who turn in repentance"; تَّوْب 1x "(of) [the] repentance"; تَٰئِبَٰت 1x "repentant"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root ت-و-ب (t-w-b) as having a single core meaning: returning / turning back (rujūʿ).

1. Usage: تَابَ مِنْ ذَنْبِهِ means "he turned back from his sin" — i.e. he withdrew from it. يَتُوبُ إِلَى اللَّهِ means "he turns/returns to God." The verbal nouns are tawba and matāb, and the agent noun is tāʾib ("one who turns back").

2. He notes that al-tawb is equivalent to al-tawba.

Qur'anic witness cited: {wa qābil al-tawb} — "and Accepter of the turning-back" (Ghāfir 40:3).

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
text:
Root ت و ر (t-w-r) — al-Zamakhsharī, Asās al-Balāgha

**1. Core meaning: "a turn, a time, an instance."**
The base word تارة (tāra), plural تارات (tārāt), means "a time/turn." Example usage: "he did that time after time" (تارات وتارة بعد أخرى), and the idiom "this is the worst of your turns" (وهذه شر تاراتك) — i.e., the worst instance of your repeated behavior.

**2. Verb تاورته (tāwartuhu)** = "I did it with him again," equated with عاودته (ʿāwadtuhu, "I repeated it with him / returned to him").

**3. التور (al-tūr) = "a small vessel/basin."**
Cited via a report: "The Messenger of God used to perform ablution (waḍūʾ) with the tūr." Al-Zamakhsharī notes this word is grammatically masculine according to the philologists.

**4. A personal note on usage.**
The author says he passed a woman near the Gate of al-ʿUmra asking her neighbor to lend her "your little tūr" (تويرتك, a diminutive) — evidence of the word's ordinary, everyday use for a small container.

**5. Why the vessel is called al-tūr — two explanations offered:**
- It gets passed around and circulated (يتعاور، يردد) from hand to hand — tying it back to the "turn/instance" sense.
- Alternatively, it is named after al-tūr in the sense of "a go-between," a messenger who shuttles back and forth (يتردد ويدور) between lovers.

**6. Supporting verse of poetry (poet unnamed, quoted with a gap in the source text):**
"The go-between is at work between us … one whom both the visited party and the sender are content with" — illustrating al-tūr as "messenger/intermediary."

**7. Root explanation tying it together.**
The go-between is called al-tūr because his derivation is from التارة (al-tāra, "a turn"): he is, at one turn, with this party, and at another turn, with that party — i.e., he shuttles between two sides.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root t-y-h (تيه) from a single core sense: bewilderment or disorientation (ḥayra).

From this core sense he gives one concrete application: al-tīh and al-tayhā' name a trackless open wasteland or desert — the kind of terrain in which a person wanders lost and loses his bearings (yatīhu fīhā al-insān, literally "in which the person tīhs/wanders-bewildered").

The entry is very short: it states the root as sound (no weak letters), gives the single abstract meaning (confusion/bewilderment), and then the one derived noun-sense (wilderness as the place where that bewilderment happens). No further senses, no shawāhid (poetic or Qur'anic citations), and no isnād are given in this entry.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris states that the letters t-y-n do not form a genuine derivational root — with one exception: the word tīn ("fig"), which is simply a known word, not something built up from an underlying root-meaning.

He adds a second, separate use of the same word: al-Tīn is also a proper name — a mountain. As evidence for this place-name sense he quotes a line of poetry (speaker unnamed) describing tawny, thirsty she-camels arriving at "al-Tīn" from an angle, driving before them a small cloud whose water is cool.

So the entry records two unrelated things sharing this spelling: (1) the fig, and (2) a mountain called al-Tīn — with no claim that either is derived from a deeper triliteral root-sense.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ث ع ب (th-ʿ-b), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: the extension and spreading-out of a thing — used of water and of other things alike.

1. thaʿabtu al-māʾ — I caused water to burst/gush forth, so it "inthaʿaba" (gushed), compared to blood gushing from the nose; from this is derived mathʿab al-maṭar, the channel or spout rainwater drains through.
2. al-thuʿbān — the large, long snake — Ibn Fāris judges this word a reasonable extension of the same root, by analogy: its long, spreading body and sinuous movement mirror the root's core sense. Illustrated with a line of poetry comparing a winding track to a thuʿbān emerging from its den.
3. māʾ thaʿb — flowing/gushing water, plural al-thuʿbān.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: ثَبَّطَ 1x "so he made them lag behind"
text:
Root ث ب ط (th-b-ṭ), al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān

1. The entry's central Qur'anic citation is al-Tawbah 9:46: "fa-thabbaṭahum wa qīla-qʿudū maʿa al-qāʿidīn" — "so He held them back, and it was said: sit with those who sit [behind]" (describing God restraining the hypocrites from joining the believers in battle) — glossed as: He detained and occupied/distracted them.
2. Al-Rāghib illustrates the ordinary usage: "thabbaṭahu al-maraḍu" / "athbaṭahu" — illness detained and hindered a person, scarcely leaving him — the same root applied to physical incapacitation as to the Qur'anic spiritual/military restraint.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats th-b-r as three separate roots rather than one:

1. **Ease, softness, level ground.**
 - الثَّبْرَة (thabra) = soft, easy ground. Thabra is also the name of a known place, cited in a rajaz verse: "I saved myself and left Ḥazra behind — an excellent young man I abandoned at Thabra."
 - Ibn Durayd's addition: a thabra is also a layer of earth like quicklime; a palm's root stops when it reaches it, hence "the palm has reached a thabra of ground."
 - ثَبِير (Thabīr) is a well-known mountain.
 - مَثْبِر (mathbir) of a she-camel = the spot where she drops her calf.
 - ثَبَرَ الْبَحْرُ = the sea ebbed — which, Ibn Fāris notes, uncovers soft level ground, tying it back to this first sense.

2. **Destruction, perishing.** الثُّبُور (thubūr) is ruin; a مَثْبُور (mathbūr) man is one destroyed. Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 25:13, "there they call out for thubūr."

3. **Persevering, keeping steadily at something.** ثَابَرْتُ عَلَى الشَّيْءِ = "I stuck to it persistently." Ibn Durayd's usage تَثَابَرَتِ الرِّجَالُ فِي الْحَرْبِ — men leaping at one another in battle — is assigned by Ibn Fāris to this third group.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: ثَبَّتْ 10x "and make firm"; تَثْبِيت 2x "strengthen(ing)"; يُثْبِتُ 2x "that they restrain you"; ثَابِت 2x "with the firm word"; ٱثْبُتُ 1x "then be firm"; ثُبُوت 1x "it is firmly planted"
text:
Ibn Sīda's entry for the root ث-ب-ت (th-b-t), whose core notion is firmness, fixity, and steadfastness.

1. Base verb: ثَبَتَ / يَثْبُتُ (thabata, "to be firm, fixed, stand fast"), with the verbal nouns thabāt and thubūt. The one who is firm is thābit or thabīt. Causatives: athbata and thabbata ("to fix, make firm, set in place"). An adjective thabt also means "firm, fixed."

2. thabbata ʿan al-amr means "to hold someone back / hinder him from a thing" — treated as equivalent to thabbaṭa.

3. Applied to a horse: faras thabīt is one sure-footed and steady in its running.

4. Of a person: rajul thabtu al-ghadar is a man steadfast in combat or in speech; the related verb thabuta has the verbal nouns thabāta and thubūta.

5. tathabbata / istathbata ("to proceed with care in a matter, act deliberately and not rush").

6. rajul thabtu al-maqām: one who does not budge from his position.

7. al-thabt / al-thabīt also denote the brave, steadfast horseman.

8. al-muthbat: one grown so heavy or incapacitated that he cannot leave his bed.

9. al-thabāt (concrete sense): a strap or thong used to bind the camel-saddle fast; plural athbita. A man tied with such a strap is muthbat. Cited verse of al-Aʿshā describes a swaying she-camel twisting the two sides of a firmly-strapped, well-fitting saddle.

10. thābata / athbata (of knowledge): "to know something thoroughly, with true knowledge."

11. In fighting: ṭaʿanahu fa-athbata fīhi al-rumḥ — "he stabbed him and drove the spear clean through."

12. athbata ḥujjatahu: "to establish one's proof and make it clear."

13. qawl thābit: a sound, valid statement. Ibn Sīda cites Qurʾān Ibrāhīm 27, {yuthabbitu llāhu lladhīna āmanū bi-l-qawl al-thābit} ("God makes firm those who believe by the firm word"), noting that all these senses stem from thabāt (firmness).

14. Proper names: Thābit and Thubayt (men's names).

15. Ithbīt: the name of a region, attested in a cited verse of al-Rāʿī describing young she-camels playing with oryx calves there on broken sandy ground.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: ث-ب-ي (th-b-y). Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) records one underlying idea for this root — "persisting/continuing upon a thing" — with two lines of derived vocabulary.

**1. Persistence (al-dawām ʿalā al-shayʾ)** — attributed to al-Khalīl.
- التَّثْبِيَة (al-tathbiyah): continuing upon a thing.
- The same word also means praising someone repeatedly during their lifetime. Cited evidence: a verse of Labīd, "he continually bestows praise from a noble man... 'Nay, live well with a goodly greeting, and drink.'"
- Ibn Fāris confirms this is a sound derivation.

**2. الثُّبَة (al-thubah) — "troop"**
- A band/troop of horsemen; plurals ثُبَات (thubāt) and ثُبُون (thubūn). Cited evidence: a verse of ʿAmr, "our horses become bands, troops," describing a day they feared for their people.
- Al-Khalīl also applies the word to ثُبَة الحوض (thubat al-ḥawḍ), the middle of a drinking-trough, where the water "returns" (from yathūbu, "to return"). On this etymology, the word originally had a wāw between the thāʾ and bāʾ that later dropped.
- This split etymology produces a dispute over the diminutive form: ordinary speakers say ثُبَيَّة (thubayyah), just following the word as pronounced; those who insist on strict analogy restore the lost wāw and say ثُوَيْبَة (thuwaybah) — the same pattern used for رُوَيِّئَة (ruwayyiʾah), the diminutive of رَوِيَّة (rawiyyah), on the grounds that it derives from رَوَّأْتُ (rawwaʾtu, "I deliberated").

**Ibn Fāris's own judgment:** he rejects treating the "trough" sense and the "troop of horsemen" sense as two separate origins — he holds they are one and the same word. He accordingly says the correct diminutive for both is ثُبَيَّة (thubayyah), tracing it back not to yathūbu ("returns") but to the root's core sense in §1, ثَبَّى عَلَى الشيء (thabbā ʿalā al-shayʾ), "to persist/continue upon a thing." He closes by noting his own reservation about the separate claim that رَوِيَّة (rawiyyah) derives from رَوَّأْتُ (rawwaʾtu).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats th-j-j as having one root meaning: the pouring out of something.

1. **thajja, to pour out.** Thajja al-māʾa means "he poured out the water", and māʾ thajjāj is water that pours out abundantly. Ibn Fāris cites Q 78:14: "And We sent down from al-muʿṣirāt water pouring out abundantly (thajjāj)."

2. **thajīj, outpouring.** Iktaẓẓa al-wādī bi-thajīj al-māʾ, "the valley was crammed with the outpouring of water", is said when the water has reached both its banks. Abū Dhuʾayb uses the word of rain: "May Umm ʿAmr be watered at the end of every night by dark rain-clouds whose water is a downpour (thajīj)."

3. **al-thajj in the ḥadīth.** A ḥadīth says: "The best ḥajj is al-ʿajj and al-thajj." Ibn Fāris explains al-ʿajj as raising the voice in the talbiyah (the call labbayka), and al-thajj as the flowing of the blood of the hady (the offering animals). He also refers to this sense the ḥadīth of the woman with continuing bleeding (al-mustaḥāḍah): "I pour it out in a torrent (athujjuhu thajjan)."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: unnamed verse ×2; Labīd (lived into Islam); Zuhayr (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats th-l-l as two distinct root meanings (aṣlān mutabāyinān): gathering together, and falling, demolition and abasement.

**Gathering**

1. al-thallah is a flock of sheep and goats. Some restrict the word to sheep alone, which is why ḥabl thallah means "a rope of wool" and a cloak of good wool is kisāʾ jayyid al-thallah. A cited verse likens a shabby man to "a soaked rope of wool".

2. al-thullah is a group of people, as in the Qur'an: "a company (thullah) of the former ones and a company of the later ones" (Q 56:39–40).

**Falling, demolition, abasement**

3. thalaltu l-bayt: "I demolished the house".

4. al-thullah: the earth of a well.

5. al-thalal: destruction. Labīd tells of an onslaught that "brought them to al-thalal".

6. thulla ʿarshuhu, literally "his throne (ʿarsh) was toppled", is said of someone whose condition has gone bad. Zuhayr addresses two people who came to the rescue of the confederates (al-aḥlāf) "when their throne had been toppled", and of Dhubyān.

7. Some say that thulla ʿarshuhu, or ʿurshuhu, means "he was killed". They cite a verse saying of ʿAbd Yaghūth, with the birds hopping around him, that "the keen steel sword has demolished his two ʿurshs". The two ʿurshs (al-ʿurshān) are the place where the neck is set into the upper back between the shoulders.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: ثَلَٰثَة 13x "(for) three"; ثَلَٰث 8x "(for) three"; ثُّلُث 6x "two thirds"; ثُلَٰث 2x "or three"; ثَالِث 2x "with a third"; ثَّالِثَة 1x "the third"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ث-ل-ث as a single root, all of it bound to the number three:

1. Number/counting. Its base sense is the numeral three, as in اثنان وثلاثة (two and three).

2. الثُّلَاثَاء — the weekday Tuesday (built on the same root). He quotes a verse in which "its Tuesday is wealth and a banquet, and all its days are like Tuesday."

3. ثالثة الأثافي ("the third trivet-stone") — the jutting rock-spur of a mountain used as the third support: two stones are set against it and the cooking-pot rests on all three. He notes this is the image al-Shammākh had in mind in a cited line describing two fire-blackened rocks over an abandoned campsite.

4. الثَّلُوث — a she-camel whose yield fills three vessels when milked.

5. المَثْلُوثة — a water-skin made of three hides.

6. حبل مَثْلوث — a rope twisted of three strands (على ثلاث قوى).

Each derived word turns on "three": the third support, the three-vessel yield, the three-hide skin, the three-ply rope.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: ثَمَن 11x "(for) a price"; ثَمَٰنِيَة 4x "eight"; ثُّمُن 1x "(is) the eighth"; ثَامِن 1x "and the eight of them"; ثَمَٰنِين 1x "(with) eighty"; ثَمَٰنِى 1x "(for) eight"
poets_named: Zuhayr (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse; al-Shammākh (lived into Islam); al-Hudhalī (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ث-م-ن (th-m-n) from two distinct roots:

1. **Price / compensation for a thing sold** — ثَمَن (thaman). Example: "I sold such-and-such and took its price (thaman)." He cites Zuhayr's line about sacrificial camels: read with ḍamma (أَثْمُن, athmun) it is the plural of thaman ("prices"); read with fatḥa (أَثْمَن, athman) it is an elative meaning "the most expensive of the camels."

2. **An eighth part** — الثُّمُن (al-thumun), one part out of eight. The verb ثَمَنْتُ الْقَوْمَ (thamantu l-qawma) means "I took the eighth of their wealth." الثَّمِين (al-thamīn) likewise denotes the eighth portion, supported by two verses of poetry: one on "when the eighth of my wealth flies off," and a line (attributed to al-Shammākh or another) contrasting the "quarter" and the "eighth" of stakes/wagers.

**Anomalous to the heading:** ثَمِينَة (Thamīna), a place-name, cited from a verse of al-Hudhalī.

**Also derived:** الْمِثْمَنَة (al-mithmana), a container resembling a feed-bag (mikhlāt).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: ثَمَرَٰت 16x "fruits"; ثَمَر 5x "its fruit"; أَثْمَرَ 2x "it bears fruit"; ثَمَرَة 1x "fruit"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives all senses of the root th-m-r (ثمر) from one core idea: something generated from another thing as a gathered, clustered mass. Further meanings, he says, are extensions from this by metaphor.

1. Fruit — الثَّمَر, the well-known sense. Forms: ثَمَرَة (one fruit), and the plurals ثَمَر, ثِمَار, ثُمُر. الشَّجَرُ الثَّامِر is a tree that has reached its fruiting season; المُثْمِر is a tree that has fruit on it (attributed to Ibn Durayd).

2. To make wealth grow — ثَمَّرَ الرَّجُلُ مَالَهُ, "he managed/tended his wealth well." In prayer: ثَمَّرَ اللَّهُ مَالَهُ, "may God make his wealth increase" (نَمَّاهُ). The link to the core sense is growth and multiplying.

3. Milk that "fruits" — الثَّمِيرَة, milk at the stage when it thickens into something like the white pith of the palm; Ibn Fāris notes this fits the root's underlying analogy (matter gathering into a mass).

4. The knot of a whip — called ثَمَرَة, which he explains as a likeness/simile (a small rounded cluster).

5. An anomaly — لَيْلَةُ ابْنِ ثَمِيرٍ, "the moonlit night," which he flags as deviating from the root's pattern, adding that he does not know its origin.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: ٱثْنَيْن 13x "two"; ٱثْنَتَيْن 7x "twice"; مَثْنَىٰ 3x "two"; ثَانِى 2x "the second"; مَّثَانِى 2x "the oft-repeated"; يَثْنُ 1x "fold up"; يَسْتَثْنُ 1x "making exception"
poets_named: unnamed verse; Maʿn and al-Namir b. Tawlab (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives ث-ن-ي (thāʾ-nūn-yāʾ) from a single core idea: doubling a thing twice, or making it into two parts — whether consecutive or distinct. The base verb is ثَنَى / ثَنْي ("to fold, double").

1. Number "two": الاثْنَان ("the two") is the well-known numeral from this root.

2. The one who ranks second. الثِّنَى / الثُّنْيَان is the man who comes after the chief, as if he were his "second." Ibn Fāris cites verse in which a man dismissed as a mere ثُنْيَان ("second-rater") is set against the بَدْء ("leader/first"), with a variant transmission reversing who is which.

3. Something done twice. الثِّنَى is an affair repeated twice. Ibn Fāris quotes the prophetic saying «لَا ثِنَى فِي الصَّدَقَةِ» — glossed as: ṣadaqa is not taken twice in a single year — plus lines by Maʿn and al-Namir b. Tawlab using ثِنَى / ثُنْيَان for blame that is repeated or that comes "second."

4. Bearing two children. A woman who has borne two is called ثِنْي; there is no parallel form for three (ثِلْث) or above.

5. الثِّنَايَة: a rope of hair or wool — possibly so named, he suggests, because it is (or can be) folded/doubled.

6. الثُّنْيَا: the part of a slaughtered camel (e.g. the head) that the owner reserves/excepts for himself. Ibn Fāris ties grammatical "exception" (استثناء) to the root's core sense of doubling: the excepted thing is named twice — once within the whole ("the people went out") and again in the detail ("except Zayd"). He notes the grammarians' view that the excepted noun has "left what it entered," governed the way عِشْرُون ("twenty") governs الدِّرْهَم (its tamyīz), and calls this sound reasoning.

7. المِثْنَاة: the end of a camel's nose-rein at the nose-peg — as if it were the "second" of the rein.

8. المَثْنَاة: a portion of Scripture that is read and repeated. Ibn Fāris connects this to Q 15:87, {…سَبْعًا مِنَ الْمَثَانِي} ("seven of the mathānī"), explaining the name as meaning that its recitation is doubled and repeated.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root ث ق ب (th-q-b), al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qur'ān

Core meaning: al-thāqib — the radiant, piercing one — that which pierces whatever it shines upon with its light.

1. Two Qur'anic citations anchor the sense: "so a piercing flame pursued him" (al-Saffat 37:10) and "the piercing star" (al-Tariq 86:2-3, glossing al-ṭāriq, the night-visitor).
2. The word's origin is traced to al-thuqbah, a hole/perforation.
3. al-mathqab — a mountain road/pass, named as though it had been "pierced through" the mountain; Abū ʿAmr notes the more correct form of the word is al-mithqab.
4. A separate idiom: thaqabtu al-nār — "I kindled the fire."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ث-ق-ف as a single root idea from which all derivatives branch: setting a thing straight — correcting what is bent in it.

1. **Straightening something crooked.** ثَقَّفْتُ الْقَنَاةَ = "I straightened the spear-shaft," i.e. removed its bend. He cites a verse (unattributed): the straightener inspects the joints of his shaft "until his straightening-tool sets right what is bent in it." The tool itself is the ثِقَاف.

2. **Grasping/acquiring accurately — of speech and knowledge.** ثَقِفْتُ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ مِنْ فُلَانٍ = "I picked this speech up from so-and-so." The phrase رَجُلٌ ثَقِفٌ لَقِفٌ describes a man quick to take in and catch hold of what he hears; Ibn Fāris explains it as attaining the knowledge of what he hears exactly, "evenly" (عَلَى اسْتِوَاءٍ) — the same notion of getting it straight.

3. **Laying hold of / overcoming a person.** ثَقِفْتُ بِهِ = "I got hold of him," in the sense of having prevailed over him. He cites a verse (unattributed): "If you get hold of me, then kill me … but if I am [not] laid hold of, you shall yet see my mettle."

**How he links sense 3 back to sense 1.** He raises the objection himself — what has "overcoming" to do with "straightening"? His answer: when one lays hold of a man he has thereby gripped and held him fast, and the one who prevails over a thing likewise holds it fast. So both usages, he concludes, are drawn from one and the same source.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: مِثْقَال 8x "(the) weight"; ثَّقَلَان 6x "their burdens"; ثَقِيل 5x "heavy"; ثَقُلَتْ 4x "(are) heavy"; مُّثْقَلُون 2x "(are) burdened"; أَثْقَلَت 1x "she grows heavy"; ٱثَّاقَلْ 1x "you cling heavily"; مُثْقَلَة 1x "a heavily laden"
poets_named: al-Khansāʾ (lived into Islam); unnamed verse; Kuthayyir ʿAzza (Umayyad); Labīd (lived into Islam) ×2; Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad)
text:
Ibn Sīda's account of the root ث ق ل (th-q-l), organized by sense.

1. Core sense — heaviness, the opposite of lightness. Verb ثَقُلَ (to be/become heavy); adjective ثَقيل (heavy), plural ثِقال. Derived: the preponderance or sinking of weight.

2. A heavy load or burden (ثِقْل, plural أثقال). Cited for Q 99:2 وأخرجت الأرض أثقالها ("the earth brings forth its burdens"), which Ibn Sīda glosses as the earth's treasures and its dead. Supporting verse of al-Khansāʾ: the earth "adorned itself" with a buried noble man — i.e. adorned its dead through him.

3. Sin or transgression (الذَّنب), same plural أثقال. Cited for Q 29:13 وليحملن أثقالهم وأثقالاً مع أثقالهم ("they shall bear their own burdens and [other] burdens with them").

4. Being heavy in the sense of befalling hard or being hidden. On Q 7:187 ثقلت في السموات والأرض, one view: its occurrence weighs heavily on the dwellers of heaven and earth; Abū ʿAlī's view: it means "it is hidden/obscure" — because what is hidden from you is also burdensome.

5. Causative and related verbs: ثَقَّلَ (to make heavy); أثقل (to load heavily) — cited for Q 52:40 فهم من مغرم مثقلون ("weighed down by debt"); استثقل (to find heavy).

6. Pregnancy: أثقلت المرأة (a woman grew heavy, her pregnancy showing) — cited for Q 7:189 فلما أثقلت ("when she grew heavy [with child]"). Such a woman is called مُثْقِل, without the feminine ة.

7. "A weighty word" — Q 73:5 قولاً ثقيلاً. Two readings Ibn Sīda records: (a) the heavy religious duty laid upon him; (b) an allusion to the gravity and excellence of the utterance. A poetic shāhid uses "not heavy in the hand" to mean yielding no benefit.

8. مِثقال — a weight-equivalent, "that whose weight is made known." Cited for Q 31:16 مثقالَ حبة من خردل ("the weight of a mustard-seed"), with a grammatical note: مثقال is in the nominative yet the verb تَكُ is feminine, because مثقال حبة reverts in sense to الحبة (the seed) — as if "though it be a mustard-seed." The point: even the smallest human deed is in God's knowledge and He brings it forth.

9. Related nouns: المِثْقَلة, a marble weight for holding down a spread/carpet.

10. Of a woman: ثَقال can mean large-hipped (مِكْفال) or, distinctly, grave and dignified (رَزان) — a deliberate distinction between what is physically heavy and what is settled/dignified in bearing (not flighty); likewise of a man, who is said to have ثِقَل (gravity) and to be ثاقِل. Shāhid from Kuthayyir ʿAzza: "a measured, weighty (ثاقل) forbearance." This form may be attributive (nasab): "possessed of weight."

11. بعير ثَقال — a slow camel; Abū Ḥanīfa [al-Dīnawarī] used this to explain a line of Labīd comparing flood-channels to "heavy poles."

12. ثَقَلَ الشيءَ بيده — to weigh/gauge a thing's weight by hand. تثاقل عنه — to be sluggish toward something. On Q 9:38 اثّاقلتم إلى الأرض ("you inclined heavily toward the earth"), Ibn Sīda notes it takes إلى ("toward") because it carries the sense of "you leaned/inclined"; al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl glossed ثقل إلى الأرض as "clung to and settled into it," which validates the construction with إلى without needing figurative reinterpretation. تثاقل القوم — a people summoned to relief who fail to rise to it.

13. الثَّقَل — baggage/goods and dependents (plural أثقال); "the people set off with their baggage," attested with several vowelings of ثَقلة. Also الثَّقْلة — the heaviness one feels in the belly from food, or heaviness felt in the body.

14. Severe illness: ثَقُلَ الرجل — his sickness grew grave; he is ثَقيل / ثاقِل. Labīd's verse describes a man who "wakes ثاقلاً," i.e. heavy with illness near death (a variant reads ناقلاً, "moved" from this world to the next). Sleep too can make one heavy (أثقله); المُستثقَل is one overcome by sleep, the state being الثَّقْلة (drowsiness).

15. Of desert shrubs (العرفج، الثمام، الضعة): ثَقَلَ — they grew rank and sappy.

16. Of hearing: ثَقُلَ سَمْعُه — his hearing partly failed; if wholly gone, one says وَقَرَ (he went deaf).

17. الثَّقَلان — mankind and the jinn. Cited for Q 55:31 سنفرغ لكم أيها الثقلان. Grammatical note: though dual in form, it means a collective plural (hence لكم, "you [pl.]"). A verse of Dhū al-Rumma calls Mayya "the fairest of the two kinds," with an extended note on why the singular pronoun أحسنه is used — in superlative constructions of this type the singular predominates ("the fairest human in face"), so the singular pronoun is idiomatic rather than the expected plural.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the three letters th-r-b as covering two entirely separate, underived words:

1. al-tathrīb (التثريب) — blame; reproaching or taking someone to task over a wrongdoing. He cites the Qur'an: "lā tathrība ʿalaykumu l-yawm" — "no blame upon you today" (Yūsuf 12:92).

2. al-tharb (الثرب) — the thin fat/membrane that covers the stomach (kirsh) and intestines. Plural: thurūb (ثروب).

He states explicitly that these two senses share no common root or derivation between them — they are simply two unrelated words that happen to use the same three letters.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
poets_named: Ibn Muqbil (lived into Islam); Jarīr (Umayyad); Ṭufayl (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse; Kuthayyir (Umayyad)
text:
Root ث ر ي (th-r-y). Source: Asās al-Balāgha by al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144 CE).

Core literal sense — moisture/dampness in earth and things:
1. A traditional trio of month-names traces the pasture season: 'a moist month,' then 'a month in which [greenery] is seen,' then 'a grazed month' — first the earth turns damp, then green growth becomes visible, then the plants grow tall enough for animals to graze.
2. Rain 'moistens' (tharā) the dust/earth; moistened earth is muthran.
3. Earth that has 'become moist' is tharin (the adjective for 'moist').
4. To 'moisten' dust or parched-barley meal (sawīq) is tharaytu — I dampened it.

Metaphorical extension (explicitly marked by al-Zamakhsharī as majāz) — moisture as a figure for wealth, abundance, affection, and trace/effect:
5. A man 'becomes athrā' (grows rich) — parallel to 'becomes atrab' (dusty) — literally 'comes to possess moist earth and soil,' figuratively 'comes to possess abundant wealth.' A wealthy man is muthrin, or 'possessor of tharwa/tharā' (riches).
6. A people 'tharaw' (grow numerous) when their numbers increase; they are 'in tharwa and tharā'' (abundance). Ibn Muqbil is cited praising a multitude of men likened to dense thickets (the verse's place-name is textually uncertain).
7. Proverb: 'the two moistures met' — for how quickly two men's affection unites, from the image of fresh rain-moisture meeting the old moisture already in the ground.
8. 'Do not let the moisture dry up between us' = do not cut off relations with me — illustrated by a line of Jarīr using the same image for a bond staying 'moist' (i.e. alive).
9. 'The moisture of water appeared on the horse' = it broke into a sweat — illustrated by a verse of Ṭufayl describing camels' flanks growing damp.
10. 'I see the moisture of anger in his face' = I see the trace of his anger — illustrated by an anonymous verse about a man who notices resentment surface in a kinsman but chooses not to provoke it further.
11. 'So-and-so is near in moisture, far in water-source' — said of someone who is generous with promises (words) but never delivers (the underlying water/substance).
12. 'I reached so-and-so's tharā' = I got what I wanted from him.
13. 'I became moist through you' (thariytu bika) = I was made glad and pleased by you — illustrated by a verse of Kuthayyir about rejoicing at being envied on someone's account (the verse's precise sense is not fully certain).
14. 'He is the son of its inner knowledge, and son of its tharā' = an idiom for someone who is a thorough expert in a matter.
15. 'Nothing moistens him,' or 'nothing thrives in him' = nothing has any effect on him, because of how hard/unyielding he is.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: ثَوَاب 13x "reward"; ثِيَاب 8x "garments"; أَثَٰبَ 3x "so rewarded them"; مَثُوبَة 2x "(as) recompense"; مَثَابَة 1x "a place of return"; ثُوِّبَ 1x "been rewarded"
poets_named: al-Jaʿdī (disputed date); Kuthayyir (Umayyad); unnamed verse; Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic)
text:
Zamakhsharī's Asās al-Balāgha treats the root ث و ب by separating literal from figurative usage. The core idea is returning / coming back.

Literal senses:
1. ثاب (thāba) — to return: companions who had scattered "return to him." The noun مثابة (mathāba) is a place people keep coming back to: "the House is a mathāba for the people." The III-form يثاوبها means to go back to someone repeatedly (used of suitors returning to a woman).
2. Form-II ثوّب (thawwaba) — to do again / repeat: to repeat the call in supplication; to perform two extra rakʿas over again after a prayer.
3. أثاب / ثوّب — to requite, reward: "God requited him." Zamakhsharī cites the Qurʾān, "have the disbelievers been requited" (83:36), and the noun مثوبة (mathūba, "reward"): "may God grant you the goodliest reward."

Figurative senses (labelled majāz):
4. Return of something that had left a person: reason and forbearance "come back" to him; the body "returns" after emaciation, i.e. one regains flesh (أثاب = God restored his body).
5. Water gathering and returning: a well's مثابة is its water-collecting basin; a well with a ثائب has water that flows back after being drawn out; a basin "thāba" = filled up.
6. ثائب of a surging influx of people arriving throng after throng — al-Jaʿdī likens such an inflow to an unbroken sea.
7. Accrual / accumulation: wealth "thāba" to a man = grew abundant; dust "thāba" = surged up and thickened; a man "thawwaba" = recovered his estate after poverty.
8. Entrenchment (a striking metaphor): "the reservoir of his ignorance filled up," said when someone's ignorance became firmly set.
9. مستثابات الرياح — auspicious, blessing-bearing winds whose good is hoped for (shāhid from Kuthayyir). By extension the best of winds is called ثواب (thawāb), and so is honey, the best product of bees — hence the saying "sweeter than thawāb (honey)."
10. استثاب — to recover lost wealth: "his wealth was lost and he recovered it"; the idiom "istathabtu bi-mālika" = I recouped my loss through what you gave me.

The garment (ثوب / ثياب):
11. Metaphor for character: "clean of garment" = free of fault; its opposite, "soiled of garments" = blameworthy.
12. Admiration formula: "li-llāhi thawbā fulān" (lit. "to God belong the two garments of so-and-so") praises the man himself — parallel to "li-llāhi bilāduhu." Shawāhid from al-Rāʿī and Laylā al-Akhyaliyya.
13. Separation idiom: "draw your garments out of mine" = withdraw and part from me (shāhid from Imruʾ al-Qays, where the garments "slip loose").
14. "He clung to the garments of God" = he clung to the covering-cloths of the Kaʿba.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ث-و-ر as two separate base meanings that, he notes, could be brought together with only a little reflection: (1) a thing rising up or bursting forth, and (2) a kind of animal.

1. Rising up / stirring up.
- ثَارَ (thāra), imperfect yathūru, with three verbal nouns — thawr, thuʾūr, thawarān: a thing rises up, stirs, breaks out.
- Used of a rash: "the measles broke out."
- Form III ثَاوَرَ (thāwara): to spring upon someone, glossed as wāthaba — as though each of the two men rose up against the other.
- Form II ثَوَّرَ (thawwara) evil against someone: to bring it out into the open, make it show.
- He suggests that thawr in the sense of pond-scum/duckweed (ṭuḥlub), reported by some, may belong under this heading, since it is something that has risen to the water's surface.

2. The bull.
- الثَّوْر (al-thawr), plural الثِّيرَان (thīrān), and also الأَثْوَار (athwār).

Extended and disputed usages:
- Calling a chief or leading man a "bull" he treats as figurative (tashbīh) — and only conditionally: he says he has found no sound transmission that the Arabs actually used it that way.
- A line of verse ("Truly I, in killing Sulayk and then paying his blood-money, am like the bull that is beaten when the cows refuse the water") is read two ways by earlier scholars: some take thawr as the animal, citing the belief that a jinnī rides the bull's back so the cows will not drink — supported by another line, "What is his fault, that the cows refused the water? — and they refuse it only so that he may be beaten." Others take thawr here as the duckweed sense noted above.
- ثَوْر is also the name of a mountain and of an Arab tribe — both, in his account, by likeness.
- الثَّوْر also denotes a piece of aqiṭ (dried curd). His derivation of this last sense is cut off in the text.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats ث-و-ي as a single sound root with one core meaning: staying, dwelling, remaining in a place. He states that every derivative traces back to this one sense.

1. Core verb: ثَوَى / يَثْوِي — to stay or dwell; the active participle ثاوٍ is "one who dwells, a resident," and the verbal noun ثَوَاء is a "stay, sojourn." Poetic witness: a line on Asmāʾ's departure — "many a dweller whose long stay grows wearisome."

2. Variant form: أَثْوَى, used in the same sense (to tarry/lodge). Witness: a verse of a traveller who "tarried and cut short his night to get provisioned, then moved on and broke a tryst with Qutayla."

3. Derived nouns of place/shelter:
- الثَّوِيَّة and الثَّايَة: a fold or shelter for sheep.
- الثَّوِيَّة is also a specific place-name.
- أُمُّ مَثْوَى الرَّجُل: the woman who keeps a man's lodging (his hostess/housekeeper).
- الثَّايَة additionally: stones set up as a marker for a shepherd, to which he returns at night — a landmark.

All of these, in his analysis, come back to the single idea of staying/settling in a place.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ث-خ-ن (th-kh-n). Ibn Fāris states the core sense is steadiness/solidity combined with heaviness.

1. Thickness/density — thakhuna ("became thick/dense"); noun thakhāna ("thickness").

2. Of a person — thakhīn describes a forbearing, composed/dignified man.

3. Of cloth — a garment is thakhīn ("thick") when its weft and warp are tightly compact, the result of fine weaving.

4. Causative — athkhantu-hu = "I weighed him down" (= aʾthqaltuhu, "I made him heavy").
   - Cited for this sense: Q8:67, {ḥattā yuthkhina fī l-arḍ} ("until he deals a crushing blow in the land"). Ibn Fāris explains this as describing the slain man weighed down (by wounds/death) to the point that no movement is left in him.

5. muthkhan — a man "left muthkhan" (taraktuhu muthkhanan) means left waqīdh, beaten down to the point of incapacity.

6. A further usage some scholars (qawm) report: thakhīn is also said of an unarmed man, one with no weapon on him — because his movement is restrained out of fear for himself. Ibn Fāris notes this fits the root's underlying logic (qiyās al-bāb) of reduced movement under heaviness/restraint.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
Root: ث ي ب — Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr, d. 1311 CE).

**Core sense.** Al-thayyib, applied to a woman, is one who married and then separated from her husband — by any means — after he had had intercourse with her.

**Defining "thayyib" more precisely — several authorities cited:**
1. Abū al-Haytham: a thayyib woman is one who had a husband who then died (leaving her a widow), or who was divorced and has since become eligible for marriage again.
2. Al-Aṣmaʿī: the term applies equally to men and women — anyone (male or female) who has had intercourse is "thayyib." Male and female are treated the same here.
3. Ibn al-Athīr: thayyib simply means "not a virgin (bikr)." He adds that the word can also be stretched, figuratively, to mean any mature/adult woman, even one who is still a virgin.

**Restriction on usage.** The author of al-ʿAyn notes the term is normally used only for women, not men — except in the set expression "child of the two thayyibs" versus "child of the two bikrs (virgins)."

**A cited report (khabar).** "The two thayyibs are stoned; the two virgins (bikrs) are flogged and exiled" — distinguishing the penalty for a previously-married offender from that for a never-married one.

**A cited ḥadīth** on the same theme: "The thayyib [paired] with the thayyib: a hundred lashes and stoning with stones." Ibn al-Athīr notes that combining flogging with stoning in this way is abrogated (no longer operative).

**Morphology.** The verb form: thuyyibat al-marʾah tathyīban — "the woman was made/became a thayyib." Once so described, she is called muthayyab. The plural of thayyib (for women) is thayyibāt.

**Qur'anic citation.** God's words "thayyibātin wa-abkāran" (Q. 66:5) — "previously-married women and virgins" — are cited as an attestation of the plural form.

**Etymology.** Ibn al-Athīr states that despite the ي in the spelling, the word's true root is و (wāw), not ي — it comes from thāba yathūbu, "to return, to revert." On this account, a thayyib is so called because she is, in a sense, one who "returns" — i.e., who has reverted to/entered that state (of no longer being a virgin).

**Toponym.** Thībān is separately noted as the name of a kūrah (district/province) — unrelated to the marital sense.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
text:
Root و-ش-ي (w-sh-y) — Tāj al-ʿArūs, al-Zabīdī

Core sense: decorative patterning/embroidery, branching into "informing/slandering," "increase or first appearance of something," and "gentle extraction."

1. Washy = the ornamental patterning of a woven garment, in any color (illustrated with a poetic image of blossoms compared to the embroidery on cushions). The washy of a sword is the wavy damascene-pattern (firind) on its blade.

2. Verb washā l-thawb / intensive washshāhu = to pattern, decorate, and beautify a garment; the doubled form marks intensity or repetition (al-Jawharī).

3. Figurative extensions of washā:
   - Of a talebearer: "he washā his speech" = he lied, i.e. he shaped, composed, and embellished a false report.
   - "washā bihi ilā l-sulṭān" (noun: wishāyah) = he informed against or intrigued against someone before the ruler. Proverb: "he keeps on walking and informing" — a pun on mashy (walking) and washy.
   - "washā banū fulān" = a people's offspring multiplied.

4. Shiyah (from the same root, the lost initial wāw replaced by a tāʾ marbūṭah) = a horse's or other animal's color — specifically a patch that differs from its main coat (al-Ṣiḥāḥ). Hence thawr ashyah, "a parti-colored bull," parallel to faras ablaq, "piebald horse." The phrase "lā shiyata fīhā" (no shiyah in her) is explained here as: no color in her differs from the rest of her coat. Also: faras ḥasan al-ushiyy = a horse with a fine blaze and white feet (called an irregular form by al-Liḥyānī); tawashshā fīhi l-shayb = grey hair appeared in his hair (= al-shiyah), with a supporting verse.

5. An idiom, "the night is long, and I will not āshī its shiyah" — meaning "I won't lie awake worrying over and planning what I intend to arrange" — from the sense "to embroider/work out in detail," used as a kind of curse formula. Al-Zabīdī devotes a long note to disputing Ibn Sīdah's claim that this word's exact form is unknown, arguing it derives either from washaytu ("I worked out") or from a reciprocal verb built on the same root.

6. Awshā (Form IV) / istawshā (Form X) — a cluster of extended, mostly figurative senses:
   - awshati l-arḍ: the land's first vegetation appeared.
   - awshati l-nakhlah: a palm tree's first ripe dates appeared.
   - awshā l-rajul: his wealth grew and multiplied. The related noun al-washāʾ means "wealth" — Ibn Jinnī explains it as literally "an ornament-pattern," since wealth, like fine embroidered cloth, is worn as adornment; al-Zabīdī supports this with Qur'an 16:6 on the beauty of grazing livestock.
   - awshā: to draw out the meaning of a speech or poem by close study.
   - awshā l-maʿdin (= istawshā l-maʿdin): a small amount of gold was found in the mine.
   - awshā l-shayʾ: to draw something out gently (cited poetry, with lexicographers disputing whether the original sense was "gently" or "forcibly").
   - awshā farasahu / istawshāhu: to urge a horse to show its full speed, e.g. with a goad, or by striking its flank with the heel.
   - awshā (fī) l-shayʾ: to make or work something.
   - awshā fī l-darāhim: to skim off/take some of a sum of money or goods.
   - awshā l-dawāʾ al-marīḍ: the medicine cured the patient (cited verse where al-wushāh = goldsmiths/gold-minters).
   - istawshā l-ḥadīth: to investigate and gather information — also used in a ḥadīth about seeking help from distant relatives in hard times.

7. ḥajar bihi washy = a stone from a gold-bearing mine.

8. al-wāshī = prolific in offspring (of any breeding animal); "this livestock hasn't washat anything for me" = hasn't given birth (a figurative use).

9. The weaver is called wāshin ("one who washī's the cloth") — one who weaves and assembles it.

10. istawshaytahu = said of anything you call or urge on so as to send it off (a dialectal sīn-variant of a related verb).

11. iʾtashā l-ʿaẓm = a broken bone knitted/healed (Form VIII from al-washy, per al-Azharī). Illustrated with a ḥadīth anecdote: a man caught by a wronged husband and injured, who later explains his injury as a fall from a young camel that "healed crooked" (fa-ʾtashā muḥdawdiban).

Additional notes appended by al-Zabīdī: plural of washy (cloth) is wishāh; a decorated garment is mawshiyy or muwashshā; the relational adjective of shiyah is washawiyy (grammarians differ on the vocalization of the shīn); the imperative is shih (a hāʾ is added because Arabic doesn't pronounce a bare single consonant); thawr muwashshā l-qawāʾim = a bull with dusky-and-white legs; a little spadix/pollen-sheath appearing on a palm is also called washy; al-washshāʾ (intensive noun) = a seller of silk cloth (also a nickname for some ḥadīth-narrators), and also means "the talebearer" and "the liar"; washāhu burdan = he clothed him in a mantle; al-Mūshiyyah = a large village west of the Nile in Upper Egypt (vocalization disputed among the geographers).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats و-ذ-ر as covering two unrelated words:

1. **A piece of flesh.** الْوَذَرَة (al-wadhara) is a lump or chunk of meat. From this comes the verb التَّوْذِير (al-tawdhīr), "to make an incision in a wound" — one says وَذَّرْتُهُ ("I lanced it"). He notes a ḥadīth in which one man insulted another as "son of the woman who sniffs the flesh-bits," an obscene innuendo (alluding to men's private parts) for which the speaker received the ḥadd penalty.

2. **"Leaving / letting be."** The second word appears in the phrase ذَرْ ذَا (dhar dhā, "leave this alone"). Ibn Fāris reports the philologists' observation that the Arabs let the past-tense form of this verb fall out of use, so they do not say وَذَرْتُهُ ("I left it") — only the imperative and imperfect survive.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root و-ء-د (w-ʾ-d) from one core sense: weighing something down with something else.

1. Camel gait: when camels walk burdened by a heavy load, their tread is called a wa'īd — a heavy, thudding walk. A citation is given: "What ails the camels, that their walking is wa'īd?" i.e., a heavy-footed walk.

2. Al-maw'ūda — the female infant buried alive: Ibn Fāris ties this term directly to the root's core sense of "weighing down" — she is called maw'ūda because, once buried alive, she is weighed down by the earth piled over her. He gives the verb pattern: wa'adahā yaʾiduhā wa'dan ("he buried her alive").

3. A further citation extends the usage: "he kept the one due to be buried alive, so she was not buried" — i.e., he spared a girl who would otherwise have been wa'ada'd.

So for Ibn Fāris, the burial-alive sense is not a separate root meaning but a specific application of the general idea of "weighing/pressing something down," via the image of earth pressing down on the one buried.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: و-أ-ل (w-ʾ-l) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris states that this root's letters (wāw, hamza, lām) point to one core idea: gathering together and taking refuge.

He supports this with three usages:

1. **اسْتَوْأَلَتِ الْإِبِلُ** (istawʾalat al-ibil) — said of camels that "gathered together" (ijtamaʿat), i.e. herded/clustered as a group.

2. **الْمَوْئِلُ** (al-mawʾil) — "a refuge" or "place of shelter," derived from the verb وَأَلَ إِلَيْهِ يَئِلُ (waʾala ilayhi, yaʾilu) — "he fled to / sought refuge in" something.

3. **الْوَأْلَةُ** (al-waʾlah) — the smell given off by a gathered/piled-up heap of camel dung — here the "gathering" sense applies to the dung itself being clustered together, with the derived word naming its odor.

So the entry ties one semantic thread — clustering/coming together, whether of animals, of dung, or (metaphorically) of a person converging toward safety — through all three attested forms.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: وَضَعَ 21x "they deliver"; مَّوَاضِع 3x "their places"; أَوْضَعُ 1x "and would have been active"; مَّوْضُوعَة 1x "put in place"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root w-ḍ-ʿ (وضع) from a single core idea: lowering something and setting it down.

1. Basic sense — to put down, lay down. وَضَعْتُهُ بِالْأَرْضِ (I laid it on the ground; verbal noun waḍʿ). Applied to birth: وَضَعَتِ الْمَرْأَةُ وَلَدَهَا (the woman delivered her child).

2. Commercial loss — the passive وُضِعَ فِي تِجَارَتِهِ (he was "brought low" in his trade) means he incurred a loss (khasira).

3. الْوَضَائِعُ (al-waḍāʾiʿ) — people relocated from one land to another to settle there.

4. الْوَضِيعُ (al-waḍīʿ) — a base or lowly man (from the sense of "low").

5. An easy gait — a riding-beast that "goes at a waḍʿ" moves at an easy, low pace, as opposed to al-marfūʿ (the raised, brisker gait). Ibn Fāris cites a verse contrasting the beast's brisk gait (a marvel) with its easy gait (like a passing rainstorm in the wind). Related forms: mawḍūʿ (that easy gait — "she is excellent in the mawḍūʿ"), the form-IV awḍaʿa (its rider drove her at that pace), and وَضَعَ الرَّجُلُ (the man traveled at that gait).

6. الْوَاضِعَاتُ (al-wāḍiʿāt) — reported as the camels that graze on khalla (a soft pasture-plant), supported by a cited verse.

7. الْمُوَضَّعُ (al-muwaḍḍaʿ, form II) — a man whose affairs are not firmly settled or sound.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
poets_named: al-Muthaqqib al-ʿAbdī (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse; Al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam)
text:
Root و ض ن (w-ḍ-n) — Tāj al-ʿArūs, al-Zabīdī

**1. Core sense — folding/doubling over, stacking:** waḍana something = he folded part of it over another part, doubling it. Applied to building: stacking stone or brick layer upon layer. A related sense given for the same verb is "arranged/set in order" (naḍḍada) — illustrated by a man telling his wife to "waḍana" the household goods, i.e. bring the pieces close together.

**2. Weaving a girth-strap (al-waḍīn):** The verb also means "he wove" a nisʿ (a woven strap). From this comes al-waḍīn: a broad band woven part-over-part from leather strips or hair, used to bind a camel's pack-saddle (raḥl) in place — some say it serves both the pack-saddle and the howdah, while the narrower biṭān-strap is reserved for the smaller qatab saddle. Al-Jawharī compares it across mounts: waḍīn : howdah :: biṭān : qatab :: taṣdīr (chest-band) : rider :: ḥizām : horse-saddle. Another view restricts waḍīn strictly to leather — if not leather, it's called ghurḍa instead — supported by a line of verse from al-Muthaqqib al-ʿAbdī about "loosening her waḍīn." Grammatically, waḍīn is noted as a faʿīl-form with a passive (mafʿūl) sense, like qatīl for maqtūl. Plural: wuḍun.

**3. A loosened girth = a worn-down mount, or an unsteady man:** "Her waḍīn grew loose" describes a camel's girth-strap slackening as she grows thin. This becomes a figure of speech: in a ḥadīth about ʿAlī, "you are one whose girth is loose" describes a man as flighty and unsteady — quick to shift, like a slack strap. A set of verses attributed (in different transmissions) to Ibn ʿUmar, or to the Prophet reciting while leaving ʿArafāt, uses the same image — "toward You her girth runs loose, her unborn young shifting within her" — for an exhausted, travel-worn she-camel.

**4. al-mawḍūna — woven mail armor:** A coat of chain mail is called mawḍūna because of how it is woven — rings interlocked one within another (compared to a near-synonym marḍūna). Al-Aʿshā's verse describes "the weave of Dāwūd" (i.e. mail armor) driving a caravan. Other lexicographers describe the weave more specifically as two rings linked at a time, or extend the word to cloth/thrones set or inlaid with jewels.

**5. Two derived verbs:** tawaḍḍana — "he humbled/abased himself" (per Ibn al-Aʿrābī). ittaḍana — "he became joined/connected" (per another source).

**6. Woven baskets:** al-mīḍāna and al-mīḍana name woven containers — one a basket-like quffa, the other a sack like a jūwāliq — both made from khūṣ, palm-leaf fiber; plural mawāḍīn.

**Supplementary notes:** al-waḍn also names the weaving of a couch/throne with pearls and cloth trim; a sarīr mawḍūn ("doubly woven couch") is the term the author links directly to the Qur'anic phrase "ʿalā sururin mawḍūna" (Q. 56:15). al-wuḍna names a woven chair or stool. al-tawaḍḍun, distinct from sense 5 above, is also glossed as "mutual affection" (per Ibn al-Aʿrābī) — the entry gives both meanings for related forms without resolving them into one.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root w-ʿ-ẓ as expressing a single idea.

1. الوَعْظ (al-waʿẓ): instilling fear or cautioning.
2. العِظَة (al-ʿiẓa): the noun formed from it.

He cites al-Khalīl's definition: it is reminding someone of the good, and of that which softens the heart.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: وَعَدَ 70x "promised"; وَعْد 49x "(the) promise"; مَّوْعِد 12x "an appointment"; مِّيعَاد 6x "the promise"; وَعِيد 6x "my threat"; وَٰعَدْ 4x "we appointed"; تُوعِدُ 1x "threatening"; تَوَاعَد 1x "you (had) made an appointment"; مَّوْعِدَة 1x "(of) a promise"; مَوْعُود 1x "promised"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats و-ع-د (w-ʿ-d) as a sound root whose core sense is holding out a prospect to someone by speech — a promise.

1. Basic verb: waʿada / aʿidu / waʿd ("to promise"). Crucially, the promise can be of good or of evil.

2. Threat (waʿīd): the form specialized to evil only. The verb here is awʿada bi- ("to threaten with"). Shāhid: a poet's line, "he threatened me with prison and iron fetters."

3. Mutual appointment (muwāʿada): derived from mīʿād, an appointed time or place.

4. Morphology of "promise": ʿida is a synonym of waʿd; its plural is ʿidāt, while waʿd itself takes no plural.

5. Extended usage — of a stallion: waʿīd al-faḥl is its rumbling growl when it is roused to charge. Shāhid: "it threatens the heart of the unarmed man."

6. Extended usage — of land: arḍ wāʿida, "promising land," when a good yield is hoped for from rain and pasture.

7. Extended usage — of a day: yawm wāʿid, a day whose early hours "promise" (give early signs of) heat or cold.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: وِعَاء 3x "(the) bag"; أَوْعَىٰ 2x "they keep within themselves"; تَعِيَ 1x "and would be conscious of it"; وَٰعِيَة 1x "conscious"
text:
Ibn Fāris's account of the root و-ع-ي:

1. Core notion. The three letters wāw, ʿayn, yāʾ point to one idea: gathering something in, enclosing or containing it.

2. Retaining knowledge. waʿaytu al-ʿilm aʿīhi waʿyan — "I took in / held the knowledge." The mind is treated as a container that keeps what is put into it.

3. Stowing goods (Form IV). awʿaytu al-matāʿ fī l-wiʿāʾ — "I packed the goods into the vessel." wiʿāʾ is the container itself. A verse of poetry (unattributed here) is cited as evidence: "and evil is the foulest thing you have stowed away as provision."

4. A separate sense: al-waʿā = clamour, a din of voices. Ibn Fāris treats this as not properly belonging to the root: he classes it under letter-substitution (ibdāl), holding that the original consonant was ghayn — i.e. it is really al-waghā (battle-din).

5. Derived from that noise-sense: al-waʿiyya, a woman who cries out or shrieks.

6. An idiom he records without further comment: lā waʿya ʿan kadhā — "there is no holding back from such-and-such."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha on the root و-ح-ش (w-ḥ-sh):

The root's core sense is "the opposite of al-ins" — that is, the opposite of what is tame, familiar, or companionable. From it comes tawaḥḥasha, "to part from the familiar/companion."

Senses recorded:

1. Al-waḥsh — the wild, as opposed to the tame (of animals/game).
2. A "waḥsh-land" (arḍ mūḥisha) — a desolate place, named from this root.
3. On a bow: the "wild" side (waḥshiyy) is its back; the "tame/near" side (insiyy) is the face turned toward the archer.
4. On a riding animal: al-Aṣmaʿī is cited as saying the waḥshiyy side is the side the rider mounts from and the milker milks from. The entry goes on to explain the related idioms "it bolted upon its waḥshiyy side" and "its waḥshiyy side swerved away" on the grounds that the animal is approached — for mounting, milking, handling — only from that (waḥshiyy) side, so its fright/skittishness shows up there too; the insiyy side is the remaining, opposite side.
5. Idiom: "I met him at a waḥsh of iṣmit" — meaning in a barren, uninhabited stretch of land.
6. Idiom: "waḥasha bi-thawbihi" — he flung away/cast off his garment.
7. Idiom: "he spent the night waḥsh" — meaning hungry, as though stranded in a desolate land with nothing to eat.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats و-ح-د (w-ḥ-d) as a single root whose core sense is singleness / being alone (al-infirād).

1. Base noun: الوَحْدة (waḥda) — oneness, solitude.

2. "Unique of his kind": one says "he is the wāḥid of his tribe" when no one among them matches him. Cited verse: "O unique one of the Arabs, who has no equal among mankind."

3. Adverbial / distributive uses: مَوْحَدَ مَوْحَدَ ("one by one, singly," as in "I met the people singly") and وَحْدَه ("alone," as in "I met him alone").

4. Grammatical note: the word waḥd is not used in a genitive construct (iḍāfa) except in fixed expressions such as نَسيجُ وَحْدِه ("uniquely woven") and its parallels ʿuyayr waḥdihi, juḥaysh waḥdihi. Nasīj waḥdihi means something so precious that nothing else is woven like it; it functions as a proverb.

5. الوَاحِد (al-wāḥid): the one who stands alone, the solitary (al-munfarid).

6. Poetic attestation (ʿUbayd b. al-Abraṣ): "By God, had I died it would not have harmed me; and I, if I live, am not in a single one." Ibn Fāris glosses this as: I do not rest on one lasting trait, since everything must come to an end.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَوْحَىٰ 72x "and we inspired"; وَحْى 6x "and our inspiration"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root w-ḥ-y (wāw, ḥāʾ, and a weak final letter) from a single core idea: conveying knowledge to another person, whether covertly or openly.

1. Core sense — al-waḥy: the act of imparting something to another until he knows it, in whatever manner it happens.

2. Related senses of al-waḥy: (a) a "sign" or gesture (ishāra); (b) "writing" and "a message" (kitāb, risāla).

3. Verb forms: both awḥā and waḥā are used, including of God. Ibn Fāris cites a line of verse: "He conveyed/prompted the settling to it, and it settled" (waḥā lahā al-qarāra fa-staqarrat).

4. Ibn Fāris states that everything falling under the heading of waḥy goes back to this one root.

5. Two further derivatives: al-waḥiyy means "swift, quick" (sarīʿ); al-waḥā means "sound, voice" (ṣawt).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root و ص ب (w-ṣ-b), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: the continuance/persistence of a thing.

1. waṣaba al-shayʾ — it persisted, continued; waṣaba al-dīn — it became obligatory (i.e. binding, ongoing).
2. mafāzah wāṣibah — an endless wasteland with no limit — an extension of "persisting without end."
3. Qur'anic citation, al-Saffat 37:9, "wa lahum ʿadhābun wāṣib" — glossed as: an unceasing, perpetual punishment.
4. al-waṣab — chronic, persistent illness; rajul waṣib / muwaṣṣab — a man continually afflicted with ailments.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha derives the whole root w-ṣ-d from one core idea: joining or bringing one thing close up against another.

1. Verb — awṣadtu al-bāb, "I awṣad-ed the door," means simply "I closed/shut it."

2. Noun waṣīd (first sense) — plant growth whose stems/roots stand close together, packed near one another.

3. Noun waṣīd (second sense) — the finā' (courtyard or forecourt) of a dwelling, called this precisely because it is joined/adjoining to the rab‘ (the living-quarters) — the same "joining" idea as the root meaning.

4. Passive participle mūṣad — something shut tight, closed up (glossed by the author as muṭbaq, "closed/sealed").

5. Qur'anic citation — Ibn Fāris cites Q104:8 (Sūrat al-Humazah): "innahā ‘alayhim mu'ṣadah" — "it is mu'ṣadah [shut/closed] over them" — as the Qur'anic instance of this same "closed/shut" sense of the root.

All senses in this entry trace back to the one idea of joining/closing something onto or against something else: a door shut, a courtyard joined to a house, plants growing close together, and something sealed shut.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats و-ص-ف (w-ṣ-f) as one root whose core sense is setting forth a thing's qualities — describing or characterizing it.

1. Basic usage: waṣaftuhu, aṣifuhu, waṣfan — "I described it / describe it / a describing."

2. al-ṣifa (a "quality, attribute") is the mark that inheres in and is bound to a thing. He draws a parallel with weighing: wazantuhu waznan ("I weighed it"), where al-zina is a thing's measure — so a ṣifa is, as it were, the measure or defining mark of a thing.

3. Derived verb: ittaṣafa al-shayʾu fī ʿayni al-nāẓir — "the thing came to be [thus] in the beholder's eye," i.e. it became something that admits of being described.

4. Related uses tied to describing at point of sale: waṣafat al-nāqa wuṣūfan is said of a she-camel that goes at an excellent pace. Ibn Fāris links this with the words for servants — waṣīf (male servant) and waṣīfa (female servant) — and with awṣafat al-jāriya (the girl reached the age/state of a waṣīfa). His stated reason: such servants have their qualities described (waṣf) when they are being sold.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: يَصِلُ 10x "be joined"; وَصِيلَة 1x "a wasilah"; وَصَّلْ 1x "we have conveyed"
poets_named: Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad); al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); al-Farazdaq (Umayyad)
text:
Root w-ṣ-l (وصل). Zamakhsharī arranges the senses from the literal act of joining to its figurative extensions.

1. Core literal sense — to join/connect one thing to another (waṣala … fa-ttaṣala, "he joined it, and it became joined"). Form II waṣṣala (tawṣīl) = to splice or link repeatedly; cited with Qurʾān 28:51, "We have joined together the discourse for them." A khayṭ muwaṣṣal is a thread with many splices.

2. Human connection vs. severance — waṣala/wāṣala = to reconnect or keep up ties (after estrangement); its opposite is ṣarama, "to cut off." The nouns for the bond are waṣl, ṣila, and wiṣāl; tawāṣul = mutual connection, opposed by taṣārum (mutual cutting-off).

3. Physical joint — mawṣil = the juncture of two ropes or two bones. awṣāl = the body's joints (singular waṣl/wiṣl), as in the curse "may God sever his joints" (with a verse of Dhū al-Rumma). Also of joining hair to hair — cited with the ḥadīth cursing "the woman who joins hair and the one who requests it."

4. The waṣīla (Qurʾān 5:103, among baḥīra and sāʾiba) — per Zamakhsharī, a ewe that "accompanied"/was paired with her brother among the flock's young and so was spared slaughter. Related idiom: to a survivor it is said "may you be no waṣīl to him" — may you not be so bound to a stricken man that his misfortune reaches you too. A waṣīl is also an inseparable intimate companion.

5. To reach/arrive — waṣala ilā (wuṣūl) = to reach; awṣala = to convey/deliver; tawaṣṣala ilā = to reach someone by gentle or artful means. A wuṣla is a means or link to something; also a travelling party that carries one to his destination. (He notes travel-provisions were called ṣulla.)

6. Figurative (majāz) senses Zamakhsharī marks explicitly:
 - A gift — "he connected him with a thousand dirhams"; a ruler's bounty is his ṣila (pl. ṣilāt).
 - Claiming affiliation — ittaṣala / waṣala ilā a tribe = to attach oneself, claim lineage (verse of al-Aʿshā).
 - Beyond remedy — a blow "that cannot be joined" = one that cannot be healed (verse of al-Farazdaq).

7. Kinship — waṣala raḥimahu, "to join one's kinship ties"; noted that God commanded ṣilat al-raḥim, the maintaining of kin bonds.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: وَصَّىٰ 11x "(he) has enjoined on you"; وَصِيَّة 8x "any will"; أَوْصَٰ 5x "and has enjoined (on) me"; تَوَاصَ 5x "and enjoin (each other)"; مُّوص 1x "(the) testator"; يُوصِي 1x "they have made"; تَوْصِيَة 1x "(to) make a will"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats و ص ي (w-ṣ-y; the third radical being the weak letter yāʾ/wāw) as a single root whose core meaning is the joining or connecting of one thing to another.

1. Basic sense — to connect. waṣaytu al-shayʾa = "I joined the thing."

2. Extended usage:
   - A land is called wāṣiya when its plant-growth is continuous and unbroken, the ground being filled with it.
   - waṣaytu al-laylata bi-l-yawmi = "I joined the night to the day," said of carrying a task on without interruption.

3. Derivation of "injunction" (waṣiyya). Ibn Fāris derives waṣiyya — an injunction or bequest — from this same idea of connecting: it is as though it were speech that is "linked/conveyed" (yūṣā) from one party to another.

4. Verb forms. The charging or enjoining sense appears in two derived forms: waṣṣā (form II, verbal noun tawṣiya) and awṣā (form IV, verbal noun īṣāʾ), both meaning "to enjoin/charge someone."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَطَـُ 3x "you may trample them"; يُوَاطِـُ 1x "to adjust"; مَوْطِئ 1x "any step"; وَطْـ 1x "and most potent"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats و-ط-أ (wāw, ṭāʾ, hamza) as a single root idea: making something level and smooth, hence making it easy.

1. To level or prepare a place — waṭṭaʾtu lahu al-makān, "I made the place smooth/ready for him."
2. al-wiṭāʾ — bedding: what one spreads to make a soft, level surface for oneself.
3. To tread — waṭiʾtuhu bi-rijlī, aṭaʾuhu, "I trod on it with my foot"; the act of setting the foot down on something, i.e. pressing it flat.
4. waṭʾa (the noun of that treading, used of pressure brought to bear) appears in the ḥadīth cited here: "Make your tread heavy upon Muḍar."
5. al-muwāṭaʾa (the mutual, form-III noun) — coming to agreement on a matter, each party smoothing/preparing the way of it for the other.

Grammatically, the entry gives the perfect/imperfect pair waṭiʾtu / aṭaʾu for the treading sense, and the doubled form waṭṭaʾa for "to level, prepare," alongside the derived nouns wiṭāʾ and muwāṭaʾa.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats w-ṭ-n as a single, coherent root idea (not two unrelated meanings folded together).

1. Al-waṭan — a person's dwelling-place, the place where one settles/resides.
2. Awṭān al-ghanam ("the awṭāns of sheep") — by extension, the resting-folds or pens where sheep bed down.
3. Awṭantu al-arḍa ("I awṭana-ed the land") — the verb form: to take a piece of land as one's settled home/dwelling.
4. Al-mīṭān — a related word given at the end of the entry, meaning the goal or finish-mark (al-ghāya), i.e. the point aimed at or reached.

The entry is brief: it establishes "settled dwelling/abode" as the core sense, extends it from human dwelling to animal resting-place, gives the corresponding verb, and closes with one further derived word (mīṭān) glossed simply as "goal."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root w-ṭ-r (وطر), per Ibn Fāris:
1. The three root letters express a single, unified meaning.
2. al-waṭar (الوَطَر) - a need or want, and a strong craving or keen desire.
3. Grammatical note: no verb is formed from this root - it exists only as a noun.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: وَبَال 4x "(the bad) consequence"; وَابِل 3x "heavy rain"; وَبِيل 1x "ruinous"
text:
Ibn Fāris gives the root w-b-l a single core idea: **intensity or severity in something, together with gathering/massing**. From that he lists:

1. **Heavy rain.** al-wabl and al-wābil = violent, pelting rain. Verb: wabalat al-samāʾ — "the sky brought down a downpour." He cites a line of verse for the escalating scale of giving-as-raining: "If they rain steadily, he rains generously; if they rain generously, he pours in a torrent."

2. **Weight, heaviness.** wabalat al-shayʾ = the heaviness of a thing. Hence shayʾ wabīl — something grievous, heavy in its consequences (he glosses it wakhīm, "unwholesome in outcome").

3. **A place that disagrees with you.** istawbaltu al-balad = I found the country unwholesome — it did not suit me, even though I was fond of it.

4. **A severe blow.** al-wabīl = a hard beating.

5. **A heavy-handed man.** al-wabīl = one who takes charge of an affair clumsily and fails to put it right.

6. **Harsh ground.** al-mawbil = rough, hard, stony terrain.

7. **A beating-club.** al-wabīl = the launderer's wooden mallet used to beat clothes.

8. **A bundle of firewood** — al-wabīl (the "gathering" side of the root).

9. **Pasture/herbage**, fresh or dry — reported with "it is said," i.e. a weaker attribution in his presentation.

10. **A knee-joint bone.** al-wābila.

The senses hold together through the two poles Ibn Fāris names at the outset: force (downpour, blow, mallet, harsh ground, grievous outcome) and massing (bundle, herbage, joint-bone).

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: مَّوْبِق 1x "a barrier"; يُوبِقْ 1x "he could destroy them"
text:
Root w-b-q, per al-Raghib al-Isfahani.

1. Core sense (verb wabaqa): said of something that is impeded or held back to the point that it perishes or is destroyed. Verbal nouns: wabaq and mawbiq.

2. Quranic citation (mawbiq): "And We placed between them a mawbiq" (18:52) -- mawbiq names a barrier or scene of destruction set between two parties.

3. Causative form (awbaqahu): Form IV, "X destroyed/ruined him/it" -- one thing bringing about another's ruin.

4. Quranic citation (yubiq): "Or He could destroy them [the ships] for what they [their people] earned" (42:34) -- the causative verb applied to God bringing ships to ruin because of the wrongdoing of their people.

The entry treats the whole root as centered on being checked or impeded and thereby brought to ruin, with mawbiq as the noun for the place or instrument of that destruction.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root w-b-r - Ibn Faris opens by marking this root as one whose senses do not reduce to a single core meaning; he lists them as separate, unrelated words that merely share the three letters.

1. Al-wabar - the soft fur/down of camels and similar animals. Given only as "well known," with no further definition.
2. Al-wabr (same letters, different vowel pattern) - "an animal," left unspecified beyond that.
3. Banat awbar ("daughters/offspring of Awbar") - a growth resembling small truffles.
4. An idiom: "ma bi-l-dari wabirun," there is not in the house a wabir, meaning there is no one in the house at all.
5. A usage reported by some: "wabbara fi manzilihi tawbiran," he did tawbir in his dwelling, meaning he did not leave or depart from it.
6. Wabr - the name of one of the "Days of the Old Woman" (ayyam al-'ajuz), a traditional set of cold days marking the tail end of winter.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مُسْتَوْدَع 2x "and a resting place"; دَعْ 1x "and disregard"; وَدَّعَ 1x "has forsaken you"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats و-د-ع as one root whose core sense is leaving off and letting be.

1. **Leaving alone.** وَدَعَهُ (wadaʿahu) = he left him/it. The common imperative دَعْ (daʿ, "leave it, let it be") belongs here. He cites a line of verse as evidence: "Would that I knew about my friend — what overcame him in love, until he left off (wadaʿah)."

2. **Taking leave / farewell.** From the same root: وَدَّعْتُهُ تَوْدِيعًا (waddaʿtuhu tawdīʿan), the second-form verb with verbal noun tawdīʿ — bidding farewell, i.e. parting from someone.

3. **Ease, repose.** الدَّعَة (al-daʿa) is ease or an unstrained low-keyed state; Ibn Fāris explains the link as a condition in which one leaves aside whatever wearies. Related forms: رَجُلٌ مُتَّدِعٌ (muttadiʿ), a man at rest and comfortable, who obtained something وَادِعًا (wādiʿan) — calmly, without exertion; and الْوَدِيع (al-wadīʿ), a still, quiet man.

4. **Truce.** الْمُوَادَعَة (al-muwādaʿa) is making peace and mutually leaving off — i.e. both sides ceasing hostilities.

5. **Laying something away.** وَدَّعْتُ الثَّوْبَ فِي صُوَانِهِ — "I put the garment away in its case"; the protective cloth/case for it is called مِيدَع (mīdaʿ).

Method: he states a single semantic origin for the root and then shows each derived form (verb, verbal noun, active participle, reciprocal form, instrument-noun pattern mīdaʿ) as a branch of that one sense.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: وَدَّ 17x "they wish"; مَّوَدَّة 8x "love"; وَدُود 2x "the most loving"; وُدّ 1x "affection"; وَدّ 1x "wadd"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats w-d-d as a word indicating affection (maḥabba, love).

1. **To love.** wadidtuhu means "I loved him". The verbal noun for this sense is al-wudd. One is someone's wadīd when one loves him.

2. **To wish.** wadidtu anna dhāka kāna means "I wished that that had been". The verbal noun for this sense is al-wadāda.

Both senses share the same imperfect, awaddu; they are told apart by their verbal nouns (wudd for love, wadāda for wishing).

3. **A separate word.** al-wadd means the peg (al-watid). Ibn Fāris says it has been dealt with already, in another place.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root w-d-q (و-د-ق) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: this root carries two linked ideas — "coming/approaching" (ityān) and "becoming familiar/at ease with" (unās).

1. Verb: wadaqtu bihi — I became familiar/at ease with someone (verbal noun: wadq).

2. Al-mawdiq — the place one approaches or comes to; also the spot where one stands feeling at ease/familiar. Applied to a gazelle (mawdiq al-ẓaby), it's the spot where it stands to browse a tree. A poetic line is cited using mawdiq for a place of rendezvous/tryst: "She effaces [the traces] with the hem of her wrap when I came to my mawdiq" (poet unnamed).

3. Atān wadīq — a she-ass "in heat," desiring the stallion; her state is called widāq — described as if she is growing familiar with him and drawing him toward familiarity with her.

4. Al-wadq — rain. Ibn Fāris links this to the "coming" sense: rain is so called because it yadiqqu, i.e., comes down from the sky.

5. Anomalous item (does not fit the root's core meaning, per the author): al-wadaq — red spots that appear in the eye, singular wadaqah.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: وَاد 7x "in the valley"; دِيَة 2x "then blood money"; أَوْدِيَة 2x "their valleys"; وَادِي 1x "a valley"
text:
Ibn Sīda gathers under the root و د ي a set of senses linked by the idea of flowing, dropping, and by-products:

1. **Blood-money (al-diya).** The compensation due for a slain person: وَدَيْتُه ("I paid his blood-money").

2. **Of a horse or donkey: to let the member down (وَدَى / أَدْلَى)** — to protrude it, either to urinate or to mate. Some distinguish: وَدَى = "to urinate," أَدْلَى = "to mate." Also said to mean simply "to drip."

3. **al-wady / al-wadiyy** — the thin white fluid discharged after urine. The lightened form (wady) is judged the more eloquent.

4. **To flow (وَدَى الشَّيءُ).** Supported by a verse cited by Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī using "when it flowed" (a coarse simile of a plaited rope).

5. **al-wādī — the valley:** any open cleft between mountains, hills, and mounds; named from "flowing," because water runs through it. A cited verse shows the poet dropping the final vowel of الوادِ, explained as elision forced when the weak letter cannot carry the extra vowel.
   - On {في كل وادٍ يهيمون} ("in every valley they roam," al-Shuʿarāʾ 225): Ibn Sīda holds this is not literal valleys but a metaphor for the poets' shifting speech — like the idiom "I am for you in one valley and you in another." The point is that poets range through praise and blame and lie, praising or reviling a man for what is not in him. The following verse (227) then excepts the believing poets who did not let verse distract them from remembering God, but defended the Prophet with hand and tongue and satirized those deserving it. He notes the exegetes name these as ʿAbd Allāh b. Rawāḥa, Kaʿb b. Mālik, and Ḥassān b. Thābit (the Anṣār).

6. **Plurals of wādī:** أَوْداء, أَوْدِية, أَوْداية. He flags a variant reading (والأَوادِيَه) as a scribal corruption, since the poem's rhyme (fixed by the preceding line) requires -āyah.
