7. **وَدَيْتُ الأَمْرَ — "I brought the matter near"** (= قَرَّبْتُه).

8. **To perish (أَوْدَى).** أَوْدَى الرَّجُلُ ("the man perished"); أَوْدَى بِه المَوْتُ ("death carried him off"). A verse of al-Aʿshā uses a masculine verb (أَوْدَى for أَوْدَتْ) because "the vicissitudes of time" (al-ḥadathān) are intended.

9. **al-wadā (shortened)** — perishing, destruction; cross-referenced to the hamzated root (w-d-ʾ).

10. **al-wadiyy — young date-palm shoots** (singular wadiyya). A verse boasts of skill at planting these over horsemanship.

11. **al-tawdiya** — the wooden peg tied over a she-camel's teat when she is bound, to stop her calf from suckling; a noun on the pattern of al-tanhiya. وَدَّيْتُها = "I fastened that peg on her."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root w-f-ḍ (وفض) as covering three unrelated words that merely share the same three letters:

1. Haste — the verb أَوْفَضَ (awfaḍa), "to hasten, hurry," with verbal noun إِيفَاض (īfāḍ). The phrase جاء على وَفْضٍ / أَوْفَاضٍ, "he came in haste," uses وَفْض in the sense of hurry (ʿajalah).

2. Groups of people — الأَوْفَاض (al-awfāḍ) denotes scattered bands or parties of people (al-firaq min al-nās).

3. The quiver — الوَفْضَة (al-wafḍah) is an arrow-case (al-kinānah), plural وِفَاض (wifāḍ).

No single unifying sense is proposed; the three are presented as separate homographic roots.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root و ف د (w-f-d), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: prominence and rising/ascending.

1. al-wāfid — people who arrive as a delegation (wafada); al-wafd — the prominent crest of a sand-ridge. al-wāfid, of camels — the one that outstrips the rest. al-īfād — haste/speed.
2. al-wāfidān — two prominent cheekbones that project during chewing; in old age, these sink and become less prominent, illustrated with a line of poetry by al-Aʿshā describing an aged, sight-impaired man with sunken cheeks.
3. Closing: "awfada ʿalā al-shayʾ" / "awfā" — he rose above and overlooked something — both verbs expressing the root's core sense of elevation/prominence.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: تَوْفِيق 2x "and reconciliation"; يُوَفِّقِ 1x "will cause reconciliation"; وِفَاق 1x "appropriate"
text:
al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's entry for the root و-ف-ق (w-f-q) is brief and turns on a single idea: two things falling into correspondence.

1. **wifq — correspondence between two things.** The base sense is one thing matching or fitting another. He cites Q 78:26, *jazāʾan wifāqan*, a recompense that corresponds to (fits) what was done.

2. **wāfaqa — to coincide with, to chance upon.** "I wāfaqtu so-and-so" and "I wāfaqtu the matter" mean to meet with or happen upon it — the encounter is a coinciding, not a plan.

3. **ittifāq — a human act coinciding with the decree (qadar).** al-Rāghib defines this form as the matching-up of what a person does with what is decreed. He notes explicitly that it is morally neutral in usage: it is said of good and of evil alike — "good ittafaqa for him," "evil ittafaqa for him."

4. **tawfīq — the same notion, but restricted by usage to the good.** He treats tawfīq as close in meaning to ittifāq, with the difference lying not in the root sense but in convention (*fī al-taʿāruf*): people apply it only to what is good. His Qur'anic witness is Q 11:88, *wa-mā tawfīqī illā bi-Llāh* — the speaker's being brought into accord comes only through God.

5. **tīfāq / mīfāq — a nominal form for the moment of coincidence.** The idiom "he came to us at the tīfāq / mīfāq of the new moon" means he came just as the moon's appearance coincided with his arrival.

Method note: the entry works by keeping one root idea (matching) and distinguishing the derived forms by what they match and by conventional restriction of scope, rather than by listing separate unrelated senses.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) derives the root و ف ر (w-f-r) as follows:

1. Core meaning: the root signals abundance and completeness/fullness.

2. Verbal usage: wafara al-shay' = "the thing became abundant/copious"; mawfūr = "made abundant" (an ample or full thing); wafarahu Allāh = "God made it abundant" — a causative use of the verb.

3. A specific hair-term: wafrat al-sha'r denotes hair that falls short of the jumma — that is, hair reaching to the earlobes, shorter/less full than the jumma, which falls to the shoulders.

4. Etymology of "wealth": the ordinary word for wealth or property, al-wafr, is said to derive from this same root (i.e., wealth as "abundance").

5. A verse is cited (unnamed poet, in the original): "I wished, out of my love for Buthayna, that we were on a raft [ramath] in a sea-inlet [al-sharm], with no wafr [wealth/abundance] belonging to us" — a wish for a simple, possession-free life together with the beloved.

6. A related derived word: al-wafrā' names a large leather water-skin (mazāda) made from a hide that has not been cut down or reduced in any part — i.e., a whole, undiminished hide.

dictionary: Muḥkam — al-Muḥkam wa-l-Muḥīṭ al-Aʿẓam, Ibn Sīda al-Mursī (d. 1066)
quran_words: تَوَفَّىٰ 24x "take them in death"; أَوْفَىٰ 18x "and fulfil"; وَفَّىٰ 18x "and will be paid in full"; أَوْفَىٰ 2x "(is) more faithful"; مُوفُون 1x "and those who fulfill"; مُتَوَفِّي 1x "(will) take you"; مُوَفُّو 1x "will surely pay them in full"; يَسْتَوْفُ 1x "they take in full"
poets_named: Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam); Ghaylān al-Rabaʿī (Umayyad); Kuthayyir (Umayyad); Ibn Jinnī (unnamed); Ibn Ḥillizah (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Sīda's entry for the root و-ف-ي (w-f-y). He gives the core sense as fulfilling and completing, then traces its branches through faith-keeping, arrival/overlooking high ground, full measure, and death.

1. Keeping faith / fulfilling. وَفَى بالعَهْدِ = to keep faith with a covenant (verbal noun wafāʾ). A man is وَفِيّ (faithful). One "fulfils a vow" in several constructions (wafā, awfā, waffā). Qurʾanic witnesses: "they fulfil the vow" (al-Insān 7) and "Abraham, who fulfilled" (al-Najm 37). On a poet's use of the rare noun وَفْي (in full measure), Ibn Sīda notes it may be genuinely attested, or a licensed coinage — Abū ʿAlī held a poet may form a faʿl for any faʿal even unheard.

2. Meeting / coming to a place. تَوَافَيْنَا في الميعاد = we met at the appointed time; وَافَيْتُهُ = I met him there. أَوْفَيْتُ المكان = I came to a place. With a shawāhid from Abū Dhuʾayb: أُوْفى here means to look out over a rise of ground and come to it — the poet calls out from each height, "O dwelling, where are your people?"

3. Completing / making full. وَفَى الشيء = it was abundant. وَفَى الدرهمُ المثقالَ = the dirham equalled the mithqāl (a wāfī = one dirham plus four dāniqs). Anything brought to completion — speech included — takes wafā; awfaytuhu = I completed it. A verse from Ghaylān al-Rabaʿī shows the verb taking two objects (like "the crop was given/granted"). Ibn Sīda notes he has elsewhere distinguished tamām (completeness) from wafāʾ.

4. Prosody. الوَافِي = a metrical foot that, in usage, fulfils the full count of its parts within its circle; alternatively, any foot that could take ziḥāf (metrical alteration) but stays free of it.

5. Length of life. الوَفَاء can mean length: in supplication, "may so-and-so die while you have wafāʾ," i.e. length of life (from Ibn al-Aʿrābī).

6. Rendering a due in full. أَوْفَى/وَفَّى الرجلَ حقَّه = paid him his due in full; tawaffā = took it in full; istawfā = left nothing of it; wafā/awfā al-kayl = made the measure full. Qurʾanic witness: "He pays him his account in full" (al-Nūr 39).

7. Looking out over / rising above. أَوْفَى على الشيء = to overlook or rise above it; a mīfāʾ keeps looking out over the heights (used of a donkey too). الوَفْي of land = a high point looked out from (shawāhid from Kuthayyir); variants mīfā, mīfāt. أَوْفَى على الخمسين = he passed fifty (al-Aṣmaʿī first rejected, then accepted this).

8. Death. الوَفَاة = death; تَوَفّاهُ اللهُ = God took him. On "when Our messengers come to them, taking them" (al-Aʿrāf 37), Ibn Sīda cites al-Zajjāj's two readings: (a) the angels of death take them, and they confess their disbelief as they die; or (b) the angels of punishment take them — either "by torment" (as one may say "I killed him by torment" though he did not die, supported by "death comes to him from every side, yet he does not die," Ibrāhīm 17), or, more weakly, "take their full number." Related: wāfāhu ḥimāmuhu (his death came to him); and a line from Ibn Jinnī where تُوْفِيَ stands for وُوْفِيَ, the wāw shifted to tāʾ (as in tAllāhi, "by God").

9. Place-name. الوَفَاء is also a location (a line from Ibn Ḥillizah). The entry closes the doubly-weak (lafīf) triliteral.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: وَهَبَ 22x "and we bestowed"; وَهَّاب 3x "(are) the bestower"
text:
Al-Zamakhsharī arranges the root و هـ ب (w-h-b) by its literal giving-sense and then its figurative extensions.

Literal sense — to give as a gift:
1. وهب (wahaba) — to give something as a gift; verbal nouns هِبة (hiba) and مَوهَب (mawhab). Derived forms: اتّهب (ittahaba, to accept a gift), أستوهب / استوهب (to ask for something as a gift), تواهبوا (they exchanged gifts). He cites the Hadith "I swore to accept a gift from none but a Qurashī or a Thaqafī," and idioms like "may God grant you well-being" and "O God, grant me [pardon for] my sins."
2. The act of vying in generosity: واهبني فوهبته ("he competed with me in giving and I outgave him").
3. Nouns and the divine name: هِبة/مَوهِبة "a gift, a grant," plurals هِبات/مَواهِب; al-Wahhāb "the abundant in gifts." A blessing said at a birth calls the child the موهوب ("the gift").

Extended sense — wahaba meaning "to make / suppose":
4. هَبْ (hab, imperative) — "suppose, reckon": "suppose him a man who erred," "suppose him dead," with a supporting verse ("suppose her a nation that perished..."). Al-Zamakhsharī links this to وهب = جعل ("to make/render"), as in "God made me your ransom," and reports a Yamāma servant-girl's "shall I put dust on it?" using أهب for "place." He notes the underlying logic: "he gave him the thing" already means "he made it his." A separate imperative to horses, هبي (habī), means "come forward."

Figurative usage (majāz):
5. Water/rain imagery: the مَواهِب of the land are rainwater and the natural pools (قِلات) that collect it; a single such pool is مَوهَبة (with fatḥa) — a vowel he says was deliberately used to distinguish this "gift of water" from ordinary gifts (مَوهِبة, with kasra). Several verses (including Abū Ṣakhr al-Hudhalī's) praise the pure water of a high mountain pool.
6. Abundance: أوهب له الطعام "the food was made plentiful for him, until some was given away"; واد موهب الحطب "a valley rich and ample in firewood" (with illustrating verses).
7. Capacity/readiness: أوهبت لأمر / أصبحت موهباً لذلك "I became fit, capable, and ready for such a matter."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root و هـ ج (w-h-j), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: al-wahaj — the heat of fire and its blazing.

1. tawahhaja al-jawhar — a gem sparkled/gleamed — a figurative borrowing of fire's blazing heat applied to light and brilliance.
2. tawahhajat rāʾiḥatu al-ṭīb / wahaj al-ṭīb — perfume's scent "blazed forth" — its fragrance and aroma, extending "heat/blaze" to the intensity of a smell.
3. sirāj wahhāj — a blazing lamp; najm wahhāj — a blazing star — the same intensifying pattern applied to light sources.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: وَهَنَ 5x "weaken"; وَهْن 2x "(in) weakness"; مُوهِن 1x "one who makes weak"; أَوْهَن 1x "the weakest"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats و-ه-ن as two separate words: one meaning weakness, the other denoting a time of night.

1. Weakness. وَهَنَ (wahana), imperfect yahinu, verbal noun wahn: "a thing grew weak." The causative أَوْهَنْتُهُ (awhantuhu) means "I weakened it."

Ibn Fāris attaches two items to this first sense:
- الْوَاهِنَة (al-wāhina): the shortest rib, the lowest one. He also cites Abū Bakr for a second use of the same word: an ailment that strikes a person in the two akhdaʿ veins of the neck.
- الْوَهْنَانَة (al-wahnāna): a woman who moves little and is slow, or heavy, in getting up and sitting down.

2. A time of night. الْوَهَن (al-wahan) and الْمَوْهِن (al-mawhin): an hour that passes during the night. From this comes the verb أَوْهَنَ (awhana) said of a man: he was present in — or travelled during — that hour of the night.

Method: the entry works by grouping derived nouns (a rib, a bodily complaint, a sluggish woman) under a single core notion of slackness or weakness, while explicitly refusing to merge the night-hour sense into it, keeping the two as distinct homonymous words.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root و-ه-ي (w-h-y) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: a slackening or loosening in something.

1. Illustrative usage: "the cloud's water-outlets (ʿazālī) grew slack (wahat) with its water" — meaning the cloud's rain-spouts loosened and let the water pour through.

2. Derived adjective: anything whose binding/tie has gone slack is called wāhin ("slack, weak").

3. Related noun al-wahy: a tear or rent in a hide (or similar material) — the physical result of something giving way/splitting open.

So the root's single underlying sense, per Ibn Fāris, is looseness/slackening, applied concretely to a binding that loosens or a hide that tears open.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root و ج ب (w-j-b), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: the falling and occurrence of a thing, from which further senses branch.

1. wajaba al-bayʿu — a sale became binding: valid and effective (the source of the modern sense "obligatory/necessary"). wajaba al-mayyitu — the dead man fell/collapsed; al-qatīl wājib — the slain person. A hadith uses this verb for death itself: "once he has wajaba, let no wailing woman weep."
2. The entry's central Qur'anic citation is al-Hajj 22:36, regarding sacrificial animals: "fa-idhā wajabat junūbuhā" — "then when their flanks fall [to the ground]" — i.e. once they have died, illustrated further with a line of poetry by Qays about a tribe's "first casualty."
3. wajaba al-ḥāʾiṭ — a wall collapsed (wajbah). al-wajībah — making a sale binding through daily installment payments, completed when "his wajībah is received in full."
4. al-wajb — a coward, so named because he "collapses" like a falling thing, illustrated with a line of poetry. al-muwajjib — a she-camel too fat to rise, or (a related sense) one whose first milk (colostrum) has clotted in her udder.
5. Closing note: wajīb al-qalb (the heart's throbbing/palpitation) is explicitly excluded from this root — Ibn Fāris identifies it as a case of consonant substitution, properly belonging to al-wajīf, discussed elsewhere.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats و-ج-د (w-j-d) as having a single origin: coming upon or finding a thing.

1. Finding / coming upon. Example: waǧadtu al-ḍāllata ("I found the stray animal"), with the verbal noun wiǧdān.

2. An emotional sense. Ibn Fāris notes that some transmitters record waǧadtu fī l-ġaḍab wiǧdānan — using the same verb, with the same verbal noun wiǧdān, for what one "finds"/feels in anger. He cites a line of verse for this: "Each of us turned his companion back in despair, upon rancor and intense wiǧdān" (i.e. deep grief or passion).

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root w-j-f, from al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's al-Mufradāt.

1. Core sense — swiftness of gait. Al-wajīf means speed of movement/pace. "awjaftu al-baʿīr" — "I made the camel go fast" — means I hastened it, drove it on quickly.

Qur'anic citation (Q59:6, al-Ḥashr): "you drove/spurred no horse or riding-camel for it" — using awjaftum (the causative verb, "you made [mounts] go fast") for the act of driving animals hard in pursuit or attack.

2. A related saying is quoted: "adalla fa-ammala, wa-awjafa fa-a'jafa" — roughly, "he presumed on closeness and so hoped [for favor], and he drove [the horse] hard and so wore it thin." Al-Rāghib glosses the wajafa/a'jafa half: it means driving a horse to make it go fast, and thereby exhausting/emaciating it through that hard driving.

3. Extended (metaphorical) sense — a trembling heart. Qur'anic citation (Q79:8, al-Nāziʿāt): "hearts, that day, will be wājifah." Al-Rāghib explains wājifah here as muḍṭaribah — agitated, quaking, throbbing — comparing it to other metaphors used for the heart, such as ṭāʾirah ("fluttering/flying") and khāfiqah ("pounding/throbbing"). So the root's basic idea of a fast, driven pace is carried over metaphorically to describe a heart in violent agitation.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: وَجْه 72x "their faces"; وَجِيه 2x "honorable"; وَجَّهْ 2x "[i] have turned"; وِجْهَة 1x "(is) a direction"; تَوَجَّهَ 1x "he turned his face"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats و-ج-ه as a single root whose core sense is facing or confronting something.

1. الوَجْه (the face) is what fronts or stands opposite anything; used of a man's face and of other things. By extension it can stand for the essence or self of a thing. Hence "my face is toward you," and the cited verse "to Him are the turning-of-the-face and the deed," where "face" marks the direction of one's devotion.

2. وَاجَهَ — to meet someone face to face, i.e. to set one's face toward theirs.

3. From the same root: وَجِيه, "eminent, of manifest standing," and الجَاه ("standing, prestige"), which Ibn Fāris explains as a metathesis (letter-transposition) of وَجْه.

4. الوِجْهَة — the direction one faces; every place turned toward. He cites Qurʾān 2:148, "and each has a direction he faces."

5. وَجَّهَ — to set a thing on a particular course or direction (جِهَة); he notes that جِهَة itself derives from وِجْهَة.

6. Specialized senses: التَّوْجِيه — to dig under a cucumber or melon and lay it on its side; تَوَجَّهَ (of an old man) — to turn away and depart; and a colt is called وَجِيه when its forelegs emerge first at birth.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root وجل (w-j-l), as al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī gives it:

1. Core sense — al-wajal is the inward sensing or feeling of fear: fear as something perceived within the self, rather than an external event.

2. Morphology — the verb runs wajila / yawjalu / wajalan; the derived descriptive form is wajil ("fearful, apprehensive").

3. Qur'anic evidence cited for this sense:
- al-Anfāl 8:2 — believers are described as those "whose hearts feel fear (wajilat qulūbuhum) when God is mentioned."
- al-Ḥijr 15:52–53 — "Indeed we are apprehensive (wajilūn) of you," answered with "Do not be afraid (lā tawjal)" — showing both the descriptive form and the prohibitive verb.
- al-Muʾminūn 23:60 — "and their hearts are fearful (wajila)."

In every citation the author anchors the word to the heart, consistent with his opening definition of it as felt, interior fear.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root و-ج-س (w-j-s) from a single core idea: perceiving something together with listening/hearkening for it.

1. Core sense — tawajjasa (تَوَجَّسَ) a thing: to sense/perceive it and thereby listen out for it. He cites the Qur'an, {فَأَوْجَسَ فِي نَفْسِهِ خِيفَةً مُوسَى} — "Mūsā sensed/conceived a fear within himself" (Ṭāhā 20:67) — as the model instance, followed by a line of the poet Dhū al-Rumma beginning "idhā tawajjasa..." (the citation is given only by its opening words in this entry).

2. An irregular, unrelated usage — Ibn Fāris flags two idioms as anomalies that don't derive from the "sense/hearken" meaning:
 - lā afʿaluhu sajīsa l-awjas — "I will never do it [for] sajīs al-awjas," where sajīs al-awjas simply means "time" / "ever, for all time" (al-dahr).
 - mā dhuqtu ʿindahu awjas(an) — "I tasted nothing (awjas) of food at his place," where awjas is used loosely for "anything" (of food).

He explicitly treats these two idioms as lexical oddities standing outside the root's main semantic thread, not as extensions of the "perceive/hearken" sense.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مُتَّكِـِين 8x "reclining"; مُتَّكَـ 1x "a banquet"; أَتَوَكَّؤُا 1x "i lean"; يَتَّكِـُ 1x "they recline"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats و-ك-ي as a small root whose core sense is binding something tight, and firmness/tightness generally.

1. الوِكَاء (wikāʾ): the tie or cord used to bind something shut. Cited in a ḥadīth instructing one to guard a lost item's "container and its tie."

2. Extended to stinginess: سَأَلْتُهُ فَأَوْكَى عَلَيَّ — "I asked him and he tied it up on me," i.e. he was miserly, as if he had bound his wealth shut. Likewise إِنَّ فُلَانًا لَوِكَاءٌ — "he is a tight-binder; nothing oozes out of him."

3. The sense of "tying off after filling": Abū ʿUbayd, on a report about al-Zubayr who "would yūkī between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwa," explains it as filling the space between them with running — just as a water-skin is tied off once it is full.

4. Also grouped here: تَوَكَّأْتُ عَلَى كَذَا — "I leaned/propped myself on such-a-thing" (= اتَّكَأْتُ), because one braces and strengthens oneself by means of it; and أَوْكَأْتُ فُلَانًا — "I set up a support/couch (مُتَّكَأ) for him to lean on."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root w-k-d (وكد) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: the root signals tightening and making something firm or secure.

1. Firming/securing something: the verbal example "awkid ʿaqdaka" (أَوْكِدْ عَقْدَكَ) means "tighten/secure your knot or contract" — make it firm.

2. Al-wikād (الوكاد): the rope used to tie a cow's leg while milking her — a concrete instance of the "binding/tightening" sense.

3. Figurative extension — intent and focus: the phrase "wakada wakdahu" (وكد وكده) is used when someone sets something as his aim and gives it his concerned attention — i.e., he means it firmly / makes it his settled purpose.

Ibn Fāris derives all three uses — physical tightening, the milking-rope, and firm intent/purpose — from the single underlying sense of binding something securely.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: تَوَكَّلْ 40x "let put (their) trust"; وَكِيل 24x "a guardian"; مُتَوَكِّلُون 4x "the ones who put trust (in him)"; وُكِّلَ 2x "has been put in charge"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats و-ك-ل (w-k-l) as a single sound root whose core meaning is relying on someone else in your own affair.

1. Weakness / dependence. الوُكَلة / الوَكَل (al-wukala / al-wakal) is the weak man; the phrase وُكَلة تُكَلة (wukala tukala) describes one who leans on others.

2. توكُّل (tawakkul). Derived from the root: admitting one's own inability in a matter and leaning on another.

3. وَاكَلَ (wākala). Of a person who neglects his own business and leaves it to someone else.

4. وكيل (wakīl, "agent"). So named because an affair is entrusted (yūkal) to him.

5. Of animals — الوِكَال (al-wikāl). A mount that habitually falls behind the other beasts, as if handing off the task of running to them. Ibn Fāris cites Imruʾ al-Qays — لا يُواكِل نَهْزَها ("it does not lag when spurred") — glossing it as "does not slacken," and traces the phrase to مواكلة (muwākala). A related sense: a beast that keeps pace with another.

6. Mutual reliance. وَاكَلْتُ الرجلَ (wākaltu al-rajul): you rely on him and he on you.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: وَكَزَ 1x "so musa struck him with his fist"
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) records the root w-k-z (وكز) as a single, regular triliteral root, glossed with three closely related senses of the verb wakaza(hu) — "he [verb]-ed him":

1. To stab or pierce (طعنه, ṭaʿanahu).
2. To strike with a clenched fist — literally, with the gathered/closed hand (ضربه بجمع كفه, ḍarabahu bi-jumʿi kaffihi).
3. To push or shove (دفعه, dafaʿahu).

The entry is very terse: no etymology, wazn/morphological discussion, or shawāhid (citations) are given — just the three-sense definition above.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: وَلَد 56x "a son"; وَالِد 14x "(by) the parents"; وَٰلِدَي 10x "to his parents"; وَلَدَ 9x "he was born"; وَلِيد 7x "and the children"; مَوْلُود 3x "a son"; وَٰلِدَة 2x "your mother"; وَٰلِدَٰت 1x "and the mothers"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats و-ل-د (w-l-d) as a single sound root whose core sense is offspring and progeny; its other uses are extended from that core by analogy.

1. وَلَد (walad) — "child, offspring." The same form covers both singular and plural; for the singular one may also say وُلْد (wuld).
2. وَلِيدَة (walīda) — the female (offspring/girl); plural وَلَائِد (walāʾid).
3. تَوَلَّدَ (tawallada) — "to be generated from" something, i.e. to result or issue from it (X came about from Y).
4. لِدَة (lida) — "a coeval, one of the same age." Ibn Fāris notes it is morphologically deficient: the missing letter is the wāw, since its underlying form is وِلْدَة (wilda) — showing it too derives from this root.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: يُولِجُ 10x "and causes to enter"; يَلِجَ 3x "penetrates"; وَلِيجَة 1x "(as) intimates"
text:
Root ولج (w-l-j), from al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's Qur'an-focused lexicon.

1. Core sense — al-wulūj: to enter into a narrow or tight place/passage. Shawāhid: "until the camel passes through the eye of the needle" (al-Aʿrāf 7:40); and the causative yūliju — "He makes the night enter into the day and the day into the night" (al-Ḥajj 22:61). Al-Rāghib reads this second verse as pointing to how God has structured the world so that night lengthens into day and day into night, following the sun's points of rising and setting.

2. al-walīja: anything a person takes on and leans upon that is not of his own kin. It comes from the saying "So-and-so is a walīja among the people" — used of one who attaches himself to a group though he does not belong to them, whether a person or otherwise. Shāhid: "and they have not taken, apart from God and His Messenger and the believers, any walīja [intimate confidant]" (al-Tawba 9:16). Al-Rāghib treats this as parallel to "do not take the Jews and Christians as awliyāʾ [allies]" (al-Māʾida 5:51).

3. Derived usage: a rajul khurajatun walijatun is a man who is forever going out and coming in — one who moves in and out a great deal.

dictionary: Ṣiḥāḥ — al-Ṣiḥāḥ, al-Jawharī (d. 1003)
quran_words: وَلِىّ 86x "protector"; تَوَلَّىٰ 78x "you turn away"; وَلَّىٰ 30x "[so] turn"; مَوْلَىٰ 18x "(is) your protector"; أَوْلَىٰ 11x "and woe"; مَوَٰلِى 2x "the successors"; وَلَٰيَت 2x "the protection"; مُوَلِّي 1x "turns towards it"; أَوْلَيَٰن 1x "the former two"; يَلُ 1x "(are) close to you"; وَال 1x "protector"; مَوَٰلِي 1x "and your friends"
poets_named: unnamed verse ×3; Labīd (lived into Islam); al-Farazdaq (Umayyad)
text:
al-Jawharī derives the root from a core sense of nearness and treats "following/adjoining" as the thread running through its many derivatives.

1. Core sense — nearness, proximity. الوَلْي = closeness; تباعد بعد ولى = "he grew distant after being near"; "كل مما يَليكَ" = eat from what is nearest you. Shāhid: وعَدَتْ عَوادٍ دون وَلْيِكَ تَشْعَبُ (obstacles arose short of access to you).

2. The verb. وَلِيَهُ يَلِيَهُ ("he was/became adjacent to it") — anomalously keeping kasra in both perfect and imperfect. أوليته الشيء فوَلِيَهُ = I set him next to it, so he adjoined it.

3. Holding office / charge. وَلِيَ الوالي البلدَ (the governor governed the town), وَلِيَ الرجلُ البيعَ (took charge of the sale) — verbal noun wilāya. وَلّاهُ الأميرُ (the amir put him in charge); تَوَلَّى العملَ = took up the office. أوْلَيْتُهُ معروفاً = I did him a kindness; exclamation ما أولاه للمعروف (how apt to kindness) is anomalous. فلان وَلِيَ ووُلِيَ عليه = governed and was governed over (paralleling ساسَ وسِيسَ عليه).

4. Turning. تَوَلَّى عنه = turned away; ولّى هارباً = turned in flight. Qur'anic shāhid: (ولكلِّ وِجهةٌ هو مُوَلِّيها) glossed as "facing it with his face."

5. al-Waliyy = the rain that falls after the first autumn rain (wasmī), so called because it follows (yalī) it. Also al-waly (patterns faʿl and faʿīl), plural أولية; verb وَلِيَتِ الأرضُ.

6. al-Walī = opposite of an enemy [ally/friend]; verb تَوَلّاهُ (took as walī).

7. al-Mawlā — a many-sided term. al-Jawharī lists: manumitter, freed slave, paternal cousin, helper, neighbor. He adds al-waliyy = in-law, and states the unifying rule: anyone who has charge of another's affair is his walī. He documents the "paternal cousin" sense with a verse (هم المولى وإن جنفوا علينا, on Abū ʿUbayda's reading, singular for plural like Qur'anic ثم يخرجكم طفلاً); the "fittest place" nuance with Labīd's مولى المخافة (the fittest seat of danger, with a note on how the line parses); and the "confederate by oath" (ḥalīf) sense with two verses, including al-Farazdaq's مولى مواليا, with a grammatical note that its accusative-without-tanwīn is a poetic license restoring the word to its base form.

8. Nisba forms. From al-mawlā → mawlawiyy; from rain-waliyy → walawiyy (paralleling ʿalawiyy), because four consecutive yāʾs were avoided by dropping the first and turning the second into wāw.

9. al-Walāʾ (fatḥa) = kinship; also the manumitter's patronage-tie (ḥadīth: the Prophet "forbade the sale of walāʾ and its gift"); also a body of supporters (هم وَلاءُ فلان).

10. Succession sense. al-Muwālāt = opposite of enmity; والى بينهما = made things follow in order; على الوِلاء = in succession; تَوالى عليه شهران = two months ran consecutively; اسْتَوْلى على الأمَد = reached the goal.

11. al-Wilāya (kasra) = rule/authority; al-walāya / al-wilāya = support (هم على ولاية = united in support). Sībawayh's distinction: walāya (fatḥa) is the verbal noun, wilāya (kasra) the concrete noun (like imāra, niqāba) — the name of the thing you take charge of.

12. al-Waliyya (per Abū ʿUbayd) = a saddle-pad, or what lies under it; plural walāyā. Illustrated by كالبلايا رؤوسها في الولايا, of the she-camel left tethered at its owner's grave with the pad over its head until it died.

13. أولى لك! = a threat/menace. Per al-Aṣmaʿī (endorsed by Thaʿlab as the best explanation) it means "destruction has drawn near / befallen him."

14. Elative أولى بكذا = more entitled, worthier. Paradigm: هو الأولى، وهم الأوالي والأولَون (like al-aʿlā/al-aʿālī/al-aʿlawn); feminine الوُليا، الوُلْيَيان، الوُلَى / الوُلْيَيات (like al-kubrā etc.).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root w-n-y - Ibn Faris, Maqayis al-Lugha

Core meaning Ibn Faris assigns to this root: weakness.

1. Verb - wana, yani, wanyan: "to flag, slacken, grow weak/languid."
2. al-wani: "the weak one" - the active-participle noun form.
3. Qur'anic citation - "wa la taniya fi dhikri", "do not (you two) flag in My remembrance" (Taha 20:42, addressed in the dual). Ibn Faris gives this as the Qur'anic attestation of the verb in its core "weakness/slackening" sense.
4. al-wana: "fatigue, weariness" - a related noun.
5. Causative form - awnaytuhu: "I wearied him / wore him out."
6. Idiomatic phrase - naqatun waniyah: "a jaded, worn-out she-camel," i.e. an animal slackened by fatigue.
7. Fixed usage - la yani yaf'alu ("he does not flag from doing...") is explained as functioning like la yazalu ("he does not cease..."), i.e. it marks continuous, unbroken action.
8. imra'atun wanah: said of a woman who shows slackness/languor (futur) when rising to stand - a description of physical sluggishness.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مَوْقُوذَة 1x "and that which is hit fatally"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root و-ق-ذ (w-q-dh) from a core sense of "striking with wood."

1. al-waqdh (الوَقْذ) — inflicting pain by striking [with wood].
2. shātun mawqūdhah (a "waqadh-ed" ewe) — a sheep beaten with wood until it died.
3. A usage the author explicitly sets apart as not fitting this root's core analogy: wuqidhati n-nāqah, said of a she-camel — she gives her milk only reluctantly/with difficulty, so that her milk becomes scant.

So the entry records two branches: (i) the literal "beaten/struck [with wood], to the point of injury or death," and (ii) an unrelated idiomatic use about a she-camel's milk drying up or being withheld.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: وَقَعَ 12x "then fall down"; وَاقِع 6x "bound to happen"; وَاقِعَة 2x "the occurrence"; يُوقِعَ 1x "cause"; مُّوَاقِعُو 1x "are to fall in it"; وَقْعَت 1x "at its occurrence"; مَوَٰقِع 1x "by setting"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats و-ق-ع (w-q-ʿ) as a single root with one core idea: the falling / dropping of something. All the branches trace back to that.

Core usage: وَقَعَ الشَّيْءُ وُقُوعًا — "the thing fell/occurred"; the active participle is وَاقِعٌ ("falling, befalling").

Senses derived from "falling":
1. الْوَاقِعَة — "that which befalls," used of the Resurrection/the Rising, because (in this author's explanation) it falls upon creation and envelops them.
2. الْوَقْعَة — the clash or shock of war; a battle-engagement.
3. الْوَقَائِع — scattered pools or water-hollows, as if the water had "fallen"/settled into them.
4. مَوَاقِع الْغَيْث — the spots where rain falls.
5. النَّسْر الْوَاقِع — the "alighting/falling vulture" (the star Vega), from a bird's alighting: it has folded its wings, as though come down to the ground. مَوْقَعَة الطَّائِر is the exact spot a bird lands on.
6. وَقَاعِ — a single circular brand burned onto part of a camel's hide, as though it had "fallen" upon it.
7. وَقَعَ فِي فُلَان — to assail someone (in speech); أَوْقَعَ بِهِ — to fall upon / attack him.

A related sub-group Ibn Fāris links by analogy — sharpening by striking against stone:
8. وَقَعْتُ الْحَدِيدَة (وَقْعًا) — to whet an iron blade, because you strike/rub it on a stone to draw it out; a whetted blade is حَدِيدَة وَقِيع. He notes this as the transitive counterpart of an intransitive "the thing happened / I did it."
9. الْحَافِر الْوَقِيع — a hoof pared down by stones; السَّيْف الْوَقِيع — a sword sharpened on a stone (same analogy).

More "falling" derivatives:
10. وَقَعَ الْغَيْث — the rain fell scattered.
11. التَّوْقِيع (a) the mark of a saddle-gall on a camel's back; (b) an annotation/endorsement appended to a document after it is finished.
12. تَوَقَّعْتُ الشَّيْء — I expected/awaited a thing, watching for when it would occur.
13. الْوَقَع — soreness of the feet; الْوَقِع — a footsore person, likened to a stone worn down on a whetstone (mīqaʿa).
14. الْوَقِع — a thin wisp of cloud, as though about to fall with its rain.

Finally, Ibn Fāris cites a report from Abū ʿAmr that الْوَقْع can mean a high place on a mountain — explained as if named so because a climber fears falling from it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root و-ق-ب (w-q-b) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core sense: a thing disappearing or sinking into a hollow or hiding-place.

1. waqaba al-shayʾ ("the thing waqaba") — it entered a waqbah, a hollow or cavity/socket in something (like a pit or depression).

2. waqabat ʿaynāhu ("his two eyes waqabatā") — they became sunken/hollowed (eyes sinking into their sockets).

3. waqaba al-shayʾ (second sense) — it descended, fell, set. Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 113:3, "and from the evil of a ghāsiq when it waqaba," and notes that exegetes explain this as the night when it descends/falls.

4. On the side, some say "al-waqb" means "the fool" — but Ibn Fāris rejects this as belonging to the root w-q-b itself; he attributes it instead to a phonetic swap (ibdāl) from the separate root w-gh-b (وغب), discussed by him elsewhere.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
quran_words: أَوْقَدُ 5x "ignite"; وَقُود 4x "(of) the fuel"; ٱسْتَوْقَدَ 1x "kindled"; مُوقَدَة 1x "kindled"
text:
Root **و ق د (w-q-d)**, from al-Zabīdī's *Tāj al-ʿArūs*. The core idea is fire and its blazing.

**1. Fire / blazing.** **الوَقَد** (al-waqad, all letters vowelled) is, per Ibn Fāris, the fire itself — hence "how great is this fire!" — and also the act of its blazing (a verbal noun). Several forms carry the "blazing" sense: **al-waqd**, **al-wuqūd** (ḍamma), **al-waqūd** (fatḥa, from Sībawayh — deemed anomalous in al-Baṣāʾir), plus **al-qidah**, **al-waqadān**, **al-waqīd**, **al-tawaqqud**, and **al-istīqād**. The usual rule: the ḍamma-form (wuqūd) is the verbal noun, the fatḥa-form (waqūd) the firewood. Al-Zajjāj notes both vowellings are attested, citing وَقَدَتِ النَّارُ وُقوداً.

**2. The verb.** وَقَدَ (waqada, like waʿada): "the fire blazed" (waqadat…wuqūdan). The root is both intransitive and transitive:
- intransitive/reflexive flaring up: waqadat, tawaqqadat, ittaqadat, istawqadat;
- transitive kindling: أَوْقَدَها (awqada), وَقَّدَها (waqqada), استَوْقَدَها, تَوَقَّدَها. Per al-Asās, awqadtuhā = "I built it up with fuel."

**3. الوَقُود (al-waqūd) — firewood/fuel** (pattern ṣabūr). Al-Zabīdī records a grammatical dispute over its Qurʾānic uses:
- In النَّارِ ذَاتِ الْوَقُودِ (Q 85:5), al-Azharī prefers reading it as a verbal noun ("the fire of the *blazing*") over "firewood"; Yaʿqūb notes a variant reading dhātu al-wuqūd (attributed to al-Ḥasan, Abū Rajāʾ, Zayd al-Naḥwī).
- In وَقُودُهَا النَّاسُ وَالْحِجَارَةُ (Q 2:24), waqūd (a noun) stands in for the verbal noun. Al-Layth distinguishes waqūd = the visible flame (noun) from wuqūd = the blazing (verbal noun). Others: anything you kindle with is waqūd, also **wiqād** (kasra) and **waqīd**. Al-Baṣāʾir records variant readings: the Prophet's وِقادُ النَّار, and ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr's وَقِيدُهَا النَّاسُ وَالْحِجَارَة.

**4. Figurative uses.**
- **al-waqqād** (of a person): witty and keenly sharp — "quick-kindling"; likewise **al-mutawaqqid**. Of a star: bright/shining. Of a heart: quick to fire up in vigour and cutting sharpness. (Some class one of these as metaphor built on metaphor.)
- **al-waqdah**: the fiercest heat of the year (ten days, or half a month) — "the blaze of summer cooked them"; waqada al-ḥaṣā = the pebbles grew scorching.

**5. Other senses.**
- **al-waqīdiyyah**: a breed of large red goats (Jarīr cites them; the better-known form is al-ruqaydiyyah).
- **Idiom "to light a fire for something"** = to abandon/bid it farewell: "I sobered and lit a fire for amusement…" A curse: أَبْعَدَ اللهُ دَارَهُ وَأَوْقَدَ نَاراً إِثْرَهُ ("…and lit a fire in his wake") = may God never bring him back. A reported custom of the ʿUqayl woman: kindling a fire behind a feared man as he departed, "so that their evil goes off with them." **Zayd mīqād** = quick to ignite; وَقَدَتْ بِكَ زِنَادِي is a blessing ("may my fire-sticks kindle through you").

**6. Derived words & names.** **al-mawqid** = the fireplace/hearth; **al-Mīqadah** = a spot near al-Mashʿar al-Ḥarām. تَوَقَّدَ = to glitter/gleam (anything that glitters "yaqidu," even a sparkling hoof); of a blind man, غائِرُ الواقِدَيْنِ ("sunken of the two gleamers," his eyes). Proper names: Wāqid, Waqqād, Waqdān. The entry closes with biographical notes on several men named Wāqid or al-Wāqidī — including the Companion Abū Wāqid al-Laythī (d. 68), a later namesake who was weak in transmission, and the historian al-Wāqidī, who was criticised as a source.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: وُقِفُ 3x "and stop them"; مَوْقُوفُون 1x "will be made to stand"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats و-ق-ف as a single root meaning to stay put, to remain in place with respect to something; every other use, in his method, is measured analogically against that core.

1. Standing still. وَقَفَ / يَقِفُ / وُقُوف (waqafa, yaqifu, wuqūf) — to stand, to halt. Also transitive: وَقَفْتُ وَقْفِي, "I set my waqf" — the thing one causes to stand fixed.

2. A grammatical restriction, and its exception. Ibn Fāris states that the form-IV verb أَوْقَفَ (awqafa) is not used of things generally — with one exception: it is said of someone who is involved in something and then pulls back from it, قَدْ أَوْقَفَ ("he has desisted"). His evidence is a line of al-Ṭirimmāḥ: "headlong in my error, then I desisted, content with mindful restraint — and the man of piety is content." Al-Shaybānī is cited for the same usage: "I spoke to them, then awqaftu from them," meaning "I fell silent"; and generally, of anything you hold back from, you say awqaftu.

3. مَوْقِف (mawqif) — the place where a person, or anything else, stands.

4. وِقَاف (wiqāf) — the same as مُوَاقَفَة: standing opposite one another, confrontation.

5. وَقِيفَة (waqīfa) — on Ibn Durayd's authority, a mountain-goat driven by dogs or archers onto a rock from which it cannot descend, until it is caught. A verse is cited: "Do not reckon me fat from a cornered quarry, driven, of the sort Salfaʿ hunts for you" — Salfaʿ being the name of a hunting bitch.

6. وَقْف (waqf) — an ivory bangle. Ibn Fāris offers this derivation tentatively: it may be so called because it has come to rest (waqafa) at that spot on the arm.

7. حِمَارٌ مُوَقَّف (muwaqqaf) — used by way of resemblance, of a donkey with white markings at the pasterns, as though it had stopped there.

8. مَوْقِفَا الْفَرَس — the horse's two "standing places": the two hollows in its flanks.

The entry closes with the standard formula, "God knows best what is correct."

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: وَقْر 6x "(is) deafness"; تُوَقِّرُ 1x "and respect him"; وِقْر 1x "a load"; وَقَار 1x "grandeur"
text:
Root و ق ر (w-q-r), as al-Zamakhsharī presents it: a literal core of "heavy load / weighing down," then a set of transfers he explicitly labels figurative (majāz).

LITERAL SENSES

1. **A load, a burden.** وِقْر (wiqr) is a load one carries; plural أَوْقَار (awqār). أَوْقَرَ (awqara) = to load an animal: "he loaded the mule or the donkey."
2. **A tree weighed down with fruit.** A palm that bears heavily is مُوقِرَة / مُوقِر / مُوَقَّرَة, plural مَوَاقِير. Poetic witness: loaded camel-litters cresting a rise look, in the forenoon, "like heavily laden palm-trees."
3. **Weighed down with one's own bulk.** اسْتَوْقَرَتِ الإبلُ شَحْماً — the camels grew laden with fat, i.e. fatness made them heavy.

FIGURATIVE SENSES (al-Zamakhsharī's own heading, "and of the figurative")

4. **Burdened by debt:** أَوْقَرَهُ الدَّيْنُ — debt loaded him down.
5. **Heaviness/dullness of hearing.** وَقْر (waqr) in the ear = heaviness, hardness of hearing; an ear so affected is وَقِرَة or مَوْقُورَة. وَقِرَتْ أُذُنِي = my ear grew heavy; and it can be constructed with عَنْ — "it grew deaf *to* listening to his speech." Verse cited: "How much foul speech my ear has been deafened against, though there is no deafness in me." Also used as an imprecation: "O God, deafen his ear."
6. **Gravity, dignified self-possession.** A man is وَقُور (waqūr), men وُقُر — رُزَنَاء, weighty and steady in bearing; the verb is وَقَرَ / وَقُرَ with the verbal noun وَقَار, and the reflexive تَوَقَّرَ. Here the entry places the sense of *staying settled in place*: "stay put in your seat," and the Qur'anic wording "and stay settled in your houses" (وَقَرْنَ فِي بُيُوتِكُنَّ) is quoted as an instance of that same imperative.
7. **To show honour.** وَقَّرَ (form II) = to treat someone as weighty — to magnify him and not make light of him.
8. **A steady heart.** جَنَان وَاقِر — a heart that panic does not unsettle. Verse fragment: "loud-voiced, possessed of a steady heart."
9. **To lodge and leave a trace.** وَقَرَ فِي قَلْبِهِ كَذَا — something "fell" into his heart and its mark stayed. Likewise a word may "settle in his ear," i.e. hold fast — the idiom being "it settled in the hearing and the heart retained it."
10. **A lasting crack or dent (physical damage).** وَقْرَة = a fissure that does not close; وَقَرَ العَظْمَ = he broke the bone. Of a riding beast, وُقِرَتْ / وَقِرَتْ (so: مَوْقُورَة, وَقِرَة) = its hoof has a هَزْمَة, a dent. A battered object is مُوَقَّر, having وَقَرَات (dents). Closing verse: gear dragged over pebbles was left dented, "yet what is there is not lost."

Method note: the entry is arranged as Asās al-Balāgha typically is — the concrete usage first, then an explicit majāz section, with the transfers (debt, deafness, gravity, honour, a word lodging in the mind, a dented hoof) all traceable back to the idea of weight pressing down or of an impression that stays.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مِيقَٰت 8x "(is) an appointed term for them"; وَقْت 3x "(of) the time"; مَّوْقُوت 1x "(at) fixed times"; أُقِّتَتْ 1x "are gathered to their appointed time"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats و–ق–ت (w-q-t) as a single root whose core sense is the limit or boundary of a thing and its essential reality — applied to time and to other things as well.

Derived words he lists:
1. الوقت (al-waqt): a known, appointed stretch of time.
2. الموقوت (al-mawqūt): something delimited or fixed.
3. الميقات (al-mīqāt): the set point or destination for an appointed time.

Verb usage: waqata lahu kadhā and its intensive form waqqatahu both mean "to delimit / fix (a thing)."

As a Qur'anic witness he cites al-Nisāʾ 4:103, {inna al-ṣalāta kānat ʿalā al-muʾminīna kitāban mawqūtan} — where mawqūtan carries the root's sense of something "fixed to set times."

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: ٱتَّقَىٰ 166x "and fear"; مُتَّقِين 49x "the righteous"; تَقْوَى 17x "(of) [the] righteousness"; وَقَىٰ 16x "and save us"; تَقِيّ 4x "righteous"; وَاق 3x "defender"; أَتْقَى 2x "(is the) most righteous of you"; تُقَىٰة 1x "(as) a precaution"
text:
Zamakhsharī's Asās al-Balāgha organizes the root و ق ي (w-q-y) around the core idea of guarding/shielding, moving from literal to figurative uses.

1. Core sense — to guard, protect. وقاه الله كلّ سوء = "God guarded him from every evil"; the noun of protection is وقاية (wiqāya). The intensive form II is وقّاه / توقية (waqqā / tawqiya, to protect thoroughly). Proverb: "the brave man is protected" (الشجاع موقّى). A line of Ruʾba plays on this: "the guarded one is as you have guarded," meaning tawqiya.

2. Reflexive forms — to guard oneself, take precaution. Forms VIII and V: اتقيته / توقّيته (ittaqaytu / tawaqqaytu). Applied to God: اتقى الله حق تقاته = to be heedful/guarded toward God as is truly His due, with the verbal nouns tuqāt, tuqāh, and taqwā (heedfulness). Its diminutive is تقيّ (tuqayy). A verse of al-Namir uses tuqā in this sense of self-guarding heedfulness. The word التّقيّة (taqiyya) denotes protective caution.

3. The active-participle "protector" (wāqiya). A cited phrase: "whoever disobeys God, no protectress will guard him from Him." The idiom "over so-and-so is a wāqiya like the wāqiya of dogs" uses wāqiya for a preserving watch.

4. Instrument of protection. وقاء / وقاية (wiqāʾ / wiqāya) = the thing by which something is guarded. Separately, الواقي (al-wāqī) names a bird, the ṣurad (shrike), from its cry.

5. Figurative (majāz):
 - A "protecting" saddle (سرج واق) = one that does not gall or wound the mount.
 - A "protecting"/wincing horse (فرس واق) = one that dreads walking because of pain in its hoof.
 - اتقاه بحجفته = he shielded himself from someone with his leather shield.
 - اتقاه بحقّه = he protected himself from someone by rendering him his due.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: وَارِد 3x "their water drawer"; وِرْد 2x "thirsty"; وَرَدَ 2x "they (would) have come to it"; أَوْرَدَ 1x "and lead them"; مَوْرُود 1x "to which (they are) led"; وَرِيد 1x "(his) jugular vein"; وَرْدَة 1x "rose-colored"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives و-ر-د from two base meanings: (1) coming or arriving at something, and (2) a particular color.

1. Coming/arriving. al-wird is the opposite of al-ṣadar — going down to water as opposed to returning from it. Hence وَرَدَتِ الإبلُ الماءَ ("the camels came to the water"). From the same sense: al-wird as the recurrent onset of a fever that seizes its sufferer at a set time; and al-mawārid, meaning roads/paths, and also the watering-places that are approached and the villages (attributed to Abū ʿUbayda). A verse of Jarīr uses al-mawārid for the roads: the Commander of the Faithful is on a path that stays straight even when the roads bend crooked. Also from this root are al-warīdān, the two thick veins flanking the front sides of the neck — so named as though the two "arrive/meet" together at that spot.

2. Color. al-ward is the rose (and its color); one says فرسٌ وَرْدٌ ("a rose-colored horse") or أسدٌ وَرْدٌ ("a rose-colored lion") when the color matches that of the rose.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: وَرَق 2x "(the) leaves"; وَرَقَة 1x "any leaf"; وَرِق 1x "with this silver coin of yours"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats و-ر-ق as two separate roots: one about good things and wealth, whose origin is the leafage of a tree, and one about a colour.

FIRST ROOT — leafage, and by extension wealth

1. waraq — the leaves of a tree.
2. waraq — wealth. He derives this by analogy: when a tree sheds its leaves it stands stripped bare, like a destitute man. He cites a verse: "To You I call, so accept my entreaty; forgive my faults and make my waraq bear fruit."
3. riqa — silver coin (dirhams). He places it under the same analogy, the two words being told apart only by their vowelling.
4. wāriqa (per Abū ʿUbayd) — a tree green of leaf and handsome.
5. warāq (per Abū ʿUbayd) — the green flush of the ground from herbage; he explicitly notes this is NOT from waraq (leafage). Shāhid: "As though their steeds, at the crag of Zumm, were locusts to which the greenery had yielded."
6. waraqtu l-shajara — I stripped a tree of its leaves.
7. awraqa (of a hunter) — he caught nothing. Ibn Fāris explains the idiom concretely: the hunter lays a snare, leaves it, and returns later to find the ground grown over and leaves fallen across the snare, so he cannot locate it — "he met with leaves" covering his trap. The usage then spread, so that anyone who sought something and failed is said to have "awraqa."
8. warqa (with a silent rāʾ) — a small hidden knot or swelling in a branch.
9. waraqa — a clot/piece of blood, plural waraq; named by likeness to falling leaves.
10. waraq — weak men, likened in their weakness to tree leaves.

SECOND ROOT — an ashen colour

11. wurqa — a colour resembling that of ashes. Hence an ash-grey camel (aʾwraq), an ash-grey dove (ḥamāma warqāʾ), and a man described the same way.
12. ʿām awraq — an "ashen year," i.e. a year of drought, as if the ground had taken the colour of ashes. Ibn Fāris says the "Year of Ashes" (ʿām al-Ramāda) was named on this basis.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: وَرِثَ 13x "will inherit it"; أَوْرَثَ 12x "and we caused to inherit them"; وَارِث 7x "(are) the inheritors"; مِيرَٰث 2x "(is the) heritage"; تُّرَاث 1x "the inheritance"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root و ر ث as expressing a single idea: al-wirth, inheritance.

1. Core sense: a thing that belongs to one group passing over to others. This happens either by nasab (lineage/kinship) or by sabab (some connecting cause or means).

2. Morphological note: the noun al-mīrāth ("heritage, legacy") has the wāw as its original root-letter — the initial mīm is a later substitution, so the underlying root is و ر ث.

3. Poetic witness (shāhid): "We inherited them from truthful forefathers, and we bequeath them, when we die, to our sons" — illustrating the movement of a possession down the generations.

dictionary: Ṣiḥāḥ — al-Ṣiḥāḥ, al-Jawharī (d. 1003)
quran_words: وَرَاء 24x "behind"; وُرِىَ 4x "was concealed"; تَوَارَتْ 2x "they were hidden"; تُورُ 1x "you ignite"; مُورِيَٰت 1x "and the producers of sparks"
text:
Al-Jawharī (al-Ṣiḥāḥ) records the following for the root و ر ي (w-r-y):

1. To eat away / consume from within: وَرى القَيْحُ جوفَه (the pus consumed his belly), verb yarī, verbal noun waryan. He cites a ḥadīth ("filled with pus until it consumes him") and verse-lines by ʿAbd Banī al-Ḥasḥās and (via al-Yazīdī) an imprecatory use — "may you be consumed." He lists the imprecation forms by addressee: to a man riyā, two men wiryā, a group rūa, a woman rī (the yāʾ being the feminine-subject ending as in "stand," "sit"), two women riyā, women rīna.

2. As a noun, الوَرى (waraā) = a disease. Per al-Farrāʾ, the curse "may God set upon him the disease and the fever of Khaybar."

3. الوَرى also = creation / mankind: "I don't know which of creation he is." Shāhid from Dhū al-Rumma ("the lands of mankind are no lands for it").

4. Of a fire-stick (zand): وَرى (with fatḥa; also the dialectal wariya with kasra) = to produce/give out fire. Transitive/causative: awraytuhu or warraytuhu (tawriya) = "I kindled it." Idiom: "he strikes the fire-sticks of error."

5. Of marrow: وَرِيَ = to become compact and full. Hence a wāriya she-camel = fat; laḥm warī (pattern faʿīl) = fat meat. Shāhid: "they eat of the fat hump-meat."

6. وَرَّى الجرحُ سابرَه = the wound struck its prober with the disease (al-warā). Shāhid from al-ʿAjjāj, glossed as the wound "infecting" from its depth and from the soul's revulsion.

7. To conceal/hide: وارَيْتُ الشيءَ = I hid the thing; تَوارى = he hid himself.

8. وَراءَ (warāʾ) = "behind," but can also mean "in front / ahead," so it belongs to the aḍdād (words with two opposite senses). Grammatical note (al-Akhfash): unannexed, it becomes an indeclinable noun ("I met him min warāʾu"), parallel to min qablu / min baʿdu; the idiom "behind you is roomier for you" is accusative under an implied verb "move back." Al-Jawharī reads the Qurʾānic "and behind them was a king" (18:79) as meaning "ahead of them." Its diminutive wurayʾa (with a hāʾ) is anomalous. الوَراء also = grandchild (a child's child).

9. Derived from that spatial sense: وَرَّيْتُ الخبر (tawriya) = to conceal a report while displaying something else — as if one puts the matter "behind" himself, out of sight (the source of the rhetorical term tawriya, double-meaning/dissimulation).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: وَٰسِع 9x "(is) all-encompassing"; سَعَة 6x "his ample means"; وَسِعَ 6x "encompasses"; وُسْع 5x "(to) its capacity"; وَٰسِعَة 4x "(is) spacious"; مُوسِع 2x "the wealthy"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root و-س-ع (w-s-ʿ) from a single core notion: the opposite of narrowness (ḍīq) and hardship/straitness (ʿusr) — i.e. width, roominess, ampleness.

1. Core verb: وَسُعَ الشَّيْءُ / اتَّسَعَ — "the thing became wide, roomy, spacious."

2. الوُسْع (al-wusʿ) as wealth: richness, affluence (al-ghinā). On this sense he glosses the divine name اللهُ الواسِعُ (al-Wāsiʿ) as al-Ghanī, "the Rich."

3. الوُسْع as capacity: means, ability, what one can manage (al-jida wa-l-ṭāqa) — as in "he spends according to the measure of his wusʿ (capacity)."

4. سَعَة (saʿa) — abundance/ampleness of means. Cited shāhid: Qur'an al-Ṭalāq 65:7, "Let the one of abundance spend out of his abundance." The verb أَوْسَعَ الرَّجُلُ likewise means "the man became possessed of ample means."

5. Applied to a horse: وَسَاعٌ (wasāʿ) describes one swift and broad of stride.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَوْسَط 2x "average"; وَسَط 1x "(of the) middle way"; وُسْطَىٰ 1x "[the] middle"; وَسَطْ 1x "then penetrate (in the) center"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats و-س-ط as a single sound root whose core idea is fairness/evenness and the middle or midpoint.

1. Core sense — middle and equitableness. The "most equitable" part of a thing is its middle: awsaṭuhu / wasaṭuhu. He cites Qur'an 2:143, ummatan wasaṭan, as an instance of this adjectival use ("a middling/balanced community").

2. Vocalisation distinguishes two uses. With fatḥa on the sīn (wasaṭ) it names the physical middle of a thing: ḍarabtu wasaṭa raʾsihi, "I struck the middle of his head." With sukūn (wasṭ) it functions adverbially, "amid": wasṭa al-qawm, "in the midst of the people."

3. Extended sense — social centrality and rank. He is awsaṭuhum ḥasaban is said of a man who stands at the centre-point (wāsiṭa) of his people and is the highest of them in station. Here "middle" carries elevation, not mediocrity.

4. Concrete derivative — al-wasūṭ, a hair-cloth tent larger than the miẓalla (awning tent).

5. Of camels — al-wasūṭ is also said of a she-camel, comparable to al-ṣafūf: one that fills the milking vessel.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris states that the root و-س-ل (w-s-l) covers two entirely unrelated meanings:

1. Desire / seeking. "Wasala" means "he desired, yearned." The one who yearns toward God is called al-wāsil. As evidence he cites the poet Labīd: "Nay, every possessor of a religion is one who yearns toward God (wāsil)." From this same sense comes al-wasīlah, "the means" (of approach/access) — the noun is derived by the same analogical pattern (qiyās).

2. Theft. The expression "akhadha ibilahu tawassulan" ("he took his camels by tawassul") means he took them by stealth, i.e. stole them.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مُتَوَسِّمِين 1x "for those who discern"; نَسِمُ 1x "we will brand him"
text:
Root و-س-م (w-s-m) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Single core sense: a trace or impression (athar) left as a distinguishing mark (maʿlam).

1. Base verb — wasamtu al-shayʾa wasman, "I marked it": to leave an imprint on something with a sīma (a mark/brand).

2. al-wasmiyy — the season's first rain, so called because it "marks" the earth with the vegetation it brings up.

3. tawassama (per al-Aṣmaʿī) — to go out in search of the pasturage produced by that wasmī rain. Cited verse: at dawn they were like graceful doom-palms, moving in the direction taken by a departing traveler who reads the tracks (mutawassim).

4. mawsim al-ḥājj, "the pilgrims' mawsim" (gathering-season) — called a mawsim precisely because it is a fixed landmark/appointed point (maʿlam) to which people converge. Ibn Fāris only explains the naming here; he does not describe any rite performed at it.

5. Marked by a quality — fulān mawsūm bi-l-khayr, "so-and-so bears the mark of goodness"; fulāna dhāt mīsam, "she carries the mark [of beauty]" — said of someone showing a visible trace of beauty. Related noun: al-wasāma, "beauty."

6. A disputed line of verse — "the troughs of ʿIrāk: the mawāsim wore them down." Two readings are given: either "the people of the seasonal gatherings" [wore them down], or "branded camels" [wore them down].

7. wassama al-nās, "the people wassama" — they attended the mawsim (seasonal gathering), on the model of ʿayyadū, "they observed the feast."

8. Qur'anic citation, 15:75 — {inna fī dhālika la-āyātin li-l-mutawassimīn}, "Indeed in that are signs for al-mutawassimīn." Ibn Fāris glosses al-mutawassimīn simply as "those who look for the telling/indicative mark" (al-nāẓirīn fī al-sima al-dālla) — discerning observers who read an outward sign — without specifying further what sign or where.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
poets_named: unnamed verse; Ḥumayd ibn Thawr (lived into Islam)
text:
ROOT و س ن (w-s-n) — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī

1. Core sense: drowsiness/dozing. Al-wasan and al-sinah (this author treats سِنَة as belonging to the same root) both name a light doze or drowsiness that overtakes a person — "drowsiness/dozing seized him," "they were in the stupor of their dozing," "a doze came over him." A drowsy man is وَسْنَان (wasnān); a drowsy woman, وَسْنى (wasnā). Idiom: a person can be "granted something in his sleep that he wasn't even drowsy for" — i.e. he received it (a vision/dream) in sleep without truly having dozed off. (One phrase describing a woman as "drowsy through the forenoon," paralleling the stock expression nawūm al-ḍuḥā, "a habitual late-morning sleeper," is textually uncertain/possibly garbled in this copy.)

2. توسّن (tawassana) — used of a phantom or night-visitor in the convention of love poetry: to come upon someone while they sleep, paralleling tanawwama ("to come upon someone as they doze"). Two shawāhid: an anonymous verse about a beloved visited in her sleep, and a verse by Ḥumayd ibn Thawr in which a rain-cloud "visits" a meadow the way a night-phantom visits a sleeper. Zamakhsharī explains the extended image: the cloud is the "bright one" (al-aghar), pictured as a bikr — a young, first-time visitor — while the already-rained-on lands are ʿawn, "seasoned/mature" ones, echoing the poetic scene of an experienced woman receiving a young suitor by night.

3. Figurative extensions (majāz):
   - سِنَة (sinah) = heedlessness/inattention: "he is in a sinah" = he is in a state of neglect; "he has buried his head in a sinah" = he is oblivious.
   - سِنَة also loosely for "need" or "concern": "it's none of my hamm (concern) or my sinah" = it's none of my business.
   - أوسان (awsān, plural) = one's fill or need, said of water: "the camels satisfied their awsān from the water" = they drank their fill. A wordplay pairs this with أرسان (arsān, "tethers/halters"): "the horses fulfilled their arsān [were tethered/restrained], until they fulfilled their awsān [got their fill of water]."

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
poets_named: unnamed verse; Labīd (lived into Islam); Jandal (pre-Islamic)
text:
Root و-س-ق (W-S-Q) — from Asās al-Balāgha by al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144 CE)

**Core sense: load, gather, carry**
- wasq (وسق): a standard measure/load-quantity — "he has a wasq of dates." Plurals: wusūq, awsāq.
- wassaqa matāʿahu: he bundled his belongings into loads (wusūq).
- awsaqa al-baʿīr / wasaqahu: to load a camel; wasaqa = ḥamala, "to carry/load." The author states the general rule plainly: "everything you gather and carry, you have wasaqtahu."
- A cited verse plays on this sense figuratively: someone "like one grasping water his fingers do not wasiqhu [hold/contain]" — using wasaqa for "to hold, contain."

**Gathering/driving (herding sense)**
- The herdsman "yasiqu" (drives) the camels until they "istawsaqat" — gathered/coalesced together.
- wasīqa / wasāʾiq: livestock driven off by an enemy raider — driven plunder (al-ṭarīda). The same word is used of a wild ass driving off its own ʿāna (herd) — "wasīqatuhu."

**Extended senses via "bearing/carrying"**
- A pregnant she-camel is called wāsiq ("she has wasaqat" = become pregnant) — pregnancy framed as "bearing a load."
- A heavily fruit-laden palm tree is mūsiqa ("it has awsaqat"). Labīd uses this in a verse describing a garden: on the day provision became abundant, the palms were mūsiqāt (heavily laden) and other growth was copious and first-yielding.

**Figurative uses (al-majāz)**
- "The moon ittasaqa" — became full/complete, its light aligned into wholeness.
- "His affair ittasaqa and istawsaqa" — became settled, ordered, brought together.
- muwāsaqa (mutual "wasaqa-ing" of one another): to be someone's match or equal, since its root idea is muḥāmala — mutually matching one another's load/pace. "He does not yuwāsiq so-and-so" = he is not his equal. Illustrated with a verse by Jandal about not matching a rival's pace or being reliably firm when tested (the exact sense of this verse is not fully certain).

**Qur'anic citation**
- Q84:17, "wa'l-layli wa-mā wasaq" — "by the night, and what it wasaq [gathers/enshrouds]" — cited as an attestation of the root, without further comment by the author.

**Idiom**
- "I will not do that so long as my eye wasaqat water" — as long as the eye can still hold/contain tears, i.e., "for as long as I live."

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's entry for the root w-s-w-s is brief and has three parts.

1. **Core sense.** *Waswasa* is defined as "the bad passing thought" — an evil notion that crosses the mind.

2. **Etymology.** He derives it from *waswās*, which he explains as a sound: the tinkling of jewellery, and faint, barely audible whispering. The mental sense is thus traced back to a sound-word for a low, indistinct murmur.

3. **Qur'anic evidence.** He cites two verses: "then the shayṭān whispered to him" (Ṭā Hā 20:120), and "from the evil of the whisperer" (al-Nās 114:4).

4. **Further usage.** He adds that the hunter's low murmur is likewise called *waswās* — a non-Qur'anic usage showing the word applied to quiet, stealthy sound.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the three letters w-t-d as expressing one single underlying notion: al-watid, "the peg" or "stake" (the kind driven into the ground, e.g. a tent-peg).

1. Core sense — the peg itself, and the verb of driving one in. He cites the usage wa-tadahu, "he drove/fixed it in as a peg," and the imperative phrase witid watidaka, "drive in your peg!" — showing the root functions as a verb (to peg/stake something down) as well as a noun.

2. Variant noun form — the noun is also said as watd, alongside watid; both name the same object.

3. Extended/figurative use — watid al-udhun, "the peg of the ear," names the part inside the ear's interior, so called because its shape resembles a peg (watid). This shows the core "peg" image extended by resemblance to an anatomical feature.

The entry is very brief and gives no further senses, morphological detail (wazn, plural), or citations beyond these.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root و ت ن (w-t-n), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: firmness/stability and constant attachment.

1. wātana al-amra — he held fast, persistently attached himself to a matter.
2. māʾ wātin — perpetual, never-drying water.
3. al-watīn — a vein constantly attached to the heart, nourishing it — i.e. the aorta, the great vessel emerging directly from the heart — the same underlying image of unbreakable attachment applied to human anatomy.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: تَتْرَا 1x "(in) succession"; يَتِرَ 1x "will deprive you"; وَتْر 1x "and the odd"
text:
Ibn Fāris opens by noting that the root w-t-r does not reduce to one governing idea (qiyās); its senses are separate and do not resemble one another. He then lists them:

1. Al-watīrah — the rounded white blaze on a horse's forehead.
2. Al-watīrah — a target/object used for practicing the spear-thrust.
3. Al-watīrah — steady persistence in something; the phrase "huwa ʿalā watīratin" means "he keeps to a [fixed] course/routine."
4. Al-watar — a grudge or blood-debt (al-dhaḥl) owed for a wrong, e.g. a killing; "wataartuhu" means "I wronged/deprived him [of a kinsman], leaving him with a vengeance-claim against me."
5. Al-witr / al-watar — the single, odd, unpaired one (opposite of paired/even).
6. Watar al-qaws — the bowstring; "wataartuhā" or "awtartuhā" means "I strung it."
7. Al-watarah — the tip/end of the nose.

He closes with a report from al-Liḥyānī distinguishing two kinds of succession: things are only called muwātarah ("successive at intervals") if a pause occurs between occurrences; if there is no pause, the correct term is mudārakah ("back-to-back, uninterrupted"). He illustrates with a she-camel called muwātirah, who sets down one knee, pauses, then sets down the other.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives wathan (idol; plural awthān) from a single underlying root-idea centered on firmness/abundance, not on divinity or worship as such:

1. al-wathan = "idol," the singular of awthān ("idols"): stones that used to be worshipped.
2. The root's origin, per Ibn Fāris, is the expression istawthana al-shay' — "the thing became strong/firmly established."
3. From the same root: awthana fulānun al-ḥimla — "so-and-so made the load heavy / increased it."
4. Also: awthantu lahu — "I gave him a large/generous amount."

So the lexical common thread he traces across these four usages is strength, firmness, or abundance/heaviness — with "idol" (a solid, firmly-set stone object) being one particular application of that core sense, alongside "making a load heavy" and "giving generously."

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: مِّيثَٰق 25x "a covenant"; مَّوْثِق 3x "a promise"; وُثْقَىٰ 2x "the most trustworthy"; وَثَاق 2x "(as) his binding"; وَاثَقَ 1x "he bound you"; يُوثِقُ 1x "will bind"
text:
al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī derives the root و-ث-ق (w-th-q) from a core sense of trusting/relying and, correspondingly, of binding firmly.

1. Verb wathiqtu bihi ("I trusted / relied on him") — to be at ease with someone and depend on him. The verbal noun is thiqa (trust, reliability).

2. awthaqtu ("I bound it fast") — to secure something firmly. From this: al-waṯāq / al-wiṯāq, a noun for the thing something is bound with (a bond or fetter). He supports the binding sense with al-Fajr 89:26 ("none binds as He binds") and Muḥammad 47:4 ("make the bond fast").

3. al-wuthqā — feminine of al-awthaq, "the firmest / most reliable."

4. al-mīthāq — a compact confirmed by an oath and covenant. Cited from Āl ʿImrān 3:81, al-Aḥzāb 33:7, and al-Nisāʾ 4:154 ("a solemn compact").

5. al-mawthiq — a noun of the same sense (a pledge / covenant), cited from Yūsuf 12:66. al-Rāghib notes al-wuthqā is close in meaning to al-mawthiq, and cites al-Baqara 2:256 ("the firmest handhold").

6. Usage: rajul thiqa ("a trustworthy man"), qawm thiqa ("trustworthy people"); the word is applied figuratively to the one who is trusted. Also nāqa mūthaqat al-khalq — a she-camel of firm, solidly-built form.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: يُوزَعُ 3x "(were) set in rows"; أَوْزِعْ 2x "grant me (the) power"
poets_named: unnamed verse ×2; Yazīd b. al-Ḥakam al-Thaqafī (Umayyad)
text:
Root: و ز ع (w-z-ʿ), as recorded by al-Zamakhsharī in Asās al-Balāgha.

1. Core sense — holding back, restraining.
- وزعته (wazaʿtuhu) = "I restrained him"; the reflexive اتزع (ittazaʿa) = "he restrained himself."
- وازعته (wāzaʿtuhu), the reciprocal form, = "I withheld from him / held out against him."

2. The wāziʿ = the restrainer, in several applications.
- الشيب وازع — "grey hair is a restrainer" (age itself curbs a man).
- وازع العسكر — the officer of an army who holds back whoever pushes forward out of line.
- لا بدّ للناس من وزعة — "people cannot do without restrainers," glossed by the author as those who hold others back from wrongdoing and aggression.
- Used reflexively of the self: وزع نفسه عن الجهل والهوى, "he restrained himself from ignorance and caprice." A verse cited (poet unnamed): if a man does not restrain himself from ignorance and youthful folly so that his learning may benefit him, his ignorance has already harmed him.
- متّزع (muttaziʿ) — a person of proud, self-guarding spirit who holds himself back.

3. Form IV أوزع — being made keen or disposed toward something.
- أوزعه الله الشكر — "God disposed him to thankfulness"; أستوزع الله شكر نعمته — asking God for that disposition.
- The author pairs this form throughout with the root و ل ع (ولع, "to be enamoured/keen"), treating the two as interchangeable: ʾawlaʿtu / ʾawzaʿtu bihi; the participles mūlaʿ / mūzaʿ; the verbal nouns wulūʿ / wuzūʿ; and the causatives ʾawlaʿtuhu / ʾawzaʿtuhu bihi. Keenness, on this account, is a companion sense to the root rather than a separate homonym.

4. Form II وزّع — dividing and distributing.
- وزّع المال والخراج توزيعاً = he apportioned property and revenue, i.e. divided it up.

5. أوزاع (ʾawzāʿ) — scattered assortments, the resulting sense of "parts divided off."
- بها أوزاع من الناس وأوشاب — mixed, scattered groups of people.
- ذهبت نفسه شعاعاً ولحمه أوزاعاً — his soul scattered and his flesh left in pieces. Shāhid from Yazīd b. al-Ḥakam al-Thaqafī: he turned back a squadron's charge from a youth whose flesh it had almost left in scattered pieces.
- Of livestock: ما لهم إلا أوزاع من الصّرم, "they have only scattered remnants of camel-herds." A supporting verse describes raiders driving off every large warm herd, the sheltered women, and scattered remnants of the camel-groups; the author glosses استدبروا as "they drove off" and الضحضاح as "numerous camels."

6. Figurative (labelled ومن المجاز by the author).
- توزّعته الأفكار — "thoughts divided him among themselves," i.e. pulled him in pieces; متوزّع القلب — a man of divided heart. The physical sense of being parcelled out is transferred to the mind.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مِيزَان 16x "his scales"; وَزْن 3x "and the weighing"; وَّزَنُ 3x "and weigh"; مَّوْزُون 1x "well-balanced"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root w-z-n from a single core idea: adjustment/balancing (taʿdīl) and straightness (istiqāma).

1. Core sense — weighing: wazantu al-shayʾa waznan, "I weighed the thing." The noun al-zina is the measure of a thing's weight; Ibn Fāris notes its original form was wazna.

2. Balance / midpoint: qāma mīzānu al-nahār ("the balance of the day stood up") is said when the day reaches its midpoint (noon).

3. Parallelism / counterpoise: hādhā yuwāzinu dhālika means one thing is level with or aligned opposite another (muḥādhī).

4. Figurative — soundness of mind: wazīn al-raʾy is a person of balanced, sound judgment; rājiḥ al-wazn ("of preponderant weight") describes someone credited with sound judgment and strong intellect.

Anomalous sense (Ibn Fāris flags it as departing from the root's core, on al-Khalīl's authority): al-wazīn as kneaded colocynth once eaten as food; and al-wazn said to mean a lump or piece of dates.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: وِزْر 12x "burden"; يَزِرُ 7x "will bear"; وَازِرَة 5x "bearer of burdens"; وَزِير 2x "a minister"; وَزَر 1x "refuge"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives وزر (w-z-r) from two sound base meanings: (1) a refuge, and (2) heaviness or weight in a thing.

1. Refuge — الْوَزَر (al-wazar): a place of refuge or shelter. He cites Qur'an 75:11, {كَلَّا لَا وَزَرَ} ("Nay, there is no refuge"). Related, per al-Shaybānī: أَوْزَرَ الشَّيْءَ means to secure or store something away.

2. Load/weight — الْوِزْر (al-wizr): a man's carried load, as when he spreads his garment, piles his belongings in it, and hauls it. From this sense of a carried burden, a sin came to be called wizr.

3. Weapons/arms — al-wizr also means arms or war-gear, plural أَوْزَار (awzār). Shāhid: al-Aʿshā — "I made ready for war its gear: long spears and stallion horses."

4. Vizier — الْوَزِير (al-wazīr) is named from this root because he carries the burden on his master's behalf.

5. Less certain senses (Ibn Fāris flags them as "perhaps sound"): أَوَزَرْتُ مَالَهُ, to carry off / take away someone's wealth; and وَزَرْتُهُ, to overcome someone. Shāhid: "their foals have outmatched their grown mares."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: خَاشِع 14x "humbled"; خَشَعَتِ 2x "and (will be) humbled"; خُشُوع 1x "(in) humility"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-ش-ع (kh-sh-ʿ) as a single root meaning to lower or abase oneself (taṭāmun).

1. Core sense: خَشَعَ (khashaʿa), verbal noun خُشُوع (khushūʿ) — to lower oneself and bow the head. He notes it is close in meaning to خُضُوع (khuḍūʿ, "submission"), but distinguishes them: khuḍūʿ concerns the body and the outward admission of being subdued, whereas khushūʿ shows in the voice and the gaze. Shāhid: Qurʾān 68:43, "their eyes downcast" (خَاشِعَةً أَبْصَارُهُمْ).

2. On the personal form (Ibn Durayd): al-khāshiʿ is the submissive one and the one who bows. The reflexive اخْتَشَعَ (iktashaʿa) is used of a person humbling himself, but not of the eye/gaze.

3. Physical idiom: خَشَعَ خَرَاشِيَّ صَدْرِهِ — to cough up thick, viscous phlegm.

4. Landscape senses: الخُشْعَة (al-khushʿa) is a rocky rise that has become mostly level/smooth; قُفٌّ خَاشِعٌ is a rise lying low and flat against the ground. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: بَلْدَةٌ خَاشِعَةٌ, a dust-covered land. Poetic shāhid (Jarīr): at the news of al-Zubayr's death, "the walls of the city and the humbled mountains sank low."

5. Of animals (al-Khalīl): خَشَعَ سَنَامُ الْبَعِيرِ — the camel's hump "sank," i.e. wasted away until barely any remained.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root idea: kh-sh-b (خ ش ب) conveys roughness and coarseness/thickness — one single underlying sense according to Ibn Fāris.

1. al-akhshab — a rough, rugged mountain. Cited via a hadith about Mecca: "It will not perish until its two akhshabs perish," meaning the two mountains [flanking the city]. Also used by a poet describing a camel so tall that, rising above the she-camels around it, it looked like a mountain (akhshab).

2. al-khashīb — a sword at the very start of its forging, while it is still rough. By the same idea, sahm makhshūb / khashīb is an arrow at the stage when it is still being roughly carved.

3. jamal khashīb — a thick, coarse camel; and ẓalīm khashīb — a thick, coarse male ostrich.

Ibn Fāris's own etymological note: he takes all of the above to be derived from al-khashab, "wood/timber."

4. takhashshabat al-ibil — said of camels when they had been feeding on dried-out pasture.

5. jabhah khashbāʾ — an unpleasant, dry, uneven forehead.

Appended note from Abū ʿUbayd: al-khashīb originally named a sword whose forging had only just begun (hence still rough), but the word came into such common use that among the Arabs al-khashīb shifted to mean the opposite — a polished sword.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris's account of the root خ-ش-ي (kh–sh–weak letter):

1. Core sense: the root denotes fear and dread (khawf, dhuʿr). From it: الخشية (al-khashya) means fear; رجل خشيان (rajul khashyān) is a fearful man. The construction خاشاني فلان فخشيته means "he contended with me in fearing and I outdid him" — i.e. I proved more intense in fear than he.

2. Comparative form: هذا المكان أخشى من ذلك ("this place is akhshā than that") means more to be feared / more intense in fear.

3. Figurative extension: خشيت (khashītu) can carry the sense of علمت — "I knew / came to realize." Ibn Fāris cites the verse "And indeed I khashītu that whoever follows the guidance dwells in the Gardens with the Prophet Muhammad," glossing khashītu here as "I knew."

4. An outlying group he treats as deviating from the chapter (though he allows a distant link): الخشو (al-khashw) — poor, spoiled dried dates (ḥashaf); the verb خشت النخلة تخشو خشواً describes a palm bearing such dates. And الخشيّ (al-khashiyy) applied to meat means the dried, desiccated kind.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
quran_words: يَخْذُلْ 1x "he forsakes you"; مَّخْذُول 1x "forsaken"; خَذُول 1x "a deserter"
poets_named: Ṭarafa (pre-Islamic); Jaʿfar ibn ʿUlba (Umayyad); al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); ʿAdī ibn Zayd (pre-Islamic)
text:
Root خ ذ ل (kh-dh-l) — Tāj al-ʿArūs (Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī, d. 1791 CE)

Core sense (per the author): the triliteral pattern signifies "leaving a thing and desisting from it."

1. khadhala-hu / khadhala ʿanhu — "he withheld his support (naṣr) from him," i.e. abandoned/failed to help him. Qur'anic citation: "If He should forsake you [yakhdhulkum], who then could help you after Him?" God's khidhlān of a servant is glossed as His not shielding him — al-Azharī adds: from wrongdoing, so that he falls into it.
