The agent-noun is khādhil ("one who forsakes"); Ibn al-Aʿrābī records khudhala(h) for a man who forsakes habitually.

2. Of a gazelle, wild cow, or other grazing animal — khadhalat: she lagged behind her herd-mates and became isolated (or lagged and could not catch up); she is then called khādhil or khadhūl. al-Aṣmaʿī confirms this sense for a gazelle falling behind its herd, illustrated with a verse of Ṭarafa. A variant tradition (in al-ʿUbāb) instead has khadhalat mean she stayed behind with her young; some lexicographers call this the reverse (maqlūb) of the "abandoned" sense, since she is really "the one left." al-Layth gives a related picture: such a doe abandons her herd-companions in grazing to flee/stay with her young — al-Azharī corrects a manuscript variant here (from "flees" to "lags behind"). Separately, khadhūl also names a mare that freezes in place when labor pains strike her.

3. takhādhalat rijlāhu — an old man's legs "give out" from infirmity (illustrated with a verse of Jaʿfar ibn ʿUlba on fallen men whose strength to rise fails). takhādhala al-qawm — people turned their backs on one another, each abandoning the rest. al-khādhil is also used for one who is routed/defeated in battle (Ibn al-Aʿrābī). al-Layth also records akhdhala said of a wild animal's young "finding" its mother to be one who abandons it.

4. Additional notes appended by the author: khadhūl describes one much given to abandoning others — cited from the Qur'an: "Satan is ever, to man, a khadhūl [forsaker]." khadhūl al-rijl describes a man whose leg fails him from weakness, illness, or drunkenness (verse of al-Aʿshā). al-takhdhīl is the verbal noun for inciting someone to abandon a companion and deterring him from helping him. Any "one who leaves" can generally be called khādhil — illustrated with ʿAdī ibn Zayd's image of a bucket whose cross-bars come loose ("are abandoned") and it breaks apart.

5. Grammatical/dialectal note: akhdhala-hu is recorded as a dialectal variant of khadhala-hu; on this basis the reciter ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr is said to have read the Qur'anic verb as "yukhdhilkum" (ḍamma-yāʾ, kasra-dhāl) rather than the more common "yakhdhulkum."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: al-ʿAjjāj (Umayyad); Zuhayr (pre-Islamic); al-Nābighah (pre-Islamic); Imruʾ al-Qays (pre-Islamic); Labīd (lived into Islam)
text:
Root خ ض ع (kh-ḍ-ʿ), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Two distinct roots gathered under this spelling:

First — bowing down/submission (the entry's main subject)
1. al-khuḍūʿ — humility, self-abasement; ikhtaḍaʿa — he humbled himself; a man or woman "content with abasement" is akhḍaʿ/khaḍʿāʾ, illustrated with a line of poetry by al-ʿAjjāj comparing himself, tormented by a mosquito, to a humbled slave.
2. rajul khuḍʿah — one who submits to everyone; al-khaḍaʿ (per al-Shaybānī) — bending the neck toward the chest, applied to a camel (Zuhayr's poetry) and, per some Bedouin informants, to ostriches' curved necks.
3. al-mukhtaḍiʿ — of predators, one whose head droops toward its snout, illustrated with a line of poetry by al-Nābighah describing a blood-stained hunting animal swooping down on its prey. Ibn al-Aʿrābī glosses al-akhḍaʿ as "the stooping one," applied in a hadith description of al-Zubayr.
4. Abū Ḥātim: al-khuḍʿān — camels bending their necks in a fast gait, the most extreme form of that pace; akhḍaʿahu al-shayb — gray hair "bowed" him.
5. ikhtaḍaʿa al-faḥlu al-nāqata — a stallion camel repeatedly mounting and pressing down a she-camel; khaḍaʿa al-najm — a star inclining toward setting, illustrated with a line of poetry by Imruʾ al-Qays about a nighttime approach timed to the stars' descent.
6. Ibn Durayd: khaḍaʿa/akhḍaʿa — of a man's speech, to soften it; a hadith citation applies this to forbidding a man from speaking softly/suggestively to a woman not his own.

Second — a kind of sound
7. al-Khalīl: al-khayḍuʿah is the intermingled roar of sound in battle; some say it instead means battlefield dust, a reading Ibn Fāris explicitly rejects as lacking valid derivational basis, allowing only that the two senses might be loosely associated. Illustrated with a line of poetry by Labīd. [The source entry continues beyond what was captured for this digest.]

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats kh-ḍ-d as a single, consistent root whose core sense is: a bending or folding in something soft/pliant.

1. Basic usage — a branch bends without breaking: inkhaḍada al-ʿūd ("the stick bent"). Transitively, khaḍadtuhu = "I bent it."

2. Extended usage — some speakers stretch the sense to mean stripping a tree of its thorns: khaḍadtu al-shajara = "I broke off the tree's thorns." From this comes the description nabātun khaḍīd, "a khaḍīd plant."

3. Ibn Fāris's judgment: the first sense (bending) is the true root meaning, not the second. He reasons that khaḍīd itself — describing a plant as lush, succulent, and soft — bends precisely because it is soft; the "bending" idea is what the word is really tracking, and the thorn-stripping sense is a secondary extension.

4. Poetic citation (al-Nābigha), describing a flash flood fed by every brimming, roaring valley, carrying with it "a heap of yanbūt [a thorny plant] and khaḍad." Here, Ibn Fāris notes, khaḍad is used as a noun meaning cut, moist/green branch-pieces swept up by the flood — not the verb "to bend."

5. Also applied to fighting camels: khaḍada al-baʿīru ʿunuqa al-baʿīr, "the camel bent the other camel's neck," used when two camels clash and one twists the other's neck.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: خُضْر 5x "green"; خَضِر 1x "green plant"; مُخْضَرَّة 1x "green"; أَخْضَر 1x "[the] green"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-ض-ر as a single, unbroken root, with the rest of its uses carried back to that one sense.

1. Core sense — the colour green. الخُضْرة is the familiar colour. الخَضْراء ("the green one") is the sky, named for its colour, on the same pattern by which the earth is called الغَبْراء ("the dust-coloured one").

2. Green shading into black. A كتيبة خضراء ("green squadron") is one whose surface is the blackness of iron. Ibn Fāris explains the overlap by a colour principle: anything that departs from white falls on the black side, so the descriptions interpenetrate and what is black may be called أخضر. He supports this from Q 55:64, مُدْهَامَّتَان, describing the two gardens, which he glosses as "two black ones" — from خضرة, since lush, well-watered vegetation looks black from a distance. On the same logic the fertile land of Iraq is called سواد ("black-land"), for its many trees, and a people called الخُضْر were so named for their dark colouring. In horse-markings, خُضرة is a dusty coat with a dark tinge mixed in.

3. Dark-skinned as "pure-blooded". On the verse "I am the green one — who knows me? — green of skin, in the house of the Arabs", he takes the speaker to mean "I am of unmixed stock", since Arab colouring is brown (سُمرة).

4. Attractive surface over bad soil. The saying "Beware the greenery of the dung-heaps" is applied to a beautiful woman of bad origin — like a verdant tree growing on a dung heap.

5. المُخاضَرة — selling fruit before its ripeness shows. Ibn Fāris notes it is forbidden.

6. خُضْر المَزاد — either waterskins that greened with age from standing water left in them, or (on another report) the stomachs/paunches of animals.

7. الخَضار — (a) the first herbage of the season; (b) milk heavily diluted with water. He accepts (b) as belonging to the root: when water predominates, and water is called الأسمر (the dusky one), it joins the black/green overlap already described — the same reason the sea is called خُضارة.

8. "ذهب دمه خِضْرًا" — said of blood shed without redress. He judges this to belong to the root as well: the blood went off "green/fresh", like cut vegetation that is of no further use once severed, and simply withers away.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats kh-ṣ-ṣ as a single, consistent root meaning an opening or a breach.

1. **Gaps.** al-khaṣāṣ are the gaps between the stones on which a cooking pot is set. Of the moon one says it "appeared through a khaṣāṣa (gap) of the clouds", and Dhū al-Rumma describes it finding its gap and showing faintly for as long as it takes to say "lā", before the rest of it slipped back in.

2. **Destitution.** al-khaṣāṣa is destitution, a breach in one's circumstances.

3. **Singling out.** From the same root: khaṣaṣtu fulānan bi-shayʾ, "I singled someone out with something", with the verbal noun khaṣūṣiyya (with a after the kh). Ibn Fāris says this fits the root's analogy: when one person is set apart, a gap is placed between him and the others, and generality (al-ʿumūm) is the opposite. al-khiṣṣīṣā means the same as khaṣūṣiyya.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: a Hudhalī poet (lived into Islam); unnamed verse
text:
Root خ ص ف (kh-ṣ-f), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: the gathering of one thing to another — described as regular and consistent across its derivations.

1. al-khaṣf — patching a sandal by applying a matching piece over it; al-mikhṣaf — the awl used for it, illustrated with a line of poetry by a Hudhalī poet comparing an eagle's nose-tip to the awl's shape.
2. al-ikhtiṣāf — a naked person covering himself with broad leaves, taken over his private parts.
3. al-khaṣīfah — curdled milk with fresh milk poured over it.
4. Ibn Fāris explicitly notes a nuance: the sense of "two things gathered by exact matching" (patching) differs from "two things gathered without exact matching" — the latter covering ḥabl khuṣayf (a rope of mixed black-and-white strands) and, more generally, khuṣayf as any two-colored thing (usually black and white); a horse is akhṣaf when its piebald marking rises from belly to sides.
5. al-khaṣafah — the wrapping/bundle for a mass of dates, illustrated with a line of poetry about a woman selling her children in exchange for date-bundles and dates (an image of desperate poverty).
6. Closing outlier: a she-camel giving birth after nine months' gestation is described as khaṣafat/khaṣūf — a usage Ibn Fāris flags as not fitting the root's main pattern.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: ٱخْتَصَمُ 8x "dispute"; خَصِيم 5x "(is) an opponent"; خَصْم 3x "(of) the litigants"; تَخَاصُم 1x "(the) quarreling"; خَصِمُون 1x "argumentative"
text:
Root kh-ṣ-m (خصم). Al-Zamakhsharī groups the usages into a literal set (built on two ideas — quarreling, and the side/edge of an object) and a figurative extension.

1. Dispute and contention. اختصموا / تخاصموا = "they quarreled with one another"; هذا يوم التخاصم = "this is the day of mutual disputation." خاصمته فخصمته = "I contended with him and got the better of him." كنا في خصومة = "we were in a dispute/litigation." Cited from the Qurʾān: "he is the most contentious of adversaries" (2:204) and "they are a contentious people" (43:58).

2. Words for an adversary. خصم and خصيم both = "opponent"; plurals خصوم and خصماء = "adversaries." أخصم صاحبه = "he coached his companion with the argument until he won the dispute." Verbal noun of the reciprocal form: مخاصمة (contending with someone).

3. The side / edge / corner of an object. خصم الفراش = "the edge of the bed." أخصام الغرارة = "the corners of a sack, where the carrying-loops are." A verse of al-Akhṭal uses خصومها for the "sides/edges" of a heavy sagging mass battered by the south wind. خصم الراوية = the lower edge/corner of a large water-skin, gripped (with its loops) to lift it.

4. Figurative use (majāz). Of an affair that keeps going wrong, the Arabs say: "no side of it is stopped up but another side opens" — plug one breach and a new one bursts. Here خصم = a corner/gap of the sack, transferred to a problem that cannot be contained.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: خَطِيـَة 8x "our sins"; خَٰطِـِين 5x "sinners"; أَخْطَأْ 2x "you made a mistake"; خَطَـ 2x "(by) mistake"; خَطِيـَٰت 2x "your sins"; خَاطِئَة 2x "sinful"; خِطْـ 1x "a sin"
text:
Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's entry for the root خطأ (kh-ṭ-ʾ).

Core sense: khaṭaʾ is "deviation from the right direction." Al-Rāghib distinguishes three kinds by how intention and deed line up:

1. Full/culpable error (al-khaṭaʾ al-tāmm): you intend what you should not, and you do it — wrong in both aim and act, and the person is held accountable. Verb: خَطِئَ / يَخْطَأُ (khaṭiʾa), verbal nouns khiṭʾ, khiṭʾa. Cited: "their killing is a great wrong" (17:31); "we were wrongdoers" (12:91).

2. Honest mistake: you intend something good, but the result comes out contrary to your intention. Here the form-IV verb أَخْطَأَ (akhṭaʾa) is used; the agent is a mukhṭiʾ — right in intention, wrong in the deed. This is the sense in the reports "error and forgetfulness are lifted from my community" and "whoever exercises judgement and errs still has a reward," and in "whoever kills a believer by mistake (khaṭaʾan)…" (4:92).

3. Blameworthy aim, accidental good: you intend what is not good, but the opposite happens — wrong in intention, right in the deed; blamed for the aim, not praised for the outcome. Illustrated by the verse "you meant to harm me but dragged in my delight," and the remark that a person may do good without realizing it.

Summary of the verb's logic: if you intend a thing and something else results, you "erred" (akhṭaʾa); if what you intended comes about, you "hit the mark" (aṣāba). Akhṭaʾa is also used simply for doing a poor deed or holding an unseemly intention. Hence the paradoxical pairings: "he hit upon the error / missed the correct / hit the correct / missed the error." Al-Rāghib flags the word as mushtarak (shared/ambiguous), wavering between senses that a careful investigator of meanings must weigh.

The noun khaṭīʾa. In "his khaṭīʾa has encompassed him" (2:81): khaṭīʾa and sayyiʾa (misdeed) are close, but khaṭīʾa is most often used of something not itself intended, where an original aim is the cause that generates the act — e.g. shooting at game and hitting a person, or drinking an intoxicant and then committing an offence while drunk. Al-Rāghib divides the causing act into two: a forbidden cause (drinking the intoxicant — the resulting error is not excused) and a non-forbidden cause (shooting at game). Cited: "no blame on you for what you erred in, only for what your hearts intended" (33:5); "whoever earns a khaṭīʾa or a sin" (4:112), where khaṭīʾa is the unintended act. Further citations of the plural and singular: 71:24–25, 26:51, 29:12, 26:82; plurals are khaṭīʾāt and khaṭāyā.

The deliberate side. In "We will forgive you your khaṭāyā" (2:58), the reference is to what IS intended. Al-khāṭiʾ is one who deliberately aims at sin — hence "none eat it but the khāṭiʾūn" (69:36–37). A sin can itself be called a khāṭiʾa, as in "the overturned cities came with the khāṭiʾa" (69:9), meaning the enormous sin — an intensifying construction like the Arabic phrase "poetry that is poetic." What is unintended, by contrast, is (per the Prophetic report) passed over.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
text:
Root خ ط ط (kh-ṭ-ṭ), al-Zamakhsharī, Asās al-Balāgha

Literal senses
1. khaṭṭa al-kitāb — to write a document. The entry's central Qur'anic citation is al-'Ankabut 29:48: "wa lā takhuṭṭuhu bi-yamīnika" — "nor did you write it with your right hand"; kitāb makhṭūṭ — a written document.
2. ikhtaṭṭa li-nafsihi dāran — he marked out boundary-lines for a house to claim it as his own; "hādhihi khaṭṭu Banī fulānin" — this is the marked-out plot of the Banū So-and-so. "jāʾa fulānun wa fī raʾsihi khuṭṭah" — so-and-so came with a wild scheme in his head; "yukallifunī khuṭṭatan mina al-khasf" — he imposes a plan of humiliation on me; "tilka khuṭṭatun laysat min bālī" — that's a scheme I don't care to pursue. "ʿalā ẓahri al-ḥimāri khuṭṭatān" — two streaks on a donkey's back; al-khuṭṭah is grammatically related to al-khaṭṭ the way al-nuqṭah relates to al-nuqaṭ (a singulative pattern).
3. ṭaʿanahu bi-l-khaṭṭiyyah / rimāḥ al-Khaṭṭ / al-qanā al-Khaṭṭī — spears named after al-Khaṭṭ, a coastal region famed for imported spear-cane.

Figurative senses (majāz)
4. "fulānun yabnī khuṭaṭa al-makārim" — so-and-so builds up structures of noble deeds. "khaṭaṭtu bi-l-sayfi wasaṭahu" — I sliced through his middle with a sword. khaṭṭa al-marʾah — to have intercourse with a woman. khaṭṭa/ikhtaṭṭa wajhuhu — his beard-hair extended along the sides of his face (ghulām mukhtaṭṭ — a boy whose beard is just showing).
5. "khaṭaṭnā fīhi khaṭṭan" — an idiom for eating only a little of food offered. "jarāhu fa-mā khaṭṭa ghubārahu" — he raced him but couldn't even reach his dust-trail (i.e. couldn't rival him), illustrated with a line of poetry by al-Nābighah about an unmatched rival at the Battle of ʿUkāẓ.
6. khaṭṭa lahu maḍjaʿan — to dig a grave for someone, illustrated with a line of poetry about spear-tips marking out a resting-place. "ilzam al-khaṭṭ" — keep to the path. khuṭūṭ min kalaʾin wa shirāk — tracts/paths of pasture; "al-ibilu tarʿā khuṭūṭa al-anwāʾ" — camels graze the tracts watered by particular rain-stars (a folk-astronomical reference). Closing: "khaṭṭaṭa ʿalayhi dhunūbahu" — he recorded someone's sins in written lines.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: خَطْب 5x "(was) your affair"; خَاطَبَ 3x "address me"; خِطَاب 3x "speech"; خِطْبَة 1x "marriage proposal"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives خ-ط-ب (kh-ṭ-b) from two distinct roots.

1. Speech / address between two parties. The verb khāṭaba–yukhāṭibu–khiṭāban means to address someone; from it comes khuṭba, an oration or formal address, and khuṭba is likewise the speech by which such an address is delivered. In the marriage context the root denotes the request to be given a woman in marriage — cited from Q 2:235, on hinting at a "proposal (khiṭba) to women." The verb ikhtaṭaba l-qawmu fulānan means a family invited a man to marry their kinswoman. Ibn Fāris also places khaṭb (a matter or affair that befalls someone) here, explaining that it is so named because of the mutual addressing (takhāṭub) and back-and-forth discussion it involves.

2. A difference or mixture of two colors. On al-Farrāʾ's authority: khaṭbāʾ is a she-donkey with a black stripe down its back, the male being akhṭab. Akhṭab is also a bird, perhaps so called because two colors alternate on it (with a poetic citation of the akhṭab screeching on a tree). Khuṭbān is the colocynth when its colors turn variegated, and akhṭab is a donkey overlaid with a greenish tinge. Any color resembling this pattern is called akhṭab.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: خَطِفَ 3x "and (had) snatched him"; يَتَخَطَّفَ 3x "we would be swept"; خَطْفَة 1x "(by) theft"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-ط-ف (kh-ṭ-f) as one consistent root with a single core meaning that all its uses can be derived from by analogy: **snatching something away quickly and lightly**.

**1. The base sense: to snatch, seize away.**
الخَطْف = snatching away. Two conjugation patterns are recorded: خَطِفْتُهُ أَخْطَفُهُ and خَطَفْتُهُ أَخْطِفُهُ.

**2. Lightning that "snatches" sight.**
بَرْقٌ خَاطِفٌ — lightning described as snatching away the light of the eyes. Qur'anic citation: "the lightning almost snatches away their sight" (2:20).

**3. Snatching by stealth — of the shayṭān.**
The shayṭān "snatches" hearing, i.e. steals it furtively. Qur'anic citation: "except one who snatches the snatch" (37:10). Ibn Fāris adds that the shayṭān is called الخَطَّاف ("the snatcher"), a name he says occurs in ḥadīth.

**4. Speed of movement.**
جَمَلٌ خَيْطَفٌ = a swift-paced camel; the speed itself is الخَيْطَفَى. Shāhid: "and a brisk stride, sustaining its steady trot, swift-snatching." The proper name الخَطَفَى derives from this. He explains the link to the base sense: a fast-moving animal keeps its legs on the ground only briefly, as though it were snatching the ground away.

**5. Leanness.**
مُخْطَفُ الحَشَا = drawn-in / lean of flank. He judges this analogically sound: it is as if the flesh had been snatched off him, leaving him thin.

**6. Missing a shot — an uncertain case.**
رمى الرميَّةَ فأخطفها = he shot at the game and missed. Ibn Fāris leaves two options open: either it belongs to this root, or the fāʾ is a substitution for a hamza (i.e. it really belongs to أخطأ, "to miss"). Shāhid: "when he hits his quarry, or misses."

**7. الخُطَّاف — two concrete nouns, both from "snatching."**
(a) A bird (the swallow); he calls the derivation sound because it snatches its prey with its talon. Relatedly, the talons of beasts of prey are called خَطَاطِيف ("snatchers"): "when the talons of his hand fasten on an opponent, he sees death with his own two eyes, black and red."
(b) A hooked iron implement, so called because things are snatched up with it; plural خَطَاطِيف. Cited from al-Nābigha: "crooked hooks on stout ropes, drawn toward you by hands pulling hard."

dictionary: Lane — Arabic-English Lexicon, Edward William Lane (d. 1876)
text:
Lane's entry for the root خ-ط-و (kh-ṭ-w), built on the sense of taking a step.

1. Basic verb — خَطَا (form I; verbal noun خَطْو), and the form VIII اِخْتَطَى, mean the same: to step, pace, or walk — the equivalent of مَشَى ("to walk"). Lane notes اِخْتَاطَ (root خ-ي-ط) as the same word with the letters transposed. Example: خَطَوْتُ خَطْوَةً وَاحِدَةً, "I took a single step"; and وَسَّعَ الخَطْوَ, "he stepped wide."

2. Form II خَطَّى — to make something pass over (i.e. bypass) something else. Used of rain withheld: خَطَّى اللّٰهُ نَوْءَهَا, "may God make the rain-star pass the land by and send it no rain" — though Lane reports that here the verb may originally have been خَطَّطَ, with the final ṭ shifting to y, linking it to the root خطأ ("to miss, err"). Al-Farrāʾ treated خَطَّى السَّهْمَ as synonymous with خطأ: to make an arrow miss its mark. In supplication for someone: خُطِّىَ عَنْهُ السُّوْءُ, "may evil be made to pass him by / be turned away from him"; also خُطِّىَ عَنْكَ, "may it be put away from thee" (an alternative reading spells it with hamza, خُطِّئَ).

3. A usage note: common speech uses خَطِّى to a she-ass or she-camel in slippery ground, meaning "step carefully"; Lane records the correct form as the feminine imperative اُخْطُِى.

4. Form IV أَخْطَاهُ — to make another person step or walk. (The spelling أَخْطَيْتُ is treated as a variant of أَخْطَأْتُ, "I erred," under the other root.)

5. Form V تَخَطَّى — to step over, or to pass over and beyond, someone or something; form VIII اِخْتَطَاهُمْ is given as equivalent. The stock phrase is تَخَطَّيْتُ رِقَابَ النَّاسِ, "I stepped over people's necks" — and a report about the Friday assembly describes a latecomer "stepping over the necks of the people" already seated in their rows. Another idiom: فُلَانٌ لَا يَتَخَطَّى عَنِ الطُّنُبِ, "he does not step past the tent-rope," said of someone too filthy to walk away from the tent to relieve himself. Lane cautions that in the sense "I passed over to such a thing," the word is تَخَطَّيْتُ, not تَخَطَّأْتُ with hamza.

6. Figurative extensions of form V (marked tropical by Lane):
   - تَخَطَّاهُ المَكْرُوهُ — harm passed over him without striking him.
   - تَخَطَّيْتُ إِلَيْهِ بِالمَكْرُوهِ — I passed over others to single him out with harm.
   - تَخَطَّى عَنِّى بَصَرُكَ — your gaze passed me by.
   - And the sense of overstepping or transgressing a limit set for one.

7. Nouns — two vowellings with distinct meanings:
   - خَطْوَةٌ (fatḥa) = one act of stepping, a single step; plurals خَطَوَاتٌ (few) and خِطَآءٌ (many). Poetic witness from Imraʾ al-Qays: she bounds like a gazelle, so that "one valley is crossed at a walk and one valley trampled as though rained upon" — i.e. she alternates measured stepping with a downpour-like gallop. Variant readings of the line are recorded (خَطِيطٌ, "a valley not rained upon," from Abū ʿUbaydah; and كَصَوْبِ الخَرِيفِ, "like autumn's pouring rain").
   - خُطْوَةٌ (ḍamma) = the span between the two feet, the stride-distance; plurals خُطْوَاتٌ / خُطُوَاتٌ / خُطَوَاتٌ (few) and خُطًى (many). Hence قَرَّبَ اللّٰهُ عَلَيْكَ الخُطْوَةَ, "may God shorten the distance for you," and the figurative بَيْنَ القَوْلَيْنِ خُطًى يَسِيرَةٌ, "between the two statements there are only a few steps," i.e. little difference.

8. Qur'anic citation — لَا تَتَّبِعُوا خُطُوَاتِ الشَّيْطَانِ (Q 2:168; 2:163 in Lane's numbering) is explained as "do not follow the ways of the Devil" (per the TA), or "the footsteps of the Devil" (per the JK). Variant readings include خُطْوَات, and a reading خُطُؤَات attributed to Layth which al-Azharī rejected as meaningless.

9. Boundary with the root خطأ — خَطِيَّةٌ is treated as a spelling of خَطِيْئَةٌ ("fault, sin") and referred to that root; Lane notes that Freytag mistakenly assigned it the sense "beloved woman," apparently from a misreading of حَظِيَّةٌ. Similarly the saying نَاقَتُكَ هٰذِهِ مِنَ المُتَخَطِّيَاتِ الجِيَفَ ("this she-camel of yours is one of those that step over carcasses"), reported from al-Azharī, also appears in the form المُتَخَطِّئَاتِ under خطأ.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: kh-b-ʾ (خبأ) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core sense: covering or concealing something (satr al-shayʾ).

1. The verb khabaʾa — "he hid/concealed" a thing (khabaʾtu al-shayʾa akhbaʾuhu khabʾan, "I hid it, hiding").

2. al-khubaʾah (الخُبَأَة) — a young girl/maiden who is kept hidden or concealed (tukhbaʾu, "she is kept out of sight").

3. Under the same root: al-khibāʾ (الخِبَاء), a tent — named from the same idea of concealment, since it screens those inside. Ibn Fāris lists the verbs used for pitching one: akhbaytu, khabbaytu, and takhabbaytu — each meaning "you set up / took a khibāʾ (tent)."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the whole root خ-ب-ط from one core idea: treading and striking.

1. **Basic physical sense.** A camel "خَبَطَ" the ground with its foreleg — it struck it. Likewise one "خَبَطَ" the leaves of a tree by striking the tree so the leaves fall.

2. **Extended to a disease resembling madness — الْخُبَاطُ.** Because the sufferer seems to be buffeted about, as if struck repeatedly. Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 2:275, on the one "whom Satan has confounded by [his] touch" (يَتَخَبَّطُهُ الشَّيْطَانُ مِنَ الْمَسِّ) — the verb يَتَخَبَّطُ here carries the same "being struck/buffeted" image.

3. **خِبْطَةٌ = leftovers** — what remains of food or other things.

4. **الْخِبْطَةُ = scant water**, because it gets stirred and churned about and offers no resistance.

5. **اخْتَبَطَ فُلَانٌ فُلَانًا — "so-and-so came to so-and-so seeking his favor."** Ibn Fāris explains the semantic path: anyone traveling to seek a person's generosity necessarily treads the ground to get there; the expression was then shortened, so a person soliciting a gift is simply called a مُخْتَبِط ("treader").

6. **الْخِبْطَةُ (second sense) = a wide, land-covering rain**, called this — in Ibn Fāris's own usage ("عندنا") — because it "treads" and beats the ground.

7. **الْخَابِطُ reported (via al-Shaybānī, on the authority of others) to mean "the sleeper."** Supporting verse: "they crush at night the treading/coiled serpent" (يَشْدَخْنَ بِاللَّيْلِ الشُّجَاعَ الْخَابِطَا). If accurate, the sleeper is called this because his body strikes/beats the ground as he lies on it.

8. **Alternative for "the treading serpent" (الشُّجَاعُ الْخَابِطُ):** it may instead mean the snake that gets trodden on by passersby, not one that treads. A supporting verse about a bird that kills a small bird by day and preys on a desert viper by night is quoted for this sense.

9. **الْخِبَاطُ = a brand-mark on the camel's/animal's thigh**, so named because the thigh is struck (branded) with it.

Throughout, Ibn Fāris keeps returning every derived sense — disease, leftover food, thin water, solicitation, heavy rain, a sleeper, a snake, a brand — back to the one physical image of treading/striking.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ḵ-b-l — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: corruption or derangement of the bodily limbs/faculties.

1. Madness. al-khabal = insanity. "The jinn ikhtabalahu" = the jinn drove him mad/possessed him. A jinnī who does this is a khābil (pl. khubbal).

2. Physical impairment. al-khabal also names damage to a limb. "Khubilat yaduhu" ("his hand was khabal-ed") is said when a hand was severed and disabled. Illustrated by a verse of the poet Aws, who describes a hand as makhbūlah ("maimed") in its upper arm — i.e., its upper arm is damaged.

3. Figurative burden. "So-and-so is a khabal on his family" means he is a dead weight/toil on them, of no use to them at all.

4. Ḥadīth phrase. "Ṭīnat al-khabāl" ("the mire of khabāl"), found in ḥadīth, is said [by others — Ibn Fāris reports the claim, not as his own assertion] to mean the pus/discharge of the people of the Fire.

5. A separate, irregular sense — Ibn Fāris explicitly flags this as falling outside the root's core meaning: al-ikhbāl. Two explanations are given:
   (a) a man splitting his camel herd in half and breeding/producing from each half in alternating years, the way land is worked in a sharecropping arrangement; or
   (b) lending someone temporary use of an animal — a she-camel to ride, or a horse to go raiding on.
   Cited for this sense is a verse of Zuhayr praising a group's generosity: when asked to lend property (yustakhbalū) they lend it (yukhbilū); when asked for anything they give; and when they play maysir (a gambling game) they pay/bid generously.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: خَبِير 45x "(is) all-aware"; أَخْبَار 3x "your news"; خُبْر 2x "any knowledge"; خَبَر 2x "some information"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root خ-ب-ر from two separate origins: (1) knowledge, and (2) softness, looseness, and abundance.

1. Knowledge. خُبْر (khubr) is knowledge or acquaintance with something: "I have khibra/khubr of so-and-so" (= knowledge of him). The divine name الخَبِير (al-Khabīr) means the one who knows everything. Qurʾanic witness: {none informs you like one who is aware (khabīr)} [Fāṭir 35:14].

2. Softness / looseness / abundance. From this second origin come several senses:
- خَبْرَاء (khabrāʾ): soft ground. Cited from a verse by ʿUbayd describing a horse "firm-footed upon the soft ground (al-khabār)."
- خَبِير (khabīr): the plowman/tiller — so called because he softens and levels the soil. To "khābara" the land is to cultivate it. The forbidden مُخَابَرَة (mukhābara) is sharecropping for a half, third, or other share of the crop (also called khibr). Ibn Fāris notes some hold mukhābara is instead derived from the place-name Khaybar.
- Abundance sense: خَبْر (khabr) = a she-camel of copious milk, and also a large waterskin (plural khubūr).
- Softness sense: خَبِير (khabīr) can mean froth/foam; soft vegetation (with the hadith "we harvest the khabīr [soft herbage]"); and fur/down (with a rājiz verse). A place is خَبِر (khabir) when it is warm/sheltered with plentiful trees and water. Ibn Fāris takes all these as the regular analogy of the root.

Deviant sense: خُبْرَة (khubra) is a sheep a group jointly buys, slaughters, and divides — illustrated by a verse. Ibn Fāris marks this as falling outside the two main origins.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَخْبَتُ 2x "and may humbly submit"; مُخْبِتِين 1x "(to) the humble ones"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives kh-b-t from one core meaning: khushūʿ — humble, lowly submission.

1. The verb: akhbata yukhbitu ikhbātan means "he showed khushūʿ" (became humbly submissive). The phrase "akhbata li-llāhi taʿālā" means he submitted humbly to God. Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'anic word al-mukhbitīn — "those who are humbly submissive" — from the verse "wa bashshiri l-mukhbitīn" (Q22:34), as an instance of this root in use.

2. The etymology: he traces this sense back to al-khabt, a physical term for a flat desert tract with no vegetation growing on it — a bare wasteland.

3. Supporting evidence: he brings a ḥadīth phrase, "wa-law bi-khabti l-jamīsh" ("even if it be in the khabt of al-jamīsh"), and reasons about the word jamīsh itself: that wasteland is called jamīsh, he notes, as if its vegetation had been "shaved" (ḥuliqa) away — reinforcing the image of a bare, stripped-down place as the root sense that the moral meaning of "humble submission" grew out of.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: خَبِيث 9x "the wicked"; خَبِيثَة 4x "evil"; خَبِيثَٰت 2x "evil women"; خَبُثَ 1x "is bad"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-ب-ث (kh-b-th) as a single root meaning the opposite of "good/wholesome" (al-ṭayyib).

1. خَبِيث (khabīth) — "vile, foul; not good." The basic adjective from the root.
2. أَخْبَثُ (akhbath) — the elative form, used of a person whose companions (aṣḥāb) are themselves vile (khubathāʾ).
3. A distinction he draws from the phrase for seeking refuge from al-khabīth al-mukhbith:
   - خَبِيث (khabīth) = one who is vile in his own person.
   - مُخْبِث (mukhbith) = one whose companions and helpers are vile.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root: kh-b-w (خبو). Source: al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān.

1. Core sense — a dying-down fire: khabat al-nāru takhbū means the fire's flame settled/subsided, and a covering (khibāʾ) of ash formed over it — i.e. an ash "veil" or film over the embers.

2. Etymological link — al-Rāghib derives khibāʾ ("tent") from this same idea of covering: its root sense is al-ghiṭāʾ, "the covering one wraps oneself in." By extension, the husk or covering sheath around an ear of grain (sunbula) is also called khibāʾ.

So the semantic thread the author draws is: khabw = a flame settling and becoming veiled/covered (by its own ash) → khibāʾ = any covering, whether a tent, a garment-covering, or a grain-husk.

3. Qur'anic citation: 17:97 — "kullamā khabat zidnāhum saʿīran" ("every time it dies down, We increase them in blazing fire") — cited as the attestation of the verb khabā/takhbū meaning a flame subsiding.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root kh-b-z from a single core meaning: to beat or strike something with the hand.

1. Camels "beating" the saʿdān plant (takhabbazat) — striking it with their forelegs, apparently to break down its thorns before eating it.
2. From that same striking/pounding sense: the baker (khabbāz) "bakes" bread (khubz) — the act of kneading/pounding the dough.
3. A cited (unattributed) rajaz verse instructing two travelers: don't spend time baking bread — pound/mix a quick trail-food (bass, a paste of dates and fat/flour) instead, and don't linger at the resting-place.
4. Also said of a camel: al-khabz is its forelegs striking the ground as it walks — i.e., its pounding gait.

All four senses are presented by Ibn Fāris as expressions of the same base idea: a hand (or a camel's foreleg) striking or pounding something.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يُخَٰدِعُ 2x "they seek to deceive"; يَخْدَعُ 2x "they deceive"; خَٰدِع 1x "who deceives them"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-د-ع as one root with a single governing sense, which he takes from al-Khalīl: **concealing something**. Everything in the chapter, he says, runs on that principle.

1. **Core sense — to hide.** إخداع (ikhdāʿ) is the concealment of a thing. Hence the storage-closet is called المَخْدَع (makhdaʿ), the place where things are put out of sight.

2. **To deceive.** خَدَعْتُ الرجل — "I deceived the man," glossed as ختلته (I tricked / caught him off guard). Cited proverb: «الحرب خُدَعة» ("war is trickery"), also vocalized خُدْعة.

3. **Saliva withdrawing.** خَدَعَ الريقُ في الفم — the saliva "khadaʿa" in the mouth, i.e. it hides in the throat and vanishes. Shāhid (unattributed half-line): طيب الريق إذا الريق خدع ("sweet of mouth when the saliva has gone").

4. **Sleep failing to come.** ما خَدَعَتْ بعينيَّ نَعْسة — "no drowsiness slipped into my eyes," i.e. sleep did not enter them. Shāhid: أرقت فلم تخدع بعينيَّ نعسة / ومن يلق ما لاقيت لا بد يأرق ("I lay awake and no drowsiness stole into my eyes; whoever meets what I have met is bound to lie sleepless").

5. **Anatomical.** الأخدع is a vein in the side of the neck — included because it is hidden. A man called مخدوع is one whose akhdaʿ vein has been cut.

6. **Feigned character.** خُلُق خادع — said of a person who affects a disposition not his own; Ibn Fāris ties it to the root because such a person conceals the opposite of what he shows.

7. **Time/fate.** Some say الخُدَعة denotes al-dahr (time), citing: يا قوم من عاذري من الخدعه ("O my people, who will excuse me from al-khudʿa?"). He classes this as figurative (tamthīl): time is spoken of as though it beguiles and deceives.

8. **The ghoul.** غول خَيْدَع — as though it snatches away and deceives.

9. **Short-weight coin.** He reports, with distance ("some people claimed"), دينار خادع, a dīnār deficient in weight — reasoning that if so, it is because the coin displays completeness and conceals its shortfall until weighing exposes it.

10. **Mirage.** الخَيْدَع is the mirage (sarāb) — and, he closes, the underlying analogy is one and the same.

Method note: Ibn Fāris's procedure throughout is to posit one semantic nucleus (hiddenness) and then show each usage — deception, vanished saliva, absent sleep, a buried vein, a feigned manner, a light coin, a mirage — as an instance of something concealed behind an appearance.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats kh-d as a single root meaning (aṣl wāḥid), which he defines as a thing's long, tapering shape and its extending downward.

1. **Cheek.** The khadd is a person's cheek, and the pillow (mikhadda) is named after it.

2. **Cleft.** Khadd also means a split or cleft; the akhādīd are the clefts in the ground.

3. **Wasting flesh.** Takhaddud is the furrowing of the flesh through emaciation; a woman described as mutakhaddida is emaciated.

4. **A brand.** Khidād is one kind of brand-mark. Ibn Fāris suggests, without certainty, that it may be placed on the cheek. A camel bearing it is called makhdūd.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: kh-d-n — Ibn Faris, Maqayis al-Lugha

Core meaning: companionship. Ibn Faris treats this as a single, unified root meaning, and everything below is a variation on "keeping company / being a companion."

1. al-khidn — "the companion" or "friend." This is the base noun.

2. khadantu al-rajula mukhadanatan — "I kept company with / befriended the man." The Form III verb khadana implies a mutual, reciprocal act of companionship, i.e. two people becoming each other's khidn.

3. khidn al-jariyah — "the young woman's confidant," specifically glossed as "the one who converses with her." So khidn here carries a nuance of a close talking-companion, not merely an acquaintance.

4. Citation from Abu Zayd: khadantu al-rajula equals sadaqtuhu, "I befriended him" / "I made him my friend," confirming khadana as synonymous with forming a bond of friendship.

5. rajulun khudanah — "a man of many companions," i.e. someone who has an abundance of akhdan (the plural of khidn). Ibn Faris notes this as a derived adjectival form built on the same root, marking a person characterized by having many such companions/friends.

No further senses, citations, or shawahid are given; the entry is short and entirely built around this one idea of companionship.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib's entry on the root خ-ف-ض (kh-f-ḍ), "lowering":

1. Core sense: khafḍ is the opposite of rafʿ ("raising, lifting up") — to bring or put something down.

2. Extended sense: it also denotes ease and a settled, untroubled life (daʿa), and a gentle, unhurried manner of travelling or moving.

3. Applied to conduct — "and lower to them the wing of humility" (Q 17:24, of one's parents): al-Rāghib reads this as urging softness of manner and yielding compliance. He sets it as the opposite of "that you not exalt yourselves over me" (Q 27:31), so the image works by contrast with self-elevation.

4. Applied to the Resurrection — "lowering, raising" (Q 56:3): the event puts one group down and lifts another up. He connects the "lowering" element to "then We returned him to the lowest of the low" (Q 95:5).

Method note: al-Rāghib fixes the sense by antonym (khafḍ vs. rafʿ, humility vs. self-exaltation) and then explains Qur'anic usages by cross-reference to other verses rather than by external citations.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: خَفَّفَ 8x "will be lightened"; خَفَّتْ 3x "(are) light"; ٱسْتَخَفَّ 3x "so he bluffed"; خَفِيف 2x "light"; تَخْفِيف 1x "a concession"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats kh-f-f as one root meaning: something contrary to heaviness and gravity.

1. **Being light.** Khaffa, yakhiffu, khiffatan: the thing became light; it is khafīf or khufāf.

2. **Akhaffa.** Said of a man whose circumstances have become light (meager), and of a man whose mount is light and quick.

3. **Moving off.** Khaffa al-qawm: the people set off.

4. **The khuff.** The boot belongs to the root because the walker is light on his feet while wearing it; the camel's foot-pad (khuff al-baʿīr) is also from it. The khuff "in the ground", a stretch longer than a naʿl, is so named by resemblance.

5. **Al-khiff.** Simply "the light one", as in the verse: "The light youth slips from its saddle-places, and it whips away the garments of the rough, heavy rider."

6. **Khafkhafa.** The sounds of dogs are called al-khafkhafa, which Ibn Fāris counts as close to the root.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: kh-f-t (khafata), from Ibn Faris's Maqayis al-Lugha.

Ibn Faris gives this root a single core meaning: lowering the voice and speaking in concealment - i.e., quiet, inaudible, or subdued speech.

1. Al-khaft = the lowering/quieting of speech - speaking so softly it can barely be heard.

2. The verb form takhafata ("they spoke in lowered voices to each other") is used of two people conversing quietly between themselves - e.g. takhafata al-rajulan, "the two men murmured to one another."

3. Qur'anic citation: yatakhafatuna baynahum - "they speak quietly among themselves" (Ta Ha 20:103) - cited as an instance of this same sense.

4. A supporting line of poetry contrasts loud speech (jahr) with khaft-speech: the poet says he addresses [someone] openly/aloud while the others around him only murmur in lowered voices, remarking on how different loud speech is from the faint, lowered kind (al-mantiq al-khaft).

So, per this entry, the root's whole semantic field is: quietness/inaudibility of the voice and the concealment that goes with speaking that way - not a technical or later devotional term, just ordinary "speaking softly/secretly."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)

text:
Ibn Fāris treats خفي (kh-f-y) as two distinct and directly opposite roots: one meaning "to conceal," the other "to make apparent."

Sense 1 — Concealment (al-satr):
- خَفِيَ الشَّيْءُ ("the thing became hidden"); أَخْفَيْتُهُ ("I hid it"). Something is فِي خِفْيَةٍ / خَفَاءٍ ("in concealment/secrecy") when hidden.
- The idiom بَرِحَ الْخَفَاءُ ("the concealment has departed") means: the secret has become plain and come out.
- Derived nouns: الْخَوَافِي (al-khawāfī) = the feathers lying below a bird's ten front (primary) wing-feathers; also the palm-fronds nearest the heart of the palm. الْخَافِي (al-khāfī) = the jinn. A man in hiding is مُسْتَخْفٍ.

Sense 2 — Making apparent / bringing out (al-iẓhār):
- خَفَا الْبَرْقُ ("the lightning gleamed") — used of a faint flash, at the lowest degree of intensity.
- خَفَيْتُ الشَّيْءَ, spelled without an alif, means "I made the thing apparent / brought it out" (contrast the alif-form أَخْفَيْتُ = "I hid").
- خَفَا الْمَطَرُ الْفَأْرَ ("the rain drove the mice out of their burrows"). Ibn Fāris cites Imruʾ al-Qays: the flood "drove them out from their burrows as though a downpour from banked cloud had driven them out."
- On this second sense, Ibn Fāris notes, the Qurʾānic أُخْفِيهَا in {إِنَّ السَّاعَةَ آتِيَةٌ أَكَادُ أُخْفِيهَا} (Ṭā Hā 20:15) is read as meaning "I make it manifest / bring it out," rather than "I hide it."

text:
Ibn Fāris states that kh-l-ʿ is a single, consistent root whose core meaning is the separation or removal of a thing from what had enveloped it or from what it had been invested with.

1. **Taking off / removing.** The base sense: khalaʿtu al-thawb, "I took off the garment." By extension, khuliʿa al-wālī, "the governor was deposed" — but Ibn Fāris notes this deposing-sense is only used when an inferior removes a superior; a ruler removing his own subordinate governor is instead called ʿazalahu ("he dismissed him"), not khalaʿahu.

2. **Wife-initiated separation (khulʿ).** A man divorcing his wife is ṭallaqa. But when the separation is initiated by the wife, it is called khālaʿathu / ikhtalaʿat — because she "ransoms" herself from the marriage by giving something up to him. He cites a ḥadīth condemning women who seek this kind of separation without cause ("al-mukhtaliʿāt hunna al-munāfiqāt" — such women are "the hypocrites"), explained as those who part from their husbands even though the husbands did them no wrong.

3. **Ripening dates and grain.** Al-khāliʿ is a date (busr) that has ripened and sheds its skin from its own moisture, compared to fasaqat al-ruṭaba (the ripe date "bursting out" of its skin). Similarly khalaʿa al-sunbul describes an ear of grain putting out its awn, as if shedding it outward.

4. **Al-khalīʿ — the disowned/outcast man.** One whose family has cast him off: they bear no liability if he commits a crime, and they seek no redress if a crime is committed against him. Ibn Fāris quotes a line of poetry comparing a howling wolf in a desolate valley to "the disowned outcast (al-khalīʿ) burdened with dependents."

5. **Al-khalīʿ — other senses.** The same word is also used for "the wolf" (with the intensifying phrase "he was cast off — what a casting-off!") and, it is said, for "the hunter."

6. **Swaying gait / limbs coming apart.** Yatakhallaʿu fī mishyatihi describes someone swaying as he walks, as if his limbs were about to come apart.

7. **Al-khāliʿ — a camel ailment.** A disease in which a camel, once it kneels, cannot rise again — as if its limbs had come apart and it collapsed to the ground.

8. **Al-khawlaʿ — a seizure of terror.** A fright that grips the heart like demonic touch; Ibn Fāris says this fits the root's underlying logic, as though the heart itself had been "unseated" (khuliʿa).

9. **Mutual renunciation of a pact.** Taxhālaʿa al-qawm — "the people renounced [their alliance] with one another" — used when a group annuls a pact (ḥilf) that had bound them.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-ل-ص (kh-l-ṣ) as a single, regular root with one core meaning: the purifying and refining of a thing.

1. Core sense — cleansing/refining something so it becomes pure or clear. Transitive: خَلَّصْتُهُ مِنْ كَذَا ("I freed/purified it from such-and-such"); intransitive: خَلَصَ ("it became pure/clear/free").

2. Illustrative usage — خُلَاصَة السَّمْن (khulāṣat al-samn), the clarified portion of cooking-fat: dates or sawīq (parched-barley meal) are thrown into the fat so that, by this process, it is purified/clarified.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-ل-ط (kh-l-ṭ) as a single root with one core idea, which he presents as the opposite of the root discussed in the immediately preceding entry.

1. Core sense — mixing, intermingling. خلطتُ الشيءَ بغيره فاختلط: "I mixed one thing with another, and it became mixed."

2. Applied to a person — مِخْلَط (mikhlaṭ): a man who is good at getting involved in affairs, at entering into them. Its counterpart is مِزْيَل (mizyal), one who separates things out. Ibn Fāris cites Aws: asked for advice by his cousin, the speaker is found to be "mikhlaṭ of the affair and mizyal" — able both to enter into a matter and to untangle it.

3. خَلِيط (khalīṭ): a neighbour, one who lives intermingled with another.

4. خِلْط (khilṭ): an arrow whose wood grew crooked, and which keeps reverting to crookedness even after being straightened. Ibn Fāris explicitly ties this back to the root's core idea: such an arrow does not mix in, does not fall in with, straightness.

5. استخلط البعير (istakhlaṭa al-baʿīr): said of a camel that cannot manage to mount the she-camel and does not find its way to it, so it is assisted to couple and dealt with gently.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives خ-ل-د from a single core sense: permanence and constant attachment/adherence.

1. To stay or remain. خَلَدَ (and أَخْلَدَ) = he stayed, remained, endured. From this comes جَنَّةُ الْخُلْد, "the Garden of eternal abiding." Cited: a line of Ibn Aḥmar contrasting the beloved's endurance with the ruined, now-desolate dwelling.

2. Slow to age. A man is called مُخْلَد or مُخْلِد when grey hair / old age is slow to reach him. Ibn Fāris fits this to the root: youth has stayed constantly with him, and he with youth.

3. To cling to the earth. أَخْلَدَ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ = he stuck fast / cleaved to the ground. Qurʾānic citation: al-Aʿrāf 7:176, "but he clung to the earth."

4. مُخَلَّدُونَ in al-Insān 76:19 ("youths مُخَلَّدُونَ circulating among them") — two readings the author records:
   - from الْخُلْد = permanence/continued existence: i.e., they do not die (immortal youths).
   - from الْخِلَد, plural of خِلَدَة meaning an earring: i.e., "adorned with earrings / ear-pendants." A cited verse describes women decked in silver. Ibn Fāris judges this analogy sound, since an earring stays constantly attached to the ear — matching the root's core sense of adherence.

5. الْخَلَد = the mind or inmost thought (al-bāl), so named because it is settled and fixed within the heart.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives خ-ل-ف from three fundamental senses: (1) one thing coming after another and taking its place; (2) "behind," the opposite of "in front"; (3) change or alteration.

FIRST SENSE — succession / coming after.
- al-khalaf: what comes afterward, a successor. One says "he is a good successor (khalaf ṣidq) of his father" or "a bad successor (khalaf sawʾ)." Without qualification, the good successor is khalaf (with fatḥa), the defective one khalf (with sukūn). Cited: Q 7:169, "then there succeeded after them a successor-generation (khalf)."
- al-khilāfa (succession, the successor's office; also al-khillīfā): so called because the second comes after the first and stands in his place. Likewise "I sat khilāfa so-and-so" = after him.
- al-khawālif in Q 9:87 ("content to be with al-khawālif") = the women, because the men are away at war, raiding, and trade while the women remain behind (yakhlufna) in the homes. Hence al-ḥayy khulūf: an encampment whose men are absent and women stay.
- Supplications: "khalafa-llāhu ʿalayk" = may God be successor/guardian over you in place of a lost father or loved one; "akhlafa-llāhu lak" = may He compensate you, for what is gone, with a replacement.
- al-khilfa: regrowth after withered growth; khilfat al-shajar: a second crop of fruit. A shāhid on aftergrowth (al-Māṭirūn / Jillaq) and a line of Zuhayr in which wild cows and antelopes "walk in alternation (khilfa)," one succeeding another, are cited to confirm the sense.
- al-khalf: drawing water, because the two drawers alternate, each after the other; akhlafa = to draw water (with a supporting verse).

SECOND SENSE — "behind" (opposite of qudddām/in front).
- "This is behind me (khalfī)" vs. "this is in front of me (qudāmī)"; a line of Labīd on danger "behind her and before her" is cited.
- al-khilf: a single teat of the udder's teats (akhlāf), so named because it sits behind what comes after it.

THIRD SENSE — change / alteration.
- khalafa fūhu / akhlafa: his breath changed (turned bad). Cited: the Prophetic saying that the fasting person's changed mouth-odor (khulūf) is more fragrant to God than musk.
- A line of Ibn Aḥmar: youth gone, "life has changed (akhlafa)," friends and time turned strange.
- al-khilāf in a promise = breaking/failing it; "the man khalafa from his father's character" = deviated. "He promised me and I found he had broken faith (akhlafanī)"; a line of al-Aʿshā on a broken tryst.
- al-khalīf: a garment whose worn-out middle is cut out and patched (khalaftu al-thawb) — an analogy Ibn Fāris links to both this sense and the first. "My two buckets are khilfān" also fits, since one alternates with the other.

DISPOSITION OF HARDER CASES.
- "People differed (ikhtalafa)" / "people are khilfa (at variance)" → assigned to the FIRST sense: each sets aside another's view and puts himself in its place.
- khalifa for a pregnant she-camel → possibly an anomaly, or loosely traced to sense one (she brings a young one, and offspring is a khalaf), which Ibn Fāris judges far-fetched; its plural is al-makhāḍ (the pregnant camels).
- Outside all three roots: al-khalīf = a mountain pass/road between two peaks.
- al-khālifa (a tent-pole) → probably at the tent's rear, so belongs to the "behind" sense; hence "so-and-so is the khālifa of his household" = not put forward among them.
- al-baʿīr al-akhlaf (a camel that walks lopsidedly to one side, from disease) → belongs to the sense of change/corruption.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats kh-l-l as a single root (aṣl wāḥid) with closely related branches, all of which, he says, go back either to **thinness** (diqqa) or to a **gap** (furja).

**A. Thinness and slenderness**

1. **Pin, toothpick.** Al-khilāl (plural akhilla) is a pin or toothpick. "He eats his khilal / khulāla" means he eats what the toothpick brings out from his teeth.

2. **Pinning a cloak.** Al-khall is fastening your cloak on yourself with a pin.

3. **Intimate friend.** Ibn Fāris places al-khalīl, the one who is your close friend (yukhālluka), under this sense: it is as if two friends had become interlaced, like a pinned cloak.

4. **Lean.** A rajul khall is a man thin of body. Two verses illustrate it: "if you see my body lean (khall), grown thin", and "my body, after my maternal uncle, is lean".

5. **Young camel.** An ibn al-makhāḍ (young camel in its second year) is called khall because its body is slender.

6. **Sand track.** Al-khall is a road through sand, because it is narrow.

7. **Unripe dates.** Al-khalāl, unripe dates (balaḥ), also comes from this.

8. **Bow-thongs.** The khilal that are leather thongs fitted over the backs of a bow's two tips are so named for their thinness, each being like a khilla (scabbard).

9. **Anklet.** Al-khalkhāl belongs here too, because it is slender.

**B. Gap**

1. **Gap.** Al-khalal is the space between two things. Khallala al-shayʾa is said of something that did not cover the whole.

2. **Poverty.** Al-khalla is poverty, as a gap in a person's circumstances. Al-khalīl is the poor man, as in the verse: "if a khalīl comes to him on a day of hunger, he says: my wealth is neither absent nor forbidden".

**C. Listed without a stated link to either sense**

1. **Scabbard.** Al-khilla is a sword's scabbard, plural khilal.

2. **Neck vein.** Al-khall is a vein in the neck connected to the head.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives خ-ل-ق (kh-l-q) from two base senses: (1) proportioning/measuring out a thing, and (2) smoothness of a thing.

FIRST BASE — measuring, proportioning to size:
1. Core usage: خَلَقْتُ الْأَدِيمَ لِلسِّقَاءِ = "I cut the hide to measure for a waterskin," i.e. sized it to proportion. He cites a verse about "the [female] shapers/measurers" whose cutting brought no shame, and Zuhayr's line contrasting one who "cuts out what he has measured" with people who "measure and then do not cut" — measuring vs. carrying it through.
2. خُلُق (khuluq) = inborn disposition or temperament (السجية), so called because its possessor has been "proportioned"/determined upon it.
3. Derived forms of aptness: فلان خليق بكذا = "apt/fit for such," and أخلق به / ما أخلقه = "how fitting he is" — i.e. someone in whom the trait is judged likely.
4. الخَلَاق (al-khalāq) = one's allotted share or portion, because each person's share has been apportioned to him.
5. رجل مختلق = a man of complete, well-formed build (تام الخلق).
6. خُلُق الكذب = the "fashioning" of a lie: its fabrication, invention, and composing in the mind (ikhtilāq, ikhtirāʿ, taqdīr fī al-nafs). Ibn Fāris cites Q 29:17, وَتَخْلُقُونَ إِفْكًا ("you fabricate falsehood"), under this sense of contriving.

SECOND BASE — smoothness:
1. صخرة خلقاء = a smooth rock; supported by a verse in which Time wears a rift into a firm smooth crag and dislodges the ibex from it.
2. اخلولق السحاب = the clouds leveled out / became even; رسم مخلولق = a trace worn level with the ground.
3. المُخَلَّق = a trued, dressed arrow — named so because it is made smooth.
4. Wearing out: أخلق الشيء / خلُق = a thing became worn out; أخلقته = I wore it out. The link to smoothness: a worn object loses its nap/fuzz (زئبر) and turns smooth. Hence ثوب خَلَق / ملحفة خَلَق = a worn-out garment or wrap (one form for masculine and feminine).
5. المُختلَق of anything = what is well-proportioned/even (ما اعتدل); cited from Ruʾba (an even cane-brake).
6. الخَلُوق (also الخِلَاق) = a known perfume/unguent, tied here to smoothness: a thing anointed with it becomes smooth.
7. الخُلَيْقاء in a horse corresponds to the bridge of the nose (العِرنين) in a human.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives خ-ل-و from a single core idea: a thing being emptied or stripped of another thing.

1. Core sense — being empty/free of something. خِلْوٌ مِنْ كَذَا = free/devoid of a thing; خَلَتِ الدَّارُ = the house became empty (imperfect takhlū).

2. Free of care. الْخَلِيُّ (al-khalī) = one free of grief.

3. Applied to divorce. امْرَأَةٌ خَلِيَّةٌ, a euphemism for a divorced woman, because once divorced she is "emptied of" her husband.

4. Clear/available for someone. خَلَا لِيَ الشَّيْءُ / أَخْلَى = the thing became free for me — with a poetic citation ("... or has death been left to us alone?").

5. The adopting she-camel. الْخَلِيَّةُ = a she-camel made to nurse a young one not her own, as though emptied of her original offspring.

6. Past time. الْقُرُونُ الْخَالِيَةُ = the bygone generations.

7. Empty place. الْمَكَانُ الْخَلَاءُ = a place with nothing in it.

8. Exceptive particle. خَلَا in مَا فِي الدَّارِ أَحَدٌ خَلَا زَيْدٍ ("no one except Zayd," Zayd in genitive or accusative) = "leave off mentioning Zayd." Likewise وَخَلَاكَ ذَمٌّ = "blame is removed / has passed you by."

Anomalous senses Ibn Fāris flags as outside the core:
- الْخَلِيَّةُ = a ship; also a beehive.
- الْخَلَا = fresh grass. He notes some say الْخَلْيُ means "to cut" (a sword يَخْتَلِي = severs), so grass may be named khalā because it is mowed.
- The word خَلَاة for something left without a guardian (هُوَ خَلَاةٌ لِكَذَا = coveted, with no protector) — which he assigns back to the original "empty of" sense.
- خَلَا بِهِ used to mean "he mocked him."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha, root خ-م-ص (kh-m-ṣ)

Core meaning: leanness/hollowness and being sunken-in.

1. khamīṣ — lean/hollow-bellied; the noun form is khamṣ.
2. khumṣāna — a woman slender/fine at the waist.
3. al-akhmaṣ — the hollow of the sole of the foot.

Ibn Fāris treats these three as one coherent group, since "leanness/hollowness" runs through all of them and fits the root's basic pattern.

4. al-makhmaṣa = hunger, famine — because a hungry person's belly is hollow/lean. A hungry man is called khamīṣ, a hungry woman khamīṣa.
   Citation (al-A'shā): people feast through winter nights while their neighbor-women go hungry (khamā'iṣ) at night.

5. A separate sense: al-khamīṣa = a black woolen cloak. Al-A'shā uses the same word figuratively for a woman's dark hair, set against the "fresh, glistening red" of her complexion.

Ibn Fāris then tackles the obvious problem himself: how does "black cloak" connect to the root's core sense of leanness? His answer is explicitly tentative ("as a matter of possibility, not certainty"): the cloak may be called khamīṣa because a person wraps it around himself at his akhmaṣ — here reinterpreted to mean the waist/middle of the body rather than the sole of the foot. He hedges openly: if this derivation holds, well and good; if not, the word should simply be counted as an exception that falls outside the root's core meaning.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) identifies two separate underlying senses for the root kh-m-ṭ.

Sense 1 — Stripping / smoothing: Khamaṭtu al-shāh means to strip the skin off a ewe and roast it. This is distinguished from al-samṭ, which means removing only the hair or wool (e.g. by singeing) while leaving the skin on. Ibn Fāris traces this sense back to al-khamṭ, a word he defines as "anything that has no thorns."

Sense 2 — Domination / raging: Takhammaṭa al-faḥl describes a stud-camel becoming aroused and bellowing. He derives this in turn from takhammaṭa al-baḥr, said of the sea when it surges and its waves crash violently together.

text:
Ibn Fāris derives خمد (kh-m-d) from a single core sense: **motion coming to a standstill; a subsiding/falling still**.

He gives three attested uses:

1. **Fire** — خَمَدَتِ النَّارُ خُمُودًا: the fire "khamadat" (subsided) when its flame died down and stopped moving.
2. **Fever** — خَمَدَتِ الْحُمَّى: the fever "khamadat" (subsided) when its heat/intensity stilled.
3. **A fainted person** — one who has lost consciousness is described as خَمَدَ ("khamada"): he has gone still/subsided.

All three uses share the same image: an active force (flame, heat, consciousness) losing its motion and settling into stillness. No shawāhid (poetic or Qurʾanic citations) are given in this entry.
