text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-م-ر (kh-m-r) as one single root meaning covering, and mingling under a cover. Everything in the entry is then derived from that one idea, with one stated exception at the end.

1. خَمْر (khamr) — the well-known drink. Quoting al-Khalīl: its اختمار (ikhtimār) is its ripening and bubbling; مُخَمِّر (mukhammir) is the one who produces it; خُمْرَة / خُمَار (khumra / khumār) is the fume that overcomes the drinker and settles on his heart. A verse is cited: a wine whose fume "struck his vital spots," so that the fumes barely cleared from his heart. Also بِهِ خُمَارٌ شَدِيدٌ — "he has a severe after-fume."

2. Crowd as cover — دخل في خَمَار الناس / خَمَرِهم: he entered the throng of people, i.e. the press in which a person is lost from sight.

3. Cover for ambush — "So-and-so creeps up on So-and-so through the khamar" is a euphemism for killing by stealth. The literal base is whatever screens a person from view, such as trees. Abū Dhuʾayb's line describes men caught unawares, "like the birds of the covert." Related: قد أخمروا, said of people who have hidden themselves in the cover of trees.

4. خِمَار (khimār) — a woman's head-covering; خِمْرَة is the manner of wearing it (a woman "good in her khimra"). Proverb: "the matron is not taught how to wear the head-covering," i.e. the experienced need no instruction.

5. تخمير (takhmīr) — covering something over.

6. Proverb "he has neither vinegar nor wine" — used to mean he has neither good nor evil in him.

7. خامر المكانَ (Abū Zayd) — to stick to a place and not leave it.

8. مُخَمَّرَة of sheep — a ewe whose head is white while the body is not. Ibn Fāris notes this follows the root's logic, since the white on the head resembles a woman's khimār.

9. Dough — خَمَّرْتُ العجين: to leave dough unused until it improves (leavens); likewise اختمر العجين. The same verb serves perfume: اختمر الطيب, of scent maturing.

10. Disease — خامره الداءُ: the illness mingles with his insides. Kuthayyir's line uses "no mingling disease" of what ʿAzza has taken of the speaker's honour.

11. مُسْتَخْمَر — reported by al-Khalīl as meaning "partner/associate" in the speech of Ḥimyar.

12. خَمَر (khamar) as terrain — a hollow in which a wolf or similar hides; a cited verse tells two travellers they have passed "the covert of the road."

13. Scent — خُمْرَة / خَمَرَة: "I found a pleasant khumra from it," meaning the smell.

14. مُخَامَرَة — drawing close. The proverb "خامري أم عامر" (keep close, O Umm ʿĀmir) is addressed to the hyena; al-Shanfarā's lines refuse burial and consign the body to her instead.

15. خُمْرَة — (a) a scented preparation a woman applies to her face to improve her complexion; (b) a small prayer-mat, cited from a ḥadīth that he used to prostrate on the khumra.

16. Exception — Ibn Fāris marks الاستخمار (istikhmār), "to enslave," as deviating from this root: استخمرت فلانًا = I enslaved him, citing the ḥadīth of Muʿādh, "whoever istakhmara a people," glossed as enslaving them.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: خَمْسَة 3x "with five"; خَٰمِسَة 2x "and the fifth"; خَمْسِين 2x "(is) fifty"; خُمُس 1x "(is) one fifth of it"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-م-س as one root whose single origin lies in the domain of number.

1. **The number five.** خَمْسَة (five) is well known; الخُمْس is one part out of five, a fifth.

2. **Verb — to take a fifth.** خَمَسْتُ القوم means "I took a fifth of the people's property."

3. **Verb — to be the fifth.** خَمَسْتُهم also means "I was the fifth of them."

4. **الخِمْس — a camel watering-interval.** One of the fixed spans of thirst between waterings. Ibn Fāris cites al-Khalīl: it is the camels' drinking on the fourth day counted from the day they left the water, because the day of departure is itself counted in.

5. **الخَمِيس — the fifth day of the week (Thursday).** Plural أَخْمِسَاء and أَخْمِسَة, on the pattern of نَصِيب → أَنْصِبَاء / أَنْصِبَة.

6. **الخُمَاسِيّ / الخُمَاسِيَّة — a young servant boy or girl five spans tall.** Ibn Fāris notes a usage restriction: one does not say سُدَاسِيّ or سُبَاعِيّ of a person who reaches six or seven spans. Outside this use, خُمَاسِيّ simply means "reaching five," and likewise سُدَاسِيّ (six) and عُشَارِيّ (ten).

7. **الخَمِيس / المَخْمُوس — a cloth five cubits long.** Attested in a line of ʿUbayd describing a spear "upon a pliant makhmūs shaft," i.e. a shaft five cubits in length. Ibn Fāris also quotes Muʿādh telling the people of Yemen to bring "a khamīs or a labīs" garment to be taken from them as ṣadaqah.
   - An alternative etymology he reports for this garment-sense: it was named after a Yemeni king called al-Khims, the first to make it — supported by a line of al-Aʿshā contrasting a thing that looks "like the cloaks of al-Khims" one day and spoiled hide the next.

8. **The outlier.** Ibn Fāris marks one sense as deviating from the numerical root: الخَمِيس meaning a large army. He cites the report that when the Prophet came in sight of Khaybar the people called out "Muḥammad — and the khamīs!", meaning the army.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: مُنْخَنِقَة 1x "and that which is strangled (to death)"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the whole root Kh-N-Q from one core idea: narrowness / constriction (ḍīq). He gives four attested senses built on that idea:

1. **al-khāniq** — a narrow mountain pass or ravine (a physically constricted defile).
2. **khāniq** (Yemeni usage, per some scholars) — also used by the people of Yemen for a narrow lane or alley — the same "tight passage" image applied to a street.
3. **khanaq** (masdar/verbal noun of khanaqa – yakhniqu) — "to strangle/throttle" someone: constricting the throat. He notes a grammatical point some scholars made: the correct verbal noun is khanaqan, not khanqan.
4. **al-mikhnaqa** — a necklace or collar, i.e. something worn tightly around the neck — again the same root sense of constriction, applied to an ornament.

All four senses trace back to the one idea of tightness/narrowness, whether of a passage, a throat, or a neck-worn object.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: خُنَّس 1x "by the retreating planets"; خَنَّاس 1x "the one who withdraws"
text:
Root خ ن س (kh-n-s), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: concealment, hiding oneself away.

1. al-khans — going away secretly; khanistu ʿanhu — I withdrew from him [secretly]; akhnastu ʿanhu ḥaqqahu — I withheld his due from him.
2. al-khunnas — the stars that "withdraw" as they set; some say they're named this because they are hidden by day and appear by night.
3. al-khannās — an epithet of Satan, so named because he withdraws/retreats whenever God is mentioned.
4. al-khanas in the nose — a sinking or lowering of the nasal bridge; Ibn Fāris notes all cattle share this feature, extending the root's core sense (retreating/receding) to a physical trait.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: unnamed verse; al-Jaʿdī (disputed date); Al-Rāʿī (Umayyad); Labīd (lived into Islam); al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Manẓūr's entry for the root خ-ن-ز-ر (kh-n-z-r) in Lisān al-ʿArab.

1. Basic sense — thickness/coarseness. الخَنْزَرَة (al-khanzara) means "thickness, coarseness." By extension the same word names a heavy, thick-bladed axe.

2. Place-names. خَنْزَرَة (Khanzara) and الخَنْزَر (al-Khanzar) are two places; Sībawayh quoted two rajaz couplets about the wild asses "of Khanzara" / that "grazed al-Khanzar" as evidence (both verses are obscene in their imagery). دارَة خَنْزَر (Dārat Khanzar) is a nearby place, on Kurāʿ's authority, and al-Jaʿdī's line about a night-phantom of Umayma places his companions "at Dārat Khanzar." Al-Rāʿī also used the name, though Ibn Manẓūr's text at that point is defective and the editor flags it. Separately, خِنْزِير (Khinzīr) is a place-name too, listed by Labīd among al-Ghurābāt, Zarrāfāt and Ḥubal, and by al-Aʿshā in a rain description where floodwater runs from the mountain-foot through Khinzīr until plain and mountain surge.

3. To look sidelong. Some authorities give the verb خَنْزَرَ (khanzara) as "he looked from the corner of his eye." They analyse it morphologically as the pattern فَنْعَلَ (fanʿala) built on الأَخْزَر (al-akhzar, "narrow- or squint-eyed") — i.e. the n is an infix, not a radical. In the same connection the entry records that any مُومِسة (prostitute) is called akhzar.

4. A synonym for "pig." Abū ʿAmr records الخَنْزُوان (al-khanzuwān, vocalised khanzuwān or khunzuwān) as meaning خِنْزِير (pig), listed among a set of similarly shaped words (haylumān, naydulān, kaydhubān).

5. As a personal name. Ibn Sīda notes خَنْزَر (Khanzar) as a man's name: he was al-Ḥalāl, cousin of the poet al-Rāʿī; the two traded lampoons, and al-Rāʿī is said to have coined the nickname. خِنْزِير (Khinzīr) is likewise given as the name of a son of Aslam b. Hunāʾa al-Asadī, which Ibn Sīda reports only tentatively ("so far as I think").

6. The animal, and a dispute over its root. الخِنْزِير (al-khinzīr) — the pig, counted among aggressive wild beasts — is well known and, on the account above, derived from this material. Kurāʿ, however, derives it from الخَزَر (al-khazar), narrowness of the eye, since that is a permanent feature of the animal; on his analysis the word is triliteral (kh-z-r) rather than quadriliteral, and Ibn Manẓūr notes he has already treated it under خزر. The denominal verb خَنْزَرَ (khanzara) then means "to behave as a pig behaves."

7. Medical sense. الخَنازير (al-khanāzīr) is a known ailment: hard ulcers/swellings arising in the neck.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-ر-ص as several origins that, in his judgement, are very sharply distinct from one another.

1. Estimating by conjecture — al-kharṣ. To khaṛaṣa the palm-trees is to appraise by guesswork how much fruit they will bear. Ibn Fāris derives al-kharrāṣ, "the liar," from this sense: such a person says what he does not know and cannot establish as true.

2. A gold ring — khurṣ. Listed as a separate origin, with no further comment.

3. Anything forming a prong or branch of a branching thing. Under this origin:
   - al-kharīṣ of the sea: an inlet branching off from it.
   - al-kharṣ: any rod or shoot of a tree; plural khirṣān. A verse is cited comparing broken spear-shafts strewn on the ground to split rods measured out by the hands of women who pare palm-leaves.
   - By extension of the same origin, the spear itself is called al-kharṣ; a second line is cited on the straightening-tool "biting" the Khaṭṭī spear-shafts.
   - al-akhrāṣ: the sticks carried by a honey-gatherer.

4. Hunger together with cold — al-kharaṣ, the description of one who is hungry and suffering from cold; verb khariṣa, verbal noun kharṣan.

The method is Ibn Fāris's standard one: identify the distinct semantic origins under a root, place each derived word under the origin it belongs to, and mark the cases — here the majority — where those origins do not reduce to a single idea.

dictionary: ʿAyn — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786)
text:
Root kh-r-ṭ-m (خرطم) — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad al-Farāhīdī (d. 786 CE)

1. **Khurṭūm** = the nose.

2. **Khurṭūm** (second sense) = the whole muzzle area — where the front of the two jaws and the nose join together as one unit (not just the nostrils, the full snout-like front).

3. **Khurṭūm** (third sense) = a name for a kind of wine that intoxicates quickly.

4. **Kharāṭīm al-qawm** ("the kharāṭīm of a people") = their chiefs, the men who lead in affairs. A verse is quoted: "from us come the kharāṭīm, and a tough head" — explained as meaning someone hard/severe in handling matters. The ʿAyn traces the usage to the idea of being "turning of heart" — i.e. resourceful, cunning, able to change tack.

5. Verb **kharṭamtuhu kharṭamatan** = "I struck him on the khurṭūm (nose)," or "I grabbed his khurṭūm and twisted it."

6. Verb **ikhranṭama**, said of an angry man = his khurṭūm (nose) went crooked and he fell silent in his anger — i.e. he sulked, nose turned up, saying nothing. A verse is quoted showing a woman doing this (ikhranṭamat), then speaking through tears — but the quoted line breaks off mid-sentence in the source text as transmitted here.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root kh-r-b (خ ر ب) from a core sense of "a breach or notch" combined with "a piercing/perforation."

1. **Hole/perforation** — al-khurbah (خُرْبَة) is simply a hole (al-thuqbah). An akhrab slave (العبد الأخرب) is one whose ear is pierced. Al-khurb (الخُرْب) is the socket/hole of the hip joint. In a related sense, al-khurbah is also the loop or handle (ʿurwah) on a large leather water-skin (mazādah) — presumably named for the perforation through which it is fastened.

2. **Ruin (the primary sense)** — Ibn Fāris identifies al-kharāb (الخراب), "ruin, desolation," as the root meaning (al-aṣl) — the direct opposite of al-ʿimārah, "habitation/cultivation." He links this back to the breach/perforation sense: something ruined is something breached or broken open.

3. **Sand-dune sense** — al-khurb also names the point where the main body (jumhūr) of a stretch of sand comes to an end — again, a "break" in the terrain.

4. **Al-khārib = camel-thief** — the active-participle form al-khārib is used specifically for a thief of camels. Ibn Fāris says this fits the underlying logic (qiyās) of the root, since theft itself is "inflicting a breach" (thulmah) on someone's property.

5. **Anomalous branch: the bustard** — al-kharab (الخرب) is flagged as outside the root's core pattern (shādhdh); it names the male of the ḥubārā bird (the houbara bustard), plural khirbān.

6. **Place-name** — Akhrub (أَخرُب) is cited as a toponym, supported by an anonymous line of verse describing hunters ranging "between Thuʿālah ... and Ruḥayyāt, to the pass of Akhrub" while chasing wild game.

dictionary: ʿAyn — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786)
text:
Root kh-r-d-l (خردل) — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786 CE)

1. Khurdūlah — a full, generous limb-portion of meat: a cut that keeps a whole joint intact, not a thin slice.

2. "To khardil meat" (khardaltu al-laḥm) — to carve meat apart limb by limb, each piece left full-sized. The entry illustrates this with a line of verse (poet unnamed in this excerpt, and the line itself is partly elided) describing someone feeding two lions dust-covered pieces of meat cut this way — khirādīl, the plural of khurdūlah.

3. Khardal — classed by the ʿAyn as a kind of ḥarf-plant. (Ḥarf is a cress-type plant; this entry places mustard as a variety within that family, rather than defining it independently.)

4. "To khardil food" (khardaltu al-ṭaʿām) — to eat only the best and choicest parts of a meal.

5. Mukhardal — someone struck down and thrown to the ground (al-maṣrūʿ al-marmī). The text notes this usage occurs in a ḥadīth, without quoting or identifying it further.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أَخْرَجَ 99x "we will bring forth"; خَرَجَ 53x "come forth"; إِخْرَاج 6x "to drive out"; خُرُوج 5x "(will be) the coming forth"; مُخْرَج 5x "an exit"; ٱسْتَخْرَجَ 4x "and bring forth"; مُخْرِج 3x "(is) the one who brought forth"; خَارِج 3x "will come out"; خَرْج 2x "(for) a payment"; خَرَاج 1x "but the payment"; مَخْرَج 1x "a way out"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives kh-r-j from two separate roots (though he notes they could arguably be unified): (1) passing or coming forth out of something, and (2) the contrast of two colours.

FIRST ROOT — coming out:
1. The base verb خَرَجَ / يَخْرُجُ / خُرُوجًا — to go or come out.
2. خُرَاج (khurāj) — an eruption or abscess on the body.
3. خَرَاج / خَرْج — tribute or levy, so called because it is wealth the payer "brings out."
4. خَارِجِيّ — a self-made man of rank, noble through his own effort with no inherited standing, as though he "came forth" by himself; compared to the proverb "ʿIṣām's own self ennobled ʿIṣām."
5. خُرُوج — also the emerging/rising of a cloud: "how fine is its emergence."
6. خِرِّيج — a pupil or graduate of a teacher, as the teacher is the one who "brought him out" of ignorance.
7. نَاقَةٌ مُخْتَرِجَةٌ — a she-camel born shaped like a [male] camel.
8. خَرُوج — a she-camel that leaves the herd and kneels off to one side; from the same "going out."
9. خَرِيج — reportedly a children's game of the Arabs, in which they chant "kharāji, kharāji." Cited with a verse of al-Hudhalī describing something like whirled cloths among which "kharīj" is called out.
10. Banū al-Khārijiyya — a tribe; its relative adjective is khārijī.

SECOND ROOT — two-toned colouring:
1. خَرَج — a mix of two colours between black and white: a piebald ostrich hen is خَرْجَاء, a piebald cock ظَلِيم أَخْرَج.
2. The خَرْجَاء is also said to be a ewe whose legs are white up to the flank.
3. أَرْضٌ مُخَرَّجَةٌ — land whose vegetation grows in patches, in one spot and not another.
4. خَرَّجَتِ الرَّاعِيَةُ الْمَرْتَعَ — grazing animals cropped the pasture unevenly, eating some and leaving some — which Ibn Fāris ties back to the idea of contrasting colours (patchiness).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: خَرَقَ 4x "have you made a hole in it"
poets_named: Ruʾba (Umayyad); unnamed verse ×4; Dhū al-Khiraq al-Ṭuhawī (pre-Islamic)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-ر-ق as a single root meaning to tear something open and to cut/pass through it. Every derived sense, on his account, traces back to that.

1. Passing through / traversing. خَرَقْتُ الأرض = "I crossed the land"; اخترقت الريحُ الأرضَ = the wind cut across it. المُخْتَرَق is the place winds sweep through — cited from Ruʾba: "and many a dust-dark waste, empty in its wind-swept expanse."

2. الخَرْق = desert waste, so named because the winds cut across it.

3. الخِرْق (kasra) = a generous, open-handed man, as if he "tears through" with kindness.

4. الخَرْق = the opposite of رِفْق (gentleness/deftness) — clumsy, blundering conduct; the doer is as if "rending" his way along.

5. التَّخَرُّق = fabricating lies (literally, manufacturing them).

6. ريح خرقاء = a wind that will not hold to one direction.

7. الخرقاء (of a woman) = one who does no work well. A verse: "Bungling at good, she finds no way to it — yet skilled at harm toward family and neighbour."

8. الخرقاء (of sheep and the like) = an animal with a pierced ear.

9. بعير أخرق = a camel whose toe-point hits the ground before its footpad.

10. الخِرْقة = a rag or piece of cloth, plural خِرَق. The poet Dhū al-Khiraq al-Ṭuhawī got his name from his line "upon it are the feathers and the rags." الخِرْقة is also used of a detached piece of a locust swarm: "there came down in Ibn Wāṣil's courtyard a piece of a swarm of descending locusts."

11. خَرِيق (from al-Farrāʾ) = a broad stretch of land between bare tracts, wide in extent and in its vegetation; plural خُرُق — "in broad tracts where they eat their fill of their ramrām."

12. الخَرَق = bewilderment and stupefaction. خَرِقَ الغزالُ: the gazelle, circled by a hunter, is dazed and presses itself to the ground; by extension خَرِقَ الرجلُ في بيته = he stayed put and would not leave. الخُرَّق is a bird that hugs the ground.

13. Extended further, الخَرَق is used of bashfulness. An Arab saying: "She has neither a height that disparages her nor a shortness that abashes her" — i.e. it does not shame her into abashment.

14. المخاريق = twisted rags that boys play with — "twisted-rag playthings in the hands of our players."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: Abū Khirāsh (lived into Islam); Ṭufayl (pre-Islamic); Labīd (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats kh-r-r as one root meaning: agitation and falling, accompanied by a sound.

1. **Sound of water.** al-kharīr is the sound of water; a spring that makes it is ʿayn kharrāra, and the verb is kharrat, takhirru.

2. **Rumbling belly.** Of a man whose belly is agitated one says takharkhara.

3. **Falling.** kharra means "he fell." Ibn Fāris cites Abū Khirāsh describing a sword: "With it I leave the armed warrior upon his hands, falling; you would take him for a qashīb vulture." He explains qashīb as a vulture whose food has been mixed with poison so it can be caught (qashaba lahu, "he mixed poison for it"). He compares a verse of Ṭufayl that mentions "every dark muqashshab," glossing muqashshab as a vulture caught by poison (qishb) put into carcasses, and nāhiḍ in the same verse as "young." He adds that a vulture turns black as it ages.

4. **Splitting the ground.** kharra al-māʾu al-arḍa: the water split the ground.

5. **Low ground.** al-akhirra (singular kharīr) are low-lying places stretching between two rises. al-Aḥmar reports hearing Arabs recite Labīd's words "in the akhirra of al-Thalabūt."

6. **Mill-hopper and ear canal.** al-khurr of a hand-mill is the opening into which wheat is poured. Ibn Fāris says this fits the root's analogy because the grain falls (yakhirru) into it. The khurr of the ear, its hole, is named by likeness to it.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: Al-Kumayt (Umayyad) ×2; Ruʾba (Umayyad) ×2; unnamed verse ×2; Al-Mumazzaq al-ʿAbdī (pre-Islamic); Ibn al-Aʿrābī (unnamed)
text:
Ibn Manẓūr treats two closely spelled roots here: خسا (with a weak/dropped final letter) and خسأ (with final hamza). He also records the view that they are ultimately one root.

**Part I — خسا: "odd" (as opposed to "even")**

1. **Core sense: the odd number, the single one.** خَسَا (khasā) means "odd, unpaired." Its plural, المَخاسي (al-makhāsī), is irregular — not formed by the standard analogy — like مَسَاوٍ and similar words. Another plural given is الأَخاسي (al-akhāsī).

2. **The paired idiom خَساً أو زَكاً ("odd or even").** خَساً is the odd, زَكاً the even — equivalent to the pair وِتْر (odd) / شَفْع (even). Al-Layth explains it as a children's guessing game played with walnuts: one hides a handful and the other calls "odd" or "even." Al-Kumayt uses the pair for tallying: noble deeds too many to be counted "odd and even." Ruʾba twice turns it into a figure for not knowing: "he did not know the even-player from the odd-player," and of a bewildered man who cannot tell whether the handful he faces is odd or even.

3. **Verbal forms of the game.** تَخاسى الرجلان — the two men played odd-and-even against each other. خَاسَيْتُ فلاناً — I played him at odd-or-even with walnuts. هو يُخَسِّي ويُزَكِّي — he plays, asking "odd or even?"

4. **Inflection (al-Farrāʾ).** Speakers differ on how to decline خَسَا / زَكَا: some treat it like فَتىً (fatan), some like the diptote زُفَر (Zufar), some like سَكْرَى (sakrā). A verse from a woman of the Dubayr recited to al-Farrāʾ uses it of a small group: "they were odd or even, fewer than four."

5. **A compound form.** خَسَا زَكَا can also be built as one indeclinable compound on the pattern of خمسة عشر ("fifteen"). A satirical verse uses it of a corrupt old man for whom perjury or an orphan's property is as light as "a boy's play with pebbles, odd-or-even."

6. **Etymology (Ibn Barrī).** The third radical of خَسا is originally a hamza — hence the usage هو يُخاسِئُ يُقامِر ("he plays odd-and-even, he gambles"). The hamza is dropped in خَساً only for phonetic assimilation to its partner زَكاً. This links Part I directly to Part II below. Al-Kumayt's verse counting years "the least odd or even… up to four" is cited here.

7. **Reported usage.** A ḥadīth report: "I do not know how many traditions my father related to me from the Messenger of God — an odd number or an even one."

8. **An extended, physical sense.** Of a mount: تَخاسَتْ قوائمُها بالحَصى — its legs flung and tossed the pebbles about. Al-Mumazzaq al-ʿAbdī describes a mare's forelegs tossing and crushing pebbles with "a dusky creaker," which the entry glosses as the tip of the hoof (مَنْسِم). A note in Ibn Manẓūr's sources records a variant reading (ḥamma vs. jamma) in the last word of the verse.

Note also the horse verse of Ibn al-Aʿrābī, where زَكَا is used for the even side of the pair: the horse "runs at five [she-asses], his legs being even" — i.e. four.

**Part II — خسأ: driving off, being driven off, and dulled sight**

1. **Core sense: to drive away, keep at a distance.** خَسَأَ الكلبَ (verbal nouns خَسْأ, خُسوء) — he drove the dog off, chased it away. It is used both transitively and intransitively: خَسَأْتُه فَخَسَأَ, "I put it far off and it went far off"; and خَسَأَ الكلبُ بنفسِه, the dog kept off of itself. The reflexive انْخَسَأَ means "to be driven off": "like the dog — if it is told 'be off!', off it goes." Al-Layth gives the imperative اخْسَأْ as the rebuke shouted at a dog. A ḥadīth uses فَخَسَأْتُ الكلبَ, "I drove the dog away." The command also occurs as اخْسَأْ إليك and اخْسَأْ عنِّي ("off with you," "away from me").

2. **الخاسِئ — the participle.** Used of dogs, swine and satans: the one kept so far off that it is not let near a person. It means the driven-away (مطرود) and the distanced (مبعد); it can also carry the sense of the abased and contemptible (صاغِر قَمِئ).

3. **Qur'anic usages recorded by this author.**
   - اخْسَؤوا فيها ولا تُكَلِّمونِ — al-Zajjāj glosses this as "a distancing of wrath," i.e. being driven off in anger.
   - كونوا قِرَدةً خاسِئين, addressed (in Ibn Manẓūr's framing) to the Jews — glossed as مدحورين, "repelled"; al-Zajjāj: "put far away."
   - يَنْقَلِبْ إليكَ البَصَرُ خاسِئاً وهو حَسير — here خاسئاً is read by al-Zajjāj as "abased," parsed grammatically as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative).

4. **A distinct sense: of the eye.** خَسَأَ بصرُه — the sight became dazzled, dull and worn out. This is the sense that stands behind the third Qur'anic citation above.

5. **Grammatical anecdote on the imperative.** Ibn Abī Isḥāq claimed never to make a grammatical slip; Bukayr b. Ḥabīb caught him twice — once on the word كَلِمة, and once when he shouted اخْسَيْ at a passing she-cat, the correct feminine imperative being اخْسَئِي. Abū Mahdiyya's اخْسَأْنانِّ عنِّي ("get away from me") is quoted as another form; al-Aṣmaʿī thought he was addressing satans.

6. **Reciprocal form.** تَخاسَأَ القومُ بالحجارة — the people pelted one another with stones; the noun for such an exchange is مُخاسَأَة. This parallels the physical sense of تَخاسَتْ in Part I.8.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats kh-s-f as one root meaning hiddenness and a sinking or caving inward. Every branch he lists is traced back to that.

1. Ground giving way. khasf / khasaf is the caving-in of the earth's surface. His Qur'anic citation is 28:81, "So We caused the earth to swallow him and his dwelling."

2. Eclipse. khusūf of the moon belongs here (the moon "sinking away"). He notes that some lexicographers restricted khusūf to the moon and kusūf to the sun.

3. A caved-in well. A well is khasīf when its rock lining breaks through and collapses inward — such a well cannot be drawn dry. He cites a verse: "a copious [well], of the deep khusuf wells."

4. An eye. inkhasafat al-ʿayn — the eye sank in, i.e. went blind.

5. A wasted body. An emaciated person is khāsif, as if his flesh had sunk inward.

6. Going hungry. bāta ʿalā al-khasf — to spend the night hungry, as though the food one wanted had vanished away.

7. Accepting abasement. raḍiya bi-l-khasf — to be content with a low, humiliating lot.

8. Soft ground. akhāsīf are soft tracts of land, so soft they nearly cave in underfoot.

9. Extended by analogy. A rain-heavy cloud is called khasīf, likened to the abundant well; likewise a nāqa khasīfa is a she-camel copious in milk.

10. A reported sense he rejects as unknown to him: that khasf means an edible walnut — he says he does not know what that is.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-س-ر (kh-s-r) as a single root whose core sense is deficiency or loss (al-naqṣ).

1. Nominal forms: from it come الخُسْر and الخُسْران ("loss"), a paired form he compares to الكُفْر / الكُفْران and الفُرْق / الفُرْقان — i.e. a base noun alongside its longer -ān form.

2. Verbal usage: خَسَرْتُ الْمِيزَانَ and أَخْسَرْتُهُ mean "I made the balance deficient" / "gave short measure" — that is, one diminished it.

He closes with the formula "and God knows best."

text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-ت-م as one single root with one basic idea: reaching the end of something. From that one idea he derives the whole cluster.

1. Reaching the end / completing. خَتَمْتُ الْعَمَلَ — "I finished the work"; خَتَمَ الْقَارِئُ السُّورَةَ — "the reciter reached the end of the sūra."

2. Sealing / stamping (الْخَتْم). Placing a seal on something. Ibn Fāris explicitly folds this back into the same root: a thing is sealed only once one has reached its end — his example being items kept secured or stored away (الأحراز).

3. The signet-ring (الْخَاتَم), derived from sense 2 because sealing is done with it. He records four variant forms of the word: خَاتَم، خَاتِم، خَاتَام، خَيْتَام. Poetic witness: أَخَذْتِ خَاتَامِي بِغَيْرِ حَقٍّ — "You took my signet-ring without right."

4. Last in a sequence. On this basis he glosses the Prophet as خَاتَمُ الْأَنْبِيَاء, "the seal of the prophets," giving the reason as: because he is the last of them.

5. The final part of a drink (خِتَامُ كُلِّ مَشْرُوبٍ = its end). Qurʾānic witness: خِتَامُهُ مِسْكٌ (83:26), which he explains as meaning that the last thing the drinkers find of it, as they drink, is the scent of musk — i.e. "end/aftertaste" rather than a stopper or wax seal.

Method to note: each sense is justified back to the single core meaning "end," including the sealing sense, rather than being listed as an independent homonym.

2. From this same core sense: al-khatr — treachery/betrayal, because a treacherous person has "gone slack" in fulfilling his commitments, sitting back from loyalty rather than upholding it. al-khattār — the treacherous one. text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-و-ض (kh-w-ḍ) as a single root whose core meaning is entering into the middle of something and penetrating it.

1. Wading / entering: خُضْتُ الْمَاءَ وَغَيْرَهُ — "I waded into the water" (or into anything else), i.e. stepped into its midst.

2. Entering jointly into talk or affairs: تَخَاوَضُوا فِي الْحَدِيثِ وَالْأَمْرِ — "they entered together into the discourse and the matter," glossed as تَفَاوَضُوا — they conferred with one another, their speech intermingling and overlapping.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-و-ف (kh-w-f) as a single root meaning fright and alarm.

1. Core sense — fear. One says khiftu al-shayʾa ("I feared the thing"), with two verbal nouns, khawf and khīfa. He notes a morphological point: the yāʾ in khīfa is a substitution for an original wāw, triggered by the preceding kasra (i-vowel).

2. Derived form (mufāʿala) — khāwafanī fulānun fa-khuftuhu: "So-and-so contended with me in fear, and I feared him more" — i.e. I outdid him in fear.

3. A form he judges genuine but etymologically separate — the expression takhawwaftu al-shayʾa meaning "I diminished it / took part of it away." Ibn Fāris calls this correct and eloquent usage, but explains it does not really belong to this root: it arises by letter-substitution (ibdāl), its original letter being nūn, from tanaqquṣ ("diminution"), and he refers the reader to its proper entry.

text:
Ibn Fāris treats kh-w-l as one root whose sense is tending, looking after, seeing to something.

1. Recurrent attention. He cites the report "he used to yatakhawwaluhum with admonition," explaining it as: he saw to them / attended to them with it at intervals.

2. Managing property. خَوْلِيُّ مَالٍ (khawlī māl) is the man who keeps property in good order — its caretaker or steward.

3. Giving. خَوَّلَكَ اللَّهُ مَالًا, "God khawwala you property," means He gave it to you. Ibn Fāris links this to the core sense: property is something that gets tended (yutakhawwal), so what is granted is what one is put in charge of caring for.

4. Dependants. خَوَل (khawal) — a man's dependants or household retainers. He derives this from the singular خَائِل (khāʾil), the herdsman/keeper, and cites يَخُولُ عَلَى أَهْلِهِ, "he khūls over his household," i.e. he tends and provides for them as a herdsman does for a flock.

5. Repeated action. As an example of eloquent usage: تَخَوَّلَتِ الرِّيحُ الْأَرْضَ, "the wind takhawwalat the land," said when it works over the land again and again — the repeated-visitation aspect of the same root sense.
