text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-و-ن (kh-w-n) as a single root whose core meaning is diminution / detraction (al-tanaqquṣ) — taking something away, falling short.

1. Core sense: خانه (khānahu), verbal noun خون (khawn), is to act treacherously or faithlessly toward someone — which he defines as a deficiency of fidelity (a falling-short of loyalty). Likewise تخوّنني فلان حقّي means "he diminished me of my right / shortchanged me." He cites Dhū al-Rumma on an abode "worn down / eroded" at times by cloud and at times by a hot, dusty west wind (bāriḥ) — the same idea of being gradually diminished.

2. الخوّان (al-khawwān) is used for "the lion"; Ibn Fāris notes it still fits the one underlying sense.

3. He dismisses the claim that in the oldest Arabic the month Rabīʿ al-Awwal was called خوّان (khawwān): he finds no derivable meaning in it and not worth pursuing.

4. On a second Dhū al-Rumma line using تخوّنه (takhawwanahu): he reports two scholarly readings. (a) If it means "tending / caring for" (al-taʿahhud), then it is a case of letter-substitution (ibdāl) — nūn standing in for an original lām, the base word being تخوّله (takhawwalahu, "he tended it"), treated under that root. (b) Others read it in the core sense: what "diminished" the animal's sleep was its mother's call.

5. On خِوان (khiwān), the table one eats at: some held it to be a foreign (non-Arabic) word. Ibn Fāris relays, via ʿAlī b. Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān, that the grammarian Thaʿlab, asked whether the khiwān could be named from the root because the food on it is "diminished / consumed," answered that this is "not far-fetched." He closes with "God knows best."

Method note: Ibn Fāris's argument is to reduce every attested use — betrayal, the lion, the eroded abode, even the table — to one abstract sense (diminution), and to explain apparent exceptions either as letter-substitution from another root or as claims not worth entertaining.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root خ و ر (kh-w-r). Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) derives two unrelated base senses.

1. A sound — specifically the lowing/bellowing of cattle. "khāra al-thawr yakhūru" = the bull lowed. He cites Q20:88, where the Israelites' golden calf is described as "a body having a khuwār" (a lowing sound).

2. Weakness — al-khawwār means "weak," applied to anything: a flexible/weak spear is rumḥ khawwār, soft yielding ground is arḍ khawwāra (plural khūr). He quotes a line of the poet al-Ṭirimmāḥ boasting of his lineage of glory-defenders, contrasted with "the weak among men" who scatter and flee in confusion (khūr al-rijāl tahīʿ) — i.e. weak men break rank under pressure.

A further application of sense 2: a she-camel called khawwāra (plural khūr) means one that is generous/plentiful [in milk]. Ibn Fāris explains why this still belongs to the "weakness" root rather than being a separate meaning: such a camel's opposite is ʿazūz, "narrow-teated" (itself derived from ʿazāz, "hard ground"). So a khawwāra camel is one in which that firmness/tightness has given way — her yielding softness is what makes her generous.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-و-ي as a single root whose governing sense is emptiness and falling/collapse. From that one principle he derives the whole entry:

1. **Emptying, falling into ruin** — خَوَتِ الدَّارُ (khawat al-dār): the house stood empty / fell in.

2. **A star setting without rain** — خَوَى النَّجْمُ, also in form IV أَخْوَى: the star sets and brings no rain with it. He cites a line of verse: the stars of *al-akhdh* set rainless, leaving only a meagre trace, "the trace of drought, whose dripping does not enrich."

3. **Stars leaning toward setting** — form II خَوَّتِ النُّجُومُ (verbal noun تَخْوِيَة, takhwiya).

4. **Hollow bellies** — خَوَّتِ الْإِبِلُ: the camels' bellies grew empty and sunken.

5. **A woman not eating at childbirth** — خَوِيَتِ الْمَرْأَةُ (verbal noun خَوًى, khawan).

6. **Holding the body clear of the ground** — خَوَّى الرَّجُلُ, of a man who keeps his limbs raised away from his sides in prostration, and of a camel that holds itself clear as it kneels. Ibn Fāris explicitly explains this as following the root's analogy (qiyās al-bāb): the man has *emptied* the space between his upper arm and his side.

7. Similarly خَوَّتِ الْمَرْأَةُ of a woman sitting raised over an incense-burner, and خَوَّى الطَّائِرُ of a bird letting its wings out wide — both keeping a space open beneath.

8. **الْخَوَاة (al-khawāt) = a sound.** Ibn Fāris sets this apart: he notes that most of this kind does not conform to the analogy, and that it is not a root-sense — i.e. he does not reduce it to "emptiness/falling."

Method worth noting: the entry works by stating one abstract principle and then justifying each concrete usage against it, flagging the single item (khawāt) that resists the derivation rather than forcing it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris's Maqāyīs al-Lugha entry for the root خ-ي-ط (kh-y-ṭ):

**Core meaning:** the extension of something in fineness/slenderness. From this core, related senses are extended to anything that stands upright or elongated.

1. **Al-khayṭ** — "thread," the everyday sense.

2. **The white and black threads of dawn** — al-khayṭ al-abyaḍ ("white thread") = the whiteness of daylight; al-khayṭ al-aswad ("black thread") = the blackness of night. Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 2:187: "until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of dawn."

3. **Khayṭ bāṭil** ("a false/vain thread") — the shimmering gossamer-like filaments seen in sunlight (poetically, "the sun's saliva"). Illustrated with an unattributed line of verse addressing "Banū Khayṭ Bāṭil" as treacherous house-builders.

4. **Khuyyiṭa** — said of someone whose hair has begun to grey, "he has been threaded/streaked," because the streaks of grey are likened to threads. A line by al-Hudhalī is cited: "until my locks became streaked with whiteness" (takhayyaṭa).

5. **Naʿāma khayṭāʾ** — an ostrich so called for its khayṭ, the length of its neck (the "thread"-like extension sense again).

6. **Al-khiyāṭa** — "sewing/tailoring," the everyday sense.

7. **Al-khiṭ** (with kasra) — a flock/group of ostriches. Ibn Fāris explains this fits the root's logic: a gathered group is like things sewn together, one part to another.

8. **Al-khayṭa** — appears in a line of al-Hudhalī's poetry describing a descent "between a sibb (rope) and a khayṭa," down a bare rock-face. Two glosses are reported for khayṭa here: (a) "the rope" — which, if correct, follows the root's regular pattern; or (b) "the tent-peg" — which Ibn Fāris says also fits the root, since a tent-peg too involves an upright, extended shape.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-ي-ب as one root with a single core notion: no benefit obtained, and being denied.

1. Root sense — the absence of any gain; deprivation, coming away empty.

2. Concrete origin of the usage — Ibn Fāris identifies the base image as the fire-stick (القِدْح) that strikes no flame; of such a stick the Arabs said هو خَيَّاب, "it is a khayyāb" (one that yields no fire).

3. Extension to human effort — from that image comes سَعَى فِي أَمْرٍ فَخَابَ, "he exerted himself in some matter and khāba": he was denied it, so he derived no good from it.

The entry gives no further senses, grammatical patterns, or poetic citations.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
poets_named: al-Farazdaq (Umayyad); Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad); al-Shammākh (lived into Islam)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-ي-ل as one root whose single idea is **movement combined with shifting appearance or colour**. Everything below he derives from that.

1. **خَيَال (khayāl) — an apparition, a figure seen.** Its base sense is what a person sees in imagination while asleep, so called because such a figure takes on likenesses and keeps changing colour.

2. **خَيَّلْتُ لِلنَّاقَةِ — to set up a khayāl for a she-camel:** planting a dummy figure beside her calf so that the wolf is scared off and will not approach.

3. **خَيْل (khayl) — horses.** Ibn Fāris passes on an anecdote (via al-Aṣmaʿī) in which Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ was asked why horses are called khayl and said he did not know; a bedouin youth present answered: "from their اخْتِيَال — their swaggering gait," and Abū ʿAmr told his students to write it down. Ibn Fāris judges the etymology sound, since a strutting walker varies his movement in many changing ways — which is exactly the root idea.

4. **الأَخْيَل (al-akhyal) — a bird**, which Ibn Fāris supposes is multicoloured (hence the name); it is identified with the شِقِرَّاق (shiqirrāq). The Arabs regarded it as a bird of ill omen. A camel is called مَخْيُول (makhyūl) when this bird has settled on its rump and torn it.

   The ill-omen sense is illustrated by three verses on the same theme — a rider telling his mount that once it has carried him to his patron, he no longer cares what becomes of it:
   - al-Farazdaq: once you have brought me to Qaṭan ibn Mudrik, may you then meet an *akhyal*, of the birds of ill omen.
   - Dhū al-Rumma: once you have brought me to Bilāl ibn Abī Mūsā, let a butcher stand over you with an axe.
   - al-Shammākh: once you have carried me and my saddle to ʿArāba, choke on the blood of your own aorta.

5. **Weather senses.** تَخَيَّلَتِ السَّمَاءُ — the sky "made ready" for rain; Ibn Fāris notes a change of colour necessarily accompanies this. مَخِيلَة (makhīla) is the cloud; مُخَيِّلَة (mukhayyila) is the cloud that gives promise of rain.

6. **Suspicion and inference.** خَيَّلْتُ عَلَى الرَّجُلِ — to direct suspicion at a man. Ibn Fāris ties this to the same root through the idiom "it looks as though it is such-and-such / it is made to appear to me (yukhayyalu ilayya) that it is so" — i.e. an impression, not a certainty. From the same line comes تَخَيَّلْتُ عَلَيْهِ, to size someone up from his outward appearance (tafarrasa).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root خيم (kh-y-m) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: the three letters kh-y-m form a single root meaning "to stay/reside" and "firmness, steadfastness."

1. al-khaymah ("tent") — well known; explicitly named for the fact that one resides (aqāma) in/at it.
2. al-khaym — the poles or sticks a tent is built on. Supported by a line of poetry describing "a stacked frame of tent-poles" left standing [of an abandoned camp].
3. khayyama bi-l-makān — "he pitched camp / stayed at a place" — given as the reason al-khaymah carries its name.
4. al-khiyam (vocalized khiyam, kasra on the khāʾ) — a person's innate disposition/character, because one is "built upon it" and always returns to it, the way one returns to a tent.
5. khāʾim — "a coward" — extended from the same root because cowardice leaves a person without movement, i.e., he stays put.
6. yakhīmu — "he lingers, holds back."
7. A poetic citation ("they saw weakness in my leg... and tried to set it, when they saw me akhīmuhā") is glossed by Ibn Fāris as meaning "raising it up" — he says the poet is comparing the raised limb to khaym, tent-poles.

A second, separate note is attached (because of a shared alif after khāʾ), where Ibn Fāris moves to words built on khāl — treating them as belonging either to a wāw-original or a yāʾ-original root:
- al-khāl (a "mole" on the face) — tied to a discoloration/variegation he discusses under another entry. Adjectives: makhīl / makhūl ("a man with a mole"), with diminutives khuyayl / khuwayl respectively.
- khāl al-rajul ("a man's maternal uncle") — derived from khāʾilu māl, "one who tends/looks after property" — i.e., the uncle as the one who looks after [his sister's children].
- khāl al-jaysh ("the army's banner/standard") — either from its changing colors, or because the army watches over it and looks to it the way a custodian looks after something.
- al-khāl also names "the black mountain," according to report — which Ibn Fāris classifies under letter-substitution (ibdāl), i.e. a phonetic variant of another word.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: خَيْر 178x "better"; خَيْرَٰت 10x "(to) the good"; ٱخْتَارَ 4x "and chooses"; خِيَرَة 2x "(any) choice"; يَتَخَيَّرُ 2x "you choose"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root خ-ي-ر from a core idea of inclining and leaning toward something (al-ʿaṭf wa-l-mayl), with all other senses traced back to it.

1. khayr (good) — the opposite of sharr (evil), so called because everyone inclines toward it and feels kindly toward the one who has it.

2. Related nouns: khīra = choice, the choicest (khiyār); khīr = generosity (karam).

3. istikhāra (seeking the good) — to ask for the better of two options for oneself. Ibn Fāris links it to the core sense of "seeking-to-incline/coax" (istiʿṭāf), and reports the saying that it comes from "the hyena's istikhāra" — poking a stick into a hyena's den to draw the animal out from one spot to another. He cites a line of al-Hudhalī using tastakhīruhā in the sense of coaxing/drawing a woman out.

4. Inflected forms for excellence in people: rajul khayyir / imraʾa khayyira = an excellent, virtuous person (fāḍil); plurals qawm khiyār and akhyār. He notes a usage distinction: khayyir describes a woman's moral righteousness (ṣalāḥ), whereas khayra describes her beauty and fine features (jamāl, mīsam). Qurʾānic citation: "In them are good/beautiful ones, comely" (55:70).

5. Comparison and choosing: khāyartu fulānan fa-khirtuhu = "I contended with him in excellence and proved the better." ikhtar (choose) as in "choose a man from so-and-so's people," with the Qurʾānic citation "And Moses chose from his people seventy men" (7:155).

6. Grammatical note: khīra (with a short vowel) is the verbal noun (maṣdar) of ikhtāra, i.e. ikhtāra khīra, on the analogy of irtāba rība.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: خَزَائِن 8x "(are the) treasures"; خَزَنَت 4x "its keepers"; خَٰزِنِين 1x "(are) retainers"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats خ-ز-ن (kh-z-n) as a single root meaning to keep something safe, to guard or store it.

1. Core sense — safekeeping. One says "I stored away the dirham and the like" (khazn = the act of storing), and by extension "I kept the secret." A cited verse makes the same link: "When a man's tongue does not keep guard over him, he is no keeper of anything else" — guarding one's speech is itself an act of khazn.

2. A note on a look-alike form. The verb khazina l-laḥm, "the meat spoiled / changed its smell," does NOT belong to this root, despite the shared letters. Ibn Fāris identifies it as metathesis (letter-transposition); its true root is خ-ن-ز (kh-n-z), handled under that entry.

3. A poetic attestation. Ṭarafa uses the passive khuzina in the storing sense: "its meat is not stored up among us; only the hoarder's meat is stored" — i.e. this root's meaning is genuinely about laying something up in store, unlike the spoilage sense in point 2.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
quran_words: أَخْزَيْ 12x "disgrace me"; خِزْى 11x "(is) disgrace"; مُخْزِى 1x "(is) the one who (will) disgrace"; نَخْزَىٰ 1x "and disgraced"; أَخْزَىٰ 1x "(is) more disgracing"
text:
Al-Rāghib treats خَزِيَ (khaziya) as denoting a "breaking" or abasement that overtakes a person, and he divides it by its source:

1. Abasement from within oneself — excessive shame or bashfulness (al-ḥayāʾ al-mufriṭ). Its verbal noun is al-khazāya; forms include khazyān (bashful man), khazyā (bashful woman), plural khazāyā. He cites the ḥadīth: "O God, gather us neither as the disgraced (khazāyā) nor as the regretful."

2. Abasement from another — a kind of belittlement or contempt (istikhfāf). Its verbal noun is al-khizy; the agent form is khazin (a disgraced man). This is the sense in the Qurʾānic uses of khizy, e.g. "that is for them a disgrace in this world" (Q 5:33); Q 16:27; Q 39:26; Q 41:16; and the verb in "before we are humbled and disgraced" (Q 20:134).

On the causative form أَخْزَى (akhzā): al-Rāghib says it can draw on both senses. "The Day God will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believed" (Q 66:8) is closer to al-khizy (abasement from another), though possibly from both. "Whoever You admit to the Fire, You have disgraced him" (Q 3:192) he assigns to al-khazāya (inner shame), while allowing al-khizy; likewise Q 11:39, Q 3:194, Q 59:5, and "do not disgrace me before my guests" (Q 11:78).

He closes with a parallel from ذلّ وهان (dhalla wa hāna, "he was lowly"): the same two-way distinction applies. When lowliness comes from the person himself it is al-hūn / al-dhull and is praiseworthy; when imposed by another it is al-hūn, al-hawān, al-dhull and is blameworthy.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَئِسَ 8x "(have) despaired"; يَـُوس 3x "(in) despair"; ٱسْتَيْـَسَ 2x "they despaired"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root y-ʾ-s (yāʾ, hamza, sīn) into two distinct senses:

1. **Despair — the cutting off of hope** (al-yaʾs). He notes a curious point of Arabic phonology: this is the only word in which an initial yāʾ is followed by a hamza. Its verb is yaʾisa, with two imperfect forms — yayʾasu and yayʾisu — reflecting both the a-stem (yafʿalu) and i-stem (yafʿilu) conjugation patterns.

2. **To know** — in the construction a-lam tayʾas ("did you not know?"). Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'anic verse {a-fa-lam yayʾasi lladhīna āmanū} (al-Raʿd 13:31) and reports the reading that its sense is "have those who believe not come to know?" He supports this second sense with a line of poetry: "I say to them in the mountain-pass, as they take me captive: Do you not know (tayʾasū) that I am the son of the horseman Zahdam?" — where tayʾasū clearly means "you know," not "you despair."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats Y–B–S as a single sound root whose one idea is dryness.

1. Core verb: يَبِسَ ("to dry out, become dry"), with the imperfect attested in two vowellings, يَيْبَسُ and يَيْبِسُ.

2. الْيَبْس (yabs): the dried-out matter of a plant. Ibn al-Sikkīt is cited as taking it to be the plural of يَابِس ("dry [thing]").

3. الْيَبَس (yabas, with fatḥa on the second radical): a place that the water withdraws from, so that it dries out.

4. Applied to land: يَبِسَتِ الْأَرْضُ — its water and moisture are gone; and the fourth-form أَيْبَسَتْ — its dryness has become extensive.

5. Of a person, on the authority of al-Shaybānī: امْرَأَةٌ يَبَسٌ, a woman from whom no good is got. The supporting verse: "…to an old woman, wizened of face, dried up."

6. يَبِيسُ الْمَاءِ (lit. "the dried-up of water"): sweat once it has dried.

7. الْأَيْبَسَانِ (dual): the fleshless parts of the shank and the ankle.

dictionary: ʿAyn — Kitāb al-ʿAyn, al-Khalīl al-Farāhīdī (d. 786)
poets_named: Labīd (lived into Islam); unnamed verse; al-ʿAjjāj (Umayyad)
text:
Kitāb al-ʿAyn's account of the root ydy (يدي), centered on yad, "hand":

1. Literal and extended "hand." The hand is well-known. The word extends by metaphor to: the handle of an axe or similar tool; the curved tip (sīya) of a bow; the "hand" of favor (yad al-niʿma) meaning an ample, abundant benefaction; the "hand" of time meaning the extent of its span; and the "hand" of the wind meaning its command or possession — cited from Labīd, where the north wind's holding the "rein" pictures its control over marshalling the clouds as "possession of the hand."

2. "In the hand of" = possession. "This estate is in so-and-so's hand" means in his ownership. Idiomatically the singular is used here — they do not say "in so-and-so's hands."

3. "bayna yaday" = before / in front of. Used for whatever lies ahead of you. Shawāhid: the Qurʾanic "from before them and from behind them" (min bayna aydīhim wa-min khalfihim); the sayings "dust stirs up before the rain" and "cursing flares up before the fighting"; and the Qurʾanic "before a severe punishment" (bayna yaday ʿadhābin shadīd).

4. Verbs and states of the hand. yadiya — for a hand to wither/become paralyzed; a maydiyy man has his hand severed at the base; yadaytu yadahu — I struck his hand; al-yudāʾ — pain of the hand.

5. "Hand" of benefaction. aydaytu ʿindahu yadan — I did him a favor; aydāhu-llāh — may God enrich/strengthen him (verbal noun al-yad or al-ayd); a "white hand" (yad bayḍāʾ) is a noble kindness. A wealthy man "extends his hand" (yaydī) and his reach (bāʿ) with his wealth.

6. Idiom "aydī / ayādī Sabaʾ" — scattered in every direction, said of people (and of the wind, etc.).

7. Plurals and grammar. The plural of the physical hand (and of bodies/forms) is aydī; the plural of the "hand" of favor is ayādin and yadiyy (poetic shāhid: "he has with me hands [favors] and blessings"). The nisba (relative adjective) of yad is yadiyy, formed on the "deficient" pattern because yad is a defective noun — contrasted with ab (father) → abawiyy: one says the dual yadāni without the yāʾ surfacing, but abawāni shows the wāw.

8. thawb yadiyy — a wide, roomy garment (cited from al-ʿAjjāj); explained either as a newly-made garment, "as if hands had just been lifted from it," or as a garment that many hands take turns handling.

9. Further idioms. "They are a single hand against others" — their cause is united. "I gave him wealth ʿan ẓahri yad" — as an outright bounty, not a loan or repayment. "He cast his hand off from obedience" — withdrew allegiance. A "garment short of hand" — too short to wrap oneself in.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats y-m-m as a word whose core meaning is aiming at something, intending it deliberately and making for it; he explicitly sets the words for the sea apart from this analogy.

1. **To aim at, make for deliberately (tayammama, yammama).** Ibn Fāris cites Q 4:43, fa-tayammamū ṣaʿīdan ṭayyiban, "then make for clean ground/earth". Al-Khalīl says tayammamtu fulānan bi-sahmī wa-rumḥī means "I aimed my arrow and spear at so-and-so", singling him out over everyone else. He cites the verse: "I aimed the spear at him sidelong, then said to him: this is valour, not the play of sliding games." Al-Khalīl rejects the variant reading ammamtuhu ("I aimed it at him head-on") here: the verse says shazran, "sidelong", and a sidelong thrust comes from one side, not from in front (amām), so ammamtuhu would not fit.

2. **Sought out; successful (muyammam).** Al-Shaybānī reports that a man is called muyammam when he attains everything he seeks, citing: "We found Aʿṣur ibn Saʿd one whose house is sought out, lofty in fortune." Ibn Fāris explains this as being sought out for good, which ties it to the core sense of aiming.

3. **The sea (outside the core analogy).** Ibn Fāris says words for the sea do not belong to this pattern of meaning. He cites al-Khalīl: yumma al-rajul, fa-huwa maymūm, "the man was taken by the sea", said when someone falls into the yamm and drowns.

4. **A bird.** al-yamām is a bird, said to be the one bred for its young in houses.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: يَمِين 65x "(of) the right"; أَيْمَن 3x "the right"; مَيْمَنَة 3x "(of) the right"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats the root ي-م-ن (y-m-n) as a cluster of words all traceable to one underlying idea.

1. **al-yamīn — the right hand.** The primary sense: the right hand of the body.

2. **al-yamīn — strength.** A reported sense, "power/strength" (al-quwwa). Al-Aṣmaʿī, however, glosses the line of the poet al-Shammākh — "When a banner is raised for glory, ʿArāba receives it with the right" — as meaning the right hand itself, not "strength."

3. **al-yumn — blessing.** The noun al-yumn means blessing (baraka); one so favored is maymūn (blessed, fortunate).

4. **al-yamīn — an oath.** The word for a sworn oath (al-ḥalif). Ibn Fāris derives all these senses from "the right hand," and explains the oath specifically: it is called yamīn because, when two parties swear a mutual pact, it is as if each strikes his right hand upon the other's right hand.

5. **al-Yaman — the country.** The place-name Yemen belongs to the same cluster; hence rajul yamānin ("a Yemeni man") and sayf yamānin ("a Yemeni sword").

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
poets_named: unnamed verse ×3; ʿAmr b. Maʿdīkarib (lived into Islam); Abū Ḥayya al-Numayrī (pre-Islamic); Al-Ḥajjāj (Umayyad); Rakkāḍ al-Dubayrī (undated)
text:
Root y-n-ʿ (ينع) — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr

1. Core sense — "to ripen." yanaʿa/yayniʿu and the more common aynaʿa/yūniʿu both mean fruit "matured and ripened" (adraka wa-naḍija). The ripe fruit itself is called yāniʿ, and the abstract noun is al-yanʿ ("ripening, maturity"). Al-Jawharī notes a grammatical point: the middle radical yāʾ, though usually dropped in weak verbs, is kept here because it's reinforced by a second yāʾ in the pattern.

2. Qur'anic citation — Q 6:99: "Look at its fruit when it bears fruit, and its yanʿ (ripening)." Ibn Manẓūr notes the word here was also read as yunʿihi and yāniʿihi in different recitations.

3. Poetic evidence for "ripe/ripening": olive trees described as "having ripened" (yanaʿā) around a manor house; a lover's line about fruit growing moist as it ripens (yāniʿuh); ʿAmr b. Maʿdīkarib comparing teeth to "ripe pomegranate" (rummān yanīʿ); Abū Ḥayya al-Numayrī describing a scent "from ripe [fruit] moist with dew." Synonyms given: yanīʿ, aynaʿ, yāniʿ — equivalent to naḍīj/nāḍij ("ripe/ripened"). The plural of yāniʿ is yanʿ (on the pattern ṣāḥib → ṣaḥb, per Ibn Kaysān). A parallel formation is noted: aynaʿa "ripen" : yāniʿ "ripe" :: awfaʿa "grow up" (of a boy) : yāfiʿ "grown."

4. Extended sense — "done" (of cooked food). Īnāʿ can mean food finishing cooking, not just fruit ripening. Ibn Manẓūr illustrates this with an anecdote (via Ibn al-Aʿrābī): Abū Simāl invites al-Najāshī to eat lamb heads stewed all night until "done" (aynaʿat) during Ramaḍān, and to drink an intoxicant with it. They get drunk, are reported to ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib, and al-Najāshī is flogged 100 lashes (80 plus 20 extra "for your presumption against God"). The story closes with a proverbial, somewhat obscure exchange about the punishment.

5. Extended sense — "ready for death." Al-Ḥajjāj's line "I see heads that have ripened (aynaʿat) and whose harvest has come" is glossed as meaning their deaths were near — their heads compared to fruit ready to be picked.

6. Sense — "red, at its fullest." Al-yāniʿ can also mean "the red of anything that has reached its full/complete state." Fruit is yāniʿ when it takes on color; a woman can be called yāniʿat al-wajnatayn ("ripe/red-cheeked"). A verse by Rakkāḍ al-Dubayrī uses the verb of a reddening complexion. Related: al-yunūʿ = "redness of blood" (Ibn Barrī), with a supporting verse about blood-stained stones (yunūʿā); Ibn al-Athīr glosses "yāniʿ blood" as blood that has turned red.

7. Sense — a red bead / a kind of carnelian. Al-yanaʿa is "a red bead" (plural yanaʿ), cited from the ḥadīth on li'ān (mutual spousal imprecation): the Prophet is reported to have said that if the disputed child is born ruddy "like the yanaʿa," he belongs to the father who denied him. Al-yanaʿa (or, per al-Azharī's al-Tahdhīb, al-yanaʿ without the tāʾ marbūṭa) is also the name of a well-known variety of carnelian/agate stone.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
text:
Root: ي ق ظ (y-q-ẓ) — "wakefulness, alertness." Source: Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144 CE).

1. Core pair: النوم "sleep" vs. اليقظة "wakefulness." Verbs ayqaẓahu / yaqqaẓahu = "he woke him up"; the person then istayqaẓa ("woke up") or tayaqqaẓa ("became watchful, alert").

2. Adjectives: yaqẓān (masc.) / yaqẓā (fem.) = "wakeful"; plural ayqāẓ = "a wakeful group." Illustrative line: "my eye stayed wakeful all night, watching over you."

3. Figurative (majāz) sense — mental alertness: yaqẓān al-fikr, mutayaqqiẓ, yaqiẓ, and yaqẓ (variant adjective patterns) all describe a sharp, watchful mind. "He is roused by [the mere sound of] his voice" — quick to notice.

4. Shāhid from al-Farazdaq (satirical verse): "They wake at their donkeys' braying ... but their eyes sleep through the twang of bowstrings" — mocking a people alert to trivial noise yet oblivious to the sounds of war.

5. Figurative extension to dust: ayqaẓa / yaqqaẓa al-turāb = "he stirred up the dust" (literally, "woke" it).

6. Shāhid from a poet in the Ḥamāsa anthology: "When we travel between east and west, the wakeful dust stirs — and its sleeping [dust] too" — dust in motion is called "awake," settled dust "asleep."

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
quran_words: يُوقِنُ 12x "believe with certainty"; يَقِين 8x "(of) certainty"; مُّوقِنِين 5x "the ones who are certain"; ٱسْتَيْقَنَتْ 2x "that may be certain"; مُسْتَيْقِنِين 1x "(are) convinced"
poets_named: Abū Sidra al-Asadī (Umayyad); al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam)
text:
Root ي-ق-ن (y-q-n), as recorded by Ibn Manẓūr.

1. Core sense. al-yaqīn is knowledge that removes doubt and settles a matter as certain — the opposite of doubt, as knowledge is the opposite of ignorance. One says "I knew it with certainty" (ʿalimtuhu yaqīnan).

2. Verb forms. Two base patterns: ayqana / yūqinu / īqānan (agent noun mūqin), and yaqina / yayqan / yaqanan (agent noun yaqin). Ibn Sīda lists many forms all meaning "to be/become certain of a matter": yaqina, ayqanahu, ayqana bihi, tayaqqanahu, istayqanahu, istayqana bihi, and with the preposition (tayaqqantu bi-, istayqantu bihi). Also the phrase "I am in certainty of it" (anā ʿalā yaqīnin minhu).

3. Morphology note. In mūqin the original yāʾ turns to wāw only because of the preceding ḍamma; the diminutive restores the root form: muyayqin.

4. Qurʾānic citations (as read by this author):
- "ḥaqq al-yaqīn" — ḥaqq is annexed to yaqīn not as a thing joined to itself, since ḥaqq is distinct: it is the pure, soundest part of yaqīn, so the grammar is "part annexed to whole."
- "worship your Lord until al-yaqīn comes to you" — glossed as "until death comes to you," i.e. worship Him always, to the point of death. Compared to the report of ʿĪsā: "He enjoined on me the ṣalāt and the zakāt so long as I live" — meaning perpetual worship.

5. Overlap with ẓann (conjecture). Sometimes yaqīn is used for ẓann and vice versa. Shāhid: Abū Sidra al-Asadī's line about a lion (hawwās) that "was certain" the poet would give up his she-camel as ransom rather than risk fighting it. (hawwās = lion, so named because it crushes its prey.)

6. Derived human epithets. A man called yaqin / yaqan believes with certainty whatever he hears — parallel to udhun ("all ear," credulous). Variant forms: yaqana (Kurāʿ), and mīqān, fem. mīqāna (al-Liḥyānī) — the latter noted as an irregular formation. Abū Zayd gives dhū yaqan and udhun yaqan for the same trait: one who is certain of, and does not disbelieve, whatever he hears.

7. Further usages. al-Layth: al-yaqan = al-yaqīn, with a shāhid from al-Aʿshā. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: al-mawqūna is a well-guarded, secluded, veiled girl.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
quran_words: يَسِير 15x "easy"; يَسَّرَ 11x "we have made easy"; يُسْر 7x "(with) ease"; مَيْسِر 3x "and [the] games of chance"; ٱسْتَيْسَرَ 2x "(can be) obtained with ease"; تَيَسَّرَ 2x "is easy"; يُسْرَىٰ 2x "to the ease"; مَيْسَرَة 1x "ease"; مَّيْسُور 1x "gentle"
poets_named: Abū Duʾād (pre-Islamic); unnamed verse ×2; Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr (lived into Islam); Ibn Muqbil (lived into Islam); al-Farazdaq (Umayyad); Labīd (lived into Islam); Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad)
text:
Zamakhsharī's Asās al-Balāgha arranges this root by moving from literal to figurative usage.

1. Core sense — ease / being made easy. The verb (yasara / yasira, and its forms tayassara, istaysara, and the causatives yassara and yāsara) means to make a thing easy or smooth. An "easy matter" (amr yasīr) is one that is not hard; cited with the Qur'anic "with hardship comes ease." Related expressions: a departure or a great conquest "became feasible" for someone; "take the easy part (maysūr) and leave the hard part (maʿsūr)"; a matter "made easy" is maysūr, cited with the Qur'anic "a gentle word." A supplication for a pregnant woman, aysarti wa-adhkarti, wishes her an easy delivery (and a male child). "God eased him toward the easier way" (yassara li-l-yusrā) means He granted him success. "He made it ready for such-and-such" (yassarahu li-kadhā) means he prepared it — cited with Abū Duʾād's line about readying a swift, sharp-speared horseman.

2. Docile / nimble (yasar, yasarāt). A man or horse called yasar is easily led and compliant; cited with a rajaz line ("hard if you handle me harshly, easy for whoever seeks my easy side"). The legs of a mount called yasarāt are light and pliant; cited with Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr and with Ibn Muqbil, where two youthful temperaments described as yasarān are glossed "easy-going, accommodating."

3. Direction of a twist or thrust. A twisting of cord that is yasr is the opposite of shazr — done toward one's own cheek; a thrust that is yasr is delivered level with one's face. Also "an easy delivery" (wilāda yasr).

4. Small / slight. Something yasīr is little and trivial (yasura is conjugated like ḥaqura, "to be paltry"). Of a flock, yassarat means its milk and offspring grew plentiful.

5. The "left" / laterality cluster. Right-and-left pairs: yamnatan wa-yasratan (sitting to the right and left), al-yumnā / al-yusrā (right/left hand), al-maymana / al-maysara (right and left wings). To "turn one's left sides toward" someone; the imperatives yāmin / yāsir (go right / go left) and reflexives tayāmanū / tayāsarū. Someone aʿsar yasar (fem. ʿasrāʾ yasara) is ambidextrous. Aymantu / aysartu ibilī = I steered my camels right and left.

6. Maysir — the gambling game with arrows. The verb yasara means to cast the divining/gambling arrows (qidāḥ) and to play at maysir; a player is yāsir or yasar (pl. aysār). The stake is the jazūr, a slaughter-camel that the players divide and eat — cited with al-Farazdaq (an "akūlat maysir," feast-beast), Labīd (giving a "fat maysir-portion" to neighbors), and a line naming "the maysir-players of Luqmān" who provide meat in a hard winter. yasarū al-jazūr / tayāsarūhā = they portioned out the slaughter-camel among themselves.

7. Figurative extension of the gambling image (min al-majāz). From dividing the slaughter-camel comes: "they took him captive and parcelled out his wealth"; and "passions parcelled out his heart among themselves" — cited with Dhū al-Rumma's line about departing howdahs that split a lover's heart. Zamakhsharī singles this out as eloquent, lofty speech whose excellence rests entirely on the metaphor (istiʿāra).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris on the root ي ت م (y-t-m):

1. Core sense — orphanhood (yutm). For human beings, a child is "orphaned" through the loss of the father; for other animals, the term is reckoned from the loss of the mother.

2. Extended sense — anything solitary or standing alone is called yatīm. So much so that a single line of poetry is called بَيْت يَتِيم (bayt yatīm), "a solitary/orphan verse."

3. Grammar/derivation — the causative verb أَيْتَمَ (aytama) means "to make orphaned." Shāhid (poetic citation): a poet describing an archer who shot a wild she-ass (atān) and left her young orphaned — "So he fastened upon her an arrow of strong edge … and her falling dead orphaned her young ones" (the falling, wujūb, being her death).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats y-w-m as yielding a single word:

1. Core sense: الْيَوْم (al-yawm), "the day" — one unit of the أيّام (ayyām, "days").

2. Extended (metaphorical) use: the word is borrowed for a momentous or grave event. Thus the expression نِعْمَ فلانٌ في اليوم ("So-and-so is excellent on the day") is used when such an event befalls. He cites a line of verse as evidence: "Excellent is the brother of battle on the day, the yamī" — praising a man in the thick of a great occasion.

Grammatical/morphological notes:
- On that verse, one group of philologists holds the rhyme-word اليَمِي to be a metathesis (maqlūb) of the original في اليَوِمِ (fī l-yawimi).
- The plural أيّام (ayyām) derives from an original أَيْوَام (aywām), the doubled form arising through assimilation (idghām).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: زَعَمَ 13x "claim"; زَعْم 2x "by their claim"; زَعِيم 2x "(is) responsible"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives z-ʿ-m from two distinct origins: (1) speaking without soundness or certainty, and (2) standing surety for or taking charge of something.

FIRST ORIGIN — assertion without proof.
1. al-zaʿm / al-zuʿm = a claim made without any grounding. Cited: Qur'an 64:7, "Those who disbelieved claimed (zaʿama) that they will never be raised"; and a line of verse mocking the tribe Ghudāna for claiming to have a "great chief" so insignificant a locust's wing could hide him.
2. Extended idiom: zaʿama fī ghayri mazʿam = "he coveted where there was nothing to covet" (glossed as ṭamiʿa fī ghayri maṭmaʿ), with a supporting hemistich.
3. al-zaʿūm = a slaughter-camel whose fatness is doubtful, so it is felt by hand to check — i.e. a thing about which one can only guess/claim.
4. al-tazaʿʿum = lying.

SECOND ORIGIN — surety and responsibility.
5. zaʿama bi-l-shayʾ = to stand surety/guarantee for something (kafala). Cited: a verse where a man says God "guaranteed" (zaʿam) the provision of His servants, glossed as "stood surety."
6. al-zaʿāma = lordship or chieftainship, so called because the chief "takes charge of affairs" (yazʿumu bi-l-umūr = yatakaffalu bihā). Ibn Fāris notes the Qur'an gives the more authoritative witness: Yūsuf 12:72, "whoever brings it shall have a camel-load, and I am surety (zaʿīm) for it."
7. al-zaʿāma also reported as the chief's share of the spoils — or, alternatively, the choicest/best portion of the wealth. Cited: a line of Labīd contrasting the ordinary lots that "fly off odd and even" with the zaʿāma reserved for the boy.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root: ز ح ف (z-ḥ-f) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core meaning: forward propulsion — moving ahead, often with effort or by dragging oneself along the ground, rather than freely striding.

Senses recorded:

1. A body of troops advancing toward the enemy is called al-zaḥf — a mass moving forward together.

2. An infant crawling on the ground before it learns to walk is described with this verb (yazḥafu).

3. A camel that has tired out and starts dragging its foot-pad along the ground is likewise said to "yazḥafu." Such camels are called zawāḥif (plural), zāḥifa (singular) — i.e., "draggers/crawlers." Ibn Fāris cites an anonymous line of verse: "upon worn-out, dragging camels we drive them along, exhausted" (ʿalā zawāḥifa nuzjīhā maḥāsīr).

4. Locusts in their young/wingless stage (al-dabā) moving forward across the ground are also described as "zaḥafa," in the sense of advancing steadily.

5. An arrow that falls short of its target and then slides/creeps the rest of the way along the ground is called al-zāḥif.

Ibn Fāris closes with the standard formula: "And God knows best what is correct."

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
quran_words: مُزَحْزِح 1x "(will) remove him"; زُحْزِحَ 1x "is drawn away"
text:
The entry gives the verbs zaḥḥa and zaḥzaḥa with examples from the Qur'an, poetry and ḥadīth, two proposed origins for the word, and a place-name.

1. **To be moved away (zuḥziḥa).** The entry opens with "whoever is moved away (zuḥziḥa) from the Fire and admitted into the Garden has succeeded" (Q 3:185), glossing zuḥziḥa as "moved aside and put at a distance".

2. **To pull in haste (zaḥḥa).** zaḥḥa l-shayʾa, yazuḥḥuhu, zaḥḥan: he pulled the thing hastily.

3. **To push aside, put at a distance (zaḥḥa, zaḥzaḥa).** zaḥḥahu and zaḥzaḥahu: he pushed him and moved him from his place, and put him at a distance from it; the one moved "moves aside" (tazaḥzaḥa). A verse of Dhū l-Rumma: "O you who take the spirit from a body that disobeyed for a time, and who forgive sin, move me away (zaḥziḥnī) from the Fire." huwa bi-zaḥzaḥin ʿan dhālika means "he is far from that". tazaḥzaḥtu ʿani l-makān and taḥazḥaztu both mean "I moved away from the place".

4. **In ḥadīth.** "Whoever fasts a day in the way of God, God will move him (zaḥzaḥahu) seventy autumns away from the Fire": that is, God puts between him and the Fire a distance that takes seventy years to cross, since each autumn that passes marks the end of a year. ʿAlī said to Sulaymān ibn Ṣurad, who came to him after he had finished with al-Jamal: "You held aside (tazaḥzaḥta) and waited; so how did you see what God did?" Of al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī it is reported that when he had finished al-fajr he would not speak until the sun rose, "even if zuḥziḥa": even if someone tried to move him from this, unsettled him and pressed him to speak.

5. **Origin.** Al-Azharī reports that some take the word as a reduplicated form belonging with the weak roots, from zāḥa, yazīḥu, "to draw back". From zāḥa come Labīd's line "he drew back (zāḥa) from a stand like mine, and moved away" and the expressions zāḥat ʿillatuhu, "his ʿilla (ailment or excuse) went away", and azaḥtuhā, "I removed it". Others say it is taken from al-zawḥ, "hard driving", and likewise al-dhawḥ.

6. **al-Zaḥzāḥ.** A place-name, cited from a line about someone who makes threats "while he is at al-Zaḥzāḥ". The entry allows that al-zaḥzāḥ there may instead be a noun from tazaḥzuḥ, "moving away, stepping aside".

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
text:
Root ز ب د (z-b-d) — al-Zamakhshari, Asas al-Balagha.

The core sense is zabad: foam/froth on a liquid, or (for milk) the cream/butter that rises and separates. Al-Zamakhshari first lists literal uses, then figurative ones built on the image of "the light substance that rises and is cast off."

LITERAL USES
1. A "foaming sea" (bahr muzbid). The sea, a boiling cooking-pot, and the mouth of a roaring camel are all described as "foaming" (azbada) — each casts off its zabad/azbad ("foam(s)").
2. Zabad can also mean fresh butter/cream: a saying calls it "more delicious than zabad with dates," and dates are described as served with an equal measure of zabad (butter) alongside.
3. Milk "zabbada" when its cream rises to the surface. A woman "zabadat" her milk-skin when she churns it until the butter (zabad) comes out.
4. Two related verbs with different imperfect vowels: "zabadtuhu, azbuduhu" = "I fed him butter"; "zabadtu al-sawiq, azbiduhu" = "I mixed the sawiq (parched-grain meal) with butter" — hence "sawiq mazbud," creamed/buttered meal.

FIGURATIVE USES
5. "It is as though meeting you is the zubda (cream, i.e. the best part) of my life" — zubda used for "the choicest part of something."
6. "He tazabbada the oath" = he gulped it down like swallowing a lump of butter, i.e. he swore hastily and rashly — compared to the proverb "he snapped it off as the wild ass snaps off the silliyan-plant," said of doing something swiftly and completely.
7. "I zabadtuhu a blow or a throw" = I delivered it to him quickly, as if feeding him a lump of butter — i.e. I dealt with him swiftly and smoothly.
8. "Zabattuhu/zabadtuhu, azbiduhu" = I gave him a rifd, a gift or material support. On this sense, the Prophet is reported to have forbidden "the zabd of the polytheists" (accepting a gift/reward from them).
9. "So-and-so yuzabidu so-and-so" = the two trade words and match wits with each other.
10. The sidr (lote-tree) "azbada" when it puts out a white fruit resembling foam floating on water; a thing "azbada" when its whiteness becomes intense — hence "abyad muzbid," a foam-white, like yaqiq (dazzling white).
11. "Zabadtu the cotton" = I carded/teased it out.
12. Closing citation from Khudayr al-Hudhali: "the hida' (camel-driving song) is the zabad of the heart" — meaning the heart throws it off the way water throws off its foam; by this he meant how effortlessly it comes.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ز-ب-ن (z-b-n) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Ibn Fāris states the root has one core meaning: pushing/repelling (al-dafʿ). He supports this with several attested usages:

1. A she-camel that kicks away her milker is called زَبُون (zabūn).

2. War is described as "pushing/thrusting people" (تَزْبِنُ النَّاسَ) when it slams into and strikes them — giving the phrase حَرْبٌ زَبُونٌ, "a fierce, crushing war."

3. A man who guards his own side and repels attacks on himself is called ذُو زَبُّونَةٍ. A line of poetry is quoted praising a man for warding off blame with his wealth and for the "thrusts" (زَبُّونَات) of a fierce-eyed, bold man.

4. From the same idea, زَبُّونَة also came to mean kibr — pride or arrogance — because Ibn Fāris notes such a trait only appears in someone who is [otherwise] a self-defender, one who pushes back for himself.

5. The Zabāniyah (the beings mentioned in the Qurʾān as driving the people of the Fire) are named from this root because they push/drive (يَدْفَعُونَ) the people of Hell into it.

6. المُزَابَنَة (muzābanah) is a specific sale — selling fruit while it is still on top of the palm tree (unharvested) — which a ḥadīth forbids. Ibn Fāris reports scholars' explanation: this kind of sale tends to lead afterward to dispute and mutual contention (pushing against each other over the deal). He also notes that some say al-zabn, in this context, means "distance/remoteness."

7. The scorpion's zubānā (its pincer/claw) may come from the same root, since it seems to use it to defend/push away threats — though Ibn Fāris allows this could instead be an irregular (unrelated) formation.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris derives z-b-r from two separate roots.

Root 1 — making a thing firm and secure:
- زَبَرْتُ الْبِئْرَ: to line/reinforce a well with courses of stone.
- زُبْرَة: a lump or piece of iron; plural زُبَر.
- الزُّبْرَة: the chest, so called because it resembles a well built up with stone.
- Of a lion, الزُّبْرَة is the mass of hair at its elbows and chest; a broad-maned lion is أَسَدٌ مَزْبَرَانِيٌّ.
- الزَّبِير: a calamity or disaster.
- أَخَذَهُ بِزَوْبَرِهِ: he took it whole, in its entirety — cited from a line by Ibn Aḥmar (عُدَّتْ عَلِيَّ بِزَوْبَرَا), glossed as "it was ascribed to me in full."
- مَا لِفُلَانٍ زَبْرٌ: he has no sense (ʿaql) or steadiness.
- ازْبَأَرَّ الشَّعْرُ: the hair bristled and stood stiff.

Root 2 — writing and reading:
- زَبَرْتُ الْكِتَابَ: I wrote the document; from this comes الزَّبُور.
- زَبَرْتَهُ can also mean "you read it."
- The saying "أَنَا أَعْرِفُ تَزْبِرَتِي" means "I know my own writing."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris describes z-f-f as a root that indicates lightness in anything, and he ties several of its uses back to that idea.

1. **Moving fast.** zaffa l-ẓalīm (verbal noun zafīf) is said of the male ostrich when it goes fast. zaffa l-qawmu fī sayrihim means the people went fast in their journeying. He cites Q 37:94, "so they came toward him, yaziffūna (hastening)".

2. **Conducting a bride.** From this, he says, comes zuffat al-ʿarūs ilā zawjihā, "the bride was conducted to her husband".

3. **Wind.** al-zafzāfa, and likewise al-zafzaf, is a strong wind that has zafzafa, which he explains as lightness.

4. **Losing one's composure.** Of someone whose forbearance (ḥilm) has turned flighty, people say qad zaffa raʾluhu, "his young ostrich has sped off".

5. **Small feathers.** The ziff of a bird is its small feathers, so called, he says, because they are light.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
poets_named: Al-Ḥuṭayʾa (lived into Islam); unnamed verse; Al-Kumayt (Umayyad); al-Rāʿī (Umayyad); al-Jaʿdī (disputed date)
text:
Root ز ف ر (zafara) — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī

1. Core verb — zafara (yazfuru): to pant/groan with a heavy exhalation, like the groan of a mother who has lost a child (zafrat al-thaklā). The noun for this groaning sound is zafīr.

2. Heavy load: a zafr (pl. azfār) is a heavy load — called that because carrying it makes one groan (yazfuru) under the weight. The verb zafara also means simply "to carry" a load (zafarahu — yazfiruhu = he carried it).

3. Water-carriers: zawāfir are slave-women who carry water-skins — "carriers," from the same carrying sense.

4. Metaphor — one's people as one's "carriers": a man's kinship-group (ʿashīra) is called his zāfira/zawāfir, because they carry his burdens for him. A tribal chief is called the zāfir of his people (or their zāfira) before the ruler, because he bears their burdens/represents their weight.

5. Metaphor — glory's supports: a clan's glory (majd) is said to have zawāfir, meaning the pillars/props that sustain it. Al-Ḥuṭayʾa's line is cited: an inherited glory "whose zawāfir have not failed it."

6. A horse's ribs: "strong in the zawāfir" describes a horse with strong ribs (zawāfir = ribs here). A verse describing a wild ass, "strong of zawāfir," is cited to illustrate.

7. Bows: zawāfir can also mean bows (qisiyy), because a drawn bow makes a groaning/twanging sound (zafīr). Al-Kumayt's verse pictures warriors with nothing between them and the enemy but their bows, "sobbing" as they're drawn.

8. A broad-ribbed animal: an animal described as "thick of flank, great of zafra [ribcage]" is illustrated with two verses — al-Rāʿī's, comparing a fine she-camel's ribs to the vaulting of arches, and al-Jaʿdī's, describing an animal "knit upon a zafra" so that it filled out and never went lean or hollow-flanked. Al-Zamakhsharī explains the image: it is as if the animal drew one deep breath (zafara zafra) and stayed fixed that way — permanently swollen in both flanks.

9. A generous man as the sea: calling a generous man a "nawfal zāfir" likens him to the sea, which zafara-heaves and roars with its swelling waves. (The source text is slightly garbled at this final word; it is read here as zāfir to match the entry's own gloss.)

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ز هـ د (z-h-d), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: the scantiness of a thing.

1. al-zahīd — something scant/little; huwa muzhid — he possesses little wealth. A hadith is cited: "the best of people is a believing muzhid [a man of scant means]"; azhada izhādan — the corresponding verb, illustrated with a line of poetry by al-Aʿshā about a woman whose modest means keep her protected rather than exploited.
2. Al-Khalīl draws a technical distinction: al-zahādah applies to worldly matters, while al-zuhd is reserved specifically for religious asceticism. Al-Liḥyānī notes rajul zahīd — a man who eats little, also narrow-tempered.
3. Extended to terrain: al-zahīd — a valley that takes in little water; al-zahād — land that floods even from the slightest rain.
4. Closing idiom: "khudh zahda mā yakfīk" — take just the measure that suffices you. Ibn Fāris notes a report (from al-Shaybānī, whose reliability he questions) that zahadtu al-nakhla means to estimate a palm-tree's fruit-yield — flagged as anomalous, departing from the root's core "scantiness" pattern if genuinely attested.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: زَهَقَ 3x "and should depart"; زَهُوق 1x "(bound) to perish"; زَاهِق 1x "vanishing"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats z-h-q as one root meaning: to move forward, to pass on, to go past a limit. He then derives every attested usage from that single idea.

1. Passing away / departing. زَهَقَتْ نَفْسُهُ — "his soul departed." Likewise زَهَقَ الْبَاطِلُ — falsehood zahaqa, glossed by him simply as "it passed away, went off."

2. Getting out in front. زَهَقَ الْفَرَسُ أَمَامَ الْخَيْلِ — a horse zahaqa ahead of the other horses, i.e. outran and outstripped them. From the same idea: فَرَسٌ ذَاتُ أَزَاهِيقَ, a mare with azāhīq — with speed, a turn of pace, and the habit of taking the lead.

3. Overshooting. زَهَقَ السَّهْمُ — the arrow zahaqa, when it flew past the target.

4. The deep hollow. الزَّهْق is the bottom or pit of a thing; Ibn Fāris links it to the root because a falling thing plunges (yuzhaq) into it. Shāhid from Ruʾba: "as though their forelegs were plunging down into the hollow." Related to this is الزَّهُوق, a well with a far-distant bottom — a deep well.

5. Filling to overflowing. أَزْهَقَ إِنَاءَهُ, "he filled his vessel." Ibn Fāris flags this one conditionally ("if it is sound"), and explains it as belonging to the root because a full vessel runs ahead of itself, overflows, spills past the brim.

6. Fatness. الزَّاهِق is the fat animal — so called, in his explanation, because it has gone past the limit of moderation until it is packed with flesh. Hence زَهَقَ مُخُّهُ, "his marrow became packed full." Shāhid from Zuhayr, contrasting the mounts of a war-leader: "among them the lean and among them the fat, grease-laden (al-zāhiq al-zahim)."

7. A doubtful case. The phrase النَّاسُ زُهَاقُ مِائَةٍ ("the people are about a hundred") he does not force into the pattern. He offers three options: it may belong to the root, as if their number ran forward until it reached that figure; it may be a case of letter-substitution (ibdāl), a hamza replaced by qāf; or it may simply be anomalous.

Method note: Ibn Fāris's characteristic procedure is on display — one governing sense, then each idiom justified back to it, with explicit hedging ("if it is sound," "it is possible") where he is unsure of the transmitted usage.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root z-h-r — Ibn Faris, Maqayis al-Lugha

Core meaning: one underlying idea combining beauty, radiance/light, and clarity/purity.

Derived senses:
1. Az-zuhara - "the star," i.e. the planet Venus.
2. Az-zahr - the blossom/flower of any plant; verb azhara = "the plant bloomed/flowered." Some lexicographers distinguished further: nur = the white blossom, zahr = the yellow blossom. The phrase zahrat ad-dunya means "the beauty/splendor of the world (worldly life)."
3. Al-azhar - the moon (i.e., the radiant/shining one).
4. Zaharat an-nar - "the fire shone/blazed," i.e. gave off light. From this comes the phrase zaharat bika nari ("my fire has brightened on your account").

An outlier usage Ibn Faris flags as departing from the core sense: izdahartu bi-sh-shay - "I took good care of / guarded something carefully." He supports this with a hadith in which the Prophet tells Abu Qatada, about a vessel he had given him: izdahir bihi fa-inna lahu sha'nan - "Take good care of it, for it has some importance." Despite calling it an outlier, Ibn Faris then proposes it may still tie back to the root after all: to guard something carefully is, in effect, to treat it as excellent/beautiful (from husn) - and he notes a brief citation using izdaharat ("it flourished/throve") as supporting evidence for the connection.

He further suggests that al-mizhar, the word for the ud (lute), may likewise derive from this root, being close to it in meaning.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris treats z-j-j as a root (aṣl) that points to thinness in a thing.

1. **Iron point.** The zujj of a spear or of an arrow is its pointed iron end-piece; the plural is zijāj, with i after the z. Zajjajtuhu means "I fitted it with a zujj", and azjajtuhu means "I removed its zujj".

2. **Fine eyebrows.** Zajaj is the fineness and beauty of the eyebrows.

3. **Ostrich.** It is said that an azajj ostrich is one with white feathers above its eye.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: زَجْرَة 2x "(will be) a shout"; زَّٰجِرَٰت 1x "and those who drive"; زَجْر 1x "strongly"; مُزْدَجَر 1x "(is) deterrence"; ٱزْدُجِرَ 1x "and he was repelled"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats z-j-r as one root with a single core idea: intihār — sharply rebuking or shouting something away.

1. Driving an animal on by shouting: زَجَرْتُ الْبَعِيرَ حَتَّى مَضَى ("I shouted at the camel until it moved off"), imperfect أَزْجُرُهُ.
2. Restraining a person from something, with the effect registered by the reflexive form VII: زَجَرْتُ فُلَانًا عَنِ الشَّيْءِ فَانْزَجَرَ ("I checked so-and-so from the thing, and he desisted" — i.e. he was deterred and stopped).
3. الزَّجُور (fem. intensive pattern faʿūl) as a camel term: the she-camel that "recognises with her eye and rejects with her nose" — she takes the young one by sight but refuses it by smell.

The entry is terse and gives no poetic or Qur'anic citations; both the animal-driving and the human-restraining uses are held together under the one sense of shouting off / repelling.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib treats z-j-w through the verbal noun al-tazjiya, which he defines as pushing a thing so that it moves along, driven.

1. **Driving along by pushing.** His examples are urging on an inferior camel and the wind driving the clouds. He cites two Qur'anic uses of yuzjī: yuzjī saḥāban, "He drives clouds along" (Q 24:43), and rabbukumu lladhī yuzjī lakumu l-fulka fī l-baḥr, "your Lord is the One who drives the ships along for you on the sea" (Q 17:66).

2. **Expressions derived from it.** rajul muzjā, literally "a man pushed along"; and azjaytu radīʾa l-tamr fa-zajā, "I pushed the inferior dates along, and they moved along".

3. **Figurative use.** He says the following are borrowed from this sense: zajā l-kharāju yazjū, "the levy moved along", and kharāj zājin, "a levy that moves along".

4. **The poetic line.** He quotes the poet: wa-ḥājatin ghayri muzjātin mina l-ḥāji, "and a need, among needs, that is not muzjāt". He explains "not muzjāt" as "not slight": a muzjāt need would be a small one that can be pushed along and driven off because little account is taken of it.
