dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: أُزْلِفَتْ 4x "and (will be) brought near"; زُلْفَىٰ 4x "surely is a near access"; زُلْفَة 2x "and (at) the approach"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the whole root z-l-f from one core idea: a forward push and an advance in the sense of coming close to something.

1. **To move forward / draw near.** ازْدَلَفَ الرَّجُلُ (izdalafa l-rajul) — the man came forward, advanced.

2. **Place-name.** Ibn Fāris explains مُزْدَلِفَة (Muzdalifa) near Mecca by this same sense: it is so called because of people's drawing near to Minā after the departure (ifāḍa) from ʿArafāt.

3. **Nearness of standing.** زُلْفَى (zulfā) = قُرْبَى, nearness — used of one person's closeness with another. His Qur'anic witness is Q "and indeed he has, with Us, zulfā."

4. **Rank / degree.** الزَّلَف and الزُّلْفَة mean a step or degree and a station or rank.

5. **Causative form.** أَزْلَفْتُ الرَّجُلَ إِلَى كَذَا — I brought the man near to such-and-such.

6. **A disputed concrete sense.** He cites an unnamed poet: "until, when the water of the cisterns had dried up / after they had been brimful, like the zalaf." Some hold zalaf here means green earthenware basins. Ibn Fāris accepts this only conditionally, and folds it back into his core sense: if so, they are named that because water does not stay put in them once they are full but pushes out over the rim.

7. **A regional term.** Some say المَزَالِف are the tracts lying between open desert and cultivated country — named, on his explanation, for their nearness to the cultivated land.

8. **Portions of the night.** الزُّلَف of the night are its successive stretches or watches, so called because each one comes close up against the next.

Method to note: at every point he tests the derived word against the single abstract sense (drawing near / pushing forward), including the two senses he reports from others rather than asserting himself.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: زَلَلْ 2x "you slip"; أَزَلَّ 1x "then made [both of] them slip"; ٱسْتَزَلَّ 1x "made them slip"
text:
Ibn Fāris calls z-l a regular root that follows a consistent analogy in the doubled form z-l-l, and likewise in every triliteral root in which zāy is followed by lām, which he counts among the remarkable features of this root.

1. **Slipping from a place.** zalla ʿan makānihi: it slipped from its place (verbal nouns zalīl and zall).

2. **Sweet water.** al-māʾ al-zulāl is fresh, sweet water, so called because its thinness lets it slip off the surface of the tongue.

3. **Error.** zalla is an error, because the one who errs has slipped from the path of what is right.

4. **Quaking.** tazalzalat al-arḍ: the earth was in commotion; zulzilat zilzālan: it was shaken.

5. **Slippery ground.** mizalla is a slippery place.

6. **The azall wolf.** The wolf called azall is the one lean in the rump (arsaḥ). Ibn al-Aʿrābī says it is named from zalla in the sense of running, and this is given as the sound derivation; a woman slight in the buttocks (raṣʿāʾ) was then likened to the wolf and called zallāʾ. Ibn Fāris adds that if azall does mean lean-rumped, as has been said, it still fits the same analogy, because the flesh has slipped away from the hindquarters, of the wolf and of the lean-rumped woman alike.

7. **Restlessness.** zulzul, one who is restless (qaliq), belongs to the same group, because he does not stay settled in his place.

8. **An exception.** Outside the pattern of the root is zalazil (household furnishings and goods), on the measure faʿalil.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ز ل م (z-l-m), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: leanness/slenderness combined with smoothness (with occasional outliers noted).

1. al-zalam/al-zulam — the divining arrow used in pre-Islamic lot-casting; the practice is named here specifically as forbidden by Qur'an 5:3, "and that you seek decision by divining arrows."
2. A citation of Labīd's poetry, "her azlām slip on the moist ground," is explained as a comparison — he means the cow's hooves, likened to divining arrows for their shape.
3. rajul muzallam — a lean man; al-zalamah — the dangling appendage on a goat's neck (a goat has two); al-zalam, in a second sense, is also the small growths behind a cloven hoof (al-zamaʿ).
4. al-muzallam, in a further extension — one poorly fed, growing lean and thin as a result.
5. The idiom "huwa al-ʿabdu zalmatan" ("he is unmistakably a slave") is explained as originally comparing someone to those small hoof-appendages — i.e. as unmistakably identifiable as its kind.
6. Closing note on al-azlam al-jadhaʿ, a name applied either to Fate/Time (al-dahr) or, in another usage, to the lion.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ز-ل-ق (z-l-q) — Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

Core idea: a single root meaning — a thing slipping or sliding away from its place. This is the source of al-zalaq, "slipperiness."

1. Miscarriage/expulsion: "azlaqati l-ḥāmil" is said of a pregnant female that expels her young [prematurely]. Ibn Fāris flags a more precise variant of this sense: it properly describes her expelling the [seminal] fluid without her womb retaining it — i.e. failing to conceive — rather than losing an already-formed fetus.

2. Al-mazlaqa / al-mazlaq: a slippery place — one where a person or animal cannot keep its footing.

3. Qur'anic citation, 68:51 — "those who disbelieve would almost make you slip with their eyes": Ibn Fāris reads this literally, not metaphorically-vague. It refers to the sheer intensity of the disbelievers' envious stare, which nearly dislodges the addressee bodily from where he stands. He supports this with a verse of poetry: "a gaze that sweeps away the footholds of the feet" — i.e. a stare so piercing it seems to knock the ground from under one's feet.

4. Al-zaliq: a term for a man who ejaculates on approaching a woman, before intercourse. Supported by a line of verse: "Indeed al-Zubayr is zaliq and zummaliq" (both words for the same condition).

5. Ibn al-Aʿrābī's addition: "zalaqa raʾsahu" means he shaved his head — a separate, unrelated usage of the same verb form.

6. In a verse of Ruʾba describing a she-camel ("as though she were dun-colored, piebald of the zalaq"), al-zalaq denotes the animal's rump/hindquarters — named this because a hand slips off it, just as rain or dew slides off it without settling.

Ibn Fāris closes with "wa-Llāhu aʿlam" (God knows best), his standard formula, not a doctrinal claim.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
quran_words: زُلْزِلُ 3x "and they were shaken"; زِلْزَال 2x "(with) its earthquake"; زَلْزَلَة 1x "(the) convulsion"
text:
Root ZLL (زلل) as recorded by Ibn Manẓūr in Lisān al-ʿArab.

1. Core sense — to slip, slide, lose footing. زَلَّ is used of an arrow sliding off a coat of mail and of a person slipping off a rock; equivalent to زَلِقَ. Causative أَزَلَّهُ عنها = "made it slip off it." Verbal nouns: زَلّ, زَلِيل, زُلُول, مَزِلَّة. Al-Farrāʾ records a second form زَلِلْت / تَزَلُّ زَلَلاً, with the nouns زَلَّة and زِلِّيلى. Al-Liḥyānī gives three verbal nouns for slipping in mud.

2. Extension to speech and conduct — a "slip." Al-Tahdhīb distinguishes: of the foot one says زَلَّ; of an utterance, or of a fault, one says زَلَّ زَلَّة. Cited verse: "Would that you had laid the slip on someone other than me…" One also زَلَّ in one's opinion and one's dīn (way). Causatives: أَزَلَّه (made him slip) and اسْتَزَلَّه (drew him into slipping).

3. Qurʾānic shāhid. The entry notes the two readings of Q 2:36 — فأَزَلَّهما الشيطانُ عنها ("Satan made the two slip from it") and فأَزالَهُما ("removed the two"). Ibn Manẓūr reports three explanations of the first: that Satan caused them to incur the زَلَّة; Thaʿlab's, that he made them slip in judgement/opinion; and al-Liḥyānī's simple أَزَلَّهما. A report about ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Sarḥ uses the same verb: Satan "carried him into the slip," glossed here as error and offence.

4. Slippery places. مَقامٌ زُلُّ, a standing-place where one slips; زُحْلُوقة زُلٌّ, a slide (with a verse, and al-Kumayt's line making youthful folly "a slippery slide"). مَزَلَّة / مَزِلَّة (both vowellings attested) = the slippery ground, the site of slipping — pattern مَفْعَلة from زَلَّ يَزِلُّ. مكان زَلُول likewise; al-Rāʿī's verse describes a place so slick a tick cannot rest on it. In a description of the Ṣirāṭ it is called مَزِلَّة مَدْحَضَة, i.e. feet slide on it and do not hold. A grammatical note from Ibn Sīdah on a line with مَزِلّ: it must be a substitute for سُلَّم rather than an adjective, since مَفْعِل does not occur as an adjectival pattern; alternatively read مُزِلّ.

5. Slipping away, being lost. زَلَّ عُمْرُه — his lifetime slipped away (with a verse on "the life that slipped away"). قوس زَلاّء, a bow the arrow slips off from, because it releases fast. زَلَّت الدراهم زُلولاً — coins poured out, or fell short in weight; دِرْهَم زالٌّ. In a weighing, في ميزانه زَلَلٌ = a shortfall (from al-Liḥyānī).

6. Transferred sense: passing a benefit on. أَزَلَّ إِليه نَعْمَةً = conferred a favour; ḥadīth: "whoever has a favour passed to him, let him thank for it." Ibn al-Athīr derives this from زَلِيل, the movement of a body from place to place, borrowed for a benefit moving from giver to receiver; Abū ʿUbayd glosses it as bestowal. Kuthayyir's verse praises a woman "for the favours she passed to us." المُزَلِّل = one lavish with gifts. Related: أَزْلَلْت فلاناً إِلى القوم, put him forward.

7. Food senses of زَلَّة. اتَّخَذَ فلان زَلَّةً = he made a feast for people; Ibn Shumayl: كنا في زَلَّة فلان = at his wedding feast. Al-Layth calls زَلَّة an Iraqi usage for food carried from the table to a relative or friend, derived from the idea of doing a kindness. Abū ʿAmr: only أَزْلَلْت له زَلّة is said, not زَلَلْت. Also listed: زِلِّيَّة, singular of زَلاليّ (rugs).

8. Lightness and speed. زَلِيل = light walking; زَلَّ زَلِيلاً وزُلُولاً = passed by swiftly. الأَزَلُّ = the swift (Ibn al-Aʿrābī). غلامٌ زُلْزُلٌ = a nimble boy. In a rajaz line, زَلَلُ النِّيَّة is explained by Ibn al-Aʿrābī either as the remoteness of the destination sought for pasture, or as people slipping from place to place in search of herbage (النِّيَّة = the place one intends to travel to).

9. Water. زَلَّ الماءُ في حلقه زُلولاً — the water slid down his throat. ماءٌ زُلال / زَلِيل: quick to go down; زُلال is also glossed cold, sweet, clear, pure — "the pure of anything" (Dhū al-Rumma's verse likens hides to pure gold). Abū Shanbal's ما زَلْزَلْت ماءً... = "I never drank"; Abū Manṣūr explains it as never let water slide down his throat.

10. Unrelated-looking lexical items grouped by form. الزَّلَزِل (pattern فَعَلِل) = household goods and furnishings; Shamir also gives الزَّلَز; the Kitāb al-Yāqūt pairs it with قُثْرُد and خُنْثُر. الزُّلْزُل = a skilled drummer.

11. زَلْزَلة / زِلْزال — shaking. The base sense is to shake a thing violently; زَلْزَلَ اللهُ الأَرْضَ … فَتَزَلْزَلَتْ. On Q 99:1 (إِذا زُلْزِلَتِ الأَرضُ زِلْزالَها), Abū Isḥāq: the meaning is "shaken with a violent shaking"; the reading is زِلْزال with kasra, though زَلْزال is possible in speech. Grammatical point: فَعْلال with fatḥa occurs only in doubled roots (صِلْصال, زَلْزال); the kasra form is the verbal noun, the fatḥa form the substantive — parallel to وِسواس (maṣdar) vs وَسْواس (noun).

12. زَلْزلة as fear and instability. Ibn al-Anbārī, on "a zalzala befell the people," takes it as frightening and warning, citing وزُلْزِلوا حتى يقول الرسول. الزَّلازل = hardships, terrors (verse of ʿImrān b. Ḥiṭṭān). Some derive زَلْزلة from زَلَل in opinion: زُلْزِل القومُ = they were turned from steadiness and fear was cast into their hearts; hence أُزِلَّ الرجل في رأيه حتى زَلَّ. The prayer "O God, rout the Confederates and shake them" is read as making their affair unsettled and unstable. In ʿAṭāʾ's ḥadīth, no shaking of a measure so it packs down and holds more. تَزَلْزَلت نفسُه = his soul quaked/recoiled in his breast at death (verse of Abū Dhuʾayb, followed by a long grammatical excursus on eliding one of two verbs even when they differ, on the principle that a word may run in the course of its opposite as it does of its like). تَرَكْت القومَ في زُلْزُول = left them in fighting (Shamir notes Abū Saʿīd did not know this).

13. إِزِلْزِلْ — a word uttered during an earthquake. Ibn Jinnī argues it cannot belong to the letters of زَلْزَلة, since quadriliterals take no initial augment except in nouns formed on their verbal nouns (مُدَحْرج); it must therefore come from أَزْل, on the pattern فِعِلْعِل. (The text has a lacuna in his reasoning.)

14. الأَزَلُّ as a bodily and animal epithet. Slender or light in the hips; = أَرْسَح (small-buttocked), or worse — one whose waist-wrapper will not stay up. Feminine زَلاّء: a woman with no buttocks (with a satirical verse). السِّمْعُ الأَزَلُّ: per al-Jawharī, the lean-haunched wolf said to be born of wolf and hyena, the epithet being inseparable from it as "lame" is of the hyena; proverb: "keener of hearing than the azall wolf." ʿAlī's letter to Ibn ʿAbbās compares seizing the community's wealth to "the azall wolf snatching a bleeding goat"; Ibn al-Athīr notes أَزَلّ is originally "small-rumped," but of the wolf means swift, possibly from زَلَّ زَلِيلاً "he ran," and that "bleeding" is specified because the wolf loves blood. Al-Tahdhīb: زَلَل is the verbal noun of أَزَلّ, plural زُلّ. In one verse Ibn al-Aʿrābī insists أَزَلّ means "moving lightly and swiftly," not "lean-haunched"; another authority takes it as an epithet of the wolf to which the horse is likened.

15. Minor notes. Ibn al-Aʿrābī: زُلَّ (passive) = it was ground fine; زَلَّ = he erred. Al-Farrāʾ: الزِّلَّة = smooth stones.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
text:
Root ز-م-ه-ر (zmhr) — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311 CE)

1. Al-zamharīr (الزَّمْهَرِيرُ) — intense, bitter cold. Illustrated with a verse of al-Aʿshā describing sheltered women who "have seen neither sun nor zamharīr" — i.e., never exposed to either scorching heat or bitter cold.

2. Al-zamharīr, in a second notice, is described as what God has prepared as a punishment for the disbelievers in the Hereafter — the entry states this as the lexicographer's report, without further elaboration.

3. Izmaharra (ازْمَهَرَّ), said of a day: it turned intensely cold. Verbal noun: izmihrār.

4. Zamharat / izmaharratā (زَمْهَرَتْ / ازْمَهَرَّتا), said of the eyes: they reddened from anger. The one so affected is called al-muzmahirr (المُزْمَهِرُّ) — "one whose eyes have reddened."

5. Izmaharrati l-kawākib (ازْمَهَرَّتِ الكواكب), said of the stars: they glimmered/flashed. A further note repeats this sense with slightly different wording — the stars "shone and glittered," and some say their light intensified.

6. Al-muzmahirr also means intensely angry — supported by a report about ʿUmar being "muzmahirr" toward a disbeliever, glossed as "fiercely angry at him." A related expression: wajhun muzmahirr, a scowling, grim face.

7. Al-muzmahirr, in yet another sense, describes one who bares the teeth in laughter or smiling.

Closing note: izmihrār in the eye is associated with anger and intensity/harshness.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) derives the root ز-م-ل (z-m-l) from two distinct original senses:

**1. Carrying a heavy load**
- الزَّامِلَة (al-zāmilah): a pack-camel a man depends on, loaded with his baggage/goods.
- ازْدَمَلْتُ الشَّيْءَ ("I izdamal-ed the thing") = I carried it.
- عِيَالَاتٌ أَزْمَلَة ("azmilah dependents") = a large, numerous household — likened to piled-up loads, i.e., people who are themselves a burden and cannot even support themselves.
- الزُّمَّيْل (al-zummayl): a weak man who, when trouble strikes, "wraps himself up" (تَزَمَّلَ, tazammala) — piling on garments until he resembles a bundled load. Ibn Fāris cites a line by the poet Uḥayḥah mocking a "lazy zummayl" among young men who is no match for the speaker.
- الْمُزَامَلَة (al-muzāmalah): two riders balanced together on a camel.

**2. A sound**
- الْأَزْمَل (al-azmal) = a sound/clamor, illustrated by a poetic line describing a sound heard "after the still coolness of the evenings."

**Outlier (not from either root)**
- الْإِزْمِيل (al-izmīl) = a blade or knife.
- From this comes the idiom أَخَذْتُ الشَّيْءَ بِأَزْمَلِهِ ("I took the thing with its azmal"), meaning I took it whole — the entirety of it.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) treats ز-م-ر (z-m-r) as having two distinct underlying senses:

**1. Scarcity/scantiness (of something)**
- زَمَر (zamar) = scantiness of hair.
- زَمِر (zamir) = a man scant of hair.
- The phrase رَجُلٌ زَمِرُ الْمُرُوءَةِ ("a man zamir of muruwwah") means a man with little manly virtue/chivalry — the word extended metaphorically from hair to character.

**2. A category of sound**
- زَمْر / زِمَار (zamr / zimār) = the cry of the ostrich, with the verb زَمَرَتْ تَزْمُرُ/تَزْمِرُ زِمَارًا ("it cried out") attested in both imperfect vocalizations.
- From this sound-sense comes زُمْرَة (zumrah), "a group/company" — Ibn Fāris derives it here because a gathered group produces a collective clamor/noise (جَلَبَة وَزِمَار), not from the scarcity-sense.

**A note on الزَّمَّارَة in a ḥadīth**
A ḥadīth forbids "the earnings of al-zammārah." Transmitters gloss zammārah as al-zāniyah (the adulteress/fornicatress). Ibn Fāris speculates that, if that gloss is correct, her voice/tone may have been compared to zamr (piping/musical sound) — hence the name. But he also notes an alternative reading: the word is really الرَّمَّازَة (al-rammāzah, from the different root r-m-z), "the woman who signals to men with her eyebrows." He states this second explanation is the more likely one.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Root ز ن م (z-n-m), Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha

One core meaning: the attachment of one thing to another.

1. al-zanīm — one falsely/illegitimately attached to a lineage (an impostor claimed as kin), likewise al-muzannam; both likened to the two zanamahs (pendant ear-flaps) of a she-goat.
2. al-zanamah — the small piece of flesh dangling in the throat.
3. Illustrated with a line of poetry describing a zanīm as one "added on" by men claiming him as kin, the way extra shanks are stitched onto the surface of a hide.

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
quran_words: زَانِيَة 3x "and the fornicatress"; زَان 3x "a fornicator"; يَزْنُ 2x "they will commit adultery"; زِّنَىٰ 1x "adultery"
poets_named: Al-Aʿshā (lived into Islam); al-Farazdaq (Umayyad); Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam); unnamed verse
text:
Ibn Manẓūr's article on z-n-y covers two groups of meaning: al-zinā (unlawful intercourse) with its forms and derived expressions, and a separate group built on narrowness and shortness.

**1. Al-zinā: forms and dialects.** The noun is spelled two ways: short, al-zinā, and long, al-zināʾ. The verb is zanā, yaznī, used of both man and woman; zānā (verbal noun muzānāh, zināʾ) and zannā mean the same. A woman who tuzānī is one who practises harlotry. Al-Aʿshā's half-line "either marriage, or uzannu" is explained by some commentators as uzannī, "I commit zinā".

According to al-Liḥyānī the short form is the dialect of the Ḥijāz, and the Qur'an uses it: "and do not come near al-zinā" (Q 17:32). The long form is the dialect of Banū Tamīm; al-Ṣiḥāḥ assigns it to the people of Najd. Lines by al-Farazdaq ("whoever commits zinā, his zināʾ becomes known") and al-Jaʿdī are cited for the long form. The relative adjectives are zinawī from the short form and zināʾī from the long.

**2. Accusing someone of zinā.** Zannāhu (verbal noun tazniya) means to call someone a fornicator, saying "O zānī!", that is, to accuse him (qadhf).

**3. Figurative use for a place.** A ḥadīth speaks of "Constantinople the fornicatress", meaning its people. The article compares Q 21:11, "how many a town that was wrongdoing", where the town stands for its people.

**4. A rare elative.** Al-Liḥyānī reports that the daughter of al-Khuss was asked "mā aznāki?", taken to mean "what brought you to zinā?" She answered, "nearness of the pillow and long intimacy." He says the expression was heard only in this story.

**5. Legitimacy of birth.** Ibn zanya or ibn zinya (the fatḥa form is better) means a child of zinā. It is the opposite of li-rishda or li-rashda, "of lawful birth". Al-Farrāʾ gives li-ghayya, li-zanya and li-ghayri rashda, all with fatḥa. Al-Kisāʾī allows both fatḥa and kasra in rashda and zinya, but only fatḥa in ghayya. A child born of zinā is also called li-zanya.

**6. Al-zanya as "last-born child".** With fatḥa or kasra, al-zanya also means the last child of a man and a woman, like al-ʿijza. A tribe is called Banū al-Zanya for this reason. When a delegation led by Mālik ibn Thaʿlaba introduced themselves to the Prophet as "Banū al-Zanya", he replied, "Rather, you are Banū al-Rishda." The article explains that he said this to clear them of the suggestion of zinā in the name. Al-rashda is the more eloquent of the two forms. Banū Zinya is also named as a tribe.

**7. A proverb.** "Neither is her chastity chastity, nor her zinā zinā." Abū Zayd says it is used of someone who holds back from good, then falls short, and keeps to no steady course.

**8. Shortness and narrowness.** The female monkey is called zannāʾa, and al-zanāʾ means "short". Abū Dhuʾayb speaks of animals pushing their heads into "the short shade". The article says the root sense of al-zanāʾ is narrowness. Examples:
- a ḥadīth forbids praying while zanāʾ, that is, while holding back urine;
- al-Akhṭal uses zanāʾ for a narrow, dark, dusty pit;
- zanā al-mawḍiʿ, yaznū, "the place became narrow", is a variant of yaznaʾu;
- a ḥadīth says the Prophet loved only the aznaʾ (narrowest) of this world;
- Ibn al-Aʿrābī transmits wiʿāʾ zanī, "a narrow vessel", without hamza.

Al-zanʾ is glossed as al-zunuww in a mountain. Zannā ʿalayhi means to press hard on someone, as in the verse "al-Ḥārith ibn Jabala pressed hard upon his father and then killed him". The article takes this verse as evidence that the hamza of al-zanāʾ is originally a yāʾ.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text:
Ibn Fāris classifies ز-ق-م (z-q-m) as a "minor root" — one with only a small, tightly-related cluster of derivations — whose core sense is a particular manner/kind of eating.

1. الزَّقْم (al-zaqm) — "the act [of eating]," specifically the eating of al-zaqqūm (a named food/plant). Cited from al-Khalīl.
2. الِازْدِقَام (al-izdiqām) — swallowing.
3. تَزَقَّمَ (tazaqqama) — reported by Ibn Duraid from some Arabic speakers: said of someone who drank milk to excess, i.e. overindulged in it.

So the root's unifying thread, per this entry, is eating/swallowing done in a marked or excessive manner, rather than ordinary neutral eating.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: زَرْع 10x "crops"; تَزْرَعُ 2x "you will sow"; زُّرَّاع 1x "the sowers"; زَّٰرِعُون 1x "the ones who grow"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root z-r-ʿ from a single core idea: causing a thing to grow.

1. زَرْع (zarʿ): the familiar word for a crop or sown growth. The place where it is grown is called المُزْدَرَع (al-muzdaraʿ), the cultivated field.

2. On the core meaning, he cites al-Khalīl: the underlying sense of zarʿ is "causing to grow" (tanmiya).

3. He also records a variant usage — that zarʿ means the act of casting seed into the ground.

4. And zarʿ is used as a noun for the plant that has sprouted (the result, not just the act).

He notes that all these uses trace back to one and the same root idea.

Finally, he adds that زَارِع (Zāriʿ) is used as the name of a dog.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root ز ر ق (z-r-q) — al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān (early 11th c. CE)

1. Core sense — a colour: zurqah is a colour between white and black — a blue-grey hue. Applied to the eye: zaraqat ʿaynuhu ("his eye turned this blue-grey colour"), with the nouns zurqah and zaraqān for the condition.

2. Qur'anic use (Ṭāhā 20:102), "zurqan yatakhāfatūn": al-Rāghib glosses zurqan here not as literal eye-colour but as "blind, their eyes having no light in them" — the word for blue-grey eyes extended to describe eyes gone sightless.

3. Az-zuraq is given as the name of a bird (the entry does not explain the naming, though it presumably echoes the colour sense).

4. A separate verb, zaraqa al-ṭāʾiru – yazriqu ("the bird zaraqa," imperfect yazriqu), is cited but left unglossed — the entry records the form without stating its meaning.

5. zaraqahu bi-l-mizrāq ("he zaraqa'd him with the mizrāq," a small javelin) is explained as ramāhu bihi, "he threw/cast it at him" — the throwing action behind the weapon called mizrāq.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
text: Ibn Faris's Maqayis al-Lugha entry for the root z-r-y. Core sense: this root, built from za, ra, and a weak third letter, conveys the idea of belittling something and treating it with contempt or disdain. Usage: (a) zaraytu alayhi, meaning I found fault with or disparaged him, used when criticizing or blaming someone. (b) azraytu bihi, meaning I belittled or slighted him, meaning I diminished him or held him in low regard. The entry is brief. It states one governing sense, contempt or disdain, and gives two related verb forms expressing it: a bare form used for finding fault with someone, and a causative form used for disparaging or diminishing someone.

dictionary: Tāj — Tāj al-ʿArūs, Murtaḍā al-Zabīdī (d. 1791)
text:
ROOT z-w-d (زود) — Tāj al-ʿArūs (al-Zabīdī, d. 1791 CE)

1. Core meaning: al-zawd is laying in provisions. Al-zād (provisions) means food for a journey or for staying at home alike — plural azwād, or (irregularly) azwida.

2. Al-mizwad = the bag/container that holds provisions.

3. Verb forms: azadtuhu / zawwadtuhu ("I provisioned him"); tazawwada ("he took provisions for himself"). Cited in verse from Abū Khirāsh, using tuzīdu ("you provision [someone]").

4. Figurative/idiomatic uses:
   - "Riqāb al-mazāwid" ("necks of the provision-sacks") — a nickname for non-Arabs, explained either by the length of their necks or their thickness (as if stuffed full like a provision-bag).
   - "Zubayda is not to be compared to Zuwayda" — a saying about a woman named Zuwaydah of the Muhallabid family (Āl Abī Ṣufra, of al-Azd).
   - "He is the caravan's zād (provision)" — and "Azwād al-rakb" ("provisions of the caravan") became the nickname of three Qurashī men (Musāfir ibn Abī ʿAmr, Zamʿa ibn al-Aswad, and Abū Umayya ibn al-Mughīra, father of Umm Salama), because anyone who travelled with them needed no provisions of his own — they fed and supplied him. A proverb says "more hospitable than Zād al-rakb," referring to one or to all three of them.

5. Two men named Zawwād are noted as ḥadīth-transmitters (a scholar from Baṣra and one known via Abū ʿAlī ibn al-Ṣawwāf), with minor manuscript variation on one name.

6. Zād al-rakb was also the name of a famous horse — one of the horses the Qur'an calls "standing, excellent runners" (Q38:31) — so named because it could outrun game; a rider on it could hunt enough for the whole travelling party. Solomon reportedly gave this horse to the tribe of al-Azd when they visited him, and it is said every Arabian horse descends from its offspring.

7. Dhū Zūd — personal name Saʿīd, a Ḥimyarite chieftain to whom Abū Bakr wrote during the second wave of the Ridda (apostasy movement) in Yemen.

8. Extended/metaphorical sense (appendix): any deed a person carries away with him — good or bad — is metaphorically called zād ("provision"). This is the sense behind the Qur'anic verse: "Provision yourselves, for indeed the best provision is taqwā" (Q2:197). Related expressions cited: "he provisioned himself from this world for the next"; "I furnished him with a letter [as his 'provision']"; "he obtained a letter from the commander to his agent"; and, figuratively, "he came away from me with a spear-thrust between his ears and a shameful brand between his eyes" (i.e., a wound/mark he 'took away' as if it were provision).

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: زَوْج 76x "kind"; زُوِّجَتْ 5x "and we will marry them"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the root z-w-j from a single core idea: the pairing or bringing-together of one thing alongside another.

1. Spouse. From this core sense, al-zawj is the woman's husband, and the woman in turn is the zawj (spouse) of her mate — Ibn Fāris notes this latter application (the woman as zawj) is the eloquent, chaste usage. He cites Q 2:35, "Dwell, you and your zawj, in the Garden."

2. Male-and-female pair. One says a man "has two zawj-s of pigeons," meaning one male and one female — each member of a matched pair is a zawj.

3. Kind or color of plant. For Q 22:5, "of every splendid zawj," describing vegetation, he reports the view that zawj here means color ("of every splendid color"). He judges this consistent with the root idea, since a color is coupled with another color close to it.

4. Litter-covering. By extension, the patterned cloth thrown over a camel-litter (hawdaj) is called a zawj, because it is the "mate" to the frame it is laid upon. He cites a verse of Labīd describing such a shrouded litter with its zawj covering, curtain, and screen.

Throughout, the unifying principle Ibn Fāris draws is muqāranah — one thing set in correspondence with another.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Al-Rāghib treats z-w-l as a thing leaving the course or place it held, and adds a grammatical discussion of mā zāla / lā yazālu ("not cease, keep on").

1. **Moving off one's course.** Zāla, yazūlu, zawālan: a thing leaves its course, veering away from it. The causative forms are azaltuhu and zawwaltuhu ("I made it move away"). Qur'anic examples: God "holds the heavens and the earth lest they move away (an tazūlā), and if they were to move away (laʾin zālatā) …" (Q 35:41); "that the mountains should be moved away by it (li-tazūla minhu al-jibāl)" (Q 14:46).

2. **Zawāl presupposes earlier fixity.** The word is used of something that was previously fixed in place. To the objection that people speak of the sun's zawāl although the sun is never fixed, al-Rāghib answers that they said so because they believed the sun held still in the middle of the sky at midday. Hence the expressions "the midday's stander stood" (qāma qāʾimu al-ẓahīra) and "the day travelled on" (sāra al-nahār).

3. **A transitive verb: zālahu, yazīluhu, zaylan ("he removed it").** A poet's phrase "zāla zawālahā" is explained as "may God take away her movement", with zawāl here meaning moving about (taṣarruf). It is also said to be like the expression "may God silence his faint sound" (askata Allāhu naʾmatahu). Another line reads: "whenever she sees us, her zawīl departs from her." Those who hold that zāla does not take an object say that zawālahā is an accusative verbal noun.

4. **Separating.** Tazayyalū (Q 48:25) means "they separated". In "then We separated them from one another" (fa-zayyalnā baynahum, Q 10:28), the doubled form expresses intensity. This holds for those who take the simple verb as transitive ("to separate"), on the pattern of miztuhu / mayyaztuhu ("I set it apart").

5. **Mā zāla and lā yazālu: "did not cease, will not cease".** These expressions have a special use and work like kāna: the subject is nominative and the predicate accusative. Al-Rāghib takes them to come from the form with yāʾ, since people say zayyaltu, and gives their meaning as that of mā bariḥtu ("I did not cease"). Qur'anic examples: "and they will not cease to differ" (Q 11:118); "their building will not cease …" (Q 9:110); "and those who have rejected will not cease …" (Q 13:31); "and you did not cease to be in doubt" (Q 40:34).

6. **Why "mā zāla … illā" is not said.** One cannot say "mā zāla Zaydun illā munṭaliqan" the way one says "mā kāna Zaydun illā munṭaliqan" ("Zayd was nothing but going off"). His reason: zāla already carries a negative sense, being the opposite of fixity, and mā or lā adds a second negation; two negations make an affirmation. So mā zāla behaves like an affirmative kāna, and since "kāna Zaydun illā munṭaliqan" is not said, neither is "mā zāla Zaydun illā munṭaliqan".

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: زُّور 4x "and a lie"; تَّزَٰوَرُ 1x "inclining away"; زُرْ 1x "you visit"
text:
Ibn Fāris derives the whole root z-w-r from one basic idea: inclining, swerving, turning aside from one direction toward another.

1. زُور (zūr) — falsehood. Named so because it leans away from the path of truth.

2. زَوَّرَ / تَزْوِير (zawwara / tazwīr) — to falsify or dress something up. Extended even to "he zawwara the thing in his own mind," i.e. he composed or prepared it, because he shapes it away from its plain form into a form the listener is likelier to accept.

3. زُور (zūr) as a name for an idol. Ibn Fāris judges this a correct application of the root sense. Shāhid: "They came with their two zūrs and we came with al-Aṣamm."

4. زَوَر (zawar) — a bend, an inclination; ازْوَرَّ عَنْ (izwarra ʿan) means to swerve away from something.

5. زَائِر (zāʾir) — a visitor, belonging to the same idea: in coming to you he has turned aside from everyone else.

6. زُوَيْر (zuwayr) — the chief of a people, the one who handles their affairs, because they turn aside from all others toward him. Shāhid: a verse describing merciless men "driving to death the obstinate chief."

7. زَوْر (zawr) in "a man who has no zawr" — he has no settled judgement to fall back on.

8. تَزْوِير (tazwīr) — in another use: showing honour to a visitor.

9. زَوْر (zawr) — a party of visitors; the same form serves for one person, two, a group, and for women. Shāhid: a verse likening women's swaying gait to visiting girls approaching one another.

10. زِوَرّ (ziwarr) — "strong, mighty." Ibn Fāris treats this as coming instead from زَوْر (zawr), the upper chest, and marks it as anomalous (shādhdh), outside the root-principle he has laid down.

dictionary: Mufradāt — al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (d. 1020)
text:
Root z-kh-r-f, as treated by al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī in his lexicon of Qurʾānic vocabulary.

1. Core sense: al-zukhruf is decoration that has been prettified or gilded — ornamentation applied to make something look fine.

2. Extended sense — gold: because of that core sense, gold itself is called zukhruf.

Qurʾānic citations given for these senses:
- "The earth has taken on its zukhruf [ornament]" (Yūnus 10:24) — the earth's adornment.
- "a house of zukhruf" (al-Isrāʾ 17:93) — which al-Rāghib glosses as ornamented (gilded) gold.
- "and zukhruf [ornament]" (al-Zukhruf 43:35).

3. Applied to speech: "zukhruf al-qawl, as delusion" (al-Anʿām 6:112) is glossed as the prettified, dressed-up parts of speech — words given an attractive surface, on the same metaphor as gilding.

dictionary: Asās — Asās al-Balāgha, al-Zamakhsharī (d. 1144)
text:
Root z-y-d, as recorded by al-Zamakhsharī, who arranges usage from the literal into the figurative.

Literal, core sense — "to increase, grow, add, exceed":
1. Of a thing growing of itself: زاد ("increased") — of water or wealth; وازداد, "it grew"; وازداد الأمر صعوبة, "the matter grew harder."
2. Of causing growth: God "increased him in wealth"; "he added to his wealth"; ازدد من الخير, "increase yourself in good."
3. Of exceeding: "he exceeded what he intended"; "he exceeded the thing by its double"; "I took it for a dirham or more."
4. istazāda = "to seek increase." A saying of exhaustive completeness: "there is nothing to be added to what you have done, no increase possible upon it."

Commercial/bidding uses:
5. tazāyada/tazayyada al-siʿr = a price "rose, mounted"; people "bid one another up" over goods until the price peaked; muzāyada = one buyer outbidding another (an auction sense).

Extended physical uses:
6. yatazayyad fī ḥadīthihi = "he embellishes/exaggerates in his talk."
7. tazayyadat al-nāqa = a she-camel "stretched herself out," extending her neck and moving beyond her ordinary pace, "as if swimming with her rider." A verse illustrates the long, rising neck drawn out "like the folds of a plaited, braided cord."

Nominal derivatives:
8. mazāda (pl. mazāyid) = a large leather water-bag; it is the rāwiya enlarged by a third hide "added" (yuzād) between the two — the root sense being the added panel.
9. ziyādat al-kabid = "the appendage of the liver," a lobe hanging attached to it (pl. ziyāʾid); given in the saying "the child is the liver of one who has a child, and the grandchild is the liver's appendage."
10. A dictum: "if you pay zakāt on your wealth it is zīd — i.e. it increases greatly." (Al-Zamakhsharī cites this as a saying about wealth growing; he does not define zakāt itself.)

Figurative (majāz), explicitly marked:
11. yastazīd someone = to reckon him to have fallen short of what was due and to complain of him; such a person is a mustazīd, and a "letter of istizāda" is a written complaint demanding more.
12. hum zīd ʿalā miʾa = "they exceed a hundred, and more." Cited from Dhū al-Iṣbaʿ al-ʿAdwānī: "you are a company exceeding a hundred; so gather your whole affair and scheme against me" — zīd here glossed as "exceeding."

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: زَاغَ 6x "deviated"; أَزَاغَ 2x "(was caused to) deviate"; زَيْغ 1x "(is) perversity"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats z-y-gh as a single root whose core idea is a thing inclining or swerving off straight.

1. Basic verb: زَاغَ / يَزِيغُ / زَيْغًا (zāgha) — to incline, lean, swerve aside.

2. Form V verbal noun التَّزَيُّغ (al-tazayyugh) — swaying, tilting to one side.

3. Applied to people: قَوْمٌ زَاغَةٌ (qawmun zāghah), glossed by him as زَائِغُونَ (zāʾighūn) — people who swerve or deviate. زَاغَة functions here as a plural of the active participle.

4. Applied to the sun: زَاغَتِ الشَّمْسُ (zāghat al-shams) — the sun declined, i.e. when it has tilted past its height and the shade has come back.

5. Qur'anic citation: he adduces 61:5, {فَلَمَّا زَاغُوا أَزَاغَ اللَّهُ قُلُوبَهُمْ} — "when they swerved, God made their hearts swerve" — as an instance of the same inclining sense, here of hearts, without further comment.

6. An excluded form: تَزَيَّغَتِ الْمَرْأَةُ (tazayyaghat al-marʾah), said of a woman adorning herself, he assigns not to this root's meaning but to إِبْدَال (letter-substitution) — the ghayn stands in for an original nūn, so the word belongs with تَزَيَّنَتْ (z-y-n, "to adorn").

dictionary: Lisān — Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr (d. 1311)
quran_words: زَالَت 8x "they will cease"; زَيَّلْ 1x "then we will separate"; تَزَيَّلُ 1x "they had been apart"
poets_named: al-Kumayt (Umayyad); al-Mutalammis (pre-Islamic); Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam); Ibn al-Aʿrābī (unnamed); Dhū al-Rumma (Umayyad); unnamed verse
text:
Root ZYL (زيل), as recorded by Ibn Manẓūr.

1. Core sense — to separate one thing from another. زِلْتُ الشيءَ أَزِيلُه زَيْلاً (ziltu l-shayʾa, azīluhu, zaylan) means "I set it apart, I sorted it out from something else." Al-Jawharī treats it as an alternative to أَزَلْتُه (azaltuhu, "I removed it") and glosses it as "I removed the thing from its place"; Ibn Barrī says the correct wording is زِلْتُه زَيْلاً meaning azaltuhu. Al-Jawharī elsewhere glosses it plainly as مِزْتُه وفَرَّقْتُه — "I set it apart and divided it."

2. The full verbal family, per Ibn Sīdah and others: زَالَ الشيءَ زَيْلاً, أَزَالَه إِزَالةً/إِزَالاً (the second verbal noun from al-Liḥyānī), and زَيَّلَه فَتَزَيَّل — all meaning "he divided it, and it became divided."

3. Morphological argument on the Qur'anic form. The verse فَزَيَّلْنا بَيْنَهم ("so We separated between them") is of the faʿʿala pattern, proved by its verbal noun تَزْيِيلاً (tazyīlan); had it been the fayʿala pattern the verbal noun would have been زَيَّلَة (zayyalatan). The doubled form is used because the action is done many times over; for a small-scale act one would simply say زِلْ ذا من ذا ("sort this from that"), parallel to مِزْ ذا من ذا. A variant reading فَزَايَلْنا بينهم is also recorded, the faʿʿala/fāʿala alternation being like لا تُصَعِّر / لا تُصَاعِرْ and عَقَّدَ / عَاقَدَ.

4. A disputed root-assignment. Al-Farrāʾ (reported by al-Azharī) holds that fazayyalnā does not belong to z-w-l (زُلْتُ) but to z-y-l (زِلْتُ … أَزِيلُ), "to separate this from that and set this apart from that." Al-Qutaybī, by contrast, glossed fazayyalnā as "we separated" but derived it from زَالَ يَزُولُ / أَزَلْتُه. Abū Manṣūr calls this a mistake: al-Qutaybī failed to distinguish zāla/yazūlu from zāla/yazīlu as al-Farrāʾ had, and although his prose style was eloquent, he was ill-served in grammar and its analogies. (Reported here as the lexicographers' dispute, not as a settled point.)

5. Sorting and sifting concretely. Murra: أَزَلْتُ الضأْنَ من المَعَز والبِيضَ من السُّود — "I separated the sheep from the goats, the white from the black" — with زِلْتُها أَزِيلُها زَيْلاً as an equivalent, glossed مَيَّزْتُ ("I distinguished/sorted"). Al-Jawharī gives the imperative زِلْ ضَأْنَك من مِعْزاك ("sort your sheep from your goats").

6. The reflexive/mutual forms — to come apart, to be distinct. تَزَيَّلَ القومُ ("the people dispersed"), verbal nouns تَزَيُّلاً and (Ḥijāzī, per al-Liḥyānī) تَزْيِيلاً; the tribe of Rabīʿa instead say تَزَايَلَ القومُ تَزَايُلاً. The Qur'anic لو تَزَيَّلوا ("had they been separated") is glossed لو تَمَيَّزوا — "had they been set apart from one another." الزِّيال = parting; التَّزايُل = mutual distinctness (tabāyun).
Shawāhid: al-Kumayt, "They wanted leather-shapers to part their hide, measuring and cutting it"; al-Mutalammis, "O Ḥārith, even were our bloods stirred together, they would separate until no blood touched blood" (also read تَزَيَلْنَ); Abū Dhuʾayb, "towards litters like dawm-palms, in which there is a drawing apart, and a swaying of interlaced loads."

7. Parting from a person. زَايَلَهُ مُزَايَلَةً وزِيالاً — he parted from him, left him; المُزَايَلَة is separation. انْزَالَ عنه likewise means he parted from him (Ibn al-Aʿrābī's line: "and he parted from her defender and his aid"). Of women, المُتَزايِلَة is one who turns her face away and screens it from you — from this same sense. A ḥadīth is cited, خالِطوا الناسَ وزايِلُوهم ("mix with people and part from them"), explained as parting from them in acts that do not please God and His Messenger.

8. Physical extension — being set apart. الزَّيَل (al-zayal) is a wide gap between the thighs, like bow-leggedness (faḥaj); رَجُلٌ أَزْيَلُ الفَخِذين is a man whose thighs are splayed apart. Ibn Manẓūr links this directly to the core sense: what stands far apart is parted. Verb: زَيِلَ يَزْيَل. Cited from a ḥadīth of ʿAlī describing the Mahdī as of al-Ḥusayn's offspring, with receding forehead-hair, aquiline nose, azyal al-fakhidhayn, parted front teeth, and a mole on his right thigh.

9. Grammatical note on mā zāla / lā yazālu. Per al-Tahdhīb, ما زالَ يفعل كذا and لا يَزالُ يفعل كذا function like ما انْفَكَّ and ما بَرِحَ ("he has not ceased doing"), and are seldom used except with a negative particle. Ibn Kaysān: in these constructions the intended sense is not that of zāla/yazūlu ("to shift from one state or place to another") but continuous adherence to something, an abiding state. Also: ما زِلْتُ به حتى فَعَل ذلك (verbal noun زِيالاً); ما زِلْتُ وزَيْداً حتى فَعَل, where "and Zayd" carries the sense of "with Zayd" (Sībawayh); and some report زِلْتُ أَفْعَلُ meaning ما زِلْتُ.

10. A restricted idiom. Al-Liḥyānī: one says زِلْتُ الشيءَ فلم يَنْزَلْ ("I tried to sort the thing out but it would not come apart") and مِزْتُه فلم يَنْمَزْ, only in these two shapes — Arabic speakers do not say زَيَّلْتُه فلم يَتَزَيَّلْ, just as they do not say مَيَّزْتُه فلم يَتَمَيَّزْ.

11. Overlap with z-w-l in the imprecation formulae. أَزالَ اللهُ زَوالَه is a curse of destruction, meaning "may God take away his motion and free activity," comparable to أَسْكَتَ اللهُ نامَّتَه; زال زَوالُه = his motion is gone; also زِيلَ زَوِيلُه. Dhū al-Rumma, of an ostrich egg: "a white one that does not shy from us, while her mother — when she sees us, her stirring is set in motion by us," i.e. her heart was displaced by fright. Ibn Barrī notes زِيلَ here may be a passive from زَالَه اللهُ (with الزَّوِيل equal to الزَّوال), or may be a variant of the active زَالَ, as كِيدَ is used for كَادَ (Hudhalī shāhid: "the hyenas of the stony ground all but ate my corpse, and Khirāsh all but was orphaned that day"). He favours the latter, since the line is also transmitted as زِيلَ مِنَّا زَوالُها and زالَ مِنَّا زَوِيلُها, which shows زِيلَ carries the active sense.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: زَيَّنَ 26x "is made fair-seeming"; زِينَة 19x "their adornment"; ٱزَّيَّنَتْ 1x "and is beautified"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats z-y-n as a single sound root whose core sense is the beauty of something and the act of making it beautiful.

1. Core meaning: الزَّيْن (al-zayn, beauty/adornment) is defined as the opposite of الشَّيْن (al-shayn, blemish or disgrace).

2. Verb usage: زَيَّنْتُ الشَّيْءَ تَزْيِينًا (zayyantu... tazyīnan) — "I adorned the thing." Of land, the forms أَزْيَنَتِ الأرض / ازَّيَّنَتْ / ازْدَانَتْ all mean the earth became beautiful, specifically when its vegetation made it so.

3. A reported extra sense: al-zayn is said — with Ibn Fāris flagging the doubt ("if it is authentic") — to mean a cock's comb (ʿurf al-dīk). He cites a line of verse mocking someone escorted on a mule, likened to a cock with a lopsided comb and one eye, as the shāhid for this usage.

dictionary: Ibn Fāris — Maqāyīs al-Lugha, Ibn Fāris (d. 1004)
quran_words: زَّيْتُون 5x "and the olives"; زَيْتُونَة 1x "an olive"; زَيْت 1x "its oil"
text:
Ibn Fāris treats z-y-t as yielding one single meaning only.

1. The root gives الزَّيْت (al-zayt), olive oil — a familiar, everyday thing needing no explanation in his view.

2. From it comes the verb زِتُّهُ (zittuhu), "I oiled/anointed it with olive oil"; the corresponding passive participle is مَزْيُوت (mazyūt), "oiled, anointed with olive oil."

The entry records no second sense and no poetic or scriptural citations.
